title: Comedies and tragedies written by Francis Beaumont and Iohn Fletcher ...
author: Beaumont, Francis, 1584-1616.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: HEalth to my Soveraigne.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Eumenes, welcome:
Welcome to Paphos souldier to our love,
And that faire health ye wish us through the Campe
May it disperse it selfe, and make all happy;
How does the Generall, the valiant Memnon,
And how his wars, Eumenes?

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: The Gods have giv'n you (royall Sir) a Souldier
Better ne're sought a danger, more approv'd
In way of war, more master of his fortunes,
Expert in leading 'em; in doing valiant,
In following all his deeds to Victories,
And holding fortune certaine there.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O Souldier,
Thou speak'st a man indeed; a Generall Generall,
A soule conceiv'd a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Ten set Battells
Against the strong usurper Diocles
Whom long experience had begot a Leader
Ambition rais'd too mighty: hath your Memnon
Won, and won gloriously, distrest and shooke him
Even from the head of all his hopes to nothing:
In three he beat the thunder-bolt his brother
Forc'd him to wall himselfe up: there not safe,
Shooke him with warlike Engines like an earthquake,
Till like a snaile he left his shell and crawl'd
By night, and hidious darknesse to destruction:
Disarm'd for ever rising more; twelve Castles,
Some though impregnable; Townes twice as many
Countries that like the wind knew no command
But savage wildnesse; hath this Generall
With losse of blood & youth, through storms & tempests
Cal'd to your faire obedience.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: O my Souldier
That thou wert now within my arms; what drums-
Are those that beat Eumenes?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: His my Soveraigne;
Himselfe i'th head of conquest drawing home,
An old man now to offer up his glories,
And endlesse conquest at your shrine,

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Goe all,
And entertaine him with all Ceremonie,
Wee'le keep him now a Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Sir, a strange one,
Pray God his language beare it; by my life, Sir
He knowes no complement, nor curious casting
Of words into fit places ere he speak 'em,
He can say fight well fellow, and i'le thanke thee:
He that must eat, must sweat; bring up the reare there,
Or charge that wing of horse home.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Goe too, goe too.
Valiant and wise are twins Sir: welcome, welcome,
Welcome my fortunate and famous Generall,
High in thy Princes favour as in fame,
Welcome to Peace and Paphos.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thanke your Grace,
And would to God my dull tongue had that sweetnesse
To thanke you as I should; but pardon me,
My sword and I speake roughly Sir: your battells
I dare well say, I have fought well; for I bring ye
That lazie end you wish for Peace, so fully,
That no more name of war is: who now thinkes
Sooner or safer these might have bin ended.
Begin 'em If ye dare againe; I'le thanke him.
Souldier and Souldiers Mate these twenty five yeares,
At length your Generall, (as one whose merit
Durst looke upon no lesse,) I have waded through
Dangers would damp't these soft soules, but to heare of
The maidenheads of thousand lives hangs here Sir,
Since which time, Prince, I know no Court but Marshall,
No oylie language, but the shock of Armes,
No dalliance but with death; No lofty measures
But weary and sad marches, cold and hunger,
Larums at midnight, Valours selfe would shake at,
Yet I ne're shrunke. Balls of consuming Wildfire,
That lickt men up like lightning, have I laught at,
And tost 'em back againe like childrens trifles
Upon the edges of my Enemies swords
I have marcht like whirle-windes, fury at this hand waiting,
Death at my right; Fortune my forlorne hope,
When I have grapled with destruction,
And tug'd with pale fac'd Ruine, Night and Mischiefe,
Frighted to see a new day breake in bloud,
And every where I conquer'd; and for you sir,
Mothers have wanted wombes to make me famous,
And blowne ambition dangers; Those that griev'd ye,
I have taken order for i'th' earth: those fooles
That shall hereafter.

speeches.speaker: K.
verse: No more wars my souldier:
We must now treat of peace sir.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: How he talkes,
How gloriously.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: A goodly timber'd fellow,
Valiant no doubt.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: If valour dwell in vaunting;
In what a phrase he speakes as if his actions
Could be set of in nothing but a noise,
Sure has a drum in's mouth.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I wonder wenches
How he would speake to us.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Nothing but larum
Tell us whose throat he cut, shew us his sword,
And blesse it for sure biting.

speeches.speaker: Lucippe.
verse: And t like your Grace,
I doe not thinke he knowes us what we are,
Or to what end; for I have heard his followers
Affirme he never saw a woman that exceeded
A Sutlers wife yet, or in execution
Old bedrid Beldames without teeth or tongues,
That would not flie his furie? how he lookes.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: This way devoutly.

speeches.speaker: Cal
verse: Sure his Lordship's viewing
Our Fortifications.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: If he mount at me,
I may chance choake his Battery.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Still his eye

Keeps quarter this way:
~enus grant his valour
Be not in love.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: If he be, presently
Expect a Herrald and a Trompet with ye
To bid ye render; we two Perdu's pay for't else.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I'le leave ye to my sister, and these Ladies
To make your welcome fuller: my good souldier
We must now turne your sternnesse into Courtship
When ye have done there; to your fair repose sir:
I know you need it Memnon, welcome gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Now he begins to march: Madam the Van's yours,
Keep your ground sure; 'tis for your spurrs.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
prose: O Venus.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: How he stares on me.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Knight him Madam, knight him
He will grow tooth' ground els.

speeches.speaker: Eumenes.
verse: Speake sir, 'tis the Princesse.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: Ye shame your selfe, speake to her

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Rise and speake sir.
Ye are welcome to the Court, to me, to all sir,

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Is he not deafe?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: The Gentleman's not well.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Fie noble Generall,

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Give him fresh aire his colour goes, how do ye?
The Princesse will be glad sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Peace, and heare me.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Command a silence there.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I love thee Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I thank your Lordship heartily: proceed sir.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Lord how it stuck in's stomack like a surfet.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: It breaks apace now from him, God be thanked,
What a fine spoken man he is.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: A choice one of singular variety in carriage.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Yes and I warrant you he knows his distance.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: With all my heart I love thee.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: A hearty gentleman,
And I were eene an arrand beast, my Lord,
But I lov'd you againe.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Good Lady kisse me.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
prose: I marry, Mars, there thou cam'st close up to her.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Kiss you at first my Lord, 'tis no faire fashion,
Our lips are like Rose buds, blowne with mens breaths,
They loose both sap and savour; there's my hand sir.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Fie, fie, my Lord, this is too rude.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Unhand me,
Consume me if I hurt her; good sweet Lady
Let me but looke upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Doe.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Yet.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Well sir.
Take your full view.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Blesse your eyes sir.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Mercie,
Is this the man they talkt of for a souldier,
So absolute and Excellent: O the Gods,
If I were given to that vanitie
Of making sport with men for ignorance,
What a most precious subject had I purchas'd?
Speake for him gentlemen: some one that knowes,
What the man ailes; and can speake sense.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Sure Madam,
This fellow has been a rare Hare finder
See how his eyes are set.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Some one goe with me,
I'le send him something, for his head, poore gentleman,
Is troubled with the staggers.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Keep him darke,
He will run March mad else, the fumes of Battell's
Ascend into his braines,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Clap to his feet
An old Drum head, to draw the thunder downward.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Look to him gentlemen: farwell, Lord I am sorry
We cannot kisse at this time, but believe it
Wee'le find an houre for all: God keep my children,
From being such sweet Souldiers; Softly wenches,
Lest we disturbe his dreame.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Why this is Monstrous.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: A strange forgetfulnesse, yet still he holds it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: Though he ne're saw a woman of great fashion
Before this day, yet my thinks 'tis possible
He might imagine what they are, and what
Belongs unto 'em; meere ^eport of others.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Pish, his head had other whimsies in't: my Lord,
Death I think y'are strook dumb; my good Lord Generall

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: That I doe love ye Madam; and so love ye
An't like your grace.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: He has bin studying this speech.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Who doe ye speake to sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why where's the Lady
The woman, the faire woman.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cap.
verse: Who?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: The Princesse,
Give me the Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Give yee counsell rather
To use her like a Princesse: Fy my Lord,
How have you borne your selfe, how nakedly
Laid your soule open: and your ignorance
To be a sport to all; report and honour;
Drew her to doe you favours, and you bluntly,
Without consideration what, or how she was
Neither collecting reason, nor distinction.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why, what did I my masters?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: All that shewes
A man unhandsome, undigested done.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Did not I kneele unto her?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Dumbe and senslesse,
As though ye had bin cut out for your fathers tombe,
Or stuck a land-marke; when she spoke unto you,
Being the excellence of all our Island,
Ye star'd upon her, as ye had seene a monster

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Was I so foolish; I confesse Eumenes,
I never saw before so brave an outside
But did I kneele so long

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Till they laught at ye,
And when you spoke, I am asham'd to tell ye
What 'twas my Lord; how farre from order;
Blesse me, is't possible the wild noise of a warre
And what she only teaches should possesse ye,
Knowledge to treat with her, and full discretion
Being at flood still in ye, and in peace,
And manly conversation smooth and civill,
Where gracefulnesse and glory twyn together
Thrust your selfe out an exile?
Doe you know sir, what state she carries?
What great obedience waits at her backe continually?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: She ne're commanded
A hundred thousand men, as I have done,
Nor ne're won battell; Say I would have kist her.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: There was a dainty offer too, a rare one.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why, she is a woman, is she not?

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: She is so.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why, very well; what was she made for then?
Is she not young and handsome bred to breed?
Doe not men kisse faire women? if they doe,
If lips be not unlawfull ware; Why a Princesse
Is got the same way that we get a begger,
Or I am cosen'd; and the selfe-same way
Shee must be handled e're she get another,
That's rudenesse is it not?

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: To her 'tis held so, & rudnes in that high degree.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: 'Tis reason,
But I will be more punctuall; pray what thought she?

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: Her thoughts were mercifull, but she laught at ye,
Pittying the poorenesse of your complement,
And so she left ye, good sir shape your selfe
To understand the place, and noble persons
You live with now.

speeches.speaker: 1. Cap.
verse: Let not those great deserts
The King hath layd up of ye, and the people,
Be blasted with ill bearing.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: The whole name of souldier, then will suffer,

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Shee's a sweet one.
And good sirs leave your exhortations
They come untimely to me, I have braines
That beate above your reaches: Shee's a Princesse,
That's all: I have killed a King, that's greater.
Come let's to dinner, if the Wine be good,
You shall perceive strange wisdome in my blood.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Well, would thou wert i'the wars again
Old Memnon, there thou wouldst talke toth' purpose,
And the proudest of all these Court Camelions
Would be glad to find it sense too: plague of this
Dead peace, this bastard breeding lowzie lazie idlenesse,
Now we must learne to pipe, and pick our livings
Out of old rotten ends: these twenty five yeares
I have serv'd my Countrie, lost my youth and bloud,
Expos'd my life to dangers more then dayes.
Yet let me tell my wants, I know their answers,
The King is bound to right me, they good people
Have but from hand to mouth, looke to your wives
Your yong trim wives, your high-day wives, your march-paines,
For if the souldiers find not recompence,
As yet there's none a hatching; I beleeve
You men of wars, the men of wars will nick ye,
For sterve nor beg they must not, my small meanes
Are gone in fumo: here to raise a better
Unlesse it be with lying, or dog flattering,
At which our Nations excellent; observing dog-dayes,
When this good Lady broyles, and would be basted
By that good Lord or such like morall learnings,
Is here impossible; Well, I will rub among 'em
If any thing for honestie be gotten,
Thou't be but bread and cheese I can be satisfied,
If otherwise the wind blow, stiffe as I am
Yet I shall learne to shuffle: There's an old Lasse
That shall be namelesse yet alive, my last hope,
Has often got me my pocket full of crownes
If all faile, Jack-Dawes, are you alive still?
Then I see the coast cleare, when fooles and boyes can prosper.

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse: Brave Lievtenant

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Haile to the man of worship.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: You are fine sirs,
Most passing fine at all points.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: As ye see sir,
Home-bred and handsome, we cut not out our clothes sir
At halfe sword as your Taylors doe, and pinck 'em
With Pikes and Partizans, we live retir'd sir
Gentlemen like, and jealous of our honours.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Very fine Foole, and fine Boy, Peace playes with you
As the wind playes with feathers, dances ye
You grind with all gusts gallants.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: We can bounce sir,
When you Soldados bend i'th' hams, and frisk too.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: When twenty of your trip-coats turn their tippets,
And your cold sallets without salt or vineger
By wambling in your stomacks, hemp and hobnailes
Will beare no price now, hanging and old harneis
Are like to over-run us.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Whores and hot houses.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Surgeons and Sirenges ring out your sance-bells.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Your Jubile, your Jubile.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Proh Deum.
How our St. Georges will bestride the Dragons
The red and ramping Dragons.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Advanc't foole.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: But then the sting i'th' taile boy.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Tanto melior.
For so much the more danger, the more honour.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: You'r very pleasant with our occupation Gent.
Which very like amongst these fierie Serpents
May light upon a Blind-worme of your blood,
A Mother or a Sister.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Mine's past saddle
You should be sure of her else: but say Sir Huon
Now the Drums doubbes, & the sticks turn'd bed-staves,
All the old Foxes hunted to their holes,
The Iron age return'd to Eribus,
And Honorificabilitudinitatibus
Thrust out o'th' Kingdome by the head and shoulders,
What trade doe you meane to follow.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's a question.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Yes and a learned question if ye marke it,
Consider and say on.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Fooling as thou dost, that's the best trade I take it.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Take it strait then
For feare your fellowes be before ye, harke ye Lievtenant
Foolings the thing, the thing worth all your fightings,
When all's done ye must foole sir.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Well, I must then.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: But doe you know what fooling is; true fooling
The circumstances that belong unto it,
For every idle knave that showes his teeth
Wants and would live can Juggle tumble, fiddle,
Make a dog face, or can abuse his fellow,
Is not a foole at first dash, you shall find sir
Strange turnings in this trade; to foole is nothing
As fooling has bin but to foole the faire way,
The new way, as the best men foole their friends,
For all men get by fooling meerely fooling,
Desert does nothing valiant, wise, vertuous,
Are things that walke by without bread or breeches,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I partly credit that.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Fine wits, fine wits sir,
There's the young Boy, he does well in his way too,
He could not live else in his Masters absence;
He tyes a Ladyes garters so, so, pretily,
Say his hand slip, but say so.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Why let it slip then.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: 'Tis ten to one the body shall come after,
And he that workes deserves his wages.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's true.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Hee riddles finely to a waiting Gentlewoman
Expounds dreames like a Prophet, dreames himselfe too,
And wishes all dreames true; they cry Amen,
And there's a Memorandum: he can sing too
Bawdy enough to please old Ladies: he lies rarely,
Pawnes ye a sute of clothes at all points, fully,
Can pick a pocket if ye please, or casket;
Lisps when he lists to catch a Chambermaid,
And calls his Hostesse mother, these are things now,
If a man meane to live, to fight and swagger,
Beaten about the Eares with bawling sheepskins,
Cut to the soule for Summer: here an arme lost,
And there a leg; his honourable head
Seal'd up in salves and searclothes, like a packet,
And so sent over to an Hospitall, stand there, charge there,
Sweare there, whore there, dead there,
And all this sport for cheese, and chines of dog-flesh,
And money when two Wednesdayes meet together,
Where to be lowzie is a Gentleman,
And he that weares a cleane shirt has his
Shrowd on.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I'le be your scholler, come if I like fooling.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: You cannot choose but like it, fight you one day
I'le foole another, when your Surgeons paid,
And all your leakes stopt, see whose slops are heaviest,
I'le have a shilling for a can of wine,
When you shall have two Sergeants for a counter.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Come learn of us Lievtenant, hang your Iron up,
Wee'le find you cooler warrs.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Come let's together,
I'le see your tricks, and as I like 'em. —

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why was there not such women in the camp then
Prepar'd to make me know 'em.

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: 'Twas no place sir.

speeches.speaker: 1. Capt.
verse: Why should they live in Tumults: they are creatures
Soft and of sober natures.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Cou'd not your wives,
Your mothers, or your sisters have been sent for
To exercise upon.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: We thanke your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: But doe you meane?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I doe meane.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: What sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: To see her,
And see thee hang'd too, and thou anger'st me,
And thousands of your throats cut, get ye from me
Ye keepe a prating of your points of manners,
And fill my head with lowzie circumstances,
Better have Ballets in 't your courtly worships,
How to put off my hat, you how to turne me,
And you forsooth to blow my nose discreetly;
Let me alone, for I will love her, see her,
Talke to her, and mine owne way.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Shee's the Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why let her be the devill, I have spoke,
When Thunder durst not check me, I must love,
I know she was a thing kept for me.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: And I know sir,
Though she were born yours, yet your strange behaviour
And want.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thou liest.

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: I doe not.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: I doe not lye sir,
I say you want faire language, nay 'tis certaine
You cannot say good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ye Dog-whelpes,
The proudest of your prating tongues.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Doe kill us,
Kill us for telling truth, for my part Generall
I would not live to see men make a may-game
Of him I have made a Master, kill us quickly,
Then ye may.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Doe what you list, draw your sword childishly
Upon your servants that are bound to tell ye
I am weary of my life.

speeches.speaker: 1 Capt.
verse: And I.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: And all sir.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Goe to the Princesse make her sport, cry to her
I am the glorious man of warre.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Pray ye leave me,
I am sorry I was angry, I'le thinke better,
Pray no more words.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Good sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Nay then.

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
prose: We are gone sir.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: How came he hither, see for heavens sake wenches,
What faces, and what postures he puts on,
I doe not thinke he is perfect.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: If your love
Have not betrayd his little wits, he's well enough.
As well as he will be.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Marke how he Muses.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Has a Battalia now in's braines, he draws out now
Have at ye Harpers.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: See, see, there the fire failes.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Look what an Alphabet of faces he runs through,

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: O love, loue, how amorously thou look'st
In an old rusty armour.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I'le away, for by my troth I feare him.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Feare the gods Madam,
And never care what man can doe, this fellow
Withall his frights about him and his furies,
His larums and his Launces, Swords and Targets,
Nay case him up in armour Cap-a-pe,
Yet durst I undertake within two houres,
If he durst charge to give him such a shake
Should shake his valour off, and make his shankes too

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: For shame no more.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Hee muses still.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: The Devill.
Why should this old dried timber chopt with thunder.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Old wood burnes quickest.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Out you would say Madam,
Give me a green stick that may hold me heat
And smoke me soundly too: a turnes, and sees ye.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: There's no avoiding now, have at ye.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Lady,
The more I looke upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: The more you may sir.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Let him alone.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I would desire your patience
The more I say I looke, the more

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: This sir, this ye slave sir,
Death ye rude rogues, ye Scarrubbs.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Hold for Heav'ns sake Lievtenant, sweet Lievtenant.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I have done sir.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You have wrung his neck off.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: No Boy, 'tis the nature
Of this strange passion when't hits to hale people
Along by th'haire, to kick 'em, breake their heads:

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Do ye call this Acting, was your part to beat me.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Yes, I must act all that he does.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Plague act yee,
I'le act no more.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: 'Tis but to shew man.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Then man
Hee should have shew'd it only, and not done it,
I am sure he beat me beyond Action,
Gowts a your heavy fist.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Ile have thee to him,
Thou hast a fine wit, fine foole, and canst play rarely.
Hele hug thee, boy, and stroke thee,

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Ile to the stockes first,
'Ere I be strokt thus.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: But how came he Chilax?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I know not that,

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Ile to him

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: He loves thee well,
And much delights to here thee sing; much taken
He has bin with thy battell songs.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: If Musique,
Can find his madnes; ile so fiddle a him,
That out it shall by'th shoulders,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: My fine fidler,
Hele firke you and ye take not heed too: t'will be rare sport
To see his owne trade triumph over him;
His Lute lac'd to his head, for creeping hedges;
For mony ther's none stirring; try good Stremon
Now what your silver sound can doe; our voices
Are but vaine Ecchoes,

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Something shall be done
Shall make him understand all; lets to'th Taverne,
I have some few Crownes left yet: my whistle wet once
Ile pipe him such a Paven -

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Hold thy head up,
Ie cure it with a quart of wine; Come Coxcombe;
Come boye take heed of napkins.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Youl'd no more acting?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: No more Chicken;

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Goe then.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: God save you sir; pray how might I see the Princess

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Why very fitly sir shees even now ready,
To wa ke out this way into'th parke; stand there,
Ye cannot misse her sight, sir,

speeches.speaker: Siphax.
verse: I much thanke ye.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Lets have a care, for ile assure ye wenches
I woo d not meet him willingly agen;
For though I doe not feare him, yet his fashion
I wood not be acquainted much wit'h.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Gentle Ladie,
Ye need not feare the walkes are viewed and emptie,
But my thinkes Madam this kind heart of his —

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Is slow a coming.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Keepe me ye blest Angells,
What killing power is this?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: VVhy dost thou looke for't?
Dost thinke he spoke in earnest?

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: My thinkes Madam,
A Gentleman should keepe his word; and to a Ladie
A Ladie of your excellencies;

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Out foole!
Send me his heart? what should we doe wo't? dance it?

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Drie it and drinke it for the wormes.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Whose that?
What man stands there?

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: VVhere?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: There.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: A Gentleman,
Which I beseech your grace to honour so much,
As know him for your servants brother.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Siphax?

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: The same an't please your grace; what does he here?
Upon what busines and I ignorant?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Hee's growne a handsome Gentleman; good Siphax
Yat wel-come from the warres; woo'd ye with us sir?
Pray speake your will: a blushes, be not fearefu l,
I can assure ye for your Sisters sake sir,
Ther's my hand on it.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Doe you heare Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Sure these Souldiers,
Are all growne senseles,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Doe ye know where ye are sir?

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Tongue-tyde,
He lookes not well too, by my life, I thinke;

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Speake, for shame speake.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: A man woo'd speake —

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: These Souldiers,
Are all dumb Saints: Consider and take time sir,
Lets forward wenches come, his pallats downe.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Dare these men charge it'h face of fire and bullets?
And hang there heads downe at a handsome Woman?
Good master Mars that 's a soule fault.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Fye beast,
No more my brother.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: Sister, honoured Sister,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Dishonoured foole,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: I doe confesse,

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Fye on thee,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: But stay till I deliver,

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Let me goe,
I am a shame to owne thee,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Fare ye well then,
Ye must nere see me more,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Why stay deare Siphax,
My angers past; I will heare ye speake

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: O Sister,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Out with it Man,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: O I have drunke my mischiefe,

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Ha? what?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: My destruction.
In at mine eyes I have drunke it; O the Princess,
The rare sweet Princess!

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: How foole? the rare Princess?
Was it the Princess that thou sed'st?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: The Princess,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Thou doest not love her sure, thou darst not.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Yes by heaven,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Yes by Heaven? I know thou darst not,
The Princess? 'tis thy life the knowledge of it,
Presumption that will draw into it all thy kinred,
And leave 'em slaves and succourles; the Princess?
Why shee's a sacred thing to see and worship,
Fixt from us as the Sun is high and glorious,
To be ador'd not doated on; desire things possible,
Thou foolish young man, nourish not a hope,
Will haile thy heart out.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: 'Tis my destinie,
And I know both disgrace and death will quit it,
If it be knowne

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Pursue it not then Syphax
Get thee good wholesome thoughts may nourish thee.
Goe home and pray

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: I cannot

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Sleep then Syphax.
And dreame away thy doting.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: I must have her
Or you no more your brother; worke Cleant he,
Worke, and worke speedilie, or I shall die wench.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Dye then, I dare forget; farewell

speeches.speaker: Syp.
verse: Farewell Sister.
Farewell for ever, see me buried.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Stay.
Pray stay? hee's all my brothers: no way Siphax.
No other Woman,

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: None, none, shee or sincking.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Goe and hope well, my life ile venture for thee
And all my art, a Woman may worke miracles;
No more, pray heartily against my fortunes,
For much I feare a maine one.

speeches.speaker: Syphax.
verse: I shall doe it.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Find him by any meanes; and good child tell him
He has forgot his old friend, give him this,
And say this night without excuse or busines
As ever he may find a friend, come to me,
He knowes the way and how, begon.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I gallop.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: I have bin looking you;

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: The faire Cleanthe,
VVhat may your busines be?

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: O holy Mother
Such busines of such strange waite, now or never.
As ye have loved me, as ye doe or may doe,
When I shall find a fit time.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: If by my meanes
Your busines may be fitted; ye know me,
And how I am tyed unto you; be bold daughter
To build your best hopes,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: O but 'tis a strange one
Stuck with as many dangers -

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Ther's the working,
Small things performe themselves and give no pleasures;
Be confident through death ile serve.

speeches.speaker: Clean
verse: Here.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Fye no corruption

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Take it; 'tis yours,
Be not so spiced, 'tis good gold
And goodnes is no gall to'th conscience,
I know you have wayes to vent it: ye may hold it

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Ile keep it for ye; when?

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: To morrow morning
Ile visit ye agen; and when occasion
Offers it selfe -

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Instruct me, and have at ye -

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Farewell till then; be sure.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: As your owne thoughts, Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: 'Tis a maine worke and full of feare.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Fooles only
Make their effects seeme fearefull: farewell daughter.
This gold was well got for my old tuff Souldier
Now I shall be his sweet agen; what busines
Is this she has a foote? some lustie lover
Beyond her line, the young wench would faine piddle
A little to revive her, must be thought of,
'Tis even so; she must have it; but how by my meanes
A devill can she drive it? I that wait still
Before the Goddesse giving Oracle
How can I profit her? 'tis her owne project,
And if she cast it false her owne fault be it.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Why this is utter madnes

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Thus it is Sir

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Only the Princesse sight?

speeches.speaker: 1. Cap.
verse: All we can judge at;

speeches.speaker: Poli.
verse: This must be loo'kt to timelie.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Yes and wiselie;

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: He do's not offer at his life

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: not yet sir
That we can heare of

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Noble Gentlemen;
Let me entreat your watches over him.
Ye cannot doe a worthier worke.

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: We came Sir
Provided for that service?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Where is Chilax?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: A little busie Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Is the foole and boye here.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: They are Sir,

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Let 'em be still so; and as they find his humors

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Now ye may behold him

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Stand close and worke no noyse;
By his eyes now, Gentlemen,
I guesse him full of anger

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Be not seene there

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: The houre's past long agoe, hees false and fearefull,
Coward goe with thy catine soule, thou our dog.
Thou cold clod, wilde fire warme thee, monstrous fearful,
I know the slave shakes but to thinke on't.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: VVhose that?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: I know not Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: But I shall catch yee rascall,
Your mangie soule is not immortall here Sir,
Ye must die, and we must meet; we must, maggot,
Be sure we must, for not a nooke of hell,
Not the most horrid pit shall harbour thee.
The Devills taile shall hide thee, but ile have thee,
And how ile use thee, whips and firebrands
Tosting thy taile against a flame of wilde fire,
And basting it with brimstone, shall be nothing,
Nothing at all; ile reach ye to be treacherous;
Was never slave so ^wing'd since hell was hell
As I will swinge thy slaves soule: and be sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Is this imagination, or some circumstance
For 'tis extreame strange.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: So is all he does Sir

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Till then ile leave ye? whose there? wheres the Surgeon.
Demagoras.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: My Lord,

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Bring the Surgeon.
And waite you too.

speeches.speaker: Poli.
verse: What wood ye with a Surgeon

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Things mustring in his head: pray marke

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Come hither.
Have you brought your Instruments.

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: They are within Sir,

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Put to the doores a while there; ye can incise
To a haires bredth without defacing;

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: And take out fairely from the flesh;

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: The least thing.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Well, come hither then; take off my doublet,
^or looke ye Surgeon, I must have ye cut
My Heart out here, and handsomly: Nay, stare not,
Nor doe not start; I'le cut your throat else Surgeon,
Come sweare to doe it.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Good sir—

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Sirra, hold him,
I'le have but one blow at his head.

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: I'le doe it,
Why what should we doe living after you sir?
Wee'le die before if yee please.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: No, No.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Living? hang living,
Is there ne're a Cat hole where I may creep through?
Woo'd I were in the Indies.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Sweare then, and after my death presently
To kill your selves and follow, as ye are honest,
As ye have faiths and loves to me.

speeches.speaker: Dema.
verse: Wee'l doe it.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Pray doe not stir yet, we are neare enough
To run between all dangers.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Here I am sir;
Come looke upon me, view the best way boldly,
Feare nothing but cut home; if your hand shake sirra,
Or any way deface my heart i'th' cutting,
Make the least scratch upon it, but draw it whole,
Excellent faire, shewing at all points, Surgeon,
The honour and the valour of the owner,
Mixt with the most immaculate love I send it,
Looke too't, I'le slice thee to the soule.

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: Ne're feare sir,
I'le doe it daintily; would I were out once.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I will not have ye smile sirra when ye do it,
As though ye cut a Ladies corne; tis scurvie;
Doe me it as thou dost thy praiers, seriously.

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: I'le doe it in a dump sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: In a dog sir,
I'le have no dumps, nor dumplins: fetch your tooles,
And then I'le tell ye more.

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: If I returne
To heare more I'le be hang'd for't.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Quick, quick.

speeches.speaker: Dema.
verse: Yes sir,
With all the heeles we have,

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Yet stand.

speeches.speaker: Poli.
verse: Hee'le doe it.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: He cannot and we here.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why when ye rascalls,
Ye dull slaves: will ye come sir? Surgeon, Serring,
Dogleach, shall I come fetch ye?

speeches.speaker: Poli.
verse: Now i'le to him,
God save ye honour'd brother

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: My deare Polidor,
Welcome from travell welcome; and how doe ye?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Well sir, would you were so.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I am, I thanke ye,
You are a better'd man much, I the same still,
An old rude Souldier, sir.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Pray be plaine brother,
And tell me but the meaning of this vision,
For to me it appeares no more: so farre
From common course and reason.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thanke thee Fortune,
At length I have found the man: the man must do it,
The man in honour bound.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: To doe what?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Harke, for I will blesse ye with the circumstance
Of that weak shaddow that appear'd.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Speake on sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: It is no storie for all eares.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: The Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Peace and heare all: how:

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Sure 'tis dangerous
He starts so at it,

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Your heart, doe ye know sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Yes, pray thee be softer.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Me to doe it?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Only Reserv'd, and dedicated.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: For shame brother
Know, what, ye are, a man.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: None of your Athens
Good sweet sir, no Philosophy, thou feel'st not
The honourable end, foole.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I am sure I feele
The shame & scorn that follows; have ye serv'd thus long
The glory of your Country, in your Conquests,
The envy of your neighbours, in your vertues,
Rul'd Armies of your owne, given Lawes to Nations,
Belov'd and fear'd as far as Fame has travel'd,
Call'd the most fortunate and happy Memnon,
To loose all here at home, poorely to loose it,
Poorely and pettishly, ridiculously
To fling away your fortune? where's your wisdome?
Where's that you govern'd others by, discretion?
Do's your Rule lastly hold upon your selfe? fie brother,
How are ye falne? get up into your honour
The top branch of your bravery, and from thence
Looke and lament how little Memnon seemes now.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Hum! tis well spoken; but do'st thou think, young scholler
The tongues of Angels from my happinesse
Could turne the end I aime at? no: they cannot;
This is no booke case brother: will ye doe it?
Use no more art, I am resolv'd.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Ye may, sir
Command me to doe any thing that's honest,
And for your noble end: but this it carries.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ye shall not be so honour'd; live an Asse still,
And learne to spell for profit: goe, goe studie.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Ye must not hold him up so, he is lost then.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Get thee to schoole agen, and talke of turnips,
And find the naturall cause out, why a dog
Turnes thrice about e're he ly downe: there's learning.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Come, I will doe it now; 'tis brave, I find it,
And now allow the reason.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: O doe ye so sir,
Doe ye find it currant?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Yes, yes, excellent.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I told ye.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I was foolish: I have here too
The rarest way to find the truth out; hark ye,
Ye shall be rul'd by me.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I will be: but—

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: I reach it,
If the worst fall, have at the worst: wee'le both goe
But two dayes, and 'tis thus; ha?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: 'Twill doe well so

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Then if not excellent, doe ye conceive it

speeches.speaker: Mem.
prose: 'Twill worke for certaine

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: O 'twill tickle her
And you shall know then by a line

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I like it
But let me not be fool'd againe

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Doubt nothing
You doe me wrong then, get ye in there privat
As I have taught ye; Basta

speeches.speaker: Mem.
prose: Worke

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I will doe

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Have ye found the cause

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Yes, and the straingest, Gentlemen,
That ere I heard of, anon ile tell ye; Stremon
Be you still neere him to affect his fancie
And keepe his thoughts off: Let the Foole and Boy
Stay him, they may doe some pleasure too; Eumenes
VVhat if he had a wench, an handsome whore brought
Rarely drest up, and taught to state it?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: VVell Sir

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: His cause is meerly heat: and made beleeve
It were the Princesse mad for him,

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: I thinke
'Twere not amisse.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cap.
verse: And let him kisse her

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: VVhat els?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: Ile be his bawde ant please you, young and holesome
I can assure ye he shall have

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Faith let him

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: A shall, I hope 'twill helpe him, walke a little
Ile tell you how his case stands, and my project
In which you must be mourners, but by all meanes
Stir not you from him: Stremon.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
prose: On our Lives Sir

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: O y'ar a pretious Man; two daies in towne
And neuer see your old friend?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Prithe pardon me

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: And in my conscience if I had not sent

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: No more I would a come; I must

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: I find ye
God a mercy want ye never care for me
But when your slops are emptie

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Nere feare that wench
Shall find good currant coyne still; is this the old house?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Have ye forgot it?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And the dore still standing
That goes into the Temple?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Still.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: The Robes to,
That I was wount to shift in here?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: All here still.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: O ye tuff rogue what troubles have I trotted through?
VVhat feares and frights, every poore mouse a monster
That I heard stir, and every stick I trod on
A sharp sting to my conscience

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Las poore conscience,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And all to liquor thy old bootes wench

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Out beast!

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: To new carine thy carkas, that's the truth on't
How does thy keele? does it need nayling? a tother
VVhen all thy linnen's up: and a more yare?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Fye Fye Sir

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Nere stem'd the straights?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: How you talke?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I am old wench,
And talking to an old Man is like a stomacher
It keepes his blood warme

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: But; pray tell me

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Any thing

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Where did the boy meet with ye, at a wench sure,
At one end of a wench, a Cup of wine sure

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Thou know'st I am too honest

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: That's your fault
And that the Surgeon knowes

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Then farewell
I will not faile ye soone

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Ye shall staye Supper
I have sworne ye shall, by this ye shall

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I will wench,
But after Supper for an houre, my busines

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: And but an houre

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: No by this kisse, that ended
I will returne and all night in thine Armes wench

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: No more, ile take your meaning; come 'tis Supper time

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Thou art not well

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Your grace sees more a great deale
Then I feele (yet I lye) o brother ^

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Marke her,
Is not the quicknes of her ey consumed, wench?
The livelye red and white?

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Nay she is much alter'd
That on my understanding, all her sleep's Ladie
Which were as sound and sweet

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Pray doe not force me
Good Madam where I am not, to be ill,
Conceit's a double sicknes; on my faith your highnes
Is meere mistaken in me

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I am glad on't
Yet this I have ever noted when thou wast thus
It still forerun some strange event: my Sister
Died when thou wast thus last: harke harke ho,
What mournefull noyse is this comes creeping forward,
Still it growes neerer, neerer, do ye heare it?

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: It seemes some Souldiers funerall: see it enters

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: What may it meane?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: The Gods keep ye faire Calis

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: This man can speake, and well; a stands and views us
Woo'd I were nere worse look't upon: how humbly
His eyes are cast now to the earth: pray marke him
And marke how rarely he has ranckt his troubles:
See now a weepes, they all weep; a sweeter sorrow
I never look't upon nor one that braver
Became his griefe; your will with us.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Great Ladie
Excellent beauty

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: He speakes handsomelie
What a rare rhetorician his greif plaies,
That stop was admirable

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: See see thou Princesse
Thou great commander of all hearts

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I have found it,
Oh how my soule shakes:

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: See, see the noble hart
Of him that was the noblest: see and glory
Like the proud God himselfe in what thou hast purchas'd
Behold the heart of Memnon: does it start ye?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Good gods, what has his wildenes done?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Looke boldlie
You boldlie sed you durst looke wretched woman,
Nay flie not back faire follie, 'tis too late now
Vertue and blooming honour bleed to death here,
Take it the Legacie of Love bequeath'd ye,
Of cruell Love, a cruell Legacie;
What was the will that wrought it? then can ye weepe?
Imbalme it in your truest teares?
If Women can weepe a truth, or ever sorrow sunck yet
Into the soule of your sex, for 'tis a Jewell
The VVorlds worth cannot weigh downe,
Take it Ladie; And with it all (I dare not curse) my sorrowes
And may they turne to Serpents.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: How she lookes
Still upon him: see now a teare steales from her

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: But still she keepes her ey firme

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Next read this,
But since I see your spirit somewhat troubled
Ile doe it for ye

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
prose:
Still she eyes him mainlie



Goe happy heart for thou shalt ly
Intomb'd in her for whom I dy
Example of her cruelty.


Tell her if she chance to chide
Me for slownes in her pride
That it was for her I died.


If a teare escape her eye
'Tis not for my memory.
But thy rights of obsequy


The Altar was my loving brest
My heart the sacrificed beast
And I was my selfe the Preist


Your body was the sacred shrine
Your cruell mind the power divine
Pleas'd with hearts of men not kine

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Now it poures downe

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I like it rarelie Ladie

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: How greedily she swallowes up his language?

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: Her eye inhabits on him

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Cruell Ladie,
Great as your beautie scornefull; had your power
But equall poise on all hearts; all hearts perish't;
But Cupid has more shafts then one more flames too
And now he must be open ey'd, 'tis Justice:
Live to injoye your longing; live and laugh at
The losses and the miseries we suffer;
Live to be spoken when your crueltie
Has cut of all the vertue from this Kingdome
Turned honour into earth, and faithfull service

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I sweare his angers excellent

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Truth and most tried love
Into disdaine and downefall,

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Still more pleasing,

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Live then I say famous for civill slaughters,
Live and lay out your triumphs, guild your glories
Live and be spoken this is she this Ladie,
This goodly Ladie, yet most killing beautie;
This with the two edg'd eyes, the heart for hardnes
Out doing rockes; and coldnes, rockes of Christall
This with the swelling soule, more coye of Courtship
Then the proud sea is when the shores embrace him
Live till the mothers find ye; read your story
And sowe their barren curses on your beauty,
Till those that have enjoy'd their loves despise ye,
Till Virgins pray against ye, old age find ye
And even as wasted coales glow in their dying
So may the Gods reward ye in your ashes:
But y'ar the Sister of my King; more prophesies
Els I should utter of ye true loves and loyall
Blesse themselves ever from ye: so I leave ye

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Prithee be angry still young man: good faire Sir
Chide me againe, what woo^d this man doe pleas'd,
That in his passions can bewitch soules stay,

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Upon my life she loves him

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Pray stay

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: No

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I doe command ye

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: No, ye cannot Ladie
I have a spell against yee, Faith and Reason,
Yee are to weak to reach me: I have a heart too,
But not for hawkes meat Ladie

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Even for Charity
Leave me not thus aflicted: you can teach me

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: How can you Preach that Charitie to others
That in your owne soule are an Athiest
Beleeving neither power nor feare: I trouble ye,
The Gods be good unto ye.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Ladie,

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: O royall Madam, Gentlemen for heav'n sake,

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: Give her fresh air she comes again: away sirs
And here stand close till we perceive the working

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Ye have undone all

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: So I feare

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: She loves ye

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: And then all hopes lost this way

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Peace she rises

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Now for my purpose Fortune

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Wher's the Gentleman

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Gone Madam

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why gone?

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Has dispatch't his busines

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: A came to speake with me
A did,

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: A did not

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: For I had many questions

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: On my Faith Madam, he
Talk't a great while to ye

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Thou conceiv'st not.
He talk't not as he should doo; o my heart
Away with that sad sight; didst thou ere love me?

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Why doe you make that question?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: If thou didst
Run run wench, run: nay see how thou stir'st

speeches.speaker: Lucip.
verse: Whither?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: If 'twer for any thing to please thy selfe
Thou wood'st run to'th devill: but I am growne

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Fie Ladie

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I aske none of your fortunes, nor your loves
None of your bent desires I slack, ye are not
In love with all men, are ye? one for shame
You will leave your honour'd mistris? why doe ye stare so
What is that ye see about mee, tell me;
Lord what am I become? I am not wilde sure,
Heaven keepe that from me: o Cleanthe help me
Or I am suncke to death

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Ye have offended and mightily, love is incenst against yee
And therefore take my Councell, to the Temple
For that's the speediest physick: before the Goddesse
Give your repentant prayers: aske her will
And from the Oracle attend your sentence
She is milde and mercifull

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: I will: o Venus
Even as thou lov'st thy selfe!

speeches.speaker: Clean.
prose: Now for my fortune

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: What shall I doe?

speeches.speaker: 1. Cap.
verse: VVhy make your selfe

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: I dare not,
No Gentlemen, I dare not be a villaine
Though her bright beauty would entice an Angell
I will to'th King my last hope: get him a Woman
As we before concluded: and as ye passe
Give out the Spartans are in armes; and terrible
And let some letters to that end be fain'd too
And sent to you, some Poets too, to the Generall
And let me worke: be nere him still,

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: We will Sir

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Farwell: and pray for all: what 'ere I will ye
Doe it, and hope a faire end

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: The Gods speed ye.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
verse: He lies quiet

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Let him lye and as I told ye
Make ready for this shew: h'as divers times
Been calling upon Orpheus to appeare
And shew the joyes: now I wilbe that Orpheus,
And as I play and sing like beasts and trees
I woo'd have you shapt and enter: thou a Dog, foole,
I have sent about your sutes: the Boy a bush,
An Asse you, you a Lion

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: I a dog?
Ile fit you for a Dog. Bow wow

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: 'Tis excellent
Steale in and make no noise

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Bow wow

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Away rogue.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Good sweet friend be not long

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Thou think'st each houre ten
Till I be ferreting

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: You know I love ye

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I will not be above an houre; let thy robe be readie
And the doore be kept

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Who knocks there?
Yet more busines?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Have ye more pensioners, the Princesse woman?
Nay then ile stay a little, what games a foote now?

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Now is the time

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: A rancke bawde by this hand, too
She grinds a both sides: hey boyes

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: How your brother Siphax?
Loves he the Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Deadlie, and you know
He is a Gentleman descended noblie.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: But a ranck knave as ever pist

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: ^old Mother
Heres more gold and some jewells

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Heres no villany
I am glad I came to'th hearing

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Alas Daughter,
What would ye have me doe?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Hold off ye old whore;
Ther's more gold comming; alls mine, all

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Doe ye shrink now,
Did ye not promise faithfully and told me
Through any danger?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Any I can wade through

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Ye shall, and easilie the sin not seene neither
Heres for a better stole and a new vaile mother
Come ye shall be my friend: if all hit

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Hang me
Ile make ye richer then the Goddesse.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Say then
I am yours, what must I doe?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: I'th morning
But very early, will the Princesse visit
The Temple of the Goddesse, being troubled
With strange things that distract her: from the Oracle
(Being strongly too in love) she will demand
The Goddesse pleasure, and a Man to cure her,
That Oracle you give: describe my Brother
You know him perfectly.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: I have seene him often

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: And charge her take the next man she shall meet with
When she comes out; you understand me

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: VVell.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Which shalbe he attending; this is all
And easily without suspition ended,
Nor none dare disobey, 'tis Heaven that does it,
And who dares crosse it then, or once suspect it?
The venture is most easie.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: I will doe it.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: As ye shall prosper;

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: As I shall prosper.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Take this too, and farewell; but first harke hither.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: What a young whores this to betray her mistris?
A thousand Cuckolds shall that husband be,
That marries thee, thou art so mischievous.
Ile put a spoke among your wheeles

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Be constant

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: 'Tis done

speeches.speaker: Chi.
prose: Ile doe no more at drop shot then

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Farewell wench.

speeches.speaker: Servant.
verse: A stirs a stirs

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Let him, I am ready for him,
He shall not this day perish, if his passions
May bee fed with Musick; are they ready

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: All, all: see where he comes

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Ile be straight for him.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: How sad he lookes and sullen.
Here are the Captaines: my feares past now.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Put case i'th other world
She doe not love me neither: I am old 'tis certaine

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: His spirit is a little quieter.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: My blood lost and my limbes stif; my embraces
Like the cold stubborne ba^kes ^hoa^ie and hear^es
My words worse: my fame only and atcheivements
Which are my strength, my blood, my youth my fashion,
Must woe her, win her, wed her; that's but wind
And Women are not brought to bed with shadowes:
I doe her wrong, much wrong; she is young and blessed,
Sweet as the spring, and as his blossomes tender,
And I a nipping north wind, my head ^ung
With hailes, and frostie Isicles: are the soules so too
When they depart hence, lame and old, and love les?
No sure, 'tis ever youth there; Time and Death
Follow our flesh no more: and that forc'd opinion
That Spirits have no sexes, I beleive not
There must be love, there is love? what art thou.

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: Orpheus, I am come from the deep's below,
To thee fond man the plagues of love to show:
To the faire fields where loves eternall dwell
Ther's none that came, but first they passe through hell:
Harke and beware unlesse thou hast loved ever,
Beloved againe, thou shalt see those joyes never.
Hark how they graone that dyed despairing,
O take heed thou:
Hark how they houle for over daring
All those were men.
They that be fooles, and dye for fame
They loose their name,
And they that bleed
Harke how they speed.
Now in cold frosts now scorching fires,
They sit and curse their lost desires:
Nor shall these soules be free from paines and feares,
Till Women wast them over in their teares.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: How should I know my passage is deni'de me
Or which of all the Devills dare

speeches.speaker: Eumon.
verse: This Song
Was rarely formed to fit him.
prose:
SONG.


Charon o Charon
Thou wafter of the soules to blisse or bant



Who calls the Fery man of Hell?



Come near
And say who lives in joye, and whom in feare.



Those that dye well; Eternall joy shall follow,
Those that dye ill; their owne soule saie shall swallow.



Shall thy black Bark those guilty spirits stow
That kill themselves for love?



O no no.
My cordage crackes when such great sins are neare
No winde blowes faire, nor I my selfe can steare



What lovers passe and in Elizium raigne?



Those gentle loves that are belov'd againe.



This Souldier Loves, and faine wood dye to win,
Shall he goe on?



No 'tis too foule a sin
He must not come a boord: I dare not rowe,
Stormes of despaire and guilty blood will blowe.



Shall time release him saye?



No, no, no no.
Nor time nor death can alter us, nor prayer;
My boate is de^ and who then d^re
But those appointed come aboord Live still,
And love by reason mor^all not by will,



And when thy Mistris shall close up thine eyes



Then come a boord and passe,



Till when be wise



Till when be wise.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: How still he sitts: I hope this Song has setled him

speeches.speaker: 1. Cap.
verse: He ^ites his lipp, and rowl^ his fierce eyes yet
I feare for all this

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: Stremon still apply to him;

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Give me more roome then, sweetlie strike divinely
Such straines and old earth moves at

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: The power I have over both Beast and plant
Thou man alone feelst miserable want
Strike your rare Spirits that attend my will,
And loose your savage wildnesse by my skill.
This Lion was a man of Warre that died,
As thou wouldst doe to guild her Ladies pride
This Dog a foole that hung himselfe for love:
This Ape with daily hugging of a glove,
Forgot to eat and died. This goodly tree,
An usher that still grew before his Ladie,
Wither'd at roote. This, for he could not wooe,
A grumbling Lawyer: This pyed Bird a page,
That melted out because he wanted age.
Still these lye houling on the stigian shore,
O love no more, o love no more.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: He steales off silently, as though he would sleep,
No more but all be nere him, feed his fancie
Good Stremon still; this may lock up his follie.
Yet Heaven knowes I must feare him; away softly.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Did I not doe most doggedly?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Most rarelie?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Hee's a brave man when shall we dog agen;

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Unty me first for Gods sake,

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Helpe the Boye; hee's in a wood poore child: good honny Stremon
Lets have a beare baiting; ye shall see me play.
The rarest for a single Dog: at head all;
And if I doe not win immortall glorie,
Play, Dog play Devill.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Peace for this time,

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Prithee.
Lets sing him a blacke Santis, then lets all howle,
In our owne beastly voices; tree keepe your time,
Untye there; bow, wow, wow.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: A way ye Asse, away,

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: VVhy let us doe something,
To satisfie the Gentleman, hee's mad;
A Gentleman like humour and in fashion,
And must have men as mad about him.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Peace
And come in quicklie, 'tis ten to one els
Heel find a staffe to beat a dog; no more words,
Ile get ye all imployment; soft soft in all,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: VVhen camest thou over wench?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: But now this evening.
And have bin ever since looking out Siphax,
Ith' warres he would have lookt me: sure has gotten
Some other Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: A thousand wench, a thousand
They are as common here as Caterpillers
Among the corne, they eat up all the Souldiers,

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Are they so hungry? yet by their leave Chilax,
Ile have a snatch too.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Dost thou love him still wench?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Why should I not? he had my Maiden head
And all my youth.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Thou art come the happiest
In the most blessed time, sweet wench the fittest,
If thou darst make thy fortune: by this light Cloe
And so ile kiss thee: and if thou wilt but let me,
For 'tis well worth a kindnes.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: What shood I let ye?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Enjoye thy miniken

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Thou art still old Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Still still and ever shalbe: if, I say,
Thou wo't strike the stroke: I cannot doe much harme wench

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Nor much good

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Siphax shall be thy Husband,
Thy very Husband woman, thy foole thy Cuckold,
Or what thou wilt make him: I am over joy'd,
Ravisht cleane ravisht with this fortune; kiss me,
Or I shall loose my self,

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: My Husband sed ye?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Sed I? and will say Cloe; nay and doe it
And doe it home to; Peg thee as close to him
As birdes are with a pinne to one another;
I have it I can doe it: thou wants clothes too,
And heel be hanged unles he marry thee
Ere he maintaine thee: now he has Ladies Courtiers
More then his back can bend at? multitudes
We are taken up for threshers, will ye bite?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Yes

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And let me -

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Yes and let ye -

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: What!

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: VVhy that ye wo't of.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: The turne the good turne?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Any turne the Roche turne;

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's the right turne for that turnes up the bellie.
I cannot stay take your instructions
And something toward howshold, come, what ever
I shall advise ye follow it exactlie
And keep your times I point ye; for ile tell ye
A strange way you must wade through.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Feare not me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Come then and lets dispatch this modicum
For I have but an howre to stay, a short one
Besides more water for another mill
An old weake over shot I must provide for,
Ther's an old Nunnerie at hand.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: VVhat's that

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: A bawdie House.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: A pox consume it

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: If the stones ('tis bui^t on)
Were but as brickle as the flesh lives in it,
Your curse came handsomlie: feare not, ther's Ladies,
And other good sad people: your pinkt Citizens
That thinke no shame to shake a sheet there: Come wench

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: A Souldier and so fearefull?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Can ye blame me;
VVhen such a waite lies on me?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Fye upon ye
I tell ye, ye shall have her: have her safelie,
And for your wife with her owne will,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Good Sister-

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: What a distrustfull man are you? to morrow,
To morrow morning -

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Is it possible?
Can there be such a happines?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Why hang me
If then ye be not married: if to morrow night,
Ye doe not -

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: O deare Sister -

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: What ye woo'd doe
What ye desire to doe; lie with her: Devill,
What a dull man are you?

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Nay I believe now,
And shall she love me?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: As her life and stroke ye,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: O I will be her servant,

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: 'Tis your dutie,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: And she shall have her whole will,

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Yes 'tis reason,
She is a Princes, and by that rule boundles

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: What wood' you be, for I woo'd have ye Sister
Chuse some great place about us: as her woman
Is not so fit.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: No, no, I shall find places:

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: And yet to be a Ladie of her bedchamber,
I hold not so fit neither,
Some great title, beleeve it shall be look't out.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Ye may a Dutchesse
Or such a toye, a small thing pleases me Sir

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: What you will Sister: if a neighbour Prince,
When we shall come to raigne -

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: We shall thinke on't,
Be ready at the time and in that place too,
And let me worke the rest, within this half houre;
The Princess will be going, 'tis almost morning
Away and mind your busines,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Fortune blesse us.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: I doe beseech your grace to banish me.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Why Gentleman is she not worthy marriage?

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: Most worthy, Sir, where worth againe shall meet her,
But I like thicke clouds sailing slow and heavy,
Although by her drawne higher, yet shall hide her
I dare not be a traitor; and 'tis treason,
But to imagin: as you love your honour —

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: 'Tis her first maiden doting and if crost,
I know it kills her.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: How knowes your grace she loves him?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Her woman told me all; beside his story
Her maid Lucippe on what reason to,
And tis beyond all but enjoying.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: Sir.
Even by your wisedome; by that great discretion
Ye owe to rule and order —

speeches.speaker: 2 Lord.
verse: This man's mad sure,
To plead against his fortune -

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: And the King too,
Willing to have it so?

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: By those dead Princes
From whose descents ye stand a starre admired at,
Lay not so base a lay upon your vertues
Take heed for honours sake take heed: the bramble
No wise man ever planted by the rose,
It canckers all her beauty; nor the vine
When her full blushes courts the sun dares any
Choke up with wanton Ivy? good my Lords,
Who builds a monument, the Basis Jasper,
And the maine body Brick?

speeches.speaker: 2 Lord.
verse: Ye wrong your worth,
Ye are a Gentleman descended nobly.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: In both bloods truly noble.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Say ye were not,
My will can make ye so.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: No, never, never;
'Tis not descent, nor will of Princes does it,
'Tis Vertue which I want, 'tis Temperance,
Man, honest man is't fit your Majesty
Should call my drunkennesse, my rashnesse brother?
Or such a blessed Maid my breach of faith,
For I am most lacivious; and fell angers
In which I am also mischievous, her husband?
O Gods preserve her! I am wild as Winter,
Ambitious as the Devill: out upon me,
I hate my selfe, sir, if ye dare bestow her
Upon a Subject ye have one deserves her.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: But him she does not love: I know your meaning.
This young mans love unto his noble brother,
Appeares a mirrour; what must now be done Lords?
For I am gravel'd, if she have not him
She dies for certaine, if his brother misse her,
Farewell to him, and all our honours.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: He is dead sir,
Your Grace has heard of that, and strangely.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: No,
I can assure ye no there was a trick in't,
Read that, and then know all; what ailes the gentleman?
Hold him; how doe ye sir?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Sick ath' the sudden,
Extreamly ill, wondrous ill.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Where did it take ye?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Here in my head sir, and my heart, for heaven sake.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Conduct him to his chamber presently,
And bid my Doctors—

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: No I shall be well sir,
I doe beseech your Grace even for the Gods sake
Remember my poore brother, I shall pray then.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Away he growes more weaker still: I will do it,
Or heaven forget me ever. Now your Counsells,
For I am at my wits end; what with you sir?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Letters from warlike Pelius.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Yet more troubles?
The Spartans are in Armes, and like to win all:
Supplies are sent for and the Generall;
This is more crosse then tother; come let's to him,
For he must have her, 'tis necessitie,
Or we must lose our honours, let's plead all,
For more then all is needfull, shew all reason
If love can heare a that side, if she yeild
We have fought best and won the noblest field.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cap.
verse: I have brought the wench, a lusty wench,
And somewhat like the Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: 'Tis the better, let's see her,
And goe you in and tell him, that her Grace
Is come to visit him? how sleeps he Stremon?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: He cannot, only thinkes, and calls on Polidor,
Swears a will not be fool'd; sometimes he rages,
And sometimes sits and muses.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: He's past all helpe sure?
How doe ye like her?

speeches.speaker: 2 Capt.
verse: Byth' masse a good round Virgin,
And at first sight resembling, she is well cloth'd too.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: But is she sound?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: Of wind and limbe, I warrant her.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: You are instructed Lady?

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: Yes, and know sir
How to behave my selfe, ne're feare.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Polibius,
Where did he get this Vermin?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cap.
verse: Hang him Badger,
There's not a hole free from him, whores and whores mates,
Doe all pay him obedience.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Indeed i'th' war,
His quarter was all whore, whore upon whore,
And linde with a whore, beshrew me 'tis a faire whore.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cap.
verse: She has smockt away her blood; but fair or foule,
Or blind or lame, that can but lift her leg up
Comes not amisse to him, he rides like a night mare,
All ages, all Religions.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: Can ye state it?

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: I'le make a shift.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: He must lie with ye, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: Let him, he's not the first man I have lain with,
Nor shall not be the last.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: A comes, no more words,
She has her lesson throughly; how he views her?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Goe forward now, so, bravely, stand!

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Great Lady,
How humbly I am bound—

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: You shall not kneele sir,
Come, I have done you wrong; stand up my Souldier,
And thus I make amends —

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: A plague confound ye,
Is this your state?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: 'Tis well enough.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: O Lady,
Your royall hand, your hand my dearest beauty
Is more then I must purchase: here divine one,
I dare revenge my wrongs: ha?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cap.
verse: A dam'd foule one.

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: The Lees of baudie prewnes: mourning gloves?
All spoyl'd by heaven.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha! who art thou?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: A shame on ye,
Ye clawing scabby whore.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I say, who art thou?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Why 'tis the Princesse sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: The divell sir,
'Tis some rogue thing.

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: If this abuse be love sir,
Or I that laid aside my modesty—

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: So far thou't never find it.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Doe not weepe,
For if ye be the Princesse, I will love ye,
Indeed I will, and honour ye, fight for ye,
Come wipe your eyes; by heaven she stinkes; who art ta?
Stinkes like a poyson'd Ratt behind a hanging?
Woman who art ta? like a rotten Cabbage.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cap.
verse: Y'ar much to blame sir, 'tis the Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: How?
Shee the Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: And the loving Princesse.

speeches.speaker: 1. Capt.
verse: Indeed the doting Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Come hither once more,
The Princesse smells like mornings breath, pure Amber,
Beyond the courted Indies in her spices
Still a dead rat by heaven; thou art a Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: What a dull whore is this?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I'le tell ye presently,
For if she be a Princesse, as she may be
And yet stink too, and strongly, I shall find her;
Fetch the Numidian Lyon I brought over,
If she be sprung from royall blood, the Lyon
He'l doe ye reverence, els

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: I beseech your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: He'l teare her all to pieces.

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: I am no Princesse, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Who brought thee hither?

speeches.speaker: 2. Capt.
verse: If ye confesse, wee'll hang ye.

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: Good my Lord;

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Who art thou then?

speeches.speaker: Who.
verse: A poore retaining whore, sir,
To one of your Lordships Captaines.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Alas poore whore,
Go, be a whore still, and stinke worse:
What fooles are these, and coxcombes?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: I am right glad yet,
He takes it with such lightnesse.

speeches.speaker: 1. Cap.
verse: Me thinkes his face too,
Is not so clouded as it was; how he lookes?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Where's your dead Rat?

speeches.speaker: 2. Cap.
verse: The divell dine upon her
Lyons, why what a medicine had he gotten
To try a whore?

speeches.speaker: Stre.
prose: Here's one from Polidor staies to speak with ye.

speeches.speaker: Eume.
verse: With whom?

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: With all; where has the Generall bin?
Hee's laughing to himselfe extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Come,
I'le tell thee how: I am glad yet he's so merry.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: What lights are those that enter there, still neerer?
Plague a your rotten itch, do you draw me hither
Into the Temple to betray me? was there no place
To satisfie your sin in? Gods forgive me,
Still they come forward;

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: Peace ye foole, I have found it,
