'Tis the young Princesse Calis.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: 'Tis the divell
To claw us for our catterwawling.

speeches.speaker: Pri.
verse: Retire softly,
I did not looke for you these two houres, Lady,
Beshrew your hast: that way,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That goes to th'Altar?
Ye old blind Beast.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: I know not any way;
Still they come nearer,
I'le in to th'Oracle;

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's well remembred Ile in with ye;

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Doe.
O faire sweet Goddesse Queene of Loves,
Soft and gentle, as thy Doves,
Humble ey'd, and ever ruing
Those poore hearts, their Loves pursuing:
O thou mother of delights,
Crowner of all happy nights,
Star of deare content, and pleasure
Of mutuall loves the endlesse treasure,
Accept this sacrifice we bring
Thou continuall youth and Spring,
Grant this Lady her desires,
And every houre, wee'll crown thy fires.

speeches.speaker: Nun.
verse: You about her all retyre,
Whilst the Princesse feedes the fire,
When your Devotions ended be
To the Oracle I will attend ye.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Hee will abroad.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: How does his humour hold him?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: He is now growne wondrous sad, weeps often too,
Talkes of his brother to himselfe, starts strangely.

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: Does he not curse?

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Eum.
verse: Nor breake out in furie,
Offering some new attempt?

speeches.speaker: Stre.
verse: Neither, toth' Temple
Is all we heare of now: what there he will doe;

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: I hope repent his folly, let's be neare him.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Where are the rest?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: About a businesse
Concernes him mainly, if heav'n cure this madnesse,
He's man for ever Stremon.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Does the King know it?

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Yes, and much troubled with it, is now gone
To seeke his sister out.
Come let's away then.

speeches.speaker: Nun.
verse: Peace to your praiers Lady, will it please ye
To passe on to the Oracle.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
prose: Most humblie.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Doe ye heare that?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Yes, lie close.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: A wildfire take ye,
What shall become of me? I shall be hang'd now.
Is this a time to shake? a halter shake ye,
Come up and juggle, come.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: I am monstrous fearfull.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Up ye old gaping Oyster, up and answer,
A mouldie mange upon your chops, ye told me
I was safe here till the Bell rung.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: I was prevented,
And did not looke these three houres for the Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Shall we be taken?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Speake for loves sake Chilax?
I can not, nor I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
prose: I'le speake treason, for I had as lieve be hang'd for that

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Good Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Must it be sung or sed? what shall I tell 'em?
They are here? here now preparing.

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: O, my conscience!

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Plague a your spurgall'd conscience, does it tyre now?
Now when it should be tuffest? I could make thee—

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Save us, wee are both undone else.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Downe ye dog then,
Be quiet, and be stanch to no inundations.

speeches.speaker: Nun.
verse: Here kneele againe, and Venus grant your wishes.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: O Divine starre of Heaven,
Thou in power above the seven:
Thou sweet kindler of desires,
Till they grow to mutuall fires:
Thou, O gentle Queen that art,
Curer of each wounded heart.
Thou the fuell, and the flame;
Thou in heaven, and here the same:
Thou the wooer, and the wood:
Thou the hunger, and the food:
Thou the prayer, and the prayed;
Thou what is, or shall be said:
Thou still young, and golden tressed,
Make me by thy Answer blessed.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: When?

speeches.speaker: Pr.
verse: Now speake handsomly, and small by all meanes,
I have told ye what.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: But I'le tell you a new tale
Now for my necke verse; I have heard thy prayers,
And marke me well.

speeches.speaker: Nun.
verse: The Goddesse is displeased much,
The Temple shakes and totters: she appeares,
Bow, Lady, bow.

speeches.speaker: Venus.
verse: Purge me the Temple round,
And live by this example henceforth sound
Virgin, I have seene thy teares,
Heard thy wishes and thy feares,
Thy holy Incence flew above,
Harke therefore, thy doome in love,
Had thy heart bin soft at first,
Now thou had'st alayd thy thirst:
Had thy stubborne will but bended,
All thy sorrows here had ended;
Therefore be just in love,
And strange fortune thou must prove,
And, for thou hast bin sterne and coy,
A dead love thou shalt enjoy.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: O gentle goddesse!

speeches.speaker: Venus.
verse: Rise, thy doome is sed,
And feare not; I shall please thee with the dead,

speeches.speaker: Nun.
verse: Goe up into the Temple and there end
Your holy rites, the Goddesse smiles upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I'le no more Oracles, nor Miracles,
Nor no more Church worke, Ile be drawn & hang'd first:
Am not I torne a pieces with the thunder?
Death, I can scarce believe I live yet,
It ga^e me on the buttocks, a cruell, a huge bang,
I had as lieue a had 'em scratcht with dog-whips;
Be quiet henceforth, now ye feele the end on't,
I would advise ye my old friends the good gentlewoman
Is strucken dumbe and there her grace sits mumping
Like an old Ape eating a Brawn; sure the good Goddesse
Knew my intent was honest, to save the Princesse.
And how we young men are entic'd to wickednesse
By these lewd women, I had paid for't els too:
I am monstrous holy now, and cruel fearefull,
O! 'twas a plaguy thump, charg'd with a vengeance.
Woo'd I were well at home; the best is 'tis not day:
Who's that? ha? Siphax? I'le be with you anon, sir,
Ye shall be Oracled I warrant ye,
And thunderd too as well as I: your Lordship
Must needs enjoy the Princesse, yes, ha! torches?
And Memnon comming this way, he's dog mad,
And ten to one appearing thus unto him,
Hee worries me, I must goe by him.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Aske me no further questions; what art thou?
How dost thou stare? stand off; nay looke upon me,
I doe not shake, nor feare thee. —

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: A will kill me,
This is for Church worke.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Why dost thou appeare now?
Thou wert fairly slain: I know thee Diocles,
And know thine envie to mine honour: but—

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Stay Memnon,
I am a Spirit, and thou canst not hurt me.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: This is the voyce of Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: What makes he thus?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: 'Tis true that I was slaine in field, but fowly
By multitudes not manhood: therefore marke me,
I doe appeare againe to quit mine honour,
And on thee single.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: I accept the challenge.
Where?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: On the Stigian banks

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: When?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Four dayes hence.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Goe noble Ghost, I will attend.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I thanke ye.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Ye have sav'd your throat and handsomly:
Farwell sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Sing me the Battell of Pelusium,
In which this Worthie died.

speeches.speaker: Eumen.
verse: This will spoile all, and make him worse
Then ere he was, sitt downe sir,
And give your selfe to rest.
ARme, arme, arme, arm, the Scouts are all come in
Keepe your rankes close and now your honours win.
Behold from yonder hill, the foe appeares,
Bowes, bills glaves arrowes shields, and Speares,
Like a darke wood he comes, or tempest powring,
O view the wings of horse, the meadows scowring,
The vant-guard marches bravely, hark the Drums—dub, dub,
They meet they meet, now the Battell comes,
See how the Arrows fly
That darken all the skie,
Harke how the Trumpets sound,
Hark how the hills rebound, — Tara-tara-tara.
Hark how the horses charge: in boyes in boyes in,-tara, tara,
The Battell totters; now the wounds begin,
O how they cry,
O how they dy.
Roome for the valiant Memnon, arm'd with thunder,
See how he breakes the rankes asunder:
They fly they flie Eumenes has the Chace,
And brave Polibius, makes good his place.
To the plaines to the Woode,
To the Rocks to the floods,
They fly for succour: Follow, follow, follow, Hey, hey.
Harke how the Souldiers hollow
Brave Diocles is dead,
And all his Souldiers fled,
The battell's won, and lost,
That many a life hath cost.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Now forward to the Temple.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Are ye gone?
How have I scapt this morning? by what miracle?
Sure I am ordain'd for some brave end.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: How is it?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Come, 'tis as well as can be.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: But is it possible
This should be true you tell me?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: 'Tis most certaine.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: Such a grosse Asse to love the Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Peace,
Pull your robe close about ye: you are perfect
In all I taught ye.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: Sure.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Gods give thee good luck,
'Tis strange my braines should still be beating knaverie
For all these dangers: but they are needfull mischiefes,
And such are Nuts to me, and I must doe 'em,
You will remember me—

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: By this kisse Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Chilax.
verse: No more of that, I feare another Thunder.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: We are not i'th' Temple man.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Peace, here he comes,
Now to our businesse handsomely: away now.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: 'Twas sure the Princesse, for he kneel'd unto her,
And she lookt every way: I hope the Oracle
Has made me happy: me I hope she lookt for.
Fortune, I will so honour thee, Love so adore thee,
She is here againe lookes round about againe too,
'Tis done, I know 'tis done; 'tis Chilax with her,
And I shall know of him; whose that?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Speake softly,
The Princesse from the Oracle.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: She views me,
By heav'n she beckens me.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Come neare, she woo'd have ye.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: O royall Lady.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: She wills ye read that, for belike she's bound to silence
For such a time; she is wondrous gracious to ye.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Heav'n make me thankfull.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: She woo'd have ye read it,

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Siphax, the will of Heaven hath cast me on thee
To be thy wife, whose will must be obay'd:
Use me with honour, I shall love thee dearly,
And make thee understand thy worths hereafter;
Convey me to a secret Ceremony,
That both our hearts and loves may be united,
And use no language, till before my brother
We both appeare, where I will shew the Oracle,
For till that time I am bound, I must not answer.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: O happy I!

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Ye are a made man.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: But Chilax
Where are her women?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: None but your Graces Sister,
Because she would have it privat to the world yet,
Knowes of this businesse.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: I shall thanke the Chilax,
Thou art a carefull man.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Your Graces servant.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: I'le find a sit place for thee.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: If you will not,
There's a good Lady will, she points yee forward,
Away and take your fortune, not a word sir,
So, you are greas'd I hope.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Stremon, Foole, Picus.
Where have you left your Lord?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: I'th' Temple, Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Why are ye from him?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Why the King is with him,
And all the Lords.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Is not the Princesse there too.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Yes,
And the strangest coile amongst 'em: She weeps bitterly;
The King entreats, and frownes, my Lord like Autumne
Drops off his hopes by handfulls, all the Temple
Sweats with this Agonie.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Where's young Polidor?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Dead as they said o'th' sudden.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Dead?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: For certaine,
But not yet knowne abroad,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: There's a new trouble;
A brave young man he was; but we must all die.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Did not the Generall meet you this morning
Like a tall stallion Nun?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: No more a that Boy.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: You had been ferreting.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: That's all one, Foole;
My Master foole that taught my wits to traffique,
What has your wisdome done? how have you profited?
Out with your Audit, come: you are not emptie,
Put out mine eye with twelve pence? do you shaker?
What thinke you of this shaking? here's with coxcombe
Ha boyes? ha my fine rascalls, here's a Ring,
How right they goe?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: O let me ring the fore-bell.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And here are thumpers, Chickens, golden rogues,
^it wit ye rascalls.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: I have a Sty here Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I have no gold to cure it, not a penny,
Not one crosse Cavalier; we are dull Sou'diers,
Grosse, heavy-headed fellowes; fight for victualls?

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Why; ye are the spirits of the time.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: By no meanes.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: The valiant firie.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Fy, fie no.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Be-lee-me sir.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I woo'd I could sir.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: I will satisfie ye.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: But I will not content you; alas poore boy,
Thou shewst an honest nature weepes for thy Master,
There's a red rogue to buy thee handkerchers.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: A was an honest Gentleman, I have lost too.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Ye have indeed your labour Foole; but Stremon,
Doest thou want money too? no virtue living?
No firking out at fingers ends?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: It seemes so.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Will ye all serve me?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: Yes, when ye are Lord Generall,
For lesse I will not goe.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: There's gold for thee then,
Thou hast a souldiers minde, Foole.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Here, your first man.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I will give thee for thy wit, for 'tis a fine wit,
A daintie diving wit, hold up; just nothing,
Goe graze i'th' commons, yet I am mercifull
There's six pence; buy a Saucer, steale an old gowne,
And beg i'th' Temple for a Prophet, come away boyes,
Let's see how things are carried, Foole, up sirra,
You may chance get a dinner: Boy your preferment
I'le undertake, for your brave Masters sake,
You shall not perish.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: Chilax.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Please me well Foole,
And you shall light my pipes: Away to th' Temple.
But stay, the Kings here, sport upon sport Boyes.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What would you have Captaine,
Speake suddenly, for I am wondrous busie.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: A Pardon, Royall sir.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: For what?

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: For that,
Which was heav'ns will, should not be mine alone sir;
My marrying with this Lady.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: It needs no Pardon,
For marriage is no sin.

speeches.speaker: Si.
verse: Not in it selfe, sir,
But in presuming too much: Yet heav'n knowes
So does the Oracle that cast it on me,
And — the Princesse, royall sir.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: O be not angrie, my dread King, your Sister.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: My sister? she's i'th' Temple man.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: She is here sir.

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: The Captain's mad, she is kneeling at the Altar.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I know she is, with all my heart good Captain,
I do forgive ye both: be unvail'd Lady;
Will ye have more forgivenes? the mans frantick,
Come let's goe bring her out: God give yee joy sir.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
prose: How? Cloe? my old Cloe?

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: Even the same sir.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Gods give your manhood much c^ntent.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: The Princesse
Lookes something mustie since her comming over.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: 'Twere good, youl'd brush her over.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: Fooles and Fidlers
Make sport at my abuse too.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: O 'tis the nature
Of us Fooles to make bold with one another,
But you are wise, brave sirs.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Cheere up your Princesse,
Believe it sir, the King will not be angry,
Or say he were; why 'twas the Oracle,
The Oracle, and like your Grace, the Oracle.

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: And who, most mighty Siphax?

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: With mine owne whore.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: With whom els should ye marry speak your conscience,
Will ye transgresse the law of Armes, that ever
Rewards the Souldier with his owne sins?

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: Devills.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: Ye had my maiden-head my youth, my sweetnes,
Is it not justice then? —

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: I see it must be,
But by this hand. I'le hang a lock upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: You shall not need, my honesty shall doe it.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: If there be wars in all the world—

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: I'le with ye,
For you know, I have bin a souldier,
Come, curse on: when I need another Oracle.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Send for me Siphax, I'le fit ye with a Princesse,
And so to both your honours.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: And your graces.

speeches.speaker: Siph.
verse: The Devill grace ye all.

speeches.speaker: Cloe.
verse: God a mercy Chilax,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Shall we laugh halfe an houre now?

speeches.speaker: Strem.
verse: No the King comes,
And all the traine.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Away then, our Act's ended.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You know he do's deserve ye, loves ye dearly,
You know what bloody violence had us'd
Upon himselfe, but that his brother crost it,
You know the same thoughts still inhabit in him
And covet to take birth: Look on him Lady,
The wars have not so far consum'd him yet,
Cold age disabled him, or sicknesse sunk him
To be abhorr'd: looke on his Honour sister,
That beares no stamp of time, no wrinkles on it,
No sad demolishment, nor death can reach it:
Looke with the eyes of heaven that nightlie waken,
To view the wonders of my glorious Maker,
And not the weaknesse: looke with your vertuous eyes,
And then clad royaltie in all his conquests;
His matchlesse love hung with a thousand merits
Eternall youth attending, Fame and Fortune,
Time and Oblivion vexing at his vertues,
He shall appeare a miracle: looke on our dangers,
Looke on the publique ruine.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: O, deare brother.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Fie, let us not like proud and greedy waters
Gaine, to give off againe: this is our Sea,
And you his Cynthia, govern him, take heed,
His stouds have bin as hie, and full as any,
And gloriously now is got up to the girdle,
The Kingdomes he hath purchas'd; noble Sister,
Take not your vertue from him, O take heed
We ebbe not now to nothing, take heed Calis.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: The wil of heaven not mine, which must not alter,
And my eternall doome for ought I know
Is fixt upon me; alas, I must love nothing.
Nothing that loves againe must I be blest with:
The gentle Vine climbs up the Oke and clips him.
And when the stroke comes, yet they fall together;
Death death must I enjoy, and live to love him,
O noble Sir!

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Those teares are some reward yet,
Pray let me wed your sorrowes.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Take 'em Souldier,
They are fruitfull ones, lay but a fight upon 'em,
And strait they will conceive to infinites;
I told ye what, ye could find 'em,
Roome before there.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How now, what's this? more drops to th'Ocean?
Whose body's this?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
verse: The noble Polidor,
This speakes his death.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: My Brother dead?

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: O Goddesse!
O cruell, cruell Venus, here's my fortune.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Read Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
prose: Read aloude: farewell my follies.

speeches.speaker: 1. Cap.
verse: Be wise, as you are beauteous, love with judgement,
And look with clear eyes on my noble Brother,
Value desert and vertue, they are Jewells,
Fit for your worth and wearing: take heed Lady,
The Gods reward ingratitude most grievous;
Remember me no more, or if you must,
Seeke me in noble Memnons love, I dwell there:
I durst not live, because I durst not wrong him,
I can no more, make mee eternall happy
With looking downe upon your loves.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: And did'st thou die for me?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Excellent vertue!
What will ye now doe?

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: Dwell for euer here sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: For me deare Polidor? ô worthy young man!
O love, love, love, love above recompence!
Infinite love, infinite honesty!
Good Lady leave, you must have no share here,
Take home your sorrowes: here's enough to store me,
Brave glorious griefes! was ever such a brother?
Turne all the stories over in the world yet,
And search through all the memories of mankind,
And find me such a friend; h'as out-done all.
Outstript 'em sheerely, all, all, thou hast Polidor,
To die for me; why, as I hope for happinesse,
'Twas one of the rarest thought on things
The bravest, and carried beyond compasse of our actions,
I wonder how he hit it, a young man too,
In all the blossomes of his youth and beautie,
In all the fulnesse of his veines and wishes
Woed by that Paradice, that would catch heaven;
It starts me extreamly, thou blest Ashes,
Thou faithfull monument, where loue and friendship
Shall while the world is, worke new miracles.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: O! let me speake too.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: No not yet, thou man,
For we are but mans shadowes, only man,
I have not words to utter him; speake Lady,
I'le thinke a while.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: The Goddesse grants me this yet,
I shall enjoy the dead: no tombe shall hold thee
But these two armes, no Trickments but my teares
Over thy Hearse, my sorrowes like sad armes
Shall hang for ever: on the tuffest Marble
Mine eyes shall weepe thee out an Epitaph,
Love at thy feet shall kneele, his smart bow broken;
Faith at thy head, youth and the Graces mourners;
O sweet young man!

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Now I begin to melt too.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Have ye enough yet Lady? roome for a gamster
To my fond Love, and all those idle fancies
A long farwell, thou diedst for me deare Polidor,
To give me peace, thou hast eternall glory,
I stay and talke here; I will kisse thee first,
And now I'le follow thee.

speeches.speaker: Pollidor.
verse: Hold, for heavens sake!

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Ha!
Does he live?
Dost thou deceive me?

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Thus farre,
Yet for your good, and honour.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Now deare sister;

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: The Oracle is ended, noble sir,
Dispose, me now as you please.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: You are mine then?

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: With all the joyes that may be.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: Your consent sir;

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Ye have it freely.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: Walke along with me then,
And as you love me, love my will.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: I will so.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: Here worthy Brother, take this vertuous Princesse,
Ye have deserv'd her nobly, she will love ye,
And when my life shall bring ye peace, as she does,
Command it, ye shall have it.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Sir, I thanke ye.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I never found such goodnesse in such yeares.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Thou shalt not over-doe me, though I die for't,
O how I love thy goodnesse, my best brother,
You have given me here a treasure to enrich me,
Would make the worthiest King alive a begger,
What may I give you back againe?

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: Your love sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: And you shall have it, even my dearest love,
My first, my noblest love, take her againe, sir,
She is yours, your honesty has over-run me,
She loves ye, lov'st her not? excellent Princesse,
Injoy thy wish, and now get Generalls.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: As ye love heaven, love him, she is only yours, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: As ye love heaven, love him, she is only yours, sir;
My Lord, the King.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: He will undoe himselfe sir,
And must without her perish; who shall fight then?
Who shall protect your Kingdome?

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Give me hearing,
And after that beliefe, were she my soule
(As I doe love her equall) all my victories,
And all the living names I have gain'd by warre,
And loving him that good, that vertuous good man,
That only worthy of the name of brother,
I would resigne all freely, 'tis all love
To me, all marriage rites, the joy of issues
To know him fruitfull, that has been so faithfull.

speeches.speaker: King.
prose: This is the noblest difference-take your choise sister.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: I see they are so brave, and noble both,
I know not which to looke on.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Chuse discreetly,
And vertue guide ye, there all the world in one man
Stands at the marke.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: There all mans honestie,
The sweetnesse of all youth —

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: O God's!

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: My Armour,
By all the God's she's yours; my armes, I say,
And I beseech your Grace, give me imployment,
That shall be now my Mistresse: here my Courtship.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Ye shall have any thing.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: Vertuous Lady,
Remember me, your servant now; Young man,
You cannot over-reach me in your goodnesse;
O love! how sweet thou look'st now? and how gentle,
I should have slubber'd thee, and stain'd thy beauty;
Your hand, your hand sir;

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Take her, and Heaven blesse her.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: So.

speeches.speaker: Po.
verse: 'Tis your will sir, nothing of my merit;
And as your royall gift, I take this blessing.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: And I from heaven this gentleman: thanks Goddess.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: So ye are pleas'd now Lady;

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Now or never.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: My cold stiffe carkasse, would have frozen ye,
Warres, warres.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Ye shall have warres.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: My next brave battell
I dedicate to your bright honour (sister,)
Give me a favour, that the world may know
I am your souldier.

speeches.speaker: Calis.
verse: This, and all faire Fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Mem.
verse: And he that beares this from me, must strike boldly.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I do forgive thee: be honest, no more wench.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Come now to Revells, this blest day shall prove
The happy crown of noble Faith and Love.

speeches.speaker: Arsenio.
verse: LEandro paid all.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: 'Tis his usuall custome,
And requisite he should: he has now put off
The Funerall black, (your rich heirs weares with joy,
When he pretends to weep for his dead Father,)
Your gathering Sires, so long heape muck together,
That their kind Sonnes, to rid them of their care
Wish them in heaven; Or if they take a taste
Of Purgatory by the way, it matters not:
Provided they remove hence; What is befalne
To his Father, in the other world, I ask not,
I am sure his prayre is heard: would I could use one
For mine, in the same method.

speeches.speaker: Arsen.
verse: Fy upon thee.
This is prophane,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Good Doctor, doe not schoole me,
For a fault you are not free from: On my life
Were all Heires in Corduba, put too their oathes
They would confesse with me, 'tis a sound Tenet:
I am sure Leandro do't.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: He is th'owner
Of a faire Estate.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: And fairly he deserves it,
He's a royall Fellow: yet observes a meane
In all his courses, carefull to on whom
He showres his bounties: he that's liberall
To all alike, may doe a Good by chance,
But never out of Judgement! This invites
The prime men of the Citie to frequent
All places he resorts to, and are happy
In his sweet Converse.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Don Jamie the Brother
To the Grandee Don Henrique, appeares much taken
With his behaviour.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: There is something more in't:
Hee needs his Purse, and knowes how to make use on't,
'Tis now in fashion for your Don, that's poore,
To vow all Leagues of friendship with a Merchant
That can supply his wants, and howsoe're
Don Jamie's noble borne, his elder Brother
Don Henrique rich and his Revenues long since
Encreasing by marrying with a wealthy Heire
Call'd Madam Violante, he yet holds
A hard hand o're Jamie, allowing him
A bare annuity onely.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Yet 'tis said
He hath no child, and by the Lawes of Spaine
If he die without issue, Don Iamie
Inherits his Estate.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Why that's the reason
Of their so many jarres: Though the young Lord
Be sick of the elder Brother, and in reason
Should flatter, and observe him, he's of a nature
Too bold and fierce, to stoop so, but beares up,
Presuming on his hopes.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: What's the young Lad
That all of em make so much of?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: 'Tis a sweet-One,
And the best condition'd youth, I ever saw yet,
So humble and so affable, that he wins
The love of all that know him, and so modest,
That (in despight of povertie) he would starve
Rather then aske a courtesie; He's the Sonne
Of a poore cast-Captaine, one Octavio
And She, that once was calld th' faire Iacinta,
Is happy in being his Mother: for his sake.
(Though in their Fortunes falne) they are esteem'd of,
And cherish'd by the best. O here they come,
I now may spare his Character, but observe him,
Hee'l justifie my report.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: My good Ascanio
Repaire more often to me: above Women
Thou ever shalt be welcome.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: My Lord your favours
May quickly teach a raw untutour'd Youth
To be both rude and sawcie.

speeches.speaker: Leandro.
verse: You cannot be
Too frequent where you are so much desir'd:
And give me leave (deare friend) to be your Rivall
In part of his Affection; I will buy it
At any rate.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Stood I but now possess'd
Of what my future hope presages to me,
I then would make it cleare thou hadst a Patron
That would not say but do: yet as I am,
Be mine, I'le not receive thee as a servant,
But as my Son (and though I want my self)
No Page attending in the Court of Spain
Shall find a kinder master.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: I beseech you
That my refusall of so great an offer
May make no ill construction, 'tis not pride
(That common vice is farre from my condition)
That makes you a denyall to receive
A favour I should sue for: nor the fashion
Which the country followes, in which to be a servant
In those that groan beneath the heavy weight
Of povertie is held an argument
Of a base and abject mind, I wish my yeares
Were fit to do you service in a nature
That might become a Gentleman (give me leave
To think my self one) My father serv'd the King
As a Captain in the field; and though his fortune
Return'd him home a poore man, he was rich
In reputation, and wounds fairly taken.
Nor am I by his ill successe deterr'd,
I rather feel a strong desire that swayes me
To follow his Profession, and if heaven
Hath marked me out to be a man, how proud,
In the service of my Country, should I be,
To traile a pike under your brave command.
There, I would follow you as a guid to honour,
Though all the horrours of the Warre made up
To stop my passage.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Thou art a hopefull Boye,
And it was bravely spoken: For this answer,
I love thee more then ever.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Pitty such seeds
Of promising courage should not grow and prosper

speeches.speaker: Aug.
verse: What ever his reputed Parents bee,
He ha^ a mind that speakes him right and noble.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: You make him blush: it needs not sweet Ascanio,
We may heare praises when they are deserv'd,
Or modestie unwounded. By my life
I would adde something to the building up
So fair a mind, and if till you are fit
To beare Armes in the field, you'l spend some yeares
In Salamanca, I'le supply your studies
With all conveniences.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Your goodnesse (Signiors)
And charitable favours overwhelm me.
If I were of your blood, you could not be
More tender of me: what then can I pay
(A poore boy and a stranger) but a heart
Bound to your service? with what willingnes
I would receive (good Sir) your noble offer,
Heaven can beare witnes for me: but alas
Should I embrace the meanes to raise my fortunes,
I must destroy the lives of my poore Parents
(To whom I ow my being) they in me
Place all their comforts, and (as if I were
The light of their dim eyes) are so indulgent
They cannot brook one short dayes absence from me;
And (what will hardly win belief) though young,
I am their steward and their nurse: the bounties
VVhich others bestow on me serves to sustain 'em,
And to forsake them in their age, in me
VVere more then murther.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: This is a kind of begging
VVould make a Broker charitable.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Here (sweet heart)
I wish that it were more.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: VVhen this is spent,
Seek for supply from me

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Thy pietie
For ever be remembred: nay take all,
Though 't were my exhibition to a Royall
For one whole yeare.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: High heavens reward your goodnes.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: So Sir, is this a slip of your own grafting,
You are so prodigall?

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: A slip Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Yes,
A slip; or call it by the proper name
Your Bastard.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: You are foul-mouth'd; do not provoke me,
I shall forget your Birth, if you proceed,
And use you, (as your manners do deserve) uncivilly.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: So brave? pray you give me hearing,
Who am I Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: My elder Brother: One
That might have been born a fool and so reputed,
But that you had the luck to creep into
The world a yeare before me.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Be more temperate.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: I neither can nor will, unlesse I learn it
By this example: let him use his harsh
Unsavoury reprehensions upon those
That are his hinds, and not on me. The Land
Our father left to him alone rewards him,
For being twelve moneths elder, let that be
Forgotten, and let his Parasites remember
One quality of worth or vertue in him
That may authorise him, to be a censurer
Of me, or of my manners, and I will
Acknowledge him for a tutor, til then, never

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: From whom have you your meanes Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: From the will
Of my dead father; I am sure I spend not
Nor give't upon your purse.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: But will it hold out
Without my help?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: I am sure it shall I'le sink else
For sooner I will seek aid from a whore,
Then a courtesie from you.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: 'Tis well; you are proud of
Your new Exchequer when you have cheated him
And worn him to the quick, I may be found
In the List of your acquaintance'

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Pray you hold
And give me leave (my Lord) to say thus much
(And in mine own defence) I am no Gull
To be wrought on by perswasion: nor no Coward
To be beaten out of my meanes, but know to whom
And why I give or lend, and will do nothing
But what my reason warrants; you may be
As sparing as you please, I must be bold
To make use of mine own, without your licence.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: 'Pray thee let him alone, he is not worth thy anger
All that he do's (Leandro) is for my good,
I think there's not a Gentleman of Spain,
That ha's a better steward, then I have of him.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Your steward Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Yes, and a provident one:
Why, he knowes I am given to large Expence,
And therefore layes up for me: could you believe els
That he, that sixteen years hath worne the yoke
Of barren wedlock, without hope of issue.
(His Coffer's full, his Lands, and Vineyards fruitfull)
Could be so sold to base, and sordid thrift,
As almost to deny himselfe, the meanes
And necessaries of life? Alas, he knowes
The Lawes of Spaine appoint me for his heire,
That all must come to me, if I out-live him,
(Which sure I must doe, by the course of Nature,)
And the assistance of good Mirth, and Seck,
How ever you prove Melancholy.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: If I live,
Thou dearly shalt repent this,

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: When thou art dead,
I am sure I shall not.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Now they begin to burn
Like oppos'd Meteors.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Give them line, and way,
My life for Don Jamie.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Continue still
The excellent Husband, and joyne Farme to Farme,
Suffer no Lordship, that in a cleare day
Falls in the prospect of your coveteous eye
To be an others; Forget you are a Grandee
Take use upon use, and cut the throats of heires
With cozening Mort-gages: rack your poore Tenants,
Till they looke like so many Skeletons
For want of Food; And when that Widowes curses,
The ruines of ancient Families, teares of Orphans
Have hurried you to the divell, ever remember
All was rak'd up, for me, (your thankfull Brother)
That will dance merrily upon your Grave,
And perhaps give a double Pistolet
To some poore needy Frier, to say a Masse
To keep your Ghost from walking.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: That the Law
Should force me to endure this!

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Verely,
When this shall come to passe (as sure it will)
If you can find a loope-hole, though in hell'
To looke on my behaviour, you shall see me
Ransack your Iron Chests, and once againe
Pluto's flame-colour'd Daughter shall be free
To dominier in Taverns, Maskes, and Revells
As she was us'd, before she was your Captive.
Me thinkes the meere conceipt of it, should make you
Goe home sick and distemper'd if it do's.
I'le send you a Doctor of mine owne, and after
Take order for your Funerall.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: You have said, sir,
I will not fight with words, but deeds to tame you,
Rest confident I will and thou shalt wish
This day thou hadst been dumb. —

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: You have given him a heat.
But with your owne distemper.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Not a whit
Now he is from mine eye, I can be merry,
Forget the cause, and him: all plagues goe with him,
Let's talke of something els: what newes is stirring?
Nothing to passe the time?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: 'Faith it is said
That the next Summer will determine much
Of that we long have talk'd of, touching the Wars.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: What have we to doe with them? Let us discourse
Of what concernes our selves. 'Tis now in fashion
To have you Gallants set downe, in a Taverne,
What the Arch-Dukes purpose is the next spring & what
Defence my Lords (the States) prepare: what course
The Emperour takes against the encroching Turke,
And whither his Moony-Standards are design'd
For Persia or Polonia: and all this
The wiser sort of State-Wormes seeme to know
Better then their owne Affaires: this is discourse
Fit for the Counsell it concernes; we are young,
And if that I might give the Theame, 'twere better
To talke of handsome women.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: And that's one,
Almost as generall.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Yet none agree
Who are the fairest.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Some prefer the French,
For their conceited Dressings: some the plump
Italian Bona-Robas some the State
That ours observe; and I have heard one sweare,
(A merry friend of mine) that once in London,
He did enjoy the company of a Gamester,
(A common Gamester too) that in one night
Met him th'Italian, French, and Spanish waies,
And ended in the Dutch; for, to coole her selfe,
She kiss'd him drunke in the morning.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Wee may spare
The travell of our tongues in forraigne Nations,
When in Corduba, if you dare give credit
To my report (for I have seene her, Gallants)
There lives a woman) of a meane birth too,
And meanly match'd) whose all-excelling Forme
Disdaines comparison with any She
That puts in for a faire one, and though you borrow
From every Country of the Earth the best
Of those perfections, which the Clymat yeilds
To help to make her up, if put in Ballance,
This will weigh-downe the Scale.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: You talke of wonders.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: She is indeed a wonder, and so kept,
And, as the world deserv'd not to behold
What curious Nature made without a patterne,
Whose Copy she hath lost too, she's shut up,
Sequestred from the world.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Who is the owner
Of such a Jem? I am fir'd.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: One Bartolus,
A wrangling Advocate.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: A knave on Record.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: I am sure he cheated me of the best part
Of my Estate.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Some Businesse calls me hence,
(And of importance) which denies me leisure
To give you his full character: In few words
(Though rich) he's covetous beyond expression,
And to encrease his heape, will dare the Divell,
And all the plagues of darknesse: and to these
So jealous, as if you would paralell
Old Argus to him, you must multiply
His Eies an hundred times: of these, none sleepe.
He that would charme the heaviest lid, must hire
A better Mercurie, then Iove made use of:
Blesse your selves from the thought of him and her
For 'twill be labour lost: So farewell Signiors.—

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Leandro? in a dreame? wake man for shame.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Trayned into a fooles paradise with a tale
Of an imagin'd Forme,

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Iamie is noble,
And with a forg'd Tale would not wrong his Friend,
Nor am I so much fired with lust as Envie,
That such a churl as Bartolus should reap
So sweet a harvest, half my State to any
To help me to a share.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Tush do not hope for
Impossibilities,

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I must enjoy her,
And my prophetique love tells me I shall,
Lend me but your assistance;

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Give it 'ore,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: I would not have thee fool'd

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I have strange Engines,
Fashioning here: and Bartolus on the Anville
Diswade me not, but help me,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Take your fortune,
If you come off well; praise your wit, if not,
Expect to be the subject of our Laughter.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: You met Don Henrique.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: Yes:

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: What comfort bring you?
Speake cheerefully: how did my Letter worke?
On his hard temper? I am sure I wrot it,
So feelingly, and with the pen of sorrow,
That it must force Co^punction,

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: You are cozen'd;
Can you with one hand prop a falling Tower?
Or with the other stop theraging maine,
When it breakes in on the usurped Shore?
Or any thing that is impossible?
And then conclude that there is some way left,
To move him to compassion.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Is there a Justice
Or thunder (my Octavio) and he
Not sunk unto the center?

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: Good Iacinta.
With your long practised patience beare afflictions,
And by provoking it call not on Heavens anger,
He did not onely scorne to read your Letter,
But (most inhumane as he is) he cursed you,
Cursed you most bitterly,

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: The bad mans charity,
Oh that I could forget there were a Tye,
In me, upon him! or the releife I seeke,
(If given) were bounty in him, and not debt,
Debt of a deere accompt!

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: Touch not that string,
Twill but encrease our Sorrow, and tame silence,
(The Balme of the oppressed) which hitherto
Hath eas'd your grieved soule, and preserv'd your fame,
Must be your Surgeon still.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: If the contagion
Of my misfortunes had not spread it self,
Upon my Son Ascanio, though my wants
Were centupli'd upon ^y self, I could be patient:
But he is so good, I so miserable,
His pious care his dutie, and obedience,
And all that can be wish'd for from a Son,
Discharg'd to me, and I, bard of all meanes,
To returne any scruple of the debt
I owe him as a Mother, is a Torment,
Too painefull to be borne.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: I suffer with you,
In that; yet find in this assurance comfort,
High heaven ordaines (whose purposes cannot alter)
Children that pay obedience to their Parents,
Shall never beg their Bread.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Here comes our joy,
Where has my dearest been?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I have made (Mother)
A fortunate voyage and brought home rich prize,
In a few houres: the owners too contented,
From whom I tooke it. See heres Gold, good store too
Nay pray you take it,

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Mens Charities are so cold,
That if I knew not, thou wert made of Goodnes,
'Twould breed a jealousie in me by what meanes,
Thou cam'st by such a sum

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Were it ill got,
I am sure it could not be employed so well,
As to relieve your wants. Some noble Friends,
(Rais'd by heavens mercy to me, not my merits)
Bestow'd it on me.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: It were a sacriledge
To rob thee of their bounty, since they gave it,
To thy use onely;

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Buy thee brave Cloathes with it
And fit thee for a fortune, and leave us,
To our necessities; why do'st thou weep?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Out of my feare, I have offended you;
For had I not, I am sure you are too kind,
Not to accept the offer of my service,
In which I am a gainer; I have heard
My tutor say of all a iereall foule
The Storke's the Embleme of true pietie,
Because when age hath seiz'd upon her dam,
And made unfit for flight, the gratefull young one
Takes her upon his back, provides her foode,
Repaying so, her tender care of him,
'Ere he was fit to fly, by bearing her:
Shall I then that have reason, and discourse
That tell me all I can doe is too litle,
Be more unnaturall then a silly Bird?
Or feed or cloth my selfe superfluously,
And know, nay see you want? holy Saints keepe me.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Can I be wretched,
And know my selfe the Mother to such Goodnes?

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: Come, let us drie our eyes, wee'll have a Feast,
Thanks to our little Steward;

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: And in him,
Beleeve that we are rich.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I am sure I am,
While I have power to comfort you, and serve you.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Is it my fault (Don Henrique) or my fate,
Wha'ts my offence? I came young to your Bed
I had a fruitfull Mother and you met me,
With equall ardour in your May of blood;
And why then am I barren?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: 'Tis not in Man
To yield a reason for the will of Heaven,
Which is inscrutable.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: To what use serve
Full fortunes, and the meaner sort of Blessings,
When that, which is the Crowne of all our wishes,
The period of humane happines,
One only Child that may possesse what's ours,
Is cruelly denide us?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: 'Tis the curse,
Of great Estates to want those Pledges which,
The poore are happy in: They in a Cottage,
With joy, behold the Modells of their youth,
And as their Roote decaies those budding Branches,
Sprout forth and flourish, to renew their age;
But this is the beginning, not the end
To me, of, that misery against my will,
(Since Heaven denies us Issue of our owne)
Must leave the fruit of all my care and travell
To an unthankfull Brother that insults,
On my Calamity.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I will rather choose,
A Bastard from the Hospitall and adopt him,
And nourish him, as mine owne.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Such an evasion
(My Violante) is forbid to us;
Happy the Romane State, where it was lawfull,
(If our owne Sonnes were vicious) to choose one
Out of a vertuous Stock, though of poore Parents,
And make him noble. But the Lawes of Spaine,
(Intending to preserve all ancient Houses)
Prevent such free elections; with this my Brothers
Too well acquainted, and this makes him bold to
Reigne 'ore me, as a Master,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I will fire
The Portion I brought with me, 'ere he spend,
A Royall of it: No Quirck left? no Quiddit
That may defeate him?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Were I but confirmed,
That you would take the meanes I use, with patience,
As I must practise it with my dishonour,
I could lay levell with the earth his hopes
That soare above the clouds with expectation
To see me to my grave.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Effect but this
And our revenge shall be to us a Son
That shall inherit for us.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Do not repent
When 'tis too late.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I feare not what may fall
He disposess'd that doe's usurpe on all

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Can any thing, but wonder?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Wonder on,
I am as ye see, and what will follow Gentlemen

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Why dost thou put on this form? what can this do?
Thou lookest most sillily,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Like a young Clerk
A half pin'd-puppy that would write for a Royall.
Is this a commanding shape to win a Beautie?
To what use, what occasion?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Peace ye are fooles,
More silly then my out-side seems ye are ignorant
They that pretend to wonders must weave cunningly.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: What manner of accesse can this get? or if gotten
What credit in her eyes?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Will ye but leave me?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Me thinks a yong man and a handsom Gentleman
(But sure thou art lunatick) me thinks a brave man
That would catch cunningly the beames of Beautie,
And so distribute 'em, unto his comfort,
Should like himself appeare young, high, and buxom.
And in the brightest form.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Ye are cozen'd (Gentlemen)
Neither doe I believe this, nor will follow it,
Thus I am, I will begin my voyage,
When you love, lanch it out in silks and velvets,
I le love in Serge, and will outgo our Sattins
To get upon my great horse and appeare.
The signe of such a man, and trot my measures,
Or fiddle out whole frosty nights (my friends)
Vnder the window, while my teeth keep tune,
I hold no handsomnesse. Let me get in
There trot and fiddle where I may have faire play,

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: But how get in?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Leave that to me, your patience,
I have some toyes here that I dare well trust to:
I have smelt a Vicar out, the call him Lopez.
You are ne're the nearer now,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: We do confesse it.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Weak simple men, this Vicar to this Lawyer
Is the most inward, Damon.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: What can this do?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: We know the fellow, and he dwells there.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: So.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: A poore, thin theef: he help? he; hang the Vicar
Can reading of an—preferre thee?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Thou art dead-sick in love, and hee'l pray for thee
Have patience (Gentlemen) I say this Vicar,
This thing I say is all one with the Close Bartolus
(For so they call the Lawyer) or his nature
Which I have studied by relation;
And make no doubt I shall hit hansomly,
Will I work cunningly and home: understand me.
Next I pray leave me, Leave me to my fortune
Difficilia pulchra, thats my Motto (Gentlemen)
I 'le win this Diamond from the rock and weare her
Or—

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Peace, the Vicar: send ye a full sail, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: There's your Confessor, but what shal be your pennance?
A fools head if I fail and so forsake me.
You shall heare from me daily.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: We will be ready,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Thin world indeed:

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I'le let him breathe and mark him:
No man would think a stranger as I am
Should reap any great commodity from his pigbelly,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Poore stirring for poore Vicars,
Diego And poore Sextons.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We pray and pray, but to no purpose
Those that enjoy our Lands, choak our Devotions.
Our poore thin stipends make us arrant dunces,

speeches.speaker: Diego
verse: If you live miserably, how shall we do (Master?)
That are fed only with the sound of prayers?
We rise and ring the Bells to get good stomacks.
And must be fain to eat the ropes with reverence,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: When was there a Christning (Diego?)

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Not this ten weekes:
Alas, they have forgot to get children (Master)
The Warres, the Seas, and usurie undoe us,
Takes off our minds, our edges, blunts our plough-shares,
They eat nothing here, but herbs, & get nothing but green sauce:
There are some poore Labourers, that perhaps
Once in seven yeare, with helping one another,
Produce some few pind—Butter—prints, that scarce hold
The christning neither.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Your Gallants, they get Honour,
A strange fantasticall Birth, to defraud the Vicar,
And the Camp Christens their Issues, or the Curtizans,
'Tis a lewd time.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: They are so hard-hearted here too,
They will not dye, there's nothing got by Burialls.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Diego, the Ayre's too pure, they cannot perish:
To have a thin Stipend, and an everlasting Parish,
Lord what a torment 'tis!

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Good sensible Master,
You are allow'd to pray against all weathers,
(Both foule, and faire, as you shall find occasion)
Why not against all ayres?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: That's not i'th' Canons,
I would it had, 'tis out of our way forty pence.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: 'Tis strange, they are starv'd too yet they wil not die here,
They will not Earth: a good stout plague amongst 'um,
Or halfe a dozen new fantasticall Fevers
That would turne up their heeles by whole-sale (Master)
And take the Doctors too, in their grave Counsells,
That there might be no naturall help for money;
How merrily would my Bells goe then?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Peace Diego
The Doctors are our friends, let's please them well,
For though they kill but slow, they are certaine (Diego)
We must remove into a muddy Ayre,
A most contagious Clymat.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: We must certaine,
An ayre that is the nursery of Agues,
Such Agues (Master) that will shake mens soules out,
Ne're stay for Possets, nor good old wives plaisters.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Gowts and dead Palsies.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: The dead doe's well at all times,
Yet Gowts will hang an arsse a long time (Master)
The Pox, or English Surfets if we had 'em;
Those are nich Marle, they make a Church-yard fat,
And make the Sexton sing, they never misse, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Then Wills and Funerall Sermons come in season,
And Feasts that makes us frolicke.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Would I could see' em.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And though I weepe i'th' Pulpit for my Brother,
Yet (Diego) here I laugh.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: The cause requires it.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Since people left to die I am dunce (Diego.)

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: 'Tis a strange thing, I have forgot to dig too.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: A pretious pair of youths; I must make toward 'em

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Who's that? look out it seemes he would speak to us.
I hope a Marriage, or some Wil to make (Diego.)

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: My friend your businesse?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: 'Tis to that grave Gentleman;
Blesse your good learning (Sir)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And blesse you also,
He beares a promising face, there's some hope toward.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I have a Letter to your worship.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Well Sir,
From whence I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: From Nova Hispania, Sir,
And from an ancient friend of yours.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Tis well (Sir)
'Tis very well: the divell a-one I know there.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Take heed of a Snap (Sir) has a cozening countenance,
I doe not like his way.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Let him goe forward.
Cantabit ~acuus, They that have nothing, feare nothing,
All I have to loose (Diego) is my learning,
And when he has gotten that, he may put it in a Nut shell,
Alonzo Tiveria very well,
A very ancient friend of mine, I take it,
For till this houre I never heard his Name, yet.
prose:
SIgnior Lopez, Since my arrivall from Cordova to these parts I have written divers Letters unto you but as yet received no Answer of any (Good, and very good) And although so great a forgetfulnesse might cause a want in my due correspondence yet the desire I have still to serve you must more prevaile with me (Better and better: the divell a man know I yet) and therefore with the present occasion offered I am willing to crave a continuance of the favours, which I have heretofore received from you and doe recommend my Son Leandro the Bearer to you with request that he may be admitted in that Universitie till such time as I shall arive at home; his studies he will make you acquainted withall: This kindnesse shall supply the want of your slacknesse: And so heaven keep you.

Yours Alonzo Tiveria.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: You looke (Sir) as if ye had forgot my Father.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: No, no, I look as I would remember him,
For that I never remembred, I cannot forget (Sir)
Alonzo Tiveria.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: The same (Sir.)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And now i'th' Indies?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He may be any where,
For ought that I consider.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Thinke againe (Sir)
You were Students both at one time in Salamanca,
And, as I take it, Chamber-fellowes.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Nay, sure you must remember.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Would I could.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I have heard him say, you were Gossips too.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Very likely,
You did not heare him say, to whom? for we Students
May often-times over-reach our memories,
Do'st thou remember (Diego) this same Signiour?
Thou hast been mine these twenty yeares.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Remember?
Why this Fellow would make ye mad: Nova Hispania?
And Signiour Tiveria? what are these?
He may as well name ye Friends out of Cataya
Take heed I beseech our worship: doe you heare, (my friend?)
You have no Letters for me?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Not any Letter,
But I was charged to doe my Fathers love
To the old honest Sexton Diego; are you he (Sir?)

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Ha? have I friends, and know'em not? my name is Diego,
But if either I remember you, or your Father,
Or Nova Hispania (I was never there Sir)
Or any kindred that you have — for heaven-sake, Master,
Let's cast about a little, and consider,
We may dreame out our time.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: It seemes I am deceiv'd (Sir)
Yet, that you are Don Lopez all men tell me,
The Curat here, and have bin some time (sir)
And you the Sexton Diego, such I am sent too,
The Letter tells as much: may be they are dead,
And you of the like names succeed: I thank ye gentlemen,
Ye have done honestly, in telling truth,
I might have bin forward els. For that Lopez
That was my Fathers friend, I had a charge,
(A charge of Money) to deliver (Gentlemen)
Five hundred Duckets, a poore small gratuity,
But since you are not he, good sir, let me thinke,
I pray ye be patient.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Pray ye stay a little,
Nay, let me remember, I beseech ye stay, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: An honest noble friend, that sends so lovingly;
An old friend too; I shall remember sure, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Thou sayst true Diego.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: 'Pray ye consider quickly,
Doe, doe, by any meanes, me thinkes already
A grave staid gentleman comes to my memory.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: He's old indeed, sir.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: With a goodly white Beard,
(For now he must be so: I know he must be)
Signior Alonzo, (Master.)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I begin to have him.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: 'Has bin from hence, about some twenty years (sir.)

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Som five and twenty (sir.)

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: You say most true (sir)
Just to an houre; 'tis now just five and twenty,
A sine straite timber'd man, and a brave souldier,
He married: let me see, —

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: De Castro's Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: The very same.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Thou art a very Rascall,
De Castro is the Turke to thee, or any thing:
The Money rubbs 'em into strange remembrances,
For as many Duckets more they wou d remember Adam.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Give me your hand, you are welcome to your countrey,
Now I remember plainly, manifestly,
As freshly, as if yesterday I had seene him,
Most heartily welcome, sinfull that I am,
Most sinfull man, why should I loose this Gentleman?
This loving old Companion? we had all one soule, sir,
He dwelt here hard by, at a handsome—

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Farme sir,
You say most true.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Alonzo Tiveria;
Lord, Lord, that time should play the treacherous knave thus?
Why, he was the onely friend, I had in Spaine (sir)
I knew your Mother too, a handsome Gentlewoman,
She was married very young: I married 'em:
I doe remember now the Maskes and Sports then,
The Fire-workes, and the fine delights; good faith, sir,
Now I looke in your face, whose eies are those Diego?
Nay, if he be not just Alonzo's picture—

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Lord how I blush for these two impudents?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Well Gentleman, I thinke your name's Leandro;

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: It is indeed (sir)
Gra'-mercy Letter, thou hadst never knowne els.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I have dandled ye, and kist ye and plaid with ye
A hundred, and a hundred times, and danc'd ye,
And swong ye in my Bell-ropes, ye lov'd swinging.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A sweet Boy.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Sweet lying knaves.
What would these doe for thousands?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A wondrous sweet Boy then it was, see now
Time that consumes us, shoots him up still sweeter.
How do's the noble Gentleman? how fares he?
When shall we see him? when will he blesse his Country?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: O, very shortly, sir, till his returne,
He has sent me over to your charge.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And welcome,
Nay, you shall know you are welcome to your friend, sir,

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: And to my Study (sir) which must be the Law,
To further which, he would entreat your care
To plant me in the favour of some man
That's expert in that knowledge: for his paines
I have three hundred Duckets more: For my Diet,
Enough (sir) to defray me: which I am charged
To take still, as I use it, from your custodie,
I have the money ready, and I am weary.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Sit down, sit down, and once more ye are most welcome,
The Law you have hit upon most happily,
Here is a Master in that Art, Bartolus,
A neighbour by, to him I will preferre ye,
A learned man, and my most loving Neighbour,
I'll doe ye faithfull service (sir.)

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: He's an Asse,
And so wee'll use him; he shall be a Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
verse: But if ever he recover this mony again: before Diego.
And get some pretty pittance: my Pupill's hungry.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Pray ye Sir, unlade me.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I'le refresh ye Sir;
When ye want, you know your Exchequer.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: If all this get me but accesse, I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Come, I am tender of ye,

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I'll goe with ye,
To have this Fort betray'd these fooles must fliece me.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: My Amaranta, a retir'd sweet life,
Private and close, and still, and houswifely.
Becomes a Wife, sets off the grace of woman
At home to be beleev'd both young, and handsome,
As Lil^ies that are casde in christall Glasses,
Makes up the wonder: shew it abroad, 'tis stale,
And still and the more eyes cheapen it, 'tis more slubberd,
And what need windowes open to inviting?
Or evening Tarrasses, to take opinions?
When the most wholsome Ayre (my wife) blowes inward,
When good thoughts are the noblest Campanions,
And old chast stories (wife) the best discourses;
But why doe I talke thus, that know thy nature?

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: You know your own disease: distrust, & jealousies,
And those two, give these Lessons, not good meaning,
What triall is there of my honestie,
When I am mew'd at home? to what end, Husband,
Serves all the vertvous thoughts, and chast behaviours
Without their uses? Then they are known most excellent
When, by their contraries the are set off, and burnish'd,
If ye both hold me faire, and chast, and vertuous,
Let me goe fearelesse out, and win that greatnesse;
These Seeds grow not to Shades, and conceal'd places
Set 'em i'th' heat of all, then they rise glorious.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Peace, ye are too soude.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: You are too covetous,
If that be rank'd a vertue, you have a rich one,
Set me (like other Lawyers wives) off handsomely,
Attended as I ought, and as they have it,
My Coach, my people, and my handsome women,
My will, in honest things.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Peace Amaranta:

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: They have content, rich clothes, and that secures 'em,
Bindes, to their carefull Husbands, their observance,
They are merry, ride abroad, meet, laugh,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Thou shalt too:

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: And freely may converse with proper Gentlemen,
Suffer temptations daily to their honour.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You are now too far again: thou shalt have any thing,
Let me but lay up for a handsome Office,
And then my Amaranta —

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: Here's a thing now,
Ye place as pleasure to me: all my retinue,
My Chamber-maid, my Kitchin-maid, my friend,
And what she failes in, I must doe my selfe.
A soyle to set my Beauty off, I thanke ye,
You will place the Devill next for a Companion,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No more such words (good wife)
What would you have (Maid?)

speeches.speaker: Moor.
verse: Master Curate, and the Sexton, & a stranger (sir)
Attend to speake with your worship.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: A stranger?

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: You had best to be jealous of the man you know not.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Pree thee no more of that.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: 'Pray ye goe out to 'em,
That will be safest for ye, I am well here,
I onely love your peace, and serve like a slave for it.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No, no, thou shalt not; 'tis some honest Client,
Rich, and litigious, the Curate has brought to me,
Pre'thee goe in (my Duck) I'll but speake to 'em,
And returne instantly.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: I am commanded,
One day you will know my sufferance.—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And reward it.
So, so, fast bind, fast find; Come in my Neighbours,
My loving Neighbours pray ye come in, ye are welcome,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Blesse your good reverence.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Good-day, good Master Curate,
And neighbour Diego, welcome: what's your businesse?
And 'pray ye be short (good friends) the time is pretious,
Welcome, good sir.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: To be short then with your Mastership.
(For I know your severall houres, are full of businesse)
We have brought ye this young-man, of honest parents,
And of an honest face.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: It seemes so (Neighbours)
But to what end?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: To be your Pupill (Sir)
Your Servant, if you please.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I have travell'd far, sir.
To seeke a worthy man,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Alas, good Gentleman,
I am a poore man, and a private too,
Unfit to keep a Servant of your Reckoning;
My house a little Cottage, and scarce able
To hold my selfe, and those poore few live under it;
Besides, you must not blame me Gentleman,
If I were able to receive a Servant,
To be a little scrupulous of his dealing
For in these times—

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Pray let me answer that (sir)
Here is fiue hundred Duckets, to secure him,
He cannot want (sir) to make good his credit,
Good gold, and coyne.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And thats an honest pledge;
Yet sure, that needs not, for his face, and carriage,
Seeme to declare an in-bred honesty,

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: And for I have a ripe mind to the Law (sir)
(In which I understand you live a Master)
The least poore corner in your house, poore Bed (sir)
(Let me not seeme intruding to your Worship)
With some Books to instruct me, and your Counsell,
Shall I rest most content with: other Acquaintance
Then your grave presence, and the grounds of Law
I dare not covet, nor I will not seeke (sir)
For surely mine owne nature desires privacie.
Next, for your monthly paines (to shew my thanks,)
I doe proportion out some twenty Duckets;
As I grow riper, more: three hundred now (sir)
To shew my love to learning, and my Master,
My diet, I'll defray too, without trouble.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Note but his mind to learning.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: I do strangely, yes, and I like it too, thankes to his money.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Would he would live with me, and learn to dig too.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A wondrous modest man (sir.)

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: So it seemes,
His deare love to his Studie must be nourish'd
Neighbour, he's like to prove.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: With your good counsell,
And with your diligence, as you will ply him;
His Parents, when they know your care—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Come hither;

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: An honester young man, your worship ne're kept,
But he is so bashfull—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: O I like him better,
Say I should undertake ee, which indeed (sir)
Will be no little straightnesse to my living,
Considering my Affaires, and my small house (sir)
For I see some promises that pull me to ye;
Could you content your selfe, at first thus meanly,
To lye hard, in an out —part of my house (sir?)
For I have not many Lodgings to allow ye;
And studie should be still remote from company;
A little fire sometimes too, to refresh ye;
A Student must be frugall: sometimes Lights too,
According to your labour.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Any thing (sir)
That's dry, and wholsome: I am no bred-wanton.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Then I receive you: but I must desire ye
To keep within your confines.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Ever sir,
There's the Gold, and ever be your servant,
Take it and give me Bookes: may I but prove (sir)
According to my wish, and these shall multiply.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Do, study hard, pray ye take him in, and settle him,
He's onely fit for you; Shew him his Cell (sir.)

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Take a good heart; and when ye are a cunning Lawyer,
I'le sell my Bells and you shall prove it lawfull,

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Come, sir, with me: neighbors I thank your diligence.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I'l come sometimes, and crack a case with ye.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Welcome —

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Here's mony got with ease: here, spend that jovially,
And pray for the Foole, the Founder.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Many more Fooles
I heartily pray may follow his example,
Lawyers, or Lubbers, or of what condition,
And many such sweet friends in Nova Hispania.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: It will do well; Let 'em but send their moneys,
Come from what quarter of the world, I care not,
I'll know 'em instantly; nay I'll be a kin to 'em;
I cannot misse a man, that sends me money:
Let him Law there, long as his Duckets last, Boy,
I'll grace him, and prefer him.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I'l turn Trade (Master) and now live by the living
Let the dead stinke, 'tis a poore stinking Trade.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: If the young Foole now
Should chance to chop upon his faire Wife (Diego.)

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: And handle her Case (Master) that's a law point,
A point would make him start, and put on his Spectacles
A hidden point, were worth the canvassing.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Now surely, surely, I should love him (Diego)
And love him heartily: nay, I should love my selfe,
Or any thing that had but that good fortune,
For to say truth the Lawyer is a dog-bolt,
An arrant worme: and though I call him worshipfull,
I wish him a canoniz'd Cuckold (Diego)
Now, if my youth doe dub him—

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: He is too demure (sir.)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: If he do sting her home.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: There's no such matter,
The woman was not borne to so much blessednesse,
He has no heate: study consumes his oyle (Master,)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Let's leave it to the will of Fate, and presently
Over a cup of lustie Sack, let's prophecie.
I am like a man that dreampt he was an Emperour,
Come Diego, hope, & whilst he lasts, we'll lay it on.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Angelo, Millanes, did you see this wonder?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Yes, yes.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: And you Arsenio?

speeches.speaker: Ar^
verse: Yes he's gon (Sir)
Strangely disguis'd, he's set upon his voyage.
Love guide his thoughts: he's a brave honest fellow,
Sit close Don Lawyer, ô that arrant knave now,
How he will stinke, will smoake againe, will burst:
He's the most arrant Beast.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: He may be more beast.

speeches.speaker: Ja,
verse: Let him beare six, and six, that all may blaze him,
The villany he has sowed into my Brother,
And from his State the Revenue he has reach'd at:
Pay him, my good Leandro, take my praiers.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: And all our wishes plough with his fine white heifer.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Marke him (my deare Friend) for a famous Cuckold,
Let it out-live his Bookes, his paines, and heare me,
The more he seeks to smother it with Justice,
Let it blaze out the more: what news Andrea?

speeches.speaker: Andr.
verse: Newes I am loth to tell ye: but I am charg'd (Sir)
Your Brother layes a strict command upon ye,
No more to know his house, upon our danger,
I am sorry (Sir.)

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: 'Faith never be: I am glad on't,
He keepes the house of pride, and foolery:
I meane to shun it: so returne my Answer,
'Twill shortly spew him out; Come, let's be merry,
And lay our heads together, carefully
How we may helpe our friend; and let's lodge neare him,
Be still at hand: I would not for my patrimony,
But he should crown his Lawyer, a learned Monster,
Come, let's away I am stark mad till I see him.

speeches.speaker: Amar.
verse: Why, will ye bring men in, and yet be jealous?
Why will ye lodge a young man, a man able,
And yet repine?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He shall not trouble thee (Sweet)
A modest poore slight thing, did I not tell thee
He was onely given to the Booke, and for that
How royally he paies? finds his owne meat too.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I will not have him here: I know your courses,
And what fits you will fall into of madnesse.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Y'faith, I will not Wife,

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I will not try ye,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He comes not neare thee: shall not dare to tread
Within thy Lodgings, in an old out-Roome
Where Logs, and Coles were layd.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Now ye lay fire; Fire to consume your quiet.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Didst thou know him,
Thou wouldst thinke as I doe: he disquiet thee?
Thou mayst weare him next thy heart, & yet not warme him,
His mind (poore man) 's o'th' Law, how to live after,
And not on lewdnesse: on my conscience
He knowes not how to looke upon a woman
More then by reading what Sex she is.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I doe not like it (Sir.)

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Do'st thou not see (Foole)
What presents he sends hourely in his gratefulnesse?
What delicate meates?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You had best trust him at your Table,
Doe and repent it doe.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: If thou be'st willing,
By my troth, I thinke he might come, he's so modest,
He never speakes: there's part of that he gave me,
He'll eat but halfe a dozen bits, and rise immediatly,
Even as he eats, he studies: he'll not disquiet thee,
Doe as thou pleasest (Wife.)

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What means this Wood-cocke?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: Retire (Sweet) there's one knocks: come in, your businesse.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: My Lord Don Henrique, would entreat ye, Sir,
To come immediatly, and speake with him,
He has businesse of some moment.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I'll attend him,
I must be gon: I pre'thee thinke the best (wife)
At my returne I'll tell thee more, good morrow;
Sir, keep ye close, and study hard: an houre hence
I'll read a new Case to ye:—

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I'll be ready.

speeches.speaker: Amar.
verse: So many hundred Duckets, to ly scurvily?
And learne the pelting law? this sounds but slenderly,
But very poorely: I would see this fellow
Very faine see him, how he lookes: I will find
To what end, and what study: there's the place:
I'll goe o'th' other side, and take my Fortune;
I think there is a window.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: He's gone out
Now, if I could but see her: she is not this way:
How nastily he keepes his house? my Chamber,
If I continue long, will choak me up,
It is so damp: I shall be mortifide
For any woman, if I stay a moneth here:
I'll in, and strike my Lute, that sound may call her.

speeches.speaker: Ama.
verse: He keeps very close: Lord, how I long to see him:
A Lute strooke handsomely, a voice too; I'll heare that:
These Verses are no Law, they sound too sweetly,
Now I am more desirous.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: 'Tis she certain.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What's that that peeps?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: O, admirable face!

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Sure 'tis the man.
