speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I will goe out a little.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Hee lookes not like a foole, his face is noble:
How still he stands?

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I am strucken dumb, with wonder,
Sure all the Excellence of Earth dwells here.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: How pale he looks? yet how his eies like torches,
Fling their beames round: how manly his face shewes?
He comes on: surely he will speak: he is made most handsomly:
This is no Clerk behaviour; Now I have seen ye,
I'l take my time: husba~d ye have brought home tinder.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Sure she has transform'd me,
I had forgot my tongue cleane,
I never saw a face yet, but this rare one,
But I was able boldly to encounter it,
And speak my mind, my lips were lock upon me,
This is divine, and onely serv'd with reverence;
O most faire cover, of a hand far fairer,
Thou blessed Innocence, that gaurds that whiteness,
Live next my heart. I am glad I have got a relick,
A relick when I pray to it, may work wonders.
Harke, there s some noyse: I must retire againe.
This blessed Apparition, makes me happy;
I'll suffer, and I'll sacrifice my substance.
But I'll enjoy: now softly to my Kennell.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: You know my cause sufficiently?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I doe (Sir.)

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: And though it will impaire my honesty,
And strike deep at my Credit, yet (my Bartolus)
There being no other evasion left to free me
From the vexation of my spightfull Brother,
That most insultingly raignes over me,
I must and will goe forward.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Doe (my Lord)
And looke not after credit, we shall cure that,
Your bended honestie, we shall set right (Sir)
We Surgeons of the Law, doe desperate cures (Sir)
And you shall see how heartily I'll handle it:
Marke how I'll knock it home: be of good cheare (Sir)
You give good Fees, and those beget good Causes,
The prerogative of your crownes will carry the matter,
(Carry it sheere) The Assistant fits to morrow,
And he's your friend, your monied men love naturally,
And as your loves are cleare, so are your Causes.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: He shall not want for that.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No, no, he must not,
Line your Cause warmly (Sir) the times are Aguish,
That holds a Plea in heart; hang the penurious,
Their Causes (like their purses) have poore Issues.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: That way, I was ever bountifull.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis true (Sir)
That makes ye fear'd forces the Snakes to kneele to ye,
Live full of money, and supply the Lawyer,
And take your choice of what mans lands you please (Sir)
What pleasures, or what profits; what revenges,
They are all your owne: I must have witnesses
Enough, and ready.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: You shall not want (my Bartolus.)

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Substantiall fearless soules, that wil swear suddenly,
That will sweare any thing.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: They shall sweare truth too.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: That's no great matter: for varietie
They may sweare truth, els 'tis not much look'd after:
I will serve Processe, presently, and strongly
Upon your Brother, and Octavio,
Jacintha and the Boy; provide your proofes (Sir)
And set 'em fairely off, be sure of Witnesses,
Though they cost money, want no store of witnesses,
I have seen a handsome Cause, so fowly lost (Sir,)
So beastly cast away for want of Witnesses.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: There shall want nothing.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Then be gone, be provident,
Send to the Judge, a secret way: you have me,
And let him understand the heart.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I shall (Sir.)

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And feele the pulses strongly beat, I'll study,
And at my houre, but mark me, goe, be happy,
Goe and beleeve i'th' Law.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I hope 'twill helpe me.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Nea'r talke to me, I will not stay amongst ye,
Debaush'd and ignorant lazie knaves I found ye,
And fooles I leave ye, I have taught these twenty yeares,
Preacht spoon-meat to ye, that a child might swallow,
Yet ye are Block-heads still: what should I say to ye?
Ye have neither faith, nor money left to save ye,
Am I a fit companion for such Beggers?

prose: If the Shepheard will suffer the sheep to be scab'd (sir)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: No, no, ye are rotten.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Would they were, for my sake.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I have nointed ye, and tar'd ye with my doctrine,
And yet the murren sticks to ye, yet ye are mangy,
I will avoid ye.
Pray ye (Sir) be not angry,
In the pride of your new Cassock, doe not part with us,
We doe acknowledge ye a carefull Curat,
And one that seldome troubles us with Sermons,
A short slice of a Reading serves us (Sir)
We doe acknowledge ye a quiet Teacher,
Before You'll vex your Audience, you'll sleep with 'em,
And that's a loving thing.
We grant ye (Sir)
The onely benefactor to our Rowling,
To all our merry Sports, the first provoker,
And at our Feasts we know there is no reason,
But you that edifie us most, should eat most.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I will not stay for all this, ye shall know me
A man borne to a more beseeming fortune
Then ringing all-in, to a rout of Dunces.
We will increase your Tithes, you shall have Egs too,
Though they may prove most dangerous to our Issues.
I am a Smith; yet thus far out of my love
You shall have the tenth horse I prick, to pray for,
I am sure I prick five hundred in a yeare (Sir.
I am a Cooke a man of a dride conscience,
Yet thus far I relent: you shall have tith porrage.

prose: Your stipend shal be rais'd too (good neighbour Diego.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Would ye have me speak for ye? I am more angry
Ten times more vex'd not to be pacified:
No there be other places for poore Sextons
Places of profit (Friends) fine stirring places,
And people that know how to use our Offices,
Know what they were made for: I speak for such Capons?
Ye shall find the Key o'th' Church,
Under the doore (Neighbours,)
You may goe in, and drive away the dawes.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: My Surplesse, with one sleeve, you shall find there,
For to that dearth of Linnen, you have driven me;
And the old Cutworke Cope, that hangs by gymitrie:
Pray ye turne em carefully, they are very tender:
The remnant of the Books, lie where they did (Neighbours)
Half puft away with the Church-wardens pipings.
Such smoaky zeales they have against hard places,
The poore-mans Box is there too: if ye find any thing
Beside the posie, and that halfe rub'd out too,
For feare it should awake too much charitie
Give it to pious uses, that is, spend it:

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: The Bell-ropes, they are strong enough to hang ye,
So we bequeath ye to your destiny.
'Pray ye be not so hastie.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I'll speake a proud word to ye,
Would ye have us stay?
We doe most hearilty pray ye.
I'll draw as mighty drinke (Sir.)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A strong motive,
The stronger still the more ye come unto me.
And I'll send for my Daughter:

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: This may stir too:
The Maiden is of age, and must be edified.
You shall have any thing: loose our learned Vicar?
And our most constant friend; honest deare Diego?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Yet all this will not do: I'll tell ye (Neighbours)
And tell ye true: if ye will have us stay,
If you will have the comforts of our companies,
You shall be bound to doe us right in these points,
You shall be bound, and this the obligation,
Dy when 'tis fit, that we may have fit duties,
And doe not seeke to draw—out our undoings,
Marry tryde women, that are free, and fruitfull,
Get children in abundance, for your Christnings,
Or suffer to be got, 'tis equall justice,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Let Weddings, Christnings, Churchings, Funerals,
And merry Gossippings goe round, go round still,
Round as a Pig, that we may find the profit.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: And let your old men fall sick handsomely:
And dy immediatly, their Sonnes may shoot up:
Let women dy oth' sullens too, 'tis naturall,
But be sure their Daughters be of age first,
That they may stock us still: your queazie young wives
That perish undeliver'd, I am vext with,
And vext abundantly, it much concernes me,
There's a childes buriall lost, looke that be mended.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
verse: Let 'em be brought to bed, then dy when they please,
These things considered (Country-men) and sworne to
All these, and all our sports againe, and gambolls.
We must dy, and we must live, and we'll be merry,
Every man shall be rich by one another.
We are here to morrow, and gone to day: for my part
If getting children can be-friend my Neighbours,
I'll labour hard but I will fill your Font (Sir.)
I have a Mother now, and an old Father,
They are as sure your own, within these two moneths—
My Sister must be prayd for too, she is desperate,
Desperate in love.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Keepe, desperate men farre from her,
Then 'twill goe hard: doe you see how melancholy?
Doe you marke the man? do you professe ye love him?
And would doe any thing to stay his fury?
And are ye unprovided to refresh him,
To make him know your loves? fie Neighbours,
We'll doe any thing,
We have brought Musick to appease his spirit,
And the best Song we'll give him.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Pray ye sit down (Sir)
They know their duties now, and they stand ready
To tender their best mirth.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Tis well, proceed Neighbours,
I am glad I have brought ye to understand good manners,
Ye had Puritan hearts a-while, spurn'd at all pastimes,
But I see some hope now.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: We are set proceed Neighbours.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: What ayles this Priest? how highly the thing takes it?

speeches.speaker: Mi.
verse: Lord how it looks? has he not bought some Prebend?
Leandro's money, makes the Rascall merry,
Merry at heart; he spies us.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
verse: Be gon Neighbours,
Here are some Gentlemen: be gone good Neighbours,
Be gon, and labour to redeeme my favour,
No more words but be gon: these two are Gentlemen,
No company for crusty-handed fellowes.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: We will stay for a yeare or two, and trie ye:

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Fill all your hearts with joy, we will stay with ye,
Be gone no more; I take your pastimes graciously:
Would ye with me (My friends?)

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: We would looke upon ye,
For me-thinks ye looke lovely.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Ye have no Letters?
Nor any kind Remembrances?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Remembrances?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: From Nova Hispania, or some part remote (Sir)
You looke like travell'd men: may be some old friends
That happily I have forgot; some Signeours
In China, or Cataya; some Companions—

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: In the Mogulls Court, or else-where.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: They are mad sure.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Ye came not from Peru? doe they look (Diego)
As if they had some mistery about 'em?
Another Don Alonzo now?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I marry,
And so much money, Sir, from one you know not,
Let it be who it will.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: They have gracious favours.
Would ye be private?

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: There's no need on't (Sir)
We come to bring ye a Remembrance from a Merchant.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Tis very well, 'tis like I know him.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: No. sir,
I doe not thinke ye doe.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A new mistake (Diego)
Let's carry it decently.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: We come to tell ye,
You have received great summes from a young Factor
They call Leandro, that has rob'd his Master,
Rob'd him, and run away.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Let's keep close (Master)
This newes comes from a cold Country.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: By my faith it freezes,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Is not this true? doe you shrink now (good man Curate)
Doe I not touch ye?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We have a hundred Duckets
Yet left, we doe beseech ye sir—

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: You'll hang both.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: One may suffice.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I will not hang alone (Master)
I had the least part, you shall hang the highest.
Plague o' this Tiveria, and the Letter,
The divell sent it post, to pepper us,
From Nova Hispania we shall hang at home now.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: I see ye are penitent, and I have compassion:
Ye are secure both; doe but what we charge ye,
Ye shall have more gold too, and he shall give it,
Yet ne're indanger ye.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Command us (Master)
Command us presently, and see how nimbly —

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: And if we doe not handsomely endeavour —

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Goe home and till ye heare more keep private,
Till we appeare againe, no words, (Vicar)
There's something added.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: For you too.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We are ready.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Goe, and expect us hourely, if ye falter,
Though ye had twenty lives—

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: We are fit to loose 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Tis most expedient that we should hang both.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: If we be hang'd, we cannot blame our fortune.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Farewell, and be your owne friends.

speeches.speaker: Lop,
verse: We expect ye. —

speeches.speaker: Oct.
prose: We cited to the Court!

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: It is my wonder,

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: But not our fear, (Iacintha) wealthy men
That have Estates to loose, whose conscious thoughts
Are full of inward guilt, may shake with horrour,
To have their Actions sifted or appeare
Before the Judge. But we that know our selves
As innocent, as poore, that have no Fleece
On which the Talons of the griping Law
Can take sure hold, may smile with scorne on all
That can be urg'd against us.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: I am confident
There is no man so covetous, that desires
To ravish our wants from us, and lesse hope
There can be so much Justice left on earth,
(Though sude and call'd upon) to ease us of
The burthen of our wrongs.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: What thinkes Ascanio?
Should we be call'd in question or accus'd
Unjustly, what would you doe to redeeme us,
From tirannous oppression?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I could pray
To him that ever has an open eare
To heare the innocent, and right their wrongs;
Nay, by my troth, I thinke I could out plead
An Advocate, and sweat as much as he
Do's for a double Fee, ere you should suffer
In an honest cause.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: Happy simplicitie!

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: My dearest, and my best one: Don Iamie,

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: And the Advocate, that caus'd us to be summond.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: My Lord is mov'd, I see it in his lookes,
And that man, in the Gowne, in my opinion
Lookes like a proaguing knave.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Peace, give them leave.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Serve me with Processe?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: My Lord, you are not lawlesse.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Nor thou honest;
One, that not long since was the buckram Scribe,
That would run on mens errands for an Aspe^,
And from such basenesse, having rais'd a Stock
To bribe the covetous Judge, call'd to the Bar,
So poore in practise too, that you would plead
A needy Clyents Cause, for a starv'd hen,
Or halfe a little loyn of Veale, though fly blowne,
And these, the greatest Fees you could arrive at
For just proceedings; but since you turn'd Rascall —

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Good words, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: And grew my Brothers Bawd
In all his vitious courses, soothing him
In his dishonest practises, you are growne
The rich, and eminent knave, in the divels name,
What am I cited for?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You shall know anon,
And then too late repent this bitter language,
Or I'll misse of my ends.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Wer't not in Court,
I would beat that fat of thine, rais'd by the food
Snatch'd from poore Clyents mouthes, into a jelly:
I would (my man of Law) but I am patient,
And would obey the Judge.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis your best course:
Would every enemy I have would beat me,
I would wish no better Action.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: 'Save your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: My numble service.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: My good Boy, how dost thou?
Why art thou call'd into the Court?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I know not,
But 'tis my Lord the Assistants pleasure
I should attend here.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: He will soone resolve us.

speeches.speaker: Offi.
verse: Make way there for the Judge.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: How? my kind Brother?
Nay then 'tis ranck: there is some villany towards.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: 'Tis Sessions purchas'd at our suit, Don Henrique,
Hath brought us hither, to heare and determine
Of what you can prefer.

speeches.speaker: Henrique.
verse: I doe beseech
The honourable Court, I may be heard
In my Advocate.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: 'Tis granted.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: humh, humh.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: That preface
If left out in a Lawyer, spoyles the Cause,
Though ne're so good, and honest.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: If I stood here,
To plead in the defence of an ill man,
(Most equall Judge) or to accuse the innocent
(To both which, I professe my selfe a stranger)
It would be requisite I should deck my Language
With Tropes and Figures, and all flourishes
That grace a Rethorician, 'tis confess'd
Adulterate Mettals, need the Gold-smiths Art,
To set 'em off; what, in it selfe is perfect
Contemnes a borrowed glosse: This Lord (my Client)
Whose honest cause, when 'tis related truly,
Will challenge Justice, finding in his conscience
A tender scruple of a fault long since
By him committed, thinkes it not sufficient
To be absolv'd of't, by his Confessor,
If that in open Court, he publish nor
What was so long conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: To what tends this?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: In his young yeares (it is no miracle
That youth, and heat of Blood, should mix together)
He look'd upon this woman, on whose face
The ruines yet remaine of excellent forme,
He look'd on her, and lov'd her.

speeches.speaker: Iac:
verse: You good Angels,
What an impudence is this?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And us'd all meanes
Of Service, Courtship, Presents, that might win her
To be at his devotion: but in vaine
Her maiden Fort impregnable held out
Untill he promis'd Marriage; and before
These Witnesses a solemne Contract pass'd
To take her as his wife.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Give them their oath.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: They are incompetent Witnesses, his own Creatures,
And will sweare any thing for halfe a royall.

speeches.speaker: Off.
verse: Silence.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Proceed.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Upon this strong assurance
He did enjoy his wishes to the full,
Which satisfied and then with eyes of Judgement
(Had winck'd with lust before) considering duly
The inequality of the Match, he being
Nobly descended, and allyed, but she
Without a name, or Family, secretly
He purchas'd a Divorce, to disanull
His former Contract, marrying openly
The Lady Violante.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: As you sit here
The Deputy of the great King, who is
The Substitute of that impartiall Judge
With whom, or Wealth, or titles prevaile nothing,
Grant to a much wrong'd Widow, or a Wife
Your patience, with liberty to speake
In her owne Cause, and let me face to face
To this bad man, deliver what he is:
And if my wrongs, with his ingratitude ballanc'd,
Move not compassion, let me die unpittied;
His teares, his oathes, his perjuries, I passe o're
To thinke of them is a disease; but death
Should I repeat them. I dare not deny,
(For Innocence cannot justifie what's false)
But all the Advocate hath alleadged concerning
His falshood and my shame in my consent,
To be most true: But now I turne to thee,
To thee Don Henrique, and if impious Acts
Have left thee blood enough to make a blush,
I'll paint it on thy cheekes. Was not the wrong
Sufficient to defeat me of mine honour,
To leave me full of sorrow, as of want,
The witnesse of thy lust, left in my womb,
To testifie thy falshood, and my shame?
But now so many yeares I had conceal'd
Thy most inhumane wickednesse, and won
This Gentleman, to hide it from the world
To Father what was thine (for yet by heaven,
Though in the City, he pas'd for my husband,
He never knew me as his wife)

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: 'Tis strange:
Give him an Oath.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: I gladly sweare, and truly.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: After all this (I say) when I had borne
These wrongs, with Saint-like patience saw another
Freely enjoy, what was (in Justice) mine,
Yet still so tender of thy rest, and quiet,
I never would divulge it, to disturb
Thy peace at home, yet thou most barbarous,
To be so carelesse of me, and my Fame,
(For all respect of thine in the first step
To thy base lust, was lost) in open Court
To publish my disgrace? and on record,
To write me up an easie-yeilding wanton?
I thinke can find no president: In my extreames,
One comfort yet is left, that though the Law
Divorce me from thy bed, and made free way
To the unjust embraces of an other,
It cannot yet deny that this thy Son
(Looke up Ascanio since it is come out)
Is thy legitimate heire.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Confederacie:
A trick (my Lord) to cheat me; e're you give
Your Sentence grant me hearing.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: New Chymera's?

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: I am (my Lord) since he is without Issue,
Or hope of any his undoubted Heire,
And this forg'd by the Advocate, to defeat me
Of what the Lawes of Spaine, confer upon me,
A meere Imposture, and conspiracie
Against my future fortunes,

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: You are too bold.
Speak to the Cause Don Henrique.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I confesse,
(Though the acknowledgement must wound mine honour,
That all the Court hath heard touching this Cause,
Or with me, or against me) is most true:
The later part my Brother urg'd, excepted:
For what I now doe, is not out of Spleene
(As he pretends) but from remorse of conscience)
And to repaire the wrong that I have done
To this poore woman: And I beseech your Lordship
To thinke I have not so far lost my reason,
To bring into my Familie, to succeed me,
The stranger—Issue of anothers Bed,
By proofe, this is my Son, I challenge him,
Accept him, and acknowledge him, and desire
By a definitive Sentence of the Court,
He may be so recorded, and full powre
To me, to take him home.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: A second rape
To the poore remnant of Content, that's left me,
If this be granted: and all my former wrongs
Were but beginnings to my miseries,
But this the height of all: rather then part
With my Ascanio, I'll deny my oath,
Professe my selfe a Strumpet, and endure
What punishment soe're the Court decrees
Against a wretch that hath forsworne her selfe,
Or plai'd the impudent whore.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: This tastes of passion,
And that must not divert the course of Justice;
Don Henrique, take your Son, with this Condition
You give him maintenance, as becomes his birth,
And 'twill stand with your honour to doe something
For this wronged woman: I will compell nothing,
But leave it to your will. Break up the Court:
It is in vaine to move me; my doom's pass'd,
And cannot be revok'd. —

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: There's your reward.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: More Causes: and such Fees. Now to my Wife,
I have too long bin absent: Health to your Lordship,

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: You all look strangely, and I feare beleeve
This unexpected fortune makes me proud,
Indeed it do's not: I shall ever pay you
The duty of a son, and honour you
Next to my Father: good my Lord, for yet
I dare not call you uncle, be not sad,
I never shall forget those noble favours
You did me being a stranger, and if ever
I live to be the master of a fortune,
You shall command it.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Since it was determi'nd
I should be cozen'd, I am glad the profit
Shall fall on thee, I am too tough to melt,
But something I will do.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Pray you take leaue
Of your steward (gentle Brother) the good husband
That takes up all for you.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Very well, mock on,
It is your turn: I may have mine—

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: But do not
Forget us deare Ascanio

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Do not feare it.
I Every day will see you: every houre
Remember you in my prayers.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: My grief's too great
To be expressed in words—

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Take that and leave us,
Leave us without reply, nay come back sirrah
And study to forget such things as these
As are not worth the knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: O good Sir.
These are bad principles—

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Such as you must learn
Now you are mine for wealth and poverty
Can hold no friendship: and what is my will
You must observe and do, though good or ill.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Where is my wife? 'fore heaven, I have done wonders
Done mighty things to day, my Amaranta,
My heart rejoyces at my wealthy Gleanings,
A rich litigious Lord I love to follow,
A Lord that builds his happinesse on brawlings,
O 'tis a blessed thing to have rich Clyents,
Why, wife I say, how fares my studious Pupill?
Hard at it still? ye are too violent
All things must have their rests they will not last els
Come out and breathe.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I do beseech you pardon me
I am deeply in a sweet point Sir,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I'le instruct ye:
I say take breath, seek health first, then your study,
O my sweet soul I have brought thee golden birds home,
Birds in abundance: I have done strange wonders:
There's more a hatching too.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Have ye done good husband?
Then 'tis a good day spent

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Good enough chicken,
I have spred the nets o'th' law, to catch rich booties,
And they come flttering in: how do's my Pupil?
My modest thing, hast thou yet spoken to him?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: As I past by his chamber I might see him,
But he is so bookish,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And so bashfull too,
I faith he is, before he will speak, he will starve there

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I pitie him a little.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: So do I too.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: And if he please to take the aire o'th gardens
Or walk i'th' inward roomes, so he molest not—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He shall not trouble thee, he dare not speak to thee
Bring out the Chesse-board —come let's have a game wife,
I'le try your masterie, you say you are cunning

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: As learned as ye are (Sir) I shall beat ye

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Here he steales out, put him not out of countenance
'Prethee look another way, he will be gone else
Walk and refresh your self I'l be with you presently,

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I'le take the aire a little.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Twill be healthfull.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Will ye be there? then here? Ile spare ye that man,

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: 'Would I were so neare too, and a mate fitting.

speeches.speaker: A.
verse: What think ye (Sir) to this? have at your Knight now

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Twas subtilly playd: your Queen lies at my service
Pre thee look off, he is ready to pop in again,
Look off I say, do'st thou not see how he blushes?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I do not blast him:

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: But ye do, and burn too.
What killing looks she steals?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I have you now close,
Now for a Mate.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: You are a blessed man that may so have her.
Oh that I might play with her—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Who's there? I come you cannot scape me now wife
I come, I come,

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Most blessed hand that calls him.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Play quickly wife.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: 'Pray ye give leave to think, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Moore
verse: An honest neighbour that dwells hard by (Sir)
Would fain speak with your worship about businesse.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: The devil blow him off.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Play.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I will study:
For if you beat me thus, you will still laugh at me—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He knocks again; I cannot stay. Leandro
'Pray thee come near.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I am well (Sir) here,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Come hither:
Be not afraid but come.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Here's none will bite (Sir)

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: God forbid Lady.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: 'Pray come nearer.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Yes forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Pre thee observe these men: just as they stand here
And see this Lady, do not alter 'em,
And be not partiall, Pupill.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: No indeed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Let her not move a pawn, I'le come back presently
Nay you shall know I am a Conquerour.
Have an eye Pupill—

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Can ye play at Chesse Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: A little Lady.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: But you cannot tell me
How to avoid this Mate, & win the Game too
Ha's noble eyes: ye dare not friend me so farre.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I dare do any thing that's in mans power, Lady,
To be a friend to such a noble beauty.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: This is no Lawyers language: I pray ye tell me,
Whether may I remove, Ye see I am set round?
To avoid my husband.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I shall tell ye happily.
But happily you will not be instructed.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Yes, and I thank ye too, shall I move this man?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Those are unseemly: move one can serve ye
Can honour ye, can love ye.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: 'Pray ye tell quickly
He will return and then

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I'le tell ye instantly
Move me, and I wil move any way to serve ye
Move your heart this way (Lady)

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: 'Pray ye heare me.
Behold the sport of Love, when he is imperious
Behold the slave of Love

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Move my Queen this way?
Sure, he's some worthy man: then if he hedge me
Or here to open him.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Do but behold me
If there be pity in you, do but view me,
But view the misery I have undertaken
For you the povertie.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: He will come presently.
Now play your best Sir, though I loose this Rook here
Yet I get Libertie.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I'le seize your fair hand
And warm it with a hundred, hundred kisses
The God of love warm your desires but equal
That shall play my game now.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What do you mean Sir?
Why do you stop me?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: That ye may intend me.
The time ha's blest us both: Love bids us use it.
I am a Gentleman nobly descended:
Young to invite your Love, rich to maintain it.
I bring a whole heart to ye, thus I give it,
And to those burning altars thus I offer,
And thus divine lips, where perpetuall Sping grows.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Take that, ye are too saucy.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: How proud Lady?
Strike my deserts?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I was too blame.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What wise, there?
Heaven keep my house from thieves.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I am wretched:
Opened, discovered, lost to my wishes.
I shall be whooted at.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What noise was this (wife?)
Why dost thou smile?

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: This proud thing will betray me.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Why these lie here? what anger (deare?)

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Why none, Sir,
Onely a chance, your pupill said he plaid well,
And so indeed he do's: he undertook for ye
Because I would not sit so long time idle
I made my Liberty avoided your mate,
And he again as cunningly endangered me,
Indeed he put me strangely to it. When presently
Hearing you come, and having broke his ambush too
Having the second time brought off my Queen fair,
I rose o'th' sudden smilingly to shew ye,
My apron caught the Chesse-board, and the men,
And there the noise was.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Thou art grown a Master,
For all this, I shall beat ye.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: Or I, Lawyer,
For now I love her more, 'twas a neat answer,
And by it hangs a mighty hope, I thank her
She gave my pate a sound knock that it rings yet,
But you shall have a sounder if I live Lawyer,
My heart akes yet I would not be in that fear—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am glad ye are a gamester, Sir, sometimes
For recreation we two shall fight hard at it.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: He will prove too hard for me,

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: I hope he shall do,
But your Ches-board is too hard for my head, line that good Lady,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I have been attoning two most wrangling neighbours,
They had no money, therefore I made even
Come, let's go in, and eat, truly I am hungry.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
prose: I have eaten already, I must intreat your pardon

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Do as ye please, we shall expect ye at supper.
He ha's got a little heart, now it seems handsomly,

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You'l get no little head, if I do not look to ye.

speeches.speaker: Lean.
verse: If ever I do catch thee again thou vanity—

speeches.speaker: Am.
prose: I was too blame to be so rash, I am sorie—

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Heare but my reasons,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: O my patience heare 'em.
Can cunning falshood colour an excuse?
With any seeming shape of borrowed truth?
Extenuate this wofull wrong, not error.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: You gave consent that to defeat my brother
I should take any course,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: But not to make
The cure more loathsome then the fowle disease:
Was't not enough you took me to your bed,
Tir'd with loose dalliance, and with emptie veines,
All those abilities spent before and wasted,
That could conferre the name of mother on me?
But that (to perfect my account of sorrow)
For my long barrennesse you must highten it
By shewing to my face, that you were fruitfull
Hug'd in the base embraces of another?
If Solitude that dwelt beneath my roofe,
And want of children was a torment to me
What end of my vexation to behold
A bastard to upbraid me with my wants?
And heare the name of father paid to ye
Yet know my self no mother,
What can I say?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: shall I confesse my fault and ask your pardon?
Will that content ye?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: If it could make void,
What is confirm'd in Court No, no, Don Henrique
You shall know that I find my self abus'd,
And adde to that I have a womans anger,
And while I look upon this Basilisk
Whose envious eyes hath blasted all my comforts
Rest confident I'le study my dark ends,
And not your pleasures,

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Noble Lady, heare me,
Not as my Fathers son, but as your servant,
Vouchsafe to heare me, for such in my duty,
I ever will appeare: And far be it from
My poore ambition, ever to looke on you,
But with that reverence; which a slave stands bound
To pay a worthy Mistris: I have heard
That Dames of highest place, nay Queenes themselves,
Disdaine not to be serv'd by such as are
Of meanest Birth: and I shall be most happie,
To be emploi'd when you please to command me
Even in the coursest Office, as your Page,
I can wayte on your trencher:: fill your wine
Carry your pontafles, and be sometimes bless'd
In all humilitie to touch your feete
Or if that you esteeme that too much grace
I can run by your Coach: observe your lookes
And hope to gaine a fortune by my service,
With your good favour, which now, as a Son,
I dare not challenge

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: As a Son,

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Forgive me
I will forget the name, let it be death
For me to call you Mother.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Still upbraided?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: No way left to appease you?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: None: now heare me,
Heare what I vow before the face of heaven,
And if I breake it all plagues in this life,
And those that after death are fear'd, fall on me,
While that this Bastard staies under my rooffe,
Looke for no peace at home, for I renounce
All Offices of a wife,

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: What am I falne to?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I will not eate, nor sleepe with you and those howres
Which I should spend in prayers for your health
Shall be emploi'd in Curses,

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Terrible.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: All the day long, i'le be as tedious to you
As lingring fevers, and i'le watch the nights,
To ring alon'd your shame and breake your sleepes
Or if you doe but slumber, i'le appeare
In the shape of all my wrongs, and like a fury
Fright you to madnes, and if all this faile
To worke out my revenge, I have friends and kinsmen,
That will not sit downe tame with the disgrace
That's offer'd to our noble familie
In what I suffer,

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: How am I devided
Betweene the duties I owe as a Husband,
And pietie of a Parent?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I am taught Sir
By the instinct of nature that obedience
Which bids me to prefer your peace of mind,
Before those pleasures that are dearest to me
Be wholy hers (my Lord) I quit all parts,
That I may challenge: may you grow old together
And no distast e're find you and before
The Characters of age are printed on you
May you see many Images of your selves,
Though I, like some false Glasse, that's never look'd in
Am cast a side, and broken from this hower
(Unles invited, which I dare not hope for)
I never will set my forbidden feete,
Over your threshold: onely give me leave
Though cast off to the world, to mention you,
In my devotions 'tis all I sue for
And so I take my last leave

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Though I am
Devoted to a wife nay allmost sol'd
A slave to serve her pleasures, yet I cannot
So part with all humanity, but I must
Shew something of a Father: thou shalt not goe
Unfurnish'd and unfriended too: take that
To guard thee from necessities; may thy goodnes
Meet many favours, and thine innocence
Deserve to be the heire of greater fortunes,
Then thou wer't borne to. Scorne me not Violante
This banishment is a kind of civill death,
And now, as it were at his Funerall
To shed a teare or two, is not unmanly
And so farewell for ever: one word more,
Though I must never see thee (my Ascanio)
When this is spent (for so the Judge decreed)
Send to me for supply: are you pleas'd now?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Yes: I have cause: to see you howle and blubber
At the parting of my torment, & your shame
'Tis well: proceed: supply his wants: doe doe:
Let the great dowre I brought serve to maintain
Your Bastards riots: send my Clothes and Jewells,
To your old acquaintance, your deare dame his Mother
Now you begin to melt, I know 'twill follow,

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Is all I doe misconstrude?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I will take
A course to right my selfe a speeding one:
By the bless'd Saints, I will; if I prove cruell
The shame to see thy foolish pitty taught me
To loose my naturall softnes, keepe off from me
Thy flateries are infectious, and i'le fle thee
As I would doe a Leaper.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Let not fury
Transport you so: you know I am your Creature,
All love, but to your self, with him, hath left me
I'le ioyne with you in any thing

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: In vaine
I'le take mine owne waies, and will have no partners,

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I will not crosse you,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Doe not, they shall find
That to a Woman of her hopes beguil'd
A viper troad on, or an Aspick's, mild.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Sits the game there? I have you by mine order,
I love Leandro for't

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: But you must shew it
In lending him your helpe, to gain him meanes
And opportunitie.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He shall want nothing,
I know my Advocate to a hayre, and what
Will fetch him from his prayers, if he use any,
I am honyed with the project: I would have him horn'd
For a most pretious Beast.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: But you loose time;

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I am gon, instruct you Diego, you will find him
A sharpe and subtle knave, give him but hints
And he will amplifie: Se all things ready
I'll fetch him with a vengeance.—

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: If he faile now,
Wee'll give him over too,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Tush he is flesh'd,
And knowes what vaine to strike for his owne credit.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: All things are ready.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Then we shall have a merry Scene, no're feare it.

speeches.speaker: Amar.
verse: Is thy Master gone out?

speeches.speaker: Moore.
verse: Even now, the Curat fetch'd him,
About a serious businesse as it seem'd,
For he snatch'd up his Cloak, and brush'd his hat strait,
Set his Band handsomely, and out he gallop'd.

speeches.speaker: Amar.
verse: 'Tis well, 'tis very well, he went out (Egla.)
As luckily, as one would say, goe Husband,
He was call'd by providence: fling this short paper
Into Leandro's Cell, and waken him,
He is monstrous vexed, and musty, at my Chesse-play;
But this shall supple him, when he has read it:
Take your owne recreation for two houres,
And hinder nothing.

speeches.speaker: Moore.
verse: If I doe, I'll hang for't.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: If that you lov'd Ascanio for himselfe,
And not your private ends, you rather should
Blesse the faire opportunitie, that restores him
To his Birth-right, and the Honours he was borne to,
Then grieve at his good Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Grieve Octavio?
I would resigne my Essence, that he were
As happy as my love could fashion him,
Though every blessing that should fall on him,
Might prove a curse to me, my sorrow springs
Out of my feare, and doubt he is not safe.
I am acquainted with Don Henrique's nature,
And I have heard too much the fiery temper
Of Madam Violante: can you thinke
That she, that almost is at war with heaven
For being barren, will with equall eyes
Behold a Son of mine?

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: His Fathers care,
That for the want of Issue tooke him home,
(Though with the forfeiture of his owne fame)
Will looke unto his safetie.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Step-mothers
Have many eyes, to find a way to mischiefe,
Though blind to goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Oct.
verse: Here comes Don Jamy,
And with him our Ascanio.

speeches.speaker: Jamy.
verse: Good youth leave me,
I know thou art forbid my company,
And onely to be seene with me, will call on
Thy Fathers anger.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Sir if that to serve you
Could loose me any thing (as indeed it cannot)
I still would follow you. Alas I was borne
To doe you hurt but not to help my selfe,
I was, for some particular end, tooke home,
But am cast off againe.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Is't possible?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: The Lady, whom my Father calls his wife
Abhors my sight, is sick of me, and forc'd him
To turne me out of dores.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: By my best hopes
I thanke her crueltie, for it comes neere
A saving charitie.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I am onely happy
That yet I can relieve you, 'pray you share:
My Father's wondrous kind, and promises
That I should be supplide: but sure the Lady
Is a malitious woman, and I feare
Meanes me no good.

speeches.speaker: Iamy.
verse: I am turn'd a stone with wonder,
And know not what to thinke.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: From my Lady,
Your private eare and this—

speeches.speaker: Iamy.
verse: New Miracles?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: She sayes, if you dare make your selfe a Fortune,
She will propose the meanes; My Lord Don Henrique
Is now from home and she alone expects you,
If you dare trust her so, if not despaire of
A second offer,

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Though there were an Ambush
Layd for my life, I,ll on and sound this secret,
Retire thee (my Ascanio) with thy Mother:
But stir not forth, some great designe's on foot,
Fall what can fall, if e're the Sun be set,
I see you not, give me dead.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: We will expect you,
And those bless'd Angels, that love goodnesse, guard you.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Is't possible he should be rich?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Most possible,
He hath bin long, though he had but little gettings,
Drawing together, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Accounted a poore Sexton,
Honest poore Diego,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I assure ye, a close Fellow,
Both close, and scraping, and that fills the bags, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: A notable good Fellow too?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Sometimes, Sir,
When he hop'd to drink a man into a surfeit,
That he might gaine by his Grave.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: So many thousands?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Heaven knowes what.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis strange,
Tis very strange; but we see by endeavour,
And honest labour—

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Milo by continuance
Grew from a silly Calfe (with your worships reverence)
To carry a Bull, from a penny, to a pound, Sir,
And from a pound, to many: 'tis the progresse.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ye say true, but he lov'd to feed well also,
And that me-thinks—

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: From another mans Trencher, Sir,
And there he found it season'd with small charge:
There he would play the Tyrant, and would devoure ye
More then the Graves he made, at home he liv'd
Like a Camelion suckt th'Ayre of misery,
And grew fat by th'Brewis of an Eg-shel,
Would smell a Cooks shop, and goe home and surfeit,
And be a moneth in fasting out that Fever.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
prose: These are good Symptomes: do's he lye so sick say ye?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Oh, very sick.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And chosen me Executor?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Onely your Worship.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No hope of his amendment?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: None, that we find.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He hath no kinsmen neither?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Truth, very few.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: His mind will be the quieter,
What Doctors has he?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: There's none sir he believes in.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They are but needlesse things, in such extremities.
Who drawes the good-man's will?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Marry that doe I, Sir.
And to my griefe.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Griefe will doe little now, Sir,
Draw it to your comfort, Friend, and as I counsell ye,
An honest man, but such men live not alwayes
Who are about him?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Many now he is passing,
That would pretend to his love, yes, and some gentlemen
That would faine counsell him, and be of his kindred;
Rich men can want no heires, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They doe ill,
Indeed they doe, to trouble him: very ill, Sir,
But we shall take a care.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Will ye come neare, Sir,
'Pray ye bring him out; Now ye may see in what state:
Give him fresh ayre.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am sorry, Neighbour Diego,
To find ye in so weake a state.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Ye are welcome,
But I am fleeting, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Me-thinkes he looks well,
His colour fresh, and strong, his eyes are chearfull.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A glimmering before death, 'tis nothing els Sir,
Do you see how he fumbles with the sheet? do ye note that

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: My learned Sir 'pray ye sit: I am bold to send for ye,
To take a care of what I leave.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Doe you heare that?

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Play the knave finely.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: So I will, I warrant ye,
And carefully.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Pray ye doe not trouble him,
You see he's weake and has a wandring fancie.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: My honest Neighbours, weep not, I must leave ye,
I cannot alwayes beare ye company,
VVe must drop still, there is no remedie:
'Pray ye Master Curat, will ye write my Testament,
And write it largely it may be remembred
And be witnesse to my Legacies good Gentlemen;
Your worship I doe make my full Executor,
You are a man of wit and understanding:
Give me a cup of wine to raise my Spirits,
For I speake low: I wou^d before these Neighbours
Have ye to sweare (Sir) that you will see it executed,
And what I give, let equally be rendred
For my soules health.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I vow it truly, Neighbours,
Let not that trouble ye before all these,
Once more I give my Oath.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Then set me higher,
And pray ye come neare me all.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: VVe are ready for ye.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Now spur the Asse, and get our friend time.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: First then,
After I have given my Body to the wormes
(For they must be serv'd first, they are seldome cozen'd)

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Remember your Parish, Neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Y u speake truly,
I doe remember it, a lewd vile Parish,
And pray it may be mended: To the Poore of it,
(VVhich is to all the Parish) I give nothing,
For nothing, unto nothing, is most naturall,
Yet leave as much space, as will build an Hospitall,
Their children may pray for me.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What doe you give to it?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Set downe two thousand Duckets,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis a good gift,
And will be long remembred.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: To your worship,
(Because you must take paines to see all finish'd)
I give two thousand more, it may be three, Sir,
A poore gratuitie for your paines-taking.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: These are large summes;

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Nothing to him that has 'em.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: To my old Master Vicar, I give five hundred,
(Five hundred, and five hundred, are too few Sir)
But there be more to serve.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: This fellow coynes sure.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Give me some more drink. Pray ye buy Books, buy Books,
You have a learned head, stuffe it with Libraries,
And understand 'em, when ye have done, 'tis Justice,
Run not the Parish mad with Controversies,
Nor preach not Abstinence to longing women,
'Twill budge the bottoms of their consciences:
I would give the Church new Organs, but I prophecie
The Church-wardens would quickly pipe'em out o'th'Parish,
Two hundred Duckets more to mend the chancel,
And to paint true Orthographie, as many,
They write Sunt with a C, which is abominable,
'Pray you set that downe, to poore Maidens marriages.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
verse: I that's wel thought of, what's your wil in that point?
A meritorious thing.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No end of this will?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I give per annum two hundred ells of Lockram,
That there be no strait dealings in their Linnens,
But the Sayles cut according to their Burthens;
To all Bell-Ringers, I bequeath new Ropes,
And let them use 'em at their owne discretions.

speeches.speaker: Ars
verse: You may remember us.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I doe, good Gentlemen,
And I bequeath ye both good carefull Surgeons
A Legacy, you have need of, more then money,
I know you want good Diets and good Lotions,
And in your pleasures good take heed.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He raves now.
But 'twill be quickly off,

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I doe bequeath ye
Commodities of pins: browne papers: pack-threds,
Rost porke & puddings: Ginger-bread, & Jewes-trumps,
Of penny Pipes, and mouldy Pepper: take 'em,
Take 'em even where you please, and be cozen'd with 'em,
I should bequeath ye Executions also,
But those I'll leave to th'Law.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Now he growes temperate.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You will give no more?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: I am loth to give more from ye,
Because I know you will have a care to execute
Onely, to pious uses, Sir, a little.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: If he be worth all these, I am made for ever,

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I give to fatall Dames, that spin mens threds out,
And poore distressed Damsells, that are militant
As members of our owne Afflictions,
A hundred Crowns to buy warm tubbs to worke in,
I give five hundred pounds to buy a Church-yard,
A spacious Church-yard, to lay Theeves and knaves in,
Rich men, and honest men, take all the roome up.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Are ye not weary?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Never of well-doing.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: These are mad Legacies.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: They were got as madly;
My Sheep, and Oxen, and my moveables,
My Plate, and Jewells, and five hundred Acres;
I have no heires.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: This cannot be, 'tis Monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Three Ships at Sea too.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You have made me full Executor.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Full, full, and totall, would I had more to give ye
But these may serve an honest mind.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ye say true,
A very honest mind, and make it rich too;
Rich, wondrous rich, but where shall I raise these monys,
About your house? I see no such great promises;
Where shall I find these summes?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Even where you please Sir,
You are wise and provident and know businesse
Ev'n raise 'em where you shal think good, I am reasonable

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Thinke good? will that raise thousands?
What doe you make me?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: You have sworn to see it done, that's all my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Where I please? this is pack'd sure to disgrace me.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Ye are just and honest, and I know you will doe it,
Ev'n where you please, for you know where the wealth is.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am abused, betrayed, I am laugh'd at, scorn'd,
Baffel'd, and boared, it seemes.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: No, no, ye are fooled.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Most finely fooled, and handsomely, and neatly,
Such cunning Masters must be fooled sometimes, Sir,
And have their worships noses wiped, 'tis healthfull,
We are but quit: you foole us of our moneys
In every Cause, in every Quiddit wipe us.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Ha, ha, ha ha, some more drink, for my heart, Gentlemen,
This merry Lawyer— ha, ha, ha, ha this Scholler—
I thinke this fitt will cure me: this Executor—
I shall laugh out my Lungs.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: This is derision above sufferance, villany
Plotted, and set against me.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Faith 'tis knavery,
In troth I must confesse, thou art fooled indeed, Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Did you thinke, had this man been rich —

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: 'Tis well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: He would have chosen such a Wolfe, a Cancker,
A Maggot-pate, to be his whole Executor.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A Lawyer, that entangles all mens honesties,
And lives like a Spider in a Cobweb lurking,
And catching at all Flies, that passe his pitt-falls?
Puts powder to all States, to make em caper?
Would he trust you?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Doe you deserve? I find, Gentlemen,
This Cataplasme of a well cozen'd Lawyer
Laid to my stomach lenifies my Fever,
Me-thinkes I could eat now and walke a little.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am asham'd to feele how flat I am cheated,
How grossely, and malitiously made a May-game,
A damned Trick; my wife, my wife, some Rascall:
My credit, and my wife, some lustfull villaine,
Some Bawd, some Rogue,

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Some craftie Foole has found ye:
This 'tis Sir, to teach ye to be too busie,
To covet all the gaines, and all the rumours
To have a stirring oare, in all mens actions.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We did this, but to vex your fine officiousnesse.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Good 'yeild ye and go'd thank ye: I am fooled, gentlemen;
The Lawyer is an Asse, I doe confesse it,
A weak dull shallow Asse: good even to your worships:
Vicar, remember Vicar, Rascall remember,
Thou notable rich Rascall.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I doe remember, Sir,
'Pray ye stay a little, I have ev'n two Legacies
To make your mouth up, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Remember Varletts,
Quake & remember, Rogues; I have brine for your Buttocks.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Oh how he frets, and fumes now like a dunghill.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: His gall containes fine stuffe now to make poysons,
Rare damned stuffe.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Let's after him, and still vex him,
And take my Friend off: by this time he has prosper'd,
He cannot loose this deere time: 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Well Diego, thou hast done.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Hast done it daintily.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: And shalt be as well paid, Boy—

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Goe, let's crucifie him.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I have told ye all my story, and how desperately.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I doe believe: let's walke on, time is pretious,
Not to be spent in words, here no more wooing,
The open Ayre's an enemy to Lovers,
Doe as I tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I'll doe any thing,
I am so over-joy'd, I'll fly to serve ye.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Take your joy moderately, as it is ministred,
And as the cause invites: that man's a foole
That at the sight o'th' Bond, dances and leapes,
Then is the true joy, when the money comes.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: You cannot now deny me.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Nay, you know not,
Women have crotchets, and strange fits.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: You shall not.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Hold ye to that and sweare it confidently,
Then I shall make a scruple to deny ye:
'Pray ye let's step in, and see a friend of mine,
The weather's sharp: we'll stay but halfe an houre,
We may be miss'd els: a private fine house 'tis, Sir,
And we may find many good welcomes.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: Doe Lady,
Doe happy Lady.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: All your mind's of doing,
You must be modester.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I will be any thing. —

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Open the dores, and give me roome to chafe in
Mine owne roome, and my liberty: why Maid there,
Open, I say, and doe not anger me,
I am subject to much fury: when ye dish-clout?
When doe ye come? a sleepe, ye lazie hell-hound?
Nothing intended, but your ease, and eating?
No body here? why wife, why wife? why jewell?
No tongue to answer me? 'pre'thee (good Pupill)
Dispence a little with thy carefull study,
And step to th' doore, and let me in; nor he neither?
Ha! not at's study? nor asleepe? nor no-body?
I'll make ye heare: the house of Ignorance,
No sound inhabits here: I have a key yet
That commands all: I feare I am metamorphiz'd.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He keepes his fury still, and may doe mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
prose: He shalbe hang'd first, we'll be sticklers there, boyes

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: The hundred thousand Dreams now, that posses him
Of jealousie, and of revenge, and frailtie
Of drawing Bills against us, and Petitions.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And casting what his credit shall recover.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Let him cast till his Maw come up, we care not.
You shall be still secured.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: We'll pay him home then;
Hark what a noyse he keeps within?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Certaine
H'as set his Chimneys o' fire, or the divell roars there.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: The Codixes o'th' Law are broke loose, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: He's fighting sure,

speeches.speaker: Di
verse: I'll tell ye that immediatly —

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Or doing some strange out-rage on himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Hang him, he dares not be so valiant.

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: There's no body at home and he chafes like a Lyon,
And stinkes withall.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: No body?

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Not a creature,
Nothing within, but he and his Law-tempest,
The Ladies, dishes, kettles, how they fly all?
And how the Glasses through the Roomes?

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: My friend sure
Has got her out and now he has made an end on't.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: See where the Sea comes? how it foams, & brussels?
The great Leviathan o'th' Law, how it tumbles?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Made every way an Asse? abus'd on all sides?
And from all quarters, people come to laugh at me?
Rise like a Comet, to be wonder'd at?
A horrid Comet, for Boyes tongues, and Ballads?
I will run from my wits.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Doe, doe, (good Lawyer)
And from thy money too, then thou wilt be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Here she comes home: now mark the salutations;
How like an Asse my friend goes?

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: She has pull'd his eares downe.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Now, what sweet voyage? to what Garden, Lady?
Or to what Cosens house?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Is this my welcome?
I cannot goe to Church but thus I am scandall'd,
Use no devotion for my soule, but Gentlemen—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: To Church?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Yes, and ye keep sweet youths to wait upon me,
Sweet bred-up youths, to be a credit to me.
There's your delight againe, pray take him to ye,
Ho^ever comes neare me more to debase me.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: How's this? how's this? good wife, how has he wrongd ye?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I was faine to drive him like a sheep before me,
I blush to thinke how people fleere, and scorn'd me,
Others have handsome men, that know behaviour,
Place, and observance: this silly thing knowes nothing,
Cannot tell ten; Let every Rascall justle me,
And still I push'd him on as he had bin comming.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ha! did ye push him on? is he so stupid?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: When others were attentive to the Priest,
Good devout Gentleman, then fell he fast
Fast, sound asleepe: then first began the Bag-pipes
The severall stops on's nose, made a rare musick,
A rare and lowd, and those plaid many an Antheme
Put out of that, he fell strait into dreaming.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: As cunning, as she is sweet; I like this carriage.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What did he then?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Why then he talked in his Sleep too,
Nay I'll divulge your morall vertues (sheeps-face)
And talk'd aloude, that every eare was fixt to him:
Did not I suffer (doe you thinke) in this time?
Talk of your bawling Law, of appellations
Of Declarations, and Excommunications:
Warrants, and Executions: and such divells
That drove all the Gentlemen out o'th' Church, by hurryes
With execrable oaths, they would never come there again
Thus am I serv'd, and man'd.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I pray ye forgive me,
I must confesse I am not fit to wait upon ye:
Alas, I was brought up —

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: To be an Asse,
A Lawyers Asse, to carry Bookes, and Buckrams.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: But what did you at Church?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: At Church, did ye aske her?
Doe you heare gentlemen, doe you mark that question?
Because you are halfe an heretique your selfe, Sir,
Would ye breed her too? this shall to the Inquisition,
A pious Gentlewoman, reprov'd for praying?
I'll see this filed, and you shall heare further, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Ye have an ill heart.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: It shall be found out Gentlemen,
There be those youths will search it.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: You are warme Signiour,
But a Faggot will warme ye better: we are witnesses.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Enough to hang him, doe not doubt.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Nay certaine,
I doe beleeve has rather no Religion.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: That must be knowne too, because shee goes to Church, sir?
O monstrum informe ingens!

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Let him goe on, sir,
His wealth will build a Nunnery, a faire one,
And this good Lady, when he is hang'd, and rotten,
May there be Abbesse.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You are cozend, honest Gentlemen,
I doe not forbid the use, but the forme, marke me.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Forme? what doe ye make of Forme?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They will undoe me,
Sweare, as I oft have done, and so betray me;
I must make faire way, and hereafter, Wife,
You are welcome home, & henceforth take your pleasure,
Goe, when ye shall thinke fit, I will not hinder ye,
My eyes are open now, and I see my errour,
My shame as great as that, but I must hide it.
The whole conveyance now I smell, but Basta,
Another time must serve: you see us friends, now
Heartily friends and no more chiding (gentlemen)
I have bin too foolish, I confesse, no more words,
No more (sweet wife.)

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You know my easie nature

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Goe get ye in: you see she has bin angry:
Forbeare her sight a while and time will pacify.
And learne to be more bold.

speeches.speaker: Lea.
verse: I would I could,
I will doe all I am able.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Doe Leandro,
We will not part, but friends of all hands.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Well said,
Now ye are reasonable, we can looke on ye,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ye have ierckt me: but for all that I forgive ye
Forgive ye hartily, and doe invite ye
To morrow to a Breakfast, I make but seldome
But now we will be merry.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Now ye are friendly,
Your doggednes and nigardize flung from ye.
And now we will come to ye

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Give me your hands, all;
You shall be wellcome hartily.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We will be,
For wee'll eate hard

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: The harder, the more wellcome,
And till the morning farewell; I have busines.

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Farewell good bountiful Bartolus 'tis a brave wench
A sudaine witty Theif, and worth all service:
Goe wee'll all goe, and crucifie the Lawyer,

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I'll clap foure tire of teeth into my mouth more
But I will grind his substance.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: Well Leandro,
Thou hast had a strange voyage, but I hope
Thou rid'st now in safe harbour,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: Lets goe drinke, Friends,
And laugh alou'd at all our merry may-games

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A match, a match 'twill whet our stomachs better.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Madam hees come.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: 'Tis well how did he looke,
When he knew from whom you were sent? was he not startled?
Or confident? or fearefull?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: As appear'd
Like one that knew his fortune at the worst,
And car'd not what could follow.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: 'Tis the better
Reach me a Chaire: So bring him in, be carefull
That none disturb us: I will try his temper,
And if I find him apt for my employments,
I'll worke him to my ends, if not I shall
Find other Engines.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Ther's my Ladie,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Leave us

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: You sent for me?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I did, and do's the favour,
Your present state considered, and my power,
Deserve no greater Ceremonie?

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Ceremonie?
I use to pay that, where I doe owe dutie,
Not to my Brothers wife: I cannot fawne,
If you expect it from me, you are cozen'd,
And so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: He beares up still; I like it,
Pray you a word

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Yes: I will give you hearing
On equall termes, and sit by you as a friend,
But not stand as a Sutour: Now your pleasure?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: You are very bold.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: 'Tis fitt: since you are proud
I was not made to feed that foolish humour,
With flattery and observance

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Yet, with your favour,
A little forme ioyn'd with respect to her,
That can add to your wants, or free you from 'em
(Nay raise you to a fate, beyond your hopes)
Might well become your wisedome,

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: It would rather
Write me a Foole, should I but onely think
That any good to me, could flow from you,
Whom for so many yeares: I have found and prov'd
My greatest Enemy: I am still the same
My wants have not transform'd me: I dare tell you,
To your new cerviz'd face, what I have spoken
Freely behind your back, what I thinke of you,
You are the proudest thing, and have the least,
Reason to be so, that I ever read of
In stature you are a Giantesse: and your Tailour
Takes measure of you, with a Iacobs staffe,
Or he can never reach you, this by the way
For your large size: Now, in a word, or two
To treat of your Complexion were decorum:
You are so far from faire, I doubt your Mother
Was too familliar with the Moore, that serv'd her,
Your Limbes and Features, I passe breifely over,
As things not worth description; and come roundly
To your soule, if you have any: for 'tis doubtfull

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I laugh at this, proceed

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: This Soule, I speake of
Or rather salt to keepe this heape of flesh,
From being a walking stench, like a large Inne,
Stands open for the entertainement of
All impious practises: but ther's no Corner
An honest thought can take up: and as it were not
Sufficient in your self to comprehend
All wicked plots, you have taught the Foole, my Brother
By your contagion, almost to put off
The nature of the man, and turn'd him Devill
Because he should be like you, and I hope
Will march to hell together: I have spoken,
And if the limming you, in your true Colours
Can make the Painter gracious, I stand readie
For my reward, or if my words distaste you
I weigh it not, for though your Groomes were ready
To cut my throat for't, be assur'd I cannot
Use other Language

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: You thinke you have said now,
Like a brave fellow: in this Womans War
You ever have bin train'd: spoke big: but suffer'd
Like a tame Asse; and when most spur'd and gall'd
Were never Master of the Spleene or Spirit,
That could raise up the anger of a man,
And force it into action,

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Yes vile Creature
Wer't thou a subject worthy of my Sword,
Or that thy death, this moment, could call home,
My banish'd hopes, thou now wer't dead: dead (woman)
But being as thou art, it is sufficient
I scorne thee, and contemne thee

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: This shewes nobly:
I must confesse it: I am taken with it
For had you kneeld, and whind and shew'd a base
And low deiected mind, I had despis'd you
This Bravery (in your adverse fortune) conquers
And do's command me, and upon the sudaine
I feele a kind of pittie, growing in me,
For your misfortunes, pittie some sayes the Parent,
Of future love, and I repent my part,
So far in what you have suffered, that I could,
(But you are cold) doe something to repaire
What your base Brother (such Iami I thinke him)
Hath brought to ruine

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Be not amaz'd,
Our injuries are equall in his Bastard
You are familliar with what I grone for
And though the name of Husband holds a tye
Beyond a Brother, I, a poore weake Woman,
Am sensible, and tender of a wrong,
And to revenge it, would break through all letts,
That durst oppose me.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Is it possible?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: By this kisse: start not: thus much, as a stranger
You may take from me; But, if you were pleas'd,
I should select you, as a bosome Friend,
I would print 'em, thus, and thus,

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Keepe off.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Come neare,
Neere into the Cabinet of my Counsailes:
Simplicity and patience dwell with Fooles,
And let them beare those burthens, which wise men
Boldly shake off; Be mine and ioyne with me,
And when that I have rais'd you to a fortune,
(Doe not deny your selfe the happie meanes)
You'l looke on me, with more iudicious eies
And sweare I am most faire,

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: What would this Woman?
The purpose of these words? speake not in ridles
And when I understand what you would counsell,
My answer shall be suddaine,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Thus then Iami,
The objects of our fury, are the same,
For young Ascanio, whom you snake like hug'd
(Frozen with wants to death) in your warme bosome,
Lives to supplant you in your certaine hopes,
And kills in me all comfort.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Now 'tis plaine,
I apprehend you: and were he remov'd —

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: You, once againe were the undoubted heire.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: 'Tis not to be denyed; I was ice before,
But now ye have fir'd me, —

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I'l add fuell to it,
And by a nearer cut, doe you but steere
As I direct you bring our Bark into
The Port of happines,

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: By Henriques death:
But you'l say hee's your Brother; in great fortunes
(Which are epitomes of States & Kingdomes)
The po^iticke brooke no Rivalls.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Excellent.
For sure I thinke out of a scrupulous feare,
To feed in expectation when I may
(Dispensing but a little with my conscience)
Come into full possession, would not argue
One that desir'd to thrive,

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Now you speake like
A man that knowes the World.

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: I needs must learne
That have so good a Tutresse: And what thinke you,
(Don Henrique and Ascanio cut off)
That none may live, that shall desire to trace us
In our black pathes, if that Octavio
His foster Father' and the sad Iacinta,
(Faith pittie her, and free her from her Sorrowes)
Should fall Companions with 'em? When we are red
With murther, let us often bath in blood,
The collour will be scarlet.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: And that's glorious,
And will protect the fact

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: Suppose this don:
(If undiscovered) we may get for money,
(As that you know buyes any thing in Rome)
A dispensation

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: And be married?

speeches.speaker: Jam.
verse: True.
Or if it be knowne, trusse up our Gold and Jewells,
And fly to some free State, and there with scorne —

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Laugh at the lawes of Spaine.
'Twere admirable.

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: We shall beget rare Children. I am rap'd with
The meere imagination —

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Shall it be don?

speeches.speaker: Iam.
verse: Shall? tis too tedious: furnish me with meanes
To hire the instruments, and to your self,
Say it is done already: I will shew you,
'Ere the Sun set, how much you have wrought upon me,
Your province is onely to use some meanes,
To send my Brother, to the Grove that's neighbour,
To the west Port of th' Citie; leave the rest,
To my owne practise; I have talk'd too long:
But now will doe: this kisse, with my Confession,
To worke a fell revenge: A mans a foole,
If not instructed in a Womans Schoole.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You are well enough disguiz'd, furnish the Table,
Make no shew, what ye are, till I discover
Not a soule knowes ye here: be quick and dilligent,
These youthes, I have invited to a Breakefast,
But what the Sawce will be, I am of opinion
I shall take off the edges of their Appetites,
And greaze their gums, for eating hartily;
This month or two they have plaid their prizes with me
And with their severall flurts they have lighted dangerously
But sure I shall be quit: I heare 'em comming
Goe off, and wait the bringing in your service,
And doe it handsomely: you know where to have it
Wellcome i'Faith,

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: That's well said, honest Lawyer,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Said like a Neighbour

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Wellcome all: all over
And let's be merry:

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: To that end we came Sir,
An hower of freedome's worth an age of juglings,

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I am come too Sir, to specifie my Stomach
A poore reteyner to your worships bountie,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And thou shalt have it fill'd, my merry Diego,
My liberall, and my bonney bounteous Diego
Even fil^d till it groane againe

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: Let it have faire play,
And if it founder then—
I'll tell ye neighbours,
Though I were angry yesterday, with ye all,
And very angry for me thought ye bobd me.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: No, no, by no meanes.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: No, when I considered
It was a jest, and carried off so quaintly
It made me merry: very merry, Gentlemen,
I doe confes I could not sleepe to thinke on't
The mirth so tickled me, I could not slumber,

speeches.speaker: Lop,
verse: Good mirth do's worke so: honest mirth,
Now, should we have meant in earnest—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You say true Neighbour,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: It might have bred such a distast and sowrenesse,
Such fond imaginations in your Braines, Sir
For things thrust home in earnest —

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Very certaine
But I know ye all for merry waggs, and ere long
You shall know me too. in another fashion
Though y'are pamper d ye shall beare part 'oth burthen.
Come Wife; Come bid 'em wellcome; Come my Jewell:
And Pupill, you shall come too; nere hang backward,
Come, come the womans pleas'd, her angers over,
Come, be not bashfull,

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What do's he prepare here?
Sure ther's no meate 'ith house at least none drest,
Do's he meane to mock 'em? or some new bred Crotchet
Come o're his braines; I doe not like his kindnes?
But silence best becomes me: if he meane foule play
Sure they are enough to right themselves and let 'em,
I'll sit by, so they beat him not to powder,

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Bring in the meate there, ha? Sit downe deare Neighbour
A little meate needs little Complement,
Sit downe I say:

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What doe you meane by this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Convay away their weapons handsomely,

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You know ther's none ith' house to answer ye,
But the poore Girle; you know ther's no meat neither

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Peace and be quiet; I shall make you smoak els
Ther's men and Meate enough, set it downe formally

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I feare some lew'd tricke, yet I dare not speake on't

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I have no dainties for ye Gentlemen,
Nor ^odes of meat, to make the roome smell of'em
Onely a dish to every man I have dedicated,
And if I have pleas'd his appetite,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: O, a Capon,
A Bird of grace, and be thy will, I honour it

speeches.speaker: Di.
verse: For me some fortie pound of lovely Beeffe,
Plac'd in a mediterranean sea of Brewisse

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Fall to, fall to that we may drinke and laugh after
Wait diligently knaves,

speeches.speaker: Mil.
verse: What rare bits this?
An execution, blesse me!

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Nay take it to ye
Ther's no avoiding it 'tis somewhat tough Sir,
