Your honours ever-springing, and your yeares.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Cozen?

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: Your Graces vassall, far unworthy
The nearnesse of your blood.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Correct me not, I know the word I speake,
And know the person.
Though I be something higher then the place
VVhere common men have motion, and discending
Down with my eye, their formes are lessened to me,
Yet from this pitch can I behold my owne,
From millions of those men that have no marke,
And in my fearfull stoop, can make them stand.
VVhen others feele my soule and perish, Cozen
Be comforted, you are very welcome, so
Is your faire wife: the charge of whom I give
To my own dearest and best beloved.
Tell me, have you resolv'd your selfe for Court,
And utterly renounce the slavish Countrey,
VVith all the cares thereof?

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: I have sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Have you dismist your eating houshold,
Sold your hangings of Nebuchadnezar, for such they were,
As I remember, with the furnitures
Belonging to your beds and chambers?

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: I Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Have you most carefully tane off the lead,
From your roofe weake with age, and so prevented
The ruine of your house, and clapt him
In a summer suite of thatch to keepe him coole?

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: All this I have perform'd.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Then lend me all your hands, I will embrace my Cozen
VVho is an understanding Gentleman,
And with a zeale mighty as is my name,
Once more I bid you welcome to the Court;
My state againe.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: As I was telling you your husband
Must be no more Commander, looke to that,
Be severall at meate, and lodging, let him have
Boord-wages and dyet 'mongst his men it'h towne
For pleasure if he be given too't let him have it,
Else as your own fancie shall direct you.
Cozen, you see this mighty man here: he was an asse
When he came first to towne: indeed he was
Just such another coxcomb as your husband,
God blesse the mark and every good mans childe!
This must not stir you Cozen.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Heaven forbid?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Sweet Maria, provide the cushion ready for it.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse: It shall be done.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Receive all your advices from our selfe,
Be once a day with us, and so farewell
For this time, my faire Cozen; Gentlemen
Conduct him to his lodging.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Farewell, and think upon my words.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I shall observe them.

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: Health, and the Kings continuall love attend you.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: O for a private place to ease my lungs!
Heaven give me patience, such a paire of Jades
Were never better ridden to this houre,
Pray heaven they hold out to the journeys end.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Twitch him aside good Monsieur, whilst I breake
Upon the body of his strength, his wife,
I have a constant promise: she is my own.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Ply her to wind-ward Monsieur, you have taken
The most compendious way to raise your selfe,
That could have been delivered by a councell.

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: I have some certaine aimes Sir: but my wife—

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Your wife? you must not let that trouble you.

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: It will Sir, to see her in a strangers armes.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: What mean you? let her alone, be wise, stir not a foot
For if you do, all your hopes are buryed:
I sweare you are a lost man if you stir.

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: I thanke you Sir, I will be more advis'd.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: But what great Office do you levell at?

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: Sir, they are kissing.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Let them kisse,
And much may do their good hearts; they must kisse
And kisse, and double kisse, and kisse againe,
Or you may kisse the post for any rising:
Had your noble Kinsman ever mounted
To these high Spheres of honour, now he moves in,
But for the kisses of his wife?

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: I Know not.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Then I doe; credite me, he had been lost,
A fellow of no mark, and no repute,
Had not his wife kist soone, and very sweetly
She was an excellent woman, and dispatcht him
To his full, being in a moment Sir—

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: But yet me thinks he should not take her Sir
Into a private roome.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Now stand and flourish,
You are a made man for ever.
I doe envy you if you stand your fortunes up,
You are the happiest man: but your great Cozen
This day in Court: well I will marry surely,
And not let every man out-run me thus.
'Tis time to be mine owne friend, I live
In towne here, and direct the readiest way,
To other men, and be a slave my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Co.
verse: Nay good Sir be not mov'd, I am your servant,
And will not be ungratefull for this knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Will you be walking home?

speeches.speaker: Co.
verse: I would de^ire to have my wife a long.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You are too raw,
Be gon and take no notice where you left her,
Let her returne at leisure, if she stay
A moneth 'twill be the better, understand me
This Gentleman can doe't.

speeches.speaker: Co.
verse: I will Sir, & wife remember me a Duke, a Duke wife.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Aboard her Longaveile shee's thine owne,
To me the fooling of this foole, is venerie.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Come, preethe come, have I not crownes? behold
And follow me, here; not a word, go in
Grope by the walls, and you shall finde a bed,
Lye downe there, see, see, a turne or two to give
My blood some heate; and I am presently
For action, darknesse by thy leave I come.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: I am perfect in my lesson, be my speed,
Thou God of marriage, this is the doore, I'le knock.

speeches.speaker: Bew. within.
verse: Whose there? I cannot come yet.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Mounsier Bewford?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Stay 'till I light a candle, who are ye?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir? a poore Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: O come in, I'le finde a time for you too, be not loude.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Sir you have found that time already, shame
On my soule therefore.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Why? what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Do you not see Sir, is your light so dim?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Do you not waite on the Lady Mount Marine?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I do Sir, but my love on you.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Poore soule! how cam'st thou by this big belly?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: By your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: By heaven I ne're toucht your body.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, unsweare that oath agen, I'le tell you all;
These two yeares I have lov'd you, but the meanes
How to enjoy you, I did never know
Till twelfe night last, when hearing of your game
To take up wenches private in the night,
I apprehended straight this course to make
My selfe as one of them, and waite your coming;
I did so, and enjoyed you, and now this child
That now is quicke within me: hide my shame,
And marry me: or else I must be forc't—

speeches.speaker: Long within.
verse: Monsieur Bewford, Monsieur Bewford.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Whose that calls?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Are you a bed?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: No Sir, the hangings.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Nay Mounsieur, I'le forbid that, we'le have faire play
Lend me your candle, are you taken Bewford?
A lecher of your practice, and close carriage
To be discovered thus? I am a sham'd
So great a Master in his art should faile,
And stagger in his grounds.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Your wide,
This woman and my selfe are man and wife,
And have been so this halfe yeare,
Where are you now? have I been discovered?
You cannot breake so easily on me Sir,
I am to wary to be opend by you.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: But these are but illusions to give couler
To your most misticke leacherie, but Sir
The belly hath betray'd you all, it must out.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Good Longavile believe me on my faith,
I am her husband.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: On my faith I cannot unlesse I saw
Your hands fast and your heartes.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Why Longavile when did I give that to your eares
That was not truth? by all the world she's mine,
She is my wife and to confirme you better
I give my selfe againe, here take my hand
And I yours, we are once more married,
Will this content you?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Yes, I am believing, and God give you joy.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: My loving wife I will not wrong thee,
Since I am thine and only loved of thee
From this houre I, vow my selfe a new man,
Be not jealous: for though I had a purpose,
To have spent an hower or two in solace otherwise,
And was provided for it, yet my love
Shall put a better temper to my blood,
Come out thou woman of unholsome life,
Be sorry for thy sinnes, and learne to mend,
Nay never hide your face, you shall be seene.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Jaques, why Jaques, art thou that Jaques,
The very staffe, and right hand of our Duke?
Speake, thou bearded Venus.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: I am he, by miracle preserv'd to be that Jaques,
Within this two houres Gentlemen, poore Jaques
Was but as coarse in grave: a man of wisedome,
That of my conscience if he had his right
Should have a pretty state, but that's all one
That noble Gentleman did save this life,
I keepe it for him, 'tis his owne.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Oh Bachus! is all the world drunke? come wee'le to the Duke
And give thankes for this delivery.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Not gon unto my Tenants to relate
My grace and honour; and the mightynesse
Of my new name which would have struck a terrour
Through their course doublets, to their very hearts?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Alas great Lord and Master, I could scarce
With safety of my life returne againe
Unto your graces house, and but for one
That had some mercie, I had sure been hang'd.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: My house?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Yes Sir, this house, your house 'ith towne.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Jaques we are displeas'd, hath it no name?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: What name?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Dull rogue; what hath the King bestowed
So many honours, open'd all his springes,
And showerd his graces downe upon my head,
And has my house no name? no title yet?
Burgundy house you Asse.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Your graces mercy,
And when I was come off, and had recover'd
Burgundy house, I durst not yet be seene,
But lay all night for feare of pursuiuants
In Burgundy privie house.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: O Sir, 'tis well,
Can you remember now? but Jaques know
Since thy intended journey is so croste,
I will go downe my selfe this morning.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Have I not said this morning?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: But consider,
That nothing is prepared yet for your journey,
Your graces teames not here to draw your cloathes;
And not a carrier yet in town to send by.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I say once more go about it,
You'r a wise man, you'de have m^ linger time,
Till I have worne these cloathes out: will ye go?
Make ye ready wife.

speeches.speaker: Dutches.
verse: I am so, mighty Duke.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Nay for the Countrey.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: How? for the Countrey?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Yes I am resolv'd to see my Tenants in this bravery
Make them a sumptuous feast, with a slight shew,
Of Dives, and Lazarus, and a squib or two,
And so returne.

speeches.speaker: Dutches.
verse: VVhy Sir? you are not mad?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: How many Dukes have ye known mad? I pray speake.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: You are the first Sir, and I hope the last,
But you are stark horne mad.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Forbeare good wife.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: As I have faith you'r mad: your hornes
Have been to heavy for you, and have broke
Your skull in pieces: If you be in earnest.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: VVell you shall know my skull and wits are whole
Ere I have done, and yet I am in earnest.

speeches.speaker: Dutches.
verse: VVhy, do you think I'le go?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I know you shall.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: I shall? by what authority shall I?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I am your husband.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: True I confesse it,
And by that name the world hath given you
A power to sway me; but Sir you shall know
There is a greater bond that tyes me here,
Alleagance to the King; has he not heapt
Those honours on you to no other end,
But to stay you here, and shall I have a hand
In the offending such a gracious Prince?
Besides, our owne undoings lyes uppon't,
Were there no other cause, I do not see,
Why you should go: If I should say you should not.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Do you thinke so?

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: Yes faith.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Now good wife make me understand that point.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: Why that you shall, did I not bring you hither?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
prose: And were not all those honours wrought out of the fire by me?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: By you?

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: By me; how strang you make it?
When you came first did you not walke the Town,
In a long cloake halfe compasse? an old hat,
Linde with vellure, and on it for a band,
A skeine of crimson cruell?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I confesse it.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: And tooke base courses?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Base?

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
prose: Base by this light, extreame base, and scurvie, monstrous base.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What were these courses, wife?

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: Why you shall know,
Did you not thus attired trot up and down,
Plotting for vild and lowsie offices,
And agreed with the Sergiant of the beares,
To buy his place? deny this if you can.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Why it is true.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: And was not that monstrous base?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Be advis'd wife, a beares a princly beast.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: A beare?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Yes wife, and one side venson.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: You'r more then one side foole, I'm sure of that

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: But since you have vext me wife, know you shall go
Nor you shall never have penny from me.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: Nay I have done, and though I know 'twill be
Your overthrow, I'le not forsake you now.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Be ready then.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: What are you married Bewford?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
prose: I as fast as words, and hearts, and hands & Priest can make us.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: O Gentlemen, we are undone.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: For what?

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: This Gentleman the Lord of lorne my husband,
Will be gon downe to shew his play fellowes,
Where he is gay.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: What, downe into the Countrey?

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: Yes faith, was ever foole but he so crosse?
I would as faine be gracious to him,
As he could wish me, but he will not let me;
Speake faithfully, will he deserve my mercy?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: According to his merits he should weare,
A guarded coate, and a great wooden dagger.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: If there be any woman that doth knowe,
The duties 'twixt a husband and his wife,
Will speake but one word for him he shall scape;
Is not that reasonable? but ther's none,
Be ready therefore, to pursue the plot
We had against a pinch, for he must stay.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: VVaite you here for him whilst I go
And make the King acquainted with your sport,
For feare he be incens'd for our attempting;
Places of so great honour.

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: Go, be speedy.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Come let me see how all things are disposed of.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: One Cart will serve for all your furniture,
With roome enough behinde to ease the footman
A capcase for your linnen, and your plate,
VVith a strange locke that opens with Amen;
For my young Lord because of easie portage,
A quiver of your graces linde with Cunney,
Made to be hang'd about the Nurses neck,
Thus with a scarfe or towell.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Very good.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Nay, 'tis well, but had you staid another weeke,
I would have had you, furnisht in such pomp,
As never Duke of Burgundy was furnisht,
You should have had a sumpter though't had cost me
The laying on my selfe: where now you are faine,
To hire a rippers mare, and buy new dossers,
But I have got them painted with your armes,
VVith a faire darnex Carpet of my owne
Laid crosse for the more state.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Jaques I thanke you: your Carpet shall be brusht
And sent you home; what, are you ready wife?

speeches.speaker: Dutch.
verse: An houre agoe

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I cannot chuse but kisse thy royall lips,
Deare Dutches mine, thou art so good a woman.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Yould say so if you knew all, goodman Duckling.

speeches.speaker: Coz.
verse: This was the happiest fortune could befall me
Now in his absence will I follow close
Mine owne preferment, and I hope e ere long,
To make my meane and humble name so strong,
As my great Couzens, when the world shall know,
I beare too hot a spirit to live low
The next Spring wil I down my wife and houshold,
I'le have My Ushers, and my foure Lacquies,
Six spare croches too: but mum, no more,
What I intend to do, I'le keep in store.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Mountye, mountye, Iaques, be our querry.

speeches.speaker: Groom.
verse: To horse there Gentlemen, and fall in couples.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Come honoured Duchesse.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Stand thou proud man.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Thieves, Iaques, raise the people.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: No, raise no people, 'tis the Kings command,
Which bids thee once more stand thou haughty man,
Thou art a monster, for thou art ungratefull,
And like a fellow of a rebell nature,
Hast flung from his embraces: and for
His honours given thee, hast not returnd
So much as thanks, and to oppose his will,
Resolv'd to leave the Court, and set the Realm
A fire, in discontent, and open action:
Therefore he bids thee stand thou proud man,
Whilst with the whisking of my sword about
I take thy honours off: this first sad whiske
Takes off thy Duke-dome, thou art but an Earl.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: You are mistaken, Longavile.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: O would I were, this second whiske divides
Thy Earldome from thee, thou art yet a Baron.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: No more whisks if you love me Longavile.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Two whisks are past, and two are yet behind,
Yet all must come, but not to linger time.
With these two whisks I end, now Mount Marine,
For thou art now no more, so says the King,
And I have done his Highnesse will with griefe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Disgraced from my honours?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: 'Tis too certaine.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I am no Traitor sure that I know of;
Speak Iaques? hast thou ever heard me utter word
Tending to treason, or to bring in the enemy?

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Alas sir I know nothing,
Why should your Worship bring me in to hang me?
God's my judge Gentlemen I never medled
But with the brushing of his cloaths, or fetching
In water in a morning for his hands.

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: Are these the honours of this place? Antony
Help me to take her gowne off quickly
Or I'le so swinge ye for't—

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Why husband? Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: I'le not loose a penny by this towne.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Why what do you meane sir, have her to her lodging,
And there undresse her, I will waite upon her.

speeches.speaker: Cous.
verse: Indeed you shall not, your moneth is out I take it,
Get you out before me wife:
Couzen farewell, I told you long agoe,
That pride begins with pleasure, ends with woe.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Goe thy way sentences, 'twill be thy fortune,
To live and dye a Cuckold and Church-warden.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: O my poor husband! what a heavy fortune
Is fallen upon him?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Me thinks 'tis strange,
That heaven fore-warning great men of their falls,
With such plaine tokens, they should not avoid them?
For the last night betwixt eleven and twelve,
Two great and hideous blazing stars were seen
To fight a long houre by the clocke, the one
Drest like a Duke, the other like a King,
Till at the last the crowned star ore-came.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Why do ye stand so dead, Monsieur Marine?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: So Caesar fell when in the Capitoll
They gave his body two and thirty wounds.
Be warned all ye Peers, and by my fall,
Hereafter learn to let your wives rule all.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Monsieur Marine, pray let me speak with you;
Sir I must wave you to conceale this party,
It stands upon my utter overthrow;
Seem not discontented, nor do not stir a foote,
For if you do, you and your hope—
I sweare you are a lost man if you stir.
And have an eye to Bewford, he'l tempt you.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Come, come, for shame goe downe;
Were I Marine, by heaven I would goe down:
And being there, I would rattle him such an answer
Should make him smoake.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Good Monsieur Bewford peace
Leave these rebellious words,
Or by the honours which I once enjoyed,
And yet may sweare by,
I'le tell the King of your proceedings;
I am satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: You talkt of going down when 'twas not fit,
But now let's see your spirit,
A thousand and a thousand will expect it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Why wife, are you mad?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: No nor drunk, but I'de have you know your own strength

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: You talk like a most foolish woman wife;
I tell you I will stay, yet I have a
Cratchet troubles me.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: More cratchets yet?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Follow me Jaq. I must have thy counsell,
I will returne againe, stay you there Wife.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I fear this losse of honour will give him some few stooles.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: No, no, he is resolv'd, he will not
Stir a foote I'le lay my life.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: I but hee's discontented, how shall we resolve that
And make him stay with comfort?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Faith Bewford we must even let nature work,
For hee's the sweetest temper'd man for that
As one can wish, for let men but goe about to foole him,
And hee'l have his finger as deep in 't as the best;
But see where he comes frowning, blesse us all!

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Off with your hats, for here doth come
The high and mighty Duke of Burgundy.
What ever you may think, I have thought
And thought, and thought upon't, and I finde it plaine,
The King cannot take backe what he has given,
Unlesse I forfeit it by course of Law.
Not all the water in the river Sene,
Can wash the blood out of these Princely veines.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: God a mercy husband, thou art the best
To worke out a thing at a pinch, in France.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I will ascend my state againe,
Duchesse take your place,
And let our Champion enter.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Has he his Champion? that's excellent.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: And let loud musick sound before his entrance.
Sound Trumpet.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: How well our Champion doth demean himselfe,
As if he had been made for such an action?
Me thinks his sturdy trunchion he doth wield,
Like Mars approaching to a bloody field.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: I think ther's no man so desperate
To dare encounter with our Champion,
But trust me, Iaques, thou hast pleas'd us well;
Once more our warlike musick, then proceed.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: What wondrous age is this? what close proceedings?
I heare the clang of Trumpets in this house,
To what intent do not our States-men search?
O no, they look not into simple truth;
For I am true, and they regard not me,
A man in armour too: God save the King
The world will end, theres nought but treachery.

speeches.speaker: Ia.
prose: I Ja. servant to the high & mighty Godfrey Duke of Burgundy, do come hither to prove by natural strength and activity of my body, without the help of sorcery, inchant~ment, or negromancy, that the said Godfrey late of Mount Marine, & now of Burgundy, hath perfect right therto, notwithstanding the Kings command to the contrary, & no other person whatsoever: & in token that I wilbe ready to make good the same: I throw down my gage, wch is my honour, pronounced the 37. of Feb. stilo novo, God save the D.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Of all the plots the King hath laid for me
This was the shrewdest, 'tis my life they seeke,
And they shall have it: if I should refuse
To accept the challenge in the Kings behalfe,
They have some cause to take away my life,
And if I do accept it, who can tell,
But I may fall by doubtfull chance of war?
'Twas shrewd, but I must take the least of evills,
I take thy gauntlet up thou treacherous man,
That stands in armed coate against the King,
Whom God preserve, and with my single sword
Will justifie whatever he commands;
I'le watch him for catching of my words.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Jaques goe on, defend our Princely title.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Why shrinkst thou backe? thou hast an evill cause;
Come forward man, I have a rocke about me,
I fight for my true Liege.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Goe forward Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: I do beeseech your Grace to pardon me,
I will not fight with him, with any else
I'le shew my resolution speedily.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Come do thy worst, for the King shall see
All is not true that is reported of me.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: I may not fight with him by law of armes.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What? shall my title fall? wilt thou not fight?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Never with him that once hath sav'd my life.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Dar'st thou not fight? behold then I doe goe
Strong with the zeale I beare my Soveraign,
And seize upon that haughty man himselfe.
Descend the steps that (thou hast thus usurpt
Against the King and State) downe to the ground,
And if thou doe utter but a syllable
To crosse the Kings intent, thou art but dead;
There, lye upon the earth and pine and dye.
Did ever any man wade through such stormes,
To save his life, as poore Shattillion?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I feare this challenge hath spoil'd all.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Ne're feare it, hee'l work it out againe servant.
See where Shattillions Love, poor Lady, comes.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
prose: Lye still sir if you love your life, I'le whistle when he's gone,

speeches.speaker: Love.
verse: O Gentlemen, I charge you by the love
Which you beare to women, take some pitty
On this distressed man, help to restore
That pretious jewell to him he hath lost.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Lady what ever power doth lye in us
By art or prayer, or danger, we are yours,

speeches.speaker: Love.
verse: A strange conceite hath wrought this malady,
Conceites againe must bring him to himselfe,
My strict denyall to his will wrought this?
And if you could but draw his wilder thoughts
To know me, he would sure recover sense.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: That charge I'le undertake.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Looke Jaques, look, for Gods sake let me rise,
This greatnesse is a Jade, I cannot sit it.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: His sword is up, and yet he watcheth you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I'le down again, pray for thy Master, Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Now the King may see all the suggestions are not true,
He hath receiv'd against my loyalty;
When all men else refuse, I fight his battails,
And thrust my body into dangers mouth;
I am become his Champion, and this sword
Has taught his enemies to know themselves;
O that he would no more be jealous of me!

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Monsieur Shattillion, the King assigns you,
That for this valiant loyall act of yours,
He hath forgot all jealousies and feares,
And never more will tempt you into danger.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: But how shall I believe this? what new token
Of reconcilement will he shew me?
Let him release my poor love from her torment,
From her hard fare and strict imprisonment.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: He hath done this to win your after-love,
And see your Lady sent you from the King
By these two Gentlemen: be thankfull for her.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: She lives, she lives, I know her by the power
Shoots from her eyes.

speeches.speaker: Love.
verse: Rise deare Sbattillion.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: I Know my duty,
Next unto my King, I am to kneele to you.

speeches.speaker: Love.
prose: I'le have you rise, fetch me a chair, sit down Shat.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: I am commanded, and faith tell me Mistris,
What usage have you had? pray be plaine?

speeches.speaker: Love.
verse: O my most lov'd Shattillion, paine enough,
But now I am free, thanks to my God and King.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: His eyes grow very heavy, not a word,
That his weak senses may come sweetly home.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: The King is honourable.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: When do you whistle Jaques?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: By and by.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Come hither Monsieur, canst thou laugh a little?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: So thou shalt then. Bewford how dost thou?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Why well.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I'me glad on't, and how does thy wife?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Why you may see her Sir, she stands behind you.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: By the mass she's there indeed, but wher's her belly?

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Belly?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: Her great belly man: what hast thou sent thee?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: A boy I'le lay my life, it tumbled so.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Catcht by this light.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I'le be a gossip Bewford.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: And I.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I have an odd Apostle spoone.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: S' foote catcht.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Why what's the matter Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: He's married to your woman.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: And I not know it?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: 'Twas a veniall sin.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Gall, gall, gall.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Forgive her Monsieur Bewford, 'twas her love.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: You may rise if you please, I must endure it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: See how my great Lord lyes upon the ground
And dare not stir yet?
Jaques, whistles?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Jaques, Jaq. is the Kings Champion gone yet,

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: No, but hee's asleep.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Is he asleep art sure?

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: I am sure he is, I heare him snore.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Then by your favours Gentlemen I rise,
And know I am a Duke still.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: And I am his Champion.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Hold thee there, and all France cannot mend thee.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I am a Prince as great within my thoughts
As when the whole state did adorn my person;
What tryall can be made to try a Prince?
I will oppose this noble corps of mine
To any danger that may end the doubt.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Great Duke and husband there is but one way
To satisfie the world of our true right,
And it is dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What may it be?
Were it to bring the great Turke bound in chaines
Through France in triumph: or to couple up
The Sophie, and great Prester Iohn together,
I would attempt it Duchesse, tell the course.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: There is a strong opinion through the world,
And no doubt grounded on experience
That Lyons will not touch a lawfull Prince,
If you be confident then of your right,
Amongst the Lions beare your naked body,
And if you come off cleare and never winch,
The world will say you are a perfect Prince.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I thank you Duchesse for your kinde advice,
But now we do not affect those ravenous beasts.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: A Lyon is a beast to try a King;
But for the triall of such a state like this
Pliny reports a mastive dog will serve.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: We will not deale with dogs at all: but men.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You shall not need to deale with them at all,
Hark you Sir, the King doth know you are a Duke:

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: No, does he?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes, and is content you shall be, but with this caution,
That none know it but your selfe:
For if ye do, he'l take it away by act of Parliament.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Here's my hand, and whilst I live or breath,
No living wight shall know I am a Duke.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Marke me directly Sir, your wife may know it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: May not Jaques?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes, he may.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: May not my countrey Couzen?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: By no meanes sir, if you love your life and state.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Well then, know all I am no Duke.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: No I'le sweare it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: See he wakes.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Where am I, or where have I been all this while?
Sleep hath not sate so sound upon mine eyes
But I remember well that face;
O thou too cruell, leave at length to scorne
Him that but looking on thy beauty dyes,
Either receive me, or put out my eyes.

speeches.speaker: Love.
verse: Dearest Shattillion see upon my knees,
I offer up my love, forget my wrongs.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Art thou mine own?

speeches.speaker: Love.
verse: By heaven I am.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Then all the world is mine.

speeches.speaker: Love.
verse: I have stranger things to tel thee, my dearest love.

speeches.speaker: Shat.
verse: Tell nothing but that thou art mine own:
I do not care to know where I have been,
Or how I have liv'd, or any thing,
But that thou art my own.

speeches.speaker: Bew.
verse: Well wife, though 'twere a trick that made us wed,
Wee'l make our selves merry soone in bed.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Know all I am no Duke.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: What saye?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Jaques?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I am a Duke.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: Are yee?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Yes faith, yes faith.
But it must only run amongst our selves,
And Jaques thou shalt be my Secretary still.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Kinde Gentlemen, leade in Shattillion,
For he must needs be weak and sickly yet.
Now all my labours have a perfect end as I could wish,
Let all young sprightly wives that have
Dull foolish Coxcombs to their husbands,
Learn by me their duties, what to doe,
VVhich is to make 'em fooles, and please 'em too.

speeches.speaker: Lodovico.
verse: THe truth is Piso, so she be a woman
And rich and holsome, let her be of what
Condition & Complection it please,
She shall please me I am sure; Those men are fooles
That make their eyes their choosers, not their needes.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Me thinks I would have her honest too, & handsom.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Yes if I could have both, but since they are
Wishes so neare impossibilities,
Let me have that that may be.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: If it were so,
I hope your conscience would not be so nice
To start at such a blessing.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: No beleeve me,
I doe not thinke I should.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: But thou would'st be
I doe not doubt upon the least suspition
Unmercifully jealous

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: No I should not,
For I believe those mad that seeke vexations,
A wife, though she be honest, is a trouble,
Had I a wife as faire as Hellen was
That drew so many Cuckolds to her cause,
These eyes should see another in my Saddle
Ere I beleeve my beast would carry double.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: So should not I by'r Lady, and I thinke
My patience (by your leave) as good as yours,
Report would stirre me mainely, I am sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Report? you are unwise; report is nothing;
For if there were a truth in what men talke,
I meane of this kind, this part of the world
I am sure would be no more cal'd Christendom.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: What then?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Why Cuckoldome, for we should loose
Our old faiths cleane, and hold their new opinions:
If talke could make me sweat, before I would marry,
I'de tie a surer knot, and hang my selfe;
I tell thee there was never woman yet,
Nor never hope there shall be, though a Saint,
But she has been a subject to mens tongues,
And in the worse sense: and that desperate husband,
That dares give up his peace, and follow humours
(Which he shall find too busie, if he seek'em)
Beside the forcing of himselfe an Asse
He dyes in chaines, eating himselfe with anger.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Having these Antidotes against opinion
I would marry any one; an arrant whore.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Thou dost not feele the nature of this phisick
Which I prescribe not to beget diseases,
But where they are, to stop them.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: I conceive ye.
What thinkest thou? thy way of the widow Lelia?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Faith thou hast found out one I must confesse
Would stagger my best patience: From that woman
As I would blesse my selfe from plagues and surfets
From men a war at Sea, from stormes, and quicksands,
From hearing Treason and concealing it,
From daring of a Madman, or a Drunkard,
From Heresie, ill wine, and stumbling post horse;
So would I pray each morning, and each night
(And if I said each houre, I should not lye)
To be delivered of all these in one,
The woman thou hast named.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Thou hast set her in a pretty Letany.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Pray take my councell.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: When I am my selfe
Ile heare you any way; love me though thus
As thou art honest, which I dare not be
Lest I despise my selfe. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Doe you heare my friend: Sir are you not a setter,
For the faire widdow here of famous memory?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Ha? am I taken for a Bawd? oh God
To mine owne child too? misery, I thanke thee
That keepes me from their knowledge: Sir beleeve me
I understand ye not.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: You love plaine dealing.
Are you not percell Bawd? confesse your Function,
It may be we would use it.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Were she worse,
As I feare strangely she is ill enough,
I would not heare this tamely.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Heer's a shilling
To strike good luck withall.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Heer's a Sword Sir
To strike a Knave withall, thou lyest, and basely,
Be what thou woult.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Why how now Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: You are many: I shall meete you, Sir, againe,
And make you understand, y'ave wrongd a woman
Compard with whom thy Mother was a sinner. Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: He has amazd me.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: With a blow?
By'r Lady twas a sound on; are ye good
At taking knocks? I shall know you hereafter:
You weare too blame to tempt a man so far
Before you knew him ce^ine: h'as not hurt ye?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: No I think.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: We were too blame indeed to goe so far,
For men may be mistaken: if he had swinged us
H'ad serv'd us right: Beshrew my heart I think,
VVe have done the Gentlewoman as much wrong too,
For hang me, if I know her
In my particular.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Nor I; this tis to credit
Mens idle tongues; I warrant they have sed
As much by our two mothers.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Like enough.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I see a beating now and then does more
Move and stir up a mans contrition
Then a sharpe Sermon, here probatum est.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: What shall I tell your Sister?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Tell her this,
Till she be better conversation'd
And leave her walking by her selfe, and whyning
To her old melancholly Lute, I'le keepe
As far from her as the Gallowes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Who's that Fredrick?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes marry is't. O Angelo how do'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Save you Sir, how does my Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She is in love I thinke, but not with you.
I can assure you, saw ye Fabritio?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Is he come over?

speeches.speaker: Fred
verse: Yes a weeke agoe: Shall we dyne?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I cannot:

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Pre'thee doe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Beleeve me I have businesse.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Have you too, gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: No sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why then let's dyne together:

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: With all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Goe then: Farewell good Angelo,
Commend me to your friend.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Doe not dissemble Franc, mine eyes are quicker
Then such observers, that do ground their faith
Upon one smile or teare; y'ar much alterd,
And are as empty of those Excellencies
That were companions to you; I meane mirth
And free disposure of your blood and Spirit,
As you were borne a mourner.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: How I pre'thee?
For I perceive no such change in my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Clora.
verse: Come, come, this is not wise, nor provident
To halt before a Cripple: If you love
Be liberall to your friend, and let her know it,
I see the way you run, and know how tedious
'Twill prove without a true companion.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Sure thou wouldst have me love.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Yes marry would I
I should not please ye else.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: And who for gods sake?
For I assure my selfe, I know not yet:
And pre'thee Clora, since thou'lt have it so
That I must love, and doe I know not what:
Let him behold a pretty handsome fellow,
And young, and if he be a little valiant
Twill be the better; and a little wise
And faith a little honest.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Well I will sound ye yet for all your craft.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Heigh ho! I'le love no more.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Then one; and him
You shall love Franck.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Which him? thou art so wise
People will take thee shortly for a witch:
But prethee tell me Clora, if I were
So mad as thou wouldst make me, what kind of man
Wouldst thou imagine him?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Faith some pretty fellow?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: With a cleane strength, that cracks a cudgell well
And dances at a wake, and plaies at nine holes.
O God what pretty commendations thou hast given him'
Faith if were in love, as I thanke God
I doe not thinke I am; this short Epistle
Before my love would make me burne the legend.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: You are too wilde, I meane some gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: So doe not I, till I can know'em wiser:
Some Gentleman, no Clora, till some Gentleman
Keepe some land, and fewer whores beleeve me
Ile keepe no love for him, I doe not long
To goe a foot yet, and solicite causes.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: What thinke you then of an adventurer?
I meane some wealthy Merchant.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Let him venture
In some decaid Crare of his owne: he shall not
Rig me out, that's the short on't; out upon't:
What young thing of my yeares would endure
To have her husband in another Country
Within a moneth after she is married
Chopping for rotten Raysons, and lye pining
At home under the mercy of his fore-man? no,
Though they be wealthy, and indifferent wise
I doe not see that I am bound to love'em.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: I see ya're hard to please; yet I will please ye.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Faith not so hard neither, if considered;
What woman may deserve as? she is worthy:
But why do we bestow our ttme so idely?
Preethee let us entertaine some other talke,
This is as sickly to me as faint weather.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Now I believe I shall content you Francke,
What thinke you of a Courtier?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Faith so ill,
That if I should be full, and speake but truth,
'Twold shew as if I wanted charity,
Prethee good wench let me not raile upon 'em,
Yet I have an excellent stomach, and must do it;
I have no mercie of these infidels;
Since I am put in minde on't, good beare with me,
Can no man fit you? I will finde him out.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: This somer fruite, that you call Courtier,
While you continue cold and frosty to him
Hangs fast, and may be found: but when youfling
Too full a heate of your affections —
Upon his roote and make him ripe too soone,
Youl' finde him rotten 'ith the handling;
His oathes and affections are all one
With his apparrell, things to set him off,
He has as many Mistrisses, as Faithes,
And all appocripha; his true beliefe
Is onely in a private Surgeon,
And for my single selfe, I'de sooner venture—
A new conversion of the Jndies,
Then to make Courtiers, able men or honest.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I do believe you love no Courtier,
And by my troth to ghesse you into love
With any I can thinke of; is beyond
Either your will, or my imagination.
And yet I am sure y'ar caught: and I will know him,
Ther's none left now worthy the thinking of;
Unles it be a Souldier, and I am sure,
I would ever blesse my selfe from such a fellow.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Why preethee?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Out upon 'em firelockes,
They are nothing 'ith world, but Buff and Scarlet,
Tough unhewne peeces, to hack swords upon;
I had as liev be courted by a Cannon,
As one of those.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Thou art too malitious,
Upon my faith me thinks they're worthy men.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Say ye so? I'le pull ye on a little further.
VVhat worth can be in those men, whose profession
Is nothing ith' world but drinke and damn me,
Out of whose violence they are possest
VVith legions of unwholsome whores and quarrels;
I am of that opinion, and will dye in't,
There is no understanding, nor can be
In a soust Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Now 'tis ignorance
I easily perceive that thus provokes thee,
And not the love of truth; I'le lay my life
If God had made thee man, thou hadst been a coward.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: If to be valiant, be to be a Souldier; I'le tel ye true,
I had rather be a Coward, I am sure with lesse sin.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: This heresie must be look'd too in time: for if it spread
'Twill grow too pestilent; were I a Scholler
I would so hamper thee for thy opinion,
That ere I left, I would write thee out of credit
VVith all the world, and make thee not beleev'd
Even in indifferent things; that I would leave thee
A reprobate out of the state of honour.
By all good things, thou hast flung aspersions
So like a foole (for I am angry with thee)
Upon a sort of men; (that let me tell thee
Thy mothers mother would have been a Saint
Had she conceiv'd a Souldier) they are people
(I may commend 'em, while I speake but truth)
Of all the old world, only left to keepe
Man as he was, valiant and vertuous:
They are the modell of those men, whose honours
VVe heave our hands at when we heare recited.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: They are, and I have all I sought for, 'tis a souldier
You love, hide it no longer; you have betray'd your selfe;
Come, I have found your way of commendations,
And what I said, was but to pull it from ye.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: 'Twas pretty, are you grown so cunning, Clora?
I grant I love a souldier; But what souldier
VVill be a new taske to ye? But all this
I doe imagine was but laid to draw me
Out of my melancholy.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I will have the man
Ere I forsake ye.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I must to my chamber.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: May not I goe along?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Yes, but good wench
Move me no more with these fond questions,
They worke like Rubarb with me.

speeches.speaker: Glo.
verse: VVell, I will not.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: How now? who was that you staid to speak withal.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: The old man forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: VVhat old man?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
prose: The poor old man that uses to come hither he that you call Father.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Have you dispatched him?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: No; he would faine speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Wilt thou never learn more manners, then to draw in such
Needy rascalls to disquiet me? goe, answer him I wil
Not be at leisure.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: He will needs speak with you; and good old man he weeps so,
That by my troth I have not the heart to deny him, pray let you are not in love
Him speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Lord how tender stomach'd you are grown of late?
With him, are ye; if ye be, strike up the match; you shal have
Three, l. & a paire of blankets; will ye goe answer him?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Pray let him speak with you, he wil not away else.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Well, let him in then if there be no remedy; I thank God I am
Able to abuse him, i shal nere come cleer else of him.
Now Sr. what is your business? pray be short; for I have other
Matters of more moment to call me from ye.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: If you but looke upon me like a daughter
And keepe that love about ye that makes good
A Fathers hope, you'l quickly finde my businesse,
And what I would say to you, and before
I aske, will be a giver: say that sleepe,
I meane that love, or be but num'd within ye,
The nature of my want is such a searcher,
And of so mighty power, that where he findes
This dead forgetfulnesse, it works so strongly,
That if the least heate of a childes affection
Remaine unperish'd, like another nature,
It makes all new againe; pray do not scorne me,
Nor seeme to make your selfe a greater businesse
Then my relieving.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: If you were not old
I should laugh at ye; what a vengeance ailes ye
To be so childish to imagine me
A founder of old fellows? make him drinke wench,
And if there be any cold meate in the Buttery,
Give him some broken bread and that, and rid him.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Is this a childs love? or a recompence
Fit for a fathers care? O Lelia,
Had I been thus unkind, thou hadst not been;
Or like me miserable: But 'tis impossible
Nature should dye so utterly within thee,
And loose her promises; thou art one of those
She set her stamp more excellently on,
Then common people, as fore-telling thee
A generall example of her goodnesse;
Or say she could lye, yet religion
(For love to parents is religious)
Would leade thee right againe: Looke well upon me
I am the roote that gave thee nourishment,
And made thee spring faire, do not let me perish
Now I am old and saplesse.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: As I live
I like ye far worse now ye grow thus holy,
I grant you are my father; am I therefore
Bound to consume my selfe and be a begger
Still in relieving you? I doe not feele
Any such mad compassion yet within me.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I gave up all my state to make yours thus.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: 'Twas as ye ought to do, and now ye cry for't
As children do for babies backe againe.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: How wouldst thou have me live?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I would not have ye,
Nor know no reason Fathers should desire
To live, and be a trouble, when children
Are able to inherit, let them dye,
'Tis sit, and lookt for, that they should do so.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Is this your comfort?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: All that I feele yet.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I will not curse thee.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: If you do I care not.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Pray you give me leave to weep

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Why pray take leave,
If it be for your ease.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Thy mother dyed,
Sweet peace be with her, in a happy time.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: She did Sir, as she ought to do, would you
Would take the paines to follow; what should you
Or any old man do wearing away
In this world with diseases, and desire
Only to live to make their children scourge-sticks,
And hoord up mill-money? me thinks a marble
Lyes quieter upon an old mans head
Then a cold fit a'th palsey.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: O good God!
To what an impudence thou wretched woman,
Ha^ thou begot thy selfe againe! well, justice
Will punish disobedience.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You mistake Sir;
Twill punish beggers, fye for shame go worke
Or serve, you are grave enough to be a Porter
In some good man of worships house, and give
Sententious answers to the commers in,
A pretty place; or be of some good Consort,
You had a pleasant touch 'ath Cithron once,
If idelnesse have not bereft you of it:
Be any thing but old, and beggarly,
Two sinnes that ever do out grow compassion;
If I might see you offer at a course
That were a likely one, and shew'd some proffit,
I would not stick for ten groates, or a noble.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Did I beget this woman?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Nay, I know not:
And 'till I know, I will not thanke you for't;
How ever, he that got me had the pleasure,
And that me thinkes, is a reward sufficient.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I am so strangly stroken with amazement,
I know not where I am, nor what I am.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You had best take fresh aire some where else, 'twill bring ye
Out of your trance the sooner.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Is all this
As you meane Lelia?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Yes believe me is it,
For yet I cannot thinke you are so foolish,
As to imagine you are young enough
To be my heire, or I so old to make
A Nurse at these yeares for you, and attend
While you sup up my State in penny pots
Of Malmsey: when I am excellent at Cawdles,
And Cullices. and have enough spare gold
To boyle away, you shall be welcome to me;
'Till when I'de have you be as merry Sir
As you can make your selfe with that you have,
And leave to trouble me with these relations;
Of what you have beene to me, or you are,
For as I heare them, so I loose them; this
For ought I know yet, is me resolution.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Well God be with thee, for I feare thy end
Will be a strange example.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Fare ye well Sir;
Now would some poore tender harted foole have wept,
Relented, and have been undone: such children
I thanke my understanding I hate truely,
For by my troth I had rather see their teares;
Then feele their pitties: my desires and ends
Are all the kindred that I have, and friends.
Is he departed?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Yes, but heer's another.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Not of his tribe I hope; bring me no more
I would wish you such as he is, If thou seest
They looke like men of worth, and state, and carry
Ballast of both sides like tall Gentlemen
Admit 'em, but no snakes to poyson us
With poverty; wench you must learne a wise rule,
Looke not upon the youthes of men, and making,
How they discend in blood, nor let their tongues
Though they strike sodainly, and sweet as musique
Corrupt thy fancy: see, and say them faire too,
But ever keep thy selfe without their distance:
Unlesse the love thou swallows be a pill,
Gilded to hide the bitternesse it brings,
Then fall on without feare wench, yet so wisely
That one encounter cloy him not; nor promise
His love hath made thee more his, then his moneyes;
Learne this and thrive,
Then let thine honour ever,
(For that's the last rule) be so stood upon,
That men may fairely see
'Tis want of meanes, not vertue makes thee fall;
And if you weepe 'twill be a great deale better,
And draw on more compassion, which includes
A greater tendernesse of love and bounty;
This is enough at once, digest it well:
Go let him in wench, if he promise proffit,
Not else.
O you are welcome my faire servant,
Upon my troth I have been longing for ye.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: This, by her rule should be a liberall man,
I see the best on's may learne every day.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Ther's none come with you.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You do the wiser,
For some that have been here (I name no man)
Out of their malice, more then truth, have done me
Some few ill offices.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: How, sweete?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Nay nothing,
Onely have talk't a little wildely of me;
As their unruly youth directed 'em:
Which though they bite me not, I would have wish'd
Had light upon some other that deserv'd 'em.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Though she deserve this of the loosest tongue,
(Which makes my sinne the more) I must not see it;
Such is my misery: I would I knew him.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: No, no, let him go,
He is not worth your anger: I must chide you
For being such a stranger to your Mistris,
Why would you be so, Servant?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I should chide,
If chiding would worke any thing upon you:
For being such a stranger to your Servant,
I meane to his desires: when my deare Mistris,
Shall I be made a happy man?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Fy Servant
What do you meane, unhand me, or by heav'n,
I shall be very angry, this is rudenesse.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: 'Twas but a kisse or two, that thus offends you

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: 'Twas more I thinke then you have warrant for.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I am sorry I deserv'd no more.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You may,
But not this rough way Servant: we are tender,
And ought in all to be respected so;
If I had been your horse, or whore, you might
Back me with this intemperance; I thought
You had lov'd as worthy men, whose faire affections
Seeke pleasures warranted, not puld by violence,
Do so no more.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I hope you are not angry?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I should be with another man, I am sure,
That durst appeare but halfe thus violent.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I did not meane to ravish ye

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You couldot.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: You are so willing—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Me thinkes this shadow,
If you had so much shame as fits a woman:
At least of your way, Mistris, long ere this
Had been lay'd of to me that understand ye.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: That understand me? Sir ye understand,
Nor shall no more of me then modesty,
Will without feare deliver to a stranger;
You understand I am honest; else I tell yee
(Though you were better far then Iulio)
You, and your understanding are two fooles,
But were we Saints, thus we are still rewarded.
I see that woman had a pretty catch on't,
That had made you the Master of a kindnesses,
She durst not answer openly; o me!
How easily we women may be cozen'd?
I tooke this Iulio as I have a faith,
(This young dissembler with the sober vizard)
For the most modest temper'd Gentleman,
The coolest, quietest, and best companion;
For such an one I could have wish'd a woman.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: You have wish'd me ill enough a conscience,
Make me no worse for shame: I see the more
I worke by way of service to obtaine ye
You worke the more upon me. Tell me truely
(While I am able to believe a woman,
For if you use me thus, that faith will perish)
What is your end, and whether will you pull me?
Tell me, but tell me that I may not start at,
And have a cause to curse ye.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Blesse me goodnesse!
To curse me did you say Sir? let it be
For too much loving you then, such a curse
Kill me withall and I shall be a Martyr;
You have found a new way to reward my doting,
And I confesse a fit one for my folly,
For you your selfe if you have good within ye,
And dare be Master of it, know how deadly
This hart has held you ever; oh good God!
That I had never seene that false mans eyes,
That dare reward me thus with feares and curses,
Nor never heard the sweetnesse of that tongue,
That will when this is knowne, yet cozen women:
Curse me good Iulio, curse me bitterly,
I do deserve it for my confidence,
And I beseech thee, if thou hast a goodnesse
Of power yet in thee to confirme thy wishes,
Curse me to earth; for what should I do here
Like a decaying flower, still withering
Under his bitter wordes, whose kindly heate
Should give my poore hart life? No, curse me Iulio,
Thou canst not do me such a benefit
As that, and well done, that the heav'ns may heare it.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Oh faire teares were you but as chast, as subtill,
Like Bones of Saints, ye would worke miracles;
What were these women to a man that knew not
The thousand, thousand wayes of their deceiving?
What riches had he found? Oh he would thinke
Himselfe still dreaming of a blessednesse,
That like continuall spring should flourish ever.
For if she were as good as she is seeming,
Or like an Eagle could renew her vertues,
Nature had made another world of sweetnesse;
Be not so greiv'd sweet Mistris, what I sed
You do, or should know, was but passion;
Pray wipe your eyes and kisse me; take these trifles,
And weare them for me, which are onely rich
When you will put them on; Indeed I love ye,
Beshrew my sicke hart, if I grieve not for ye.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Will you dissemble still? I am a foole,
And you may easily rule me, if you flatter,
The sin will be your owne.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: You know I doe not.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: And shall I be so childish once againe,
After my late experience of your spight
To credit you? you doe not know how deepe
(Or if you did, you would be kinder to me,)
This bitternesse of yours have strooke my heart.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I pray no more.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Thus you would doe I warrant,
If I were married to you.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Married to me?
Is that your end?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Yes, Is not that the best end,
And as all hold, the noblest way of love?
Why doe you looke so strange Sir? doe not you
Desire it should be so?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Stay.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Answer me.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Farwell.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I, are you there? are all these teares lost then?
Am I so overtaken by a foole
In my best daies and tricks? my wise fellow
Ile make you smart for't as I am a woman,
And if thou beest not timber, yet Ile warme thee:
And is he gon?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: He's not so lightly strooke
To be recovered with a base repentance,
I should be sorry then: Fortune I pre'thee
Give me this man but once more in my armes,
And if I loose him, women have no charmes.

speeches.speaker: Iaco.
verse: SEigneur, What thinke you of this sound of warrs?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: As onely of a sound; they that intend
To doe are like deepe waters that run quietly
Leaving no face of what they were behind 'em,
This rumour is too common and too loude
To carry truth.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Shall we never live to see
Men looke like men againe,
Upon a march?
This cold dull rusty peace makes us appeare
Like empty Pictures, onely the faint shadowes
Of what we should be:
Would to God my Mother
Had given but halfe her will to my begetting
And made me woman, to sit still and sing,
Or be sicke when I list, or any thing
That is too idle for a man to thinke of:
Would I had been a whore 'thad been a course
Certaine, and of my conscience of more gaine
Then two commands, as I would handle it:
Faith I could wish I had been any thing
Rather then what I am, a Soldier
A Carriere, or a Cobler, when I knew
What 'twas to weare a Sword first; for their trades
Are and shall be a constant way of life,
While men send cheeses up, or weare out buskins.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Thou art a little too impatient,
And mak'st thy anger a far more vexation
Then the not having warrs: I am a Soldier
Which is my whole Inheritance, yet I
Though I could wish a breach with all the world
If not dishonourable, I am not so malitious,
To curse the faire peace of my Mother Countrey;
But thou want'st money; and the first supply
Will bury these thoughts in thee.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Pox a peace.
It fills the Kingdome full of holydayes,
And onely feedes the wants of whores and pipers;
And make the idle drunken Rogues, get Spinsters.
'Tis true I may want money, and no litle,
And almost cloathes too: of which if I had both
In full abundance: yet against all peace,
That brings up mischiefe thicker then a showre,
I would speake louder then a Lawyer;
By heaven it is the surfet of all youth,
That makes the toughnesse, and the strength of nations
Melt into women. 'Tis an ease that broodes
Theeves, and basterds onely.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: This is more,
(Though it be true) then we ought to lay open,
And seasons onely of an indiscretion,
Believe me Captaine such distemper'd spirits
Once out of motion, though they be proofe valiant,
If they appeare thus violent and fierie,
Breed but their owne disgraces; and are nearer
Doubt, and suspect in Princes, then rewardes.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: 'Tis well they can be neere 'em any way,
But call you those true spirits, ill affected
That whil'st the warres were, serv'd like walls and ribs,
To girdle in the Kingdome?
And now falne
Through a faint peace into affliction,
Speake but their miseryes? come, come, Fabritio
You may pretend what patience ye please,
And seeme to yoake your wants like passions;
But while I know thou art a Souldier,
And a deserver, and no other harvest
But what thy Sword reapes for thee to come in,
You shall be pleas'd to give me leave to tell ye,
You wish a Devill of this musty peace:
To which prayer,
As one that's bound in conscience, and all
That love our trade, I cry, Amen.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Prethee no more, we shall live well enough,
There's wayes enough besides the warrs to men
That are not loggs, and lye still for the handes
Of others to remove 'em.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: You may thrive Sir,
Thou art young and handsome yet, and well enough
To please a widdow: thou canst sing, and tell
These foolish love-tales; and indite a little,
And if need be, compile, a pretty matter
And dedicate it to the honourable,
Which may a waken his compassion,
To make ye Clarke a'th kitchen, and at length
Come to be married to my Ladyes woman,
After she's crack't 'ith ring.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: 'Tis very well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: But what dost thou thinke shall become of me,
With all my imperfections? let me dye
If I thinke I shall ever reach above
A forlorne Tapster, or some frothy fellow,
That stincks of stale beere.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Captaine Jacamo,
Why should you thinke so hardly of your vertues?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: What vertues? by this light I have no vertue,
But downe right buffeting: what can my face
That is no better then a ragged Map now
Of where I have marcht and traveled profit me?
Unlesse it be for Ladyes to abuse, and say
'Twas spoil'd for want of a Bongrace when I was young,
And now 'twill make a true prognostication
Of what man must be? Tell me of a fellow
That can mend noses, and complaine,
So tall a souldier should want teeth to his stomach?
And how it was great pitty, that it was,
That he that made my body, was so busied
He could not stay to make my leggs too? but was driven
To clap a paire of cat-skins to my knees, for which
I am indebted to two Schoole-boyes? this
Must follow necessary.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Ther's no such matter.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Then for my morals, and those hidden pieces,
That art bestowes upon me, they are such
That when they come to light: I am sure will shame me.
For I can neither write, nor read, nor speake
That any man shall hope to proffet by me,
And for my Languages, they are so many
That put them altogether, they will scarce
Serve to beg single beere in: the plaine truth is,
I love a Souldier, and can lead him on,
And if he fight well I dare make him drunk:
This is my vertue, and if this will do
I'le scramble yet amongst 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: 'Tis your way
To be thus pleasant still, but feare not man
For though the warrs fail, we shall screw our selves
Into some course of life yet.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Good Fabritio,
Have a quick eye upon me, for I feare
This peace will make me something that I love not;
For by my troth though I am plaine and dudgion,
I would not be an Asse: and to sell parcels,
I can as soone be hang'd; preethee bestowe me
And speake some little good, though I deserve not.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Come wee'l consider more: stay, this
Should be another winde-fall of the warrs.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: He lookes indeed like an old tater'd Colours,
That every winde would borrow from the Staffe;
These are the hopes we have for all our hurts:
They have not cast his tongue too.

speeches.speaker: Father.
verse: They that say
Hope never leaves a wretched man that seekes her,
I thinke are either patient fooles, or lyers,
I am sure I finde it so, for I am master'd,
With such a misery and griefe together
That that stay'd Anchor men lay hold upon
In all their needs, is to me lead that bowes,
Or breakes, with every strong sea of my sorrowes.
I could now question heaven, (were it well
To looke into their justice) why those faultes,
Those heavy sinnes, other provoke 'em with
Should be rewarded on the heads of us,
That hold the least alliance to their vices?
But this would be too curious; for I see
Our suffering, not disputing, is the end,
Reveal'd to us of all these miseryes.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Twenty such holy Hermits in a Campe,
Would make 'em all Carthusians, I'le be hang'd
If hee know what a whore is: or a health,
Or have a nature liable to learne,
Or so much honest nurture to be drunke.
I do not thinke he has the spleene to sweare
A greater oath then Sempsters utter Sockes with,
S'pur him a question.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: They are strangers both
To me, as I to them I hope: I would not have
Me and my shame together known by any,
I'le rather lye my selfe unto another.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I need not aske you Sir your Countrey,
I heare you speake this tongue: pray what more are ye?
Or have you been? if it be not offensive
To urge ye so far, misery in your yeares,
Gives every thing a tongue to question it.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Sir, though I could be pleas'd to make my ills
Only mine owne, for grieving other men,
Yet to so faire and courteous a demander
That promises compassion, at worst, pity,
I will relate a little of my story.
I am a Gentleman, however thus
Poore and unhappy; which beleeve me sir
Was not borne with me: for I well have tri'd
Both the extreams of fortune; and have found
Both dangerous: my younger yeares provok'd me,
Feeling in what an case I slept at home,
Which to all stirring spirits is a sicknesse,
To see far Countreyes, and observe their Customes.
I did so; and I travelld till that course
Stor'd me with language, and some few slight manners,
Scarce worth my money; when an ich possest me
Of making armes my active end of travell.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: But did you so?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I did; and twenty winters
I wore the Christian Cause upon my sword
Against his enemies, at Buda siege
Full many a cold night have I lodg'd in armour
When all was frozen in me but mine honour:
And many a day, when both the Sun and Canon
Strove, who should most destroy us: have I stood
Malld up in steele, when my rough sinews shrunke,
And this parch'd body ready to consume
As soone to ashes, as the pike I bore:
Want has been to me as another nature,
Which makes me with this patience still professe it;
And if a Souldier may without vaine-glory
Tell what h'as done, beleeve me Gentlemen
I could turne over annals of my dangers:
With this poor weaknesse have I mann'd a breach,
And made it firme with so much blood, that all
I had to bring me off alive was anger.
Thrice was I made a slave, and thrice redeem'd
At price of all I had; The miseries
Of which times, if I had a heart to tell,
Would make ye weep like children; But I'le spare ye

speeches.speaker: Ja
verse: Fabricio, we two have been souldiers
Above these fourteen yeares, yet a my conscience
All we have seen, compar'd to his experience
Has been but cudgel-play, or Cock-fighting.
By all the faith I have in armes, I reverence
The very poverty of this brave fellow:
Which were enough it selfe, and his to strengthen
The weakest towne against halfe Christendome.
I was never so asham'd of service
In all my life before, now I consider
What I have done; and yet the rogues would sweare
I was a valiant fellow; I do finde
The greatest danger I have brought my life through,
Now I have heard this worthy, was no more
Then stealing of a May-pole, or at worst,
Fighting at single billet with a Barge-man.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I do believe him Jacamo.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Beleeve him?
I have no faith within me, if I doe not.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I see they are souldiers?
And if we may judge by affections
Brave and deserving men: how they are stir'd
But with a meer relation of what may be?
Since I have wonne beliefe, and am not known,
Forgive me honour, i'le make use of thee.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Sir would I were a man, or great, or able
To looke with liberall eyes upon your vertue.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Let's give him all we have, and leave off prating:
Here Souldier, there's even five months pay: be merry,
And get thee handsome cloths.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: What meane you Jacamo?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Ye are a foole.
The very story's worth a hundred pound.
Give him more money.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Gentlemen, I know not
How I am able to deserve this blessing.
But if I live to see faire dayes againe,
Something i'le doe in honour of your goodnesse,
That shall shew thankfulnesse, if not desert.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: If you please Sir, till we procure ye place,
To eate with us, or weare such honest garments
As our poor meanes can reach to, you shall be
A welcome man; to say more, were to feede ye
Only with words; we honour what y'ave been,
For we are souldiers, though not neere the worth
You spake of lately.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I do ghesse ye so,
And knew, unlesse he were a souldier,
He could not find the way to know my wants.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: But me thinks all this while y'are too temperate;
Do you not tell men sometimes of their dulnesse
When you are grip't, as now you are with need?
I do, and let them know those silkes they weare
The Warre weaves for 'em: and the bread they eate
We sow, and reape again to feed their hunger:
I tell them boldly, they are masters of
Nothing but what we fight for: their faire women
Lye playing in their armes, whilst we like Lares
Defend their pleasures: I am angry too,
And often raile at these forgetfull great men
That suffer us to sue for what we ought
To have flung on us, ere we aske.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I have
Too often told my griefes that way, when all
I reapt, was rudenesse of behaviour;
In their opinions men of Warre that thrive,
Must thank 'em when they raile: and wait to live.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Come Sir, I see your wants need more relieving,
Then looking what they are: pray goe with us.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I thanke you Gentlemen: since you are pleas'd
To do a benefit, I dare not crosse it,
And what my service or endeavours may
Stand you in need, you shall command, not pray.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
prose: So you shall us; i'le to the Taylors with you bodily

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Well, if this be true; I'le believe a woman
When I have nothing else to do.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: 'Tis certaine; if there be a way of truth,
In blushes, smiles, and commendatious;
For by this light, have heard her praise you fellow
In such a pitch, as if sh'ad studied
To croude the worths of all men into him,
And I imagine these are seldome us'd
Without their speciall ends, and by a maide
Of her desires and youth.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: It may be so.
She's free as you or I am, and may have
By that prerogative, a liberall choise
In the bestowing of her love.

speeches.speaker: Lod
verse: Bestowing?
If it be so, she has bestowed her selfe
Upon a trim youth: Piso, what do you call him?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Why, Captain Jacamo.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: O Captaine Jack-boy,
That is the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I thinke he be
A Gentleman at worst.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: So think I too,
Would he would mend Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And a tall one too.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Yes of his teeth; for of my faith I thinke
They are sharper then his sword, and dare do more
If the Beuffe meet him fairely.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Very well.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Now do I wonder what she meanes to doe
When she has married him.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Why well enough,
Traile his pike under him, and be a Gentlewoman
Of the brave Captaines company.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Doe you heare me?
This woman is my sister, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I am glad she is none of mine: but Fredericke,
Thou art not such a foole sure to be angry
Unlesse it be with her; We are thy friends man.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I thinke ye are.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Yes faith, and do but tell thee
How shee will utterly orethrow her credit,
If she continue gracing of this pot-gun.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: I thinke she was bewitcht, or mad, or blinde,
She would never have taken such a scar-crow else
Into protection: of my life he lookes
Of a more rusty swarth complexion
Then an old arming doublet.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I would send
His face to the Cutlers then, and have it sanguin'd,
'Twill looke a great deale sweeter; then his nose
I would have shorter, and my reason is,
His face will be ill mounted else.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: For his body,
I will not be my own Judge, least I seeme
A railer, but let others look upon't,
And if they finde it any other thing
Then a trunke-seller, to send wines downe in,
Or a long walking-bottle, I'le be hang'd for't:
His hide, (for sure he is a beast) is ranker
