Then the Muscovy leather: and grain'd like it.
And by all likeli-hoods he was begotten
Between a stubborn paire of winter boots.
His body goes with straps, he is so churlish.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Hee's poor and beggerly besides all this:
And of a nature farre uncapable
Of any benefit: for his manners cannot
Shew him a way to thanke a man that does one,
He's so uncivill: you may do a part
Worthy a brother, to perswade your sister
From her undoing: if she prove so foolish
To marry this cast Captaine, looke to finde her
Within a month, where you, or any good man
Would blush to know her: selling cheese and prunes,
And retayl'd bottle ale: I grieve to think
Because I lov'd her, what a march this Captaine
Will set her into.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You are both, beleeve me,
Two arrant Knaves; and were it not for taking
So just an execution from his hands
You have beli'd thus, I would swaddle ye,
Till I could draw off both your skins like scaberds.
That man that you wrong'd thus, though to me
He be a stranger, yet I know, so worthy,
However low in fortune, that his worst parts,
The very wearing of his cloths, would make
Two better Gentlemen then you dare be,
For there is vertue in his outward things.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Belike you love him then.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes marry do I.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: And will be angry for him.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: If you talke
Or pull your face into a stich againe,
As I love truth I shall be very angry.
Do not I know thee, though thou hast some land
To set thee out thus among Gentlemen,
To be a prating and vain-glorious asse?
I do not wrong thee now, for I speake truth.
Doe not I know thou hast been a cudgel'd coward,
That has no cure for shame but cloath of silver?
And thinkst the wearing of a gawdy suite
Hides all disgraces?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I understand you not, you hurt not me
Your anger flies so wide.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Signeur Frederick,
You much mistake this Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: If you would please to be lesse angry,
I would tell you how.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You had better study Sir
How to excuse your selfe if ye be able,
Or I shall tell you once againe.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Not me Sir;
For I protest what I have said, was only
To make you understand your sisters danger.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: He might if it pleas'd him conceive it so.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I might if it pleas'd me stand still and heare
My sister made a may-game, might I not?
And give allowance to your liberall jests
Upon his person, whose least anger would
Consume a legion of such wretched people,
That have no more to justifie their actions
But their tongues ends? that dare lye every way
As a mill grindes? From this houre I renounce
All part of fellowship that may hereafter
Make me take knowledge of ye, but for Knaves;
And take heed, as ye love whole skins, and coxcombs,
How, and to whom ye prate thus; for this time
I care not if I spare ye: do not shake,
I will not beat ye, though ye doe deserve it
Richly.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: This is a strange course Fredericke;
But sure you do not, or you would not know us,
Beate us?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: 'Tis somewhat low Sir, to a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I'le speak but few words, but I'le make 'em truths;
Get you gone both, and quickly, without murmuring,
Or looking big: and yet before you goe
I will have this confest, and seriously,
That you two are two rascalls.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Two Rascals.
Come speake it from your hearts, or by this light
My sword shall flye among ye; answer me,
And to the point directly.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: You shall have
Your will for this time: since we see y'are grown
So far untemperate; Let it be so Sir
In your opinion.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Do not mince the matter,
But speake the words plaine; and you Lodovick
That stand so tally on your reputation,
You shall be he shall speake it.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: This is pretty,

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Let me not stay upon't.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Well we are rascalls,
Yes Piso, we are rascals.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Get ye gone now, not a word more, y'are rascals.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: That should be Fredericke.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: 'Tis he: Fredericke?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: A friend Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: It is so, by the voyce
I have sought you Gentlemen, and since I have found you,
So neare our house, I'le force ye stay a while,
I pray let it be so.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: It is too late,
Wee'l come and dine to morrow with your sister,
And do our services.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Who were those with you?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: We met two came from hence:
Two idle fellows,
That you shall beate hereafter, and I'le tell ye
Some fitter time a cause sufficient for it.

speeches.speaker: Fabr.
verse: But Fredericke, tell me truly; do you thinke
Shee can affect my friend?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No certainer
Then when I speake of him, or any other,
She entertaines it with as much desire
As others do their recreations.

speeches.speaker: Fabr.
verse: Let not him have this light by any meanes;
He will but thinke he's mockt, and so grow angry,
Even to a quarrell: he's so much distrustfull
Of all that take occasion to commend him—
Women especially: for which he shuns
All conversation with 'em, and beleeves
He can be but a mirth to all their Sex.
Whence is this musique?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: From my sisters chamber.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: The touch is excellent' let's be attentive.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Harke, are the waights abroad?

speeches.speaker: Fabr.
verse: Be softer prethee,
'Tis private musicke.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: What a dyn it makes?
I had rather hear a Jews-trump then these Lutes,
They crye like Schoole-boyes.

speeches.speaker: Fabr.
verse: Prethee Jacamo.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Well I heare, or sleepe, I care not whether.
TEll me dearest what is Love?
'Tis a lightning from above,
'Tis an arrow, 'tis a fire,
'Tis a boy they call Desire.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: 'Tis a grave,
Gapes to have
Those poore fooles that long to prove.
Tell me more, are women true?
Yes, some are, and some as you.
Some are willing, some are strange,
Since you men first taught to change.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: And till troth
Be in both,
All shall love, to love anew.
Tell me more yet, can they grieve?
Yes, and sicken sore, but live:
And be wise, and delay,
When you men are as wise as they.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: Then I see
Faith will be,
Never till they both beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Franc.
verse: Clora, come hither; who are these below there?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: There.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Ha? I should know their shapes
Though it be darkish; there are both our brothers,
What should they make thus late here?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: What's the tother?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: What tother?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: He that lyes along there.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: O, I see him
As if he had a branch of some great Petigree
Grew out on's belly.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: That should be,
If I have any knowledge in proportion.—

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: They see us.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis no matter.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: VVhat a log
Is this, to sleep such musique out?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No more let's heare 'em.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: If I have any knowledge in proportion,
The Captaine Jacamo, those are his legs
Upon my conscience.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: By my faith, and neate ones.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: You mean the boots, I thinke they are neate by nature,

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: As thou art knavish, would I saw his face!

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: 'Twould scare you in the dark.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: A worse then that
Has never scar'd you Clora to my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Clora.
verse: 'Tis true, for I never have seen a worse;
Nor while I say my prayers heartily,
I hope I shall not.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: VVell, I am no tell tale:
But is it not great pitty, tell me Clora,
That such a brave deserving Gentleman
As every one delivers this to be,
Should have no more respect, and worth flung on him
By able men? VVere I one of these great ones,
Such vertues should not sleep thus.

speeches.speaker: Clora.
verse: VVere he greater
He would sleep more I thinke: I'le waken him.

speeches.speaker: Frank.
verse: Away ye foole.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Is he not dead already, and they two taking order
About his Blacks? me thinks they are very busie,
A fine cleane coarse he is: I would have him buried
Even as he lyes, crosse legg'd, like one o'th Templers
(If his west-phaly gammons will hold crossing)
And on his brest, a buckler with a pike in't,
In which I would have some, learned Cutler
Compile an Epitaph, and at his feete
A musquet, with this word upon a Labell
VVhich from the cocks mouth thus should be delivered,
I have discharg'd the office of a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Frank.
verse: VVell, if thy Father were a Souldier
Thus thou wouldst use him.

speeches.speaker: Clora.
verse: Such a Souldier,
I would indeed.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: If he heare this, not all
The power of man could keep him from the windowes
^ill they were downe and all the dores brok open:
For Gods sake make her cooler: I dare not venture
To bring him else: I know he will goe to buffetts
Within five words with her, if she holds this spirit;
Let's waken him, and away, we shall heare worse else.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Well if I be not even with thee Clora
L^t m^ be hang'd for this: I know thou dost it
Onely to anger me, and purge your witt
Which would breake out else.

speeches.speaker: Clora.
verse: I have found ye,
Ile be no more crosse, bid'em good night

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: No, no, they shall not know, we have seen'em;
Shut the window.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Will you get up Sir?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Have you paid the Fidlers?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: You are not left to doe it: Fie upon thee,
Hast thou forsworne manners?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Yes unlesse
They would let me eate my meate without long graces
Or drinke without a preface to the pledger;
Oft will it please you, shall I be so bold sir
Let me remember your good bedfellow,
And lye and kisse my hand unto my Mistris
As often as an Ape does for an Aple;
These are meere Schismes in Soldiers; wher's my friend?
These are to us as bitter as purgations,
We love that generall freedome we are bred to;
Hang these faint fooleries, they smell of peace,
Doe they not friend?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Faith Sir to me they are
As things indifferent, yet I use'em not,
Or if I did, they would not prick my conscience.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Come, shall we goe? 'tis late.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Yes any whether,
But no more Musick, it has made me dull.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Faith any thing but drinking disturbs thee Jacomo
Wee'l ev'n to bed.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Content.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Thou wilt dreame of wenches.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I never thinke of any I thanke God
But when I am drunke, and then tis but to cast
A cheape way how they may be all destroyd
Like vermine; let's away I am very sleepy.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: I, thou art ever so, or angry, come.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I Will but see her once more Angilo
That I may hate her more, and then I am
My selfe againe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I would not have thee tempt lust,
Tis away dangerous, and will deceive thee
Hadst thou the constancy of all men in thee.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Having her sins before me, I dare see her
Were she as catching as the plague, and deadly,
And tell her she is fouler then all those
And far more pestilent, if not repentant,
And like a stronge man, chide her well, and leave her.

speeches.speaker: Arg.
verse: 'Tis easily said, of what complexion is she?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Make but a curious frame unto thy selfe
As thou wouldst shape an Angell in thy thought
Such as the Poets, when their fancies sweat
Imagine Iuno is, or faire eyde Pallas
And one more excellent, then all those figures
Shalt thou finde her; shees browne, but of a sweetnes,
(If such a poore word may expresse her beauty)
Beleeve me Angilo would doe more mischiefe
With a forc't smile, then twenty thousand Cupids
With their love quivers, full of Ladies eyes,
And twice as many flames, could fling upon us.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Of what age is she?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: As a Rose at fairest,
Neither a bud, nor blown, but such a one,
Were there a Hercules to get againe
With all his glory, or one more then he
The god would choose out mongst a race of women
To make a mother of; she is outwardly
All that bewitches sense; all that entises,
Nor is it in our vertue to uncharme it.
And when she speakes, oh Angilo, then musick
(Such as old Orpheus made, that gave a soule
To aged mountaines, and made rugged beasts
Lay by their rages; and tall trees that knew
No sound but tempests, to bow downe their branches
And heare, and wonder; and the Sea, whose surges
Shooke their white heads in heaven, to be as midnight
Still, and attentive; steales into our soules
So suddenly, and strangely, that we are
From that time no more ours but what she pleases.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Why looke, how far you have thrust your selfe againe
Into your old disease? are you that man
With such a resolution, that would venture
To take your leave of folly, and now melt
Even in repeating her?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I had forgot me.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: As you will still doe.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: No, the strongest man
May have the grudging of an ague on him,
This is no more; let's go, I would faine be fit
To be thy friend againe, for now I am no mans.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Goe you, I dare not goe, I tell you truely
Nor were it wise I should.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I am well.
And if I can, will keepe my selfe so.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Ha? thou mak'st me smile, though I have little cause,
To see how prettily thy feare becomes thee;
Art thou not strong enough to see a woman?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Yes, twenty thousand: but not such a one
As you have made her; Ile not lye for'th matter:
I know I am fraile, and may be cosen'd too
By such a Syren.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Faith thou shalt goe, Angilo

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Faith but I will not; no I know how far Sir
I am able to hold out, and will not venture
Above my depth: I doe not long to have
My sleepe ta'ne from me, and goe pulingly
Like a poore wench had lost her market money;
And when I see good meat, sit still and sigh,
And call for small beere; and consume my wit
In making Anagrams, and faithfull poses;
I doe not like that Itch, I am sure I had rather
Have the maine pox, and safer.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Thou shalt goe,
I must needs have thee as a witnesse with mee
Of my repentance; as thou lov'st me goe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Well I will goe, since you will have it so,
But if I prove a foole too, looke to have me
Curse you continually, and fearefully.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And if thou seest me fall againe, good Angilo
Give me thy councell quickly least I perish.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Pray God I have enough to save my selfe,
For as I have a soule, I had rather venture
Upon a savage Island, then this woman.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: From whom Sir, comes this bounty? for I thinke
You are mistaken.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: No Sir, 'tis to you,
I am sure my Mistris sent it.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Whoes your Mistris,
That I may give her thanks?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The vertuous Widow,

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: The vertuous widow Sir? I know none such:
Pray what's her name?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Laelia.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I knew you err'd
'Tis not to me I warrant ye; there Sir,
Carry it to those she feedes fat with such favours,
I am a stranger to her.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Good Sir take it,
And if you will, I'le sweare she sent it to you,
For I am sure mine eye never went off ye
Since you forsook the Gentlemen you talk'd with
Just at her doore.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Indeed I talkt with two
Within this halfe houre in the street.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: 'Tis you Sir,
And none but you I am sent to: wiser men
Would have been thankfull sooner, and receiv'd it,
'Tis not a fortune every man can brag of,
And from a woman of her excellence.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Well Sir, I am Chatechiz'd; what more belongs to 't?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: This only Sir; she would intreat you come
This evening to her without faile.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You ghesse where.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Sir I have a tongue else.
She is down-right Devill; or else my wants
And her disobedience have provok't her
To looke into her foule selfe, and be sorry.
I wonder how she knew me? I had thought
I had been the same to all, I am to them
That chang'd me thus: God pardon me for lying,
For I have paid it home: many a good man
That had but found the profit of my way
Would forsweare telling true againe in hast.
Here are my praters; now if I did well
I should be labour 'em, but I have found
A way to quiet 'em, worth a thousand on't.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: If we could get a fellow that would do it.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: What villany is now in hand?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: 'Twill be hard to be done in my opinion
Unlesse we light upon an English-man
With seven-score surfets in him.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Are the English-men such stubborn drinkers?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Not a leake at Sea
Can sucke more liquor; you shall have their children
Christned in mull'd sacke, and at five yeares old, able
To knocke a Dane downe: Take an English-man
And cry St. George, and give him but a rasher,
And you shall have him upon even terms
Defy a hogshead; such a one would do it
Home boy, and like a work-man: at what weapon?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Sherry sack: I would have him drinke stark dead,
If it were possible: at worst past pottage.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: What is the end then?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Dost thou not perceive it?
If he be drunke dead, ther's a faire end of him.
If not, this is my end, or by enticing,
Or by deceiving, to conduct him where
The foole is, that admires him; and if sober,
His nature be so rugged, what wilt be
When he is hot with wine? come lets about it,
If this be done but handsomely, I'le pawne
My head she hath done with souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: This may do well.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Here's a new way to murther men alive,
I'le choake this traine: God save ye Gentlemen.
It is to you, stay: yes it is to you.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: What's to me?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: You are fortunate,
I cannot stand to tell you more now, meete me
Here soone, and you'l be made a man.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: What Vision's this?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: I know not.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Well, I'le meet it,
Think you ot'h other, and let me a while
Dreame of this fellow.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: For the Drunkard, Lodowicke,
Let me alone.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Come, let's about it then.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, pray let me laugh extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Why? prethee why? hast thou such cause?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: Yes faith, my brother wil be here straightway, &—

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: The other party: ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: VVhat party?
VVench thou art not drunke.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: No faith.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Faith thou hast been among the bottles Clora;

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Faith but I have not Franke: Prethee be handsom,
The Captaine comes along too, wench.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: O is that it?
That tickles ye.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Yes, and shall tickle you too,
You understand me?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: By my troth thou art grown
A strange lewd wench: I must e'ne leave thy company,
Thou wilt spoile me else.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Nay, thou art spoil'd to my hand;
Hadst thou been free, as a good wench ought to be,
VVhen I went first a birding for thy Love,
And roundly said, that is the man must doe it,
I had done laughing many an houre agoe.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: And what dost thou see in him, now thou knowst him,
To be thus laught at?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Prethee be not angry
And I'le speake freely to thee.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Doe, I will not.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Then as I hope to have a handsome husband,
This fellow in mine eye, and Franke I am held
To have a shrewd ghesse at a pretty fellow,
Appeares a strange thing.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Why how strange for Gods sake?
He is a man, and one that may content
(For any thing I see) a right good woman:
And sure I am not blinde.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: There lyes the question?
For, but you say he is a man, and I
Will credit you, I should as soone have thought him
Another of Gods creatures; out upon him,
His body, that can promise nothing
But lazinesse and long strides.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: These are your eyes;
Where were they Clora, when you fell in love
With the old foot-man, for singing of Queen Dido?
And swore he look'd in his old velvet trucks
And his slyc't Spanish Jerkin, like Don Iohn?
You had a parlous judgment then, my Clora.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Who told you that?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I heard it.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Come, be friends,
The Souldier is a Mars, no more, we are all
Subject to slide away.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Nay, laugh on still.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: No faith, thou art a good wench, and 'tis pity
Thou shouldst not be well quarred at thy entring,
Thou art so high flown for him: Look, whose there?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Prethee goe single, what should I do there,
Thou knowst I hate these visitations,
As I hate peace or perry.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Wilt thou never
Make a right man?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: You make a right foole of me
To lead me up and down to visit women,
And be abus'd and laugh'd at; let me sterve
If I know what to say, unlesse I aske 'em
What their shooes cost?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Fye upon thee, coward,
Canst thou not sing?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Thou knowest I can sing nothing
But Plump^on parke.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Thou't be bold enough,
When thou art enterd once.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I had rather enter
A breach: If I miscarry, by this hand
I will have you by'th eares for't.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Save ye Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Clora.
verse: Sweet brother I dare sweare, you'r welcome hither,
So is your Friend;

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Come, blush not, but salute 'em.

speeches.speaker: Franck.
verse: Good Sir beleeve your Sister; you are most welcome,
So is this worthy Gentleman whose vertues
I shall be proud to be acquainted with.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: She has found me out already, and has paid me;
Shall we be going?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Peace;
Your goodnesse Lady
Will ever be afore us, for my selfe
I will not thanke you single, lest I leave
My friend, this Gentleman, out of acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: More of me yet?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Would I were able Sir,
From either of your worths to merit thankes.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: But brother, is your friend thus sad still? me thinks
'Tis an unseemly nature in a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: What hath she to do with me, or my behaviour?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: He do's but shew so, prethee to him Sister.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: If I do not breake thy head, I am no Christian,
If I get off once.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Sir, we must intreat you
To thinke your selfe more welcome, and be merry,
'Tis pitty a faire man of your proportion
Should have a soule of sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Very well;
Pray Gentlewoman what would you have me say?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Do not you know Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: Not so well as you
That talke continually.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: You have hither, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I thank him, so he has,
Faire fall his sweet face for't.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Let my face
Alone, I would wish you, least I take occasion
To bring a worse in question.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Meaning mine?
Brother, where was your friend brought up? h'as sure
Been a great lover in his youth of pottage,
They lye so dull upon his understanding.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: No more of that, thou'lt anger him at heart.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Then let him be more manly, for he lookes
Like a great School-boy that had been blown up
Last night at dust-point.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: You will never leave
Till you be told how rude you are, fye Clora.
Sir will it please you sit?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: And I'le sit by you.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Woman be quiet, and be rul'd I would wish you.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I have done, Sir Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Art thou not asham'd?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: You are an asse, I'le tell you more anon.
You had better ha been hang'd then brought me hither.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: You are grown a sullen foole; either be handsom,
Or by this light I'le have wenches baite thee;
Goe to the Gentlewoman, and give her thanks,
And hold your head up; what?

speeches.speaker: Ia.
verse: By this light I'le brain thee.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Now ô my faith this Gentleman do's nothing
But it becomes him rarely; Clora, look
How well this little anger, if it be one,
Shews in his face.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Yes, it shewes very sweetly.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Nay do not blush Sir, ô my troth it does,
I would be ever angry to be thus.
Fabritio, ô my conscience if I ever
Do fall in love, as I will not forswear it
Till I am something wiser, it must be,
I will not say directly with that face,
But certainly, such another as that is,
And thus dispose my chance to hamper me.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Dost thou heare this, and stand still?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: You will prate still;
I would you were not women, I would take
A new course with ye.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Why couragious?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: For making me a stone to whet your tongues on.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Prethee sweet Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Goe, goe spin, goe hang.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Now could I kisse him.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: If you long for kicking,
You'r best come kisse me, do not though, I'de wish ye,
I'le send my Foot-man to thee, he shall leap thee,
And thou wantst horsing: I'le leave ye Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Beshrew my heart you are unmannerly
To offer this unto a Gentleman
Of his deserts, that comes so worthily
To visite me, I cannot take it well.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: I come to visite you, you foolish woman?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I, though you did Sir, and for that I thanke you,
I would be loth to loose those thankes; I knowe
This is but some odd way you have, and faith
It do's become you well to make us merry;
I have heard often of your pleasant veine.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: What wouldst thou ask more?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Pray thou scurvy fellowe
Thou hast not long to live; adieu deare Damsels,
You silthy women farewell, and be sober,
And keepe your chambers.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Farewell old Don Diego.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Away, away, you must not be so angry,
To part thus roughly from us; yet to me
This do's not shew, as if 'twere yours, the wars
May breed men something plain I know,
But not thus rude; give me your hand good Sir
I know 'tis white, and—

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: If I were not patient,
What would become of you two prating houswives?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: For any thing I know, we would in to supper,
And there begin a health of lusty Claret
To keep care from our hearts, and it should be—

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Faith to whom? Mark but this Jacamo.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Even to the handsomest fellow now alive.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Do you know such a one?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: He may be ghest at,
Without much travel.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: There's another item.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: And he should be a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: 'Twould be better.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: And yet not you sweet Captaine

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Why not he?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Well; I shall live to see your husbands beate you,
And hisse 'em on like ban-dogs.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Green sicknesses and serving-men light on ye
With greasy Codpieces, and woollen stockings,
The Devill (if he dare deal with two women)
Be of your counsels: Farewell Plaisterers—

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: This fellow will be mad at Mid-sumer
Without all doubt.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I thinke so too.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I am sorry
Hee's gone in such a rage; but sure this holds him
Not every day.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Faith every other day
If he come neare a woman.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: I wonder how his mother could endure
To have him in her belly he's so boysterous.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: He's to be made more tractable I doubt not.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Yes, if they taw him as they do whit-leather
Upon an iron, or beate him soft like Stock-fish.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Art sure 'tis he?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Yes, and another with him.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: The more the merryer; did you give that money
And charg'd it to be delivered where I shewed you?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Yes, and what else you bad me.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: That brave fellow,
Though he be old, what e're he be, shews toughnesse,
And such a one I long for, and must have
At any price; these young soft melting gristles
Are only for my safer ends.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: They are here.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Give me my vaile, and bid the boy goe sing
That song above, I gave him: the sad Song:
Now if I misse him, I am curst, goe wench
And tell 'em I have utterly forsworn
All company of men; yet make a venture
At last to let 'em in; thou knowst these things,
Doe 'em to'th life.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: I warrant you I am perfect.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Some ill woman for her use would give
A million for this wench, she is so subtle.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Good Sir desire it not, I dare not do it,
For since your last being here, Sir, beleeve me
She has griev'd her selfe out of all company,
And (sweet soule) almost out of life too.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Prethee,
Let me but speake one word.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: You will offend Sir
And yet your name is more familiar with her
Then any thing but sorrow, good Sir goe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: This little varlet hath her lesson perfect,
These are the baites they bob with.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Faith I will not.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: I shal be chidden cruelly for this;
But you are such a Gentleman—

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: No more.

speeches.speaker: Aug.
verse: There's a new Tyre-wench; peace, thou art well enough.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: What, has she musique?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Yes; for Gods sake stay,
'Tis all she feedes upon.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Alas poore soule.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Now will I pray devoutly, for there's need ont.
AWay delights, goe seeke some other dwelling,
For I must dye.
Farewell false Love, thy tongue is ever telling
Lye after lye.
For ever let me rest now from thy smarts,
Alas, for pitty goe,
And fire their hearts
That have been hard to thee, mine was not so.
Never againe deluding love shall know me,
For I will dye:
And all those griefes that thinke to over-grow me
Shall be as I.
For ever will I sleepe, while poore maids cry,
Alas for pity stay
And let us dye
With thee, men cannot mocke us in the day.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Mistris? not one word, Mistris if I grieve ye
I can depart againe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Let's goe then quickly,
For if she get from under this darke cloud,
We shall both sweate I feare for't.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Do but speake
Though you turne from me, and speake bitterly,
And I am gone, for that I think will please you.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Oh that all women were thus silent ever,
What fine things they were.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: You have look'd on me,
When (if there be beliefe in womens words
Spoken in teares) you swore you lov'd to do so.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: O me my heart!

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Now Julio play the man,
Or such another will undoe thee:
Would I had any thing to keepe me busie
I might not heare her; thinke but what she is,
Or I doubt mainly, I shall be i'th mash too.

speeches.speaker: Jul
verse: Pray speake againe;

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Where is my woman?

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Here.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Mercy upon me! what a face she has?
Would it were vail'd againe.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Why did you let
This flattering man in to me? did not I
Charge thee to keep me from his eyes againe,
As carefully as thou wouldst keep thine owne?
Thou hast brought me poyson in a shape of heaven
Whose violence will breake the hearts of all,
Of all weake women, as it has done mine,
That are such fooles to love, and looke upon him.
Good Sir be gone, you know not what an ease
Your absence is.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: By heaven she is a wonder,
I cannot tell what 'tis, but I am squeamish.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Though I desire to be here more then heaven
As I am now, yet if my sight offend you,
So much I love to be commanded by you
That I will goe: Farewell—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I should say something
E're you depart, and I would have you heare me:
But why should I speak to a man that hates me?
And will but laugh at any thing I suffer?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: If this be hate—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Away, away deceiver.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Now help me Angilo!

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I am worse then thou art.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Such teares as those might make another woman
Believe thee honest Julio: almost me
That know their ends, for I confesse they stir me.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: What will become of me? I cannot goe now
If you would hang me, from her: o brave eye!
Steale me away for Gods sake Julio.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Alas poor man! I am lost againe too strangely.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: No, I will sooner trust a Crocadile
When he sheds teares, for he kills sodainly,
And ends our cares at once; or any thing
That's evill to our natures, then a man;
I finde there is no end of his deceivings,
Nor no avoyding 'em, if we give way:
I was requesting you to come no more,
And mocke me with your service, 'tis not well,
Nor honest to abuse us so far: you may love too;
For though, I must confesse I am unworthy
Of your love every way: yet I would have you
Thinke I am somewhat too good to make sport of.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Will you believe me?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: for your vows and oaths,
And such deceiving teares as you shed now,
I will as you doe, study to forget 'em.

speeches.speaker: Jul
verse: Let me be most despis'd of men—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: No more;
There is no new way left, by which your cunning
Shall once more hope to catch me; no, thou false man
I will avoid thee, and for thy sake all
That beare thy stamp; as counterfeit in love.
For I am open ey'd againe, and know thee.
Goe, make some other weepe, as I have done,
That dare believe thee: goe, and sweare to her
That is a stranger to thy cruelty,
And knowes not yet what man is, and his lyings,
How thou di'st daily for her: poure it out
In thy best lamentations; put on sorrow,
As thou canst, to deceive an Angell, Julio,
And vow thy selfe into her heart, that when
I shall leave off, to curse thee for thy falshood,
Still a forsaken woman may be found,
To call to heaven for vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: From this houre,
I heartily despise all honest women;
I care not if the world tooke knowledge on't,
I see there's nothing in them, but that folly
Of loving one man only: give me henceforth
(Before tne greatest blessing can be thought of)
If this be one, a whore; that's all I aime at.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Mistris, the most offending man is heard
Before his sentence, why will you condemn me
E're I produce the truth to witnesse with me
How innocent I am of all your angers?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: There is no trusting of that tongue, I know't,
And how far if it be believed it kills; no more Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: It never lyed to you yet; if it did
'Twas only when it cal'd you mild and gentle.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Good Sir no more; make not my understanding
After I have suffered thus much evill by you,
So poor to thinke I have not reach'd the end
Of all your forc'd affections; yet because
I once lov'd such a sorrow too too dearly,
As that would strive to be; I do forgive ye
Even heartily, as I would be forgiven,
For all your wrongs to me; my charity
Yet loves you so far, (though againe I may not)
And wish when that time comes, you will love truly
(If you can ever doe so) you may finde
The worthy fruit of your affections,
True love againe, not my unhappy harvest,
Which like a foole I sow'd in such a heart
So drye and stonie, that a thousand showres
From these two eyes, continually rayning,
Could never ripen.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Y'ave conquer'd me:
I did not thinke to yield, but make me now,
Even what you will my Lelia, so I may
Be but so truly happy to enjoy you.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: No, no, those fond imaginations,
Are dead and buried in me, let 'em rest.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I'le marry you.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: The Devill thou wilt Iulio
How that word waken'd me? come hither friend,
Thou art a foole, looke stedfastly upon her
Though she be all that I know excellent
As she appeares, though I could fight for her,
And run through fire; though I am starke mad too
Never to be recover'd, though I would
Give all I had l'th world to lye with her
Even to my naked soule, I am so far gone,
Yet me thinks still we should not doate away
That that is something more then ours, our honours
I would not have thee marry her by no meanes,
Yet I should do so; is she not a whore?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: She is; But such a one—

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: 'Tis true, she's excellent,
And when I well consider, Iulio
I see no reason we should be confin'd
In our affections; when all creatures else
Enjoy stil where they like.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And so will I then,

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: He's fast enough I hope now, if I hold him.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: You must not do so though, now I consider
Better what 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Do not consider Angilo,
For I must do it.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: No I'le kill thee first.
I love thee so well that the wormes shall have thee
Before this woman, friend.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I was your counsell.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: As I was a knave,
Not as I lov'd thee.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: All this is lost upon me Angilo,
For I must have her: I will marry yee
When you please; pray looke better on me.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Nay then no more friend; farewell Iulio,
I have so much discretion left me yet
To know, and tell thee thou art miserable.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Stay thou art more then she, and now I finde it.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Is he so?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
prose: No, I'le see thee sterv'd first.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Friend.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Fly her as I do, Iulio, she's a witch.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Beate me away then, I shall grow heere still else.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: That were the way to have me grow there with thee
Farewell for ever.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Stay, I am uncharm'd,
Farewell thou cursed house, from this houre be
More hated of me then a Leprosie.

speeches.speaker: Lelia.
verse: Both gon? a plague upon 'em both,
Am I deceiv'd againe? Oh I would raile
And follow 'em; but I feare the spight of people,
'Till I have emptied all my gall; the next
I seize upon, shall pay their follies
To the last penny; This will worke me worse
He that comes next, by heav'n shall feele their curse.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: O yee are a sweet youth, so uncivilly
To rayle and run away?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: O are you there Sir?
I am glad I have found ye, you have not now your Ladies
To shew your wit before.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Thou woult not, woult 'a?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: What a sweet youth I am, as you have made me,
You shall know presently.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Put up your sword
I have seene it often, 'tis a Fox.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: It is so,
And you shall feele it too; will you dispatch Sir?
And leave your mirth out? or I shall take occasion
To beate ye, and disgrace you too.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Well since, there is no other way to deale with you
Let's see your sword, I am sure you scorne all odds,
I will fight with you —

speeches.speaker: Jac.
prose: How now?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Nay stand out,
Or by this light I'le make yee.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: This is scurvy
And out of feare done.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: No Sir out of judgement,
For he that deales with thee, thou'rt growne so boystrous
Must have more wits, or more lives then another,
Or alwayes be in Armor, or inchanted;
Or he is miserable.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Your end of this Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: My end is only mirth to laugh at thee,
Which now I'le do in safety; ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Shart? then I am growne ridiculous.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Thou art,
And wilt be shortly sport for little children,
If thou continuest this rude stubbornenesse.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: O God, for any thing that had an edge?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Fye, what a shame it is,
To have a lubber shew his teeth?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Why dost thou laugh at me thou wretched fellow?
Speake with a pox; and looke ye render me
Iust such a reason —

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I shall dye with laughing.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: As no man can finde fault with: I shall have
Another Sword; I shall ye fleering puppy.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Does not this testiness shew finely in thee?
Once more take heed of children, if they finde thee
They'le breake up schoole, to beare thee company,
Thou wilt be such a pastime, and whoo'te at thee:
And call thee bloody bones, and Spade, and Spitfire,
And Gaffer Madman; and go by Ieronimo,
And will with wispe and come aloft, and crack rope,
And old Saint Dennis with the dudgeon Codpeeece:
And twenty such names.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: No I thinke they will not.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Yes but they will: and Nurses still their children
Onely with thee, and ^ere take him Iacanio.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Gods pretious, That I were but over thee
One Steeple height: I would fall and breake thy neck.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: This is the reason I laugh at thee,
And while thou art thus, will do: tell me one thing.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I wonder how thou durst thus question me,
Pre'thee restore my Sword.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Tell me but one thing,
And it may be I will: Nay Sir; keep out

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Well I will be your foole now, speake your minde Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Art thou not breeding Teeth?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: How? Teeth?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Yes Teeth, thou would'st not be so froward else.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Teeth?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Come, 'twill make thee
A little reumatique, but that's all one,
Weel'e have a Bib, for spoyling of thy doublet;
And a fring'd Muckender, hang at thy girdle,
I'le be thy Nurse, and get a Corall for thee:
And a fine Ring of Bells.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Faith this is somewhat
Too much Fabritio, to your friend that loves you;
Me thinkes your goodnesse, rather should invent,
A way to make my follies lesse, then breed 'em;
I should have been more moderate to you,
But I see ye despise me.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Now I love yee,
There, take your Sword, continue so: I dare not
Stay now to try your patience, Soone I'le meet yee,
And as you love your honours, and your state,
Redeeme your selfe well to the Gentlewoman,
Farewell 'till soone.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Well I shall thinke of this.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Nothing 'ith world but a dri'd Tongue or two—

speeches.speaker: Host
verse: Tast him and tell me.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Is a valiant wine,
This must be he mine Host.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: This shall be Ipse,
Oh he 's a develish bitten wine, a Tyrant;
Where he layes hold Sir, This is he that scornes
Small Beere should quench him, or a foolish Caudell
Bring him to bed; no if he flinch I'le shame him,
And draw him out to mull amongst old Midwives.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: There is a Souldier, I would have thee better
Above the rest, because he thinkes there's no man
Can give him drinke enough.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: What kinde of man?

speeches.speaker: Pis.
verse: That thou mayst know him perfectly, hee's one
Of a left-handed making, a lanck thing,
As if his belly were tane up with straw,
To hunt a match.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Has he no beard to shew him?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Faith but a little; yet enough to note him,
Which growes in parcells here, and there a remnant:
And that thou maist not misse him, he is one
That weares his fore-head in a vellet scabberd.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: That note's enough, he's mine, I'le fuddle him
Or lye 'ith sudds; you will be here too?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Yes, till soone, farewell and beare up.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: If I do not,
Say I am recreant; I'le get things ready.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: 'TIs strange thou should'st be thus, with thy discretion

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I am sure I am so.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I am well you see.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Keep your selfe warme then, & go home, & sleepe,
And pray to God thou maist continue so;
Would I had gon to'th Devill of an arrant,
When I was made a foole to see her: Leave me
I am not fit for conversation.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Why, thou art worse then I was.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Therefore leave me,
The nature of my sicknesse is not eas'd
By company, or councell, I am mad,
And if you follow me with questions
Shall shew my selfe so.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: This is more then errour.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Pray be content, that you have made me thus,
And do not wonder at me.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Let me know, but what you meane to do and I am gon
I would be lo'ath to leave you thus else.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Nothing
That needs your feare, that is sufficient;
Farewell, and pray for me.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I would not leave you.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: You must and shall.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I will then: would yon woman
Had been ten fathom under ground, when first
I saw her eyes.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Yet she had been dangerous,
For to some wealthy Rocke of pretious stone,
Or mine of gold as tempting, her faire body
Might have been turn'd; which once found out by labour
And brought to use, having her spells within it,
Might have corrupted States, and ruin'd Kingdomes
Which had been fearefull (Friend) Go, when I see thee
Next, I will be as thou art, or no more.
Pray do not follow me, you'l make me angry.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Heav'n grant you may be right againe.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
prose: Score a gallon of Sack, and a pinte of Olives to the Vnicorne.

speeches.speaker: Above within.
verse: Why drawer?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: A non, a non.

speeches.speaker: Another boy.
verse: Looke into the Nags head there.

speeches.speaker: 2. Boy.
verse: Score a quart of Claret to the Bar,
And a pound of Sausages into the flower-pott.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: The Divell's in their throates, anon, anon.

speeches.speaker: 2. Ser.
verse: And Robbin fetch Tobacco for the Peacock, they will not
Drunke till midnight else: how now how does my Master.
prose: Mull a pinte of Sack there for the women in the Flower-deluce, & put in ginger enough, they belch like potguns,

speeches.speaker: 2 Boy.
verse: Faith he lyes drawing on a pace.

speeches.speaker: 1. Boy.
verse: That's an ill signe.

speeches.speaker: 2. Boy.
verse: And fumbles with the pots too.

speeches.speaker: 1. Boy.
verse: Then ther's no way but one with him.

speeches.speaker: 2. Boy.
verse: All the rest.
Except the Captaine are in Limbo patrum,
Where they lye sod in sack.

speeches.speaker: 1. Boy.
verse: Does he beare up still.

speeches.speaker: 2. Boy.
verse: Afore the winde still, with his lightes up bravely
All he takes in I think he turnes to Iuleps,
Or has a world of Stoage in his belly,
The rest looke all like fire-drakes, and lye scatter'd
Like rushes round about the roome. My Master
Is now the louing'st man, I thinke above ground,

speeches.speaker: 1. Boy.
verse: Would he were always drunke then.
Drawer.

speeches.speaker: 2. B.
verse: Anon, anon Sir,

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: And swears I shall be free to morrovv, and so vveeps
And calls upon my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Then he's right.

speeches.speaker: 1. B.
verse: And svvears the Captain must lye this night with her
And bad me breake it to her vvith discretion,
That he may leave an issue after him:
Able to entertaine a dutch Ambassador,
And tells him feelingly how sweete she is,
And hovv he stoole her from her friendes i'th Countrey;
And brought her up disguiz'd vvith the Carriers,
And vvas nine nights bereaving her her maiden head,
And the tenth got a dravver, here they come.
Anon, anon, speake to the Tyger, Peter.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Ther's my Bells boyes, my silver Bell.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Would he vvere hang'd
As high as I could ring him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Hoe Boy.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Robin, sufficient single Beere, as cold as christall,
Quench Robin, quench.

speeches.speaker: 1. Boy.
verse: I am gon Sir.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Shall vve beare up still? Captaine hovv I love thee?
Sweete Captaine let me kisse thee, by this hand
I love thee next to Malmesey in a morning,
Of things transitory.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: I love thee too, as far as I can love a fatt man.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Do'st thou Captaine?
Sweetly? and hartily?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: With all my heart Boy.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Then welcome death, come close mine eyes sweet Captaine
Thou shalt have all.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: What shall your wife have then?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Why she shall have besides my blessing, and a silver spoone
Enough to keepe her stirring in the world,
Three little Children, one of them was mine
Upon my conscience, th'other two are Pagans.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: 'Twere good she had a little foolish money,
To rub the time a way with.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Not a rag,
Not a Deniere, no let her spin a Gods name:
And raise her house againe,

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Thou shalt not dye though,
Boy see your Master safe delivered,
He's ready to lye in.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: God night.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: God morrow,
Drinke tell the Cow come home, 'tis all pay'd boyes.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: A pox of Sack.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Marry God blesse my Buts, Sack is a jewell,
'Tis comfortable Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: More Beere boy.
Uery sufficient single Beere.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Here Sir.
How is it Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: But ev'n so, so.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Go before finely Robin, and prepare
My wife, bid her be right and streight, I come boy
And Sirha, if they quarrell let 'em use,
Their owne discretions, by all meanes, and stir not,
And he that's kill'd shall be as sweetly buried;
Captaine, adieu, adieu sweet bully Captai ne,
One kisse before I dye, one kisse.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Farewell Boy.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: All my sweet boyes farewell.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Go sleep, you are drunke.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Come Gentlemen, I'le see you at your Lodging,
You looke not lustily, a quart more.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: No Boy.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Get us a Torch.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: 'Tis day Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: That's all one.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Are not those the stars, thou scurvy Boy?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Is not Charle-waine there, tell me that, there?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Yes;
I have paid 'em truely: do not vex him Sirha.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Confesse it Boy, or as I live I'le beate
Midnight into thy braines.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I do confesse it.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Then live, and draw more small Beere presently.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Come Boyes, let's hug together, and be loving,
And sing, and do brave things cheerely my hearts,
A pox a being sad; now, could I fly
And turne the world about upon my finger,
Come ye shall love me, I am an honest fellow:
Hang care and fortune, we are friendes.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: No Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Do not you love me? I love you too dearely.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: No by no meanes; you are a fighting Captaine,
And kill up such poore people as we are, by'th dozens.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: As they kill flyes with Fox-tailes, Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Me thinkes now as I stand, the Captaine shewes,
To be a very mercifull young man.
(And pre'thee Piso, let me have thy opinion)

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Then he shall have mercy, that mercifull is,
Or all the Painters are Apocrypha.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: I am glad you have your witts yet, will ye go?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: You had best say we are drunke.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Ye are.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Yee lye.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Y'are Rascalls, drunken rascalls.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: 'Tis sufficient.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: And now I'le tell you why, before I beate yee,
You have been tampring any time these three dayes,
Thus to disgrace me.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: That's a lye too.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Well Sir,
Yet I thanke God I have turn'd your points on you,
For which I'le spare yee somewhat, halfe a beating.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: I'le make you fart fire Captaine, by this hand,
And ye provoke, do not provoke I'de wish you.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: How do you like this?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Sure I am inchanted.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Stay till I draw.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Despatch then, I am angry.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: And thou shalt see how sodainly I'e kil thee.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Thou darst not draw, ye cold, tame, mangy Cowards
Ye drunken Rogues, can nothing make you valiant?
Not wine, nor beating?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: If this way be sufferd
'Tis very well.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Go ther's your way, go and sleep:
I have pitty on you, you shall have the rest
To morrow when wee meete.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Come Lodowick,
Hee's monstrous drunke now, ther's no talking with him.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: I am so, when I am sober, I'le do more.
Boy wher's mine Host?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Hee's on his bed a sleepe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Let him alone then: Now am I high proofe
For my action, now could I fight bravely,
And charge into a wilde fire; or I could love
Any man living now, or any woman,
Or indeed any creature that loves Sack
Extreamly, monstrously; I am so loving,
Iust at this instant, that I might be brought
I feele it, with a little labour, now to talke
With a justice of peace, that to my nature
I hate next an ill Sword: I will do
Some strange brave thing now, and I have it here:
Pray God the ayre keepe out; I feele it buzing.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Shee loves him too much, that's the plaine truth Fredrick
For which if I might be beleev'd, I thinke her
A strange forgetter of her selfe; ther's Iulio,
Or twenty more—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: In your eye I believe you,
But credit me the Captaine is a man:
Lay but his rough affections by, as worthy.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: So is a resty Iade, a horse of service,
If he would leave his nature, give me one
By your leave Sir to make a husband of
Not to be wean'd, when I should marry him;
Me thinkes a man is misery enough,

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You are too bitter,
I would not have him worse.
Yet I shall see you hamper'd one day Lady,
I do not doubt it, for this heresie

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: I'le burne before; come pre'thee leave this sadnesse;
This walking by thy selfe to see the Divell,
This mumps, this Lachrimae, this love in sippets;
It fitts thee like a French-hood.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Does it so?
I am sure it fits thee to be ever talking,
And nothing to the purpose, take up quickly;
Thy witt will founder of all foure else wench,
I thou hold'st this pace; take up when I bid thee.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Before your Brother fly?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I can endure it.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Heer's Raw-head come againe; Lord how he lookes?
Pray God we scape with broken pates.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Were I hee,
Thou should'st not want thy wish, he has been drinking
Has he not Fredrick?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes but do not finde it.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Peace and let's heare his wisedome.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You will mad him.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I am somewhat bold, but that's all one.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: A short and pithy saying of a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: As I live
Thou art a strange mad wench.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: To make a parson.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Ladyes I meane to kisse yee

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: How he wipes his mouth like a young Preacher;
We shall have it.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: In order as you ly before me; first
I'le begin with you.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: With me Sir?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Yes
If you will promise me to kisse in ease.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I care not if I venture.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I will kiss according to mine owne inventions
As I shall see cause; sweetly I would wish you,
I love ye.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Do you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Yes indeed do I,
Would I could tell you how.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I would you would Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I would to God I could, but 'tis sufficient,
I love you with my heart.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Alas poore heart.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: And I am sorry; but wee'l talk of that,
Hereafter if it please God.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Ev'n when you will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Hee's dismall drunk, would he were musled.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: You
I take it are the next.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Go to him foole.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Not I, 'a will bite me.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: When witt? when?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Good Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Nay, and you play boa-peepe; I'le ha, no mercy
But catch as catch may.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Nay, I'le not defend ye.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Good Captaine do not hurt me, I am sorry
That ere I anger'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: I'le tew you for't
By this hand witt, unlesse you kisse discreetly.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: No more Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Yes a little more sweet witt,
One tast more o' your office: go thy wayes
With thy small kettle Drumes; upon my conscienc
Thou art the best, that e're man laid his leg o'er.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: He smells just like a Cellar,
Fye upon him.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Sweete Lady now to you.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: For loves sake kisse him.

speeches.speaker: Fred
verse: I shall not keep my countenance.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Trye pre'thee.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Pray be not coy sweet woman, for I'le kisse ye,
I am blunt
But you must pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: O God my sides.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Why ha, ha, ha? why laugh?
Why all this noyse sweet Ladyes?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Lusty Laurence,
See what a Gentlewoman you have saluted;
Pray God she prove not quick.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Where were thine eyes
To take me for a woman, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Who art 'a, art 'a mortall?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I am Fredrick

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Then Fredrick is an Asse,
A scurvy Fredrick to laugh at me.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Sweet Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: A way woman;
Go stich and serve God, I despise thee woman,
And Fredrick shall be beaten; S'blood ye Rogue
Have you none else to make your puppies of, but me?

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: I pre'thee be more patient
Ther's no hurt done.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: S'blood but there shall be, Scab.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Help, help for loves sake.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Whose within there?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: So now you have made a faire hand.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You have kill'd me—

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Call in some Officers, and stay the Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: You shall not need.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: This is your drunkennesse.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: O me unhappy Brother, Fredrick,
Looke but upon me, do not part so from me,
Set him a little higher he is dead.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: O villaine, villaine.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: How now what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: O Sir my Brother! o my dearest Brother!

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: This drunken trowgh has kill'd him.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Kill'd him?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Yes.
For heaven God sake hang him quickly, he will do
Ev'ry day such a murder else. there is nothing
But a strong Gallowes that can make him quiet,
I finde it in his nature too late.

speeches.speaker: Fabr.
verse: Pray be quiet,
Let me come to him.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Some go for a Surgeon.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Oh what a wretched woman has he made me!
Let me alone good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: To what a fortune,
Hast thou reserv'd thy life.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Fabritio.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Never entreat me, for I will not know thee,
Nor utter one word for thee, unlesse it be
To have thee hang'd; for God sake bee more temperate.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I have a sword still, and I am a villaine.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: &c. Hold, hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Away with him for heavens sake
He's too desperate for our enduring.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Come, you shall sleepe, come strive not
Ile have it so, here take him to his lodging, and
See him laid before you part.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: We will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ne're wonder, I am living yet, and well,
I thanke you sister for your griefe, pray keepe it
Till I am fitter for it.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Do you live Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes, but 'twas time to counterfeit, he was grown
To such a madnesse in his wine.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: 'Twas well Sir,
You had that good respect unto his temper,
That no worse followd.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: If I had stood him, certaine one of us must have perish'd,
How now Franke?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Beshrew my heart I tremble like an aspine.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Let him come here no more for heavens sake
Unlesse he be in chaines.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I would faine see him
After he has slept, Fabritio, but to try
How he wil be; chide him, and bring him backe.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: You'l never leave till you be worried with him.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Come brother, wee'l walke in, and laugh a little.
To get this Fever off me.

speeches.speaker: Clo
verse: Hang him squib,
Now could I grinde him into priming powder.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Pray will you leave your fooling?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Come, all friends.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Thou art enough to make an age of men so,
Thou art so crosse and peevish.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I will chide him,
And if he be not gracelesse, make him cry for't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I would goe a mile (to see him cry) in slippers
He would looke so like a whay cheese;

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Would we might see him once more.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: If you dare
Venture a second tryall of his temper
I make no doubt to bring him.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: No good Franke
Let him alone, I see his vaine lyes only
For falling out at Wakes and Beare-baitings,
That may expresse him sturdy.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Now indeed
You are too sharp sweet sister, for unlesse
It be this sin, which is enough to drown him,
I meane this sowrnesse, he's as brave a fellow,
As forward, and as understanding else
As any He that lives.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I doe beleeve you,
And good Sir when you see him, if we have
Distasted his opinion any way,
Make peace againe.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I will: I'le leave ye Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Take heed you had best, h'as sworn to pay you else.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I warrant you, I have been often threatned.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: When he comes next, I'le have the cough or tooth-ach,
Or something that shall make me keepe my chamber,
I love him so well.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Would you would keepe your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I cannot keepe from this ungodly woman,
This Lelia, whom I know too, yet am caught,
Her looks are nothing like her; would her faults
Were all in Paris print upon her face,
Cum Privilegio, to use 'em still.
I would write an Epistle before it, on the inside of her masque
And dedicate it to the whore of Babilon, with a preface upo~
Her nose to the gentle Reader; & they should be to be sold
At the signe of the Whores head i'th pottage pot, in what
Street you please: But all this helps not me;—I
Am made to be thus catch'd, past any redresse, with a thing
I contemn too.
I have read Epictetus twice over against the
Desire of these outward things, and still her face runs in
My mind, I went to say my prayers, and they were
So laid out o'th way, that if I could finde any prayers I
Had, I'me no Christian.
This is the doore, and the short
Is, I must see her againe.—

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: 'Tis I, I would speake with your Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Did she send for you?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: No, what then? I would see her, prethee by thy leave.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Not by my leave; for she will not see you, but doth hate you, and
Your friend, and doth wish you both hang'd, wch being so proper
Men, is great pitty, that you are not.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: For your sweet self in particular, who she resolvs perswaded your
Friend to neglect her, she deemeth whip-cord the most
Convenient unction for your backe and shoulders.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Let me in, I'le satisfie her.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: And if it shal happen that you are in doubt of these my speeches,
Insomuch that you shal spend more time in arguing at the
Dore, I am fully perswaded that my Mistris in person from
Above, will utter her mind more at large by way of
Urine upon your head, that it may sink the more soundly
Into your understanding faculties.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: This is the strangest thing, good pretty soul, why dost thou use me so?
I pray thee let me in sweet heart.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Indeed I cannot sweet-heart.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Thou art a handsome one, and this crosseness do's become thee.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Alas I cannot help it.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Especially to me; thou knowst when I was here, I said I lik'd thee of
All thy Mistriss servants.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: So did I you, though it be not my fortune to express
It at this present: for truly if you would cry, I cannot
Let you in.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Pox on her, I must goe the down-right way: looke you
Here is ten pound for you, let me speak with her.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: I like your gold well, but it is a thing by heaven
I cannot doe, shee
Will not speake with you, especially at this time, she has affaires.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: This makes her leave her jesting yet, but take it
And let me see her, bring me to a place
Where undiscern'd of herselfe I may
Feede my desiring eyes but halfe an houre.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Why faith I think I can, and I wil stretch my wits
And body too for gold: if you will sweare as you
Are gentle, not to stir, or speake, where you shall
See or hear, now, or hereafter: give me your gold, I'le plant you

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Why, as I am a Gentleman, I will not.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: Enough, quicke, follow me.
Why where's this maid, she ha's much care of her business. Nell?
I thinke she be sunke;—why Nell—whiew—

speeches.speaker: Maid within.
verse: Whats the matter?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I pray you heartily come away, oh, come, come, the Gentleman,
My Mistris invited, is comming down the street, and the banquet
Not yet brought out?—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
prose: Nell, Sirha?

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: I come forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Now must I walk: when ther's any fleshly matters in hand, my
Mistris sends me of a four hours errand: but if I goe not
About mine own bodily businesse as well as shee, I am a Turke.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: What, all wide open? 'Tis the way to sin
Doubtlesse; but I must on; the gates of hell
Are not more passable then these; how they
Will be to get out, God knows, I must try.
'Tis very strange, if there be any life
Within this house, would it would shew it selfe.
What's here? a Banquet? and no mouth to eate,
Or bid me do it? this is something like
The entertainment of adventurous Knights
Entring enchanted Castles: For the manner
Though there be nothing dismall to be seene
Amazes me a little; what is meant
By this strange invitation? I will sound
My Daughters meaning, e're I speake to her,
If it be possible, for by my voyce—
She will discover me! hark, whence is this.
COme hither you that love, and heare me sing
of joyes still growing
Green, fresh, and lusty, as the pride of Spring,
and ever blowing.
Come hither youths that blush, and dare not know
what is desire,
And olde men worse then you, that cannot blow
one sparke of fire.
And with the power of my enchanting Song,
Boyes shall be able men, and old men young.
Come hither you that hope, and you that cry,
leave off complaining,
Youth, strength, and beauty, that shall never dye,
are here remaining.
Come hither fooles, and blush, you stay so long
from being blest,
And mad men worse then you, that suffer wrong,
Yet seeke no rest.
And in an houre, with my enchanting Song,
You shall be ever pleas'd, and yovng maids long.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Sir you are welcome hither, as this kisse
Given with a larger freedome then the use
Of strangers will admit, shall witnesse to you.
Put the gowne on him, in this chaire sit downe;
Give him his slippers: be not so amaz'd,
Here's to your health, and you shall feele this wine
Stir lively in me, in the dead of night.
Give him some wine; fall to your banquet Sir,
And let us grow in mirth; though I am set
Now thus far off you, yet four glasses hence
I will sit here,
And try, till both our bloods
Shoote up and downe to finde a passage out,
Then mouth, to mouth will we walke up to bed,
And undresse one another as we goe;
Where both my treasure, body, and my soule
Are your's to be dispos'd of.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
prose: Umh, umh.—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You are old,
Is that your meaning? why, you are to me
The greater novelty, all our fresh youth
Are daily offer'd me, though you performe
As you thinke little, yet you satisfie
My appetite: from your experience
I may learn something in the way of lust
I may be better for. But I can teach
These young ones;
But this day I did refuse
A paire of 'em, Julio, and Angilo,
And told them they were as they were
Raw fooles and whelps.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
prose: Pray God he speak not

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Why speak you not sweet Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
prose: Umh.—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Peace there, that musique, now Sir speak
To me.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Umh.—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Why? would you have her gone? you need not keep
Your freedome in for her; she knows my life
That she might write it;
Thinke she is a stone?
Shee is a kinde of bawdy Confessor,
And will not utter secrets.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Umh.—

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Be gone then, since he needs will have it so,
Tis all one.
'Is all now as you would? come meet me then,
And bring a thousand kisses on thy lips,
And I will rob thee of 'em, and yet leave
Thy lips as wealthy as they were before.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Yes, all is as I would but thou.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: By heaven 'tis my Father.—

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: And I do beseech thee
Leave these unheard of lusts which worse become thee,
Then mocking of thy Father; let thine eyes
Reflect upon thy soule, and there behold
How loathed blacke it is; and whereas now
Thy face is heavenly faire, but thy minde foule,
Goe but into thy Closet, and there cry
Till thou hast spoil'd that face, and thou shalt finde
How excellent a change, thou wilt have made
For inward beauty.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Though I know him now
To be my Father, never let me live
If my lust do abate.
I'le take upon me
To have known him all this while.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Looke, dost thou know me?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I knew yee Sir before.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: What didst thou do?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Knew you, and so unmov'dly have you borne
All the sad crosses that I laid upon you,
With such a noble temper, which indeed
I purposely cast on you, to discern
Your carriage in calamity, and you
Have undergone 'em with that brave contempt,
That I have turn'd the reverence of a childe
Into the hot affection of a Lover.
Nor can there on the earth be found but yours
A spirit fit to meete with mine.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: A woman? thou art not sure.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Looke and beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Thou art
Something created to succeed the Devill
When be growes weary of his envious course,
And compassing the world; but I beleeve thee
Thou didst but meane to try my patience,
And do'st so still; but better be advis'd:
And make thy tryall with some other things
That safelier will admit a dalliance:
And if it should be earnest, understand
How curst thou art, so far from heaven, that thou
Beleev'st it not enough to damn alone,
Or with a stranger, but wouldst heape all sins
Unnaturall upon this aged head
And draw thy Father to thy Bed, and hell.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You are deceiv'd Sir, 'tis not against nature
For us to lye together; if you have
An arrow of the same tree with your bow,
Is't more unnaturall to shoot it there
Then in another? 'Tis our generall nature
To procreate, as fires is to consume,
And it will trouble you to finde a sticke
The fire will turne from: If't be natures will
We should not mixe, she will discover to us
Some most apparant crossenesse, as our organs
Will not be fit; which if we do perceive
Wee'l leave, and thinke it is her pleasure
That we should deale with others.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: The dores are fast; thou shalt not say a prayer,
'Tis not Gods will thou shouldst; when this is done
I'le kill my selfe, that never man may tell me
I got thee.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I pray you Sir, help ther, for Gods sake Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Hold reverend Sir, for honour of your age.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Whoe's that?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: For safety of your soule, and of the soule
Of that too wicked woman yet to dye.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: What art thou? and how cam'st thou to that place?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I am a man so strangely hither come,
That I have broke an oath in speaking this,
But I believe 'twas better broke then kept,
And I desire your patience; let me in,
And I protest I will not hinder you
In any act you wish, more then by word,
If so I can perswade you, that I will not
Use violence, I'le throw my sword down to you:
This house holds none but I, only a maid
Whom I will locke fast in as I come downe.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I do not know thee, but thy tongue doth seeeme
To be acquainted with the truth so well
That I will let thee in: throw down thy sword.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: There 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: How came he there? I am betraid to shame,
The feare of sodaine death strook me all over
So violently, that I scarce have breath
To speake yet: But I have it in my head,
