And out it shall, that (Father) may perhaps
O're-reach you yet.

speeches.speaker: Fat.
verse: Come Sir, what is't you say?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: My Angilo, by all the joyes of love
Thou art as welcome as these plyant arms
Twin'd round, and fast about thee, can perswade thee.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Away.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I was in such a fright before thou cam'st,
You old mad fellow, (it will make thee laugh
Though it feared me) has talkt so wildly here—
Sirrha, he rusht in at my dores, and swore
He was my Father, and I thinke beleev'd it:
But that he had a sword, and threatned me—
I'faith he was good sport, good, thrust him out
That thou and I may kisse together; wilt thou?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Are you her Champion? & with these fair words,
Got in to rescue her from me.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Hold sir,
I sweare I doe not harbour such a thought,
I speake it not, for that you have two swords,
But for tis truth.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Two swords my Angilo?
Thinke this, that thou hast two young brawny armes
And ne're a sword, and he has two good swords
And ne're an arme to use 'em; rush upon him,
I could have beaten him with this weake body,
If I had had the spirit of a man.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Stand from me, and leave talking, or by heaven
I'le trample thy last damning word out of thee.

speeches.speaker: Fa^.
verse: Why do you hinder me then? stand away
And I will rid her quickly.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Would I were
Cleare of this businesse, yet I cannot pray.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Oh be advis'd, why you were better kill her
If she were good; Convey her from this place
Where none but you, and such as you appoint
May visite her; where let her heare of nought
But death and damning, which she hath deserv'd,
Till she be truly, justly sorrowful,
And then lay mercy to her, who does know
But she may mend?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: But whither should I beare her?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: To my house,
'Tis large, and private, I will lend it you.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I thanke you Sir, and happily it fits
With some designe I have, but how shall we
Convey her?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Will they cary me away?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: For she wil scratch and kick, & scream so loud
That people will be drawn to rescue her.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Why? none can hear her here, but her own maid,
Who is as fast as she.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: But in the streete?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Why, we will take 'em both into the Kitchin,
There binde 'em, and then gag 'em, and then throw 'em
Into a Coach I'le bring to the backe-dore,
And hurry 'em away.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: It shall be so,
I owe you much for this; and I may pay you,
There is your sword, lay hold upon her quickly,
This way with me, thou disobedient childe.
Why do's thy stubborn heart beat at thy breast?
Let it be still, for I will have it search'd
Till I have found a well of living teares
Within it, that shall spring out of thine eyes,
And flow all o're thy body foul'd with sin,
Till it have wash'd it quite without a stain.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Help! help! ah! ah!
Murther, I shall be murthered, I shall be murthered.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: This helps thee not.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Basely murdered, basely.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: THis roguy Captaine has made fine work with us.

speeches.speaker: Pi^o
verse: I would the Devill in a storm would carry him
Home to his Garison againe; I ake all over,
That I am sure of; Certainly my body
Is of a wild-fire, for my head rings backward,
Or else I have a morise in my braines.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I'le deale no more with souldiers: wel remembred,
Did not the Vision promise to appeare
About this time again?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Yes, here he comes:
He's just on's word.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: O, they be here together,
Shee's penitent, and by my troth I stagger
Whether (as now she is) either of these
Two fooles be worthy of her; yet because
Her youth is prone to fall againe, ungovern'd,
And marriage now may stay her, one of 'em:
And Piso, since I understand him abler,
Shall be the man; the other beare the charges,
And willingly, as I will handle it.
I have a Ring here, which he shall believe
Is sent him from a woman I have thought of:
But e're I leave it, I'le have one of his
In pawne worth two on't: for I will not loose
By such a messe of sugar-sops as this is:
I am too old.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: It moves againe, let's meet it.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Now if I be not out, we shall have fine sport,
I am glad I have met you Sir, so happily,
You do remember me, I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I doe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: This is a short praeludium to a challenge.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I have a message Sir, that much concerns you,
And for your speciall good; Nay you may heare too.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: VVhat should this fellow meane?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: There is a Lady,
(How the poore thing begins to warme already)
Come to this Towne, (as yet a stranger here Sir)
Faire, young, and rich, both in possessions,
And all the graces that make up a woman,
A widow, and a vertuous one: It workes,
He needs no broath upon't,

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: VVhat of her Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: No more but this; she loves you.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Loves me?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Yes.
And with a strong affection, but a faire one,
If ye be wise and thankfull, you are made: ther's the whole matter.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I am sure I heare this.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Here is a Ring Sir, of no little value:
Which after she had seen you at a window,
She bad me hast, and give it, when she blush'd
Like a blown rose.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: But pray Sir by your leave—
Me thinks your yeares should promise no ill meaning.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I am no Bawd, nor cheater, nor a coarser
Of broken-winded women: if you feare me
I'le take my leave: and let my Lady use
A fellow of more forme; an honester
I am sure she cannot.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Stay, you have confirm'd me,
Yet let me feele, you are in health.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I hope so,
My water's well enough, and my pulse.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Then
All may be excellent: pray pardon me;
For I am like a boy that had found money,
Afraid I dreame still.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Sir, what kind of woman?
Of what proportion is your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I,

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: I'le tell you presently her very picture,
Do you know a woman in this towne they call,
Stay, yes, it is so, Lelia?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Not by sight.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Nor you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Neither.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: These are precious Rogues
To raile upon a woman they never saw;
So they would use their Kindred.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: We have heard though
She is very faire and goodly.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Such another,
Just of the same complexion, making, speech,
But a thought sweeter is my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Then
Shee must be excellent indeed.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Indeed she is,
And you will finde it so; you do beleeve me?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Yes marry do I, and I am so alter'd —

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Your happinesse will alter any man.
Do not delay the time Sir: at a house
Where Don Valasco lay, the Spanish Signior
(Which now is Signieur Angelos) she is.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I know it.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: But before you shew your selfe,
Let it be night by all meanes, willingly
By day she would not have such gallants seene
Repair unto her 'tis her modesty.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I'le goe and fit my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Doe, and be sure
You send provision in, in full abundance,
Fit for the marriage; for this night I know
Shee will be yours: Sir, have you never a token
Of worth to send her backe againe? you must,
Shee will expect it.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Yes, pray give her this,
And with it all I have; I am made for ever.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Well, thou hast fooles lucke; should I live as long
As an old oake, and say my prayers hourly
I should not be the better of a penny.
I think the Devill be my ghostly Father;
Upon my conscience I am full as handsome,
I am sure I have more wit, and more performance,
Which is a pretty matter.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Do you thinke sir,
That your friend Signeur Piso will be constant
Unto my Lady? you should know him well.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Who? Signieur Piso?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Yes, the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: VVhy, you are wide Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Is not his name Piso?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: No, mine is Piso.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: 'Tis indeed Sir,
And his is Lodowicke.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Then I am undone Sir,
For I was sent at first to Piso; what a rascall
VVas I, so ignorantly to mistake you?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Peace.
There is no harme done yet.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Now 'tis too late,
I know my errour:
At turning of a Street,
For you were then upon the right hand of him,
You chang'd your places sudainly: where I
(Like a crosse Block-head) lost my memory:
What shall I do? my Lady utterly
Will put me from her favour.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Never feare it,
I'le be thy guard, I warrant thee, O, O,
Am I at length reputed? for the Ring,
I'le fetch it back with a light vengance from him:
Had better keep tame Devills, then that Ring;
Art thou not Steward?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Thou shalt be shortly

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Lord how he takes it?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: I'le go shift me streight;
Art sure it was to Piso?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: O too sure Sir.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: I'le mount thee if I live for't,
Give me patience heav'n to be are this blessing I beseech thee;
I am but man; I pre'thee breake my head
To make me understand, I am sensible.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Lend me your dagger, and I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: No
I believe now like a good Christian.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Good Sir make hast; I dare not go without ye
Since I have so mistaken.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: 'Tis no matter,
Meet me within this halfe houre at St. Margrets.
Well go thy wayes old leg, thou hast the trick on't.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: How now? the newes?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Well, passing well, I have 'em,
Both in a leash and made right for my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I am glad on't I must leave you.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Whether man?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: If all go right, I may be fast enough too.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I cry you mercie Sir, I know your meaning,
Clora's the woman, she's Francks bedfellow,
Commend me to 'em, and go Julio
Bring 'm to supper all, to grace this matter;
They serve for witnesses.

speeches.speaker: Ju.
prose: I will, Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Sister, I brought you Jacamo to the doore,
He has forgot all that he said last night:
And shame of that makes him more loath to come,
I left Fabritio perswading him, but 'tis in vaine.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Alas my fortune Clora.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Now Franck, See what a kind of man you love,
That loves you when hee's drunk; If so
Faith I would marry him; My friends I hope
Would make him drink.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: 'Tis well consider'd Franck, he has such pretty humours then,
Besides being a Souldier, 'tis better he should love
You when hee's drunck, then when hee's sober, for then he
Will be sure to love you, the greatest part on's life.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: And were not I a happy woman then?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: That ever was borne Franck. y'faith—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: How now? what sayes hee?

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Faith you may as well tice a dog up with a whip, and bell
As him, by telling him of love and women, he sweares
They mock him.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Looke how my Sister weepes.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: VVhy who can helpe it?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes, you may safly sweare she loves him.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: VVhy so I did; and may do all the oathes,
Arithmatique can make, ere he believe me,
And since he was last drunk, he is more jealous
They would abuse him: If we could perswade him
She lov'd, he would embrace it.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She her selfe
Shall bate so much of her owne modesty
To sweare it to him; with such teares as now
You see raine from her.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I believe 'twould worke,
But would you have her do't i'th open street?
Or if you would hee'le run away from her,
How shall we get him hither?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: By entreaty.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: 'Tis most impossible, No, If we could
Anger him hither, as ther is no way
But that to bring him; and then hold him fast
Women, and men, whilst she delivers to him the truth
Seal'd with her teares, he would be plaine
As a pleas'd child; he walkes below for me
Under the window.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: VVee'le anger him I warrant ye,
Let one of the maides take a good bowle of water,
Or say it be a piss-pott, and power't on's head.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Content hang me If I like not the cast of it rarely, for no question it,
Is an approv'd receipt to fetch such a fellow
Take all the women-kind in this house, betwixt the age of one,
And one hundred, & let them take unto them a pott or a
Bowle containing seven quarts or upwards, & let them
Never leave, till the above named,
Pott or Bowle become full, then let one of them stretch out
Her arme and power it on his head, add Probatum est, it
VVill fetch him, for in his anger he will run up, & then let
Us alone.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Go you and do it.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Good Clora, no.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Away I say & do it; never feare, we have enough of that
Water ready distill'd.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Why this will make him mad Fabritio,
Hee'le neither love me drunke, nor sober now.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I warrant you: what, is the wench come up?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Art thou there wench?

speeches.speaker: Wench.
verse: I.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Looke out then if thou canst see him.

speeches.speaker: Wench.
verse: Yes I see him, & by my troth he stands so faire I could not
Hold were he my Father; his hat's of too, & he's scratching
His head.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: O wash that hand I pre'thee. (I have throwne thee

speeches.speaker: Wench.
verse: God send thee good luck, this the second time,
Out to day, ha, ha, ha, just on's head.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Alas!

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: What does he now?

speeches.speaker: Wench.
prose: He gathers stones, God's light, he breakes all the Street windows

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Whore's Bawdes, your windowes, your windowes.

speeches.speaker: Wench.
verse: Now he is breaking all the low windowes with his Sword,
Excellent sport, Now he's beating a fellow that laugh'd at him;
Truely the man takes it patiently; Now he goes downe the Street
Gravely, looking on each side, ther's not one more dare laugh.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Does he go on?

speeches.speaker: Wench.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Fabritio, you have undone a Maid
By treachery; know you some other better,
You would prefer your friend to? If you do not
Bring him againe, I have no other hope,
But you that made me loose hope, If you faile me,
I ne're shall see him, but shall languish out
A discontented life, and dye contemn'd.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: This vexes me, I pray you be more patient
If I have any truth, let what will happen,
I'le bring him presently, Do you all stand
At the Street dore, the Maides, and all, to watth
When I come backe, and have some private place
To shuffle me into, for he shall follow
In fury, but I know I can out run him:
As he comes in, clap all fast hold on him,
And use your owne discretions.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Wee will do it.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: But sudainly for I will bring him hither,
With that unstop'd speed that you shall run over
All that's in's way: and though my life be ventur'd
'Tis no great matter, will do't.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I thanke you,
Worthy Fabritio.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: I ever knew no woman could abide me,
But am I growne so contemptible, by being once drunke
Amongst 'em, that they begin to throw pisse on my head?
For surely it was pisse huh, huh.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Jacamo, how do'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Well, something troubled with watrish humours.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Foh, how thou stinck'st; pre'thee stand further of me
Me things these humours become thee better then thy dry
Chollerick humours, or thy wine-wet humours; ha?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: You'r pleasant, but Fabrito know I am not in the wood of
Suffering jest.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: If you be not i'th mood I hope you will not be moody
But truely I cannot blame the Gentlewoman, you stood evesdropping,
Under their window, and would not come up.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Sir, I suspect now, by your idle talke
Your hand was in't, which if I once believe,
Be sure you shall account to me.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: The Gentlewomen and the Maides have counted to you already
The next turne I see is mine.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Let me dye but this is very strange; good Fabritio
Do not provoake me so.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Provoke you? you'r growne the strongest fellow; ther's no
Keeping company with you, phish; take you that.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
prose: O all the Devills? stand Slave.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: follow me if thou dar'st.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
prose: Stay coward, stay.—

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Be ready for I see Fabritio running,
And Jacamo behind him.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Wher's the place.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
prose: That way Fabritio.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Where art thou treacher?
What is the matter Sirs?
Why do you hold me? I am basely wrong'd,
Torture, and hell, be with you; let me go.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Good Iacamo be patient, and but heare
What I can say, you know I am your friend,
If you yet doubt it, by my soule I am.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: S'death stand away;
I would my breath were poyson.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: As I have life that which was throwne on you,
And this now done, were but to draw you hither
For causes weighty, that concerne your selfe
Uoid of all malice, which this Maid my Sister
Shall tell you.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Puh, a pox upon you all; you will not hold me
For ever here, and till you let me go,
I'le talke no more.

speeches.speaker: Franck.
verse: As you'r a Gentleman
Let not this boldnesse make me be beleev'd,
To be immodest; If there were a way
More silently to be acquainted with you
God knowes, that I would choose, But as it is
Take it in plainesse: I do love you more
Then you do your content, If you refuse
To pitty me, I'le never cease to weepe,
And when mine eyes be out I will be told
How fast the teares I shed for you do fall,
And if they do not flow abundantly,
I'le fetch a sigh shall make 'em start, and leap,
As if the fire weare under.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Fine mocking, fine mocking.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Mocking? looke how she weepes.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Do's she counterfeit crying too.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Behold how the teares flow, or pitty her
Or never more be call'd a man.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: How's this? soft you, soft you my Masters: Is't possible thinke you,
She should be in earnest?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Earnest? I in earnest: she's a foole to breake so many sleepes,
That would have been sound ones, & venture such a face, &
So much life, for ere an humorous asse i'th world.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Why Clora? I have knowne you cry as much?
For Julio, that has not halfe his worth,
All night you write and weepe too much I feare
I do but what I should.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: If I do write
I am answer'd Franck.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I would I might be so.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Good Fredrick let me go I would faine trye
If that thing do not counterfeit.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Give me your Sword then.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: No, but take my word,
As I am man, I will not hurt a creature
Under this roofe, before I have deliver'd
My selfe, as I am now into your handes,
Or have your full consent.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: It is enough.

speeches.speaker: Ja
verse: Gentlwoman, I pray you let me fele your face; I am an
Infidell, if she do not weepe: Stay, wher's my handkerchife?
I'le wipe the old wett off, the fresh teares come, pox on't
I am a handsome, gratious fellow amongst women, and
Knew't not Gentlewoman; how should I know these
For me? Is not your Mother dead?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: By heaven they are for you.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Slight I'le have my head corld, and powderd to teares are morrow
By breake of day; If you love me, I pray you kisse me,
For If I love you, it shall be such love, as I will not be
A sham'd of, If this be a mock—
It is the hartiest, and the sweetest mock
That ere I tasted, mock me so againe

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Fy Iacamo? why do you let her kneele
So long?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: It's true I had forgot it
And should have done this twelve-moneth; pray you rise
Fredrick, If I could all this while have been perswaded she could
Have lov'd me, dost thou thinke I had not rather kisse her
Then another should? and yet you may gull me for ought
I know, but if you do, hell take me If I do not cutt
All your throates sleeping.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Oh do not thinke of such a thing.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Otherwise, If she be in earnest, the short is I am.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Alas, I am.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: And I did not think it possible any woman
Could have lik'd this face, it's good for nothing, is't?

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: Yes it's worth forty shillings to pawne, being lind almost quite
Through with velvet.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: 'Tis better then your Iulio's.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Thou thinkest so,
But otherwise, in faith it is not Franck

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Hist Iacamo; How do'st thou Boy? ha?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Why very well, I thank you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Do'st thou perceive the reason of matters, and passages,
Yet Sirah, or no?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: 'Tis wondrous good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I have done simply for you, but now you are beatten to some
Understanding, I pray you dally not with the Gentlewoman
But dispatch your Matrimony, with all convenient speed.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: He gives good counsell.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: And I will follow it.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: And I you, prethee do not take it unkindly,
For trust me I boxt thee for thy advancement,
A foolish desire I had to joggle thee into preferment.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: I apprehend you Sir, & if I can study out a course
How a bastinadoing may any waies raise your fortunes
In the State, you shall be sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Oh Sir keepe your way, God send you much joy.

speeches.speaker: Clor.
verse: And me my Iulio.
O God I heare his voyce, now he is true,
Have at a marriage Franck, as soone as you

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Sir I would speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What is your hasty busines friend?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: The Duke commandes your present attendance at Court.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: The cause?

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: I know not in particular; but this
Many are sent for more, about affaires
Forraigne I take it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I will be there
Within this houre, returne my humble service.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: I will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Farewell friend, what new's with you?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: My Mistris would desire you Sir to follow
With all the hast you can, she is gon to Church,
To marry Captaine Iacamo, and Iulio,
To do as much for the young merry Gentlewoman,
Faire Mistris Clora.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Julio, marry Clora?
Thou art deceiv'd I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: No sure Sir,
I saw their lips as close upon the bargaine
As Cockles.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Give 'em joy, I cannot now goe,
The Duke hath sent for me in hast.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: This note Sir: when you are free, will bring you where they are.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You shall finde us all at Signeur Angilo's,
Where Piso, and the worthy Lelia
Of famous memory are to be married,
And we not far behinde.
Would I had time
To wonder at this last couple in hell.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: You are staid for Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I come, pray God the businesse
Hold me not from this sport, I would not loose it.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: God give you joy, and make you live together
A happy paire.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: I do not doubt we shall.
There was never poore Gentleman had such a sodaine fortune,
I could thrust my head betwixt 2. pales, & strip me out of
My old skin like a Snake: will the guests come thou saidst
Thou sentest for to solemnize the Nuptials?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: They will, I looke for em ere this.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: By your leave all.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: They'r here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Especially faire Lady
I aske your pardon, to whose marriage bed
I wish all good successe, I have here brought you
Such guests as can discerne your happinesse,
And best do know how to rejoyce at it;
For such a fortune they themselves have run,
The worthy Iacamo, and his faire Bride,
Noble Fabritio, whom this age of peace
Has not yet aught to love ought but the warrs,
And his true friends, this Lady who is but
A piece of me.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Sir, you are welcome all,
Are they not Sir?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Bring in some wine, some of the wine Lodwick the foole.
Sent hither: who ever thou bid'st welcome shall finde it

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: An unexpected honour you have done
To our too hasty wedding.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Faith Madam, our weddings were as hasty as yours
We'ar glad to run up & downe any whether, to see where
We can get meat to our wedding.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: That Lodwick hath provided too, good Asse.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: I thought you Iulio, would not thus have stollen a marriage
Without acquainting your friends.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Why I did give thee incklings.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: If a marriage should be thus slubberd up in a play, er'e almost
Any body had taken notice you were in love, the Spectators
Would take it to be but ridiculous.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: This was the first, and I will never hide
An other secret from you.

speeches.speaker: Father.
verse: Sir, yonder's your friend Lodwick, hide your selfe
And 'twill be the best sport—

speeches.speaker: Piso
verse: Gentlemen, I pray you take no notice, I'm here.
The coxcomb Lodwick is coming in.

speeches.speaker: Lodwick.
verse: Is that that Lady?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: That is my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: As I live she's a faire one; what make al these heere?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: O Lord Sir she is so pesterd—

speeches.speaker: Fab.
prose: Novv vvill the sport be, it runnes right as Iulio told us

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Faire Lady health to you; some vvords I have, that
Require an utterance more private,
Then this place can afford.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I'le call my husband
All businesse I heare vvith his eares novv.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Good Madam no, bet I perceive your jest,
You have no husband, I am the very man
That vvalk'd the streetes so comely.

speeches.speaker: Lel
verse: Are you so?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Yes faith, vvhen Cupid first did prick your heart
I am not cruell, but the love began
I'th Street I'le satisfie i'th chamber fully.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: To aske a Madman vvhether he be mad
Were but an idle question, if you be,
I do not speake to you, but if you be not
Walke in the Streetes againe and there perhaps
I may dote on you, here I not endure you.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Good Madam stay do not you know this Ring?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Yes it vvas mine, I sent it by my Man,
To change and so he did, it has a blemish,
And this he brought me for it; did you change it?
Are you a Goldsmith?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Sure the world is mad,
Sirrah, did you not bring me this ring from your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Yes surely Sir, did I, but your worship must ev'n beare with me;
For there was a mistaking in it, and so: as I was
Saying to your worship, my Lady is now married.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Married? to whom?

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: To your worships friend Piso.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: S'death to Piso?

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: within. Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: Yes Sir I can assure you she's maried to him, I saw't
With these gray eyes.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Why what a Rogue art thou then? thou hast made
Me send in provision too.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: O a Gentleman should not have such fowle wordes in's mouth
But your Worships provision could not have come in at a fitter time;
Will it please you to tast any of your owne wine?
It may be the Vintner has cozend you.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Pox I am mad.

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: You have alwayes plots Sir, & see how they fall out.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: You had a plott upon me, how do you like this?

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: I do not speake to you.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Because you dare not.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
prose: But I will have one of that old Rogues teeth sett in this Ring

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: Do'st not thou know that I can beate thee?
Dost thou know it now? (discovers himselfe)

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: He beate me once indeed.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: And if you have forgot it, I can call a witnesse.
Come forth Piso—remember you it?

speeches.speaker: Piso
verse: Faith I do call to minde such a matter.

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: And if I cannot still do't, you are young
And will assist your Father in law.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: My Father in law?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
prose: Your Father in law, as sure as this is widow Lelia.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: How widow Lelia?

speeches.speaker: Fath.
verse: I faith 'tis she, Sonne.

speeches.speaker: Lod.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, let my provision go, I am glad I
Have mist the woman.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: Have you put a whore upon me?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: By heaven you do me wrong, I have a heart
As pure as any womans, and I meane
To keep it so for ever.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: There is no starting now, Son, if you offer't
I can compell you, her estate is great,
But all made o're to me, before this match,
Yet if you use her kindly, as I sweare
I thinke she will deserve, you shall enjoy it
During your life, all save some slender piece
I will reserve for my own maintenance,
And if God blesse you with a childe by her,
It shall have all.

speeches.speaker: Piso.
verse: So I may have the meanes
I doe not much care what the woman is:
Come my sweet heart, as long as I shall finde
Thy kisses sweet, and thy meanes plentifull,
Let people talke their tongues out.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: They may talke
Of what is past, but all that is to come
Shall be without occasions.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
prose: Shall we not make Piso, and Lodwick friends?

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Hang'em they dare not be Enemies, or if they be,
The danger is not greate, vvelcome Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Fredrick.
verse: First joy unto you all; and next I think
We shall haue vvarres.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Give me some vvine, I'le drinke to that.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: I'le pledge.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: But I shall loose you then.

speeches.speaker: Iac.
prose: Not a vvhit vvench; I'le teach thee presently to be a Souldier

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Fabritios command, and yours are both restor'd

speeches.speaker: Iac.
verse: Bring me foure glasses then.

speeches.speaker: Fab.
verse: Where are they?

speeches.speaker: Ang.
verse: You shall not drink 'em here, 'tis supper time,
And from my house no creature here shall stir,
These three dayes, mirth shall flow as well as wine.

speeches.speaker: Fa.
verse: Content, within I'le tell you more at large
How much I am bound to all, but most to you,
Whose undeserved liberality
Must not escape thus unrequited,

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: 'Tis happinsse to me, I did so well:
Of every noble action, the intent
Is to give worth reward, vice, punishment.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: IS he then taken?

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: And brought back even now sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: He was not in disgrace?

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: No man more lov'd,
Nor more deserv'd it, being the onely man.
That durst be honest in this Court.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Indeed
We have heard abroad sir, that the State hath suffered,
A great change, since the countesse death.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: It hath sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: My five yeares absence, hath kept me a stranger
So much to all the occurrents of my Country,
As you shall bind me for some short relation
To make me understand the present times.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: I must begin then with a war was made
And seven yeares with all cruelty continued
Upon our Flanders by the Duke of Brabant,
The cause grew thus: during our Earles minority,
Woolfort, (who now usurps) was employed thither
To treat about a match betweene our Earle
And the daughter and Heire of Brabant: during which treaty
The Brabander pretends, this daughter was
Stolne from his Court, by practice of our State,
Though we are all confirm'd, 'twas a sought quarrell
To lay an unjust gripe upon this Earledome,
It being here beleev'd the Duke of Brabant
Had no such losse. This war upon't proclaim'd,
Our Earle, being then a Child, although his Father
Good Gerrard liv'd, yet in respect he was
Chosen by the Countesse favour, for her Husband
And but a Gentleman, and Floriz holding
His right unto this Country from his Mother,
The State thought fit in this defensive war,
Woolfort being then the only man of marke,
To make him Generall.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Which place we have heard
He did discharge with honour.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: I, so long,
And with so blest successes, that the Brabander
Was forc't (his treasures wasted, and the choyce
Of his best men of Armes tyr'd, or cut off)
To leave the field, and sound a base retreat
Back to his Countrey: but so broken both
In minde and meanes, er'e to make head againe,
That hitherto he sitts downe by his losse,
Not daring, or for honour, or revenge
Againe to tempt his fortune. But this Victory
More broke our State, and made a deeper hurt
In Flanders, then the greatest overthrow
She ever receiv'd: For Woolfort, now beholding
Himselfe, and actions in the flattering glasse
Of selfe-deservings, and that cherish't by
The strong assurance of his power, for then
All Captaines of the Army, were his creatures,
The common Souldier too at his devotion,
Made so by full indulgence to their rapines
And secret bounties, this strength too well knowne
And what it could effect, soone put in practice,
As furtherd by the child-hood of the Earle
And their improvidence, that might have peirc't
The heart of his designes, gave him occasion
To sieze the whole, and in that plight you find it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Sir, I receive the knowledge of thus much
As a choyce favour from you

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: Onely I must add
Bruges holds out.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Whether sir, I am going
For there last night I had a ship put in,
And my horse waits me.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: I wish you a good journey.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: What? Hubert stealing from me? who disarm'd him,
It was more then I commanded; take your sword,
I am best guarded with it in your hand,
I have seene you use it nobly.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: And will turne it
On mine owne bosom, ere it shall be drawne
Vnworthily or rudely.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: VVould you leave me
VVithout a farwell Hubert? fly a friend
Vnwearied in his study to advance you?
VVhat have I ev'r possessed which was not yours?
Or either did not court you to command it?
Who ever yet arriv'd to any grace,
Reward or trust from me, but his approaches
Wereby your faire reports of him prefer'd?
And what is more I made my selfe your Servant,
In making you the Master of those secrets
Which not the rack of conscience could draw from me,
Nor I, when I askt mercy, trust my prayers with;
Yet after these assurances of love,
These tyes and bonds of freindship, to forsake me,
Forsake me as an enemie? come you must
Give me a reason.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, and so I will,
If I may do't in privat: and you heare it.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: All leave the roome: you have your will, set downe
And use the liberty of our first friendship.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Friendship? when you prov'd Traitor first, that vanish'd
Nor do I owe you any thought, but hate,
I know my flight hath forfeited my head;
And so I may make you first understand
What a strange monster you have made your selfe,
I welcome it.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: To me this is strange language.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: To you? why what are you?

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: Your Prince and Master,
The Earle of Flaunders.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: By a proper title,
Rais'd to it by cunning circumvention, force,
Blood, and proscriptions.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: And in all this wisedome;
Had I not reason? when by Gerrards plotts
I should haue first been call'd to a strict accop
How, and which way I had consum'd that masse
Of money, as they terme it in the warr,
VVho underhand, had by his Ministers
Detracted my great action, made my faith
And loyalty so suspected in which failing
He sought my life by practice.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: With what fore-head,
Do you speake this to me? who (as I know't)
Must, and will say 'tis false,

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: My guard there.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, you bad me sit, & promis'd you would heare
Which I now say you shall, not a sound more,
For I that am contemner of mine owne,
Am Master of your life; then heer's a Sword
Betweene you, and all aydes Sir, though you blind
The credulous beast, the multitude, you passe not
These grosse untruthes on me.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: How? grosse untruthes.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I, and it is favourable language,
They had bin in a meane man lyes, and foule ones.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: You take strange licence.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Yes, were not those rumours
Of being called unto your answers, spread
By your owne followers; and weake Gerrard wrought
(But by your cunnig practise) to be beleeve
That you were dangerous; yet not to be
Punish'd by any formall course of law,
But first to be made sure, and have your crimes
Layd open after, which your queint traine taking
You fled unto the Campe, and there crav'd humbly
Protection for your innocent life, and that,
Since you had scap'd the fury of the warr,
You might not fall by treason, and for proofe,
You did not for your owne ends make this danger;
Some that had been before, by you subornd,
Came forth and tooke their oathes they had been hir'd
By Gerrard to your murther. This once heard,
And easily beleev'd, th'inraged Souldier
Seeing no further then the outward man,
Snatch'd hastily his Armes, ran to the Court,
Kill'd all that made resistance, cut in pieces
Such as were Servants, or thought friends to Gerrard,
Vowing the like to him.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: Will you yet end?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Which he foreseeing, with his Sonne, the Earle,
Forsooke the Citty; and by secret wayes
As you give out, and we would gladly have it,
Escap'd their fury: though 'tis more then fear'd
They fell among the rest; Nor stand you there
To let us onely mourne, the impious meanes
By which you got it, but your cruelties since
So farr transcend your former bloody ills,
As if compar'd, they onely would appeare
Essayes of mischiefe; do not stop your eares,
More are behind yet.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: O repeat them not,
'Tis hell to heare them nam'd.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: You should have thought,
That hell would be your punishment when you did them,
A Prince, in nothing but your princely lusts,
And boundlesse rapines.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: No more I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Who was the Lord of house or land, that stood
Within the prospect of your coveteous eye?

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: You are in this to me a greater Tyrant,
Then ere I was to any.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I end thus
The generall griefe, now to my private wrong;
The losse of Gerrards daughter Jaqueline:
The hop'd for partner of my lawfull bed,
Your cruelty hath frighted from mine armes;
And her, I now was wandring to recouer.
Thinke you that I had reason now to leave you,
When you are growne so justly odious,
That ev'n my stay here with your grace and favour,
Makes my life ircksome? here surely take it,
And do me but this fruite of all your frendship,
That I may dye by you, and not your hang-man.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: Oh Hubert, these your wordes and reasons have
As well drawne drops of blood from my griev'd hart,
As these teares from mine eyes;
Despise them not
By all that's sacred, I am serious Hubert,
You now have made me sensible, what furyes,
Whips, hangmen, and tormentors a bad man
Do's ever beare about him: let the good
That you this day have done, be ever numberd,
The first of your best actions;
Can you think,
Where Floriz is or Gerrard, or your love,
Or any else, or all that are proscrib'd?
I will resigne, what I usurpe, or have
Unjustly forc'd; the dayes I have to live
Are too too few to make them satisfaction
With any penitence: yet I vow to practise
All of a man.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: O that your hart and tongue
Did not now differ!

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: By my griefes they do not
Nake the good paines to search them out; 'tis worth it,
You have made cleane a Leper: trust me you have,
And made me once more fit for the society,
I hope of good men.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, do not abuse
My aptnesse to beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: Suspect not you
A faith that's built upon so true a sorrow,
Make your owne safetyes: aske them all the ties
Humanity can give, Hemskirick too shall
Along with you to this so wish'd discovery,
And in my name profess all that you promise;
And I will give you this helpe to't: I have
Of late receiv'd certaine intelligence,
That some of them are in or about Bruges
To be found out: which I did then interpret,
The cause of that Townes standing out against me;
But now am glad, it may direct your purpose
Of giving them their safety, and mee peace.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
prose: Be constant to your goodnesse, & you have it.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: T'is much that you deliver of this Goswin.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: But short of what I could, yet have the Country
Confirmd it true, and by a generall oath,
And not a man hazard his credit in it:
He beares himselfe with such a confidence
As if he were the Master of the Sea;
And not a winde upon the Sailers compasse,
But from one part or other, was his factor,
To bring him in the best commodities,
Merchant e're venturd for:
'Tis strange,
And yet;
This do's in him deserve the least of wonder,
Compared with other his peculiar fashions,
Which all admire: he's young, and rich, at least
Thus far reputed so, that since he liv'd
In Bruges, there was never brought to harbour
So rich a Bottome, but his bill would passe
Unquestion'd for her lading.

speeches.speaker: 3 M^r.
verse: Yet he still
Continues a good man.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: So good, that but
To doubt him, would be held an injury
Or rather malice, with the best that traffique;
But this is nothing, a great stocke, and fortune,
Crowning his judgement in his undertakings
May keep him upright that way: But that wealth
Should want the power to make him dote on it,
Or youth teach him to wrong it, best commends
His constant temper; for his outward habit
'Tis sutable to his present course of life:
His table furnish'd well, but not with dainties
That please the appetite only for their rarenesse,
Or the deare price: nor given to wine or women,
Beyond his health, or warrant of a man,
I meane a good one: and so loves his state
He will not hazard it at play; nor lend
Upon the assurance of a well-pen'd Letter,
Although a challenge second the denyall
From such as make th'opinion of their valour
Their meanes of feeding.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: These are wayes to thrive,
And the meanes not curs'd.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: What follows this,
Makes many Venturers with him, in their wishes,
For his prosperity: for when desert
Or reason leads him to be liberall,
His noble mind and ready hand contend
Which can add most to his free curtesies,
Or in their worth, or speed to make them so.
Is there a Virgin of good fame wants dowre?
He is a father to her; or a Souldier
That in his Countreyes service, from the warre
Hath brought him only scars, and want? his house
Receives him, and relieves him, with that care
As if what he posses'd had been laid up
For such good uses, and he steward of it.
But I should loose my selfe to speake him further
And stale in my relation, the much good
You may be witnesse of, if your remove
From Brugis, be not speedy.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: This report
I do assure you will not hasten it,
Nor would I wish a better man to deale with
For what I am to part with.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Never doubt it,
He is your man and ours, only I wish
His too much forwardnesse to embrace all bargains
Sucke him not in the end.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: Have better hopes,
For my part I am confident; here he comes.

speeches.speaker: Flor.
verse: I take it at your own rates: your wine of Cyprus,
But for your Candy sugars, they have met
With such foule weather, and are priz'd so high
I cannot save in them.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mer.
verse: I am unwilling
To seeke another Chap-man: make me offer
Of something near my price, that may assure me
You can deale for them.

speeches.speaker: Flor.
verse: I both can, and will,
But not with too much losse; your bill of lading
Speakes of two hundred chests, valued by you
At thirty thousand gilders. I will have them
At twenty eight; so, in the payment of
Three thousand sterling, you fall only in
Two hundred pound.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mar.
verse: You know, they are so cheape.—

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Why looke you; I'le deale fairly, ther's in prison,
And at your suite, a Pirat, but unable
To make you satisfaction, and past hope
To live a weeke, if you should prosecute
What you can prove against him: set him free,
And you shall have your money to a Stiver,
And present payment.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mar.
verse: This is above wonder,
A Merchant of your ranke, that have at Sea
So many Bottoms in the danger of
These water-Theeves, should be a meanes to save 'em
It more importing you for your owne safety
To be at charge to scoure the Sea of them
Then stay the sword of Justice, that is ready
To fall on one so conscious of his guilt
That he dares not deny it.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: You mistake me,
If you thinke I would cherish in this Captaine
The wrong he did to you, or any man;
I was lately with him, (having first, from others
True testimony been assured, a man
Of more desert never put from the shore)
I read his letters of Mart from this State granted
For the recovery of such losses, as
He had receiv'd in Spain, 'twas that he aim'd at,
Not at three tuns of wine, bisket, or beefe,
Which his necessity made him take from you.
If he had pillag'd you neare, or sunke your ship,
Or thrown your men o'r-boord, then he deserv'd
The Lawes extreamest rigour: But since want
Of what he could not live without, compel'd him
To that he did (which yet our State calls death)
I pitty his misfortune; and to worke you
To some compassion of them, I come up
To your own price: save him, the goods are mine;
If not, seeke else-where, I'le not deale for them.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mar.
verse: Well Sir, for your love, I will once be lead
To change my purpose.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: For your profit rather.

speeches.speaker: 4 Mar.
verse: I'le presently make meanes for his discharge,
Till when, I leave you.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mar.
verse: What do you thinke of this?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mar.
verse: As of a deed of noble pitty: guided
By a strong judgement.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mar.
verse: Save you Master Goswin.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Good day to all.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mar.
verse: We bring you the refusall
Of more Commodities.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Are you the owners
Of the ship that lastnight put into the Harbour?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mar.
verse: Both of the Ship, and lading.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What's the fraught?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mar.
prose: Indico, Quitchineel, choise Chyna stuffs.

speeches.speaker: 3 Mar.
verse: And cloath of Gold brought from Camball.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Rich lading,
For which I were your Chapman, but I am
Already out of cash.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mar.
verse: I'le give you day
For the moiety of all.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How long?

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Sixe moneths.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Tis a faire offer: which (if we agree
About the prizes) I, with thanks accept of,
And will make present payment of the rest;
Some two hours hence I'le come aboord.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: The Gunner shall speake you welcome.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I'le not faile,

speeches.speaker: 3 Mer.
verse: Good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Heaven grant my Ships a safe returne, before
The day of this great payment: as they are
Expected three moneths sooner: and my credite
Stands good with all the world.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Blesse my good Master,
The prayers of your poor Beads-man ever shall
Be sent up for you.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: God 'a mercy Clause,
Ther's something to put thee in minde hereafter
To thinke of me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: May he that gave it you
Reward you for it, with encrease, good Master.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I thrive the better for thy prayers.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I hope so.
This three yeares have I fed upon your bounties,
And by the fire of your blest charity warm'd me,
And yet, good Master, pardon me, that must,
Though I have now receiv'd your almes, presume
To make one sute more to you.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What is't Clause?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Yet do not think me impudent I beseech you,
Since hitherto your charity hath prevented
My begging your reliefe, 'tis not for money
Nor cloaths (good Master) but your good word for me.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose: That thou shalt have, Clause, for I think thee honest.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: To morrow then (dear Mr.) take the trouble
Of walking early unto Beggars Bush,
And as you see me, among others (Brethren
In my affliction) when you are demanded
Which you like best among us, point out me,
And then passe by, as if you knew me not.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: But what will that advantage thee?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: O much Sir,
'Twill give me the preheminence of the rest,
Make me a King among 'em, and protect me,
From all abuse, such as are stronger, might
Offer my age; Sir, at your better leizure
I will informe you further of the good
It may do to me.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Troth thou mak'st me wonder;
Have you a King and Common-wealth among you?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: We have, & there are States are governd worse.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Ambition among Beggars?

speeches.speaker: Ger
verse: Many great ones
Would part with halfe their States, to have the place,
And credit to beg in the first file, Master:
But shall I be so much bound to your furtherance
In my Petition?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: That thou shalt not misse of,
Nor any worldly cane make me forget it,
I will be early there.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Heaven blesse my Master.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: COme Princes of the ragged regiment,
You 'o the blood, Prig my most upright Lord,
And these (what name or title, e're they beare)
Jarkman, or Patrico, Cranke, or Clapperdudgeon.
Frater, or Abram-man; I speake to all
That stand in faire Election for the title
Of King of Beggars, with the command adjoyning,
Higgen, your Orator, in this Inter-regnum,
That whilom was your Dommerer, doth beseech you
All to stand faire, and put your selves in ranke,
That the first Commer, may at his first view
Make a free choise, to say up the question.

speeches.speaker: Fer. Pr.
verse: 'Tis done Lord Higgen.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Thankes to Prince Prig, Prince Ferret.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Well, pray my Masters all, Ferret be chosen
Ye'ar like to have a mercifull mild Prince of me.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A very tyrant, I, an arrant tyrant.
If e're I come to reigne; therefore looke to't,
Except you do provide me hum enough
And Lour to bouze with: I must have my Capons
And Turkeys brought me in, with my green Geese,
And Ducklings i'th season: fine fat chickens,
Or if you chance where an eye of tame Phesants
Or Partridges are kept, see they be mine,
Or straight I seize on all your priviledge,
Places, revenues, offices, as forfeit,
Call in your crutches, wooden legs, false bellyes,
Forc'd eyes and teeth, with your dead arms; not leave you
A durty clout to beg with o' your heads,
Or an old rag with Butter, Frankinsence,
Brimstone and Rozen, birdlime, blood, and creame,
To make you an old sore; not so much sope
As you may fome with i'th Falling-sicknesse;
The very bag you beare, and the brown dish
Shall be escheated. All your daintiest dells too
I will deflowr, and take your dearest Doxyes
From your warme sides; and then some one cold night
I'le watch you what olde barne you goe to roost in,
And there I'le smoother you all i'th musty hay.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: This is tyrant-like indeed: But what would Ginkes
Or Clause be here, if either of them should raigne?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Best aske an asse, if he were made a Camell,
What he would be; or a dog, and he were a Lyon.

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: I care not what you are, Sirs, I shall be
A Begger, still, I am sure, find my selfe there.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: O here a Judge comes.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Cry, a Judge, a Judge.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What aile you Sirs? what means this out cry?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Master
A sort of poor soules met: Gods fools, good Master,
Have had some little variance amongst our selves
Who should be honestest of us; and which lives
Uprightest in his call: Now, 'cause we thought
We ne're should gree on't our selves, because
Indeed 'tis hard to say: we all dissolv'd, to put it
To whom that should come next, and that's your Mastership,
Who, I hope, will termine it as your mind serves you,
Right, and no otherwise we aske it: which?
Which does your Worship thinke is he? sweet Master
Looke over us all, and tell us; we are seven of us,
Like to the seven wise Masters, or the Planets.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I should judge this the man with the grave beard,
And if he be not—

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Blesse you, good Master, blesse you.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I would he were: there's something too, amongst you
To keep you all honest.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: King of heaven goe with you.

speeches.speaker: Omn.
verse: Now good reward him,
May he never want it, to comfort still the poor, in a good houre.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: What is 't? see: Snap ha's got it.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: A good crown, marry:

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A crown of gold.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: For our new King: good luck.

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: To the common treasury with it; if 't be gold,
Thither it must.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Spoke like a Patriot, Ferret—
King Clause. I bid God save thee first, first, Clause,
After this golden token of a crowne;
Wher's Oratour Higgen with his gratuling speech now,
In all our names?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Here he is pumping for it.

speeches.speaker: Gin.
verse: H' has cough'd the second time, 'tis but once more
And then it comes.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: So, out with all: expect now—

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: That thou art chosen, venerable Clause,
Our King and Soveraign; Monarch o'th Maunders.
Thus we throw up our Nab-cheats, first for joy,
And then our filches; last, we clap our fambles,
Three subject signes, we do it without envy:
For who is he here did not wish thee chosen
Now thou art chosen? aske 'em: all will say so,
Nay swear't: 'tis for the King, but let that passe;
When last in conference at the bouzing ken
This other day we sate about our dead Prince
Of famous memory: (rest, goe with his rags:)
And that I saw thee at the tables end,
Rise mov'd, and gravely leaning on one Crutch,
Lift the other like a Scepter at my head,
I then presag'd thou shortly wouldst be King
And now thou art so: but what need presage,
To us, that might have read it, in thy beard,
As well, as he that chose thee? by that beard
Thou wert found out, and mark'd for Soveraignty.
O happy beard! but happier Prince, whose beard,
Was so remark'd, as marked out our Prince,
Not bating us a haire. Long may it grow,
And thick, and faire, that who lives under it,
May live as safe, as under Beggars Bush,
Of which this is the thing, that but the type.

speeches.speaker: Om.
verse: Excellent, excellent oratour, forward good Higgen
Give him leave to spit: the fine, well-spoken Higgen.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: This is the beard, the bush, or bushy-beard,
Under whose gold and silver raigne 'twas said
So many ages since, we all should smile
On impositions, taxes, grievances,
Knots in a State, and whips unto a Subject,
Lye lurking in this Beard, but all hem'd out:
If now, the Beard be such, what is the Prince
That owes the Beard? a Father; no, a Grandfather;
Nay the great Grand-father of you his people.
He will not force away your hens, your bacon,
When you have ventur'd hard for't, nor take from you
The fattest of your puddings: under him
Each man shall eate his own stolne eggs, and butter,
In his owne shade, or sun-shine, and enjoy
His owne deare Dell, Doxy, or Mort, at night
In his own straw, with his owne shirt, or sheet,
That he hath filch'd that day, I, and possesse
What he can purchase, backe, or belly-cheats
To his own prop: he will have no purveyers
For Pigs, and poultry.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: That we must have, my learned Oratour,
It is our will, and every man to keep
In his own path and circuite.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Do you heare?
You must hereafter maund on your own pads he saies.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: And what they get there, is their owne, besides
To give good words.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Do you marke? to cut bene whids,
That is the second Law.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: And keepe a-foote
The humble, and the common phrase of begging,
Lest men discover us.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes; and cry sometimes,
To move compassion: Sir, there is a table,
That doth command all these things, and enjoyns 'em;
Be perfect in their crutches: their fain'd plaisters,
And their true pas-ports, with the ways to stammer,
And to be dumb, and deafe, and blind, and lame,
There, all the halting paces are set downe,
I'th learned language.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Thither I refer them,
Those, you at leisure shall interpret to them,
We love no heapes of lawes, where few will serve.

speeches.speaker: Om.
prose: O gracious Prince, 'save, 'save the good K. Clause.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: A Song to crowne him.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Set a Centinell out first.

speeches.speaker: Sn.
verse: The word?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
prose: A Cove comes, and fumbumbis to it.—

verse: CAst our Caps and cares away: this is Beggars Holli-day,
At the Crowning of our King, thus we ever dance & sing.
In the world looke out and see: where so happy a Prince as he?
Where the Nation live so free, and so merry as do we?
Be it peace, or be it war, here at liberty we are,
And enjoy our ease and rest; To the field we are not prest;
Nor are called into the Towne, to be troubled with the Gowne.
Hang all Offices we cry, and the Magistrate too, by;
When the Subsidies encreast, we are not a penny ceast.
Nor will any goe to law, with the Beggar for a straw.
All which happinesse he brags, he doth owe unto his rags.

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: A Cove: Fumbumbis.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: To your postures; arme:

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Yonder's the Towne: I see it.

speeches.speaker: Hemsk.
verse: Ther's our danger
Indeed afore us, if our shadows save not.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Blesse your good Worships:

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: One small piece of money.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Amongst us all poore wretches:

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Blinde, and lame,

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: For his sake that gives all.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Pittifull Worships;

speeches.speaker: Snap.
verse: One little doyt.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: King, by your leave, where are you?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: To buy a litle bread,

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: To feed so many
Mouths, as will ever pray for you.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Here be seven of us.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Seven, good Master, ô remember seven,
Seven blessings.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Remember, gentle Worship.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Gainst seven deadly sins,

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And seven sleepers.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: If they be hard of heart, and will give nothing—
Alas, we had not a charity this three dayes.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Ther's amongst you all?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Heaven reward you.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Lord, reward you?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The Prince of pitty blesse thee.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Do I see? or is't my fancy that would have it so?
Ha? 'tis her face: come hither Maid.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: What ha', you
Bells for my squirrell? I ha' giv'n Bun meat,
You do not love me, do you? catch me a butterfly,
And I'le love you againe; when? can you tell?
Peace, we go a birding: I shall have a fine thing.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Her voyce too sayes the same; but for my head
I would not that her manners, were so chang'd,
Heare me thou honest fellow; what's this Mayden,
That lives amongst you here?

speeches.speaker: Gincks.
verse: Ao, ao, ao, ao.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: How? nothing but signes?

speeches.speaker: Gin.
verse: Ao, ao, ao, ao.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This strange,
I would saine have it her, but not her thus.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
prose: He is de-de-de-de-de-de-deafe, and du-du-dude—dumb Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Slid they did all speak plain ev'n now me thought
Do'st thou know this same Maid?

speeches.speaker: Sn.
verse: Why, why, why, why, which, gu, gu, gu, gu, Gods foole
She was bo-bo-bo-bo-borne at the barne younder,
By-be-be-be-be-Beggars Bush-bo-bo-Bush
Her name is, My-my-my-my-my-match: so was her Mo-mo-mo-Mothers too-too

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I understand no word she sayes; how long
Has she been here?

speeches.speaker: Sn.
prose: Lo-lo-long enough to be ni-ni-nigled: and she ha' go-go-go-good luck,

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I must be better inform'd, then by this way.
Here was another face too, that I mark'd
O the old mans: but they are vanish'd all
Most sodainly: I will come here againe,
O, that I were so happy, as to finde it,
What I yet hope? it is put on.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What meane you Sir,
To stay there with that stammerer?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Farewell friend,—
It will be worth returne, to search: Come,
Protect us our disguize now, pre'thee Hemskirck
If we be taken, how do'st thou imagine
This Towne will use us, that hath stood so long
Out, against Woolfort?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Ev'n to hang us forth
Upon their walls a sunning, to make Crowes meate,
If I were not assur'd 'o the Burgomaster,
And had a pretty skuys, to see a niece there,
I should scarce venture.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Come 'tis now too late
To looke back at the ports: good luck, and enter.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Still blow'st thou there? and from all other parts,
Do all my Agents sleepe? that nothing comes?
Ther's a conspiracy of windes, and servants:
If not of Elements, to ha' me breake;
What should I thinke unlesse the Seas, and Sandes
Had swallow'd up my ships? or fire had spoyl'd
My ware-houses? or death devour'd my Facto
I must ha' had some returnes;

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: 'Saue you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Save you.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: No newes, yet 'o your Ships?

speeches.speaker: o.
verse: Not any yet Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: 'Tis strange.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Tis true Sir: what a voyce was here now?
This was one passing bell, a thousand ravens
Sung in that man now, to presage my ruines.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
prose: Goswin, good day, these winds, are very constant.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: They are so Sir; to hurt—

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: Ha? you had no letters,
Lately from England, nor from Denmark?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Neither.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: This winde brings them; nor no newes over land,
Through Spaine, from the Straights?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Not any.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: I am sorry Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: They talke me downe: and as 'tis said, of Vultures
They sent a feild fought, and do smell the carkasses
By many hundred miles: So do these, my wracks
At greater distances: why thy will heaven
Come on, and be: yet if thou please, preserve me;
But in my owne adventure, here at home,
Of my chast love, to keep me worthy of her,
It shall be put in scale against all ill fortunes:
I am not broken yet: nor should I fall,
Me thinkes with lesse then that, that ruines all.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Captaine you are welcome; so is this your friend
Most safely welcome, though our Towne stand out
Against your Master; you shall finde good quarter:
The troth is, we not love him: Meg: some wine,
Let's talke a little treason, If we can
Talk treason, gain' the Traitors; by your leave, Gentlemen
We here in Brugis, thinke he do's usurpe,
And therefore I am bold with him.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, your boldnesse,
Happely becomes your mouth, but not our eares,
While we are his servants; And as we come here,
Not to aske questions, walke forth on your walls;
Visit your courtes of guard, view your Munition,
Aske of your corne-provisions, nor enquire
Into the least, as spies upon your strengthes,
So let's entreate, we may receive from you
Nothing in passage or discourse, but what
We may with gladnesse, and our honesties here,
And that shall seale our welcome.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Good: let's drinke then,

speeches.speaker: Mage:
verse: fill out, I keep mine old pearle still Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I hang fast man.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Old Iewels, commend their keeper, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Heer's to you with a hart, my Captaines friend,
With a good heart, and if this make us speake
Bold words, anon: 'tis all under the Rose
Forgotten: drowne all memory, when we drinke

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: 'Tis freely spoken noble Burgomaster,
I'le do you right.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Nay Sir mine heire Van-dunck,
Is a true Statesmen.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Fill my Captaines cup there, ô that your Master Woolfort.
Had been an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Under the Rose.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Heer's to you Marget.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Welcom; welcom Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Well said my pearle still,

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Well said, my pearl still,

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: And how does my Niece?
Almost a woman; I thinke? This friend of mine,
I drew along with me, through so much hazard,
Only to see her: she was my errand.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I, a kinde Uncle you are (fill him his glasse)
That in seven yeares, could not find leizure.—

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No,
It's not so much.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I'le bate you nev'r an houre on't,
I was before the Brabander gan his war,
For moone-shine, i'th water there, his daughter
That never was lost: yet you could not finde time
To see a Kinswoman: But shee is worth the seeing Sir.
Now you are come, you aske if she were a woman?
Shee is a woman Sir; fetch her forth Margee.
And a fine woman, and has Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: How?
What Suitors are they.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Bachellors: young Burgers:
And one, a gallant, the young Prince of Merchants,
We call him here, in Bruges.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: How? a Merchant?
I thought Van-doncke, you had understood me better,
And my Niece too, so trusted to you by me:
Then t'admit of such in name of Suitors.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Such? he is such a such, as were she mine
I'de give him thirty thousand crownes with her.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
prose: But the same things Sir, fit not you and me.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Why, give's some wine, then; This will fit us all:
Here's to you still, my Captains friend: All out:
And still, would Woolfort were an honest man,
Under the Rose, I speake it: but this Merchant
Is a brave boy: he lives so, i'the towne here,
We know not what to thinke on him: At sometimes
We feare he will be Bankrupt; he do's stretch
Tenter his credite so; embraces all,
And too't, the winds have been contrary, long.
But then, if he should have all his returnes,
We thinke he would be a King, and are halfe sure on't.
Your Master is a Traytor, for all this
Under the Rose: here's to you; and usurps
The Earldome ftom a better man.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I marry Sir,
Where is that man?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Nay soft: and I could tell you
'Tis ten to one I would not: here's my hand,
I love not Woolfort: sit you still, with that:
Here comes my Captaine againe, and his fine Niece,
And ther's my Merchant: view him well, fill wine here.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You must not only know me for your Uncle,
Now, but obey me; you, goe cast your selfe
Away, upon a dunghill here? a Merchant?
A petty fellow? one that makes this trade
With oathes and perjuries?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What is that you say Sir?
If it be me you speake of; as your eye
Seemes to direct: I wish you would speake to me, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Sir, I do say, she is no Merchandize,
Will that suffice you?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Merchandize good Sir,
Though ye be Kinsman to her: take no leave thence
To use me with contempt: I ever thought
Your Niece above all price.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: And do so still, Sir,
I assure you, her rate's at more then you are worth.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: You do not know, what a Gentleman's worth sir,
Nor can you value him.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Well said Merchant.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Nay,
Let him alone, and ply your matter.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: A Genntleman?
What, o' the wool-pack? or the Sugar-chest?
Or lists of Velvet? which is't? pound, or yard,
You vent your Gentry by?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: O Hemskirke, fye.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Come, do not mind 'em drink, he is no Woolfort,
Captaine, I advise you.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Alas, my pretty man,
I think't be angry, by its looke: Come hither,
Turne this way, a little: if it were the blood
Of Charlemaine, as 't may (for ought I know)
Be some good Botchers issue, here in Bruges.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Nay: I'me not certaine of that; of this I am,
If it once buy, and sell, its Gentry is gone.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Ha, ha:

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You are angry, though ye laugh.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No, now 'tis pitty
Of your poor argument. Do not you, the Lords,
Of land (if you be any) sell the grasse,
The corne, the straw, the milke, the cheese?

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: And butter:
Remember butter; doe not leave out butter.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: The Beefs and Muttons that your grounds are stor'd with?
Swine, with the very mast, beside the woods?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No, for those sordid uses, we have Tenants,
Or else our Bayliffs.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Have not we Sir, Chap-men,
And Factors, then to answer these? your errour
Fetch'd from the Heralds A B C. and said over
With your Court faces, once an houre, shall never
Make me mistake my selfe. Do not your Lawyers
Sell all their practise, as your Priests their prayers?
What is not bought, and sold? The company
That you had last, what had you fort, y'faith?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You now grow sawcy.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Sure I have been bred
Still, with my honest liberty, and must use it.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Upon your equals, then.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Sir, he that will
Provoke me first, doth make himselfe my equall.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Do ye heare? no more.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Yes Sir, this little, I pray you,
And't shall be aside, then after, as you please,
You appeare the Uncle, s^ir, to her I love,
More then mine eyes; and I have heard your scorns
With so much scoffing, and so much shame,
As each strive which is greater: But, beleeve me
I suck'd not in this patience with my milke.
Do not presume, because you see me young,
Or cast despights on my profession
For the civility and tamenesse of it.
A good man beares a contumely worse
Then he would do an injury. Proceed not
To my offence: wrong is not still successefull,
Indeed it is not: I would approach your Kins-woman
With all respect, done to your selfe and her.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Away Companion: handling her? take that.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Nay, I do love no blows, sir, there's exchange.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Hold sir,

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: O murther.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Help, my Goswin.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Man.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Let 'em alone; my life for one.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Nay come
If you have will.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: None to offend you, I, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: He that had, thank himself: not hand her? yes Sir,
And claspe her, and embrace her; and (would she
Now goe with me) bear her through all her race,
Her Father, Brethren, and her Uncles, arme'd,
And all their Nephews, though they stood a wood
Of pikes, and wall of Canon: kisse me Gertrude,
Quake not, but kisse me.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Kisse him, girle, I bid you;
My Merchant royall; feare no Uncles: hang 'em,
Hang up all Uncles: Are we not in Bruges?
Under the Rose here?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: In this circle, Love,
Thou are as safe, as in a towre of brasse;
Let such as do wrong, feare.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I, that's good,
Let Woolfort looke to that.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Sir, here she stands,
Your Niece, and my beloved. One of these titles
She must apply to; if unto the last,
Not all the anger can be sent unto her,
In frowne, or voyce, or other art, shall force her,
Had Hercules a hand in't: Come, my Joy,
Say thou art mine, aloud Love, and professe it.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Doe: and I drinke to it.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Prethee say so, Love.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: 'Twould take away the honour from my blushes:
Doe not you play the Tyrant, sweet: they speake it.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I thanke you Niece.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Sir, thanke her for your life,
And fetch your sword within.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You insult too much
With your good fortune, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: A brave cleare spirit;
Hemskirke, you were too blame: a civill habit
Oft covers a good man: and you may meete
In person of a Merchant, with a soule
As resolute, and free, and all wayes worthy,
As else in any file of man-kinde: pray you,
What meant you so to slight him?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: 'Tis done now,
Aske no more of it; I must suffer.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This,
Is still the punishment of rashnesse, sorrow;
Well; I must to the woods, for nothing here
Will be got out. There, I may chance to learne
Somewhat to help my enquiries further.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Ha?
A Looking-glasse.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: How now, brave Burgo-master?

speeches.speaker: Van.
prose: I love no Woolforts, and my names Vandoncke,

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Van-drunke it's rather: Come, go sleep within.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Earle Florez is right heir, and this same Woolfort
Under the Rose I speake it. —

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Very hardly.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Usurpes: and a ranke Traitor, as ever breath'd,
And all that do uphold him. Let me goe,
No man shall hold me, that upholds him;
Doe you uphold him?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Then hold me up.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Sir, I presume, you have a sword of your owne,
That can so handle anothers.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Faith you may Sir.

speeches.speaker: He.
verse: And ye have made me have so much better thoughts of you
As I am bound to call you forth.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: For what Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: To the repairing of mine honour, & hurt here.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Expresse your way.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: By fight, and speedily.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: You have your will: Require you any more?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: That you be secret: and come single.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: As you are the Gentlema~ you would be thought.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Without the Conjuration: and I'le bring
Only my sword, which I will fit to yours,
I'le take his length within.

speeches.speaker: Hem
