verse: Your place now Sir?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: By the Sand-hills.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Sir, nearer to the woods,
If you thought so, were fitter.

speeches.speaker: Flor.
verse: There, then.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: good.
Your time?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Twixt seven and eight.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You'l give me Sir
Cause to report you worthy of my Niece,
If you come, like your promise.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: If I do not
Let no man think to call me unworthy first,
I'le doe't my selfe: and justly wish to want her.—

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
prose: COme, English beer Hostess, English beer bi'th belly

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Start beer boy, stout & strong beer: so, sit downe Lads,
And drinke me upsey-Dutch:
Frollicke, and feare not.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Have ye any worke for the Sow-gelder, boa,
My horne goes to high to low, to high to low.
Have ye any Piggs, Calves, or Colts,
Have ye any Lambs in your holts
To cut for the Stone
Here comes a cunning one.
Have ye any braches to spade,
Or e're a faire maide
That would be a Nun,
Come kisse me, 'tis done.
Harke how my merry borne doth blow,
Too high too low, too high too low.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: O excellent! two-pence a piece boyes, two-pence a piece:
Give the boys some drink there. Piper, wet your whistle.
Canst tell me a way now, how to cut off my wives Concupiscence?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I'le sing ye a Song for't.
prose:
The Song.
TAke her, and hug her,
And turn her & tug her,
And turn her again boy, again,
Then if she mumble,
Or if her taile tumble,
Kisse her amain boy, amain.
Do thy endeavour,
To take off her feaver,
Then her disease no longer will raign.
If nothing will serve her,
Then thus to preserve her,
Swinge her amain boy amaine.
Give her cold jelly
To take up her belly,
And once a day swinge her again
If she stand all these paines
Then knock out her brains,
Her disease no longer will reign.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bo.
verse: More excellent, more excellent, sweet Sow-gelder.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bo.
verse: Three-pence a peice, three-pence a peice.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Will you heare a Song how the Divel was gelded?

speeches.speaker: 3 Bo.
verse: I, I, lets heare the Divell roare, Sow-gelder.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bo.
verse: Groats a piece, groats a piece, groats a piece,
There sweet Sow-gelder.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Will ye see any feates of activity,
Some sleight of hand, leigerdemaine? hey passe,
Presto, be gone there?

speeches.speaker: 2 Bo.
verse: Sit downe Jugler.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Sirha, play you your art well; draw neer piper:
Looke you, my honest friends, you see my hands;
Plaine dealing is no Divel: lend me some money;
Twelve-pence a piece will serve.

speeches.speaker: 1. 2. B.
verse: There, there.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: I thanke you,
Thanke ye heartily: when shall I pay ye?

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, by'th masse this was a fine trick.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A merry sleight toy: but now I'le shew your Worships
A tricke indeed.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Marke him well now my Masters.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Here are three balls,
These balls shall be three bullets,
One, two, and three: ascentibus malentibus.
Presto, be gone: they are vanish'd: faire play Gentlemen,
Now these three, like 3. bullets, from your three noses
Will I plucke presently: feare not, no harme boyes,
Titere, tu patule.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Oh, oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Recubans sub jermine fagi.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Ye pull too hard; ye pull too hard.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Stand faire then:
Silvertramtrim-tram.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Hold, hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Prig
verse: Come aloft bullets three, with a whim-wham:
Have ye their moneys?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes, yes.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Oh rare Jugler.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Oh admirable Jugler,

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: One tricke more yet;
Hey, come aloft: sa, sa, flim, flum, taradumbis?
East, west, north, south, now flye like Jacke with a bumbis.
Now all your money's gone: pray search your pockets.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Humh.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: He,

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: The Divell a penny's here.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: This was a rare tricke.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: But 'twould be a far rarer to restore it.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: I'le doe ye that too: looke upon me earnestly,
And move not any wayes your eyes from this place,
This button here: pow, whir, whiss, shake your pockets

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: By'th masse 'tis here againe boyes.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Rest ye merry;
My first tricke has paid me.

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: I, take it, take it,
And take some drinke too.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Not a drop now I thanke you;
Away, we are discoverd else.
BRing out your Cony-skins, faire maids to me,
And hold 'em faire that I may see;
Grey, blacke, and blew: for your smaller skins,
I'le give ye looking-glasses, pins.
And for your whole Coney, heer's ready ready money.
Come gentle Jone, do thou begin
With thy blacke, blacke, blacke Cony-skin.
And Mary then, and Jane will follow,
With their silver-hair'd skins, and their yellow.
The white Cony-skin, I will not lay by,
For though it be faint, tis faire to the eye,
The grey it is warme, but yet for my money,
Give me the bonny, bonny blacke Coney.
Come away faire maides, your skins will decay:
Come, and take money maids, put your ware away.
Cony-skins, Cony-skins, have ye any Cony-skins,
I have fine brace-lets, and fine silver pins.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Buy any brand wine, buy any brand wine?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Have ye any Cony-skins.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: My fine Canary-bird, ther's a cake for thy worship,

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Come, fill, fill, fill, fill suddenly: let's see Sir,
What's this?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: A penny Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Fill till't be six-pence,
And there's my pig.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: This is a counter Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: A counter? stay ye, what are these then?
O execrable Jugler! ô damn'd Jugler!
Look in your hose, hoa: this comes of looking forward.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Divell a Dunkirke! what a rogue's this Jugler,
This hey passe, repasse, h'as repast us sweetly.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Doe ye call these tricks.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Have ye any ends of gold or silver.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: This fellow comes to mock us; gold or silver? cry copper.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Yes my good friend,
We have e'ne an end of all we have.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Ts well Sir,
You have the lesse to care for: gold and silver,

speeches.speaker: Pr.
prose: Have ye any old cloaks to sel, have ye any old clokes to sel.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Cloakes? looke about ye boyes: mine's gone.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: A —juggle 'em?
— o' their Prestoes: mine's gone too.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: Here's mine yet.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: Come, come, let's drink then: more brand wine.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: If e're I catch your Sow-gelder, by this hand I'le strip him;
Were ever fooles so ferkt? we have two cloakes yet,
And all our caps; the Divell take the flincher.

speeches.speaker: All B.
verse: Yaw, yaw, yaw, yaw.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Good do'n my honest fellows,
You are merry here I see.

speeches.speaker: 3 B.
verse: 'Tis all we have left Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What hast thou? Aquavitae?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Fill out then,
And give these honest fellows round.

speeches.speaker: All b.
verse: We thanke ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: May I speake a word in private to ye?

speeches.speaker: All b.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I have a businesse for you, honest friends,
If you dare lend your help, shall get you crownes.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Ha?
Lead me a little nearer, boy.

speeches.speaker: 1 B.
verse: What is't Sir?
If it be any thing to purchase money,
Which is our want, command us.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: All, all, all Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You know the young spruce Merchant in Brugis.

speeches.speaker: 2 B.
verse: Who? Master Goswin?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: That: he owes me money,
And here in towne there is no stirring of him.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Say ye so?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: This day, upon a sure appointment,
He meets me a mile hence, by the Chase side
Under the row of Okes, do you know it?

speeches.speaker: All b.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Give 'em more drinke: there if you dare but venture
When I shall give the word to seize upon him,
Here's twenty pound.

speeches.speaker: 3 Boy.
verse: Beware the Jugler.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: If he resist, downe with him, have no mercy.

speeches.speaker: 1 Boy.
verse: I warrrant you: wee'l hamper him.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: To discharge you,
I have a warrant here about me.

speeches.speaker: 3 Boy.
verse: Her's our warrant,
This carries fire i'the tayle.

speeches.speaker: H^m.
verse: Away with me then,
The time draws on,
I must remove so insolent a Suitor,
And if he be so rich, make him pay ransome
Ere he see Bruges towres againe: thus wise men
Repaire the hurts they take by a disgrace,
And piece the Lyons skyn with the Foxes case.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I am glad I have heard this sport yet.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Ther's for thy drink; come pay the house within boyes,
And loose no time.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Away with all our hast too.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No winde blow faire yet? no returne of moneys?
Letters? nor any thing, to hold my hopes up?
Why then 'tis destin'd, that I fall, fall miserably,
My credite I was built on, sinking with me.
Thou boystrous North-wind, blowing my mis-fortunes,
And frosting all my hopes to cakes of coldnesse,
Yet stay thy fury: give the gentle South
Yet leave to court those sailes that bring me safety,
And you auspicious fires, bright twins in heaven
Daunce on the shrowds: he blows still, stubbornly,
And on his boystrous racke rides my sad ruine;
There is no help, there can be now no comfort,
To morrow with the Sun-set sets my credite.
Oh misery! thou curse of man, thou plague,
In the midst all our strength thou strik'st us;
My vertuous Love is toss'd too: all, what I have been,
No more hereafter to be seen then shadow;
To prison now? well, yet ther's this hope left me,
I may sinke fairely under this dayes venture
And so to morrow's cross'd, and all those curses:
Yet manly I'le invite my fate, base fortune
Shall never say, she has cut my throate in feare.
This is the place his challenge call'd me too,
And was a happy one at this time for me,
For let me fall before my foe i'the field,
And not at Bar, before my Creditors,
Ha's kept his word: now Sir, your swords tongue only
Loud as you dare, all other language—

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Well Sir,
You shall not be long troubled: draw.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Tis done Sir,
And now have at ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Now.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Betray'd to Villains?
Slaves ye shall buy me bravely,
And thou base coward.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now upon 'em bravely,
Conjure 'em soundly boyes.

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: Hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Lay on still,
Down with that Gentleman rogue, swinge him to sirrup:
Retire Sir, and take breath: follow and take him,
Take all, 'tis lawfell prize.

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: We yield.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Downe with 'em
Into the wood, and rifile 'em, tew 'em, swinge 'em,
Knocke me their braines into their breeches.

speeches.speaker: Boors.
verse: Hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What these men are I know not, nor for what cause
They shou^d thus thrust themselves into my danger,
Can I imagine. But sure heavens hand was in't,
Nor why this coward knave should deale so basely
To eate me up with slaves: but heaven, I thanke thee,
I hope thou hast reserv'd me to an end
Fit for thy creature, and worthy of thine honour:
Would all my other dangers here had suffered,
With what a joyfull heart should I goe home then?
Wher now, heaven knows, like him that waits his sente~ce
Or heares his passing bell; but ther's my hope still.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Blessing upon you Master.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Thanke ye; leave me,
For by my troth I have nothing now to give thee.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Indeed I do not aske Sir, only it grieves me
To see ye looke so sad; now goodnesse keepe ye
From troubles in your minde.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: If I were troubled
What could thy comfort do? prethee Clause, leave me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good Master be not angry; for what I say
Is out of true love to ye..

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I know thou lov'st me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good Mr. blame that love then, if I prove so sawcy
To aske ye why ye are sad.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Most true, I am so,
And such a sadnesse I have got will sinke me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Heaven shield it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Faith thou must loose thy Master.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I had rather loose my neck Sir: would I knew—

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What would the knowledg do thee good, so miserable,
Thou canst not help thy selfe? when all my ways
Nor all the friends I have—

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: You do not know Sir,
What I can doe: cures sometimes, for mens cares
Flow, where they least expect 'em.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I know thou wouldst doe,
But fare-well Clause, and pray for thy poore Master.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I will not leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I dare not leave ye,
And till ye beate me dead, I must not leave ye.
By what ye hold most pretious, by heavens goodnesse,
As your faire youth may prosper, good Sir tell me:
My minde beleeves yet something's in my power
May ease you of this trouble.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I will tell thee
For a hundred thousand crownes upon my credit,
Taken up of Merchants to supply my traffiques,
The windes and weather envying of my fortune,
And no returne to help me off, yet shewing
To morrow, Clause, to morrow, which must come
In spron, thou shalt finde me poore, and broken.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I cannot blame your griefe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Now, what say'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I say you should not shrinck, for he that gave ye,
Can give you more; his power can bring ye off Sir,
When friends and all forsake ye, yet he sees you.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: That's all my hope.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Hope still Sir, are you tide
Within the compasse of a day, good Master,
To pay this masse of money?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Ev'n to morrow;
But why do I stand mocking of my misery?
Is't not enough the floods, and friends forget me?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Will no lesse serve?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What if it would?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Your patience,
I do not aske to mock ye: 'tis a great sum,
A sum for mighty men to start, and stick at;
But not for honest: have ye no friends left ye,
None that have felt your bounty? worth this duty?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Duty? thou know'st it not.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: It is a duty,
And as a duty, from those men have felt ye,
Should be return'd againe: I have gain'd by ye,
A daily ^lmes these seven yearess you have showr'd me,
Will half^ supply your want.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Why do'st thou foole me?
Can'st thou worke miracles?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: To save my Master,
I can worke this.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Thou wilt make me angry with thee.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: For doing good?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What power hast thou?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Enquire not:
So I can do it, to preserve my Master;
Nay if it be three parts.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: O that I had it,
But good Clause, talke no more, I feele thy charity,
As thou has felt mine: but alas!

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Distrust not.
'Tis that that quenches ye: pull up your spirit,
Your good, your honest, and your noble spirit;
For if the fortunes often thousand people
Can save ye, rest assur'd; you have forgot Sir,
The good ye did, which was the power you gave me;
Ye shall now know the King of Beggars treasure:
And let the windes blow as they please, the Seas roare,
Yet, here to morrow, you shall finde your harbour,
Here faile me not, for if I live I'le fit ye.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How faine I would believe thee.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: If I ly Master,
Believe no man hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I will trye thee,
But he knowes, that knowes all.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Know me to morrow,
And if I know not how to cure ye, kill me;
So passe in peace, my best, my worthiest Master.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Thus have I stolne away disguiz'd from Hemskirck
To try these people, for my heart yet tells me
Some of these Beggars, are the men I looke for
Appearing like my selfe, they have no reason
(Though my intent is faire, my maine end honest)
But to avoyde me narrowly, that face too,
That womans face, how neere it is: ô may it
But prove the same, and fortune how I'le blesse thee;
Thus, sure they cannot know me, or suspect me,
If to my habit I but change my nature;
As I must do; this is the wood they live in,
A place fit for concealement: where, 'till fortune
Crowne me with that I seeke, I'le live amongst 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Come bring 'em out, for here we sit in justice:
Give to each one a cudgell, a good cudgell:
And now attend your sentence, that you are rogues,
And mischeivous base rascalls, (ther's the point now)
I take it, is confess'd.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Deny it if you dare knaves.

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: We are Rogues Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: To amplify the matter then rogues as ye are,
And lamb'd, ye shall be ere we leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And to the open handling of our justice,
Why did ye this upon the proper person
Of our good Master? were you drunk when you did it?

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: Yes indeed were we.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: You shall be beaten sober.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Was it for want you undertooke it?

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: You shall be swing'd aboundantly.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And yet for all that,
You shall be poore rogues still.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Has not the Gentleman,
Pray marke this point Brother Prig, that noble Gentleman
Releiv'd ye often, found ye meanes to live by,
By imploying some at Sea, some here; some there;
According to your callings?

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: 'Tis most true Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Is not the man, an honest man?

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: Yes truly.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: A liberall Gentleman? and as ye are true rascalls
Tell me but this, have ye not been drunk, and often,
At his charge?

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: Often, often.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Ther's the point then,
They have cast themselves, brother Prig.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: A shrew'd point Brother.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Brother, proceed you now; the cause is open,
I am some what weary.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Can you do these things?
You most abhominable stincking Rascalls,
You turnip-eating Rogues.

speeches.speaker: Boores.
verse: We are truly sorry.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Knock at your hard harts Rogues, and presently
Give us a signe you feele compunction,
Every man up with's cudgell, and on his neighbour
Bestow such almes, 'till we shall say sufficient,
For there your sentence lyes without partiality;
Either of head, or hide, Rogues, without sparing,
Or we shall take the paines to beat you dead else:
You shall know your doom.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: One, two, and three about it.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: That fellow in the blew, has true compunction,
He beates his fellowes bravely, oh, well struck boyes,

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Up with that blew breech, now playes he the Divell,
So get ye home, drink small beere, and be honest;
Call in the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Do, bring him presently,
His cause I'le heare my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Prig. With all due reverence,
We do resigne Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now huffing Sir, what's your name?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What's that to you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: It shall be ere we part.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: My name is Hemskirk,
I follow the Earle, which you shall feele.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: No threatning,
For we shall coole you Sir; why did'st thou basely
Attempt the murder of the Merchant Go swin?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What power hast thou to aske me?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I will know it.
Or flea thee till thy paine discover it.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: He did me wrong, base wrong.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: That cannot save ye,
Who sent ye hither? and what further villanies
Have ye in hand?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Why would'st thou know? what profit,
If I had any private way, could rise
Out of my knowledge, to do thee commodity?
Be sorry for what thou hast done, and make amends foole
I'le talke no further to thee: nor these rascalls.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Tye him to that tree.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I have told you whom I follow.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: The Divell you should do, by your villanies,
Now he that has the best way, wring it from him.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I undertake it: turne him to the Sun boyes;
Give me a fine sharpe rush, will ye confesse yet?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Ye have rob'd me already, now you'le murder me

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Murder your nose a little: does your head purge Sir?
To it againe, 'twill do ye good.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Oh,
I cannot tell you any thing.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Proceed then.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Ther's maggots in your nose, I'le fetch em out Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: O my head breakes.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The best thing for the rhewme Sir,
That falls into your worships eyes.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Hold, hold.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Speake then.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I know not what.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: It lyes in 's braine yet,
In lumps it lyes, I'le fetch it out the finest;
What pretty faces the foole makes? heigh!

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Hold,
Hold, and I'le tell ye all, looke in my doublet;
And there within the lining in a paper,
You shall finde all.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Go fetch that paper hither,
And let him loose for this time.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Good ev'n my honest feiends.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good ev'n good fellow.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: May a poore huntsman, with a merry hart,
A voyce shall make the forrest ring about him,
Get leave to live amongst ye? true as steele, boyes?
That knowes all chases, and can watch all howres,
And with my quarter staffe, though the Divell bid stand,
Deale such an almes, shall make him roare again?
Prick ye the fearefull hare through crosse wayes, sheepe walkes
And force the crafty Reimald climb the quiksetts;
Rouse ye the lofty Stag, and with my bell-horne,
Ring him a knell, that all the woods shall mourne him,
'Till in his funerall teares, he fall before me?
The Polcat, Marterne, and the rich skin'd Lucerne,
I know to chase, the Roe, the winde out-stripping
Isgrin himselfe, in all his bloody anger;
I can beate from the bay, and the wild Sounder
Single, and with my arm'd staffe, turne the Boare,
Spight of his fomy tushes, and thus strike him;
'Till he fall downe my feast.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: A goodly fellow.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: What mak'st thou here, ha?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: We accept thy fellowship.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
prose: Hemskirck, thou art not right I feare, I feare thee.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Here is the paper: and as he said we found it.

speeches.speaker: Ger,
verse: Give me it, I shall make a shift yet, old as I am
To finde your knavery: you are sent here, Sirra
To discover certaine Gentlemen, a spy-knave
And if ye finde 'em, If not by perswasion
To bring 'em back, by poyson to dispatch 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: By poyson, ha?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Here is an other, Hubert;
What is that Hubert Sir?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: You may perceive there.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I may perceive a villany and a ranke one,
Was he joyn'd partner of thy knavery?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No.
He had an honest end, would I have had so,
Which makes him scape such cut throates.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: So it seemes,
For here thou art commanded, when that Hubert
Has done his best and worthiest service, this way
To cut his throat, for here he's set downe dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This is most impious.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I am glad we have found ye,
Is not this true?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Yes? what are you the better;

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: You shall perceive Sir, ere you get your fredome:
Take him aside, and friend, we take thee to us,
Into our company, thou dar'st be true unto us?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I, and obedient too?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: As you had bred me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Then take our hand: thou art now a servant to us,
Welcom him all.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Stand off, stand off: I'le do it,
We bid yee welcome three wayes; first for your person,
Which is a promising person, next for your quallity,
Which is a decent, and a gentle quality,
Last for the frequent meanes you have to feed us,
You can steale 'tis to be presum'd.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Yes, venson,
Or if I want —

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Tis well you understand right,
And shall learne dayly: you can drink too?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Soundly.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And ye dare know a woman from a weathercock?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Yes, if I handle her.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now sweare him.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: You are welcom Brother.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Welcom, welcom, welcom, but who shall have the keeping
Of this fellow?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Thank ye friends,
And I beseech ye, if you dare but trust me;
For if I have kept wilde doggs and beastes for wonder,
And made 'em tame too: give into my custody
This roaring rascall I shall hamper him,
With all his knacks and knaveryes, and I feare me
Discover yet a further villany in him;
O he smells ranck 'oth rascall.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Take him to thee,
But if he scape—

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Let me be ev'n hang'd for him,
Roome Sir, I'le tye ye to my leash.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: A way Rascall.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Be not so stubborne: I shall swindge ye soundly,
And ye play tricks with me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now sweare him.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I crowne thy nab, with a gag of benbouse,
And stall thee by the salmon into the clowes,
To mand on the pad, and strike all the cheates;
To mill from the Ruffmans, commision and states,
Twang dell's, i' the stiromell, and let the Quire Cuffin:
And Herman Beck strine, and trine to the Ruffin.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now interpret this unto him.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I powre on thy pate a pot of good ale,
And by the Rogues oth a Rogue thee install:
To beg on the way, to rob all thou meetes;
To steale from the hedge, both the shirt and the sheetes:
And lye with thy wench in the straw till she twang,
Let the Constable, Iustice, and Divell go hang.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: So, now come in,
But ever have an eye Sir, to your prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: He must blinde both mine eyes, if he get from me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Go, get some victualls, and some drink, some good drink
For this day wee'le keep holly to good fortune,
Come and be frollick with us.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: ye are a stanger.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Indeed yae'r welcom: I have hard your scape,
And therefore give her leave, that onely loves you;
(Truely and dearely loves ye) give her joy leave,
To bid ye welcom: what'ist makes you sad man?
Why do you looke so wilde? is 't I offend ye?
Be shrew my heart, not willingly.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No Jertred.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Is't the delay of that ye' long have look'd for,
A happy marriage? now I come to urge it:
Now when ye please to finish it.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No newes yet?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Do you heare Sir?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Do you love me?

speeches.speaker: Flo..
verse: Have I liv'd,
In all the happinesse fortune could seat me,
In all mens faire opinions?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I have provided
A Priest, that's ready for us.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: And can the Divell,
In one ten dayes, that Divell chance devour me?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Wee'le fly to what place you please.

speeches.speaker: Flo
verse: No star prosperous?
All at a swoope?

speeches.speaker: Ber:
verse: You do not love me Goswin?
You will not looke upon me?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Can mens prayers
Shot up to heaven, with such a zeale as mine are,
Fall back like lazy mists, and never prosper?
Geyves, I must weare, and cold must be my comfort;
Darknesse, and want of meat; alas she weepes too,
Which is the top of all my sorrowes, Jertred.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: No, no, you will not know me; my poore beauty,
Which has been worth your eyes.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: The time growes on still:
And like a tumbling wave, I see my ruine,
Come rolling over me.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Yet will ye know me?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: For a hundred thousand crownes.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Yet will ye love me?
Tell me but how I have deserv'd your slighting.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: For a hundred thousand crownes?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Farewell dissembler.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Of which I have scarce ten: ô how it starts me.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: And may the next you love, hearing my ruine.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I had forgot my selfe, ô my best Gertred,
Crowne of my joyes, and comforts.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: sweet what ayle ye?
I thought you had been vext with me.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: My minde wench,
My minde o're flow'd with sorrow, sunck my memory.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Am I not worthy of the knowledge of it?
And cannot I as well affect your sorrowes,
As your delights? you love no other woman?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No I protest.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: You have no ships lost lately?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: None that I know of.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I hope you have spilt no blood: whose innocence
May lay this on your conscience.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Cleare, by heaven.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Why should you be thus then?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Good Jertred, aske not,
Ev'n By the love you beare me.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I am obedient.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Go in my faire; I will not be long from ye,
Nor long I feare me with thee, At my returne
Despise me as you please.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: The good gods guide ye.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Now for my selfe which is the least I hope for,
And when that failes, for mans worst fortune, pitty.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: WHy Gentlemen, 'tis but a week more I intreat you
But 7. short daies, I am not runnig from ye,
Nor, if you give me patience, is it possible
All my adventures faile; you have ships abroad,
Endure the beating both of winde, or weather:
I am sure 'twould vex your hearts, to be protested
Ye are all faire Merchants,

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: Yes, and must have faire play;
There is no lying here else, one howres failing
Failes us of all our friends, of all our credits:
For my part I would stay; but my wants tell me,
I must wrong others in't.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No mercy in ye?

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: 'Tis foolish to depend on others mercy:
Keepe your selfe right, and even, out your cloth Sir,
According to your calling: you have liv'd here
In Lordlike prodigality; high, and open,
And now ye finde what 'tis: the liberall spending
The summer of your youth, which you should gleane in,
And like the labouring Ant, make use and gaine of,
Has brought this bitter stormy winter on ye,
And now you cry.

speeches.speaker: 3. Mer.
verse: Alas before your poverty,
We were no men, of no marke, no endeavour;
You stood alone, tooke up all trade, all business,
Running through your hands, scarce a sayle at Sea,
But loaden with your goods: we poore weak pedlers,
When by your leave, and much intreaty to it:
We could have stoage for a little cloth,
Or a few wines, put of and thanke your worship
Lord, how the world's chang'd with ye? now I hope Sir,
We shall have sea-roome

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Is my misery,
Become my scorne too? have ye no humanity,
No part of men left? are all the bountyes in me
To you, and to the Towne; turn'd my reproaches?

speeches.speaker: 4. Mer.
verse: Well, get your monyes ready: 'tis but 2. howres
We shall protest ye else, and sodainly.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: But two dayes.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: Not an howre, ye know the hazard.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How soone my light's put out: hard harted Bruges;
Within thy walls, may never honest Merchant
Venture his fortunes more: ô my poore wench too;

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Good fortune Master.

speeches.speaker: Flo
verse: Thou mistak'st me Clause,
I am not worth thy blessing.

speeches.speaker: Cer.
verse: Stil a sad man?
No beliefe gentle Master? come bring it in then,
And now believe your Beadesman.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Is this certaine?
Or do'st thou work upon my troubled sence?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Tis gold Sir,
Take it and try it.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Certainely 'tis treasure,
Can there be yet this blessing?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Cease your wonder,
You shall not sinke, for nev'r a sowst Flap-dragon:
For nere a pickell'd pilcher of 'em all Sir,
'Tis there your full summ, a hundred thousand crownes,
And good sweet Master, now Be merry: pay 'em
Pay the poore pelting knaves, that know no goodnesse:
And cheere your heart up handsomely.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Good Clause,
How cam'st thou by this mighty summ? if naughtily
I must not take it of thee, 'twill undo me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Feare not: you have it by as honest meanes
As though your father gave it: Sir, you know not
To what a masse, the little we get dayly,
Mounts in seven yeares; we beg it for heavens charity,
And to the same good, we are bound to render it.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What great security?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Away with that Sir,
Were not ye more then all the men in Bruges;
And all the money in my thoughts—

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: But good Clause,
I may dye presently.

speeches.speaker: Ger,
verse: Then this dyes with ye-
Pay when you can good Master, I'le no parchments,
Onely this charity I shall intreat ye,
Leave me this Ring.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Alas, it is to poore Clause.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Tis all I aske, and this with all, that when
I shall deliver this back, you shall grant me
Freely one poore petition.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: There I confesse it,
And may my faith forsake mee when I shun it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Away, your time drawes on. Take up the money
And follow this young Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Farewell Clause,
And may thy honest memory live ever.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Heaven blesse ye and still keep ye, farewell Master.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I have lockt my youth up close enough for gadding
In an olde tree, and set watch over him.
Now for my Love, for sure this wench must be she,
She follows me; Come hither, pretty Minche.

speeches.speaker: Jac,
verse: No, no, you'l kisse,

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: So I will.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Y'ded law?
How will ye kisse me, pray you?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Thus: soft as my loves lips.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: What's your Fathers name?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: He's gone to heaven.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Is it not Gerrard, sweet?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I'le stay no longer,
My mother's an olde woman, and my Brother
Was drown'd at sea, with catching Cockles. O love:
O how my heart melts in me: how thou fir'st me!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: 'Tis certain she: pray let me see your hand, sweet,

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: No, no, you'l bite it.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sure I should know that Gymmall;

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: 'Tis certaine he: I had forgot my ring too.
O Hubert, Hubert.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Ha? me-thought she nam'd me—
Doe you know me, Chicke?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: No indeed, I never saw ye,
But me-thinks you kisse finely.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Kisse againe then;
By heaven 'tis she.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: O what a joy he brings me.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: You are not Minche?

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Yes pretty Gentleman,
And I must be married to morrow to a Capper.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Must ye my sweet, and doe's the Capper love ye?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Yes, yes, he'l give me pye, & look in mine eys thus:
Tis he: 'tis my deare Love; ô blest fortune.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: How fain she would conceal her selfe? yet shew it,
Will ye love me, and leave that man? I'le serve.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: O I shall loose my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I'le waite upon ye,
And make ye dainty Nose-gayes.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: And where will ye sticke 'em?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Here in bosome, and make a crown of Lillies
For your faire head.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: And will ye love me, deed-law?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: With all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: Call me to morrow then,
And we'l have brave chear, and goe to Church together:
Give you good ev'n Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: But one word faire Minche.

speeches.speaker: Jac.
verse: I must be gone a milking.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Ye shall presently.
Did you never heare of a young Maid called Jaculine?

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: I am discovered: hark in your eare, I'le tell ye;
You must not know me: kisse and be constant ever.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Heaven curse me else: tis she, and now I am certain
They are all here: now for my other project.—

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: Nay if it would do you courtesy.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: None at all Sir;
Take it 'tis yours: ther's your ten thousand for ye,
Give in my Bills: your sixteene.

speeches.speaker: 3. Mer.
verse: Pray be pleas'd Sir,
To make a further use.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: 3. Mer.
verse: What I have Sir,
You may command; pray let me be your Servant.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Put your hatts on: I care not for your courtisies,
They are most untimely don, and no truth in 'em.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: I have a frought of pepper.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Rot your pepper,
Shall I trust you againe? ther's your seven thousand.

speeches.speaker: 4. Mer.
verse: Or if you want fine suger, 'tis but sending.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No, I can send to Barbary, those people
That never yet knew faith, have nobler freedoms:
These carry to Vanlock, and take my Bills in
To Peter Zuten these: bring back my Iewells;
Why are these peices?

speeches.speaker: Saylor.
verse: Health to the noble Merchant,
The Susan is return'd.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Well?

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Well, and rich Sir,
And now put in.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Heaven thou hast heard my prayers.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: The brave Rebecca too: bound from the straights,
With the next tide is ready to put after.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What newes o'th' fly-boate?

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: If this winde hold till midnight,
She will be here, and wealthy, scap't fairely.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How, pre'thee Saylor?

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Thus Sir, she had fight
Seven howers together, with six Turkish Gallyes,
And she fought bravely: but at length was borded:
And over lai'd with strength: when presently
Comes boring up the winde Captaine Van-noke,
That valiant Gentleman, you redeem'd from prison;
He knew the Boate, set in: and fought it bravely:
Beate all the Gallies off; sunk three, redeem'd her,
And as a service to ye, sent her home Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: An honest noble Captaine, and a thankfull;
Ther's for thy new's: go drink the Merchants health, Saylor

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: I thanke your bounty, and I'le do it to a doyt, Sir,

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: What miracles are powr'd upon this fellow?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: This ye are I hope my friends, I shall scape prison,
For all your cares to catch me.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer
verse: You may please Sir
To think of your poor servants in displeasure,
Whose all they have, goods, monyes, are at your service.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I thank you,
When I have need of you I shall forget you:
You are paid I hope.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We joy in your good fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Come Sir, come take your ease you must go home
With mee, yonder is one weepes and howles.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Alas how does she?

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: She will be better soone I hope.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Why soone sir?

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Why when you have her in your armes, this night,
My boy she is thy wife

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: With all my hart I take her.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: We have prepar'd, all thy friends will be there,
And all my Roomes shall smoake to see the revell;
Thou hast been wrong'd and no more shall my seruice,
Waite on the knaue her Vncle, I have hard all,
All his baites for my Boy, but thou shalt have her;
Hast thou dispatch't thy businesse?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Most.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: By the masse Boy,
Thou tumblest now in wealth, and I joy in it,
Thou art the best Boy, that Bruges ever nourish'd
Thou hast been sad, I'le cheere thee up with Sack,
And when thou art lusty I'le fling thee to thy Mistris.
Shee'l hug thee, sirha.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I long to see it,
I had forgot you: ther's for, you my friends:
You had but heavy burthens, commend my love
To my best love, all the love I have
To honest Clause, shortly I will thanke him better.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: By the masse a royall Merchant,
Gold by the handfull, here will be sport, soone Prig.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: It partly seemes so, and here will I be in a trice.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And I boy,
Away a pace we are look'd for.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Oh these bak'd meates,
Me thinkes I smell them hither.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Thy mouth waters.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I Must not,

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: Why? 'tis in thy power to do it, and in mine
To reward thee to thy wishes.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I dare not, nor I will not.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Gentle Huntsman,
Though thou hast kept me hard: though in thy duty,
Which is requir'd to do it, th' hast used me stubbornly;
I can forgive thee freely.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: You the Earles servant.

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: I sweare I am neare as his owne thoughts to him;
Able to doe thee—

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Come, come, leave your prating.

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: If thou dar'st but try.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I thanke you hartily, you will be
The first man that will hang me, a sweet recompence,
I could do, but I do not say I will,
To any honest fellow that would thinke on't:
And be a benefactor.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: If it be not recompenc'd, and to thy owne desires,
If within these ten dayes I do not make thee—

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: What, a false knave?

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: Prethee, prethee conceive me rightly, any thing
Of profit or of place that may advance thee.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Why what a Goosecap would'st thou make me,
Do not I know that men in misery will promise
Any thing, more then their lives can reach at?

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: Beleeve me Huntsman,
There shall not one short sillable
That comes from me, passe
Without it's full performance.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Say you so Sir?
Have ye e're a good place for my quality.

speeches.speaker: H^m.
verse: A thousand Chases, Forrests, Parks: I'le make thee
Chiefe ranger over all the games.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: When?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Presently.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: This may provoke me: and yet to prove a knave too.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: 'Tis to prove honest: 'tis to do good service,
Service for him thou art sworn to, for thy Prince,
Then for thy selfe that good; what fool would live here,
Poore, and in misery, subject to all dangers,
Law, and lewd people can inflict, when bravely
And to himselfe he may be law, and credit?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Shall I believe thee?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: As that thou holdst most holy;

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Ye may play tricks.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Then let me never live more.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Then you shall see Sir, I will do a service
That shall deserve indeed.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: 'Tis well said, hunts-man,
And thou shalt be well thought of.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I will do it: 'tis not your letting free, for that's meer nothing,
But such a service, if the Earl be noble,
He shall for ever love me.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What is't hunts-man?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Do you know any of these people live here?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: You are a foole then: here be those to have 'em,
I know the Earl so well, would make him caper.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Any of the old Lords that rebel'd?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Peace, all,
I know 'em every one, and can betray 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: But wilt thou doe this service?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: If you'l keep
Your faith, and free word to me.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Wilt thou swear me?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No, no, I will beleeve ye: more then that too,
Here's the right heire.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: O honest, honest hunts-man!

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Now, how to get these Gallants, ther's the matter,
You will be constant, 'tis no work for me else.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Will the Sun shine agen?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: The way to get 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Propound it, and it shall be done.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No sleight;
(For they are Devillish crafty, it concerns 'em,)
Nor reconcilement, (for they dare not trust neither)
Must doe this tricke.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: By force?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I, that must doe it.
And with the person of the Earl himselfe,
Authority (and mighty) must come on 'em:
Or else in vaine: and thus I would have ye do it.
To morrow-night be here: a hundred men will bear 'em,
(So he be there, for he's both wise and valiant)
And with his terrour will strike dead their forces,
The houre be twelve a clock, now for a guide
To draw ye without danger on these persons,
The woods being thicke, and hard to hit, my selfe
With some few with me, made unto our purpose,
Beyond the wood, upon the plain, will wait ye
By the great Oke.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: I know it: keep thy faith hunts-man,
And such a showr of wealth—

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I warrant ye:
Misse nothing that I tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Farewell;
You have your liberty, now use it wisely;
And keep your houre, goe closer about the wood there,
For feare they spy you.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: And bring no noyse with ye.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
prose: All shall be done to'th purpose: farewel hunts-ma~.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now, what's the news in towne?

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: No news, but joy Sir;
Every man wooing of the noble Merchant,
Who has his hearty commendations to ye.

speeches.speaker: Fer
verse: Yes, this is news, this night he's to be married.

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: By'th masse that's true, he marryes Vandoncks daughter
The dainty black-ey'd bell.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I would my clapper
Hung in his baldricke, what a peale could I ring?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Marryed?

speeches.speaker: Gin.
verse: 'Tis very true Sir, ô the pyes,
The piping-hot mince-pyes.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: O the Plum-pottage.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: For one leg of a goose now would I ventura limb boys,
I love a fat goose, as I love allegiance,
And—upon the Boors, too well they know it,
And therefore starve their powltry.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: To be married
To Vandonks daughter?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: O this pretious Merchant:
What sport he will haue? but hark ye brother Prig,
Shall we do nothing in the fore-said wedding?
Ther's money to be got, and meate I take it,
What thinke ye of a morise?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: No, by no meanes,
That goes no further then the street, there leaves us,
Now we must think of something that must draw us
Into the bowels of it, into'th buttery,
Into the Kitchin, into the Cellar, something
That that old drunken Burgo-master loves,
What think ye of a wassell?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: I think worthily.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And very fit it should be, thou, and Ferret,
And Ginks to sing the Song: I for the structure,
Which is the bowle.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Which must be up-sey English,
Strong, lusty London beer; let's think more of it,

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: He must not marry.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: By your leave in private,
One word Sir, with ye; Gerrard: do not start me,
I know ye, and he knows ye, that best loves ye:
Hubert speakes to ye, and you must be Gerrard,
The time invites you to it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Make no show then,
I am glad to see you Sir; and I am Gerrard.
How stands affaires?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Faire, if ye dare now follow,
Hemskirke I have let goe, and these my causes,
I'le tell ye privately, and how I have wrought him,
And then to prove me honest to my friends,
Looke upon these directions; you have seen his.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Then will I speak a speech, and a brave speech
In praise of Merchants, where's the Ape

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: —Take him,
A gowty Beare-ward stole him the other day.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: May his Beares worry him, that Ape had paid it,
What dainty tricks? —o' that whorson Bear-ward:
In his french doublet, with his baster'd bullions,
In a long stock ty'd up; o how daintily
Would I have made him waite, and change a trencher,
Cary a cup of wine? ten thousand stinks
Waite on thy mangy soule, thou lowzy Bear-ward.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Tis passing well, I both beleeve and joy in't
And will be ready; keepe you here the meane while,
And keepe this in, I must a while forsake ye,
Upon mine anger no man stir, this two houres.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Not to the wedding sir?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Not any whither.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The wedding must be seene sir; we want meat too,
VVe be monstrous out of meat.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Shall it be spoken,
Fatt Capon shak't their tailes at's in defiance?
And turkey toombs such honorable monuments,
Shall piggs, sir, that the Persons selfe would envy,
And deintie Ducks?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Not a word more, obey me.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: VVhy then come dolefull death, this is flat tyrany
And by this hand —

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: VVhat?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Ile goe sleepe upon't.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Nay, and there be a wedding, and we wanting
Farewell our happie daies: we doe obey sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mer.
verse: VVell met sir, you are for this lusty wedding.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: I am so, so are you I take it.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: Yes,
And it much glads me, that to doe him service
Who is the honour of our trade, and luster,
VVe meet thus happily.

speeches.speaker: 2. Mer.
verse: He's a noble fellow,
And well becomes a bride of such a beauty.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: She is passing faire indeed, long may their loves
Continue like their youths, in spring of sweetnesse,
All the young Merchants will be here
No doubt on't,
For he that comes not to attend this wedding
The curse of a most blind one fall upon him,
A lowd wife, and a lazie: here's Vanlock.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: VVell overtaken gentlemen: save ye.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
verse: The same to you sir; save ye faire Mistris Francis,
I would this happie night might make you blush too.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: She dreames a pace,

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: That's but a drowsie fortune.

speeches.speaker: 3. Mer.
verse: Nay take us with ye too; we come to that end,
I am sure ye are for the wedding.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: Hand and heart man:
And what their feet can doe, I could have tript it
Before this whorson gout

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Blesse ye Masters.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: Clause? how now Clause; thou art come to see thy Master,
(And a good master he is to all poore people)
In all his joy, tis honestly don of thee.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Long may hee live sir, but my businesse now is
If you would plase to doe it, and to him too.

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: He's heere himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Stand at the doore my friends?
I pray walke in: welcome faire Mistris Francis,
See what the house affords, ther's a young Lady
VVill bid you welcome,

speeches.speaker: Vanl.
verse: VVe joy your happinesse.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I hope It will be so: Clause nobly welcome,
My honest, my best friend, I have been carefull
To see thy monys—

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Sir, that brought not me,
Do you know this Ring againe?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Thou hadst it of me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: And do you well reme~ber yet, the boone you gave me
Upon returne of this?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Yes, and I grant it,
Be it what it will: aske what thou can'st, I'le do it;
Within my power.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Ye are not married yet

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No,

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Faith I shall aske you that that will disturb ye,
But I must put ye to your promise.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Do,
And if I faint and flinch in't—

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Well said Master,
And yet it grieves me too: and yet it must be.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Prethee distrust me not.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: You must not marry,
That's part of the power you gave me: which to make up,
You must presently depart, and follow me.

speeches.speaker: Flo
verse: Not marry Clause?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Not if you keep your promise,
And give me power to aske.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Pre'thee thinke better,
I will obey, by heaven.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I have thought the best Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Give me thy reason, do'st thou feare her honesty?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Chaste as the yee, for any thing I know, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose: Why should'st thou light on that then? to what purpose?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I must not now discover.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Must not marry?
Shall I breake now when my poore hart is pawn'd?
When all the preparation?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now or never.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose: Come, 'tis not that thou would'st: thou dost but fright me

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Upon my soule it is Sir, and I binde ye.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Clause, can'st thou be so cruell?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: You may breake Sir,
But never more in my thoughts, appeare honest.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Did'st ever see her?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: No:

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: She is such a thing,
O Clause, she is such a wonder, such a mirror,
For beauty, and faire vertue, Europe has not:
Why hast thou made me happy, to undo me?
But looke upon her; then if thy heart relent not,
I'le quit her presently, who waites there?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Bid my faire love come hither, and the company,
Pre'thee be good unto me; take a mans hart
And looke upon her truly: take a friends hart
And feele what misery must follow this,

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Take you a noble hart and keep your promise;
I forsooke all I had, to make you happy.
Can that thing call'd a woman, stop your goodnesse?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Looke there she is, deale with me as thou wilt now
Did'st ever see a fayrer?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: She is most goodly.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Pray ye stand still.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: What ayles my love?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Did'st thou ever,
By the faire light of heaven, behold a sweeter?
O that thou knew'st but love, or ever felt him,
Looke well, looke narrowly upon her beauties.

speeches.speaker: 1. Mer.
prose: Sure h'as some strange designe in hand, he starts so.

speeches.speaker: 2 Mer.
verse: This Beggar has a strong power over his pleasure

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: View all her body.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Tis exact and excellent.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Is she a thing then to be lost thus lightly?
Her mind is ten times sweeter, ten times nobler,
And but to heare her speak, a Paradise,
And such a love she beares to me, a chaste love,
A vertuous, faire, and fruitfull love: 'tis now too
I am ready to enjoy it; the Priest ready: Clause,
To say the holy words shall make us happy,
This is a cruelty beyond mans study,
All these are ready, all our joyes are ready,
And all the expectation of our friends,
Twill be her death to do it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Let her dye then.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Thou canst not: 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: It must be.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Twill kil me too, 'twil murder me: by heaven Claus
I'le give thee halfe I have; come thou shalt save me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Then you must goe with me: I can stay no longer
If ye be true, and noble.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Hard heart, I'le follow:
Pray ye all goe in againe, and pray be merry,
I have a weighty businesse, give my cloake there.
Concerns my life, and state; make no enquiry,
This present houre befaln me: with the soonest
I shall be here againe: nay pray goe in Sir,
And take them with you, tis but a night lost, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: Come, come in, we will not loose our meat yet,
Nor our good mirth, he cannot stay long from her
I am sure of that.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I will not stay; beleeve Sir.
Gertrud, a word with you;

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Why is this stop, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I have no more time left me, but to kisse thee,
And tell thee this, I am ever thine: farewell wench.

speeches.speaker: Be.
verse: And is that all your ceremony? Is this a wedding?
Are all my hopes and prayers turnd to nothing?
Well, I will say no more, nor sigh, nor sorrow; oh me,
Till to thy face I prove thee false.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: LEad, if thou thinkst we are right: why dost thou make
These often stands? thou saidst thou knewst the way

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: Fsar nothing, I doe know it: would twere homeward.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Wrought from me, by a Beggar? at the time
That most should tye him? Tis some other Love
That hath a more command on his affections,
And he that fetcht him, a disguised Agent,
Not what he personated; for his fashion
Was more familiar with him, and more powerfull
Then one that ask'd an almes: I must finde out
One, if not both: kind darknesse be my shrowd
And cover loves too curious search in me,
For yet, suspition, I would not name thee.

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Mistris, it grows some-what pretty and dark.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: What then?

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Nay, nothing; do not thinke I am afraid,
Although perhaps you are.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I am not, forward.

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: Sure but you are: give me your hand, fear nothing.
There's one leg in the wood, do not pull backward:
What a sweate one on's are in, you or I?
Pray God it do not prove the plague; yet sure
It has infected me; for I sweat too,
It runs out at my knees, feele, feele, I pray you.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: What ailes the fellow?

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Hark, hark I besech you,
Doe you heare nothing?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Lyst: a wilde hog,
He grunts: now 'tis a beare: this wood is full of 'em,
And now, a wolfe Mistris, a wolfe a wolfe,
It is the howling of a wolfe.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: The braying of an asse, is it not.

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Oh, now one has me;
Oh, my left ham, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Looke to your shankes,
Your breech is safe enough, the wolfe's a Fern-brake.

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: But see, see, see. There is a serpent in it,
It has eyes as broad as platters; it spits fire;
Now it creeps towards us, help me to say my prayers:
It hath swallowed me almost, my breath is stopt,
I cannot speake; do I speake Mistris? tell me.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Why, thou timerous Sot, canst thou perceive
Any thing i'the bush, but a poore glo-worme?

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: It may be tis but a glo-worm now, but 'twill
Grow to a fire-drake presently.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Come thou from it:
I have a pretious guide of you; and a courteous
That gives me leave to lead my selfe the way thus.

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: It thunders, you heare that now.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: I heare one hollow.

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: 'Tis thunder, thunder:
See, a flash of Lightning:
Are you not blasted Mistris? pull your maske off,
It has plaid the barber with me here: I have lost
My beard, my beard, pray God you be not shaven,
'Twill spoile your marriage Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: What strange wonders,
Feare fancies in a Coward?

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Now, the earth opens.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Prethee hold thy peace.

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Will you on then?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Both love and jealousie have made me bold,
Where my fate leads me, I must goe.

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: God be with you then.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: It was the fellow sure, he that should guide me,
The hunts-man that did hollow us.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Best make a stand
And listen to his next: ha?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Who goes there?

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Mistris, I am taken.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Mistris? look forth souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: What are you sirha?

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: Truly all is left
Of a poore Boore, by day-light, by night no body,
You might have spar'd your drum, and guns, & pikes too
For I am none that will stand out Sir, I.
You may take me in with a walking sticke
Euen when you please, and hold me with a pack-threed.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: What woman was't you call'd to.

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: VVoman? none Sir.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: None? did you not name Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Boor.
verse: Yes, but shee's
No woman yet! she should have been this night,
But that a Beggar stole away her Bridegroome,
VVhom we were going to make hue and cry after;
I tell you true Sir, she should ha'bin maried to day,
And was the Bride, and all; but in came Clause,
The old lame Beggar, and whips up Mr. Goswin;
Under his arme; away with him as a Kite,
Or an old Fox, would swoope a way a gosling.

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: 'Tis she, 'tis she, 'tis she, Niece?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: She Sir,
This was a noble entrance to your fortune,
That being on the point thus to be married:
Upon her venture here: you should surprise her.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: I begin Hemskirck, to believe my fate,
Works to my ends.

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Yes Sir, and this adds trust,
Unto the fellow our guide, who assur'd me Floris,
Liv'd in some Merchants shop, as Gerrard did:
I' the old beggars, and that he would use
Him for the traine, to call the other forth,
All which we finde is done—That's he againe—

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Good we sent out to meet him.

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: Heer's the Oke.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O I am miserably lost, thus falne
Into my vncles hands from all my hopes,
Can I not thinke away my selfe and dye?
O I am miserably lost; thus fallen
Into my Uncles hands, from all my hopes:
No matter now, where thou be false or no,
Goswin, whether thou love an other better;
Or me alone; or where thou keep thy vow,
And word, or that thou come, or stay: for I
To thee from henceforth, must be ever absent,
And thou to me: no more shall we come neere,
To tell our selves, how bright each other eyes were,
How soft our language, and how sweet our kisses,
Whil'st we made one our food, th' other our feast,
Not mix our soules by sight, or by a letter
Hereafter, but as small relation have,
As two new gon to in habiting a grave:
Can I not thinke away my selfe and dye?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I like your habits well: they are safe, stand close

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: But what's the action we are for now? ha?
Robbing a Ripper of his fish?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Or taking,
A poultrer prisoner, without ransome, Bullyes?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Or cutting off a convoy of butter?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Or surprising a Boores ken, for granting cheates?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Or cackling cheates?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Or mergery-praters, Rogers,
And Tibs o'th the Buttry?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: O' I could drive a Regiment
Of geese afore me, such a night as this
Ten leagues with my hatt, and staff, and not a hisse
Heard, or a wing of my troopes disordered.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Tell us,
If it be milling of a lag of duds,
The fetching of a back of clothes or so;
We are horribly out of linnen.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No such matter.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Let me alone for any Farmers dog,
If you have a minde to the cheese-loft: 'tis but thus:
And he is a silenc'd Mastiff, during pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Would it would please you to be silent.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Mum.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: A friend, the Huntsman.

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: O 'tis he.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I have kept touch Sir, which is the Earle of these?
Will ye know a man now?

speeches.speaker: Hems,
verse: This my Lord's the friend,
Hath undertooke the service.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: If 't be worth
His Lordships thanks anon, when 'tis done
Lording, I'le looke for't, a rude woodman,
I know how to pitch my toyles, drive in my game:
And I have don't, both Floriz and his Father
Old Gerrard, with Lord Arnold of Benthuisen,
Cozen, and Jaqueline, young Floris Sister;
I haue 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: Thou speak'st too much, too happy,
To carry faith with it.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: I can bring you
Where you shall see, and finde 'em.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: We will double,
What ever Hemskirck then hath promis'd thee.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: And I'le deserve it treble; what horse ha you?

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: A hundred.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: That's well: ready to take
Upon surprise of 'em?

speeches.speaker: Hems.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Devide then,
Your force into five Squadrous; for there are
So many out lets, wayes, thorough the wood,
That issue from the place: where they are lodg'd;
Five severall wayes, of all which passages
We must posses our selves, to round 'em in,
For by one starting hole, they'll all escape else;
I and 4. Boores here, to me will be guides,
The Squadron, where you are, my selfe will lead:
And that they may be more secure, I'le use
My wonted whoopes, and hollowes, as I were
A hunting for 'em; which will make them rest,
Careles of any noyse, and be a direction
To the other guides, how we approch 'em still.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: 'Tis orderd well, and relisheth the Souldier,
Make the division Hemskirck: you are my charge
Faire one, I'le looke to you.

speeches.speaker: Boo.
verse: Shall no body need
To looke to me? I'le looke unto my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: 'Tis but this, remember.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Say 'tis don boy.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: By this time Sir I hope you want no reasons
Why I broke off your marriage, for though I
Should as a Subject study you my Prince
In things indifferent, it will not therefore
Discredit you, to acknowledge me your Father,
By harkning to my necessary counsells.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Acknowledge you my Father? Sir I do,
And may impiety, conspiring with
My other Sinnes, sinck me, and sodainly
When I forget to pay you a Sonnes duty
In my obedience, and that help'd forth
With all the cheerefullnesse.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I pray you rise,
And may those powers that see and love this in you,
Reward you for it: Taught by your example
Having receiv'd the rights due to a Father,
I tender you th' allegance of a Subject:
Which as my Prince accept of.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Kneele to me?
May mountaines first fall down beneath their valleys,
And fire no more mount upwards, when I suffer
An act in nature so preposterous;
I mu^t o'recome in this, in all things else
The victory be yours: could you here read me,
You should perceive how all my faculties
Triumph in my blest fate, to be found yours;
I am your son, your son Sir, and am prouder
To be so, to the Father, to such goodnesse
(Which heaven be pleas'd, I may inherit from you)
Then I shall ever of those specious titles
That plead for my succession in the Earldome
(Did I possesse it now) left by my mother.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: I do beleeve it: but—

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: O my lov'd Father,
Before I knew you were so, by instinct,
Nature had taught me, to look on your wants,
Not as a strangers: and I know not how,
What you call'd charity, I thought the payment
Of some religious debt, nature stood bound for;
And last of all, when your magnificent bounty
In my low ebb of fortune, had brought in
A flood of blessings, though my threatning wants
And feare of their effects, still kept me stupid,
I soone found out, it was no common pitty
That lead you to it.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Thinke of this hereafter
When we with joy may call it to remembrance,
There will be a time, more opportune, then now
To end your story, with all circumstances,
I add this only: when we fled from Woolfort
I sent you into England, and there placed you
With a brave Flanders Merchant, call'd rich Goswin,
A man supplyed by me unto that purpose,
As bound by oath never to discover you,
Who dying, left his name and wealth unto you
As his reputed Son, and yet receiv'd so;
But now, is Florez, and a Prince, remember
The countreys, and the subjects generall good
Must challenge the first part in your affection:
The faire maid, whom you chose to be your wife,
Being so far beneath you, that your love
Must grant shee's not your equall.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: In discent
Or borrowed glories, from dead Ancestors,
But for her beauty, chastity, and all vertues
Ever remembred in the best of women,
A Monarch might receive from her, not give,
Though she were his Crownes purchase; In this only
Be an indulgent Father: in all else,
Use my authority.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Sir, here be two of 'em,
The Father and the Son, the rest you shall have
As fast as I can rouze them.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Who's this? Woolfort?

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: I Criple, your faigned crutches wil not help you,
Nor patch'd disguise that hath so long conceal'd you,
It's now no halting. I must here finde Gerrard,
And in this Merch^nts habit, one called Florez
Who would be an Earl.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: And is, wert thou a subject.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Is this that Traitor Woolfo^t?

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Yes, but you
Are they that are betraid: Hemskirke;

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: My Goswin
Turn'd Prince? ô I am poorer by this greatnesse,
Then all my former jealousies or misfortunes.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Gertrud?

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Stay Sir, you were to day too neare her,
You must no more ayme at those easy accesses,
Lesse you can do 't in aire, without a head,
Which shall be sodainly tri'de.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: O take my heart, first,
And since I cannot hope now to enjoy him,
Let me but fall a part of his glad ransome.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: You know not your own value, that entreat

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: So proud a fiend as Woolfort.

speeches.speaker: VVoolf.
verse: For so lost
A thing as Florez.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: And that would be so
Rather then she should stoop againe to thee;
There is no death, but's sweeter then all life,
When VVoolfort is to give it: O my Gertrude,
It is not that, nor Prince dome that I goe from,
It is from thee, that losse includeth all.

speeches.speaker: Wool
verse: I, if my young Prince knew his losse, hee would say so,
VVhich that he yet may chew on, I will tell him
This is no Gertrude, nor no Hemskirks Niece,
Nor Vandoncks daughter; this is Bertha, Bertha,
The heir of Brabant, she that caus'd the warr,
Whom I did steale, during my treaty there,
For your minority, to raise my selfe;
I then fore-seeing 'twould beget a quarrell.
That, a necessity of my employment,
The same employment, make me master of strength,
That strength, the Lord of Flanders, so of Brabant,
By marrying her: which had not been to doe Sir,
She come of years, but that the expectation
First of her Fathers death, retarded it,
And since the standing out of Bruges, where
Hemskirke had hid her, till she was neer lost:
But Sir, we have recover'd her: your Merchantship
May breake, for this was one of your best bottoms
I thinke

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Insolent Devill!

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Who are these, Hemskirke?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: More, more, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How they triumph in their treachery?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: Lord Arnold of Benthusin, this Lord Costin,
This Jaqueline the sister unto Florez.

speeches.speaker: Wol.
verse: All found? why here's brave game, this was sport-royall,
And puts me in thought of a new kind of death for 'em.
Hunts-man, your horn: first wind me Florez fall,
Next Gerrards, then his daughter Jaquelins,
Those rascalls, they shall dye without their rights:
Hang 'em Hemskirke on these trees; Il'e take
The assay of these my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: Not here my Lord,
Let 'em be broken up, upon a scaffold,
Twill shew the better when their arbour's made.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Wretch art thou not content thou hast betraid us
But mocke us too?

speeches.speaker: Ginks.
verse: False Hubert, this is monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Wool.
verse: Hubert?

speeches.speaker: Hem.
verse: VVho, this?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Yes, this is Hubert, Woolfort,
I hope he ha's helpt himselfe to a tree.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: The first,
The first of any, and most glad I have you Sir,
I let you goe before, but for a traine;
Is't you have done this service?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: As your Hunts-man,
But now as Hubert; save your selves, I will,
The Woolf's a foote, let slip; kill, kill, kill, kill.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Betray'd?

speeches.speaker: Hub.
verse: No, but well catch'd and I the Huntsman.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: How do you Woolfort? Rascal, good knave Wool:
I speake it now without the Rose, and Hemskirck,
Rogue Hemskirck, you that have no neice, this Lady
Was stolen by you, and tane by you, and now
Resign'd by me, to the right owner here:
Take her my Prince.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Can this be possible,
Welcom my love, my sweet, my worthy love.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: I ha' giv'n you her twice: now keep her better & thanke
Lord Hubert, that came to me in Gerrards name,
And got me out, with my brave Boyes, to march
Like Caesar, when he bred his Comentaryes,
So I, to end my Chronicle, came forth
Caesar Van-donck, & veni, vidi, vici,
Give me my Bottle, and set downe the drum;
You had your tricks Sir, had you? we ha' tricks too,
You stole the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And we led your Squadrons
Where they ha' scratch'd their leggs a little, with brambles,
If not their faces.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Yes, and run their heads
Against trees.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: 'Tis Captaine Prig, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And Coronell Higgen.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: We have fill'd a pitt with your people some with leggs
Some with armes broken, and a neck, or two
I think be loose.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The rest too, that escap'd,
Are not yet out o'the briars,

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And your horses, Sir,
Are well set up in Bruges all by this time:
You looke as you were not well Sir, and would be
Shortly let blood; do you want a scarfe?

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: A halter.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: 'Twas like your selfe, honest, and noble Hubert:
Can'st thou behold these mirrors altogether,
Of thy long, false, and bloody usurpation?
Thy tyrranous proscription, and fresh treason:
And not so see thy selfe, as to fall downe
And sincking, force a grave, with thine owne guilt,
As deep as hell, to couer thee and it?

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: No, I can stand: and praise the toyles that tooke me
And laughing in them dye, they were brave snares.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Twer truer valour, if thou durst repent
The wrongs th' hast don, and live.

speeches.speaker: Woolf.
verse: Who, I repent?
And say I am sorry? yes, 'tis the fooles language
And not fot Woolfort.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Woolfort thou art a Divell,
