And speaks his language, oh that I had my longing
Under this rew of trees now would I hang him.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No let him live, untill he can repent,
But banish'd from our State, that is thy doome.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: Then hang his worthy Captaine here, this Hemskirck
For profit of th' example.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No let him,
Enjoy his shame too: with his conscious life,
To shew how much our innocence contemnes;
All practise from the guiltiest, to molest us.

speeches.speaker: Van-d.
verse: A noble prince.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Sir, you must helpe to joyne
A paire of hands, as they have don their heartes here,
And to their loves with joy.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: As to mine owne,
My gratious Sister, worthiest Brother:

speeches.speaker: Van.
verse: I'le go afore, and have the bon-fire made,
My fire-workes, and flap dragons, and good backrack,
With a peck of little fishes, to drink downe
In healthes to this day.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Slight, here be changes,

The Bells ha' not so many, nor a dance,
^rig.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Our Company's growne horrible thin by it,
What think you Ferret?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Marry I do thinke,
That we might all be Lords now, if we could stand for't

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Not I if they should offer it: I'le dislodge first,
Remove the Bush to another climat.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Sir, you must thanke this worthy Burgomaster,
Here be friends aske to be look'd on too:
And thank'd, who though their trade, and course of life
Be not so perfect, but it may be betterd,
Have yet us'd me with curtesy, and bin true
Subjects unto me, while I was their King,
A place I know not well, how to resigne.
Nor unto whom: But this I will entreat
Your grace, command them, follow me to Bruges;
Where I will take the care on me, to finde
Some manly, and more profitable course
To fit them, as a part of the Republique.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Do you heare Sirs? do so.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Thankes to your good grace.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: To your good Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: May you both live long.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
prose: Attend me at Van-doncks, the Burgomasters.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes, to beat hemp, and be whipt twice a weeke,
Or turne the wheele, for Crab the Rope-maker:
Or learne to go along with him, his course;
That's a fine course now, i' the Common-wealth, Prig,
What say you to it?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: It is the backwardst course,
I know i'the world.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Then Higgen will scarce thrive by it,
You do conclude?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: 'Faith hardly, very hardly.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Troth I am partly of your minde, Prince Prig.
And therefore farewell Flanders, Higgen will seek
Some safer shelter, in some other Clymat:
With this his tatterd Colony: Let me see
Snap, Ferret, Prig, and Higgen, all are left
O the true blood: what? shall we into England?

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Agreed,

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Then beare up bravely with your Brute my lads
Higgen hath prig'd the prancers in his dayes,
And sold good peny-worthes; we will have a course,
The spirit of Bottom, is growne bottomlesse.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: I'le mand no more, nor cant.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Yes, your sixpenyworth
In private, brother, sixpence is a summ,
I'le steale you any mans dogg for

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: For Sixpence more,
You'l tell the owner where he is.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: Tis right,
Higgen must practise, so must Prig to eat;
And write the Letter: and gi' the word, But now
No more, as either of these.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: But as true Beggars,
As ere we were.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: We stand here, for an Epilogue;
Ladyes, your bountyes first; the rest will follow,
For womens favours, are a leading almes,
If you be pleas'd look cheerely throw your eyes:
Out at your maskes.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And let your beauties sparkle.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: So may you neer want dressings, Iewells, gownes
Still i' the fashion.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: Nor the men you love,
VVealth nor discourse to please you.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: May you Gentlemen,
Never want good fresh suites nor liberty.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: May every Merchant here see safe his ventures.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And every honest Citizen his debts in.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The Lawyers gaine good Clyents.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: And the Clyents good Councell.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: All the Gamesters here good fortune.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The Drunkards too good wine.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The eaters meate
Fit for their tasts and pallats.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The good wives kind Husbands.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: The young maides choyce of Sutors.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: The Midwives merry hearts.

speeches.speaker: Prig.
verse: And all good cheere.

speeches.speaker: Hig.
verse: As you are kinde unto us and our Bush,
We are the Beggars and your dayly Beadsmen,
And have your money, but the Almes we aske
And live by, is your Grace, give that and then
VV'eel boldly say our word is, Come agen.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: LEt us make use of this stolne privacy,
And not loose time in protestation, mistris,
For twere in me a kind of breach of faith,
To say againe I love you.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Sweet speake softly
For though the venture of your love to me,
Meetes with a willing, and a full returne:
Should it arrive unto my Fathers knowledge;
These were our last discourse.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: How shall he know it?

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: His watching cares are such, for my advancement,
That every where his eye is fix'd upon me:
This night that does afford us some small freedom,
At the request and much entreaty of,
The mistris of the house, was hardly given me:
For I am never sufferd to stir out,
But he hath spies upon me, yet I know not
You have so won upon me, that could I thinke
You would love faithfully (though to entertaine
Another thought of you, would be my death)
I should adventure on his utmost anger.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why, do you thinke I can be false?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: No faith,
You have an honest face, but if you should—

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Let all the stored vengeance of heavens justice—

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: No more, I do believe you, the dance ended,
Which this free womans ghests have vow'd to have
Ere they depart, I will make home, and store me
With all the Iewells, Chaines, and gold are trusted
Unto my custody, and at the next corner,
To my Fathers house, before one at the farthest,
Be ready to receive me.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I desire
No bond beyond your promise, let's go in,
To talke thus much before the doore, may breed,
Suspition.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: Here are company too.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Away,
Those powers that prosper true and honest loves
Will blesse our undertakeings.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: 'Tis my wish Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Nay, Sir, excuse me, I have drawne you to,
Too much expence already in my travell:
And you have been to forward in your love;
To make my wants your owne, allow me manners
Which you must grant I want, should I encrease,
The bond in which your courtisyes have tide me:
Be still consuming you, give me leave
To take mine owne wayes now; and I shall often
With willingnesse come to visit you, and then thanke you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: By this hand I could be angry, what do you thinke me?
Must we that have so long time, beene as one
Seene Cityes, Countryes, Kingdomes, and their wonders
Beene bedfellowes, and in our various journey
Mixtall our observations, part (as if
We were 2. Carriers at 2. severall wayes,
And as the forehorse guides, cry God be with you)
Without or complement, or cerimony?
In travelers that know transalpine garbes,
Though our designes are neere so serious, friend,
It were a capitall crime; it must not be,
Nay what is more, you shall not, you ere long
Shall see my house, and finde what I call mine
Is wholly at your service.

speeches.speaker: Mer,
verse: 'Tis this tires me,
Sir I were easily woo'd if nothing else
But my will lay in the choyce, but 'tis not so
My friends and kindred that have part of me,
And such on whom my chiefest hopes depend,
Iustly expect the tender of my love
After my travell, then mine owne honesty
Tells me 'tis poore, having indifferent meanes
To keep me in my quallity and rank,
At my returne to tire anothers bounty,
And let mine owne grow lusty, pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I will not, cannot, to conclude I dare not:
Can any thing confer'd upon my friend
Be burthensome to me? for this excuse
Had I no reason else you should not leave me,
By a travellers faith you should not, I have said,
And then you know my humour, ther's no contending.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Is there no way to scape this Inundation?
I shall be drown'd with folly if I go:
And after 9. dayes men may take me up,
With my gall broken.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Are you yet resolv'd?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Wood you would spare me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: By this light I cannot
By all, that may be sworne by.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Patience helpe me,
And heaven grant his folly be not catching:
If it be, the townes undone, I now would give
A reasonable sum of gold to any sheriff,
That would but lay an execution on me,
And free me from his company; while he was abroad,
His want of witt and language kept him dumbe:
But Balaam's Asse will speake now without spurring.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Speake, have I won you?—

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: You are not to be resisted.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Be ready I entreat you the dance done,
Besides a liberall reward I have,
A bottle of sherry in my power shall beget
New crotchets in your heads.

speeches.speaker: Musit.
verse: Tush feare not us, wee'le do our parts.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Go in,

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I know this fellow.
Belong you to the house?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I serve the Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Pretty, and short, pray you sir then informe her,
Two Gentlemen are covetous to be honour'd,
With her faire presence.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: She shall know so much,
This is a merry night with us, and forbid not
Welcom to any that lookes like a man:
I'le guide you the way.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nay follow, I have a trick in't.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: Come wher's this masque? fairest for our cheare,
Our thankes and service, may you long surviue,
To joy in many of these nights.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I thanke you.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: We must have musique too, or ells you give us,
But halfe a welcom.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Pray you Sir excuse me.

speeches.speaker: Silu.
verse: By no meanes Lady.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: Weele crowne your liberall feast,
With some delightfull straine fitting your love:
And this good company.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Since you enforce it,
I will not plead the excuse of want of skill
Or be, or nice, or curious, every year,
I celebrate my marriage night; and will
'Till I see my absent husband.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: 'Tis fit freedome.

speeches.speaker: Silu.
verse: Richardo thou art dull—

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I shall be lighter,
When I have had a heate.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now Sir, the newes?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Mistris there are 2. Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Complementing who should first enter.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What are they?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Heaven knowes, but for their strangenesse, have you never seen a Cat wash her face?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Iust such a stir they keep if you make but hast,
You may see 'em yet before they enter.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Let 'em be what they will, wee'le give them faire
Entertaine, and gentle welcome.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It shall be so.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Then let it be your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let's stand a side and you shall see us have
Fine sport anon.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: A faire society, do you know these Gentle women?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: What are they?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse:
The second is a neighbours daughter, her name is
~iola.
There is my kinsmans wife, Portia her name, and a
Friend too.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Let her—what's she that leades the dance?

speeches.speaker: 1. Ser.
verse: A Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I see that.

speeches.speaker: 1. Ser.
verse: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: 1. Ser.
verse: A Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Udsfoote, good Sir what's she that leades the dance?

speeches.speaker: 2. Ser.
verse: My Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: VVhat els?

speeches.speaker: 2. Ser.
verse: My Mistris, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Your Mistris? a pox on you, What a fry of fooles are here? I see 'tis treason to understa~d in this house; if nature were not better to them, then they can be to themselves, they would scant hitt their mouthes; my Mistris? Is there any one with so much witt in 's head, that can tell me at the first sight, what Gentlewoman that is that leades the dance?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis my wife.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Hum.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How do'st thou like her?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: VVell, a pretty Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Prethee be quiet.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I would I could
Let never any hereafter that's a man,
That has affections in him and free passions,
Receive the least tye from such a foole as this is,
That holds so sweet a wife, 'tis lamentable to consider truly
What right he robbs himselfe of, and what wrong
He doth the youth of such a Gentlewoman?
That knowes her beauty is no longer hers,
Then men will please to make it so, and use it
Neither of which lyes freely in a husband,
O what have I don, what have I don, Coxcomb?
If I had never seen, or never tasted
The goodnesse of this kix, I had beene a made man,
But now to make a Cuckold is a sinne
Against all forgivenesse, worse then a murther;
I have a Woolfe by the eares, and am bitten both wayes.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How now friend, what are you thinking of?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Nothing concerning you, I must be gone.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Pardon me, Ile have no going sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Then good sir give me leave to goe to bed,
I am very weary and ill tempered.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You shall presently, the dance is done.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Mistris, these are the gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: My husband will come home, deare sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: She's faire still, O that I were a knave or durst be one,
For thy sake coxco~be; he that invented honesty, undid me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I had you had not knowne me, y'are merry tis well thought,
And how ist with these worthy Gent?

speeches.speaker: Vb. & Sil.
verse: We are glad to see you here againe

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Oh Gent, what ha'you lost? but get you into travells,
There you may learne, I cannot say what hidden vertues.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Hidden from you I am sure,
My blood boyles like a furnace,
Shees a faire one.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Pray entertaine this Gent. with all the curtesie,
Fitting my most especiall friend.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What this poore house may yeild,
To make you welcome deare sir command
Without more complement.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I thanke you:
Shee's wise and speakes well too, oh what a blessing
Is gone by me neere to be recovered?
prose: Well, twas an old shame the Devill laid up for mee, and now has hit me home; if there be any waies to bee dishonest and save my selfe yet, — No it must not bee, why should I bee a foole to —Yet those eyes would tempt another Adam, how they call to me, and tell me — Sfoote they shall not tell me any thing, sir will you walke in.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How ist Signior?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Crazie a litle.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What ayle you sir?
Whats in my power pray make use of, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Tis that must doe me good, she do's not mock me sure,
An't please you nothing, my disease is only wearinesse.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: Come Gent. weele not keepe you from your bedds too long.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I ha some businesse, and tis late, and you far from your lodging.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Come my deare Mercury, ile bring you to your chamber, and then I am for you, Maria, thou art a new wife to me now, and thou shalt finde it, ere I sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: This foole, and his faire wife have made me franticke
From two such physickes for the soule, deliver me.
prose:
And I, an old asse to my selfe, mine owne rod whips me, — good sir no more of this, tis tedious, you
are the best guide in your owne house — goe sir —

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: VVell, you must have this wench then.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: I hope so, I am much o'th bow hand else.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: VVood I were hangd, tis a good loving little foole that dares venture her selfe upon a coast she never knew yet, but these women, when they are once thirteene, god speede the plough.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Faith they'le venture further, so their lading then a Merchant, and through as many stormes, but theyle bee franghted, they are made like Carrecks only strength and storage.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Come, come, you talke, you talke.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: VVe doe so, but tell me Richardo, woote thou marry her?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Marry her? why what should I do with her?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Pox, I thought we should have had all shares in her like lawfull prize.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: No by my faith sir, you shall pardon me, I lancht her at my owne charge without partners, and so ile keepe her.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: VVhats the houre?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Twelve.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: VVhat shall we doe the while? tis yet scarce eleven.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Theres no standing here, is not this the place?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: And to go back unto her fathers house, may breede suspition lets slip into a Taverne, for an houre, tis very cold.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
prose: Content, there is one hard by, a quart of burnt sack will recover us, I am as cold as Chri^mas, this stealing flesh in the frosty weather, may be sure 'ith eating, but sure the woodmen have no great catch on't; shalls go?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Thou art the strangest lover of a taverne, what shall we doe there now? loose the hower and our selves too?

speeches.speaker: Vb.
prose: Loose a pudding; what do'st thou talke of the howre; will one quart muzle us? have wee not eares to heare, and tongues to aske the drawers, but wee must stand here like bawds to watch the minuts?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Prethee content thy selfe, we shall scout here, as though we went a haying, and have some mangey prentice, that cannot sleepe for scratching, over eare us, come will you goe sirs? when your love fury is a little frozen, youle come to us.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: VVill you drinke but one quart then?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: No more I faith.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Content.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: VVhy then, have with you, but letts be very watchfull

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: The night is terrible and I enclos'd
With that my vertue and my self hate most,
Darkenesse; yet must I feare that which I wish,
Some company, and every step I take
Sounds louder in my fearefull eares to night
Then ever did, the shrill and sacred bell
That rang me to my prayers; the house will rise
When I unlock the doore, were it by day
I am bold enough, but then a thousand eyes
Warne me from going, might not God have made
A time for envious prying folke to sleepe
Whilst lovers met, and yet the sunne have shone?
Yet I was bold enough, to steale this key
Out of my fathers Chamber, and dare yet
Venture upon mine enemy, this night,
Arm'd onely with my love, to meet my friend.
Alas how valiant, and how fraid at once
Love makes a Virgin? I will throw this key
Back through a windowe, I had wealth enough
In Iewels with me, if I hold his love
I steale e'm for; farewell my place of birth,
I never make account to looke on thee againe;
And if there be as I have heard men say,
These houshold gods, I doe beseech them looke
To this my charge, blesse it from theeves and fire,
And keepe till happily my love I win
Me from thy doore, and hold my Father in.
prose: As watchfull as the belman, come Ile lead, because I hate good manners, they are too tedious.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: No more for God sake, how is the night boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Faith sir tis very late.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
prose: Faith sir you lye, is this your jack i'th clock-house? will you strike sir? gi's some more sack, you varlet.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Nay, if you love me, good Vberto goe,
I am monstrous hot with wine.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
prose: Quench it againe with love, Gent. I will-drinke one health more, and then if my leggs say mee not shamefully nay, I will goe with you, give me a singular quart.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Of what wine sir?

speeches.speaker: Vber.
prose: Of Sack, you that speake confusion at the bar, of sack I say, and every one his quart, what a devill letts be merry.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: You shall sir.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: We will sir, and a dryed tongue.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: And an Olive, boy, and a whole bunch of fidlers, my head swimmes plaguely, vds pretious I shall be claud.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: Pray goe, I can drinke no more, thinke on your promise, tis midnight Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
prose: O that it were dum midnight now, not a word more, every man on's knees, and betake himselfe to his saint, heer's to your wench, seigneour, all this, & then away.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I cannot drinke it.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Tis a toy, a toye, away wo't.

speeches.speaker: Vber.
prose: Now dare I speake any thing, to any body living, come whers the fault? off with it.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: I have broke my wind, call you this sack?— I wonder who made it? he was a sure workeman, for tis plaguy strong worke, is it gone round?

speeches.speaker: Vb.
prose: Tis at the last out of my way, good boy, is the moon up yet?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: Where is she boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: There sir.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: We shall have raine and thunder, boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: When sir?

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: I cannot tell, but sure we shall, boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: The Gent. is wine wise.

speeches.speaker: Vber.
verse: Drawer?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Here sir.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: Can you procure?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: What sir?

speeches.speaker: Vber.
verse: A whore or two or three as need shall serve, boy?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I, a good whore were worth money, boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: I protest sir we are all together unprovided.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: The mor's the pitty, boy, can you not vize us where my child?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Neither, in troth sir.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Why where were you brought up boy? no jugling of a whore? no ayme my boy?

speeches.speaker: Vber.
prose: It cannot sink in my head now, that thou shouldst marry, why shouldst thou marry, tell me?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I marry? Ile be hang'd first: some more wine boy.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Is she not a whore translated? & she be, lets repaire to her.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
prose: I cannot tell, she may be an offender; but signior Silvio I shall scratch your head, indeed I shall.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Judge me I do most jest with thee, what an she were inverted with her heeles upward, like a traitors Coate? what care I.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: I, hang her, shall we fall out for her?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I am a little angry, but these wenches, did you not talke of wenches?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Boy lend me your candle.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: VVhy Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: To set fire to your rotten feeling, you'le keep no
Whores, Rogue, no good members;

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: VVhores Sir?

speeches.speaker: Silu.
prose: I, whores, Sir, do you think we come to lye with your hogsheads?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: I must beate the watch, I have long'd for't any time this three weekes.

speeches.speaker: Silu.
prose: VVee'le beate the towne too, and thou wilt, we are proofe boy; shall wee kill any body?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: No but wee'le hurt 'em dangerously.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: Silu. Now must I kill one, I cannot avoide it, boy easily afore there with your candle; wher's your Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: A bed, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: VVith whom?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: VVith my Master.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
prose: You lye Boy, shee's better brought up then to lye with her husband, has he not cast his head yet? next yeare he will be a velvet-headed Cuckold.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: You are a merry Gentleman, there Sir, take hold

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: This is the place I have out told the Clock,
For hast, he is not here. Richardo? no;
Now every power that loves and is belov'd:
Keep me from shame to night, for all you know
Each thought of mine is innocent, and pure,
As flesh and blood can hold: I cannot back;
I threw the key within, and ere I raise
My Father up, to see his daughters shame,
I'le set me downe, and tell the Northern winde,
That it is gentler then the curling West;
If it will blow me dead, but he will come;
I faith 'tis cold; if hee deceive mee thus,
A woman will not easily trust a man. Hark what's that?

speeches.speaker: Sil within.
prose: Th'art over long at thy pott, tom, tom, thou art over long at the pott tom.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: Blesse me! whose that?

speeches.speaker: Pedro within.
verse: Whoo!

speeches.speaker: ~ber. within.
verse: There Boyes.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: Darkenesse be thou my cover, I must fly,
To thee I hast for help —

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: They have a light,
Winde if thou lov'st a virgine blow it out,
And I will never shut a window more,
To keep thee from me.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why Boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: What say you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why boy? art thou drunk boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: What would you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why very good, where are wee?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: I, that's the point.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Why Sir, you will be at your lodging presently.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I'le go to no lodging Boy.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: VVhether will you go then Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I'le go no farther.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: For Gods sake Sir, do not stay here all night.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: No more I will not boy, lay me downe, and rowle me to a whore.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: And mee.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: There spoke an —

speeches.speaker: Silvio.
verse: Then set your foote to my foote, & up tailes all.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: That is Richardo, what a noyse they make?
'Tis ill don on 'em: heere Sirs, Richardo?

speeches.speaker: Rich..
verse: What's that Boy?

speeches.speaker: Dra.
verse: 'Tis a wench Sir, pray Gent. come away.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: O my deare love! how doest thou?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: My sweet hart? even as thou seest.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Wher's thy wench?

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: VVher's this bed worme?

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: Speake softly for the love of heaven.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: Mistris get you gone, and doe not entice the gent. now you see thei're drunke, or Ile call the watch, and lay you fast enough.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Alas what are you? or what doe you meane?
Sweet love wher's the place?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Marry sweet love, ee'n here, lye downe Ile feese you.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Good god! what meane you?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Ile have the wench.

speeches.speaker: Vber.
verse: If you can get her.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: No Ile lye with the wench to night, and she shall be yours to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Let goe the wench.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Let you goe the wench.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: O Gent. as you had mothers!

speeches.speaker: Vber.
verse: They had no mothers, they are the sons of bitches

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Let that be maintain'd.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Marry then.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Oh blesse me heaven!

speeches.speaker: Vber.
verse: How many is there ons?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: About five.

speeches.speaker: Vber.
prose: Why then lets fight three to three.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Content.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: The watch? the watch? the watch? where are you?

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Where are these cowards?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Ther's the whore.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I never saw a drunken man before,
But these I thinke are so.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I mist you narrowly there.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: My state is such, I know not how to thinke,
A prayer fit for me, only I could move,
That never maiden more might be in love.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
verse: Where are they, boy?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Make no such hast sir, they are no runners.

speeches.speaker: Vb.
verse: I am hurt, but that's all one, I shall light upon some of ye,
Pedro thou art a tall Gent. let me kisse thee.

speeches.speaker: Watch.
verse: My friend.

speeches.speaker: Vber.
verse: Your friend? you ly.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Stand further off, the watch, you are full of fleas.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: Gent either be quiet, or we must make you quiet.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Nay good Mr. Constable, be not so Rigorous.

speeches.speaker: Vber.
verse: Mr. Constable lend me thy hand of justice.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: That I will sir.

speeches.speaker: Vber.
prose: Fy Mr. Constable what golls you have? is justice so blind she cannot see to wash your hands? I cry you mercy Sir; Your gloves are one.

speeches.speaker: Dra.
verse: Now you are up Sir, will you go to bed?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I'le truckle heere Boy, give me another pillow.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: VVill you stand up and let me lay it on then?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Draw.
prose: There hold him two of yee, now they are up be going Mr. Constable

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: And this way, and that way, tom.

speeches.speaker: ~ber.
verse: And heere away and there away tom.

speeches.speaker: Silu.
verse: This is the right way the others the wrong.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Th' others the wrong.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Thou art over long at the pott tom, tom.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Lead valiantly sweet Constable, whoop! ha Boyes!

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: This wine hunts in their heads.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Give me the bill, for I'le bee the Sergeant.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: Looke to him Sirs.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Keep your Ranks you Rascalls, keep your Ranks.

speeches.speaker: Mercury.
prose: I Cannot sleep for thinking of this Asses wife, I'le be gon presently, ther's no staying heere, with this Divell about me? hoe, this is the house of sleep, hoe? againe ther's foote the darknesse, and this love together, will make mee lunaticke; ho?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Who calls there?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Pray take the paines to rise and light a candle.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Presently,

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Was ever man but I in such a stockes? well this shal be a warning to me, and a faire one too, how I betray my selfe to such a dunce, by way of benefit.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Did you call?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Yes, pray doe me the kindnesse sir, to let me out and not to enquire why, for I must needs be gone.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Not to night, I hope sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good sir to night, I would not have troubled you else, pray let it be so.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Alas sir, my Master will be offended.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: That I have businesse? no I warrant yee.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Good sir take your rest.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Pray my good friend let me appoint my owne rest.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Then shew me the way out, I'le consider you.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Good Lord, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If I had not an excellent tempered patience, now should I breake this fellowes head, and make him understand 'twere necessary; the onely plague of this house is the unhandsome love of servants, that neere doe their duty in the right place, but when they muster before dinner, and sweep the table with a wodden dagger, and then they are troublesom too, to all mens shoulders, the Woodcocks flesht agen, now I shall have a new stir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: VVhy how now friend? what do you up so late? are you well? do you want any thing? pray speake.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Onely the cause I rise for.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What knaues are these? what do you want? why sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nothing i'the world, but the keyes to let me out of dores; I must be gon, bee not against it, for you cannot stay me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Begon at this time? that were a merry jest.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If there be any mirth in't, make you use on't, but I must go.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Why for loves sake?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: 'Twill benefit your understanding nothing to know the cause, pray go to bed, I'le trouble your man only.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Nay Sir you have rais'd more, that has reason to curse you, and you knew all, my wifes up, and comming downe too.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Alas it will be a trouble, pray go up to her and let me disturbe no more, 'tis unmannerly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Shee's here already; sweet hart: how say you by this Gentleman? he would away at midnight.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: That I am sure hee will not.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Indeed I must.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
prose: Good Sir let not your homely entertainement presse you to leave your bed at midnight; if you want, what my house or your towne may afford you, make it your own fault if you call not for it pray go to bed again; let me compell you, I am sure you have no power to denye a woman; the ayre is piercing, & to a body beaten with long travell, 'twill prove an ill Physitian.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If she speake longer I shall be a knaue, as ranke as ever sweat for't; Sir if you will send your wife up presently, I will either stay with you, d'ye marke, me or deliver you, so just a cause, that you your selfe, shall thrust me out of doores, both suddainly and willingly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I would faine heare that faith, pray thee go up sweet hart, I have halfe perswaded him, besides, he hath some private businesse with mee.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good night Sir, and what content you would have, I wish with you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Could any man that had a back aske more? o me! o me!

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Now deale directly with me: why should you go?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If you be wise do not enquire the cause, 'twill trouble you:

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVhy? prithee why?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Faith I would not have you know it, let me go, 'twill be far better for you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Who's that, that knocks there? i'st not at the street doore?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Who's there, cannot you speake?

speeches.speaker: Within Vio.
verse: A poore distressed maid, for gods sake let me in.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Let her in and me out together, 'tis but one labour, tis pity shee should stand ith' street, it seemes she knowes you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: There shee shall stand for me, you are ignorant; this is a common custome of the Rogues that lie about the loose parts of the City.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: As how?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: To knock at doores in dead time of night, and use some fained voyce to raise compassion, and when the doores are open, in they rush, and cut the throats of all and take the booty, we cannot be too carefull.

speeches.speaker: Within ~i.
verse: As ever you had pity let me in, I am undone else.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Who are you?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: My name is Viola, a Gentlewoman, that ill chance hath distressed, you know my father,

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Alas of god we'll let her in, 'tis one of the Gentlewomen were here ith' evening, I know her by her name, (poore soule) shee's cold I warrant her, let her have my warme Bed, and Ile take her fortune; come, pray come.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: It is not Viola that's certaine, she went home to her fathers, I am sure,

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Will not you be so good to let me in?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Ile be so good to have you whipt away if you stay a litle longer: Shee's gone I warrant her, now let mee know your cause for I will heare it, and not repent the knowing.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Since you are so importunate, I'le tell you, I love your wife extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Uery well.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: And so well that I dare not stay.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVhy?

speeches.speaker: M^r.
prose: For wronging you, I know I am flesh and blood, and you have done me friendships infinite and often, that must require me honest and a true man, and I will be so or I'le breake my heart.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVhy, you may stay for all this, me thinks.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No, though I wood be good, I am no saint, nor is it safe to try mee, I deale plainely.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Come I dare try you, do the best you can.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: You shall not when I am right agen, I'le come and see you, till when, I'le use all Countryes and all meanes, but I will loose this folly, 'tis a Divell.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Is there no way to stay you?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No, unles you will have me such a villaine to you as all men shall spit at mee.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Do's she know you love her?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No I hope not, that were recompence fit for a Rogue to render her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: If ever any had a faithfull friend I am that man, and I may glory in't, this is he, that ipse, he that passes all Christendome for goodnesse, hee shall not over go me in his friendship twere recreant and base, and I'le be hang'd first, I am resolv'd, go thy wayes, a wife shall never part us, I have consider'd and I finde her nothing to such a friend as thou art; I'le speake a bold word, take your time and woe her, you have overcome me cleerely, and do what's fitting with her, you conceive mee, I am glad at hart you love her: by this light, ne're stare upon me for I will not flye from it, if you had spoken sooner, sure you had bin serv'd; Sir, you are not every man, now to your taske, I give you free leave, and the sinne is mine if there be any in it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Hee will be hang'd before he makes this good, hee cannot be so innocent a Coxcombe, he can tell ten sure, if I had never knowne you as I have done, I might be one, as others perhaps sooner, but now 'tis impossible ther's too much good betweene us.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Well thou art een the best man—I can say no more, I am, so over joy'd, you must stay this night, and in the morning go as earely as you please, I have a toy for you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I thought this pill would make you sicke.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: But where you meane to be I must have notice,
And it must be hard by too, do you marke me?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Why? what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: There is a thing in hand.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Why? what thing?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: A sound one, if it take right, and you be not peevish We two will be—you would little thinke it; as famous for our friendship—

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: If God please, as ever Damon was and Pytheas or Pylades, and Orestes, or any two that ever were: do you conceive me yet?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: No by my troth Sir; he will not help me up sure.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: You shall anon, and for our names, I thinke they shal live after us, and be remember'd while there is a story; or I loose my aime.

speeches.speaker: Mer
verse: What a vengeance ailes hee? how do you?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Yes faith, wee two wilbe such friends as the world shall ring off.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: And why is all this?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You shall enjoy my wife.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: The wonder must begin, so I have cast it, 'twill be scurvy else, you shall not stirr a foote i'nt, pray be quiet 'till I have made it perfect.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: What shall a man do with this wretched fellow? there is no mercy to be used towards him, he is not capable of any pitty, he will in spight of course be a Cuckold, And who can help it? must it begin so needs Sir?— thinke agen.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Yes marry must it, and I my selfe will woe this woman for you, do you perceive it now? ha?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Yes now I have a little sight i'th matter; o that thy head should be so monstrous, that al thy Servants hatts may hang upon't! but do you meane to do this?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Yes certaine, I will woe her, and for you, strive not against it, 'tis the overthrow of the best plott that ever was then.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Nay I'le assure you Sir, I'le do no harme, you have too much about you of your owne.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Have you thought of a place yet?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: A place?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I a place where you will bide, pre'thee no more of this modesty, 'tis foolish, and we were not determinde to be absolute friends indeed, 'twere tolerable.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I have thought, and you shall heare from me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why? this will gaine me everlasting glory; I have the better of him, that's my comfort, good night.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Good night, well go thy wayes, thou art the tydiest wittall this day I thinke above ground, and yet thy end for all this must bee mottly.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: 'Tis bitter cold; a plague upon these Rogues, how wary they are growne? not a doore open now, but double bard, not a window, but up with a case of wood like a spice box, and their locks unpickable, the very smithes that were halfe venturers, drink penitent single Ale, this is the Iron age, the Ballad sings of; well I shall meet with some of our loose Linnen yet, good fellowes must not starve; heer's he shall shew you God a mighties dog bolts, if this hold.

speeches.speaker: Dorathy.
prose: Faith thou art but too mercifull, that's thy fault thou art as sweete a thiefe, that sin excepted ever sufferd, that's a proud word and I'le maintaine it.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Come prethee let's shogg off, & brouze an hower or two, ther's ale will make a Cat speake, at the harrow, we shall get nothing now, without we batter, 'tis growne too neere morning, the Rogues sleep sober, and are watchfull.

speeches.speaker: Dorit.
prose: Wee want a Boy extreamely for this function kept under for a yeare, vvith milke and knott-grasse; in my time I have seene a boy do vvonders Robbin the red Tincker had a boy Rest his soule he sufferd this time 4. yeares for two spoones, & a Pevvter Candlestick, that svveet man had a Boy as I am Curstend Whore, vvould have run through a Cat hole, he vvold have boulted such a peece of linen in an evening—

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Well, vve vvill have a Boy, prethee lets go, I am vengeance cold I tell thee.

speeches.speaker: Dorithy.
prose: I'le be hang'd before I stirr vvithout some purchase by these ten bones, I'le turne she ape and untile a house, but I'le have it, it may be I have an humour to bee hang'd, I cannot tell

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
prose: Peace, you flead vvhore, thou hast a mouth like a Bloodhounde, heere comes a night shade.

speeches.speaker: Dorit.
prose: A Gentlevvoman vvhore, by this darkenesse I'le case her to the skin.

speeches.speaker: Tinck.
verse: Peace I say.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: What feare have I endured this dismall night?
And vvhat disgrace if I vvere seene and knovvne?
In vvhich this darkenesse, onely is my friend,
That onely has undone me; a thousand curses
Light on my easy, foolish childish, love,
That durst so lightly lay a confidence
Upon a man, so many being false;
my wearinesse, and weeping makes me sleepie, I must lye downe.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: VVhats this? a prayer, or a homilie, or a Ballad of good councell? she has a gowne, I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Knock out her braines and then shee'le neere byte

speeches.speaker: Tin.
verse: Yes I will knock her, but not yet, you? woman?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: For gods sake what are you?

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: One of the groomes of your wardrobe, come uncase, uncase; byr lady a good Kersey.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Pray doe not hurt me sir.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Lets have no pitty, for if you doe, heres that shall cutt your whistle.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
prose: Alas what would you have? I am as miserable as you can mak me any way.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: That shall be tryde.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Here, take my gowne if that will doe you pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Yes marry will it, looke in the pockets Doll, there may be birds.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: They are flown a pox goe vvith them, I'le have this Hatt, and this Ruffe too, I like it, novv vvill I flourish like a Lady, brave I faith boy.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Y'are so gentle people to my seeming,
That by my truth I could live vvith you.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Could you so? a pretty young round vvench, vvell bloudded, I am for her, theeves.

speeches.speaker: Dor
prose: But by this I am not, coole your Godpiece, Rogue, or Ile clap a spell upon't, shall take your edge off with a very vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Peace horse-flesh, peace, Ile cast off my Amazon, she has walked too long, and is indeede notorious, sheele fight and scould, and drinke like one of the worthies.

speeches.speaker: Dort.
prose: Vds pretious you young contagious whore must you be ticing? and is your flesh so wrank sir, that two may live upon't? I am glad to heare your cortall growne so lusty; he was dry foundered tother day, wee hee my pampered lade of Asia.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Good woman doe not hurt me, I am sorry that I have given any cause of anger.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Either binde her quickly and come away, or by this steele Ile tell though I trusse for company; now could I eate her broyld, or any way, without vinegar, I must have her nose.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: By any thing you love best, good sir, good woman.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
verse: Why her nose Dorithy?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: If I have it not and presently and warme, I loose that I goe withall.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Wood the Devill had that thou goest withall, and thee together, for sure he got thy whelps if thou hast any, shees thy deere dad, whore! put up your cutpurse; an I take my swich up, twill be a black time with you else sheth your bung whore.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
prose: Will you binde her? we shall stand here prating and be hang both.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
verse: Come I must bind you, not a word, no crying.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Doe what you will, indeed I will not cry.

speeches.speaker: Tin.
prose: Hurt her not, if thou dost by Ale and Beare Ile clout thy old bald braine pan, with a peece of brasse, you bitch incarnate.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: O God to what am I reserved, that knew not
Through all my childish howers and actions
More sinne then poore imagination,
And too much loving of a faithlesse man?
For which I am paid, and so, that not the day
That now is rising to protect the harmelesse,
And give the innocent a sanctuary
From theeves and spoylers, can deliver me
From shame, at least suspition—

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Sirrah leade downe the horses easily, I'le walke a foot till I be downe the hill, tis very early, I shall reach home betimes. How now, whose there?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Night that was ever friend to lovers, yet
Has rais'd some weary soule, that hates his bed
To come and see me blush, and then laugh at me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: H'ad a rude heart that did this.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Gentle sir,
If you have that which honest men call pitty,
And be as far from evill as you shew;
Helpe a poore maide, that this night by bad fortune
Has beene thus us'd by Robbers.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: A pox upon his heart that would not helpe thee, this theefe was halfe a Lawyer, by his bands, how long have you bin tyed here?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: Alas this hower, and with cold and feare am almost perisht.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Where were the watch the while? good sober Gent. they were like carefull members of the City, drawing in diligent ale and singing catches, while Mr. Constable contrived the tosts: these fellowes would bee more severely punisht then wandring Gipsies, that every stat^te whipps, for if they had every one two eyes a peece more, three pots would put them out.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I cannot tell I found no Christian to give me succour.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: When they take a theefe, I'le take Ostend agen; the whorsons drinke opium in their Ale, & then they sleep like topps; as for their bills, they onely serve to reach downe Bacon to make Rashers on; now let mee know whom I have done this courtesie too, that I may thanke my early rising for it?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Sir, All I am, you see.

speeches.speaker: Val
prose: You have a name I'm sure, and a kindred, a father, friend or something that must owne you; shee's a handsome young wench; what Rogues were these to Rob her?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Sir you see all I dare reveale,
And as you are a Gent presse me no further;
For there begins a griefe whose bitternesse
Will breake a stronger heart then I have in me,
And twill but make you heavie with the hearing,
For your owne goodnesse sake desire it not.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: If you would not have me enquire that, how do you live then?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: How I have lived, is still one question,
Which must not be resolu'd—
How I desire to live, is in your liking,
So worthy an opinion I have of you,

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: Is in my liking? how I pray thee? tell me, ifaith I'le do you any good lys in my power; she has an eye would raise a bedrid man; come leave your feare and tell mee, thats a good wench.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: Sir I would serve—

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Who wouldst thou serve? doe not weepe and tell me.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
prose: Faith sir even some good woman, and such a wife if you be married, I doe imagine yours.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: Alas! thou art young and tender, let me see thy hand, this was neere made to wash or wind up water, beate cloaths, or rub a floore, by this light, for one use that shall be namelesse, tis the best wanton hand that ere I looke on.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Dare you accept me sir, my heart is honest,
Among your vertuous charitable deeds,
This will not be the least.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Thou canst in a Chamber.

speeches.speaker: ~io
verse: In a Chamber sir.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: I meane waite there upon a Gentlewoman,
How quick she is, I like that mainely too;
Ile have her, though I keepe her with maine strength
like a besieged towne, for I know I shall have the enemy afore me within a weeke.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: Sir I can sow too, and make pretty laces,
Dresse a head handsome, teach young gentlewomen,
For in all these I have a little knowledge.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: Tis well, no doubt I shall encrease that knowledge; I like her better still, how she provokes me; pritty youngmaid you shall serve a good Gentlewoman, though I say't that will not be unwilling you should please mee, nor I forgetfull if you doe.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
verse: I am the happier.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: My man shall make some shift to carry you behind him, can you ride well?

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: But I'le hold fast for catching of a fall.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: That's the next way to pull another on you, I'le worke her as I go I know shee's wax, now, now, at this time could I begett a worthy on this wench.

speeches.speaker: ~iol.
prose: Sir for this Gentlenesse, may heaven requite you tenfold.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: 'Tis a good vvench hovv ever others use thee, be sure I'le bee a loving master to thee, come.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I hope I am vvilde enough for being knovvne I have vvrit a letter here, and in it have abus'd my selfe most bitterly, yet all my feare is not enough, for that must do it, that must lay it on, I'le vvin her out i'th flint, 'tvvill be more famous, novv for my language.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Now Sir vvho vvould you speake vvith?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Where be thy Mastres man? I vvould speake vvith her.
I have a letter.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Cannot I deliver it?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No by my trot and fait can'st thou not man.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Well Sir I'le call her to you, pray shake your eares vvithout a little.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Cran a Cree do it quickly; this rebbell tonge sticks in my teeth vvorse then a toughe hen, sure it vvas nere knovvne at Babell, for they soul'd no apples, and this vvas made for certaine at the first planting of Orchards 'tis so crabbed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Whats he wood speake with me?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: A kill kenny ring, there he stands Madam.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What would you have with me, friend?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: He has a letter for other women, wilt thou read it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: From whence?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: De Crosse creest from my Master.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Who is your Master?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I pray do you looke.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Doe you know this fellow?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: No Maddam not I; more then an Irish footman stand further friend, I doe not like your roperunners, what stallion Rogues are these, to weare such dovvsetts, the very Cotton may commit adultery.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: I cannot find whose hand this should be, Ile reade, to the beauteous vvife of Don Antonio, sure this is some blind scrib —vvell novv vvhat follovves?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Pray God it take, I have given her, that will stirr her conscience, how it workes with her; hope if it be thy will let the flesh have it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: This is the most abhor'd, intollerable knavery, that ever slave entertain'd, sure there is more then thine owne head in this villany, it goes like practic'd mischeife, disabled in his body? o good God, as I live he lyes fearefully, and basely, ha? I should know that Iewell, 'tis my husband, come hither shat, are you an Irish man?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sweete woman a Cree I am an Irish man.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Now I know it perfectly; is this your trick Sir? I'le trick you for it; how long have you serv'd this Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Please thee a little day, o my Mac dermond put me to my mastree, 'tis don I know.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: By my faith he speakes as well as if he had been lousy for the language a yeare or two; well Sir, you had bin better have kept your owne shape as I will use you, what have I don that should deserve this tryall, I never made him cuckold to my knowledge, Sirrah com hither.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Now will she send some Iewell, or some letter
I know her minde as well; I shall be famous.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Take this Irish bawde heere.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And kicke him till his breeches and breech bee of one colour a bright blew both.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I may be well swing'd thus, for I dare not reveale my selfe, I hope shee does not meane it, o hone o hone, o St. Patricke, o a Cree, o sweet woman.

speeches.speaker: Mar,
verse: No turne him and kick him o tother side, that's well

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: O good waiting man, I beseech thee good waiting man, a pox fyre your leggs.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: You Rogue you enimy to all, but little breeches how darst thou come to me with such a letter?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Prethee pitty the poore Irishman, all this makes for me, if I win her yet, I am still more glorious.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: Now could I weep at what I have don, but I'le harden my hart agen, go shut him up, 'till my husband comes home, yet thus much ere ye go, sirrah thatch'd head, would'st not thou be whipt & think it justice? well Aquavitae Barrell, I will bounce you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I pray do, I beseech you be not angry.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: O you hobby headed Raskall, I'le have you flead, and trossers made of thy skin to tumble in, go a way with him, let him see no sun, 'till my husband come home, sir I shall meet with you for your knavery, I feare it not.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Wilt thou not let mee go? I do not like this.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Away with him.

speeches.speaker: Servingman.
prose: Come I'le lead you in by your Iacke a lent haire, go quietly or I'le make your crupper cracke.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
prose: And do you heare me sirrah? and when you have done, make my Coach ready.

speeches.speaker: Serving.
prose: Yes forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Locke him up safe enough I'le to this Gentleman,
I know the reason of all this businesse, for I do suspect it,
If he have this plott, I'le ring him such a peale, shall make his eares deafe for a moneth at least.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Am I not mad? can this weake temper'd head,
That will be mad with drink, endure the wrong
That I have done a virgin and my love?
Be mad, for so thou ought'st, or I vvill beate
The vvalls and trees, dovvne vvith thee, and vvill let
Either thy memory out or madnesse in,

But sure I never lov'd faire
~iola:
I never lov'd my Father nor my Mother,
Or any thing but drinke; had I had love;
Nay, had I knovvne so much charity,
As would have sav'd an Infant from the fire,
I had bin naked, raving in the street:
With halfe a face, gashing my selfe with knives,
Two howers ere this time.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Good morrow Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Good morrow Gentlemen, shal we go drink agen?
I have my witts.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: So have I but they are unsetled ones, would I had some porrige.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: The taverne boy was here this morning with mee
And told me that there was a Gentlewoman,
Which he tooke for a whore that hung on me:
For whom we quarrel'd, and I know not what.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I faith nor I.

speeches.speaker: ~be.
verse: I have a glimmering of some such thing.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Was it you Silvio,
That made me drinke so much? 'twas you or Pedro.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I know not who.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: We were all apt enough.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: But I wil lay the fault on none but me,
That I would be so entreated, come Silvio,
Shall we goe drinke agen, come Gentlemen,
Why do you stay, let's never leave off now,
Whilst we have Wine and throates, I'le practise it,
Till I have made it my best quality;
For what is best for me to do but that?
For Gods sake come and drinke; when I am nam'd
Men shall make answer, which Richado meane you?
The excellent drinker? I will have it so,
Will you goe drinke?

speeches.speaker: Silv.
verse: We drunke too much too lately.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why there is then the lesse behind to drinke,
Let's end it all, dispatch that, wee'l send abroad,
And purchase all the Wine the world can yield,
And then drinke it off, then take the fruits o'the earth,
Distill the Juice from them, and drinke that off;
Wee'l catch the raine before it fall to ground,
And drinke off that that never more may grow;
Wee'l set our mouths to Springs, and drinke them off,
And all this while wee'l never thinke of those
That love us best, more then we did last night.
We will not give unto the poore a drop
Of all this drinke, but when we see them weepe,
Wee'l run to them, and drinke their teares off too,
Wee'l never leave whilst there is heate or moysture,
In this large globe, but suck it cold and dry,
Till we have made it Elementall earth,
Meerly by drinking.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Is't flattery to tell you, you are mad?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: If it be false,
There's no such way to bind me to a man;
He that will have me, lay my goods and lands,
My life down for him, need no more, but say
Richardo thou art mad, and then all these
Are at his service, then he pleases me,
And makes me thinke that I had vertue in me,
That I had love, and tendernesse of heart,
That though I have committed such a fault,
As never creature did, yet runinng mad,
As honest men should doe for such a crime,
I have exprest some worth, though it be late:
But I alas have none of these in me,
But keep my wits still like a frozen man,
That had no fire within him.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Nay good Richardo leave this wild talk, and send a letter to her, I'le deliver it.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: 'Tis to no purpose; perhaps she's lost last night,
Or she got home agen, she's now so strictly
Look'd to, the wind can scarce come to her, or admit
She were her selfe; if she would hear from me,
From me unworthy, that have us'd her thus,
She were so foolish, that she were no more
To be beloved.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Sir, we have fou~d this night-gown she took with her.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Where? where? speake quickly.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Searching in the Suburbs, we found a Tinker and his whore, that had in it a sap-house, whom we apprehended, and they confest they stole it from her.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: And murthered her?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: What aile you Man?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why all this doth not make me mad.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: It does, you would not offer this else, good Pedro looke to his sword.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: They do deny the killing of her, but swore they left her tyed to a tree, in the fields, next those Suburbs that are without our Ladies gate, neer day, & by the rode, so that some passinger must needs unty her quickly.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: The will of heaven be done? Sir I wil only entreat you this, that as you were the greatest occasion of her losse, that you will be pleased to urge your friends, and be your selfe earnest in the search of her; if she be found, she is yours, if she please, I my selfe only, see these people better examin'd, and after follow some way in search, God keepe you Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Alas good man!

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: VVhat think you now of me, I think this lump
Is nothing but a piece of fleagme congeal'd
VVithout a soule, for where theres so much spirit
As would but warm a flea, those faults of mine
VVould make it glow and flame in this dull heart,
And run like molten gold through every sin,
Till it could burst these walls and fly away.
Shall I intreat you all to take your horses,
And search this innocent?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: VVith all our hearts.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Do not devide your selves till you come there,
VVhere they say she was ty'd, I'le follow too,
But never to return till she be found.
Give me my sword good Pedro, I will do
No harme believe me with it, I am now
Farre better temper'd, If I were not so,
I have enow besides, God keep you all,
And send us good successe.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: WHo is it? can you tell?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: By my troth Sir I know not, but 'tis a Gentlewoman

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: A Gentleman I'le lay my life you puppy, h'as sent his wife to me: if he have, fling up the bed.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Here she is Sir.

speeches.speaker: VVife.
verse: VVhy should you dare to imagine me
So light a huswife, that from four hours knowledge
You might presume to offer to my credite
This rude and ruffian tryall, I am sure
I never courted you, nor gave you tokens,
That might concerne assurance, you are a foole.
prose: I am glad I found you Sir, there take your letter and keepe it till you have another friend to wrong, 'tis too malicious false to make me sin, you have provoked mee to be that I love not, a talker, and you shall heare me.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I cannot blame you now, I see this letter
Though you be angry, yet with me you must not,
Unlesse you'l make me guilty of a wrong,
My worst affections hate—

speeches.speaker: VVife.
verse: Did not you send it?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose:
No upon my faith, which is more, I understand
it not; the hand is as far from my knowledg, as the malice.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: This is strange.

speeches.speaker: Mer
verse: It is so, and had been stranger, and indeed more hatefull,
Had ^, that have receiv'd such courtesies, & owe so many
Thanks, done this base office.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Your name is at it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Yes, but not my nature, and I shall hate my name worse then the manner, for this base broking; you are wise and vertuous, remove this fault from me; for on the love I beare to truth and goodnesse, this letter dare not name me for the author.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Now I perceive my husbands knavery, if my man can but finde where he has been, I will goe with this Gentleman whatsoever comes on't: and as I meane to carry it both he and all the world shall thinke it fit, and thank me for it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I must confesse I loved you, at first, however this made me leave your house unmannerly, that might provoke me to do something ill, both to your honour & my faith, and not to write this letter, which I hold so truly wicked, that I will not thinke on't.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I do beleeve you, and since I see you are free, my words were not meant to you, but this is not the halfe of my affliction.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: 'Tis pitty you should know more vexation; may I enquire?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Faith Sir I feare I have lost my husband.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Your husband? it cannot be: I pitty her, how shee's vext?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: How now? what news? nay speake, for we must know.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Faith I have found at length by chance where he has been

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: In a blind out-house in the Suburbs, pray God all be well with him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: There are his cloaths, but what's become of him, I cannot yet enquire.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I am glad of this; sure they have murtherd him, what shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Be not so grieved before you know the truth, you have time enough to weepe, this is the sodainst mischiefe; did you not bring an Officer to search there, where you say you found his cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Yes, and wee searcht it, and charg'd the fellow with him: but he like a rogue, stubborn rogue, made answer, he knew not where he was; he had been there, but where he was now, he could not tell: I tell you true I fear him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Are all my hopes and longings to enjoy him,
After this 3 yeares travell, come to this?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: It is the rankest house in all the City, the most cursed roguy bawdi-house? hell fire it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: This is the worst I heard yet; will you go home? I'le beare you company, and give you the best help I may: this being here will wrong you.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: As you are a Gentleman, and as you loved your dead friend, let me not goe home, that will but heape one sorrow on another.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why purpose any thing and I'le perform't; I am at my wits end too.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: So am I, O my deare Master!

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Peace you great foole.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Then good Sir cary me to some retired place, far from the sight of this unhappy City, whether you will indeed, so it be far enough.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If I might councel you, I think 'twere better to go home, and try what may be done yet, hee may bee at home afore you, who can tell?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: O no, I know he's dead, I know hee's murder'd; tell me not of going home, you murder me too.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Well, since it pleases you to have it so, I will no more perswade you to go home, I'le be your guide in the Countrey, as your griefe doth command me, I have a Mother dwelling from this place some 20. miles, the house though homely, yet able to shew something like a welcome: thither I'le see you safe with all your sorrows.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: With all the speed that may be thought upon; I have a Coach here ready, good Sir quickly; I'le fit you my fine husband.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: It shall be so; if this fellow be dead, I see no band of any other man, to tye me from my will, and I will follow her with such carefull service, that she shall either be my Love or Wife; will you walke in?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I thank you Sir, but one word with my man, and I am ready; keepe the Irish fellow safe, as you love your life, for he I feare has a deep hand in this, then search agen, & get out warrants for that naughty man, that keeps the bad house, that he may answer it, if you find the body, give it due buriall; farewell. You shall heare from mee, keep all safe.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: O my sweet Mr!

speeches.speaker: Ant. within.
prose: Man-a-cree, the Devill take thee, wilt thou kill me here, I prethee now let me goe seeke my Mr. I shall be very cheel else.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Do you hear man-a-cree, i'le cree your coxcombe, and you keep not still, down you rogue.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Good sweet fact serving-man, let me out I beseech de, and by my trot I will give dye Worship 2. shillings in good argott, to buy dy VVorship pippines.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: This rogue thinks all the worth of man consists in Peepins; by this light I'le beate rebellion out of you for ever.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Wilt thou not heare me man? is fet, i'le give thee all I have about me.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I thank you Sir, so I may have picking worke,

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Here is five shillings man,
Here is a cudgell, a very good one.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: How now, what's the matter, wher's the Irishman.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: There, a wyth take him, he makes more noyse alone there, then ten Lawyers can do with double & a scurvy Case.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Let him out, I must talke with him.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Wilt thou give me some drinke, ô hone? I am very dry man.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
prose: You shall have that shall quench your thirst, my friend.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Fate dost thou meane man.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Even a good tough halter.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: A halter? ô hone!

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Sirha you are a mischievous rogue, that'^ the truth.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No fet I am not.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser
prose: Shall I knocke out his braines? I have kill'd dogs have been worth three of him for all uses.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
prose: Sirah, the truth on't is, you must with mee to a Justice. O Roger, Roger.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Why, what's the matter William?

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Heavy newes Roger, heavy newes, God comfort us.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: What is't man?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: What's the matter now? I am e'ne weary of this way, wouldl were out on't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: My Mr. sure is murdered, Roger, and this cursed rogue feare has had a hand in't.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No fet not.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: Stand away, i'le kickt out of him: come sirha, mount, i'le make you dance, you Rascall, kill my Master? If thy breech were cannon proofe, having this good cause on my side, I would encounter it; hold faire, Shamrocke.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Why how now sirs? you wil not murder me indeed.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Blesse us Roger!

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nay, I am no spirit.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: How do you Sir, this is my very Master.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Why well enough yet, but you have a heavy foote of your owne; where's my wife?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: Alas poor sorrowfull Gentlewoman, she thinks you are dead, and has given o're house-keeping.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Whether is she gone then?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: Into the Countrey with the Gentleman your friend Sir, to see if she can wear her sorrows out there; she weeps and takes on too too —

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: This falls out pat; I shall be everlasting for a name: doe you hear? upon your lives and faiths to me, not one word I am living, but let the same report passe along, that I am murther'd still; I am made for ever.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Why Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I have a Cause Sir that's enough for you; well, if I be not famous, I am wrong'd much; for any thing I know I will not trouble him this weeke at least, noe, let them take their way one of another.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Sir, will you be still an Irish-man.?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes a while.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: But your Worship will be beaten no more?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No I thanke you William.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: In truth Sir, if it must be so, I'le doe it better then a stranger.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Goe, you are Knaves both, but I forgive you, I am almost mad with the apprehension of what I shall be, not a word I charge you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Come pretty soul, we now are neer our home,
And whilst our horses are walkt downe the hill,
Let thou and I walke here over this Close:
The foot-way is more pleasant, 'tis a time
My pretty one, not to be wept away,
For every living thing is full of love;
Art not thou so too? hah?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Nay, there are living things empty of love,
Or I had not been here, but for my selfe!
Alas, I have too much.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: It cannot be, that so much beauty, so much youth and grace should have too much of love.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Pray what is love? for I am full of that I doe not know.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Why, love faire maid is an extream desire,
That's not to be examin'd but fulfil'd,
To aske the reason why thou art in love,
Or what might be the noblest end in love,
Would overthrow that kindly rising warmth,
That many times slides gently o're the heart,
'Twould make thee grave, & staid thy thoughts would be,
Like a thrice married Widow, full of ends,
And void of all compassion, and to fright thee
From such enquiry, whereas thou art now
Living in ignorance, mild, fresh, and sweet,
And but sixteen, the knowing what love is,
Would make thee sixe and forty.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Would it would make me nothing, I have heard
Schollers affirme the world is upheld by love,
But I beleeve women maintain all this,
For ther's no love in men.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Yes, in some men.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I know them not.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Why, there is love in me.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Ther's charity I am sure towards me.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: And love; which I will now expresse, my pretty maide,
I dare not bring thee home, my Wife is foule,
And therefore envious, she is very old,
And therefore Jealous; thou art faire and young,
A subject fit, for her unlucky vices.
To worke upon, she never will endure thee.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Shee may endure
If she be ought, but Divell, all the friendship
That I will hold with you; can she endure
I should be thankfull to you? may I pray
For you and her, will she be brought to thinke
That all the honest industry I have
Deserves browne bread? if this may be endur'd,
Shee'l picke a quarrell with a sleeping childe,
E're she fall out with me.

speeches.speaker: Val
verse: But trust me she doe's hate all handsomenesse.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: How fell you in love with such a creature?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I never lov'd her.

speeches.speaker: Vio,
verse: And yet married her?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Shee was a rich one.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: And you swore I warrant you, she was a faire one then too.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Or beleeve me I thinke I had not had her.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Are you men all such? wood you wood wall us in a place
Where all we women, that are innocent,
Might live together.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Do not weep at this,
Although I dare not for some weighty reason
Displease my Wife, yet I forget not thee.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
