verse: VVhat will you do with me?

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Thou shalt be plac'd
At my mans house, and have such food and rayment
As can be bought with money: these white hands
Shall never learn to worke, but they shall play
As thou saist they were wont, teaching the strings
To move in order, or what else thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: I thanke you Sir, but pray you cloath me poorly,
And let my labour get me meanes to live.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: But faire one, you I know do so much hate
A foule ingratitude, you will not looke
I should do this for nothing.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: I will worke as much out as I can, and take as litle
That you shall have as duly paid to you
As ever servant did.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: But give me now a tryall on't, I may beleeve
We are alone, shew me how thou wilt kisse
And hug me hard, when I have stolne away
From my too clamorous Wife that watches me,
To spend a blessed houre or two with thee.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Is this the love you mean? you would have that
Is not in me to give, you would have lust.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Not to dissemble, or to mince the word,
'Tis lust I wish indeed.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: And by my troth I have it not for heavens sake use mee kindely.
Though I be good, and shew perhaps a monster,
As this world goes.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I doe
But speak to thee, thy answers are thy owne,
I compell none, but if thou refuse this motion,
Thou art not then for me, alas good soule?
What profit can thy worke bring me.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: But I feare: I pray goe, for lust they say will grow
Outragious being deni'd, I give you thankes
For all your courtesies, and there's a Jewell
That's worth the taking, that I did preserve
Safe from the robbers, pray you leave me here
Just as you found me, a poor innocent,
And Heaven will blesse you for it.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Pretty maid I am no Robber nor no Ravisher,
I pray thee keepe thy Jewel, I have done
No wrong to thee, though thou beest vertuous
And in extremity, I doe not know,
That I am bound to keepe thee.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: No sir, for gods sake if you know an honest man in all these countries, give me some directions to find him out.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: More honest then my selfe good sooth I doe not know; I would have lain with thee with thy consent, and who would not in all these parts, is past my memory, I am sorry for thee, farwell gentle maid, god keepe thee safe.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I thanke you sir, and you;
Woman they say, was onely made of man,
Me thinks tis strange they should be so unlike,
It may be all the best was cut away
To make the woman and the nought was left
Behind with him, I'le sit me downe and weepe,
All things have cast me from 'em but the earth;
The evening comes and every little flower
Droops now, as well as I.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Good Madg lets rest a little, by my troth I am weary, this new pail is a plaguy heavie one, would Tom were hang'd for choosing it, 'tis the antowardst foole in a Country.

speeches.speaker: Mag.
verse: With all my heart, and I thanke you too, Nan.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: What true contented happinesse dwells here,
More then in Cities? wood to God my father
Had lived like one of these and bred me up
To milke and doe as they doe: me thinks
Tis a life that I wood choose, if I were now
To tell my time agen, above a princes; maids for charity
Give a poore wench one draught of Milke
That wearinesse and hunger have nigh famisht.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: If I had but one Cows Milke in all the world, you should have some on't; there drink more, the cheese shall pay for it, alas poore heart! shees dry.

speeches.speaker: Mag.
verse: Doe you dwell here abouts?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: No, would I did.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Madge if she do not looke like my cosen Sue o'th more lane as one thing can looke like another—

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: Nay Sue has a hazell eye, I know Sue well, and by your leave not so trim a body neither, this is a feate bodied thing I tell you.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: She laces close by the masse I warrant you, and so does Sue too.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I thanke you for your gentlenesse faire maids.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: Drinke agen pray thee.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I am satisfied, and heaven reward thee for't, yet thus far I will compell you to accept these trifles, toyes onely that expresse my thanks, for greater worth, I'm sure they have not in them; indeed you shall, I found e'm as I came.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: Madge, look you here Madge.

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: Nay I have as fine a one as you, mine's all gold and painted, and pretious stone in't; I warrant it cost a crowne wench.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: But mine is the most sumptuous one that ere I saw.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
prose: One favour you must doe me more, for you are well acquainted here.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: Indeed wee'le doe you any kindnesse sister.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Onely to send me to some honest place, where I may finde a service.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Vds me, our Dorithy went away but last weeke and I know my Mistris wants a Maid, and why may shee not be placed there? this is a likely wench I tell you truly, and a good wench I warrant her.

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: And tis a hard case if wee that have served four yeares a piece cannot bring in one servant, we will preferr her; harke you sister, pray what's your name?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Melvia.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: A feate name ifaith, and can you milke a Cow? and make a merry-bush? that's nothing.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I shall learne quickly.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: And dresse a house with flowers? and serve a pigg? this you must doe, for we deale in the dary, and make a bed or two?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I hope I shall.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: But be sure to keepe the men out, they will mar all that you make else, I know that by myselfe; for I have been so touz'd among e'm in my days, come you shall een home with us and be our fellow, our house is so honest, and we serve a very good woman, and a Gentlewoman, and we live as merrily, and dance a good dayes after even-song, our wake shall be on Sunday; doe you know what a wake is? we have mighty cheer then, and such a coyle, 'twould blesse ye; you must not be so bashfull, you'l spoile all.

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: Let's home for Gods sake, my Mistris thinkes by this time we are lost, come wee'l have a care of you, I warrant you; but you must tell my Mistris where you were borne, and every thing that belongs to you, & the strangest things you can devise, for she loves those extreamly, 'tis no matter whether they be true or no, shee's not so scrupulous; you must be our sister, and love us best, and tell us every thing, and when cold weather comes wee'l ly together, will you do this?

speeches.speaker: Viola.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: Then home again a gods name, can you go apace.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
verse: HOw now, any good newes yet?

speeches.speaker: Siluio.
verse: Faith not any yet.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: This comes a tipling; would 'twere treason an^ pleas'd God to drinke more then three draughts at a meale.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: When did you see Richardo?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I crost him twice to day.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: You have heard of a young wench that was seen last night?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Has Richard hard of this?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Yes and I thinke hee's ridden after, farewell I'le have another round.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: If you heare any thing, pray spare no horse-fleshe
I'le do the like.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Do.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Sir, I did thinke 'twas you by all discriptions.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Tis so,
I tooke her up indeed, the manner how
You have heard already, and what she had about her,
As Iewels, gold and other trifling things:
And what my end was, which because she slighted,
I left her there i'the feildes.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Left i'th feildes? could any but a Rogue
That had despis'd humanity and goodnesse,
God, law and credit? and had set himselfe
To loose his noblest part, and be a beast,
Have left so innocent, unmatch'd a virtue,
To the rude mercy of a wildernesse?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Sir If you come to raile, pray quit my house,
I do not use to have such language given;
Within my doores to me; for your wench,
You may go seeke her with more patience,
Shee's tame enough I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Pray forgive me.
I do confesse my much forgetfullnesse;
And weigh my words no farther I beseech you,
Then a meere madnesse; for such a griefe has seiz'd mee
So strong and deadly, as a punishment,
And a just one too,
That 'tis a greater wonder I am living,
Then any thing I utter; yet let me tel you thus much,
'Twas a fault for leaving her
So in the fieldes.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Sir I will thinke so now, and credit me,
You have so wrought me with your griefe, that I
Do both forgive and pitty you:
And if youle please to take a bed this night heere;
Too morrow I'le bring you where I left her.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I thanke you, no, shall I be so unworthy,
To think upon a bed, or ease or comfort,
And have my heart stray from me God knowes where,
Cold and forsaken, destitute of friends,
And all good comforts else, unlesse some tree
Whose speechlesse charity must better ours,
With which the bitter east winds made thier sport
And sung through hourely, hath invited her
To keep off halfe a day? shall shee be thus,
And I draw in soft slumbers? God forbid.
No, night and bitter coldnesse I provoke thee,
And all the dewes that hang upon thy locks,
Showers, hailes, snowes, frosts, & two edged windes that prime
The maiden blossoms, I provoke you all,
And dare expose this body to your sharpnesse,
'Till I be made a land marke.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Will you then stay and eate with mee?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Y'are angry with me, I know you'r angry,
You would not bid me eate else; my poore Mistris,
For ought I know thou art famish't, for what else
Can the feilds yeeld thee, and the stubborne season,
That yet holds in the fruite? good Gentle Sir,
Thinke not ill manners in mee for denying
Your offer'd meate, for sure I cannot eate
While I do thinke she wants; well I'me a rascall;
A villaine, slave, that onely was begotten,
To murder women and of them the best.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: This is a strange affliction.
If you'le accept no greater courtisy, yet drink Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ric.
verse: Now I am sure you hate me, and you knew
What kinde of man I am, as indeed 'tis fitt,
That every man should know me to avoide me.
If you have peace within you Sir, or goodnesse
Name that abhor'd word drinke no more unto mee,
You had safer strike me.
I pray you do not, if you love me do not.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Sir, I meane no ill by it.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: It may be so,
Nor let me see
None sir, if you love heaven;
You know not what offence it is unto mee,
Nor good now, do not aske me why:
And I warne you once againe, let no man else speake of't,
I feare your servants will be prating to me.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Why Sir what aile you?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I hate drinke, ther's the end on't,
And that man that drinkes with meate is dambn'd
without an age of prayers and repentance,
And ther's a hazard too; good Sir no more,
If you will do me a free courtisy;
That I shall know for one, go take your horse,
And bring me to the place where you left her:

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Since you are so importunate I will;
But I will wish Sir you had stay'd to night
Upon my credit, you shall see no drinke.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Be gon the heating of it makes me giddy,
Sir will you be intreated to forbeare it,
I shall be mad else.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I pray no more of that, I am quiet,
I'le but walke in and away straight.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Now I thanke you,
But what you do, do in a twinckling, Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: As soone as may bee.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: Is this the wench? you have brought me some catch I warrant;
How injuringly she looks upon the matter?

speeches.speaker: Madge.
verse: Yes forsooth this is the maiden.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: Come hither, wood you serve?

speeches.speaker: Viola
prose: If it shalt please you to accpt my service I hope I shall do something that shall like you, though it be but truth, and often praying for you.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: You are very curious of your hand me thinks,
You preserve it so with gloves, let me see it;
I marry, here's a hand of march-pane wenches:
This pretty palme never knew sorrow yet;
How soft it is I warrant you, and supple:
O' my word this is fitter for a pocket to filch withall
Then to worke, I feare me little one,
You are no better then you should be; goe too.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: My Conscience yet is but one witnesse to me,
And that heaven knows is or mine innocence,
Tis true, I must confesse, with shame enough,
The time that I have lead yet never taught me
What t'was to breake a sleep, or to be weary.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: You can say well: if you be mine, Wench, you must doe well too, for words are but slow workers, yet so much hope I have of you, that I'le take you so you'l bee diligent, and do your duty: how now?

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: There is a messenger come from your son
That brings you word he is return'd from travell,
And will be here this night.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: Now joy upon thee for it, thou art ever
A bringer of good tidings, there, drinke that:
In troth thou hast much contented me, my son?
Lord how thou hast pleas'd me, shall I see my Son
Yet e're I dye? take care my house be handsome,
And the new stooles set out, and boughes and rushes,
And flowers for the window, and the Turky Carpet,
And the great parcell salt, Nan, with the Cruets,
And prethee Alexander goe to the Cooke,
And bid him spare for nothing, my son's come home,
Who's come with him?

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: I heare of none yet, but a Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: A Gentlewoman? what Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: I know not but such a one there is, he sayes.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: Pray God he have not cast away himselfe
Upon some snout-faire piece, I do not like it.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
verse: No sure, my Master has more discretion.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: Well, be it how it will, he shall be welcome.
Sirs, to your tasks, and shew this little novice
How to bestir her selfe, I'le sort out things.

speeches.speaker: Madg.
prose: We will forsooth, I can tell you my mistris is a s^irring woman.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Lord how shee'le talke some times? tis the maddest cricket—

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Mee thinks she talkes well, and shewes a great deale of good huswifry, pray let me deck the chambers, shall I?

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Yes you shall, but doe not scorne to be avis'd sister, for there belongs more to that then you are aware on; why would you venture so fondly upon the strowings? ther's mighty matters in them I'le assure you, and in the spreading of a bough pot, you may misse if you were ten yeares elder, if you take not a speciall care before you.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: I will learne willingly, if that be all.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Sirrah where is't they say my young master hath beene?

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: Faith I know not, beyond the sea, where they are borne without noses.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: lesse blesse us! without noses? how doe they doe for handkerchers?

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: So Richard saies, and sirrah, their feet stands in their foreheads.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Thats fine by my troth, these men have pestilence running heads then; doe they speake as we doe?

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: No, they never speake.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Are they cursend?

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: No they call them Infidells, I know not what they are.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Sirrah we shall have fine courting now my young master is come home, were you never courted sister?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: Alas I know it not.

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: What is that courting sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: I can tell, for I was once courted in the matted chamber, you know the party Madge, faith hee courted finely.

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: Pray thee what ist?

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: Faith nothing but he was some what figent with me, faith tis fine sport, this courting.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Where be the Maids there?

speeches.speaker: Mag.
prose: We shall be hang'd anon, away good wenches, and a care you dight things handsomely, I will looke over you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If your sorrow will give you so far leave, pray thinke your selfe most welcome to this place, for so upon my life you are, and for your owne faire sake, take truce a while with these immoderate mournings.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: I thanke you sir, I shall doe what I may;
Pray leade me to a chamber.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Presently,
Before your blessing mother, I entreate ye
To know this Gentlewoman, and bid her welcome,
The vertuous wife of him that was my selfe
In all my travells.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: Indeed she is most welcom, so are you son
Now all my blessing on thee; thou hast made me
Younger by 20 yeares, then I was yesterday,
Will you walke in? what ayles this Gentlewoman?
Alas I feare she is not well, good Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: You feare right.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: She has fasted over long,
You shall have supper presently o'th boord.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: She will not eate I can assure you mother,
For Gods sake let your maide conduct her up
Into some faire becomming Chamber
Fit for a woman of her being and
As soone as may be,
I know shee's very ill, and wood have rest.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: There is one ready for her, the blew chamber.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Tis well, I'le leade you to your Chamber doore
And there I'le leave you to your quiet, Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: I thanke you Sir, good rest to every one,
You'le see me once againe to night I hope.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: When you shall please, I'le waite upon you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Where are these maides attend upon the Gentlewoman, and see she want no good thing in the house? goodnight with all my heart forsooth, good Lord how you are growne? is he not Alexander?

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Yes truly he's shot up finely god be thanked.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: An ill weed Mother will do so.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: You say true Sir, an ill weede growes a pace.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Allexander the sharpe, you take me very quickly.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Nay I can tell, Allexander will do it, do you reade madcapp still?

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Some times forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: But faith son what countries have you traveld?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why many, Mother, as they lay befor me, France, Spaine, Italy and Germany, and other Provinces that I am, sure you are not betterd by, when you heare of them.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: And can you these tongues perfectly?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Of some a little, Mother.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Pray spout some french sonne.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: You understand it not, and to your eares 'twill go like an unshod cart upon the stones, onely a rough unhandsome sound.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Faith I would faine heare some french.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Good Sir speake some french to my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: At your entreaty Allexander, I will, who shall speake to?

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: If your worship will do me the favour Sir, to me.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Mounseir, Poultron, Coukew, Cullione, Besay, Man cur.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Awe Mounseir.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, this fine indeed, gods blessing 'on thy hart Son, by my troth thou art growne a proper Gentleman, cullen and pullen, good god what aucey words they use beyond the seas, ha, ha, ha?

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Did not you sweare right?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Yes good Allexander, if you had done so to
But good Mother I am very hungry and have rid farr to day and am fasting.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: You shall have your supper presently my sweet Sonne.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: As soone as you please, which once ended,
I'le go and visit you sicke gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: Come then.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I have ridden like a fury to make up this worke and I will do it bravely ere I leave it, this is the house I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Whood you speake with Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Marry Sir I would speake with a Gentlewoman, came this night late heere from the City, I have some letters of Importance to her, I am a Post Sir and would bee dispatch'd in hast.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Sir, cannot I deliver 'em? for the truth is shee's ill and in her chamber.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Pray pardon me I must needes speake with her, my businesse is so weighty.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: I'le tell her so, and bring you present word.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Pray do so, and I'le attend her, pray god the griefe of my imaginde death spoyle not what I intend, I hope it will not.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
verse: Though she be very ill, and desires no trouble,
Yet If your businesse be so urgent, you may come up and speake with her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I thanke you Sir, I follow you.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: What should this fellow be i'th name of heaven that comes with such Post businesse? sure my husband hath reveal'd himselfe, and in this hast sent after me, are you the Post my friend?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Yes for sooth Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: What good newes hast thou brought me gentle Post?
For I have woe and griefe too much already.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I would you had lesse, Mistris, I could wish it, beshrow my hart she moves me cruelly.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Have I found you once more Iugler? well Iewell, thou hast onely vetrtue in thee, of all I read of yet; what eares has this asse to betray him with? well, what's your businesse then?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I have brought a letter from your servant, Mistris, in hast.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Pray give it me, I hope the best still.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: This is the upshot and I know I have hit it,
Well if the spirits of the dead do walke, I shall
Heare more of this one hundred yeares hence.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: By any meanes you must have speciall care, for now the Citty is possest for certaine, my Master is made away, which for ought I knowe is a truth indeed; good Mistris leave your griefe and see your danger, and let that wise and noble Gentleman with whome you are, bee your right hand in all things.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Now do I know I have the better on't by the languishing of her eye at this neere instant, 'tis stil simming in her blood, in coyning somewhat to turne Mercury I know it.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: He is my husband, and 'tis reasonable he should command in all things, since he will be an asse again the haire at his one perill be it, in the morne you shall have a packet, 'till I must intreate you stay, you shall not loose by it.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I do not doubt it, Mistris; I'le leave you to your rest and waite your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Do, and speake out the Gentleman of the house, bid him come to me presently.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Who, Mr. Mercury?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Do you know him, post?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Onely by sight forsooth, now I remember your servant wild me to let you know he is the onely man, you and your fortunes, are now to rest upon.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Prethee no more, I know all this already.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I'le take my leave now, I am made for ever.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Good night I am provided for you my fine youth

speeches.speaker: Mother.
prose: I'le make thee have more care.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: Good Mistris pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Thou't neere be good I warrant thee, can your fine fingers hold no faster?

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: Indeed it was against my will.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Allexander, let's see the glasse, as, I am true kirsome woman, it is one of the christall glasses my cozen sent mee and the baggage hath broake it where it cannot bee mended, Allexander, can Humfrey mend this thinke you?

speeches.speaker: All^x.
prose: No truly this will neere be mended.

speeches.speaker:
~
^ola.
prose: T^uly I meant but to wash it for the Gentlewoman, that is sick above, and shaking out the water, knockt it against the paile side.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Did you so? be sure I'le stop it, 'twill make a good gap in your quarters wages, can tell you.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: I pray forgive me, and let me have no wages this first quarter.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Go whimling, and fetch two or three grating loaves out of the kitching, to make gingerbread of, 'tis such an untoward thing.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: Shee's somewhat simple indeed, she knew not what a kimnell was, she wants good nurture mightily.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: My Sonne tells me, Allexander, that this young widdow meanes to sojourne here, she offers largly for her board, I may offer her good cheere, prey thee make a step i'th morning downe to the parsonage for some Pigions? what are you mad there; what noyse is that? are you at bowles within? why do you whine?

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: I have done another fault, I beseech you sweete Mistris ofrgive me.

speeches.speaker: Mother.
prose: What's the matter.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: As I was reaching for the bread that lay upon the shelfe, I have throwne downe the minct meate, that should have made the pyes to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Get thee out of my house thou filthy destroying Harlot, thou, I'le not keepe thee an howre longer.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: Good Mistris beate me rather for my fault as much as it deserves, I do not know whether to go.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: No I warrant thee, out of my dores.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: Indeed I'le mend, I pray speake you for me.

speeches.speaker: Allex.
prose: If thou had'st hurl'd downe any thing but the pye meate, I would have spoake for thee, but I cannot finde in my hart now.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Art thou here yet? I thinke I must have an officer to thrust thee out of my dores, must I?

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: Why you may stop this in my wages too,
For Gods sake do, I'le finde my selfe this yeare;
And let me stay.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Thou't spoyle ten times as much, I'le cudgell thee out of my dores.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: I am assur'd you are more mercifull,
Then thus to beate me and discharge me too.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Dost thou dispute with mee, Allexander carry the prating hilding forth.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: Good Mistris heare me I have heere a Jewell,
My Mother left me and 'tis something worth:
Receive it and when all my faultes together
Come to the worth of that, then turne me forth,
'Till then I pray you keep mee.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: What giggombob have wee here? pray god you have not pilfer'd this some where; th'art such a puling thing, wipe your eyes, and rise go your wayes, Allexander, bid the Cook mince some more meate, come and get you to bed quickly that you may up betime i'th morning a milking or you and I shall fall out worse yet.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: She has hurt my arme; I am a fraid, she is a very angry woman, but blesse him heaven that did me the most wrong, I am a fraide Antonious wife should see mee, she will knowe mee

speeches.speaker: Mother within.
prose: Melvia.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
prose: I am coming, shee's not angry agen I hope.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Now what am I the better for enjoying
This woman that I lov'd? so all I finde,
That I before immaginde to be happy:
Now I have done, it turnes to nothing else
But a poore pittied and a base repentance,
Udsfoote I am monstrous angry with my selfe:
Why should a man that has discourse and reason,
And knowes how neere he looses all in these things,
Covet to have his wishes satisfied;
Which when they are, are nothing but the shame
I do begin to loath this woman straingly,
And I thinke justly too, that durst adventure,
Flinging away her modesty to take
A stranger to her bed, her husbands body
Being scarce cold in the earth for her content,
It was no more to take my sences with,
Then if I had an idle dream had in sleep
Yet I have made her promises: which grieves me,
And I must keep 'em too, I thinke she hunts me:
The Devill cannot keep these women off,
When they are fletched once.

speeches.speaker: VVife.
verse: To bed for gods sake Sir, why do you stay heer?
Some are up i'th house, I hard the wife,
Good deare sweete hart to bed.

speeches.speaker: Merc.
verse: Why I am going? why do you follow me?
You would not have it knowne I hope, pray get you
Back to your chamber, the dores hard by for mee,
Let me alone I warrant you, this it is
To thresh well, have got a customer,
Will you go to bed?

speeches.speaker: VVife.
verse: Will you?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Yes I am going.

speeches.speaker: VVife.
verse: Then remember your promise you made to marry mee.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I will, but it was your fault, that it came
To this pinch now, that it must neede remembrance:
For out of honesty I offer'd you
To marry you first, why did you slacke that offer?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Alas I told you the inconvenience of it,
And what wrong it would appeare to the world
If I had married you in such post hast
After his death: beside, the foolish people
VVould have beene bold to have thought wee had lyen
together in his time, and like enough imagin'd
VVe two had murthered him.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I love her tongue yet,
If I were a Saint
A gilded Saint, and such a thing as this
Should prate thus wittily and feelingly
Unto my holinesse, I cannot tell,
But I feare shrewdly I should doe something
That would quite scratch me out o'the Kallender,
And if I stay longer talking with her,
Though I am mad at what I have done already,
Yet I shall forget my selfe againe;
I feele the Divell
Ready to hold my stirrop; pray to bed, god-night.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: This kisse, god-night sweet Love,
And peace goe with thee: thou hast prov'd thy selfe
The honestest man that ever was entic'd
To that sweet sin as people please to call it,
Of lying with anothers VVife, and I,
I thinke the honestest woman without blushing,
Th^t ever lay with another man, I sent my husband
Into a Cellar, post, fearing, and justly,
He should have knowne him, which I did not purpose
Till I had had my end.
VVell, now this plot is perfect, let him bragge on't.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: BIrlady Sir you have rid hard that you have.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: They that have businesse must do so I take it.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: You say true, when set you out my friend?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: About ten a clock and I have rid all night.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: By the masse you are tough indeed, I have seene the day, I would have rid too with the proudest of them and fling durt in their faces, and I have don't with this foolish boy sir many a time; but what can last alwayes? 'tis done, 'tis done now Sir, age, care, and office, brings us to our footecloathes, the more the pitty.

speeches.speaker: Curio.
prose: I believe that Sir, but will it please you to read the businesse?

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: My friend I can read an I can tell you when.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Would I could too Sir, for my hast requires it.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Whence comes it do you say?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Sir from the Citty.

speeches.speaker: Justice.
prose: O from the City 'tis a reverent place.

speeches.speaker: Curio.
verse: And his justice bee as short as his memory,
A Dudgion Dagger will serve him to mow downe sinne withall,
What clod pole Commissioner is this?

speeches.speaker: Just.
verse: And by my faith govern'd by worthy member,
Discreete and upright.

speeches.speaker: Curio.
prose: Sir they are beholding to you, you have given some of them a commendations, they were not worthy of this twenty yeares.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Go to go to, you have a merry meaning, I have found you sir ifaith, you are a wag, away, fye, now I'le read Your letter.

speeches.speaker: Curio.
verse: Pray do sir; what a misery 'tis,
To have an urgent businesse, wait the Justice,
Of such an old Tuff taffity that knowes not,
Nor can be brought to understand more sence,
Then how to restore supprest Ale-houses,
And have his man compound small trespasses,
For ten groates.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Sir it seems here your businesse is of deeper circumstance then I conceiv'd it for; what do you meane Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: 'Tis for mine owne ease I'le assure your VVorship.

speeches.speaker: Just.
verse: It shall not be ifaith friend, here I have it,
That one Antonio a Gentleman, I take it so,
Yes it is so, a Gentleman is lately thought to
Have been made away, and by my faith upon a
Perles ground too, if you consider; wel, there's
Knavery in't, I see that without spectacles.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Sure this fellow deals in revelation he's so hidden,
Goe thy wayes, thou wilt sicke a bench spit as formally,
And shew thy agot, and hatch'd chaine
As well as the best of them.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: And now I have consider'd, I beleeve it.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: VVhat Sir?

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: That he was murdered.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Did you know him?

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: No.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Nor how it is suppos'd.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose:
No, nor I care not two-pence, those are toyes and yet I verily beleeve hee was murdered, as sure as I beleeve thou art a man, I never failde in these things yet, weare a man that's beaten to these matters, experience is a certaine conceal'd thing that failes not; pray let me aske you one
thing, why doe you come to me?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Because the letter is addrest to you, being the nearest Justice.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: The nearest? is that all?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: I thinke it be Sir, I would be Ioth you should bee the wisest.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Well Sir, as it is, I will endeavour in it; yet if it had come to me by name, I know not, but I thinke it had beene as soone dispatcht as by another, and with as round a wisedome, I, and as happily, but that's all one: I have borne this place this thirty yeares, and upwards, and with sufficient credit: and they may when they please, know me better; to the nearest? well.

speeches.speaker: Curio.
prose: Sir, it is not my fault, for had I knowne you sooner—

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: I thanke you Sir, I know it.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: I'le besworne you should have plaid for any businesse now.

speeches.speaker: Iustice
prose: And further, they have specified unto mee, his Wife is sorely suspected in this matter, as a maine cause,

speeches.speaker: Curio
prose: I thinke she be Sir, for no other cause can be yet found.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: And one Mercury a traveller, with whom they say directly shee is runne away, and as they thinke this way.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: I knew all this before.

speeches.speaker: Iustice.
prose: Well Sir, this Mercury I know, and his breeding, a neighbours childe hard by, you have been happy Sir in comming hither.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Then you know where to have him Sir?

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: I do Sir, he dwells neare me.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: I doubt your Worship dwels neare a Knave then.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
verse: I think so; pray put on: but 'tis a wonder
To see how gracelesse people are now given,
And how base vertue is accounted with them
That should be all in all as sayes a wise man.
prose: I tell you Sir, and it is true, that there have beene such murthers, and of late dayes, as 'twould make your very heart bleede in you, and some of them as I shall bee enabled I will tell you, it fell out of late dayes.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: It may be so, but will it please you to proceede in this?

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: An honest Weaver, and as good a work-man as ere shot shuttle, and as close: but every man must dye; this honest Weaver being a little mellow in his Ale, that was the evidence verbatim, Sir, God blesse the marke, sprung his necke just ^n this place: wel Iarvis, thou hadst wrongs, & if I ^ve some of the best shall sweat fort, then a wench—

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: But Sir you have forgot my businesse.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: A sober pretty maide about 17. they say, certainly howsoever 'tis shuffled, shee burst her selfe, and fondly, if it be so, with Furmety at a Churching, but I thinke the Divell had another agent in't: either of which if I can catch shall stretch for't.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: This is a mad Justice that will hang the Devill; but I would you would be short in this, before that other notice can be given?

speeches.speaker: Iustice.
prose: Sir I will doe discreetly what is fitting; what, Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Your Worship?

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Put on your best coate, and let your fellow Marke goe to the Constable & bid him aide me with all the speed hee can, and all the power, and provide pen and inke to take their Confessions, and my long sword, I cannot tell what danger wee may meete with; you'le goe with us?

speeches.speaker: Curio.
prose: Yes, what else? I came to that end to accuse both parties.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: May I crave what you are?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Faith Sir one that to be knowne would not profit you, more then a meere Kinsman of the dead Antonio's.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: 'Tis well, I am sorry for my neighbour, truly, that hee had no more grace, 'twill kill his Mother; shee's a good olde woman, will you walke in? I'le but put my Cloake on, and my Chaine off, and a cleane band, and have my shooes blackt over, and shift my Jerkin, and wee'l to our businesse, and you shall see how I can bolt these matters.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: As soone as't please you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: This is the place; here did I leave the Maid
Alone las^ night drying her tender eyes,
Uncertaine what to do, and yet desirous
To have me gone.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: How rude are all we men,
That take the name of Civill to our selves?
If she had set her foote upon an earth
Where people live that we call barbarous;
Though they had had no house to bring her too,
They would have spoil'd the glory that the spring
Has deckt the trees in, and with willing hands
Have torne their branches downe, and every man
Would have become a builder for her sake.
What time left you her there?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I left her, when the Sun had so much to set,
As he is now got from his place of rise.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: So near the night she could not wander far;
Faire Viola?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: It is in vaine to call, she sought a house
Without all question.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Peace, faire Viola?
Faire Viola? who should have left her here
On such a ground? if you had meant to loose her,
You might have found there were no Inches here
To take her name and carry it about,
When her true Lover came to mourn for her,
Till all the neighbouring valleys and the hills,
Resounded Viola,—
And such a place,
You should have chose—
You pity us because
The dew a little wets our feete,
Unworthy far to seeke her in the wet;
And what becomes of her? where wandred she,
With 2 showers raining on her, from her eyes
Continually, abundantly, from which
There's neither tree nor house to shelter her;
Will you goe with me to travell?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Whither?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Over all the world.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: No by my faith, I'le make a shorter journey
When I do travell.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: But theres no hope
To gaine my end in any shorter way.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Why, what's your end?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: It is to search the earth,
Till we have found two in the shapes of men,
As wicked as our selves.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Twere not so hard to find out those.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why, if we finde them out,
It were the better; for what brave villany,
Might wee 4. do? wee wood not keepe together:
For every one has treachery enough
For 20. Countryes, one should trouble Asia,
Another should sowe strife in Affrica;
But you should play the knave, at home in Europ,
And for America let me alone.

speeches.speaker: ~ale.
verse: Sir I am hones^e^,
Then you know how to bee, and can no more
Bee wrong'd but I shall finde my selfe a right.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: If you had any sparke of honesty,
You would not think that honester then I,
Were a praise high enough to serve your turne:
If men were commonly so bad as I,
Theeves would be put in Callenders for Saints;
And bones of murderers would worke miracles.
I am a kinde of knave, of knave so much —
There is betwixt mee and the vilest else,
But the next place of all to mine is yours.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: That last is she, 'tis shee.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Let us away, we shall infect her, let her have the winde,
And wee will kneele downe here.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: Wenches away for here are men.

speeches.speaker: ~alerio.
verse: Faire maide I pray you stay.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Alas, agen?

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Why do you lay hold on her? I pray hartily let her go.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: With all my heart, I do not meane to hurt her.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: But stand away then for the purest bodyes
VVill soonest take infection, stand away,
But for infecting her my selfe, by heaven,
I would come there and beate thee further off.

speeches.speaker: ~iola.
verse: I know that voyce and face.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
prose: You are finely mad, godbwy Sir, now you are here together, I'e leave you so, god send you good lucke, both when you are soberer, you'le give me thanks.

speeches.speaker: Madge.
prose: VVilt thou go milke? come.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: VVhy dost not come?

speeches.speaker: Madge.
prose: She nods, shee's a sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: VVhat, wert up so early?

speeches.speaker: Madge.
prose: I think your man's mad to kneele there, nay come away ves body, Nan, help she looks black 'ith face, Shee's in a sound.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: And you bee a man com hither, & helpe a woman.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
prose: Come thither? you are a foole.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: And you a knave and a beast that you are.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Come hither? 'twas being my now so neare,
That made her sowne, and you are wicked people,
Or you wood do so too, my venom eyes
Strike innocency dead at such a distance,
Here I'le kneele for this is out of distance.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: Th'art a prating Asse ther's no goodnesse in thee,
I warrant, how dost thou?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Why? well.

speeches.speaker: Madge.
prose: Art thou able to go?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: No, pray go you and milke, if I be able to come
I'le follow you, if not I'le sit here,
'Till you come back.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
prose: I am loth to leave thee here with you wild foole.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: I know him well, I warrant thee, he will not hurt mee.

speeches.speaker: Madge.
prose: Come then Nan.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: How do you? be not fearefull, for I hold my hands
Before my mouth and speake, and so
My breath can never blast you.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: 'Twas enough to use me ill, though you had never sought me too mock me to, why kneele you so farr Off, were not that gesture better us'd in prayer, had dealt so with you, I should not sleep, till God and you had both forgiven me.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: I do not mock, nor lives there such a villane
That can do any thing contemptible,
To you, but I do kneele because it is,
An action very fit, and reverent,
In presence of so pure a creature,
And so farr off, as fearefull to offend,
One too much wrong'd already.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: You confesse you did the fault, yet scorne to come,
So far as hither to aske pardon for't;
Which I could willingly afford to come,
To you to grant, good Sir if you have
A better love, may you be blest together,
Shee shall not wish you better then I will,
I but offend you; there are all the Iewels
I stole, and all the love I euer had,
I leave behinde with you, I'le carry now
To give another, may the next maide you try
Love you no worse, nor be no worse then I.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Do not leave me yet for all my fault,
Search out the next things too impossible,
And put me on them when they are effected,
I may with better modesty receive
Forgivenesse from you.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: I will set no pennance,
To gaine the great forgivenesse you desire:
But to come hither and take me and it,
Or else I'le come and beg so you will grant,
That you will be content to be forgiven.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: Nay I will come since you will haue it so,
And since you please to pardon me I hope
Free from infection, here I am by you;
A carelesse man, a breaker of my faith,
A lothsome drunkard and in that wild fury:
A hunter after whores I do beseech you,
To pardon all these faultes, and take me up
An honest sober and a faithfull man.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: For gods sake urge your faultes no more, but mend,
All the forgivenesse I can make you is,
To love you which I will do and desire,
Nothing but love againe, which if I have not,
Yet I will love you still.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse: O women that some one of you will take,
An everlasting pen into your hands:
And grave in paper which the writ shall make,
More lasting then the marble monuments,
Your matchlesse vertues to posterityes:
Which the defective race of envious man,
Strive to conceale.

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: Me thinkes I would not now for any thing,
But you had mist me, I have made a story,
Will serve to wast many a winters fier
When we are old, I'le tell my daughters then,
The miseryes their Mother had in love:
And say my girles bee wiser, yet I would not
Have had more witt my selfe, take up those Iewells,
For I thinke I heare my fellowes coming.

speeches.speaker: Madge.
verse: How dost thou now?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
prose: Why? very well I thanke you, 'tis late shall I hast home?

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: I prethee vvee shall be shent soundly.

speeches.speaker: Madge.
verse: VVhy doe's that railing man go vvith us?

speeches.speaker: ~io.
verse: I preythee speake vvell of him, on my vvord,
Hee's an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: There was never any so one's complexion, a Getleman?
I'de be asham'd to have such a foule mouth.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: How now Alexander, what Gentleman is this?

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Indeed forsooth I know not, I found him at the market full of woe, crying a lost daughter, and telling all her tokens to the people; and wot you what? by all subscription in the world, it should be our new maid Melvia, one would little thinke it, therefore I was bold to tel him of her Mistriss.

speeches.speaker: Mother.
prose: Melvia? it cannot be, foole, alas you know shee is a poore wench, and I tooke her in upon meere charity.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: So seem'd my daughter when shee went away, as she had made her selfe.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: What stature was your childe of, Sir?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Not high, and of a browne complexion, Her haire aborne, a round face, which some friends that flattered mee, would say 'twould bee a good one.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: This is still Melvia, Mistriss, that's the truth on't.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: It may be so I'le promise you.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Well, goe thy wayes, the flower of our towne, For a hand and a foote, I shall never see thy fellow.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: But had shee not such toyes, as bracelets, rings, and Jewels?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Shee was something bolde indeed, to take such things that night she left me.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Then belike she run away?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Though she be one I love, I dare not lye, shee did indeed.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: What thinke you of this Jewel?

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: Yes, this was one of them, and this was mine, you have made mee a new man, I thanke you for it.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Nay, and she be given to filching, there is your Jewell, I am cleare on't: but by your leave Sir, you shall answer me for what is lost since she came hither, can tell you there lye things scattering in every place about the house.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: As I am vertuous, I have the lyingst olde Gentlewoman to my Mistris, and the most malicious, the Devill a good word will shee give a servant, that's her olde rule; and God be thanked they'l give her as few, there is perfect love on both sides, it yearns my heart to heare the wench misconstrued, a carefull soule shee is i'le besworne for her, and when shee's gone, let them say what they will, they may cast their Capps at such another.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: What you have lost by her, with all my heart
I'le see you double paid, for you have sav'd
With your kinde pitty two that must not live
Unlesse it be to thanke you; take this Jewell,
This strikes off none of her offences, Mistris,
Would I might see her.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Alexander, runne, and bid her make hast home, shee's at the milking Close; but tell her not by any means whoe's here, I know shee'l be too fearfull.

speeches.speaker: Alex.
prose: Wel, wee'l have a posset yet at parting, that's my comfort, and one round, or else i'le loose my will.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: You shall finde Silvio, ~berto, and Pedro enquiring for the Wench at the next Towne, tell them shee is found, and where I am, and with the favour of this Gentlewoman, desire them to come hither,

speeches.speaker: Mo.
prose: I pray doe, they shall be all welcome.

speeches.speaker: Justice.
prose: By your leave forsooth you shall see me find the parties by a slight.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: who's that? Mr. Justice? how do you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Why very well, and busie, wher's your son.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Hee's within Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Hum, and how does the young woman my Cozen that came downe with him.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Shee's above, as a woman in her case may be.

speeches.speaker: Iustice.
prose: You have confest it? then sirha call in the Officers; shee's no Couzen of mine; a meere tricke to discover all.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: To discover? what?

speeches.speaker: Iustice.
prose: You shall know that anon: I thinke you have over reached you; ô welcome, enter the house, and by vertue of my warrant which you have there, seize upon the bodily persons of those whose names are there written, to wit, one Mercury, and the wife of one Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: For what.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
verse: Away I say,
This Gentleman shall certifie you for what.

speeches.speaker: Mother.
prose: Hee can accuse my Sonne of nothing, hee came from travell but within these two dayes?

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: There hangs a tale.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: I should be sorry this should fall out at any time: but especially now Sir; will you favour mee so much, as to let me know of what you accuse him?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: Upon suspition of murther.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Murther? I defie thee.

speeches.speaker: Curio.
prose: I pray GOD hee may prove himselfe innocent.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Fye, say not so, you shew your selfe to be no good Common-wealths man: for the more are hang'd, the better 'tis for the Common-wealth.

speeches.speaker: Mother.
prose: By this rule you were best hang your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
verse: I forgive your honest mirth ever: O, welcome, welcome Marke.
Your penne, inke, and paper to take their examinations.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why do you pull me so? I'le goe alone.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Let them stand, let them stand quietly, whilst they are examin'd?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: What will you examine us of?

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Of Antonio's murther.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: Why, he was my friend.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: He was my husband.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: The more shame for you both; Marke, your penne and inke.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
prose: Pray God all be well, I never knew any of these Travellers come to good; I beseech you, Sir, be favourable to my Sonne.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Gentlewoman hold you content, I would it were come to that?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: For gods sake mother why kneele you to such a pig bribe fellow? he has surfetted of geese, and they have put him into a fit of Justice, let him do his worst.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Is your paper ready?

speeches.speaker: Mark.
prose: I am ready Sir.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Accuse them Sir, I command thee to lay down accusations against these persons in behalfe of the State, and ^irst looke upon the parties to be accus'd, and deliver your name.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: My name is Curio, my murthered Kinsman
If he were living now, I should not know him,
Tis so long since we saw one another.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: My cozen Curio?

speeches.speaker: Cur
prose:
But thus much from the mouths of his servants, & others, whose examinations I have in writing about me, I can accuse them of; this Mercury, the last night, but this last, lay in Antonio's house, and in the night he rose, raising Antonio, where privately they were in talke an houre, to what end I know not: but of likely-hood, finding An
^onio's house not a fit place to murther him in, hee suffered him to goe to bed againe, but in the morning early, he train'd him I think forth, after which time hee never saw his home; his cloathes were found neere the place where Mercury was, and the people at first denyed they saw him: but at last he made a frivolous tale, that there he shifted himselfe into a foote-mans habit: but in short, the next houre this woman went to Mercury, and in her Coach they posted hither; true accusations, I have no more, and I will make none.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: No more? wee need no more, Sirha, be drawing heir Mittimus before wee heare their answer. What say you Sir? are you guilty of this murther?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Whether you are or no, confesse, it will bee the better for you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: If I were guilty, your Rhetoricke could not fetch it forth: but though I am innocent, I confesse, that if I were a stander by, these circumstances urg'd, which are true, would make me doubtless beleeve the accused parties to be guilty.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Write downe, that hee being a stander by, for so you see he is, doth doubtlessely beleeve the accused parties, which is himselfe, to be guilty.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I say no such thing.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Write it downe I say, wee'l try that.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I care not what you write, pray God you did not kill him for my love, though I am free from this, we both deserve.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Govern your tongue I pray you, all is well, my husband lives, I know it, and I see him.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: They whisper, sever them quickly I say Officers why do you let them prompt one another, Gentlewoman, what say you to this, are not you guilty?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: No as I hope for mercy.

speeches.speaker: Jus.
prose: But are not those circumstances true, that this Gentleman hath so shortly and methodically deliver'd?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: They are; and what you do with me I care not,
Since he is dead, in whome was all my care:
You knew him not.

speeches.speaker: Jus.
prose: No an't bin better for you too, and you had never knew'd him.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
verse: Why then you did not know the worlds chiefe joy
His face so manly, as it had been made,
To fright the world, yet he so sweetly temper'd;
That he would make himselfe a naturall foole,
To do a noble kindnesse for a friend,
He was a man whose name I'le not out live,
Longer then heaven whose will must be obay'd;
Will have me do.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: And I will quit thy kindnesse.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Before me she has made the teares s^and in mine eyes, but I must be austere Gentlewoman, you must confesse this murder.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: I cannot Sir, I did it not, but I de sire to see those examinations which this Gentleman acknowledges to have about him, for but late last night I receiv'd letters from the Citty, yet I heard of no confession, then.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: You shall see them time enough I warrant you, but letters you say you had, where are those letters?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Sir they are gon.

speeches.speaker: Just.
verse: Gone? whether are they gone?
How have you dispos'd of 'em?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Why Sir they are for womens matters, and so I use 'em.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Who writ em?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: A man of mine.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: VVho brought 'em?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: A Post.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: A Post? there was some great hast sure, a ha where is that Post?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: Sir there he stands.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Doe's hee so? bring hither that Post, I am afraid that Po^t will prove a knave; come hither Post, what? what can you say con^erning the murder of Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: VVhats that to you?

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: O Post, you have no answer ready have you? I'le have one from you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: You shall have no more from mee then you have, you examine an honest Gentleman and Gentlewoman heere, 'tis pitty such fooles as you should bee i'the commission.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Say you so Post, take away that Post, whip him and bring him againe quickly, I'le hamper you Post.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: 'Tis Antonio, I know him now as well, what an irregular foole is this?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: VVhip me? hold off.

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: O good Sir whip him, by his murmuring he should know some thing of my husbands death; that may quit me, for gods sake fetch't out.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: Whip him I say.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: who 'ist dares whip me now?

speeches.speaker: Wife.
prose: O my lou'd husband.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: My most worthy friend? where have you been so long?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I cannot speake for joy.

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: VVhy, what's the matter now, and shall not law then have her course?

speeches.speaker: Andra.
prose: It shall have no other course then it has I thinke

speeches.speaker: Just.
prose: It shall have other course before I go, or I'le beate my braines, and I say it was not honestly done of him to discover himselfe before the parties accus'd were executed that law might have had her course, for then the kingdome flourishes.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: But such a wife as thou, had never any man, and such a friend as he, beleeve me wife, shall never be a good wife, love my frend, friend love my wife, harke friend.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: Mark. if wee can have nothing to doe, you shall sweare the peace of some body.

speeches.speaker: Mark.
prose: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: By my troth I am sorry my wife is so obstinate, sooth if I could yet doe thee any good, I wood, faith I wood.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: I thanke you Sir, I have lost that passion.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Couzen Curio, you and I must be better acquainted.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: It is my wish Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose:
I should not have known you neither, 'tis so long
since we saw, we were but children then: but you have shewd your selfe an honest man to me.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: I would be ever so.

speeches.speaker: Moth.
verse: Looke you, whoe's there.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: Say nothing to me, for thy peace is made.

speeches.speaker: Kic.
verse: Sir, I can nothing say,
But that you are her Father, you can both
Not only pardon, when you have a wrong,
But love where you have most injury.

speeches.speaker: Iust.
prose: I think I shall heare of no hanging this yeare, there A Tinker and a Whore yet, the Cryer said that rob'd her, and are in prison, I hope they shall be hang'd.

speeches.speaker: And.
verse: No truly sir, they have broke prison.

speeches.speaker: Inst.
verse: 'Tis no matter, then the Jaylor shall be hang'd.

speeches.speaker: And.
prose: You are deceiv'd in that to sir, 'twas known to bee against his will, and he hath got his pardon, I thinke for nothing, but if it doth cost him any thing, 'Ile pay it.

speeches.speaker: Just.
verse: Marke up with your papers, away.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
prose: O you shal stay dinner, I have a couple of brawling neighbours, that I'le assure you will not agree, and you shall have the hearing of their matter.

speeches.speaker: Just.
verse: With all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Go, Gentlemen, go in.

speeches.speaker: Rich.
verse:
O
~iola, that no succeeding age,
Might loose the memory of what thou wert,
But such an overswayed sex is yours,
That all the vertuous actions you can do,
Are but as men will call them, and I sweare,
'Tis my beliefe that women want but wayes;
To praise their deeds, but men want deeds to praise.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: I Love the K. nor do dispute his power,
For that is not confin'd, nor to be censurd
By me, that am his Subject) yet allow me
The liberty of a man, that still would be
A friend to Justice, to demand the Motives
That did induce young Ptolomy, or Photinus
(To whose directions he gives up himselfe,
And I hope wisely) co commit his Sister
The Princesse Cleopatra (if I said
The Queen (Achillas) twere (I hope) no treason,
Shee being by her Fathers testament
(Whose memory I bow to) left Co-heire
In all he stood possest of.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Tis confest
(My good Achoreus) that in these Eastern Kingdomes
Women are not exempted from the Scepter,
But claime a priviledge, equall to the Male;
But how much such divisions have tane from
The Majesty of Egypt, and what factions
Have sprung from those partitions, to the ruine
Of the poor Subject, (doubtfull which to follow,)
We have too many and too sad examples,
Therefore the wise Photinus, to prevent
The murthers, and the massacres, that attend
On dis-united Government, and to shew
The King, without a partner, in full splendor,
Thought it convenient, the faire Cleopatra,
(An attribute not frequent in this Clymate)
Should be committed to safe custody,
In which she is attended like her Birth,
Untill her Beauty, or her royall Dowre,
Hath found her out a Husband.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: How this may
Stand with the rules of policy, I know not;
Most sure I am, it holds no correspondence
With the rites of Aegypt, or the lawes of Nature;
But grant that Cleopatra can sit downe
With this disgrace (though insupportable)
Can you imagine, that Romes glorious Senate
(To whose charge, by the will of the dead King
This government was deliverd) or great Pompey,
(That is appointed Cleopatra's Guardian
As well as Ptolomies) will ere approve
Of this rash Counsell, their consent not sought for,
That should authorize it?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: The Civill war
In which the Roman Empire is embarq'd
On a rough Sea of danger, does exact
Their whole care to preserve themselves, and give them
No vacant time to think of what we do,
Which hardly can concern them.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: What's your opinion
Of the successe? I have heard, in multitudes
Of souldiers, and all glorious pomp of war,
Pompey is much superiour.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: I could give you
A Catalogue of all the severall Nations
From whence he drew his powers: but that were tedious
They have rich armes, are ten to one in number,
Which makes them think the day already wonne;
And Pompey being master of the Sea,
Such plenty of all delicates are brought in,
As if the place on which they are entrench'd,
Were not a Camp of souldiers, but Rome,
In which Lucullus and Apicius joyn'd
To make a publique Feast: they at Dirachium
Fought with successe; but knew not to make use of
Fortunes faire offer: so much I have heard
Caesar himselfe confesse.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: Where are they now?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: In Thessalie, neere the Pharsalian plains
Where Caesar with a handfull of his Men
Hems in the greater number: his whole troops
Exceed not twenty thousand, but old Souldiers
Flesh'd in the spoiles of Germany and France,
Enur'd to his Command, and only know
To fight and overcome; And though that Famine
Raignes in his Camp, compelling them to tast
Bread made of rootes, forbid the use of man,
(Which they with scorne threw into Pompeys Camp
As in derision of his Delicates)
Or corne not yet halfe ripe, and that a Banquet:
They still besiege him, being ambitious only
To come to blows, and let their swords determine
Who hath the better Cause.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: May Victory
Attend on't, where it is.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: We every houre
Expect to heare the issue.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Save my good Lords;
By Isis and Osiris, whom you worship;
And the foure hundred gods and goddesses
Ador'd in Rome, I am your Honours servant.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: Truth needs (Seprinius) no oaths.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: You are cruell,
If you deny him swearing, you take from him
Three full parts of his language.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Your Honour's bitter,
Confound me, where I love I cannot say it,
But I must swear't: yet such is my ill fortune,
Nor vowes, nor protestations win beliefe,
I think, and (I can finde no other reason)
Because I am a Roman.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: No Septinius,
To be a Roman, were an honour to you,
Did not your manners, and your life take from it,
And cry aloud, that from Rome, you bring nothing
But Roman Vices, which you would plant here,
But no seed of her vertues.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: With your reverence
I am too old to learn.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: Any thing honest,
That I beleeve, without an oath.

speeches.speaker: Sept.
verse: I feare
Your Lordship has slept ill to night, and that
Invites this sad discourse: 'twill make you old
Before your time: —o' these vertuous Moralls,
And old religious principles, that foole us;
I have brought you a new Song, will make you laugh,
Though you were at your prayers.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: What is the subject?
Be free Septinius.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: 'Tis a Catalogue
Of all the Gamsters of the Court and City,
Which Lord lyes with that Lady: and what Gallant
Sports with that Merchants wife; and does relate
Who sells her honour for a Diamond,
Who, for a tissew robe: whose husband's jealous,
And who so kind, that, to share with his Wife
Will make the match himselfe?
Harmlesse conceits,
Though fooles say they are dangerous: I sang it
The last night at my Lord Photinus table.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: How? as a Fidler?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: No Sir, as a Guest,
A welcome guest too: and it was approv'd of
By a dozen of his friends, though they were touch'd in't:
For looke you, 'tis a kind of merriment,
When we have laid by foolish modesty
(As not a man of fashion will weare it)
To talke what we have done: at least to heare it:
If merrily, set down, it fires the blood,
And heightens Crest-falne appetite.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: New doctrine!

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Was't of your owne composing?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: No, I bought it
Of a skulking Scribler for two Ptolomies:
But the hints were mine owne; the wretch was fearfull:
But I have damnd my selfe, should it be question'd,
That I will owne it.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: And be punished for it:
Take heed: for you may so long exercise
Your scurrilous wit against authority,
The Kingdomes Counsels: and make profane Jests,
(Which to you (being an atheist) is nothing)
Against Religion, that your great maintainers
(Unlesse they would be thought Co-partners with you)
Will leave you to the Law: and then (Septinius)
Remember there are whips.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: For whores I grant you,
Till they are out of date, till then are safe too,
Or all the Gallants of the Court are Eunuchs,
And for mine owne defence I'le only add this,
I'le be admitted for a wanton tale
To some most private Cabinets, when your Priest-hood
(Though laden with the mysteries of your goddesse)
Shall waite without unnoted: so I leave you
To your pious thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: 'Tis a strange impudence,
This fellow does put on.

speeches.speaker: A^h.
verse: The wonder great,
He is accepted of.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Vices, for him,
Make a^ free way as vertues doe for others.
'Tis the times fault: yet great ones still have grace'd
To make them sport, or rub them o're with flattery,
Observes of all kinds.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: No more of him,
He is not worth our thoughts: a Fugitive
From Pompeys army: and now in a danger
When he should use his service.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: See how he hangs
On great Photinus Eare.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Hell, and the furies,
And all the plagues of darknesse light upon me:
You are my god on earth: and let me have
Your favour here, fall what can fall hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Thou art beleev'd: dost thou want money?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: No Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Or hast thou any suite? these ever follow
Thy vehement protestations.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: You much wrong me;
How can I want, when your beames shine upon me,
Unlesse employment to expresse my zeale
To do your Greatnesse service? doe but thinke
A deed so darke, the Sun would blush to looke on,
For which Man-kind would curse me, and arme all
The Powers above, and those below against me:
Command me, I will on.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: When I have use,
I'le put you to the test.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: May it be speedy,
And something worth my danger: you are cold,
And know not your own powers: this brow was fashion'd
To weare a Kingly wreath, and your grave judgment,
Given to dispose of Monarchies, not to govern
A childes affaires, the peoples eyes upon you,
The Souldier courts you; will you weare a garment
Of sordid loyalty when 'tis out of fashion?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: When Pompey was thy Generall (Septinius)
Thou saidst as much to him.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: All my love to him,
To Caesar, Rome, and the whole world is lost
In the Ocean of your Bounties: I have no friend,
Project, designe, or Countrey, but your favour,
Which I'le preserve at any rate.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: No more;
When I call on you, fall not off: perhaps
Sooner then you expect, I may employ you,
So leave me for a while.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Ever your Creature.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Good day Achoreus; my best friend Achillas,
Hath fame delivered yet, no certaine rumour
Of the great Roman action.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: That we are
To enquire, and learn of you Sir: whose grave care
For Egypts happinesse; and great Ptolomies good,
Have eyes and eares in all parts.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: I'le not boast,
What my Intelligence costs me: but 'ere long
You shall know more. The King, with him a Roman,

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: The scarlet livery of unfortunate war
Dy'de deeply on his face.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: 'Tis Labienus
Caesars Lieutenant in the wars of Gaul,
And fortunate in all his undertakings:
But since these Civill Jars he turn'd to Pompey,
And though he followed the better Cause
Not with the like successe.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Such as are wise
Leave falling buildings, flye to those that rise;
But more of that hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Lab.
verse: In a word (Sir,)
These gaping wounds, not taken as a slave,
Speake Pompeys osse: to tell you of the Battaile,
How many thousand severall bloody shapes
Death wore tha day, in triumph: how we bore
The shocke of Caesars charge: or with what fury
His souldiers came on as if they had been
So many Caesars, and like him ambitious,
To tread upon the liberty of Rome:
How Fathers kill'd their Sons, or Sons their Fathers,
Or how the Roman Peils on either side
Drew Roman blood, which spent, the Prince of weapons,
(The sword) succeeded, which in Civill wars,
Appoints the Tent, on which wing'd victory
Shall make a certaine Stand, then, how the Plaines
Flowd o're with blood, and what a cloud of vulturs
And other birds of prey, hung o're both armies,
Attending when their ready Servitors,
(The souldiers, from whom the angry gods
Had tooke all sense of reason, and of pity)
Would serve in their owne carkasses for a feast.
How Caesar with his Javelin force'd them on
That made the least stop, when their angry hands
Were lifted up against some known friends face;
Then comming to the body of the army
He shews the sacred Senate, and forbids them
To waste their force upon the Common souldier,
Whom willingly, if ere he did know pity,
He would have spar'd.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: The reason Labienus?

speeches.speaker: Lab.
verse: Full well he knows, that in their blood he was
To passe to Empire, and that through their bowels,
He must invade the Laws of Rome, and give
A period to the liberty of the world.
Then fell the Lepidi, and the bold Corvini,
The fam'd Torquati, Scipio's, and Marcelli,
(Names next to Pompeys, most renown'd on earth)
The Nobles, and the Commons lay together,
And Pontique, Punique, and Assyrian blood
Made up one crimson Lake: which Pompey seeing,
And that his, and the fate of Rome had left him
Standing upon the Ramper of his Camp,
Though scorning all that could fall on himselfe,
He pities them whose fortunes are embarqu'd
In his unlucky quarrell; cryes aloud too
That they should sound retreat, and save themselves:
That he desir'd not, so much noble blood
Should be lost in his service, or attend
On his misfortunes: and then, taking horse
With some few of his friends, he came to Lesbos,
And with Cornelia, his Wife, and Sons,
He's touch'd upon your shore: the King of Parthia
(Famous in his defeature of the Crassi)
Offer'd him his protection, but Pompey
Relying on his Benefits, and your Faith,
Hath chosen Aegypt for his Sanctuary,
Till he may recollect his scattered powers,
And try a second day: now Ptolomy,
Though he appeare not like that glorious Thing,
That three times rode in triumph, and gave lawes
To conquer'd Nations, and made Crownes his guift
As this of yours, your noble Father tooke
From his victorious hand, and you still weare it
At his devotion) to do you more honour
In his declinde estate, as the straightst Pyne
In a full grove of his yet flourishing friends,
He flyes to you for succour, and expects
The entertainment of your Fathers friend,
And Guardian to your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: To say I grieve his fortune
As much as if the Crowne I weare (his gift)
Were ravish'd from me, is a holy truth,
Our Gods can witnesse for me: yet, being young,
And not a free disposer of my self;
Let not a few hours, borrowed for advice,
Beget suspition of unthankfulnesse,
(Which next to hell I hate) pray you retire,
And take a little rest, and let his wounds
Be with that care attended, as they were
Carv'd on my flesh: good Labienus, thinke
The little respite, I desire shall be
Wholly emploid to find the readiest way
To doe great Pompey service.

speeches.speaker: Lab.
verse: May the gods
(As you intend) protect you.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Sit: sit all,
It is my pleasure: your advice, and freely.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: A short deliberation in this,
May serve to give you counsell to be honest,
Religious and thankfull, in themselves
Are forcible motives, and can need no flourish
Or glosse in the perswader, your kept faith,
(Though Pompey never rise to the height he's fallen from)
Caesar himselfe will love; and my opinion
Is (still committing it to graver censure)
You pay the debt you owe him, with the hazard
Of all you can call yours.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: What's yours (Photinus?)

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Achoreus (great Ptolomy) hath counsaild
Like a religious, and honest man,
Worthy the honour that he justly holds
In being Priest to Isis: But alas,
What in a man, sequesterd from the world,
Or in a private person, is preferd,
No policy allows of in a King,
To be or just, or thankfull, makes Kings guilty,
And faith (though prais'd, is punish'd) that supports
Such as good Fate forsakes: joyne with the gods,
Observe the man they favour, leave the wretched,
The Stars are not more distant from the Earth
Then profit is from honesty; all the power,
Prerogatives, and greatnesse of a Prince
Is lost, if he descend once but to steere
His course, as what's right, guides him; let him leave
The Scepter, that strives only to be good,
Since Kingdomes are maintain'd by force and blood.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: Oh wicked.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Peace: goe on.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Proud Pompey shews how much he scorns your youth,
In thinking that you cannot keepe your owne
From such as are ore-come. If you are tired
With being a King, let not a stranger take
What nearer pledges challenge: resigne rather
The government of Aegypt and of Nyle
To Cleopatra, that has title to them,
At least defend them from the Roman gripe,
What was not Pompeys, while the wars endured,
The Conquerour will not challenge, by all the world
Forsaken and despis'd, your gentle Guardian
His hopes and fortunes desperate, makes choise of
What Nation he shall fall with: and pursu'd
By their pale Ghosts, slaine in this Civill War,
He flyes not Caesar only, but the Senate,
