verse: Let me alone; I am not for your purpose,
I am no wa new man.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: We have new affairs for thee
Those that would raise thy head.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I would 'twere off,
And in your bellies for the love you beare me.
I'le be no more Knave: I have stings enough
Already in my breast.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Thou shalt be noble:
And who dares thinke then that thou art not honest?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Thou shalt command in Chief, all our strong Forces
And if thou serv'st an use, must not all justifie it?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I am Rogue enough.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Thou wilt be more, and baser:
A poor Rogue is all rogues: open to all shames:
Nothing to shadow him: dost thou think crying
Can keep thee from the censure of the Multitude?
Or to be kneeling at the altar save thee?
'Tis poore and servile:
Wert thou thine own Sacrifice
'Twould seeme so low, people would spit the fire out.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Keep thy self glorious stil, though ne're so staind,
And that will lessen it, if not work it out
To goe complaining thus: and thus repenting
Like a poore Girle that had betraid her maiden-head—

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I'le stop mine eares.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Will shew so in a souldier,
So simply, and so ridicolously, so tamely—

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: If people would believe thee, 'twer some honesty,
And for thy penitence would not laugh at thee
(As sure they will) and beat thee, for thy poverty:
If they would allow thy foolery, there were some hope.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: My foolery?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Nay, more then that, thy misery,
Thy monstrous misery.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: He begins to hearken:
Thy misery so great, men will not bury thee.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: That this were true!

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Why does this conquering Caesar
Labour through the worlds deep Seas of toyls & troubles,
Dangers, and desperate hopes? to repent afterwards?
Why does he slaughter thousands in a Battell,
And whip his Countrey with the Sword? to cry sor't?
Thou killdst great Pompey: hee'l kil all his kinred,
And justifie it: nay raise up Trophies to it,
When thou hearest him repent: (he's held most holy too)
And cry for doing daily bloody murthers,
Take thou example, and goe aske forgivenesse,
Call up the thing thou nam'st thy conscience,
And let it work: then 'twill seeme well Septinius.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: He does all this.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Yes: and is honoured for it;
Nay call'd the honoured Caesar, so maist thou be:
Thou wert born as neere a Crowne as he.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: He was poore.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: And desperate bloody tricks got him this credit.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I am afraid you will once more—

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Help to raise thee:
Off with thy pining blacke, it dulls a Souldier,
And put on resolution like a man,
A noble Fate waits on thee.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I now feele
My selfe returning Rascall speedily.
O that I had the power—

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Thou shalt have all:
And doe all through thy power, men shall admire thee,
And the vices of Septinius, shall turn vertues.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Off: off: thou must off: off my cowardize,
Puling repentance off.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Now thou speakst nobly.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Off my dejected looks: and welcome impudence:
My daring shall be Deity, to save me:
Give me instructions, and put action on me:
A glorious cause upon my swords point (Gentlemen)
And let my wit, and valour work: you will raise me,
And make me out-dare all my miseries?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: All this, and all thy wishes.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Use me then,
Womanish feare farewell: I'le never melt more,
Lead on, to some great thing, to weale my spirit:
I cut the Cedar Pompey, and I'le fell
This huge Oake Caesar too.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Now thou singst sweetly:
And Ptolomy shall crowne thee for thy service:

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: He's well wrought: put him on apace for cooling.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: THe tumult still encreases.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: O my fortune!
My lu^full folly rather! but 'tis well,
And worthily I am made a bondmans prey,
That after all my glorious victoryes,
In which I pass'd so many seas of dangers:
When all the Elements conspir'd against me,
Would yeild up the dominion of this head
To any mortall power; so blinde and stupid:
To trust these base Egyptians, that proclaim'd
Their per^uries, in noble Pompeys death,
And yet that could not warn me.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: Be still, Caesar,
Who ever lov'd to exercise his fate,
Where danger look't most dreadfull.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: If you fall,
Fall not alone: let the King and his Sister
Be buried in your ruines: on my life
They both are guilty: reason may assure you
Photinus nor Achillas durst attempt you,
Or shake one Dart, or Sword, aim'd at your safety,
Without their warrant.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: For the young King I know not
How he may be missed; but for his Sister
(Unequall'd Cleopatra) 'twere a kinde
Of blasphemy to doubt her: ougly treason
Durst never dwell in such a glorious building,
Nor can so cleare and great a spirit, as hers is,
Admit of falsehood.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let us seize on him then:
And leave her to her fortune.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: If he have power
Use it to your security, and let
His honesty acquit him; if he be fase,
It is too great an honour he should dye
By your victorious hand.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: He comes: and I
Shall do as I finde cause.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Let not great Caesar
Impute the breach of hospitality,
To you (my guest) to me; I am contemn'd,
And my rebellious subjects lift their hands
Against my head: and would they aim'd no farther,
Provided that I fell a sacrifice
To gaine you safety: that this is not faign'd,
The boldnesse of my innocence may confirme you:
Had I bin privy to their bloody plot,
I now had led them on, and given faire glosse
To their bad cause, by being present with them:
But I that yet taste of the punishment,
In being false to Pompey, will not make
A second fault to Caesar uncompell'd
With such as have not yet shooke off obedience,
I yeild my selfe to you, and will take part
In all your dangers.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: This pleades your excuse,
And I receive it.

speeches.speaker: Ach.
verse: If they have any touch,
Of justice, or religion, I will use
The athority of our Gods, to call them back,
From their bad purpose.

speeches.speaker: Ap.
verse: This part of the pallace,
Is yet defensible: we may make it good,
Till your powers rescue us.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Caesar beseig'd?
Ostaine to my great actions: 'twas my custome
An Army routed, as my feete had wings
To be first in the chase: nor walls, nor Bulworkes
Could guard those that escap'd the Battailes fury
From this strong Arme, and I to be enclos'd
My heart! my hart! but 'tis necessity,
To which the Gods must yeild, and I obey,
'Till I redeeme it, by some glorious way.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Ther's no retiring now, we are broke in:
The deed past hope of pardon: if we prosper
A will be stilde lawfull, and we shall give lawes
To those that now command us: stop not at
Or loyalty, or duty, bold Ambition,
To dare and power to do, gave the first difference
Betweene the King, and subject, Caesars Motto,
Aut Caesar aut Nihil, each of us must claime,
And use it as our owne.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: The deed is bloody
If we conclude in Ptolomies death.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: The better
The globe of Empire must be so manur.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Rome, that from Romulus first tooke her name
Had her walls watered with a Crymson showr
Draind from a Brothers heart: nor was she rais'd
To this prodigious height, that overlooks
Three full parts of the Earth, that pay her tribute,
But by enlarging of her narrow bounds
By the Sack of Neighbour Cities, were made hers
Till they were Cemented with the Blood of those
That did possesse 'em: Cesar, Ptolomy,
(Now I am steeld) to me are empty names
Esteem'd as Pompeys was.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Well said Septinius,
Thou now art right againe.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: But what course take we
For the Princesse Cleopatra?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Let her live
A while to make us sport: she shall authorize
Our undertakings to the ignorant people,
As if what we do were by her command:
But our triumvirat Government once confirm'd,
Shee beares her Brother company, that's my Province:
Leave me to work her.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: I will undertake
For Ptolomy.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Cesar shall be my taske,
And as in Pompey I began a names
I'le perfect it in Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: 'Tis resolv'd then
Wee'l force our passage.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: See: they do appeare
As they desir'd a parley.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: I am proud yet
I have brought them to capitulate.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Now Photinus?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Now Ptolomy?

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: No addition?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: We are equall,
Though Caesars name were put into the scale,
In which our worth is weighd.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Presumptuous Villaine,
Upon what grounds hast thou presum'd to raise
Thy servile hand against the King, or me,
That have a greater name?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: On those, by which
Thou didst presume to passe the Rubicon
Against the Laws of Rome; and at the name
Of traytor smile, as thou didst when Marcellus
The Consull, with the Senats full consent
Pronounc'd thee for an enemy to thy Country,
Yet thou wentst on, and thy rebellious Cause
Was crown'd with fair success: why should we fear then?
Thinke on that Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: O the gods! be brav'd thus?
And be compelld to beare this from a slave
That would not brooke great Pompey his Superiour?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Thy glories now have touch'd the highest point,
And must descend.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Despaire, and thinke we stand
The Champions of Rome, to wreak her wrongs
Upon whose liberty thou hast set thy foote.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: And that the ghosts of all those noble Romans
That by thy sword fell in this Civill warre,
Expect revenge.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Dar'st thou speak, and remember
There was a Pompey?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: There is no hope to scape us:
If that against the odds we have upon you
You dare come forth and fight, receive the honour
To dye, like Romans, if ye faint, resolve
To starve, like wretches: I disdain to change
Another syllable with you.

speeches.speaker: An^.
verse: Let us dye nobly:
And rather fall upon each others sword
Then come into these villains hands.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: That Fortune
Which to this howre hath been a friend to Caesar,
Though for a while she cloath her brow with frowns
Will smile again upon me; who will pay her,
Or sacrifice or vowes, if she forsake
Her best of works in me? or suffer him
Whom, with a strong hand she hath led triumphant
Through the whole Western world, & Rome acknowledgd
Her Soveraign Lord, to end in gloriously,
A life admir'd by all? the threatned danger
Must by a way more horrid, be avoided,
And I will run the hazard: Fire the Pallace,
And the rich Magazines that neighbour it,
In which the wealth of Aegypt is contain'd:
Start not, it shall be so; that while the people
Labour in quenching the ensuing flames,
Like Caesar, with this handfull of my friends
Through fire, and swords, I force a passage to
My conquering Legions. King, if thou darst follow
Where Caesar leads, or live, or dye a Free-man;
If not, stay here a bond-man to thy slave,
And dead, be thought unworthy of a grave.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I feele my resolution melts againe,
And that I am not knave alone, but foole
In all my purposes. This Devill Photinus
Employs me, as a property, and grown uselesse
Will shake me off againe: he told me so
When I kill'd Pompey: nor can I hope better
When Caesar is dispatch'd: Services done
For such as only study their owne ends,
Too great to be rewarded, or return'd
With deadly hate: I learnd this principle
In his own Schoole: yet still he fooles me: well:
And yet he trusts me; Since I in my nature
Was fashion'd to be false, wherefore should I
That kill'd my Generall, and a Roman, one
To whom I owe all nourishments of life
Be true to an Aegyptian? to save Caesar,
And turn Photinus plots on his own head,
As it is in my power, redeem my credit,
And live, to lye, and swear again in fashion,
Oh, 'twere a Master-piece? ha? — me Ceasar,
How's he got off?

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: The fire has tooke,
And shews the City, like a second Troy,
The Navy too is scorch'd, the people greedy
To save their wealth, and houses, while their souldiers
Make spoile of all: only Achillas troops
Make good their guard: break through them, we are safe:
I'le lead you like a Thunder-bolt.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Stay Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Who's this? the dog Septinius?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Cut his throat.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: You barkt but now, fawne you so soone?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: O heare me,
What I'le deliver is for Caesars safety,
For all your good.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Good from a moneth like thine,
That never belch'd but blasphemy & treason, on Festivall dayes

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I am an altered man: altered indeed,
And I will give you cause to say I am a Roman.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: Rogue, I grant thee.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Trust me, I'le make the passage smooth and easy,
For your escape.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I'le trust the Devill sooner,
And make a safer bargaine.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: I am trusted,
With all Photinus secrets.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: There's no doubt then,
Thou wilt be false.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Still to be true to you.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: And very likely.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Be breife, the meanes?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Thus Caesar:
To me alone, but bound by terrible oathes
Not to discover it, he hath reveal'd
A dismall vault, whose dreadfull mouth do's open
A mile beyond the Citty: in this cave
Lye but two houres conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant
verse: If you believe him,
Hee'le bury us alive.

speeches.speaker: Dol.
verse: I'le fly in the ayre first.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Then in the dead of night, I'le bring you backe
Into a private roome, where you shall finde
Photinus, and Achillas, and the rest
Of their Commanders, close at Counsell.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Good: what followes?

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Fall me fairly on their throates,
Their heads cut off and shorn, the multitude
Will easily disperse.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: O Devill! away with him:
Nor true to friend nor enemy? Caesar scornes
To find his safety, or revenge his wrongs
So base a way: or owe the meanes of life
To such a leaprous Traytor. I have towr'd
For victory like a Faulcon in the clouds,
Not dig'd for't like a Moale: our Swords, and Cause
Make way for us; and that it may appeare
We tooke a noble course, and hate base Treason,
Some souldiers, that would merit Caesars favour,
Hang him on yonder turret, and then follow
The lane, this sword makes for you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: Here's a Belt,
Though I dye for it I'le use it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: Tis too good
To trusse a Cur in.

speeches.speaker: Sep.
verse: Save me, here's gold.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: If Rome
Were offered for thy ransome, it could not help thee.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: Hang not an arse.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sold.
verse: Goad him on with thy sword:
Thou dost deserve a worser end; and may
All such conclude so, that their friends betray.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: We are lost.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: Undon.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Confusion, Fire, and Swords,
And fury in the souldiers face, more horrid
Circle us round.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: The Kings command they laugh at,
And jeere at Caesars threats.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: My brother seizd on
By the Roman, as thought guilty of the tumult,
And forc'd to beare him company, as mark'd out
For his protection, or revenge.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: They have broke
Into my Cabinet: my Trunks are ransak'd.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I have lost my Jewels too; but thats the least:
The barbarous Rascalls, against all humanity,
Or sense of pity, have kill'd my little dog,
And broke my monkeys chaine.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: They rufled me:
But that I could endure, and tire 'em too,
Would they proceed no further.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: O my sister!

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: My Queen, my Mistresse!

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Can you stand unmov'd
When an Earth-quake of rebellion shakes the City?
And the Court trembles?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Yes Arsino,
And with a masculine constancy deride
Fortunes worst malice, as a servant to
My Vertues, not a Mistress: then we forsake
The strong fort of our selves, when we once yield,
Or shrink at her assaults; I am still my selfe,
And though dis-roab'd of Sovereignty, and ravisht
Of ceremonious duty, that attends it,
Nay, grant they had slav'd my body, my free mind
Like to the Palm-tree, walling fruitfull Nyle,
Shall grow up straighter, and enlarge it selfe
Spight of the envious weight that loads it with:
Think of thy birth (Arsino) common burthens
Fit common shoulders; teach the multitude
By suffering nobly what they feare to touch at:
The greatnesse of thy mind does soare a pitch,
Their dim eyes (darkned by their narrow soules)
Cannot arrive at.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I am new created,
And owe this second being to you (best sister)
For now I feele you have infus'd into me
Part of your fortitude.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: I still am fearfull:
I dare not tell a lye: you that were born
Daughters, and Sisters unto Kings, may nourish
Great thoughts, which I, that am your humble handmaid
Must not presume to ryvall.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Yet (my Eros)
Though thou hast profited nothing, by observing
The whole course of my life, learn in my death,
Though not to equall, yet to imitate
Thy fearlesse Mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: O, a man in armes?
His weapon drawn too?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Though upon the point
Death sate, I'le meete it, and out-dare the danger.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Keep the watch strong, and guard the passage sure
That leads unto the Sea.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: What sea of rudenesse
Breaks in upon us? or what Subjects breath
Dare raise a storme, when we command a calm?
Are duty, and obedience fled to heaven,
And in their roome, ambition and pride
Sent into Aegyt? that face speaks thee Photinus,
A thing thy Mother brought into the world:
My Brothers, and my Slave: but thy behaviour,
Oppos'd to that an insolent Intruder
Upon that Soveraignty thou shouldst bow to,
If in the gulph of base ingratitude,
All loyalty to Ptolomy the King
Be swallowed up, remember who I am,
Whose Daughter, and whose Sister: or suppose
That is forgot too; let the name of Caesar
Which Nations quake at, stop the desperate madnesse
From running headong on to thy confusion.
Throw from thee quickly those rebellious armes,
Tnd let me read submission in thine eyes,
Ahy wrongs to us, we will not only pardon,
But be a ready advocate, to plead for thee
To Caesar, and my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Plead my pardon?
To you I bow, but scorn as much to stoop thus
To Ptolomy, to Caesar? Nay the gods,
As to put off the figure of a man,
And change my Essence, with a sensuall beast:
All my designes, my counsels, and dark ends
Were aym'd to purchase you.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: How durst thou, being
The scorne of basenesse, nourish such a thought?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: They that have power are royall: and those base
That live at the devotion of an other,
What birth gave Ptolomy, or fortune Caesar,
By Engines fashiond in this Protean Anvill
I have made mine: and onely stoop at you,
Whom I would still preserve free to command me;
For Caesars frownes, they are below my thoughts,
And but in these faire eyes, I still have read
The story of a supreame Monarchy,
To which all hearts with mine, gladly pay tribute,
Photinus name, had long since bin as great
As Ptolomies ere was, or Caesars is,
This made me as a weaker tye to unloose
The knot of loyalty, that chain'd my freedom;
And slight the feare that Caesars threats might cause,
That I and they might see no Sun appeare
But Cleopatra, in th' Egyptian Spheare.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: O giantlike Ambition! married to
Cymerian darknesse! in considerate foole,
(Though flatter'd with selve love) could'st thou beleeve,
Were all Crownes on the earth, made into one,
And that (by Kings) set on thy head: all Scepters,
Within thy graspe, and laid downe at my feete,
I would vouchsafe a kisse to a no-man?
A guelded Evenuch?

speeches.speaker: Phot.
verse: Fairest, that makes for me:
And shewes it is no sensuall appetite,
But true love to the greatnesse of thy spirit,
That when that you are mine shall yeild me pleasures:
Hymen, though blessing a new married paire
Shall blush to thinke on, and our certaine Issue,
The glorious splendour of dread Majesty:
Whose beames shall dazell Rome, and awe the world:
My wants in that kinde, others shall supply,
And I give way to it.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Baser then thy birth:
Can there be Gods, and heare this, and no thunder,
Ram thee into the earth?

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: They are a sleepe,
And cannot heare thee:
Or with open eyes,
Did Jove looke on us, I would laugh and sweare
That his artillary is cloid by me:
Or if that they have power to hurt, his Bolts
Are in my hand.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Most impious!

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: They are dreames,
Religious fooles shake at: yet to assure thee,
If Nemesis, that scourges pride, and scorne,
Be any thing but a name she lives in me:
For by my selfe (an oath to me more dreadfull
Then Stix is to your Gods) weake Ptolomy dead,
And Caesar (both being in my toile) remov'd
The poorest Rascalls, that are in my Camp
Shall, in my presence, quench their Iustfull heate
In thee, and young Arsinoe; while I laugh
To heare you howle in vaine:
I deride those Gods,
That you thinke can protect you,

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: To prevent thee,
In that I am the Mistress of my fate:
So hope I of my Sister, to confirme it,
I spit at thee, and scorne thee.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: I will tame,
That haughty courage, and make it stoop too.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Never:
I was borne to command and I will dye so.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: The King dead? this is a faire entrance to,
Our future happinesse.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: O my Deare Brother?

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Weepe not Arsinoe, common women do soe,
Nor loose a teare for him, it cannot helpe him:
But study to dye nobly.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: Caesar fled?
'Tis deadly aconite to my cold heart:
It choakes my vitall spirits: where was your care?
Did the guardes sleepe?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: He rowz'd them with his sword:
We talke of Mars, but I am sure his courage
Admits of no comparison but it selfe,
And (as inspir'd by him) his following friends
With such a confidence, as you Eagletss prey
Under the large wing of their feircer dam,
Brake through our troopes, and scatterd 'em, he went on:
But still pursude by us: when on the sudaine,
He turn'd his head, and from his eyes flew terrour;
Which strooke in us no lesse feare, and amazement,
Then if we had encounter'd with the lightning,
Hurld from Joves clowdy brow.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: 'Twas like my Caesar.

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: We falne back, he made on, and as our feare
Had parted from us, with his dreadfull lookes,
Againe we follow'd: but got neare the sea:
On which his navy anchord; in one hand
Holding a scroll he had, above the waves,
And in the other grasping fast his sword

As it had bin a trident, forg'd by
~ulcan,
To calme the raging Ocean, he made away
As if he had bin Neptune: his friends like
So many Tritons follow'd their bold showts,
Yeilding a chearefull musique; we showr'd darts,
Upon them but in vaine, they reach'd their ships,
And in their safety we are sunck; for Caesar
Prepares for war.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: How fell the King?

speeches.speaker: Achil.
verse: Unable,
To follow Caesar, he was trod to death
By the pursuers, and with him the Priest,
Of Isis good Achoreus.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: May the Earth,
Lye gently on their ashes.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: I feele now,
That there are powers above us: and that 'tis not
Within the searching policies of man,
To alter their decrees.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: I laugh at thee:
Where are thy threates now, (foole) thy scoffs, and scornes
Against the Gods? I see calamity
Is the best Mistris of Religion,
And can convert an Atheist.

speeches.speaker: Pho.
verse: O they come,
Mountaines fall on me! O, for him to dye
That plac'd his heaven on earth, is an assurance
Of his descent to hell; where shall I hide me?
The greatest daring to a man dishonest,
Is but a bastard courage, ever fainting.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
prose: Looke on your Caesar; banish feare (my fairest) You now are safe.

speeches.speaker: Sce.
verse:
By
~enus, not a kisse
Till our worke be done: the Traitors once dispatch'd
To it, and wee'le cry aime.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I will be speedy.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: Farewell againe Arsinoe; how now Eros,
Ever faint-harted?

speeches.speaker: Eros.
verse: But that I am assur'd,
Your excellency can command the Generall,
I feare the Souldiers, for they looke as if
They would be nibling too.

speeches.speaker: Cleo.
verse: He is all honour,
Nor do I now repent me of my favours;
Nor can I thinke nature e're made a woman,
That in her prime deserv'd him.

speeches.speaker: Ars.
verse: He's come backe,
Pursue no farther; curb the Souldiers fury.
See (beauteous Mistris) their accursed heads,
That did conspire against us.

speeches.speaker: Sceva.
verse: Furies plague 'em,
They had too faire an end, to dye like Souldiers,
Pompey fell by the sword; the crosse, or halter
Should have dispatch'd them.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: All is but death (good Sceva)
Be therefore satisfied, and now (my dearest)
Looke up on Caesar, as he still appear'd
A Conquerour, and this unfortunate King
Entomb'd with honour, wee'le for Rome, where Caesar
Will shew he can give Kingdome: for the Senate,
(Thy brother dead) shall willingly decree
The Crowne of Egypt, (that was his) to thee.

speeches.speaker: Peter.
verse: I Would we were remov'd from this Town, Anthony
That we might taste some quiet: for mine owne part,
I'me almost melted with continuall trotting
After enquities, dreames, and revelations,
Of who knowes, whom or where? serve wenching soldiers,
That know no other Paradice but Plackets:
Ile serve a Priest in Lent, first and eate Bell-ropes.

speeches.speaker: Anth.
verse: Thou art the froward'st foole —

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why good tame Anthony?
Tell me but this: to what end came we hither?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: To wait upon our Masters.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: But how Anthony?
Answer me that; resolve me there good Anthony?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: To serve their uses.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Shew your uses Anthony.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: To be imploy'd in any thing.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: No Anthony,
Not any thing I take it; nor that thing
We travell to discover, like new Islands;
A salt itch serve such uses; in things of moment,
Concerning things I grant yee, not things errant,
Sweet Ladies things, and things to thank the Surgeon:
In no such things, sweet Anthony, put case —

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Come, come, all will be mended: this invisible woman
Of infinite report for shape and vertue,
That bred us all this trouble to no purpose,
They are determin'd now no more to thinke on,
But fall close to their studies.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Was there ever
Men knowne to run mad with report before?
Or wonder after that they know not where
To finde? or if found, how to enjoy? are mens braines
Made now a dayes of Malt, that their affections
Are never sober? but like drunken people
Founder at every new fame? I do believe too
That men in love are ever drunke, as drunken men
Are ever loving.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Prethee be thou sober,
And know, that they are none of those, not guilty
Of the least vanity of love, onely a doubt
Fame might too farre report, or rather flatter
The graces of this woman, made them curious
To finde the truth, which since they finde so blotted
And lock'd up from their searches, they are now setled
To give the wonder ever.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Would they were setled
To give me some new shooes too: for I'le be sworne
These are e'ne worne out to the reasonable soules
In their good worships businesse: and some sleep
Would not doe much amisse, unlesse they meane
To make a Bell-man on me: and what now
Meane they to study, Anthony, Morall Philosophy
After their mar-all women?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Mar a fooles head.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Twill mar two fools heads, & they take not heed,
Besides the Giblets to 'em.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Will you walke Sir,
And talke more out of hearing? your fooles head
May chance to finde a wooden night-cap else.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
prose: I never lay in any.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Then leave your lying,
And your blinde Prophesying: here they come,
You had best tell them as much.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I am no tell-tale.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: I would we could have seen her though: for sure
She must be some rare creature, or report lyes,
All mens reports too,

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I could well wish I had seen her;
But since she is so conceal'd, so beyond venture
Kept and preserv'd from view, so like a Paradice,
Plac't where no knowledg can come near her; so guarded
As 'twere impossible, though knowne to reach her,
I have made up my beliefe.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Hang me from this houre
If I more thinke upon her, or believe her,
But as she came a strong report unto me,
So the next Fame shall loose her.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis the next way:
But whither are you walking?

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: My old round
After my meat, and then to bed.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis healthfulll.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Will not you stir?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I have a little businesse.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Upon my life this Lady still—

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Then you will loose it.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Pray let's walke together.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Now I cannot.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: I have something to impart.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: An houre hence
I will not misse to meet you.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Ith' high street;
For not to lye, I have a few Devotions
To doe first, then I am yours.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Remember.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Cut his winde-pipe, I say.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Fie Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Or knock his brains out first, then forgive him
If you doe thrust, be sure it be to th' hilts,
A Surgeon may see through him.
You are too violent,
Too open, undiscreet.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Am I not ruin'd?
The honour of my house crack'd? my bloud poyson'd?
My credit, and my name?
Be sure it be so,
Before ye use this violence. Let not doubt,
And a suspecting anger so much sway ye,
Your wisedome may be question'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I say kill him,
And then dispute the cause; cut off what may be,
And what is, shall be safe.
Hang up a true man,
Because 'tis possible he may be theevish:
Alas, is this good Justice?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: I know as certaine,
As day must come againe; as cleare as truth.
And open as beliefe can lay it to me,
That I am basely wrong'd, wrong'd above recompence;
Malitiously abus'd, blasted for ever
In name and honour, lost to all remembrance,
But what is smear'd, and shamefull; I must kill him,
Necessitie compells me.
But think better

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: There is no other cure left: yet witnesse with me
All that is faire in man, all that is noble,
I am not greedy of this life I seek for,
Nor thirst to shed mans bloud; and would 'twere possible
I wish it with my soule, so much I tremble
To offend the sacred Image of my Maker,
My sword could onely kill his crimes: no 'tis honour,
Honour, my noble friends, that idoll honour,
That all the world now worships, not Petruchio
Must doe this justice.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let it once be done,
And 'tis no matter, whether you, or honour,
Or both be accessarie.
Doe you weigh Petruchio
The value of the person, power, and greatnesse,
And what this sparke may kindle?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: To performe it,
So much I am ty'd to reputation,
And credit of my house, let it raise wild-sires,
That all this Dukedome smoak, and stormes that tosse me
Into the stormes of everlasting ruine,
Yet I must through; if yee dare side me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Dare?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Ye're friends indeed, if not.
Here's none flies from you,
Doe it in what designe ye please, wee'll back ye.
But then be sure yee kill him.
Is the cause
So mortall, nothing but his life?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Beleeve me,
A lesse offence has been the desolation
Of a whole name.
No other way to purge it?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: There is, but never to be hoped for,
Thinke an houre more,
And if then ye finde no safer road to guide yee,
Wee'll set up our rests too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Mine's up already,
And hang him for my part,
Goes lesse than life.
If we see noble cause, 'tis like our swords
May be as free and forward as your words.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: The civill order of this Towne Bellonia
Makes it belov'd, and honour'd of all travellers,
As a most safe retirement in all troubles;
Beside the wholsome seat, and noble temper
Of those mindes that inhabit it, safely wise,
And to all strangers vertuous: But I see
My admiration has drawne night upon me,
And longer to expect my friend may pull me
Into suspition of too late a stirrer,
Which all good Governments are jealous of.
Ile home, and thinke at liberty: yet certaine,
'Tis not so farre night as I thought; for see,
A faire house yet stands open, yet all about it
Are close, and no lights stirring: there may be foule play:
Ile venture to look in: if there be knaves,
I may doe a good office.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: Signieur?

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: What? how is this?

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: Signieur Fabritio?

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: Ile goe nearer.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: Fabritio?

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: This is a womans tongue, here may be good done.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: Who's there?
Fabritio?

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: I.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: Where are ye?

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Here.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: O come, for heavens sake!

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: I must see what this meanes,

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: I have stay'd this long houre for you, make no noise,
For things are in strange trouble: here, be secret,
'Tis worth your care; begone now; more eyes watch us,
Then may be for our safeties.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Harke ye?

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: Peace: good night.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: She is gone, and I am loaden; fortune for me;
It weighes well, and it feeles well; it may chance
To be some pack of worth: by th' masse 'tis heavie;
If it be Coyne or Jewels, 'tis worth welcome:
Ile ne're refuse a fortune: I am confident
'Tis of no common price: now to my lodging:
If it hit right, Ile blesse this night.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis strange,
I cannot meet him; sure he has encountred
Some light o' love or other, and there meanes
To play at In and In for this night. Well Don John,
If you doe spring a leak, or get an itch,
Til ye claw off your curl'd pate, thank your night-walks:
You must be still a bootehalling: one round more,
Though it be late, Ile venture to discover ye,
I doe not like your out-leaps.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Welcome to Towne, are ye all fit?
To point Sir,

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Where are the horses?
Where they were appointed.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Be private, and whatsoever fortune
Offer it selfe, let's stand sure.
Feare not us,
'Ere ye shall be endangered, or deluded,
Wee'll make a black night on't.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No more, I know it;
You know your Quarters?
Will you goe alone sir?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Ye shall not be farre from me, the least noise
Shall bring ye to my rescue.
We are counsell'd.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
verse: Was ever man so paid for being curious?
Ever so bob'd for searching out adventures,
As I am? did the devill lead me? must I needs be peeping
Into mens houses where I had no businesse,
And make my selfe a mischiefe? 'Tis well carried;
I must take other mens occasions on me,
And be I know not whom: most finely handled:
What have I got by this now? what's the purchase?
A piece of evening Arras worke, a childe,
Indeed an Infidell: this comes of peeping:
A lumpe got out of lazinesse; good white bread
Let's have no bawling with yee: 'sdeath, have I
Knowne Wenches thus long, all the wayes of wenches,
Their snares and subtilties? have I read over
All their Schoole learnings, div'd into their quiddits,
And am I now bum-fidled with a Bastard?
Fetch'd over with a Carde of five, and in mine old dayes,
After the dire massacre of a million
Of Maiden-heads? caught the common way, ith'night too
Under anothers name, to make the matter
Carry more weight about it? well Don Iohn,
You will be wiser one day, when ye have purchas'd
A beavy of these Butter prints together,
With searching out conceal'd iniquities,
Without commission: why, it would never grieve me,
If I had got this Ginger-bread: never stirr'd me,
So I had had a stroak for't: 't had been Justice
Then to have kept it; but to raise a dayrie
For other mens adulteries, consume my selfe in candles,
And scowring works, in Nurses Bells and Babies,
Onely for charity, for meere I thank you,
A little troubles me: the least touch for it,
Had but my breeches got it, had contented me.
Whose e're it is, sure t' had a wealthy mother,
For 'tis well cloathed, and if I be not cozen'd,
Well lin'd within: to leave it here were barbarous,
And ten to one would kill it: a more sin
Then his that got it: well, I will dispose on't,
And keep it, as they keep deaths heads in rings,
To cry, memento to me; no more peeping.
Now all the danger is to qualifie
The good old gentlewoman, at whose house we live,
For she will fall upon me with a Catechisme
Of foure houres long: I must endure all;
For I will know this mother: Come good wonder,
Let you and I be jogging: your starv'd trebble
Will waken the rude watch else: All that bee
Curious night-walkers, may they finde my fee.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Sure hee's gone home:
I have beaten all the purlewes,
But cannot bolt him: if he be a bobbing
'Tis not my care can cure him: To morrow morning
I shall have further knowledge from a Surgeons—
Where he lyes moord, to mend his leaks.

speeches.speaker: Con,
verse: I'me ready,
And through a world of dangers am slown to yee.
Be full of haste and care, we are undone else:
Where are your people? which way must we travell?
For heaven sake stay not here sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What may this prove?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Alas I am mistaken, lost, undone.
For ever perish'd. Sir, for heaven sake tell me,
Are ye a Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I am.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Of this place?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No, borne in Spain.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: As ever you lov'd honour,
As ever your desires may gaine their ends,
Doe a poore wretched woman but this benefit,
For I am forc'd to trust yee.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Y'ave charm'd me,
Humanity and honour bids me helpe ye;
And if I faile your trust.—

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: The time's too dangerous
To stay your protestations: I beleeve ye,
Alas, I must believe ye: From this place,
Good noble Sir, remove me instantly,
And for a time, where nothing but your selfe,
And honest conversation my come neare me,
In some secure place settle me. What I am,
And why thus boldly I commit my credit
Into a strangers hand, the feares and dangers,
That force me to this wilde course, at more leisure
I shall reveale unto you.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Come, be hearty,
He must strike through my life that takes ye from me.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: He will sure come. Are yee well arm'd?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Never feare us.
Here's that will make 'em dance without a Fiddle.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: We are to look for no weak foes, my friends,
Nor unadvised ones.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Best gamsters make the best game,
We shall fight close and handsome then.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Antonio,
You are a thought too bloudy.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Why? all Physitians
And penny Almanacks allow the opening
Of veines this moneth: why doe ye talke of bloudy?
What come we for, to fall to cuffes for apples?
What, would ye make the Cause a Cudgell quarell?
On what termes stands this man? is not his honour
Open'd to his hand, and pickt out like an Oyster?
His credit like a quart pot knockt together,
Able to hold no liquor? cleare but this point.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Speak softly, gentle Couzen.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ile speak truely;
What should men doe ally'd to these disgraces,
Lick o're his enemie, sit downe, and dance him?
You are as farre o'th' bow hand now.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And crie;
That's my fine boy, thou wilt doe so no more child.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Here are no such cold pitties.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: By Saint Jaques
They shall not finde me one: here's old tough Andrew,
A speciall friend of mine, and he but hold,
He strike 'em such a horne-pipe: knocks I come for,
And the best bloud I light on; I profes it,
Not to scarre Coster-mongers; If I loose mine owne,
Mine audits lost, and fare-well five and fifty.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Let's talke no longer, place your selves with silence,
As I directed yee; and when time calls us,
As ye are friends, so shew your selves.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: So be it.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Nay Son, if this be your regard.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Good mother.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Good me no goods; your Cozen, and your self
Are welcome to me, whilst you beare your selves
Like honest and true Gentlemen: Bring hither
To my house, that have ever been reputed
A gentlewoman of a decent, and faire carriage,
And so behav'd my self?

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: I know ye have.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Bring hither, as I say, to make my name
Stinke in my neighbours nostrills? your Devises,
Your Brats, got out of Alligant, and broken oathes?
Your Linsey Woolsey worke, your hasty puddings?
I fosler up your filch'd iniquities?
Y'are deceiv'd in me, Sir, I am none
Of those receivers.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Have I not sworne unto you,
'Tis none of mine, and shew'd you how I found it?

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Ye found an easie foole that let you get it,
She had better have worne pastornes.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Will yee heare me?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Oathes? what doe you care for oathes to gaine your ends,
When ye are high and pamper'd? What Saint know ye?
Or what Religion, but your purpos'd lewdnesse,
Is to be look'd for of ye? nay, I will tell ye,
You will then sweare like accus'd Cut-purses,
As far of truth too; and lye beyond all Faulconers:
I'me sick to see this dealing.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Heaven forbid Mother.

speeches.speaker: Lat.
verse: Nay, I am very sick.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Who waits there?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Bring down the bottle of Canary wine.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Exceeding sick, heav'n helpe me.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Haste ye sirrah,
I must ev'n make her drunk; nay gentle mother;

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Now sie upon ye, was it for this purpose
You fetch'd your evening walks for your digestions,
For this pretended holinesse? no weather,
Not before day could hold ye from the Matins.
Were these your bo-peep prayers? ye have praid well,
And with a learned zeale: watcht well too; your Saint
It seems was pleas'd as well: still sicker, sicker.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: There is no talking to her till I have drencht her.
Give me: here mother take a good round draught,
'Twill purge spleen from your spirits: deeper mother.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: I, I, sonne; you imagine this will mend all.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: All y'faith Mother.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: I confesse the Wine
Will doe his part.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Ile pledge ye.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: But sonne John.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: I know your meaning mother; touch it once more,
Alas you look not well; take a round draught,
It warmes the bloud well, and restores the colour,
And then wee'll talke at large.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: A civill gentleman?
A stranger? one the Town holds a good regard of?

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Nay I will silence there.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: One that should weigh his faire name? oh, a stichl

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: There's nothing better for a stitch, good mother,
Make no spare of it, as you love your health,
Mince not the nutter.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: As I said, a gentleman,
Lodge in my house? now heav'ns my comfort, Signior!

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: I look'd for this.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: I did not thinke you would havo us'd me thus;
A woman of my credit: one, heaven knowes,
That lov'd you but too tenderly.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Deare mother,
I ever found your kindnesse, and acknowledge it.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: No, no, I am a fool to counsell yee. Where's the infant?
Come, lets see your Workmanship.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: None of mine, Mother.
But there 'tis, and a lusty one.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Heaven blesse thee,
Thou hadst a hasty making; but the best is,
'Tis many a good mans fortune: as I live
Your owne eyes Signior, and the nether lip
As like yee, as ye had spit it.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: I am glad on't.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Blesse me, what things are these?

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: I thought my labour
Was not all lost, 'tis gold, & these are jewels,
Both rich, and right I hope.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Well, well sonne Iohn,
I see ye are a wood-man, and can chuse
Your Deere, though it be i'th darke, all your discretion
Is not yet lost; this was well clapt aboard:
Here I am with you now; when as they say
Your pleasure comes with profit; when ye must needs do,
Doe where ye may be done to, 'tis a wisedome
Becomes a young man well: be sure of one thing,
Loose not your labour and your time together,
It seasons of a foole, sonne, time is pretious,
Worke wary whilst ye have it; since ye must traffick
Sometimes this slippery way, take sure hold Signior,
Trade with no broken Merchants, make your lading,
As you would make your rest, adventurously,
But with advantage ever.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: All this time mother,
The childe wants looking too, wants meat and Nurses.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Now blessing o' thy care; it shall have all,
And instantly; Ile seek a Nurse my selfe, sonne;
'Tis a sweet childe: ah my young Spaniard;
Take you no further care sir.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Yes of these Jewels,
I must by your leave Mother: these are yours,
To make your care the stronger: for the rest
Ile finde a Master; the gold for bringing up on't,
I freely render to your charge.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: No more words,
Nor no more children, (good sonne) as you love me,
This may doe well.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: I shall observe your Morals.
But where's Don Ferdinand (Mother)

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Ten to one
About the like adventure: he told me.
He was to finde you out.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Why should he stay thus?
There may be some ill chance in't: sleep I will not,
Before I have found him: now this woman's pleas'd,
Ile seek my friend out, and my care is eas'd.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Beleeve sir, 'tis as possible to doe it,
As to remove the City; the maine faction,
Swarm throgh the streets like hornets, arm'd with angers
Able to ruine States: no safety left us,
Nor meanes to dye like men, if instantly
You draw not back againe,

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: May he be drawne
And quarter'd too, that turnes now; were I surer
Of death then thou art of thy fears, and with death
More then those feares are too.
Sir, I feare not.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I would not crack my vow, start from my honour,
Because I may finde danger; wound my soule,
To keep my body safe.
I speak not sir,
Out of a basenesse to you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No, nor doe not
Out of a basenesse leave mo: what is danger,
More then the weaknesse of our apprehensions?
A poor cold part o'th bloud? who takes it hold of?
Cowards, and wicked livers: valiant mindes
Were made the Masters of it, and as hearty Seamen
In desperate stormes, stem with a little Rudder
The tumbling ruines of the Ocean:
So with their cause & swords do they do dangers.
Say we yere sure to dye all in this venture,
As I am confident against it: is there any
Amongst us of so fat a sense, so pamper'd,
Would chule luxuriously to lye a bed,
And purge away his spirit, send his soule out
In Sugar-lops, and Syrups? give me dying,
As dying out to be, upon mine enemy,
Parting with man-kinde, by a man that's manly:
Let 'em be all the world, and bring along
Cain's envy with 'em, I will on.
You may sir,
But with what safety?
Since 'tis come to dying,
You shall perceive sir, here be those amongst us
Can dye as decently as other men,
And with as little ceremony: on brave sir.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: That's spoken heartily.
And he that flinches
May he dye lowzie in a ditch.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No more dying,
There's no such danger in it:
What's a clock?
Somewhat above your houre.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Away then quickly,
Make no noise, and no trouble will attend us.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Give me the candle: so goe you out that way.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: What have we now to doe?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And o' your life sirrah,
Let none come neare the doore without my knowledge,
No not my Land lady, nor my friend.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Tis done sir.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Nor any serious businesse that concerns me.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Is the winde there agen?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Be gone.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I am sir.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Now enter without feare.—And noble Lady
That safety and civility yee wish'd for
Shall truely here attend you: no rude tongue
Nor rough behaviour knows this place, no wishes
Beyond the moderation of a man,
Dare enter here: your owne desires and Innocence,
Joyn'd to my vow'd obedience, shall protect you,
Were dangers more then doubts.

speeches.speaker: Coast.
verse: Ye are truely noble,
And worth a womans trust: let it become me,
(I doe beseech you sir) for all your kindnesse,
To render with my thanks, this worthlesse trifle;
I may be longer troublesome.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Faire offices
Are still their owne rewards: Heav'n blesse me Lady
From selling civill courtesies: may it please ye,
If ye will force a favour to oblige me,
Draw but that cloud aside, to satisfie me
For what good Angel I am engag'd,

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: It shall be.
For I am truely confident yee are honest:
The Piece is scarce worth looking on.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Trust me
The abstract of all beauty, soule of sweetnesse,
Defend me honest thoughts, I shall grow wilde else:
What eyes are there, rather what little heavens,
To stirre mens contemplations? what a Paradice
Runs through each part she has? good bloud be temperate:
I must look off: too excellent an object
Confounds the sense that sees it Noble Lady,
If there be any further service to cast on me,
Let it be worth my life, so much I honour ye,
Or the engagement of whole Families.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: Your service is too liberall, worthy sir,
Thus farre I shall entreat.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Command me Lady.
You make your power too poore.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: That presently
With all convenient haste, you would retire
Unto the street you found me in.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis done.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: There, if you finde a gentleman opprest
With force and violence, doe a mans office,
And draw your sword to rescue him.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Hee's safe,
Be what he will, and let his foes be devills,
Arm'd with your pitty, I shall conjure 'em.
Retire, this key will guide ye: all things necessary
Are there before ye.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: All my prayers goe with ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ye clap on proof upon me: men say gold
Do's all, engages all, works through all dangers:
Now I say beauty can do more: The Kings Exchequer,
Nor all his wealthy Indies, could not draw me
Through halfe those miseries this peece of pleasure
Might make me leap into: we are all like sea-Cards,
All our endeavours and our motions,
(As they doe to the North) still point at beauty,
Still at the fairest: for a handsome woman,
(Setting my soule a side) it should goe hard,
But I would straine my body: yet to her,
Unlesse it be her owne free gratitude,
Hopes ye shall dye, and thou tongue rot within me,
E're I infringe my faith: now to my rescue.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: YOu will not all oppresse me?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Kill him ith' wanton eye: let me come to him.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Then yee shall buy me dearely.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Say you so sir?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I say cut his Wezand spoile his peeping.
Have at your love-sick heart sir.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: Sure 'tis fighting.
My friend may be engag'd: fie gentlemen,
This is unmanly oddes.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: Ile stop your mouth sir.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: Nay, then have at thee freely:
Ther's a plumb sir to satisfie your longing.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Away: I hope I have sped him: here comes rescue.
We shall be endangered: where's Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I must have one thrust more sir.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Come up to me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: A mischiefe confound your fingers.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: How is't?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Well:
Ha's giv'n me my quiet us est, I felt him
In my small guts, I'me sure, has feez'd me:
This comes of siding with ye.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Can you goe sir?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I should goe man, and my head were of,
Never talke of going.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Come, all shall be well then.
I heare more rescue comming.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let's turne back then;
My skull's uncloven yet, let me but kill.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Away for heaven sake with him.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: How is't?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Well sir,
Onely a little stagger'd.

speeches.speaker: Faction Du.
verse: Lets pursue 'em.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No not a man, I charge ye: thanks good coat,
Thou hast sav'd me a shrewd welcome: 't was put home too,
With a good minde I'me sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Are ye safe then?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: My thanks to you brave sir, whose timely valour,
And manly courtesie came to my rescue,

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Ye' had foule play offer'd ye, and shame befall him
That can passe by oppression.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: May I crave sir,
But thus much honour more, to know your name?
And him I am so bound to?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: For the Bond sir,
'Tis every good mans tye: to know me further
Will little profit ye; I am a stranger,
My Countrey Spaine; my name Don Iohn, a gentleman
That lyes here for my study.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I have heard sir,
Much worthy mention of ye, yet I finde
Fame short of what ye are.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: You are pleas'd sir,
To expresse your courtesie: may I demand
As freely what you are, and what mischance
Cast you into this danger?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: For this present
I must desire your pardon: you shall know me
Ere it be long sir, and a nobler thanks,
Then now my will can render.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Your will's your owne sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What is't you look for sir, have yee lost any thing?

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Onely my hat i'th scuffle; sure these fellowes
Were night-snaps.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No, believe sir: pray ye use mine,
For 'twil be hard to finde your owne now.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: No sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Indeed ye shall, I can command another:
I doe beseech ye honour me.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: I will sir,
And so Ile take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Within these few dayes
I hope I shall be happy in your knowledge.
Till when I love your memory.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: I yours.
This is some noble fellow.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis his tongue sure.
Don Iohn?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Don Fredrick?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ye' are fairely met sir:
I thought ye had been a Bat-fowling: prethee tell me,
What Revelations hast thou had to night,
That home was never thought of?

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Revelations?
Ile tell thee Fredrick. but before I tell thee,
Settle thy understanding.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis prepar'd, sir.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Why then mark what shall follow. This night Fredr.
This bawdy night.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I thought no lesse.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: This blinde night,
What dost think I have got?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: The Pox it may be.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Would 'twere no worse: ye talke of Revelations,
I have got a Revelation will reveale me,
An arrant Coxcombe while I live.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What is't?
Thou hast lost nothing?

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: No, I have got I tell thee.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: What hast thou got?

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: One of the Infantry, a childe.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: A chopping child, man.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Give ye joy, sir.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: A lump of lewdnesse Fredrick, that's the truth on't:
This Town's abominable.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: I still told ye Iohn
Your whoring must come home; I counsell'd ye:
But where no grace is—

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: 'Tis none o'mine, man.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Answer the Parish so.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Cheated introth.
Peeping into a house, by whom I know not,
Nor where to find the place agen: no Fredricke,
Had I but kist the ring fort; 'tis no poor one,
That's my best comfort, for't has brought about it
Enough to make it man.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Where is't?

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: At home.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: A saving voyage: But what will you say Signior,
To him that searching out your serious Worship,
Has met a stranger fortune?

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: How, good Frederick?
A militant girle now to this boy would hit it?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No, mine's a nobler venture: What do you think Sir
Of a distressed Lady, one whose beauty
Would oversell all Italy?

speeches.speaker: Joh,
verse: Where is she—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: A woman of that rare behaviour,
So qualified, as admiration
Dwels round about her: of that perfect spirit—

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: I marry Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: That admirable carriage,
That sweetnes in discourse; young as the morning,
Her blushes staining his.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: But where's this Creature?
Shew me but that.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: That's all one, shee's forth comming,
I have her sure Boy.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Harke ye Fredrick.
What truck betwixt my Infant?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis too light Sir,
Stick to your charges good Don John, I am well.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: But is there such a wench?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: First tell me this,
Did ye not lately as ye walk'd along,
Discover people that were arm'd, and likely
To doe offence?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Yes mary, and they urg'd it
As far as they had spirit.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Pray goe forward.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: A Gentleman I found ingag'd amongst e'm,
It seemes of noble breeding, I'm sure brave mettall,
As I return'd to looke you, I set in to him,
And without hurt (I thanke heaven) rescued him,
And came my selfe off safe too.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: My work's done then:
And now to satisfie you, there is a woman,
Oh Iohn, there is a woman—

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Oh, where is she?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And one of no lesse worth then I assure ye;
And which is more, falne under my protection.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
prose: I am glad of that: forward sweet Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And which is more then that, by this nights wandring,
And which is most of all, she is at home too Sir.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Come, lets be gone then.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes, but 'tis most certaine,
You cannot see her, Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She has sworne me
That none else shall come neare her: not my Mother
Till some few doubts are clear'd.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Not look upon her? What chamber is she in?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: In ours.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Let's goe I say:
A womans oathes are wafers, breake with making,
They must for modestie a litle: we all know it.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No, I'le assure you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Not see her?
I smell an old dog trick of yours, well Fredrick,
Ye talkt to me of whoring, let's have faire play,
Square dealing I would wish ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: When 'tis come.
Which I know never will be, to that issue,
Your spoone shall be as deep as mine Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Tell me,
And tell me true, is the cause honourable,
Or for your ease?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: By all our friendship, Iohn,
'Tis honest, and of great end.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: I am answer'd:
But let me see her though: leave the doore open
As yee goe in.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Not wide open,
But just so, as a jealous husband
Would levell at his wanton wife through.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: That courtesie,
If ye desire no more, and keep it strictly,
I dare afford yee: come, 'tis now neare morning.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Nay the old woman's gone too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Shee's a Catterwauling
Among the gutters: But conceive me, Peter,
Where our good Masters should be?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Where they should be,
I doe conceive, but where they are, good Anthony—

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I, there it goes: my Masters bo-peep with me,
With his slye popping in and out agen,
Argued a cause, a frippery cause.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Beleeve me,
They bear up with some carvell.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I doe believe thee,
For thou hast such a Master for that chase,
That till he spend his maine Mast—

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Pray remember
Your courtesie good Anthony; and withall,
How long 'tis since your Master sprung a leak,
He had a sound one since he came.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Harke.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Doest not hear a Lute?
Agen?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Where is't?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Above in my Masters chamber.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: There's no creature: he hath the key himself man.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: This is his Lute: let him have it.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I grant you; but who strikes it?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: An admirable voice too, harke ye.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Anthony,
Art sure we are at home?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Without all doubt, Peter.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Then this must be the Devill.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let it be.
Good Devill sing againe: O dainty devill,
Peter beleve it, a most delicate devill,
The sweetest Devill—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: If ye could leave peeping.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I cannot by no meanes.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Then come in softly,
And as ye love your faith, presume no further
Then yee have promised.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Basto.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: What make you up so early sir?

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: You sir in your contemplations.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: O pray ye peace sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why peace sir?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Doe you heare?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: 'Tis your Lute.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Pray yee speak softly.
She's playing on't.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: The house is haunted sir,
For this we have heard this halfe yeare.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ye saw nothing;

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Not I.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Nor I Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Get us our breakfast then,
And make no words on't; wee'll undertake this spirit,
If it be one.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: This is no devill Peter.
Mum, there be Bats abroad.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Stay, now she sings.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: An Angels voice Ile sweare.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why did'st thou shrug so?
Either allay this heat; or as I live
I will not trust ye.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Passe: I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: To curse those starres, that men say governe us,
To raile at fortune, fall out with my Fate,
And taske the generall world, will helpe me nothing:
Alas, I am the same still, neither are they
Subject to helpes, or hurts: Our owne desires
Are our owne fates, our owne stars, all our fortunes,
Which as we sway 'em, so abuse, or blesse us.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Peace to your meditations.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Pox upon ye,
Stand out oth' light.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: I crave your mercy sir,
My minde o're-charg'd with care made me unmannerly.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Pray yee set that minde at rest, all shall be perfect.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: I like the body rare; a handsome body,
A wondrous handsome body: would she would turne:
See, and that spightfull puppy be not got
Between me and my light againe,

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Tis done,
As all that you command shall bee: the gentleman
Is safely off all danger.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: O de dios.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: How shall I thank ye sir? how satisfie?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Speak softly, gentle Lady, all's rewarded,
Now does he melt like Marmalad.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Nay, 'tis certaine,
Thou art the sweetest woman I e're look'd on:
I hope thou art not honest.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: None disturb'd yee?

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: Not any sir, nor any sound came neare me,
I thank your care.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: I would faine pray now,
But the Devill and that flesh there, o' the world,
What are we made to suffer?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Hee'll enter;
Pull in your head and be hang'd.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Harke ye Fredricke,
I have brought ye home your Pack-saddle.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Pox upon yee.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Nay let him enter: fie my Lord the Duke,
Stand peeping at your friends.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Ye are cozen'd Lady,
Here is no Duke.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: I know him full well Signior.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Hold thee there wench.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: This mad-brain'd foole will spoile all.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I doe beseech your grace come in.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: My Grace,
There was a word of comfort.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Shall he enter,
Who e're he be?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Well follow'd Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: With all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Come in then.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: 'Blesse yee Lady:

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Nay start not, though he be a stranger to ye,
Hee's of a Noble straine, my kinsman, Lady,
My Countrey-man, and fellow Traveller,
One bed containes us ever, one purse feeds us,
And one faith free between us; do not fear him,
Hee's truely honest.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: That's a lye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And trusty:
Beyond your wishes: valiant to defend,
And modest to converse with, as your blushes.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Now may I hang my self; this commendation
Has broke the neck of all my hopes: for now
Must I cry, no forsooth, and I forsooth, and surely,
And truely as I live,, and as I am honest.
Has done these things for 'nonce too; for hee knowes,
Like a most envious Rascall as he is,
I am not honest, nor desire to be,
Especially this way: h'as watch'd his time,
But I shall quit him.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: Sir, I credit ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Goe kisse her John.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Plague o' your commendations.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Sir, I shall now desire to be a trouble.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Never to me, sweet Lady: Thus I seale
My faith, and all my service.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: One word Signeur.

speeches.speaker: Jo.
verse: Now 'tis impossible I should be honest,
She kisses with a conjuration
Would make the devill dance: what points she at?
My leg I warrant, or my well knit body:
Sit fast Don Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Twas given him by that gentleman
You took such care of; his owne being lost ith' scuffle.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: With much joy may he weare it: 'tis a right one,
I can assure ye Gentleman, and right happy
May you be in all fights for that faire service.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why doe ye blush?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: 'T had almost cozen'd me,
For not to lye, when I saw that, I look'd for
Another Master of it: but 'tis well.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Who's there?
Stand ye a little close: Come in Sir,
Now what's the newes with you?

speeches.speaker: Anth.
verse: There is a gentlemen without,
Would speak with Don John,

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Who sir?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I do not know Sir, but he shews a man
Of no meane reckoning.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Let him shew his name,
And then returne a little wiser.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: How doe you like her Iohn?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: As well as you Fredrick,
For all I am honest: you shall finde it so too.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Art thou not honest?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Art thou an Asse?
And modest as her blushes? What a block-head
Would e're have popt out such a dry Apologie,
For his deare friend? and to a Gentlewoman,
A woman of her youth, and delicacy.
They are arguments to draw them to abhorre us.
An honest morall man; 'tis for a Constable:
A handsome man, a wholsome man, a tough man,
A liberall man, a likely man, a man
Made up like Hercules, unslak'd with service:
The same to night, to morrow night, the next night,
And so to perpetuitie of pleasures,
These had been things to hearken too, things catching:
But you have such a spiced consideration,
Such qualmes upon your worships conscience,
Such-chil-blaines in your bloud, that all things pinch ye,
Which nature, and the liberall world makes custome,
And nothing but faire honour, O sweet honour,
Hang up your Eunuch honour: That I was trusty,
And valiant, were things well put in; but modest!
A modest gentleman I ô wit where wast thou?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I am sorrie John,

speeches.speaker: John
verse: My Ladies gentlewoman
Would laugh me to a Schoole-boy, make me blush
With playing with my Codpeece point: fie on thee,
A man of thy discretion?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: It shall be mended:
And henceforth yee shall have your due.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: I look fort: How now, who is't?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: A gentleman of this towne
And calls himselfe Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Ile attend him.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: How did he call himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Petruchio,
Doe's it concerne you ought?

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: O gentlemen,
The houre of my destruction is come on me,
I am discover'd, lost, left to my ruine:
As ever ye had pitty—

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Doe not feare,
Let the great devill come, he shall come through me:
Lost here, and we about ye?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Fall before us?

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: O my unfortunate estate, all angers
Compar'd to his, to his—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Let his, and all mens,
Whilst we have power and life: stand up for heaven sake.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I have offended heaven too; yet heaven knows—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: We are all evill:
Yet heaven forbid we should have our deserts.
What is a?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Too too neare to my offence sir;
O he will cut me peece-meale.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Tis no Treason?

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Let it be what it will: if a cut here,
Ile finde him cut-worke.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: He must buy you deare,
With more than common lives.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Feare not, nor weep not:
By heaven Ile fire the Towne before yee perish,
And then, the more the merrier, wee'll jog with yee.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Come in, and dry your eyes.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Pray no more weeping:
Spoile a sweet face for nothing? my returne
Shall end all this I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Heaven grant it.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: This man should be of speciall rank:
For these commends carry no common way,
No slight worth with 'em:
A shall be he.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: 'Save yee sir: I am sorrie
My businesse was so unmannerly, to make ye
Wait thus long here.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Occasions must be serv'd sir:
But is your name Don John?

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: It is Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Then,
First, for your owne brave sake I must embrace yee:
Next, from the credit of your noble friend
Hernando de Aluara, make yee mine:
Who layes his charge upon me in this Letter
To look yee out, and for the goodnesse in yee,
Whilst your occasions make yee resident
In this place, to supply yee, love and honour yee;
Which had I knowne sooner—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Noble sir,
You'll make my thanks too poore: I weare a sword, sir,
And have a service to be still dispos'd of,
As you shall please command it.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Gentle sir,
That manly courtesie is half my businesse:
And to be short, to make ye know I honour ye,
And in all points believe your worth like Oracle,
And how above my friends, which are not few,
And those not slack, I estimate your vertues,
Make your selfe understand, This day Petruchio,
A man that may command the strength of this place,
Hazzard the boldest spirits; hath made choice
Onely of you, and in a noble office.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Forward, I am free to entertaine it.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Thus then:
I doe beseech ye mark me.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: I shall doe it.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Ferrara's Duke, would I might call him wort hie,
But that he has raz'd out from his family,
As he has mine with Infamie, This man,
Rather this powerfull Monster, we being left
But two of all our house, to stock out memories,
My Sister, and my selfe; with arts, and witch-crafts,
Vowes, and such oathes heaven has no mercy for,
Drew to dishonour this weak maid, by stealthes,
And secret passages I knew not of,
Oft he obtain'd his wishes, oft abus'd her:
I am asham'd to say the rest: This purchas'd,
And his hot bloud allay'd, as friends forsake us
At a miles end upon our way, he left her,
And all our name to ruine.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: This was foule Play,
And ought to be rewarded so.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: I hope so;
He scap'd me yester-night: which if he dare
Againe adventure for, heaven pardon him,
I shall with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: For me, brave Signior,
What doe yee intend?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Onely, faire sir, this trust,
Which from the commendations of this Letter,
I dare presume well placed, nobly to beare him
By word of mouth a single challenge from me,
That man to man, if he have honour in him,
We may decide all difference.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Faire, and noble,
And I will doe it home: When shall I visite ye?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Please you this after-noon, I will ride with yee:
For at a Castle six mile hence, we are sure
To finde him.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
verse: Ile be ready.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: To attend ye,
My man shall wait: with all my

speeches.speaker: John
verse: My service shall not faile yee.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: How now?

speeches.speaker: John
verse: All's well: who dost thou think this wench is?
Ghesse, and thou canst?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I cannot.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Be it knowne then,
To all men by these presents, this is she,
She, she, and only she, our curious coxcombs
Were errant two moneths after.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Who, Constantia?
Thou talk'st of Cocks and Bulls.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: I talke of wenches,
Of Cocks and Hens Don Frerdick; this is the Pullet
We two went proud after.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: It cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: It shall be;
Sister to Don Petruchio: I know all man.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Now I beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Goe to, there has been stirring,
Fumbling with Linnen Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis impossible,
You know her faine was pure as fire.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: That pure fire
Has melted out her maiden-head: she is crickt:
We have all that hope of our side, boy.

speeches.speaker: Fred,
verse: Thou tell'st me,
To my imagination, things incredible:
I see no loose thought in her.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: That's all one,
She is loose ith' hilts by heaven: but the world must know
A faire way, upon vow of marriage.
