speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: There may be such a slip.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: And will be Fredrick,
Whil'st the old game's a foot: I feare the boy too
Will prove hers too I took up.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Good circumstance
May cure all this yet.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: There thou hitst it, Fredrick:
Come, let's walke in and comfort her: her being here
Is nothing yet suspected: anon Ile tell thee
Wherefore her brother came, who by this light
Is a brave noble fellow, and what honour
H'as done to me a stranger: there be Irons
Heating for some, will histe into their heart blouds,
'Ere all be ended; so much for this time.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Well sir

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: CCome ye doe know.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I do not by this hand Mistris.
But I suspect.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: That if egges continue
At this price, women wil ne're be sav'd
By their good works.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: I will know.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Yee shall, any thing
Lyes in my power: The Duke of Loraine now
Is seven thousand strong: I heard it of a fish-wife,
A woman of fine knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Sirrah, sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Pe.
verse: The Popes Buls are broke loose too and 'tis suspected
They shall be baited in England.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Very well sir.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: No, 'tis not so well neither.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: But I say to yee,
Who is it keeps your Master company?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I say to you, Don Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: I say what woman?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I say so too.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: I say againe, I will know.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I say 'tis fit yee should.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: And I tell thee
He has a woman here.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: And I tell thee
'Tis then the better for him.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: You are no Bawd now?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Would I were able to be call'd unto it:
A worshipfull vocation for my elders;
For as I understand it is a place
Fitting my betters farr.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Was ever Gentlewoman
So frumpt off with a foole? well sawcy sirrah,
I will know who it is, and for what purpose;
I pay the rent, and I will know how my house
Comes by these Inflamations: if this geere hold,
Best hang a signe-post up, to tell the Signiors,
Here ye may have lewdnesse at Liverie.

speeches.speaker: Pet,
verse: 'Twould be a great ease to your age.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: How now?
Why what's the mater Land-lady?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: What's the matter?
Ye use me decently among ye gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Who has abus'd her, you sir?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: 'Ods my witnesse
I will not be thus treated, that I will not.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I gave her no ill language.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Thou lyest lewdly,
Thou tookst me up at every word I spoke,
As I had been a Mawkin, a flurt Gillian;
And thou thinkst, because thou canst write & read,
Our noses must be under thee.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Dare you sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Let but the truth be known Sir, I beseech ye,
She raves of wenches, and I know not what sir:

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Go to, thou know'st too well, thou wicked varlet,
Thou instrument of evill.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: As I live Sir,
She is ever thus till dinner.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Get ye in,
Ile answer you anon sir.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: By this hand
Ile break your Possit pan.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Then by this hood
Ile lock the meat up.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Now your grief, what is't?
For I can ghesse—

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Ye may with shame enough,
If theer were shame amongst yee; nothing thought on,
But how yee may abuse my house: not satisfi'd
With bringing home your Bastards to undoe me,
But you must drill your whores here too; my patience
Because I beare, and beare, and carry, all,
And as they say am willing to groan under)
Must be your make-sport now.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No more of these words.
Nor no more murmurings Lady: for you know
That I know something. I did suspect your anger,
But turne it presently and handsomely,
And beare your selfe discreetly to this woman,
For such a one there is indeed.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: 'Tis well sonne.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Leaving your devils Matins, and your melanchollies,
Or we shall leave our lodgings.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: You have much need
To use these vagrant wayes, and to much profit:
Ye had that might content
(At home within your selves too) right good gentlemen,
Wholsome, and yee said handsome: But you gallants,
Boast that I was to beleeve ye—

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Leave your suspicion:
For as I live there's no such thing.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Mine honour;
And 'twere not for mine honour.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: Come, your honour,
Your house, and you too, if you dare beleeve me
Are well enough: sleek up your self, leave crying,
For I must have yee entertain this Lady
With all civility, she well deserves it,
Together with all secresie: I dare trust yee,
For I have found ye faithfull: when you know her
You will find your owne fault; no more words, but doe it.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: You know you may command me.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: Worshipfull Lady,
How does thy Velvet scabbard? by this hand
Thou look'st most amiably: now could I willingly
And 'twere not for abusing thy Geneva print there,
Venture my body with thee.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: You'll leave this roperie,
When you come to my yeares.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: By this light
Thou art not above fifteen yet, a meere girle,
Thou hast not half thy teeth: come—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Prethee Iohn
Let her alone, she has been vex'd already:
Shee'll grow starke mad man.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: I would see her mad,
An old mad woman

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Prethee be patient.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Is like a Millers Mare, troubled with tooth-ache.
Shee'll make the rarest faces.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Goe, and doe it,
And doe not mind this fellow.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Well Don John.
There will be times agen; when O good Mother,
What's good for a carnosity in the Bladder?
O the green water, mother.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: Doting take yee,
Doe ye remember that?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: She has payd ye now sir.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Clarry, sweet mother, Clarry.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Are ye satisfied?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Ile never whore againe; never give Petticoats
And Wastcoats at five pound a peece; good Mother,
Quickly Mother: now mock on Son.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: A devill grinde your old chaps.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: By this hand wench
Ile give thee a new hood for this.
Has she met with your Lordship?
Touch-wood rake her.
Shee's a rare ghostly mother.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Below attends yee
The Gentlemans man sir that was with yee.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: Well Sir;
My time is come then: yet if my project hold,
You shall not stay behinde: Ile rather trust.
A Cat with sweet milk Fredrick; by her face
I feele her feares are working.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: Is there no way,
I doe beseech yee think yet, to divert
This certaine danger?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
verse: 'Tis impossible:
Their honours are engag'd.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Then there must be murther,
Which, Gentlemen, I shall no sooner heare of,
Then make one int: you may, if you please sir,
Make all goe lesse yet.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: Lady wer't mine owne cause,
I could dispence: but loaden with my friends trust,
I must go on; though generall massacres
As much I feare—

speeches.speaker: Const,
verse: Doe ye heare sir; for heavens pittie
Let me request one love of you.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes any thing.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: This gentleman I find too resolute,
Too hot, and fiery for the cause, as ever
You did a vertuous deed, for honours sake
Go with him, and allay him: your fair temper
And noble disposition, like wish'd showres,
May quench those eating fires, that would spoile all else.
I see in him destruction.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I will doe it;
And 'tis a wise consideration,
To me, a bounteous favour: harke ye John,
I will goe with yee.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Indeed I will,
Ye goe upon a hazard: no denyall;
For as I live, Ile goe.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: Then make ye ready,
For I am straight a horse-back.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: My sword on,
I am as ready as you: what my best labour,
With all the Art I have can work upon 'em,
Be sure of, and expect faire end: the old gentlewoman
Shall wait upon you; she is both grave and private,
And yee may trust her in all points.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: Ye are noble:
And so I kisse your hand.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: That seale for me too,
And I hope happy issue Lady.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: All heavens care upon yee, and my prayers.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: So,
Now my mind's at rest.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Away, 'tis late John.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Come sir. be hearty: all the worst is past.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Give me some Wine.

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: 'Tis death Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis a horse sir.
'Sbloud, to be drest to the tune of Ale onely,
Nothing but sawces to my sores.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gen.
verse: Fie Antonio,
You must be govern'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Has given me a dam'd Glister,
Only of sand and snow water, gentlemen,
Has almost scour'd my guts out.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: I have giv'n you that sir
Is fittest for your state.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And here he feeds me
With rotten ends of rooks, and drown'd chickens,
Stewd Pericraniums, and Pia-maters;
And when I goe to bed, by heaven 'tis true gentlemen,
He rolls me up in Lints, with Labels at 'em,
That I am just the man ith' Almanack,
In head and face, is Aries place.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Wilt please ye
To let your friends see ye open'd?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Will it please you sir
To let me have a wench: I feele my body
Open enough for that yet?

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: How, a wench?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Why look yee gentlemen; thus I am us'd still,
I can get nothing that I want.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Leave these things,
And let him open ye.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: De'ye heare Surgeon?
Send for the Musick, let me have some pleasure
To entertaine my friends, beside your Sallads,
Your green salves, and your searches, and some wine too,
That I may onely smell to it: or by this light
Ile dye upon thy hand, and spoyle thy custome.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Let him have Musick.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: 'Tis ith' house, and ready,
If he will aske no more: but wine—

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: He shall not drink it.

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: Will these things please yee?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes, and let 'em sing
John Dorrie.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: 'Tis too long.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ile have John Dorrie,
For to that warlike tune I will be open'd.
Give me some drinke, have yee stopt the leakes well Surgeon,
All will runne out else?

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Feare not.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sit downe Gentlemen:
And now advance your plaisters.
Give 'em ten shillings friends: how doe ye finde me?
What Symptomes doe you see now?

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: None Sir, dangerous:
But if you will be rul'd—

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What time?

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: I can cure ye
In forty dayes, so you will not transgresse me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I have a dog shall lick me whole in twenty:
In how long canst thou kill me?

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Presently.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Doe it; there's more delight in't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: You must have patience.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Man, I must have busines; this foolish fellow
Hinders himselfe: I have a dozen Rascalls
To hurt within these five dayes: good man mender,
Stop me up with Parsley, like stuft Beefe,
And let me walke abroad.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Ye shall walke shortly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: For I must finde Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
verse: Time enough.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Come lead him in, and let him sleep: within these three dayes
Wee'll beg yee leave to play.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: And then how things fall,
Wee'll certainly informe yee.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: But Surgion promise me
I shall drinke Wine then too.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: A little temper'd.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nay, Ile no tempering Surgion,

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: Well, as't please ye,
So ye exceed not.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Farewell: and if ye finde
The Mad slave, that thus slasht me, commend me to him,
And bid him keep his skin close.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Take your rest sir.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I have told yee all I can, and more then yet
Those Gentlemen know of me; ever trusting
Your Councell and concealement: for to me
You seem a worthy woman; one of those
Are seldome found in our sex, wise and vertuous,
Direct me I beseech ye.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Ye say well Lady,
And hold yee to that poynt; for in these businesses
A womans councell that conceives the matter,
(Doe ye marke me, that conceives the matter Lady)
Is worth ten mens engagements: She knows something'
And out of that can worke like wax: when men
Are giddy-headed, either out of wine,
Or a more drunkennesse, vaine ostentation,
Discovering all: there is no more keep in 'em,
Then hold upon an Eeles taile: nay 'tis held fashion
To defame now all they can.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I, but these gentlemen—

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Doe not you trust to that: these gentlemen
Are as all Gentlemen of the same Barrell:
I, and the selfe same pickle too. Be it granted,
They have us'd yee with respect and faire behaviour,
Yet since ye came: doe you know what must follow?
They are Spaniards, Lady, Gennets of high mettle,
Things that will thrash the devill, or his dam,
Let 'em appeare but cloven.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Now heaven blesse me.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Mad Colts will court the wind: I know 'em Lady
To the least haire they have; and I tell you,
Old is I am, let but the pinte pot blesse 'em,
They'll offer to my yeares—

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Such rude gambolls—

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: To you?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: I, and so handle me, that oft I am forc'd
To fight of all foure for my safety: there's the yonger,
Don John, the arrantst Jack in all this City:
The other, time has blasted, yet he will stoop,
If not ore-flowne, and freely on the quarry;
Has been a Dragon in his dayes. Bur Tarmont,
Don Jenkin is the Devill himselfe, the Dog-dayes,
The most incomprehensible whore-master,
Twenty a night is nothing: Beggers, Broom-women,
And those so miserable, they look like famine,
Are all sweet Ladies in his drink.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: He's a handsome Gentleman.
Pitty he should be master of such follies.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Hee's ne're without a noise of Sirrenges
In's pocket, those proclame him; birding pills,
Waters to coole his conscience, in small Viols;
With thousand such sufficient emblemes: the truth is,
Whose chastily he chops upon, he cares not.
He flies at all; Bastards upon my conscience,
He has now in making multitudes; The last night
He brought home one; I pitty her that bore it,
But we are all weake vessels, some rich woman
(For wise I dare not call her) was the mother,
For it was hung with Jewels: the bearing cloath
No lesse then Crimson Velvet.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: 'Tis true Lady.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Was it a Boy too?

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: A brave Boy; deliberation
And judgement shewd in's getting, as I'le say for him,
He's as well paced for that sport—

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: May I see it?
For there is a neighbour of mine, a Gentlewoman,
Has had a late mischance, which willingly
I would know further of; now if you please
To be so curteous to me.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Ye shall see it:
But what do ye thinke of these men now ye know 'em,
And of the cause I told ye of? Be wise,
Ye may repent too late else; I but tell ye
For your owne good, and as you will find it Lady.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I am advis'd.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: No more words then; do that,
And instantly, I told ye of be ready:
Don Iohn, I'le fit ye for your frumps,

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I shall be:
But shall I see this Child?

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Within this halfe houre,
Let's in, and there thinke better; she that's wise,
Leapes at occasion first; the rest pay for it.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Sir, he is worth your knowledg; and a Gentleman
If I that so much love him, may commend him,
Of free and vertuous parts; and one, if soule play
Should fall upon us, for which feare I brought him,
Will not flie backe for phillips.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Ye much honour me,
And once more I pronounce ye both mine.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Stay, what Troope
Is that below i'th valley there?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Hawking I take ir.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: They are so; 'tis the Duke, 'tis even he Gentlemen,
Sirrah, draw backe the Horses till we call ye,
I know him by his company.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I thinke too
He bends up this way.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: So he does.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Stand you still
Within that Covert till I call: you Fredrick,
By no meanes be not seen, unlesse they offer
To bring on odds upon us; he comes forward,
Here will I waite him fairely: to your Cabins.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I need no more instruct ye?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Feare me not,
I'le give it him, and boldly.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Feed the Hawkes up,
Wee'l flie no more to day: O my blest fortune,
Have I so fairely met the man!

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Ye have Sir,
And him you know by this,

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Sir all the honour,
And love—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I do beseech your Grace stay there,
(For I know you too now) that love and honour
I come not to receive; nor can you give it,
Till ye appeare faire to the world; I must beseech ye
Dismisse your traine a little.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Walke aside,
And out of hearing I command ye: Now Sir,

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Last time we met, I was a friend.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: And Nobly
You did a friends office: let your businesse
Be what it may, you must be still—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Your pardon,
Never a friend to him, cannot be friend
To his own honour.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: In what have I transgress'd it?
Ye make a bold breach at the first Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Bolder,
You made that breach that let in infamy
And ruine, to surprize a noble stocke.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Be plaine Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I will, and short;
Ye have wrong'd a Gentleman
Little behind your selfe, beyond all justice,
Beyond mediation of all friends.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: The man, and manner of wrong?
Iohn Petruchio,
The wrong, ye have whord his Sister.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: What's his will in't?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: His will is to oppose you like a Gentleman,
And single, to decide all.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Now stay you Sir,
And heare me with the like beliefe: this Gentleman
His Sister that you named, 'tis true I have long loved,
Nor was that love lascivious, as he makes it;
As true, I have enjoy'd her: no lesse truth
I have a child by her: But that she, or he,
Or any of that family are tainted
Suffer disgrace, or ruine, by my pleasures,
I weare a Sword to satisfie the world no,
And him in this cause when he please; for know Sir,
She is my wife, contracted before Heaven,
(Witnesse I owe more tye to, then her Brother)
Nor will I flye from that name, vvhich long since
Had had the Churches approbation,
But for his jealous danger.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Sir, your pardon,
And all that was my anger, now my service.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Faire sir, I knew I should convert ye; had we
But that rough man herd now too—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: And ye shall Sir
Whoa, hoa, hoo.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: I hope ye have laid no Ambush?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Only friends.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: My noble Brother welcome:
Come put your Anger off, we'l have no fighting,
Unlesse you will maintaine I am unworthy
To beare that name.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Do you speake this hartely?

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: upon my soule, and truly; the first Priest
Shall put you out of these doubts.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Now I love ye;
And I beseech you pardon my suspitions,
You are now more then a Brother, a brave friend too.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: The good man's over-joyd

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: How now, how goes it?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Why, the man 'has his mare agen, and all's well Fredrick,
The Duke professes freely hee's her husband.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis a good hearing.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Yes, for modest Gentlemen.
I must present ye: may it please your Grace
To number this brave Gentleman, my friend
And noble kinsman, amongst those your servants.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: O my brave friend! you showre your bounties on me
Amongst my best thoughts Signior, in which number
You being worthily dispos'd already,
May place your friend to honour me.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: My love sir,
And where your Grace dares trust me, all my service.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why? this is wondrcus happy: But now Brother,
Now comes the bitter to our sweet: Constantia.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Why, what of her?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Nor what, nor where, do I know?
Wing'd with her feares last night, beyond my knowledge,
She quit my house, but whether—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Let not that—

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: No more good Sir, I have heard too much.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Nay sinke not,
She cannot be so lost.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Nor shall not Gentlemen;
Be free agen, the Ladie's found; that smile Sir,
Shewes ye distruct your Servant.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: I do beseech ye.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Ye shall beleeve me: by my soule she is safe.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Heaven knows, I would beleeve Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ye may safely.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: And under noble usage: this faire Gentleman
Met her in all her doubts last night, and to his guard
(Her feares being strong upon her) she gave her person,
who waited on her, to our lodging; where all respect,
Civill and honest service now attend her.

speeches.speaker: Pet
verse: Ye may beleeve now.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Yes, I do, and strongly:
Well my good friends, or rather my good Angels,
For ye have both preserved me; when these vertues
Dye in your friends remembrance—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Good your grace
Lose no more time in complement, 'tis too pretious,
I know it by my selfe, there can be no hell
To his that hangs upon his hopes; especially
In way of lustly pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: He has hit it.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: To horse againe then, for this night I'le crowne
With all the joyes ye wish for.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Happy Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: This is the maddest mischiefe: never foole
Was so fubd off, as I am; made ridiculous,
And to my selfe, mine owne Asse: trust a woman,
I'le trust the Devill first; for he dare be
Better then's word sometime: what faith have I broke?
In what observance failed? Let me consider,
For this is monstrous usage.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Let them talke,
Wee'll ride on faire and softly.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Well Constantia,

speeches.speaker: Fred.
prose: Constantia, what's this fellow? stay by all means.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Ye have spun your selfe a faire thred now.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Stand still Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: What cause had you to fly? what feare possest ye?
Were you not safely lodg'd from all suspition?
Us'd with all gentle meanes? did any know
How ye came thether, or what your sin was.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Iohn.
smell some juggling John.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Yes, Fredricks, I feare it will be found so.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: So strangely,
Without the counsell of your friends; so desperatly
To put all dangers on ye?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis she.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: So deceitfully
After a strangers lure?

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Did ye marke that Fredrick?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: To make ye appeare more monster; and the Law
More cruell to reward ye? to leave all,
All that should be your safegard, to seeke evils?
Was this your wisedome? this your promise? well
He that incited ye—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Marke that too.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: 'Had better have plough'd farther off; now Lady,
What will your last friend, he that should preserve ye,
And hold your credit up, the brave Antonio,
Thinke of this slip? he'll to Petruchio,
And call for open justice.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: 'Tis she Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: But what that he is John.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: I do not doubt yet
To bolt ye out, for I know certainly
Ye are about the Towne still: ha, no more words.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Very well.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Discreetly.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Finely carried.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You have no more of these tricks?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Ten to one Sir,
I shall meet with 'em if ye have.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Is this honest?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Was it in you a friends part to deale double?
I am no asse Don Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And Don Iohn,
It shall appeare I am no foole;
Disgrace me to make yourselfe a lecher?
'Tis boyish, 'tis base.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: 'Tis false, and most unmanly to upbraid me,
Nor will I be your boister Sir,

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Thou wanton boy, thou hadst better have been Eunuch,
Thou common womans curtesie, then thus
Lascivious, basely to have bent mine honour.
A friend? I'le make a horse my friend first!

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Holla, holla,
Ye kicke to fast sir: what strange braines have you got,
That dare crow out thus bravely? I better been a Eunuch?
I privy to this dog tricke? cleare your selfe,
For I know where the wind sits, and most nobly,
Or as I have a life—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No more: they'r horses.
Nor shew no discontent: to morrow comes;
Let's quietly away: if she be at home,
Our jealousies are put off.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: The fellow
We have lost him in our spleenes, like fooles.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Come Gentlemen,
Now set on roundly; suppose ye have all mistresses,
And mend your pace according,

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Then have at ye.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: NOw to Bollonia, my most honoured brother,
I dare pronounce yea hearty, and safe welcome,
Our loves shall now way-lay ye; welcome Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: The same to you brave Sir; Don Fredrick
Will ye step in, and give the Lady notice
Who comes to honour her?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Bid her be suddain,
We come to see no curious wench: a night-gowne
Will serve the turne: here's one that knowes her neerer.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I'le tell her what ye say Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: My deare brother,
Ye are a merry Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Now will the sport be
To observe her alterations; how like wildfire
She'll leap into your bosome; then seeing me,
Her conscience, and her feares creeping upon her
Dead as a fowle at souse, she'll sinke.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Faire brother,
I must entreat you—

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I conceive your mind Sir,
I will not chide her: yet ten duckets Duke,
She falls upon he knees, ten more she dare not—

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: I must not have her frighted.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Well you shall not:
But like a summers evening against heate,
Marke how I'le guild he cheekes?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: How now.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ye may Sir:
Not to abuse your patience, noble friends,
Nor hold ye off with tedious circumstance,
For you must know,—

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Where is she?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Gone Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: What did you say Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Gone, by heaven removed,
The woman of the house too.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Well Don Fredrick.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Don Iohn, it is not well, but—

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Gone?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: This fellow
Can testifie I lye not.

speeches.speaker: Peter
verse: Some foure houres after
My Master was departed with this Gentleman,
My fellow and my selfe, being sent of businesse,
(As we must thinke) of purpose—

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Hang these circumstances,
They appeare like owles, to ill ends.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Now could I eate
The devil in his own broath, I am so tortur'd.
Gone?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Gone?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
prose: Directly gone, fled, shifted: what would you have me say?

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Well Gentlemen,
Wrong not my good opinion.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: For your Dukedome
I will not be a knave Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: He that is
A rot run in his bloud.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: But harke ye Gentlemen,
Are ye sure ye had her here, did ye not dreame this.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Have you your nose Sir?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Then we had her.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Since you are so short, beleeve your having her
Shall suffer more construction.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Let it suffer,
But if I be not cleere of all dishonour,
Or practice that may taint my reputation,
And ignorant of where this woman is,
Make me your Cities monster.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: I beleeve ye.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: I could lye with a witch now, to be reveng'd
Upon that Rascall did this.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Only thus much
I would desire your Grace, for my minde gives me
Before night yet she is yours: stop all opinion,
And let no anger out, till full cause call it,
Then every mans owne work's to justifie him,
And this day let us give to search: my man here
Tels me, by chance he saw out of a window
(Which place he has taken note of) such a face
As our old Landladies, he beleeves the same too,
And by her hood assures it: Let's first thether,
For she being found, all's ended.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Come, for heavens sake,
And Fortune, and thou beest not ever turning,
If there be one firme step in all thy reelings,
Now settle it, and save my hopes: away friends.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: With all my jewels?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: All Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And that money
I left i'th' trunke?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The Trunke broke, and that gone too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Franscisco of the plot?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Gone with the wench too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: The mighty poxe go with 'em: belike they thought
I was no man of this world, and those trifles
Would but disturbe my conscience.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Sure they thought Sir,
You would not live to persecute 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Whore and Fidler,
Why, what a consort have they made? Hen and bacon?
Well my sweet Mistris, well good Madam martaile?
You that have hung about my neck, and lick't me,
I'le try how handsomely your Ladyship
Can hang upon a Gallowes, there's your Master-piece;
But harke ye Sirrah, no imagition
Of where they should be?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: None Sir, yet we have search'd
All places we suspected; I beleeve Sir,
They have taken towards the Ports.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Get me a conjurer,
One that can raise a water devill, I'le port 'em;
Play at duck and drake with my money? take heed Fidler;
I'le dance ye by this hand, your Fidle-sticke
I'le grease of a new fashion, for presuming
To medle with my degamboys: get me a Conjurer,
Enquire me out a man that lets out devils:
None but my C. Cliffe serve your turne?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I know not—

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: In every street, Tom foole, any bleare-eyd people
With red heads, and flat noses can performe it;
Thou shalt know 'em by their half gowns & no breeches:
Mount my mare Fidler? ha boy? up at first dash?
Sit sure, I'le clap a nettle, and a smart one,
Shall make your filly firck: I will find Fidier,
I'le put you to your plundge boy: Sirrah meet me
Some two houres hence at home; In the meane time
Find out a conjurer and know his price,
How he will let his devils by the day out,
I'le have 'em, and they be above ground.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Now blesse me,
What a mad man is this? I must do something
To please his humour: such a man I'le aske for,
And tell him where he is: but to come neare him,
Or have any thing to do with his don devills,
I thanke my feare, I dare not, nor I will not.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Whether wilt thou lead us?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Tis hard by sir.
And ten to one this wine goes thether.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Forward.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Are they growne so merry.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: 'Tis most likely
She has heard of this good fortune, and determines
To wash her sorrowes off.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Tis so; that house sir
Is it: out of that window certainly
I saw my old Mistrisses face.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: They are merry indeed,
Harke I here Musicke too.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Excellent Musick.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Would I were ev'n among 'em and alone how,
A pallat for the purpose in a corner,
And good rich wine within me; what gay sport
Could I make in an houre now?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Harke a voice too;
Let's not stir yet by any meanes.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Was this her owne voyce?

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Yes sure.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis a rare one.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: The Song confirmes her here too: for if ye marke it,
It spake of liberty, and free enjoying
The happy end of pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Looke ye there sir,
Do ye know that head?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis my good Landlady,
I find feare has done all this.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Shee I sweare,
And now do I know by the hanging of her hood,
She is parcell drunke: shall we go in?

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Not yet Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: No, let 'em take their pleasure,

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: When it is highest,
Wee'll step in, and amaze 'em: peace more Musicke.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: This Musick murders me; what bloud have I now?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
prose: I should know that face.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: By this light 'tis he Fredricks,
That bred our first suspitions, the same fellow.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: He that we overtooke, and overheard too
Discoursing of Constantia.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Still the same;
Now he slips in.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She must be here Sir:
This is the very fellow, I told your Grace
We found upon the way; and what his talke was.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Why, sure I know this fellow; yes, 'tis he,
Francisco, Antonio's Boy, a rare Musitian,
He taught my Sister on the Lute, and is ever
(She loves his voice so well) about her: certaine,
Without all doubt she is here: it must be so.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Here? that's no question: what should our hen o'th game else
Do here without her? if she be not here
(I am so confident) let your Grace beleeve,
We two are arrant Rascalls, and have abus'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I say so too.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Why there's the hood againe now,
The guard that guides us; I know the fabricke of it.
And know the old tree of that saddle yet, 'twas made of
A hunting hood, observe it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Who shall enter?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: I'le make one.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: I, another.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: But so carry it,
That all her joyes flow not together.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: If we told her,
Your Grace would none of her?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: By no meanes Signior,
'Twould turne her wild, starke frantick.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Or assur'd her—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Nothing of that? starve nature? this ye may sir.
That the conditions of our feare yet stand
On nyce and dangerous knittings: or that a little
I seeme to doubt the child.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Would I could draw her
To hate your Grace with these things.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Come let's enter,
And now he sees me not, I'le search her soundly.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Now lucke of all sides.

speeches.speaker: Fred
verse: Doubt it not: more Musicke:
Sure she has heard some comfort.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Yes, stand still sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: This is the maddest song.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Applyed for certaine
To some strange mellancholly she is loden with.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Now all the sport begins—harke?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: They are amongst'em,
The feares now, and the shakings?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Our old Lady
(Harke how they run) is euen now at this instant
Ready to loose her head peice by Don Iohn,
Or creeping through a Cat hole.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Bring 'em downe,
And you sir, follow me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Hee's angry with 'em,
I must not suffer this.
Bowle downe the Bawd there
Old Erra mater: you Lady leachery
For the good will I beare to'th game, most tenderly
Shall be lead out, and lash'd.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Is this Constantia?
Why Gentlemen? what do you meane? is this she?

speeches.speaker: Whore
verse: I am Constantia sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A Whore ye are sir.

speeches.speaker: Whore
verse: 'Tis very true: I am a Whore indeed sir.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: She will not lye yet, though she steale.

speeches.speaker: Whore
verse: A plaine whore,
If you please to imploy me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And an impudent—

speeches.speaker: Whore
verse: Plaine dealing now is impudence.
One if you will sir, can shew ye as much sport
In one halfe houre, and with as much variety,
As a far wiser woman can in halfe a yeare:
For there my way lies.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Is she not drunk too?

speeches.speaker: Whore
verse: A little guilded o're sir,
Old sack, old sacke boyes.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: This is saliant.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: A brave bold queane.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Is this your certainty?
Do ye know the man ye wrong thus, Gentlemen?
Is this the woman meant?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: That your Landlady?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I know not what to say.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Am I a person
To be your sport Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I do beleeve now certaine
I am a knave; but how, or when—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What are you?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Bawd to this peece of pye meat.

speeches.speaker: Bawd
verse: A poore Gentlewoman
That lyes in Towne, about Law businesse,
And't like your worships.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: You shall have Law, beleeve it.

speeches.speaker: Bawd
verse: I'le shew your mastership my case.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: By no meanes,
I had rather see a Custard.

speeches.speaker: Bawd
verse: My dead husband
Left it even thus sir.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Blesse mine eyes from blasting,
I was never so frighted with a case.

speeches.speaker: Bawd
verse: And so sir—

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Enough, put up good velvet head.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What are you two now,
By your owne free confessions?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What you shall thinke us,
Though to my selfe I am certaine, and my life
Shall make that good and perfect, or fall with it.

speeches.speaker: Io.
verse: We are sure of nothing (Fred) that's the truth on't:
I do not think my nam's Don John, nor dare not
Beleeve any thing that concernes me, but my debts,
Nor those in way of payment: things are so carried,
What to entreat your Grace, or how to tell ye
We are, or we are not, is past my cunning,
But I would faine imagine we are honost,
And o' my conscience, I should fight in't—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thus then,
For we may be all abus'd.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: 'Tis possible,
For how should this concerne them?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Here let's part—
Untill to morrow this time: we to our way,
To make this doubt out, and you to your way;
Pawning our honours then to meet againe,
When if she be not found.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: We stand engaged
To answer any worthy way we are cald to.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: We aske no more.

speeches.speaker: Whore
verse: Ye have done with us then?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: No Dame.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: But is her name Constantia?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Yes a moveable
Belonging to a friend of mine: come out Fidler,
What say you to this Lady; be not fearfull?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Saving the reverence of my Masters pleasure,
I say she is a whore, and that she has robb'd him,
Hoping his hurts would kill him.

speeches.speaker: Whore.
verse: Who provok't me?
Nay sirrah squeak, Ile see your treble strings
Ty'd up too; if I hang, Ile spoyle your piping,
Your sweet face shall not save yee.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Thou dam'd impudence,
And thou dry'd devill; where's the Officer?

speeches.speaker: Peter
verse: Hee's here sir.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Lodge these safe till I send for 'em;
Let none come to 'em, nor no noise be heard
Of where they are, or why: away.

speeches.speaker: John.
verse: By this hand
A handsome whore: Now will I be arrested,
And brought home to this officers: a stout whore,
I love such stirring ware: pox o' this businesse,
A man must haunt out morsells for another,
And starve himself: a quick-ey'd whore, that's wild-fire,
And makes the bloud dance through the veines like billowes.
I will reprive this whore.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Well, good luck with ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: As much attend your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: To morrow certaine—

speeches.speaker: John
verse: If we out-live this night sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Come Don John,
We have something now to doe.

speeches.speaker: Ioh.
verse: I am sure I would have.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: If she be not found, we must fight.

speeches.speaker: Joh.
verse: I am glad on't,
I have not fought a great while.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: If we dye—

speeches.speaker: Jo.
prose: Ther's so much money sav'd in lecherie.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: IT should be here abouts.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Your grace is right,
This is the house I know it.

speeches.speaker: Voch.
verse: Grace?

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: 'Tis further
By the description we received.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Good my Lord the Duke,
Believe me, for I know it certainly,
This is the very house.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: My Lord the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Pray heaven this man Prove right now.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Beleeve it, hee's a most sufficient Scholler,
And can doe rare tricks this way; for a figure,
Or raising an appearance, whole Christendome
Has not a better; I have heard strange wonders of him.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: But can he shew us where she is?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Most certaine,
And for what cause too she departed.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Knock then,
For I am great with expectation,
Till this man satisfie me: I feare the Spaniards,
Yet they appeare brave fellowes: can he tell us?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: With a wet finger, whether they be false.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Away then.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Who's within here?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Your Grace may enter.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How can he know me?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: He knowes all.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: And you sir.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: What do you call his name?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why, Peter Vechio.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: They say he can raise devills,
Can he make 'em
Tell truth too, when he has rais'd 'em? for beleeve it,
These devils are the lyingst Rascalls.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: He can compell 'em.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: With what? can he
Tye squibs in their tailes, and fire the truth out?
Or make 'em eate a bawling Puritan,
Whose sanctified zeale shall rumble like an Earthquake?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: With Spels man?

speeches.speaker: John
verse: I with spoones as soone, dost thou thinke
The devill such an Asse as people make him?
Such a poore coxcomb? such a penny foot post?
Compel'd with crosse and pile to run of errands?
With Asteroth, and Behemoth, and Belfagor?
Why should he shake at sounds, that lives in a smiths forg?
Or if he do—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Without all doubt he do's Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Why should not Bilbo raise him, or a paire of bullyons,
They go as big as any? or an unshod Car,
When he goes tumble, tumble o're the stones,
Like Anacreons drunken verses, make us tremble?
These make as fell a noyse; me thinkes the collick
Well handled, and fed with small beere—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis the vertue—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: The vertue? nay, and goodnesse fetch him up once,
Has lost a friend of me; the wise old Gentleman
Knowes when, and how; I'le lay this hand to two pence,
Let all tho Conjurers in Christendome,
With all their spells, and vertues call upon him,
And I but thinke upon a wench, and follow it,
He shall be sooner mine then theirs; where's vertue?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Thou art the most sufficient, (I'le say for thee)
Not to beleeve a thing —

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: O sir, slow credit
Is the best child of knowledge; I'le go with ye,
And if he can do any thing, I'le thinke
As you would have me.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Let's enquire a long,
For certaine we are not far off.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Nor much nearer.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: You lost her yesternight.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: How thinke you sir?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Is your name Vechio?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And you can shew me
These; things you promise.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Your graces word bound to me,
No hand of Law shall seize me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: As I live sir—

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: And as I live, that can do something too sir.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: I take your promises: stay here a little,
Till I prepare some Ceremonies, and I'le satisfie ye.
The Ladies name's Constantia?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Yes

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: I come straight.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Sure hee's a learned man.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: The most now living;
Did your grace marke when we told all these circumstances,
How ever and anon he bolted from us
To use his studies helpe?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Now I thinke rather
To talke with some familiar.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Not unlikely,
For sure he has 'em subject.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How could he else
Tell when she went, and who went with her?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: True.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Or hit upon mine honour: or assure me
The Lady lov'd me dearely?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Twas so.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Now,
I do beseech your Grace sit downe, and you sir;
Nay pray sit close like brothers.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: A rare fellow.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: And what ye see, stir not at, nor use a word,
Untill I aske ye; for what shall appeare
Is but weake apparition and thin ayre
Not to be held, nor spoken too.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: We are counselled—

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: What noise is that without there?

speeches.speaker: Fred. Within.
verse: We must speake with him.

speeches.speaker: Ser. Within.
verse: Hee's busie Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Iohn. Within.
verse: That's all one friend,
We must, and will speake with him.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Let 'em in sir,
We know their tongues and businesse, 'tis our owne,
And in this very cause that we now come for,
They also come to be instructed.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Let 'em in then:
Sit down, I know your meaning.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: The Duke before us,
Now we shall sure know something.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Not a question,
But make your eyes, your tongues—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: This is a strange jugler,
Neither indent before hand for his payment,
Nor know the breadth of the businesse; sure his devell
Comes out of Lapland were they sell men winds,
For dead drinke, and old doublets.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Peace, he conjures.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Let him, he cannot raise my devill.

speeches.speaker: Fred,
verse: Prethee peace.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Appeare, appeare,
And you soft winds so cleare,
That dance upon the leaves, and make them sing
Gentle love-layes to the Spring,
Gilding all the vales below
With your verdure as ye blow,
Raise these formes from under ground
With a soft and happy sound.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
verse: This is an honest Conjurer, and a pretty Poet;
I like his words well, there's no bumbast in 'em,
But do you thinke now, he can cudgell up the devill,
With this short staffe of Verses?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
prose: Peace the spirits—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Nay, and they be no worse—

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Do ye know these faces?

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Sit still upon your lives then: and marke what follows:
Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: These devils do not paint sure?
Have they no sweeter shapes in hell?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Harke now Iohn.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I marry, this moves something like, this devill
Carries some metall in her gate.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: I find ye,
You would see her face unvail'd?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Be uncovered.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O heaven!

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Peace.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: See how she blushes.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Fredrick,
This devill for my money; this is she Boy,
Why thou shake? I burne.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Sit still, and silent.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: She lookes back at me; now she smiles sir.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Silence.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I must rise, or burst.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Ye see what followes—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O gentle sir this shape agen.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: I cannot,
'Tis all disolv'd againe: this was the figure.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: The very same sir.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: No hope once more to see it?

speeches.speaker: Ve.
verse: You might have kept it longer, had ye spar'd it,
Now 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No meanes to find it?

speeches.speaker: Ve.
verse: Yes that there is: sit still a while, there's wine
To thaw the wonder from your hearts: drinke well sir.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: This Conjurer is a right good fellow too,
A lad of mettle; two such devils more
Would make me a Conjurer: what wine is it?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Hollock.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
verse: The devil's in it then, looke how it dances?
Well, if I be—

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: We are all before ye,
That's your best comfort sir.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Byth' mas brave wine;
Nay, and the Devils live in this hell, I dare venture
Within these two months yet to be delivered
Of a large legion of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Here 'a comes,
Silence of all sides Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Vec.
verse: Good your grace,
Observe a stricter temper, and you too gallants,
You'l be deluded all else. This merry devill
That next appeares, for such a one you'l find it,
Must be cal'd up by a strange incantation,
A Song, and I must sing it: pray beare with me,
And pardon my rude pipe; for yet ere parting
Twenty to one I please ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: We are arm'd Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Nor shall you see us more transgresse.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What think'st thou
Now Iohn?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Why, now do I thinke Fredrick,
(And it I thinke amisse heaven pardon me,)
This honest Conjurer, with some foure or five
Of his good fellow devils, and my selfe,
Shall be yet drunke ere midnight.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Peace, he conjures.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Why, this is the Song Fredrick: twenty pound now
To see but our Don Gillian.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Peace it appeares.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I cannot peace: devils in French hoods Fredrick?
Sathans old Siringes?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What's this?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Peace.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: She, Boy.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What dost thou meane?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: She, Boy, I say.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: She, boy.
The very child too Fredrick;

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She laughes on us
Aloud Iohn, has the devill these affections?
I do beleeve 'tis she indeed.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Stand still.

speeches.speaker: Iohn.
verse: I will not;
Who calls Jeronimo from his naked bed?
Sweet Lady, was it you? If thou beest the devill,
First, having crost my selfe, to keep out wildfire,
Then said some speciall prayers to defend me
Against thy most unhallowed hood: have at thee.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Hold sir, I am no devill.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: That's all one.

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: I am your very Landlady.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I defie thee:
Thus as St. Dunstan blew the devils nose
With a paire of tongs, even so right worshipfull—

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Sweet son, I am old Gillion.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: This is no spirit.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Art thou old Gillian, flesh and bone?

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: I am Son.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
prose: Sit still sir, now I'le shew you all.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Where's thy bottle?

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: Here, I beseech ye son—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: For I know the devill
Cannot assume that shape.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Tis she Iohn, certaine—

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: A hogs poxe o'your mouldy chaps, what make you
Tumbling and juggling here?

speeches.speaker: Land.
verse: I am quit now Signior,
For all the prankes you plaid, and railings at me,
For to tell true, out of a trick I put
Upon your high behaviours, which was a lye,
But then it serv'd my turne, I drew the Lady
Unto my kinsmans here, only to torture
Your Don-ships for a day or two; and secure her
Out of all thoughts of danger: here she comes now.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: May I yet speake?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Yes, and embrace her too,
For one that loves you deerer—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O my sweetest.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Blush not, I will not chide ye.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: To add more
Unto the joy I know, I bring ye, see sir,
The happy fruit of all our vowes.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Heavens blessing
Be round about thee ever.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Pray blesse me to,
For if your grace be well instructed this way,
You'l find the keeping halfe the getting.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How sir?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I'le tell ye that anon.

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: 'Tis true this Gentleman
'Has done a charity worthy your favour,
And let him have it deare sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: My best Lady
She has, and ever shall have: so must you sir,
To whom I am equall bound, as to my being.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Your Graces humble servants—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why kneele you sir?

speeches.speaker: Ve.
verse: For pardon for my boldnesse: yet 'twas harmlesse
And all the art I have sir; those your grace saw
Which you thought spirits, were my neighbours children
Whom I instruct in Grammer, here, and Musick;
Their shapes, the peoples fond opinions,
Beleeving I can conjure, and oft repairing
To know of things stolne from 'em, I keepe about me,
And alwaies have in readinesse; by conjecture
Out of their owne confessions, I oft tell 'em
Things, that by chance have fallen out so: which way
(Having the persons here, I knew you sought for)
I wrought upon your grace: my end is mirth,
And pleasing, if I can, all parties.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I beleeve it,
For you have pleas'd me truly: so well pleas'd me,
That when I shall forget it—

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Here's old Antonio,
I spide him at a window, comming mainely
I know about his whore, the man you light on,
As yon discovered unto me: good your Grace,
Let's stand by all, 'twill be a mirth above all,
To observe his pelting fury.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: About a wench sir?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: A young whore that has rob'd him,

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: But do you know sir,
Where she is?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Yes, and will make that perfect—

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: I am instructed well then.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: If he come
To have a devill shew'd him, by all meanes
Let me be he, I can rore rarely.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Be so,
But take heed to his anger.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Slip in quickly,
There you shall find suites of all sorts: when I call,
Be ready and come forward.
Who's there come in?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Are you the Conjurer?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Sir I can do a little
That way, if you please to imploy me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Presently shew me a devill that can tell—

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Where your wench is.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You are i'th'right; as also where the Fidler
That was consenting to her.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Sit ye there sir,
Ye shall know presently: can ye pray heartily?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Why, is your devill so furious?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: I must shew ye
A forme, may chance affright ye.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: He must fart fire then:
Take you no care for me.

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Ascend Asterth,
Why, when, appeare I say—Now question him.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Where is my whore Don devill?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Gone to China,
To be the great Chams Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: That's a lye devill:
Where are my jewels?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Pawn'd for Peticoates.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: That may be; where's the Fidler?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: Condemn'd to th' Gallowes,
For robbing of a Mill.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: The lyingst devill
That e're I dealt withall, and the unlikeliest:
What was that Rascall hurt me?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: I.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Who was he?

speeches.speaker: John
verse: I.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Do ye here conjurer,
Dare you venture your devill?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Then I'le venture my dagger;
Have at your devils pate; do ye mew?

speeches.speaker: Vech.
verse: Hold.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Hold there,
I do command ye hold.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Is this the devill?
Why Conjurer—

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Has been a devill to you sir.
But now you shall forget all: your whores safe,
And all your Jewels: your Boy too.

speeches.speaker: John
verse: Now the devill indeed
Lay his ten claws upon thee, for my pate
Finds what it is to be a fend.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: All safe?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Pray ye know this person: all's right now.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Your grace
May now command me then: but where's my whore?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Ready to goe to whiping.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: My whore whipt?

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Yes, your whore without doubt Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Whipt? pray Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why, would you have her once more rob ye? the young boy
You may forgive, he was intic'd.

speeches.speaker: Iohn
verse: The Whore sir,
Would rather carry pitty: a hansome Whore.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: A Gentleman I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: Petr.
verse: Let's in all.
And if we see contrition in your whore sir,
Much may be done.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Now my deare faire, to you,
And the full consummation of my Vow.

speeches.speaker: Theodor.
verse: CAptaine, your friend's prefer'd, the Princesse has her,
Who, I assure my selfe, will use her nobly;
A prettie sweet one 'tis indeed.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Well bred Sir,
I doe deliver that upon my credit,
And of an honest stock.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: It seemes so Captaine,
And no doubt will doe well.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Thanks to your care sir;
But tell me Noble Colonell, why this habit
Of discontent is put on through the Army?
And why your valiant father, our great Generall,
The hand that taught to strike, the Love that lead all;
Why he, that was the father of the warte,
He that begot, and bred the Souldier,
Why he sits shaking of his Armes, like Autumne,
His Collours folded, and his Drums cas'd up,
The tongue of war for ever ty'd within us?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: It must be so: Captaine you are a stranger,
But of a small time here a souldier,
Yet that time shewes ye a right good, and great one,
Else I could tell yee houres are strangely alterd:
The young Duke has too many eyes upon him,
Too many feares 'tis thought too, and to nourish those,
Maintains too many Instruments.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Turne their hearts,
Or turn their heeles up, heaven: 'Tis strange it should be.
The old Duke lov'd him dearely.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: He deserv'd it;
And were he not my Father, I durst tell yee,
The memorable hazzards he has run through
Deserv'd of this man too; highly deserv'd too;
Had they been lesse, they had been safe Putskie,
And sooner reach'd regard.

speeches.speaker: Put
verse: There you strook sure sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Did I never tell thee of a vow he made
Some yeares before the old Duke dyed?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I have heard yee
Speake often of that vow; but how it was,
Or to what end, I never understood yet?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Ile tell thee then: and then thou wilt finde the reason:
The last great Muster, ('twas before ye serv'd here,
Before the last Dukes death, whose honour'd bones
Now rest in peace) this yong Prince had the ordering,
(To Crowne his fathers hopes) of all the Army:
Who (to be short) put all his power to practise;
Fashion'd, and drew 'em up: but alas, so poorely
So raggedly and loosely, so unsouldier'd,
The good Duke blush'd, and call'd unto my father,
Who then was Generall: Goe Archus speedily,
And chide the Boy, before the souldier finde him,
Stand thou between his ignorance and them,
Fashion their bodies new to thy direction;
Then draw thou up, and shew the Prince his errours.
My Sire obey'd, and did so; with all duty
Inform'd the Prince, and read him all directions:
This bred distaste, distaste grew up to anger,
And anger into wilde words broke out thus:
Well Archus, if I live but to command here,
To be but Duke once, I shall then remember,
I shall remember truely, trust me, I shall,
And by my Fathers hand; the rest his eyes spoke.
To which my Father answer'd (somewhat mov'd too)
And with a vow he seal'd it: Royall sir,
Since for my faith and fights, your Icorne and anger
Onely pursue me; if I live to that day,
That day so long expected to reward me,
By his so ever noble hand you swore by,
And by the hand of Justice, never Armes more
Shall rib this body in, nor sword hang here, sir:
The Conflicts I will doe you service then in,
Shall be repentant prayers. So they parted.
The time is come; and now you know the wonder.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I finde a feare too, which begins to tell me,
The Duke will have but poore and slight defences
If his hot humour raigne, and not his honour:
How stand you with him, Sir?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: A perdue Captaine,
Full of my fathers danger.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: He has rais'd a young man,
They say a slight young man, I know him not,
For what desert?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Beleeve it, a brave Gentleman,
Worth the Dukes respect, a cleere sweet Gentleman,
And of a noble soule: Come, let's retire us,
And wait upon my father, who within this houre
You will finde an alter'd man.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I am sorry for't sir.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Is't not a handsome wench?

speeches.speaker: 2. Wom.
verse: She is well enough, Madam:
I have seen a better face, and a straiter body,
And yet she is a pretty Gentle-woman.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: What thinkst thou Petesca?

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: Alas, Madam, I have no skill, she has a black eye,
Which is of the least too, and the dullest water;
And when her mouth was made, for certaine Madam,
Nature intended her a right good stomach.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: She has a good hand.

speeches.speaker: 2 Wom.
verse: 'Tis good enough to hold fast.
And strong enough to strangle the neck of a Lute.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: What thinke ye of her colour?

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: If it be her owne
'Tis good black bloud: right weather-proofe
I warrant it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Wom.
verse: What a strange pace she has got?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: That's but her breeding.

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: And what a manly body? me thinks she looks
As though she would pitch the Barre, or goe to Buffets.

speeches.speaker: 2 Wom.
verse: Yet her behaviour's utterly against it,
For me thinks she is too bashfull.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Is that hurtfull?

speeches.speaker: 2 Wo.
verse: Even equall to too bold: either of 'em Madam
May doe her injurie when time shall serve her.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: You discourse learnedly, cal in the wench.
What envious fooles are you? Is the rule generall,
That women can speak handsomely of none,
But those they are bred withall?

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: Scarce well of those Madam,
If they believe they may out-shine 'em any way:
Our natures are like oyle, compound us with any thing,
Yet stil we strive to swim o'th' top:
Suppose there were here now,
Now in this court of Mosco, a stranger Princesse,
Of bloud and beauty equall to your excellence,
As many eyes and services stuck on her;
What would you think?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I would thinke she might deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: Your grace shall give me leave not to believe ye;
I know you are a woman, and so humourd:
Ile tell yee Madam, I could then get more gownes on ye,
More caps & feathers, more scarfs, & more silk stockings,
With rocking you a sleep with nightly railings
Upon that woman, then if I had nine lives
I could weare out: by this hand ye'would scratch her eyes out.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Thou art deceiv'd foole;
Now let your own eyes mock ye.
Come hither girle: hang me & she be not a handsom one.

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: I feare it will prove indeed so.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Did you ever serve yet
In any place of worth?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: No Royall Lady.

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: Hold up your head; sie.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Let her alone, stand from her.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: It shall be now,
Of all the blessings my poore youth has pray'd for,
The greatest and the happiest to serve you;
And might my promise carrie but that credit
To be believ'd, because I am yet a stranger,
Excellent Lady, when I fall form dutie,
From all the service that my life can lend me,
May ever-lasting miserie then finde me.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: What think ye now? I doe believe, and thank ye;
And sure I shall not be so farre forgetfull,
To see that honest faith die unrewarded:
What must I call your name?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Alinda Madam.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Can yee sing?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: A little, when my griefe will give me leave, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Olm.
verse: VVhat griefe canst thou have wench?
Thou art not in love?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: If I be Madam, 'tis onely with your goodnesse;
For yet I never saw that man I sighed for.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Of what yeares are you?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: My mother oft has told me,
That very day and houre this land was blest
With your most happy birth, I first saluted
This worlds faire light: Nature was then so busie,
And all the Graces to adorne your goodnesse,
I stole into the world poore and neglected.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Something there was, when I first look'd upon thee,
Made me both like and love thee: now I know it;
And you shall find that knowledge shall not hurt you:
I hope ye are a Maid?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I hope so too, Madam;
I am sure for any man: and were I otherwise,
Of all the services my hopes could point at,
I durst not touch at yours.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: The great Duke, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Good morow, sister.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: A good day to your highnesse.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I am come to pray you use no more perswasions
For this old stubborne man: nay to command ye:
His saile is swell'd too full: he is grown too insolent,
Too self-affected, proud: those poore slight services
He has done my father, and my self, has blowne him
To such a pitch, he flyes to stoop our favours.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I am sorry sir: I ever thonght those services
Both great and noble.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: However, may it please yee
But to consider 'em a true hearts servants,
Done out of faith to you, and not selfe-fame:
But to consider royall sir, the dangers;
When you have slept secure, the mid-night tempests,
That as he marcht sung through his aged locks;
When you have sed at full, the wants and famines;
The fires of heaven, when you have found all temperate,
Death with his thousand doores—

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I have consider'd;
No more: and that I will have, shall be.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: For the best,
I hope all still.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: What handsome wench is that there?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: My servant, sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Prethee observe her Burris.
Is she not wondrous handsome? speak thy freedome.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Shee appeares no lesse to me sir.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Of whence is she?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Her father I am told is a good gentleman,
But farre off dwelling: her desire to serve me
Brought her to th' Court, & here her friends have left her.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: She may find better friends:
Ye are welcome faire one,
I have not seen a sweeter: By your Ladies leave:
Nay stand up sweet, we'll have no superstition:
You have got a servant; you may use him kindly,
And he may honour ye:
Good morrow sister.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Good morrow to your Grace. How the wench blushes?
How like an Angel now she looks?

speeches.speaker: 1 VVom.
verse: At first jumpe
Jumpe into the Dukes armes? we must look to you,
Indeed we must, the next jump we are journeymen.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I see the ruine of our hopes already,
Would she were at home again, milking her fathers cows

speeches.speaker: 1 Wo.
verse: I feare shee'll milke all the great Courtiers first.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: This has not made yee proud?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: No certaine, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: It was the Duke that kist yee.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Twas your brother,
And therefore nothing can be meant but honour.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: But say he love ye?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That he may with safety:
A Princes love extends to all his subjects.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: But say in more particular?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Pray feare not:
For vertues sake deliver me from doubts, Lady:
'Tis the name of King, nor all his promises,
His glories, and his greatnsse stuck about me,
Can make me prove a Traitor to your service:
You are my Mistris, and my noble Master,
Your vertues my ambition, and your favour
The end of all my love, and all my fortune:
And when I faile in that faith—

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I beleeve thee,
Come wipe your eyes; I doe: take you example—

speeches.speaker: Pets.
verse: I would her eyes were out.

speeches.speaker: 1 Wom.
verse: If the winde stand in this doore,
We shall have but cold custome: some trick or other,
And speedily.

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: Let me alone to think on't,

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Come, be you neare me still.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: With all my duty.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: This is the heaviest march we e're trod Captain,

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: This was not wont to be: these honour'd pieces
The fierie god of warre himselfe would smile at,
Buckl'd upon that body, were not wont thus,
Like Reliques to be offer'd to long rust,
And heavy-ey'd oblivion brood upon 'em

speeches.speaker: Arch.
verse: There set 'em downe: and glorious war fare well;
Thou childe of honour and ambitious thoughts,
Begot in bloud, and nurs'd with Kingdomes ruines;
Thou golden danger, courted by thy followers
Through fires and famines, for one title from thee,
Prodigall man-kinde spending all his fortunes;
A long farewell I give thee: Noble Armes,
You ribs for mighty mindes, you Iron houses,
Made to defie the thunder-claps of Fortune,
Rust and consuming time must now dwell with yee:
And thou good Sword that knewst the way to conquest,
Upon whose fatall edge despaire and death dwelt,
That when I shooke thee thus, fore-shew'd destruction,
Sleep now from bloud, and grace my Monument:
Farewell my Eagle; when thou flew'st, whole Armies
Have stoopt below thee: At Passage I have seen thee,
Ruffle the Tartars, as they fled thy furie;
And bang 'em up together, as a Tassell,
Upon the streach, a stock of fearefull Pigeons.
I yet remember when the Volga curl'd,
The aged Volga, when he heav'd his head up,
And rais'd his waters high, to see the ruines,
The ruines out Swords made, the bloudy ruines;
Then flew this Bird of honour bravely, Gentlemen;
But these must be forgotten: so must these too,
And all that tend to Armes, by me for ever.
Take 'em you holy men; my Vow take with 'em,
Never to weare 'em more: Trophies I give 'em,
And sacred Rites of warre to adorne the Temple:
There let 'em hang, to tell the world their master
Is now Devotions souldier, fit for prayer,
Why doe ye hang your heads? why look you sad friends?
I am not dying yet.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Ye are indeed to us sir.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Dead to our fortunes, Generall.

speeches.speaker: Arch.
verse: Youll finde a better,
A greater, and a stronger man to lead yee,
And to a stronger fortune: I am old friends,
Time, and the wars together make me stoop, gentlemen,
Stoop to my grave: my minde unfurnish'd too,
Emptie and weak as I am: my poore body,
Able for nothing now but contemplation,
And that will be a taske too to a Souldier:
Yet had they but encourag'd me, or thought well
Of what I have done, I thinke I should have ventur'd
For one knock more, I should have made a shift yet
To have broke one staffe more handsomly, and have dyed
Like a good fellow, and an honest souldier,
In the head of ye all, with my sword in my hand,
And so have made an end of all with credit.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Well, there will come an houre, when all these injuries
These secure slights—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ha! no more of that sirrah,
Not one word more of that I charge ye.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: I must speak sir.
And may that tongue forget to found your service,
That's dumbe to your abuses.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Understand foole,
That voluntary I sit downe.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: You are forced sir,
Forced for your safety: I too well remember
The time and cause, and I may live to curse 'em,
You made this vow, and whose un-noblenesse,
Indeed forgetfulnesse of good—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No more,
As thou art mine no more.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Whose doubts and envies—
But the devill will have his due.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Good yentle Colonell.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: And though disgraces, and contempt of honour
Reigne now, the wheele must turne againe.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Peace sirrah,
Your tongue's too saucy: doe ye stare upon me?
Downe with that heart, downe suddenly, down with it,
Downe with that disobedience; tye that tongue up.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Tongue?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Doe not provoke me to forget my vow, sirrah,
And draw that fatall sword againe in anger.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: For heavens sake, Colonell.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Doe not let me doubt
Whose Sonne thou art, because thou canst not suffer:
Doe not play with mine anger; if thou dost,
By all the loyalty my heart holds—

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: I have done sir,
'Pray pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I pray ye be worthy of it:
Beshrew your heart, you have vext me.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am sorrie sir.

speeches.speaker: Arch.
verse: Goe to, no more of this: be true and honest,
I know ye are man enough, mold it to just ends,
And let not my disgraces; then I am miserable,
When I have nothing left me but thy angers.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: And't please ye sir, the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Duk
verse: Now, what's all this?
The meaning of this ceremonious Embleme?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Your Grace should first remember—

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: There's his nature.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I doe, and shall remember still that injury,
