That at the Muster, where it pleas'd your greatnesse
To laugh at my poore souldiership, to skorne it;
And more to make me seem ridiculous,
Took from my hands my charge.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: O thinke not so Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And in my Fathers sight.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Heaven be my witnesse
I did no more, (and that with modestie,
With love and faith to you) then was my warrant,
And from your Father seal'd: nor durst that rudenesse
And impudence of scorne fall from my haviour,
I ever yet knew duty.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: We shall teach yee:
I well remember too, upon some words I told ye,
Then at that time, some angrie words ye answer'd,
If ever I were Duke, you were no souldier.
You have kept your word, and so it shall be to you.
From henceforth I dismisse ye; take your ease sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I humbly thanke your Grace; this wasted body,
Beaten and bruis'd with Armes, dry'd up with troubles,
Is good for nothing else but quiet, now sir,
And holy prayers; in which, when I forget
To thanke high heaven for all your bounteous favours,
May that be deafe, and my Petitions perish.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: What a smooth humble cloak he has cas'd his pride in?
And how he has pull'd his clawes in? ther's no trusting—

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Speake for the best.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Beleeve I shall doe ever.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: To make yee vnderstand we feele not yet
Such dearth of valour, and experience,
Such a declining age of doing spirits,
That all should be confin'd within your Excellence,
And you, or none be honour'd, take Boroskie
The place he has commanded, lead the Souldier;
A little time will bring thee to his honour,
Which has been nothing, but the worlds opinion,
The souldiers fondnesse, and a little fortune,
Which I believe his sword had the least share in.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: O that I durst but answer now.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Good Colonell.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: My heart wil break else: Royal sir, I know not
What you esteem mens lives, whose hourely labours,
And losse of bloud, consumptions in your service,
Whose bodies are accquainted with more miseries,
And all to keep you safe, then Dogs or slaves are.
His sword the least share gain'd?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You will not fight with me?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: No Sir, I dare not,
You are my Prince: but I dare speake to yee,
And dare speak truth, which none of their ambitions,
That be informers to you dare once thinke of;
Yet truth will now but anger yee: I am sorry for't.
And so I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Ev'n when you please Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Sirrah, see me no more.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And so may you too:
You have a house ith' Countrey, keep you there Sir,
And when you have rull'd your self, teach your son manners.
For this time I forgive him.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Heaven forgive all:
And to your Grace a happie and long rule here.
And you Lord Generall, may your fights be prosperous.
In all your course, may Fame and Fortune Court you.
Fight for your Countrey, and your Princes safetie;
Boldly, and bravely face your enemie,
And when you strike, strike with that killing vertue,
As if a generall plague had seiz'd before ye;
Danger, and doubt, and labour cast behinde yee,
And then come home an old and noble storie.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: A little comfort sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: As little as may be:
Farewell, you know your limit.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Alas, brave gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I doe, and will observe it suddenly:
My grave; I, that's my limit: 'tis no new thing,
Nor that can make me start, or tremble at it,
To buckle with that old grim souldier now:
I have seen him in his sowrest shapes and dreadfull'st;
I, and I thanke my honestie, have stood him:
That audits cast: Farewell my honest souldiers,
Give me your hands. Farewell, fare-well good Ancient,
A stout man, and a true, thou art come in sorrow.
Blessings upon your swords, may they ne're faile yee.
You doe but change a man: your fortunes constant;
That by your ancient valours is ty'd fast still:
Be valiant still and good; and when ye fight next,
When flame and furie make but one face of horror,
When the great rest of all your honour's up,
When you would thinke a spell to shake the enemy,
Remember me: my prayers shall be with yee.
So once againe farewell.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Let's wait upon yee.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No, no, it must not be: I have now left me
A single fortune to my selfe, no more,
Which needs no traine, nor complement: good Captain,
You are an honest and a sober gentleman,
And one I thinke has lov'd me.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: I am sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Look to my boy he's grown too head-strong for me,
And if they think him fit to carrie Armes still,
His life is theirs: I have a house ith' Countrey,
And when your better houres will give ye liberty
See me: you shall be welcome. Fortune to ye.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Ile cry no more, that will doe him no good,
And 'twill but make me drie, and I have no money:
Ile fight no more, and that will doe them harme;
And if I can do that I care not for money:
I could have curst reasonable well, and I have had the luck too
To have 'em hit sometimes: Whosoever thou art,
That like a devill didst possesse the Duke
With these malitious thoughts; mark what I say to thee,
A plague upon thee, that's but the Preamble.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: O take the pox too:

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: They'll cure one another:
I must have none but kills, and those kill stinking:
Or look ye, let the single pox possesse them,
Or pox upon pox.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: That's but ill i'th' Armes sir,

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Tis worse ith' legs, I would not wish it else:
And may those grow to scabs as big as Mole-hils,
And twice a day, the devill with a Currie-combe
Scratch 'em, and scrub em. I warrent him he has 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: May he be ever lowzie.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: That's a pleasure,
The Beggars Leacherie: sometime the Souldiers:
May he be ever lazie, stink where he stands,
And Maggots breed in's braines.

speeches.speaker: 2 Soul.
verse: I marrie sir,
May he fall mad in love with his Grand-mother,
And kissing her, may her teeth drop into his mouth,
And one fall crosse his throat, then let him gargell.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Now, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Post.
verse: Where's the Duke pray gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Keep on your way, you cannot misse.

speeches.speaker: Post.
verse: I thanke yee.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: If he be married, may he dreame hee's Cuckol'd,
And when he wakes, believe, and sweare he saw it:
Sue a divorce, and after finde her honest:
Then in a pleasant Pigsty with his owne garters,
And a fine running knot, ride to the devill.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: If these would doe —

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Ile never trust my minde more,
If all these faile.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sould.
verse: What shall we doe now Captaine?
For by this honest hand Ile be torne a pieces,
Unlesse my old Generall goe, or some that love him,
And love us equall too, before I fight more:
I can make a shooe yet, and draw it on too,
If I like the legge well.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Fight? 'tis likely.
No, there Will be the sport boyes, when ther's need on's.
They thinke the other Crowne will doe, will carry us,
And the brave golden coat of Captain Cankro

speeches.speaker: Boroskie:
verse: What a noyse his very name carries?
'Tis gun enough to fright a nation,
He need no souldiers: if he doe, for my part,
I promise ye, he's like to seek 'em: so I thinke you thinke too,
And all the Army: No honest brave old Archas,
We cannot so soon leave thy memory,
So soon forget thy goodnesse: he that does,
The scandall, and the scumme of Armes be counted.

speeches.speaker: Pu.
verse: You much rejoice me: now you have hit my meaning:
I durst not presse ye, till I found your spirits.
Continue thus.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
prose: Ile goe and tell the Duke on't.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: No, no, hee'll finde it soone enough, and feare it,
When once occasion comes: Another Packet.
From whence friend come yee?

speeches.speaker: 2 Post.
verse: From the borders sir.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: What newes sir, I beseech yee?

speeches.speaker: 2 Post.
verse: Fire and sword gentlemen;
The Tartar's up, and with a mighty force,
Comes forward like a tempest, all before him
Burning and killing.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Brave boyes; brave newes boyes.

speeches.speaker: 2 Post.
verse: Either we must have present helpe—

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Still braver.

speeches.speaker: 2 Post.
verse: Where lyes the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Hee's there.

speeches.speaker: 2 Post.
verse: 'Save ye gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: We are safe enough, I warrant thee:
Now the time's come.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I now 'tis come indeed, and now stand firm boyes,
And let 'em burne on merrily.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: This City would make a marvelous fine bone-fire:
'Tis old dry timber, and such wood has no fellow.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sold.
verse: Here will be trim piping anon and whining,
Like so many Pigs in a storme,
When they heare the newes once,

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Here's one has heard it already,
Room for the Generall.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: Say I am falne exceeding sick oth' suddain,
And am not like to live.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: If ye goe on Sir,
For they will kill yee certainly: they look for yee.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: I see your Lordships bound, take a suppository,
Tis I Sir; a poor cast Flag of yours. The foolish Tartars
They burne and kill, and 't like your honour, kill us,
Kill with Guns, with Guns my Lord, with Guns Sir.
What sayes your Lordship to a chick in sorrell sops?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Go, go thy wayes old true-peny;
Thou hast but one fault, Thou art ev'n too valiant.
Come toth' Army gentlemen, and let's make them acquainted.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Away, we are for ye.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why whither run ye fools, wil ye leave my Lady?

speeches.speaker: Petes.
verse: The Tartar comes, the Tartar comes.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why let him,
I had thought you had feard no men: upon my conscience
You have try'd their strengths already: stay for shame.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Shift for thy selfe Alinda.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Beauty blesse ye:
Into what Grooms Feather-bed will yee creep now?
And there mistake the enemy: sweet youths ye are,
And of a constant courage: are you afraid of foyning?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: O my good wench, what shall become of us?
The Posts come hourely in, and bring new danger;
The Enemy is past the Volga, and beares hither
With all the blond and crueltie he carries,
My brother now will find his fault.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I doubt me.
Somewhat too late to Madam: but pray feare not,
All will be well I hope. Sweet Madam shake not.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: How cam'st thou by this spirit? our Sex tremble.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I am not unacquainted with these dangers:
And you shall know my truth; for e're you perish,
A hundred swords shall passe through me: 'tis but dying,
And Madam we must doe it: the manner's all:
You have a Princely Birth, take Princely thoughts to ye,
And take my councell too; goe presently,
With all the haste yee have, (I will attend ye)
With all the possible speed, to old Lord Archas,
He honours yee: with all your art perswade him,
('I will be a dismall time else) wooe him hither,
But hither Madam; make him see the danger;
For your new Generall looks like an Asse;
There's nothing in his face but losse.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Ile doe it,
And thank thee sweet Alinda: O my Jewell.
How much I am bound to love thee: by this hand wench
If thou wert a man—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I would I were to fight for yee.
But haste deare Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I need no spurres Alinda.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: The Lord Generall sick now? is this a time
For men to creep into their beds? what's become Post
Of my Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Post.
verse: Beaten, and 't please your Grace.
And all his forces sparkled.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: That's but cold newes.
How now, what good newes? are the souldiers ready?

speeches.speaker: Ge.
verse: Yes, sir, but fight they wil not, nor stir from that place
They stand in now, unlesse they have Lord Archas
To lead 'em out: they raile upon this Generall,
And sing songs of him, scurvy songs to worse tunes:
And much they spare not you sir: here they sweare
They'll stand and see the Citie burnt, & dance about it,
Unlesse Lord Archas come before they fight for't.
It must be so sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I could wish it so too:
And to that end I have sent Lord Burris to him;
But all I feare will faile: we must dye gentlemen,
And one stroak wee'll have for't.
What bringst thou Burris?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: That I am loath to tell: he will not come sir.
I found him at his prayers: there he tells me,
The enemy shall take him, sit for heaven:
I urg'd to him all our dangers, his owne worthes,
The Countries ruine: nay, I kneeld and pray'd him;
I se shooke his head, let fall a teare, and pointed
Thus with his finger to the ground; a grave
I think he meant; and this was all he answer'd.
Your Grace was much too blame.
Where's the new Generall?

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: He is sick poore man

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Hee's a poore man indeed Sir:
Your Grace must needs goe to the souldier.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: They have sent me word
They will not stirre: they raile at me,
And all the spight they have—
What shout is that there?
Is the enemy come so neare?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I have brought him Sir;
At length I have woo'd him thus farre.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Happy sister;
O blessed woman!

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Use him nobly brother;
You never had more need: And gentlemen,
All the best powers yee have, to tongues turn presently,
To winning and perswading tongues: all my art,
Onely to bring him hither, I have utter'd;
Let it be yours to arme him: And good my Lord,
Though I exceed the limit you allow'd me,
Which was the happinesse to bring ye hither,
And not to urge yee farther: yet, see your Countrey,
Out of your owne sweet spirit now behold it:
Turne round, and look upon the miseries,
Of every side the seares: ô see the dangers;
We finde 'em soonest, therefore heare me first sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Next heare your Prince;
You have said you lov'd him Archas,
And thought your life too little for his service:
Thinke not your vow to great now, now the time is,
And now you are brought toth'test, touch right now souldier,
Now shew the manly pureness of thy mettle:
Now if thou beest that valued man, that vertue,
That great obedience teaching all, now stand it.
What I have said forget, my youth was hasty,
And what you laid your selfe forgive, you were angry.
If men could live without their faults, they were gods Archas.
He weeps, & holds his ha~ds up: to him Burris.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You have shew'd the Prince his faults:
And like a good Surgeon you have laid
Tha^ to 'em makes 'em smart: hee feeles it,
Let 'em not sester now sir: your owne honour,
The bountie of that minde, and your allegeance,
'Gainst which I take it, heaven gives no command sir,
Nor seales no vow, can better teach ye now
What yee have to doe, then I, or this necessity:
Onely this little's left: would ye doe nobly,
And in the eye of honour truely triumph?
Conquer that minde first, and then men are nothing.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Last, a poor virgin kneels: for loves sake General,
If ever you have lov'd; for her sake, sir,
For your owne honesty, which is a virgin,
Look up, and pitty us, be bold and fortunate.
You are a Knight, a good, and noble souldier,
And when your spurs were given ye, your sword buckl'd,
Then were you sworne for vertues cause, for beauties,
For chastity to strike: strike now, they suffer:
Now draw your sword, or else you are recreant,
Onely a Knight ith' heeles, ith' heart a Coward:
Your first vow honour made, your last but anger.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: How like my vertuous wife this thing looks, speaks too?
So would she chide my dulnesse: faire one I thank yee:
My gracious sir, your pardon, next your hand:
Madam, your favour, and your prayers: gentlemen,
Your wishes and your loves; and pretty sweet one,
A favour for your Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Give him this wench.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Thus doe I tye on victory.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: My Armour,
My horse, my sword, my tough staffe, and my fortune,
And Olin now I come to shake thy glorie.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Goe brave and prosperous, our loves go with thee.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Full of thy vertue, and our prayers attend thee.

speeches.speaker: Bur. &c.
verse: Loden with victory, and we to honour thee.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Come home the son of honour,
And Ile serve ye.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: No newes of Archas yet?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: But now, and't please ye
A Post came in, Letters he brought none with him,
But this deliver'd: He saw the Armies joyne,
The game of bloud begun, and by our Generall,
Who never was acquainted, but with Conquest,
So bravely fought, he saw the Tartars shaken,
And there he said he left 'em.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Where's Boroskie?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: He is up againe, and't please ye.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Sir, me thinks
This newes should make yee lightsome, bring joy to ye,
It strikes our hearts with generall comfort.
Gone? What should this meane, so suddenly?
Hee's well?

speeches.speaker: 2. Gen.
verse: We see no other.
Would the rest were well too,
That put these starts into him.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Ile goe after him.
'T will not be fit Sir: h'as some secret in him
He would not be disturb'd in: know you any thing
Has crost him since the Generall went?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Not any.
If there had been, I am sure I should have found it;
Onely I have heard him oft complaine for money;
Money he sayes he wants.
It may be that then.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: To him that has so many wayes to raise it,
And those to honest, it cannot be.
He comes back,
And Lord Boroskie with him.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: There the game goes,
I feare some new thing hatching.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come hether Burris,
Go see my Sister, and commend me to her,
And to my litle Mistrisse give this token;
Tell her I'le see her shortly.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Yes, I shall sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Waite you without: I would yet try him further.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: 'Twill not be much amisse: has your grace heard yet
Of what he has done i'th' field?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A Post but now
Came in, who saw 'em joyne, and 'has deliver'd,
The enemy gave ground before he parted.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: 'Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come, speake thy mind man: 'tis not for fighting
And noise of War I keepe thee in my bosome;
Thy ends are nearer to me; from my childhood
Thou brought'st me up: and like another nature,
Made good all my necessities: speake boldly.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Sir, what I utter, will be thought but envy
Though I intend, high heaven knows, but your honour,
When vaine and empty people shall proclaime me—
Good sir excuse me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Do you feare me for your enemy?
Speake on your dutie.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Then I must, and dare sir.
When he comes home, take heed the Court receive him not,
Take heed he meet not with their loves, and praises,
That glasse will shew him ten times greater Sir,
And make him strive to make good that proportion,
Then ere his fortune bred him, he is honourable,
At least I strive to understand him so,
And of a nature, if not this way poyson'd,
Perfect enough, easie, & sweet, but those are soone seduc'd sir;
He's a great man, and what that pill may worke,
Prepar'd by generall voyces of the people,
Is the end of all my councell: only this sir,
Let him retire a while, there's more hangs by it
Then you know yet: there if he stand a while well,
But till the Souldier coole, who, for their service
You must pay now most liberally, most freely,
And shewrd your selfe into 'em; 'tis the bounty
They follow with their loves, and not the bravery.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: But wher's the money? how now?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Sir the Collonell,
Son to the Lord Archas, with most happy newes
Of the Tartars overthrow, without here
Attends your graces pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Be not seen sir,
He's a bold fellow, let me stand his thunders,
Toth' Court he must not come: no blessing here sir,
No face of favour, if you love your honour.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Do what you thinke is meetest; I'le retire sir.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Conduct him in sir—welcome noble Collonell,

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: That's much from your Lordship: pray where's the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: We heare you have beat the Tartar.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Is he busie sir?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Have ye taken Olin yet?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I would faine speake with him,

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: How many men have ye lost?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Do's he lye this way?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I am sure you fought it bravely.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I must see him.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You cannot yet, ye must not, what's your Commission.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: No gentleman o'th' Chamber here?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Why pray ye sir?
Am not I fit to entertaine your businesse?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I thinke you are not sir; I am sure ye shall not.
I bring no tales, nor flatteries: In my tongue sir,
I carry no fork'd stings.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You keepe your bluntnesse.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You are deceiv'd: it keeps me: I had felt else
Some of your plagues ere this: but good sir trifle not,
I have businesse to the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: He's not well sir,
And cannot now be spoke withall.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Not well sir?
How would he ha' been, if we had lost? not well sir?
I bring him newes to make him well: his enemie
That would have burnt his City here, and your house too,
Your brave gilt house, my Lord, your honours hangings,
Where all your Ancestors, and all their battles,
Their silke and golden battles are descipher'd:
That would not only have abus'd your buildings,
Your goodly buildings sir, and have drnnke dry your butteries,
Purlcin'd your Lordships plate, the Duke bestow'd on you,
For turning hansomely o'th toe, and trim'd your Virgins,
Trim'd 'em of a new cut, and't like your Lordship,
'Tis ten to one, your wife too, and the curse is
You had had no remedy against these Rascals,
No Law, and't like your honour; would have kil'd you too
And roasted ye, and eaten ye, ere this time:
Notable knaves my Lord, unruly Rascals:
These youths have we tide up, put muzzels on 'em,
And pair'd their nailes, that honest civill Gentlemen,
And such most noble persons as your selfe is,
May live in peace, and rule the land with a twine thread.
These newes I bring,

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: And were they thus deliver'd ye?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: My Lord, I am no pen-man, nor no Orator,
My tongue was never oyl'd with Here and't like ye,
There I beseech yee, weigh, I am a souldier,
And truth I covet onely, no fine termes sir;
I come not to stand treating here; my businesse
Is with the Duke, and of such generall blessing—

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You have overthrowne the enemy, we know it,
And we rejoyce in't; ye have done like honest subjects,
You have done handsomely and well.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: But well sir?
But handsomly and well? what are we juglers?
Ile doe all that in cutting up a Capon.
But handsomely and well? does your Lordship take us
For the Dukes Tumblers? we have done bravely sir,
Ventur'd our lives like men.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Then bravely be it.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: And for as brave rewards we look, and graces,
We have sweat and bled for't sir.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: And ye may have it,
If you will stay the giving. Men that thank themselves first,
For any good they doe, take off the lustre,
And blot the benefit.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Are these the welcomes,
The Bells that ring out our rewards? pray heartily,
Early and late, there may be no more enemies:
Doe my good Lord, pray seriously, and sigh too,
For if there be—

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: They must be met, and fought with.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: By whom? by you? they must be met & flattererd.
Why, what a devill aild ye to do these things?
With what assurance dare ye mocke men thus?
You have but single lives, and those I take it
A Sword may find too: why do ye dam the Duke up?
And choake that course of love that like a River
Should fill our empty veines againe with comforts?
But it ye use these knick knacks,
This fast and loose, with faithfull men and honest,
Youl be the first will find it.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: You are too untemperate.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Better be so, and theese too, then unthankfull:
Pray use this old man so, and then we are paid all.
The Duke thanks ye for your service, & the Court thanks ye,
And wonderfull desirous they are to see ye;
Pray heaven we have roome enough to march for May-games,
Pageants, & bonfires for your welcome home Sir;
Here your most noble friend the Lord Boroskey,
A Gentleman too tender of your credit,
And ever in the Dukes eare, for your good Sir,
Crazie and sickly, yet to be your servant,
Has leapt into the open aire to meet ye.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The best is your words wound not, you are welcome home Sir.
Hartily welcome home, and for your service,
The noble overthrow you gave the Enemy,
The Duke salutes ye too with all his thanks Sir.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Sure they will now regard us.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: There's a reason:
But by the changing of the Colonels countenance,
The rolling of his eyes like angry billowes;
I feare the wind's not downe yet, Ancient.

speeches.speaker: Arch.
verse: Is the Duke well Sir?

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: Not much unhealthy,
Only a little grudging of an ague,
Which cannot last: he has heard, which makes him fearful,
And loath as yet to give your worth due welcome,
The sicknesse hath been somewhat hot i'th' Army,
Which happily may prove more doubt, then danger,
And more his feare then fate: yet howsoever,
An honest care—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ye say right, and it shall be;
For though upon my life 'tis but a rumor,
A meere opinion, without faith or feare in't;
For Sir, I thanke heaven, we never stood more healthy,
Never more high and lusty; yet to satisfie,
We cannot be too curious or too carefull
Of what concernes his state, wee'l draw away Sir,
And lodge at further distance, and lesse danger.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: It will be well.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: It will be very scurvy.
I smell it out, it stinks abominably,
Stir it no more.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: The Duke Sir would have you too,
For a short day or two, retyre to your owne house,
Whither himselfe will come to visit ye,
And give ye thanks.

speeches.speaker: Arch.
verse: I shall attend his pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: A trick, a lowsie trick: so hoa, a trick boyes.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: How now, what's that?

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: I thought I had found a Hare Sir,
But 'tis a Fox, an old Fox, shall we hunt him?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No more such words.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: The souldier's growne too sawcy,
You must tie him straiter up.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I doe my best Sir;
But men of free-born minds sometimes will flie out.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: May not we see the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: Not at this time Gentlemen,
Your Generall knowes the cause.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: We have no plague Sir,
Unlesse it be in our pay, nor no pox neither;
Or if we had, I hope that good old Courtier
Will not deny us place there.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Certaine my Lord,
Considering what we are and what we have done;
If not, what need ye may have, 'twould be better,
A great deale nobler, and taste honester
To use us with more sweetnes; men that dig
And lash away their lives at the Carts taile,
Double our comforts; meat, and their Masters thanks too,
When they worke well, they have: Men of our qualitie,
When they doe well, and venture for't with valor,
Fight hard, lye hard, feed hard, when they come home Sir,
And know these are deserving things, things worthy,
Can you then blame 'em if their minds a little
Be stirr'd with glory? 'tis a pride becomes 'em,
A litle season'd with ambition,
To be respected, reckon'd well, and honour'd
For what they have don: when to come home thus poorly,
And met with such unjointed joy, so looked on,
As if we had done no more but drest a horse well;
So entertain'd, as if I thank ye Gentlemen,
Take that to drinke, had pow'r to please a souldier?
Where be the shouts, the bels rung out, the people?
The Prince himself?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Peace: I perceive your eye Sir
Is fixt upon this Captaine for his freedome,
And happily you find his tongue too forward;
As I am Master of the place, I carry,
'Tis fit I thinke so too, but were I this man,
No stronger tye upon me, then the truth
And tongue to tell it, I should speake as he do's,
And thinke with modestie enough, such Saints
That daily thrust their loves & lives through hazards,
And fearelesse for their Countries peace, march hourely
Through all the doores of death, and know the darkest,
Should better be canoniz'd for their service:
What labour would these men neglect, what danger
Where honour is, though seated in a billow,
Rising as high as heaven, would not these souldiers,
Like to so many Sea-gods charge up to it?
Doe you see these swords? times Sithe was ne're so sharp Sir;
Nor ever at one harvest mow'd such handfuls:
Thoughts ne're so sudden, nor beliefe so sure,
When they are drawne, and were it not sometimes,
I swim upon their angers to allay 'em,
And like a calme depresse their fell intentions;
They are so deadly sure, nature would suffer —
And whose are all these glories? why, their Princes,
Their Countries, and their Friends? Alas, of all these,
And all the happy ends they bring, the blessings,
They only share the labors, a little joy then,
And outside of a welcome, at an upshot
Would not have done amisse Sir; But howsoever
Between me and my duty, no crack Sir
Shall dare appeare: I hope by my example
No discontent in them: without doubt Gentlemen,
The Duke will both looke suddenly and truly
On your deserts: Methinks 't were good they were paid Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: They shall be immediately; I stay for mony;
And any favour else—.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: We are all bound to ye;
And so I take my leave Sir; when the Duke pleases
To make me worthy of his eyes—

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Which will be suddenly,
I know his good thoughts to ye.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: With all duty,
And all humility, I shall attend Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: Once more you are welcome home: these shall be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Be sure we be: and hansomely.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Waite you on me sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And honestly: no jugling.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Will ye come sir?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Pray do not doubt.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
prose: We are no Boyes.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Well sir.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Here's money from the Duke, and 't please your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: 'Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: How sowre the Souldiers looke?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Is't told?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yes: and for every company a double pay,
And the Dukes love to all.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: That's worth a ducket.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You that be Officers, see it discharg'd then,
Why do not ye take it up?

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: 'Tis too heavy:
'Body o'me, I have strain'd mine arme.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Do ye scorne it?

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Has your Lordship any dice about ye? sit round Gentlemen.
And come on seaven for my share.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Do you thinke sir,
This is the end we fight? can this durt draw us
To such a stupid tamenesse, that our service
Neglected, and look'd lamely on, and skewd at
With a few honourable words, and this, is righted?
Have not we eyes and eares, to heare and see Sir,
And minds to understand the slights we carry?
I come home old, and full of hurts, men looke on me
As if I had got 'em from a whore, and shun me;
I tell my griefes, and feare my wants, I am answer'd,
Alas 'tis pity I pray dine with me on Sunday:
These are the sores we are sicke of, the minds malladies,
And can this cure 'em? you should have us'd us nobly,
And for our doing well, as well proclam'd us,
To the worlds eye, have shewd and fainted us,
Then ye had paid us bravely: then we had shin'd sir,
Not in this gilded stuffe but in our glory:
You may take backe your money.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: This I fear'd still.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Consider better Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Thanke your Lordship:
And now I'l put on my considering cap:
My Lord, that I am no Courtier, you may guesse it
By having no sute to you for this money:
For though I want, I want not this, nor shall not,
Whilst you want that civility to ranke it
With those rights we expected; money growes sir,
And men must gather it, all is not put in one purse.
And that I am no Carter, I could never whistle yet:
But that I am a Souldier, and a Gentleman,
And a fine Gentleman, and't like your honour,
And most pleasant companion: all you that are witty,
Come list to my ditty: come set in boyes,
With your Lordships patience.
How do you like my Song, my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Even as I like your self, but 'twould be a great deale better,
You would prove a great deale wifer, and take this mony,
In your owne phrase I speake now sir, and 'tis very well
You have learn'd to sing; for since you prove so liberall, To refuse such meanes as this, maintaine your voice still,
Twill prove your best friend.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: 'Tis a singing age sir,
A merry moone here now: I'le follow it:
Fidling, and fooling now, gaines more then fighting.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
prose: What is't you blench at? what would you aske? speak freely.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: And so we dare: a triumph for the Generall.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: And then an honour speciall to his vertue.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: That we may be prefer'd that have serv'd for it,
And cram'd up into favour like the worshipfull,
At least upon the Cities charge made drunke
For one whole year; we have done 'em ten yeares service;
That we may enjoy our lechery without grudging,
And mine, or thine be nothing, all things equall,
And catch as catch may be proclaimed: that when we borrow,
And have no will to pay againe, no Law
Lay hold upon vs, nor no, Court controule us.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Some of these may come to passe; the Duke may do 'em,
And no doubt will: the Generall will find too,
And so will you, if you but stay with patience: I have no power.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Nor will: come fellow Souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Pray be not so distrustfull.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: There are waies yet,
And honest waies; we are not brought up Starues.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: If your Lordship
Have any silke stockings, that have holes i'th'heeles,
Or ever an honourable Cassock that wants buttons,
I could have cur'd such malladies: your Lordships custome
And my good Ladies, if the bones want setting
In her old bodies—

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: This is disobedience.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Eight pence a day, and hard Eggs.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Troop off Gentlemen,
Some Coine we have, whilst this lasts, or our credits,
Wee'll never sell our Generalls worth for six-pence.
Ye are beholding to us.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Fare ye well Sir,
And buy a pipe with that: doe ye see this skarfe sir?
By this hand Ile cry Brooms in't, birchen Brooms sir,
Before I eate one bit from your benevolence.
Now to our old occupations againe.
By your leave Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You will bite when ye are sharper; take up the money.
This love I must remove, this fondnes to him,
This tendernesse of heart; I have lost my way else.
There is no sending man, they will not take it,
They are yet too full of pillage,
They'll dance for't ere't belong:
Come, bring it after.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: How now, refus'd their money?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Very bravely,
And stand upon such termes 'tis terrible.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Where's Archas?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Hee's retir'd Sir, to his house,
According to your pleasure, full of dutie
To outward shew: but what within—

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Refuse it?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Most confidently: 'tis not your revenewes
Can feed them sir, and yet they have found a Generall
That knowes no ebbe of bountie: there they eate Sir,
And loath your invitations.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: 'Tis not possible,
Hee's poor as they.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You'll find it otherwise.
Pray make your journey thither presently,
And as ye goe Ile open yee a wonder.
Good sir this morning.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Follow me, Ile doe it.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: But doe you thinke my brother loves her.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Certaine Madam,
He speaks much of her, and sometimes with wonder,
Oft wishes she were nobler borne.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Doe you thinke him honest?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Your Grace is nearer to his heart, then I am,
Upon my life I hold him so.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: 'Tis a poore wench,
I would not have her wrong'd: methinks my Brother—
But I must not give rules to his affections;
Yet if he weigh her worth—

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You need not feare Madam.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I hope I shall not: Lord Burris
I love her well; I know not, there is something
Makes me bestow more then a care upon her:
I doe not like that ring, from him to her;
I meane to women of her way, such tokens
Rather appeare as baits, then royall bounties:
I would not have it so.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You will not find it,
Upon my troth I thinke his most ambition
Is but to let the world know 'has a hansome Mistris:
Will your Grace command me any service to him?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Remember all my duty.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Blessings crowne ye:
What's your will Lady?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Anything that's honest;
And if you thinke it sits so poore a service,
Clad in a ragged vertue, may reach him,
I doe beseech your Lordship speake it humbly.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Faire one I will: in the best phrase I have too,
And so I kisse your hand

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Your Lordships servant.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Come hither wench, what art thou doing with that Ring.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I am looking on the posie, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: What is't?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: The Jewels set within.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: But where the joy wench,
When that invisible Jewel's lost? why dost thou smile so?
What unhappy meaning hast thou?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Nothing Madam,
But only thinking what strange spels these Rings have,
And how they worke with some.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I feare with you too.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: This could not cost above a Crowne.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Twill cost you
The shaving of your crowne, if not the washing.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: But he that sent it, makes the vertue greater.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I and the vice too Madam: goodnes blesse me:
How sit 'tis for my finger.

speeches.speaker: 2 W.
verse: No doubt you'l find too
A finger fit for you.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Sirrah, Petesca,
What wilt thou give me for the good that followes this?
But thou hast Rings enough, thou art provided:
Heigh ho, what must I doe now?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: You'l be taught that,
The easiest part that e're you learn't, I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ay me, ay me.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: You will divide too, shortly,
Your voice comes finely forward.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Come hither wanton,
Thou art not surely as thou saist.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I would not:
But sure there is a witchcraft in this Ring, Lady,
Lord how my heart leaps.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Twill goe pit a pat shortly.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: And now methinks a thousand of the Dukes shapes.

speeches.speaker: 2 W.
verse: Will no lesse serve ye?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: In ten thousand smiles.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Heaven blesse the wench.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: With eyes that will not be denide to enter;
And such soft sweet embraces; take It from me,
I am undone else Madam: I 'm lost else.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: What ailes the girle?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How suddenly I 'm alter'd?
And growne my selfe againe? doe not you feele it?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: Weare that, and I'le weare this:
I'le try the strengthon't.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How cold my bloud growes now?
Here's sacred vertue:
When I leave to honour this,
Every houre to pay a kisse,
When each morning I arise,
Or I forget a sacrifice:
When this figure in ray faith,
And the purenes that it hath,
I pursue not with my will,
Nearer to arrive at still:
When I lose, or change this Jewell,
I lie me faith, and heaven be cruell.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: You have halfe confirm'd me,
Keep but that way sure,
And what this charme can doe, let me endure.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Carry your selfe discreetly, it concernes me,
The Duke's come in, none of your froward passions,
Nor no distastes to any: Prethee Theodor,
By my life, boy, 'twill mine me.

speeches.speaker: The,
verse: I have done Sir,
So there be no foule play he brings along with him.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: What's that to you?
Let him bring what please him,
And whom, and how.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: So they meane well—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Is't sit you be a Judge sirrah,

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis sfit I feele Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Get a banquet ready,
And trim your selves up hansomly.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: To what end?
Doe you meane to make 'em whores?
Hang up a signe then,
And set 'em out to Livery.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Whose sonne art thou?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Yours Sir, I hope: but not of yonr disgraces.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Full twenty thousand men I have commanded,
And all their minds with this, calm'd all their angers;
And shall a boy of mine owne breed too, of mine owne bloud,
One crooked stick—

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Pray take your way, and thrive in't,
I'le quit your house; if taint or black dishonour
Light on ye, 'tis your owne, I have no share in't.
Yet if it doe fall out so, as I feare it,
And partly find it too—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Hast thou no reverence?
No dutie in thee?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: This shall shew I obey ye:
I dare not stay: I would have shew'd my love too,
And that you aske as duty, with my life sir,
Had you but thought me worthy of your hazzards,
Which heaven preserve ye from, and keep the Duke too:
And there's an end of my wishes, God be with ye.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stubborne, yet full of that we all love, honesty,
Lord Burris, where's the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: In the great chamber Sir,
And there stayes till he see you, ye 'have a fine house here.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: A poore contented lodge, unsit for his presence,
Yet all the joy it hath.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I hope a great one, and for your good, brave Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I thanke ye Lord:
And now my service to the Duke.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I'le wait on ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: May this be credited?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Disgrace me else,
And never more with favour looke upon me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: It seemes impossible.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: It cannot chuse Sir,
Till your owne eies behold it; but that it is so,
And that by this meanes the too haughtie souldier
Has been so cramm'd and fed, he cares not for ye;
Beleeve, or let me perish: Let your eyes
As you observe the house, but where I point it,
Make stay, and take a view, and then you have found it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I'le follow your direction: welcome Archas,
You are welcome home brave Lord, we are come to visit ye,
And thanke ye for your service.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Twas so poore Sir,
In true respect of what I owe your Highnesse,
It merits nothing.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Are these faire ones yours Lord?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Their Mother made me thinke so Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Stand up Ladies:
Beshrew my heart they are faire ones; methinks fitter
The lustre of the Court, then thus live darken'd:
I would see your house Lord Archas, it appeares to me,
A hansome pile.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis neate but no great structure;
I'le be your Graces guide, give me the keyes there.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Lead on, wee'l follow ye: begin with the Gallery,
I think that's one.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis so, and't please ye Sir,
The rest above are lodgings all.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Goe on Sir.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: The Duke gone thither, doe you say?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Yes marry doe I,
And all the ducklings too: but what the'l doe there.—

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I hope they'l crowne his service.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: With a Custard;
This is no weather for rewards; they crowne his service?
Rather, they goe to shave his crowne: I was rated,
As if I had been a dog had worried sheep, out of doores,
For making but a doubt.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: They must now grace him.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Marke but the end.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: I am sure they should reward him, they cannot want him.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They that want honesty, want any thing.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: The Duke is so noble in his owne thoughts.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: That I grant ye,
If those might only sway him: but 'tis most certaine,
So many new borne slyes, his light gave life too,
Buzze in his beames, flesh slies, and Butterflies,
Hornets, and humming Scarrabs, that not one honey Bee
That's loden with true labour, and brings home
Encrease, and credit, can scape rifling,
And what she sucks for sweet, the turne to bitternesse.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: Shall we go see what they do, & talke our minds to 'em?

speeches.speaker: 'P.
verse: That we have done too much, & to no purpose.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Shall we be hang'd for him?
I have a great mind to be hangd now
For doing some brave thing for him; a worse end will take me
And for an action of no worth; not honour him?
Upon my conscience even the devill, the very devill
(Not to belye him) thinkes him an honest man,
I am sure he has sent him soules any times these twenty yeares,
Able to furnish all his fishmarket.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Leave thy talking
And come, let's go to dinner and drinke to him,
We shall heare more ere supper time: if he be honour'd,
He has deserv'd it well, and we shall sight for't:
If he be ruin'd, so, we know the worst then,
And for my selfe I'le meet it.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I ne're feare it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: They are handsome roomes all, well contriv'd and fitted,
Full of covenience, the prospects excellent.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Now will your Grace passe downe, and do me but the honour
To taste a Country banket?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What roome's that?
I would see all now; what conveyance has it?
I see you have kept the best part yet; pray open it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ha? I misdoubted this: 'tis of no receipte sir,
For your eyes most unfit—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I long to see it,
Because I would judge of the whole peece: some excellent paintings,
Or some rare spoiles you would keep to entertaine me
An other time, I know.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: In troth there is not,
Nor any thing worth your sight: below I have
Some fountaines, and some ponds.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I would see this now.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Borosky, thou art a knave; It containes nothing
But rubbish from the other roomes and unnecessaries:
Wil't please you see a strange Clocke?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: This, or nothing:
Why should you barre it up thus with defences
Above the rest, unlesse it contain'd something
More excellent, and curious of keeping:
Open't, for I will see't.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: The keyes are lost sir;
Do's your grace thinke if it were fit for you,
I could be so unmannerly?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I will see it, and either shew it—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Good sir—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thanke ye Archas,
You shew your love abundantly,
Do I use to entreat thus? force it open,

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: That were inhospitable: you are his guest sir,
And with his greatest joy, to entertaine ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Hold thy peace foole; will ye open it?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Sir, I cannot.
I must not if I could.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Goe breake it open.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: I must withstand that force: Be not too rash Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Unarme him first, then if he be not obstinate,
Preserve his life.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I thanke your grace, I take it:
And now take you the keyes, goe in and see Sir;
There feed your eyes with wonder, and thanke that traytor,
That thing that sels his faith for favor.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Sir, what moves ye?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I have kept mine pure: Lord Burris there's a Judas,
That for a smile will sell ye all: a Gentleman?
The Devill 'has more truth, and has maintain'd it;
A whores heart more beliefe in't.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What's all this Archas?
I cannot blame ye to conceale it so,
This most inestimable treasure.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Yours Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Nor doe I wonder now the souldier sleights me.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Be not deceiv'd; he has had no favor here Sir,
Nor had you knowne this now, but for that pickthank,
That lost man in his faith, he has reveal'd it,
To suck a little honey from ye has betray'd it.
I sweare he smiles upon me, and forsworne too,
Thou crackt, uncurrant Lord: I'le tell ye all Sir:
Your Sire, before his death, knowing your temper,
To be as bounteous as the aire, and open,
As flowing as the Sea to all that follow'd ye,
Your great mind sit for war and glory, thriftily
Like a great husband, to preserve your actions,
Collected all this treasure: to our trusts,
To mine I meane, and to that long-tongu'd Lords there,
He gave the knowledge, and the charge of all this,
Upon his death-bed too: And on the Sacrament
He swore us thus, never to let this treasure
Part from our secret keepings, till no hope
Of subject could relieve ye, all your owne wasted,
No help of those that lov'd ye could supply ye,
And then some great exploit afoot; my honestie
I would have kept till I had made this usefull;
I shew'd it, and I stood it to the tempest,
And usefull to the end 'twas left: I am cozen'd,
And so are you too, if you spend this vainly;
This worme that crept into ye has abus'd ye,
Abus'd your fathers care, abus'd his faith too:
Nor can this masse of money make him man more,
A stea'd dog has more soule, an Ape more honestie:
All mine ye have amongst it, farwell that,
I cannot part with't nobler; my hearts cleare,
My conscience smooth as that, no rub upon't,
But O thy hell.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I seeke no heaven from you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thy gnawing hell Boroskey, it will find thee:
Would ye heape coles upon his head has wrong'd ye,
'Has ruin'd your estate? give him this money,
Melt it into his mouth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What little Trunck's that,
That there o'th' top, that's lockt?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: You'l find it rich Sir,
Richer I think then all.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You were not covetous,
Nor wour to weave your thoughts with such a coursenes;
Pray racke not honestie.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Be sure ye see it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Bring out the Trunck.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You'l find that treasure too,
All I have left me now.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What's this a poore gowne?
And this a peece of Seneca?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Yes sure Sir,
More worth then all your gold, yet ye have enough on't,
And of a Mine far purer, and more precious:
This sels no friends, nor searches into counsels,
And yet all counsell and all friends live here Sir,
Betrayes no faith, yet handles all that's trusty;
Wilt please ye leave me this.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: With all my heart Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: What sayes your Lordship to't?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I dare not rob ye.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Poore miserable men, you have rob'd your selves both;
This gown, and this unvalu'd treasure, your brave Father,
Found me a childe at schoole with, in his progresse,
Where such a love he tooke to some few answers,
Unhappie boyish toyes hit in my head then,
That suddenly I made him thus as I was;
For here was all the wealth I brought his Highnes:
He carried me to Court, there bred me up,
Bestow'd his favours on me, taught me Armes first,
With those an honest mind; I serv'd him truly,
And where he gave me trust, I thinke I fail'd not;
Let the world speake: I humbly thanke your Highnes,
You have done more, and nobler, eas'd mine age Sir;
And to this care, a faire quietus given:
Now to my Booke againe.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You have your wish Sir,
Let some bring off the treasure.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Some is his sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: None, none my Lord: a poore unworthy reaper,
The harvest is his graces.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thanke ye Archas.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: But will not you repent Lord? when this is gone,
Where will your Lordship?—

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Pray take you no care sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Do's your Grace like my house?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Wondrous well Archas,
You have made me richly welcome.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I did my best sir,
Is there any thing else may please your Grace?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Your daughters
I had forgot, send them to Court.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: How's that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I said your daughters; see it done: I'le have 'em
Attend my sister, Archas.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thanke your Highnes.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Through all the waies I dare,
I'le serve your temper, though you try me too far.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I wonder we heare no newes.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Heere's your fathers servant,
He comes in haste too, now we shall know all sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: How now?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I am glad I have met you sir; your father
Intreats ye presently make haste unto him.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What newes?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: None of the best Sir, I am asham'd to tell it,
Pray aske no more.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Did not I tell ye Gentlemen?
Did not I prophesie? he is undone then.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Not so Sir, but as neare it —

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: There's no help now;
The Armye's scatter'd all, though discontent,
Not to be rallied up in haste to help this.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Plague of the devill; have ye watch'd your seasons?
We shall watch you ere long.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Farewell, there's no cure,
We must endure all now: I know what I'le doe.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Nay there's no striving, they have a hand upon us,
A heavy, and a hard one.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Now I have it,
We have yet some Gentlemen, some boyes of mettle,
(What, are we bob'd thus still, colted, and carted?)
And one mad trick wee'l have to shame these vipers;
Shall I blesse 'em?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Farwell: I have thought my way too.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Were never such rare cryes in Christendome,
As Mosco shall affoord: wee'l live by fooling,
Now lightings gone, and they shall find & feele it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No more: it must be so; do you think I would send ye
Your father, and your friend —

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Pray Sir be good to us,
Alas, we know no Court, nor seeke that knowledge;
We are content like harmles things at home,
Children of your content, bred up in quiet,
Only to know our selves, to seeke a wisedome
From that we understand, easie, and honest;
To make our actions worthy of your honour,
Their ends as innocent as we begot 'em:
What shall we looke for Sir, what shall we learne there,
That this more private sweetnesse cannot teach us?
Vertue was never built upon ambition,
Nor the soules beauties bred out of braverie:
What a terrible Father would you seeme to us,
Now you have moulded us, and wrought our tempers
To easie and obedient waies, uncrooked,
Where the faire minde can never lose, nor loiter,
Now to divert our Natures, now to stem us
Roughly against the tide of all this treasure?
Would ye have us proud? 'tis sooner bred, then buried;
Wickedly proud? for such things dwell at Court Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Would you have your children learn to forget their father,
And when he dies dance on his Monument?
Shall we seeke vertue in a Sattin gowne,
Imbroider'd vertue? faith in a well-curl'd feather?
And set our credits to the tune of green sleeves?
This may be done; and if you like, it shall be.
You should have sent us thither, when we were younger,
Our Maiden-heads at a higher rate, our Innocence
Able to make a Mart indeed: we are now too old Sir,
Perhaps they'l think too cunning too, and slight us,
Besides we are altogether unprovided,
Unfurnish'd utterly of the rules should guide us:
This Lord comes licks his hand; and protests to me:
Compares my beauty to a thousand fine things;
Mountaines, and fountaines, trees, and stars, and goblins;
Now have not I the fashion to beleeve him,
He offers me the honourable curtesie,
To lye with me all night, what a miserie is this?
I am bred up so foolishly alas I dare not,
And how madly these things will shew there.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I send ye not,
Like parts infected, to draw more corruption;
Like Spiders to grow great, with growing evill:
With your owne vertues season'd, and my prayers,
The card of goodnes in your minds, that showes ye
When ye saile false; the needle touch'd with honour,
That through the blackest stormes, still points at happines:
Your bodies the tall barks, rib'd round with goodnes;
Your heavenly soules the Pilots, thus I send you;
Thus I prepare your voyage, sound before ye,
And ever as you saile through this worlds vanitie,
Discover sholes, rocks, quicksands, cry out to ye,
Like a good Master tack about for honour:
The Court is vertue's schoole; at least it should be;
Nearer the Sun the Mine lies, the mettels purer:
Be it granted, if the Spring be once infected.
Those branches that flow from him must run muddy;
Say you find some sins there, and those no small ones,
And they like lazie fits begin to shake ye:
Say they affect your strengths, my happy children,
Great things through greatest hazards are atchiev'd still,
And then they shine, then goodnes has his glory,
His Crowne fast rivited, then time moves under,
Where, through the mist of errors, like the Sun,
Through thicke and pitchie clouds, he breaks out nobly.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I thanke you Sir, you have made me half a souldier,
I will to court most willingly, most fondly.
And if there be such stirring things amongst 'em,
Such travellers into Virginia,
As fame reports, if they can win me, take me:
I thinke I have a close ward, and a sure one;
A honest mind I hope, 'tis petticote-proofe,
Chaine proofe, and jewell-proof: I know 'tis gold proof,
A Coach and foure horses cannot draw me from it:
As for your hansome faces, and filed tongues,
Curl'd Millers heads; I have another word for them,
And yet I'le slatter too, as fast as they doe,
And lye, but not as lewdly: Come, be valiant sister,
She that dares not stand the push o'th' Court, dares nothing,
And yet come off ungrased: Sir, like you,
We both affect great dangers now; & the world shall see
All glory lies not in mans victorie.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Mine owne Honora.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I am very fearfull,
Would I were stronger built? you would have me honest?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Or not at all my Viola.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I'le thinke on't,
For 'tis no easie promise, and live there;
Doe you thinke we shall doe well?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Why what should aile us?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Certaine they'l tempt us strongly: beside the glory
Which women may affect: they are hansome gentlemen,
Every part speaks: nor is it one deniall,
Nor two, nor ten: from every looke we give 'em,
They'le frame a hope: even from our prayers, promises,

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Let 'em feed so, & be fat: there is no feare wench,
If thou bee'st fast to thy self.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: I hope I shall be:
And your example will work more.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thou shalt not want it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: How doe you Sir, can you lend a man an Angell?
I heare you let out money.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Very well Sir,
You are pleasantly dispos'd: I am glad to see it,
Can you lend me your patience, and be rul'd by me?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Is't come to Patience now?

speeches.speaker: Arch.
verse: Is t not a vertue?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: I know not. I ne're found it so.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: That's because
Thy anger ever knowes, and not thy judgement.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: I know you have been rifl'd.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Nothing lesse boy:
Lord what opinions these vaine people publish?
Rifl'd of what?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Study your vertue patience,
It may get Mustard to your meat. Why in such haste sir,
Sent ye for me?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: For this end onely, Theodore,
To wait upon your sisters to the Court;
I am commanded they live there.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Toth' Court sir?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Toth' Court I say.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And must I wait upon 'em?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Yes, 'tis most fit yee should, ye are their brother.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Is this the businesse? I had thought your mind sir
Had been set forward on some noble action,
Something had truely stirr'd ye. Toth' Court with these?
Why they are your daughters sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: All this I know sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: The good old woman on a bed he threw.
Toth' Court?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thou art not mad.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Nor drunke as you are:
Drunke with your duty sir: doe you call it duty?
A pox o' duty, what can these doe there?
What should they doe? Can ye look Babies sisters
In the young Gallants eyes, & twirle their Band-strings?
Can ye ride out to ayre your selves? pray sir,
Be serious with me: doe you speake this truely?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Why didst thou never heare of women
Yet at Court boy?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Yes, and good women too, very good women,
Excellent honest women: but are you sure sir,
That these will prove so?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: There's the danger brother.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: God a mercy wench, thou hast a grudging of it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Now be you serious sir, and observe what I say,
Doe it, and doe it handsomely: goe with 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: With all my heart sir; I am in no fault now;
If they be thought whores for being in my company;
Pray write upon their backs, they are my sisters,
And where I shall deliver 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ye are wondrous jocund,
But prethee tell me, art thou so lewd a fellow,
I never knew thee faile a truth,

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am a souldier,
And spell you what that meanes.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: A Souldier?
What dost thou make of me?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Your Pallat's downe sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I thanke yee sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Come, shall we to this matter?
You will to Court?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: If you will please to honour us.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Ile honour yee, I warrant: Ile set yee off
With such a lustre wenches: Alas poore Viola,
Thou art a foole, thou criest for eating white-bread:
Be a good huswife of thy teares, and save 'em,
Thou wilt have time enough to shed 'em sister.
Doe you weep too? nay then Ile foole no more.
Come worthy sisters, since it must be so,
And since he thinks it fit to trie your vertues,
Be you as strong to truth, as I to guard yee,
And this old gentleman shall have joy of ye.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Burris take you ten thousand of those Crowns,
And those two chaines of Pearle they hold the richest,
I give 'em yee.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I humbly thanke your grace;
And may your great example worke in me
That noble charity to men more worthy,
And of more wants.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: You beare a good minde Burris;
Take twenty thousand now: Be not so modest,
It shall be so, I give 'em: goe, there's my ring for't.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
prose: Heaven blesse your Highnesse ever.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: You are honest.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: They're comming now to Court, as faire as vertue:
Two brighter starres ne're rose here.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Peace, I have it,
And what my Art can doe; the Duke—

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I am gone,
Remember.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I am counsell'd to the full sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: My prettie Mistris, whither lyes your businesse?
How kindly I should take this, were it to me now?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I must confesse immediately to your grace,
At this time.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You have no addresse, I doe believe ye,
I would yee had.

speeches.speaker: Al
verse: 'Twere too much boldnesse Sir,
Upon so little knowledge, lesse deserving.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You'll make a perfect Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: A very poore one.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A very faire one sweet: come hither to me.
What killing eyes this wench has? in his glorie
Not the bright Sun, when the Sirian starre reignes,
Shines halfe so fierie.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why does your grace so view me?
Nothing but common handsomenesse dwells here sir,
Scarce that: your grace is pleas'd to mock my meanness.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thou shalt not goe: I doe not lie unto thee,
In my eye thou appear'st—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Dim not the sight sir,
I am too dull an object.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Canst thou love me?
Canst thou love him will honour thee?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I can love,
And love as you doe too: but 'twill not shew well:
Or if it doe shew here where all light lustres,
Tinsell affections, make a glorious glistering,
Twill halt ith' handsome way.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Are yee so cunning?
Dost think I love not truely?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: No, ye cannot,
You never travell'd that way yet: pray pardon me,
I prate so boldly to you.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: There's no harme done:
But what's your reason, sweet?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I would tell your grace,
But happily—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: It shall be pleasing to me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I should love you again, & then you would hate me.
With all my service I should follow yee,
And through all dangers.

speeches.speaker: Du
verse: This would more provoke me,
More make me see thy worthes,
More make me meet 'em.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You should doe so, if yee did well and truely.
But though yee be a Prince, and have power in ye,
Power of example too, ye have fail'd and falter'd.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Give me example where?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You had a Mistris,
Oh heaven, so bright, so brave a dame, so lovely,
In all her life so true.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That serv'd yee with that constancy, that care,
That lov'd your will, and woo'd it too.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That nus'rd your honour up, held fast your vertue,
And when she kist encreas'd, not stole your goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And I neglected her?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Lost her, forsook her,
Wantonly slung her off.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What was her name?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Her name as lovely as her selfe, as noble,
And in it all that's excellent.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What was it?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Her name was Beau-desert:
Doe you know her now sir?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Beau-desert? I not remember—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I know you doe not:
Yet she has a plainer name; Lord Archas service;
Do you yet remember her? there was a Mistris
Fairer then women, far fonder to you sir,
Then Mothers to their first-borne joyes: Can you love?
Dare you professe that truth to me a stranger,
A thing of no regard, no name, no lustre,
When your most noble love you have neglected,
A beautie all the world would wooe and honour?
Would you have me credit this? thinke ye can love me,
And hold ye constant, when I have read this storie?
Is't possible you should ever favour me,
To a slight pleasure prove a friend, and fast too,
When, where you were most ty'd, most bound to benefit,
Bound by the chaines of honesty and honour,
You have broke and boldly too? I am a weak one,
Arm'd onely with my feares: I beseech your Grace
Tempt me no further.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Who taught you this Lesson?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Woefull experience Sir: if you seek a faire one,
Worthy your love, if yet you have that perfect,
Two daughters of his ruin'd vertue now
Arive at Court, excellent faire indeed sir,
But this will be the plague on't, they'r excellent honest.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: I love thy face.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Upon my life yee cannot.
I doe not love it my selfe Sir, 'tis a lewd one,
So truely ill Art cannot mend it; 'sod if 'twere handsome,
At least if I thought so, you should heare me talke sir
In a new straine; and though ye are a Prince,
Make ye Petition to me too, and wait my answers;
Yet o' my conscience I should pitty yee,
After some ten yeares siege.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Prethee doe now.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: What would ye doe?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why I would lye with yee.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I doe not think yee would.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Introth I would wench.
Here, take this Jewell.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Out upon't that's scurvee.
Nay, if we doe, sure wee'll doe for good fellowship,
For pure love, or nothing: thus you shall be sure sir
You shall not pay too deare for't.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Sure I cannot.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: By'r Lady but yee may: when ye have found me able,
To doe your work well, ye may pay my wages.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why does your Grace start back?

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I ha' seen that shakes me:
Chills all my bloud: O where is faith or goodnesse?
Alinda thou art false, false, false thou faire one,
Wickedly false; and (woe is me) I see it.
For ever false.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: I am glad't has taken thus right.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Ile goe aske my Lady, sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Whether I shall lye with ye, or no: If I find he— willing—r
For look ye sir, I have sworn, while I am in her service—
('Twas a rash oath I must confesse.)

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Thou mockst me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why, would yee lye with me, if I were willing?
Would you abuse my weaknesse?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I would peece it,
And make it stronger.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I humbly thank your highnesse,
When you piece me, you must piece me to my Coffin:
When you have got my Maiden-head, I take it,
'Tis not an inch of an Apes taile will restore it;
I love ye, and I honour yee, but this way
Ile neither love nor serve yee:
Heaven change your minde sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: And thine too:
For it must be chang'd, it shall be.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: They are goodly gentlewomen.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: They are,
Wondrous sweet women both.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Does your Lordshid like 'em?
They are my sisters sir; good lusty Lasses,
They'll doe their labour well, I warrant yee
You'll finde no bed-straw here sir.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thanke yee brother.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: This is not so strongly built: but she is good mettle,
Of a good stirring straine too: she goes tith sir.
Here they be gentlemen must make ye merry,
The toyes you wot of: doe you like their complexions?
They be no Moors: what think ye of this hand gentlemen?
Here's a white Altar for your sacrifice:
A thousand kisses here. Nay, keep off yet gentlemen,
Let's start first, & have fair play: what would ye give now
To turne the globe up, and finde the rich Moluccas?
To passe the straights? here (doe ye itch) by St. Nicolas,
Here's that will make ye scratch and claw,
Claw my fine Gentlemen, move ye in divers sorts:
Pray ye let me request yee, to forget
To say your prayers, whilst these are Courtiers;
Or if yee needs will thinke of heaven, let it be no higher
Then their eyes?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: How will ye have 'em bestow'd sir?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Even how your Lordship please,
So you doe not bake 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Bake 'em.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: They are too high a meat that way, they run to gelly.
But if you'l have 'em for your own dyet, take my counsel,
Stew 'em between two feather-beds.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Please you Colonell
To let 'em wait upon the Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Yes sir,
And thanke your honour too: but then happily,
These noble Gentlemen shall have no accesse to 'em,
And to have 'em buy new cloathes, studdy new faces,
And keep a stinking stirre with themselves for nothing,
'Twill not be well y'faith: they have kept their bodies,
And bin at charge for Bathes: do you see that shirt there?
Way but the morall meaning, 'twill be grievous:
Alas, I brought 'em to delight these gentlemen,
I weigh their wants by mine: I brought 'em wholsome,
Wholsome, and young my Lord, and two such blessings
They will not light upon againe in ten yeare.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: 'Tis fit they wait upon her.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They are fit for any thing.
They'll wait upon a man, they are not bashfull,
Carrie his cloak, or untie his points, or any thing,
Drink drunk, and take Tobacco; the familiarst fooles—
This wench will leap over stools too, & sound a Trumpet,
Wrastle, and pitch the Bar; they are finely brought up,

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ladies, ye are bound to your brother,
And have much cause to thank him:
Ile ease ye of this charge, and to the Princesse,
So please you, Ile attend 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thank your Lordship:
If there be e're a private corner as yee goe Sir,
A foolish lobbie out oth' way, make danger,
Trie what they are, trie.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ye are a merrie gentleman.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I would faine be your honours kinseman.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ye are to curst sir.

speeches.speaker: Th.
prose: Farewel wenches, keep close your ports, y'are washt else.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Brother bestow your fears where they are needfull.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Honor thy name is, and I hope thy nature.
Goe after, Gentlemen, goe, get a snatch if you can,
Yond'old Erra Pater will never please 'em.
Alas I brought 'em for you, but see the luck on't,
I sweare I meant as honestlie toward ye—
Nay doe not crie good gentlemen: a little counsell
Will doe no harme: they'll walke abroad ith' evenings,
Ye may surprize 'em easily, they weare no Pistols.
Set downe your mindes in Metre, flowing Metre,
And get some good old linnen woman to deliver it,
That has the trick on't: you cannot faile:
Farewell gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You have frighted off these flesh-flies.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Flesh-flies indeed my Lord.
And it must be verie stinking flesh they will not seize on.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Your Lordship bid me bring this Casket.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Yes. Good Colonell
Commend me to your worthy father, and as a pledge
He ever holds my love, and service to him,
Deliver him this poore, but hearty token,
And where I may be his—

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Ye are too noble;
A wonder here my Lord, that dare be honest,
When all men hold it vitious: I shall deliver it,
And with it your most noble love. Your servant.
Were there but two more such at Court, 'twere Sainted,
This wil buy brawn this Christmas yet, & Muscadine.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Broom, Broom, the bonnie Broom,
Come buy my Birchen Broom,
Ith' warres we have no more room,
Buy all my bonnie Broom.
For a kisse take two;
If those will not doe,
For a little, little pleasure,
Take all my whole treasure:
If all these will not do't,
Take the Broom-man to boot.
Broom, Broom, the bonnie Broome.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: The wars are done and gone,
And Souldiers now neglected, Pedlers are,
Come maidens, come alone,
For I can shew you handsome, handsome ware.
Powders for, for the head,
And drinks for your bed,
To make yee blith and bonney.
As well in the night we souldiers can fight,
And please a young wench as any.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: I have fine Potato's,
Ripe Potato's.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
verse: Will ye buy any Honesty, come away,
I sell it openly by day,
I bring no forced light, nor no Candle
To cozen yee; come buy and handle:
This will shew the great man good,
The Trades-man where he sweares and lyes,
Each Lady of a noble bloud,
The Citie dame to rule her eyes:
Ye are rich men now: come buy, and then
Ile make yee richer, honest-men.

speeches.speaker: 4 Sol.
verse: Have ye any crackt maiden-heads, to new leach or mend?
