Have ye any old maiden-heads to sell or to change?
Bring 'em to me with a little pretty gin,
Ile clout 'em, Ile mend 'em, Ile knock in a pin,
Shall make 'em as good maids agen,
As ever they have bin.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: What means all this, why do y' sel Brooms Ancient?
Is it in wantonnesse, or want?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: The onely reason is,
To sweep your Lordships conscience: here's one for the nonce.
Gape sir, you have swallowed many a goodlier matter—
The onely casting for a crazie conscience.

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
prose: Will your Lordship buy any honestie? 'twill be worth your money.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: How is this?

speeches.speaker: 3 Sol.
verse: Honestie my Lord, 'tis here in a quill.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Take heed you open it not, for 'tis so subtle,
The least puffe of wind will blow it out oth' kingdome.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: Will your Lordship to taste a fine Potato?
'Twill advance your wither'd state.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Fill your honour full of most noble itches,
And make Jack dance in your Lordships breeches.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: If your daughters on their beds,
Have bow'd, or crackt their maiden-heads;
If in a Coach with two much tumbling,
They chance to crie, fie, fo, what fumbling;
If her foot slip, and downe fall shee,
And break her leg 'bove the knee,
The one and thirtieth of Februarie let this be tane,
And they shall be arrant maids againe.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ye are brave souldiers; keep your wantonnesse,
A winter will come on to shake this wilfulnesse.
Disport your selves, & when you want your money—

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Broom, Broom, &c.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You must not be so fearefull, little one,
Nor Lady you so sad, you will ne're make Courtiers
With these dull sullen thoughts; this place is pleasure,
Preserv'd to that use, so inhabited;
And those that live here, live delightfull, joyfull:
These are the Gardens of Adonis, Ladies,
Where all sweets to their free and noble uses,
Grow ever young and courted.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Blesse me heaven,
Can things of her yeares arrive at these rudiments?
By your leave fair gentlewoman, how long have you bin here?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Faith much about a week.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: You have studied hard,
And by my faith arriv'd at a great knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Were not you bashfull at first?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I, I, for an houre or two:
But when I saw people laugh'd at me for it,
And thought it a dull breeding—

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: You are govern'd here then
Much after the mens opinions.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ever Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: And what they think is honourable.—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Most precisely
We follow with all faith.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: A goodly Catechisme.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: But bashfull for an houre or two?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Faith to say true,
I do not think I was so long: for look yee,
Tis to no end here, put on what shape ye will,
And soure your selfe with ne're so much austeritie,
You shall be courted in the same, and won too,
'Tis but some two houres more; and so much time lost,
Which we hold pretious here: In so much time now
As I have told you this, you may lose a servant,
Your age, nor all your Art can e're recover.
Catch me occasion as she comes, hold fast there,
Till what you doe affect is ripn'd to yee.
Has the Duke seen yee yet?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: What if he have not?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You doe your beauties too much wrong, appearing
So full of sweetnesse, newnesse; set so richly,
As if a Councell beyond nature fram'd yee.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: If we were thus? say heaven had given these blessings,
Must we turne these to sin-oblations?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How foolishly this Countrey way shewes in ye?
How full of flegme? doe you come here to pray Ladies.
You had best crie, stand away, let me alone gentlemen,
Ile tell my father else.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: This woman's naught sure,
A verie naughtie woman.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Come, say on friend,
Ile be instructed by ye.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You'll thank me for't.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Either I or the devil shal: The Duke you were speaking of.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Tis well remembred: yes, let him first see you,
Appeare not openly till he has view'd yee.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Hee's a very noble Prince they say.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: O wondrous gracious;
And as you may deliver your selfe at the first viewing.
For look ye, you must beare your selfe; yet take heed
It be so season'd with a sweet humilitie,
And grac'd with such a bountie in your beautie—

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: But I hope he will offer me no ill?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: No, no:
'Tis like he Will kisse ye, and play with ye.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Plaie with me, how?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why, good Lord, that you are such a foole now.
No harme assure your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Will ye play with me too?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Look babies in your eyes, my prettie sweet one:
Ther's a fine sport: doe you know your lodgings yet?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I heare of none.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I doe then, they are handsome,
Convenient for accesse.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Accesse?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Yes little one,
For visitation of those friends and servants,
Your beauties shall make choice of: friends and visits:
Doe not you know those uses? Alas poore novice;
There's a close Cowch or two, handsomely placed too.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: What are those I pray you?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Who would be troubled with such raw things? they are to lie upon,
And your love by ye; and discourse, and toy in.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Alas I have no love.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You must by any meanes:
You'll have a hundred, feare not.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Honestie keep me:
What shall I doe with all those?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You'll finde uses:
Ye are ignorant yet, let time work; you must learne too,
To lie handsomly in your bed a mornings, neatly drest
In a most curious VVastcoat, to set ye off well,
Play with your Bracelets, sing you must learn to rhime to,
And riddle neatlie; studie the hardest language,
And 'tis no matter whether it be sense, or no,
So it goe seemlie off. Be sure yee profit
In kissing, kissing sweetly: there lies a maine point,
A key that opens to all practick pleasure;
Ile helpe yee to a friend of mine shal teach ye,
And suddenlie: your Countrey way is fulsome.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Have ye schooles for all these mysteries?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: O yes,
And severall houres prefix'd to studie in:
Ye may have Kalanders to know the good houre,
And when to take a jewell: for the ill too,
VVhen to refuse, with observations on 'em;
Under what Signe 'tis best meeting in an Arbor,
And in what Bower, and houre it works; a thousand,
VVhen in a Coach, when in a private lodging,
VVith all their vertues.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Have ye studied these?
How beastly they become your youth? how bawdily?
A woman of your tendernesse, a teacher,
Teacher of these lewd Arts? of your full beauty?
A man made up in lust would loath this in yee:
The rankest Leacher, hate such impudence.
They say the devill can assume heavens brightnesse,
And so appeare to tempt us: sure thou art no woman.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I joy to finde ye thus.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thou hast no tendernesse,
No reluctation in thy heart: 'tis mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: All's one for that; read these and then be satisfi'd,
A few more private rules I have gather'd for ye,
Read 'em, and well observe 'em: so I leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: A wondrous wicked woman: shame go with thee.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: What new Pandoras box is this? Ile see it,
Though presently I teare it. Read Thine Viola,
'Tis in our owne wills to believe and follow.
How's this? Read yours out sister: this amazes me.
prose:
Worthy Honora, as you have begun
In vertues spotlesse schoole, so forward run:
Pursue that noblenesse, and chaste desire
You ever had, burne in that holy fire;
And a white Martyr to faire memorie
Give up your name, unsoil'd of infamy.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: Feare not thou yet unblasted Violet,
Nor let my wanton words a doubt beget,
Live in that peace and sweetnessr of thy bud,
Remember whose thou art, and grow still good.
Remember what thou art, and stand a storie
Fit for thy noble Sex, and thine owne glorie.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: I know not what to thinke.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Sure a good woman,
An excellent woman, sister.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: It confounds me;
Let 'em use all their arts, if these be their ends,
The Court I say breeds the best foes and friends.
Come, let's be honest wench, and doe our best service.

speeches.speaker: Vio.
prose: A most excellent woman, I will love her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: MAdam, the Duke has sent for the two Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Olim.
verse: I prethee go: I know thy thoughts are with him.
Go, go Alinda, do not mock me more.
I have found thy heart wench, doe not wrong thy Mistris,
Thy too much loving Mistris: doe not abuse her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: By your owne faire hands I understand ye not.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: By thy own faire eyes I understand thee too much,
Too farre, and built a faith there thou hast ruine.
Goe, and enjoy thy wish, thy youth, thy pleasure,
Enjoy the greatnesse no doubt he has promised,
Enjoy the service of all eyes that see thee,
The glory thou hast aim'd at, and the triumph:
Onely this last love I aske, forget thy Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Oh, who has wrong'd me? who has ruin'd me?
Poore wretched Girle, what poyson is slung on thee?
Excellent vertue, from whence flowes this anger?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Go, ask my Brother, ask the faith thou gav'st me,
Aske all my favours to thee, aske my love,
Last, thy forgetfulnesse of good: then flye me,
For we must part Alinda.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You are wearie of me;
I must confesse, I was never worth your service,
Your bounteous favours lesse; but that my duty,
My ready will, and all I had to serve ye—
O heaven thou know'st my honestie.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: No more:
Take heed, heaven has a justice: take this ring with yee,
This doting spell you gave mee: too well Alinda,
Thou knew'st the vertue in't; too well I feele it:
Nay keep that too, it may sometimes remember ye,
When you are willing to forget who gave it,
And to what vertuous end.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Must I goe from yee?
Of all the sorrowes sorrow has—must I part with yee?
Part with my noble Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Or I with thee wench.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: And part stain'd with opinion? Farewell Lady,
Happy and blessed Lady, goodnesse keep yee:
Thus your poore servant full of griefe turnes from yee,
For ever full of griefe, for ever from yee.
I have no being now, no friends, no Countrey,
I wander heaven knowes whither, heaven knows how.
No life, now you are lost: onely mine innocence,
That little left me of my selfe, goes with me,
That's all my bread and comfort. I confesse Madam,
Truely confesse, the Duke has often courted me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: And powr'd his soule into thee, won thee.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Doe you think so?
Well, time that told this tale, will tell my truth too,
And say ye had a faithfull, honest servant:
The businesse of my life is now to pray for ye,
Pray for your vertuous loves; Pray for your children,
When heaven shall make ye happy.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: How she wounds me?
Either I am undone, or she must go: take these with yee,
Some toyes may doe ye service; and this money;
And when ye want, I love ye not so poorely,
Not yet Alinda, that I would see ye perish.
Prethee be good, and let me heare: look on me,
I love those eyes yet dearely; I have kiss'd thee,
And now Ile doe't againe: farewell Alinda,
I am too full to speak more, and too wretched.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You have my faith,
And all the world my fortune.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I would faine heare
What becomes of these two Wenches:
And if I can, I will doe 'em good.
Doe you heare my honest friend?
He knowes no such name:
What a world of businesse,
Which by interpretation are meere nothings,
These things have here? 'Masse now I think on't better,
I wish he be not sent for one of them
To some of these by-lodgings: me thought I saw
A kinde of reference in his face to Bawderie.
He has her, but 'tis none of them: hold fast theefe:
An excellent touzing knave. Mistris
You are to suffer your penance some half hour hence now
How farre a fine Court Custard with Plumbs it
Will prevaile with one of these waiting gentlewomen,
They are taken with these soluble things exceedingly;
This is some yeoman oth' bottles now that has sent for hir,
That she calls father: now woe to this Ale incence.
By your leave sir.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Well sir; what's your pleasure with me?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You do not know the way to the maids lodgings?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes indeed doe I sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: But you will not tell me?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: No indeed will not I, because you doubt it.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: These are fine gim-cracks: hey, here comes another,
A Haggon full of wine in's hand, I take it.
Well met my friend, is that wine?

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Yes indeed is it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Faith Ile drink on't then.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Ye may, because ye have sworne sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis very good, Ile drinke a great deale now sir.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: I cannot helpe it sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Ile drinke more yet.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: 'Tis in your owne hands.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: There's your pot, I thank ye.
Pray let me drinke againe.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Faith but ye shall not.
Now have I sworn I take it. Fare ye well sir.

speeches.speaker: Th.
verse: This is the fin'st place to live in I e're enterd.
Here comes a gentle woman, & alone; Ile to her.
Madam, My Lord my Master.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Who's your Lord sir?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: The Lord Boroskie, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Pray excuse me:
Here's something for your paines: within this houre sir,
One of the choise young Ladies shall attend him:
Pray let it be in that Chamber juts out to the water;
'Tis private and convenient: doe my humble service
To my honourable good Lord, I beseech ye sir;
If it please you to visit a poore Lady—
You carrie the 'haviour of a noble Gentleman,

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I shall be bold.

speeches.speaker: Lady
verse: 'Tis a good aptnesse in ye.
I lye here in the Wood-yard, the blew lodgings sir;
They call me merily the Lady of the—Sir;
A little I know what belongs to a gentleman,
And if it please you take the paines.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Deare Lady, take the paines?
Why a horse would not take the pains that thou requir'st now,
To cleave old crab-tree? one of the choise yong Ladies:
I would I had let this Bawd goe, she has frighted me;
I am cruelly afraid of one of my Tribe now;
But if they will doe, the devill cannot stop 'em.
Why should he have a young Lady? are women now
Oth' nature of Bottles, to be stopt with Corks?
O the thousand little furies that flye here now?
How now Captaine?

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: I come to seek you out sir,
And all the Town I have travell'd.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What's the newes man?

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: That that concernes us all, and very neerely:
The Duke this night holds a great feast at Court,
To which he bids for guests all his old Counsellors,
And all his favourites: your Father's sent for.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Why he is neither in councell, nor in favour.

speeches.speaker: Pu.
verse: Thats it: have an eye now, or never, & a quick one,
An eye that must not wink from good intelligence.
I heard a Bird sing, they mean him no good office.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Art sure he sups here?

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Sure as 'tis day.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis like then:
How now, where hast thou been Ancient?

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Measuring the City:
I have left my Brooms at gate here;
By this time the Porter has stole 'em to sweep out rascals.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Brooms?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: I have been crying Brooms all the towne over,
And such a Mart I have made, there's no trade neare it.
O the young handsome wenches, how they twitter'd,
When they but saw me shake my ware, and sing too;
Come hither Master Broom-man I beseech ye:
Good Master Broom-man hither cries another.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thou art a mad fellow.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: They are all as mad as I: they all have trades now,
And roare about the streets like Bull-beggers.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What company of souldiers are they?

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: By this meanes I have gather'd
Above a thousand tall and hardy souldiers,
If need be Colonell.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: That need's come Ancient,
And 'twas discreetly done: goe, draw 'em presently,
But without suspition: this night we shall need 'em;
Let 'em be neare the Court, let Putskie guide 'em;
And wait me for occasion: here Ile stay still.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: If it fall out we are ready; if not we are scatter'd:
Ile wait ye at an inch.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Doe, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Are the Souldiers still so mutinous?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: More then ever,
No Law nor Justice frights 'em: all the Towne over
They play new pranks and gambols: no mans person,
Of what degree soever, free from abuses:
And durst they doe this, (let your grace consider)
These monstrous, most offensive things, these villanies,
If not set on, and fed? if not by one
They honour more then you? and more aw'd by him?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Happily their owne wants.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: I offer to supply 'em,
And every houre make tender of their moneyes:
They scorne it, laugh at me that offer it:
I feare the next device will be my life sir;
And willingly Ile give it, so they stay there.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Doe you think Lord Archas privie?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: More then thought,
I know it Sir, I know they durst not doe
These violent rude things, abuse the State thus,
But that they have a hope by his ambitions—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No more: he's sent for?

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: Yes, and will be here sure.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Let me talke further with you anon.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ile wait sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Did you speak to the Ladies?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: They'll attend your grace presently.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How doe you like 'em?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: My eyes are too dull Judges.
They wait here sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Be you gone then: Come in Ladies.
Welcom toth' court sweet beauties; now the court shines,
When such true beames of beauty strike amongst us:
Welcome, welcome, even as your owne joyes welcome.
How doe you like the Court? how seems it to you?
Is't not a place created for all sweetnesse?
Why were you made such strangers to this happinesse?
Barr'd the delights this holds? the richest jewels
Set ne're so well, if then not worne to wonder,
By judging eyes not set off, lose their lustre:
Your Countrey shades are faint; blasters of beauty;
The manners like the place, obscure and heavie;
The Rose buds of your beauties turne to cankers,
Eaten with inward thoughts: whilst there ye wander.
Here Ladies, here, you were not made for Cloisters,
Here is the Sphere you move in: here shine nobly,
And by your powerfull influence command all:
What a sweet modestie dwells round about 'em,
And like a nipping morne pulls in their blossoms?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Your grace speaks cunningly, you doe not this,
I hope sir, to betray us, wee are poore triumphs;
Nor can our losse of honour adde to you sir:
Great men, and great thoughts, seek things great & worthy,
Subjects to make 'em live, and not to lose 'em;
Conquests so nobly won, can never perish;
We are two simple maids, untutor'd here sir;
Two honest maids, is that a sin at Court sir?
Our breeding is obedience, but to good things,
To vertuous and to faire: what wou'd you win on us?
Why doe I aske that question, when I have found yee?
Your Preamble has pow'rd your heart out to us;
You would dishonour us; which in your translation
Here at the Court reads thus, your grace would love us,
Most dearely love us: sticke us up for mistresses:
Most cerraine, there are thousands of our Sex sir
That would be glad of this, and handsome women,
And crowd into this favour, faire young women,
Excellent beauties sir: when ye have enjoyd 'em,
And suckt those sweets they have, what Saints are these then?
What worship have they won? what name you ghesse sir,
What storie added to their time, a sweet one?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: A brave spirited wench.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Ile tell your grace,
And tell yee true: ye are deceiv'd in us two,
Extreamly cozend sir: And yet in my eye
You are the handsomst man I evet lookt on,
The goodliest gentleman; take that hope with yee;
And were I fit to be your wife (so much I honour yee)
Trust me I would scratch for ye but I would have yee.
I would wooe you then.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: She amazes me:
But how am I deceiv'd?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: O we are too honest,
Believe it sir, too honest, far too honest,
The way that you propound too ignorant,
And there is no medling with us; for we are fooles too,
Obstinate, peevish fooles: if I would be ill,
And had a wantons itch, to kick my heeles up,
I would not leap into th'Sun, and doe't there,
That all the world might see me: an obscure shade sir,
Darke as the deed, there is no trusting light with it,
Nor thats that lighter far, vain-glorious greatnesse.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You will love me as your friend?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: I will honour yee,
As your poore humble handmaid serve, and pray for ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What sayes my little one; you are not to obstinate?
Lord how the blushes: here are truely faire soules:
Come you will be my love?

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: Good sir be good to me,
Indeed Ile doe the best I can to please yee;
I doe beseech your grace: Alas I feare ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What shouldst thou feare?

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Fie sir, this is not noble.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why doe I stand entreating, where my power—

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: You have no power, at least you ought to have none
In bad and beastly things: arm'd thus, Ile dye here,
Before she suffer wrong.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Another Archas?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: His childe sir, and his spirit.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Ile deale with you then,
For here's the honour to be won: sit down sweet,
Prethee Honora sit.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Now ye intreat I will sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I doe, and will deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: That's too much kindnesse.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Prethee look on me.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Yes: I love to see yee,
And could look on an age thus, and admire ye:
Whilst ye are good and temperate I dare touch ye,
Kisse your white hand.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why not my lips?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: I dare sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I doe not thinke ye dare.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: I am no coward.
Doe you believe me now? or now? or now sir?
You make me blush: but sure I mean no ill sir:
It had been fitter you had kiss'd me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: That Ile doe too.
What hast thou wrought into me?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: I hope all goodnesse:
Whilst ye are thus, thus honest, I dare doe any thing,
Thus hang about your neck, and thus doat on yee;
Blesse those faire lights: hell take me if I durst not—
But good Sir pardon me. Sister come hither,
Come hither, feare not wench: come hither, blush not,
Come kisse the Prince, the vertuous Prince, the good Prince:
Certaine he is excellent honest.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thou wilt make me—

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Sit downe, and hug him softly.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Fie Honora,
Wanton Honora; is this the modesty,
The noble chastity your on-set shew'd me,
At first charge beaten back? Away.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Thank ye:
Upon my knees I pray, heaven too may thank ye;
Ye have deceiv'd me cunningly, yet nobly
Ye have cozen'd me: In all your hopefull life yet,
A Scene of greater honour, you ne're acted:
I knew Fame was a lyar, too long, and loud tongu'd,
And now I have found it: O my vertuous Master.

speeches.speaker: Viol.
verse: My vertuous Master too.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Now you are thus,
What shall become of me let Fortune cast for't.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Ile be that fortune, if I live Honora,
Thou hast done a cure upon me, counsell could not.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Here take your ring sir, & whom ye mean to ruine,
Give it to her next; I have paid for't dearely.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: A Ring to her?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why frownes my faire Alinda?
I have forgot both these againe.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Stand still sir,
Ye have that violent killing fire upon ye,
Consumes all honour, credit, faith.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: My Royall Mistris favour towards me,
Woe-worth ye sir, ye have poyson'd, blasted.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: I sweet?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You have taken that unmanly liberty,
Which in a worse man, is vaine-glorious feigning,
And kild my truth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Upon my life 'tis false wench.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ladies,
Take heed, ye have a cunning gamster,
A handsome, and a high; come stoar'd with Antidotes,
He has infections else will fire your blouds.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Prethee Alinda heare me.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Words steept in honey,
That will so melt into your mindes, buy Chastity,
A thousand wayes, a thousand knots to tie ye;
And when he has bound ye his, a thousand ruines.
A poore lost woman ye have made me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Ile maintaine thee,
And nobly too.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That Gin's too weak to take me:
Take heed, take heed young Ladies: still take heed,
Take heed of promises, take heed of gifts,
Of forced feigned sorrowes, sighes, take heed.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: By all that's mine, Alinda—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Sweare
By your mischiefes:
O whither shall I goe?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Goe back againe,
Ile force her take thee, love thee.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Fare ye well Sir,
I will not curse ye; onely this dwell with ye,
When ever you love, a false beliefe light on ye.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Wee'll take our leaves too sir.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Part all the world now,
Since she is gone.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: You are crooked yet, deare Master,
And still I feare—

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: I am vext,
And some shall finde it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis strange
To me to see the Court, and welcome:
O royall place, how have I lov'd and serv'd thee?
Who lies on this side, know'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The Lord Burris.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thou hast nam'd a gentleman
I stand much bound to.
I think he sent the Casket sir?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The same Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: An honest minded man, a noble Courtier:
The Duke made perfect choice when he took him.
Goe you home, I shall hit the way
Without a guide now.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You may want something sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Onely my horses,
Which after Supper let the Groom wait with:
Ile have no more attendance here.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Your will sir?

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: You are well met here sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: How now boy,
How do'st thou?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I should aske
You that question: how doe you sir?
How doe you feele your selfe?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Why well, and lustie.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What doe you here then?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Why I am sent for
To Supper with the Duke.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Have you no meat at home?
Or doe you long to feed as hunted Deere doe,
In doubt and feare?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I have an excellent stomach,
And can I use it better
Then among my friends boy?
How doe the wenches?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They doe well enough sir,
They know the worst by this time: pray be rul'd sir,
Goe home againe, and if ye have a Supper
Eate it in quiet there: this is no place for ye,
Especially at this time,
Take my word for't.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: May be they'll drink hard;
I could have drunk my share Boy.
Though I am old, I will not out.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I hope you will.
Hark in your eare: the Court's
Too quick of hearing.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Not mean me wel?
Thou art abus'd and cozen'd.
Away, away.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: To that end sir I tell ye.
Away, if ye love your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Who dare doe these things,
That ever heard of honesty?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Old Gntleman,
Take a fooles counsell.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis a fooles indeed;
A very fooles: thou hast more of
These flams in thee, these musty doubts:
Is't fit the Duke send for me,
And honour me to eate within his presence,
And I, like a tal fellow, play at bo-peep
With his pleasure?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Take heed
Of bo-peep with your pate, your pate sir,
I speak plain language now.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: If 'twere not here,
Where reverence bids-me hold,
I would so swinge thee, thou rude,
Unmanner'd knave; take from his bounty,
His honour that he gives me, to beget
Sawcy, and sullen feares?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You are not mad sure:
By this faire light, I speak
But what is whisper'd,
And whisper'd for a truth.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: A dog: drunken people,
That in their Pot see visions,
And turne states, mad-men and children:
Prethee doe not follow me;
I tell thee I am angrie:
Doe not follow me.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am as angrie
As you for your heart.
I and as wilfull too: goe, like a Wood-cock,
And thrust your neck ith' noose.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ile kill thee.
And thou speakst but three words more.
Doe not follow me.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: A strange old foolish fellow: I shall heare yet,
And if I doe not my part hisse at me.

speeches.speaker: 1. Ser.
verse: Beleeve me fellow here will be lusty drinking.
Many a washt pate in wine I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: I am glad the old Generall's come: upon my conscience
That joy will make half the Court drunk. Hark the Trumpets,
They are comming on; away.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Wee'll have a rowse too.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
prose: Come seat your selves: Lord Archas sit you there.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis farre above my worth.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Ile have it so:
Are all things ready?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: All the Guards are set,
The Coutt gates shut.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Then doe as I prescrib'd yee.
Be sure no further.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I shall well observe ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come bring some wine: here's to my sister gentlemen;
A health, and mirth to all.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Pray fill it full sir.
'Tis a high health to vertue: here Lord Burris,
A maiden health: you are most fit to pledge it,
You have a maiden soule, and much I honour it.
Passion o'me, ye are sad man.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How now Burris.
Goe to, no more of this.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Take the rowse freely,
'Twill warme your bloud, and make ye fit for jollity.
Your graces pardon: when we get a cup sir,
We old men prate a pace.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Mirth makes a banque^;
As you love me no more.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I thank your grace.
Give me it; Lord Boroskie.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: I have ill braines sir.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Damnable ill, I know it.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: But Ile pledge sir
This vertuous health.

speeches.speaker: Bu.
verse: The more unfit for thy mouth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come, bring out Robes, & let my guests look nobly,
Fit for my love, and presence: begin downward.
Off with your cloaks, take new.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Your grace deales truely
Like a munificent Prince, with your poor subjects,
Who would not fight for you? what cold dull coward
Durst seek to save his life when you would aske it?
Begin a new health in your new adornments,
The Dukes, the Royall Dukes: ha, what have I got
Sir? ha! the robe of death!

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: You have deserv'd it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: The livorie of the grave? do you start all from me?
Doe I smell of earth already? Sir look on me,
And like a man; is this your entertainment?
Doe you bid your worthiest guests to bloudy Banquets.
A Guard upon me too? this is too foule play
Boy to thy good, thine honour; thou wretched Ruler,
Thou sonne of fooles and flatterers, heire of hypocrites,
Am I serv'd in a hearse that sav'd ye all?
Are ye men or devills? doe ye gape upon me,
Wider, and swallow all my services?
Entombe them first, my faith next, then my integritie,
And let these struggle with your mangy mindes,
Your sear'd, and seal'd up consciences, till ye burst.

speeches.speaker: Boros.
verse: These words are death.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No those deeds that want rewards, sirrah,
Those Battells I have fought, those horrid dangers,
Leaner then death, and wilder then destruction,
I have march'd upon, these honour'd wounds, times story,
The bloud I have lost, the youth, the sorrowes suffer'd,
These are my death, these that can ne're be recompenced,
These that ye sit a brooding on like Toads,
Sucking from my deserts the sweets and favours,
And render me no pay againe but poisons.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The proud vaine souldier thou hast set—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Thou lyest.
Now by my little time of life lyest basely,
Malitiously and loudly: how I scorne thee?
If I had sweld the souldier, or intended
As act in person, leaning to dishonour,
As ye would faine have forced me, witnesse heaven,
Where clearest understanding of all truth is,
(For these are spightfull men, and know no piety)
When Olin came, grim Olin, when his marches,
His last Incursions made the City sweat,
And drove before him, as a storme drives Haile,
Such showrs of frosted fears, shook all your heart-strings;
Then when the Volga trembled at his terrour,
And hid his seven curl'd heads, afraid of bruising,
By his arm'd horses hoofes; had I been false then,
Or blowne a treacherous fire into the souldier,
Had but one sparke of villanie liv'd within me,
Ye'ad had some shadow for this black about me.
Where was your souldiership? why went not you out?
And all your right honourable valour with ye?
Why met ye not the Tartar, and defi'd him?
Drew your dead-doing sword, and buckl'd with him?
Shot through his Squadrons like a fierie Meteor?
And as we see a dreadfull clap of thunder
Rend the stiffe hearted Oakes, and tosse their roots up:
Why did not you so charge him? you were sick then,
You that dare taint my credit slipt to bed then,
Stewing and fainting with the feares ye had,
A whorson shaking fit opprest your Lordship:
Blush Coward knave, and all the world hisse at thee.

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Exceed not my command.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: I shall observe it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Are you gone too? Come weep not honest Burris,
Good loving Lord, no more teares: 'Tis not his malice,
This fellowes malice, nor the Dukes displeasure,
By bold bad men, crowded into his nature,
Can startle me: fortune ne're raz'd this Fort yet:
I am the same, the same man, living, dying;
The same mind to 'em both, I poize thus equall;
Onely the jugling way that told me to it,
The Judas way, to kisse me, bid me welcome,
And cut my throat, a little sticks upon me.
Farewell, commend me to his grace, and tell him,
The world is full of servants, he may have many:
And some I wish him honest: hee's undone else:
But such another doating Archas never,
So try'd and touch'd a faith: farewell for ever.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Be strong my Lord: you must not go thus lightly.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Now, what's to doe? what sayes the Law unto me?
Give me my great offence that speaks me guilty,

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Laying aside a thousand petty matters,
As scornes, and insolencies both from your selfe and followers,
Which you put first fire to, and these are deadly,
I come to one maine cause, which though it carries
A strangenesse in the circumstance, it carries death too,
Not to be pardon'd neither: ye have done a sacriledge.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: High heaven defend me man: how, how Borosky?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Ye have tooke from the Temple those vow'd Arms,
The holy Ornament you hung up there,
No absolution of your vow, no order
From holy Church to give 'em backe unto you
After they were purified from war, and rested
From bloud, made cleane by ceremony: from the Altar
You snatch'd 'em up againe, againe ye wore 'em,
Againe you staind 'em, staind your vow, the Church too,
And rob'd it of that right was none of yours sir,
For which the Law requires your head, ye know it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Those Armes I fought in last?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: The same.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: God a mercy,
Thou hast hunted out a notable cause to kill me:
A subtle one: I dye, for saving all you;
Good sir remember if you can, the necessitie,
The suddainesse of time, the State all stood in;
I was entreated to, kneel'd to, and prai'd to,
The Duke himselfe, the Princes, all the Nobles,
The cries of Infants, bedrid fathers, virgins;
Prethee find out a better cause, a hansomer,
This will undo thee too; people will spit at thee,
The devill himselfe would be asham'd of this cause;
Because my hast made me forget the ceremony,
The present danger every where, must my life satisfie?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: It must, and shall.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: O base ungratefull people,
Have ye no other Sword to cut my throat with
But mine owne noblenesse? I confesse, I tooke 'em,
The vow not yet absolv'd, I hung 'em up with:
Wore 'em, fought in 'em, gilded 'em againe
In the fierce Tartars blouds; for you I tooke 'em,
For your peculiar safety, Lord, for all,
I wore 'em for my Countries health, that gron'd then:
Tooke from the Temple, to preserve the Temple;
That holy place, and all the sacred monuments,
The reverent shrines of Saints, ador'd and honour'd,
Had been consum'd to ashes, their owne sacrifice,
Had I been slacke, or staid that absolution.
No Priest had liv'd to give it; my owne honour
Cure of my Country murder me?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: No, no sir,
I shall force that from ye, will make this cause light too,
Away with him: I shall plucke downe that heart sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Breake it thou maiest; but if it bend, for pitty,
Doggs, and Kits eate it: come I am honours Martyr.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Exceed my warrant?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You know he loves him not.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He dares as well meet death, as do it, eat wildfire,
Through a few feares I meane to trye his goodnesse,
That I may find him fit, to weare here Burris;
I know Boroskie hates him, to death hates him,
I know he's a Serpent too, a swolne one
But I have puld his sting out; what noise is that?

speeches.speaker: The.
prose: Down with 'em, down with 'em, down with the gates.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
prose: Stand, stand, stand.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
prose: Fire the Pallace before ye.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Upon my life the Souldier, sir, the Souldier,
A miserable time is come.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Oh save him,
Upon my knees, my hearts knees, save Lord Archas,
We are undone else.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Dares he touch his body?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: He racks him fearefully, most fearefully.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Away Burris,
Take men, and take him from him; clap him up,
And if I live, I'le find a strange death for him:
Are the Souldiers broke in?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: By this time sure they are sir,
They beate the gates extreamely, beate the people.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Get me a guard about me; make sure the lodgings
And speake the Souldiers faire.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Pray heaven that take sir.

speeches.speaker: Put,
verse: Give us the Generall, wee'l fire the Court else,
Render him safe and well,

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Do not fire the Cellar,
There's excellent wine in't Captain, and though it be cold whether,
I do not love it mul'd; bring out the Generall,
Wee'll light ye, such a bonefire else; where are ye?
Speak, or wee'l tosse your Turrets, peep out of your hives
Wee'l smoake ye else: is not that a nose there?
Put out that note againe, and if thou dar'st
But blow it before us: now he creepes out on's but rough.

speeches.speaker: Puts.
verse: Give us the Generall.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yes, Gentlemen;
Or any thing ye can desire.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: You musk-cat
Cordevan-skin, we will not take your answer.

speeches.speaker: Put.
prose: Where is the Duke? speak suddenly, and send him hether.

speeches.speaker: Anc
verse: Or wee'l so frie your buttucks.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Good sweet Gentlemen—

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: We are neither good, nor sweet, we are Souldiers
And you miscreants that abuse the Generall,
Give fire my boyes 'tis a darke evening,
Let's light 'em to their lodgings.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Good brother be not fierce.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I will not hurt her,
Feare not sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: 'May do what you please sit,
I have a sorrow that exceeds all yours,
And more, contemnes all danger.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Where is the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He's here; what would ye Souldiers? wherefore troop ye
Like mutinous mad-men thus?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Give me my father.

speeches.speaker: Put. Anc.
verse: Give us our Generall.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Set him here before us,
Ye see the pledge we have got; ye see these torches;
All shall to ashes, as I live, immediately,
A thousand lives for one.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: But heare me?

speeches.speaker: Put.
prose: No, we come not to dispute.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: By heaven I sweare he's rackt and whipt.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Oh my poore father!

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Burne, kill, and burne.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Hold, hold I say: hold Souldiers,
On your allegeance hold.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: We must not.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Hold:
I sweare by heaven he it a barbarous Traitour stirs first,
A villaine, and a stranger to obedience,
Never my Souldier more, nor friend to honour:
Why did you use your old man thus? thus cruelly
Torture his poore weake body? I ever lov'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Forget me in these wrongs, most noble Archas.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I have balme enough for all my hurts: weep no more sir,
A satisfaction for a thousand sorrowes:
I do beleeve ye innocent, a good man,
And heaven forgive that naughty thing that wrong'd me.
Why looke ye wild my friends? why stare ye one me?
I charge ye as ye are men, my men, my lovers,
As ye are honest faithfull men, faire Souldiers,
Let downe your anger: Is not this our Soveraigne,
The head of mercie, and of Law? who dares then,
But Rebels scorning Law, appeare thus violent?
Is this a place for Swords? for threatning fires?
The reverence of this house dares any touch,
But with obedient knees, and pious duties?
Are we not all his Subjects? all sworn to him?
Has not he power to punish our offences?
And do not we dayly fall into 'em? assure your selves
I did offend and highly, grievously,
This good sweet Prince I offended, my life forfeited,
Which yet his mercy, and his old love met with,
And only let me feele his light rod this way:
Ye are to thanke him for your Generall,
Pray for his life, and fortune: sweat your blouds for him.
You are offenders too, daily offenders,
Proud insolencies dwell in your hearts, and ye do 'em,
Do 'em against his peace, his Law, his Person;
Ye see he only sorrowes for your sins,
And where his power might persecute, forgives ye:
For shame put up your Swords, for honesty,
For orders sake and whose ye are, my Souldiers,
Be not so rude.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They have drawne bloud from ye sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: That was the bloud rebel'd, the naughty bloud,
The proud provoking bloud; 'tis well 'tis out boy;
Give you example first; draw out, and orderly.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Good brother doe.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Honest and high example,
As thou wilt haue my blessing follow thee,
Inherit all mine honours: thanke ye Theodore,
My worthy son.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: If harme come, thanke your selfe sir;
I must obey ye.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Captaine, you know the way now:
A good man, and a valiant, you were ever,
Inclind to honest things: I thanke ye Captaine.
Souldiers, I thanke ye all: and love me still,
But do not love me so you lose allegeance,
Love that above your lives: once more I thanke ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Bring him to rest, and let our cares waite on him;
Thou excellent old man, thou top of honour,
Where justice, and obedience onlie build,
Thou stocke of vertue, how am I bound to love thee?
In all thy noble waies to follow thee?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Remember him that vext him sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Remember?
When I forget that villaine, and to pay him
For all his mischiefes, may all good thoughts forget me.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I am very sore,

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Bring him to bed with ease Gentlemen,
For everie stripe I'le drop a teare to wash 'em,
And in my sad repentance—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Tis too much,
I have a life yet left to gaine that love sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: HOw do's Lord Archas yet?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: But weake and't please ye,
Yet all the helpes that art can, are applied to him;
His heart's untouch't, and whole yet; and no doubt sir,
His minde being found, his body soone will follow.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: O that base knave that wrong'd him, without leave too;
But I shall find an houre to give him thankes for't;
He's fast I hope?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: As fast as irons can keep him:
But the most fearefull wretch—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He has a conscience,
A cruell stinging one I warrant him,
A loaden one: But what newes of the Souldier?
I did not like their parting, 'twas too sullen.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: That they keep still, and I feare a worse clap:
They are drawn out of the Towne, and stand in counsels,
Hatching unquiet thoughts, and cruell purposes:
I went my selfe unto 'em, talk't with the Captaines,
Whom I found fraught with nothing but loud murmurs,
And desperate curses, sounding these words often
Like trumpets to their angers: we are ruin'd,
Our services turn'd to disgraces, mischiefes,
Our brave old Generall, like one had pilfer'd,
Tortur'd, and whipt: the Collonells eyes like torches,
Blaze everie where and fright faire peace.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yet worse sir:
The newes is currant now, they meane to leave ye,
Leave their allegiance: and under Olins charge
The bloudy Enemy march strait against ye.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I have heard this too sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: This must be prevented,
And suddenly, and warily.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: 'Tis time sir,
But what to minister, or how?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Go in with me,
And there wee'l thinke upon't: such blows as these,
Equall defences aske, else they displease.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Lord, what a coile has here been with these Souldiers?
They are cruell fellowes.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: And yet me thought we found 'em
Hansome enough; I'le tell thee true Petesca,
I look'd for other manner of dealings from 'em,
And had prepar'd my selfe; but where's my Lady?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: In her old dumps within: monstrous mellancholly;
Sure she was mad of this wench.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: And she had been a man,
She would have been a great deale madder, I am glad she is shifted.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Twas a wicked thing for me to betray her,
And yet I must confesse she stood in our lights,
What young thing's this?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Good morrow beuteous Gentlewomen:
Pray you is the Princesse stirring yet?

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: He has her face.

speeches.speaker: Pe.
verse: Her very tongue, and tone too: her youth upon him.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I ghesse ye to be the Princesse women.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Yes, We are sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Pray is there not a Gentlewoman waiting on her Grace,
Ye cal Alinda?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: The devill sure in her shape.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: I have heard her tell my Lady of a brother,
An only brother that she had: in travell—

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: 'Mas, I remember that: this may be he too:
I would this thing would serve her.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: So would I wench,
We should love him better sure: sir, here's the Princes,
She best can satisfie ye.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How I love that presence!
O blessed eyes how nobly shines your comforts!

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: What Gentleman is that?

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: We know not Madam:
He ask'd us for your Grace: and as we guesse it,
He is Al ndas Brother.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Ha? let me marke him:
My griefe has almost blinded me: her brother?
By Venus, he has all her sweetnesse upon him:
Two silver drops of dew, were never liker.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Gratious Lady—

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: That pleasant pipe he has too.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Being my happinesse to passe by this way,
And having as I understand by Letters,
A sister in your vertuous service Madam—

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: O now my heart, my heart akes.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: All the comfort
My poore youth has, all that my hopes have built me,
I thought it my first duty, my best service
Here to arive first, humbly to thanke your Grace
For my poore first, humbly to thanke your noblenesse,
That bounteous goodnesse in ye.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: 'Tis he certainly.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That spring of favour to her; with my life Madam
If any such most happy meanes might meet me,
To shew my thankefulnesse.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: What have I done foole?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: She came a stranger to your Grace, no Courtier;
Nor of that curious breed besits your service,
Yet one I dare assure my soule, that lov'd ye
Before she saw ye; doated on your vertues;
Before she knew those faire eyes long'd to read 'em,
You only had her prayers, you her wishes;
And that one hope to be yours once, preserv'd her,

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I have done wickedly.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: A little beauty,
Such as a Cottage breeds, she brought along with her;
And yet our Countrie eyes esteem'd it much too:
But for her beauteous mind forget great Lady
I am her brother, and let me speake a stranger,
Since she was able to beget a thought, 'twas honest,
The dayly studdy how to fit your services,
Truly to tread that vertuous path you walke in,
So fir'd her honest soule, we thought her Sainted;
I presume she is still the same: I would faine see her,
For Madam, 'tis no little love I owe her.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Sir, such a maid there was, I had—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: There was Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: O my poore wench: eyes, I will ever curse ye
For your credulity. Alinda.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That's her name, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Give me a little leave sir to lament her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Is she dead Lady?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Dead sir, to my service.
She is gone, pray ye aske no further,

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I obey Madam:
Gone? now must I lament too: said ye gone, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Gone, gone for ever.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: That's a cruell saying:
Her honour too?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Prethee looke angry on me,
And if thou ever lovedst her, spit upon me;
Doe something like a brother, like a friend,
And do not only say thou lov'st her—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ye amaze me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I ruin'd her, I wrong'd her, I abus'd her;
Poore innocent soule, I flung her; sweet Alinda,
Thou vertuous maid, my soule now cals thee vertuous.
Why do ye not raile now at me?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: For what Lady?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Call me base treacherous woman.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Heaven defend me.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Rashly I thought her false, and put her from me,
Rashly, and madly I betrai'd her modesty,
Put her to wande, heaven knows where: nay, more sir,
Stucke a blacke brand upon her.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: 'Twas not well Lady,

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: 'Twas damnable: she loving me so deerely,
Never poore wench lov'd so: Sir, beleeve me,
'Twas the most dutious wench, the best companion,
When I was pleas'd, the happiest, and the gladdest,
The modestest sweet nature dwelt within her:
I saw all this, I knew all this. I lov'd it,
I doated on it too, and yet I kil'd it:
O what have I forsaken? what have I lost?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Madam, I'le take my leave, since she is wandring,
'Tis fit I know no rest.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Will you go too sir?
I have not wrong'd you yet, if you dare trust me,
For yet I love Alinda there, I honour her,
I love to looke upon those eyes that speake her,
To read that face againe, modesty keepe me,
Alinda, in that shape: but why should you trust me,
'Twas I betray'd your sister, I undid her;
And beleeve me, gentle youth, 'tis I weep for her:
Appoint what pennance you please: but stay then,
And see me performe it; aske what honour this place
Is able to heape on ye, or what wealth:
If following me will like ye, my care of ye,
Which for your sisters sake, for your owne goodnesse—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Not all the honour earth h'as, now she's gone Lady,
Not all the favour; yet if I sought preferment,
Under your bounteous Grace I would only take it.
Peace rest upon ye: one sad teare every day
For poore Alindas sake, 'tis fit ye pay,

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: A thousand noble youth, and when I sleep,
Even in my silver slumbers still I'le weep.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Have ye been with 'em?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Yes, and 't please your Grace,
But no perswasion serves 'em, nor no promise,
They are fearefull angry, and by this time sir,
Upon their march to the enemy-

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: They must be stopt.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I, but what force is able? and what leader—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How now, have you been with Archas?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Yes, and't please ye,
And told him all: he frets like a chas'd Lyon,
And cals for his Armes: and all those honest Courtiers
That dare draw Swords.

speeches.speaker: Du
verse: Is he able to do any thing?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: His mind is well enough; and where his charge is,
Let him be ne're so sore, 'tis a full Army.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Who commands the Rebels?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: The young Collonell,
That makes the old man almost mad: he sweares sir,
He will not spare his Sons head for the Dukedome.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Is the Court in Armes?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: As fast as they can bussell,
Every man mad to goe now: inspir'd strangely,
As if they were to force the Enemie,
I beseech your Grace to give me leave.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Pray go sir,
And looke to the old man well; take up all fairely,
And let no bloud be spilt; take generall pardons,
And quench this fury with faire peace.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I shall sir,
Or seale it with my service; they are villaines;
The Court is up: good sir, go strengthen 'em,
Your Royall sight will make 'em scorne all dangers;
The Generall needs no proofe.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come let's go view 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Tis known we are up, and marching: no submission,
No promise of base peace can cure our maladies,
We have suffer'd beyond all repaire of honour:
Your valiant old man's whipt; whipt Gentlemen,
Whipt like a slave: that flesh that never trembled,
Nor shrunke one sinew at a thousand charges,
That noble body rib'd in armes, the Enemy
So often shooke at, and then shun'd like thunder,
That bodies torne with lashes.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Let's turne head.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Turne nothing Gentlemen, let's march on fairely,
Unlesse they charge us.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thinke still of his abuses,
And keep your angers.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: He was whipt like a top,
I never saw a whore so lac'd: Court schoole-butter?
Is this their diet? I'le dresse 'em one running banquet:
What Oracle can alter us? did not we see him?
See him we lov'd?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And though we did obey him,
Forc'd by his reverence for that time; is't fit Gentlemen?
My noble friends, is't fit we men, and Souldiers,
Live to endure this, and looke on too?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Forward:
They may call backe the Sun as soone, stay time,
Prescribe a Law to death, as we endure this.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: They will make ye all faire promises.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: We care not.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Use all their arts upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Hang all their arts.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: And happily they'l bring him with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: March apace then,
He is old and cannot overtake us.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Say he doe.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: Wee'l run away with him: they shall never see him more:
The truth is, wee'l heare nothing, stop at nothing,
Consider nothing but our way; beleeve nothing,
Not though they say their prayers: be content with nothing,
But the knocking out their braines: and last, do nothing
But ban 'em and curse 'em, till we come to kill 'em.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Remove then forwards bravely; keep your minds whole,
And the next time we face 'em, shall be fatall.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
prose: Peace to your Grace; take rest sir, they are before us.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: They are sir, and upon the ma^ch

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Lord Burris,
Take you those horse and coast 'em: upon the first advantage,
If they will not slacke their march, charge 'em up roundly,
By that time I'le come in.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: I'le do it truly.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: How do you feele your selfe sir?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Well, I thanke ye;
A little weake, but anger shall supply that;
You will all stand bravely to it?

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Whilst we have lives sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ye speake like Gentlemen; I'le make the knaves know,
The proudest, and the strongest hearted Rebell,
They have a law to live in, and they shall have;
Beat up a pace, by this time he is upon 'em,
And sword, but hold me now, thou shalt play ever.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Stand, stand, stand close, and sure;
The horse will charge us.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Let 'em come one, we have provender sit for 'em.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Here comes Lord Burris sir, I thinke to parley.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You are welcome noble sir, I hope to our part.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: No, valiant Collonell, I am come to chide ye,
To pitty ye; to kill ye, if these faile me;
Fie, what dishonour seeke ye? what blacke infamy!
Why do ye draw out thus? draw all shame with ye?
Are these sit cares in subjects? I command ye
Lay downe your armes againe, move in that peace,
That faire obedience you were bred in.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Charge us?
We come not here to argue.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Charge up bravely,
And hotly too, we have hot spleenes to meet ye,
Hot as the shames are offer'd us.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Looke behind ye.
Do you see that old man? do you know him Souldiers?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Your father sir, beleeve me—

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: You know his marches,
You have seene his executions: is it yet peace?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Wee'l dye here first.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Farewell: you'l heare on's presently.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stay Burris: this is too poore, too beggerly a body
To beare the honour of a charge from me,
A sort of tatterd Rebels; go provide Gallowses;
Ye are troubled with hot heads, I'le coole ye presently:
These looke like men that were my Souldiers
Now I behold 'em neerly, and more narrowly,
My honest friends: where got they these faire figures?
Where did they steale these shapes?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: They are strooke already.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Do you see that fellow there; that goodly Rebell?
He lookes as like a Captaine, I lov'd tenderly:
A fellow of a faith indeed.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: He has sham'd him.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: And that that beares the Collors there, most certaine
So like an Ancient of mine owne, a brave fellow,
A loving and obedient, that beleeve me Burris,
I am amaz'd and troubled: and were it not
I know the generall goodnesse of my people,
The duty, and the truth, the steadfast honestie,
And am assur'd they would as soone turne devils
As Rebells to allegeance, for mine honour.

speeches.speaker: Bu.
verse: Here needs no wars.

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: I pray forgive us sir.

speeches.speaker: Anc.
verse: Good Generall forgive us, or use your sword,
Your words are double death.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Good noble Generall.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Pray sir be mercifull.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Weep out your shames first,
Ye make me foole for companie: fie Souldiers,
My Souldiers too, and play these tricks: what's he there?
Sure I have seen his face too; yes, most certaine
I have a son, but I hope he is not here now,
'Would much resemble this man, wondrous neare him,
Just of his height and making too, you seeme a Leader.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Good sir, do not shame me more: I know your anger,
And lesse then death, I looke not for.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You shall be my charge sir, it seemes you want foes,
When you would make your friends your Enemies:
A running bloud ye have, but I shall cure ye.

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Good sir—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No more good Lord: beate forward Souldiers:
And you, march in the reare, you have lost your places.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You shall not be thus sullen still, with me sister
You doe the most unnobly to be angry,
For as I have a soule, I never touch'd her,
I never yet knew one unchast thought in her:
I must confesse, I lov'd her: as who would not?
I must confesse I doated on her strangely,
I offer'd all, yet so strong was her honour,
So fortifi'd as faire, no hope could reach her,
And whilst the world beheld this, and confirmd it,
Why would you be so jealous?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Good sir pardon me,
I feele sufficiently my follies pennance,
And am asham'd, that shame a thousand sorrowes
Feed on continually, would I had never seen her,
Or with a clearer judgement look'd upon her,
She was too good for me, so heavenly good sir,
Nothing but heaven can love that soule sufficiently,
Where I shall see her once againe.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No more teares,
If she be within the Dukedome, wee'l recover her:
Welcome Lord Burris, faire newes I hope.

speeches.speaker: Bu.
verse: Most faire sir,
Without one drop of bloud these wars are ended,
The Souldier coold againe, indeed asham'd sir,
And all his anger ended.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Where's Lord Archas?

speeches.speaker: Bur.
verse: Not far off sir: with him his valiant son,
Head of this fire, but now a prisoner,
And if by your sweet mercie not prevented,
I feare some fatall stroke.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I heare the drums beate,
Welcome, my worthy friend.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stand where ye are sir,
Even as you love your Country, move not forward,
Nor plead for peace, till I have done a justice,
A justice on this villaine; none of mine now,
A justice on this Rebell.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: O my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: This fatall firebrand—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Forget not old man,
He is thy son of thine owne bloud.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: In these veines
No treacherie e're harbour'd yet, no mutinie,
I ne're gave life to lewd and headstrong Rebels.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: 'Tis his first fault.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Not of a thousand sir,
Or were it so, it is a fault so mightie,
So strong against the nature of all mercie,
His mother were she living, would not weep for him,
He dare not say he would live.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I must not sir,
Whilst you say 'tis not fit: your Graces mercy
Not to my life appli'd, but to my fault sit,
The worlds forgivenesse next, last, on my knees sir,
I humbly beg,
Do not take from me yet the name of father,
Strike me a thousand blowes, but let me dye yours.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: He moves my heart: I must be suddaine with him,
I shall grow faint else, in my execution;
Come, come sir, you have seen death; now meet him bravely.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Hold, hold I say, a little hold, consider
Thou hast no more sons Archas to inherit thee.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Yes sir, I have another, and a nobler:
No treason shall inherit me: young Archas
A boy, as sweet as young, my brother breeds him,
My noble brother Briskie, breeds him nobly,
Him let your favour find: give him your honour.

speeches.speaker: Pu.
verse: Thou hast no child left Archas, none to inherit thee
If thou strikst that stroke now: behold young Archas;
Behold thy brother here, thou bloudy brother,
As bloudy to this sacrifice as thou art:
Heave up thy sword, and mine's heav'd up: strike Archas,
And I'le strike too, as suddenly, as deadly:
Have mercy, and I'le have mercy: the Duke gives it,
Looke upon all these, how they weep it from thee,
Choose quickly, and begin.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: On your obedience,
On your allegeance save him.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Take him to ye,
And sirha, be an honest man, ye have reason:
I thanke ye worthy Brother; welcome child,
Mine owne sweet child.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why was this boy concealed thus?

speeches.speaker: Put.
verse: Your graces pardon:
Fearing the vow you made against my brother
And that your anger would not only light
On him, but find out all his familie,
This young boy, to preserve from after danger,
Like a young wench, hether I brought; my selfe
In the habit of an ordinarie Captaine
Disguis'd, got entertainement, and serv'd here
That I might still be ready to all fortunes:
The boy your Grace tooke, nobly entertain'd him,
But thought a Girle, Alinda, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: Stand away,
And let me looke upon him.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: My young Mistris?
This is a strange metamorphosis, Alinda?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Your graces humble servant.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come hether sister:
I dare yet scarce beleeve mine eyes? how they view one another?
Dost thou not love this boy wel?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I should lye else,
Trust me, extreamely lye sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Didst thou never wish Olimpia,
It might be thus?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: A thousand times.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Here take him:
Nay, do not blush: I do not jest; kisse sweetly:
Boy, ye kisse faintly boy; heaven give ye comfort;
Teach him, he'l quickly learne: there's two hearts eas'd now.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You do me too much honour sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: No Archas,
But all I can, I will; can you love me? speake truly.

speeches.speaker: Hon.
verse: Yes sir, dearly.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come hether Viola, can you love this man?

speeches.speaker: Vio.
verse: I'le do the best I can sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Seale it Burris:
Wee'l all to Church together instantly:
And then a vse for boyes; stay, bring Boroskie.
I had almost forgot that lumpe of mischiefe.
There Archas, take the enemie to honour,
The knave to worth: do with him what thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Then to my sword againe; you to your prayers;
Wash off your villanies, you feele the burthen.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Forgive me ere I die, most honest Archas;
'Tis too much honour that I perish thus;
O strike my faults to kill them, that no memorie,
No blacke and blasted infamy heareafter—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Come, are ye ready?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: And truly penitent, to make your way straight?

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: Thus I wash off my sins.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stand up, and live then,
And live an honest man; I scorne mens ruin's:
Take him againe, Sir, trie him: and beleeve
This thing wil be a perfect man.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I take him.

speeches.speaker: Bor.
verse: And when I faile those hopes, heavens hopes faile me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: You are old: no more wars Father:
Theodore take you the charge, be Generall.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: All good blesse ye.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: And my good father, you dwell in my bosome,
From you rise all my good thoughts: when I would think
And examine time for one that's fairely noble,
And the same man through all the straights of vertue,
Upon this silver booke I'le looke, and read him.
Now forward merrily to Hymens rights,
To joyes, and revels, sports, and he that can
Most honour Archas, is the noblest man.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: SIr, you'r the very friend I wish'd to meet with,
I have a large discourse invites your eare
To be an Auditor.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: And what concernes it?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: The sadly thriving progresse of the loves
Betweene my Lord the Prince, and that great Lady,
Whose in^olencie, and never-yet-match'd pride,
Can by no Character be well exprest,
But in her onlie name, the prow'd Erota.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Alas Melitus, I should ghesse, the best
Successe your Prince could find from her, to be
As harsh as the event doth prove: but now
'Tis not a time to pity passionate griefes,
When a whole Kingdome in a manner lies
Upon its death-bed bleeding.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Who can tell
Whether or no, these many plagues at once
Hang over this unhappie Land, for her sake,
That is a monster in it.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Here's the miserie
Of having a child our Prince: else I presume
The bold Venecians had not dar'd to attempt
So bloudie an Invasion.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Yet I wonder
Why, Master Secretarie, still the Senate
So almost superstitiouslie adores,
Gonzalo the Venetian Lord, considering
The outrage of his Countrymen—

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: The Senate
Is wise, and therein just, for this Gonzalo,
Upon a Massacre performed at Sea
By the Admirall of Venice, on a Merchant
Of Candy, when the cause was to be heard
Before the Senate there, in open Court
Professed, that the crueltie the Admirall
Had shewed, deserved not only fine, but death:
For Candy then, and Venice were at peace:
Since when upon a motion in the Senate,
For conquest of our Land, 'tis known for certaine,
That only this Gonzalo dar'd to oppose it,
His reason was, because it too much savoured
Of Lawlesse, and unjust ambition.
The wars were scarce begun, but he (in feare
Of quarrels 'gainst his life) fled from his Countrie,
And hether came, where (to confirme his truth)
I know (Melitus) he, out of his owne store,
Hath monied Cassilanes the Generall.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: What, without other pledges then Cassilanes
Bare promise of payment?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: No, it may be
He has some pettie Lordship to retire to:
But this he hath done; now 'tis fit Melitus,
The Senate should be thankefull, otherwise,
They should annihilate one of those Laws,
For which this Kingdome is throughout the world
Unfollowed, and admired.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: What Lawes are these? sir,
Let me so much importune you.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: You shall,
And they be worth your knowledge; briefly thus:
Who ere he be that can detect apparantly
Another of ingratitude, for any
Received benefit, the Plaintiffe may
Require the offenders life; unlesse he please
Freely, and willingly to grant remission.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: By which strict Law the Senate is in danger,
Should they neglect Gonzalo.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Right; the Law
Permits a like equalitie to Aliens,
As to a home-borne Patriot.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Pray sir the other?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Know Melitus,
The elder Cretans flourished many yeares,
In War, in Peace, unparalel'd, and they
(To spurre heroicke spirits on to vertue)
Enacted that what man so ere he were,
Did noblest in the field against his enemie,
So by the generall voice approv'd, and knowne,
Might at his home-returne, make his demand
For satisfaction, and reward.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: They are
Both famous Lawes indeed.

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: Master Secretarie,
The Senate is about to sit, and crave
Your presence.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: What, so suddenly?

speeches.speaker: Mes.
verse: These Letters
Will shew the causes why.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Heaven thou art great,
And worthie to be thanked.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Your countenance sir
Doth promise some good tidings.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: O the best
And happiest for this land, that e're was told!
All the Venetian Forces are defeated.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: How Sir?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: And what doth adde some delight more,
There is amongst the Souldiers a contention
Who shall be the triumpher and it stands
Doubtfull betweene a Father and his Son,
Old Cassilanes, and young Antinous.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Why may not both demand it?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: The Law denies it:
But where the Souldiers do not all consent,
The parties in contention, are refer'd
To plead before the Senate; and from them,
Upon an open Audience, to be judg'd
The Chiefe, and then to make demands.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: You ravish me
With wonder and delight,

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Come: as we walke,
I shall more fully informe you.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Admit no Souldier neare us, till the Senate
Have tooke their places.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: You are obey'd, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Decius, fall off.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: I shall.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Give leave Arcanes:
Young-man come nearer to me: who am I?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It were a sin against the piety
Of filiall duty, If I should forget
The debt I owe my father on my knee;
Your pleasure?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: What, so low? canst thou finde joynts,
Yet be an Elephant? Antinous, rise:
Thou wilt belye opinion, and rebate
The ambition of thy gallantry, that they
Whose confidence thou hast bewitched, should see
Their little God of War, kneele to his father,
Though in my hand I did graspe Thunder.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir,
For proofe that I acknowledge you the Author
Of giving me my birth, I have discharg'd
A part of my obedience. But if now
You should (as cruell fathers do) proclame
Your right, and Tyrant like usurp the glory
Of my peculiar honours, not deriv'd
From successary, but purchas'd with my bloud,
Then I must stand first Champion for my selfe,
Against all interposers.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Boldly urg'd,
And proudly, I could love thee, did not anger
Consult with just disdaine, in open language
To call thee most ungratefull. Say freely,
Wilt thou resigne the flatteries, whereon
The reeling pillars of a popular breath,
Have rais'd thy Giant-like conceit; to adde
A suffrage to thy fathers merit, speake?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir, heare me: were there not a Chronicle
Well pend by all their tongues, who can report
What they have seene you do; or had you not
Best in your owne performance writ yourselfe,
And been your own Text, I would undertake
Alone, without the helpe of Art, or Character,
But only to recount you deeds in Armes,
And you should ever then be fam'd a president
Of living victory: But as you are
Great, and well worthy to be stiled great,
It would betray a povertie of spirit
In me to obstruct my fortunes, or discent,
If I should coward-like surrender up
The interest, which the inheritance of your vertue,
And mine owne thriftie fate can claime in honour:
My Lord, of all the masse of fame, which any
That weares a sword, and hath but seen me fight,
Gives me, I will not share, nor yeild one jot,
One tittle.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Not to me?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You are my father,
Yet not to you.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Ambitious boy, how darst thou
To tell me, that thou wilt contend?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Had I
Been sloathfull, and not followed you in all
The streights of death, you might have justly then
Reputed me a bastard; 'tis a cruelty,
More then to murther Innocents, to take
The life of my yet Infant-honour from me.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Antinous, looke upon this badge of age,
Thy fathers gray-hair'd beard: full fifty yeares,
(And more then halfe of this, ere thou wert borne)
I have been knowne a Souldier, in which time
I found no difference 'twixt War and Peace,
For War was peace to me, and Peace was war;
Antinous, marke me well; there hath not liv'd
These fifty yeares, a man whom Creet prefer'd
Before thy farher; let me boldly boast,
Thy father, both for Discipline, and Action,
Hath so long been the first of all his Nation;
Now canst thou thinke it honest, charitable,
Nay humane, being so young, my son, my child,
Begot, bred, taught by me, by me thy father,
For one dayes service, and that on thy first,
To rob me of a glory which I fought for
A halfe of hundred yeares.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: My case observes
Both equity, and presidents; for sir,
That very day whereon you got your fame,
You tooke it from some other, who was then
Chiefe in repute, as you are now; and had been
Perhaps as many yeares deserving that,
Which you gain'd in a day, as I have mine.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: But he was not my father then Antinous.
Thou leav'st out that.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir had he been your father,
