Of our impartiality? be sure
Wee'l flatter no mans injuries.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: 'Tis well;
You have a Law (Lords) that without remorse
Dooms such as are belcapred with the curse
Of foule ingratitude unto death.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: We have.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Then do me justice.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Mad-man, whether run'st thou?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Peace Decius, I am deafe.

speeches.speaker: Hyp.
verse: Will you forget
Your greatnesse and your modesty?

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Hyparcha leave, I will not heare,

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Lady; great, gentle, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Prethee young-man forbeare to interrupt me,
Triumph not in thy fortunes; I will speake.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: More uproares yet; who are they that disturb us?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: The viper's come; his feares have drawn him hether,
And now (My Lords) be Chronicled for ever,
And give me justice against this vile Monster,
This bastard of my bloud.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: 'Tis justice fathers,
I sue for too: and though I might command it,
(If you remember Lords, whose child I was)
Yet I will humbly beg it; this old wretch
'Has forfeited his life to me.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Tricks, tricks;
Complots, devices, 'twixt these paire of young-ones,
To blunt the edge of your well temper'd Swords,
Wherewith you strike offendors, (Lords) but I
Am not a baby to be fear'd with bug-beares,
'Tis justice I require.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: And I.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You speak too tenderly; and too much, like your self
To meane a cruelty; which would make monstrous
Your Sexe: yet for the loves sake, which you once
Pleas'd to pretend, give my griev'd father leave
To vrge his owne revenge; you have no cause
For yours: keep peace about ye.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Will you heare me?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Here's some strange novelty.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Sure we are mock'd,
Speake one at once: say wherein hath your Son
Transgress'd the Law?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: O the grosse mists of dulnesse;
Are you this Kingdomes Oracles, yet can be
So ignorant? first heare, and then consider,
That I begot him, gave him birth and life,
And education, were I must confesse,
But duties of a father: I did more;
I taught him how to manage Armes, to dare
An Enemy; to court both death and dangers;
Yet these were but additions to compleate
A well accomplish'd Souldier: I did more yet.
I made him chiefe Commander in the field
Next to my selfe, and gave him the full prospect
Of honour, and preferment; train'd him up
In all perfections of a martiallist:
But he unmindfull of his gratitude,
You know with what contempt of my deserts,
First kick'd against mine honour, scorn'd all
My services; then got the palme of glory
Unto himselfe: yet not content with this,
He (lastly) hath conspir'd my death, and sought
Means to engage me to this Lady's debt,
Whose bounty, all my whole estate could never
Give satisfaction too: now honoured fathers,
For this cause only, if your Law be law,
And you the Ministers of justice; then
Thinke of this strange ingratitude in him.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Can this be so Antinous?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis all true,
Nor hath my much wrong'd father limn'd my faults
In colours halfe so black, as in themselves,
My guilt hath dyed them: were there mercy left,
Yet mine owne shame would be my Executioner:
Lords, I am guilty.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Thou beliest Antinous,
Thine innocence: alas (my lords) hee's desperate,
And talkes he knowes not what: you must not credit
His lunacy; I can my selfe disprove
This accusation: Cassilane, be yet
More mercifull; I beg it.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Time, nor fate,
The world, or what is in it, shall not alter
My resolution; he shall dye.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: The Senats
Prayers; or weeping Lovers, shall not alter
My resolution: thou shalt dye.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Why Madam,
Are ye all Marble?

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Leave your shifts Antinous,
What plead you to your fathers accusation?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Most fully guilty.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: You have doom'd your selfe,
We cannot quit you now.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: A burthen'd conscience
Will never need a hang-man: hadst thou dar'd
To have denide it, then this Sword of mine
Should on thy head have prov'd thy tongue a lyar.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Thy sword? wretched old man, thou hast liv'd too long
To carry peace or comfort to thy grave;
Thou art a man condemn'd: my Lords this tyrant
Had perish'd but for me, I still suppli'd
His miserable wants; I sent his daughter
Mony to buy him food; the bread he eate,
Was from my purse: when he (vaingloriously)
To dive into the peoples hearts, had pawn'd
His birth-right, I redeemed it, sent it to him,
And for requitall, only made my suite,
That he would please to new receive his son
Into his favour, for whose love I told him
I had been still so friendly: But then he
As void of gratitude, as all good nature,
Distracted like a mad man, poasted hether
To pull this vengeance on himselfe, and us;
For why, (my Lords) since by the Law, all meanes
Is blotted out of your commission,
As this hard hearted father hath accus'd
Noble Antinous, his unblemished Son,
So I accuse this father, and crave judgement.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: All this is but deceit, meere trifles forg'd
By combination to defeat the processe
Of Justice, I will have Antinous life.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: Sir, what do ye meane?

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: I will have Cassilane's.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Cunning and cruell Lady, runs the streame
Of your affections this way? have you not
Conquest enough by treading on my grave?
Unlesse you send me thether in a shrowd
Steept in my fathers bloud? as you are woman,
As the protests of love you vow'd were honest;
Be gentler to my father.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Cassilane,
Thou hast a heart of flint: let my intreates,
My teares, the Sacrifice of griefes unfained,
Melt it: yet be a father to thy son,
Unmaske thy long besotted judgement, see
A low obedience kneeling at the feet
Of nature: I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Pish you cosen
Your hopes: your plots are idle: I am resolute.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Antinous, urge no further.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Hence thou Sorcery
Of a beguiling softnesse, I will stand,
Like the earths Center, unmoved; Lords your breath
Must finish these divisions: I confesse
Civility doth teach I should not speake
Against a Lady of her birth, so high
As great Erota, but her injuries
And thankelesse wrongs to me, urge me to cry
Alowd for justice, Fathers.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Whether run you?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: For (honoured fathers) that you all may know
That I alone am not unmatchable
In crimes of this condition, lest perhaps
You might conceive, as yet the case appeares,
That this foule staine, and guilt runs in a bloud;
Before this presence, I accuse this Lady
Of as much vile ingratitude to me.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Impudent Traitor!

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Her? O spare Antinous;
The world reputes thee valiant, do not soyle
All thy past noblenesse with such a cowardize,
As murthering innocent Ladies will stamp on thee?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Brave Prince, with what unwillingnesse I force
Her follies, and in those her sin, be witnesse,
All these about me: she is bloudy minded.
And turnes the justice of the Law to rigor:
It is her cruelties, not I accuse her:
Shall I have Audience?

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Let him speake my Lords.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Your memory will rot.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Cast all your eyes
On this, what shall I call her? truthlesse woman,
When often in my discontents, the sway
Of her unruly bloud, her untam'd passion,
(Or name it as you list) had houre by houre
Sollicited my love, she vow'd at last
She could not, would not live unlesse I granted
What she long sued for: I in tender pitty,
To save a Lady of her birth, from ruine
Gave her her life, and promis'd to be hers:
Nor urg'd I ought from her, but secresie,
And then enjoyn'd her to supply such wants
As I perceiv'd my fathers late engagements
Had made him subject to; what, shall I heape up
Long repetitions? she to quit my pitty,
Not only hath discover'd to my father
What she had promis'd to conceale, but also
Hath drawne my life into this fatall forfeit;
For which, since I must dye, crave a like
Equality of justice against her;
Not that I covet bloud, but that she may not
Practice this art of falsehood on some other,
Perhaps more worthy of her love hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: If this be true—

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: My Lords, be as the Law is,
Indifferent, upright, I do plead guilty:
Now sir, what glory have you got by this?
'Las man, I meant not to outlive thy doome;
Shall we be friends in death?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Heare me, the villaine
Scandals her, honour'd Lords.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Leave off to doate,
And dye a wise man.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I am over-reach'd,
And master'd in my own resolution.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Will ye be wilfull Madam? here's the curse
Of loves disdaine.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Why sit you like dumb Statues?
Demur no longer.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Cassilane, Erota,
Antinous, death ye aske; and 'tis your doomes,
You in your follies liv'd, dye in your follies.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I am reveng'd, and thanke you for it.

speeches.speaker: Er.
verse: Yes, and I: Antinous hath been gratious.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sir, may I presume to crave a blessing from you
Before we part.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Yes, such a one as Parents
Bestow on cursed sons now, now, I laugh
To see how those poore younglings are both cheated
Of life and comfort: looke ye, lookeye, Lords,
I go but some ten minutes (more or lesse)
Before my time, but they have fiuely coz'nd
Themselves of many, many hopefull yeares
Amidst their prime of youth and glory; now
My vengeance is made ful. Welcome my joy,
Thou comst to take a seasonable blessing
From thy halfe buried fathers hand; I am dead
Already girle, and so is she and he,
We all are wormes-meat now.

speeches.speaker: Anno.
verse: I have heard all;
Nor shall you dye alone: Lords on my knees
I beg for justice too.

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: 'Gainst whom, for what?

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: First let me be resolv'd; does the Law favour
None, be they ne're so mighty?

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: Not the greatest.

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: Then justly I accuse of foule ingratitude
(My Lords) you of the Senate all, not one
Excepted.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Porp. Us?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Annophill—

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: You are the Authors
Of this unthrifty bloud-shed; when your enemies
Came marching to your gates, your children suck'd not
Safe at their mothers breasts, your very Cloysters
Were not secure, your starting-holes of refuge
Not free from danger, nor your lives your owne:
In this most desperate Extasie, my father,
This aged man, not onely undertook
To guard your lives, but did so; and beat off
The daring foe; for you he pawn'd his lands,
To pay your souldiers, who without their pay
Refus'd to strike a blow: but (Lords) when peace
Was purchas'd for you, and victorie brought home;
Where was your gratitude, who in your Coffers
Hoarded the rustie treasure which was due
To my unminded father? he was glad
To live retir'd in want, in penurie,
Whilst you made feasts of surfeit, and forgot
Your debts to him: The sum of all is this,
You have been unthankfull to him; and I crave
The rigor of the Law against you all.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: My Royall spirited daughter!

speeches.speaker: Fro.
verse: Annophill.
Thou art a worthy wench; let me embrace thee.

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: Lords, why doe ye keep your seats? they are no places
For such as are offenders.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Though our ignorance
Of Cassilanes engagements might asswage
Severity of justice, yet to shew
How no excuse should smooth a breach of Law,
I yeeld me to the triall of it.

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: So must I:
Great Prince of Cyprus, you are left
The onely Moderator in this difference;
And as you are a Prince be a Protector
To wofull Candy.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What a Scene of miserie
Hath thine obdurate frowardnesse (old man)
Drawne on thy Countries bosome? and for that
Thy proud ambition could not mount so high
As to be stil'd thy Countries onely Patron,
Thy malice hath descended to the depth
Of hell, to be renowned in the Title
Of the destroyer? dost thou yet perceive
What curses all posterity will brand
Thy grave with? that at once hast rob'd this kingdome
Of honour and of safety.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: Children yet unborne
Will stop their eares when thou art nam'd.

speeches.speaker: Arc.
verse: The world will be too little to containe
The memorie of this detested deed;
The Furies will abhorre it.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: What the sword
Could not enforce, your peevish thirst of honour
(A brave, cold, weak, imaginarie fame)
Hath brought on Candy: Candy groans, not these
That are to die.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: 'Tis happinesse enough
For them, that they shall not survive to see
The wounds wherewith thou stab'st the land that gave
Thee life and name.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: 'Tis Candy's wrack shall feele—

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: The mischief of your folly.

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: Pos. Annophill—

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: I will not be entreated.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Prethee Annophill.

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: Why would ye urge me to a mercy which
You in your selfe allow not?

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: 'Tis the Law,
That if the party who complaines, remit
The offender, he is freed: is't not so Lords?

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: Pos. 'Tis so.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Antinous, By my shame observe
What a close witch-craft popular applause is:
I am awak'd, and with cleare eyes behold
The Lethargie wherein my reason long
Hath been be-charm'd: Live, live, my matchlesse sonne,
Blest in thy fathers blessing; much more blest
In thine owne vertues: let me dew thy cheeks
With my unmanly teares: Rise, I forgive thee:
And good Antinous, if I shall be thy father
Forgive me: I can speak no more.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Deare Sir,
You new beget me now—Madam your pardon,
I hartily remit you.

speeches.speaker: Ero.
verse: I as freely
Discharge thee Cassilane.

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: My gracious Lords,
Repute me not a blemish to my Sex,
In that I strove to cure a desperate evill
With a more violent remedy: your lives,
Your honours are your owne.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Then with consent
Be reconcil'd on all sides: Please you fathers
To take your places.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Let us againe ascend,
With joy and thankfulnesse to heaven: And now
To other businesse Lords.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: Two howres and more Sir,
The Senate hath been set.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: And I not know it?
Who sits with them?

speeches.speaker: Mel.
verse: My Lord, the Prince of Cyprus.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Gaspero,
VVhy how comes that to passe?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Some waighty cause
I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Now Lords the businesse? ha?
VVho's here, Erota?

speeches.speaker: Porp.
verse: Secretarie doe your charge
Upon that Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Traytor?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Yes, Gonzalo, Traitor,
Of treason to the peace and state of Candy,
I doe arrest thee.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Me? thou dog?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: With License
From this grave Senate, I arrest thee likewise
Of Treason to the State of Venice.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Ha?
Is Michael here? nay then I see
I am undone.

speeches.speaker: Ero.
verse: I shall not be your Queen,
Your Dutchesse, or your Empresse.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: Dull, dull braine.
O I am fool'd?

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Look Sir, do you know this hand?

speeches.speaker: Mic.
verse: Do you know this Seale? First (Lords) he writes to Venice,
To make a perfect league, during which time
He would in private keep some Troops in pay,
Bribe all the Centinells throughout this kindom,
Corrupt the Captaines; at a Banquet poyson
The Prince, and greatest Peeres, and in conclusion
Yield Candy slave to Venice.

speeches.speaker: Gas.
verse: Next, he contracted
With the Illustrious Princesse, the Lady Erota,
In hope of marriage with her, to deliver
All the Venetian gallantry, and strength,
Upon their first arrivall, to the mercy
Of her and Candy.

speeches.speaker: Erot.
verse: This is true Gonzalo.

speeches.speaker: Gon.
verse: Let it be true: what then?

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: My Lord Ambassadour,
What's your demand?

speeches.speaker: Mich.
verse: As likes the State of Candy,
Either to sentence him as he deserves
Here, or to send him like a slave to Venice.

speeches.speaker: Porph.
verse: We shall advise upon it.

speeches.speaker: Gonz.
verse: O the devills,
That had not thrust this trick into my pate—
A Politician foole? destruction, plague
Candy and Venice both.

speeches.speaker: Pos.
verse: Porp. Away with him.

speeches.speaker: Mel.
prose: Come sir, Ile see you safe.

speeches.speaker: Ero.
verse: Lords, e're you part
Be witnesse to another change of wonder;
Antinous, now be bold, before this presence,
Freely to speak, whether or no I us'd
The humblest meanes affection could contrive,
To gaine thy love.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Madam, I must confesse it,
And ever am your servant.

speeches.speaker: Ero.
verse: Yes Antinous,
My servant, for my Lord thou shalt be never:
I here disclaim the interest thou hadst once
In my too passionate thoughts. Most noble Prince,
If yet a relique of thy wonted flames
Live warme within thy bosome, then I blush not
To offer up the assurance of my faith,
To thee that hast deserv'd it best.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: O Madam,
You play with my calamity.

speeches.speaker: Ero.
verse: Let heaven
Record my truth for ever.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: With more joy
Then I have words to utter, I accept it.
I also pawne you mine.

speeches.speaker: Ero.
verse: The man that in requitall
Of noble and un-sought affection
Growes cruell, never lov'd, nor did Antinous.
Yet herein (Prince) ye are beholding to him;
For his neglect of me humbled a pride,
Which to a vertuous wife had been a Monster.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: For which Ile ranke him my deserving friend.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Much comfort dwell with you, as I could wish
To him I honour most.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: O my Antinous,
My owne, my owne good son.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: One suit I have to make.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: To whom Fernando?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Lord Cassilane to you.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: To me?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: This Lady
Hath promised to be mine.

speeches.speaker: Ann.
verse: Your blessing sir;
Brother your love.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You cannot sir bestow her
On a more noble gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: Saist thou so?
Antinous I confirm it. Here Fernando,
Live both as one; she is thine.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And herein sister,
I honour you for your wise setled love.
This is a day of Triumph, all Contentions
Are happily accorded: Candy's peace
Secur'd, and Venice vow'd a worthy friend.

speeches.speaker: Malfort.
verse: AND as I told you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I understand you,
Clarinda's still perverse.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Shee's worse, obdurate,
Flinty relentlesse, my love-passions jeer'd at,
My presents scorn'd.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: 'Tis strange a waiting-woman,
In her condition apt to yield, should hold out,
A man of your place, reverend beard and shape,
Besieging her.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: You might adde too my wealth,
Which she contemnes, five hundred Crowns per annum,
For which I have ventur'd hard, my conscience knows it,
Not thought upon, though offer'd for a Joyinture:
This Chaine which my Lords Pesants worship, stouted;
My solemne hums and ha's, the servants quake at,
No Rhetorick with her; every houre she hangs out
Some new flag of defiance to torment me:
Last Lent my Lady cal'd me her poor John,
But now I am growne a walking Skelliton,
You may see through and through me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Indeed you are much falne away.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: I am a kinde of nothing,
As she hath made me: love's a terrible glister,
And if some Cordiall of her favours help not,
I shall like an Italian dye backward,
And breath my last the wrong way.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: As I live you have my pity; but this is cold comfort,
And in a friend lip-physick; and now I think on't,
I should doe more, and will, so you deny not
Your selfe the meanes of comfort.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Ile be hang'd first: one dram of't I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: You are not jealous of any mans accesse to her?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: I would not receive the Dor, but as a bosome friend
You shall direct me, still provided that
I understand who is the man, and what
His purpose that pleads for me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: By all meanes.
First, for the undertaker I am he:
The meanes that I will practise, thus—

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Pray you forward,

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You know your Lady chaste Caliste loves her.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Too well, that makes her proud.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Nay, give me leave.
This beauteous Lady, I may stile her so,
(Being the paragon of France for feature)
Is not alone contented in her selfe
To seeem, and be good, but desires to make
All such as have dependance on her like her;
For this Clarinda's liberty is restrain'd;
And though her kinsman the gate's shut against me;
Now if you please to make your selfe the doore,
For my conveyance to her, though you run
The hazard of a check for't, 'tis no matter.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: It being for mine owne ends.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ile give it o're,
If that you make the least doubt otherwise:
Studying upon't? good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Pray you stay sir;
You are my friend: yet as the Proverb saies,
When love puts in, friendship is gone: suppose
You should your selfe affect her?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Do you think Ile commit Incest; for it is no lesse,
She being my cousin Germane. Fare you well sir.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: I had forgot that; for this once forgive me.
Onely to ease the throbbing of my heart,
(For I doe feele strange pangs) instruct me what
You will say for me.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: First, Ile tell her that
She hath so far besotted you, that you have
Almost forgot to cast accompt.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Meere truth sir.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: That of a wise and provident Steward,
You are turn'd starke Asse.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Urge that point home, I am so.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: That you adore the ground she treads upon,
And kisse her foot-steps.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: As I doe when I finde their print in the Snow.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: A loving foole I know it,
By your bloudlesse-frosty lips: then having related
How much you suffer for her, and how well
You doe deserve it—

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: How? to suffer?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No sir, to have your love return'd.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: That's good, I thank you.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I will deliver her an Inventorie
Of your good parts: as this your precious nose,
Dropping affection: your high-forehead, reaching
Almost to the crowne of your head; your slender waste,
And a back not like a threshers, but a bending
And Court-like back, and so forth, for your body.
But when I touch your minde, for that must take her,
(Since your out-side promises little) Ile enlarge it,
(Though ne're so narrow) as your Arts to thrive,
Your composition with the Cook, and Butler,
Fory Coney-skins and Chippings, and halfe a share
With all the under-officers of the house,
In strangers bounties, that she shall have all,
And you as 'twere her Bailiffe.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: As I will be.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: As you shall, so Ile promise. Then your qualities.
As playing on a Gytterne, or Jewes Trumpe.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: A little too on the Viall.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I care you nothing.
Then singing her asleep with curious catches
Of your owne making: for as I have heard,
You are Poeticall.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Something given that way.
Yet my works seldome thrive: and the main reason
The Poets urge for't, is, because I am not
As poore as they are.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Very likely: fetch her,
While I am in the vaine.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: 'Tis an apt time, my Lady being at her prayers.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Let her pray on.
Nay goe, and if upon my intercession
She doe you not some favour, Ile disclaime her;
Ile ruminate on't the while.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: A hundred Crownes is your reward.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Without 'em—nay, no trifling.
That this dull clod of ignorance should know
How to get money, yet want eyes to see
How grossely hee's abus'd, and wrought upon,
When he should make his will, the rogues turn'd rampant,
As he had renew'd his youth: A handsome wench
Love one a spittle-whore would run away from?
Well Master Steward, I will plead for you
In such a Method, as it shall appeare
You are fit to be a propertie.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Yonder he walks
That knowes my worth and value, though you scorn it.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: If my Lady know not this—

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Ile answer it:
If you were a Nun, I hope your cousin German
Might talke with you through a grate, but you are none,
And therefore may come closer: ne're hang off,
As I live you shall bill: you may salute as strangers,
Custome allowes it. Now, now, come upon her
With all your Oratory, tickle her to the quick,
As a young advocate should, and leave no vertue
Of mine unmentioned, Ile stand Centinell;
Nay keep the doore my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: How have you work'd
This piece of motley to your ends?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Of that at leasure, Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Lower, you are too loud,
Though the fool be deaf some of the house may hear you.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Suppose they should, I am a gentleman,
And held your kinseman, under that I hope
I may be free.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: I grant it, but with caution;
But be not seen to talke with me familiarly,
But at fit distance, or not seen at all,
It were the better: you know my Ladies humour,
Shee is all honour, and compos'd of goodnesse,
(As she pretends) and you having no businesse,
How jealous may she grow?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I will be rul'd.
But you have promis'd, and I must enjoy you.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: We shall finde time for that; you are too hastie:
Make your selfe fit, and I shall make occasion,
Deli^eration makes best in that businesse,
And contents every way.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: But you must feed
This foolish Steward with some shadow of
A future favour, that we may preserve him
To be our instrument.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Hang him.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: For my sake sweet,
I undertook to speak for him, any bauble,
Or slight employment in the way of service,
Will feed him fat.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Leave him to me,

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: She comes. My Lady.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: I will satisfie her.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: How far have you prevail'd?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Observe.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Mounsieur Malfort.
I must be briefe, my cousin hath spoke much
In your behalfe, and to give you some proof,
I entertaine you as my servant,
You shall have the grace.

speeches.speaker: Leon
verse: Upon your knee receive it,

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: And take it a speciall favour from me,
To tye my shooe.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: I am ore-joy'd.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Good reason.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: You may come higher in time.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: No more, the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: She frownes.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: I thanke you for this visit cousin,
But without leave hereafter from my Lady,
I dare not change discourse with you.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Pray you take your mornings draught.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I thank you:
Happinesse attend your honour.

speeches.speaker: Calist.
verse: Who gave warrant to this private parle?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: My innocence; I hope
My conference with a kinseman cannot call
Your anger on me.

speeches.speaker: Calist.
verse: Kinsman? Let me have
No more of this, as you desire you may continue mine.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Why Madam (under pardon)
Suppose him otherwise: yet comming in
A lawfull way it is excusable.

speeches.speaker: Calist.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: I grant you are made of purenesse,
And that your tendernesse of honour holds
The soveraigntie o're your passions. Yet you have
A noble Husband, with allow'd embraces,
To quench lascivious fires, should such flame in you,
As I must ne're believe. Were I the wife
Of one that could but zanie brave Cleander,
Even in his least perfections, (excuse
My ore-bold inference) I should desire
To meet no other object.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: You grow saucie. Doe I look further?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: No, deare Madam: and
It is my wonder or astonishment rather,
You could deny the service of Lisandar;
A man without a rivall: one the King
And Kingdome gazes on with admiration,
For all the excellencies a mother could
Wish in her onely sonne.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Did not mine honour
And Obligation to Cleander, force me
To be deafe to his complaints?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: 'Tis true; but yet
Your rigor to command him from your presence,
Argu'd but small compassion; the Groves
Witnesse his grievous sufferings, your faire name
Upon the rhinde of every gentle Poplar,
And amorous Myrtle, (trees to Venus sacred)
With adoration carv'd, and kneel'd unto,
This you (unseen of him) both saw and heard
Without compassion, and what receiv'd he
For his true sorrowes? but the heavy knowledge,
That 'twas your peremptory will and pleasure,
(How e're my Lord liv'd in him) he should quit
Your sight and house for ever.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I confesse I gave him a strong potion to worke
Upon his hot bloud, and I hope 'twill cure him:
Yet I could wish the cause had concern'd others,
I might have met his sorrowes with more pittie;
At least have lent some counsell to his miseries,
Though now for honour sake, I must forget him,
And never know the name more of Lisander:
Yet in my justice I am bound to grant him,
(Laying his love aside) most truely noble.
But mention him no more, this instant houre
My brother Lidian, new return'd from travaile,
And his brave friend Clarange, long since rivalls
For faire and rich Olinda, are to heare
Her absolute determination, whom
She pleases to elect: see all things ready
To entertain 'em: and on my displeasure
No more words of Lisander.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: She endures to heare him nam'd by no tongue but her owne:
How e're she carries it, I know she loves him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Hard nature: hard condition of poore women!
That where we are most su'd too, we must flye most.
The trees grow up, and mixe together freely,
The Oke not envious of the sailing Cedart
The lustie Vine not jealous of the Ivie
Because she clips the Elme; the flowers shoot up,
And wantonly kisse one another hourely,
This blossome glorying in the others beauty,
And yet they smell as sweet, and look as lovely:
But we are ty'd to grow alone. O honour,
Thou hard Law to our lives, chaine to our freedomes;
He that invented thee had many curses;
How is my soule divided? O Cleander,
My best deserving husband! O Lisander!
The truest lover that e're sacrific'd
To Cupid against Hymen: O mine honour;
A Tyrant, yet to be obey'd, and 'tis
But justice we should thy strict Lawes endure,
Since our obedience to thee keeps us pure.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: How insupportable the difference
Of deare friends is, the sorrow that I feele
For my Lisanders absence, one that stampes
A reverend print on friendship, does assure me
You are rivals for a Lady, a faire Lady,
And in the acquisition of her favours,
Hazard the cutting of that Gordion knot
From your first childhood to this present houre,
By all the tyes of love and amity fastend,
I am blest in a wife (heaven make me thankefull)
Inferiour to none (sans pride I speake it)
Yet if I were a free-man, and could purchase
At any rate the certainty to enjoy
Lisanders conversation while I liv'd,
Forgive me my Caliste and the Sexe,
I never would seeke change.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: My Lord and brother,
I da e not blame your choice, Lisanders worth,
Being a Mistris to be ever courted;
Nor shall our equall suit to faire Olinda
Weaken, but adde strength to our true affection,
With zeale so long continued.

speeches.speaker: Claran.
verse: When we know
Whom she prefers, as she can choose but one,
By our so long tride friendship we have vow'd
The other shall desist.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: 'Tis yet your purpose,
But how this resolution will hold
In him that is refus'd, is not alone
Doubtfull, but dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: The rich heire is come sir.

speeches.speaker: Cleand.
verse: Madam Olinda.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Yes sir, and makes choice,
After some little conference with my Lady,
Of this room to give answer to her suitors.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Already both look pale, between your hopes
To win the prize, and your despaire to lose
What you contended for.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: No sir, I am arm'd.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: I confident of my interest.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Ile beleeve ye when you have endur'd the test.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Is not your garter
Unty'd? you promis'd that I should grow higher
In doing you service.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Fall off or you lose mee.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Nay take your place, no Paris now sits judge
On the contending goddesses. You are
The Deitie that must make curst or happy,
One of your languishing servants.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
verse: I thus look with equal eyes on both, either deserves
A fairer fortune then they can in reason
Hope for from me; from Lidian I expect,
When I have made him mine, all pleasures that
The sweetnesse of his manners, youth, and vertues
Can give assurance of: but turning this way
To brave Clarange, in his face appeares
A kinde of majesty which should command,
Not sue for favour. If the fairest Lady
Of France, set forth with natures best endowments
Nay should I adde a Princesse of the bloud,
Did now lay claime to either for a husband,
So vehement my affection is to both,
My envie at her happinesse would kill me.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: The strangest love I ever heard.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: You can enjoy but one.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: The more I say the merrier.

speeches.speaker: Olin.
verse: Witnesse these teares I love both, as I know
You burne with equall flames, and so affect me;
Abundance makes me poore; such is the hard
Condition of my fortune; be your owne judges;
If I should favour both, 'twill taint my honour,
And that before my life I must prefer,
If one I leane to, the other is disvalewed;
You are fierie both, and love will make you warmer,

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: The warmer still the fitter. You are a foole Lady.

speeches.speaker: Oli.
verse: To what may love, and the devill jealousie spur you
Is too apparent: my name's cal'd in question:
Your swords flie out, your angers range at large:
Then what a murther of my modesty followes?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Take heed of that by any meanes: O innocent,
That will deny a blessing when 'tis offer'd,
Would I were murther'd so, I would thank my modesty.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: What pause you on?

speeches.speaker: Oli.
verse: It is at length resolved.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: We are on the Rack, uncertain expectation,
The greatest torture.

speeches.speaker: Lidian.
verse: Command what you please,
And you shall see how willingly we will execute.

speeches.speaker: Olinda
verse: Then heare what for your satisfaction,
And to preserve your friendship I resolve
Against my selfe, and 'tis not to be alter'd:
You are both brave gentlemen, Ile still professe it,
Both noble servants, for whose gentle offers,
The undeserving, and the poore Olinda
Is ever bound; you love both, faire, and vertuously;
Would I could be so happy to content both:
Which since I cannot, take this resolute answer;
Goe from me both contentedly, and he
That last makes his returne, and comes to visit,
Comes to my bed. You know my will: farewell;
My heart's too big to utter more: come friend.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Ile wait on you to your Coach.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: You both look blank, I cannot blame you.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: We have our dispatches.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Ile home.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
prose: And Ile abroad again, Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Farewell to yee.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Their blunted departure troubles me: I feare
A suddaine and a dangerous division
Of their long love will follow: have you took
Your leave of faire Olinda?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: She is gone sir.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Had you brought news Lisander were return'd too,
I were most happy.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: ^till upon L^sander?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: I know he loves me, as he loves his health:
And heaven knowes I love him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I finde it so:
For me you have forgot, and what I am to you.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: O think not so If you had lost a sister,
You lock'd all your delights in, it would grieve you:
A little you would wander from the fondnesse,
You ow'd your husband: I have lost a friend,
A noble friend, all that was excellent
In man, or man-kinde, was contain'd within him.
That loste my wife—

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Madam, your noble Father—
A see for my good newes.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why? what of him sir?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Is lighted at the doore, and longs to see you.

speeches.speaker: Calist.
verse: Attend him hither.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: O my deare Lisander.
But Ile bee merry: lets meet him my Caliste.

speeches.speaker: Cal
verse: I hope Lasanders love will now be buried:
My father will bring joy enough for one moneth,
To put him out of his memorie.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: How doe you sonne?
Blesse my faire child, I am come to visit yee,
To see what house you keep, they say you are bountifull,
I like the noyse well, and I come to trie it.
Ne're a great belly yet? how have you trifl'd?
If I had done so (sonne) I should have heard on't
On both sides by Saint Denis.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: You are nobly welcome sir:
We have time enough for that.

speeches.speaker: Dorilaus.
verse: See how she blushes:
'Tis a good signe you'll mend your fault, how dost thou,
My good Caliste?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Well, now I see you sir;
I hope you bring a fruitfulnesse along with ye.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Good luck, I never misse, I was ever good at it:
Your mother groand for't wench, so did some other,
But I durst never tell.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: How does your arme sir?

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Have you been let bloud of late?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Against my will sir.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: A fall deare father?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: No, a Gun, deare daughter;
Two or three Guns; I have one herein my buttock,
'Twould trouble a Surgeons teeth to pull it out.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: O me! O me!

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Nay, if you fall to fainting,
'Tis time for me to trudge: art such a coward,
At the meere name of hurt to change thy colour?
I have been shot that men might see clean through me
And yet I fainted not: besides my selfe,
Here are an hospitall of hurt men for yee.

speeches.speaker: Cloan.
verse: What should this wonder be?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I am amaz'd at it.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: What think ye of these? they are every one hurt soundly,
Hurt to the proof, they are through, & through I assure ye;
And that's good game, they scorne your puling scratches.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Who did this sir?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Leave crying, and Ile tell you,
And get your plaisters, and your warme stupes ready:
Have you ne're a Shepheard that can tarre us over?
'Twill proove a businesse else, we are so many.
Comming to see you, I was set upon,
I and my men, as we were singing frolickly,
Not dreaming of an ambush of base rogues,
Set on ith' forrest, I have forgot the name—

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: 'Twixt this, and Fountaine-Bleiu?
In the wilde Forrest?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: The same, the same, in that accursed Forrest,
Set on by villaines, that make boot of all men.
The Peeres of France are pillage there, they shot at us,
Hurt us, un-hors'd us, came to the sword, there plide us,
Opprest us with fresh multitudes, fresh shot still,
Rogues that would hang themselves for a fresh doublet,
And for a Skarlet Caslock kill their fathers.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Lighted you among these?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Among these murtherers,
Our poore blouds were ingag'd: yet we strook bravely,
And more then once or twice we made them shun us,
And shrink their rugged heads: but we were hurt all.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: How came you off? for I even long to hear that.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: After our prayers made to heaven to help us,
Or to be mercifull unto our soules,
So neare we were. Alas poore wench, wipe, wipe.
See heaven sends remedy.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I am glad 'tis come sir,
My heart was even a bleeding in my body.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: A curl'd haire gentleman stept in, a stranger,
As he rod by, belike he heard our bickering,
Saw our distresses, drew his sword, and prov'd
He came to execute, and not to argue.
Lord what a lightning me thought flew about him,
When he once toss'd his blade; in face Adonis,
While peace inhabited between his eye-browes:
But when his noble anger stirr'd his mettle,
And blew his firie parts into a flame,
Like Pallas, when she sits between two armies,
Viewing with horrid browes their sad events,
Such then hee look'd: and as her shield had arm'd him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: This man sir were a friend to give an age for.
This gentleman I must love naturally:
Nothing can keep me off; I pray you goe on sir.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: I will, for now you please me: this brave youth,
This bud of Mars, for yet he is no riper,
When once he had drawne bloud, and flesh'd his sword,
Fitted his manly mettle to his spirit,
How he bestirr'd him? what a lane he made?
And through their fierie Bullets thrust securely:
The hardned villaines wondring at his confidence,
Lame as I was I follow'd, and admir'd too,
And stirr'd, and laid about me with new spirit,
My men too with new hearts thrust into action,
And down the rogues went.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: I am strook with wonder.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Remember but the storie of strong Hector,
When like to lightning he broke through his van-guard,
How the Greeks frighted ran away by Troops,
And trod downe Troops to save their lives: so this man,
Dispers'd these slaves: had they been more and mightier,
He had come off the greater, and more wonder.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Where is the man, good sir, that we may honor him?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: That we may fall in superstition to him.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: I know not that, from me he late departed,
But not without that pious care to see safe
Me, and my weak men lodg'd, and dress'd; I urg'd him
First hither, that I might more freely thanke him:
He told me he had businesse crav'd my pardon,
Businesse of much import.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Know you his name?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: That he deny'd me too: a vow had bard him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: In that he was not noble to be namelesse.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Daughter you must reme~ber him when I am dead,
And in a noble sort requite his piety,
'Twas his desire to dedicate this service
To your faire thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: He knowes me then?

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: I nam'd you,
And nam'd you mine: I think that's all his knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: No name, no being?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Now I am mad to know him:
Saving mine honour, any thing I had now
But to enjoy his sight, but his bare picture;
Make me his Saint, I must needs honour him.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: I know his name.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: There's thy reward for't; speak it.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: His man told me, but he desir'd my silence.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: O Jasper speak, 'tis thy good Masters cause too:
We all are bound ingratitude to compell thee.

speeches.speaker: Serv
prose: Lisander, Yes, I am sure it was Lisander.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Lisander? 'twas Lisander.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: 'Tis Lisander. O my base thoughts? my wicked?
To make question this act could be another mans:
'Tis Lisander, a handsome timber'd man.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
prose: My Lisander! was this friends absence to bee mourn'd?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I grant it:
Ile mourne his going now, and mourne it seriously:
When you weep for him, sir, Ile beare you company.
That so much honour, so much honesty
Should be in one man, to doe things thus bravely,
Make me his Saint, to me give this brave service:
VVhat may I doe to recompence his goodnesse?
I cannot tell.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Come sir, I know you are sickly, so are your men.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: I must confesse I am weake,
And fitter for a bed then long discourses.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: You shall hear to morrow, to morrow provide Surgeons.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Lisander—

speeches.speaker: Cal.
prose: VVhat new fire is this?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: PRethee good Lancelot remember that
Thy Masters life is in thy trust, and therefore
Be very careful.

speeches.speaker: Lance.
verse: I will lose mine owne, rather then hazard yours.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Take what disguise
You in your owne discretion shall think fittest,
To keep your selfe unknowne.

speeches.speaker: * Lanc.
verse: I warrant yee;
'Tis not the first time I have gone invisible:
I am as fine a Fairie in a businesse
Concerning night-worke—

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Leave your vanities:
VVith this purse (which deliver'd,
You may spare your Oratory) convey this Letter to
Caliste's woman.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
verse: 'Tis a handsome girle, Mistris Clarinda.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I have made her mine. You know your work.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
verse: And if I sweat not in it,
At my returne discarde me.

speeches.speaker: Lisand.
verse: O Caliste! the fairest! cruellest!

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: So early stirring? a good day to you.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I was viewing sir,
The site of your house, and the handsomnesse about it:
Believe me it stands healthfully and sweetly.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: The house and master of it really
Are ever at your service.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I returne it:
Now if you please goe forward in your storie
Of your deare friend and Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: I will tell it,
And tell it short, because 'tis breakfast time,
(And love a tedious thing to a quick stomach)
You eate not yester-night.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I shall endure sir.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: My selfe (and as I then deliver'd to you)
A gentleman of noble hope, one Lidian,
Both brought up from our infancy together,
One company, one friendship, and one exercise,
Ever affecting, one bed holding us,
One griefe, and one joy parted still between us,
More then companions, twins in all our actions,
VVe grew up till we were men, held one heart still:
Time call'd us on to Armes, we were one souldier,
Alike we sought our dangers and our honours,
Gloried alike one in anothers noblenesse:
VVhen Armes had made us fit, we were one lover,
VVe lov'd one woman, lov'd without division,
And woo'd a long time with one faire affection;
And she, as it appeares, loves us alike too.
At length considering what our love must grow to,
And covet in the end, this one was parted,
Rivalls and honours make men stand at distance.
VVe then woo'd with advantage, but were friends still,
Saluted fairely, kept the peace of love,
We could not both enjoy the Ladies favour,
Without some scandall to her reputation,
We put it to her choice, this was her sentence,
To part both from her, and the last returning
Should be her Lord; we obey'd, and now you know it;
And for my part, (so truely I am touch'd with't)
I will goe farre enough, and be the last too,
Or ne're returne:

speeches.speaker: Lisand.
verse: A sentence of much cruelty;
But milde, compar'd with whats pronounc'd on me.
Our loving youth is borne to many miseries.
What is that Lidian pray ye?

speeches.speaker: Claran.
prose: Caliste's brother, if ever you have heard of that faire Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: I have seen her sir.

speeches.speaker: Claran.
verse: Then you have seen a wonder.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: I doe confesse: of what yeares is this Lidian?

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: About my years: there is not much between us.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: I long to know him.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: 'Tis a vertuous longing,
As many hopes hang on his noble head,
As blossoms on a bough in May, and sweet ones.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Ye are a faire storie of your friend.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Of truth sir: now, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: There is a gentleman
At doore, would speak with you on private businesse.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: With me?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: He saies so, and brings haste about him.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Wait on him in.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: I will retire the while, to the next room.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
prose: We shall not long disturbe you.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Save ye sir.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: The like to you fair sir: pray you come neare.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Pray you instruct me for I know you not.
With Monsieur Clarange I would speake.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: I am he sir:
Ye are nobly welcome; I wait your businesse.

speeches.speaker: Alcid.
verse: This will informe you.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Will you please to sit down?
He shall command me sir, Ile wait upon him
Within this houre.

speeches.speaker: Alcid.
verse: Y'are a noble gentleman,
Wil't please you bring a friend? we are two of us,
And pitty either sir should be unfurnish'd.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: I have none now, and the time is set so short,
'Twill not be possible.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Doe me the honour:
I know you are so full of brave acquaintance,
And worthy friends, you cannot want a partner:
I would be loath to stand still sir; besides,
You know the custome, and the vantage of it,
If you come in alone.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: And I must meet it.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Send, wee'l defer an houre, let us be equall:
Games won and lost on equall tearmes shew fairest.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: 'Tis to no purpose to send any whither,
Unlesse men be at home by Revelation:
So please you breath a while; when I have done with him
You may be exercis'd too: Ile trouble no man.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: They are very loud. Now what's the newes?

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: I must leave you,
Leave you a while, two houres hence Ile returne friend.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: Why, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: A little businesse.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: And't be but a little, you may take me with ye.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: 'Twill be a trouble to you.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: No indeed, to do you service, I account a pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: I must alone.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Clarang.
verse: 'Tis necessity—
Before you passe the walks, and back agen,
I will be with ye.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: If it be not unmannerly
To presse you, I would goe.

speeches.speaker: Claran.
verse: Ile tell you true sir,
This gentleman and I upon appointment,
Are going to visit a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lisond.
verse: I am no Capuchin, why should not I goe?

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Take the gentleman,
Come he may see the gentlewoman too,
And be most welcome, I do beseech you take him.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: By any means, I love to see a gentlewoman,
A prettie wench too.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Well sir, wee'll meet you,
And at the place: My service to the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: I kisse your hand.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Prethee read o're her Letter.

speeches.speaker: Lisander
verse: Is this your wench? you'll finde her a sharp Mistris.
What have I thrust my selfe into? is this that Lidian
You told me of?
prose:
Monsieur,


I Know you have consider'd the dark sentence Olinda gave us, and that (however she disguis'd it) it pointed more at our swords edges then our bodies banishments; the last must enjoy her: if we retire, our youths ars lost in wandring; in emulation we shall grow old men, and feeble, Which is the scorne of love, and rust of honour, and so return more fit to wed our Sepulchers, then the Saint we aime at; let us therefore make our journey short, and our hearts ready, and with ou^ swords in our hands put it to fortune, which shall be worthy to receive that blessing, Ile stay you on the mountaine, our old hunting place, this gentleman alone runs the hazzard with me, and so I kisse your hand.

Your servant Lidian.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: The same.

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: My Ladies brother?
No cause to heave my sword against but his?
To save the father yesterday, and this morning,
To help to kill the son? this is most courteous?
The onely way to make the daughter doat on me.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Why doe you muse? would ye goe off?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: No, no, I must on now; this will be kindly taken;
No life to sacrifice, but part of hers?
Doe you fight straight?

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Yes, presently.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: To morrow then,
The balefull tidings of this day will break out,
And this nights Sun will set in bloud; I am troubl'd:
If I am kill'd, I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: VVill you goe friend?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
prose: I am ready sir, fortune thou hast made me monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Malf.
verse: Your cousin, and my true friend, lusty Leon,
Shall know how you use me.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Be more temperate,
Or I will never use, nor know you more
Ith' way of a seruant: all the house takes notice
Of your ridiculous fopperie; I have no sooner
Perform'd my duties in my Ladies chamber,
And she scarce down the staires, but you appeare
Like my evill spirit to me.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Can the fish live out of the water, or the Salamander
Out of the fire? or I live warme, but in
The frying-pan of your favour?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Pray you forget
Your curious comparisons, borrowed from
The pond, and kitchin, and remember what
My Ladies pleasure is forth' entertainment
Of her noble father.

speeches.speaker: Ma
verse: I would learn the art of memory in your table book.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Very good sir, no more but up and ride, I apprehend
Your meaning, soft fire makes sweet mault sir:
I'le answer you in a Provetbe,

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: But one kisse from thy honey lippe.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You sight too high, my hand is
A faire ascent from my foot, his slavering kisses
Spoyle me more gloves,—enough for once, you'l surfet
With too much grace.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Have you no imployment for me?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Yes, yes, go send for Leon, and convey him
Into the private Arbour, from his mouth
I heare your praises with more faith.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: I am gone-yet one thing ere I go, there's at the dore
The rarest Fortune-teller, he hath told me
The strangest things; he knows ye are my Mistris,
And under seale deliver'd how many children
I shall beget on you, pray you give him hearing,
He'l make it good to you.

speeches.speaker: Gla.
verse: A cunning man
Of your own making, howsoe're I'le heare him
At your intreaty.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Now I perceive ye love me,
At my entreaty, come in friend—remember
To speake as I directed, he knows his lesson,
And the right way to please her; this it is
To have a head-peece.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Tis said you can tell Fortunes to come.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Yes Mistris, and what's past;
Unglove your hand, by this straight line, I see
You have laine crooked.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: How? laine crooked?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Yes; and in that posture plaid at the old game,
(No body heares me, and I'le be no blab)
And at it lost your maiden-head.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: A shrewd fellow;
'Tis truth, but not to be confess'd; in this
Your palmestry deceaves you, some thing else sir.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Ye are a great woman with your Lady, and
Acquainted with her counsels.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Still more strange.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: There is a noble Knight Lisander loves her,
Whom she regards not. and the destinies
With whom I am familiar, have deliver'd
That by your meanes alone, he must enjoy her.
Your hand agen, Yes, yes; you have already
Promis'd him your assistance, and what's more,
Tasted his bounty, for which, from the skye
There are 200. crownes dropp'd in a Purse,
Looke backe, you'l find it true; nay, open it,
'Tis good Gold I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: How, two Letters? the first indors'd to me? this to my Lady?
Subscrib'd Lisander.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: And the Fortuneteller, his servant Lancelot.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: How had I lost my eyes,
That I could not know thee? not a word of the losse
Of my virginity.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
verse: Nor who I am.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I'le use all speedy meanes for your dispatch,
With a welcome answer, but till you receive it,
Continue thus disguis'd, Mounsieur Malfort
(You know the way to humour him) shall provide
A lodging for you, and good entertainment;
Nay, since we trade both one way, thou shalt have
Some feeling with me, take that.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Bountifull wench may'st thou ne're want imployment.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nor such pay boy.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: You'r welcome.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Let us do our office first,
And then make choice of a new peece of ground
To try our fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: All's faire here.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: And here, their swords are equall.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: If there be any odds in mine, we will exchange.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: Wee'l talke of that
When we are farther off, farwell.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Farewell friend.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: Come let us not be idle?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I will find you imployment, feare not.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: You know sir, the cause that brings us hether

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: There needs no more discoursing,
No time, nor place for repetition now.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: Let our Swords argue, and I wish Clarange,
The proud Olinda saw us.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Would she did;
What ever estimation she holds of me,
She should behold me like a man fight for her.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: 'Tis nobly said; set on love; and my fortune—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: The same for me, come home brave Lidian,
'Twas manly thrust, this token to the Lady,
Ye have it sir, deliver it, take breath,
I see ye bleed apace, ye shall have faire play.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: You must lye there a while, I cannot help you,

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: Nay, then my fortunes gone, I know I must dye:
Yet dearely will I sell my love, come on both,
And use your fortunes, I expect no favour;
Weake as I am, my confidence shall meet ye.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Yeild up your cause and live.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: What dost thou hold me?
A recreant, that prefers life before credit?
Though I bleed hard, my honour finds no Issue,
That's constant to my heart.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Have at your life then.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Hold, or I'le turne, and bend my sword against ye;
My cause Clarange too, view this brave Gentleman,
That yet may live to kill you, he stands nobly,
And has as great a promise of the day
As you can tye unto your selfe, he's ready,
His Sword as sharpe, view him with that remembrance,
That you deliver'd him to me Clarange:
And with those eyes, that clearnesse will become ye:
View him, as you reported him; survey him,
Fixe on your friendship sir, I know you are noble,
And step but Inward to your old affection,
Examine but that soule grew to your bosome,
And try then if your Sword will bite, it cannot,
The edge will turne againe, asham'd, and blunted;
Lidian, you are the patterne of faire friendship,
Exampled for your Love, and imitated,
The Temple of true hearts, stor'd with affections,
For sweetnesse of your spirit made a Saint,
Can you decline this noblenesse to anger?
To mortall anger? 'gainst the man ye love most?
Have ye the name of vertuous, not the nature?

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: I will sit downe.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: And I'le sit by you Lidian.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: And I'le go on, can heaven be pleas'd with these things?
To see two hearts that have been twin'd together
Married in friendship to the world, to wonder,
Of one growth, of one nourishment, one health,
Thus mortally divorc'd for one weake woman?
Can love be pleas'd? love is a gentle spirit,
The wind that blowes the Aprill flowers, not softer;
She is drawne with doves to shew her peacefulnesse,
Lions and bloudy Pards are Mars's servants;
Would ye serve love? do it with humblenesse,
Without a noise, with still prayers, and soft murmurs;
Upon her Altars offer your obedience,
And not your brawles; she's won with teares, not terrors:
That fire ye kindle to her deity,
Is only gratefull when it blowes with sighs,
And holy Incense flung with white hand-innocence;
Ye wound her now; ye are too superstitious,
No sacrifice of bloud, or death she longs for:

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: Came he from heaven?

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: He tels us truth good Lidian.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: That part of Noble love which is most sweet,
And gives eternall being to faire beauty,
Honour. You hack a peeces with your swords,
And that ye fight to crowne, ye kill faire credit.

speeches.speaker: Clara.
verse: Thus we embrace, no more fight, but all friendship,
And where love pleases to bestow his benefits,
Let us not argue.

speeches.speaker: Lid.
verse: Nay brave sir, come in too;
You may love also, and may hope, If he do,
And not rewarded for't, there is no justice;
Farwell friend, here let's part upon our pilgrimage,
It must be so, Cupid draws on our sorrowes.
And where the lot lights—

speeches.speaker: Claran.
verse: I shall count it happinesse,
Farewell deare friend.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: First, let's relieve the Gentleman
That lyes hurt in your cause, and bring him off,
And take some cure for your hurts, then I will part too,
A third unfortunate, and willing wanderer.

speeches.speaker: Olin.
verse: My feares foresaw't would come to this.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I would your sentence had been milder.

speeches.speaker: Olin.
verse: 'Tis past helpe now.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I share in your despaire, and yet my hopes
Have not quite left me, since all possible meanes
Are practised to prevent the mischiefe following
Their mortall meeting, my Lord is coasted one way,
My father, though his hurts forbad his travell,
Hath tooke another, my brother in Law Beronte,
A third, and every minute we must looke for
The certaine knowledge, which we must endure
With that calme patience heav'n shall please to lend us.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Dead both?

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: Such is the rumour, and 'tis generall.

speeches.speaker: Olin.
verse: I heare my passing-bell.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I am in a feavour.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: They say their seconds too; but what they are,
Is not known yet, some worthy fellows certain.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Where had you knowledge?

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: Of the Country people, 'tis spoken every where.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: I heard it so too;
And 'tis so common, I do halfe beleeve it,
You have lost a brother wench, he lov'd you well,
And might have liv'd to have done his countrie service,
But he is gone, thou feld'st untimely Lidian,
But by a valiant hand, that's some small comfort,
And tooke him with thee too, thou lov'st brave company,
Weeping will do no good, you lost a servant,
He might have liv'd to have been your Master Lady,
But you fear'd that.

speeches.speaker: Olind.
verse: Good sir, be tender to me,
The newes is bad enough, you need not presse it.
I lov'd him well, I lov'd 'em both.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: It seemes so.
How many more have you to love so Lady?
They were both fooles to fight for such a Fidle;
Certaine there was a dearth of noble anger,
When a slight woman was thought worth a quarrell.

speeches.speaker: Olin.
verse: Pray you thinke nobler.

speeches.speaker: Do.
verse: I'le tell thee what I thinke, the plague, war, famine,
Nay put in dice and drunkennesse, and those
You'l grant are pretty helpes, kill not so many
(I meane so many noble) as your loves do,
Rather your lewdnesse, I crave your mercy women.
Be not offended if I anger ye.
I am sure ye have touch'd me deep, I came to be merry,
And with my children, but to see one ruin'd
By this fell accident—are they all dead?
If they be, speake?

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: What newes?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: What dead? ye pose me;
I understand you not.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: My brother Lidian, Clarange, and their seconds.

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Here is one of 'em, and sure this Gentleman's alive.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: I hope so, so is your son sir, so is brave Clarange:
They fought indeed, and they were hurt sufficiently;
We were all hurt, that bred the generall rumour,
But friends againe all, and like friends we parted.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: Heard ye of Lisander?

speeches.speaker: Ber.
verse: Yes, and miss'd him narrowly:
He was one of the combatants, fought with this Gentleman,
Second against your brother, by his wisdome
(For certainly good fortune followes him)
All was made peace, I'le tell you the rest at dinner,
For we are hungry.

speeches.speaker: Alc.
verse: I before I eate
Must pay a vow I am sworne to; my life Madam
Was at Lisander's mercy, I live by it;
And for the noble favour, he desir'd me
To kisse your faire hand for him, offering
This second service as a Sacrifice
At the Altar of your vertues.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Come, joy on all sides;
Heaven will not suffer honest men to perish.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Be proud of such a friend.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: Forgive me Madam,
It was a griefe might have concern'd you neare too.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: No worke of excellence but still Lisander,
Go thy waies worthy.

speeches.speaker: Olin.
verse: Wee'l be merry too,
Were I to speake againe, I would be wiser. *

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Too much of this rare cordiall makes me sick,
However I obey you.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: Now or never is an apt time to move her, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Cal
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Clari.
verse: Your servant, I would speake with your Ladyship.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why dost thou looke about?

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: I have private businesse
That none must heare but you. Lisander—

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Where?

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: Nay, is not here, but would entreat this favor,
Some of your Balsome from your own hand given,
For he is much hurt, and that he thinkes would cure him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: He shall have all, my prayers too.

speeches.speaker: Clarind.
verse: But conceive, me,
It must be from your selfe immediately,
Pitty so brave a Gentleman should perish,
He is superstitious, and he holds your hand
Of infinite power: I would not urge this Madam,
But only in a mans extreames, to helpe him.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Let him come (good wench) 'tis that I wish, I am happy in't,
My husband his true friend, my noble father,
The faire Olinda, all desire to see him;
He shall have many hands.

speeches.speaker: Clarind.
verse: That he desires not,
Nor eyes, but yours to looke upon his miseries,
For then he thinkes 'twould be no perfect cure (Madam)
He would come private.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: How can that be here?
I shall do wrong unto all those that honour him,
Besides my credit.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: Dare ye not trust a hurt man?
Not straine a curtesie to save a Gentleman?
To save his life that has sav'd all your family?
A man that comes like a poore mortifi'd Pilgrim;
Only to beg a blessing, and depart againe?
He would but see you, that he thinkes would cure him.
But since you find fit reasons to the contrary,
And that it cannot stand with your cleare honour,
Though you best know how well he has deserv'd of ye:
I'l send him word backe, though I grieve to do it,
Grieve at my soule, for certainly 'twill kill him,
What your will is.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Stay, I will thinke upon't; where is he wench?

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: If you desire to see him,
Let not that trouble you, he shall be with ye,
And in that time, that no man shall suspect ye;
Your honour Madam, is in your own free keeping;
Your care in me, in him all honesty;
If ye desire him not, let him passe by ye:
And all this businesse reckon but a dreame.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Go in, and counsell me, I would faine see him,
And willingly comfort him.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: 'Tis in your power.
And if you dare trust me, you shall do it safely,
Read that, and let that tell you, how he honours you.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: THis happy night.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: Preserve this eagernesse
Till we meet nearer, there is something done
Will give us opportunity.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Witty girle, the plot?

speeches.speaker: Clarind,
verse: You shall heare that at leasure,
The whole house reeles with joy at the report
Of Lidians safety, and that joy increas'd
From their affection to the brave Lisander,
In being made the happy instrument to compound
The bloudy difference.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: They will heare shortly that
Will turne their mirth to mourning, he was then
The principall meanes to save two lives, but since
There are two falne, and by his single hand,
For which his life must answer, if the King,
Whose arme is long, can reach him.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: We have now no spare time to heare stories, take this key,
'Twill make your passage to the banquetting house
I' the garden free.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: You will not faile to come?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
prose: For mine owne sake ne're doubt it? now for Lisander.

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: To bed, to bed, 'tis very late.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: To bed all, I have dranke a health too much,

speeches.speaker: Dor.
verse: You'l sleep the better,
My usuall phisicke that way.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Where's your Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: She is above, but very ill and aguish:
The late fright of her brother, has much troubl'd her;
She would entreate to lye alone.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: Her pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Do.
verse: Commend my love to her, and my prayers for her health,
I'le see her ere I goe.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: All good rest to ye:
Now to my watch for Lisander, when he's furnish'd,
For mine own friend, since I stand Centinell,
I love to laugh i'th' evenings too, and may,
The priviledge of my place will warrant it.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: You have done well hetherto; where are we now?

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: Not far from the house, I heare by th'owles,
There are many of your welch falkoners about it;
Here were a night to choose to run away with
Another mans wife, and do the feate.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Peace knave,
The house is here before us, and some may heare us;
The candles are all out.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
verse: But one i'the parlor,
I see it simper hether, pray come this way.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Step to the garden doore, and feele and 't be open.

speeches.speaker: Lan.
verse: I am going, lucke deliver me from the saw pits,
Or I am buried quicke: I heare a dog,
No, 'tis a cricket, ha? here's a cuckold buried,
Take heed of his horns sir, here's the doore, 'tis open.

speeches.speaker: Clarinda
verse: Whose there?

speeches.speaker: Lisan.
verse: Friend.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Sir, Lisander?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: Ye are welcome, follow me, and make no noise.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Go to your horse, and keep your watch with care, sirah
And be sure ye sleep not.

speeches.speaker: Lanc.
verse: Send me out the dairy-maid
To play at trump with me, and keep me waking,
My fellow horse, and I now must discourse
Like two learned Almanack-makers, of the stars,
And tell what a plentifull year 'twil prove of drunkards,
If I had but a pottle of Sacke, like a sharp prickle,
To knock my nose against when I am nodding,
I should sing like a Nightingall, but I must
Keepe watch without it, I am apt to dance,
Good fortune guide me from the faires circles.

speeches.speaker: Clarin.
verse: Come neare,
I'le leave ye now, draw but that Curtaine,
And have your wish; now Leon I am for thee.
We that are servants must make use of stoln houres,
And be glad of snatch'd occasions.

speeches.speaker: Lisand.
verse: Shee is asleepe,
Fierce love hath clos'd his lights, I may looke on her,
Within her eyes 'has lock'd his graces up,
I may behold and live; how sweet she breathes?
The orient morning breaking out in odors,
Is not so full of perfumes, as her breath is;
She is the abstract of all excellence, and scornes a paralell.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Who's there?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Your servant, your most obedient slave (adored Lady)
That comes but to behold those eyes againe,
And pay some vowes I have to sacred beauty,
And so passe by; I am blind as ignorance,
And know not where I wander, how I live,
Till I receive from their bright influence
Light to direct me, for devotions sake,
You are the Saint I tread these holy steps to.
And holy Saints are all relenting sweetnesse;
Be not imag'd nor be not angry with me;
The greatest attribute of heaven is mercy;
And 'tis the crowne of justice, and the glory
Where it may kill with right, to save with pitty.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Why do you kneele, I know you come to mock me,
T' upbraid me with the benefits you have giv'n me,
Which are too many, and too mighty sir,
For my returne; and I confesse 'tis justice,
That for my cruelty you should despise me,
And I expect however you are calme now,
A foyle you strive to set your cause upon,
It will breake out; Caliste is unworthy,
Coy, proud, disdaine full, I acknowledge all,
Colder of comfort than the frozen North is,
And more a stranger to Lisanders worth,
His youth and faith then it becomes her gratitude,
I blush to grant it, yet take this along,
A soveraigne medicine to allay displeasure,
May be an argument to bring me off too;
She is married, and she is chaste; how sweet that sounds?
How it perfumes all ayre 'tis spoken in?
O deare Lisander, would you breake this union?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: No, I adore it: let me kisse your hand,
And seale the faire faith of a Gentleman on it.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: You are truly valiant, would it not afflict you
To have the horrid name of coward touch you?
Such is the whore to me.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I nobly thanke ye;
And may I be the same when I dishonour ye;
This I may do againe.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Ye may, and worthily;
Such comforts maids may grant with modesty,
And neither make her poore, nor wrong her bounty;
Noble Lisander, how fond now am I of ye?
I heard you were hurt.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: You dare not heale me Lady?
I am hurt here; how sweetly now she blushes?
Excellent objects kill our sight, she blinds me;
The roses in the pride of May shew pale to her;
O tyrant custome! and O coward honour!
How ye compell me to put on mine owne chaines?
May I not kisse ye now in superstition?
For you appeare a thing that I would kneele to:
Let me erre that way.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Ye shall erre for once, I have a kind of noble pity on you,
Among your manly sufferings, make this most,
To erre no farther in desire, for then sir,
Ye adde unto the gratitudes I owe you;
And after death, your deare friends soule shall blesse you.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I am wondrous honest.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I dare try.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: I have tasted a blessednesse too great for dull mortality
Once more and let me dye.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: I dare not murther,
How will maids curse me if I kill with kisses?
And young men flye th' embraces of faire virgins?
Come pray sit down, but let's talke temperately.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Is my deare friend a bed?

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Yes, and asleep;
Secure asleep, 'tis midnight too Lisander,
Speake not so loud.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: You see I am a Statue,
I could not stand else as I had eaten Ice,
Or tooke into my bloud a drowzie poyson,
And natures noblest, brightest flame burne in me;
Midnight? and I stand quietly to behold so?
The alarme rung, and I sleep like a coward?
I am worne away, my faith, and dull obedience
Like crutches, carry my decayed body
Down to the grave, I have no youth within me,
Yet happily you love too.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Love with honour.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Honour? what's that? 'tis but a specious title
We should not prize too high.

speeches.speaker: Cal.
verse: Dearer than life.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: The value of it, is as time has made it,
