verse: Peace, peace, you are fool'd sir;
Things of these natures have strange outsides Pedro,
And cunning shadowes, set 'em far from us,
Draw 'em but neare, they are grosse, and they abuse us;
They that observe her close, shall find her nature,
Which I doubt mainly will not prove so excellent;
She is a Princesse, and she must be faire,
That's the prerogative of being royall:
Let her want eyes and nose, she must be beautious,
And she must know it too, and the use of it,
And people must beleeve it, they are dam'd else:
Why, all the neighbour Princes, are mad for her,

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: Is she not faire then?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: But her hopes are fairer,
And there's a haughty Master, the King of Bakan,
That lofty sir, that speakes far more, and louder
In his own commendations then a Cannon:
He is strucken dumbe with her.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Beshrew me she is a sweet one.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: And there's that hopefull man of Syana,
That spritely fellow, he that's wise and temperate,
He is a lover too.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: Wou'd I were worth her looking
For; by my life I hold her a compleate one,
The very Sun I thinke, affects her sweetnesse,
And dares not as he does to all else, dye it
Into his tauny Livery.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: She dares not see him,
But keepes her selfe at distance from his kisses,
And weares her complexion in a case; let him but like it
A week or two, or three, she would looke like a Lion;
But the maine sport on't is, or rather wonder
The Governour of Ternata her mortall enemie,
He that has catcht her brother King is strooke too,
And is arriv'd under safe conduct also,
And hostages of worth delivered for him;
And he brought a letter from his prisoner,
Whether compel'd, or willingly delivered
From the poore King, or what else dare be in't.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: So it be honourable, any thing, 'tis all one,
For I dare thinke she'l do the best.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: 'Tis certaine
He has admittance, and sollicites hourely.
Now if he have the tricke—

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: What trick?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: The true one,
To take her too, if he be but skil'd in bat-fowling,
And lime his bush right.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: I'le be hang'd when that hits,
For 'tis not a compel'd, or forc'd affection,
That must take her, I guesse her stout and vertuous,
But where's your unckle sir, our valiant Captaine,
The brave Ruy Dias all this while?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I marry,
He is amongst 'em too.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: A Lover.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Nay,
I know not that, but sure he stands in favour,
Or wou'd stand stifly, he is no Portugall else.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: The voyce says in good favour, in the list too
Of the privy woers, how cunningly of late
I have observ'd him, and how privately
He has stolne at all houres from us, and how readily
He has feign'd a businesse to bid the Fort farewell
For five or sixe daies, or a month together,
Sure there is something—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Yes, yes, there is a thing in't,
A thing would make the best on's all dance after it;
A dainty thing; Lord how this unckle of mine
Has read to me, and rated me for wenching,
And told me in what desperate case 'twould leave me,
And how 'twould stew my bones.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: You car'd not for it.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I faith, not much, I ventur'd on still easily,
And tooke my chance, danger is a Souldiers honour;
But that this man, this herbe of Grace, Ruy Dias,
This father of our faculties should slip thus,
For sure he is a ferriting, that he
That would drinke nothing to depresse the spirit,
But milke and water, eate nothing but thin ayre
To make his bloud obedient, that his youth
In spight of all his temperance, should tickle,
And have a love mange on him.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: 'Tis in him sir
But honourable courtship, and becomes his ranke too.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: In me 'twere abominable Lecherie, or would be,
For when our thoughts are on't, and misse their levell,
We must hit something.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Well, 'is a noble Gentleman,
And if he be a suitor, may he speed in't.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Let him alone, our family ne're fail'd yet.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: Our mad Lieutenant still merry Pyniero,
Thus wou'd he do if the Surgeon were searching of him.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Especially if a warme wench had shot him.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: But harke Christophero; come hether Pedro;
When saw you our brave countryman Armusia?
He that's arriv'd here lately, and his gallants?
A goodly fellow, and a brave companion
Me thinkes he is, and no doubt truly valiant,
For he that dares come hether, dares fight any where.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: I saw him not of late, a sober Gentleman
I am sure he is, and no doubt bravely sprung,
And promises much noblenesse.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I love him,
And by my troath wou'd faine be inward with him;
Pray lets go seeke him.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Wee'l attend you sir.

speeches.speaker: Py.
prose: By that time we shalheare the burst of businesse.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Aunt I much thanke you for your curtesie,
And the faire liberty you still allow me,
Both of your house and service, though I be
A Princesse, and by that Prerogative stand free
From the poore malice of opinion,
And no waies bound to render up my actions,
Because no power above me can examine me;
Yet my deare brother being still a prisoner,
And many wandring eyes upon my waies,
Being left alone a Sea-marke, it behoves me
To use a little caution, and be circumspect.

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: You'r wise and noble Lady.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Often Aunt
I resort hether, and privately to see you,
It may be to converse with some I favour;
I wou'd not have it knowne as oft, nor constru'd,
It stands not with my care.

speeches.speaker: Quis^n.
verse: You speake most fairely,
For even our pure devotions are examin'd.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: So mad are mens minds now.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Or rather monstrous;
They are thick dreams, bread in foggs that know no fairnesse.

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: Madam the house is yours, I am yours, pray use me,
And at your service all I have lyes prostrate;
My care shall ever be to yeild ye honour,
And when your fame fals here, 'tis my fault Lady;
A poore and simple banquet I have provided,
Which if you please to honour with your presence —

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I thanke ye Aunt, I shall be with you instantly,
A few words with this Gntleman.

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: I'le leave ye,
And when you please retire, I'le wait upon you.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Why, how now Captaine, what affraid to speak to me?
A man of armes, and danted with a Lady?
Commanders have the power to parle with Princes.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Madam, the favours you have still showr'd on me,
Which are so high above my meanes of merit,
So infinite, that nought can value 'em
But their owne goodnesse, no eyes looke up to 'em
But those that are of equall light; and lustre,
Strike me thus mute, you are my royall Mistris,
And all my services that aime at honour,
Take life from you, the Saint of my devotions;
Pardon my wish, it is a faire ambition,
And well becomes the man that honours you;
I wou'd I were of worth, of something neare you,
Of such a royall peece, a King I wou'd be,
A mighty King that might command affection,
And bring a youth upon me might be witch ye,
And you a sweet sould Christian.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Now you talke sir;
You Portugals, though you be rugged Souldiers,
Yet when you list to flatter, you are plaine courtiers;
And could you wish me Christian brave Ruy Dias?

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: At all the danger of my life great Lady,
At all my hopes, at all—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Pray ye stay a little,
To what end runs your wish?

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: O glorious Lady,
That I might — but I dare not speake.

speeches.speaker: Quisar,
verse: I dare then,
That you might hope to marry me; nay blush not,
An honourable end needs no excuse;
And would you love me then?

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: My soule not dearer.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Do some brave thing that may entice me that way,
Some thing of such a meritorious goodnesse,
Of such an unmatcht noblenesse, that I may know
You have a power beyond ours that preserves you,
'Tis not the person, nor the royall title,
Nor wealth, nor glory that I looke upon,
That inward man I love that's lin'd with vertue,
That well deserving soule workes out a favour;
I have many Princes suiters, many great ones,
Yet above these I love you, you are valiant,
An active man, able to build a fortune;
I do not say I dote, nor meane to marry,
Only the hope is something may be done,
That may compell my faith, and aske my freedom,
And leave opinion faire.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Command deare Lady,
And let the danger be as deep as hell,
As direfull to attempt —

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Y'are too sudden,
I must be rul'd by you, find out a fortune
Wisely and hansomely, examine time,
And court occasion that she may be ready;
A thousand uses for your forward spirit
Ye may find daily, be sure ye take a good one,
A brave and worthy one that may advance ye,
Forced smiles reward poore dangers; you are a Souldier,
I wou'd not talke so else, and I love a Souldier,
And that that speakes him true, and great, his vallour;
Yet for all these which are but womens follies,
You may do what you please, I shall still know ye,
And though ye weare no sword.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Excellent Lady,
When I grow so cold, and disgrace my nation,
That from their hardy nurses sucke adventures,
'Twere fit I wore a Tombstone; you have read to me
The story of your favour, if I mistake it,
Or grow a tenant in the study of it,
A great correction Lady—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Let's toth' banquet,
And have some merrier talke, and then to Court,
Where I give audience to my generall Suiters;
Pray heaven my womans wit hold; there brave Captain,
You may perchance meet something that may startle ye;
I'le say no more, come be not sad—
I love ye.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: You are welcome gentlemen, most worthy welcom,
And know there's nothing in our power may serve ye,
But you may freely challenge.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Sir we thanke ye,
And rest your servants too.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Ye are worthy Portugals,
You shew the bravery of your minds and spirits;
The nature of our country too, that brings forth
Stirring, unwearied soules to seeke adventures;
Minds never satisfied with search of honour
Where time is, & the sunne gives light, brave countrimen,
Our names are known, new worlds disclose their riches,
Their beauties, and their prides to our embraces;
And we the first of nations find these wonders.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: These noble thoughts sir, have intic'd us forward,
And minds unapt for ease to see these miracles,
In which we find report a poore relater;
We are arriv'd among the blessed I stands,
Where every wind that rises blowes perfumes;
And every breath of aire is like an Incence:
The treasure of the Sun dwels here, each tree
As if it envied the old Paradice,
Strives to bring forth immortall fruit; the spices
Renewing nature, though not deifying,
And when that fals by time, scorning the earth,
The sullen earth should taint or sucke their beauties,
But as we dreamt, for ever so preserve us:
Nothing we see, but breeds an admiration;
The very rivers as we floate along,
Throw up their pearles, and curle their heads to court us;
The bowels of the earth swell with the births
Of thousand unknowne gems, and thousand riches;
Nothing that beares a life, but beings a treasure;
The people they shew brave too, civill manner'd,
Proportioned like the Mastres of great minds,
The women which I wonder at—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Ye speake well.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Of delicate aspects, faire, clearly beauteous,
And to that admiration, sweet and courteous.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: And is not that a good thing? brave Armusia
You never saw the Court before?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: No certaine,
But that I see a wonder too, all excellent,
The Government exact.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: Ye shall see anon,
That that will make ye start indeed, such beauties,
Such riches, and such forme.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: We are fire already;
The wealthy Magazine of nature sure
Inhabits here.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: These sure are all Ilanders.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Yes, and great Princes too, and lusty lovers.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: They are goodly persons; what might he be signeor
That beares so proud a state?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: King of Bakam,
A fellow that farts terrour,

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: He lookes highly,
Sure he was begot o'th top of a steeple.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: It may well be,
For you shall heare him ring anon.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: That is Syana,
And a brave temper'd fellow, and more valiant.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: What rugged face is that?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: That's the great Governour,
The man surpriz'd our friend, I told ye of him.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: 'Has dangerous eyes.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: A perilous theefe, and subtle.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: And to that subtlety a heart of Iron.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Yet the young Lady makes it melt.

speeches.speaker: Ar,
verse: They start all,
And thunder in the eyes.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Away ye poore ones,
Am I in competition with such bubbles?
My vertue, and my name rank'd with such trifles?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Ye speake loud.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Young-man, I will speake louder;
Can any man but I, deserve her favour,
You petty Princes?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: He will put 'em all in's pocket.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Thou proud mad thing be not so full of glory,
So full of vanity.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: How: I contemne thee,
And that fort-keeping fellow,

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: How the dog lookes,
The bandog Governour?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Ha, why?

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Away thing,
And keepe your ranke with those that fit your toyalty;
Call out the Princesse.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Dost thou know me bladder,
Thou insolent impostume?

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: I despise thee;

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Art thou acquainted with my nature baby?
Let my revenge for injuries? darst thou hold me
So far behind thy file, I cannot reach thee?
What canst thou merit?

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Merit? I am above it;
I am equall with all honours, all atchievements,
And what is great and worthy; the best doer
I keepe at my command, fortune's my servant,
'Tis in my power now to despise such wretches,
To looke upon ye slightly, and neglect ye,
And but she daines at some houres to remember ye,
And people have bestowed some titles one ye,
I should forget your names—

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Mercy of me;
What a blowne foole has selfe affection
Made of this fellow? did not the Queene your mother,
Long for bellows, and bagpipes when she was great with ye,
She brought forth such a windy birth?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: 'Tis ten to one
She eate a Drum, and was deliver'd of alarum,
Or else he was swadled in an old saile when he was yong.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: He swels too mainly with his meditations;
Faith talke a little hansomer, ride softly
That we may be able to hold way with ye, we are Princes,
But those are but poore things to you; talke wiser,
'Twill well become your mightinesse; talke lesse,
That men may thinke ye can do more.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Talke truth,
That men may thinke ye are honest, and beleeve ye,
Or talke your selfe asleep, for I am weary of you.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Why? I can talke and do.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: That wou'd do excellent.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: And tell you, only I deserve the Princesse,
And make good only I, if you dare, you sir,
Or your Syanas Prince.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Heres a storme toward,
Me thinkes it sings already, to him Governour.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Here lies my proofe.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: And mine.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I'le be short with ye,
For these long arguments I was never good at.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: How white the boaster lookes?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I see he lackes faith.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: For shame forbeare great Princes, rule your angers,
You violate the freedome of this place,
The state and royalty—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: He's well contented
It seemes, and so I have done.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Is this she signior?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: This is the Princesse sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: She is sweet and goodly,
An admirable forme, they have cause to justle.
Quisar. Ye wrong me and my court, ye forward Princes;
Comes your love wrapt in violence to seeke us?
Is't fit though you be great, my pretence should be
Staind, and polluted with your bloudy rages?
My privacies affrighted with your swords?
He that loves me, loves my command; be temper'd,
Or be no more what ye professe, my Servants.

speeches.speaker: Omnes
verse: We are calme as peace.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: What command she carries?
And what a sparkling Majesty flyes from her?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Is it ye love to do? ye shall find danger,
And danger that shall start your resolutions,
But not this way; 'tis not contention,
Who loves me to my face best, or who can flatter most
Can carry me, he that deserves my favour,
And will enjoy what I bring, love and Majesty,
Must win me with his worth; must travell for me;
Must put his hasty rage off, and put on
A well confirm'd, temperate, and true vallour.

speeches.speaker: Omnes
verse: But shew the way.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: And will, and then shew you
A will to tread the way, I'le say ye are worthy.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: What taske now
Will she turne 'em to? these hot youths,
I feare will find a coolling card, I read in her eyes
Something that has some swinge must flye amongst 'em;
By this hand I love her a little now.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: 'Tis not unknown to you
I had a royall brother, now miserable,
And Prisoner to that man; if I were ambitious,
Gap'd for that glory was ne're borne with me,
There they should lye as miseries upon him:
If I were covetous, and my heart set
On riches, and those base effects that follow
On pleasures uncontroul'd, or safe revenges,
There he should dye, his death would give me all these;
For then stood I up absolute to do all;
Yet all these flattering shews of dignity,
These golden dreames of greatnesse cannot force
To forget nature and my faire affection.
Therefore that man that would be known my lover,
Must be known his redeemer, and must bring him
Either alive or dead to my embraces,
For even his bones I scorne shall feele such slavery,
Or seeke another Mistris, 'twill be hard
To do this, wondrous hard, a great adventure,
Fit for a spirit of an equall greatnesse;
But being done, the reward is worthy of it.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: How they stand gaping all?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Ruy Dias cold?
Not flye like fire into it? may be you doubt me,
He that shall do this is my husband Prince;
By the bright heavens he is, by whose justice
I openly proclame it; if I lye,
Or seeke to set you on with subtilty,
Let that meet with me, and reward my falshood.
No stirring yet, no start into a bravery?

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Madam, it may be, but being a maine danger,
Your Grace must give me leave to looke about me,
And take a little time, the cause will aske it,
Great acts require great counsells.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Take your pleasure,
I feare the Portugall.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: I'le raise an Army
That shall bring backe his Island fort and all,
And fixe it here.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: How long will this be doing?
You should have begun in your Grandfathers dayes.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: What may be,
And what my power can promise noblest Lady,
My will I am sure standsfaire.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Faire be your fortune,
Few promises are best, and faire performance.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: These cannot doe,
Their power and arts are weake ones.
'Tis in my will, I have this King your brother,
He is my prisoner, I accept your prisoner,
And blesse the faire occasion that atchiev'd him:
I love ye, and I honor ye, but speake
Whether alive or dead he shall be rendred,
And see how readily, how in an instant,
Quicke as your wishes Lady—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: No, I scorne ye,
You and your courtesie; I hate your love sir;
And ere I would so basely win his liberty,
I would study to forget he was my brother;
By force he was taken; he that shall enjoy me,
Shall fetch him backe by force, or never know me.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: As I live, a rare wench.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: She has a noble spirit.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: By force?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Yes sir by force, and make you glad too
To let him goe.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: How? you may looke nobler on me,
And thinke me no such boy; by force he must not,
For your love much may be.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Put up your passion,
And pack ye home, I say, by force, and suddenly.
He lies there till he rots else, although I love him
Most tenderly and dearly, as a brother,
And out of there respects would joy to see him;
Yet to receive him as thy courtelie,
With all the honour thou couldst adde unto him
From his hands that most hate him, I had rather
Though no condition were propounded for him,
See him far sunke i'th earth, and there forget him.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Your hopes are gelt good Governour.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: A rare woman.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Lady,
I'le pull this pride, I'le quench this bravery,
And turne your glorious scorne to teares and howlings;
I will proud Princesse; this neglect of me
Shall make thy brother King most miserable;
Shall turne him into curses 'gainst thy crueltie:
For where before I us'd him like a King,
And did those Royall Offices unto him,
Now he shall lie a sad lump in a dungeon,
Loden with chaines and fetters, colds and hunger,
Darknesse and lingring death for his companions;
And let me see who dare attempt his rescue,
What desperate foole; looke toward it; farwell,
And when thou know'st him thus, lament thy follies,
Nay I will make thee kneele to take my offer:
Once more farwell, and put thy trust in puppits.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: If none dare undertake it, I'le live a mourner.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: You cannot want.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: You must not.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: 'Tis most dangerous,
And wise men wou'd proceed with care & counsell,
Yet some way would I knnw—
Walke with me Gentlemen—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: How doe you like her spirit?

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: 'Tis a cleare one,
Clod with no dirty stuffe, she is all pure honor.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: The bravest wench I ever look'd upon,
And of the strongest parts, she is most faire,
Yet her mind such a mirrour—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: What an action
Wou'd this be to put forward one, what a glory,
And what an everlasting wealth to end it?
Methinkes my soule is strangely rais'd.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: To step into it,
Just while they thinke, and ere they have determin'd
To bring the King off.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Things have been done as dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: And prosper'd best when they were least considerd.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Blesse me my hopes,
And you my friends assist me.
None but our companions.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: You deale wisely,
And if we shrinke the name of slaves dye with us.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Stay not for second thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I am determin'd;
And though I lose, it shall be sung, I was valiant,
And my brave offer shall be turn'd to story,
Worthy the Princesse tongue. A boat that's all
That's unprovided, and habits like to merchants,
The rest wee'l councell as we goe.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Away then,
Fortune lookes faire on those, make haste to win her.

speeches.speaker: Kee.
verse: I Have kept many a man, and many a great one,
Yet I confesse, I nere saw before
A man of such a sufferance; he lies now
Where I would not lay my dog, for sure 'twou'd kill him.
Where neither light or comfort can come neare him;
Nor aire, nor earth that's wholsome; it grieves me
To see a mighty King with all his glory,
Sunke o'th' sudden to the bottome of a dungeon.
Whether should we descend that are poore Rascals
If we had our deserts?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mo.
verse: 'Tis a strange wonder,
Load him with Irons, oppresse him with contempts,
Which are the Governors commands, give him nothing,
Or so little, to sustaine life, 'tis next nothing;
They stir not him, he smiles upon his miseries,
And beares 'em with such strength as if his nature
Had been nurs'd up, and foster'd with calamities.
He gives no ill words, curses, nor repines not,
Blames nothing, hopes in nothing we can heare of;
And in the midst of all these frights, feares nothing.

speeches.speaker: Kee.
verse: I'le be sworne
He feares not, for even when I shake for him,
As many times my pitty will compell me,
When other soules that beare nor halfe his burthen,
Shrinke in their powers, and burst with their oppressions;
Then will he sing, wooe his afflictions,
And court 'em in sad aires, as if he wou'd wed 'em.
That's more then we have heard yet, we are only
Appointed for his guard, but not so neare him,
If we could heare that wonder—

speeches.speaker: Kee.
verse: Many times
I feare the Governour should come to know it;
For his voice so affects me, so delights me,
That when I find his houre, I have Musicke ready,
And it stirs me infinitely, be but still and private,
And you may chance to heare.
King appeares loden with chaine, his head, arms only above
We will not stir sir;
This is a suddaine change, but who darres blame it.

speeches.speaker: Kee.
verse: Now harke and melt, for I am sure I shall;
Stand silent, what stubbourne weight of chaines—
Yet he lookes temperately.
His eyes not sunke, and his complexion firme still,
No wildnesse, no distemper'd touch upon him.
How constantly he smiles, and how undanted?
With what a Majesty he heaves his head up?

speeches.speaker: Ke.
verse: Now marke, I know he wil sing; do not disturb him.
Your allowance from the Governor, wou'd it were more sir,
Or in my power to make it hansomer.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Do not transgresse thy charge, I take his bounty,
And fortune, whilest I beare a mind contented,
Not leavend with the glory I am falne from,
Nor hang upon vaine hopes, that may corrupt me.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Thou art my slave, and I appeare above thee.

speeches.speaker: Kee.
verse: The Governor himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: What, at your banquet?
And in such state, and with such change of service?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Nature's no glutton sir, a little serves her.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: This diet's holsome then.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I beg no better.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: A calme contented mind, give him lesse next;
These full meales will oppresse his health, his Grace
Is of a tender, and pure constitution,
And such repletions—

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Mocke, mock, it moves not me sir,
Thy mirthes, as do thy mischiefes flie behind me.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Ye carry it handsomely, but tell me patience,
Do not you curse the brave and royall Lady
Your gratious sister? do not you damn her pitty,
Damn twenty times a day, and dam it seriously?
Do not you sweare aloud too, cry and kick?
The very soule sweat in thee with the agony
Of her contempt of me? couldst not thou eate her
For being so injurious to thy fortune,
Thy faire and happy fortune? couldst not thou wish her
A Bastard, or a whore, fame might proclame her
Black ugly fame, or that thou hadst had no sister?
Spitting the generall name out, and the nature;
Blaspheming heaven for making such a mischiefe;
For giving power to pride, and will to woman?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: No Tyrant, no, I blesse and love her for it;
And though her scorne of thee, had laid up for me
As many plagues as the corrupted aire breeds,
As many mischiefes as the houres have minutes.
As many formes of death, as doubt can figure;
Yet I should love her more still, and more honour her;
All thou canst lay upon me, cannot bend me,
No not the stroke of death, that I despise too:
For if feare could possesse me, thou hadst won me;
As little from this houre I prize thy flatteries,
And lesse then those thy prayers, though thou wouldst kneele to me;
And if she be not Mistris of this nature,
She is none of mine, no kin, and I contemne her.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Are you so valiant sir?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Yes, and so fortunate;
For he that holds my constancy still conquers;
Hadst thou preserv'd me as a noble enemy,
And as at first, made my restraint seeme to me
But only as the shadow of captivity,
I had still spoke thee noble, still declar'd thee
A valiant, great, and worthy man, still lov'd thee,
And still prefer'd thy faire love to my sister;
But to compell this from me with a misery,
A most inhumane, and unhansome slavery —

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You will relent for all this talke I feare not,
And put your wits a worke agen.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: You are cozen'd;
Or if I were so weake to be wrought to it,
So fearefull to give way to so much poverty,
How I should curse her heart if she consented.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You shall write and entreat or —

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Do thy utmost,
And e'ne in all thy tortures I'le laugh at thee,
I'le thinke thee no more valiant, but a villaine;
Nothing thou hast done brave, but like a theefe,
Atchiev'd by craft, and kept by cruelty;
Nothing thou canst deserve, thou art unhonest;
Nor no way live to build a name, thou art barbarous.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Down with him low enough, there let him murmur,
And see his dyet be so light and little,
He grow not thus high hearted on't, I will coole ye,
And make ye cry for mercy, and be ready
To worke my ends, and willingly; and your sister taken downe,
Your scornefull, cruell sister shall repent too,
And sue to me for grace.
Give him no liberty,
But let his bands be doubled, his ease lessened;
Nothing his heart desires, but vexe and torture him:
Let him not sleepe, nothing that's deare to nature
Let him enjoy; yet take heed that he dye not;
Keepe him as neere death, and as willing to embrace it,
But see he arrive not at it; I will humble him,
And her stout heart that stands on such defiance;
And let me see her champions that dare venture
Her high and mighty wooers, keepe your guards close,
And as yon love your lives be diligent,
And what I charge, observe.

speeches.speaker: Omnes
verse: We shall be dutifull.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I'le pull your courage King and all your bravery.
Most certaine he is resolved nothing can stir him;
For if he had but any part about him
Gave way to feare or hope, he durst not talke thus,
And do thus stoutly too, as willingly,
And quietly he sunke downe to his sorrows,
As some men to their sleepes.

speeches.speaker: Kee.
verse: Yes, and sleepes with 'em;
So litle he regards them, ther's the wonder,
And often soundly sleepes, wou'd I durst pitty him,
Or wou'd it were in my will, but we are servants,
And tyed unto command.
I wish him better,
But much I feare has found his tombe already,
We must observe our guards.
He cannot last long,
And when he is dead, he is free.

speeches.speaker: Kee.
verse: That's the most cruelty,
That we must keepe him living.
That's as he please;
For that man that resolves, needs no Phisitian.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Our prosperous passage was an omen to us,
A lucky and a faire omen.

speeches.speaker: Omnes
verse: We beleeve it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: The sea and wind strove who should most befriend us,
And as they favourd our designe and lov'd us,
So lead us forth—where lies the boat that brought us?

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Safe lodg'd within the Reeds, close by the Castle,
That no eye can suspect, nor thought come neare it.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: But where have you been, brave sir?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I have broke the Ice boyes:
I have begun the game, faire fortune guide it,
Suspectlesse have I travell'd all the towne through,
And in this Merchants shape won much acquaintance,
Survey'd each strength and place that may befriend us,
View'd all his Magazines, got perfect knowledge
Of where the prison is, and what power guards it.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: These will be strong attempts.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Courage is strong:
What we began with policy, my deare friends,
Let's end with manly force; there's no retiring,
Unlesse it be with shame.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Shame his that hopes it

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Better a few, and clearer fame will follow us,
However, lose or win, and speak our memories,
Then if we led our Armies; things done thus,
And of this noble waight, will stile us worthyes.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Direct, and we have done, bring us to execute,
And if we flinch, or faile—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I am sure ye dare not.
Then further know, and let no eare be neare us
That may be false.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Speak boldly on, we are honest;
Our lives and fortunes yours.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Hard by the place then
Where all his treasure lies, his armes, his women,
Close by the prison too where he keeps the King,
I have hir'd a lodging, as a trading merchant,
A Celler to that too, to stow my wares in,
The very wall of which, joynes to his store-house.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: What of all this?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Ye are dull, if ye apprehend not:
Into that Celler, elected friends, I have convey'd
And unsuspected too that will doe it;
That that will make all shake, and smoak too.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: My thoughts have not been idle, nor my practice:
The fire I brought here with me shall doe something,
Shall burst into materiall flames, and bright ones,
That all the Island shall stand wondring at it,
As if they had been stricken with a Comet:
Powder is ready, and enough to worke it,
The match is left a-fire, all, all husht, and lockt close,
No man suspecting what I am but Merchant:
An houre hence, my brave friends, look for the fury,
The fire to light us to our honour'd purpose,
For by that time 'twill take.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: What are our duties?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: When all are full of feare and fright, the Governour
Out of his wits, the to see flames so imperious,
Ready to turne to ashes all he worships,
And all the people there to stop these ruines,
No man regarding any private office;
Then flie we to the prison suddenly,
Here's one has found the way, and dares direct us.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Then to our swords and good hearts,
I long for it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Certaine we shall not find much opposition,
But what is must be forced.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: 'Tis bravely cast sir,
And surely too I hope.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: If the fire faile not,
And powder hold his nature, some must presently
Upon the first cry of the amazed people,
(For nothing will be markt then, but the miserie)
Be ready with the boat upon an instant,
And then all's right and faire.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Blesse us deare fortune.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Let us be worthie of it in our courage,
And fortune must befriend us, come all sever,
But keep still within fight, when the flame rises
Let's meet, and either doe, or dye.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: So be it.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: No Captaine, for those troops we need 'em not,
The Towne is strong enough to stand their furies;
I wou'd see 'em come, and offer to doe something.
They are high in words.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: 'Tis safer sir then doing.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Dost thinke they dare attempt.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: May be by treaty
But sure by force they wil not prove so forward.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: No faith, I warrant thee, they know me wel enough,
And know they have no child in hand to play with:
They know my nature too, I have bit some of 'em,
And to the bones, they have reason to remember me,
It makes me laugh to think how glorious
The fooles are in their promises, and how pregnant
Their wits and powers are to bring things to passe;
Am I not growne leane with losse of sleep and care
To prevent these threatnings, Captaine?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: You look well sir:
Upon my conscience you are not like to sicken
Upon any such conceit.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I hope I shall not:
Well wou'd I had this wench, for I must have her,
She must be mine; and there's another charge Captaine;
What betwixt love and brawling I got nothing,
All goes in maintenance—
Heark what was that,
That noyse there? it went with a violence.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Some old wall belike sir,
That had no neighbour helpe to hold it up,
Is fallen suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Gov,
verse: I must discard these Rascals,
That are not able to maintaine their buildings,
They blur the beauty of the Town.

speeches.speaker: Within,
verse: Fire, fire.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I heare another tune, good Captaine,
It comes on fresher still, tis loud and fearefull,
Look up into the Towne, how bright the ayre shewes;
Upon my life some suddaine fire.
The bell too?
I heare the noyse more cleare

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Fire, fire.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Where? where?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Suddenly taken in a Merchans house sir,
Fearefull and high it blazes; helpe good people.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Pox o'their paper-houses, how they smother,
They light like candles, how the rore still rises?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Your Magazine's a fire sir, help, help suddenly,
The Castle too is in danger, in much danger,
All will be lost, get the people presently,
And all that are your guard, and all helpe, all hands sir,
Your wealth, your strenth, is burnt else, the town perisht;
The Castle now begins to flame.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: My soule shakes.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: A Merchants house next joyning? shame light on him,
That ever such a neighbour, such a villaine—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Raise all the garrison, and bring 'em up.
And beat the people forward—Oh I have lost all
In one house, all my hopes: good worthy Citizens
Follow me all, and all your powers give to me,
I will reward you all. Oh cursed fortune—
The flame's more violent: arise still, help, helpe Citizens,
Freedome & wealth to him that helps: follow, oh follow.
Fling wine, or any thing, Ile see't recompenc'd.
Buckets, more Buckets; fire, fire, fire.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Let it flame on, a comely light it gives up
To our discovery.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Hearke, what a merry crye
These hounds make? forward fairely,
We are not seen in the mist, we are Not noted. Away,
Away. Now if we lose our fortune —

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Up souldiers, up, and deale like men.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: More water, more water, all is consum'd else.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: All's gone, unlesse you undertake it straight, your
Wealth too, that must preserve, & pay your labor bravely.
Up, up, away.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: So, thou art open, keep the way cleare
Behinde still. Now for the place.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: 'Tis here sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Sure this is it.
Force ope the doore—A miserable creature!
Yet by his manly face — The King discover'd.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Why stare ye on me?
You cannot put on faces to afright me:
In death I am a King still, and contemne ye:
Where is that Governour? me thinks his man-hood
Should be well pleas'd to see my Tragedy,
And come to bath his sterne eyes in my sorrowes;
I dare him to the fight, bring his scornes with him,
And all his rugged threats: here's a throat, souldiers;
Come, see who can strike deepest.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Break the Chain there.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: What does this mean?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Come, talke of no more Governours,
He has other businesse sir, put your legs forward,
And gather up your courage like a man,
Wee'll carrie off your head else: we are friends,
And come to give your sorrowes ease.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: On bravely;
Delayes may lose agen,

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: The Guard.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Upon 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Make speedy, and sure work.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: They flye.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Up with him, and to the Boat; stand fast, now be speedy,
When this heat's past, wee'll sing our History.
Away, like thoughts, sudden as desires, friends;
Now sacred chance be ours.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Pray when we have done sir.
What is the fire allaid?
'Tis out, tis out,
Or past the worst, I never did so stoutly
I'le assure you neighbours since I was a man:
I have been burnt at both ends like a squib:
I liv'd two hovres in the fire, 'twas a hideous matter;
But when men of understanding come about it,
Men that judge of things, my wife gave me over,
And tooke her leave a hundred times, I bore up still,
And tost the Buckets boyes.
We are all meere Martins.
I heard a voice at latter end o'th hurry,
Or else I dreamt I heard it, that said treason.
'Tis like enough, it might cry murder to, for there was
Many without a joint, but whats that to us: Lets home
And fright our wives. for we looke like Devils.
Here come some of 'em to fright us.

speeches.speaker: 1 W.
verse: Mine's alive neighbor— oh sweet hony husband.
Thou liest I thinke abominably, and thou hadst bin
In my place, thou wouldst have stunke at both ends.
Get me some drinke, give me whole tuns of drinke,
Whole cisternes, for I have foure dozen of fine firebrands
In my belly, I have more smoke in my mouth, then would
Blote a hundred herrings.

speeches.speaker: 2 Wo.
verse: Art thou come safe agen?

speeches.speaker: 3 Wo.
verse: I pray you what became of my man, is he in a wel?
At hearts ease in a Well, is very well neighbour;
We left him drinking of a new dozen of Buckets;
Thy husbands happy, he was through roasted,
And now hee's basting of himselfe at all points:
The Clarke and he are cooling their pericraniums;
Body O me neighbors there's fire in my codpiece.

speeches.speaker: 1 Wo.
verse: Blesse my husband.
Blow it out wife—blow, blow, the gable end a'th' store-house.

speeches.speaker: Women.
verse: Some water, water, water.
Peace, tis but a sparkle;
Raise not the Towne again, 'twill be a great hinderance,
I'm glad tis out, and 't had tane in my hayloft?
What frights are these, marry heaven blesse thy modicum.

speeches.speaker: 3 Wo.
verse: But is a drown'd outright, pray put me out of Feare neighbor.
Thou wouldst have it so, but after a hundred fires
More, hee'l live to see thee burnt for brewing musty Liquor.
Come lets goe neighbor.
For I would very faine turne downe this liquor;
Come, come, I fry like a burnt marry-bone:
Women get you afore, and draw upon us;
Run wenches run, and let your taps run with ye;
Run as the fire were in your tailes, cry ale, ale.

speeches.speaker: Wom.
verse: Away lets nourish the poore wretches.
Wee'l Rallie up the rest of the burnt Regiment.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: The fire's quencht Captain, but the mischief hangs still;
The Kings redeem'd, & gon too; a trick, a dam'd one:
Oh I am overtaken poorely, tamely.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Where were the guard that waited upon the prison?

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Most of 'em slaine, yet some scap't sir, and they deliver,
They saw a little boat ready to receive him,
And those redeem'd him, making such haste and fighting;
Fighting beyond the force of men.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I am lost Captaine,
And all the world will laugh at this, and scorne me:
Count me a heavy sleepy foole, a coward,
A coward past recovery, a confirm'd coward,
One without carriage, or common sense.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Hee's gone sir,
And put to sea amaine, past our recovery,
Not a Boat ready to pursue; if there were any,
The people stand amazed so at their valour,
And the sudden fright of fire, none knowes to execute.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Oh, I could tear my limbs, & knock my boys brains
'Gainst every post I meet; fool'd with a fire?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: It was a crafty trick.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: No, I was lazy,
Confident sluggish lazie, had I but met 'em,
And chang'd a dozen blowes, I had forgiv'n 'em,
By both these hands held up, and by that brightnesse
That gildes the worldwith light, by all our worships,
The hidden ebbes and flowes of the blew Ocean,
I will not rest; no mirth shall dwell upon me,
Wine touch my mouth, nor any thing refresh me,
Till I be wholy quit of this dishonour:
Make ready my Barrato's instantly,
And what I shall intend—

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: We are your servants.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Never tell me, you never car'd to win me,
Never for my sake to attempt a deed,
Might draw me to a thought you sought my favour:
If not for love of me, for love of armes sir,
For that cause you professe, for love of honour,
Of which you stile your selfe the mighty Master,
You might have stept out nobly, and made an offer,
As if you had intended something excellent,
Put on a forward face.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Deare Lady hold me—

speeches.speaker: Quisar,
verse: I hold ye, as I finde yee, a faint servant.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: By—I dare doe—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: In a Ladies chamber
I dare beleeve ye, there's no mortall danger:
Give me the man that dares doe, to deserve that:
I thought you Portugalls had been rare wonders,
Men of those haughty courages and credits,
That all things were confin'd within your promises,
The Lords of fate and fortune I beleev'd yee,
But well I see I am deceiv'd Ruy Dias,
And blame too late my much beliefe.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I am asham'd, Lady,
I was so dull, so stupid to your offer:
Now you have once more school'd me, I am right,
And something shall be thought on suddenly,
And put in act as soone, some preparation —

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: And give it out?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Yes, Lady, and so great too:
In which, the noyse of all my Countrey-men—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Those will doe well, for they are all approv'd ones,
And though he be restor'd alive.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I have ye.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: For then we are both servants.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I conceive ye,
Good Madam give me leave to turne my fancies.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
prose: Do, & make all things fit, & then Ile visit you.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: My selfe, the cozen, and the Garrison,
The neighbours of the out-Isles of our nation,
Syana's strength, for I can humour him:
And proud Bekamus, I shall deceive his glory.
What ringing sound of joy is this? whence comes it?
May be the Princes are in sport.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Where are ye?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Now Pyniero, what's the haste you seek me?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Doe you know this signe sir?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Doe you know this embleme?
Your nose is boar'd.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Boar'd? what's that?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Y'are topt sir:
The Kings come home againe, the King.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: The devill?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Nay sure he came a gods name home:
Hee's return'd sir.

speeches.speaker: Christ.
verse: And all this joy yee heare—

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Who durst attempt him?
The Princes are all here.

speeches.speaker: Chry.
verse: They are worthy Princes,
They are speciall Princes, all they love by ounces.
Believe it sir, 'tis done, and done most bravely and easily.
What fortune have ye lost sir?
What justice have ye now unto this Lady?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: How stands your claime?
That ever man should be fool'd so,
When he should doe and prosper; stand protesting,
Kissing the hand, and farting for a favour,
When he should be about his businesse sweating;
She bid you goe, and pickt you out a purpose,
To make your selfe a fortune by, a Lady, a Lady, and a lusty one,
A lovely, that now you may goe look, she poynted ye,
Knowing you were a man of worth and merit,
And bid you fly, you have made a faire flight on't,
You have caught a goose.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: How dare you thus molest me?
It cannot bee.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: Heark how the generall joy rings!

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Have you your hearing left? is not that drunk too?
For if you had been sober, you had been wise sure.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Done? who dares doe?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: It seems an honest fellow,
That has ended his Market before you be up.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: The shame on't 's a stranger too.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: 'Tis no shame,
He took her at her word, and tyed the bargaine,
Dealt like a man indeed, stood not demurring,
But clapt close to the cause, as he will doe to the Lady:
'Is a fellow of that speed and handsomnesse,
He will get her with childe too, ere you shall come to know him,
Is it not brave, a gentleman scarce landed,
Scarce eating of the aire here, not acquainted,
No circumstance of love depending on him,
Nor no command to shew him, must start forth,
At the first sight to—

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I am undone.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Like an Oyster:
She neither taking view, nor value of him,
Unto such deeds as these — Pox o'these,
These wise delayings—
They make men cowards.
You are undone as a man would undoe an egge,
A hundred shames about ye.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Can it be possible,
A stanger that I have not knowne, not seen yet,
A man I never grac'd; O Captaine, Captaine,
What shall I doe? I am betray'd by fortune,
It cannot be, it must not be.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: It is Lady,
And by my faith a hansome Gentleman;
'Tis his poore Schollers prize.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Must I be given
Unto a man I never saw, ne're spoke with,
I know not of what Nation?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Is a Portugall,
And of as good a pitch he will be given to you Lady,
For hee's given much to hansome flesh.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Oh Ruy Dias,
This was your sloth, your sloth, your sloth Ruy Dias.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Your love sloth, Unckle doe you find it now?
You should have done at first, and faithfully:
And then the tother had lyed ready for ye;
Madam, the generall joy comes.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: We must meet it—but with what comfort?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Oh my deare brother what a joy runs through me,
To see you safe again, your selfe, and mighty,
What a blest day is this?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Rise up faire sister,
I am not welcome till you have embraced me.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: A generall gladnes sir flies through the City,
And mirth possesses all to see your Grace arrive,
Thus happily arrived againe, and fairely;
'Twas a brave venture who so e're put for it,
A high and noble one, worthy much honor;
And had it failed, we had not failed great sir,
And in short time too to have forc'd the Governor,
In spight of all his threats.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I thanke ye Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: And all his subtilties to set you free,
With all his heart and will too.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I know ye love me.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: This had bin good with something done before it,
Somthing set off to beautifie it, now it sounds emptie like
A Barbers bason, pox there's no mettall in't, no noble marrow.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: I have an army sir, but that the Governor,
The foolish fellow was a little provident,
And wise in letting slip no time, became him too,
That would have scoured him else, and all his confines;
That would have rung him such a peale —

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Yes backward,
To make doggs houle, I know thee to a farthing,
Thy armye's good for hawkes, there's
Nothing but sheeps hearts in it.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: I have done nothing sir, therefore
I thinke it convenient I say little what I purposed,
And what my love intended.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I like your modestie,
And thanke ye royall friends, I know it griev'd ye
To know my miserie; but this man Princes,
I must thanke heartily indeed and truly,
For this man saw me in't, and redeemed me:
He lookt upon me sinking, and then caught me.
This sister this, this all man, this all valour,
This pious man.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: My countenance, it shames me,
One scarce arrived, not harden'd yet, not
Read in dangers and great deeds, sea-sick, not season'd —
Oh I have boy'd my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: This noble bulwarke,
This launce and honor of our age and Kingdome;
This that I never can reward, nor hope
To be once worthy of the name of friend to,
This, this man from the bowels of my sorrowes
Has new begot my name, and once more made me:
Oh sister, if there may be thanks for this,
Or any thing neere recompence invented.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You are too noble sir, there is reward
Above my action too by millions:
A recompence so rich and glorious,
I durst not dreame it mine, but that 'twas promised;
But that it was propounded, sworne and sealed
Before the face of heaven, I durst not hope it,
For nothing in the life of man, or merit,
It is so truly great, can else embrace it.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: O speake it, speake it, blesse mine eares to heare it,
Make me a happy man, to know it may be,
For still methinkes I am a prisoner,
And feele no libertie before I find it.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Then know it is your sister, she is mine sir,
I claime her by her owne word, and her honour;
It was her open promise to that man
That durst redeeme ye; Beauty set me on,
And fortune crownes me faire, if she receive me.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Receive ye sir — why sister — ha — so backward,
Stand as you knew me not, nor what he has ventured
My dearest sister.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Good sir pardon me,
There is a blushing modestie becomes her,
That holds her back; women are nice to wooe sir;
I would not have her forced, give her faire libertie;
For things compell'd and frighted of soft natures,
Turne into feares, and flye from their owne wishes.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Looke on my Quisara such another,
Oh all ye powers, so excellent in nature,
In honour so abundant.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I confesse sir,
Confesse my word is past too, he has purchased;
Yet good sir give me leave to thinke, but time
To be acquainted with his worth and person;
To make me fit to know it; we are both strangers,
And how we should beleeve so suddenly,
Or come to fasten our affections —
Alas, love has his complements.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Be sudden
And certaine in your way, no womans doubles,
Nor coy delayes, you are his, and so assure it,
Or cast from me and my remembrance ever;
Respect your word, I know you will, come sister,
Lets see what welcome you can give a prisoner,
And what faire lookes a friend — Oh my most noble
Princes, no discontents, but all be lustie,
He that frownes this day is an open enemie:
Thus in my armes my deare.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: You make me blush sir.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: And now lead on —
Our whole Court crowned with pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Madam, despaire not, something shall be done yet,
And suddenly and wisely.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: O Ruy Dias.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Well he's a brave fellow, & he has deserv'd her richly,
And you have had your hands full I dare swear Gentleme~.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: We have done something sir, if it hit right.

speeches.speaker: Ch.
verse: The woman has no eyes else, nor no honesty,
So much I think.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Come, let's goe bounce amongst 'em,
To the Kings health, and my brave country-mans.
My uncle looks as though he were sick oth'
Worms friends.
MIne uncle haunts me up & down, looks melancholy,
Wondrous proof melancholy, sometimes sweares,
Then whistles, starts, cries, & groans, as if he had the Bots.
As to say truth, I think h'as little better,
And wo'd fain speak; bids me good morrow at midnight,
And good night when 'tis noon, has something hovers
About his braines, that would faine finde an issue,
But cannot out, or dares not: stil he followes;
How he looks still, and how he beats about,
Like an old Dog at a dead sent? I marry,
There was a sigh wou'd a set a ship a sayling:
These winds of love and honour blow at all ends.
Now speak and't be thy will: good morrow Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Good morrow sir.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: This is a new salute:
Sure h'as forgot me: this is pur-blinde Cupid.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: My Nephew?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Yes sir, it I be not chang'd.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I wou'd faine speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I wou'd faine have ye sir,
For to that end I stay.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: You know I love yee,
And I have lov'd you long, my deare Pyniero,
Bred and supply'd you.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Whither walks this Preamble?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: You may remember, though I am but your Uncle,
I sure had a fathers care, a fathers tendernesse.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Sure he would wrap me into something now suddenly,
He doubts my nature in, for mine is honest,
He windes about me so.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: A fathers deligence.
My privat benefits, I have forgot sir,
But those you might lay claime to as my follower;
Yet some men wou'd remember—

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: I doe dayly.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: The place which I have put ye in, which is no weak one,
Next to my selfe you stand in all employments,
Your counsells, cares, assignements with me equall,
So is my study still to plant your person;
These are small testimonies I have not forgot ye,
Nor wou'd not be forgotten.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: Sure you cannot.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: O Pyniero—

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: Sir; what hangs upon you,
What heavy weight oppresses ye, ye have lost,
(I must confesse, in those that understand ye)
Some little of your credit, but time will cure that;
The best may slip sometimes.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Oh my best Nephew—

speeches.speaker: Pyn
verse: It may be yee feare her too, that disturbs ye,
That she may fall her selfe, or be forc'd from ye.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: She is ever true, but I undone for ever.
Oh that Armusia, that new thing, that stranger,
That flag stuck up to rob me of mine honor;
That murdring chaine shot at me from my Country;
That goodly plague that I must court to kill me.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: Now it comes flowing from him, I feared this,
Knew, he that durst be idle, durst be ill too,
Has he not done a brave thing?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I must confesse it nephew, must allow it,
But that brave thing has undone me, has sunke me,
Has trod me like a name in sand to nothing,
Hangs betwixt hope and me, and threatens my ruine:
And if he rise and blaze, farewell my fortune;
And when thats set, where's thy advancement Cozen?
That were a friend, that were a noble kinsman,
That would consider these; that man were gratefull;
And he that durst doe something here durst love me.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: You say true, 'tis worth consideration,
Your reasons are of weight, and marke me Unckle,
For I'le be sudden, and to'th' purpose with you.
Say this Armusia then wert taken off,
As it may be easily done
How stands the woman?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: She is mine for ever;
For she contemnes his deed and him.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: Pox on him,
Or if the single pox be not sufficient,
The hogs, the dogs, and devils pox possesse him:
'Faith this Armusia stumbles me, is a brave fellow;
And if he could be spared Unckle—

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I must perish:
Had he set up at any rest but this,
Done any thing but what concern'd my credit,
The everlasting losing of my worth.—

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: I understand you now, who set you on too;
I had a reasonable good opinion of the devill
Till this houre; and I see he is a knave indeed,
An arrant stinking knave, for now I smell him;
I'le see what may be done then, you shall know
You have a kinsman, but no villaine Unckle,
Nor no betrayer of faire fame, I scorne it;
I love and honour vertue; I must have
Accesse unto the Lady to know her mind too,
A good word from her mouth you know may stir me;
A Ladies looke at setting on—

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: You say well;
Here Cozen, here's a Letter readie for you,
And you shall see how nobly shee'l receive you,
And with what care direct.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: Farewell then Unckle,
After I have talked with her, I am your servant,
To make you honest if I can — else hate you.
Pray ye no more complements, my head is busie, heaven blesse me;
What a malicious soule does this man carry?
And to what scurvy things this love converts us?
What stinking things, and how sweetly they become us?
Murther's a morall vertue with these Lovers,
A speciall peece of Divinitie I take it:
I may be mad, or violentlie drunke,
Which is a whelp of that litter; or I may be covetous,
And learne to murther mens estates, thats base too;
Or proud, but thats a Paradise to this;
Or envious, and sit eating of my selfe
At others fortunes; I may lye, and damnably,
Beyond the patience of an honest hearer;
Couzen, Cut purses, sit i'th' stocks for apples.
But when I am a lover, Lord have mercy,
These are poore pelting sins, or rather plagues,
Love and Ambition draw the devills Coach.
How now! who are these? Oh my great Ladies followers,
Her riddle-founders, and her fortune-tellers,
Her readers of her love-lectures, her inflamers:
These doors I must passe through, I hope they are wide.
Good day to your beauties, how they take it to 'em?
As if they were faire indeed.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: Good morrow to you sir.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: That's the old Hen, the brood-bird? how she busies?
How like an Inventory of Lecherie she looks?
Many a good peece of iniquity
Has past her hands, I warrant her—I beseech you,
Is the faire Princesse stirring?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Yes marry is she sir,
But somewhat private: have you a businesse with her?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Yes forsooth have I, and a serious businesse.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: May not we know?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Yes, when you can keep counsell.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: How prettily he looks? he's a souldier sure,
His rudenesse sits so handsomly upon him.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: A good blunt gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Yes marry am I:
Yet for a push or two at sharp, an't please you —

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: My honest friend, you know not who you speak to:
This is the Princesse Aunt.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: I like her th' better
And she were her Mother, (Lady) or her grandmother,
I am not so bashfull but I can buckle with her.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Of what size is your businesse?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Of the long sixteens,
And will make way I warrant yee.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: How fine he talks?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Nay in troth I talke but coursely, Lady,
But I hold it comfortable for the understanding:
How faine they won'd draw me into ribaldry?
These wenches that live easily, live high,
And love these broad discourses, as they love possets;
These dry delights serve for preparatives.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Why doe you look so on me?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: I am ghessing
By the cast of your face, what the property of your place should be,
For I presume you turne a key sweet beauty,
And you another gravity, under the Princesse,
And by my — I warrant ye good places,
Comely commodious feates.

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: Prethee let him talke still,
For me thinkes he talkes hansomely.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: And truly
As neare as my understanding shall enable me
You look as if you kept my Ladies secrets:
Nay doe not laugh, for I meane honestly,
How these young things tattle, when they get a toy by th' end?
And how their hearts goe pit a pat and look for it?
Wou'd it not dance too, if it had a Fiddle?
Your gravity I ghesse, to take the Petitions,
And heare the lingring suits in love dispos'd,
Their sighes and sorrowes in their proper place,
You keep the ayme office.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Prethee suffer him,
For as I live hee's a pretty fellow.
I love to here sometimes what men think of us:
And thus deliver'd freely, 'tis no malice:
Proceed good honest man.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: I will, good Madam.
According to mens states and dignities,
Moneyes and moveables, you rate their dreames,
And cast the Nativity of their desires,
If he reward well, all he thinks is prosperous:
And if he promise place, his dreams are Oracles;
Your ancient practique Art too in these discoveries,
Who loves at such a length, who a span farther,
And who drawes home, yeeld you no little profit,
For these yee milk by circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Yee are cunning.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: And as they Oyle ye, and advance your spindle,
So you draw out the lines of love, your doores too,
The doores of destiny, that men must passe through;
These are faire places.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: He knowes all.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Your trap doores,
To pop fooles in it, that have no providence,
Your litle wickets, to work wise men, like wires throgh at,
And draw their states and bodies into Cobwebs,
Your Posterne doores, to catch those that are cautelous,
And would not have the worlds eye finde their knaveries:
Your doores of danger, some men hate a pleasure,
Unlesse that may be full of feares; your hope doores,
And those are fine commodities, where fooles pay
For every new encouragement, a new custome;
You have your doores of honour, and of pleasure;
But those are for great Princes, glorious vanities,
That travell to be famous through diseases;
There be the doores of povertie and death too:
But these you doe the best you can to damme up,
For then your gaine goes out.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: This is a rare lecture.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Read to them that understand.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Beshrew me,
I dare not venture on ye, yee cut too keen sir.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: We thank you sir for your good mirth
You are a good Companion.
Here comes the Princesse now, attend your businesse.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Is there no remedy? no hopes can help me?
No wit to set me free? whose there hoe?

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: Troubled? her looks are almost wilde:
What ailes the Princesse?
I know nothing she wants.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Who's that there with you?
Oh Signeur Piniero? you are most welcome:
How does your noble uncle?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: Sad as you are Madam:
But he commends his service, and this Letter.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Goe off, attend within—Faire sir, I thank ye,
Pray be no stranger, for indeed you are welcome;
For your owne vertues welcome.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: We are mistaken,
This is some brave fellow sure.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I'me sure hee's a bold fellow:
But if she hold him so, we must beleeve it.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Doe you know of this faire sir?

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: I ghesse it Madam,
And whither it intends: I had not brought it else.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: It is a businesse of no common reckoning.

speeches.speaker: Pin.
verse: The handsomer for him that goes about it;
Slight actions are rewarded with slight thanks:
Give me a matter of some waight to wade in.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: And can you love your Uncle so directly,
So seriously, and so full, to undertake this?
Can there be such a faith?

speeches.speaker: Pyn:
verse: Dare you say I to it,
And set me on? 'tis no matter for my Uncle,
Or what I owe to him, dare you but wish it.

speeches.speaker: Ouisar.
verse: I wou'd faine—

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: Have it done; say but so Lady.

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: Conceive it so.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: I will, 'tis that I am bound too:
Your will that must command me, and your pleasure,
The faire aspects of those eyes, that must direct me:
I am no Uncles agent, I am mine owne, Lady;
I scorne my able youth should plough for others,
Or my ambition serve for pay; I ayme,
Although I never hit, as high as any man,
And the reward I reach at shall be equall,
And what love spurs me on to, this desire,
Makes me forget an honest man, a brave man,
A valiant, and a vertuous man, my country-man, Armusia,
The delight of all the Minions,
Is love of you, doting upon your beauty, the admiration of your excellence;
Make me but servant to the poorest smile,
Or the least grace you have bestow'd on others,
And see how suddenly Ile worke your safety,
And set your thoughts at peace; I am no flatterer,
To promise infinitely, and out-dream dangers;
To lye a bed, and sweare men into Feavers,
Like some of your trim suters; when I promise,
The light is not more constant to the world,
Then I am to my word — She turnes for millions.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I have not seen a braver confirm'd courage.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: For a tun of Crownes she turns: she is a woman,
And much I feare a worse then I expected.
You are the object Lady, you are the eye
In which all excellence appears, all wonder,
From which all hearts take fire, all hands their valour:
And when he stands disputing, when you bid him,
Or but thinks of his estate, Father, Mother,
Friends, Wife, and Children,
'Is a foole, and I scorne him,
And be but to make cleane his sword: coward
Men have forgot their fealty to beauty.
Had I the place in your affections,
My most unworthy uncle is fit to fall from,
Liv'd in those blessed eyes, and read the stories
Of everlasting pleasures figur'd there,
I wou'd finde out your co~mands before you thought 'em,
And bring 'em to you done, ere you dream't of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: I admire his boldnesse.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: This, or any thing;
Your brothers death, mine uncles, any mans,
No state that stands secure, if you frowne on it.
Look on my youth, I bring no blastings to you,
The first flower of my strength, my faith.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: No more sir;
I am too willing to believe, rest satisfi'd;
If you dare doe for me, I shall be thankfull:
You are a handsome gentleman, a faire one,
My servant if you please; I feale it thus sir.
No more, till you deserve more.

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: I am rewarded:
This woman's cunning, but she's bloudy too;
Although she pulls her Tallons in, she's mischievous;
Form'd like the face of heaven, cleare and transparent;
I must pretend still, beare 'em both in hopes,
For feare some bloudy slave thrust in indeed,
Fashion'd and flesh'd to what they wish: well uncle,
What will become of this, and what dishonour
Follow this fatall shaft, if shot, let time tell,
I can but only feare, and crosse to crosse it.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Why are you thus sad? what can grieve or vex you
That have the pleasures of the world, the profits,
The honour, and the loves at your disposes?
Why should a man that wants nothing, want his quiet?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I want what beggars are above me in, content:
I want the grace I have merited,
The favour, the due respect.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Does not the King allow it?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Yes and all honors else, all I can aske,
That he has power to give; but from his sister,
The scornfull crueltie, forgive me beauty,
That I transgresse from her that should looke on me,
That should a little smile upon my service,
And foster my deserts for her owne faiths sake;
That should at least acknowledge me, speake to me.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: And you goe whining up and downe for this sir,
Lamenting and disputing of your grievances;
Sighing and sobbing like a sullen Schoole-boy,
And cursing good-wife fortune for this favor.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: What would you have me doe?

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Doe what you should doe,
What a man would doe in this case, a wise man,
An understanding man that knowes a woman;
Knowes her and all her tricks, her scorns & all her trifles:
Goe to her and take her in your armes and shake her,
Take her and tosse her like a barre.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: But be sure you pitch her upon a feather-bed,
Shake her between a paire of sheets sir,
There shake these sullen fits out of her, spare her not there,
There you may breake her will, and bruise no bone sir.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Goe to her.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Thats the way.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: And tell her and boldly,
And doe not mince the matter, nor mocke your selfe,
With being too indulgent to her pride:
Let her heare roundly from ye, what ye are,
And what ye haue deserved, and what she must be.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: And be not put off like a common fellow,
With the Princesse would be private,
Or that she has taken phisicke, and admits none,
I would talke to her any where.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: It makes me smile.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Now you looke hansomely:
Had I a wench to win, I would so flutter her,
They love a man that crushes 'em to verjuice;
A woman held at hard meat is your spanniel.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Pray take our counsell sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I shall doe something,
But not your way, it shewes too boisterous,
For my affections are as faire and gentle,
As her they serve.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: The King.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Why, how now friend?
Why doe you rob me of the companie
I love so dearly sir, I have bin seeking you;
For when I want you, I want all my pleasure:
Why sad? thus sad still man; I will not have it;
I must not see the face I love thus shadowed.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: And't please your Grace, methinks it ill becomes him,
A souldier should be joviall, high and lustie.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: He shall be so, come, come, I know your reason,
It shall be none to crosse you, ye shall have her,
Take my word, ('tis a Kings word) ye shall have her,
She shall be yours or nothing, pray be merry.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Your grace has given me cause, I shall be sir,
And ever your poore servant.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Me my selfe sir,
My better selfe, I shall finde time, and suddenly,
To gratifie your loves too gentlemen,
And make you know how much I stand bound to you:
Nay 'tis not worth your thanks, no further complement;
Will you goe with me friend?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I beseech your grace,
Spare me an houre or two, I shall wait on you,
Some little private businesse with my selfe sir,
For such a time.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Ile hinder no devotion,
For I know you are regular, Ile take you gentlemen,
Because hee shall have nothing to disturbe him,
I shall look for your friend.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I dare not faile sir:
What shal I doe to make her know my misery,
To make her sensible? This is her woman,
I have a toy come to me suddenly,
It may worke for the best, she can but scorne me,
And lower then I am I cannot tumble,
Ile trye what ere my fate be—Good even faire one,

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: 'Tis the brave stranger—A good night to you sir.
Now by my Ladies hand a goodly gentleman!
How happy shall she be in such a husband?
Wou'd I were so provided too.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Good pretty one,
Shall I keep you company for an houre or two?
I want employment for this evening.
I am an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I dare beleeve yee:
Or if yee were not sir, that's no great matter,
We take mens promises, wou'd ye stay with me sir?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: So it please you; pray let's be better acquainted,
I know you are the Princesse gentlewoman,
And wait upon her neere.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: 'Tis like I doe so.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: And may befriend a man, do him faire courtesies,
If he have businesse your way.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I understand yee.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: So kinde an office, that you may bind a gentleman
Hereafter to be yours, and your way too,
And ye may blesse the houre you did this benefit,
Sweet handsome faces should have courteous mindes,
And ready faculties.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Tell me your businesse,
Yet if I thinke it be to her, your selfe sir,
For I know what you are, and what we hold ye,
And in what grace ye stand, without a second
For that but darkens, you wou'd doe it better,
The Princesse must be pleas'd with your accesses,
I'me sure I should.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I want a Courtiers boldnesse,
And am yet but a stranger, I wou'd faine speak with her:

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: 'Tis very late, and upon her houre of sleep sir.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Pray ye weare this, and believe my meaning civil,
My businesse of that faire respect and carriage:
This for our more acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: How close he kisses?
And how sensible the passings of his lips are?
I must do it, and I were to be hang'd now, and I will do it,
He may doe as much for me, that's all I ayme at,
And come what will on't, life or death, I'le do it,
For ten such kisses more, and 'twere high treason.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I wou'd be private with her.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: So you shall,
'Tis not worth thankes else, you must dispatch quick.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: And I must leave you in my chamber sir,
Where you must locke your selfe that none may see you,
'Tis close to her, you cannot misse the entrance,
When she comes downe to bed.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I understand ye, and once more thanke ye Lady.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Thanke me but thus.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: If I faile thee—
Come close then.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: 'Tis late good Aunt, to bed, I am ene unready,
My! woman will not be long away.

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: I wou'd have you a little merrier first,
Let me sit by ye, and read or discourse
Something that ye fancy, or take my instrument.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: No, no I thanke you,
I shall sleep without these, I wrong your age Aunt
To make ye waite thus, pray let me entreat ye,
To morrow I'le see ye, I know y'are sleepy,
And rest will be a welcome guest, you shall not,
Indeed you shall not stay; oh here's my woman,
Good night, good night, and good rest Aunt attend you.

speeches.speaker: Qui.
verse: Sleep dwell upon your eyes, & faire dreams court ye.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Come, where have you been wench? make me unready;
