I slept but ill last night.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: You'l sleep the better
I hope too night Madam.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: A little rest contents me;
Thou lovest thy bed Panura.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I am not in love Lady,
Nor seldome dreame of devils, I sleep soundly.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I'le sweare thou dost, thy husband wou'd not take it so well
If thou wert married wench.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Let him take Madam
The way to waken me, I am no dormouse.
Husbands have larum bels, if they but
Ring once.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Thou art a merry wench.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I shall live the longer.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Prethee fetch my booke.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I am glad of that.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I'le read a while before I sleep.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I will Madam.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: And if Ruy Dias meet you and be importunate,
He may come in.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I have a better fare for you,
Now least in sight play I.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Why should I love him?
Why should I doat upon a man deserves not,
Nor has no will to worke it? who's there wench?
What are you? or whence come you?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ye may know me,
I bring not such amazement noble Lady.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Who let you in?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: My restles love that serves ye.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: This is an impudence I have not heard of,
A rudenesse that becomes a theefe or russin;
Nor shall my brothers love protect this boldnesse,
You buil'd so strongly on, my roomes are sanctuaries,
And with that reverence they that seeke my favours,
And humble feares, shall render their approches.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Mine are no lesse.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I am Mistris of my selfe sir,
And will be so, I will not be thus visited;
These feares and dangers thrust into my privacy,
Stand further off, I le cry out else.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Oh deare Lady!

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I see dishonour in your eyes.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: There is none:
By all that beauty they are innocent;
Pray ye tremble not, you have no cause.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I'le dye first;
Before you have your will, be torne in peeces;
The little strength I have left me to resist you,
The gods will give me more, before I am forc'd
To that I hate, or suffer—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You wrong my duty.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: So base a violation of my liberty?
I know you are bent unnobly; I'le take to me
The spirit of a man, borrow his boldnesse,
And force my womans feares into a madnesse,
And ere you arrive at what you aime at—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Lady,
If there be in you any womans pitty?
And if your feares have not proclam'd me monstrous?
Looke on me and beleeve me; is this violence?
Is it to fall thus prostrate to your beauty,
A ruffins boldnesse? is humility a rudenesse?
The griefes and sorrowes that grow here an impudence?
These forcings, and these feares I bring along with me,
These impudent abuses offered ye;
And thus high has your brothers favour blowne me:
Alas deare Lady of my life, I came not
With any purpose rough, or desperate,
With any thought that was not smooth and gentle
As your faire hand, with any doubt or danger,
Far be it from my heart to fright your quiet;
A heavy curse light on it when I intend it.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Now I dare heare you.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: If I had been mischievous,
As then I must be mad; or were a monster,
If any such base thought had harbour'd here,
Or violence that became not man,
You have a thousand bulwarkes to assure you,
The holy powers beare shields to defend chastity;
Your honour and your vertues are such armours;
Your cleare thoughts such defences; if you misdoubt still,
And yet retaine a feare I am not honest,
Come with impure thoughts to this place;
Take this, and sheath it heare; be your own safety;
Be wise, and rid your feares, and let me perish;
How willing shall I sleepe to satisfie you.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: No, I beleeve now, you speake worthily;
What came you then for?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: To complaine, me beauty,
But modestly.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Of what?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Of your feirce cruelty,
For though I dye, I will not blame the doer:
Humbly to tell your grace, ye had forgot me:
A little to have toucht at, not accused,
For that I dare not do, your scornes, pray pardon me
And be not angry, that I use the liberty
To urge that word, a little to have shew'd you
What I have been, and what done to deserve ye,
If any thing that love commands may reach ye,
To have remembred ye, but I am unworthy,
And to that misery fals all my fortunes,
To have told ye, and by my life ye may beleeve me,
That I am honest, and will only marry
You, or your memory; pray be not angry.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I thanke you sir, and let me tell you seriously,
Ye have taken now the right way to befriend ye,
And to beget a faire and cleare opinion,
Yet to try your obedience—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I stand ready Lady,
Without presuming to aske any thing.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Or at this time to hope for further favour;
Or to remember services, or smiles;
Dangers you have past through, and rewards due to 'em;
Loves or dispaires, but leaving all to me:
Quit this place presently.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I shall obey ye.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Who's this?
What art thou?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: A Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Thou art no more I'm sure: oh 'tis Ruy Dias;
How high he lookes, and harsh?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Is there not doore enough,
You take such elbow roome?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: If I take it, I'le carry it.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Does this become you Princesse?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: The Captain's jealous,
Jealous of that he never durst deserve yet;
Go freely, go I'le give thee leave.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Your leave sir?

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Yes my leave sir, I'le not be troubled neither,
Nor shall my heart ake, or my head be jealous,
Nor strange suspitious thoughts reigne in my memory;
Go on, and do thy worst, I'le smile at thee;
I kisse your faire hand first, then farewell Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: What a pure soule inherits here? what innocence?
Sure I was blind when I first lov'd this fellow,
And long to live in that fogg stil: how he blusters!

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Am I your property? or those your flatteries,
The banquets that ye bid me to, the trust
I build my goodly hopes on?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Be more temperate.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Are these the shewes of your respect and favour?
What did he here? what language had he with ye?
Did ye invite? could ye stay no longer?
Is he so gratious in your eye?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: You are too forward.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Why at these private houres?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: You are too saucy,
Too impudent to taske me with those erours:
Do ye know what I am sir, and my prerogative?
Though you be a thing I haue cal'd bith' name of friend,
I never taught you to dispose my liberty;
How durst you touch mine honour? blot my meanings?
And name an action, and of mine but noble?
Thou poore unworthy thing, how have I grac'd thee?
How have I nourisht thee, and raised thee hourely?
Are these the gratitudes you bring Ruy Dias?
The thankes? the services? I am fairely paid;
Was't not enough I saw thou wert a Coward,
And shaddowed thee? no noble sparkle in thee?
Dayly provok'd thee, and still found thee coward?
Rais'd noble causes for thee, strangers started at;
Yet still, still, still a Coward, ever Coward;
And with those taints, dost thou upbraid my vertues?

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: I was too blame
Lady.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: So blindly bold to touch at my behaviour?
Durst thou but looke amisse at my allowance?
If thou hadst been a brave fellow, thou hadst had some licence,
Some liberty I might have then allowed thee
For thy good face, some scope to have argued with me;
But being nothing but a sound, a shape,
The meere signe of a Souldier — of a Lover,
The dregs and draffy part, disgrace and jealousie,
I scorne thee, and contemne thee.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Dearest Lady,
If I have been too free—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Thou hast been too foolish,
And goe on still, I'le study to forget thee,
I would I could, and yet I pitty thee.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I am not worth it, if I were, that's misery,
The next doore is but death, I must aime at it.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: SOe far and truly you have discovered to me
The former currents of my life and fortune,
That I am bound to acknowledge ye most holy,
And certainly to credit your predictions
Of what are yet to come.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I am no lyer,
'Tis strange I should, and live so neare a neighbour;
But these are not my ends.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Pray ye sit good father,
Certaine a reverend man, and most religious.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I, that beliefe's well now, and let me worke then,
I'le make ye curse religion ere I leave ye;
I have liv'd a long time son, a mewd up man,
Sequester'd by the speciall hand of heaven
From the worlds vanities, bid farewell to follies,
And shooke hands with all heats of youth and pleasures,
As in a dreame these twenty yeares I have slumber'd,
Many a cold moone have I in meditation,
And searching out the hidden wils of heaven,
Laine shaking under, many a burning Sun
Has fear'd my body, and boyl'd up my bloud,
Feebl'd my knees, and stampt a Meagernesse
Upon my figure, all to find out knowledge,
Which I have now attained too, thankes to heaven,
All for my countries good too, and many a vision,
Many a misticke vision have I seen son,
And many a sight from heaven which has been terrible,
Wherein the goods and evils of these Islands
Were lively shadowed; many a charge I have had too,
Still as the time grew ripe to reveale these,
To travell and discover, now I am come son,
The houre is now appointed,
My tongue is touch'd, and now I speake.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Do holy man, I'le heare ye.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Beware these Portugals, I say beware 'em,
These smooth fac'd strangers, have an eye upon 'em.
The cause is now the God's, heare, and beleeve King.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I do heare, but before I give rash credit,
Or hang too light on beliefe, which is a sin father;
Know I have found 'em gentle, faithfull, valiant,
And am in my particular, bound to 'em,
I meane to some for my most strange deliverance.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: O Son, the future aimes of men, observe me,
Above their present actions, and their glory,
Are to be look'd at: the stars shew many turnings,
If you could see, marke but with my eyes pupill;
These men came hether as my vision tels me,
Poore, weatherbeaten, almost lost, starv'd, feebled,
Their vessels like themselves, most miserable;
Made a long sute for traffique, and for comfort,
To vent their childrens toyes, cure their diseases:
They had their sute, they landed, and too th'rate
Grew rich and powerfull, suckt the fat, and freedome
Of this most blessed Isle, taught her to tremble,
Witnesse the Castle here, the Cittadell,
They have clapt upon the necke of your Tidore,
This happy town, till that she knew these strangers,
To check her when shee's jolly.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: They have so indeed father.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Take heed, take heed, I find your faire delivery,
Though you be pleas'd to glorifie that fortune,
And thinke these strangers Gods, take heed I say,
I find it but a hansome preparation,
A faire fac'd Prologue to a further mischiefe:
Marke but the end good King, the pin he shootes at
That was the man deliver'd ye; the mirrour,
Your Sister is his due; what's she, your heire sir?
And what's he a kin then to the Kingdome?
But heires are not ambitious, who then suffers?
What reverence shall the Gods have? and what justice
The miserable people? what shall they doe?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: He points at truth directly.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Thinke of these son:
The person, nor the manner I mislike not
Of your preserver, nor the whole man together,
Were he but season'd in the faith we are,
Ne, our devotions learn'd.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You say right father.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: To change our worships now, and our Religion?
To be traytor to our God?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You have well advised me,
And I will seriously consider father,
In the meane time you shall have your faire accesse
Unto my sister, advise her to your purpose,
And let me still know how the Gods determine.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I will, but my maine end is to advise
The destruction of you all, a generall ruine,
And then I am reveng'd, let the Gods whistle.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Indeed, I am right glad ye were not greedie,
And suddaine in performing what I wild you,
Upon the person of Armusia,
I was affraid, for I well knew your valour,
And love to me.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: 'Twas not a faire thing unckle,
It shewd not hansome, carried no man in it.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: I must confesse 'twas ill, and I abhor it,
Only this good has risen from this evill;
I have tried your honestie, and find proofe,
A constancie that will not be corrupted,
And I much honour it.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: This Bell sounds better.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: My anger now, and that disgrace I have suffer'd,
Shall be more manly vented, and wip'd off,
And my sicke honour cur'd the right and straight way;
My Swords in my hand now nephew, my cause upon it,
And man to man, one vallour to another,
My hope to his.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Why? this like Ruy Dias?
This carries something of some substance in it;
Some mettle and some man, this sounds a gentleman;
And now methinkes ye utter what becomes ye;
To kill men scurvily, 'tis such a dog tricke,
Such a ratcatchers occupation —

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: It is no better,
But Pyniero now—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Now I do bravely.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: The difference of our states slung by forgotten,
The full opinion I have won in service,
And such respects that may not shew us equall,
Laid hansomely aside, only our fortunes,
And single manhoods—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: In a service sir,
Of this most noble nature, all I am,
If I had ten lives more, those and my fortunes
Are ready for ye, I had thought ye had forsworn fighting,
Or banish'd those brave thoughts were wont to waite upon you Shews a Challenge
I am glad to see 'em cal'd home agen.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: They are nephew,
And thou shall see what fire they carry in them,
Here, you guesse what this meanes.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Yes, very well sir,
A portion of Scripture that puzzels many an interpreter.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: As soone as you can find him—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: That will not be long unckle,
And o' my conscience heele be ready as quickly.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: I make no doubt good Nephew, carry it so
If you can possible that we may sight.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Nay, you shall fight assure your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Pray ye heare me
In some such place where it may be possible
The Princesse may behold us.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I conceive ye,
Upon the sand behind the Castle sir,
A place remote enough, and there be windows
Out of her lodgings too, or I am mistaken.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Y'are i'th' right, if ye can worke that hansomly —

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Let me alone, and pray be you prepar'd
Some three houres hence.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: I will not faile.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Get you home,
And if you have any things to dispose of,
Or a few light prayers
That may befriend you, run 'em over quickely,
I warrant, I'le bring him on.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Farewell Nephew,
And when we meet againe —

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I, I, fight handsomely;
Take a good draught or two of wine to settle ye,
'Tis an excellent armour for an ill conscience Unckle;
I am glad to see, this mans conversion,
I was affraid faire honour had been bedrid,
Or beaten out o'th' Island, souldiers and good ones,
Intended such base courses? he will fight now;
And I beleeve too bravely; I have seene him
Curry a fellowes carkasse hansomely:
And in the head of a troope stand as if he had been rooted there,
Dealing large doles of death; what a rascall was I
I did not see his will drawn?
What does she here?
If there be any mischief toward, a woman makes one stil;
Now what new businesse is for me?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I was sending for ye,
But since we have met so faire,
You have sav'd that labour; I must entreat you sir—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Any thing Madam,
Your wils are my commands.

speeches.speaker: Qusar.
verse: Y'are nobly courteous;
Upon my better thoughts Signeor Pyniero,
And my more peaceable considerations.
Which now I find the richer ornaments;
I wou'd desire you to attempt no farther
Against the person of the noble stranger,
In truth I am ashamd of my share in't;
Nor be incited further by your unckle,
I see it will sit ill upon your person;
I have considered, and it will shew ugly
Carried at best, a most unheard of cruelty;
Goood sir desist—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: You speake now like a woman,
And wondrous well this tendernesse becomes ye;
But this you must remember—your command
Was laid on with a kisse, and seriously
It must be taken off the same way Madam,
Or I stand bound still.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: That shall not endanger ye,
Looke ye faire sir, thus I take off that duty.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Byth' masse 'twas soft and sweet,
Some blouds would bound now,
And run a tilt; do not you thinke bright beauty,
You have done me in this kisse a mighty favour,
And that I stand bound by vertue of this honour,
To do what ever you command me?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I thinke sir,
From me these are unusuall curtesies,
And ought to be respected so; there are some,
And men of no mean ranke, would hold themselves
Not poorely blest to taste of such a bounty.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I know there are that wou'd do many unjust things
For such a kisse, and yet I hold this modest;
All villanies body and soule dispence with,
For such a provocation, kill their kindred,
Demolish the faire credits of their Parents;
Those kisses I am not acquainted with, most certaine Madam
The appurtenance of this kisse wou'd not provoke me
To do a mischief, 'tis the devils owne dance,
To be kiss'd into cruelty.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I am glad you make that use sir.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I am gladder
That you made me beleeve you were cruell,
For by this hand I know I am so honest,
However I deceiv'd ye, 'twas high time too,
Some common slave might have been set upon it else,
That willingly I wou'd not kill a dog
That could but fetch and carry for a woman,
She must be a good woman made me kick him,
And that will be hard to find, to kill a man,
If you will give me leave to get another,
Or any she that plaid the best game at it,
And fore a womans anger prefer her fancy.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I take it in you well.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I thanke ye Lady,
And I shall study to confirme it.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Do sir,
For this time, and this present cause I 'low it,
Most holy sir.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Blesse ye my royall daughter,
And in you, blesse this Island heaven.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Good Aunt,
What thinke ye of this man?

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: Sure 'is a wise man,
And a religious, he tels us things have hapned
So many yeares agoe almost forgotten,
As readily, as if they were done this houre.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Does he not meet with your sharpe tongue?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: He tels me Madam,
Marriage, and mouldy cheese will make me tamer.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: A stubborne keeper, and worse fare,
An open stable, and cold care,
Will tame a Jade, may be your share.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Bir Lady, a sharp prophet, when this proves good
I'le bequeath you a skin to make ye a hood.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Lady I would talke with you.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Do reverend sir.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: And for you good, for that that must concerne ye,
And give eare wisely to me.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I shall father.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You are a Prinresse of that excellence,
Sweetnesse, and grace, that Angell-like faire feature,
Nay, do not blush, I doe not flatter you,
Nor do I dote in telling this, I am amazed Lady,
And as I thinke the gods bestow'd these on ye,
The gods that love ye.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I confesse their bounty.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Apply it then to their use, to their honour,
To them, and to their service give this sweetnesse;
They have an instant great use of your goodnesse;
You are a Saint esteem'd here for your beauty,
And may a longing heart —

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I seeke no fealty,
Nor will I blemish that heaven has seal'd on me,
I know my worth, indeed the Portugals
I have at those commands, and their last services,
Nay, even their lives, so much I thinke my hansomnesse,
That what I shall enjoyne —

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Use it discreetly,
For I perceive ye understand me rightly,
For here the gods regard your helpe, and suddenly;
The Portugals like sharpe thornes (marke me Lady)
Sticke in our sides, like razors, wound religion,
Draw deep, they wound, till the life bloud followes,
Our gods they spurne at, and their worships scorne,
A mighty hand they beare upon our government,
These are the men your miracle must worke on,
Your heavenly forme, either to roote them out,
Which as you may endeavour will be easie,
Remember whose great cause you have to execute,
To nip their memory, that may not spring more,
Or fairely bring 'em home to our devotions,
Which will be blessed, and for which, you sainted,
But cannot be, and they go; let me buzzle.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Go up with me,
Where wee'l converse more privately;
I'le shew ye shortly how I hold their temper;
And in what chaine their soules.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Keep fast that hold still,
And either bring that chaine, and those bound in it,
And linke it to our gods, and their faire worships,
Or daughter pinch their hearts a peeces with it,
I'le waite upon your grace.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Come reverend father.
Waite you below.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: If this prophet were a young thing,
I should suspect him now, he cleaves so close to her;
These holy coats are long, and hide in iniquities.

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: Away, away foole, a poore wretch,

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: These poore ones
Warme but their stomakes once —

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
prose: Come in, thou art foolish.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I am sorry sir my fortune is so stubborne,
To court my sword against my countriman,
I love my nation well, and where I find
A Portugall of noble name and vertue,
I am his humble servant. Signeor Pyniero,
Your person, nor your unckles am I angry with,
You are both faire Gentlemen in my opinion,
And I protest, I had rather use my sword
In your defences, then against your safeties;
'Tis me thinkes, a strange dearth of enemies,
When we seeke foes among our selves.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: You are injured,
And you must make the best on't now, and readiest—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: You see I am ready in the place; and arm'd
To his desire that cald me.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Ye speake honestly,
And I could wish ye had met on tearmes more friendly,
But it cannot now be so.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Turne sir, and see.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I have kept my word with ye unckle,
The Gentleman is ready.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ye are welcome.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Bid those fooles welcome that affect your curtesie,
I come not to use complement, ye have wrongd' me,
And ye shall feele proud man ere I part from ye,
The effects of that, if fortune do not foole me;
Thy life is mine, and no hope shall redeeme thee.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: That's a proud word,
More then your faith can justifie.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Sure they will fight.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: She's there, I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Let 'em alone, let 'em kill one another,
These are the maine postes, if they fall, the buildings
Will tumple quickely.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: How temperate Armusia?
No more, be quiet yet.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I am not bloudy,
Nor do not feele such mortall malice in me,
But since we cannot both enjoy the Princesse,
I am resolv'd to fight.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Fight home Armusia,
For if thou faint'st, or fall'st—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Do ye make all vantages?

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Alwaies; unto thy life I will not spare thee,
Nor looke not for thy mercy.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I am arm'd then.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Stand still I charge ye nephew, as ye honour me.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: And good Emanuel—not—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Ye speake fitly,
For we had not stood idle else.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I am sorry for't.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: But since you will have it so—

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: Come sir.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I waight ye.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I marry this looks hansomely,
This is warme worke.

speeches.speaker: Gov
verse: Both fall an't be thy will.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: My Unckle dead?

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Stand still, or my swords in—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Now brave Ruy Dias,
Now Where's your confidence, your prayers? quickly
Your owne spite has condemn'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Hold Armusia.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Most happy Lady.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Hold and let him rise,
Spare him for me.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: A long life may he enjoy Lady.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: What ha' you done? 'tis better they had all perisht.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Peace father, I worke for the best; Armusia,
Be in the garden an houre hence.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I shall Madam.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Now as I live a Gentleman at all inches,
So brave a mingled temper saw I never.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Why are ye sad sir? how would this have griev'd you,
If ye had falne under a profest enemie?
Under one had taken vantage of your shame too?
Pray ye be at peace, I am so far from wronging ye,
Or glorying in the pride of such a victorie,
That I desire to serve ye, pray look cheerfully

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Doe you heare this sir? this love sir? do you see this Gentleman
How he courts ye? why doe you hold your head downe?
Tis no high treason I take it, to be equal'd,
To have a slip i'th' field, no sinne that's mortall;
Come, come, thanke fortune and your friend.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: It may be
You thinke my tongue may prove your enemie;
And though restrain'd sometimes, out of a braverie
May take a license to disable ye:
Beleeve me sir, so much I hate that libertie,
That in a strangers tongue 't will prove an injurie,
And I shall right you in't.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Can you have more Unckle?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Sir you have beate me both wayes, yet so nobly,
That I shall ever love the hand that did it:
Fortune may make me worthie of some title
That may be neere your friend.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Sir I must leave ye,
But with so hearty love, and pray be confident,
I carry nothing from this place shall wrong ye.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Come, come, you are right agen, sir love your honor,
And love your friend, take heed of bloudy purposes,
And unjust ends, good heaven is angry with 'm;
Make your faire vertues, and your fame your mistres,
And let these trinkets goe.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: You teach well nephew,
Now to be honorable even with this Gentleman,
Shall be my businesse, and my ends his.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Sir, sir, you must doe something suddenly,
To stop his pride so great and high, he is shot up,
Upon his person too, your state is sunke else:
You must not stand now upon termes of gratitude,
And let a simple tendernesse besot ye:
I'le bring ye suddenly where you shall see him,
Attempting your brave sister privately;
Marke but his high behaviour then.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I will Father.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: And with scorne, I feare contempt too.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I hope not.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I will not name a lust;
It may be that also;
A little force must be applyed upon him,
Now, now applyed, a little force to humble him.
These sweet intreaties doe but make him wanton.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Take heed ye wrong him not.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Take heed to your safety,
I but fore warne ye King; if you mistrust me,
Or thinke I come unsent—

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: No I'le goe with you.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Madam, you see there's nothing I can reach at,
Either in my obedience, or my service,
That May deserve your love, or win a liking,
But a poore thought, but I pursue it seriously,
Take pleasure in your wils, even in your anger,
Which other men would grudge at, and grow stormy;
I study new humility to please ye,
And take a kind of joy in my afflictions,
Because they come from ye, I love my sorrowes:
Pray Madam but consider—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Yes, I do sir,
And to that honest end I drew ye hether;
I know ye have deserv'd as much as man can,
And know it is a justice to requite you:
I know ye love.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: If ever love was mortall,
And dwelt in man, and for that love command me,
So strong I find it, and so true, here Lady,
Something of such a greatnesse to allow me,
Those things I have done already, may seem foyles too:
'Tis equity that man aspires to heaven,
Should win it by his worth, and not sleepe to it.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Now stand close King and heare, and as you find him,
Beleeve me right, or let religion suffer.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I dare beleeve your worth without additions;
But since you are so liberall of your love sir,
And wou'd be farther tried, I do intend it,
Because you shall not, or you wou'd not win me
At such an easie rate.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I am prepared still,
And if I shrinke—

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I know ye are no coward,
This is the utmost triall of your constancy,
And if you stand fast now, I am yours, your wife sir;
You hold there's nothing deare that may atchieve me,
Doubted or dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: There's nothing, nothing:
Let me but know, that I may straight flie to it.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I'le tell you then, change your religion,
And be of one beleefe with me.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Marke,
Worship our Gods, renounce that faith you are bred in;
'Tis easily done, I'le teach ye suddenly;
And humbly on your knees—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Ha! I'le be hang'd first.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Offer as we do.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: To the Devill Lady?
Offer to him I hate? I know the devill,
To dogs and cats? you make offer to them;
To every bird that flies, and every worme.
How terribly I shake? Is this the venture?
The tryall that you talkt off? where have I bin?
And how forgot my selfe? how lost my memorie?
When did I pray or looke up stedfastly?
Had any goodnes in my heart to guide me?
That I should give this vantage to mine enemie;
The enemie to my peace, forsake my faith.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Come, come, I know ye love me.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Love ye this way?
This most destroying way? sure you but jest Lady.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: My love and life are one way.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Love alone then, and mine another way,
I'le love diseases first,
Doate on a villaine that would cut my throat,
Wooe all afflictions of all sorts, kisse crueltie;
Have mercy heaven, how have I been wandring?
Wandring the way of lust, and left my maker?
How have I slept like Corke upon a water,
And had no feeling of the storme that tost me?
Trod the blinde paths of death? forsooke assurance,
Eternitie of blessednesse for a woman?
For a young hansome face hazard my being?

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: Are not our powers eternall so their comforts?
As great and full of hopes as yours?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: They are puppits.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Now marke him sir, and but observe him nearly,

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Their comforts like themselves, cold senseles outsides;
You make 'em sicke, as we are, peevish, mad,
Subject to age; and how can they cure us,
That are not able to resine themselves?

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: The Sun & Moon we worship, those are heavenly,
And their bright influences we beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Away foole,
I adore the Maker of that Sun and Moone,
That gives those bodies light and influence,
That pointed out their paths, and taught their motions;
They are not so great as we, they are our servants,
Plac'd there to teach us time, to give us knowledge
Of when and how the swellings of the maine aire,
And their returnes agen; they are but our stewards
To make the earth fat with their influence,
That she may bring forth her increase and feed us.
Shall I fall from this faith to please a woman?
For her embraces bring my soule to ruine?
I lookd you should have said, make me a Christian,
Worke that great cure, for 't is a great one woman;
That labour truly doe performe, that venture
The crowne of all great triall, and the fairest:
I lookd ye should have wept and kneel'd to beg it,
Washt off your mist of ignorance, with waters
Pure and repentant, from those eyes; I lookt
You should have brought me your chief god ye worship,
He that you offer humane bloud and life to,
And made a sacrifice of him to memorie,
Beat downe his Altars, ruin'd his false Temples.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Now you may see.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: Take heed, you goe too far sir,
And yet I love to heare him; I must have ye,
And to that end I let you storme a little;
I know there must be some strife in your bosome
To coole and quiet ye, ere you can come backe:
I know old friends cannot part suddenly,
There wil be some let still, yet I must have ye,
Have ye of my faith too, and so injoy ye.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Now I contemne ye, and I hate my selfe
For looking on that face lasciviously,
And it lookes ugly now methinkes.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: How Portugall?

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: It lookes like death it selfe, to which 'twou'd lead me;
Your eyes resemble pale dispaire, they fright me,
And in their rounds a thousand horrid ruines,
Methinkes I see; and in your tongue heare fearefully
The hideous murmurs of weake soules have suffer'd;
Get from me, I despise ye, and know woman,
That for all this trap you have laid to catch my life in,
To catch my immortall life, I hate and curse ye,
Contemne your deities, spurne at their powers,
And where I meet your maumet Gods, I'le swing 'em
Thus o're my head, and kick 'em into puddles,
Nay I will out of vengeance search your Temples,
And with those hearts that serve my God, demolish
Your shambles of wild worships.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Now, now you heare sir.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I will have my faith since you are so crafty,
The glorious crosse, although I love your brother;
Let him frowne too, I will have my devotion,
And let your whole State storme.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Enter and take him;
I am sorry friend that I am forc'd to do this.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Be sure you bind him fast.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: But use him nobly.

speeches.speaker: King
verse: Had it to me been done, I had forgiven it,
And still preserv'd you faire, but to our Gods sir —

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Methinkes I hate 'em now,

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: To our Religion,
To these to be thus stubborne, thus rebellious
To threaten them.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Use all your violence,
I aske no mercy, nor repent my words;
I spit at your best powers; I serve one,
Will give me strength to scourge your gods.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Away with him.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: To grind 'em into base dust, and disperse 'em,
That never more their bloudy memories—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Clap him close up.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Good friend be cooler.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Never;
Your painted sister I despise too.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Softly.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: And all her devillish arts laugh and scorne at,
Mocke her blind purposes.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: You must be temperate;
Offer him no violence I command you strictly.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Now thou art up I shall have time to speake too.

speeches.speaker: Quis.
verse: Oh how I love this man, how truly honour him.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: DDo you know the newes Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Wou'd we knew as well sir
How to prevent it.

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Is this the love they beare us,
For our late benefit? taken so maliciously,
And clapt up close? is that the thankes they render?

speeches.speaker: Ch.
verse: It must not be put up thus, smother'd sleightly,
'Tis such a base unnaturall wrong.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I know,
They may thinke to doe wonders, aime at all,
And to blow us with a vengeance out o'th' Islands:
But if we be our selves honest and resolute,
And continue but Masters of our ancient courages,
Sticke close and give no vantage to their villanies—

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Nay if we faint or fall apeeces now,
We are fooles and worthy to be markt for miserie;
Begin to strike at him they are all bound to?
To cancell his deserts? what must we looke for
If they can carry this?

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: I'le carry coales then;
I have but one life, and one fortune Gentlemen,
But I'le so husband it to vexe these rascalls,
These barbarous slaves.

speeches.speaker: Ch.
verse: Shall we goe charge 'em presently?

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: No that will be too weake, and too foole-hardy,
We must have grounds that promise safety friends,
And sure offence, we loose our angers else,
And worse then that, venture our lives too lightly.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Did you see mine Uncle? plague 'a these Barbarians,
How the rogues sticke in my teeth, I know ye are angry,
So I am too, monstrous angry Gentlemen,
I am angry that I choke agen.
You heare Armusias up, honest Arm:
Clapt up in prison friends, the brave Arm:
Here are fine boyes.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: We hope he shall not stay there.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Stay? no he must not stay, no talke of staying,
These are no times to stay; are not these Rascals?
Speake, I beseech ye speake, are they not Rogues?
Thinke some abominable names — are they not Devils?
But the devil's a great deale too good for 'em — fusty villaines.

speeches.speaker: Ch.
verse: They are a kind of hounds.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Hounds were their fathers,
Old blear-eyed bob-tail'd hounds — Lord where's my Unckle?

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: But what shall be done sir?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Done?

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Yes to relieve him;
If it be not sudden they may take his life too.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: They dare as soone take fire and swallow it,
Take stakes and thrust into their tailes for glisters:
His life, why 'tis a thing worth all the Islands,
And they know will be rated at that value;
His very imprisonment will make the Town stinch,
And shake and stinke, I have phisick in my hand for 'em
Shall give the goblins such a purge —

speeches.speaker: Ped
verse: Your Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I heare strange newes, and have bin seeking ye;
They say Armusia's prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: 'Tis most certaine.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Upon what cause?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: He has deserv'd too much sir;
The old heathen policie has light upon him,
And paid him home.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: A most unnoble dealing.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: You are the next if you can carry it tamely,
He has deserved of all.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I must confesse it,
Of me so nobly too.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I am glad to heare it,
You have a time now to make good your confession,
Your faith will shew but cold else, and for fashion,
Now to redeeme all, now to thanke his courtesie,
Now to make those beleeve that held you backward,
And an ill instrument, you are a Gentleman,
An honest man, and you dare love your Nation,
Dare sticke to vertue though she be opprest,
And for her owne faire sake step to her Rescue:
If you live ages sir, and lose this houre,
Not now redeeme, and vindicate your honour,
Your life will be a murmure, and no man in't.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: I thanke ye nephew, come along with me Gentlemen,
Wee'l make 'em dancing sport immediately:
We are Masters of the Fort yet, we shall see
What that can doe.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Let it but spit fire finely,
And play their turrets, and their painted Palaces,
A frisking round or two, that they may trip it,
And caper in the aire.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Come, wee'l doe something
Shall make 'em looke about, wee'l send 'em plumbes
If they be not too hard for their teeth.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: And fine Potatoes
Roasted in gunpowder, such a banquet sir
Will prepare their unmannerly stomacks.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: They shall see
There is no safe retreat in villanie;
Come be high hearted all.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: We are all on fire sir.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I am ungratefull, and a wretch, perswade me not,
Forgetfull of the mercy he show'd me,
The timely noble pitty — why should I
See him fast bound and fetter'd, whose true curtesie,
Whose manhood, and whose mighty hand set me free?
Why should it come from me? why I command this?
Shall not all tongues and truths call me unthankfull?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Had the offence bin thrown on you, 'tis certaine
It had been in your power, and your discretion
To have turn'd it into mercy, and forgiven it,
And then it had show'd a vertuous point of gratitude,
Timely and nobly taken; but since the cause
Concernes the honour of our gods, and their title,
And so transcends your power, and your compassion,
A little your owne safety if you saw it too,
If your too fond indulgence did not dazle you,
It cannot now admit a private pitty;
'Tis in their wils, their mercies, or revenges,
And these revolts in you shew meere rebellious.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: They are milde and pittifull.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: To those repent.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Their nature's soft and tender.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: To true hearts
That feele compunction for their trespasses:
This man defies 'em still, threatens destruction
And demolition of their armes and worship,
Spits at their powers; take heed ye be not found sir,
And markt a favourer of their dishonour;
They use no common justice.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: What shall I doe
To deserve of this man —

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: If ye more bemoane him,
Or mitigate your power to preserve him,
I'le curse ye from the gods, call up their vengeance,
And fling it on your Land and you, I have charge for't;
I hope to wracke you all.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What ailes my sister?
Why is she bound? why looks she so distractedly?
Who does doe this?

speeches.speaker: Quisan.
verse: We did it, pardon sir,
And for her preservation — She is growne wilde,
And raving on the strangers love and honour,
Sometimes crying out, help, help, they will torture him,
They will take his life, they will murder him, presently,
If we had not prevented, violently
Have laid hands on her owne life.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: These are tokens
The gods displeasure is gone out, be quicke,
And ere it fall doe something to appease 'em,
You know the sacrifice — I am glad it works thus.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: How low and base thou lookst now that wert noble?
No figure of a King methinks showes on you,
No face of Majestie, foule swarth ingratitude
Has taken off thy sweetnesse, base forgetfulnesse
Of mighty benefits, has turned thee Devill:
Thou hast persecuted goodnes, innocence,
And laid a hard and violent hand on vertue,
On that faire vertue that should teach and guide us;
Thou hast wrong'd thine owne preserver, whose least merit
Pois'd with thy maine estate, thou canst not satisfie,
Nay put thy life in too, 'twill be too light still:
What hast thou done?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Goe for him presently.
And once more wee'l try it we can win him fairely:
If not, let nothing she sayes hinder ye, or stir ye;
She speaks distractedly — Do that the gods command ye:
Doe you know what ye say Lady?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: I could curse thee too,
Religion and severitie has steel'd thee,
Has turnd thy heart to stone; thou hast made the gods hard too,
Against their sweet and patient natures, cruell:
None of ye feele what braverie ye tread on?
What innocence? what beauty?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Pray be patient.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: What honorable things ye cast behind ye?
What monuments of man?

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Once more Armusia,
Because I love ye tenderly and dearly,
And would be glad to win ye mine, I wish ye,
Even from my heart I wish and wooe ye—

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: What sir,
Take heed how ye perswade me falsely, then ye hate me;
Take heed how ye intrap me.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I advise ye,
And tenderly and truly I advise ye,
Both for your soules health and your safetie.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Stay,
And name my soule no more, she is too precious,
Too glorious for your flatteries, too secure too.

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: Consider the reward sir, and the honor
That is prepared, the glory you shall grow to.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: They are not to be consider'd in these cases,
Not to be nam'd when soules are questioned;
They are vaine and flying vapors — touch my life,
'Tis ready for ye, put it to what test
It shall please ye, I am patient; but for the rest
You may remove rocks with your little fingers,
Or blow a mountaine out o'th' way, with bellowes,
As soon as stir my faith; use no more arguments.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: We must use tortures then.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Your worst and paineful'st
I am joyfull to accept.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You must the sharpest,
For such has been your hate against our deities
Delivered openly, your threats and scornings,
And either your repentance must be mighty,
Which is your free conversion to our customes,
Or equall punishment, which is your life sir.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: I am glad I have it for ye, take it Priest,
And all the miseries that shall attend it:
Let the Gods glut themselves with Christian bloud,
It will be ask'd againe, and so far followed,
So far reveng'd, and with such holy justice,
Your Gods of gold shall melt and sinke before it;
Your Altars, and your Temples shake to nothing;
And you false worshippers, blind fooles of ceremony,
Shall seeke for holes to hide your heads, and feares in,
For seas to swallow you from this destruction,
Darkenesse to dwell about ye, and conceale ye,
Your mothers wombes agen—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Make the fires ready,
And bring the severall tortures out.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Stand fast sir,
And feare 'em not, you that have stept so nobly
Into this pious triall start not now,
Keepe on your way, a virgin will assist ye,
A virgin won by your faire constancy,
And glorying that she is won so, will dye by ye;
I have touch'd ye every way, tried ye most honest,
Perfect, and good, chaste, blushing chaste, and temperate,
Valiant, without vaineglory, modest, stayed,
No rage, or light affection ruling in you:
Indeed, the perfect schoole of worth I find ye,
The temple of true honour.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Whether will she?
What do you infer by this faire argument Lady?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Your faith, and your religion must be like ye,
They that can shew you these, must be pure mirrours,
When the streames flow cleare and faire, what are fountaines?
I do embrace your faith sir, and your fortune;
Go one, I will assist ye, I feele a sparkle here,
A lively sparke that kindles my affection,
And tels me it will rise to flames of glory:
Let 'em put on their angers, suffer nobly,
Shew me the way, and when I faint instruct me;
And if I follow not—

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: O blessed Lady,
Since thou art won, let me begin my triumph,
Come clap your terrors on.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: All your fell tortures.
For there is nothing he shall suffer brother,
I sweare by new faith which is most sacred,
And I will keepe it so, but I will follow in,
And follow to a scruple of affliction,
In spight of all your Gods without prevention.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Death she amazes me.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: What shall be done now?

speeches.speaker: Go.
verse: They must dye both,
And suddenly, they will corrupt all else;
This woman makes me weary of my mischiefe,
She shakes me, and she staggers me, go in sir.
I'le see the execution.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Not so suddaine:
If they goe all my friends and sisters perish.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Wou'd I were safe at home agen.

speeches.speaker: Mes
verse: Arme, arme sir,
Seek for defence, the Castle playes and thunders,
The Towne Rocks, and the houses flye ith' aire,
The people dye for feare—Captaine Ruy Dias,
Has made an Oath he will not leave a stone here;
No not the memory, here has stood a City,
Unlesse Armusia be deliver'd fairely.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: I have my feares: what can our gods do now for us?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Be patient, But keep him still: he is a cure sir
Against both rage and Cannon: goe and fortifie,
Call in the Princesse, make the Pallace sure,
And let 'em know you are a King: look nobly;
And take your courage to ye; keep close the prisoner,
And under command, we are betray'd else.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: How ioyfully I goe?

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Take my heart with thee.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I hold a Wolfe by the eare now:
Fortune free me.
Heaven blesse us,
What a thundring's here? what fire-spitting?
We cannot drinke, but our Cans are mald amongst us.
I wou'd they would mall our skores too:
Shame o'their Guns, I thought they had been bird-pots,
Or great Candlecases, how devilishly they bounce,
And how the Bullets borrow a piece of a house here,
There another, and mend those up agen
With another parish; here flyes a poudring-tub,
The meat ready roasted & there a barrel pissing vinegar,
And they two over-taking the top of a high Steeple,
Newly slic'd off for a sallet.
A vengeance fire 'em.
Nay they fire fast enough;
You need not help 'em.
Are these the Portugall Bulls—
How loud they bellow?
Their horns are plaguie strong, they push down Pallaces
They tosse our little habitations like whelps,
Like grindle-tailes, with their heeles upward;
All the windowes ith' town dance a new trench-more,
'Tis like to prove a blessed age for Glasiers,
I met a hand, and a Letter in't in great haste,
And by and by a single leg running after it,
As if the Arme had forgot part of his arrant,
Heads she like foot-balls every where.
What shall we doe?
I care not, my shop's cancell'd,
And all the Pots and earthen pans in't vanish't:
There was a single Bullet and they together by the eares;
You would have thought Tom Tumbler had been there,
And all his troop of devills.
Let's to the King,
And get this gentleman deliver'd handsomely;
By this hand there's no walking above ground else.
By this leg—Let me sweare nimbly by it,
For I know not how long I shall owe it,
If I were out oth' Towne once, if I came in agen to
Fetch my breakfast, I will give 'em leave to cram me
With a Portugall pudding: Come, let's doe any thing
To appease this thunder,

speeches.speaker: Pyn.
verse: Art sure it was that blinde priest?

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Yes most certaine,
He has provok't all this; the King is mercifull,
And wondrous loving; but he fires him on still,
And when he cooles enrages him, I know it,
Threatens new vengeance, and the gods fierce justice
When he but looks with faire eyes on Armusia,
Will lend him no time to relent; my royall Mistris,
She has entertain'd a Christian hope.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Speake truely.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Nay 'tis most true, but Lord, how he lies at her,
And threatens her, and flatters her, and dams her,
And I feare, if not speedily prevented,
If she continue stout, both shall be executed.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Ile kisse thee for this newes: nay more Panura,
If thou wilt give me leave, Ile get thee with Christian,
The best way to convert thee.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: Make me believe so.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I will y'faith. But which way cam'st thou hither?
The Pallace is close guarded, and barricado'd.

speeches.speaker: Pan.
verse: I came through a private vault, which few there know of;
It rises in a Temple not farre hence,
Close by the Castle here.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: How—To what end?

speeches.speaker: Pan
verse: A good one:
To give ye knowledge of my new-borne Mistris,
And in what doubt Armusia stands,
Thinke any present meanes, or hope to stop 'em
From their fell ends: the Princes are come in too,
And they are hardn'd also.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: The damn'd Priest—

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Sure he's a cruell man, methinks Religion
Should teach more temperate lessons.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: He the fire-brand?
He dare to touch at such faire lives as theirs are?
Well Prophet, I shall prophesie, I shall catch ye,
When all your Prophecies will not redeem yee?
Wilt thou doe one thing bravely?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Any good I am able.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: And by thine owne white hand Ile sweare thou art vertuous,
And a brave wench, durst thou but guide me presently
Through the same vault thou cam'st into the Pallace,
And those I shall appoynt, such as I thinke fit.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Yes, I will doe it, and suddenly, and truely.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I wou'd faine behold this Prophet.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Now I have yee;
And shall bring yee where ye shall behold him,
Alone too, and unfurnish'd of defences:
That shall be my care; but you must not betray me.

speeches.speaker: Py.
prose: Dost thou think we are so base? such slaves, rogues?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: I doe not:
And you shall see how fairely Ile worke for ye.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I must needs steale that Priest,
Steale him, and hang him.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Do any thing to remove his mischife, strangle him—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Come prethee love.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: You'll offer me no foule play?
The Vault is darke.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: 'Twas well remember'd.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: And ye may —
But I hold ye honest.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Honest enough, I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: I am but a poore weak wench; and what with the place,
And your perswasions Sir — but I hope you will not;
You know we are often cozn'd.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: If thou dost feare me,
Why dost thou put me in minde?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: To let you know sir,
Though it be in your power, and things fitting to it,
Yet a true gent—

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I know what hee'll doe:
Come and remember me, and Ile answer thee,
Ile answer thee to the full; wee'll call at th'Castle,
And then my good guide do thy will; sha't finde me
A very tractable man.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: I hope I shall sir.

speeches.speaker: Bak.
verse: Let my men guard the gates.

speeches.speaker: Syan.
verse: And mine the Temple,
For feare the honour of our gods should suffer,
And on your lives be watchfull.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: And be valiant;
And let's see, if these Portugalls dare enter;
What their high hearts dare doe: Let's see how readily,
The great Ruy Dias will redeem his Countrey-men;
He speaks proud words, and threatens.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: He is approv'd sir,
And will put faire for what he promises;
I could wish friendlier termes,
Yet for our Liberties, and for our gods,
We are bound in our best service
Even in the hazard of our lives.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Come up Princes,
And give your counsells, and your helpes, the Fort still
Playes fearfully upon us, beats our buildings,
And turnes our people wild with feares.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Send for the prisoner,
And give us leave to argue.

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Come on nobly,
And let the Fort play still, we are
Strong enough to look upon 'em,
And returne at pleasure; it may
Be on our view they will returne him.

speeches.speaker: Chr.
verse: We will returne 'em such thanks else,
Shall make 'im scratch where it itches not.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: How the people stare,
And some cry, some pray, and some curse heartily:
But it is the King —

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: I cannot blame their wisedomes,
They are all above, Armusia chain'd and bound too?
O these are thankfull Squiers.

speeches.speaker: Ba.
verse: Heare us Ruy Dias,
Be wise and heare us, and give speedy answer,
Command thy Cannon presently to cease,
No more to trouble the afflicted People,
Or suddenly Armusias head goes off,
As suddenly as seeaid.

speeches.speaker: Em.
verse: Stay Sir, be moderate.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: Doe nothing that's dishonourable Ruy Dyas,
Let not the feare of me master thy valour;
Pursue 'em still, they are base malitious people.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Friend be not desperate.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: I scorne your courtesies;
Strike when you dare, a faire arme guide the Gunner,
And may he let flye still with fortune: friend,
Doe me the honour of a souldiers funeralls,
The last faire Christian right, see me ith' ground,
And let the pallace burne first, then the Temples,
And on their scorn'd gods erect my monument:
Touch not the Princesse, as you are a souldier.

speeches.speaker: Quisar.
verse: Which way you go, sir,
I must follow necessary.
One life, and one death.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: Will you take a truce yet?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: No, no, goe on:
Look here your god, your Prophet.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How came he taken?

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: I Conjur'd for him King.
I am sure Curre at an old blinde Prophet.
Ile haunt ye such a false knave admirably,
A terrier I; I eartht him, and then snapt him;

speeches.speaker: Soz.
verse: Saving the reverence of your grace, we stole him
E'ne out of the next chamber to yee.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: Come, come, begin King,
Begin this bloudy matter when you dare;
And yet I scorne my sword should touch the rascall,
Ile teare him thus before ye. Ha!
What art thou?

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: How's this!
Art thou a Prophet?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: Come downe Princes.

speeches.speaker: Kin.
verse: VVe are abus'd—
Oh my most deare Armusia—
Off which his chaines. And now my noble sister,
Rejoyce with me, I know yee are pleas'd as I am.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: This is a pretious Prophet. Why Don Governour,
What make you here? how long have you taken orders?

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: VVhy what a wretch
Art thou to work this mischiefe?
To assume this holy shape to ruine honour,
Honour and chastity?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I had paid you all,
But fortune plaid the slut. Come,
Give me my doome.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I cannot speak for wonder.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Nay, 'tis I sir,
And here I stay your sentence.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Take her friend,
You have halfe perswaded me to be a Christian,
And with her all the joyes, and all the blessings.
VVhy what dreame have we dwelt in?

speeches.speaker: Ru.
verse: All peace to yee,
And all the happinesse of heart dwell with ye,
Children as sweet and noble as their Parents.

speeches.speaker: Py.
verse: And Kings at least.

speeches.speaker: Ar.
verse: Good Sir forget my rashnesse.
And noble Princesse, for I was once angrie,
And out of that might utter some distemper,
Think not 'tis my nature.

speeches.speaker: Sya.
verse: Your joy is ours sir,
And nothing we finde in ye, But most noble.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: To prison with this dog, there let him houle,
And if he can repent, sigh out his villanies:
His Island we shall seize into our hands,
His father and himselfe have both usurp'd it,
And kept it by oppression; the Towne and Castle,
In which I lay my selfe most miserable,
Till my most honourable friend redeem'd me,
Signeur Pyniero I bestow on you,
The rest of next command upon these gentlemen,
Upon ye all my love.

speeches.speaker: Arm.
verse: O brave Ruy Dias.
You have started now beyond me. I must thank ye,
And thank ye for my life, my wife and honour.

speeches.speaker: Ruy.
verse: I am glad I had her for you sir.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Come Princes,
Come friends and lovers all, come noble gentlemen,
No more guns now, nor hates but joyes and triumphes,
An universall gladnesse flye about us:
And know however subtill men dare cast,
And promise wrack, the gods give peace at last.

speeches.speaker: 1. Usher.
verse: ROund, round, perfume it round, quick, loook ye
Diligently the state be right, are these the richest
Cushions? Fie, fie, who waits i'th' wardrobe?

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: But pray tell me, do you thinke for certaine
These Ambassadours shall have this morning audience?

speeches.speaker: 1. Ush.
verse: They shall have it: Lord that you live at Court
And understand not? I tell you they must have it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: Upon what necessity?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Still you are of the tricke of Court, sell your place
And sow your grounds, you are not for this tillage.
Madams, the best way is the upper lodgings,
There you may see at ease.

speeches.speaker: Ladies.
verse: We thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Would you have al these slighted? who should report then
The Embassadors were hansome men? his beard
A neat one? the fire of his eyes quicker then lightning,
And when it breaks, as blasting? his legs, though litle ones,
Yet movers of a masse of understanding?
Who shall commend their cloaths: who shall take notice
Of the most wise behaviour of their feathers?
Ye live a raw man here.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: I thinke I doe so.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Why, whether would you all presse?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: Good Master Usher.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: My wife, and some few of my honest neighbours, here.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Prethee begon thou and thy honest neighbours,
Thou lookst like an asse, why, whether would you fish face

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: If I might have
But the honour to see you at my poore house sir,
A Capon bridled, and sadled I'le assure your worship,
A shoulder of mutton, and a pottle of wine sir;
I know your brother, he was as like ye,
And shot the best at buts—

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: A—upon thee.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: Some musick I'le assure you too,
My toy sir, can play o'th' virginals.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Prethee good toy,
Take away thy shoulder of mutton, it is flie blowne,
And shoulder take thy flap along, here's no place for ye;
Nay then you had best be knock'd.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I wou'd faine see him
The glory of this place, makes me remember,
But dye those thoughts, dye all but my desires,
Even those to death are sicke too; he's not here,
Nor how my eyes may guide me—

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: What's your businesse?
Who keeps the outward doore there? here's fine shufling,
You wastcoater you must go backe.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: There is not,
There cannot be, sixe dayes and never see me?
There must not be desire; sit do you thinke
That if you had a Mistris—

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Death, she is mad.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: And were your selfe an honest man? it cannot—

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: What a devill hast thou to do with me or my honesty?
Will you be jogging, good nimble tongue,
My fellow doore keeper.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: Prethee let her alone.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: The King is comming,
And shall we have an agent from the suburbs
Come to crave audience too?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Before I thought ye
To have a little breeding, some tang of Gentry;
But now I take ye plainly,
Without the helpe of any perspective,
For that ye cannot alter.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: An asse sir, you bray as like one,
And by my troth, me thinkes as ye stand now,
Considering who to kick next, you appeare to me
Just with that kind of gravity, and wisdome;
Your place may beare the name of Gentleman,
But if ever any of that butter stick to your bread—

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: You must be modester.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Let him use me nobler,
And weare good cloaths to do good offices;
They hang upon a fellow of his vertue,
As though they hung on Gibbets.

speeches.speaker: 2. Ush.
verse: A perilous wench.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Thrust her into a corner, I'le no more on her.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: You have enough, goe pretty maid, stand close,
And use that little tongue, with a little more temper.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I thanke ye sir.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: When the shews are past,
I'le have ye into the cellar, there wee'l dine
A very pretty wench, a witty rogue,
And there wee'l be as merry, can ye be merry?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: O very merry.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: Only our selves; this churlish fellow shall not know.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: By no meanes.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: And can you love a little?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Love exceedingly:
I have cause to love you deare sir.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: Then I'le carry ye,
And shew you all the pictures, and the hangings,
The lodgings, gardens, and the walkes: and then (sweet)
You shall tell me where you lye.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Yes marry will I.

speeches.speaker: 2. Ush.
verse: And't shall go hard but I'le send ye a venison pastie,
And bring a bottle of wine along.

speeches.speaker: 1. Ush.
verse: Make roome there.

speeches.speaker: 2. Ush.
verse: Room there afore, stand close, the train is coming

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Have I yet left a beauty to Catch fooles?
Yet, yet, I see him not, O what a miserie
Is love, expected long, deluded longer!

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Conduct in the Embassadors.

speeches.speaker: 1. Ush.
verse: Make roome there.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: They shall not wait long answer —

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Yet he comes not.
Why are eyes set on these, and multitudes
Follow to make these wonders? O good gods!
What would these looke like if my love were here?
But I am fond, forgetfull.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Now your grievance,
Speake short, and have as short dispatch.

speeches.speaker: 1. Em.
verse: Then thus sir:
In all our Royall Masters names, We tell you
Ye have done injustice, broke the bonds of concord,
And from their equall shares, from Alexander
Parted, and so possess'd, not like a brother,
But as an open Enemie, Ye have hedged in
Whole Provinces, man'd and maintain'd these injuries;
And daily with your sword (though they still honor ye)
Make bloudy roades, take Townes, and ruine Castles,
And still their sufferance feeles the waight.

speeches.speaker: 2. Em.
verse: Think of that love great sir, that honor'd friendship
Your selfe hold with our Masters, thinke of that strength
When you were all one body, all one minde;
When all your swords strook one way, when your angers,
Like so many brother billowes rose together,
And curling up your foaming crests, defied
Even mighty Kings, and in their fals, entomb'd 'em;
O thinke of these; and you that have been Conquerours,
That ever led your fortunes open ey'd,
Chain'd fast by confidence; you that fame courted,
Now ye want enemies and men to match ye;
Let not your owne swords seeke your ends to shame ye.

speeches.speaker: 3 Emb.
verse: Choose which you will, or peace or war,
We come prepar'd for either.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Roome for the Prince there.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: was it the Prince they said? how my heart trembl'd!
'Tis he indeed; what a sweet noble fiercenesse
Dwels in his eyes? young Meleager like,
When he returnd from slaughter of the Boare,
Crown'd with the loves and honours of the people,
With all the gallant youth of Greece, he lookes now,
Who could deny him love?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Haile Royall Father.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Ye are welcome from your sport sir, do you see this, gent.
You that bring thunders in your mouthes, and earthquakes
To shake and totter my designes? can you imagine
(You men of poore and common apprehensions)
Whilst I admit this man, my son, this nature
That in one looke carries more fire, and fiercenesse,
Then all your masters in their lives: dare I admit him,
Admit him thus, even to my side, My bosome,
When he is fit to rule, when all men cry him,
And all hopes hang about his head; thus place him,
His weapon hatcht in bloud, all these attending
When he shall make their fortunes, all as sudden
In any expedition he shall point 'em,
As arrowes from a Tartars bow, and speeding,
Dare I do this, and feare an enemy?
Feare your great Master? yours? or yours?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: O Hercules,
Who saies you do sir? Is there any thing
In these mens faces, or their Masters actions,
Able to worke such wonders?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Now 'a speakes:
O I could dwell upon that tongue for ever.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You call 'em Kings, they never wore those roialties
Nor in the progresse of their lives ariv'd yet
At any thought of King: emperiall dignities,
And powerfull god-like actions, fit for Princes
They can no more put on, and make 'em sit right,
Then I can with this mortall hand hold heaven:
Poore petty men, nor have I yet forgot
The chiefest honours time, and merit gave 'em:
Lysimachus your Master, at his best,
His highest, and his hopefull'st dignities
Was but grand-master of the Elephants;
Seleucus of the Treasure; and for Ptolomy,
A thing not thought on then, scarce heard of yet,
Some master of amunition: and must these men—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: What a brave confidence flowes from his spirit?
O sweet young man!

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Must these hold pace with us,
And on the same field hang their memories?
Must these examine what the wils of Kings are?
Prescribe to their designes, and chaine their actions
To their restraints? be freinds, and foes when they please?
Send out their thunders, and their menaces,
As if the fate of mortall thinge were theirs?
Go home good men, and tell your masters from us,
We do 'em too much honour to force from 'em
Their barren countries, ruine their vast Cities,
And tell 'em out of love, we meane to leave 'em
(Since they will needs be Kings) no more to tread on,
Then they have able wits, and powers to manage,
And so we shall befriend 'em: ha? what does she there?

speeches.speaker: Emb.
verse: This is your answer King.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis like to prove so.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Fie sweet, what make you here?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Pray ye do not chide me.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You do your selfe much wrong, and me.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Pray you pardon me,
I feele my fault, which only was committed
Through my deare love to you: I have not seen ye,
And how can I live then? I have not spoke to ye—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I know this weeke ye have not; I will redeem all.
You are so tender now: thinke where you are, sweet.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: What other light have I left?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Prethee Celia,
Indeed, I'le see ye presently.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I have done sir:
You will not misse?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: By this, and this, I will not.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: 'Tis in your will: and I must be obedient.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: No more of these assemblies.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I am commanded.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ush.
verse: Roome for the Lady there: Madam, my service—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: My Coach and't please you Lady.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ush.
verse: Roome before there.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: The honour Madam, but to waite upon you—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: My servants, and my state:
Lord, how they flocke now?
Before I was affraid they would have beat me;
How these flies play i'th Sunshine? pray ye no services,
Or if ye needs must play the hobby horses,
Seek out some beautie that affects 'em: farewell,
Nay pray ye spare: Gentlemen I am old enough
To go alone at these yeares, without crutches.

speeches.speaker: 2. Ush.
verse: Wel, I could curse now: but that will not help me,
I made as sure account of this wench now, immediately,
Do but consider how the devill has crost me,
Meate for my Master she cries, well —

speeches.speaker: 3 Em.
verse: Once more sir,
We aske your resolutions: peace or war yet?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: War, war, my noble father.

speeches.speaker: 1 Em.
verse: Thus I fling it:
And faire ey'd peace, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You have your answer;
Conduct out the Embassadours, and give 'em convoies.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Tell your high hearted Masters, they shall not seek us,
Nor coole i'th' field in expectation of us,
Wee'l ease your men those marches: In their strengths,
And full abilities of mind and courage,
Wee'l ffnd 'em out, and at their best trim buckle with 'em

speeches.speaker: 3 Em.
verse: You will find so hot a Souldiers welcome sir,
Your favor shall not freeze,

speeches.speaker: 2 Em.
verse: A forward Gentleman,
Pitty the wars should bruise such hopes—

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Conduct 'em —
Now, For this preparation: where's Leontius?
Call him in presently: for I meane in person Gentlemen
My selfe, with my old fortune—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Royall sir:
Thus low I beg this honour: fame already
Hath every where rais'd trophies to your glory,
And conquest now grown old, and weake with following
The weary marches, and the bloudy shockes
You daily set her in: 'tis now scarce honour
Fo you that never knew to fight, but conquer,
To sparkle such poore people: the roiall Eagle
When she hath tri'd her young ones gainst the Sun,
And found 'em right; next teacheth 'em to prey,
How to command on wing, and check below her
Even birds of noble plume; I am your owne sir,
You have found my spirit, trie it now, and teach it,
To stoop whole kingdomes: leave a little for me;
Let not your glory be so greedy sir,
To eate up all my hopes; you gave me life,
If to that life you adde not what's more lasting,
A noble name, for man you have made a shadow:
Blesse me this day: bid me go on, and lead,
Bid me go on, no lesse fear'd, then Antigonus,
And to my maiden sword, tye fast your fortune;
I know 'twill fight it selfe then: deare sir honour me:
Never faire virgin long'd so.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Rise, and command then,
And be as fortunate as I expect ye:
I love that noble will; your young companions
Bred up and foster'd with ye, I hope Demetrius.
You will make souldiers too: they must not leave ye.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Never till life leave us sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: O Leontius,
Here's worke for you in hand.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: I am ev'n right glad sir.
For by my troath, I am now grown old with idlenesse;
I heare we shall abroad sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes, and presently,
But who thinkes you commands now?

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Who commands sir?
Methinkes mine eye should guide me: can there be
(If you your selfe will spare him so much honour)
Any found out to lead before your armies,
So full of faith, and fire as brave Demetrius?
King Philips Son, at his yeares was an old Souldier,
'Tis time his fortune be a wing, high time sir,
So many idle houres, as here he loyters,
So many ever-living names he loses,
I hope 'tis he.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis he indeed, and nobly
He shall set forward: draw you all those Garrisons
Upon the frontiers as you passe: to those
Joyne these in pay at home, our ancient souldiers,
And as you go presse all the Provinces.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: We shall not need;
Beleeve, this hopefull Gentleman
Can want no swords, nor honest hearts to follow him,
We shall be full, no feare sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You Leontius,
Because you are an old, and faithfull servant,
And know the wars, with all his vantages,
Be neare to his instructions, least his youth
Lose valours best companion, staid discretion,
Shew where to lead, to lodge, to charge with safetie;
In execution not to breake, nor scatter,
But with a provident anger, follow nobly:
Not covetous of bloud, and death, but honour,
Be ever neare his watches; cheere his labours,
And where his hope stands faire, provoke his valour;
Love him, and thinke it no dishonour (my Demetrius)
To weare this Jewell neare thee; he is a tri'd one,
And one that even in spight of time, that sunke him,
And frosted up his strength, will yet stand by thee.
And with the proudest of thine enemies
Exchange for bloud, and bravely: take his counsell.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Your grace hath made me young again, and wanton.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: She must be known and suddenly; when you have done
Come in and take your leave sir, and some few
Prayers along.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Do ye know her?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Char. No, beleeve sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Did you observe her Tymon?

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: I look'd on her,
But what she is —

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I must have that found.

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: Well sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I know my duty,
You shall be halfe my father.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: All your Servant:
Come Gentlemen, you are resolv'd I am sure
To see these wars.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: We dare not leave his fortunes,
Though most assured death hung round about us.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: That bargaines yet to make;
Be not too hasty, when ye face the Enemie,
Nor too ambitious to get honour instantly,
But charge within your bounds, and keepe close bodies,
And you shall see what sport wee'l make these mad-caps;
You shall have game enough, I warrant ye,
Every mans Cock shall fight.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I must go see sir:
Brave sir, as soone as I have taken leave,
I'le meet you in the Parck;
Draw the men thether,
Waite you upon Leontius.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Wee'l attend sir.
