speeches.speaker: Lie.
verse: But I beseech your Grace, with speed; the sooner
We are i'th' field—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You could not please me better.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: You never saw the wars yet?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Not yet Collonell.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: These foolish Mistrisses do so hang about ye,
So whimper, and so hug, I know it Gentlemen,
And so intice ye, now ye are i'th' bud;
And that sweet tilting war, with eies and kisses,
Th' allarums of soft vowes, and sighes, and fiddle faddles,
Spoiles all our trade: You must forget these knick knacks,
A woman at some time of yeare, I grant ye
She is necessarie; but make no busines of her;
How now Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Oh sir, as ill as eves;
We shall have wars they say; they are mustring yonder:
Would we were at it once: fie, how it plagues me.

speeches.speaker: Le.
verse: Here's one has served now under Captaine Cupid,
And crackt a Pike in's youth: you see whats come on't.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: No, my disease will never prove so honourable.

speeches.speaker: Le.
verse: Why sure, thou hast the best pox.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: If I have'em,
I am sure I got 'em in the best companie;
They are pox of thirty Coates.

speeches.speaker: Le.
verse: Thou hast mewed 'em finely:
Here's a strange fellow now, and a brave fellow,
If we may say so of a pockie fellow,
(Which I beleeve we may) this poore Lieutenant;
Whether he have the scratches, or the scabs,
Or what a devill it be, I'le say this for him,
There sights no braver souldier under Sun, gentlemen;
Show him an Enemie, his paine's forgot straight;
And where other men, by beds and bathes have ease,
And easie rules of phisick, set him in a danger,
A danger, thats a fearfull one indeed,
Ye rock him, and he will so play about ye,
Let it be ten to one, he ne're comes off againe;
Ye have his heart: and then he works it bravely,
And throughly bravely: not a pang remembred:
I have seen him do such things, beliefe would shrinke at.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: 'Tis strange he should do all this, and diseas'd so.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I am sure 'tis true: Lieutenant, canst thou drink wel?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Would I were drunk, dog-drunk, I might not feele this.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I would take Phisicke.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: But I would know my disease first.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Why? it may be the Collique: canst thou, blow backward?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: There's never a bag-pipe in the kingdom better.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Is't not a pluresie?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: 'Tis any thing
That has the devill, and death in't: will ye march Gentlemen?
The Prince has taken leave.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How know ye that?

speeches.speaker: Lie.
verse: I saw him leave the Court, dispatch his followers,
And met him after in a bye street: I thinke
He has some wench, or such a toy, to lick over
Before he goe: would I had such another
To draw this foolish paine downe.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Let's away Gentlemen,
For sure the Prince will stay on us.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Wee'l attend sir.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Must ye needs go?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Or stay with all dishonour.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Are there not men enough to fight?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Fie Celia,
This ill becomes the noble love you beare me;
Would you have your love a coward?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: No; beleeve sir,
I would have him fight, but not so far off from me.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Wouldst have it thus? or thus?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: If that be fighting—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Ye wanton foole: when I come home againe
I'le fight with thee, at thine weapon Celia,
And conquer thee too.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: That you have done already,
You need no other Armes to me, but these sir;
But will you fight your selfe sir?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Thus deep in bloud wench,
And through the thickest rankes of Pikes.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Spur bravely,
Your firie Courser, beat the troopes before ye,
And crambe the mouth of death with executions.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I would do more then these: But prethee tell me,
Tell me my faire, where got'st thou this male spirit?
I wonder at thy mind.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Were I man then,
You would wonder more.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Sure thou wouldst prove a Souldier,
And some great Leader.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Sure I should do somewhat;
And the first thing I did, I should grow envious,
Extreamely envious of your youth, and honour.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: And fight against me?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Ten to one, I should do it.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Thou wouldst not hurt me?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: In this mind I am in,
I thinke I should be hardly brought to strike ye,
Unlesse 'twere thus; but in my mans mind—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I should be friends with ye too,
Now I thinke better.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Ye are a tall Souldier:
Here, take these, and these;
This gold to furnish ye, and keepe this bracelet;
Why do you weep now?
You a masculine spirit?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: No, I confesse I am a foole, a woman:
And ever when I part with you —

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You shall not,
These teares are like prodigious signes, my sweet one,
I shall come backe, loden with fame, to honour thee.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I hope you shall:
But then my deare Demetrius,
When you stand Conquerour, and at your mercy
All people bow, and all things waite your sentence;
Say then your eye (surveying all your conquest)
Finds out a beautie, even in sorrow excellent,
A constant face, that in the midst of ruine
With a forc'd smile, both scornes at fate, and fortune:
Say you find such a one, so nobly fortified,
And in her figure, all the sweets of nature?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Prethee,
No more of this, I cannot find her.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: That shews as far beyond my wither'd beauty;
And will run mad, to love ye too.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Do you feare me,
And do you thinke, besides this face, this beauty,
This heart, where all my hopes are lock'd—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I dare not:
No sure, I think ye honest; wondrous honest.
Pray doe not frowne, Ile swear ye are.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Ye may choose.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: But how long will ye be away?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I know not.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I know you are angry now: pray look upon me:
Ile aske no more such questions.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: The Drums beat,
I can no longer stay.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: They doe but call yet:
How faine you would leave my company.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I wou'd not,
Unlesse a greater power then love commanded,
Commands my life, mine honour.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: But a little.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Prethee farewell, and be not doubtfull of me.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I would not have ye hurt: and ye are so ventrous—
But good sweet Prince preserve your selfe, fight nobly,
But do not thrust this body; 'tis not yours now,
'Tis mine, 'tis onely mine: doe not seek wounds, Sir,
For every drop of bloud you bleed —

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I will Celia,
I will be carefull.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: My heart, that loves ye deerely.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Prethee no more, we must part:
Harke, they march now.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Pox on these bawling Drums: I am sure you'll kisse me,
But one kisse? what a parting's this?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Here take me,
And doe what thou wilt with me, smother me;
But still remember, if your fooling with me,
Make me forget the trust—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I have done: farewell sir,
Never look back, you shall not stay, not a minute.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I must have one farewell more.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: No, the Drums beat;
I dare not slack your honour; not a hand more,
Onely this look; the gods preserve, and save ye.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What have ye found her out?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: We have hearkned after her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What's that to my desire?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Your grace must give us time,
And a little meanes.

speeches.speaker: Ty.
verse: She is sure a stranger,
If she were bred or knowne here—

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Your dull endeavours
Should never be employ'd. Welcome Menippus.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: I have found her sir,
I meane the place she is lodg'd in; her name is Celia,
And much a doe I had to purchase that too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Dost think Demetrius loves her?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Much I feare it,
But nothing that way yet can win for certaine.
Ile tell your grace within this houre.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: A stranger?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: VVithout all doubt.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: But how should he come to her?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: There lies the marrow of the matter hid yet.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Has't thou been with thy wife?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: No sir, I am going to her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Goe and dispatch, and meet me in the garden,
And get all out ye can.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Ile doe my best sir.

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: Blest be thy wife, thou wert an arrant asse else.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I, she is a stirring woman indeed:
There's a braine brother.

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: There's not a handsome wench of any mettle
VVithin an hundred miles, but her intelligence
Reaches her, and out reaches her, and brings her
As confidently to Court, as to a sanctuary:
VVhat had his mouldy braines ever arriv'd at,
Had not she beaten it out oth' Flint to fasten him?
They say she keeps an office of Concealements:
There is no young wench, let her be a Saint,
Unlesse she live ith' Center, but she findes her,
And every way prepares addresses to her:
If my wife would have followed her course Charinthus,
Her lucky course, I had the day before him:
O what might I have been by this time, Brother?
But she (forsooth) when I put these things to her,
These things of honest thrift, groans, ô my conscience,
The load upon my conscience, when to make us cuckolds,
They have no more burthen then a brood-goose, brother;
But let's doe what we can, though this wench faile us,
Another of a new way will be lookt at:
Come, let's abroad, and beat our brains, time may
For all his wisedome, yet give us a day.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I will not see 'em fall thus, give me way sir,
I shall forget you love me else.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: VVill ye lose all?
For me to be forgotten, to be hated,
Nay never to have been a man, is nothing,
So you, and those we have preserv'd from slaughter
Come safely off.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I have lost my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: You are cozn'd.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: And am most miserable.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: There's no man so, but he that makes himself so.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I will goe on.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: You must not: I shall tell you then,
And tell you true, that man's unfit to governe,
That cannot guide himselfe: you lead an Army?
That have not so much manly suff'rance left yee,
To beare a losse?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Charge but once more Leontius,
My friends and my companions are engag'd all.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Nay give 'em lost, I saw 'em off their horses,
And the enemy master of their Armes; nor could then,
The policie, nor strength of man redeem 'em.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: And shall I know this, and stand fooling?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: By my dead fathers soule you stir not, sir,
Or if you doe, you make your way through me first.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Thou art a Coward.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: To prevent a Madman.
None but your fathers Son, durst call me so,
'Death if he did—Must I be scandall'd by ye,
That hedg'd in all the helps I had to save ye?
That, where there was a valiant weapon stirring,
Both search'd it out, and singl'd it, unedg'd it,
For feare it should bite you, am I a coward?
Goe, get ye up, and tell 'em ye are the Kings Sonne;
Hang all your Ladies favours on your Crest,
And let them fight their shares; spurre to destruction,
You cannot misse the way: be bravely desperate,
And your young friends before ye, that lost this battell,
Your honourable friends, that knew no order,
Cry out, Antigonus, the old Antigonus,
The wise and fortunate Antigonus,
The great, the valiant, and the fear'd Antigenus,
Has sent a desperate sonne, without discretion
To bury in an houre his age of honor.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I am ashamed.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: 'Tis ten to one, I die with ye:
The coward will not long be after ye;
I scorne to say I saw you fall, sigh for ye,
And tell a whining tale, some ten yeares after
To boyes and girles in an old chimney corner,
Of what a Prince we had, how bravely spirited;
How young and faire he fell: wee'l all goe with ye,
And ye shall see us all, like sacrifices
In our best trim, fill up the mouth of ruine,
Will this faith satisfie your folly? can this show ye,
Tis not to die we feare, but to die poorely,
To fall, forgotten, in a multitude?
If you will needs tempt fortune now she has held ye,
Held ye from sinking up.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Pray doe not kill me,
These words pierce deeper then the wounds I suffer,
The smarting wounds of losse.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ye are too tender;
Fortune has houres of losse, and houres of honor,
And the most valiant feele them both: take comfort,
The next is ours, I have a soule descries it:
The angry bull never goes backe for breath,
But when he meanes to arme his fury double.
Let this day set but not the memorie,
And we shall find a time: How now Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I know not: I am mall'd: we are bravely beaten,
All our young gallants lost.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Thou art hurt.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I am pepper'd,
I was i'th' midst of all: and bang'd of all hands:
They made an anvile of my head, it rings yet;
Never so thresh'd: do you call this fame? I have fam'd it;
I have got immortall fame, but I'le no more on't;
I'le no such scratching Saint to serve hereafter;
O my conscience I was kill'd above twenty times,
And yet I know not what a Devil's in't,
I crawled away, and lived againe still; I am hurt plaguily,
But now I have nothing neere so much paine Colonell,
They have sliced me for that maladie.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: All the young men lost?

speeches.speaker: Lie.
verse: I am glad you are here: but they are all i'th' pound sir,
They'l never ride o're other mens corne againe, I take it,
Such frisking, and such flaunting with their feathers,
And such careering with their mistres favours;
And here must he be pricking out for honor,
And there got he a knocke, and downe goes pilgarlike,
Commends his soule to his she-saint, and exit.
Another spurres in there, cryes make roome villaines,
I am a Lord, scarce spoken, but with reverence
A rascall takes him o're the face, and fels him;
There lyes the Lord, the Lord be with him.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Now sir,
Doe you find this truth?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I would not.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Pox upon it,
They have such tender bodies too; such Cullisses,
That one good hansome blow breaks 'em a pieces.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How stands the Enemie?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Even coole enough too:
For to say truth, he has bin shrewdly heated,
The gentleman no doubt will fall to his jewlips.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: He marches not i'th' taile on's.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: No, plague take him,
Hee'l kisse our tailes as soone; he lookes upon us,
As if he would say, if ye will turne againe, friends,
We will belabor you a little better,
And beat a little more care into your coxcombs.
Now shall we have damnable Ballads out against us,
Most wicked madrigals: and ten to one Colonell,
Sung to such lowsie, lamentable tunes.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Thou art merrie,
How e're the game goes: good sir be not troubled,
A better day will draw this backe againe.
Pray goe, and cheere those left, and lead 'em off,
They are hot, and wearie.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I'le doe any thing.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Lieutenant, send one presentlie away
To 'th' King, and let him know our state: and harke ye,
Be sure the messenger advise his Majestie
To comfort up the Prince: hee's full of sadnes.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: When shall I get a Surgeon? this hot weather,
Unlesse I be well pepper'd, I shall stinke Colonel.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Goe, I'le prepare thee one.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: If ye catch me then,
Fighting againe, I'le eat hay with a horse.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Have ye written to Merione?

speeches.speaker: 1. Ma.
verse: Yes, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: And let her understand the hopes she has
If she come speedilie —

speeches.speaker: 1. Ma.
verse: All these are specified,

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: And of the chaine is sent her,
And the rich stuffe to make her shew more hansome here?

speeches.speaker: 1 Maid.
verse: All this is done, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What have you dispatcht there?

speeches.speaker: 2 Mai.
verse: A letter to the Countrey maid, and't please ye.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: A pretty girle, but peevish, plaguy peevish:
Have ye bought the embroydered gloves, and that purse for her,
And the new Curle?

speeches.speaker: 2. Maid.
verse: They are ready packt up Madam.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Her maiden-head will yeeld me; let me see now,
She is not fifteen they say: for her complexion—
Cloe, Cloe, Cloe, here, I have her,
Cloe, the Daughter of a Countrey gentleman;
Her age upon fifteen: now her complexion,
A lovely browne; here 'tis; eyes black and rolling,
The body neatly built: she strikes a Lute well,
Sings most inticingly: these helpes consider'd,
Her maiden-head will amount to some three hundred,
Or three hundred & fifty crowns; 'twil bear it handsomly.
Her father's poore, some little share deducted,
To buy him a hunting Nag; I, 'twill be pretty:
VVho takes care of the Merchants wife?

speeches.speaker: 1 Mai.
verse: I have wrought her.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You know for whom she is?

speeches.speaker: 1. Maid.
verse: Very well, Madam,
Though very much adoe, I had to make her
Apprehend that happinesse.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: These kinde are subtile:
Did she not cry and blubber when ye urg'd her.

speeches.speaker: 1. Maid.
prose: O most extremly, & swore she would rather perish.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Good signes, very good signes,
Symptomes of easie nature.
Had she the plate?

speeches.speaker: 1. Maid.
verse: She lookt upon't, and left it,
And turn'd againe, and view'd it.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Very well still.

speeches.speaker: 1 Maid.
verse: At length she was content to let it lye there,
Till I call'd for't, or so,

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: She will come?

speeches.speaker: 1. Maid.
verse: Doe you take me
For such a foole, I would part without that promise?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: The Chambers next the park.

speeches.speaker: 2. Maid.
verse: The Widdow Madam,
You bad me look upon.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Hang her, she is mustic:
She is no mans meat; beside, she is poore and sluttish:
Where lies old Thisbe now, you are so so long now—

speeches.speaker: 2. Ma.
verse: Thisbe, Thisbe, This. agent Thisbe, ô I have her,
She lyes now in Nicopolis.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Dispatch a packet,
And tell her, her superiour here commands her,
The next Mon'th not to faile, but see deliver'd
Here to our use, some twenty young and handsome,
As also able maids, for the Court service,
As she will answer it: we are out of beautie,
Utterly out, and rub the time away here,
With such blown stuff, I am asham'd to send it.
Who's that? look out, to your businesse maid,
There's nothing got by idlenesse: There is a Lady,
Which if I can but buckle with, Altea,
A, A, A, A, Altea, young, and marrried,
And a great lover of her husband, well,
Not to be brought to Court: say ye so? I am sorry,
The Court shall be brought to you then: how now, who is't?

speeches.speaker: 1. Maid.
verse: An ancient woman, with a maid attending,
A pretty girle, but out of cloathes; for a little money,
It seemes she would put her to your bringing up, Madam,

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Let her come in. Would ye ought with us, good woman?
I pray be short, we are full of businesse.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: I have a tender girle here, and't please your honour.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Very well.

speeches.speaker: VVom.
verse: That hath a great desire to serve your worship.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: It may be so; I am full of Maids.

speeches.speaker: VVom.
verse: She is young, forsooth—
And for her truth; and as they say her bearing.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Ye say well: come ye hither maid, let me feel your pulse,
'Tis some what weak, but nature will grow stronger,
Let me see your leg, she treads but low ith' pasternes.

speeches.speaker: VVom.
verse: A cork heele Madam.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: We know what will doe it,
Without your aime good woman: what do you pitch her at?
Shee's but a slight toy—cannot hold out long.

speeches.speaker: VVom.
verse: Even what you think is meet.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Give her ten Crowns, we are full of businesse,
Shee is a poore woman, let her take a Cheese home:
Enter the wench ith' office.

speeches.speaker: 2. Maid.
verse: What's your name, sister?

speeches.speaker: Phe.
verse: Phebe forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: A pretty name; 'twill doe well:
Goe in, and let the other maid instruct ye Phebe;
Let my old velvet skirt be made fit for her,
I'le put her into action for a wascoate,
And when I have rigg'd her up once, this small Pinnace
Shall saile for gold, and good store too: who's there?
Lord, shall we never have any ease in this world?
Still troubled? still molested? what would you have?
I cannot furnish ye faster then I am able
And ye were my husband a thousand times, I cannot do it;
At least a dozen poasts are gone this morning
For severall parts of the Kingdome: I can do no more
But pay 'em, and instruct 'em.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Prethee, good sweet heart,
I come not to disturbe thee, nor discourage thee,
I know thou labour'st truly: harke in thine eare.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Ha?
What do you make so dainty on't? looke there,
I am an Asse, I can do nothing.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Celia?
I, this is she; a stranger borne.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: What would you give for more now?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Prethee, my best Leucippe, ther's much hangs ont
Lodg'd at the end of Marse's street? thats true too;
At the sacke of such a Towne, by such a Souldier
Preserv'd a prisoner: and by Prince Demetrius
Bought from that man againe, maintain'd, and favourd:
How came you by this knowledge?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Poore weake man,
I have a thousand eyes, when thou art sleeping,
Abroad, and full of businesse.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: You never tri'd her?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: No, she is beyond my levell; so hedg'd in
By the Princes infinite love, and favour to her—

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: She is a hansome wench.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: A delicate, and knowes it;
And out of that proofe armes her selfe.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Come in then;
I have a great designe from the King to you,
And you must worke like waxe now.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: On this Lady?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: On this, and all your wits call home.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I have done.
Toyes in my time of some note; old as I am,
I thinke my braines will worke without barme,
Take up the Bookes.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: As we goe in, I'le tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No face of sorrow for this losse? 'twill choake him,
Nor no man misse a friend, I know his nature
So deep imprest with griefe, for what he has suffer'd,
That the least adding to it, adds to his ruine;
His losse is not so infinite, I hope Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: Faith neither great, nor out of discretion,
The young men out of heate.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I ghesse the manner.

speeches.speaker: Lord Men.
verse: The Prince and't like your Grace—

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You are welcome home sir;
Come, no more sorrow, I have heard your fortune,
And I my self haue tride the like: cleare up man,
I will not have ye take it thus; if I doubted.
Your feare had lost; and that you had turn'd your back to 'em,
Basely besought their mercies—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: No, no, by this hand sir,
We fought like honest and tall men.

speeches.speaker: Antig.
verse: I know't Leontius; or if I thought
Neglect of rule, having his councell with ye,
Or too vaine-glorious appetite of fame,
Your men forgot, and scatter'd.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: None of these sir,
He shew'd himselfe a noble gentleman,
Every way apt to rule.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: These being granted;
Why should you think you have done an act so hainous,
That nought but discontent dwells round about ye?
I have lost a Battaile.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I, and fought it hard too.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: With as much meanes as man—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Or devill could urge it.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Twenty to one of our side now.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Turne Tables,
Beaten like dogs againe, like Owles, you take it
To hart for flying but a mile before 'em,
And to say truth, 'twas no flight neither sir,
'Twas but a walke, a handsome walke,
I have tumbl'd with this old body, beaten like a stock-fish,
And stuck with arrowes, like an arming Quiver,
Blouded and bang'd, almost a day before 'em,
And glad I have got off then. Here's a mad shaver,
He fights his share I am sure, when ere he comes to't;
Yet I have seen him trip it tithely too,
And cry the devill take the hindmost ever.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I learn'd it of my betters.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Boudge at this?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Has fortune but one face?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: In her best vizard,
Me thinks she looks but lowzily.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Chance, though she faint now,
And sink below our expectations,
Is there no hope left strong enough to boy her?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: 'Tis not this day, I fled before the enemie,
And lost my people, left mine honour murder'd,
My mayden honour, never to be ransom'd,
(VVhich to a noble soule is too too sencible)
Afflicts me with this sadnesse; most of these,
Time may turne straight againe, experience perfect,
And new swords, cut new wayes to nobler fortunes.
O I have lost—

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: As you are mine forget it:
I doe not think it losse.

speeches.speaker: Demet.
verse: O sir, forgive me,
I have lost my friends, those worthy soules bred with me,
I have lost my selfe, they were the pieces of me;
I have lost all Arts, my Schooles are taken from me,
Honour and Armes, no emulation left me:
I liv'd to see these men lost, look'd upon it;
These men that twin'd their loves to mine, their vertues,
O shame of shames, I saw, and could not save 'em,
This carries sulphure in't, this burnes and boyles me,
And like a fatall Tombe bestrides my memorie.

speeches.speaker: Antig.
verse: This was hard fortune, but if alive, and taken,
They shall be ransom'd; let it be at Millions.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: They are dead, they are dead.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: VVhen would he weep for me thus?
I may be dead, and powder'd.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Good Prince, grieve not:
VVe are not certaine of their deaths: the enemy,
Though he be hot, and keene,
Yet holds good Quarter.
VVhat noyse is this?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: He doe's not follow us?
Give me a steeple top.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: They live, they live sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Hold up your manly face;
They live, they are here, Son.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: These are the men.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: They are, and live to honour ye.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: How scap't ye noble friends? me thought I saw ye
Even in the jawes of death.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
verse: Thanks to our folly,
That spurr'd us on; we were indeed hedg'd round in't,
And ev'n beyond the hand of succour beaten,
Unhors'd, disarm'd: and what we lookt for then sir,
Let such poore weary soules that heare the Bell knoll,
And see the grave a digging, tell.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: For heaven sake
Delude mine eyes no longer: how came ye off?

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
verse: Against all expectation: the brave Seleucus,
I thinke this day enamour'd on your vertue,
VVhen, through the Troops, he saw ye shoot like lightning;
And at your manly courage all tooke fire,
And after that, the miserie we fell too,
The never-certaine fate of war considering,
As we stood all before him, fortunes ruines,
Nothing but death expecting, a short time
He made a stand upon our youths and fortunes,
Then with an eye of mercy inform'd his judgement,
How yet unripe we were, unblowne, unhardend,
Unfitted for such fatall ends; he cryed out to us,
Goe Gentlemen, commend me to your Master,
To the most high, and hopefull prince Demetrius,
Tell him the valour that he showed against me
This day, the virgin valour, and true fire
Deserves, even from an Enemie, this courtesie;
Your lives and Armes freely I'le give 'em: thanke him,
And thus we are return'd Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Faith 'twas well done;
'Twas bravely done; was't not a noble part Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Had I been there up had I gone, I am sure on't;
These noble tricks, I never durst trust 'em yet.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Let me not live, and't were not a famed honestie,
It takes me such a tickling way: now would I wish heaven,
But ee'n the happines, ee'n that poore blessing
For all the sharp afflictions thou hast sent me,
But ee'n i'th' head o'th' field to take Seleucus.
I should doe something memorable: fie, sad still.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
verse: Doe you grieve we are come off?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Unransom'd, was it?

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
verse: It was sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: And with such a fame to me?
Said ye not so?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ye have heard it.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: O Leontius,
Better I had lost 'em all: my selfe had perished,
And all my fathers hopes,

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Mercy upon ye,
VVhat ayle ye Sir? 'death, doe not make fooles on's,
Neither goe to Church, nor tarry at home,
That's a fine Horne-pipe?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVhat's now your griefe Demetrius?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Did he not beat us twice?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: He beate a pudding;
Beate us but once.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Has beate me twice, and beat me to a coward,
Beat me to nothing.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Is not the devill in him?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I pray it be no worse.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Twice conquer'd me.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Bear witnesse all the world, I am a dunce here.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: With valour first he strook me, then with honour;
That stroak Leontius, that strook, do'st thou not feele it?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Where abouts was it? for I remember nothing yet.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: All these gentlemen
That were his prisoners—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Yes, he set 'em free sir,
With Armes and honour.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: There, there, now thou hast it;
At mine owne weapon, Courtesie, h'as beaten me,
At that I was held a Master in, he has cow'd me,
Hotter then all the dint oth' fight he has charg'd me:
Am I not now a wretched fellow? think on't;
And when thou hast examin'd all wayes honourable,
And find'st no doore left open to requite this,
Conclude I am a wretch, and was twice beaten.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I have observ'd your way, and understand it,
And equall love it as Demetrius,
My noble childe thou shalt not fall in vertue,
I and my power will sink first: you Leontius,
Wait for a new Commission, ye shall out againe,
And instantly: you shall not lodge this night here,
Not see a friend, nor take a blessing with ye,
Before ye be ith'field: the enemy is up still,
And still in ful dnsigne: Charge him againe, Son,
And either bring home that againe thou hast lost there,
Or leave thy body by him.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Ye raise me,
And now I dare look up againe, Leontius.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I, I, sir, I am thinking who we shall take of 'em,
To make all straight; and who we shall give toth' devill.
VVhat saist thou now Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I say nothing.
Lord what aile I, that I have no minde to fight now?
I finde my constitution mightily alter'd
Since I came home: I hate all noises too,
Especially the noise of Drums; I am now as well
As any living man; why not as valiant?
To fight now, is a kinde of vomit to me,
It goes against my stomack.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Good sir, presently;
You cannot doe your Son, so faire a favour.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis my intent: Ile see ye march away too;
Come, get your men together presently, Leontius,
And presse where please you, as you march.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: VVe goe sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVait you on me, Ile bring ye to your command,
And then to fortune give you up.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Ye love me.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Goe, get the drums, beat round, Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Harke ye, sir,
I have a foolish businesse they call marriage.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: After the wars are done.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: The partie staies sir,
I have giv'n the Priest his money too: all my friends sir,
My father, and my mother.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: VVill you goe forward?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: She brings a pretty matter with her.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Halfe a dozen Bastards.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Some fortie sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: A goodly competency.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I meane sir, pounds a year; Ile dispatch the matter,
'Tis but a night or two; Ile overtake ye sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: The 2 old legions, yes: where lies the horse-quarter?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: And if it be a boy, Ile even make bold sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Away with your whore,
A plague o'your whore, you damn'd rogue,
Now ye are cur'd and well; must ye be clicketing?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I have broke my minde to my Ancient, in my absence,
Hee's a sufficient gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Get forward.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Onely receive her portion.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Get ye forward;
Else Ile bang ye forward.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Strange sir,
A Gentleman and an officer cannot have the libertie
To doe the office of a man.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Shame light on thee,
How came this whore into thy head?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: This whore sir?
'Tis strange, a poore whore.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Doe not answer me:
Troop, Troop away; doe not name this whore againe,
Or think there is a whore.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: That's very hard sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: For if thou dost, look to't, Ile have thee guelded,
Ile walk ye out before me: not a word more.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Ye are the Mistris of the house ye say,
Where this young Ladie lies.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: For want of a better.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You may be good enough for such a purpose:
When was the Prince with her? answer me directly.

speeches.speaker: Gover.
verse: Not since he went a warring.

speeches.speaker: Leuc.
verse: Very well then:
What carnall copulation are you privie too
Between these two? be not afraid, we are women,
And may talke thus amongst our selves, no harme in't.

speeches.speaker: Gover.
verse: No sure, there's no harme in't, I conceive that;
But truely, that I ever knew the gentlewoman
Otherwise given, then a hopefull gentlewoman—

speeches.speaker: Leuc.
verse: You'll grant me the Prince loves her?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: There I am with ye.
And the gods blesse her, promises her mightily.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Stay there a while. And gives her gifts?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Extreamly;
And truely makes a very Saint of her.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I should think now,
(Good woman let me have your judgement with me,
I see 'tis none of the worst: Come sit down by me)
That these two cannot love so tenderly.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Being so young as they are too.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You say well—
But that methinks some further promises —

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Yes, yes,
I have heard the Prince sweare he would marry her.

speeches.speaker: Leuc.
verse: Verie well still: they doe not use to fall out?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: The tenderest Chickens to one another,
They cannot live an houre assunder.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I have done then;
And be you gone; you know your charge, and doe it.
You know whose will it is; if you transgresse it—
That is, if any have accesse, or see her,
Before the Kings will be fulfill'd—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Not the Prince, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You'll be hang'd if you it, that Ile assure ye.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: But ne're the lesse, Ile make bold to obey ye.

speeches.speaker: Leuc.
verse: Away, and to your businesse then.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: 'Tis done, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: THou hast taken wondrous pains; but yet Menippus,
You understand not of what bloud, & countrey.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: I labour'd that, but cannot come to know it.
A Greek I am sure she is, she speaks this language.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Is she so excellent handsome?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Most inticing.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Sold for a prisoner?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Yes sir,
Some poore creature.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: And he loves tenderly?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: They say extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis well prevented then: yes, I perceiv'd it:
When he took leave now, he made a hundred stops,
Desir'd an houre, but halfe an houre, a minute,
Which I with anger cross'd; I knew his businesse,
I knew 'twas she he hunted on; this journey, man,
I beat out suddenly for her cause intended,
And would not give him time to breath. When comes she?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: This morning sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Lodge her to all delight then:
For I would have her try'd toth' test: I know,
She must be some crackt coyne, not fit his traffique,
Which when we have found, the shame will make him leave her,
Or we shal work a nearer way: Ile bury him,
And with him all the hopes I have cast upon him,
Ere he shall dig his owne grave in that woman:
You know which way to bring her: Ile stand close there,
To view her as she passes: and doe you hear Menippus,
Observe her with all sweetnesse: humour her,
'Twill make her lie more carelesse to our purposes.
Away, and take what helpes you please.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: I am gone sir.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Governesse, from whom was this Gown sent me?
Prethee be serious true; I will not wear't else:
'Tis a handsome one.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: As though you know not?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: No faith:
But I believe, for certaine too, yet I wonder,
Because it was his caution, this poore way,
Still to preserve me from the curious searchings
Of greedy eyes.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You have it: does it please you?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: 'Tis very rich, methinks too, prethee tell me?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: From one that likes you wel, never look coy, Lady;
These are no gifts, to be put off with poutings.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Powtings, and gifts? is it from any stranger?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You are so curious, that there is no talk to ye.
What if it be I pray ye?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Unpin good Governesse,
Quick, quick.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Why, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Quick, good Governesse:
Fie on't, how beastly it becomes me? poorely?
A trick put in upon me? well said Governesse:
I vow I would not weare it—out, it smells musty.
Are these your tricks? now I begin to smell it
Abominable musty; will ye help me?
The Prince will come againe—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You are not mad sure?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: As I live ile cut it off: a pox upon it;
For sure it was made for that use; do you bring me Livories?
Stales to catch Kites? dost thou laugh too, thou base woman?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I cannot chuse, if I should be hang'd.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Abuse me,
And then laugh at me too?

speeches.speaker: Gover.
verse: I doe not abuse ye:
Is it abuse, to give him drink that's thirsty?
You want cloathes; is it such a hainous sin I beseech ye,
To see you stor'd?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: There is no greater wickednesse
Then this way.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: What way?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I shall curse thee fearefully,
If thou provok'st me further: and take heed, woman;
My curses never misse.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Curse him that sent it.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Tell but his name—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You dare not curse him.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Dare not?
By this faire light—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You are so full of passion—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Dare not be good? be honest? dare not curse him?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I think you dare not: I beleeve so.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Speak him.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Up with your valour then, up with it bravely,
And take your full charge.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: If I doe not, hang me;
Tell but his name.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: 'Twas Prince Demetrius sent it:
Now, now, give fire, kill him ith' eye now Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Is he come home?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: It seems so; but your curse now.

speeches.speaker: Col.
verse: You doe not lie, I hope.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: You dare not curse him.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Prethee do not abuse me: is he come home indeed?
For I would now with all my heart beleeve thee.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Nay, you may chuse: alas, I deale for strangers,
That send ye scurvie musty Gownes, stale Livories:
I have my tricks.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: 'Tis a good gowne, a handsome one;
I did but jest; where is he?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: He that sent it—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: How? he that sent it? is't come to that againe?
Thou canst not be so foolish: prethee speak out,
I may mistake thee.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I said he that sent it.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Curse o' my life: why dost thou vex me thus?
I know thou meanst Demetrius, dost thou not?
I charge thee speak truth: if it be any other,
Thou knowst the charge he gave thee, and the justice
His anger will inflict, if 'ere he know this,
As know he shall, he shall, thou spightfull woman,
Thou beastly woman; and thou shalt know too late too,
And feele too sensible, I am no ward,
No sale stuffe for your money Merchants that sent it?
Who dare send me, or how durst thou, thou—

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: What you please:
For this is ever the reward of service.
The Prince shall bring the next himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: 'Tis strange
That you should deale so peevishly: beshrew ye,
You have put me in a heat.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I am sure ye have kild me:
I ne're receiv'd such language: I can but wait upon ye,
And be your drudge; keep a poore life to serve ye.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: You know my nature is too easie, Governesse,
And you know now, I am sorry too: how does he?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: O God, my head.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Prethee be wel, and tell me,
Did he speak of me, since he came? nay, see now,
If thou wilt leave this tyranny? good sweet governesse,
Did he but name his Celia? look upon me,
Upon my faith I meant no harme: here, take this,
And buy thy selfe some rrifles: did a good wench?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: He loves yee but too dearely.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: That's my good Governesse.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: There's more cloathes making for yee.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: More cloathes?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: More:
Richer and braver; I can tell yee that newes;
And twenty glorious things.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: To what use sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Ye are too good for our house now: we poore wretches
Shall lose the comfort of ye.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: No, I hope not.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: For ever lose ye Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Lose me? wherefore?
I heare of no such thing.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: 'Tis sure it must be so:
You must shine now at Court: such preparation,
Such hurrie, and such hanging roomes—

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Toth' Court wench?
Was it toth' Court thou saidst?

speeches.speaker: Gox.
verse: You'll finde it so.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Staie, stay, this cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I say it must be:
I hope to finde ye still the same good Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Toth' Court? this stumbles me: art sure for me, wench,
This preparation is?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: She is peilous crafty:
I feare too honest for us all too. Am I sure I live?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Toth' Court? this cannot down: what should I do there?
Why should he on a suddain change his mind thus,
And not make me acquainted? sure he loves me;
His vow was made against it, and mine with him:
At least while this King liv'd: he will come hither,
And see me ere I goe?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Wou'd some wise woman
Had her in working: that I think he will not,
Because he means with all joy there to meet ye.
Ye shall heare more within this houre?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: A Courtier?
What may that meaning be? sure he will see me
If he be come, he must: Hark ye good Governesse,
What age is the King of?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Hee's an old man, and full of businesse.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I feare too full indeed: what Ladies are there?
I would be loath to want good company.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Delicate young Ladies, as you would desire;
And when you are acquainted, the best company.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: 'Tis very well: prethee goe in, let's talk more.
For though I feare a trick, Ile bravely try it.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I see he must be cunning,
Knoks this Doe downe.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: You shal not have your wil, sirrah, are ye running?
Have ye gotten a toy in your heeles? Is this a season,
When honour pricks ye on, to prick your eares up,
After your whore, your Hobby-horse?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Why look ye now:
What a strange man are you? would you have a man fight
At all houres all alike.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Doe but fight something;
But halfe a blow, and put thy stomack to't:
Turne but thy face, and do but make mouthes at 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: And have my teeth knockt out; I thank ye heartily,
Ye are my deare friend.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: What a devill ailes thee?
Dost long to be hang'd?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Faith Sir, I make no suit for't:
But rather then I would live thus our of charity,
Continually in brawling—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Art thou not he?
I may be cozn'd—

speeches.speaker: Lie.
verse: I shall be discover'd.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: That in the midst of thy most hellish pains,
When thou wert crawling sick, didst aime at wonders,
When thou wert mad with paine?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Ye have found the cause out;
I had ne're been mad to fight else: I confesse sir,
The dayly torture of my side that vext me,
Made me as dayly carelesse what became of me,
Till a kinde sword there wounded me, and eas'd me;
'Twas nothing in my valour fought; I am well now,
And take some pleasure in my life, methinks now,
It shewes as mad a thing to me to see you scuffle,
And kill one another foolishly for honour,
As 'twas to you, to see me play the cox-combe.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And wilt thou ne're fight more?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Ith' minde I am in,

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Nor never be sick againe?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I hope I shall not.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Prethee be sick againe; prethee, I beseech thee,
Be just so sick againe.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Ile just be hang'd first.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: If all the Arts that are can make a Chollique,
Therefore look to't: or if imposthumes, marke me,
As big as foot-bals—

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Deliver me.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Or stones of ten pound weight ith' kidneyes,
Through ease and ugly dyets may be gather'd;
Ile feed ye up my selfe sir, Ile prepare ye,
You cannot fight, unlesse the devill teare ye,
You shall not want provocations, Ile scratch ye,
Ile have thee have the tooth-ach, and the head-ach.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Good Colonell, Ile doe any thing.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: No, no, nothing—
Then will I have thee blowne with a paire of Smiths bellowes,
Because ye shall be sure to have a round gale with ye,
Fil'd full of oyle, o' devill, and Aqua fortis,
And let these worke, these may provoke.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Good Colonell.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: A coward in ful bloud; prethee be plain with me,
Will roasting doe thee any good?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Nor basting neither, sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Marry that goes hard.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Where are you Colonell?
The Prince expects ye sir; has hedg'd the enemy
Within a straight, where all the hopes and valours
Of all men living cannot force a passage,
He has 'em now.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I knew all this before sir,
I chalk'd him out his way: but do you see that thing there?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Nay good sweet Colonell, Ile fight a little.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: That thing?

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
verse: What thing? I see the brave Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Rogue, what a name hast thou lost?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: You may helpe it?
Yet you may help't: Ile doe ye any courtesie:
I know you love a wench well.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Look upon him;
Doe you look too.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
verse: What should I look on?
I come to tell yee, the Prince stayes your direction,
We have 'em now ith Coop, sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Let 'em rest there,
And chew upon their miseries: but look first—

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I cannot fight for all this.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Look on this fellow.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I know him; 'tis the valiant brave Lieutenant.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Canst thou heare this, and play the rogue? steal off quickly,
Behinde me quickly, neatly doe it,
And rush into the thickest of the enemy,
And if thou kill'st but two.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: You may excuse me,
'Tis not my fault: I dare not fight.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Be rul'd yet
Ile beat thee on; goe wink and fight: a plague upon your sheeps heart.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: What's all this matter?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Nay I cannot shew yee.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Here's twenty pound, goe but smell to 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Alas sir,
I have taken such a cold I can smell nothing.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I can smell a rascall, a ranke rascall:
Fye, how he stinks, stinkes like a tyred Jade.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: What sir?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Why, that sir, doe not you smell him?

speeches.speaker: 2. Gent.
verse: Smell him?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I must endure.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Stinks like a dead dog, Carrion—
There's no such damnable smell under heaven,
As the faint sweat of a Coward: will ye fight yet?

speeches.speaker: Lie.
verse: Nay, now I defie ye; ye have spoke the worst, ye can
Of me, and if every man should take what you say
To the heart. —

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: God a mercy,
God a mercy with all my heart; here I forgive thee;
And fight, or fight not, doe but goe along with us,
And keep my dog.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I love a good dog naturally.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: What's all this stir, Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Lieut.
verse: Nothing Sir,
But a slight matter of argument.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Pox take thee.
Sure I shall love this rogue, he's so pretty a Coward,
Come gentlemen, let's up now, and if fortune
Dare play the slut againe, Ile never more Saint her,
Come play fellow, come, prethee come up; come chicken,
I have a way shall fit yet: A tame knave.
Come, look upon us.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Ile tell ye who does best boyes.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: I saw her comming out,

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVho waits upon her?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Tymon, Charinthus, and some other gentlemen,
By me appointed.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVhere's your wife?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Shee's ready
To entertaine her here sir; and some Ladies
Fit for her lodgings.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: How shews she in her trim now?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Oh most divinely sweet.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Prethee speak softly.
How does she take her comming?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: She beares it bravely;
But what she thinks—I or heaven sake sir preserve me—
If the Prince chance to finde this.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Peace ye old foole;
She thinks to meet him here.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: That's all the Project.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: VVas she hard to bring?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: No, she believ'd it quickly,
And quickly made her selfe fit, the Gowne a little,
And those new things she has not been acquainted with,
At least in this place, where she liv'd a prisoner,
Troubled and stirr'd her minde, But believe me sir,
She has worne as good, they sit so apted to her;
And she is so great a Mistris of disposure:
Here they come now: but take a full view of her.
How cheerefully she looks? how she salutes all?
And how she viewes the place? she is very yong sure:
That was an admirable smile, a catching one,
The very twang of Cupids bow sung to it:
She has two-edg'd eyes, they kill o' both sides.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: She makes a stand, as though she would speak.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Be still then.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Good Gentlemen, trouble your selves no further,
I had thought sure to have met a noble friend here.

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: Yee may meet many Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Such as you are
I covet few or none, sir.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: VVill you walk this way,
And take the sweets oth' garden? coole and close, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Methinks this open aire's farre better, tend ye that way.
Pray where's the woman came along?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: VVhat woman?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: The woman of the house I lay at.

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: Woman?
Here was none came along sure.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Sure I am catcht then:
Pray where's the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: He will not be long from yee,
We are his humble servants.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I could laugh now,
To see how finely I am cozn'd: yet I feare not,
For sure I know a way to scape all dangers.

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: Madam, your lodgings lye this way.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: My Lodgings?
For heaven sake sir, what office doe I beare here?

speeches.speaker: Ty.
prose: The great co~mander of all hearts

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: You have hit it.
I thank your sweet-heart for it. Who are these now?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Ladies that come to serve yee.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Well consider'd,
Are you my servants?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Servants to your pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I dare believe ye, but I dare not trust ye:
Catch'd with a trick? well, I must beare it patiently:
Methinkes this Court's a neat place: all the people
Of such refin'd a size—

speeches.speaker: Tym.
verse: This is no poore rogue.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Were it a Paradice to please your fancy,
And entertaine the sweetnesse you bring with ye;

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Take breath;
You are fat, and many words may melt ye,
This is three Bawdes beaten into one; blesse me heaven,
What shall become of me? I am i'th' pitfall:
O' my conscience, this is the old viper, and all these little ones
Creep every night into her belly; do you heare plumpe servant
And you my litle sucking Ladies, you must teach me,
For I know you are excellent at carriage,
How to behave my selfe, for I am rude yet:
But you say the Prince will come?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Will flie to see you.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: For look you if a great man, say the King now
Should come and visit me?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: She names ye.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Peace foole.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: And offer me a kindnesse, such a kindnesse.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: I, such a kindnesse.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: True Lady such a kindnesse,
What shall that kindnesse be now?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: A witty Lady,
Learne little ones, learne.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Say it be all his favour.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: And a sweet saying 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: And I grow peevish?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You must not be neglectfull.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: There's the matter,
There's the maine doctrine now, and I may misse it.
Or a kind hansome Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: You say well.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: They'l count us basely bred.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Not freely nurtur'd.

speeches.speaker: Cel
verse: I'le take thy counsell.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: 'Tis an excellent woman.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: I find a notable volume here, a learnd one;
Which way? for I would faine be in my chamber;
In truth sweet Ladies, I grow weary; fie,
How hot the aire beats on me?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: This way Madam?

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Now by mine honour, I grow wondrous faint too.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Your fans sweet Gentlewomen, your fans.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: Since I am foold,
I'le make my self some sport, though I pay deare for't.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: You see now what a manner of woman she is sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Thou art an asse.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Is this a fit love for the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: A coxcombe:
Now by my crowne a deintie wench, a sharpe wench,
And a matchlesse spirit: how she Jeer'd 'em?
How carelesly she scoff'd 'em? use her nobly;
I would I had not seen her: waite anon,
And then you shall have more to trade upon.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: We must keep a round, and a strong watch to night,
The Prince will not charge the Enemy till the morning:
But for the trick I told ye for this rascall,
This rogue, that health and strong heart makes a coward.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I, if it take.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ne're feare it, the Prince has it,
And if he let it fall, I must not know it;
He will suspect me presently: but you two
May helpe the plough.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: That he is sicke again.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Extreamely sicke: his disease growne incurable,
Never yet found, nor touch'd at.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Well, we have it
And here he comes.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: The Prince has been upon him,
What a flatten face he has now? it takes beleeve it;
How like an asse he lookes?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I feele no great paine,
At least, I thinke I do not; yet I feele sensibly
I grow extreamely faint: how cold I sweat now?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: So, so, so.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: And now 'tis ev'n too true, I feele a pricking,
A pricking, a strange pricking: how it tingles?
And as it were a stitch too: the Prince told me,
And every one cri'd out I was a dead man;
I had thought I had been as well—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Upon him now boyes,
And do it most demurely.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: How now Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I thanke ye Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent
verse: Life, how lookes this man?
How dost thou good Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I ever told ye
This man was never cur'd, I see it too plaine now;
How do you feele your selfe? you looke not perfect,
How dull his eye hangs?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: That may be discontent.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Beleeve me friend, I would not suffer now
The tith of those paines this man feeles; marke his forehead
What a cloud of cold dew hangs upon't?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I have it,
Againe I have it; how it growes upon me?
A miserable man I am.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ha, ha, ha,
A miserable man thou shalt be,
This is the tamest trout I ever tickell^.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phis.
verse: This way he went.

speeches.speaker: 2 Phis.
verse: Pray heaven we find him living,
He's a brave fellow, 'tis pitty he should perish thus.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: A strong hearted man, & of a notable sufferance.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: How now? how is it man?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Oh Gentlemen,
Never so full of paine.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Did I not tell ye?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Never so full of paine Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: He is here;
How do you sir?

speeches.speaker: 2 Phi.
verse: Be of good comfort Souldier,
The Prince has sent us to you.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Do you thinke I may live?

speeches.speaker: 2 Phi.
verse: He alters hourely, strangely.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: Yes, you may live: but—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Finely butted Doctor.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Do not discourage him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: He must be told truth,
'Tis now too late to trifle.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Here the Prince comes.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: How now Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Be wailing sir, a Souldier,
And one I thinke, your Grace will grieve to part with,
But every living thing—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: 'Tis true, must perish,
Our lives are but our martches to our graves,
How dost thou now Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Faith 'tis true sir,
We are but spans, and candles ends.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: He's finely mortified.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Thou art heart whole yet; I see he alters strangely,
And that a pace too; I saw it this morning in him,
When he poore man, I dare sweare—

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: No beleev't sir,
I never felt it.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Heres lies the paine now: how he is swel'd?

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: The Impostume
Fed with a new malignant humour now,
Will grow to such a bignesse, 'tis incredible,
The compasse of a bushell will not hold it,
And with such a hell of torture it will rise too.—

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Can you endure me touch it?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Oh, I beseech you sir:
I feele you sensibly ere you come neare me.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: He's finely wrought, he must be cut, no cure else,
And suddenlie, you see how fast he blowes out.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Good Master Doctor, let me be beholding to you,
I feele I cannot last.

speeches.speaker: 2 Phi.
verse: For what Lieutenant?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: But ev'n for halfe a dozen Cans of good wine,
That I may drinke my will out: I faint hideously.

speeches.speaker: De.
verse: Fetch him some wine; and since he must go gentlemen
Why let him take his journey merrily.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: That's ev'n the nearest way.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I could laugh dead now.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Here, off with that.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: These two I give your Grace,
A poore remembrance of a dying man sir,
And I beseech you weare 'em out.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I will Souldier,
These are fine legacies.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Among the Gentlemen,
Even all I have left; I am a poore man, naked,
Yet something for remembrance: foure a peece Gentlemen,
And so my body where you please.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: It will worke.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I make your Grace my executor, and I beseech ye
See my poore will fulfill'd: sure I shall walke else.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: As full as they can be sill'd, here's my hand Souldier.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: The wine will tickle him.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I would heare a drum beat,
But to see how I could endure it.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Beat a drum there.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Oh heavenly musick, I would heare one sing to't,
I am very full of paine.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Sing? 'tis imposible.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Why, then I would drinke a drum full:
Where lies the Enemie?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Why, here close by.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Now he begins to muster.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: And dare ye fight?
Dare ye fight Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: You must not cut him:
He's gone then in a moment; all the hope left, is
To worke his weakenesse into suddaine anger,
And make him raise his passion above his paine,
And so dispose him on the enemie;
His body then, being stir'd with violence,
Will purge it selfe and breake the sore.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: 'Tis true sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: And then my life for his.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: I will not dye thus.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: But he is too weake to doe—

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Dye like a dog?

speeches.speaker: 2 Phi.
verse: I, he's weake, but yet he's heart whole.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Hem.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: An excellent signe.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Hem.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Stronger still, and better.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Hem, hem; tan, tan, tan, tan, tan.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: Now he's i'th' way on't.

speeches.speaker: De.
verse: Well go thy waies, thou wilt do something certain.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And some brave thing, or let mine eares be cut off.
He's finely wrought.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Let's after him.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I pray Sir;
But how this rogue, when this cloud's melted in him,
And all discover'd. —

speeches.speaker: Dem.
prose: That's for an after mirth, away, away, away.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Let no man feare to dye: we love to sleep all,
And death is but the sounder sleep; all ages,
And all houres call us; 'tis so common, easie,
That little children tread those paths before us;
We are not sicke, nor our soules prest with sorrows,
Nor go we out like tedious tales, forgotten;
High, high we come, and hearty to our funerals,
And as the Sun that sets, in bloud let's fall.

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: 'Tis true, they have us fast, we cannot scape 'em,
Nor keeps the brow of fortune one smile for us,
Dishonourable ends we can scape though,
And (worse then those, captivities) we can die,
And dying nobly, though we leave behind us
These clods of flesh, that are too massie burthens,
Our living soules flie crown'd with living conquests.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: They have begun, fight bravely, and fall bravely;
And may that man that seekes to save his life now
By price, or promise, or by feare fals from us,
Never again be blest with name of Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: How now? who charged first? I seek a brave hand
To set me off in death.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: We are not charg'd sir,
The Prince lies still.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: How comes this Latum up then?

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: There is one desperate fellow, with the devill in him
(He never durst do this else) has broke into us,
And here he bangs ye two or three before him,
There five or sixe; ventures upon whole companies.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: And is not seconded?

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: Not a man followes.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Nor cut a peeces?

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: Their wonder yet has staid 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Let's in, and see this miracle?

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: I admire it.

speeches.speaker: Leon.
verse: Fetch him off, fetch him off; I am sure he's clouted;
Did I not ^ you how 'twould take?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Tis admirable.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Follow that blow, my friend, there's at your coxcombs,
I fight to save me from the Surgeons miseries.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How the knave curries 'em?

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: You cannot rogues,
Till you have my diseases, flie my furie,
Ye bread and butter rogues, do ye run from me?
And my side would give me leave, I would so hunt ye,
Ye porredge gutted slaves, ye veale-broth boobies.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
prose: Enough, enough Lieutenant, thou hast done bravely.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Mirrour of man.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: There's a flag for ye sir,
I tooke it out o'th' shop, and never paid for't,
I'le to 'em againe, I am not come to th' text yet.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: No more my souldier: beshrew my heart he is hurt sore.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Hang him, hee'l lick all those whole.

speeches.speaker: 1 Phi.
verse: Now will we take him,
And cure him in a trice.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Be carefull of him.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: Let me live but two yeares,
And doe what ye will with me;
I never had but two houres yet of happinesse;
Pray ye give me nothing to provoke my valour,
For I am ev'n as weary of this fighting—

speeches.speaker: 2 Phi.
verse: Ye shall have nothing; come to the Princes Tent
And there the Surgeons presently shall search ye,
Then to your rest.

speeches.speaker: Lieu.
verse: A little hansome litter
To lay me in, and I shall sleepe.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Looke to him.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I do beleeve a horse begot this fellow,
He never knew his strength yet; they are our owne.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I thinke so, I am cozen'd else; I would but see now
A way to fetch these off, and save their honours.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Only their lives.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Pray ye take no way of peace now,
Unlesse it be with infinite advantage.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I shall be rul'd;
Let the battels now move forward,
Our selfe will give the signall:
Now Herold, what's your message?

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: From my Masters
This honourable courtesie, a Parley
For halfe an houre, no more sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Let 'em come on,
They have my princely word.

speeches.speaker: Her.
verse: They are here to attend ye.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Now Princes, your demands?

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Peace, if it may bee
Without the too much tainture of our honour:
Peace, and wee'l buy it too.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: At what price?

speeches.speaker: Ly.
verse: Tribute.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: At all the charge of this war.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: That will not do.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Leontius, you and I have serv'd together,
And run through many a fortune with our swords,
Brothers in wounds, and health; one meat has fed us,
One tent a thousand times from cold night cover'd us:
Our loves have been but one; and had we died then,
One monument had held our names, and actions:
Why do you set upon your friends such prizes?
And sacrifice to giddy chance such Trophies?
Have we forgot to dye? or are our vertues
Lesse in afflictions constant, than our fortunes?
Ye are deceiv'd old souldier.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I know your worths,
And thus low bow in reverence to your vertues:
Were these my wars, or lead my power in chiefe here,
I knew then how to meet your memories:
They are my Kings imployments; this man fights now,
To whom I owe all dutie, faith, and service;
This man that sled before ye; call backe that,
That bloudy day againe, call that disgrace home,
And then an easie peace, may sheath our swords up.
I am not greedy of your lives and fortunes,
Nor do I gape ungratefully to swallow ye,
Honour the spur of all illustrious natures,
That made you famous Souldiers, and next Kings,
And not ambitious envy strikes me forward,
Will ye unarme, and yeild your selves his prisoners?

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: We never knew what that sound meant: no gives
Shall ever bind this body, but embraces;
Nor weight of sorrow here, till earth fall on me.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Expect our charge then.

speeches.speaker: Lys.
verse: 'Tis the nobler curtesie:
And so we leave the hand of heaven to blesse us.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Stay, have you any hope?

speeches.speaker: Cel
verse: We have none left us,
But that one comfort of our deaths together;
Give us but room to sight.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Win it, and weare it.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Call from the hils those companies hang ore us
Like bursting clouds; and then breake in, and take us.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Find such a Souldier will forsake advantage,
And wee'l draw off, to shew I dare be noble,
And hang a light out to ye in this darkenesse,
The light of peace; give up those Cities, forts,
And all those frontire Countries to our uses.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Is this the peace? traitours to those that feed us,
Our Gods and people? give our Countries from us?

speeches.speaker: Lis.
verse: Begin the knell, it sounds a great deale sweeter.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Let loose your servant death.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Fall fate upon us,
Our memories shall never stinke behind us.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Seleucus, great Seleucus,

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: The Prince cals sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Thou stocke of noblenesse, and curtesie,
Thou father of the war —

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: What meanes the Prince now?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Give me my Standard here.

speeches.speaker: Lys.
verse: His angers melted.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: You Gentlemen that were his prisoners,
And felt the bounty of that noble nature,
Lay all your hands, and beare these Colours to him,
The Standard of the Kingdome; take it souldier.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: What will this meane?

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Thou hast won it, beare it off,
And draw thy men home whilst we waite upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: You shall have all our countries.

speeches.speaker: Lys. Ptol.
verse: All by heaven sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I will not have a stone, a bush, a bramble,
No, in the way of curtesie, I'le start ye;
Draw off, and make a lane through all the Armie,
That these that have subdu'd us, may martch through us.

speeches.speaker: Sel.
verse: Sir, do not make me surfet with such goodnesse,
I'le beare your Srandard for ye; follow ye.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I sweare it shall be so, martch through me fairely,
And thine be this daies honour, great Seleucus.

speeches.speaker: Ptol.
verse: Mirrour of noble minds.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Nay then ye hate me.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I cannot speake now:
Well, go thy wayes, at a sure peece of bravery
Thou art the best, these men are won by th' neckes now:
I'le send a post away.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: NO aptnesse in her?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Not an immodest motion,
And yet when she is as free, and when she is courted,
Makes as wild witty answers.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: This more fires me,
I must not have her thus.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: We cannot alter her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Have ye put the youths upon her?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: All that know any thing,
And have been studied how to catch a beauty,
But like so many whelps about an Elephant—
The Prince is coming home sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I heare that too,
But that's no matter; am I alter'd well;

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Not to be knowne I thinke sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: I must see her.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I offered all I had, all I could thinke of,
I tri'd her through all the points o'th' compasse, I thinke.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: She studies to undo the Court, to plant here
The enemy to our age, chastitie;
She is the first, that ere bauked a close Arbour,
And the sweet contents within: She hates curl'd heads too,
And setting up or beards she sweares, is Idolatrie.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I never knew so faire a face so froze;
Yet she would make one thinke—

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: True by her carriage,
For she's as wanton as a kid toth' out side,
As full of mocks and taunts: I kiss'd her hand too,
Walkt with her halfe an houre.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: She heard me sing,
And sung her selfe too; she sings admirably;
But still, when any hope was, as 'tis her trick
To minister enough of those, then presently
With some new slam or other, nothing to th' matter,
And such a frowne, as would sinke all before her,
She takes her chamber; come we shal not be the last fools.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Not by a hundred I hope; 'tis a strange wench.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
prose: This screwes me up still higher.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Here she comes sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Then be you gone: and take the women with ye,
And lay those Jewels in her way.

speeches.speaker: Cel.
verse: If I stay longer
I shall number as many lovers as Lais did;
How they slocke after me? upon my conscience,
I have had a dozen horses given me this morning,
I'le ev'n set up a troop, and turne she-souldier.
A good discreet wench now, that were not hidebound
Might raise a fine estate here, and suddenly:
For these warme things will give their soules— I can go no where
Without a world of offerings to my excellence:
I am a Queene, a Goddesse, I know not what—
And no constellation in all heaven, but I outshine it;
And they have found out now I have no eyes
Of mortall lights, but certaine influences,
Strange vertuous lightnings, humane nature starts at,
And I can kill my twenty in a morning,
With as much case now—
Ha? what are these? new projects?
Where are my honourable Ladies? are you out too?
Nay then I must buy the stocke, send me good carding:
I hope the Princes hand, be not in this sport;
I have not seen him yet, cannot heare from him,
And that, that, troubles me: all these were recreations
