speeches.speaker: Sh.
verse: We are your servants.

speeches.speaker: VVife.
verse: Hee's but a gentleman oth' chamber, he might have kist me:
Faith, where shall one finde lesse courtesie, then at Court?
Say I have an undeserver to my husband:
That's ne're the worse for him: well strange lipt men,
'Tis but a kisse lost, there'll more come agen.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gen.
verse: Look who comes here sir, his love fit's upon him;
I know it, by that set smile, and those congies.
How courteous hee's to nothing? which indeed,
Is the next kin to woman; onely shadow
The elder Sister of the twaine, because 'tis seen too.
See how it kisses the fore-finger still;
Which is the last edition, and being come
So neare the thumbe every Cobler has got it?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: What a ridiculous peice, humanity
Here makes it selfe?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Nay, good give leave a little sir,
Y'are so precise a manhood—

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: It afflicts me
When I behold unseemelinesse in an Image
So neare the Godhead, 'tis an injurie
To glorious Eternity.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Pray use patience sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I do confesse it freely precious Lady,
And loves suit'is so, the longer it hangs
The worse it is; better cut off sweet Madam;
O that same drawing in your nether lip there,
Foreshewes no goodnesse Lady: make you question on't?
Shame on me but I love you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Who is't sir,
You are at all this paines for? may I know her?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: For thee thou fairest, yet the falsest woman,
That ever broke mans heart-strings.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: How? how's this sir?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: What, the old tricke of Ladies? mans apparrell,
Wil't nere be left amongst you? steale from Court in't?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I see the fit growes stronger.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Pray let's talke a little.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: I can endure no more.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Good, let us alone a little:
You are so exact a worke: love light things somewhat sir.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Th'are all but shames.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: What is't you'd say to me sir?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Can you be so forgetfull to enquire it Lady?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Yes truly sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: The more I admire your stintinesse:
What cause have I given you, illustrious Madam,
To play this strange part with me?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Cause enough,
Do but looke backe sir into your memorie,
Your love to other women ô lewd man,
'Tas almost kil'd my heart, you see I'm chang'd with it,
I ha' lost the fashion of my Sexe with griefe on't,
When I have seen you courting of a Dowdie;
Compar'd with me, and kissing your fore-finger
To one o'th' black-guards Mistresses: would not this
Cracke a poore Ladies heart, that beleev'd love,
And waited for the comfort? but 'twas said sir,
A Lady of my haire cannot want pittying:
The Countries coming up, farewell to you sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Whither intend you sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: A long journey sir:
The truth is, I'm with child, and goe to travell.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: With child? I never got it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I heard you were busie
At the same time sir, and was loath to trouble you.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Why, are not you a whore then, excellent Madam?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: O by no meanes, 'twas done sir in the state
Of my beliefe in you, and that quits me,
It lies upon your falshod.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Does it so?
You shall not carry her though sir, she's my contract.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I prethee thou four Elements ill brued,
Torment none but thy selfe; away I say
Thou beast of passion, as the drunkard is
The beast of wine; dishonour to thy making,
Thou man in fragments.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Heare me pretious Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Kneele for thy wits to heaven.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Lady, I'le father it,
Who ere begot it: 'tis the course of greatnesse.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: How vertue groanes at this?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I'le raise the Court, but I'le stay your slight.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: How wretched is that peice?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: He's the Dukes kinsman sir.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: That cannot take a passion away sir,
Nor cut a fit, but one poore houre shorter,
He must endure as much as the poorest begger,
That cannot change his money; there's the equality
In our impartiall essence:
What's the newes now?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Your worthy brother sir, has left his charge,
And come to see you.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: O the noblest welcome
That ever came from man, meet thy deservings:
Methinkes I've all joyes treasure in mine armes now,

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: You are so fortunate in prevention brother,
You alwaies leave the answerer barren sir,
You comprehend in few words so much worth—

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: 'Tis all too little for thee: come th'art welcome,
So I include all: take especiall knowledge pray,
Of this deare Gentleman, my absolute friend,
That loves a Souldier far above a Mistris,
Thou excellently faithfull to 'em both.
But love to manhood, ownes the purer troath.

speeches.speaker: Lady
verse: THere should be in this gallery—on th'are here,
Pray sit downe; beleeve me sir I'm weary.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: It well becomes a Lady to complaine a little
Of what she never feeles: your walke was short Madam,
You can be but affraid of wearinesse;
Which well employes the softnesse of your Sexe,
As for the thing it selfe, you never came to't.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Y'are wonderously well read in Ladies sir.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: Shall I thinke such a creature as you Madam,
Was ever borne to feele paine, but in travell?
There's your full portion,
Besides a little toothache in the breeding,
Which a kind husband too, takes from you Madam.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: But where do Ladies sir, find such kind husbands?
Perhaps you have heard
The Rhumaticke story of some loving Chandler now,
Or some such melting fellow, that you talke
So prodigall of mens kindnesse: I confesse sir,
Many of those wives are happy, their ambition
Does reach no higher, then to love and ignorance,
Which makes an excellent husband, and a fond one:
Now sir, your great ones aime at height, and cunning,
And so are oft deceiv'd, yet they must venture it;
For 'tis a Ladies contumely sir,
To have a Lord an Ignorant; then the worlds voice
Will deeme her for a wanton ere she taste on't:
But to deceive a wise man, to whose circumspection,
The world resignes it selfe with all his envy;
'Tis lesse dishonour to us then to fall,
Because his beleev'd wisdome keepes out all.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: Would I were the man Lady, that should venture
His wisedome to your goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: You might faile
In the returne, as many men have done sir:
I dare not justifie what is to come of me,
Because I know it not, though I hope vertuously;
Marry what's past or present, I durst put
Into a good mans hand, Which if he take
Upon my word for good, it shall not couzen him.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: No, nor her after?

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: It may hap so too sir:
A womans goodnesse, when she is a wise,
Lies much upon a mans desert, believe it sir,
If there be fault in her, Ile pawn my life on't,
'Tis first in him, if she were ever good,
That makes one; knowing not a husband yet,
Or what he may be, I promise no more vertues,
Then I may well performe, for that were cousenage.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Happy were he that had you with all feares,
That's my opinion, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: What say you now sir?
Dare you give confidence to your owne eyes?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Not yet I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: No?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Scarce yet, or yet:
Although I see 'tis he. Why can a thing,
That's but my selfe divided be so false?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Nay doe but marke how the chaire plaies his part too:
How amorously 'tis bent.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Hell take thy bad thoughts,
For they are strange ones. Never take delight
To make a torment worse. Look on 'em heaven,
For that's a brother: send me a faire enemy,
And take him; for a fouler fiend there breathes not:
I will not sin, to think there's ill in her,
But what's of his producing.
Yet goodnesse, whose inclosure is but flesh,
Holds out oft times but sorrily. But as black sir,
As ever kindred was: I hate mine owne bloud,
Because it is so neare thine. Live without honesty,
And maist thou dye with an unmoistned eye,
And no teare follow thee.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: Y'are wondrous merry sir; I would your Brother heard you.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: O my sister
I would not out oth' way, let fall my words Lady,
Por the precizest humour.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Yea, so close.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Th'are merry, that's the worst you can report on 'em;
Th'are neither dangerous, nor immodest.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: So sir,
Shall I believe you, think you?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Who's this Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: O the Dukes Cousen; he came late from travel sir.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Respect belongs to him.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: For as I said Lady,
Th'are merry that's the worst you can report of em:
Th'are neither dangerous, nor immodest.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: And there I think I left.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Abuses me.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Now to proceed, Lady; perhaps I swore I lov'd you,
If you believe me not, y'are much the wiser.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: He speaks still in my person, and derides me.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: For I can cog with you.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: You can all doe so.
We make no question of mens promptness that way.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: And smile, & wave a chair with comely grace too,
Play with our Tastle gently, and doe fine things,
That catch a Lady sooner then a vertue.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: I never us'd to let man live so long
That wrong'd me.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Talke of Battalions, wooe you in a skirmish;
Divine my mind to you Lady; and being sharp set,
Can court you at halfe pike: or name your weapon,
We cannot faile you Lady.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Now he dies:
Were all succeeding hopes stor'd up within him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ge.
verse: O fie, i'th' Court sir?

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: I most dearely thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ge.
verse: Tis rage ill spent upon a passionate mad-man.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: That shall not priviledge him for ever sir:
A mad-man call you him? I have found too much reason
Sound in his injurie to me, to beleeve him so.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ge.
verse: If ever truth from mans lips may be held
In reputation with you, give this confidence;
And this his love-fit, which we observe still,
By's flattering and his finenes: at some other time,
Hee'l goe as slovenly as heart can wish.
The love and pity that his Highnesse shewes to him,
Makes every man the more respectfull of him:
Has never a passion, but is well provided for,
As this of Love, he is full fed in all;
His swinge as I may tearme it: have but patience,
And ye shall witnesse somewhat.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Still he mocks me:
Looke you, in action, in behaviour sir;
Hold still the chaire, with a grand mischiefe to you,
Or Ile set so much strength upon your heart sir—

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: I feele some power has restrain'd me Lady:
If it be sent from love, say, I obey it,
And ever keep a voice to welcome it.
THou Deitie, swift winged love,
Sometimes below, sometimes above,
Little in shape, but great in power,
Thou that makest a heart thy Tower,
And thy loop-holes, Ladies eyes,
From whence thou strik'st the fond and wise.
Did all the shafts in thy faire quiver
Stick fast in my ambitious liver;
Yet thy power would I adore,
And call upon thee to shoot more.
shoot more, shoot more.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I prethee hold though, sweet Caelestiall boy;
I'm not requited yet with love enough,
For the first arrow that I have within me:
And if thou be an equall archer Cupid,
Shoot this Lady, and twenty more for me.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: Me sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Tis nothing but device, feare it not Lady;
You may be as good a maid after that shaft Madam,
As ere your mother was at twelve and halfe:
Tis like the boy that drawes it, 'tas no sting yet.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: Tis like the miserable maid that drawes it—aside.
That sees no comfort yet, seeing him so passionate.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Strike me the Duchesse of Valois in love with me,
With all the speed thou canst, and two of her women.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: You shall have more.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Tell 'em I tarry for 'em.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Who would be angry with that walking trouble now
That hurts none but it selfe?

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: I am better quieted.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ile have all women-kind strucke in time for me
After thirteene once:
I see this Cupid will not let me want,
And let him spend his forty shafts an houre,
They shall be all found from the Dukes Exchequer;
He's come already.
O turne thy bow,
Thy power we feele and know,
Faire Cupid turne away thy bow:
They be those golden Arrowes,
Bring Ladies all their sorrowes,
And till there be more truth in men,
Never shoot at maid agen.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: What a felicity of whores are here?
And all my concubines, strucke bleeding new:
A man can in his life time make but one woman,
But he may make his fifty Queanes a month.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: Have you remembred a Priest honest brothers?

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Yes sister, and this is the young gentleman,
Make you no question of our faithfulnesse.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: His growing shame sister provokes our care.

speeches.speaker: Priest.
verse: He must be taken in this fit of love Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: What else sir? he shall do't.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: Enough.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Be cheerefull wench.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Now by the stroake of pleasure, a deep oath,
Nimbly hopt Ladies all; what height they beare too?
A story higher then your common statures;
A little man must go up staires to kisse 'em:
What a great space there is
Betwixt loves dyning Chamber, and his Garret?
Ile trie the utmost height—the Garret stoopes methinkes;
The roomes are made all bending, I see that,
And not so high as a man takes 'em for.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: Now if you'l follow me sir, I've that power,
To make them follow you.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Are they all shot?

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: All, all sir, every mothers daughter of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Then there's no feare of following; if they be once shot,
They'l follow a man to th' devill—As for you sir—

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: Me sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Nay sweet sir.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: A noise, a threatning; did you not heare it sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Without regard sir, so would I heare you.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: This must come to something, never talke of that Sir,
You never saw it otherwise.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Nay deare merit —

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: Me above all men?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Troth you wrong your anger.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: I will be arm'd my honourable Letcher.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: O fie sweet sir.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: That devoures womens honesties by lumps,
And never chawst thy pleasure.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: What do you meane sir?

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: What does he meane t'ingrosse all to himselfe?
There's others love a whore, as well as he sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Oh an' that be part o'th furie, we have a Citty
Is very well provided for that case;
Let him alone with her, sir we have women
Are very charitable to proper men,
And to a Souldier that has all his limbes;
Marry the sicke and lame gets not a penny:
Right womens charity, and the husbands follow't too:
Here comes his highnesse sir.

speeches.speaker: Soul.
verse: Ile walke to coole my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: The brother of Shamont.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He's Brother then
To all the Courts love, they that love discreetly,
And place their friendlinesse upon desert:
As for the rest, that with a double face
Looke upon merit, much like fortunes visage,
That lookes two waies, both to lifes calmes and stormes,
Ile so provide for him, chiefly for him,
He shall not wish their loves, nor dread their envies.
And here comes my Shamont.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: That Ladies vertues are my only joyes,
And he to offer to lay siedge to them?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Shamont.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Her goodnesse is my pride; in all discourses,
As often as I here rash tongued gallants,
Speake rudely of a woman, presently
I give in but her name, and th'are all silent:
O who would lose this benefit?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come hether sir.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: 'Tis like the gift of healing, but diviner;
For that but cures diseases in the body,
This workes a cure on fame, on reputation:
The noblest piece of Surgery upon earth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Shamont; he minds me not.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: A Brother do't?

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Shamont I say. Gives him a touch with his switch.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Ha?
If he be mortall, by this hand he perishes;
Unlesse it be a stroake from heaven, he dies for't.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why, how now sir? 'twas I.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: The more's my miserie.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Why, what's the matter prethee?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Can you aske it sir?
No man else should; stood forty lives before him
By this I would have op'd my way to him;
It could not be you sir, excuse him not,
What ere he be, as y'are deere to honour,
That I may find my peace agen.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Forbeare I say.
Upon my love to truth, 'twas none but I.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Still miserable?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come, come, what ailes you sir?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Never sate shame cooling so long upon me,
Without a satisfaction in revenge,
And heaven has made it here a sin to wish it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Harke you sir?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: O y'ave undone me.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Cruelly undone me;
I have lost my peace, and reputation by you:
Sir pardon me, I can never love you more.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What language call you this sirs?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Truth my Lord, I've seldome heard a stranger.—

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent,
verse: He is a man of a most curious valour,
Wondrous precise, and punctuall in that vertue.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: But why to me so punctuall? my last thought
Was most intirely fixt on his advancement:
Why, I came now to put him in possession
Of his faire fortunes: what a mis-conceiver 'tis?
And from a Gentleman of our Chamber meerely,
Made him Vice-Admirall; I was setled in't,
I love him next to health: call him Gentlemen;
Why would not you, or you ha' taken as much,
And never murmur'd?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Troath, I thinke we should my Lord,
And there's a fellow walkes about the Court,
Would take a hundred of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I hate you all for't,
And rather praise his high pitch'd fortitude,
Though in extreames for nicenesse: now I thinke on't,
I would I had never done't.—Now sir, where is he?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: His sute is only sit to be excus'd.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He shall not be excus'd, I love him dearelier:
Say we intreat him; goe, he must not leave us.
So vertue blesse me, I nere knew him parraleld;
Why, he's more pretious to me now, then ever.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: With much faire language, w'ave brought him?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Thankes—Where is he?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Yonder sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come forward man.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Pray pardon me, I'm asham'd to be seene sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Was ever such a touchie man heard of?
Prethee come nearer.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: More into the light?
Put not such crueltie into your requests my Lord,
First to disgrace me publikely, and then draw me
Into mens eyesight, with the shame yet hot
Upon my reputation.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: What disgrace sir?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: What?
Such as there can be no forgivenesse for,
That I can find in honour.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: That's most strange sir.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Yet I have seartch'd my bosome to find one,
And wresled with my inclination,
But 't will not be: would you had kild me sir,
With what an ease had I forgiven you then?
But to endure a stroke from any hand
Under a punnishing Angels, which is justice,
Honour disclame that man, for my part chiefly:
Had it been yet the malice of your sword.
Though it had cleft me, 'thad been noble to me;
You should have found my thankes paid in a smile
If I had fell unworded; but to shame me,
With the correction that your horse should have,
Were you ten thousand times my royall Lord,
I cannot love you never, nor desire to serve you more.
If your drum call me. I am vowed to valour,
But peace shall never know me yours agen,
Because I've lost mine owne, I speake to dye sir;
Would you were gratious that way to take off shame,
With the same swiftnesse as you powre it on:
And since it is not in the power of Monarches
To make a Gentleman, which is a substance
Only begot of merit, they should be carefull
Not to destroy the worth of one so rare,
Which neither they can make; nor lost, repaire.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Y'ave set a faire light sir before my judgement,
Which burnes with wondrous clearnes; I acknowledge it,
And your worth with it: but then sir, my love,
My love — what gone agen?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: And full of scorne my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: That language will undoe the man that keeps it,
Who knows no difference twixt contempt and manhood.
Upon your love to goodnes, gentlemen,
Let me not lose him long: how now?

speeches.speaker: Hunts.
verse: The game's at height my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Confound both, thee and it: hence breake it off;
He hates me brings me newes of any pleasure:
I felt not such a conflict since I cou'd;
Distinguish betwixt worthinesse and bloud

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: I I heartily commend your project Gentlemen,
'Twas wise and vertuous.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: 'Twas for the safety
Of pretious honour sir, which neere bloud binds us to:
He promis'd the poore easie foole there marriage,
There was a good maiden-head lost i'th' beliefe on't,
Beshrew her hasty confidence.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: O no more sir,
You make her weep agen; alas poore Cupid:
Shall she not shift her selfe?

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: O by no meanes sir:
We dare not have her seen yet, all the while
She keepes this shape, 'tis but thought device,
And she may follow him so without suspition,
To see if she can draw all his wilde passions,
To one point only, and that's love, the maine point:
So far his highnesse grants, and gave at first,
Large approbation to the quicke conceit,
Which then was quicke indeed.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: You make her blush insooth.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: I feare 'tis more the flagg of shame, then grace sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: They both give but one kind of colour sir:
If it be bashfulnesse in that kind taken,
It is the same with grace; and there she weepes agen.
In truth y'are too hard, much, much too bitter sir,
Unlesse you meane to have her weepe her eyes out,
To play a Cupid truly.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Come, ha' done then:
We should all feare to sin first; for 'tis certaine,
When 'tis once lodg'd, though entertain'd in mirth,
It must be wept out, if it ere come forth.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Now 'tis so well, I'le leave you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Faithfully welcome sir,
Go Cupid to your charge; hee's your owne now;
If he want love, none will be blam'd but you.

speeches.speaker: Cu.
verse: The strangest marriage, and unfortunat'st Bride
That ever humane memory contain'd;
I cannot be my selfe for't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Oh Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: How now sir, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: His melancholly passion is halfe spent already,
Then comes his angry fit at the very taile on't,
Then comes in my pain gentlemen; 'has beate me e'ne to a Cullis.
I am nothing, right worshipfull, but very pap,
And jelly: I have no bones, my body's all one busines,
They talk of ribs, & chines most freely abroad i'th' world,
Why, I have no such thing; who ever lives to see me dead
Gentlemen, shall find me all mummie good to fill galipots
And long dildo glasses: I shall not have a bone to throw
At a dog.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Alas poore vassall, how he goes?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: O Gentlemen,
I am unjoynted, do but thinke o' that:
My breast is beat into my mawe, that what I eate,
I am faine to take't in all at mouth with spoones;
A lamentable hearing; and 'tis well knowne, my belly
Is driven into my backe.
I earn'd foure Crowns a month, most dearely Gentlemen,
And one he must have when the fit's upon him,
The privy purse allowes it, and 'tis thriftinesse,
He would breake else some fourty pounds in casements,
And in five hundred yeares undo the Kingdome:
I have cast it up to a quarrell.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: There's a fellow kickt about court, I would
He had his place brother, but for one fit of his indignation.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: And suddenly I have thought upon a means for't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: I Prethee how?

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: 'Tis but preferring Brother
This stockfish to his service, with a letter
Of commendations, the same way he wishes it,
And then you win his heart: for o' my knowledge
He has laied waite this halfe yeare for a fellow
That will be beaten; and with a safe conscience
We may commend the carriage of this man in't;
Now servants he has kept, lusty tall feeders,
But they have beate him, and turn'd themselves away:
Now one that would endure, is like to stay,
And get good wages of him; and the service too
Is ten times milder Brother, I would not wish it else.
I see the fellow has a sore crush'd body,
And the more need he has to be kickt at ease.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I sweet Gentlemen, a kick of ease, send me to such a Master.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: No more I say, we have one for thee, a soft footed Master,
One that weares wooll in's toes.

speeches.speaker: Ch.
verse: O Gentlemen, soft garments may you weare,
Soft skins may you wed,
But as plump as pillowes, both for white and red.
And now will I reveale a secret to you,
Since you provide for my poore flesh so tenderly,
'Has hir'd meere Rogues, out of his Chamber window,
To beate the Souldier, Mounsier Shamonts Brother.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: That nothing concernes us sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: For no cause Gentlemen,
Unlesse it be for wearing shoulder points,
With longer taggs then his.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: Is not that somewhat?
Billakin sir, the difference of long taggs,
Has cost many a mans life, and advanc'd other some,
Come follow me.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: See what a gull am I:
Oh every man in his profession;
I know a thumpe now, as juditiously,
As the proudest he that walkes, I'le except none;
Come to a tagge, how short I fall? I'm gone.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I have been ruminating with my selfe,
What honour a man loses by a kicke:
Why, what's a kicke? the fury of a foote,
Whose indignation commonly is stampt
Upon the hinder quarter of a man;
Which is a place very unfit for honour,
The world will confesse so much:
Then what disgrace I pray, does that part suffer
Where honour never comes, I'd faine know that?
This being well forc'd, and urg'd, may have the power
To move most Gallants to take kickes in time,
And spurne out the duelloes out o'th' kingdome,
For they that stand upon their honour most,
When they conceive there is no honour lost,
As by a table that I have invented
For that purpose alone, shall appeare plainly,
Which shewes the vanity of all blowes at large,
And with what ease they may be tooke of all sides,
Numbring but twice one the Letters Patience
From C.P. to E. I doubt not but in small time
To see a dissolution of all bloudshed,
If the Reform'd Kick do but once get up:
For what a lamentable folly 'tis,
If we observ't, for every little justle,
Which is but the ninth part of a sound thump,
In our meeke computation, we must fight forsooth, yes,
If kill, I'm hang'; if I be kil'd my selfe,
I dye for't also: is not this trim wisdome?
Now for the Con, a man may be well beaten,
Yet passe away his fourescore yeares smooth after:
I had a father did it, and to my power
I will not be behind him.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: O well met.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Now a fine punch or two, I looke for't duly.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: I've been to seeke you.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Let me know your lodging sir,
I'le come to you once a day, and use your pleasure sir.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: I'm made the fittest man for thy Society:
I'le live and dye with thee: come shew me a Chamber;
There is no house but thine, but only thine,
That's fit to cover me: I've tooke a blow sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I would you had indeed: why, you may see sir;
You'l all come to't in time, when my booke's out.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Since I did see thee last, I've tooke a blow.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
prose: Pha sir that's nothing; I ha' tooke fourty since.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: What? and I charg'd thee thou shouldst not?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I sir, you might charge your pleasure,
But they would giv't me, whether I would or no.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Oh I walke without my peace, I've no companion now;
Prethee resolve me, for I cannot aske
A man more beaten to experience,
Then thou art in this kind, what manner of blow
Is held the most disgracefull, or distastefull?
For thou dost only censure 'em by the hurt,
Not by the shame they do thee: yet having felt
Abuses of all kindes, thou mayst deliver,
Though't be by chance, the most injurious one.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: You put me to't sir; but to tell you truth,
Th'are all as one with me, little exception.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: That little may do much, let's have it from you.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: With all the speed I may: first then, and formost,
I hold so reverently of the Bastinado sir,
That if it were the dearest friend i'th' world,
I'd put it into his hand.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Go too, I'le passe that then.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Y'are the more happy sir,
Would I were past it too:
But being accustom'd to't, It is the better carried.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Will you forward?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Then there's your sowce, your wherrit, and your dowst,
Tuggs on the haire, your bob o'th' lips, a whelpe on't,
I nere could find much difference: Now your thumpe,
A thing deriv'd first from your Hemp-beaters,
Takes a mans wind away, most spitefully:
There's nothing that destroyes a Collicke like it,
For't leaves no wind i'th' body.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: On sir, on.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Pray give me leave, I'm out of breath with thinking ont.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: This is far off yet.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: For the twinge byth' nose,
'Tis certainly unsightly, so my tables saies,
But helpes against the head-ache, woundrous strangely.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Is't possible?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: O your crush'd nostrils slakes your opilation
And makes your pent powers flush to wholsome sneezes.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: I never thought there had been halfe that vertue
In a wrung nose before.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: O plenitude sir:
Now come we lower, to our moderne kick,
Which has been mightily in use of late,
Since our young men dranke Coltsfoot: and I grant you,
'Tis a most scornefull wrong, cause the foot plaies it;
But marke agen, how we that take't, requite it
With the like scorne, for we receive it backeward;
And can there be a worse disgrace retorted?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: And is this all?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: All but a lugg byth' eare,
Or such a trifle.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Happy sufferer,
All this is nothing to the wrong I beare:
I see the worst disgrace, thou never felt'st yet;
It is so far from thee, thou canst not thinke on't;
Nor dare I let thee know, it is so abject.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I would you would though, that I might prepare for't,
For I shall ha't at one time or another:
If't be a thwacke, I make account of that;
There's no new fashion'd swappe that ere came up yet,
But I've the first on 'em, I thanke 'em for't.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: Hast thou enquir'd?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: But Can heare nothing Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: If there be but so much substance in thee
To make a shelter for a man disgrac'd,
Hide my departure from that glorious woman
That comes with all perfection about her:
So noble, that I dare not be seene of her,
Since shame tooke hold of me: upon thy life
No mention of me.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I'le cut out my tongue first,
Before I'le loose my life, there's more belongs to't.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: See there's a Gentleman, enquire of him.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: For Mounsier Shamont Madam?

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: For whom else sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Why, this fellow dares not see him.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Shamont Madam?
His very name's worse then a feavour to him,
And when he cries, there's nothing stils him sooner;
Madam, your Page of thirteene is to hard for him,
'Twas trid i'th' wood-yard.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: Alas poore grieved Merit!
What is become of him? if he one faile,
Vertue shall find small friendship: farewell then
To Ladies worths, for any hope in men,
He lov'd for goodnesse, not for Wealth, or lust,
After the worlds foule dotage, he nere courted
The body but the beauty of the mind,
A thing which common courtship never thinkes on:
All his affections were so sweet and faire,
There is no hope for fame if he dispaire.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Good morrow to you agen most heartily sir,
Crie you mercy I heard you not, I was somewhat busie.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: He takes it as familiarly, as an Ave,
Or pretious salutation: I was sicke till I had one,
Because I am so us'd to't.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: How ever you deserve, your friends & mine, here
Give you large commendations i' this Letter,
They say you will endure well.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I'd be loath
To prove 'em liers: I've endur'd as much
As mortall pen and Inke can set me downe for.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Say you me so?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I know and feele it so sir,
I have it under black and white already;
I need no pen to paint me out.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: He fits me,
And hits my wishes pat, pat: I was nere
In possibility to be better man'd,
For he's halfe lam'd already, I see't plaine,
But take no notice on't, for feare I make
The Rascall proud, and deare, to advance his wages;
First let me grow into particulars with you;
What have you indur'd of worth? let me heare.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Marry sir, I'm almost beaten blind.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: That's pretty well for a begining,
But many a milhorse has endur'd as much.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Shame o' the millers heart for his unkindnesse then.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Well sir, what then?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
prose: I've been twice throwne down staires, just before supper.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Puh, so have I, that's nothing.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I but sir,
Was yours pray before supper?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: There thou posest me.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I marry, that's it, 't'ad been lesse griefe to me,
Had I but fil'd my bellie, and then tumbled,
But to be flung downe fasting, there's the dolour.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: It would have griev'd me, that indeed: proceed sir.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: I have been pluck'd & tugg'd bith' haire o'th' head
About a gallerie, halfe an Acre long.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Yes, that's a good one, I must needs confesse,
A principall good one that, an absolute good one,
I have bin trod upon, and spurn'd about,
But never tugg'd byth' haire, I thanke my fates.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: O 'tis a spitefull paine.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Peace, never speake on't,
For putting men in mind on't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: To conclude,
I'm bursten sir: my belly will hold no meat.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: No? that makes amends for all.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Unlesse't be puddings,
Or such fast food, any loose thing beguiles me, I'm nere the better for't.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Sheepheads will stay with thee?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Yes sir, or Chaldrons.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Very well sir:
Any your bursten fellowes must take heed of surfets:
Strange things it seemes, you have endur'd;

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Too true sir.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: But now the question is, what you will endure
Hereafter in my service?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Any thing
That shall be reason sir, for I'm but froath;
Much like a thing new calv'd, or come more nearer sir,
Y'ave seen a Cluster of Frog-spawns in April,
E'ne such a starche am I, as weak and tender
As a green woman yet.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Now I know this,
I will be very gently angry with thee,
And kick thee carefully.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: O I sweet sir.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Peace, when thou art offer'd well, lest I begin now.
Your friends and mine have writ here for your truth,
They'll passe their words themselves, and I must meet 'em.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Then have you all:
As for my honesty there is no feare of that,
For I have ne're a whole bone about me,

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: Think upon love, which makes all creatures handsome,
Seemly for ey-sight; goe not so disfusedly,
There are great Ladies purpose sir to visit you.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Grand plagues, shut in my casements, that the breaths
Of their Coach-mares reek not into my Nostrills;
Those beasts are but a kinde of Bawdy fore-runners.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: It is not well with you,
When you speak ill of faire Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Faire mischiefs, give me a nest of Owles, and take 'em;
Happy is he say I, whose window opens
To a browne Bakers chimney, he shall be sure there
To heare the Bird sometimes after twi-light:
What a fine thing 'tis me thinks to have our garments
Sit loose upon us thus, thus careleslely,
It is more manly, and more mortifying;
For w'are so much the readier for our shrouds:
For how ridiculous wer't, to have death come,
And take a fellow pinn'd up like a Mistris?
About his neck a Ruffe, like a pincht Lanthorne,
Which Schoole-boyes make in winter; and his dublet
So close and pent, as if he fear'd one prison
Would not be strong enough, to keep his soule in;
But's Tailor makes another:
And trust me, for I know't when I lov'd Cupid,
He does endure much paine, for the poore praise
Of a neat sitting suit.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: One may be handsome sir,
And yet not pain'd, nor proud.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: There you lie Cupid,
As bad as Mercurie: there is no handsomenesse,
But has a wash of Pride and Luxury,
And you goe there too Cupid. Away dissembler,
Thou tak'st the deeds part which befooles us all;
Thy Arrow heads shoot out sinners: hence away,
And after thee Ile send a powerfull charme,
Shall banish thee for ever.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: Never, never,
I am too sure thine owne.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: HEnce all you vaine Delights,
As short as are the nights,
Wherein you spend your folly,
Ther's nought in this life sweet,
If man were wise to see't,
But onely Melancholy,
O sweetest melancholy.
Welcome folded Armes, and fixed eyes,
A sigh that piercing mortifies,
A look that's fastned to the ground,
A tongue chain'd up without a sound.
Fountaine heads, and pathlesse Groves,
Places which pale passion loves:
Moon-light walkes, when all the fowles
Are warmly hous'd, save Bats and Owles;
A mid-night Bell, a parting groane,
These are the sounds we feed upon;
Then stretch our bones in a still gloomy valley,
Nothing's so daintie sweet as lovely melancholy.

speeches.speaker: 1 Br.
verse: So, so, the Wood-cock's gin'd;
Keep this doore fast brother.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: Ile warrant this.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Ile goe incense him instantly;
I know the way to't.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: Wil't not be too soon think you,
And make two fits break into one?

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Pah, no, no; The taile of his melancho
Is alwayes the head of his anger, and followes as close,
As the Report followes the powder.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: This is the appoynted place, and the houre struck,
If I can get security for's truth,
Ile never minde his honesty: poore worme,
I durst lay him by my wife, which is a benefit
Which many masters ha' not: I shall ha' no maid
Now got with childe, but what I get my selfe,
And that's no small felicity: In most places
Th'are got by th' men, and put upon the Masters:
Nor shall I be resisted when I strike,
For he can hardly stand; these are great blessings.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I want my food, deliver me a varlet.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: How now: from whence comes that?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I am allow'd a Carcasse to insult on;
Where's the villaine?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: He meanes not me I hope.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: My maintenance rascals; my Bulk, my exhibition.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Blesse us all,
What names' are these? would I were gone agen.
A Curse upon thee for a slave,
Art thou here, and heard'st me rave?
Fly not sparkles from mine eye,
To shew my indignation nye?
Am I not all foame, and fire?
With voice as hoarse, as a Towne-crier?
How my back opes and shuts together,
VVith furie, as old mens with weather?
Could'st thou not heare my teeth knash hither?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: No truely sir, I thought t'had been a Squirrell,
Shaving a Hazle-nut.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Death, hell, fiends, and darknesse,
I will thrash thy mangy carcasse.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: O sweet sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: There cannot be too many Tortures,
Spent upon those louzie Quarters.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Hold, oh.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Thy bones shall rue, thy bones shall rue,
prose:
Thou nafly, scurvie, mongrill Toad,

Mischief on thee;
Light upon thee,
All the plagues
That can confound thee
Or did ever raigne abroad:
Better a thousand lives it cost,
Then have brave Anger spilt or lost.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: May I open mine eyes yet, and safely peep?
Ile trie a groane first—oh—Nay then hee's gone.
There was no other policy but to dye,
He would ha' made me else. Ribs are you sore?
I was ne're beaten to a tune before.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Lapet.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Agen?

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Look, look, hee's flat agen,
And stretched out like a Coarse a handfull longer
Then he walks trust me brother. Why Lapet.
I hold my life we shall not get him speak now.
Monsieur Lapet; it must be a privie token,
If any thing fetch him, hee's so far gone.
We come to passe our words for your mans truth.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: O gentlemen y'are welcom: I have been thrasht i'faith.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: How? thrasht sir?

speeches.speaker: Lap
verse: Never was Shrove-tuesday Bird
So cudgel'd gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Pray how? by whom sir?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Nay that I know not.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: Not who did this wrong?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Only a thing came like a walking song.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bro.
verse: What beaten with a Song?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Never more tightly, gentlemen:
Such crotchets happen now and then, methinks,
He that endures well, of all waters drinks.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: YEs, yes, this was a Madman, sir, with you,
A passionate Madman.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
verse: Who would ha' lookt for this sir?

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: And must be priviledg'd? a pox priviledge him:
I was never so dry beaten since I was borne,
And by a litter of rogues, meer rogues, the whole twenty
Had not above nine elbowes amongst 'em all too:
And the most part of those left-handed rascalls,
The very vomit, Sir, of hospitalls,
Bridewells, and Spittle-houses; such nasty smellers,
That if they'd been unfurnish'd of Club-Trunchions,
They might have cudgel'd me with their very stinks,
It was so strong, and sturdy: and shall this,
This filthy injurie, be set off with madnesse?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Nay take your owne blouds councel sir, hereafter,
Ile deale no further in't: if you remember,
It was not come to blowes, when I advis'd you.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: No, but I ever said, 'twould come to something,
And 'tis upon me, thank him: were he kin
To all the mighty Emperours upon earth,
He has not now in life three houres to reckon;
I watch but a free time.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
prose: Your noble brother, sir, Ile leave you now.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Souldier I would I could perswade my thoughts
From thinking thee a brother, as I can
My tongue from naming on't: thou hast no friend here,
But fortune and thy owne strength, trust to them.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: How? what's the incitement, sir?

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Treacherie to vertue;
Thy treacherie, thy faithlesse circumvention:
Has Honour so few daughters, never fewer,
And must thou aime thy treacherie at the best?
The very front of vertue? that blest Lady? the Dukes sister?
Created more for admirations cause,
Then for loves ends; whose excellency sparkles
More in divinity, then mortall beauty;
And as much difference 'twixt her minde and bodie,
As 'twixt this earths poore center and the Sun:
And couldst thou be so injurious to faire goodnesse,
Once to attempt to court her down to frailty?
Or put her but in minde that there is weaknesse,
Sin, and desire, which she should never heare of?
Wretch, thou'st committed worse then Sacrilege,
In the attempting on't, and oughtst to dye for't.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: I rather ought to doe my best, to live, sir;
Provoke me not; for I've a wrong sits on me,
That makes me apt for mischiefe; I shall lose
All respects suddainly of friendship, Brother-hood,
Or any sound that way.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: But 'ware me most;
For I come with a two-edg'd injurie;
Both my disgrace, and thy apparent falshood,
Which must be dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: I courted her, sir:
Love starve me with delayes when I confesse it not.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: There's nothing then but death
Can be a pennance fit for that confession.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: But farre from any vitious taint.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: O sir,
Vice is a mighty stranger growne to courtship.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: Nay then the fury of my wrong light on thee.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Forbeare, the Duke's at hand.
Here, hard at hand, upon my reputation.

speeches.speaker: Sold.
verse: I must doe something now.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Ile follow you close sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: We must entreat you must not; for the Duke
Desires some conference with you.

speeches.speaker: Sh.
verse: Let me goe,
As y'are gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Faith we dare not sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Dare ye be false to honour, and yet dare not
Doe a man justice? give me leave—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Good sweet sir.
H'as sent twice for you.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Is this brave, or manly?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I prethee be conform'd.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: 'Death—

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Peace, hee's come introth.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Oh have you betraid me to my shame afresh?
How am I bound to loath you?

speeches.speaker: Duk.
verse: Shamont, welcome,
I sent twice.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: But my Lord, he never heard on't.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Pray pardon him, for his falsenesse, I did Sir,
Both times; I'de rather be found rude then faithlesse.

speeches.speaker: Du
verse: I love that bluntnesse darely: ha's no vice,
But is more manly then some others vertue,
That lets it out onely for shew or profit.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Wil't please you quit me sir, I've urgent busines?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Come, you'r so hasty now: I sent for you
To a better end.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: And if it be an end,
Better or worse, I thank your goodnesse for't.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I've ever kept that bounty in condition,
And thankfulnesse in bloud, which well becomes
Both Prince and Subject, that where any wrong
Beares my impression, or the hasty figure
Of my repented anger, I'me a Law
Ev'n to my selfe, and doome my selfe most strictly
To Justice, and a noble satisfaction:
So that, what you in tendernesse of honour,
Conceive to be losse to you, which is nothing
But curious opinion, Ile restore agen,
Although I give you the best part of Genoa,
And take to boot but thanks for your amends.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: O miserable satisfaction,
Ten times more wretched then the wrong it selfe;
Never was ill better made good with worse:
Shall it be said that my posterity
Shall live the sole heires of their fathers shame?
And raise their wealth and glorie from my stripes?
You have provided nobly bounteous sir,
For my disgrace, to make it live for ever,
Out-lasting Brasse or Marble:
This is my feares construction, and a deep one,
Which neither argument nor time can alter:
Yet I durst sweare, I wrong your goodnesse in't sir,
And the most faire intent on't, which I reverence
With admiration, that in you a Prince,
Should be so sweet and temperate a condition,
To offer to restore where you may ruine,
And do't with justice, and in me a servant,
So harsh a disposition, that I cannot
Forgive where I should honor, and am bound to't.
But I have ever had that curiosity
In bloud, and tenderness of reputation,
Such an antipathy against a blow,
I cannot speak the rest: Good sir discharge me,
It is not fit that I should serve you more,
Nor come so neare you; I'me made now for privacy,
And a retir'd condition, that's my suit,
To part from Court for ever, my last suit.
And as you professe bounty, grant me that, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I would deny thee nothing.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Health reward you; sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: He's gone agen already, and takes hold
Of any opportunity, not riches
Can purchase him, nor honours, peaceably,
And force were brutish: what a great worth's gone with him,
And but a gentleman? well, for his sake,
Ile nere offend more those I cannot make:
They were his words, and shall be deare to memorie.
Say I desire to see him once agen;
Yet stay, hee's so well forward of his peace,
'Twere pitty to disturbe him: he would groane
Like a soule fetch'd agen; and that were injurie,
And I've wrong'd his degree too much already.
Call forth the gentlemen of our chamber instantly.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: I shall my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: I may forget agen,
And therefore will prevent: The strain of this
Troubles me so, one would not hazard more:

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Your will my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Yes; I discharge you all.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: My Lord—

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Your places shall be otherwise dispos'd of.

speeches.speaker: 4 Gent.
verse: Why sir?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Reply not, I dismisse you all:
Y'are gentlemen, your worths will find you fortunes;
Nor shall your farewell taxe me of ingratitude,
Ile give you all noble remembrances,
As testimonies 'gainst reproach and malice,
That you departed lov'd.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gen.
verse: This is most strange, sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: But how is your grace furnish'd, these dismis'd?

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Seek me out Grooms.
Men more insensible of reputation,
Lesse curious and precise in termes of honour,
That if my anger chance let fall a stroak,
As we are all subject to impetuous passions,
Yet it may passe unmurmur'd, undisputed,
And not with braver fury prosecuted.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: It shal be done, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gen.
verse: Know you the cause sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Not I kinde gentlemen, but by conjectures,
And so much shall be yours, when you please.
Thanks sir.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gen.
verse: VVe shall ith' mean time think our selves guilty
Of some foule fault, through ignorance committed.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: No, 'tis not that, nor that way.

speeches.speaker: 4 Gen.
verse: For my part.
I shall be dis-inherited, I knew so much.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Why sir, for what?

speeches.speaker: 4 Gen.
verse: My sire's of a strange humour,
Hee'll forme faults for me, and then sweare 'em mine,
And commonly the first begins with leacherie.
He knowes his owne youthes trespasse.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Before you goe,
Ile come and take my leave, and tell you all sirs.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gen.
verse: Thou wer't ever just and kinde.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: That's my poore vertue sir,
And parcell valiant; but it's hard to be perfect:
The chusing of these fellowes now will puzzle me,
Horribly puzzle me; and there's no judgement,
Goes true upon mans out-side, there's the mischiefe:
He must be touch'd, and try'd, for gold or drosse;
There is no other way for't, and that's dangerous too;
But since I'me put in trust, I will attempt it:
The Duke shal keep one daring man about him:
Soft, who comes here? a pretty bravery this:
Every one goes so like a gentleman,
'Tis hard to finde a difference, but byth' touch.
Ile trie your mettall sure.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Why what doe you meane sir?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Nay, and you understand it not, I doe not.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Yes, would you should well know,
I understand it for a box o'th' eare Sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: And o' my troth, that's all I gave it for.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: 'Twere best it be so.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: This is a brave Coward,
A jolly threatning Coward; he shall be Captaine:
Sir, let me meet you an houre hence i'th' Lobby.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Meet you? the world might laugh at me then i'faith.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ge.
verse: Lay by your scorn & pride, the're scurvy qualities,
And meet me, or Ile hox you while I have you,
And carrie you gambril'd thither like a Mutton.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Nay, and you be in earnest, here's my hand
I will not faile you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: 'Tis for your owne good.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Away.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Too much for your own good, sir, a pox on you.

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: I prethee curse me all day long so.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Hang you.

speeches.speaker: Gal:
verse: Ile make him mad; hee's loth to curse too much to me;
Indeed I never yet took box oth' eare,
But it redounded, I must needs say so—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Will you be gone?

speeches.speaker: Gal.
verse: Curse, curse, and then I goe.
Look how he grins, I've anger'd him toth' kidnyes.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Was ever such a prigging coxcombe seen?
One might have beat him dumbe now in this humour,
And hee'd ha' grind it out still:
O here's one made to my hand,
Methinks looks like a Craven;
Lesse paines will serve his triall: some slight justle.

speeches.speaker: Pl. f.
verse: How? take you that sir:
And if that content you not—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Yes very well sir, I desire no more.

speeches.speaker: Pl. f.
verse: I think you need not;
For you have not lost by't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Who would ha' thought this would have prov'd a gentleman?
Ile never trust long chins and little legs agen,
Ile know 'em sure for gentlemen hereafter:
A gristle but in shew, but gave his cuffe
With such a fetch, and reach of gentrie,
As if h'had had his armes before the floud;
I have took a villanous hard taske upon me;
Now I begin to have a feeling on't.
O here comes a tri'd piece, now, the reformed kick.
The millions of punches, spurnes, and nips
That he has endur'd? his Buttock's all black Lead,
He 's halfe a Negro back-ward; he was past a Spaniard
In eighty eight, and more Egyptian-like;
His Table and his Book come both out shortly,
And all the Cowards in the Towne expect it;
So, if I faile of my full number now,
I shall be sure to finde 'em at Church corners,
Where Dives, and the suff'ring Ballads hang.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Well, since thou art of so milde a temper,
Of so meek a spirit, thou maist live with me,
Till better times doe smile on thy deserts.
I am glad I am got home againe.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I am happy in your service, sir,
You'll keep me from the Hospitall.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: So, bring me the last proofe, this is corrected.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I, y'are too full of your correction, sir.

speeches.speaker: Lap
verse: Look I have perfect Books within this half houre.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Bid him put all the Thumps in Pica Roman,
And with great Tees, (you vermin) as Thumps should be.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Then in what Letter will you have your Kicks?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: All in Italica, your Backward blowes
All in Italica, you Hermophrodite:
When shall I teach you wit?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: O let it alone,
Till you have some your selfe sir.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: You mumble?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: The Victualls are lockt up;
I'me kept from mumbling.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: He prints my Blows upon pot-paper too, the rogue,
Which had been proper for some drunken Pamphlet.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Monsieur Lapet? how the world rings of your sir?
Your name sounds far and neare.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: A good report it beares, for an enduring name—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: What luck have you sir?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Why, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I'me but thinking on't.
I've heard you wish this five yeare for a place.
Now there's one fall'n, and freely without money too;
And empty yet, and yet you cannot hav't.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: No? what's the reason? Ile give money for't,
Rather then goe without sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: That's not it, sir;
The troth is, there's no gentleman must have it
Either for love or money: 'tis decreed so;
I was heartily sorrie when I thought upon you,
Had you not been a gentleman I had fitted you.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Who I a gentleman? a pox I'me none, sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: How? why did you ever think I was?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: What? not a gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I would thou'dst put it upon me i'faith.
Did not my Grand-father cry Coney-skins?
My father Aquavitae? a hot gentleman:
All this I speak on i' your time and memorie too;
Onely a rich Unckle dy'd and left me chattells,
You know all this so well too—

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Pray excuse me, sir, ha' not you Armes?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Yes, a poore couple here.
That serve to thrust in wild-fowle.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Heralds Armes,
Symbols of gentrie, sir: you know my meaning;
They've been shewn and seen.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: They have.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: I fex have they.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Why I confesse, at my wives instigation once,
(As women love these Heralds kickshawes naturally)
I bought 'em: but what are they think you? puffs.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Why, that's proper to your name being Lapet.
Which is La fart, after the english letter.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: The Herald, sir, had much a doe to finde it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: And can you blame him?
Why 'tis the onely thing that puzzles the devill.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: At last he lookt upon my name agen,
And having well compar'd it, this he gave me,
The two Cholliques playing upon a winde instrument.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: An excellent proper one: but I pray tell me,
How does he expresse the Cholliques?
They are hard things.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: The Cholliques? with hot trenchers at their bellies,
There's nothing better, Sir, to blaze a Chollique.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: And are not you a gentleman by this sir?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: No, I disclaime't: no belly-ake upon earth
Shall make me one: he shall not think
To put his gripes upon me,
And wring out gentrie so, and ten pound first.
If the winde instrument will make my wife one,
Let her enjoy't, for she was a Harpers Grand-childe:
But sir, for my particular, I renounce it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Or to be call'd so?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I sir, or imagin'd.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: None fitter for the place: give me thy hand.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: A hundred thousand thanks, beside a Bribe sir.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: You must take heed
Of thinking toward a gentleman, now.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Pish, I am not mad, I warrant you: nay more sir,
If one should twit me i'th' teeth that I'me a gentleman,
Twit me their worst, I am but one since Lammas,
That I can prove, if they would see my heart out.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Marry in any case keep me that evidence.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Here comes my servant, Sir, Galoshio,
Has not his name for nought, he will be trod upon:
What sayes my Printer now?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Heres your last proof Sir.
You shal have perfect Books now in a twinkling.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: These marks are ugly.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: He sayes, sir, they're proper:
Blows should have marks, or else they are nothing worth.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: But why a Peel-crow here?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I told 'em so sir:
A Scar-crow had been better.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: How Slave? looke you Sir,
Did not I say, this Whirrit, and this Bob,
Should be both Pica Roman.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: So said I Sir, both Picked Romans,
And he has made 'em Welch Bills,
Indeed I know not what to make on 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Hay-day; a Souse, Italica?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Yes, that may hold Sir,
Souse is a bonaroba, so is Flops too.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: But why stands Bastinado so farre off here?

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Alas you must allow him room to lay about him, sir.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Why lyes this Spurne lower then that Spurn, sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Marry this signifies one kickt downe staires, sir,
The other in a Gallerie: I ask'd him all these questions.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Your Books name?
Prethee Lapet minde me, you never told me yet.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Marrie but shall sir: 'tis call'd The up-rising of the kick,
And the downfall of the Duello.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Bring that to passe you'll prove a happy member,
And doe your Countrey service: your young blouds
Will thank you then, when they see foure-score.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I hope
To save my hundred Gentlemen a month by't,
Which will be very good for the private house.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Look you, your Table's finish'd sir already.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Why then behold my Master-piece: see, see, sir,
Here's all your Blowes, and Blow-men whatsoever,
Set in their lively colours, givers, and takers.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Troth wondrous fine, sir.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Nay, but mark the postures,
The standing of the takers I admire more then the givers,
They stand scornfully, most contumeliously, I like not the~,
Oh here's one cast into a comely figure.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: My Master meanes him there that's cast downe headlong.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: How sweetly does this fellow take his Dowst?
Stoops like a Cammell, that Heroick beast,
At a great load of Nut-megs; and how meekly
This other fellow here receives his Whirrit?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Oh Master here's a fellow stands most gallantly,
Taking his kick in private behinde the hangings,
And raising up his hips to't. But oh, sir,
How daintily this man lies trampled on?
Would I were in thy place, what e're thou art:
How lovely he endures it?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
prose: But will not these things, sir, be hard to practise, think you?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Oh, easie, sir: Ile teach 'em in a Dance.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: How? in a dance?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Ile lose my new place else,
What ere it be; I know not what 'tis yet.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: And now you put me in minde, I could employ it well,
For your grace, specially: For the Dukes cozen
Is by this time in's violent fit of mirth,
And a devise must be sought out for suddainly,
To over-cloy the passion.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Say no more, sir,
Ile fit you with my Schollers, new practitioners,
Endurers of the time.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Whereof I am one sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: You carry it away smooth; give me thy hand, sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: Hark, hark, how lowd his fit's growne.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: 1. Bro.
verse: Now let our sister lose no time, but ply it
With all the power she has.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: Her shame growes big, brother;
The Cupids shape will hardly hold it longer,
'Twould take up half an Ell of China Damask more,
And all too little: it struts per'lously:
There is no tamp'ring with these Cupids longer,
The meere conceit with woman-kinde works strong.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: The laugh comes nearer now,
'Twere good we were not seen yet.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.
And was he bastinado'd to the life? ha, ha, ha.
I prethee say, Lord Generall, how did the Rascals
Entrench themselves?

speeches.speaker: Base
verse: Most deeply, politickly, all in ditches.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: 'Tis thought he'll ne're beare armes ith' field agen,
Has much adoe, to lift 'em to his head, sir.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I would he had.

speeches.speaker: Base
verse: On either side round Truncheons plaid so thick,
That Shoulders, Chines, nay Flanks were paid toth' quick.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Well said Lord Generall: ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: But pray how grew the difference first betwixt you?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: There was never any sir; there lies the jest man;
Onely because he was taller then his brother;
There's all my quarrell to him; and me thought
He should be beaten for't, my minde so gave me, sir,
I could not sleep for't; Ha, ha, ha, ha.
Another good jest quickly, while 'tis hot now;
Let me not laugh in vaine: ply me, O ply me,
As you will answer't to my Cozen Duke.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Alas, who has a good jest?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I fall, I dwindle in't.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Ten Crowns for a good jest: ha' you a good jest, sir?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: A pretty morall one.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Let's ha't, what ere it be.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: There comes a Cupid
Drawne by six fooles.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: That's nothing.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Help it, help it then.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: I ha' known six hundred fooles drawn by a Cupid.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: I that, that, that's the smarter Morall: ha, ha, ha.
Now I begin to be Song-ripe methinks.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Ile sing you a pleasant aire, sir, before you ebb.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Oh how my Lungs doe tickle? ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Oh how my Lungs doe tickle? oh, oh, ho, ho.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Set a sharp Jest
Against my breast,
Then how my Lungs doe tickle?
As Nightingales,
And things in Cambrick railes,
Sing best against a prickle.
Ha, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Ho, ho, ho, ho, ha.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Laugh.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Laugh.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Laugh.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Laugh.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Wide.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Loud.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: And vary.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: A smile is for a simpering Novice.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: One that ne're tasted Caveare,

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Nor knowes the smack of deare Anchovis.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Ho, ho, ho, ho, ho.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: A gigling waiting wench for me,
That shewes her teeth how white they be.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: A thing not fit for gravitie,
For theirs are foule and hardly three.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Ho, ho, ho.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Democritus, thou ancient Fleerer,
Now I misse thy laugh, and ha' since.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: There you nam'd the famous Geerer,
That ever geer'd in Rome, or Athens.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: Ho, ho, ho.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: How brave lives he that keeps a foole,
Although the rate be deeper?

speeches.speaker: Pas.
verse: But he that is his owne foole sir,
Does live a great deale cheaper.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
prose: Sure I shal burst, burst, quite break thou art so witty.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: 'Tis rare to break at Court for that belongs toth' City.

speeches.speaker: Pas.
prose: Ha, ha, my spleen is almost worne to the last laughter.

speeches.speaker: Bas.
verse: O keep a corner for a friend, a jest may come hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Twinge all now, twinge, I say.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Downe derry.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: Not angry Law, nor doores of Brasse shal keep me
From my wrongs expiation, to thy Bowels,
I returne my disgrace; and after turne
My face to any death that can be sentenc'd.

speeches.speaker: Base
verse: Murder, O murder, stop the murderer there—

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: I am glad hee's gone; h'as almost trod my guts out;
Follow him who list for me, Ile ha' no hand in't.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: Oh 'twas your luck and mine to be squelch'd Mr.
Has stamp'd my very Puddings into Pancakes.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: O Brothers, oh, I fear 'tis mortall: help, O helpe,
I'me made the wretched'st woman, by this accident,
That ever love beguil'd.

speeches.speaker: 2 Bro.
verse: We are undone Brother,
Our shames are too apparent: Away receptacle
Of Luxury, and dishonour, most unfortunate,
To make thy selfe but luckie to thy spoile,
After thy Sexes manner: lift him up Brother;
He breathes not to our comfort, hee's too wasted
Ever to cheere us more: A Chirurgeon speedily;
Hence; the unhappiest that ere stept aside,
Shee'll be a Mother before shee's known a Bride.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: Thou hadst a most unfortunate conception,
What ere thou prov'st to be; in midd'st of mirth
Comes ruine, for a welcome, to thy birth.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: This is a beautifull life now; privacie
The sweetnesse and the benefit of essence:
I see there is no man, but may make his paradice;
And it is nothing, but his love, and dotage
Upon the worlds fowle joyes, that keeps him out on't:
For he that lives retir'd in minde, and spirit,
Is still in paradice, and has his innocence,
Partly allow'd for his companion too,
As much as stands with justice: here no eyes
Shoot their sharp pointed scornes upon my shame;
They know no termes of reputation here,
No punctuall limits, or precise dimensions;
Plaine downe-right honestie is all the beauty
And elegancy of life found amongst shepheards;
For knowing nothing nicely, or desiring it,
Quits many a vexation from the minde,
With which our quainter knowledge does abuse us;
The name of envy is a stranger here,
That dries mens blouds abroad, robs health and rest,
Why here's no such fury thought on: no, nor falsehood,
That brotherly disease, fellow-like devill,
That plaies within our bosome, and betrayes us.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Oh are you here?

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: La Nove, 'tis strange to see thee.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: I ha' rid one horse to death,
To finde you out, sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: I am not to be found of any man
That saw my shame, nor seen long.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Good, your attention:
You ought to be seen now, and found out sir,
If ever you desire before your ending
To performe one good office, nay a deare one,
Mans time can hardly match it.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Bee't as pretious
As reputation; if it come from Court
I will not heare on't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: You must heare of this, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Must?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: You shall heare it.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: I love thee, that thoul't dye.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: 'Twere nobler in me,
Then in you living: you will live a murderer,
If you deny this office.

speeches.speaker: Sha.
verse: Ev'n to death sir.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gen.
verse: Why then you'l kill your brother.

speeches.speaker: Sham,
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Your Brother sir:
Beare witnesse heaven, this man destroyes his brother
When he may save him, his least breath may save him:
Can there be wilfuller destruction?
He was forc'd to take a most unmanly wrong,
Above the suffring vertue of a Soldier,
Has kill'd his Injurer, a work of honour;
For which, unlesse you save him, he dyes speedily
My conscience is discharg'd, I'me but a friend,
A Brother should goe forward where I end.

speeches.speaker: Sham.
verse: Dyes?
Say he be naught, that's nothing to my goodnesse,
Which ought to shine through use, or else it loses
The glorious name 'tis knowne by: hee's my brother;
Yet peace is above bloud: Let him goe; I,
But where's the noblenesse of affection then?
That must be car'd for too, or I'me imperfect,
The same bloud that stood up in wrath against him,
Now in his miserie runs all to pity;
I'de rather dye than speak one sillable
To save my selfe: but living as I am,
There's no avoiding on't, the worlds humanity
Expects it hourely from me: curse of fortune,
I took my leave so well too: Let him dye,
'Tis but a brother lost; so pleasingly,
And swiftly I came off, 'twere more then irksomnesse,
To tread that path agen; and I shall never
Depart so handsomly: But then where's posterity?
The consummation of our house and name?
I'me torne in pieces betwixt love and shame.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Good morrow fellow Poltrot, and Moulbazon,
Good morrow fellowes all.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: Mounsieur Lapet?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Look, I've remembred you, here's books a piece for you.

speeches.speaker: Moul.
verse: O sir, we dearely thank you.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: So you may;
There's two impressions gone already sirs.

speeches.speaker: Pol.
verse: What no? in so short a time?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: 'Tis as I tell you sir,
My Kick sells gallantly, I thank my stars.

speeches.speaker: Clo.
verse: So does your Table; you may thank the Moon too.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: 'Tis the Book sells the Table.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: But 'tis the Book-seller
That has the money for 'em, I'me sure o'that.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: 'Twill much enrich the Company of Stationers,
'Tis thought 'twill prove a lasting benefit,
Like the Wise Masters, and the Almanacks,
The hundred Novells, and the Book of Cookerie,
For they begin already to engrosse it,
And make it a stock-book, thinking indeed
'Twill prove too great a benefit, and help,
For one that's new set up: they know their way,
And make him Warden, ere his beard be gray.

speeches.speaker: Moul.
verse: Is't possible such vertue should lye hid,
And in so little paper?

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: How? Why there was the Carpenter,
An unknowne thing, an odoriferous Pamphlet,
Yet no more Paper, by all computation,
Then Ajax Telamon would use at once,
Your Herring prov'd the like, able to buy
Another Fishers Folly, and your Pasquill
Went not below the mad-caps of that time,
And shall my elaborate Kick come behinde think you?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Yes, it must come behinde, 'tis in Italica too,
According to your humour.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: Not in sale, varlet.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: In sale, sir? it shall saile beyond 'em all I troe.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: What have you there now? oh, Page, 21.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: That Page is come to his yeares, he should be a serving-man.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Mark how I snap up the Duello there:
One would not use a dog so,
I must needs say; but's for the common good.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Nay sir, your Commons seldome fight at sharp,
But buffet in a ware-house.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: This will save
Many a gentleman of good bloud from bleeding sirs,
I have a curse from many a Barber Surgeon;
They'd give but too much money to call't in;
Turne to Page 45. see what you finde there.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: O out upon him,
Page 45. that's an old theefe indeed.

speeches.speaker: Lap.
verse: The Duke, clap down your Books; away Galoshio.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Indeed I am too foule to be ith' presence,
They use to shake me off at the chamber door still.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Good my Lord, grant my suit; let me not rise
Without the comfort on't: I have not often
Been tedious in this kinde.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Sister, you wrong your selfe,
And those great vertues that your fame is made of,
To waste so much breath for a Murderers life.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: You cannot hate th' offence more then I doe, sir,
Nor the offender, the respect I owe
Unto his absent brother, makes me a suitor,
A most importunate sister; make me worthy
