speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I'll keep thee like a woman.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I'll keep my self Sir,
Keep my self honest Sir; there's the brave keeping:
If you will marry me.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Alas poor Florimell.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I do confesse I am too course and base Sir
To be your wife, and it is fit you scorn me,
Yet such as I have crown'd the lives of great ones:
To be your whore, I am sure I am too worthy,
(For by my troth Sir, I am truly honest)
And that's an honour equal to your greatnes.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I'll give thee what thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Tempt me no more then:
Give me that peace, and then you give abundance,
I know ye do but try me, ye are noble,
All these are but to try my modestie,
If you should find me easie, and once coming,
I see your eies already how they would fright me:
I see your honest heart how it would swell
And burst it self into a grief against me:
Your tongue in noble anger, now, even now Sir,
Ready to rip my loose thoughts to the bottom,
And lay my shame unto my self, wide open:
You are a noble Lord: you pity poor maids,
The people are mistaken in your courses:
You, like a father, try'em to the uttermost.
As they do gold: you purge the drosse from them,
And make them shine.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: This cunning cannot help ye:
I love ye to enjoy ye: I have stolne ye
To enjoy ye now, not to be fool'd with circumstance,
Yeeld willingly, or else.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I will force ye.
I will not be delay'd, a poor base wench
That I in curtesie make offer to,
Argue with me?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Do not, you will lose your labour,
Do not (my Lord) it will become ye poorly
Your curtesie may do much on my nature,
For I am kind as you are, and as tender:
If you compell, I have my strengths to fly to,
My honest thoughts, and those are guards about me:
I can cry too, and noise enough I dare make,
And I have curses, that will call down thunder,
For all I am a poor wench, heaven will hear me:
My body you may force, but my will never;
And be sure I do not live if you do force me,
Or have no tongue to tell your beastly Story,
For if I have, and if there be a Justice.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Pray ye go in here: I'll calme my self for this time.
And be your friend again.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I am commanded.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: You cannot scape me, yet I must enjoy ye,
I'll lie with thy wit, though I misse thy honesty:
Is this a wench for a Boors hungry bosom?
A morsel for a Peasants base embraces?
And must I starve, and the meat in my mouth?
I'll none of that.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: How now my Lord, how sped ye?
Have ye done the deed?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: No, pox upon't, she is honest.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Honest? what's that? you take her bare deniall,
Was there ever wench brought up in a mill, and honest?
That were a wonder worth a Chronicle,
Is your belief so large? what did she say to ye?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: She said her honesty was all her dowry,
And preach'd unto me, how unfit, and homely,
Nay how dishonourable it would seem in me
To act my will; popt me i'th mouth with modestie.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: What an impudent Quean was that? that's their trick ever.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: And then discours'd to me very learnedly
What fame and loud opinion would tell of me:
A wife she touch'd at.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Out upon her Varlet.
Was she so bold? these home spun things are devils,
They'll tell ye a thousand lies, if you'll beleeve'em;
And stand upon their honours like great Ladies,
They'll speak unhappily too: good words to cozen ye,
And outwardly seem Saints: they'll cry down-right also,
But 'tis for anger that you do not crush 'em.
Did she not talk of being with child?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: She toucht at it,

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: The trick of an arrant whore to milk your Lordship
And then a pension nam'd?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: No, no, she scorn'd it:
I offer'd any thing, but she refus'd all,
Refus'd it with a confident hate.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: You thought so,
You should have taken her then, turn'd her, and tew'd her
I'th' strength of all her resolution, flattered her,
And shak't her stubborn will: she would have thank'd ye,
She would have lov'd ye infinitely, they must seem modest,
It is their parts: if you had plaid your part Sir.
And handled her as men do unmand Hawks,
Cast her, and malde her-up in good clean linnen:
And there have coyed her, you had caught her heart-strings
These tough Virginities they blow like white thornes
In Stormes and Tempests.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: She is beyond all this,
As cold, and harden'd, as the Virgin Crystal.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Oh force her, force her, Sir, she longs to be ravishd
Some have no pleasure but in violence;
To be torne in pieces is their paradise:
'Tis ordinary in our Country, Sir, to ravish all
They will not give a penny for their sport
Unlesse they be put to it, and terribly,
And then they swear they'll hang the man comes neer'em,
And swear it on his lips too.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: No, no forcing,
I have an other course, and I will follow it,
I command you, and do you command your fellows,
That when you see her next, disgrace, and scorn her,
Ill seem to put her out o'th' dores o'th' sodain
And leave her to conjecture, then seize on her
Away, be ready straight.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: We shall not fail, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Florimell.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I am sure you have now consider'd
And like a wise wench weigh'd a friends displeasure,
Repented your prowd thoughts, and cast your scorn off.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: My Lord, I am not proud, I was never beautifull.
Nor scorn I any thing that's just and honest.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Come, to be short, can ye love yet? you told me
Kindnes would far compell ye: I am kind to ye,
And mean to exceed that way.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I told ye too, Sir,
As far as it agreed with modestie,
With honour, and with honesty I would yeeld to yee:
Good my Lord, take some other Theam: for Love,
Alas, I never knew yet what it meant,
And on the sudden Sir, to run through volumes
Of his most mystick art, 'tis most impossible;
Nay, to begin with lust, which is an Herisie,
A foul one too; to learn that in my childhood.
O good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: You will not out of this song,
Your modestie, and honestie, is that all?
I will not force ye.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Ye are too noble, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Nor play the childish fool, and marry ye,
I am yet not mad.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: If ye did, men would imagine.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Nor will I woo ye at that infinite price
It may be you expect.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I expect your pardon,
And a discharge (my Lord) that's all I look for.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: No, nor fall sick for love.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: 'Tis a healthful year Sir.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Look ye, I'l turn ye out o'dores, and scorn ye.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Thank ye my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: A proud slight Peat I found ye,
A fool (it may be too.)

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: An honest woman,
Good my Lord think me.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: And a base I leave ye,
So fare-ye-well.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Blessing attend your Lordship;
This is hot love, that vanisheth like vapors;
His Ague's off, his burning fits are well quench'd,
I thank heaven for't: his men, they will not force me.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: What dost thou stay for? dost thou not know the way,
Thou base unprovident whore?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Good words, pray ye Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: Has my Lord smoak'd ye over, good wife Miller?
Is your Mill broken that you stand so uselesse?

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: An impudent Quean, upon my life she is unwholsome;
Some base discarded thing my Lord has found her,
He would not have turnd her off o'th'sudden else.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Now against every sack (my honest sweet-heart)
With every Sim and Smug.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I must be patient.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: And every greasie guest, and sweaty Rascall
For his Royal hire between his fingers, Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
prose: I feare thou hast given my Lord the— thou damn'd thing.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: I have seen her in the Stewes.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: The knave her father
Was Bawd to her there, and kept a Tipling house,
You must even to it again: a modest function.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: If ye had honesty, ye would not use me
Thus basely wretchedly, though your Lord bid ye,
But he that knows.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Away thou carted impudence,
You meat for every man: a little meal
Flung in your face, makes ye appear so proud.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: This is inhumane. Let these tears perswade you
If ye be men, to use a poor girle better:
I wrong not you, I am sure I call you Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: What busines is here? away, are not you gone yet?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: My Lord, this is not well: although you hate me,
For what I know not: to let your people wrong me,
Wrong me maliciously, and call me

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Peace,
And mark me what we say advisedly;
Mark, as you love that that you call your credit;
Yeeld now, or you are undone: your good name's perish'd
Not all the world can buy your reputation;
Tis sunk for ever els, these peoples tongues will poison ye
Though you be white as innocence, they'll taint ye,
They will speak terrible and hideous things,
And people in this age are prone to credit,
They'll let fell nothing that may brand a woman,
Consider this, and then be wise and tremble:
Yeeld yet, and yet I'll save ye.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I'll show ye,
Their mouthes I'll seal up, they shall speak no more
But what is honourable and honest of ye,
And Saintlike they shall worship ye: they are mine,
And what I charge 'em Florimell.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I am ruind,
Heaven will regard me yet, they are barbarous wretches:
Let me not fall (my Lord.)

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: You shall not Florimell:
Mark how I'll work your peace, and how I honour ye.
Who waits there? come all in.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: Your pleasure Sir.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Who dare say this sweet beauty is not heavenly?
This virgin, the most pure, the most untainted,
The holiest thing?

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: We know it (my dear Lord)
We are her slaves: and that proud impudence
That dares disparage her, this sword (my Lord.)

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: They are rascals, base, the sons of common women
That wrong this vertue, or dare owne a thought
But fair and honourable of her: when we slight her,
Hang us, or cut's in pieces: let's tug i'th' Gallies.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Brand us for villains.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Why sure I dream: these are all Saints.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Go, and live all her slaves.

speeches.speaker: Ger.
verse: We are proud to do it.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: What think ye now? am not I able Florimell
Yet to preserve ye?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I am bound to your Lordship,
Ye are all honour, and good my Lord but grant me
Untill to morrow leave to weigh my Fortunes,
I'll give you a free answer, perhaps a pleasing,
Indeed I'll do the best I can to satisfie ye.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
prose: Take your good time, this kisse, till then farewell, Sweet.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: By all means discharge your follower.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: If we can get him off: Sirrha Bustofa.
Thou must needs run back.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: But I must not unlesse you send
A Bier, or a Lictor at my back, I do not use to run
From my friends.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Well, go will serve turne: I have forgot.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: What Sir,

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: See if I can think on't now.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I know what 'tis now?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: A Pistolet of that.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Done, you have forgot a device to send me away,
You are going a smocking perhaps.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: His owne, due, due i'faith Antonio,
The Pistolet's his owne.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I confesse it,
There 'tis: now if you could afford out of it
A reasonable excuse to mine Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Yes, I can:
But an excuse will not serve your turn: it must be a lie,
A full lie, 'twill do no good else: if you'll go to
The price of that?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Is a lie dearer then an excuse?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Oh, treble; this is the price of an excuse: but a lye is two more:
Look how many foyles go to a fair fall, so many excuses to
A full lye, and lesse cannot serve your turn, let any Tailor
I'th' Towne make it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Wie, 'tis reasonable, give him his price:
Let it be large enough now.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I'll warrant you, cover him all over.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I would have proof of one now.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: What? scale my invention before hand? you shall pardon
Me for that: well, I'll commend you to your Uncle, and
Tell him you'll be at home at supper with him.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: By no means, I cannot come to night (man)

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I know that too, you do not know a lye when you see it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Remember it must stretch for all night.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: I shall want stuffe, I doubt 'twill come to the other Pistolet.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Well, lay out, you shall be no loser Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: It must be faced, you know, there will be a yard of dissimulation
At least (City-measure) and cut upon an untroth or two: Lyned
With Fables, that must needs be, cold weather's coming, if it had
A galloon of hypocrisie, 't would do well: and hooked
Together with a couple of conceits,
That's necessity; well, I'll bring in my
Bill: I'll warrant you as fair a lye by that time I have done
With it, as any gentleman i'th' Town can swear too: if he
Would betray his Lord and Master.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: So, so, this necessary trouble's over.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I would you had bought an excuse of him
Before he went: you'll want one for Ismenia.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Tush, there needs none, there's no suspition yet,
And I'll be arm'd before the next encounter,
In a fast tye with my fair Isabel.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, you'll find your errand is before you now.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Oh Gentlemen, look to your selves, ye are
Men of another world else: your enemies are upon you;
The old house of the Bellides will fall upon your heads:
Signior Lisauro.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Lisauro?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: And Don what call you him? he's a Gentleman:
Yet he has but a Yeomans name,
Don Tarso, Tarso, and a dozen at their heels.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Lisauro, Tarso, nor a dozen more
Shall fright me from my ground, nor shun my path,
Let'em come on in their ablest fury.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis worthily resolved: I'll stand by you Sir,
This way, I am thy true friend.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I'll be gone Sir, that one may live to tell what's become of you.
Put up, put up, will you never learn to know a lye
From an Esop's fables? there's a taste for you now.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Look Sir, what time of day is it?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I know not, my eies go false, I dare not trust'em now,
I prethee tell me (Martin) if thou canst,
Is that Ismenia, or Isabella.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: This is the Lady, forget not Isabella.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: If this face may be borrowed and lent out,
If it can shift shoulders, and take other tyres,
So, 'tis mine where ere I find it

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Be sudden:
I cannot hold out long.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Beleeve't she frowns.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Let it come, she cannot frown me off on't:
How prettily it wooes me to come neerer?
How do you (Lady) since yesterdaies pains?
Were you not weary? of my faith.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: I think you were.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What Lady?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Weary of your faith, 'tis a burthen
That men faint under, though they bear little of it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: So, this is to the purpose.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You came home
In a fair hour I hope?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: From whence Sir?

speeches.speaker: Am.
prose: Sir, there's a Gentlewoman without desires to speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: They were pretty homely toyes: but your presence
Made them illustrious.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: My Cosen speaks to you.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: A Gentlewoman Sir, Isabella
She names her self.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: So, so, it hits finely now.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Name your self how you please: speak what you please,
I'll hear you cheerfully.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: You are not well,
Request her in: she may have more acquaintance
With his passions, and better cure for'em.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: She's nice in that (Madam) poor soul it seems
She's fearfull of your displeasure.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: I'll quit her
From that presently, and bring her in my self.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: How carelesly do you behave your self?
When you should call all your best faculties
To councell in you: how will you answer
The breach you made with fair Ismenia?
Have you forgot the retrograde vow you took
With her, that now is come in evidence?
You'll die upon your shame, you need no more
Enemies of the house, but the Lady now:
You shall have your dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Give me that face,
And I am satisfied upon whose shoulders
So ere it growes: Juno deliver us
Out of this amazement: Beseech you Goddesse
Tell us of our friends, how dos Ismenia?
And how does Isabella? both in good health
I hope, as you your self are.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: I am at farthest
In my counterfeit: my Antonio
I have ma^ter against you may need pardon,
As I must crave of you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Observe you Sir,
What evidence is come against me? what think you
The Hydra-headed Jury will say to't?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis I am foold,
My hopes are pour'd into the bottomles tube,
Tis labour for the house of Bellides:
I must not seem so yet: but in sooth (Lady)
Did you imagine your changeable face
Hid you from me? by this hand I knew you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I went by the face: and by these eies I
Might have been deceived.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: You might indeed (Antonio)
For this Gentleman did vow to Isabella,
That he it was that lov'd Ismenia,
And not Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Good, and was not that
A manifest confession that I knew you?
I else had been unjust unto my friend:
Twas well remembred, there I found you out
And speak your conscience now.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: But did he so protest?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Yes, I vow to you, had Antonio
Wedded Isabella, Ismenia
Had not been lost, there had been her lover.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Why much good do you friend, take her to you:
I crave but one, here have I my wish full,
I am glad we shall be so neer Neighbours.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Take both Sir, Juno to boote: three parts in one,
S. Hilarie blesse you, now oportunitie
Beware to meet with falshood, if thou canst
Shun it, my friends faith's turning from him.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Might I not justly accuse Antonio
For a love-wanderer? you know no other
But me, for another, and confesse troth now?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Here was my guide, where ere I find this face,
I am a Lover, marry, I must not misse
This freckle then, I have the number of 'em,
Nor this dimple: not a silk from this brow,
I carry the full Idea ever with me;
If Nature can so punctually paralel,
I may be cozened.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Well, all this is even:
But now, to perfect all, our love must now
Come to our Enemies hands, where neither part
Will ever give consent to't.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Most certain:
For which reason it must not be put to'em:
Have we not prevention in our owne hands.
Shall I walk by the tree? desire the fruit,
Yet be so nice to pull till I ask leave
Of the churlish Gardner, that will deny me?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: O Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: 'Tis manners to fall to
When grace is said.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: That holy act 's to come.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You may ope an oyster or two before grace.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Are there not double vows, as valuable
And as well spoke as any Frier utters?
Heaven has heard all.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Yes: but stayes the blessing,
Till all dues be done: heaven is not serv'd by halfs.
Wee shall have ne'r a fathers blessing here,
Let us not lose the better, from above.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You take up weapons of unequal force,
It shows you cowardly: heark in your ear.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Have I lost all imployment? Would this proffer
Had been made to me, though I had paid it
With a reasonable pennance.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Have I past
All thy fore-lock (Time)? I'll stretch a long arm
But I'll catch hold again: Doe but look back
Over thy shoulder, and have a pull at thee.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: I hear you (Sir) nor can I hear too much
While you speak well: You know th' accustom'd place
Of our night parley: if you can ascend,
The window shall receive you. You may finde there
A corrupted Church-man to bid you welcome.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I would meet no other man.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Aminta, you hear this.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: With joy (Madam) 'cause it pleases you.
It may be mine own case another time:
Now you go the right way: ask the Banes out,
Put it past father, or friends, to forbid it,
And then you're sure. Sir, your Hymen Taper
I'll light up for you: the window shall show you
The way to Sestos.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I'll venture drowning.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: The Simile holds not; 'tis hanging rather.
You must ascend your Castle by a ladder;
To the foot I'll bring you.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Leave mee to climb it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If I do turn you off?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Till night fare-well:
Then better.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Best it should be;
But peevish hatred keeps back that degree.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I never look'd so smooth as now I purpose:
And then beware: Knave is at worst of knave
When he smiles best, and the most seems to save.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: My mind's unquiet; while Antonio
My Nephew's abroad, my heart is not at home,
Only my fears stay with me; bad company;
But I cannot shift 'em off. This hatred
Betwixt the House of Bellides and us,
Is not fair war: 'tis civill, but uncivill.
We are neer neighbours, were of love as neer,
Till a crosse misconstruction ('twas no more
In conscience) put us so far asunder:
I would 'twere reconcil'd; it has lasted
Too many Sun-sets, if grace might moderate:
Man should not lose so many dayes of peace
To satisfie the anger of one minute.
I could repent it heartily. I sent
The knave to attend my Antonio too,
Yet he rerurns no comfort to me neither.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: No: I must not.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Hah; hee's come.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I must not: 'twill breake his heart to hear it.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: How? there's bad tidings: I must obscure & hear it;
He will not tell mee for breaking of my heart,
'Tis half split already.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: I have spi'd him: Now to knock down a Don with a lie, a silly harmlesse lie; 'twill be valiantly done, and nobly perhaps.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I cannot hear him now.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Oh the bloody dayes that wee live in; the envious, malitious, deadly dayes that we draw breath in!

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Now I hear too loud.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: The children that never shall be born may rue it; for men that are slain now might have liv'd to have got children, that might have curs'd their fathers.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh, my posterity is ruin'd.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Oh sweet Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh deer Antonio.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Yet it was nobly done of both parts: When hee and Lisauro met,

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh, death has parted 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Welcome my mortall foe (sayes one), Welcome my deadly enemy (sayes th'other:) off go their doublets, they in their shirts, and their swords stark naked; here lies Antonio, here lies Lisauro: hee comes upon him with an Embroccado, that hee puts by with a puncta reversa; Lisauro recoils mee two paces and some six inches back, takes his career, and then, oh.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Runs Antonio quite thorow,

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh villain.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Quite thorow between the arme and the body: so yet he had no hurt at that bout.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Goodnesse be praised.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: But then, at next encounter, he fetches me up Lisauro; Lisauro makes out a Long at him, which he thinking to be a Passado, Antonio's foot slipping: down: oh down.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: O now thou art lost.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Oh, but the quality of the thing: both Gentlemen, both Spanish Christians, yet one man to shed

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Say his enemies blood.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: His hair may come by divers casualties, though he never go into the field with his foe: but a man to lose nine ounces and two drams of blood at one wound, thirteen and a scruple at another, and to live till he die in cold blood: yet the Surgeon (that cur'd him) said, if Pia-mater had not been perish'd, he had bin a lives man til this day.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: There hee concludes he is gone.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: But all this is nothing: now I come to the point.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I the point, that's deadly: the ancient blow
Over the buckler ne'r went half so deep.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose:
Yet pitie bids mee keep in my charitie: for mee to pull an old mans ears from his head with telling of a Tale: oh fowle Tale! No, be silent Tale. Furthermore, there is the charge of Buriall; every one will cry Blacks, Blacks, that had but the least finger dipt in his blood, though ten degrees remov'd when 'twas done. Moreover,
the Surgeon (that made an end of him) will be paid: Sugar-plums and sweet breads; yet I say, the man may recover again, and die in his bed.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: What motley stuffe is this? Sirrha, speak truth
What hath befallen my deer Antonio?
Restrain your pity in concealing it;
Tell mee the danger full; take off your care
Of my receiving it: kill me that way,
I'll forgive my death: what thou keepst back from truth
Thou shalt speak in pain; doe not look to find
A limb in his right place, a bone unbroke,
Nor so much flesh unbroil'd of all that mountain
As a worm might sup on; dispatch, or be dispatch'd.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Alas Sir, I know nothing, but that Anton. is a man of Gods making to this hour, 'tis not two since I left him so.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Where didst thou leave him?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: In the same clothes he had on when he went from you.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Does he live?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I saw him drink.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Is he not wounded?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: He may have a cut i'th' leg by this time; for Don Martin and he were at whole slashes.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Met he not with Lisauro?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I doe not know her.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Her? Lisauro is a man, as he is.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I saw ne'r a man like him.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Didst thou not discourse a fight betwixt Ant. & Lis.?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: I to my self; I hope a man may give himself the lie if it please him.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Didst thou lie then?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: As sure as you live now.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I live the happier by it: when will he return?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: That he sent me to tel you, within these ten daies at farthest.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ten daies? he's not wont to be absent two.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Nor I think he wil not: he said he would be at home to morrow; but I love to speak within my compasse.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: You shall speak within mine Sir, now. Within there:
Take this fellow into custodie, keep him safe
I charge you.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Safe? do you hear? take notice what plight you find me in, if there want but a collop or a steak o'me, look to't.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: If my nephew return not in his health to morrow,
Thou goest to th' Rack.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Let me go to th' manger first; I had rather eat oats then hay.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: By your leave, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: For ought I know yet, you are welcom Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Read that, and tell me so: or if thy spectacles be not easie,
Keep thy nose unsadled, and ope thine ears;
I can speak thee the contents, I made 'em;
'Tis a challenge, a fair one, I'll maintain 't:
I scorn to hire my Second to deliver 't,
I bring 't my self: Dost know me, Julio?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Bellides?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Yes: Is not thine hair on end now?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Somwhat amaz'd at thy rash hardines;
How durst thou come so neer thine enemie?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Durst?
I dare come neerer: thou'rt a fool, Julio.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Take it home to thee with a knave to boot.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Knave to thy teeth again: and all that's quit:
Give me not a fool more then I give thee,
Or if thou dost, look to hear on't again.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: What an encounter's this?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: A noble one:
My hand is to my words, thou hast it there,
There I do challenge thee, if thou dar'st be,
Good friends with me; or I'll proclaim thee coward.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Be friends with thee?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I'll shew thee reasons for't:
A pair of old coxcombs (now wee go together)
Such as should stand examples of discretion,
The rules of Grammar to unwilling youth
To take out lessons by; we that should check
And quench the raging fire in others bloods,
We strike the battell to destruction?
Read 'em the black art? and make 'em beleeve
It is divinitie? Heathens, are we not?
Speak thy conscience, how hast thou slept this month,
Since this Fiend haunted us?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Sure, some good Angell
Was with us both last night: speak thou truth now,
Was it not last nights motion?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Dost not think
I would not lay hold of it at first proffer?
Should I ne'r sleep again?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Take not all from me;
I'll tell the doctrine of my vision.
Say that Antonio (best of thy blood)
Or any one, the least allyed to thee,
Should be the prey unto Lisauro's sword,
Or any of the house of Bellides?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Mine was the just inversion: on, on.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: How would thine eys have emptied thee in sorrow,
And left the condiment of Nature drie?
Thy hands have turn'd rebellious to the balls,
And broke the glasses, with thine own curses
Have torn thy soul, left thee a Statue
To propagate thy next posterity.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Yes, and thou causer? so it said to me,
They fight but your mischiefs: the yong men were friends,
As is the life and blood coagulate
And curded in one body; but this is yours,
An inheritance that you have gatherd for 'em,
A Legacie of blood, to kill each other
Throughout your Generations. Was't not so?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Word for word.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Nay, I can go farther yet.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: 'Tis far enough; Let us attone it here.
And in a reconciled circle fold
Our friendship new again.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: The signe's in Gemini,
An auspicious house, 't has joyn'd both ours again.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: You cannot proclaim me coward now, Don Bellides

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No: thou 'rt a valiant fellow: so am I:
I'll fight with thee at this hug, to the last leg
I have to stand on, or breath or life left.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: This is the salt unto humanity,
And keeps it sweet.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Love! oh life stinks without it.
I can tell you news.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Good has long been wanting.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I do suspect, and I have some proof on't,
(So far as a Love Epistle comes to)
That Antonio (your nephew) and my daughter
Ismenia are very good friends before us.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: That were a double wall about our houses,
Which I could wish were builded.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I had it
From Antonio's Intimate, Don Martin:
And yet (me thought) it was no friendly part
To show it me.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Perhaps 't was his consent:
Lovers have policies as well as Statesmen:
They look not alwaies at the mark they aime at.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Wee'll take up cudgels, and have one bowt with'em,
They shall know nothing of this union:
And till they find themselves most desperate,
Succour shall never see'em.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I'll take your part Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: It grows late; there's a happy day past us.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: The example I hope to all behind it.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Stand fair, light of Love, which epithite and place
Adds to thee honour, to me it would be shame,
We must be weight in love, no grain too light;
Thou art the Land-mark, but if love be blind,
(As many that can see have so reported)
What benefit canst thou be to his darknesse?
Love is a Jewel (some say) inestimable,
But hung at the eare, deprives our owne sight,
And so it shines to others, not our selves.
I speak my skill, I have onely heard on't,
But I could wish a neerer document,
Alas, the ignorant desire to know:
Some say Love's but a toy, and with a but.
Now me thinks I should love it ne'r the worse,
A toy is harmelesse sure, and may be plaid with,
It seldom goes without his adjunct, pretty,
A pretty toy we say, 'tis meeter to joy too.
Well, here may be a mad night yet for all this,
Here's a Priest ready, and a Lady ready:
A chamber ready, and a bed ready,
'Tis then but making unready, and that's soone done:
My Lady is my Cosen; I, my self,
Which is neerest then? My desires are mine,
Say they be hers too, is't a hanging matter?
It may be ventur'd in a worser cause,
I must go question with my conscience:
I have the word; Centinel, do thou stand,
Thou shalt not need to call, I'll he at hand.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Are we not dog'd behind us, thinkst thou friend?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I heard not one bark, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: There are that bite
And bark not (man) me-thought I spy'd two fellows
That through two streets together walk'd aloof,
And wore their eies suspiciously upon us.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Your Jealousie, nothing else; or such perhaps
As are afraid as much of us, who knows
But about the like busines? but for your fears sake
I'll advise and entreat one curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What's that friend?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I will not be denyed, Sir,
Change your upper garments with me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It needs not.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I think so too, but I will have it so,
If you dare trust me with the better Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Nay then.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If there should be danger towards,
There will be the main mark I'm sure.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Here thou tak'st from me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Tush, the General
Must be safe, how ere the Battel goes:
See you the Beacon yonder?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes, we are neer shore.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Come, Land, land, you must clamber by the cliffe,
Here are no staires to rise by.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I, are you there?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes Ismenia.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Thine owne.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Quench the light, thine eies are guides illustrious.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: 'Tis necessary.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Your legs have sav'd your lives, who ere you are,
Friend. Martin? where art thou? not hurt I hope:
Sure I was farthest in the pursuit of 'em:
My pleasures are forgotten through my fears:
The lights extinct, it was discreetly done:
They could not but have notice of the broile,
And fearing that might call up company,
Have carefully prevented, and closed up:
I do commend the heed; oh, but my friend,
I fear his hurt: friend? friend? it cannot be
So mortal, that I should lose thee quite, friend?
A groan, any thing that may discover thee:
Thou art not sunk so far, but I might hear thee:
I'll lay mine ear as low as thou canst fall:
Friend, Don Martin, I must answer for thee,
'Twas in my cause thou fell'st, if thou beest downe,
Such dangers stand betwixt us and our joyes,
That should we forethink ere we undertake,
Wee'ld sit at home, and save. What a night's here?
Purpos'd for so much joy, and now dispos'd
To so much wretchednes? I shall not rest in't:
If I had all my pleasures there within,
I should not entertain'em with a smile.
Good night to you: Mine will be black and sad,
A friend cannot, a woman may be bad.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: O thou false,

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Do your daringst, he's mine owne,
Soul and body mine, church and chamber mine,
Totally mine.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Darst thou face thy falshood?

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Shall I not give a welcom to my wishes
Come home so sweetly: farewell your company
Till you be calmer woman.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Oh what a heap
Of misery has one night brought with it.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Where is he? do you turn your shame from me?
You'r a blind Adultresse, you know you are.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: How's that Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Till I have vengeance,
Your sin's not pardonable: I'll have him,
If hell hide him not: y'have had your last of him.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: What did he speak? I understood him not,
He calld me a foul name, it was not mine,
He took me for another sure.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Hah? are you there?
Where's your sweet heart? I have found you Traytor
To my house: wilt league with mine enemie?
You'll shed his blood, you'll say: hah? will you so?
And fight with your heels upwards? No Minion,
I have a husband for you, since y'are so ranck,
And such a husband as thou shalt like him,
Whether thou wilt or no: Antonio?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: It thunders with the storm now.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: And to night
I'll have it dispatch'd: I'll make it sure, I,
By to morrow this time thy Maiden-head
Shall not be worth a Chicken, if it were
Knockt at an out-cry: go, I'll ha'ye before me:
Shough, shough, up to your coop, peay Hen.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Then I'll try my wings.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
prose: I, are you good at that? stop, stop thief, stop there.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Now having leisure, and a happy wind,
Thou maist at pleasure cause the stones to grind,
Sayles spread, and grift here ready to be ground.
Fie, stand not idely, but let the Mill go round.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Why dost thou sing and dance thus? why so merry?
Why dost thou look so wantonly upon me?
And kisse my hands?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: If I were high enough,
I would kisse your lips too.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Do, this is some kindnes,
This tastes of willingnesse, nay, you may kisse
Still, but why o'th' sudden now does the fitt take ye,
Unoffered, or uncompell'd? why these sweet curtesies?
Even now you would have blush'd to death to kisse thus:
Prethee let me be prepar'd to meet thy kindnes,
I shall be unfurnish'd else to hold thee play, wench:
Stay now a little, and delay your blessings:
If this be love, me-thinks it is too violent:
If you repent you of your strictnesse to me,
It is so sudden, it wants circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Fy, how dull?
prose:
2. Song.
How long shall I pine for love?
how long shall I sue in vaine?
How long like the Turtle-Dove
shall I heavily thus complain?
Shall the sayles of my love stand still?
Shall the grists of my hopes be unground?
Oh fie, oh fie, oh fie,
let the Mill, let the Mill go round.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Prethee be calme a little,
Thou mak'st me wonder, thou that wert so strange,
And read such pious rules to my behaviour
But yesternight: thou that wert made of modestie,
Shouldst in a few short minutes turn thus desperate.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: You are too cold.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I do confesse I freeze now,
I am another thing all over me:
It is my part to wooe, not to be courted:
Unfold this Riddle, 'tis to me a wonder,
That now o'th' instant ere I can expect,
Ere I can turn my thoughts, and think upon
A separation of your honest carriage
From the desires of youth, thus wantonly,
Thus beyond expectation.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I will tell ye,
And tell ye seriously, why I appear thus,
To hold ye no more ignorant and blinded,
I have no modestie, I am truly wanton:
I am that you look for Sir; now come up roundly:
If my strict face and counterfeited stalednesse
Could have won on ye, I had caught ye that way,
And you should ne'r have come to have known who hurt ye.
Prethee (sweet Count) be more familiar with me.
How ever we are open in our natures,
And apt to more desires then you dare meet with,
Yet we affect to lay the glosse of good on 't:
I saw you toucht not at the baite of chastity,
And that it grew distastefull to pour palate
To appear so holy, therefore I take my true shape:
Is your bed ready Sir? you shall quickly find me.
prose:
3. Song.
On the bed Ile throw thee, throw thee downe;
Down being laid, shall we be afraid
to try the rights that belong to love?
No, no, there Ile wooe thee with a Crown,
crown our desires, kindle the fires,
when love requires we should wanton prove:
We'll kisse, we'll sport, we'll laugh, we'll play,
If thou com'st short, for thee Ile stay,
If thou unskilfull art the ground,
Ile kindly teach, we'll have the Mill go round.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Are ye no maid?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Alas (my Lord) no certain:
I am sorry you are so innocent to think so,
Is this an age for silly maids to thrive in?
It is so long too since I lost it Sir,
That I have no belief I ever was one:
What should you do with maiden-heads? you hate'em,
They are peevish pettish things, that hold no game up,
No pleasure neither, they are sport for Surgeons:
I'll warrant you I'll fit you beyond Maiden-head:
A fair and easie way men travel right in,
And with delight, discourse, and twenty pleasures,
They enjoy their journey; mad men creep through hedges.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I am metamorphosed: why do you appeare,
I conjure ye, beyond belief thus wanton?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Because I would give ye
Pleasure beyond belief.
prose:
4. Song.
Think me still in my Fathers Mill,
where I have oft been found-a
Thrown on my back, on a well-fill'd sack,
while the Mill has still gone round-a:
Prethee sirrha try thy skill,
and again let the mill go round-a.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Then you have traded?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Traded? how should I know else how to live Sir,
And how to satisfie such Lords as you are,
Our best guests, and our richest?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: How I shake now?
You take no base men?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Any that will offer,
All manner of men, and all Religions Sir,
We touch at in our time: all States and Ages,
We exempt none.
prose:
5. Song.
The young one, the old one, the fearful, the bold one,
the lame one, though nere so unsound,
The Jew or the Turk, have leave for to work,
the whilest that the Mill goes round,

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: You are a common thing then.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No matter since you have your private pleasure,
And have it by an Artist excellent,
Whether I am thus, or thus, your men can tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: My men? Defend me, how I freeze together,
And am on ice? do I bite at such an Orange
After my men? I am preferr'd.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Why stay ye?
Why do we talk my Lord, and lose our time?
Pleasure was made for lips, and sweet embraces,
Let Lawyers use their tongues: pardon me Modestie,
This desperate way must help, or I am miserable.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: She turns, and wipes her face, she weeps for certain,
Some new way now, she cannot be thus beastly,
She is too excellent fair to be thus impudent:
She knows the elements of common loosenesse,
The art of lewdnesse: that, that, that, how now, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: The King (and't please your Lordship) is alighted Close at the gate.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: The King?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: And calls for ye Sir.
Means to break-fast here too.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Then I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Stolne so suddenly? go lock her up,
Lock her up where the Courtiers may not see her,
Lock her up closely, sirrha, in my closet.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I will (my Lord) what does she yeeld yet?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Peace:
She is either a damnd divel, or an Angel,
No noise (upon your life Dame) but all silence.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Your Majesty he^ps too much honour on me,
With such delight to view each several corner
Of a rude pile: there's no proportion in't, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Me-thinks 'tis hansom, and the rooms along
Are neat, and well contriv'd: the Gallery
Stands pleasantly and sweet: what rooms are these?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: They are sluttish ones.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Nay, I must see.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Pray ye do Sir,
They are lodging-chambers over a homely garden.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Fit still, and hansom; very well: and those?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
prose: Those lead to the other side o'th' house, and't like ye.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Let me see those.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Ye may, the dores are open.
What should this view mean? I am half suspicious.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: This little Room?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Tis mean: a place for trash Sir,
For rubbish of the house.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I would see this too:
I will see all.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I beseech your Majesty,
The savour of it, and the course appearance.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: 'Tis not so bad, you would not offend your house with it,
Come, let me see.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Faith Sir,

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I'faith I will see.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: My Groom has the key Sir, and 'tis ten to one

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: But I will see it: force the lock (my Lords)
There be smithes enough to mend it: I perceive
You keep some rare things here, you would not show Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ter.
verse: Here's a fair maid indeed.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: By my faith is she
A hansom girle: come forward, do not fear wench.
I marry, here's a treasure worth concealing:
Call in the Miller.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Then I am discovered.
I confesse all before the Miller comes Sir,
'Twas but intention, from all act I am cleer yet.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Is this your daughter?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: Yes, and 't please your Highnesse.
This is the shape of her, for her substance Sir,
Whether she be now honourable or dishonourable:
Whether she be a white-rose, or a canker, is the question:
I thank my Lord, he made bold with my Philly,
If she be for your pace, you had best preserve her Sir,
She is tender mouthed, let her be broken hansomly.
Maid, were you stolne?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I went not willingly,
And 't please your Grace, I was never bred so boldly.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: How has he us'd ye?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Yet Sir, very nobly.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Be sure ye tell truth, and be sure (my Lord)
You have not wrongd her: if ye have, I tell ye
You have lost me, and your self too: speak again (wench)

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: He has not wrong'd me, Sir; I am yet a maid:
By all that's white and innocent, I am Sir,
Onely I sufferd under strong temptations
The heat of youth; but heaven deliverd me.
My Lord, I am no whore, for all I faign'd it,
And faign'd it cunningly, and made ye loath me:
'Twas time to out-do you: I had been robd else,
I had been miserable, but I forgive ye.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What recompence for this?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: A great one Sir,
First a repentance, and a hearty one.
Forgive me Sweet.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: I do my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: I thank ye;
The next take this, and these: all I have Florimell.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: No good my Lord, these often corrupt maidens:
I dare not touch at these; they are lime for Virgins;
But if you'll give me.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Any thing in my power.
Or in my purchase.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Take heed (noble Sir)
You'll make me a bold asker.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Aske me freely.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Ask you? I do ask you, and I deserve ye,
I have kept ye from a crying sin would damne ye
To Men and Time: I have preserv'd your credit,
That would have died to all posterity:
Curses of maids shall never now afflict ye,
Nor Parents bitter tears make your name barren:
If he deserves well that redeems his Countrey,
And as a Patriot be remembred nobly,
Nay, set the highest: may not I be worthy
To be your friend, that have preservd your honor?

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: You are, and thus I take ye: thus I seal ye
Mine owne, and onely mine.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Count, she deserves ye,
And let it be my happines to give ye,
I have given a vertuous maid, now I dare say it,
'Tis more then blood; I'll pay her portion Sir,
And't shall be worthy you.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I'll sell my Mill,
I'll pay some too: I'll pay the Fidlers,
And we'll have all i' th' Country at this wedding,
Pray let me give her too, here my Lord take her,
Take her with all my heart, and kisse her freely,
Would I could give you all this hand has stolne too,
In portion with her, 'twould make her a little whiter.
The wind blows fair now, get me a young Miller.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Shee must have new clothes.

speeches.speaker: Tir.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Yes marry must she.
If't please ye (Madam) let me see the state of you body.
I'll fit you instantly.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Art not thou gone yet?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: And 't please your Grace, a gown, a handsome gown now,
An orient gown.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Nay, take thy pleasure of her.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Of cloth of Tissew I can fit ye (Madam)
My Lords, stand out o'th' light, a curious body,
The neatest body in Spain this day: wth embroidred flowrs,
A clinquant Petticoat of some rich stuffe,
To catch the eye: I have a thousand fashions.
O sleeve, O sleeve: I'll study all night (Madam)
To magnifie your sleeve.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Do, superstitious Tailor,
When yee have more time.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
verse: Make me no more then woman,
And I am thine.

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: Sir, haply my Wardrobe with your help
May fit her instantly: will you try her?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: If I fit her not, your Wardrobe cannot.
But if the fashion be not there, you marre her.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Is my offence so great, ere I be convict,
To be torn with Rascals? If it be Law,
Let 'm be wild horses, rather then these.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: This is a man suspected of murder, if it please your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: It pleases me not (friend). But who suspects him?

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: We that are your Highnes extraordinary officers,
We that have taken our oaths to maintain you in peace.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: 'Twill be a great charge to you.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: 'Tis a great charge indeed; but then we call our neighbours to help us. This Gentleman and another were fallen out (yet that's more then I am able to say, for I heard no words between 'em, but what their weapons spoke, Clash, and Clatter) which we seeing, came with our Bils of government, and first knock'd down their weapons, and then the men.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: And this you did to keep the peace?

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Yes, and 't like your Grace, we knock'd 'em down to keep the peace: this we laid hold on, the other we set in the stocks. That I could do by mine own power, without your Majestie.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: How so, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Const.
verse: I am a Shoo-maker by my Trade.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Oh my husband!
Why stands my husband as a man endanger'd?
Restore him me, as you are mercifull,
I'll answer for him.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: What woman's this? what husband? hold thy bawling,
I know thee for no wife.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You married me last night.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Thou lyest: I neither was in Church nor house
Last night, nor saw I thee: a thing that was my friend,
I scorne to name now, was with Ismenia,
Like a thief, and there he violated
A sacred trust. This thou maist know (Aminta).

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Are not you hee?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: No; nor a friend of his:
Would I had kill'd him: I hope I have.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: That was my husband (Royall Sir) that man,
That excellent man.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: That villain, that theefe.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Have I caught you Sir? well overtaken.
This is mine enemie: pardon (my Soveraigne).

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Good charitie, to crave pardon for your enemie.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Mine own pardon (Sir) for my joyes rudenesse:
In what place better could I meet my foe,
And both of us so well provided too?
Hee with some black blood-thirstie crime upon him,
That (ere the horse-leech burst) will suck him dry:
I with a second accusation,
Enough to break his neck, if need should be,
And then to have even Justice self to right us:
How should I make my joyes a little civill,
They might not keep this noyse?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Here is some hope.
Should the ax be dull, the halter's preparing.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: What's your accusation, Sir? We have heard the former.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Mine (My Lord)? a strong one.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: A false one, Sir.
At least malicious: an evidence
Of hatred and despight: He would accuse
My poor kinsman of that he never dream'd of,
Nor waking saw; the stealing of his daughter,
She whom, I know, he would not look upon.
Speak Antonio, Didst thou ever see her?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Yes Sir, I have seen her.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Ah ha, friend Julio.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: He might, but how? with an unheedfull eye,
An accidentall view, as men see multitudes
That the next day dare not precisely say
They saw that face, or that amongst 'm all,
Didst thou so look on her?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Guilty, guilty:
His looks hang themselves.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Your patience (Gentleman).
I pray you tell me if I be in errour,
I may speak often when I should but hear:
This is some Show you would present us with,
And I do interrupt it: Pray you speak,
(It seems no more) Is 't any thing but a Show?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: My Lord, this Gentlewoman can show you all,
So could my daughter too, if shee were here;
By this time they are both immodest enough:
Shee's fled me, and I accuse this thief for't.
Don Martin, his own friend 's my testimony:
A practis'd night-work.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: That Martin's the other
In your custodie; he was forgotten:
Fetch him hither.

speeches.speaker: Const.
prose: Wee'll bring the Stocks and all else, and't please your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: That man's my husband certain, instead of this:
Both would have deceiv'd, and both beguil'd.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Soh hoh, Miller, Miller, look out Miller: is there nere a Miller amongst you here, Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Tir.
verse: Yes Sir, here is a Miller amongst Gentlemen,
A Gentleman Miller.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: I should not be far off then; there went but a pair of sheers and a bodkin between us. Will you to work Miller? Here's a maid has a sack full of newes for you, shall your stones walk? will you grind Miller?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: This your son, Franio?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: My ungratious, my disobedient,
My unnaturall, my rebell son (my Lord).

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Fie, your hopper runs over, Miller.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: This villain (of my own flesh & blood) was accessary
To the stealing of my daughter.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Oh mountain,
Shalt thou call a molehill a scab upon the face
Of the earth? Though a man be a thief, shall a Miller call
Him so? Oh egregious!

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Remember Sirha, who you speak before.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I speak before a Miller,
A thief in grain; for he steals corn: He that steals
A wench, is a true man to him.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: Can you prove that? you may help another cause that was in pleading.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I'll prove it strongly.
He that steals corn, steals the bread of the Co~mon-wealth;
He that steals a wench, steals but the flesh.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: And how is the bread stealing more criminall then the flesh?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Hee that steals bread, steals that which is lawfull every day:
He that steals flesh, steals nothing from the fasting day:
Ergo, To steal the bread is the arranter theft.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: This is to some purpose.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Again, He that steals flesh, steals for his own belly full:
He that steals bread, robs the guts of others:
Ergo, The arranter theef the bread-stealer.
prose: Again, He that steals flesh, steals once, and gives over; yes, and often payes for it: the other steals every day, without satisfaction. To conclude, Bread-stealing is the more capitall crime: for what he steals hee puts it in at the head: hee that steals flesh (as the Dutch Author sayes) puts it in at the foot, (the lower member.) Will you go as you are now, Miller?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: How has this satisfied you, Don Bellides?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Nothing (my Lord,) my cause is serious.
I claim a daughter from that loving theefe there.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I would I had her for you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Ah ha, Julio.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: How said you (Antonio)? Wish you you had his daughter?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: With my soul I wish her; and my body
Shall perish, but I'll enjoy my souls wish.
I would have slain my friend for his deceit,
But I do find his own deceit hath paid him.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Will you vex my soul forth? no other choice
But where my hate is rooted? Come hither Girl,
Whose pretty maid art thou?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: The child of a poor man, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: The better for it. With my Soveraigns leave,
I'll wed thee to this man, will hee, nill he.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Pardon me, Sir, I'll be no Love enforcer:
I use no power of mine unto those ends.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Wilt thou have him?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Not unlesse he love me.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I do love thee: Farewell all other Beauties:
I settle here: You are Ismenia.

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: The same I was: better nor worse (Antonio)

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: I shall have your consent here, I'm sure, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: With all my heart, Sir. Nay, if you accept it,
I'll do this kindnesse to mine enemie,
And give her as a Father.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: Shee'll thank you as a Daughter.
Will you not, Ismenia?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: How? Ismenia?

speeches.speaker: Ism.
verse: Your daughter, Sir.

speeches.speaker: B^l
verse: ssiPoble? Away you feeble witted things,
You thought you had caught the old ones: You wade, you wade
In shallow fords: Wee can swim, we: look here,
We made the match: we are all friends, good friends;
Thin, thin: why the fool knew all this, this fool.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Keep that to your self, Sir; What I knew I knew: This Sack is a witnesse. Miller, this is not for your thumming. Here's gold lace: you may see her in her holliday clothes if you will; I was her ward-robe-man.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You beguil'd me well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Did you speak to me, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: It might seem to you (Martin), your conscience
Has quick ears.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: My sight was a little dim i'th' dark, indeed,
So was my feeling cozen'd; yet I'm content:
I am the better understander now,
I know my wife wants nothing of a woman;
There y'are my Junior.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You are not hurt?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Not shrewdly hurt; I have good flesh to heal, you see,
Good round flesh: these cherries wil be worth chopping,
Crack stones and all; I should not give much to boot
To ride in your new, and you in my old ones now.

speeches.speaker: Ant.
verse: You mistake the weapon: are you not hurt?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A little scratch: but I shal claw it off wel enough.

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: I can no longer own what is not mine
With a free conscience: My Liege, your pardon.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: For what? Who knows this woman?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I best (my Lord),
I have been acquainted with her these fortie Summers,
And as many Winters, were it Spring agen;
She's like the Gout, I can get no cure for her.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Oh, your wife, Franio?

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: 'Tis oh my wife indeed (my Lord,)
A painfull stitch to my side; would it were pick'd out.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Well Sir, your silence.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Wil you be older and older every day then other? the longer you live the older still? Must his Majestie command your silence ere you'l hold your tongue?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Your reprehension runs into the same fault:
Pray Sir, will you be silent.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I have told him of this before now (my Liege) but
Age will have his course, and his weaknesses,

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Good Sir, your forbearance.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: And his frailties, and his follies (as I may say) that cannot hold his tongue ere he be bidden.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Why Sirha?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: But I beleeve your Majestie will not be long troubled with him: I hope that woman has something to confesse will hang 'em both.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Sirha, you'll pull your destinie upon you
If you cease not the sooner.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Nay, I have done, my Liege; yet it grieves me that I should call that man Father, that should be so shamelesse, that being commanded to hold his tongue.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: To th' Porters Lodge with him.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: I thank your Grace, I have a friend there.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Speak woman, if any interruption meet thee more,
It shall be punish'd sharply.

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: Good my Liege (I dare not)
Ask you the question why that old man weeps.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Who? Count Julio? I observ'd it not.
You hear the question Sir, will you give the cause?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh my Lord, it hardly will get passage,
It is a sorrow of that greatnesse grown,
'Lesse it dissolve in tears, and come by parcels.

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: I'll help you Sir, in the delivery,
And bring you forth a joy. You lost a daughter.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: 'Twas that recounted thought brought forth these sorrows.

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: Shee's found again. Know you this mantle Sir?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Hah?

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: Nay leave your wonder, I'll explain it to you.
This did enwrap your childe (whom ever since.
I have call'd mine) when Nurse Amaranta
In a remove from Mora to Corduba
Was seiz'd on by a fierce and hungry Bear,
She was the Ravins prey, as heaven so would,
He with his booty fill'd, forsook the babe:
All this was in my sight: and so long I saw,
Untill the cruell creature left my sight,
At which advantage I adventur'd me
To rescue the sweet Lamb: I did it Sir,
And ever since I have kept back your joy,
And made it mine: but age hath wearied me,
And bids me back restore unto the owner
What I unjustly kept these fourteen yeers.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh, thou hast ta'n so many yeers from mee,
And made me young, as was her birth-day to me.
Oh (good my Liege) give my joyes a pardon,
I must go powre a blessing on my child,
Which here would be too rude and troublesome.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Franio, you knew this before.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Oh, oh; Item for you Miller.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: I did (my Liege) I must confesse I did,
And I confesse, I ne'r would have confess'd,
Had not that womans tongue begun to me:
We poor ones love, and would have comforts, Sir,
As well as great: this is no strange fault, Sir,
There's many men keep other mens children
As though they were their own.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: It may stretch farther yet, I beseech you (my Liege) let this woman be a little farther examin'd; let the words of her conscience be search'd. I would know how she came by me: I am a lost childe, if I be theirs: though I have been brought up in a mill, yet I had ever a minde (me thought) to be a greater man.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Shee will resolve you sure.

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: I, I Boy: thou art mine own flesh and blood,
Born of mine own body.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: 'Tis very unlikely that such a body should bear me; There's no trust in these millers. Woman, tell the truth: my father shall forgive thee, whatsoever he was, were hee Knight, Squire, or Captain; lesse he should not be.

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: Thou art mine own child, Boy.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: And was the Miller my Father?

speeches.speaker: Gill.
verse: Wouldst thou make thy mother a whore, Knave?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: I, if she make me a Bastard. The rack must make her confesse (my Lord) I shall never come to know who I am else. I have a worshipfull mind in mee sure: mee thinks I do scorn poor folks.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Here comes the brightest glory of the day:
Love yoak'd with love, the best equality,
Without the levell of estate or person.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: You both shall be rewarded bountifully,
Wee'll be a-kin too; Brother and Sister
shall be chang'd with us ever.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
prose: Thank you (Unkle) my sister is my cosen yet at the last cast: Farewell sister foster. If I had known the Civill law would have allowed it, thou hadst had another manner of husband then thou hast: but much good doe thee; I'll dance at thy wedding, kisse the Bride, and so.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Why, how now sirha?

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: 'Tis lawfull now, she's none of my Sister.
It was a Miller and a Lord
That had a scabberd and a sword,
He put it up in the Country word
The Miller and his daughter.
Shee has a face, and she can sing,
Shee has a Grace, and she can spring,
Shee has a place with another thing
Tradoodle.

speeches.speaker: Fra.
verse: A knavish Brother of yours (my Lord).

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: would I were acquainted with your Tailor (Noble Brother).

speeches.speaker: Otr.
verse: You may, there he is a mine, newly entertain'd.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: If you have any work for me, I can fit you Sir,
I fitted the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: My Sister (Tailor,) what fits her wil hardly fit me.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Who fits her may fit you Sir, the Tailor can do both.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: You have a true yard (Tailor.)

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Ne'r a whit too long, I warrant you.

speeches.speaker: Bust.
verse: Then (Tailor) march with me away,
I scorn these robes, I must be gay,
My Noble Brother, he shall pay
Tom Tailor.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Your recovered friendships are sound, Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: At heart, at heart (my Lord) the worm shall not
Beyond many ages find a breach to enter at.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: These Lovers unities I will not doubt of:
How happy have you made our Progresse then,
To be the witnesse of such fair Accords?
Come, now we'll eat with you (my Lord Otrante,)
'Tis a charge sav'd: You must not grudge your guest,
'Tis both my Welcome, and your Wedding-Feast.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: YOu buz into my head strange likelihoods,
and fill mee full of doubts; But what proofes (Niger,)
what certainties, that my most noble Brother
came to his end by murther? Tel me that,
assure me by some circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Niger
verse: I will Sir.
And as I tell you truth, so the gods prosper me.
I have often nam'd this Aper.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: True, ye have done:
and in mysterious senses I have heard ye
break out o'th' sudden, and abruptly.

speeches.speaker: Niger
verse: True, Sir.
Fear of your unbeliefe, and the Times giddinesse
made me I durst not then go farther. So your Grace please
out of your wonted goodnesse to give credit,
I shall unfold the wonder.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Do it boldly:
you shall have both our hearty loves, and hearings.

speeches.speaker: Niger
verse: This Aper then, this too much honourd villain,
(for he deserves no mention of a good man)
great Sir, give ear: This most ungratefull, spightfull,
above the memory of mankind mischievous,
with his owne bloody hands.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Take heed.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: I am in, Sir;
and if I make not good my Storie.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Forward:
I see a Truth would break out: be not fearfull.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: I say, this Aper, and his damn'd Ambition,
cut off your Brothers hopes, his life, and fortunes:
the honourd Numerianus fell by him,
fell basely, most untimely, and most treacherously:
For in his Litter, as he bore him company,
most privately and cunningly he kill'd him;
yet still hee fils the faithfull Souldiers ears
with stories of his weaknesse; of his life;
that he dare not venture to appear in open,
and shew his warlike face among the souldiers;
the tendernesse and weaknesse of his eyes,
being not able to endure the Sun yet.
Slave that he is, he gives out this infirmitie
(because hee would dispatch his honour too)
to arise from wantonnesse, and love of women,
and thus he juggles still.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: O most pernitious,
most bloody, and most base! Alas, deer Brother,
art thou accus'd, and after death thy memory
loaden with shames and lies? Those pious tears
thou daily showerdst upon my fathers Monument,
(when in the Persian Expedition
he fell unfortunately by a stroak of thunder)
made thy defame and sins? Those wept out eyes,
the fair examples of a noble Nature,
those holy drops of Love, turn'd by depravers
(malitious poyson'd tongues) to thy abuses?
We must not suffer this.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: It shows a truth now:
and sure this Aper is not right nor honest,
hee will not now come neer me.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: No, he dare not:
He has an inmate here, thats call'd a conscience,
bids him keep off.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: My Brother honourd him,
made him first Captain of his Guard, his next friend;
then to my mother (to assure him neerer)
he made him husband.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: And withall ambitious:
for when he trod so nigh, his false feet itch'd Sir,
to step into the State.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: If ye beleeve, Brother,
Aper a bloody knave (as 'tis apparant)
Let's leave disputing, and do something Noble.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Sister be rul'd, I am not yet so powerfull,
to meet him in the field: He has under him
the flower of all the Empire, and the strength,
the Brittain and the Germain Cohorts; pray ye be patient.
Niger, how stands the Souldier to him?

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: In fear, more Sir,
then love or honour: he has lost their fair affections,
by his most covetous and greedy griping.
Are ye desirous to do something on him,
that all the world may know ye lov'd your Brother?
and do it safely too, without an Army?

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Most willingly.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: Then send out a Proscription,
send suddenly: And to that man that executes it,
(I mean, that brings his head) add a fair payment,
no common summe: then ye shall see, I fear not,
even from his own camp, from those men that follow him,
follow, and flatter him, we shall find one,
and if he misse, one hundred that will venture it.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: For his reward, it shall be so, deer Brother,
so far I'll honour him that kils the villain:
for so far runs my love to my dead Brother,
let him be what he will; base, old, or crooked,
hee shall have Me: Nay, which is more, I'll love him.
I will not be denyde.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: You shall not, Sister.
But ye shall know, my Love shall go along too:
See a Proscription drawn; And for his recompence,
my Sister, and half partner in the Empire:
and I will keep my word.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: Now ye do bravely.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: And though it cost my life, I'll see it publish'd.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Away then, for the businesse.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: I am gone, Sir:
you shall have all dispatch'd to night.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Be prosperous.

speeches.speaker: Aur.
verse: And let the villain fall.

speeches.speaker: Nig.
verse: Fear nothing Madam.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: 'Tis true, that Diocles is courteous,
and of a pleasant nature, sweet and temperate:
his Cosen Maximinian, proud and bloody.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Yes: and mistrustfull too (my Girl) take heed,
although he seem to love thee, and affect
like the more Courtier, curious complement,
yet have a care.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: You know all my affection,
and all my heart-desires is set on Diocles.
But (Aunt) how coldly he requites this courtesie,
how dull and heavily he looks upon me,
although I woo him sometimes beyond modestie,
beyond a Virgins care: how still he flights me,
and puts me still off with your Prophecie,
and the performance of your late Prediction,
that when he is Emperor, then he will marry me,
alas, what hope of that?

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Peace, and be patient,
for though he be now a man most miserable,
of no rank, nor no badge of honour on him,
bred low and poor, no eye of favour shining:
And though my sure Prediction of his Rising
(which can no more faile, then the day or night do's,
nay, let him be asleep, will overtake him)
have found some rubs and stops, yet hear me Neece,
and hear me with a faith, it shall come to him.
I'll tell thee the occasion.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Do good Aunt:
for yet I am ignorant.

speeches.speaker: Del.
verse: Chiding him one day
for being too neer, and sparing for a Souldier,
too griping, and too greedy: he made answer,
When I am Caesar, then I will be liberall.
I presently inspir'd with holy fire,
and my Prophetick spirit burning in me,
gave answer from the gods; and this it was,
Imperator eris Romae, cum Aprum grandem interfeceris:
Thou shalt be Emperor, O Diocles,
when thou hast kill'd a mighty Boar. From that time
(as giving credit to my words) hee has imploy'd
much of his life in hunting. Many Boars
hideous and fierce, with his own hands he has kild too,
but yet not lighted on the fatall one,
should raise him to the Empire: Be not sad Neece,
ere long he shall: Come, lets go entertain him;
for by this time, I ghesse, he comes from hunting:
And by my art, I find this very instant
some great designe 's afoot.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: The gods give good, Aunt.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Lay down the Boar.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: With all my heart; I am weary on't:
I shall turn Jew, if I carry many such burthens.
Do you think (Master) to be Emperor
with killing Swine? ye may be an honest Butcher,
or allied to a seemly Family of Sowse-wives.
Can you be such an asse, my reverend Master,
to think these Springs of Pork will shoot up Caesars?

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: The fool sayes true.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Come leave your fooling, Sirha,
and think of what thou shalt be when I am Emperor.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Would it would come with thinking: for then o' my conscience
I should be at least a Senator.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: A Sowter:
for that's a place more fitted to thy nature,
if there could be such an expectation.
Or say the Divel could perform this wonder,
Can such a Rascall as thou art hope for honour?
such a log-carrying Lowt?

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Yes, and bear it too,
and bear it swimmingly. I am not the first Asse, Sir,
has born good Office, & perform'd it reverendly.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
prose: Thou being the son of a Tanner, canst thou hope to be a Senator?

speeches.speaker: Get.
prose: Thou being son of a Tanner, canst thou hope to be an Emperour?

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: Thou saist true Geta, there's a stop indeed;
but yet the bold and vertuous —

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: Ye are right, Master,
right as a gun: For we the vertuous,
though we be kennel-rakers, scabs, and scowndrels,
wee the discreet and bold: and yet, now I remember it,
We Tilers may deserve to be Senators;
and there we step before you thick-skin'd Tanners,
for we are born three Stories high; no base ones,
none of your groundlings, Master.

speeches.speaker: Dio.
verse: I like thee well,
thou hast a good mind, as I have, to this Honour.

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: As good a mind Sir, of a simple plaisterer—
and when I come to execute my Office,
then you shall see.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Get.
verse: An Officer in fury;
