speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Bid me be wise, and keep me where I am,
and so be safe: not come, because commanded;
Was it not thus?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: It was, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: What now think ye?

speeches.speaker: Swet.
prose: Must come, so hainous to him, so distastefull?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Give me my money.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: I confesse 'tis due Sir,
and presently I'll pay it.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: His obedience
so blind at his yeers and experience,
it cannot find where to be tendred?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: Sir,
the Regiment was willing, and advanc'd too,
the Captains at all points steel'd up; their preparations
full of resolve, and confidence; Youth and fire,
like the fair breaking of a glorious day,
guilded their Falanx: when the angrie Penyus
stept like a stormy cloud 'twixt them and hopes.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: And stopt their resolutions?

speeches.speaker: Ma.
verse: True: his reason
to them was ods, and ods so infinite,
discretion durst not look upon.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Well Penyus,
I cannot think thee coward yet; and treacherous
I dare not think: thou hast lopt a limb off from me,
and let it be thy glory, thou wast stubborn,
thy wisdome, that thou leftst thy Generall naked:
Yet ere the Sun set, I shall make thee see,
all valour dwels not in thee; all command
in one experience. Thou wilt too late repent this,
and wish, I must come up, had been thy blessing.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Let's force him.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: No, by no means; he's a torrent
we cannot easily stemme.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I think, a Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: No il words: let his own shame first revile him.
That wine I have, see it (Demetrius)
distributed amongst the souldiers,
to make 'em high and lustie: when that's done,
Petillius, give the word through, that the Eagles
may presently advance: no man discover,
upon his life, the enemies full strength,
but make it of no value: Decius,
are your starv'd people yet come home?

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: I hope so.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Keep 'em in more obedience: This is no time
to chide, I could be angry else, and say more to ye:
But come, let's order all: whose sword is sharpest,
and valour equall to his sword this day,
shall be my saint.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: We shall be holy all then.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Captain, Captain, I have brought 'em off again;
the drunkenest slaves.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: — confound your Rogueships;
I'll call the Generall, and have ye hang'd all.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Pray who will you command then?

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: For you, sirha,
that are the ring-leader to these devises,
whose maw is never cramm'd, I'll have an engine.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: A wench, sweet Captain.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Sweet Judas, even the Forks.
where ye shall have two Lictors with two whips
hammer your hide.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Captain, good words, fair words,
sweet words, good Captain; if you like not us,
farewell, we have imployment.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Where hast thou been?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: There where you dare not be with all your valour.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Where's that?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: With the best good-fellow living.

speeches.speaker: 1 Soul.
verse: The king of all good-fellows.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Caratach.
Shake now, and say, wee have done something worthie,
mark me; with Caratach: By this — Caratach:
Do you asmuch now and you dare: sweet Caratach.
Ye talk of a good fellow, of true drinking;
wel, go thy waies, old Caratach: besides the drink Captain,
the bravest running banquet of black puddings,
peeces of glorious beef.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: How scapt ye hanging?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Hanging's a dogs death: we are Gentlemen,
and I say still, Old Caratach.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Belike then,
you are turn'd Rebels all.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: We are Roman boyes all,
and boyes of mettle: I must doe that Captain,
this day, this very day.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Away, ye Rascal.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Fair words, I say again.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: What must you doe, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: I must do that my heart-strings yern to do:
but my word's past.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: What is it?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Why, kill Caratach.
that's all he ask'd us for our entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: More then you'll pay.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Would I had sold my self
unto the skin, I had not promis'd it:
for such another Caratach.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Come Fool,
have ye done your Country service?

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: I have brought that
to Captain Iunius.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: I think will doe all:
I cannot tell, I think so.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: How? to Iunius?
I'll more enquire of this: You'll fight now?

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Promise:
take heed of promise, Captain.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Away, and rank then.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: But heark ye Captain, there is wine distributing,
I would fain know what share I have.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Be gone,
ye have too much.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Captain, no wine, no fighting.
there's one call'd Caratach, that has wine.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Well Sir,
if you'll be rul'd now, and doe well.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Doe excellent.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Ye shall have wine, or any thing: goe file;
I'll see ye have your share: drag out your dormise,
and stow 'em somwhere, where they may sleep handsomly,
they'l hear a hunt's up shortly.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Now I love thee:
but no more Forks nor Whips.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Deserve 'em not then:
up with your men, I'll meet ye presently;
and get 'em sober quickly.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Arm, arm, Bullyes;
all's right again and straight; and which is more,
more wine, more wine: Awake ye men of Memphis,
be sober and discreet, we have much to do boyes.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: Prepare there for the Sacrifice, the Queen comes.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Ye powerfull gods of Britain, hear our prayers;
hear us you great Revengers, and this day
take pitie from our swords, doubt from our valours,
double the sad remembrance of our wrongs
in every brest; the vengeance due to those
make infinite and endlesse: on our pikes
this day pale terror sit, horrors and ruines
upon our executions; claps of thunder
hang on our armed carts, and 'fore our Troops
despair and death; shame beyond these attend 'em.
Rise from the dust, ye relicks of the dead,
whose noble deeds our holy Druids sing,
oh rise, ye valiant bones, let not base earth
oppresse your honours, whilest the pride of Rome
treads on your Stocks, and wipes out all your stories.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: Thou great Tiranes, whom our sacred Priests,
armed with dreadfull thunder, place on high
above the rest of the immortall gods,
send thy consuming fires and deadly bolts,
and shoot 'em home; stick in each Roman heart
a fear fit for confusion; blast their spirits,
dwell in 'em to destruction; thorow their Phalanx
strike, as thou strik'st a proud tree; shake their Bodies,
make their strengths totter, and their toplesse fortunes
unroot, and reel to ruine.

speeches.speaker: 1. Daugh.
verse: O thou god,
thou feared god, if ever to thy justice
insulting wrongs, and ravishments of women,
women deriv'd from thee, their shames, the suffrings
of those that daily fill'd thy Sacrifice
with virgin incense, have accesse, now hear me,
now snatch thy thunder up, now on these Romans,
despisers of thy power, of us defacers,
revenge thy self: take to thy killing anger,
to make thy great work full, thy justice spoken,
an utter rooting from this blessed Isle
of what Rome is or has been.

speeches.speaker: Bon.
verse: Give more incense,
the gods are deafe and drowsie; no happy flame
rises to raise our thoughts: Pour on.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: See heaven,
and all you pow'rs that guide us, see, and shame
we kneel so long for pitie over your Altars;
since 'tis no light oblation that you look for,
no incense offring, will I hang mine eyes;
and as I wear these stones with hourly weeping,
so will I melt your pow'rs into compassion.
This tear for Prosutagus my brave Father,
ye gods, now think on Rome; this for my Mother,
and all her miseries; yet see, and save us:
but now ye must be open ey'd. See, heaven,
O see thy showrs stoln from thee; our dishonours,
O sister, our dishonours: can ye be gods,
and these sins smother'd?

speeches.speaker: Bon.
verse: The fire takes.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: It does so,
but no flame rises. Cease your fetrfull prayers,
your whinings, and your tame petitions;
the gods love courage arm'd with confidence,
and prayers fit to pull them down: weak tears
and troubled hearts, the dull twins of cold spirits,
they sit and smile at. Hear how I salute 'em:
Divine Audate, thou who hold'st the reins
of furious Battels, and disordred War,
and proudly roll'st thy swarty chariot wheels
over the heaps of wounds, and carcasses,
sailing through seas of bloud; thou sure-steel'd sternnesse,
give us this day good hearts, good enemies,
good blowes o' both sides, wounds that fear or flight
can claim no share in; steel us both with angers,
and warlike executions fit thy viewing;
let Rome put on her best strength, and thy Britain,
thy little Britain, but as great in fortune,
meet her as strong as shee, as proud, as daring;
and then look on, thou red ey'd god: who does best,
reward with honour; who despair makes flie,
unarme for ever, and brand with infamie:
Grant this, divine Audate, 't is but Justice;
and my first blow thus on thy holy Altar
I sacrifise unto thee.

speeches.speaker: Bon.
verse: It flames out.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Now sing ye Druides.

speeches.speaker: Bon.
verse: 'Tis out again.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: H'as given us leave to fight yet; we ask no more,
the rest hangs in our resolutions:
tempt him no more.

speeches.speaker: Bon.
verse: I would know further Cosen,

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: His hidden meaning dwels in our endeavours;
our valours are our best gods. Cheer the souldier,
and let him eat.

speeches.speaker: Mess.
verse: He's at it, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Away then;
when he has done, let's march. Come, fear not Lady,
this day the Roman gains no more ground here,
but what his body lies in.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Now I am confident.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: We dare not hazzard it: beside our lives,
it forfeits all our understandings.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Gentlemen,
Can ye forsake me in so just a service,
a service for the Common-wealth, for honour?
Read but the Letter; you may love too.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Read it:
if there be any safety in the circumstance,
or likelihood 'tis love, we will not faile ye.
Read it good Curius.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Willingly.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Now mark it.

speeches.speaker: Cur. reads.
verse: Health to thy heart, my honourd Junius,
and all thy love requited: I am thine,
thine everlastingly, thy love has won me,
and let it breed no doubt; our new acquaintance
compels this, 'tis the gods decree to blesse us.
The times are dangerous to meet; yet fail not,
by all the love thou bear'st me I conjure thee,
without distrust of danger, to come to me,
for I have purpos'd a delivery
both of my self and fortune this blest day
into thy hands, if thou thinkst good: to shew thee
how infinite my love is, even my Mother
shall be thy prisoner, the day yours without hazzard;
for I beheld your danger like a Lover,
a just affecter of thy faith: Thy goodnesse,
I know, will use us nobly, and our marriage,
if not redeem, yet lessen Romes Ambition.
I am weary of these miseries: Use my Mother,
(if you intend to take her) with all honour,
and let this disobedience to my parents
be laid on love, not me. Bring with thee, Junius,
spirits resolv'd to fetch me off, the noblest,
forty will serve the turn; just at the joyning
of both the Battels, we will be weakly guarded;
and for a guide, within this hour shall reach thee
a faithfull friend of mine: the gods, my Junius,
keep thee, and me to serve thee: Young Bonvica.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: This letter carries much belief, and most objections
answer'd, we must have doubted.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Is that fellow
come to ye for a guide yet?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: And examin'd?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Far more then that; he has felt tortures, yet
he vows he knows no more then this truth.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Strange.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: If she mean what she writes, as 't may be probable,
'twill be the happiest vantage we can lean to.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I'll pawn my soul she means truth.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Think an hour more,
then if your confidence grow stronger on ye,
we'll set in with ye.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Nobly done; I thank ye;
ye know the time.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: We will be either ready
to give ye present counsell, or joyne with ye.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: No more as ye are Gentlemen. The Generall.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Draw out a pace, the enemy waits for us;
Are ye all ready?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: All our Troops attend, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: I am glad to hear you say so, Junius.
I hope ye are dispossest.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I hope so too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Continue so. And Gentlemen, to you now;
To bid you fight is needlesse, ye are Romans,
the name will fight it self; To tell ye who
you go to fight against, his power, and nature,
but losse of time: ye know it, know it poor,
and oft have made it so. To tell ye further,
his Bodie showes more dreadfull then it has done,
to him that fears, lesse possible to deal with,
is but to stick more honour on your Actions,
load ye with vertuous names, and to your memories
tie never dying time, and fortune constant.
Go on in full assurance, draw your swords
as daring and as confident as Justice;
the gods of Rome fight for ye; loud Fame calls ye,
pitch'd on the toplesse Perinine, and blows
to all the under world: all Nations,
the seas, and unfrequented deserts, where the snow dwels,
wakens the ruin'd monuments, and there
where nothing but eternall death and sleep is,
informs again the dead bones. With your vertues,
go on, I say, valiant and wise, rule heaven,
and all the great aspects attend 'em. Do but blow
upon this Enemy, who, but that we want foes,
cannot deserve that name; and like a myst,
a lazie fog, before your burning valours
you'll finde him flie to nothing. This is all,
We have swords, and are the sons of ancient Romans,
heirs to their endlesse valours, fight and conquer.

speeches.speaker: De. Dem.
verse: 'Tis done.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: That man that loves not this day,
and hugs not in his arms the noble danger,
may he die famelesse and forgot.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Sufficient,
up to your Troops, and let your drums beat thunder,
march close, and sudden like a tempest: all executions
done without sparkling of the Body: keep your phalanx
sure lin'd, and piec'd together; your pikes forward,
and so march like a moving Fort: ere this day run,
we shal have ground to add to Rome, wel won.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: The Roman is advanc'd from yound' hils brow,
we may behold him, Caratach.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Let's thither,
I see the dust flie. Now I see the Body,
observe 'em, Nennius; by — a handsome Body,
and of a few, strongly and wisely joynted
Swetonius is a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: As I take it,
that's hee that gallops by the Regiments,
viewing their preparations.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Very likely,
he shews no lesse then Generall: see how bravely
the Body moves, and in the head how proudly
the Captains stick like plumes: hee comes apace on;
good Nennius go, and bid my stout Leutenant
bring on the first square Bodie to oppose 'em,
and as he charges, open to enclose 'em:
the Queen move next with hers, and wheel about,
to gain their backs, in which I'll lead the Vantguard.
We shall have bloody crowns this day, I see by 't;
Haste thee good Nennius, I'll follow instantly.
How close they march, as if they grew together?
no place but lin'd alike: sure from oppression;
they will not change this figure: we must charge 'em,
and charge 'em home at both ends, Van and Rere,
they never totter else. I hear our Musick,
and must attend it: Hold good sword, but this day,
and bite hard where I hound thee, and hereafter
I'll make a relique of thee, for young Souldiers
to come like Pilgrimes to, and kisse for Conquests.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Now is the time, the fellow stayes.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: What think yee?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: I think 'tis true.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Alas, if 'twere a question,
if any doubt or hazzard fell into 't,
do ye think mine own discretion so self-blinde,
my care of you so naked, to run headlong?

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Let's take Petillius with us.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: By no means:
hee's never wise but to himself, nor courteous,
but where the end's his own: we are strong enough,
if not too many. Behind yonder hill
the fellow tels me she attends, weak guarded,
her Mother and her Sister.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: I would venture.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Wee shall not strike five blows for't: weigh the good,
the generall good may come.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Away, I'll with ye,
but with what doubt?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Fear not, my soul for all.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Here ye may see 'em all, Sir; from this hill
the Country shews off levell.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Gods defend me,
what multitudes they are, what infinites?
the Roman power shews like a little Star
hedg'd with a double halloa. Now the knell rings,
Heark how they shout to th' battell; how the air
totters and reels, and rends apieces, Drusus,
with the huge vollied clamours.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Now they charge.
oh gods, of all sides, fearfully.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Little Rome,
stand but this growing Hydra one short hour,
and thou hast out-done Hercules.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: The dust hides 'em,
we cannot see what follows.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: They are gone,
gone, swallow'd, Drusus; this eternall Sun
shall never see 'em march more.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: O turn this way,
and see a modell of the field, some forty,
against four hundred.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Well fought, bravely follow'd;
O nobly charg'd again, charg'd home too: Drusus,
they seem to carry it: now they charge all,
close, close, I say; they follow it: ye gods,
Can there be more in men? more daring spirits?
stil they make good their fortunes. Now they are gone too,
for ever gone: see Drusus, at their backs
a fearfull Ambush rises. Farewell valours,
excellent valours: O Rome, Where's thy wisdome?

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: They are gone indeed, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Look out toward the Army,
I am heavie with these slaughters.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: 'Tis the same still,
cover'd with dust and fury.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: Bring 'em in,
tie 'em, and then unarm 'em.

speeches.speaker: 1. Daugh.
verse: Valiant Romans,
ye are welcome to your Loves,

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: Your death, fools.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: We deserve 'em,
and women do your worst.

speeches.speaker: 1. Daug.
verse: Ye need not beg it.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daug.
verse: Which is kinde Junius?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: This.

speeches.speaker: 2 Dau.
verse: Are you my sweet heart?
It looks ill on't: how long is 't, pretty soul,
since you and I first lov'd? Had we not reason
to doat extreamly upon one another?
How does my Love? this is not he: my chicken
could prate finely, sing a love-song.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Monster.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: Oh, now it courts.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Arm'd with more malice
then he that got thee has the divell.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: Good.
Proceed, sweet Chick.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I hate thee, that's my last.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daug.
verse: Nay, and ye love me, forward: No? Come sister,
let's prick our answers on our arrows points,
and make 'em laugh a little. Ye damn'd Leachers,
ye proud improvident fools, have we now caught ye?
are ye i'th'noose? Since ye are such loving creatures,
wee'll be your Cupids: Do ye see these arrows?
wee'll send 'em to your wanton livers, goats.

speeches.speaker: 1. Dau.
verse: O how I'll trample on your hearts, ye villains,
ambitious salt-itcht slaves: Romes master sins,
the mountain Rams topt your hot mothers.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: Dogs,
to whose brave Founders a salt whore gave suck;
theeves, honours hangmen, do ye grin? perdition
take me for ever, if in my fell anger,
I doe not out-doe all example.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Where,
where are these Ladies? ye keep noble quarter,
your mother thinks ye dead or taken; upon which,
she will not move her Battell. Sure these faces
I have beheld and known, they are Roman Leaders,
How came they here?

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: A trick Sir, that we us'd,
a certain policie conducted 'em
unto our snare: we have done ye no small service;
these us'd as we intend, we are for th' battell.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: As you intend? taken by treachery?

speeches.speaker: 1. Daugh.
verse: Is't not allow'd?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Those that should gild our Conquest,
make up a Battell worthie of our winning,
catch'd up by craft?

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: By any means that's lawfull.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: A womans wisdome in our triumphs? Out,
out ye sluts, ye follies; from our swords
filch our revenges basely? Arm again, Gentlemen:
Souldiers, I charge ye help 'em.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daugh.
verse: By — Uncle,
we will have vengeance for our rapes.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: By —
you should have kept your legs close then: dispatch there.

speeches.speaker: 1. Daugh.
verse: I will not off thus.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: He that stirs to execute,
or she, though it be your selves, by him that got me,
shall quickly feel mine anger: one great day given us,
not to be snatch'd out of our hands but basely;
and must we shame the gods from whence we have it,
with setting snares for Souldiers? I'll run away first,
be hooted at, and children call me coward,
before I set up scales for Victories:
Give 'em their swords.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daug.
verse: O gods.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Bear off the women
unto their Mother.

speeches.speaker: 2. Daug.
verse: One shot, gentle Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: One cut her fiddle-string: Beat'em off I say.

speeches.speaker: 1. Dau.
verse: The — take this fortune.

speeches.speaker: Cara.
verse: Learn to spin,
and curse your knotted hemp: goe Gentlemen,
safely go off, up to your troops: be wiser,
there thank me like tall Souldiers: I shall seek ye.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: A noble worth.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Well Junius.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Pray ye no more.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: He blushes, do not load him.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Where's your love now?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Puffe, there it flies: Come, let's redeem our follies.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Awake, Sir; yet the Roman Bodie's whole,
I see 'em cleer again.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Whole? 'tis not possible:
Drusus, they must be lost.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: By — they are whole, Sir,
and in brave doing; see, they wheel about
to gain more ground.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: But see there Drusus, see,
see that huge Battell moving from the mountains,
their gilt coats shine like Dragons scales, their march
like a rough tumbling storm; see them, and view 'em,
and then see Rome no more: say they faile; look,
look where the armed carts stand; a new Army:
look how they hang like falling rocks, as murdring
death rides in triumph Drusus: fell destruction
lashes his fiery horse, and round about him
his many thousand wayes to let out soules.
Move me again when they charge, when the mountain
melts under their hot wheels, and from their Ax'trees
huge claps of thunder plough the ground before 'em,
till then I'll dream what Rome was.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: O bravely fought; honour till now nere show'd
her golden face i'th' field. Like lions, Gentlemen,
y' have held your heads up this day: Where's yong Junius,
Curius, and Decius?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Gone to heaven, I think, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sw.
verse: Their worths go with 'em: breath a while: How do ye?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Wel; some few scurvie wounds, my heart's whole yet.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Would they would give us more ground.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Give? wee'll have it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Have it? and hold it too, despight the divell.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
prose: Lead up to th' head, and line sure: the Qs. Battell begins to charge like wild-fire: Where's the Generall?

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Oh, they are living yet. Come, my brave souldiers,
come, let me powr Romes blessing on ye; Live,
live, and lead Armies all: ye bleed hard.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Best:
wee sh^ll appear the sterner to the foe.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: More wounds, more honour.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Lose no time.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Away then,
and stand this shock, ye have stood the world.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Wee'll grow to't.
Is not this better now then lowsie loving?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I am my self, Petillius.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: 'Tis I love thee.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose: Charge 'em i'th' flanks: O ye have plaid the fool, the fool extremely, the mad fool.

speeches.speaker: Bon.
verse: Why Cosin?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: The woman fool. Why did you give the word
unto the carts to charge down, and our people
in grosse before the Enemie? we pay for't,
our own swords cut our throats: why? — on't,
Why do you offer to command? the divell,
the divell, and his dam too, who bid you
meddle in mens affairs?

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I'll help all.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Home,
home and spin woman, spin, go spin, ye trifle.
Open before there, or all's ruine. How,
now comes the tempest; on our selves, by—
O woman, scurvie woman, beastly woman.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Victoria, Victoria.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: How's that, Drusus?

speeches.speaker: Dru.
prose: They win, they win, they win; oh look, look, look, Sir, for heavens sake look, the Britains fly, the Britains fly. Victoria.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Soft, soft, pursue it soft; excellent Souldiers,
close, my brave fellows, honourable Romans:
oh cool thy mettle Junius, they are ours,
the world cannot redeem 'em: stern Petillius,
govern the conquest nobly: soft, good Souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Shame, whither flie ye, ye unluckie Britains?
Will ye creep into your mothers wombs again? Back cowards,
Hares, fearfull Hares, Doves in your angers; leave me?
leave your Queen desolate? her haplesse children
to Roman rape again and fury?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Flie, ye buzzards,
ye have wings enough, ye fear: get thee gone, woman,
shame tread upon thy heels: all's lost, all's lost, heark,
heark how the Romans ring our knels.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Good Uncle,
let me go too.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: No boy, thy fortune's mine,
I must not leave thee; get behind me; shake not,
I'll breech ye, if ye do boy: Come, brave Romans,
all is not lost yet.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
prose: Now I'll thank thee, Caratach.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou art a Souldier: strike home, home; have at ye.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: His blows fall like huge sledges on an anvil.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: I am weary.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: So am I.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Send more swords to me.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Let's sit and rest.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: What think ye now?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: O Drusus,
I have lost mine honour, lost my name,
lost all that was my light: these are true Romans,
and I a Britain coward, a base coward;
guide me where nothing is but desolation,
that I may never more behold the face
of man, or mankind know me: O blind Fortune,
hast thou abus'd me thus?

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Good Sir, be comforted;
it was your wisdome rul'd ye; pray ye go home,
your day is yet to come, when this great fortune
shall be but foile unto it.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
prose: Fool, fool, Coward.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Draw in, draw in: wel have ye fought, and worthie
Romes noble recompence; look to your wounds,
the ground is cold and hurtfull: the proud Queen
has got a Fort, and there she and her Daughters
defie us once again. To morrow morning
wee'll seek her out, and make her know, our Fortunes
stop at no stubborn walls: Come, sons of honour,
true vertues heirs; thus hatch'd with Britain blood,
let's us march to rest, and set in gules like Suns.
Beat a soft march, and each one ease his neighbours.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Smooth was his cheek,

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: And his chin it was sleek,

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: With whoop, he has done wooing.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Junius was this Captains name,
A lad for a lasses viewing,

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Ful black his eye, & plump his thigh.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Made up for loves pursuing:

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Smooth was his cheek,

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And his chin it was sleek.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: With whoop, he has done wooing.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: O my vex'd thief, art thou come home again?
are thy brains perfect?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Sound as bels.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Thy back-worm
quiet, and cast his sting, boy?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Dead, Petillius,
dead to all folly, and now my anger only.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Why, that's wel said: hang Cupid and his quiver,
a drunken brawling Boy; thy honour'd saint
be thy ten shillings, Junius; there's the money,
and there's the ware; square dealing: this but sweats thee
like a nesh nag, and makes thee look pin buttock'd;
the other runs thee whining up and down
like a pig in a storm, fils thy brains full of ballads,
and shews thee like a long Lent, thy brave body
turn'd to a tail of green-fish without butter.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: When thou lov'st next, love a good cup of wine,
a Mistris for a King, she leaps to kisse thee,
her red and white's her own; she makes good blood,
takes none away; what shee heats sleep can help,
without a groping Surgeon.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I am counsell'd,
and henceforth, when I doat again, —

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Take heed,
ye had almost paid for't.

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: Love no more great Ladies,
thou canst not step amisse then; there's no delight in 'em;
all's in the whistling of their snatcht up silks;
they're onely made for handsome view, not handling;
their bodies of so weak and wash a temper,
a rough-pac'd bed will shake 'em all to pieces;
a tough hen puls their teeth out, tyres their souls;
plenae rimarum sunt, they are full of rynnet,
and take the skin off where they are tasted; shun 'em,
they live in cullisses like rotten cocks
stew'd to a tendernesse, that holds no tack:
Give me a thing I may crush.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Thou speak'st truly:
the Warres shall be my Mistris now.

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: Well chosen,
for she's a bownsing lasse, she'll kisse thee at night, boy,
and break thy pate i'th' morning.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Yesterday
I found those favours infinite.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Wench good enough,
but that she talks too loud.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: She talks to th' purpose,
which never woman did yet: shee'll hold grapling,
and he that layes on best, is her best servant:
all other loves are meer catching of dotrels,
stretching of legs out onely, and trim lazinesse.
Here comes the Generall.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: I am glad I have found ye:
Are those come in yet that pursu'd bold Caratach?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Not yet Sir, for I think they mean to lodge him;
take him I know they dare not, 'twill be dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Then haste Petillius, haste to Penyus,
I fear the strong conceit of what disgrace
h'as pull'd upon himself, will be his ruine:
I fear his souldiers fury too; haste presently,
I would not lose him for all Britain. Give him, Petillius,

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: That that shall choak him.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: all the noble counsell,
his fault forgiven too, his place, his honour,

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: For me, I think, as handsome.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: all the comfort;
and tell the Souldier, 'twas on our command
hee drew not to the Battell.

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: I conceive Sir,
and will doe that shall cure all.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Bring him with ye
before the Queens Fort, and his Forces with him,
there you shall find us following of our Conquest:
Make haste.

speeches.speaker: Petil.
verse: The best I may.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: And noble Gentlemen,
Up to your Companies: wee'll presently
upon the Queens pursuit: There's nothing done
till she be seiz'd; without her nothing won.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: How does my Boy?

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I would doe well, my heart's well;
I doe not fear.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: My good boy.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: I know, Uncle,
we must all die; my little brother dy'd,
I saw him die, and he dy'd smiling: sure,
there's no great pain in't Uncle. But pray tell me,
Whither must we goe when we are dead?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Strange questions!
why, to the blessed'st place Boy: ever sweetnesse
and happinesse dwels there.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Will you come to me?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Yes, my sweet boy.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: Mine Aunt too, and my Cosins?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: All, my good childe.

speeches.speaker: Hen.
verse: No Romans, Uncle?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: No, boy.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: I should be loth to meet them there.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: No ill men,
that live by violence, and strong oppression,
come thither: 't is for those the gods love, good men.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Why, then I care not when I go; for surely
I am perswaded they love me: I never
blasphem'd 'em, Uncle, nor transgrest my parents;
I always said my prayers.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou shalt go, then,
indeed thou shalt.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: When they please.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: That's my good boy.
Art thou not weary, Hengo?

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Weary, Uncle?
I have heard you say you have march'd all day in Armour.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I have, boy.

speeches.speaker: Hengo.
verse: Am not I your kinsman?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: And am not I as fully alli'd unto you
in those brave things, as blood?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou art too tender.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: To go upon my legs? they were made to bear me:
I can play twenty mile a day; I see no reason
but, to preserve my Countrey and my self,
I should march fourty.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: What, wouldst thou be
living to wear a mans strength?

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Why a Caratach,
a Romane-hater, a scourge sent from heaven
to whip these proud theeves from our kingdom. Heark,
heark, Uncle, heark, I hear a Drum.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Beat softly,
softly, I say; they are here: who dare charge?

speeches.speaker: 1 Sould.
verse: He
that dares be knockt o' th' head: I'll not come neer him.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Retire again, and watch then. How he stares!
h' as eyes would kill a dragon: mark the boy well;
if we could take or kill him. A — on ye,
how fierce ye look? see how he broods the boy;
the devil dwells in's scabbard. Back, I say,
apace, apace, h' as found us.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Do ye hunt us?

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Uncle, good Uncle see, the thin starv'd Rascal,
the eating Romane, see where he thrids the thickets:
kill him, dear Uncle, kill him; one good blow
to knock his brains into his breech: strike's head off,
that I may pisse in 's face.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Do ye make us Foxes?
Here, hold my charging-staff, and keep the place, boy.
I am at bay, and like a bull I'll bear me.
Stand, stand, ye Rogues, ye Squirrels.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Now he pays 'em:
O that I had a mans strength.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Here's the boy;
mine own, I thank my Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Uncle, uncle;
famine is faln upon me, uncle.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Come, Sir,
yeeld willingly, your uncle 's out of hearing;
I'll tickle your young tail else.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: I defie thee,
thou mock-made man of mat: charge home, sitha:
hang thee, base slave, thou shakest.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Upon my conscience
the boy will beat me: how it looks, how bravely,
how confident the worm is: a scabb'd boy
to handle me thus? yeeld, or I cut thy head off.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Thou dar'st not cut my finger: here 't is, touch it.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: The boy speaks sword and buckler. Prethee yeeld, boy:
come, here 's an apple; yeeld.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: By— he fears me.
I'll give you sharper language: When, ye coward,
when come ye up?

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: If he should beat me—

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: When, Sir?
I long to kill thee; come, thou canst not scape me,
I have twenty ways to charge thee; twenty deaths
attend my bloody staff.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Sure 't is the devil,
a dwarf, devil in a doubler.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
prose: I have kill'd a Captain, sirha, a brave Captain, and when I have done. I have kickt him thus. Look here, see how I charge this staff.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: Most certain
this boy will cut my throat, yet.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sould.
verse: Flee, flee, he kills us.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sould.
verse: He comes, he comes.

speeches.speaker: Iud.
verse: The devil take the hindmost.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Run, run, ye Rogues, ye precious Rogues, ye rank Rogues.
A comes, a comes, a comes, a comes: that 's he, boys.
What a brave cry they make?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: How does my chicken?

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: 'Faith, uncle, grown a Souldier, a great Souldier;
for by the vertue of your charging-staff,
and a strange fighting face I put upon 't,
I have outbrav'd hunger.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: That's my boy, my sweet boy.
Here, here's a Romane 's head for thee.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Good provision.
Before I starve, my sweet-fac'd Gentleman,
I'll trie your favour.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: A right compleat souldier.
Come, chicken, let's go seek some place of strength
(the Countrey 's full of Scouts) to rest a while in,
thou wilt not else be able to endure.
The journey to my Countrey, fruits, and water,
must be your food a while, boy.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Any thing:
I can eat mosse, nay, I can live on anger,
to vex these Romanes. Let 's be wary, Uncle.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I warrant thee; come chearfully.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: And boldly.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: The souldier shall not grieve ye.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Pray ye forsake me;
look not upon me, as ye love your Honours;
I am so cold a coward, my infection
will choke your vertues like a damp else.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Dear Captain.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Most honour'd Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Most hated, most abhor'd;
say so, and then ye know me, nay, ye please me.
O my dear credit, my dear credit.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Sure
his minde is dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: The good gods cure it.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: My honour got thorow fire, thorow stubborn, breaches
thorow battels that have been as hard to win as heaven,
thorow death himself, in all his horrid trims,
is gone for ever, ever, ever, Gentlemen,
and now I am left to scornful tales and laughters,
to hootings at, pointing with fingers, That's he,
that's the brave Gentleman forsook the battel,
the most wise Penyus, the disputing coward.
O my good sword, break from my side, and kill me;
cut out the coward from my heart.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Ye are none.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: He lyes that says so: by— he lyes, lyes basely,
baser then I have done. Come, souldiers, seek me,
I have robb'd ye of your vertues: Justice, seek me,
I have broke my fair obedience, lost: shame take me,
take me, and swallow me, make ballads of me;
shame, endlesse shame: and pray do you forsake me.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: What shall we do?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Good Gentlemen forsake me:
you were not wont to be commanded. Friends, pray do it,
and do not fear; for as I am a coward
I will not hurt my self: when that minde takes me,
I'll call to you, and ask your help. I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Good morrow, Gentlemen; where's the Tribune?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: There.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Whence come ye, good Petillius?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: From the General.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: With what, for heavens sake?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: With good counsel, Drusus,
and love, to comfort him.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Good Regulus
step to the souldier, and allay his anger;
for he is wilde as winter.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: O, are ye there? have at ye. Sure he 's dead,
it cannot be he dare out live this fortune:
he must die, 't is most necessary; men expect it;
and thought of life in him, goes beyond coward.
Forsake the field so basely? fie upon 't:
so poorly to betray his worth? so coldly
to cut all credit from the souldier? sure
if this man mean to live, as I should think it
beyond belief, he must retire where never
the name of Rome, the voice of Arms, or Honour
was known or heard of yet: he 's certain dead,
or strongly means it; he 's no Souldier else,
no Romane in him; all he has done, but outside,
fought either drunk or desperate. Now he rises.
How does Lord Penyus?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: As ye see.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I am glad on 't;
continue so still. The Lord General,
the valiant General, great Swetonius—

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: No more of me is spoken; my name's perish'd.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: He that commanded fortune and the day
by his own valour and discretion,
when, as some say, Penyus refused to come,
but I believe 'em not, sent me to see ye.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Ye are welcom; and pray see me; see me well,
ye shall not see me long.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I hope so, Penyus;
the gods defend, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: See me, and understand me: This is he
lef^ to fill up your triumph; he that basely
whistled his honour off to th' winde; that coldly
shrunk in his politick head, when Rome like reapers
sweat blood, and spirit, for a glorious harvest,
and bound it up, and brought it off: that fool,
that having gold and cupper offer'd him,
refus'd the wealth, and took the waste: that souldier
that being courted by loud fame and fortune,
labour in one hand, that propounds us gods,
and in the other, glory that creats us,
yet durst doubt, and be damned.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: It was an errour.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A foul one, and a black one.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Yet the blackest
may be washt white again.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Never.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Your leave, Sir,
and I beseech ye note me; for I love ye,
and bring along all comfort: Are we gods,
alli'd to no infirmities? are our natures
more then mens natures? when we slip a little
out of the way of vertue, are we lost?
is there no medicine called Sweet mercie?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: None, Petillius;
there is no mercie in mankinde can reach me,
nor is it fit it should; I have sinn'd beyond it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Forgivenesse meets with all faults.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: 'T is all faults,
all sins I can commit, to be forgiven:
't is losse of whole man in me, my discretion
to be so stupid, to arrive at pardon.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: O but the General—

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: He's a brave Gentleman,
a valiant, and a loving; and I dare say
he would, as far as honour durst direct him,
make even with my fault: but 't is not honest,
nor in his power: examples that may nourish
neglect and disobedience in whole bodies,
and totter the estates and faiths of armies,
must not be plaid withal; nor out of pitie
make a General forget his duty:
nor dare I hope more from him then is worthy.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: What would ye do?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Die.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: So would sullen children,
women that want their wils, slaves, disobedient,
that fear the law, die. Fie, great Captain; you
a man to rule men, to have thousand lives
under your regiment, and let your passion
betray your reason? I bring you all forgivenesse,
the noblest kinde commends, your place, your honour.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Prethee no more; 't is foolish: didst not thou?
by — thou didst, I over-heard thee, there,
there where thou standst now, deliver me for rascal,
poor, dead, cold coward, miserable, wretched,
if I out-liv'd this ruine?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: And thou didst it nobly,
like a true man, a souldier: and I thank thee,
I thank thee, good Petillius; thus I thank thee.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Since ye are so justly made up, let me tell ye
'tis fit ye die indeed.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: O how thou lovest me!

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: For say he had forgiven ye; say the peoples whispers
were tame again, the time run out for wonder,
what must your own Command think, from whose Swords
ye have taken off the edges, from whose valours
the due and recompence of Arms; nay, made it doubtful
whether they knew obedience? must not these kill ye?
Say they are won to pardon ye, by meer miracle
brought to forgive ye; what old valiant Souldier,
what man that loves to fight, and fight for Rome,
will ever follow you more? dare ye know these ventures?
if so, I bring ye comfort; dare ye take it?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: No, no, Petillius, no.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: If your minde serve ye,
ye may live still; but how? yet pardon me,
you may outwear all too; but when? and certain
there is a mercy for each fault, if tamely
a man will take 't upon conditions.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: No, by no means: I am onely thinking now, Sir,
(for I am resolved to go) of a most base death,
fitting the basenesse of my fault. I'll hang,

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Ye shall not; y' are a Gentleman I honour,
I would else flatter ye, and force ye live,
which is far baser. Hanging? 't is a dogs death,
an end for slaves.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The fitter for my basenesse.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
prose: Besides, the man that 's hang'd, preaches his end, and sits a signe for all the world to gape at.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: That's true: I'll take a fitter poison.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: No,
't is equal ill; the death of rats, and women,
lovers, and lazie boys, that fear correction.
Die like a man.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Why my sword then.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I, if your sword be sharp, Sir,
there 's nothing under heaven that 's like your sword;
your sword 's a death indeed.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: It shall be sharp, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Why Mithridates was an arrant asse
to die by poison, if all Bosphorus
could lend him swords: your sword must do the deed:
't is shame to die choak'd, fame to die and bleed.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Thou hast: confirmed me: and, my good Petillius,
tell me no more I may live.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: 'T was my Commission;
but now I see ye in a nobler way,
a way to make all even.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Fare-well, Captain:
be a good man, and fight well: be obedient:
command thy self, and then thy men. Why shakest thou?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I do not, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I would thou hadst, Petillius:
I would finde something to forsake the world with
worthy the man that dies: a kinde of earth-quake
thorow all stern valours but mine own.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I feel now
a kinde of trembling in me.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Keep it still,
as thou lov'st vertue, keep it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And brave Captain,
the great and honoured Penyus.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: That again:
O how it heightens me! again, Petillius.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Most excellent Commander.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Those were mine,
mine, onely mine.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: They are still.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Then to keep 'em
for ever falling more, have at ye, heavens,
ye everlasting powers, I am yours: The work's done,
that neither fire, nor age, nor melting envie
shall ever conquer. Carry my last words
to the great General: kisse his hands, and say,
My soul I give to heaven, my fault to justice
which I have done upon my self: my vertue,
if ever there was any in poor Penyus,
made more, and happier, light on him. I faint.
And where there is a foe, I wish him fortune.
I die: lie lightly on my ashes, gentle earth.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And on my sin. Fare-well, great Penyus,
the souldier is in fury. Now I am glad
't is done before he comes. This way, for me,
the way of toil; for thee, the way of honour.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: Kill him, kill him, kill him.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: What will ye do?

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Good souldiers, honest souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: Kill him, kill him, kill him.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Kill us first; we command too.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Valiant Souldiers,
consider but whose life ye seek. O Drusus,
bid him be gone, he dies else. Shall Rome say
(ye most approved souldiers) her dear children
devoured the fathers of the fights? shall rage
and stubborn fury guide those swords to slaughter,
to slaughter of their own, to Civil ruine?

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: O let 'em in: all 's done, all 's ended, Regulus,
Penyus has found his last eclipse. Come, Souldiers,
come, and behold your miseries: come bravely,
full of your mutinous and bloody angers,
and here bestow your darts. O onely Romane,
O father of the Wars.

speeches.speaker: Reg.
verse: Why stand ye stupid?
where be your killing furies? whose sword now
shall first be sheath'd in Penyus? do ye weep?
Howl out, ye wretches, ye have cause: howl ever.
Who shall now lead ye fortunate? whose valour
preserve ye to the glory of your Countrey?
who shall march out before ye, coy'd and courted
by all the mistrisses of War, care, counsel,
quick-ey'd experience, and victory twin'd to him?
who shall beget ye deeds beyond inheritance
to speak your names, and keep your honours living,
when children fail, and time that takes all with him,
build houses for ye to oblivion?

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: O ye poor desperate fools: no more now, souldiers;
go home, and hang your arms up; let iust rot'em;
and humble your stern valours to soft prayers;
for ye have sunk the frame of all your vertues;
the sun that warm'd your bloods is set for ever:
I'll kisse thy honour'd cheek. Fare well, great Penyus,
thou thunder-bolt, fare-well. Take up the body:
to morrow morning to the Camp convey it.
there to receive due Ceremonies. That eye
that blindes himself with weeping, gets most glory.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Bring up the Catapults and shake the wall,
we will not be out-brav'd thus.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: Shake the earth,
ye cannot shake our souls. Bring up your Rams,
and with their armed heads, make the Fort totter,
ye do but rock us into death.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: See Sir,
see the Icenian Queen in all her glory
from the strong battlements proudly appearing,
as if she meant to give us lashes.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Yeeld, Queen.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I am unacquainted with that language, Roman.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Yeeld, honour'd Lady, and expect our mercie,
we love thy noblenesse.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I thank ye, ye say well;
but mercie and love are sins in Rome and hell.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Ye cannot scape our strength; ye must yeeld, Ladie,
ye must adore and fear the power of Rome.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: If Rome be earthly, why should any knee
with bending adoration worship her?
She's vitious; and your partiall selves confesse,
aspires the height of all impietie:
therefore 'tis fitter I should reverence
the thatched houses where the Britains dwell
in carelesse mirth, where the blest houshold gods
see nought but chaste and simple puritie.
'Tis not high power that makes a place divine,
nor that the men from gods derive their line.
But sacred thoughts in holy bosoms stor'd,
make people noble, and the place ador'd.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Beat the wall deeper.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Beat it to the center,
we will not sink one thought.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: I'll make ye.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: 2. Dan.
verse: O mother, these are fearfull hours: speak gently
to these fierce men, they will afford ye pitie.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Pitie? thou fearful girl; 'tis for those wretches
that miserie makes tame. Woulest thou live lesse?
Wast not thou born a Princesse? Can my blood,
and thy brave fathers spirit, suffer in thee
so base a separation from thy self,
as mercie from these Tyrants? Thou lov'st lust sure,
and long'st to prostitute thy youth and beautie
to common slaves for bread. Say th y had mercie;
the divel a relenting conscience:
the lives of Kings rest in their Diadems,
which to their bodies lively souls do give,
and ceasing to be Kings, they cease to live.
Show such another fear, and —
I'll fling thee to their furie.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: He is dead then?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I think so certainly; yet all my means, Sir,
even to the hazzard of my life —

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: No more:
wee must not seem to mourn here.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: There's a breach made,
is it your will we charge, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Once more mercie,
mercie to all that yeeld.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I scorn to answer:
Speak to him girle; and hear thy sister.

speeches.speaker: 1. Daugh.
verse: Generall,
hear me, and mark me well, and look upon me
directly in my face, my womans face,
whose onely beautie is the hate it bears ye;
see with thy narrowest eyes, thy sharpest wishes,
into my soul, and see what there inhabits;
see if one fear, one shadow of a terrour,
one palenesse dare appear but from my anger,
to lay hold on your mercies. No, ye fools,
poor Fortunes fools, we were not born for triumphs,
to follow your gay sports, and fill your slaves
with hoots and acclamations.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Brave behaviour.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: The children of as great as Rome, as noble,
our names before her, and our deeds her envie;
must we gild ore your Conqu st, make your State,
that is not fairly strong, but fortunate?
No, no, ye Romanes, we have ways to scape ye,
to make yee poor again, indeed our prisoners,
and stick our triumphs full.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: 's death, I shall love her.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: To torture ye with suff^ring, like our slaves;
to make ye curse our patience, wish the world
were lost again, to win us onely, and esteem
the end of all ambitions.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Do ye wonder?
we'll make our monuments in spite of fortune,
in spight of all your E gles wings: we'll work
a pitch above ye; and from our height we'll stoop
as fearlesse of your bloody fears; and fortunate,
as if we prey'd on heartlesse doves.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Strange stiffnesse.
Decius, go charge the breach.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Charge it home, Romane,
we shall deceive thee else. Where 's Nennius?

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: They have made a mighty breach.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Stick in thy body,
and make it good but half an hour.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: I'll do it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: And then be sure to die.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: It shall go hard else.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Fare well with all my heart; we shall meet yonder,
where few of these must come.

speeches.speaker: Nen.
verse: Gods take thee, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Bring up the swords, and poison.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: O my fortune!

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: How, how, ye whore?

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: Good mother, nothing to offend ye.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Here, wench:
behold us, Romanes.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Mercy yet.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: No talking:
puff; there goes all your pitie. Come, short prayers,
and let 's dispatch the businesse: you begin,
shrink not; I'll see ye do 't.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: O gentle mother,
O Romanes, O my heart; I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Woman, woman,
unnatural woman.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: O perswade her, Romanes:
alas, I am young, and would live. Noble mother,
can ye kill that ye gave life? are my yeers
fit for destruction?

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Yeeld, and be a Queen still,
a mother, and a friend.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Ye talk: come, hold it,
and put it home.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Fie, sister, fie,
what would you live to be?

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: A whore still.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: Mercie.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Hear her, thou wretched woman.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: Mercie, mother:
O whither will you send me? I was once
your darling, your delight.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: O gods,
fear in my family? do it, and nobly.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: O do not frown then.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Do it, worthy sister:
't is nothing, 't is a pleasure; we'll go with ye.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: O if I knew but whither.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: To the blessed,
where we shall meet our father.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Woman.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Talk not.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Where nothing but true joy is.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
prose: That 's a good wench, mine own sweet girl; put it close to thee.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: O comfort me still, for heavens sake.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Where eternal
our youths are, and our beauties; where no Wars come,
nor lustful slaves to ravish us.

speeches.speaker: 2 Daugh.
verse: That steels me:
a long farewel to this world.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Good: I'll help thee.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: The next is mine.
Shew me a Romane Lady in all your stories,
dare do this for her honour: they are cowards,
eat coals like compell'd Cats: your great Saint Lucrece
di'd not for honour; Tarquin topt her well,
and mad she could not hold him, bled.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: By—
I am in love: I would give an hundred pound now
but to lie with this womans behaviour. O the devil.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: Ye shall see me example. All your Rome,
if I were proud, and lov'd ambition;
if I were lustful, all your ways of pleasure;
if I were greedie, all the wealth ye conquer—

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: Make haste.

speeches.speaker: 1 Daugh.
verse: I will. Could not intice to live
but two short hours this frailty: would ye learn
how to die bravely, Romanes, to fling off
this case of flesh, lose all your cares for ever?
live as we have done, well, and fear the gods,
hunt Honour, and not Nations with your swords,
keep your mindes humble, your devotions high;
so shall ye learn the noblest part, to die.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: I come, wench; to ye all Fates hang-men; you
that case the aged destinies, and cut
the threds of Kingdoms, as they draw 'em: here,
here 's a draught would ask no lesse then Caesar
to pledge it for the glories sake.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Great Lady.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Make up your own conditions.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: So we will.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Stay.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Stay.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Be any thing.

speeches.speaker: Bond.
verse: A Saint, Swetonius,
when thou shalt fear, and die like a slave. Ye foole,
ye should have ti'd up, death first, when ye conquer'd,
ye sweat for us in vain else: see him here,
he 's ours still, and our friend; laughs at your pities;
and we command him with as easie reins
as do our enemies. I feel the poison.
Poor vanquish'd Romanes, with what matchlesse tortures
could I now rack ye? But I pitie ye,
desiring to die quiet: nay, so much
I hate to prosecute my victory,
that I will give ye counsel ere I die.
If you will keep your Laws and Empire whole,
place in your Romane flesh a Britain soul.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Desperate and strange.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: 'T is won, Sir, and the Britains
all put to th' sword.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Give her fair Funeral;
she was truely noble, and a Queen.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: —take it,
a love-mange grown upon me? what, a spirit?

speeches.speaker: Iun.
verse: I am glad of this, I have found ye.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: In my belly,
O how it tumbles?

speeches.speaker: Iun.
verse: Ye good gods, I thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thus we afflicted Britains climb for safeties,
and to avoid our dangers, seek destructions;
thus we awake to sorrows. O thou woman,
thou agent for adversities, what curses
this day belong to thy improvidence?
to Britanie by thy means, what sad millions
of widows weeping eyes? The strong mans valour
thou hast betraid to fury; the childes fortune
to fear, and want of friends: whose pieties
might wipe his mournings off, and build his sorrows
a house of rest by his blest ancestore:
the virgins thou hast rob'd of all their wishes,
blasted their blowing hopes, turn'd their songs,
their mirthful Marriage songs to Funerals,
the Land thou hast left a wildernesse of wretches.
The boy begins to stir: thy safety made,
would my soul were in heaven.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: O noble Uncle,
look out; I dream'd we were betraid.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: No harm, boy;
't is but thy emptinesse that breeds these fancies;
thou shalt have meat anon.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: A little, Uncle,
and I shall hold out bravely. What are those?
look, Uncle, look, those multiutdes that march there?
they come upon us stealing by.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: I see 'em;
and prethee be not fearful.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Now ye hate me,
would I were dead.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou know'st I love thee dearly.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Did I ere shrink yet, Uncle? were I a man now,
I should be angry with ye.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: My sweet chicken,
see, they have reach'd us, and as it seems they bear
some Souldiers body, by their solemn gestures,
and sad solemnities; it well appears too
to be of eminence. Most worthy Souldiers,
let me intreat your knowledge to inform me
what noble body that is which you bear
with such a sad and ceremonious grief,
as if ye meant to woo the world and nature
to be in love with death? Most honourable
excellent Romanes, by your ancient valours,
as ye love fame, resolve me.

speeches.speaker: Sould.
verse: 'T is the body
of the great Captain Penyus, by himself
made cold and spiritlesse.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: O stay, ye Romanes,
by the religion which you owe those gods
that lead ye on to Victories, by those glories
which made even pride a vertue in ye.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Stay:
what 's thy will, Caratach?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Set down the body,
the body of the noblest of all Romanes,
as ye expect an offering at your graves
from your friends sorrows, set it down a while,
that with your griefs an enemy may mingle;
a noble enemy that loves a Souldier;
and lend a tear to vertue: even your foes,
your wild foes, as you call'd us, are yet stor'd
with fair affections, our hearts fresh, our spirits,
though sometimes stubborn, yet when vertue dies,
soft and relenting as a virgins prayers.
O set it down.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Set down the body, souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou hallowed relique, thou rich diamond
cut with thine own dust; thou for whose wide fame
the world appears too narrow, mans all thoughts,
had they all tongues, too silent; thus I bow
to thy most honour'd ashes; though an enemy,
yet friend to all thy worths: sleep peaceably;
happinesse crown thy soul, and in thy earth
some Lawrel fix his seat, there grow, and flourish,
and make thy grave an everlasting triumph.
Fare well all glorious Wars, now thou art gone,
and honest Arms adieu: all noble Battels
maintain'd in thirst of honour, not of blood,
fare well for ever.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Was this Romane, Uncle,
so good a man?

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Thou never knew'st thy father.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: He di'd before I was born.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: This worthy Romane
was such another piece of endlesse honour,
such a brave soul dwelt in him: their proportions
and faces were not much unlike, boy: excellent natures,
see how it works into his eyes, mine own boy.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: The multitudes of these men, and their fortunes,
could never make me fear yet: one mans goodnesse—

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: O now thou pleasest me: weep still, my childe,
as if thou saw'st me dead; with such a flux
or flood of sorrow: still thou pleasest me.
And worthy souldiers, pray receive these pledges,
these hatchments of our griefs, and grace us so much
to place 'em on his Hearse. Now if ye please,
bear off the noble burden; raise his pile
high as Olympus, making heaven to wonder
to see a star upon earth outshining theirs.
And ever loved, ever living be
thy honoured and most sacred memory.

speeches.speaker: Dru.
verse: Thou hast done honestly, good Caratach,
^nd when thou di^st, a thousand vertuous Romanes
shall sing thy soul to heaven. Now march on, souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Now dry thine eyes, my boy.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Are they all gone?
I could have wept this hour yet.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Come, take cheer,
and raise thy spirit, childe: if but this day
thou canst bear out thy faintnesse, the night coming
I'll fashion our escape.

speeches.speaker: Heng.
verse: Pray fear not me;
indeed I am very heartie.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Be so still;
his mischiefs lessen, that controls his ill.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: What do I ail, i' th' name of heaven? I did but see her,
and see her die: she stinks by this time strongly,
abominably stinks: she was a woman,
a thing I never car'd for: but to die so,
so confidently, bravely, strongly; O the devil,
I have the bots, by—; she scorn'd us, strangely,
all we could do, or durst do; threatned us
with such a noble anger, and so governed
with such a fiery spirit—; the plain bots;
a—upon the bots, the love-bots: hang me,
hang me even out o' th' way, directly hang me.
O pennie pipers, and most painful penners
of bountiful new ballads, what a subject,
what a sweet subject for your silver sounds,
is crept upon ye?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Here he is; have at him.
She set the sword unto her brest,
great pitie it was to see,
That three drops of her life-warm blood,
run trickling down her knee.
Art thou there, bonny boy? and ifaith how dost thou?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Well, gramercie, how dost thou? h' as found me,
sented me out: the shame the devil ow'd me,
h' as kept his day with. And what news, Junius?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: It was an old tale ten thousand times told,
of a young Lady was turn'd into mold,
her life was lovely, her death it was bold.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: A cruel rogue; now h' as drawn pursue on me,
he hunts me like a devil. No more singing;
thou hast got a cold: come, let's go drink some Sack, boy.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Why dost thou laugh?
what Mares nest hast thou found?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.
I cannot laugh alone: Decius, Demetrius,
Curius: O my sides. Ha, ha, ha, ha,
the strangest jest.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Prethee no more.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: The admirablest fooling.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Thou art the prettiest fellow.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Sirs.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Why Junius,
prethee away, sweet Junius.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Let me sing then.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
prose: Whoa, here's a stir now: sing a song o' six pence, by—(if) prethee; — on 't: Junius.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I must either sing, or laugh.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And what 's your reason?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: What 's that to you?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And I must whistle.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Do so.
O, I hear 'em coming.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I have a little businesse.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
prose: Thou shalt not go, believe it: what a Gentleman of thy sweet conversation?

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Captain Junius,
sweet Captain, let me go with all celerity;
things are not always one: and do not question,
nor jeer, nor gybe: none of your doleful ditties,
nor your sweet conversation: you will finde then
I may be anger'd.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: By no means, Petillius;
anger a man that never knew passion?
'tis most impossible: a noble Captain,
a wise and generous Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: Tom puppie,
leave this way to abuse me: I have found ye,
but for your mothers sake I will forgive ye.
Your subtil understanding may discover
(as you think) some trim toy to make you merry;
some straw to tickle ye; but do not trust to 't;
y' are a young man, and may do well; be sober;
carry your self discreetly.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Yes forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: How does the brave Petillius?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Monstrous merry:
we two were talking what a kinde of thing
I was when I was in love; what a strange monster
for little boys and girls to wonder at;
how like a fool I lookt.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: So they do all,
like great dull slavering fools.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Petillius saw too.

speeches.speaker: Pet.
verse: No more of this; 'tis scurvie: peace.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: How nastily,
indeed how beastly all I did became me?
how I forgot to blow my nose? there he stands,
an honest and a wise man; if himself
(I dare avouch it boldly, for I know it)
should finde himself in love—

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: I am angry.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Surely his wise self would hang his beastly self,
his understanding self so mawl his asse-self—

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: He's bound to do it; for he knows the follies,
the poverties, and basenesse that belongs to 't,
h' as read upon the reformations long.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: He has so.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: 'T is true, and he must do 't:
nor is it fit indeed any such coward—

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: You'll leave prating.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Should dare come neer the Regiments, specially
those curious puppies (for believe there are such)
that onely love behaviours: those are dog-whelps,
dwindle away, because a woman dies well;
commit with passions onely: fornicate
with the free spirit meerly: you, Petillius,
for you have long observ'd the world.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Dost thou hear?
I'll beat thee damnably within these three hours:
go pray; may be I'll kill thee. Farewel, Jack daws.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: What a strange thing he's grown?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I am glad he is so:
and stranger he shall be, before I leave him.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Is 't possible her meer death—.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I observ'd him,
and found him taken, infinitely taken
with her bravery: I have follow'd him,
and seen him kisse his sword since, court his scabbard,
call dying, dainty deer; her brave minde, mistris;
casting a thousand ways, to give those forms,
that he might lie with 'em, and get old Armors:
he had got me o' th' hip once: it shall go hard, friends,
but he shall find his own coin.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: How now Macer?
is Judas yet come in?

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: Yes, and has lost
most of his men too. Here he is.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: What news?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: I have lodg'd him; rouze him he that dares.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Where, Judas?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: On a steep rock, i' th' woods, the boy too with him,
and there he swears he will keep his Christmas, Gentlemen,
but he will come away with full conditions,
bravely, and like a Britain: he paid part of us,
yet I think we fought bravely: for mine own part,
I was four several times at half sword with him,
twice stood his partizan: but the plain truth is,
he's a meer devil, and no man: i' th' end he swing'd us,
and swing'd us soundly too: he fights by With-craft:
yet for all that I see him lodg'd,

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Take more men,
and scout him round. Macer, march you along.
What victuals has he?

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Not a piece of Bisket,
not so much as will stop a tooth; nor water,
more then they make themselves: they lie
just like a brace of bear-whelps, close, and crafty,
sucking their fingers for their food.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Cut off then
all hope of that way: take sufficient forces.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: But use no foul play, on your lives: that man
that does him mischief by deceit, I'll kill him.

speeches.speaker: Macer.
verse: He shall have fair play, he deserves it.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Heark ye,
what should I do there then? you are brave Captains,
most valiant men; go up your selves; use vertue,
see what will come on 't: pray the Gentleman
to come down, and be taken. Ye all know him,
I think ye have felt him too: there ye shall finde him,
his sword by his side, plums of a pound weight by him
will make your chops ake: you'll finde it a more labour
to win him living, then climbing of a Crowes nest.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Away, and compasse him; we shall come up
I am sure within these two hours. Watch him close.

speeches.speaker: Macer.
verse: He shall flee thorow the air, if he escape us.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: What's this loud lamentation?

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: The dead body
of the great Penyus is new come to th' Camp Sir.

speeches.speaker: Dem.
verse: Dead!

speeches.speaker: Macer
verse: By himself, they say.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: I fear'd that fortune.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Peace guide him up to heaven.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
prose: Away good Macer.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: If thou be'st guilty,
some sullen plague thou hat'st most light upon thee:
the Regiment return on Junius,
hee well deserves it.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: So.

speeches.speaker: Swet.
verse: Draw out three Companies,
yours Decius, Junius, and thou Petillius,
and make up instantly to Caratach,
he's in the wood before ye; we shall follow
after due ceremony done to the dead,
the noble dead: Come, let's go burn the body.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: The Regiment given from me; disgrac'd openly;
in love too with a trifle to abuse me?
A merry world, a fine world: serv'd seven yeers
to be an asse o' both sides, sweet Petillius,
you have brought your hogs to a fine market: you are wise, Sir,
your honourable brain-pan full of crotchets,
an understanding Gentleman; your projects
cast with assurance ever: wouldst not thou now
be bang'd about the pate, Petillius?
answer to that sweet souldier; surely, surely,
I think ye would; pull'd by the nose, kick'd; hang thee,
thou art the arrant'st rascall: trust thy wisdome
with any thing of weight; the winde with feathers.
Out ye blind puppie; you command? you govern?
dig for a groat a day, or serve a swine-herd;
too noble for thy nature too. I must up;
but what I shall do there, let time discover.

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: Hang it o'th' side o'th' rock, as though the Britains
stole hither to relieve him; who first ventures
to fetch it off, is ours. I cannot see him.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: He lies close in a hole above, I know it,
gnawing upon his anger: ha? no, 'tis not he,

speeches.speaker: Macer
verse: 'Tis but the shaking of the boughs.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: — shake 'em,
I am sure they shake me soundly. There.

speeches.speaker: Macer
verse: 'Tis nothing.

speeches.speaker: Jud.
verse: Make no noise: if he stir, a deadly tempest
of huge stones fall upon us: 'tis done: away close.

speeches.speaker: Car.
verse: Sleep stil, sleep sweetly child, 'tis all thou feedst on.
No gentle Britain neer; no valiant charitie
to bring thee food? poor knave, thou art sick, extreme sick,
almost grown wild for meat; and yet thy goodnesse
will not confesse, nor show it. All the woods
are double lin'd with souldiers; no way left us
to make a noble scape: I'll sit down by thee,
and when thou wak'st, either get meat to save thee,
or lose my life i'th' purchase. Good gods comfort thee.

speeches.speaker: Guide
verse: Ye are not far off now, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Draw the Companies
the closest way thorow the woods; we'll keep on this way.

speeches.speaker: Guide
verse: I will Sir: half a furlong more you'll come
within the sight o'th' Rock; keep on the left side,
you'll be discoverd else: I'll lodge your Companies
in the wilde vines beyond ye.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: Do ye mark him?

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Yes, and am sorry for him.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Junius,
pray let me speak two words with you.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Walk afore,
I'll overtake ye straight.

speeches.speaker: Dec.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Now, Captain.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: You have oft told me, you have lov'd me, Junius.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: Most sure I told you truth then.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: And that love
should not deny me any honest thing.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
verse: It shall not.

speeches.speaker: Petill.
verse: Dare ye swear it?
I have forgot all passages between us
that have been ill, forgiven too, forgot you.

speeches.speaker: Jun.
