verse: I am well enough serv'd,
That must be offring jointures, Jewels,
And precious stones more then I brought with me.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Why, shoote ye not?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Heare me deere Mother;
And when the greatest cruelty, is Justice,
Do not shew mercy: death to these starv'd wretches
Is a reward, not punishment: let 'em live
To undergoe the full weight of your displeasure.
And that they may have sence to feel the torments
They have deserv'd: allow 'm some small pittance,
To linger out their tortures.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Tis well counsell'd.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: And wee'l follow it;
Heare us speake.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Peace dogs.
Bind 'em fast: when fury hath given way to reason,
I will determine of their sufferings,
Which shall be horrid. Vengeance, though slow pac'd,
At length oretakes the guilty; and the wrath
Of the incensed powers will fall most sure
On wicked men, when they are most secure.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sayl.
verse: Heres nothing, sir, but poverty and hunger;
No promise of inhabitance; neither tract of Beast,
Nor foot of man: we have searcht
All this Rocky desart, yet cannot discover any assurance
Here is or hath been such men.

speeches.speaker: 2. Sayl.
verse: Not a relique of any thing they wore;
Nor marke left by 'em, either to finde reliefe,
Or to warne others from the like misfortune.
Believe it, these fellows are both false,
And to get a little succour in their misery,
Have fram'd this cunning tale.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: The ship, I know, is French, and own'd by Pirats,
If not by Albert my arch enemy.
You told me too there was a woman with 'em.
A young and handsome woman.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: There was so sir.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: And such and such young gallants.

speeches.speaker: Nic.
verse: We told ye true sir,
That they had no means to quit this Island.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: And that amidst their mutiny to save your lives
You got their ship.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: All is most certaine sir.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Where are they then? where are these men
Or woman? we are landed where your faiths
Did assure us we could not misse their sights.
For this news we tooke ye to our mercy,
Reliev'd ye, when the furious Sea and famine
Strove which should first devoure ye;
Cloath'd, and cherisht ye; us'd ye as those ye say ye are.
Faire Gentlemen, now keep your words,
And shew us this company, your own free pitties spoke of;
These men ye left in misery; the woman.
Men of those noble breedings you pretend to.
Should scorn to lie, or get their food with falshood;
Come, direct us.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Alasse sir, they are gone,
But by what means or providence, we know not.

speeches.speaker: 2. Sayl.
verse: Was not the Captain
A fellow of a fiery, yet brave nature,
A middle stature, and of brown complexion?

speeches.speaker: Nic.
verse: He was sir.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: 'Twas Albert,
And my poore wretched sister.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sayl.
verse: Twas he certain,
I ha been at Sea with him; many times at Sea.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Come shew us these men;
Shew us presently, and do not dally with us.

speeches.speaker: Sab.
verse: We left 'em here; what should we say, sir?
Here in this place.

speeches.speaker: 2. Sayl.
verse: The earth cannot swallow 'em;
They have no wings, they cannot fly sure.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: You told us too
Of heapes of treasure, and of sums conceald,
That set their hearts a fire; we see no such thing,
No such sign; what can ye say to purge ye?
What have ye done with these men?

speeches.speaker: Nic.
verse: We, sir?

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: You sir;
For certain I believe ye saw such people.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: By all that's good,
By all that's pure and honest,
By all that's holy.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: I dare not credit ye,
Ye have so abus'd my hope, that now I hate ye.

speeches.speaker: 1. Sayl.
verse: Lets put 'em in their ragged clothes again Captain,
For certain they are knaves, lets e'en deliver 'em
To their old fruitfull Farm; here let 'em walk the Island.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: If ye do so, we shall curse your mercies.

speeches.speaker: Nic.
verse: Rather put us to Sea again.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Not so.
Yet this Ile do, because ye say ye are Christians,
Though I hardly credit it: bring in the boat,
And all aboord again, but these two wretches;
Yet leave 'em four daies meat. If in that time,
(For I will search all nookes of this strange Island)
I can discover any tract of these men,
Alive or dead, Ile beare ye off, and honour ye;
If not, ye have found your graves; so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Nic.
verse: That goodnes dwels above, & knows us innocent,
Comfort our lives, and at his pleasure quit us.

speeches.speaker: Sebast.
verse: Come cousin, come; old time will end our story:
But no time (if we end well) ends our glory.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Use 'em with all the austerity that may be,
They are our slaves; turn all those pitties,
Those tender reluctations that should become your sex,
To stern anger; and when ye look upon 'em,
Looke with those eyes that wept those bitter sorrows,
Those cruelties ye sufferd by their rapines.
Some five daies hence that blessed houre comes,
Most happy to me, that knit this hand to my deare husbands,
And both our hearts in mutuall bands.
That houre Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What of that houre?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Why, on that houre daughter,
And in the height of all our celebrations,
Our deere remembrances of that deere man,
And those that suffered with him, our faire kinsmen,
Their lives shall fall a sacrifice to vengeance,
Their lives that ruind his; tis a full justice.
I will looke glorious in their bloods;
And the most Noble spirit of Sebastian,
That perisht by the pride of these French Pirates,
Shall smile in Heaven, and blesse the hand that kild 'em.
Looke strictly all unto your prisoners;
For he that makes a scape beyond my vengeance,
Or entertaines a hope by your faire usage;
Take heed, I say, she that deceives my trust,
Again take heed: her life, and thats but light neither;
Her life in all the tortures my spirit can put on.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We shall be carefull.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Do so.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Your are angry mother, and ye are old too,
Forgetting what men are: but we shall temper ye.
How fare your prisoners, Ladies? in what forms
Do they appeare in their afflictions?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Mine fare but poorly;
For so I am commanded: tis none of their fault.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Of what sort are they?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: They say they are Gentlemen.
But they shew Mungrels.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: How do they suffer?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Faith like boyes;
They are fearfull in all fortunes; when I smile
They kneele, and beg to have that face continued;
And like poore slaves, adore the ground I goe on.
When I frown, they hang their most dejected heads,
Like fearfull sheephounds; shew 'em a crust of bread
Theyl Saint me presently, and skip like Apes
For a sup of Wine. Ile whip 'em like hackneys,
Saddle 'em, ride 'em, do what I will with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Tush, these are poore things.
Have they names like Christians?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Very faire names: Franvile, Lamure, and Morillat;
And brag of great kindreds too. They offer very handsomely,
But that I am a foole, and dare not venture.
They are sound too i'my conscience,
Or very neere upon 't.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Fy, away foole.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: They tell me
If they might be brought before you,
They would reveale things of strange consequence.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Their base poore feares.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I, that makes me hate 'em too;
For if they were but manly to their sufferance,
Sure I should strain a point or two.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: An houre hence Ile take a view of 'em,
And heare their businesse. Are your men thus too?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Mine? No gentle Maddam, mine were not cast
In such base molds; afflictons, tortures,
Are names and natures of delight, to my men;
All sorts of cruelties they meet like pleasures.
I have but two; the one they call Du-pont,
Tibalt Du-pont; the other the ship-master.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Have they not lives, and feares?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Lives they have Maddam;
But those lives never linkt to such companions
As feares or doubts.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Use 'em Nobly;
And where you finde fit subjects for your pitties
Let it become ye to be courteous;
My mother will not alwaies be thus rigorous.

speeches.speaker: Hip
verse: Mine are Saylors Maddam,
But they sleep soundly, and seldom trouble me, unlesse it be when
They dream sometimes of fights and tempests;
Then they rore and whistle for Cans of Wine,
And down they fling me; and in that rage,
(For they are violent fellows) they play such reaks.
If they have meat, they thank me;
If none, they heartily desire to be hangd quickly.
And this is all they care.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Look to 'em diligently, and where your pitties tels ye
They may deserve, give comfort.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We will.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Come hither, be not frighted;
Think not ye steale this liberty, for we give it,
Your tender innocence assures me, Virgin,
Ye had no share in those wrongs these men did us;
I finde ye are not hardned in such mischieves.
Your brother was mis-led sure,
Foully mis-led.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: How much I feare these pities!

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Certain he was, so much I pity him;
And for your sake, whose eyes plead for him;
Nay, for his own sake.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: For I see about him
Women have subtill eyes, and look narrowly;
Or I am much abusd: many faire promises;
Nay beyond those, too many shadowed vertues.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I think he is good.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I assure my selfe he will be;
And out of that assurance take this comfort,
For I perceive your feare hath much dejected ye.
I love your brother.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Maddam.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nay, do not take it for a dreamt of favour,
That comforts in the sleepe, and awake vanishes;
Indeed I love him.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Do ye indeed?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You doubt still, because ye feare his safety;
Indeed he is the sweetest man I ere saw;
I think the best. Ye may heare without blushes,
And give me thanks, if ye please, for my curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Maddam, I ever must;
Yet witnesse Heaven, they are hard pul'd from me.
Believe me, Maddam, so many imperfections I could find,
(Forgive me Grace for lying) and such wants,
(Tis to an honest use) such poverties,
Both in his main proportion, and his mind too;
There are a hundred handsomer; (I lie leudly)
Your noble usage, Maddam, hath so bound me to ye,
That I must tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Come tell your worst.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: He is no husband for ye.
I think ye mean in that fayr way.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ye have hit it.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I am sure ye have hit my heart.
You will finde him dangerous, Maddam;
As fickle as the flying ayre, proud, jealous,
Soon glutted in your sweets, and soon forgetfull;
I could say more, and tell ye I have a brother,
Another brother, that so far excels this,
Both in the ornaments of man, and making.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: If you were not his sister, I should doubt ye mainly;
Doubt ye for his love, ye deale so cunningly.
Do not abuse me, I have trusted ye with more then life,
With my first love; be carefull of me.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: In what use, Maddam?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: In this Lady,
Speak to him for me, you have power upon him;
Tell him I love him, tell him I dote on him.
It will become your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Become my grave.
O fortune, O cursed fortune.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Tell him his liberty,
And all those with him; all our wealth and Jewels.
Good sister, for Ile call ye so.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I shall Lady,
Even die, I hope.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Here's Meat and Wine, pray take it,
And there he lies; give him what liberty you please;
But still conceald. What pleasure you shall please, sister.
He shall nere want again. Nay, see an you'l take it;
Why do you studdy thus?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: To avoyd mischiefes, if they should happen.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Goe and be happy for me.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: O blind fortune;
Yet happy thus far, I shall live to see him,
In what strange desolation lives he here now?
Sure this Curtaine will reveale.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Who's that? ha!
Some gentle hand, I hope, to bring me comfort.
Or if it be my death, tis sweetly shaddowed.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Have ye forgot me sir?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: My Aminta?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: She sir,
That walks here up and down an empty shadow,
One that for some few houres
But wanders here, carrying her own sad Coffin,
Seeking some Desart place to lodge her greifes in.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Sweet sorrow welcome, welcome noble griefe;
How got you this faire liberty to see me?
For sorrows in your shape are strangers to me.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I come to counsell ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Ye are still more welcome;
For good friends in afflictions give good councels.
Pray then proceed.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Pray eate first, ye shew faint;
Here's Wine to refresh ye too.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: I thank ye deere.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Drinke again.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Here's to our loves.
How, turn and weepe!
Pray pledge it: this happinesse we have yet left,
Our hearts are free. Not pledge it? why,
And though beneath the axe this health were holy,
Why doe ye weep thus?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I come to woe ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: To woe me Sweet? I am woe'd and wonne already,
You know I am yours. This pretty way becomes ye.
But you would deceive my sorrows; that's your intent.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I would I could, I should not weep, but smile.
Do ye like your Meat and Wine?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Like it?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Do you like your liberty?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: All these I well may like.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Then pray like her that sent'em.
Doe ye like wealth, and most unequal'd beauty?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Peace, indeed you'l make me angry.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Would I were dead that aske it,
Then ye might freely like, and I forgive ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: What like, and who? adde not more misery
To a man that's fruitfull in afflictions.
Who is't you would have me like?
Who sent these comforts?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I must tell.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Be bold.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: But be you temperate.
If you be bold I die. The young fair Virgin;
(Sorrow hath made me old.) O hearken,
And wisely harke, the Governesse daughter:
That Star that strikes this Island full of wonder,
That blooming sweetnesse.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: What of her?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: She sent it: and with it,
It must be out, she dotes on ye,
And must enjoy ye: else no joy must find ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: And have you the patience to deliver this?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: A sister may say much, and modestly.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: A Sister?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Yes, that name undid ye;
Undid us both: had ye nam'd wife, she had fear'd ye;
And fear'd the sin she followed; She had shun'd, yea
Her Virgin modesty had not touch'd at ye.
But thinking you were free, hath kindled a fire,
I feare will hardly be extinguisht.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Indeed I played the foole.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: O my best sir, take heed,
Take heed of lies. Truth though it trouble some minds,
Some wicked minds, that are both darke and dangerous:
Yet it preserves it selfe, comes off pure, innocent,
And like the Sunne, though never so ecclips'd,
Must breake in glory. O sir, lie no more.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Ye have read me a faire Lecture,
And put a spell upon my tongue for fayning.
But how will you counsell now?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Ye must study to forget me.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Be patient.
Be wise and patient, it concerns ye highly.
Can ye lay by our loves? But why should I doubt it?
Ye are a man, and men may shift affections,
Tis held no sin. To come to the poynt,
Ye must lose me; many and mighty reasons.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Heare me Aminta,
Have you a man that loves you to, that feeds ye,
That sends ye liberty? has this great Governesse
A noble sonne too, young, and apt to catch ye?
Am I because I am in bonds, and miserable,
My health decay'd, my youth, and strength halfe blasted,
My fortune like my wayning selfe, for this despis'd?
Am I for this forsaken? a new love chosen,
And my affections, like my fortunes wanderers?
Take heed of lying, you that chid me for it;
And shew'd how deep a sin it was, and dangerous.
Take heed, your selfe, you swore you lov'd me deerly;
No few, nor little oathes you swore Aminta,
Those seal'd with no small faith, I then assur'd my selfe.
O seek no new waies to cozen truth.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I do not.
By Love it selfe I love thee,
And ever must, nor can all deaths dissolve it.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Why do you urge me thus then?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: For your safety,
To preserve your life.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: My life I do confesse is hers,
She gives it,
And let her take it back, I yeild it.
My loves intirely thine, none shall touch at it;
None, my Aminta, none.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Ye have made me happy,
And now I know ye are mine. Fortune, I scorn thee.
Go to your rest, and Ile sit by ye;
Whilst I have time Ile be your mate, and comfort ye,
For onely I am trusted: you shall want nothing,
Not a liberty that I can steal ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: May we not celebrate our loves Aminta?
And where our wishes cannot meet

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: You are wanton,
But with cold kisses Ile allay that feavor;
Look for no more, and that in private too.
Believe me I shall blush else.
But let's consider, we are both lost else.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Let's in, and prevent fate.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: You do well to ayre us Ladies, we shal be musty else.
What are your wise wils now?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You are very cranck still.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: As cranck as a holy Fryer, fed with hayl-stones.
But do ye bring us out to baite, like Buls?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Or are you weary of the charge ye are at?
Turn us abroad again, let's jog Ladies;
We are grosse, and course, unfit for your sweet pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Knock off our shoos, and turn's to grasse.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You are determined
Still to be stubborn then: it well becomes ye.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: An humour Lady that contents a prisoner.
A sullen fit sometimes serves for a second course.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ye may as well be kind,
And gain our favours; gain meat, and drink,
And lodging to rest your bones.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: My bones have bore me thus long,
And had their share of pains, and recreations;
If they fayl now, they are no fayr companions.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Are ye thus harsh to all our sex?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We cannot be merry without a Fidler.
Pray strike up your Tabors, Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: The fools despise us.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: We know ye are very hungry now.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Yes, tis very wholsome Ladies;
For we that have grosse bodies, must be carefull.
Have ye no piercing ayre to stir our stomacks?
We are beholding to ye for our Ordinary.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Why slaves, tis in our power to hang ye.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Very likely.
Tis in our powers then to be hang'd, and scorn ye.
Hanging's as sweet to us, as dreaming to you.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Come, be more courteous.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
prose: Do, and then ye shal be pleas'd, and have all necessaries.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Give me some Rats-bane then.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: And why Rats-bane, Mounsier?

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: We live like vermin here, & eate up your Cheese,
Your mouldy Cheese, that none but Rats would bite at;
Therefore tis just that Rats-bane should reward us.
We are unprofitable, and our Ploughs are broken;
There is no hope of Harvest this yeere, Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ye shall have all content.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I, and we'l serve your uses.
I had rather serve hogs, there's more delight in't;
Your greedy appetites are never satisfied;
Just like hungry Camels, sleeping or waking
You chew the cud still.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: By this hand we'l starve ye.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Tis a Noble courtesie.
I had as liefe ye should famish me, as founder me,
To be jaded to death is onely fit for a hackney.
Here be certain tarts of tar about me,
And parcels of potargo in my Jerkin,
As long as these last.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Which will not last ever.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Then we'l eate one another like good fellows,
A shoulder of his for a hanch of mine.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Tis excellent.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Twill be, as we'l dresse it Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Why sure ye are not men.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Ye had best come search us,
A Seaman is seldome without a salt Eele.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: I am bad enough,
And in my nature a notorious wencher;
And yet ye make me blush at your immodesty.
Tell me good Master, didst ever see such things?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I could like 'em though they were lewdly given,
If they could say no; but fie on 'em,
They gape like Oysters.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Well, ye may hang, or starve us;
But your commanding impudence shall never feare us.
Had ye by blushing signs, soft cunnings, crept into us,
And shew'd us your necessities: we had met your purposes,
Supply'd your wants. We are no Saints Ladies;
I love a good wench, as I love my life,
And with my life I will maintain my love:
But such a sordid impudence Ile spit at.
Let's to our dens again. Come noble Master.
You know our minds Ladies:
This is the faith in which we'l die.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: I doe admire 'em.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: They are noble fellows,
And they shall not want, for this.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: But see, Clarinda comes.
Farewell, Ile to my charge.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Bring out those prisoners now,
And let me seee 'em, and heare their businesse.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I will, Maddam.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I hope she hath prevail'd upon her brother.
She has a sweet tongue, and can describe the happinesse
My love is ready to fling on him.
And sure he must be glad, and certain wonder
And blesse the houre that brought him to this Island.
I long to heare the full joy that he labours with.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Blesse thy Divine beauty.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Mirror of sweetnesse.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Ever springing brightnesse.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nay, stand up Gentlemen, and leave your flatteries.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: Shee cals us Gentlemen, sure we shall have some meat now.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I am a mortall creature,
Worship Heaven, and give these attributes
To their Divinities. Methinks ye look but thin.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: O we are starv'd, immortall beauty.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: We are all poor starv'd knaves.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Neither liberty nor meat Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: We were handsome men, and Gentlemen, & sweet men,
And were once gracious in the eyes of beauties,
But now we look like rogues;
Like poore starv'd rogues.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What would ye do if ye were to die now?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Alas we were prepar'd. If you will hang us,
Let's have a good meale or two to die with,
To put's in heart.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Or if you'l drown us,
Let's be drunk first, that we may die merrily,
And blesse the founders.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ye shal not die so hastily.
What dare ye do to deserve my favour?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Put us to any service.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Any bondage,
Let's but live.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Wee'l get a world of children,
For we know, ye are hainously provided that way;
And ye shal beat us when we offend ye;
Beat us abundantly, and take our meat from us.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: These are weak abject things, that shew ye poor ones.
What's the great service ye so oft have threatned,
If ye might see me, and win my favour?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: That businesse of discovery.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: O, Ile tell ye Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: and so will I.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: And I,
Pray let me speak first.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Good, no confusion.
We are before a Lady that knows manners;
And by the next, meat I shall eate, tis certain.
This little Gentlewoman that was taken with us

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Your Captains sister, she you mean.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: I, I, she's the businesse that we would open to ye.
You are cousned in her.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How, what is't you would open?

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: She is no sister.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Good sirs, how quick you are.
She is no sister, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: She is his.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Peace I say.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What is she?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Faith, sweet Lady,
She is, as a man would say, his.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: His Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Or, as some new translators read, his.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: O me!

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: And why he should delude you thus,
Unlesse he meant some villany? these ten weeks
He has had her at Sea for his own propes appetite.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: His Cabin-mate, Ile assure ye.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: No sister, say ye?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: No more then I am brother to your beauty.
I know not why he should juggle thus.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Do not lie to me.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: If ye find me lie, Lady, hang me empty.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: How am I fool'd!
Away with 'em, Juletta, and feed 'em
But hark ye, with such food as they have given me.
New misery!

speeches.speaker: Fran.
verse: Nor meat, nor thanks for all this.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Make 'em more wretched.
O I could burst! curse and kill now,
Kill any thing I meet. Juletta, follow me,
And call the rest along.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: We follow Maddam.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: I must be gone now, else she may suspect me;
How shall I answer her?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Tell her directly.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: That were too sudden, too improvident;
Fires of this nature must be put out cunningly,
They'l waste all come neere 'em else.
Farewell once more.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Farewell.
And keep my love entire.
Nay kisse me once again, me thinks we should not part.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: O be wise, sir.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Nay, one kisse more.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Indeed you'r wanton;
We may be taken too.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Out thou base woman.
By Heaven Ile shoot 'em both.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Nay stay, brave Lady, hold;
A sudden death cuts of a Nobler vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Am I made Bawd to your lascivious meetings?
Are ye grown so wise in sin?
Shut up that villaine: and sirra,
Now expect my utmost anger.
Let him there starve.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: I, mock at your mischiefes.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Tie that false witch unto that Tree,
There let the savage beasts
Gnaw of her sweetnesse, and Snakes
Embrace her beauties; tie her, and watch
That none relieve her.

speeches.speaker: Hip.
verse: We could wish ye better fortune Lady,
But dare not help ye.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Be your own friends, I thank ye.
Now onely my last audit, and my greatest,
O Heaven, be kind unto me,
And if it be thy wil, preserve.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Who is this?
Sure tis a woman; I have trod this place,
And found much footing: now I know tis peopl'd.
Ha, let me see! tis her face.
O Heaven! turn this way mayd.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: O Raymond, O brother.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Her tongue to: tis my sister; what rude hand!
Nay kisse me first, O joy!

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Fly, fly deere brother,
You are lost else.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: A man, a man, a new man.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
prose: What are these?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: An Enemy, an Enemy.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Dispatch him,
Take him off, shoot him straight.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: I dare not use my sword, Ladies,
Against such comely foes.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: O brother brother!

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Away with 'em, and in darke prisons bind 'em.
One word replyd, ye die both.
Now brave mother follow thy Noble Anger,
And Ile help thee.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I am deaf to all your intreaties: she that moves me
For pity or compassion to these Pirates,
Digs up her fathers, or her brothers Tombe,
And spurns about their ashes.
Couldst thou remember what a father thou hast once,
Twould steele thy heart against foolish pity.
By his memory, and the remembrance of his deere embraces,
I am taught, that in a Noble cause revenge is Noble;
And they shal fall the sacrifices to appease
His wandering Ghost, and my incensed fury.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: The new come prisoner to?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Him to. Yet that we may learn
Whether they are the same, or neere ally'd
To those that forc'd me to this cruell course,
Better their poore allowance, and permit'em
To meet together and confer,
Within the distance of your eare; perhaps
They may discover something that may kill
Despaire in me, and be a means to save 'em
From certain ruine.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: That shal be my charge.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yet to prevent
All hope of rescue: for this new come Captain
Hath both a ship and men not far off from us,
Though ignorant to find the onely Port,
That can yeeld entrance to our happy Island,
Guard the place strongly, and ere the next Sunne
Ends his diurnall progresse, I wil be
Happy in my revenge, or set 'em free.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: So serve it plentifully,
And lose not time to enquire the cause;
There is a main design that hangs upon this bounty.
See the Table furnisht with Wine too,
That discovers secrets which tortures cannot open:
Open the doores too of the severall prisons,
And give all free entrance into this room.
Undiscover'd I can here marke all.
Here's Captain carelesse, and the tough Ship-master,
The slaves are nos'd like Vultures
How wilde they look.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Ha, the mystery of this,
Some good Hobgoblin rise and reveale.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I am amazed at it: nor can I sound the intent.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Is not this Bread,
Substantiall bread, not painted?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: But take heed,
You may be poysoned.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: I am sure I am famisht;
And as the wise man says,
Gripes the guts as much as any Minerall.
This may be Treacle sent to preserve me
After a long fast: or be it Vipers spittle,
Ile run the hazzard.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We are past all feare, Ile take part with ye.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Do: and now yfaith, how d'e feel your selfe?
I finde great ease in't. What's here?
Wine, and it be thy will;
Strong lusty Wine. Well, fooles may talke
Of Metridate, Cordials, and Elixars.
But from my youth this was my onely Physick.
Here's a colour, what Ladies cheek,
Though ceruss'd over, comes neere it?
It sparkles too: hangs out Diamonds.
O my sweet heart, how I will hug thee,
Again, and again! They are poor drunkards,
And not worth thy favours,
That number thy moyst kisses in these Christals.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: But Mounsiuer,
Here are Suckets, and sweet dishes.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Tush, boys meat,
I am past it; here's strong food fit for men:
Nectar, old lad. Mistris of merry hearts,
Once more I am bold with you.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Take heed (man)
Too much will breed distemper.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Hast thou liv'd at Sea
The most part of thy life, where to be sober
While we have Wine aboord, is capitall treason;
And dost thou preach sobriety?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: prethee forbeare,
We may offend in it; we know not for whom
It was provided.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: I am sure for me: therefore footra,
When I am full, let 'em hang me, I care not.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: This has been his temper ever.
See, provoking dishes, candid Eringoes,
And Potatoes.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Ile not touch 'em, I will drink;
But not a bit on a march, Ile be an Eunuch rather.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Who are these?

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Marry, who you will;
I keep my text here.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Raymond!

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Albert!

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Away, Ile be drunke alone;
Keep off rogues, or Ile belch ye into ayre;
Not a drop here.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: Deere brother, put not in your eyes such anger;
Those looks poyson'd with fury shot at him,
Reflect on me. O brother looke milder, or
The Christall of his temperance
Will turn 'em on your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Sir have sought ye long
To finde your pardon: you have ploughed the Ocean
To wreak your vengeance on me, for the rape
Of this faire virgin. Now our fortune guides us
To meet on such hard terms, that we need rather
A mutuall pitty of our present state,
Then to expostulate of breaches past,
Which cannot be made up. And though it be
Far from your power to force me to confesse,
That I have done ye wrong, or such submission
Failing to make my peace, to vent your anger;
You being your selfe slav'd, as I to others:
Yet for your sisters sake, her blessed sake,
In part of recompence of what she has suffered
For my rash folly; the contagion
Of my black actions catching hold upon
Her purer innocence: I crave your mercy,
And wish however severall motives kept us
From being friends while we had hope to live,
Let death which we expect, and cannot fly from,
End all contention.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Drink upon't, 'tis a good motion;
Ratifie it in Wine, and tis authenticall.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: When I consider
The ground of our long difference, and look on
Our not to be avoyded miseries,
It doth beget in me I know not how
A soft religious tendernesse; which tels me,
Though we have many faults to answer for
Upon our own account, our fathers crimes
Are in us punisht. O Albert, the course
They took to leave us rich was not honest,
Nor can that friendship last, which vertue joyns not.
When first they forc'd the industrious Portugals,
From their Plantations in the happy Islands.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: This is that I watch for.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: And did omit no tyranny, which men
Inured to spoyle and mischiefe could inflict,
On the griev'd sufferers; when by lawlesse rapine
They reapt the harvest, which their labours sowed;
And not content to force 'em from their dwelling,
But layd for 'em at Sea, to ravish from 'em
The last remainder of their wealth; then, then,
After a long pursuit, each doubting other,
As guilty of the Portugals escape,
They did begin to quarrell, like ill men;
(Forgive me piety, that I call em so)
No longer love, or correspondence holds,
Then it is cimented with prey or profit:
Then did they turn those Swords they oft had bloodied
With innocent gore, upon their wretched selves,
And payd the forfeit of their cruelty
Shown to Sebastian, and his Collonie,
By being fatall Enemies to each other.
Thence grew Amintas rape, and my desire
To be reveng'd. And now observe the issue:
As they for spoyle ever forgot compassion
To women, (who should be exempted
From the extremities of a lawfull war)
We now, young able men, are faln into
The hands of women; that, against the soft
Tendernesse familiar to their sex,
Will shew no mercy.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: None, unlesse you shew us
Our long lost husbands.
We are those Potugals you talk'd of.

speeches.speaker: Raym.
verse: Stay,
I met upon the Sea in a tall ship
Two Portugals, famisht almost to death.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Our ship by this Wine.
And those the rogues that stole her,
Left us to famish in the barraine Islands.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: Some such tale they told me,
And something of a woman, which I find,
To be my sister.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Where are these men?

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: I left 'em,
Supposing they had deluded me with forg'd tales,
In the Island where they sayd
They had liv'd many years the wretched owners
Of a huge masse of treasure.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: The same men: and that the fatall muck
We quarreld for.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: They were Portugals you say.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: So they profes'd.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: They may prove such men as may save your lives,
And so much I am taken with faire hope,
That I will hazard life to be resolv'd on't:
How came you hither?

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: My ship lies by the rivers mouth,
That can convey yee to these wretched men,
Which you desire to see.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Back to your prisons,
And pray for the successe: if they be those
Which I desire to finde, you are safe;
If not, prepare to die to morrow:
For the world cannot redeem ye.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: How ever, we are armd
For either fortune,

speeches.speaker: Ti.
verse: What must become of me now
That I am not dismis'd?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: O sir, I purpose
To have your company.

speeches.speaker: Ti.
verse: Take heed wicked woman,
I am apt to mischiefe now.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You cannot be so unkind,
To her that gives you liberty.

speeches.speaker: Ti.
verse: No, I shall be too kind, thats the devil on't;
I have had store of good wine: and when I am drunk,
Joane is a Lady to me, and I shall
Lay about me like a Lord: I feele strange motions:
Avoid me temptation.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Come sir, i'le help yee in.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: VVhat may that be
That mooves upon the Lake?

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: Still it drawes neerer,
And now I plainly can descerne it.
Tis the French ship.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: In it a woman,
VVho seemes to invite us to her,

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: Still she cals with signes of Love to hasten to her;
So lovely hope doth still appeare:
I feele nor age nor weaknesse.

speeches.speaker: Nicu.
verse: Though it bring death,
To us tis comfort: and deserves a meeting.
Or els fortune tyrd with what we have suffer'd,
And in it overcome, as it may be,
Now sets a period to our misery.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: What dreadfull sounds are these?

speeches.speaker: Amin
verse: Infernall Musick,
Fit for a bloody Feast.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: It seemes prepar'd
To kill our courages, e're they divorse
Our soules and bodies.

speeches.speaker: Ray.
verse: But they that fearelesse fall,
Deprive them of their triumph.

speeches.speaker: Aminta
verse: See the furies,
In their full Trym of cruelty.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Tis the last
Duty that I can pay to my dead Lord,
Set out the Altar, I my selfe wilbe
The Priest, and boldly do those horrid Rites
You shake to think on: lead these Captaines neerer,
For they shall have the honour to fall first
To my Sebastians ashes: and now wretches,
As I am taught already that you are,
And lately by your free confession,
French pirats, and the sons of those I hate,
Even equall with the devil; here with horror,
What tis invites me to this cruell course,
And what you are to suffer; no Amazons we,
But women of Portugall, that must have from you
Sebastian and Nicusa; we are they
That groan'd beneath your fathers wrongs:
VVe are those wretched women,
Their injuries pursu'd, and overtook;
And from the sad remembrance of our losses
We are taught to be cruell; when we were forc'd
From that sweet ayre we breathed in, by their rapine,
And sought a place of being; as the Seas
And winds conspird with their ill purposses,
To load us with afflictions, in a storme
That fell upon us; the two ships that brought us,
To seek new fortunes in an unknown world
Were severed: the one bore all the able men,
Our treasure and our Jewels: in the other,
We women were imbarq'd: and fell upon,
After long tossing in the troubled maine,
This pleasant Island: But in few moneths,
The men that did conduct us hither died,
We long before had given our husbands lost:
Remembring what we had suffred by the French,
We took a solemn Oath never to admit
The curs'd society of men: necessity
Taught us those arts not usuall to our sex:
And the fertile Earth yeelding abundance to us,
We did resolve thus shapt like Amazons
To end our lives; but when you ariv'd here,
And brought as presents to us our own Jewels;
Those which were boorn in the other ship,
How can ye hope to scape our vengeance?

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: It boots not then to swear our inocence?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Or that we never forc'd it from the owners?

speeches.speaker: Ray
verse: Or that there are a remnant of that wrack,
And not far off?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: All you affirme, I know,
Is but to win time; therefore prepare your throats,
The world shall not redeem ye: and that your cries
May find no entrance to our eares,
To moove pitty in any: bid lowd Musick sound
Their fatall Knels; if ye have prayers use 'em quickly,
To any power will own yea; but ha!
Who are these? what spectacles of misfortun?
Why are their looks
So full of Joy and wonder?

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Oh! lay by
These instruments of death, and welcome
To your armes what you durst never hope to imbrace:
This is Sebastian, this Nicusa Maddam:
Preserv'd by miracle: look up deer sir,
And know your own Rossellia: be not lost
In wonder and amazment; or if nature
Can by instinct instruct you what it is,
To be blessed with the name of Father,
Freely injoy it in this faire Virgin.

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: Though my miseries,
And many years of wants, I have indur'd,
May well deprave me of the memory
Of all joyes past; yet looking on this building,
This ruind building of a heavenly forme
In my Rossella; I must remember, I am Sebastian.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: O my joyes!

speeches.speaker: Seba.
verse: And here,
I see a perfect modell of thy selfe,
As thou wert when thy choyce first made thee mine:
These cheecks and fronts though wrinkled now with time
Which art cannot restore: had equall purenesse,
Of naturall white and red, and as much ravishing:
Which by fayre order and succession,
I see descend on her: and may thy vertues
Winde into her forme, and make her a perfect dower:
No part of thy sweet goodnesse wanting to her.
I will not now Rossellia aske thy fortunes,
Nor trouble thee with hearing mine;
Those shall hereafter serve to make glad howers
In their relation: All past wrongs forgot;
I am glad to see you Gentlemen; but most,
That it is in my power to save your Lives;
You sav'd ours when we were neer starv'd at Sea,
And I despaire not, for if she be mine?
Rossellia can deny Sebastian nothing.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: She do's give up her selfe,
Her power and joyes, and all, to you,
To be discharged of 'em as to burthensome;
Wellcome in any shape.

speeches.speaker: Sabast.
verse: Sir in your looks,
I read your sute of my Clarinda: she is yours:
And Lady if it be in me to confirme
Your hopes in this brave Gentleman,
Presume I am your servant.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: We thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Amin.
verse: O Happy houre!

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: O my deer Aminta;
Now all our feares are ended.

speeches.speaker: Tib.
verse: Here I fix: she's mettle,
Steele to the back: and will cut my leaden dagger,
If not us'd with discretion.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: You are still no changling.

speeches.speaker: Sabast.
verse: Nay,
All look cheerfully, for none shalbe
Denyd their lawfull wishes; when a while
We have here refresht our selves; wee'l returne
To our severall homes; and well that voyage ends,
That makes of deady enemies faythfull friends.

speeches.speaker: ~irolet.
verse: BOy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: If my wife seek me, tell her that
Designes of weight, too heavy for her knowledge,
Exact my privacy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I shall, sir.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Do then,
And leave me to my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Tis a raw morning,
And would you please to interpret that for duty
Which you may construe boldnesse, I could wish
To arme your selfe against it, you would use
More of my service.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: I have heate within here,
A noble heat (good boy) to keep it off,
I shall not freeze; deliver my excuse,
And you have done your part.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: That is prevented,
My Lady follows you.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Since I must be crost then,
Let her perform that office.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I obey you.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Prethee to bed; to be thus fond's more tedious
Then if I were neglected.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Tis the fault then
Of love and duty which I would fall under,
Rather then want that care which you may challenge
As due to my obedience.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I confesse
This tendernesse argues a loving wife,
And more deserves my hearts best thanks then anger.
Yet I must tell ye Sweet, you do exceed
In your affection, if you would ingrosse me
To your delights alone.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I am not jealous,
If my embraces have distasted you,
As I must grant you every way so worthy
That tis not in weak woman to deserve you,
Much lesse in miserable me, that want
Those graces some more fortunate are stor'd with.
Seek any whom you please, and I will study
With my best service to deserve those favours,
That shall yeeld you contentment.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: You are mistaken.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: No, I am patient sir, and so good morrow;
I will not be offensive.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Heare my reasons.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Though in your life a widdows bed receives me,
For your sake I must love it. May she prosper
That shall succeed me in it, and your ardour
Last longer to her.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: By the love I beare
First to my Countries peace, next to thy selfe
To whom compar'd, my life I rate at nothing;
Stood here a Lady that were the choyce abstract
Of all the beauties nature ever fashion'd,
Or Art gave ornament to, compar'd to thee,
Thus as thou art obedient and loving,
I should contemne and loath her.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I do believe ye.
How I am blest
In my assur'd beliefe? this is unfain'd;
And why this sadnesse then?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Why Juliana,
Believe me, these my sad and dull retirements,
My often, nay almost continued fasts,
Sleep banisht from my eyes, all pleasures strangers,
Have neither root nor growth from any cause
That may arrive at woman. Shouldst thou be,
As chastity forbid, false to my bed,
I should lament my fortune, perhaps punish
Thy falshood, and then study to forget thee:
But that which like a never emptied spring,
Feeds high the torrent of my swelling griefe,
Is what my Countrey suffers; there's a ground
Where sorrow may be planted, and spring up,
Though yeelding rage and womanish despaire,
And yet not shame the owner.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I do believe it true,
Yet I should think my selfe a happy woman,
If in this generall and timely mourning,
I might or give to you, or else receive
A little lawfull comfort.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Thy discretion
In this may answer for me; look on Naples
The Countrey where we both were born and bred,
Naples the Paradise of Italy,
As that is of the earth; Naples, that was
The sweet retreat of all the worthiest Romans,
When they had shar'd the spoyles of the whole world;
This flourishing Kingdom, whose inhabitants
For wealth and bravery liv'd like petty Kings,
Made subject now to such a tyranny,
As that faire City that receiv'd her name
From Constantine the great, now in the power
Of barbarous Infidels, may forget her own,
To look with pity on our miseries,
So far in our calamities we transcend her.
For since this Arragonian tyrant Ferrand,
Ceaz'd on the government, there's nothing left us
That we can call our own, but our afflictions,

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: And hardly those; the Kings strange cruelty,
Equals all presidents of Tyranny.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Equall say you:
He has out gone, the worst compar'd to him;
Nor Phalaris, nor Dionisius,
Caligula, nor Nero can be mention'd;
They yet as Kings, abus'd their regall power;
This as a Marchant, all the Countries fatt,
He wholy does ingrosse unto himself;
Our Oyles he buyes at his own price, then sels them
To us, at dearer rates; our Plate and Jewels,
Under a fayn'd pretence of publique use,
He borrows; which deny'd, his Instruments force.
The rases of our horses, he takes from us;
Yet keeps them in our pastures; rapes of Matrons,
And Virgins, are too frequent; never man
Yet thank'd him for a pardon; for Religion,
It is a thing he dreames not off.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I have heard,
How true it is, I know not; that he sold
The Bishop-prick of Tarent to a Jew,
For thirteene thousand Duckets.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I was present,
And saw the money paid. the day would leave me,
Ere I could number out his impious actions;
Or what the miserable Subject suffers;
And can you entertaine in such a time,
A thought of dalliance? teares, and sighes, and groanes,
Would better now become you.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: They indeed are,
The onely weapons, our poor Sex can use,
When we are injur'd, and they may become us;
But for men that were born free men, of Ranck;
That would be registred Fathers of their Country;
And to have on their Tombs in Golden Letters,
The noble stile of Tyrant killers, written;
To weepe like fooles, and women and not like wise men.
To practise a redresse, deserves a name,
Which fits not me to give.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Thy grave reproofe:
If what thou dost desire, were possible
To be effected? might well argue it,
As wise as loving; but if you consider,
With what strong guards, this Tyrant is defended:
Ruffins, and malecontents drawne from all quarters;
That onely know, to serve his impious will;
The Citadels built by him in the neck
Of this poor City; the invincesible strength,
Nature by Art assisted, gave this Castle;
And above all his feare; admitting no man
To see him, but unarm'd; it being death
For any to approach him with a weapon.
You must confesse, unlesse our hands were Canons,
To batter down these walls; our weake breath mines,
To blow his Forts up; or our curses lightning,
To force a passage to him; and then blast him;
Our power is like to yours, and we like you;
Weepe our misfortunes.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Walls of Brasse resist not
A noble undertaking: nor can vice,
Raise any Bulwrack, to make good the place,
Where vertue seekes to enter; then to fall
In such a brave attempt, were such an honour;
That Brutus, did he live again would envy.
Were my dead Father in you, and my Brothers;
Nay, all the Ancestors I am deriv'd from;
As you, in being what you are, are all these.
I had rather weare a mourning Garment for you,
And should be more proud of my widdow-hood;
You dying for the freedome of this Country;
Then if I were assur'd, I should injoy
A perpetuity of life and pleasure,
With you the Tyrant living.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Till this minute,
I never heard thee speake; O more then woman!
And more to be belov'd; can I finde out
A Cabinet, to lock a secret in,
Of equall trust to thee? all doubts, and feares,
That scandalize your sex, be farre from me;
Thou shalt pertake my neer and dearest councels,
And further them with thine.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I will be faithfull.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Know then this day, stand heaven propitious to us,
Our liberty begins.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: In Ferrands death?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: 'Tis plotted love, and strongly, and beleeve it,
For nothing else could doe it; 'twas the thought,
How to proceed in this designe and end it,
That made strange my embraces.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Curs'd be she,
That's so indulgent to her own delights,
That for their satisfaction, would give
A stop to such a glorious enterprize:
For me, I would not for the world, I had been
Guilty of such a crime; goe on and prosper.
Goe on my dearest Lord, I love your Honour
Above my life; nay, yours; my Prayers go with you;
Which I will strengthen with my teares: the wrongs
Of this poor Country, edge your sword; O may it
Peirce deep into this Tyrants heart, and then
When you return bath'd in his guilty bloud,
I'le wash you cleane with fountaines of true joy.
But who are your assistants? though I am
So covetous of your glory, that I could wish
You had no sharer in it.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Be not curious.
They come, how ever you command my bosome,
To them I would not have you seene.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I am gon Sir,
Be confident; and may my resolution
Be present with you.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Such a Masculine spirit,
With more then womans vertues, were a dower
To waigh down a Kings fortune.

speeches.speaker: Briss.
prose: Good day to you.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: You are an early stirrer.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: What new face,
Bring you along?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: If I stand doubted Sir?
As by your looks I guesse it: you much injure
A man that loves, and truly loves this Country,
With as much zeale as you doe; one that hates
The Prince by whom it suffers, and as deadly;
One that dares step as farre to gaine my freedome,
As any he that breathes; that weares a sword
As sharp as any's.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Nay, no more comparisons.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: What you but whisper, I dare speake aloud,
Stood the King by; have meanes to put in act too
What you but coldly plot; if this deserve then
Suspition in the best, the boldest, wisest?
Pursue your own intents, il'e follow mine;
And if I not out-strip you—

speeches.speaker: Briss.
verse: Be assur'd Sir,
A conscience like this can never be allide
To treachery.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Who durst speake so much,
But one that is like us a sufferer,
And stands as we affected?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: You are cozend
And all undone; every Intelligencer
Speakes treason with like licence; is not this
Ronvere, that hath for many yeeres been train'd
In Ferrands Schoole, a man in trust and favour,
Rewarded too and highly?

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Grant all this,
The thought of what he was, being as he is now;
A man disgrac'd, and with contempt thrown o^f;
Will spurre him to revenge, as swift as they,
That never were in favour.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Poore and childish.

speeches.speaker: Briss.
verse: His regiment is cast, that is most certain;
And his command in the Castle given away.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: That on my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Grosser still, what shepheard
Would yeeld the poor remainder of his flock,
To a known wolfe; though he put on the habit,
Of a most faithfull dogge, and barke like one?
As this but onely talkes.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Yes, he has meanes too.

speeches.speaker: Virol.
verse: I know it to my griefe, weake men I know it;
To make his peace, if there were any warre
Between him and his Master, betraying
Our innocent lives.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: You are too suspitious;
And I have born too much, beyon'd my temper,
Take your own wayes, i'le leave you.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: You may stay now;
You have enough, and all indeed you fisht for;
But one word Gentlemen: have you discover'd
To him alone our plot?

speeches.speaker: Briss.
verse: To him and others, that are at his devotion.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Worse and worse:
For were he onely conscious of our purpose,
Though with the breach of Hospitable lawes,
In my own house, ide silence him for ever:
But what is past my help, is past my care,
I have a life to loose.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Have better hopes.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: And when you know, with what charge I have further'd
Your noble undertaking, you will sweare me
Another man; the guards I have corrupted:
And of the choyce of all our noblest youths,
Attir'd like virgins; such as Hermits would
Welcome to their sad cells, prepar'd a Maske;
As done for the Kings pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: For his safety
I rather feare; and as a pageant to
Usher our ruine.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: We as Torch-bearers
Will waite on these, but with such art and cunning;
I have convei'd sharp poniards in the Wax,
That we may passe, though search't through all his guards
Without suspition, and in all his glory,
Oppresse him, and with safety.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: 'Tis most strange.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: To be effected.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: You are doubtfull still.

speeches.speaker: Briss.
verse: But we resolv'd to follow him, and if you
Desist now Virolet, we will say 'tis feare,
Rather then providence.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: And so we leave you,

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: To your wise doubts, and to my better councels;
Oh! pardon me my Lord, and trust me too;
Let me not like Cassandra prophesie truths,
And never be beleiv'd, before the mischiefe:
I have heard all; know this Ronvere a villaine,
A villaine that hath tempted me, and plotted
This for your ruine, onely to make way
To his hopes in my embraces; at more leisure
I will acquaint you, wherefore I conceil'd it
To this last minute; if you stay you are lost,
And all prevention too late. I know,
And 'tis to me known onely, a darke cave
Within this house, a part of my poor dower,
Where you may lye conceal'd, as in the center,
Till this rough blast be ore; where there is ayre,
More then to keep in life; Ferrand will find you,
So curious his feares are.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: 'Tis better fall
Then hide my head, now 'twas thine own advice,
My friends ingag'd too.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: You stand further bound,
Then to weake men that have betray'd themselves,
Or to my Councell, though then just and loyall:
Your phansie hath been good, but not your judgement,
In choyce of such to side you, wil you leape
From a steep Tower, because a desperate foole
Does it, and trusts the wind to save his hazard?
There's more expected from you; all mens eyes are fixt
On Viriolet, to help not hurt them;
Make good their hopes and ours, you have sworn often,
That you dare credit me; and allow'd me wise
Although a woman; even Kings in great Actions,
Waite opportunity and so must you Sir,
Or loose your understanding.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Thou art constant;
I am uncertain foole, a most blinde foole;
Be thou my guide.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I. I faile to direct you,
For torment or reward, when I am wretched,
May constancy forsake me.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I've my satety.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Why are you rapt thus?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Peace, thou art a foole.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: But if I were a flatterer like your worship,
I should be wise and rich too;
There are few else that prosper, baudes excepted,
They hold an equall place there.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: A shrew'd knave;
But O the King, the happy King!

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Why happy?
In bearing a great burthen.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: What beares he,
That's born on Princes shoulders?

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: A Crownes waight,
Which sets more heavy on his head, then the ore
Slaves digge out of the Mines, of which 'tis made.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Thou worthily art his fool, to think that heavy
That carryes him in the ayre; the reverence due
To that most sacred Gold, makes him ador'd,
His Foot-steps kist, his smiles to raise a begger
To a Lords fortune; and when he but frownes,
The City quakes.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Or the poor Cuckolds in it,
Cox-combs I should say, I am of a foole.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Grown a Philosopher, to heare this parasite.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: The delicates he is serv'd with see and envy,

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: I had rather have an Onyon with a stomack,
Then these without one.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: The Celestiall Musick,
Such as the motion of the eternall spheares
Yeelds Iove, when he drinkes Nectar.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Here's a fine knave, yet hath to many fellowes.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Then the beauties,
That with variety of choyce embraces,
Renew his age.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Help him to croutch rather,
And the French Cringe, they are excellent Surgeons that way.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: O Majesty! let others think of heaven,
While I contemplate thee.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: This is not Atheisme, but Court observance.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Now the God appears, usher'd with earth-quakes.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
prose: Base Idolatry.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: These meates are poysoned, hang
The Cookes; no note more, on
Forfeit of your fingers; doe you
Envy me a minutes slumber, what are these?

speeches.speaker: 1. Gu.
verse: The Ladies appointed by your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: To the purpose, for what appointed?

speeches.speaker: 1. Gu.
verse: For your graces pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: To sucke away the little bloud is left me,
By my continuall cares; I am not apt now,
Injoy them first, ta^e of my dyet once;
And your turne serv'd, for fifty Crownes a peece
Their Husbands may redeem them.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
verse: Great Sir, mercy.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I am deafe, why stare you? is what we command
To be disputed? who's this? bring you the dead
T'upbrai'd me to my face?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Hold Emperour;
Hold mightest of Kings, I am thy vassell,
Thy Foot-stool, that durst not presume to look
On thy offended face.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Castruchio rise.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Let not the lightning of thy eye consume me,
Nor heare that Musicall tongue, in dreadfull thunder,
That speak^s all mercy.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Here's no slattering rogue.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Ferrand, that is the Father of his people,
The glory of mankinde.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: No more, no word more;
And while I tell my troubles to my selfe,
Be Statues without motion or voyce,
Though to be flatter'd, is an itch to greatnesse,
It now offends me.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Here's the happy man;
But speake who dares.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: When I was innocent;
I yet remember, I could eat and sleepe,
Walke unaffrighted, but now terrible to others:
My guards cannot keepe feare from me
It still pursues me; Oh! my wounded conscience,
The Bed I would rest in, is stuft with thornes;
The grounds strow'd o're with adders, and with aspicks
Where ere I set my foot, but I am in,
And what was got with cruelty, with blood,
Must be defended, though this lifes a hell,
I feare a worse hereafter. ha!

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Welcome Ronvere, welcome my golden plummet
With which I sound mine enemies depthes and angers,
Hast thou discover'd.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: All as you could wish Sir,
The Plot, and the contrivers; was made one
Of the conspiracie.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Is Virolet in?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: The head of all, he onely scented me:
And from his feare, that I plaid false is fled;
The rest I have in fetters

speeches.speaker: Fer
verse: Death and hell.
Next to my mortall foe the pyrat Sesse,
I aym'd at him; he's vertuous, and wise,
A lover of his freedome and his countries
Dangerous to such as govern by the sword,
And so to me: no tract which way he went,
No meanes to overtake him?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Ther's some hope left;
But with a rough hand, to be seas'd upon.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: What is't?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: If any know, or where he is,
Or which way he is fled, it is his wife;
Her with his Father I have apprehended,
And brought among the rest.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: 'Twas wisely order'd,
Go fetch them in, and let my executioners
Appeare in horrour with the racke.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: I take it signeur, this is no time for you to flatter,
Or me to foole in.

speeches.speaker: Cast
verse: Thou art wise in this, let's off, it is unsafe to be nere Jove,
When he begins to thunder.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Good morality.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I that have peirc'd into the hearts of men;
Forc'd them to lay open with my lookes,
Secrets whose leas^ discovery was death,
Will rend for what concernes my life, the fortresse,
Of a weake womans faith.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
verse: What ere we suffer,
The waight, that loads a Traytors
Heart sit ever, heavy on thine.

speeches.speaker: Briss
verse: As we are caught by thee,
Fall thou by others.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Pish poor fools, your curses will
Never reach me.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse:
Now by my
~irolets life;
Father, this is a glori^us stage of murther.
Here are five properties too, and such spectators,
As will expect good action, to the life;
Let us performe our parts, and we shall live,
When these are rotten, would we might begin once;
Are you the Master of the company?
Troth you are tedious now.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: She does deride me.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Thee and thy Power, if one poor syllable
Could win me, an assurance of thy favour,
I would not speake it, I desire to be
The great example of thy cruelty,
To whet which one, know Ferrand, I alone
Can make discovery, where my Virolet is,
Whose life, I know thou aym'st at, but if tortures
Compell me to't, may hope of heaven for sake me;
I dare thy worst.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Are we contemn'd.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Thou art,
Thou and thy Ministers, my life is thine;
But in the death, the Victory shall be mine.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: We have such a Mistresse here to teach us courage,
That cowards might learn from her.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: You are slow;
Begin the Scene thou miserable foole
For so I'le make thee.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: 'Tis not in thy reach;
I am happy in my sufferings, thou most wretched.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: So brave! Ile tame you yet, pluck hard villains;
Is she insensible? no sigh nor groan? or is she dead?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: No tyrant, though I suffer
More then a woman, beyond flesh and blood;
Tis in a cause so honourable, that I scorn
With any sign that may expresse a sorrow
To shew I do repent.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Confesse yet,
And thou shal be safe.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Tis wrapt up in my soule,
From whence thou canst not force it.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I will be
Ten daies a killing thee.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Be twenty thousand,
My glory lives the longer.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Tis a miracle,
She tires th'executioners,
And me.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Unloose her, I am conquer'd, I must take
Some other way; reach her my chaire, in honour
Of her invincible fortitude.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Will you not
Dispatch the rest?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: When I seem mercifull,
Assure thy selfe Ronvere, I am most cruell.
Thou wonder of thy sex, and of this Nation,
That hast chang'd my severity to mercy,
Not to thy selfe alone, but to thy people,
In which I do include these men, my enemies:
Unbind them.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: This is strange.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: For your intent
Against my life, which you dare not deny,
I onely aske one service.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Above hope.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: There rides a Pyrate neer, the Duke of Sesse,
My enemy and this Countries, that in bonds
Holds my deere friend Ascanio: free this friend,
Or bring the Pyrats head; besides your pardon,
And honour of the action, your reward
Is forty thousand Ducates. And because
I know that Virolet is as bold as wise,
Be he your Generall, as pledge of your faith,
That you wil undertake it: let this old man,
And this most constant Matron stay with me;
Of whom, as of my selfe, I wil be carefull;
She shall direct you where her husband is.
Make choice of any ship you think most useful.
They are rig'd for you.

speeches.speaker: Bris.
verse: We with joy accept it.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: And wil proclaim King Ferrant mercifull.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: The mysterie of this, my Lord? or are you
Chang'd in your nature?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Ile make thee private to it.
The lives of these weake men, and desperate woman,
Would no way have secur'd me, had I took them;
Tis Virolet I aime at; he has power,
And knows to hurt. If they encounter Sesse,
And he prove conquerour, I am assur'd
They'l finde no mercy: if that they prove victors,
I shall recover with my friend; his head
I most desire of all men.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Now I have it.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Ile make thee understand the drift of all.
So we stand sure, thus much for those that fall.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Ley here before the wind; up with her Canvase
And let her work, the wind begins to whis^le;
Clap all her streamers on, and let her dance,
As if she were the Minion of the Ocean.
Let her bestride the billows till they rore,
And curle their wanton heads. Ho, below there:
Ho, ho, within.
Ley her North-east, and thrust her missen out,
The day grows faire and cleare, and the wind Courts us.
O for a lusty saile now, to give chase to.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: A stubborn Barke, that wo'd but bear up to us,
And change a broadside bravely.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Where's the Duke?

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: I have not seen him stir to day.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: O Gunner,
What bravery dwels in his age, and what valour?
And to his friends, what gentlenesse and bounty?
How long have we been inhabitants at Sea here?

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Some fourteen yeers.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: By fourteen lives I swear then,
This Element never nourisht such a Pirate;
So great, so fearlesse, and so fortunate,
So patient in his want, in Act so valiant.
How many saile of wel man'd ships before us,
As the Bonuto does the flying fish,
Have we pursued and scowerd, that to outstrip us,
They have been fain to hang their very shirts on?
What Gallies have we bang'd, and sunke, and taken;
Whose onely fraughts were fire, and stern defiance?
And nothing spoke but Bullet in all these.
How like old Neptune have I seen our Generall
Standing ith' Poope, and tossing his steel Trident,
Commanding both the Sea and Winds to serve him?

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: His daughter too, which is the honour, Boteswain,
Of all her sex; that Martiall mayd.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: A brave wench.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: How oftentimes, a fight being new begun,
Has she leap'd down, and took my Linstock from me,
And crying, now fly right, fir'd all my chasers?
Then like the Image of the warlike Goddesse,
Her Target brac'd upon her arme, her Sword drawn,
And anger in her eyes, leap'd up again,
And bravely hal'd the Barke. I have wondred Botswain,
That in a body made so delicate,
So soft for sweet embraces, so much fire,
And manly soule, not starting at a danger.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Her Noble father got her in his fury,
And so she proves a souldier.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: This to I wonder at,
Taking so many strangers as he does,
He uses them with that respect and coolnesse,
Not making prize, but onely borrowing
What may supply his want: nor that for nothing;
But renders back what they may stand in need of,
And then parts lovingly: Where, if he take
His Countreyman, that should be neerest to him,
And stand most free from danger, he sure pays for't:
He drownes or hangs the men, ransacks the Barke,
Then gives her up a Bonfire to his fortune.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: The wrongs he has receiv'd from that dull Countrey,
That's all I know has purchas'd all his cruelty.
We fare the better; cheerly, cheerly boys,
The ship runs merrily; my Captain's melancholy,
And nothing cures that in him but a Sea-fight:
I hope to meet a saile boy, and a right one.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: That's my hope too; I am ready for the pastime.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: I'th mean time let's bestow a song upon him,
To shake him from his dumps, and bid good day to him.
Ho, in the hold.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Here, here.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
verse: To th' main top boy.
And thou kenst a ship that dares defie us,
Here's Gold.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I am gon.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Come sirs, a queint Levet.
To waken our brave Generall. Then to our labour.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: I thank you loving mates; I thank you all.
There's to prolong your mirth, & good morrow to you.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: Take this from me, you'r honest valiant friends;
And such we must make much of. Not a sayle stirring?

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Not any within ken yet.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
verse: Without doubt Lady,
The wind standing so faire and full upon us,
We shal have sport anon. But noble Generall,
Why are you still so sad? you take our edge off;
You make us dull, and spirit-lesse.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Ile tell ye,
Because I wil provoke you to be fortunate;
For when you know my cause, twill double arme you.
This woman never knew it yet; my daughter,
Some discontents she has.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: Pray sir go forward.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: These fourteen yeeres, I have stoed it here at Sea,
Where the most curious thought could never find it.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Call up the Master, and all the Mates.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Good morrow to our Generall, good one,
And to that Noble Lady all good wishes.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: I thank you Master.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Mark me, thus it is then;
Which I did never think to have discovered,
Till full revenge had wooed me; but to satisfie
My faithfull friends, thus I cast off my burden.
In that short time I was a Courtier,
And followed that most hated of all Princes,
Ferrant the full example of all mischiefes,
Compel'd to follow to my soule a stranger,
It was my chance one day to play at Chesse
For some few Crowns, with a mynion of this Kings,
A mean poor man, that onely serv'd his pleasures;
Removing of a Rook, we grew to words;
From this to hotter anger: to be short,
I got a blow.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: How, how my Noble father?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: A blow my girle, which I had soon repayd,
And sunk the slave for ever, had not odds
Thrust in betwixt us. I went away disgrac'd—

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: For honours sake not so sir.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: For that time, wench;
But calld upon him, like a Gentleman,
By many private friends; knockt at his valour,
Courted his honour hourely to repaire me;
And tho he were a thing my thoughts made sleight on,
And onely worth the fury of my footman,
Still I pursued him Nobly.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: Did he escape you?
My old brave father, could you sit down so coldly?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Have patience, and know all. Pursued him fairly,
Till I was laught at, scornd, my wrongs made maygames.
By him unjustly wrong'd, should be all justice,
The slave protected; yet at length I found him,
Found him, when he suppos'd all had been buried;
And what I had received durst not be questioned;
And then he fell, under my Sword he fell,
For ever sunk; his poore life, like the ayre,
Blown in an empty bubble, burst, and left him,
No Noble wind of memory to raise him.
But then began my misery, I fled;
The Kings frowns following, and my friends dispaires;
No hand that durst relieve: my Countrey fearfull,
Basely and weakly fearfull of a tyrant;
Which made his bad wil worse, stood still and wondred,
Their vertues bedrid in e'm; then my girle,
A little one, I snatch'd thee from thy nurse,
The modell of thy fathers miseries:
And some small wealth was fit for present carriage,
And got to Seal; where I profest my anger,
And wil do, whilst that base ungratefull Countrey,
And that bad King, have blood or means to quench me.
Now ye know all.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We know all, and admire all;
Go on and do all still, and still be fortunate.

speeches.speaker: Daught.
verse: Had you done lesse, or lost this Noble anger,
You had been worthy then mens empty pities,
And not their wonders. Go on, and use your justice;
And use it still with that fell violence
It first appeared to you; if you go lesse,
Or take a doting mercy to protection,
The honour of a father I disclaim in you,
Call back all duty, and will be prowder of
The infamous and base name of a whore,
Then daughter to a great Duke and a coward.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Mine own sweet Martia, no; thou knowst my nature,
It cannot, must not be.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: I hope it shal not.
But why sir, do you keep alive still young Ascanio,
Prince of Rossana, King Ferrants most belov'd one,
You took two moneths agoe?
Why is not he flung overboord, or hang'd?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Ile tell thee girle:
It were a mercy in my nature now,
So soon to break the bed of his afflictions;
I am not so far reconcil'd yet to him
To let him die, that were a benefit.
Besides, I keep him as a bayt and dyet,
To draw on more, and neerer to the King,
I look each hour to heare of his Armados,
And a hot welcome they shall have.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: But hark you?
If you were overswayed with oddes —

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: I find you:
I would not yield; no girle, no hope of yeelding,
Nor fling my self one houre into their mercies,
And give the tyrant hope to gain his Kingdom.
No, I can sink wench, and make shift to die;
A thousand doores are open, I shal hit one.
I am no niggard of my life, so it goe Nobly:
All waies are equall and all houres; I care not.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: Now you speak like my father.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Noble General,
If by our means they inherit ought but bangs,
