The mercy of the main yard light upon us.
No, we can sinke too sir, and sinke low enough,
To pose their cruelties, to follow us:
And he that thinks of life, if the world go that way,
A thousand cowards suck his bones.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Let the worst come,
I can unbreech a Canon, and without much help
Turn her into the Keele; and when she has split it,
Every man knows his way, his own prayers,
And so good night I think.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We have liv'd all with you,
And will die with you Generall.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: I thank you Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Boy above.
verse: A Sayle, a Sayle.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: A cheerfull sound.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: A Sayle.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Of whence? of whence boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: A lusty sayle.

speeches.speaker: Daugh.
verse: Look right, and look again.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: She plows the Sea before her,
And fomes i'th mouth.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Of whence?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I ken not yet sir.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: O may she prove of Naples.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Prove the Divell,
We'l spit out fire as thick as she.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Hoy.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Brave boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Of Naples Naples, I think of Naples, Master,
Me thinks I see the Armes.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Up, up another,
And give more certain signes.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: All to your businesse,
And stand but right and true.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Hang him that halts now.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sh'as us in chase.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We'l spare her our main top-saile,
He shall not look us long, we are no starters,
Down with the fore-saile too, we'l spoom before her.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Gunner, good noble Gunner, for my honour
Load me but these two Minions in the chape there;
And load 'em right, that they may bid faire welcome,
And be thine eye and level as thy heart it.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Madam, Ile scratch 'em out, Ile pisse 'em out else.

speeches.speaker: Sayl. above.
verse: Ho.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Of whence now?

speeches.speaker: Sayl.
verse: Of Naples, Naples, Naples.
I see her top flag how she quarters Naples.
I heare her Trumpets.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Down, she's welcome to us.
Every man to his charge, man her i'th bowe wel.
And place your rakers right, daughter be sparing.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I sweare Ile be above sir, in the thickest,
And where most danger is, Ile seek for honour.
They have begun, harke how their Trumpets call us.
Hark how the wide mouth'd Cannons sing amongst us.
Heark how they saile; out of our shels for shame sir.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Now fortune and my cause.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Be bold and conquer.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: They'l board us once again, they'r tuffe & valiant.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
verse: Twice we have blown 'em into th'ayre like feathers.
And made 'em dance.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Good boys, fight bravely, manly.
They come on yet; clap in her stern, & yoke 'em.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: You shall not need, I have provision for 'em;
Let 'em boord once again, the next is ours.
Stand bravely to your Pikes, away, be valiant.
I have a second course of service for 'em,
Shall make the bowels of their Barke ake, hoy
The Duke fights like a Dragon. Who dares be idle.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Down with 'em, stow 'em in.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Cut their throats, tis brotherhood to fling em into the Sea.
The Duke is hurt, so is his lovely daughter Martia.
We have the day yet.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
prose: Pox fire'em, they have smok'd us, never such plumbs yet flew.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: They have rent the ship, & bor'd a hundred holes,
She swims still lustily.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: She made a brave fight, and he shall be cur'd,
And make a braver yet.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
prose: Bring us some Cans up, I am hot as fire.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
verse: I am sure I am none o'th coolest.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: My Cannons rung like Bels. Here's to my Mistris.
The dainty Sweet brasse Minion, split their fore-mast,
She never failed.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Ye did all well, and truly, like faithfull honest men.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
prose: But is she rich Master?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Rich for my Captains purpose howsoever,
And we are his. —How bravely now he shows,
Heated in blood and anger? how do you sir?
Not wounded mortally I hope?

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: No Master, but onely weare the livery of fury.
I am hurt, and deep.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: My Mistris too?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: A scratch man,
My needle would ha done as much good sir,
Be provident and carefull.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Prethee peace girle,
This wound is not the first blood I have blusht in,
Ye fought all like tall men, my thanks among ye,
That speaks not what my purse means, but my tongue, souldiers.
Now sir, to you that sought me out, that found me,
That found me what I am, the Tyrants Tyrant;
You that were imp'd the weak arme to his folly,
You are welcome to your death.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I do expect it,
And therefore need no complement, but waite it.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Thou bor'st the face once of a Noble Gentleman,
Rankt in the first file of the vertuous,
By every hopefull spirit, shewed and pointed,
Thy Countries love; one that advanc'd her honour,
Not taynted with the base and servile uses

The Tyrant ties mens soules too. Tell me
~irolet,
If shame have not forsook thee, with thy credit.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: No more of these Racks; what I am I am.
I hope not to go free with poore confessions;
Nor if I show ill, will I seem a monster,
By making my mind prisoner; do your worst.
When I came out to deale with you, I cast it,
Onely those base inflictions fit for slaves,
Because I am a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Thou art none.
Thou wast while thou stoodst good, th'art now a villain
And agent for the divell.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: That tongue lies.
Give me my Sword again, and stand all arm'd;
He prove it on ye all, I am a Gentleman,
A man as faire in honour; rate your prisoners;
How poore and like a Pedagogue it shews?
How far from Noblenesse? tis fair, you may kil's;
But to defame your victory with foule language.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Go, fling him overboord; Ile teach you sirra.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: You cannot teach me to die. I could kill you now
With patience, in despising all your cruelties.
And make you choke with anger.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Away I say.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay sir, h'as given you such bold language,
I am not reconcil'd to him yet, and therefore
He shall not have his wish observ'd so neerly,
To die when he please; I beseech you stay sir.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Do with him what thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Carry him to th'Bilboes,
And clap him fast there, with the Prince.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Do Lady,
For any death you give, I am bound to blesse you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now to your Cabin, sir; pray lean upon me,
And take your rest, the Surgeons waite all for you.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Thou makest me blush to see thee bear thy fortuns;
Why, sure I have no hurt, I have not fought sure?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: You bleed apace, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Ye grow cold too.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: I must be ruld, no leaning,
My deepest wounds scorn Crutches.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: A brave Generall.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sayl.
verse: Will they not moore her?

speeches.speaker: 2 Sayl.
verse: Not till we come to the Fort,
This is too weak a place for our defences,
The Carpenters are hard at worke; she swims well,
And may hold out another fight. The ship we took
Burns there to give us light.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sayl.
verse: She made a brave fight.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sayl.
verse: She put us all in feare.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sayl.
verse: Beshrew my heart did she.
Her men are gone to Candy, they are pepper'd,
All but this prisoner.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sayl.
verse: Sure he's a brave fellow.

speeches.speaker: 1 Say.
verse: A stubborn knave, but we have pul'd his bravery.
Look how he looks now: come let's go serve his dyet,
Which is but bread and water.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sayl.
verse: He'l grow fat on't.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: I must confesse I have endured much misery,
even almost to the ruine of my spirit,
But ten times more grows my affliction,
To finde my friend here.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Had we serv'd our Countrey,
Or honesties, as we have serv'd our follies,
We had not been here now?

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: Tis to true Virolet.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: And yet my end in ventring for your safety,
Pointed at more then Ferrants will, a base one;
Some service for mine own, some for my Nation,
Some for my friend; but I am rightly payd,
That durst adventure such a Noble office,
From the most treacherous command of mischiefe;
You know him now?

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: And when I neerer knew him,
Then when I waited, Heaven be witnesse with me,
(And if I lie my miseries still load me)
With what teares I have woed him, with what prayers,
What weight of reasons I have layd, what dangers;
Then, when the peoples curses flew like storms;
And every tongue was whetted to defame him,
To leave his doubts, his tyrannies, his slaughters,
His fell oppressions. I know I was hated too.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: And all mankind that knew him: these confessions
Do no good to the world, to Heaven they may.
Let's study to die well, we have liv'd like coxcombs.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: That my mis-fortune, should lose you too.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Yes;
And not onely me, but many more, and better:
For my life, tis not this; or might I save yours,
And some brave friends I have engag'd, let me go;
It were the meritorious death I wish for,
But we must hang or drown like whelps.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: No remedy.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: On my part I expect none. I know the man,
And know he has been netled to the quick too,
I know his nature.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: A most cruell nature.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: His wrongs have bred him up. I cannot blame him.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: He has a daughter too, the greatest scorner,
And most insulter upon misery.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: For those, they are toyes to laugh at, not to lead men:
A womans mirth or anger, like a meteor
Glides and is gone, and leaves no crack behind it;
Our miseries would seem like masters to us,
And shake our manly spirits into feavors,
If we respected those; the more they glory,
And raise insulting Trophies on our ruines;
The more our vertues shine in patience.
Sweet Prince, the name of death was never terrible
To him that knew to live; nor the loud torrent
Of all afflictions, singing as they swim,
A gall of heart, but to a guilty conscience:
Whilst we stand faire, but by a two-edg'd storm,
We find untimely fals, like early Roses;
But to the earth, we beare our native sweetnesse.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: Good sir go on.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: When we are little children,
And cry and fret for every toy comes crosse us;
How sweetly do we shew, when sleep steales on us?
When we grow great, but our affections greater,
And struggle with this stubborn twin, born with us;
And tug and pull, yet still we finde a Giant:
Had we not then the priviledge to sleep,
Our everlasting sleep? he would make us ideots;
The memory and monuments of good men
Are more then lives, and tho their Tombs want tongues,
Yet have they eyes, that daily sweat their losses;
And such a teare from stone, no time can value.
To die both young and good, are natures curses,
As the world says; ask truth, they are bountious blessings:
For then we reach at Heaven, in our full vertues,
And fix our selves new Stars, crown'd with our goodnes.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: You have double arm'd me.
Hark, what noyse is this?
What horrid noyse is the Sea pleas'd to sing,
A hideous Dirg to our deliverance?

speeches.speaker: Viro.
prose: Stand fast now.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I am fixt.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: We feare ye not.
Let death appear in all shapes, we smile on him.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: The Lady now.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: The face oth' Maske is alter'd.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: What will she doe?

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Do what she can, I care not.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: She looks on you sir.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Rather she looks through me,
But yet she stirs me not.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Poore wretched slaves,
Why do you live? or if ye hope for mercy,
Why do not you houle out, and fill the hold
With lamentations, cries, and base submissions,
Worthy our scorn?

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Madam, you are mistaken;
We are no slaves to you, but to blind fortune;
And if she had her eyes, and durst be certain,
Certain our friend, I would not bow unto her;
I would not cry, nor aske so base a mercy:
If you see any thing, in our appearance,
Worthy your sexes softnes and your own glory?
Do it for that; and let that good reward it:
We cannot beg.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Ile make you beg, and bow too.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Madam for what?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: For life; and when you hope it,
Then will I laugh and triumph on your basenesse.

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Madam tis true, there may be such a favour,
And we may aske it too; aske it with honour;
And thanke you for that favour, nobly thank you,
Tho it be death; but when we beg a base life,
And beg it of your scorn—

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Y'are couzened woman,
Your handsomnesse may do much, but not this way;
But for your glorious hate—

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Are ye so stubborn?
Death, I will make you bow.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: It must be in your bed then;
There you may worke me to humility.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Why, I can kill thee.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: If you do it handsomely;
It may be I can thank you, else—

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: So glorious?

speeches.speaker: Asca.
verse: Her cruelty now workes.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Yet woot thou?

speeches.speaker: Virt.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Wilt thou for life sake?

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: No, I know your subtilty.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: For honour sake?

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: I will not be a Pageant,
My mind was ever firm, and so Ile lose it.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Ile starve thee to it.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Ile starve my selfe, and crosse it.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Ile lay thee on such miseries—

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Ile weare 'em,
And with that wantonnesse, you do your Bracelets.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Ile be a moneth a killing thee.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Poore Lady,
Ile be a moneth a dying then: what's that?
There's many a Callenture outdoes your cruelty.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: How might I do, in killing of his body,
To save his Noble mind? Who waites there?

speeches.speaker: Sayl.
verse: Maddam.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Unbolt this man, and leave those things behind you,
And so away. Now put 'em on. Uunbolt him.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: To what end?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: To my end, to my will.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I thank you.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Nay, now you thank me, Ile do more. Ile tell ye,
I am a servant to your curtesie,
And so far will be wooed: but if this triumph
Be onely aym'd, to make your mischiefe glorious;
Lady, y'ave put a richer shroud upon me,
Which my strong mind shall suffer in.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Come hither,
And all thy bravery put into thy carriage,
For I admire thee.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Whither will this woman?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Take heed my friend.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Look as thou scorndst my cruelty:
I know thou doest.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I never fear'd, nor flatter'd.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: No if thou hadst, thou hadst died, & I had gloried.
I suffer now, and thou which art my prisoner,
Hast Nobly won the free power to despise me.
I love thee, and admire thee for thy Noblenesse;
And for thy manly sufferance, am thy servant.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Good Lady, mock me not.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: By Heaven I love thee;
And by the soule of love, am one piece with thee.
Thy mind, thy mind; thy brave, thy manly mind:
That like a Rock stands all the storms of fortune,
And beats 'em roaring back they cannot reach thee:
That lovely mind I dote on, not the body;
That mind has rob'd me of my liberty:
That mind has darken'd all my bravery,
And into poor despis'd things, turn'd my angers.
Receive me to your love sir, and instruct me;
Receive me to your bed, and marry me:
Ile wait upon you, blesse the houre I knew you.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Is this a new way?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: If you doubt my faith.
First take your liberty; Ile make it perfect,
Or any thing within my power.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: I love you;
But how to recompence your love with marriage?
Alas, I have a wife.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Dearer then I am?
That will adventure so much for your safety?
Forget her fathers wrongs, quit her own honour,
Pull on her for a strangers sake, all curses?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Shall this Prince have his freedom too?
Else all I love is gone, all my friends perish.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: He shall.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: What shall I do?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: If thou despise my curtesie,
When I am dead, for griefe I am forsaken,
And no soft hand left to asswage your sorrows;
Too late, but too true, curse your own cruelties.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: Be wise; if she be true, no thred is left else,
To guide us from this laborinth of mischiefe;
Nor no way for our friends.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Thus then, I take you:
I bind ye to my life, my love.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I take you,
And with the like bond tye my heart your servant;
W'are now almost at Harbour, within this houre,
In the dead watch, Ile have the long boat ready;
And when I give the word, be sure you enter,
Ile see ye furnisht both immediately,
And like your selfe; some trusty man shall wait you,
The watch Ile make mine own; onely my love
Requires a stronger vow, which Ile administer
Before we go.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: Ile take it to confirm you.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Go in, there are the Keys, unlock his fetters,
And arme ye Nobly both; Ile be with you presently,
And s^ this loving kisse.

speeches.speaker: As^n.
verse: Be constant Lady.

speeches.speaker: Surg.
verse: You grow so angry sir, your wound goes backward.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: I am angry at the time, at none of you,
That sends but one poor subject for revenge;
I would have all the Court, and all the villany,
Was ever practiz'd under that foule Ferrand
Tyrant, and all to quench my wrath.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Be patient,
Your grace may find occasion every houre,
For certaine they will seeke you, to satisfy,
And to the full, your anger.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Death, they dare not:
They know that I command death, feed his hunger,
And when I let him loose—

speeches.speaker: Sur.
verse: You'l never heale sir,
If these extreames dwell in you, you are old,
And burn your spirits out with this wild angers.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Thou liest, I am not old, I am as lusty
And full of manly heat as them, or thou art.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: No more of that.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: And dare seek out a danger;
And hold him at the swords point, when thou tremblest
And creepest into thy box of salves to save thee.
O Master, I have had a dreadfull dream to night!
Me-thought the ship was all on fire, and my lov'd Daughter,
To save her life, leapt into th' Sea; where suddainly
A stranger snatch'd her up, and swom away with her.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
prose: 'Twas but the heate o'th fight sir.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
verse: Look out, what's that?

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: The long bote as I live.

speeches.speaker: Bote.
prose: Ho, there, ith long Bote.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: What noise is that?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I hear sir —

speeches.speaker: Boats.
verse: The devill or his dam; haile her agen boyes.

speeches.speaker: Ssail.
verse: The long boate, ho, the long boate.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Why, the long boate?
Where is the long Boate?

speeches.speaker: Boat.
verse: She is stolne off.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Who stole her?
O my prophetique soule!

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Your daughter's gone sir;
The prisoners, and six Saylors, rogues.

speeches.speaker: Ses
verse: Mischief, six thousand plagues sale with 'em;
They'r in her yet, make out.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We have ne'r a Boate.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Who knew of this trick?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Weigh Anchors and away.

speeches.speaker: Boat.
verse: We ha' no winde sir,
They'l beate us with their Oares.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Then sinke 'em Gunner,
O sink 'em, sink 'em, sink 'em, claw 'em Gunner;
As ever thou hast lov'd me.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: I'le do reason,
But i'le be hangd before I hurt the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
prose: Who knew of this?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We stand all clear.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: What divel
Put this base trick into her tayle? my daughter,
And run away with rogues! I hope she's sunk,
Or torne to pieces with the shot; rots find her,
The leprosy of whore, stick ever to her,
O she has ruind my revenge.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: She is gone sir,
I cannot reach her with my shot.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Rise winds, blow till you burst the aire,
Blow till ye burst the aire, and swell the Seas,
That they may sink the starres, O dance her, dance her;
Shes impudently wanton, dance her, dance her,
Mount her upon your surges, coole her, coole her
She runs hot like a whore, coole her, coole her;
O now a shot to sink her; come, cut Cables;
I will away, and where she sets her foote
Although it be in Ferrants court, ile follow her,
And such a fathers vengeance shall she suffer—
Dare any man stand by me?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: All, all.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
verse: All sir.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: And the same cup you taste.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Cut Cables then;
For I shall never sleep, nor know what peace is,
Till I have pluckt her heart out;

speeches.speaker: All within.
verse: O maine there.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: You are too gentle sir.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: You are too carelesse:
The creatures I have made, no way regard me:
VVhy should I give you names, titles of honour
Rob families, to fill your private houses
For your advancement, draw all curses on me,
VVake tedious winter nights, to make them happy
That for me break no slumber?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: VVhat we can,
VVe dare doe

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: VVhy is your Soveraignes life then
(In which you live, and in whose fall your honours,
Your wealth, your pomp, your pride and all must suffer)
No better guarded? O my cruell Stars,
That marke me out a King, raising me on
This pinnacle of greatnesse, only to be
The neerer blasting!

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: VVhat think you now Castruchio?
Is not this a merry life?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Still thou art couzend;
It is a glorious royall discontentment;
How bravely it becomes him!

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: To be made
The common butt, for every slave to shoot at;
No peace, no rest I take, but their alarams
Beat at my heart: why do I live, or seek then,
To adde a day more to these glorious troubles?
Or to what end when all I can arrive at,
Is but the summing up of feares and sorrowes,
VVhat power has my command, when from my bosom
Ascanio my most dear, and lov'd Ascanio,
Was snatch'd, spite of my wil, spite of my succor,
And by mine own proud slave reteind most miserable?
And still that villains lives to nip my pleasures,
It being not within my power to reach him.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Time may restore all this; and would you hear
VVhose counsell never faild you.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Tell me no more,
I faint beneath the burthen of my cares,
And yeild my selfe most wretched.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: On my Knees
I beg it might sir, vouchsafe me hearing.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Speak, speak, and I thus low, such is my fortune,
VVill hear what thou canst say.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Look but on this,
Has not a man that has but means to keep
A Hawk, a Grayhound, and a hunting Nag,
More pleasure then this King?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: A dull foole still,
Make me a King, and let me scratch with care,
And see who'l have the better; give me rule,
Command, obedience, pleasure of a King,
And let the devil rore; The greatest corrosive
A King can have, is of more pretious tickling,
And handled to the height more dear delight,
Then other mens whole lives, let 'em be safe too.

speeches.speaker: ~il.
verse: Think of the mutinous people.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Hang the people,
Give me the pleasure, let me do all, awe all,
Enjoy their wives and states at my discretion,
And peg 'em when I please, let the slaves mumble.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: But say they should be vex'd, and rise against thee?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Let 'em rise, let 'em rise: give me the bridle here,
And see if they can crack my girths: ah Villio,
Under the Sun, ther's nothing so voluptuous
As riding of this monster, till he founder.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: VVho's that so low^?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: I am dumb: is not this rare?
Kings looks make Pythagoreans; is not this
A happinesse Villio?

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Yes, to put to silence
A fawning sycophant.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Thou speak'st truth in all,
And mercy is a vice, when there needs rigour,
VVhich I with all severity will practise;
And since as subjects they pay not obedience.
They shall be forc'd as slaves: I wil remove
Their meanes to hurt, and with the means, my fears:
Goe you the fatall executioners
Of my commands, and in our name proclame,
That from this houre I do forbid all meetings,
All private conferences in the City:
To feast a neighbour shall be death; to talke,
As they meete in the streetes, to hold discourse,
By writing, nay by signes; see this perform'd,
And I wil call your cruelty, to those
That dare repine at this, to me true service.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gard.
verse: This makes for us.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gard.
verse: I now we have imployments,
If we grow not rich 'twere fit we should be beggers.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Ronvere.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Thou enemy to Majesty?
VVhat think'st thou of a Kingdome?

speeches.speaker: ~il.
verse: As of a man
That hath power to doe ill.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Of a thing rather
That does divide an Empire with the Gods;
Observe but with how little breath he shakes
A populous City, which would stand unmov'd
Against a whirlewind.

speeches.speaker: ~il.
verse: Then you make him more
Then him that rules the winds.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: For me I doe professe it,
Were I offerd to be any thing on Earth,
I would be mighty Ferrant.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Ha? who names me?
Deliver thy thoughts slave, thy thoughts, and truly,
Or be no more.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: They rather will deserve.
Your favour then your fury; I admire,
(As who does not, that is a loyall subject?)
Your wisdom, power, your perfect happinesse,
The most blest of mankind.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Didst thou but feele
The weighty sorrowes, that sit on a Crown,
Tho thou shouldst find one in the streets Castruchio,
Thou wouldst not think it worth the taking up;
But since thou art enamour'd of my fortune,
Thou shalt ere long taste of it.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: But one day,
And then let me expire.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Goe to my wardrop,
And of the richest things I wear, cull out,
What thou thinkst fit: do you attend him sirra.

speeches.speaker: ~il.
verse: I warrant you, I shall be at his elbow,
The foole wil never leave him.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Made for ever.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: What shout is that? draw up Guards.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Those rather
Speake joy then danger.
Bring her to my house,
I would not have her seen here.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: My Ascanio!
The most desir'd of all the men, let me die
In these embraces; how wert thou redeem'd?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: Sir, this is my preserver.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: At more leasure,
I will inquire the manner, and the meanes,
I cannot spare so much time now from my

More strickt embraces:
~irolet, welcome too,
This service weighes down your entended treason;
You long have bin mine enemy, learn now
To be my friend and loyall, I aske no more,
And live as free as Ferrant; let him have
The forty thousand crowns I gladly promis'd,
For my Ascanios freedom, and deliver
His Father, and his wife to him in safety,
Something hath passed which I am sorry for,
But 'twill not now be help'd; come my Ascanio,
And reap the harvest of my winter travels.
My best Ascanio, my most lov'd Ascanio.

speeches.speaker: ~iro.
verse: My Lord, all former passages forgot,
I am become a suitor.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse:
To me
~irolet?

speeches.speaker: ~irol.
verse: To you, yet will not beg the courtesie,
But largely pay you for it.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: To the purpose.

speeches.speaker: ~irol.
verse: The forty thousand crownes the King hath given me,
I will bestow on you, if by your meanes
I may have liberty for a divorce
Between me and my wife.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Your Julicana?
That for you hath indur'd so much, so nobly?

speeches.speaker: ~irol.
verse: The more my sorrow; but it must be so.

speeches.speaker: Ron
verse: I will not hinder it: without a bribe,
For mine own ends, I would have further'd this.
I will use all my power.

speeches.speaker: ~irol.
verse: 'Tis all I aske:
Oh my curs'd fate, that ever man should hate
Himselfe for being belov'd, or be compeld
To cast away a Jewell, Kings would buy,
Tho with the losse of Crown and Monarchy!

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: How do I look?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: You are so strangely alterd,
We scarce can know you, so young againe, and utterly
From that you were, figure, or any favour.
Your friends cannnot discern you.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: I have none,
None but my faire revenge, and let that know me.
You are finely alterd too.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
verse: To please your humour,
But we may passe without disguise, our living
Was never in their element.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: This Jew sure,
That alter'd you, is a made knave.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: O! a most excellent fellow.

speeches.speaker: Gun,
verse: How he has mew'd your head, has rub'd the show off,
And run your beard into a peak of twenty!

speeches.speaker: Boat.
verse: Stopt all the crannies in your face.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Most rarely.

speeches.speaker: Boat.
verse: And now you look as plump, your eyes as sparkling,
As if you were to leap into a Ladies saddle.
Has he not set your nose awry?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: The better.

speeches.speaker: Boat.
verse: I think it be the better, but tis awry sure;
North and by East. I ther's the point it stands in;
Now halfe a point to th'Southward.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: I could laugh,
But that my businesse requires no mirth now;
Thou art a merry fellow.

speeches.speaker: Boat.
verse: I would the Jew sir,
Could steer my head right, for I have such a swimming in't,
Ever since I went to Sea first.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Take wine and purg it.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: I have had a thousand pils of Sack, a thousand;
A thousand pottle pils.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Take more.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: Good Doctor,
Your patient is easily perswaded.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: The next faire open weather
Me thinks this Jew,
If he were truly known to founder'd Courtiers,
And decaied Ladies, that have lost their fleeces
On every bush, he might pick a pretty living.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: The best of all our gallants, now be glad of him;
For if you marke their marches, they are tender,
Soft, soft, and tender; then but observe their bodies,
And you shall find 'em cemented by a Surgeon,
Or some Physitian for a year or two,
And then toth'tub again, for a new pickle.
This Jew might live a Gentile here.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: What are these?
Stand close and marke?

speeches.speaker: Boat.
verse: These are no men, th'are motions.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: What sad and ruthfull faces!

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: How they duck!
This sencelesse, silent courtesie me thinks,
Shewes like two Turkes, salu^ing one another,
Upon two French porters backs.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: They are my Countrymen,
And this, some forc'd infliction from the tyrant;
What are you? why is this? why move thus silent
As if you were wandring shadowes? why so sad?
Your tongues seald up; are yee of severall Countries?
You understand not one another?

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: That's an English man,
He lookes as though he had lost his dog.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Your habits
Shew ye all Neapolitanes, and your faces
Deliver you oppressed things: speak boldly:
Do you groan, and labor under this stiffe yoak?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: They shake their heads and weep.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: O misery!
Give plenteous sorrow, and no tongues to shew 'em!
This is a studied cruelty.

speeches.speaker: 1. Citi.
verse: Be gon sir,
It seemes you are a stranger and your selfe;

speeches.speaker: 2. Citi.
verse: You wonder here at us, as much we wonder
To hear you speak so openly, and boldly,
The Kings command being publisht to the contrary;
Tis death here, above two to talk together;
And that must be but common salutation neither,
Short and so part.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: How should a man buy mustard,
If he be forc'd to stay the making of it?
Cleare all the streetes before the King:

speeches.speaker: 1. Cit.
verse: Get off Sir,
And shift as we must do.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: I'le see his glory.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
prose: Stand fast now and like men,

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Begin the game sir,
And pluck me down, the Row
Of houses there.
They hide the view oth' hill; and sink those merchants,
Their ships are foule and stinke.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: This is a sweete youth.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: All that are taken in assemblies,
Their houses and their wives, their wealthes are foreit,
Their lives at your devotion. Villaines, Knaves,
I'le make you bow & shake, i'le make you kneele Rogues.
How brave tis to be a King?

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Here's fine tumbling.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: No man shall sit i'th' temple neer another.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: Nor lie with his own wife.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: All upon paine
Of present death, forget to write.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: That's excellent,
Carriers and foot-Posts, wil be arrant Rebels.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: No Character, or stamp that may deliver
This mans intention, to that man i'th' Country.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Nay, an you cut off, after my hearty commendations
Your friend and Oliver. No more.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: No man smile,
And wear a face of mirth; that fellowes comming,
And hides a double heart, he's your prize, smoke him.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: What base abuse is this? Ha? tis her face sure,
My prisoners with her too? by heaven wild whore
Now is my time.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Do what you will.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Stay hold yet,
My Country shall be serv'd first, let her go,
Wee'l have an hour for her to make her tremble.
Now shew your selves, and blesse you with your valors.

speeches.speaker: Guard
prose: Here's a whole plump of Rogues.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Now for your Country.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Away with 'em and hang 'em; no, no mercy,
I say no mercy.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Be it so upon 'em.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Treason, treason, treason.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: Cut the slaves to giggets.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Down with the bul-beefes.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Hold, hold, I command you—look here

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: A miserable thing. I am no King sir.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Sirra, your fooles face has preserv'd your life.
Wear no more Kings coates, you have scap'd a scouring.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: I'st not the King.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: No, tis a prating Rascall,
The puppy makes him mirth.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Yes sir, I am a puppy.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: I beseech you let me hang him,
I'le do't in my belt straight.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: As you are honorable,
It is enough you may hang me.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: I'le hang a squib at's taile
That shall blow both his buttocks, like a petar.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Do any thing.
But do not kill me Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Boate.
verse: Lets flea h^m, and have him flye blowen.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Away, and save your lives.
The King himselfe is conning on. if you stay,
You are lost for ever; let not so much noblenesse
Willfully perish.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: How neer?

speeches.speaker: 2. Citiz.
prose: He's here behind you.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: We thank you.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Double the Guards and take in men that dare,
These slaves are frighted; where are the proud Rebels,
To what protection fled, what villain leads 'em?
Under our nose disturb our rest?

speeches.speaker: Ronver.
verse: We shall heare,
For such a search I have sent, to hunt the Traytors.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Yet better men I say, we stand too open:
How now Castruchio? how do you like our glory?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: I must confesse, 'twas somewhat more then my match Sir;
This open glory agrees not with my body,
But if it were ith' Castle, or some strength,
Where I might have my swing.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: You have been swing'd brother;
How these delights have tickled you? you itch yet;
Will you walke out again in pomp?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Good Foole.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: These rogues must be rebuked, they are too sawcy,
These peremptory Knaves. Will you walk out Sir,
And take the remnant of your Coronation?
The people stay to see it.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Do not vex him;
Ha's griefe enough in's bones; you shall to th' Citadell,
And like my selfe command, there use your pleasure,
But take heed to your person.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: The more danger;
Still the more honour Brother.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: If I reign not then,
And like a King, and thou shalt know it fool,
And thou shalt feel it foole.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Fooles still are freemen,
I'le sue for a protection, till thy reigne's out.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: The people have abus'd the liberty
I late allowed, I now proclaime it straighter,
No men shall walk together, nor salute;
For they that doe shall dye.

speeches.speaker: Ronver.
verse: You hit the right Sir;
That liberty cut off, you are free from practise.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Renew my guards.

speeches.speaker: Ronver.
verse: I shall.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: And keep strict watches;
One houre of joy I aske.

speeches.speaker: Ronver.
verse: You shall have many.

speeches.speaker: 1. Guard.
verse: You are now at liberty, in your own house Lady,
And here our charge takes end.

speeches.speaker: Pandul.
verse: 'Tis now a Custome.
We must even wooe those men deserve worst of us,
And so we thanke your labours; there's to drinke,
For that, and mischiefe are your occupations;
And to meane well to no man, you Chief'st harvests.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gard.
verse: You give liberally; we hope Sir, er't be long,
To be oftner acquainted with your bounty,
And so we leave you.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Doe, for I dote not on ye;

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: But where's my Husband? what should I do here?
Or what share have I in this joy, cal'd liberty,
Without his company? Why did you flatter me,
And tell me he was return'd, his service honour'd?

speeches.speaker: 1. Gard.
verse: He is so, and stands high in the Kings favour,
His friends redeemd, and his own liberty,
From which yours is deriv'd, confirm'd; his service,
To his own wish rewarded: so fare-well Lady.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Go persecute the good, and hunt ye hell-hounds;
Ye Leeches of the time, suck till ye burst slaves;
How does my girle?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Weake yet, but full of comfort;

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Sit down, and take some rest;

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: My heart's whole Father;
That joyes, and leaps, to heare my Virolet,
My Deer, my life, has conquer'd his afflictions.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Those rude hands, and that bloody will that did this,
That durst upon thy tender body Print
These Characters of cruelty; heare me heaven.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: O Sir be sparing.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: I'le speake it, tho I burst;
And tho the ayre had eares, and serv'd the Tyrant,
Out it should goe: O heare me thou great Justice;
The miseries, that waite upon their mischiefs,
Let them be numberlesse, and no eye pitty
Them when their soules are loaden, and in labour,
And wounded through, and through, with guilt & horror,
As mine is now with griefe; let men laugh at 'em
Then, when their monstrous sins, like earth-quaks, shake 'em;
And those eyes, that forgot heaven would look upward,
The bloody 'larms, of the conscience beating,
Let mercy flye, and day strook into darknesse,
Leave their blind soules, to hunt out their own horrors.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Enough, enough, we must forget deare Father;
For then we are glorious formes of heaven; and live,
When we can suffer, and as soon forgive.
But where's my Lord? me thinkes I have seen this house,
And have been in't before.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Thine own house jewell.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Mine, without him? or his, without my company?
I thinke it cannot be; it was not wont Father.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Some businesse with the King (let it be good heaven)
Reteines him sure.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: It must be good and noble,
For all men that he treats with taste of vertue;
His words and actions are his own; and Honour's
Not bought, nor compel'd from him.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Here's the Boy.
He can confirme us more, how sad the child looks?
Come hither Lucio; how, and where's thy Master?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Speak gentle Boy.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Is he return'd in safety?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: If not, and that thou knowest is miserable,
Our hopes and happinesse declin'd for ever;
Study a sorrow, excellent as thy Master,
Then if thou canst live, leave us.

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: Noble Madam,
My Lord is safe return'd, safe to his friends, and fortune,
Safe to his Country, entertain'd with honour,
Is here within the house.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Doe not mock me.

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: But such a melancholy hangs on his mind,
And in his eyes inhabit such sad shadowes;
But what the cause is—

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Goe tell him we are here Boy,
There must be no cause now.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Hast thou forgot me?

speeches.speaker: Lucio.
verse: No, noblest Lady.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Tell him I am here,
Tell him his wife is here, sound my name to him,
And thou shalt see him start; speake Iuliana,
And like the Sunne that labors through a tempest,
How suddainly he will disperse his sadnesse?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Goe I command thee instantly,
And charge him on his duty.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: On his Love Boy:
I would faine goe to him.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Away, away, you are foolish.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Beare all my service sweet Boy.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Art thou here still?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: And tell him what thou wilt that shall become thee.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Ith' house; and know we are here.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: No, no, he did not;
I warrant you he did not: could you think
His Love had lesse then wings, had he but seen me;
His strong affection any thing but fire
Consuming all weak lets, and rubs before it,
Till he had met my flame, and made one body?
If ever heavens high blessings met in one man,
And there erected to their holy uses.
A sacred mind, fit for their services,
Built all of polisht honour, 'twas in this man:
Misdoubt him not.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: I know he's truly noble;
But why this sadnesse, when the generall cause
Requires a Jubile of joy?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I know not.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Pray heaven you find it not.

speeches.speaker: Jul
verse: I hope I shall not:
O here he comes, and with him all my happinesse;
He staies and thinks, we may be too unmannerly;
Pray give him leave.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: I doe not like this sadnesse.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: O hard condition of my misery!
Unheard of plagues! when to behold that woman,
That chaste and vertuous woman, that preserv'd me,
That pious wife, wedded to my afflictions,
Must be more terrible then all my dangers.
O fortune, thou hast rob'd men of my making,
The noble building of a man, demolisht,
And flung me headlong, on a sin so base
Man and mankind contemn; even beasts abhor it,
A sin more dull then drinke, a shame beyond it;
So foule, and farre from faith; I dare not name it,
But it will cry it self out, loud ingratitude.
Your blessing Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: You have it in abundance;
So is our joy, to see you safe.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: My Deere one;

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: H'as not forgot me yet: O take me to you Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Must this be added to increase my misery,
That she must weep for joy, and loose that goodnesse?
My Iuliana, even the best of women,
Of wives the perfectest, let me speak this,
And with a modesty declare thy vertues,
Chaster then Christall, on the Scythian Clifts
The more the proud winds Court, the more the purer.
Sweeter in thy obedience, then a sacrifice;
And in thy mind a Saint, that even yet living,
Producest miracles, and women daily
With crooked and tame soules creep to thy goodnesse,
Which having toucht at, they become examples.
The fortitude of all their sex, is Fable
Compar'd to thine; and they that fill'd up glory,
And admiration, in the age behind us,
Out of their celebrated urns, are started,
To stare upon the greatnesse of thy spirit;
Wondring what new Martyr heaven has begot,
To fill the times with truth, and ease their stories:
Being all these, and excellent in beauty,
(For noble things dwell in the noblest buildings)
Thou hast undone thy husband, made him wretch'ed,
A miserable man, my Juliana,

Thou hast made thy
~irolet.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Now goodnesse keep me;
Oh! my dear Lord.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: She wrong you? what's the meaning?
Weep not, but speake, I charge you on obedience;
Your Father charges you; she make you miserable?
That you your self confesse.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: I doe, that kils me;
And far lesse I have spoke her. then her merit.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: It is some sinne of weaknesse, or of Ignorance?
For sure my Will—

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: No, 'tis a sinne of excellence:
Forgive me heaven, that I prophane thy blessings:
Sit still; I'le shew you all.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: What meanes this madnesse?
For sure there is no taste of right man in it;
Greives he our liberty, our preservation?
Or has the greatnesse of the deed he has done,
Made him forget, for whom, and how he did it,
And looking down upon us, scorne the benefit?

Well
~irolet if thou beest proud, or treacherous

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: He cannot Sir, he cannot; he will shew us,
And with that reason ground his words.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: He comes.
What Masque is this? what admirable beauty?
Pray heaven his heart be true.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: A goodly woman.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Tell me my Dear; and tell me without flattery,
As you are nobly honest, speak the truth;
What thinke you of this Lady?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: She is most excellent.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Might not this beauty tell me that it's a sweet one,
Without more setting off, as now it is,
Thanking no greater Mistresse then meer nature?
Stagger a constant heart?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: She is full of wonder;

But yet; yet
~irolet.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Pray; by your leave Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: She would amaze:

speeches.speaker: ~ir
verse: O! would she so? I thanke you;
Say to this beauty, she have all additions,
Wealth, noble birth.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: O hold there.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: All vertues,
A mind, as full of Candor as the truth is,
I, and a loving Lady.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: She must needs
(I am bound in conscience to confesse) deserve much.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Nay, say beyond all these, she be so pious,
That even on slaves condemn'd she showre her benefits,
And melt their stubborn Bolts with her soft pitty,
What thinke you then?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: For such a noble office,
At these yeares, I should dote my self; take heed Boy,

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: If you be he, that have received these blessings,
And this the Lady: love her, honour her;
You cannot doe too much, to shew your gratitude,
Your greatest service will shew off too slender.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: This is the Lady; Lady of that bounty,
That wealth, that noble name, that all I spoke of:
The Prince Ascaino and my selfe, the slaves
Redeem'd, brought home, still guarded by her goodnes,
And of our liberties you taste the sweetnes;
Even you she has preserv'd too, lengthen'd your lives.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And what reward doe you purpose? it must be a maine one;
If love will do it we'll all, so love her, serve her.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: It must be my love.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Ha!

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Mine, my onely love,
My everlasting love:

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Pray have patience.
The recompence she ask'd, and I have render'd.
Was to become her husband: then I vowed it,
And since I have made it good.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Thou durst not.

speeches.speaker: Virol.
verse: Done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Be what you please, his happinesse yet stayes with me,
You have been mine; Oh my unhappy fortune.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Nay, break and dye;

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: It cannot yet: I must live,
Till I see this man, blest in his new love,
And then:

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: What hast thou done? thou base one tell me,
Thou barren thing of honesty, and honour;
What hast thou wrought? Is not this she, looke on her,
Look on her, with the eyes of gratitude,
And whipe thy false teares off; Is not this she,
That three times on the Rack, to guard thy safety,
When thou stood'st lost, and naked to the Tyrant;
Thy aged Father here, that shames to know thee Tirant,
Ingag'd ith' jawes of danger; was not this she,
That then gave up her body to the torture?
That tender body, that the wind sings through;
And three times, when her sinewes, crack'd & torter'd,
The beauties of her body turn'd to ruines,
Even then, within her patient heart, she lock'd thee;
Then hid thee from the Tyrant; then preserv'd thee;
And canst thou be that slave?

speeches.speaker: Martia.
verse: This was but duty;
She did it for her Husband, and she ought it;
She has had the pleasure of him, many an houre;
And if one minutes paine cannot be suffer'd;
Mine was above all these, a nobler venter,
I speake it boldly, for I lost a Father.
He has one still; I left my friends, he has many;
Expos'd my life, and honour to a cruelty,
That if it had seiz'd on me, racks and tortures,
Alas, they are Triumphs to it: and had it hit,
For this mans love, it should have shewed a triumph,
Twise lost, I freed him; Rossana lost before him,
His fortunes with him; and his friends behind him:
Twise was I rack'd my selfe for his deliverance,
In honour first and name, which was a torture
The Hang-man never heard of; next at Sea,
In our escape, where the proud waves took pleasure
To tosse my little Boat up like a Bubble,
Then like meteor in the ayre he hung,
Then catcht, and hug him in the depth of darknesse;
The Canon from my incensed Fathers Ship,
Ringing our Knell, and still as we peep'd upward,
Beating the raging surge, with fire and Bullet,
And I stood fixt for this mans sake, and scorn'd it;
Compare but this:

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: 'Tis too true; O my fortune!
That I must equally be bound to either:

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: You have the better, and the nobler Lady;
And now I am forc'd, a lover of her goodnesse.
And so far have you wrought for his deliverance,
That is my Lord, so lovingly and nobly,
That now me thinks I stagger in my Title.
But how with honesty? for I am poor Lady,
In all my dutious service but your shadow,
Yet would be just; how with faire fame and credit,
I may goe off; I would not be a strumpet:
O my dear Sir you know:

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: O truth, thou knowest too.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Nor have the world suspect, I fell to mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Law.
verse: Take you no care for that, here's that has don it;
A faire divorce, 'tis honest too.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: The devill,
Honest? to put her off.

speeches.speaker: Law.
verse: Most honest Sir,
And in this point, most strong.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: The cause, the cause Sir?

speeches.speaker: Law.
verse: A just cause too.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: As any is in hell, Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Law.
verse: For barrennesse, she never brought him children.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
verse: Why art not thou divorc'd? thou canst not get 'em;
Thy neigbours, thy rank neighbours: O base jugling,
Is she not young?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Woemen at more yeares Sir,
Have met that blessing. 'tis in heavens high power.

speeches.speaker: Law.
verse: You never can have any:

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Why quick Lawyer?
My Philosophicall Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Law.
verse: The Rack has spoil'd her
The distentions of those parts, hath stopt all fruitfulnes.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: O I could curse.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And am I grown so miserable,
That mine own pitty must make me wretched?
No cause against me, but my love and duty?
Farewell Sir. like obedience, thus I leave you,
My long farewell: I doe not grudge, I grieve Sir,
And if that be offensive, I can dye,
And then you fairely free: good Lady love him;
You have a noble, and an honest Gentleman,
I ever found him so, the world has spoke him;
And let it be your part still to deserve him:
Love him no lesse then I have done; and serve him,
And heaven shall blesse you; you shall blesse my ashes;
I give you up the house; the name of wife,
Honour, and all respect I borrowed from him,
And to my grave I turn: one farewell more;
Nothing divide your Loves, not want of Children,
Which I shall pray against, and make you fruitfull;
Grow like two equall flames, rise high and glorious;
And in your honor'd age, burn out together:
To all I know, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Ronver.
verse: Be not so grie'vd Lady;
A nobler fortune.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Away thou parasite.
Disturbe not my sad thoughts; I hate thy greatnesse.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: I hate not you; I am glad she's off these hinges,
Come, let's pursue.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: If I had breath to curse thee;
Or could my great heart utter; farewell villaine,
Thy house, nor face agen.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Let 'em all goe.
And now let us rejoyce; now freely take me,
And now embrace me Virolet; give the rites
Of a brave Husband to his love.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I'le take my leave too.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: How, take you leave too?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: The house is furnish'd for you;
You are Mistresse, may command.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Will you to bed Sir?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: As soone to hell, to any thing I hate most;
You must excuse me, I have kept my word.
You are my wife, you now enjoy my fortune,
Which I have done to recompence your bounty:
But to yeeld up those chaste delights and pleasures,
Which are not mine, but my first vowes.

speeches.speaker: Mat.
verse: You jeast.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: You will not find it so, to give you those;
I have divorc'd, and lost with Iuliana,
And all fires of that nature.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Are you a Husband;

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: To question hers, and satisfie your flames,
That held an equall beauty, equall bounty.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Good heaven forgive; no, no, the strict forbearance,
Of all those joyes, like a full sacrifice,
I offer to the suffrings of my first love;
Honour, and wealth, attendance, state, all duty,
Shall waite upon your will, to make you happy;
But my afflicted mind, you must give leave Lady;
My weary Trunk must wander.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Not enjoy me?
Goe from me too?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: For ever thus I leave you;
And how so e're I fare, live you still happy.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Since I am scorn'd, I'le hate thee, scorn thy gifts too;
Thou miserable fool, thou fool to pitty;
And such a rude, demolisht thing, I'le leave thee,
In my revenge: for foolish love, farewell now,
And anger, and the spite of woman enter,
That all the world shall say, that read this story,
My hate, and not my love, begot my glory.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: He that feares death, or tortures, let him leave me.
The stops that we have met with, Crown our Conquest:
Common attempts are fit for common men;
The rare, the rarest spirits. Can we be daunted?
We that have smil'd at Sea at certain ruines,
Which men on shore; but hazarded would shake at
We that have liv'd free, in despite of fortune,
Laught at the out-stretch'd Arme of Tyranny,
As still too short to reach us, shall we faint now?
No my bravemates, I know your fiery temper,
And that you can, and dare, as much as men:
Calamity, that severs worldly friendships,
Could ne'r divide us, you are still the same;
The constant followers of my banisht fortunes;
The Instruments of my revenge; the hands
By which I work, and fashion all my projects.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: And such we will be ever.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: 'Slite Sir, Cramme me
Into a Canons mouth, and shoot me at
Proud Ferrands head; may onely he fall with me,
My life I rate at nothing.

speeches.speaker: Boatsw.
verse: Could I but get,
Within my swords length of him; and if then
He scape me, may th'account of all his diinnes
Be added unto mine.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: 'Tis not to dye Sir,
But to dye unreveng'd, that staggers me:
For were your ends serv'd, and our Country free,
We would fall willing sacrifices.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: To rise up,
Most glorious Martyrs.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
verse: But the reason why
We weare these shapes?

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Onely to get accesse:
Like honest men, we never shall approach him,
Such are his feares, but thus attir'd like Switzers,
And fashioning our language to our habits;
Bold, bloody, desperate, we may be admitted
Among his guard. But if this faile, I'le try
A thousand others, out doe Proteus
In various shapes, but I will reach his heart.
And seale my anger on't.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: The Lord Ronero.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
verse: Shall we begin with him?

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: He is not ripe yet,
Nor fit to fall: as you see me begin,
Withall care imitate.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: We are instructed.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
verse: Would we were at it once.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Keepe a strict watch,
And let the guards be doubled, this last night
The King had fearefull dreames.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: 'Tis a good Omen
To our attempts.

speeches.speaker: Roner.
verse: What men are these? What seek you?

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Imployment.

speeches.speaker: Roner.
verse: Of what nature?

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: We are Souldiers;
We have seen towns and Churches set on fire;
The Kennels running blood, coy virgins ravish'd;
The Altars ransack'd, and the holy reliques,
Yea, and the Saints themselves, made lawfull spoyles,
Unto the Conquerors: but these good dayes are past,
And we made Beggars, by this Idle Peace,
For want of action. I am Sir no stranger
To the Government of this state, I know the King
Needs men, that onely doe what he commands,
And search no further: 'tis the profession
Of all our Nation, to serve faitnfully,
Where th'are best payed: and if you entertaine us,
I doe not know the thing you can command,
Which we'le not put in act.

speeches.speaker: Roner.
verse: A goodly Parsonage.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: And if you have an Enemy, or so
That you would have dispatch'd.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: They are here, can fit you.

speeches.speaker: Boats.
verse: Or if there be an Itch, though to a man,

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: You shall tye
Our consciences in your purse-strings.

speeches.speaker: Roner.
verse: Gentlemen,
I like your freedome: I am now in haste,
But waite for my return. I like the Rascals,
They may be usefull.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: We'l attend you Sir:

speeches.speaker: Roner.
verse: Doe; and be confident, of entertainment;
I hope ye will deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: O, no doubt Sir:
Thus farre we are prosperous; we'l be his guard,
Till Tyranny and pride finde full reward:

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: My blessing? no; a Fathers heavy curse,
Pursue, and overtake him.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Gentle Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: My name, and Family; end in my self
Rather then live in him.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Deare Sir forbeare,
A fathers curses, hit far off, and kill too.
And like a murthering-piece aymes not at one,
But all that stand within the dangerous level.
Some bullet may return upon your selfe too,
Though against nature, if you still go on
In this unnaturall course.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Thou art not made
Of that same stuffe as other women are:
Thy injuries would teach patience to blaspheme;
Yet still thou art a Dove.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I know not malice, but like an innocent, suffer.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: More miraculous!
He have a woman Chronicled, and for goodnesse,
Which is the greatest wonder. Let me see,
I have no sonne to inherit after me;
Him I disclaime.
What then? He make thy vertues my sole heire;
Thy story Ile have written, and in Gold to;
In prose and verse, and by the ablest doers:
A word or two of a kind step-father
He have put in, good Kings and Queens shal buy it.
And if the actions of ill great women,
And of the modern times too, are remembred,
That have undone their husbands, and their families,
What will our story do? It shal be so,
And I wil streight about it.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Such as love
Goodnesse for glory, have it for reward;
I love mine for it selfe: let innocence
Be written on my Tomb, though ne're so humble,
Tis all I am ambitious of. But I
Forget my vows.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: 'Fore me, you are not modest,
Nor is this Courtlike. Would you take it wel,
If she should rudely presse into your Clolst,
When from your several Boxes you choose paint,
To make a this daies face with?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Pray know her pleasure first.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: To whom speak you Boy?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Your Ladiships pardon. That proud Lady theife,
That stole away my Lord from your embraces,
(Wrinckes at two and twenty on her cheekes for't,
Or Mercury unallayed, make blisters on it)
Would force a visit.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: And dare you deny her,
Or any else that I call mine? No more,
Attend her with all reverence and respect;
The want in you of manners, my Lord may
Construe in me for malice. I wil teach you
How to esteem and love the beauty he dotes on;
Prepare a banquet.
Madam, thus my duty
Stoops to the favour you vouchsafe your servant,
In honouring her house.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Is this in scorn?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: No by the life of Virolet: give me leave
To sweare by him, as by a Saint I worship,
But am to know no further, my heart speaks that
My servants have been rude, and this boy (doting
Upon my sorrows) hath forgot his duty:
In which, that you may think I have no share,
Sirra, upon your knees, desire her pardon.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I dare not disobey you.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Prethee rise,
My anger never looks so low: I thank you.
And wil deserve it, If we may be private,
I came to see and speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Be gone.
Good Madam sit.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I rob you of your place then.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: You have deserv'd a better, in my bed;
Make use of this too: Now your pleasure Lady.
If in your breaard there be a worthy pitty,
That brings you for my comfort, you do nobly:
But if you come to triumph in your conquest,
Or tread on my calamities, 'twil wrong
Your other excellencies. Let it suffice,
That you alone enjoy the best of men,
And that I am forsaken.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: He the best?
The scum and shame of mankind.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Virolet, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Blest in him? I would my youth had chosen
Consuming feavers, bed-rid age
For my companions, rather then a thing
To lay whose basenesse open, would even poyson
The tongue that speaks it.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Certainly from you
At no part he deserves this; and I tell you,
Durst I pretend but the least title to him,
I should not hear this.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: He's an impudent villaine,
Or a malicious wretch: to you ungratefull;
To me, beyond expression barbarous.
I more then hate him; from you, he deserves
A death most horrid: from me, to die for ever,
And know no end of torments. Would you have comfort?
Would you wash off the stain that sticks upon you,
In being refus'd? Would you redeem your fame,
Shipwrack'd in his base wrongs? if you desire this,
It is not to be done with slavish suffering,
But by a Noble anger, making way
To a most brave revenge, we may call justice;
Our injuries are equal; joyn with me then,
And share the honour.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I scarce understand you,
And know I shal be most unapt to learn
To hate the man I stil must love and honour.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: This foolish dotage in soft-hearted women,
Makes proud men insolent: but take your way,
Ile run another course.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: As you are noble,
Deliver his offence.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: He has denied
The rites due to a wife.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: O me most happy,
How largely am I payd for all my sufferings?
Most honest Virolet, thou just performer
Of all thy promises: I call to mind now,
When I was happy in those joyes you speak of,
In a chast bed, and warranted by Law too,
He oft would swear, that if he should survive me,
(Which then I knew he wisht not) never woman
Should taste of his imbraces; this one act
Makes me again his debtor.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: And was this
The cause my youth and beauty were contemn'd?
If I sit down here! wel —;

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I date thy worst,
Plot what thou canst, my piety shal guard him
Against thy malice. Leave my house and quickly,
Thou wilt infect these innocent walls. By vertue
I wil inform him of thy bloody purpose,
And turn it on thine own accursed head;
Believ't I wil.

speeches.speaker: Mart
verse: But tis not in thy power
To hinder what I have decreed against him.
He set my selfe to sale, and live a strumpet;
Forget my birth, my father, and his honour,
Rather then want an instrument to help me
In my revenge. The Captain of the guard;
Blest opportunity courts me.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Sad and troubled?
How brave her anger shews? how it sets off
Her naturall beauty? under what happy star
Was Virolet born, to be belov'd and sought to,
By two incomparable women? Noblest Lady,
I have heard your wrongs and pity them: and if
The service of my life could give me hope
To gain your favour, I should be most proud
To be commanded.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Tis in you, my Lord,
To make me your glad servant.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Name the means.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Tis not preferment, Jewels, Gold, or Courtship.
He that desires to reap the harvest of
My youth and beauty, must begin in blood,
And right my wrongs.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: I apprehend you Madam,
And rest assur'd tis done; I am provided
Of instruments to fit you: To the King,
Ile instantly present you; if I faile,
He shal make good your aymes: he's lesse then man,
That to atchieve your favour, would not doe
Deeds, friends would fear to put their agents to.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Quid invitus facis, non est scelus. Tis an axiome,
Now whether willingly I have departed
With that I lov'd: with that, above her life
Lov'd me again, crownd me a happy husband,
Was full of children: her afflictions
That I begot, that when our age must perish,
And all our painted frailties turn to ashes,
Then shal they stand and propagate our honors.
Whether this done, and taking to protection
A new stange beauty, it was a useful one:
How to my lust? if it be so, I am sinful;
And guilty of that crime I would fling from me.
Was there not in it this fair course of vertue?
This pious course, to save my friends, my Countrey,
That even then had put on a mourning garment,
And wept the desolation of her children?
Her noblest children? Did not she thrust me on,
And to my duty clapt the spur of honour?
Was there a way, without this woman, left me
To bring 'em off? the marrying of this woman?
If not, why am I stung thus? why tormented?
Or had there been a wild desire joyn'd with it,
How easily, both these, and all their beauties
Might I have made mine own? why am I toucht thus,
Having perform'd the great redemption,
Both of my friends and family? fairly done it?
Without base and lascivious ends O Heaven,
Why am I still at war thus? why this a mischiefe,
That honesty and honour had propounded,
I, and absolv'd my tender wil, and chid me,
Nay then unwillingly flung me on.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: He's here Madam;
This is the melancholy walk he lives in,
And chooses ever to encrease his sadnesse.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Stand by.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Tis she: how I shake now and tremble?
The vertues of that mind are torments to me.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Sir, if my hated face shal stir your anger,
Or this forbidden path I tread in vex you;
My love, and faire obedience let behind me,
Your pardon asked, I shal return and blesse you.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Pray stay a little, I delight to see you;
May not we yet, though fortune have divided us,
Ana set an envious stop between our pleasures,
Look thus one at another? sigh and weep thus?
And read in one anothers eyes, the Legends,
And wonders of our old loves? be not fearful,
Though you be now a Saint, I may adore you:
May I not take this hand, and on it sacrifice
The sorrows of my heart? white seale of vertue.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: My Lord, you wrong your wedlock.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Were she here,
And with her all severe eyes to behold us,
We might do this; I might name Julian,
And to the reverence of that name, bow thus:
I might sigh Juliana, she was mine once;
But I too weak a guard for that great Treasure—
And whilst she has a name, believe me Lady,
This broken heart shal never want a sorroW.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Forget her sir, your honour now commands you
You are anothers, keep those griefes for her,
She richly can reward 'em. I would have spoken with you

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: What is your wil? for nothing you can aske,
So ful of goodnesse are your words and meanings,
Must be denied: speak boldly.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I thank you sir. I come not
To beg, or flatter, onely to be believ'd,
That I desire: for I shal tell a story,
So far from seeming truth, yet a most true one;
So horrible in nature, and so horrid;
So beyond wickednesse, that when you heare it,
It must appeare the practice of another,
The cast & malice of some one you have wrongd much;
And me, you may imagine me accus'd to,
Unlesse you call to mind my daily sufferings;
The infinite obedience I have born you,
That hates all name and nature of revenge.
My love, that nothing but my death can sever,
Rather then hers I speak of.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Juliana,
To make a doubt of what you shall deliver,
After my full experience of your vertues,
Were to distrust a providence; to think you can lie,
Or being wrong'd, seek after foule repairings,
To forge a Creed against my faith.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I must do so, for it concernes your life sir;
And if that word may stir you, heare and prosper:
I should be dumb else, were not you at stake here.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: What new friend have I found, that dares deliver
This loden Trunke from his afflictions?
What pitying hand, of all that feeles my miseries,
Brings such a benefit?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Be wise and manly,
And with your honour fall, when Heaven shall call you,
Not by a Hellish mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Speak my blest one,
How weak and poor I am, now she is from me?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Your wife.

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Your wife.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Be tender of her, I shal believe else —

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I must be true: your eare, sir;
For tis so horrible, if the ayre catch it,
Into a thousand plagues, a thousand monsters,
It will disperse it selfe, and fright resistance,

speeches.speaker: Viro.
verse: She seeke my life with you? make you her agent?
Another love? O speake but truth.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Be patient,
Deare as I love you, else I leave you wretched.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Forward, tis well, it shal be welcome to me;
I have liv'd too long, numbred too many daies,
Yet never found the benefit of living;
Now when I come to reap it with my service,
And hunt for that my youth and honour aimes at,
The Sunne sets on my fortune red and bloody,
And everlasting night begins to close me,
Tis time to die.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: She comes her selfe.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Believe Lady,
And on this Angel hand, your servant seales it,
You shal be Mistris of your whole desires,
And what ye shal command.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Ha mynion,
My precious dame, are you there? nay go forward,
Make your complaints, and poure out your faind pities,
Slave, like to him you serve: I am the same still,
And what I purpose, let the world take witnesse,
Shal be so finisht, and to such example,
Spite of your poore preventions; my deare Gentleman,
My honourable man, are you there too?
You and your hot desire? Your mercy sir,
I had forgot your greatnesse.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Tis not wel Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Lord, how I hate this fellow now; how desperately
My stomack stands against him, this base fellow,
This gelded foole!

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Did you never heare of modesty?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Yes, when I heard of you and so believ'd it,
Thou bloodlesse, brainlesse foole.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Thou despis'd foole,
Thou onely sign of man, how I contemn thee!
Thou woven worthy in a piece of Arras,
Fit onely to enjoy a wall; thou beast
Beaten to use; Have I preserv'd a beauty,
A youth, a love, to have my wishes blasted?
My dotings, and the ioyes I came to offer,
Must they be lost, and sleighted by a dormouse?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Use more respect; and woman, twill become you;
At least, lesse tongue.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: He use all violence,
Let him look for't.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Dare you staine those beauties,
Those Heavenly stamps, that raise men up to wonder,
With harsh and crooked motions? are you she
That overdid all ages, with your honour;
And in a little houre dare lose this triumph?
Is not this man your husband?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: He's my halter;
Which (having sued my pardon) I fling off thus,
And with him all I brought him, but my anger;
Which I wil nourish to the desolation,
Not onely of his folly, but his friends,
And his whole name.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Tis wel, I have deservd it.
And if I were a woman, I would raile too.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Nature nere promis'd thee a thing so Noble.
Take back your love, your vow, I give it freely;
I poorly scorn it; graze now where you please:
That that the dulnesse of thy soule neglected,
Kings sue for now. And mark me, Virolet;
Thou image of a man, observe my words well.
At sucn a bloody rate Ile sell this beauty,
This handsomnesse thou scornst, and flingst away,
Thy proud ungrateful life shal shake at: take your house;
The petty things you left me give another;
And last, take home your trinket: fare you wel, sir.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: You have spoke like your selfe;
Y'are a brave Lady.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Why do you smile, sir?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: O my Juliana,
The happinesse this womans scorn has given me,
Makes me a man again; proclaimes it selfe,
In such a generall joy, through all my miseries,
That now methinks —

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Looke to your selfe deere sir,
And trifle not with danger, that attends you;
Be ioyfull when y'are free.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Did you not heare lier?
She gave me back my vow, my love, my freedom;
I am free, free as aire; and though to morrow
Her bloody wil meet with my life, and sink it,
And in her execution teare me peecemeale:
Yet have I time once more to meet my wishes,
Once more to embrace my best, my noblest, truest,
And time that's warranted.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Good sir, forbeare it:
Though I confesse, equall with your desires
My wishes rise, as covetous of your love,
And to as warm alarams spur my wil to:
Yet pardon me, the Seal oth'Church dividing us,
And hanging like a threatning flame between us;
We must not meet, I dare not.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: That poore disjoynting
