That onely strong necessity thrust on you,
Not crime, nor studied cause of mine: how sweetly,
And nobly I wil bind again and cherish;
How I wil recompence one deare imbrace now,
One free affection! how I burn to meet it~
Looke now upon me.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I behold you willingly,
And willingly would yield, but for my credit.
The love you first had was preserv'd with honour,
The last shal not cry whore; you shal not purchase
From me a pleasure, that have equally
Lov'd your faire fame as you, at such a rate:
Your honesty and vertue must be banquerout,
If I had lov'd your lust, and not your lustre;
The glorious lustre of your matchlesse goodnesse,
I would compel you now to be! — forgive me,
Forgive me sir; how fondly stil I love you!
Yet Nobly too; make the way straight before me,
And let but holy Hymen once more guide me,
Under the Ax, upon Rack again,
Even in the bed of all afflictions,
Where nothing sings our Nuptials but dire sorrows,
With all my youth and pleasure Ile imbrace you,
Make tyranny and death stand stil affrighted,
And at our meeting foules amaze our mischiefes;
Til when, high Heaven defend you, and peace guide you.
Be wise and manly, make your fate your own,
By being master of a providence,
That may controle it.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Stay a little with me,
My thoughts have chid themselves: may I not kisse you?
Upon my truth I am honest.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I believe ye;
But yet what that may raise in both our fancies,
What issues such warm parents breed.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I obey you,
And take my leave as from the Saint that keeps me.
I will be right again, and once more happy
In thy unimitable love.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ile pray for ye,
And when you fall I have not long to follow.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Now we have got free credit with the Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Soft, soft, he's here again: Is not that Lady —
Or have I lost mine eyes? a salt rhume seizes 'em;
But I should know that face.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Make him not madder,
Let him forget the woman; steere a lar boord.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: He wil not kill her.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Any thing he meets;
He's like a Hornet now, he hums, and buzzes;
Nothing but blood and horror.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I would save the Lady,
For such another Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: There's the point;
And you know there want women of her mettle.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Tis true, they bring such children now,
Such demilances,
Their fathers socks wil make them Christning clothes.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: No more, they view us.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: You shal play a while,
And sun your selfe in this felicity,
You shal you glorious whore; I know you still.
But I shal pick an houre when most securely —
I say no more.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Do you see those? those are they
Shall act your will; come hither my good fellows:
You are now the Kings. Are they not goodly fellows?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: They have bone enough, if they have stout heart to it.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Still the old wench.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Pray Captaine, let me aske you
What Noble Lady's that? tis a rude question,
But I desire to know.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: She is for the King, sir;
Let that suffice for answer.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Is she so sir?
In good time may she curse it.
Must I breed hackneys for his grace?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: What wouldst thou do
To merit such a Ladies favour?

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Any thing.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: That can supply thy wants, and raise thy fortuns?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Let her command, and see what I dare execute.
I keep my conscience here; if any man
Oppose her wil, and she would have him humbled,
Whole families between her and her wishes —

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We have seen bleeding throats sir, Cities sackt,
And infants stuck upon their Pikes.

speeches.speaker: Botes.
verse: Houses a fire, and handsome mothers weeping.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Which we have heaped upon the pile like sacrifices.
Churches and Altars, Priests and all devotions,
Tumbled together into one rude Chaos.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: We know no feare sir, but want of imployment.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Nor other faith but what our purses preach.
To gain our ends we can do any thing,
And turn our soules into a thousand figures;
But when we come to do —

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: I like these fellowes.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Be ready and waite here within this houre
Ile shew you to the King, and he shall like ye:
And if you can devise some entertainment
To fill his mirth, such as your Countrey uses,
Present it, and Ile see it grac'd.
After this Comicke Scene we shall imploy you,
For one must die.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: What is he sir? speak boldly,
For we dare boldly do.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: This Ladies husband;
His name is Virolet.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: We shall dispatch it.
O damned, damned thing: a base whore first,
And then a murtherer; Ile look to you.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Can she be grown so strange?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: She has an itch;
Ile scratch you my deare daughter, Ile so claw you;
Ile curry your hot hide; married and honour'd?
And turn those holy blessings into brothels?
Your beauty into blood? Ile hunt your hotnesse.
Ile hunt you like a traine.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We did all pity her.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Hang her, she is not worth mans memory;
She's false and base, and let her fright all stories.
Wel, though thou beest mine enemy, Ile right thee,
And right thee Nobly.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Faith sir, since she must goe,
Let's spare as few as may be.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: We'l take all,
And like a torrent sweep the slaves before us.
You dare endure the worst?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: You know our hearts sir,
And they shal bleed the last, erst we start from ye.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: We can but die, and ere we come to that,
We shal pick out some few examples for us.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Then wait the first occasion, and like Curtius,
Ile leap the gulph before you, fearlesse leap it:
Then follow me like men, and if our vertues
May boy our Countrey up, and set her shining
In her first state; our fair revenges taken,
We have our Noble ends, or else our ashes.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: As you are Noble, keep me from discovery,
And let me onely run a strangers fortune;
For when the King shall find I am his daughter
He ever holds most ominous, and hates most:
With what eyes can he look, how entertain me,
But with his feares and cruelties?

speeches.speaker: Asc.
verse: I have found you,
Suspect not. I am bound to what you like best,
What you intend. I dare not be so curious
To question now; and what you are, lies hid here.
The King comes, make your fortune, I shall joy in't.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: All things are ready sir to make you merry,
And such a King you shall behold him now.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I long for't,
For I have need of mirth.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: The Lady sir.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Now as I am a King, a sprightly beauty,
A goodly sweet aspect! my thanks Ronvere,
My best thanks; on your lips I seale your wishes,
Be what you can; imagine mine, and happy.
And now sit downe and smile; come my Ascanio;
And let this Monarch enter.

speeches.speaker: Rover.
verse: These are the Switzers.
I told your grace of.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Goodly promising fellowes,
With faces to keep fooles in awe, I like 'em;
Goe guard the presence well, and doe your duties,
To morrow I shall take a further view:

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: You shall Sir,
Or I shall loose my will; how the whore's mounted?
How she sits thron'd? thou blasing muddy meteor,
That frightest the underworld, with lustfull flashes,
How I shall dash thy flames? away, no word more:

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Now, here he comes in glory, be merry Masters, meat conveyed away.
A Banquet too?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: O, he must sit in State Sir!

speeches.speaker: Asca.
verse: How rarely he is usher'd? can he thinke now
He is a King indeed?

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: Mark but his countenance.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Let me have pleasures infinite, and to the height,
And women in abundance, many women,
I will disport my grace,
Stand there and long for me.
What have ye brought me here? is this a Feast
Fit for a Prince? a mighty Prince? are these things,
These preparations, ha?

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: May it please your grace?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: It does not please my grace: where are the Marchpanes,
The Custards double royall, and the subtleties?
Why, what weak things are you to serve a Prince thus?
Where be the delicates oth' earth and ayre?
The hidden secrets of the Sea? am I a Plow-man,
You pop me up with porridge? hang the Cooks.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: O most Kingly:
What a majestique anger.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Give me some wine.

speeches.speaker: Asca.
verse: He cooles agen now.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Foole, where are my Players?
Let me have all in pomp; let 'em play some love matter,
To make the Ladies itch, I'le be with you anon Ladies;
You black eyes, I'le be with you
Give me some wine I say,
And let me have a Masque of Cuckolds enter:
Of mine own Cuckolds,
And let 'em come in, peeping and rejoycing.
Just as I kisse their wives, and somewhat glorying.
Some wine I say, then for an excellent night-peece,
To shew my glory to my loves, and minions:
I will have some great Castle burnt.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Harke you brother:
If that be to please these Ladies, tenne to one
The fire first takes upon your own, look to that;
Then you may shew a night peece.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Where's this wine?
Why shall I choak? doe yee long all to be tortur'd?

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Why, what is this? why Doctor,
Wine and water Sir.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: 'Tis Soveraign for your heat, you must endure it.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Most excellent to coole your nigh-peece Sir.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: You are of a high and cholericke complexion,
And you must have allayes.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Shall I have no sheere wine then?

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Not for a world: I tender your deare life Sir;
And he is no faithfull Subject—

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: No, by no meanes:
Of this you may drinke; and never hang, nor quarter,
Nor never whip the fool, this liquors mercifull.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: I will sit down ahd eat then: Kings when th'are hungry,
May eat I hope.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Yes, but they eat discreetly.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Come, taste this dish, and cut me liberally;
I like sauce well.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Fie 'tis too hot Sir:
Too deeply season'd with the spice, away with 't,
You must acquaint your stomack wih those diets
Are temperately nourishing.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: But pray stay Doctor,
And let me have my meat agen.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: By no meanes:
I have a charge concerns my life.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: No meat neither;
Doe Kings never eat Doctor?

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Very little Sir.
And that too very choice.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Your King never sleeps Brother,
He must not sleep, his cares still keep him waking.
Now he that eats and drinkes much, is a dormouse;
The third part of a wafer, is a weeks diet.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Appoint me something then.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: There.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: This I feel good,
But it melts too suddainly; yet, how, that gone too! take away.
Ye are not mad! I charge you:

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: For your health Sir,
A little quickens nature, much depresses.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Eat nothing for my health? that's a new dyet;
Let me have something, something has some savour.
Why thou uncourteous Doctor, shall I hang thee?

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: 'Tis better Sir, then I should let you surfet;
My death were nothing.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: To loose a King, were terrible.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Nay, then I'le carve my self, I'le stay no ceremonies.
This is a Partridge Pye, I am sure that's nourishing,
Or Galen is an Asse: 'tis rarely season'd:
Ha Doctor have I hit right? a mark, a mark there?

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: What ailes thy grace?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Retrive those Partridges.
Or as I am a King—

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Pray Sir be patient,
They are flowen too farre.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: These are breath'd pyes an't please you,
And your hawkes are such Buzzards.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: A King and have nothing.
Nor can have nothing!

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: What think you of pudding?
A pudding Royall?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: To be royally starv'd,
Whip me this foole to death; he is a blockhead.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Let 'em think they whip me, as we think you a King:
'Twill be enough.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: As for you dainty Doctor, the Table taken away,
All gone, all snatch'd away, and I unsatsfied,
Without my wits being a King and hungry?
Suffer but this thy treason? I tell thee Doctor,
I tell it thee, in earnest, and in anger,
I am damnably hungry, my very grace is hungry.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: A hungry grace is fittest to no meale Sir.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Some two houres hence, you shall see more: but still Sir,
You must retaine a strict and excellent dyet.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: It sharpens you, and makes your wit so poynant,
Your very words will kill.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: A bit of Marmalade
No bigger then a Pease.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: And that well butter'd,
The ayre thrice purified, and three times spirited,
Becomes a King: your rare conserve of nothing
Breeds no offence.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Am I turn'd King Camelion,
And keep my Court ith' ayr?

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: They vex him cruelly.

speeches.speaker: Asca.
verse: In two dayes more they'l starve him.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Now the women, there's no food left but they.

speeches.speaker: Asca.
verse: They'l prove small nourishment.
Yet h'as another stomack and a great one,
I see by his eye.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: I'le have mine own power here;
Mine own Authority; I need no tutor.
Doctor this is no dyet.

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: It may be Sir

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: Birlady, it may turne to a dry dyet;
And how thy grace, will ward that—

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Stand off Docttor;
And talke to those that want faith,

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Hot and mighty.

speeches.speaker: Asca.
verse: He will coole apace, no doubt.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Faire, plump, and red,
A forehead high; an eye revives the dead;
A lip like ripest fruit, inviting still.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: But O, the rushy well, below the hill,
Take heed of that, for though it never faile
Take heed I say, for thereby hangs a taile.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: I'le get ye all with Childe.

speeches.speaker: Vil.
verse: With one Childe Brother,
So many men in a Blew Coat.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Had I fed well.
And drank good store of wine, ye had been blest all,
Blest all with double Births; come kisse me greedily,
And think no more upon your foolish Husbands,
They are transitory things: a Kings fame meets you,

speeches.speaker: Doct.
verse: Vanish away.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: How, they gone too? my guard there:
Take me this devill Doctor, and that foole there,
And sow 'em in a sack; bring back the women,
The lovely women, drown these rogues or hang 'em.

speeches.speaker: Asca.
verse: He is in earnest Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: In serious earnest,
I mist needs take him off.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Now, now be free.
Now liberty, now Country-men, shake from ye
The Tyrants yoake.
All Liberty, liberty, liberty.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Treason, treason, treason.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: We are betrayed, fly to the town, cry Treason,
And raise our faithfull friends; O my Ascanio.

speeches.speaker: sca.
verse: Make haste, we have way enough.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
prose: Treason, treason.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Spare none, put all to th' sword: a vengeance shake thee;
Art thou turn'd King againe?

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: I am a rascall:
Spare me but this time, if ever I see King more,
Or once beleeve in King.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: The ports are ours.
The treasure and the port, fight bravely Gentlemen;
Cry to the Town, cry liberty and honour;
Waken their persecuted soules, cry loudly,
We'l share the wealth among ye.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Doe you heare Captaine?
If ever you heare me, name a King.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: You shall not.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Or though I live under one, obey him.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: This rogue againe.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Away with him good Gunner.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Why look ye Sir? I'le put you to no charg;
I'le never eat.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: I'le take a course, you shall not.
Come, no more words.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Say nothing when you kill me.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: He's taken to the Towers strength;
Now stand sure Gentlemen.
We have him in a pen, he cannot scape us,
The rest oth'Castle's ours; liberty, liberty:
What is this City up?

speeches.speaker: Boatsw.
verse: They are up and glorious,
And rouling like a storm they come; their Tents
Ring nothing but liberty and freedome.
The women are in Arms too.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Let 'em come all.
Honour and liberty.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Honour and liberty.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: This womans threats, her eyes, even red with fury
Which like prodigious meteors, foretold
Assur'd destruction, are still before me.
Besides I know such natures unacquainted
With any meane, or in their love, or hatred,
And she that dar'd all dangers to possesse him,
Will check at nothing, to revenge the losse
Of what she held so deare, I first discover'd
Her bloody purposes, which she made good,
And openly profess'd 'em; that in me
Was but a cold affection; charity
Commands so much to all; for Virolet
Me thinks I should forget my Sexes weaknesse,
Rise up, and dare beyond a womans strength;
Then doe, not counsell: he is too secure,
And in my judgement, 'twere a greater service
To free him from a deadly Enemy,
Then to get him a friend. I undertooke too,
To crosse her plots, oppos'd my piety,
Against her malice; and shall vertue suffer?
No Martia, wer't thou here equally armed,
I have a cause, spite of thy masculine breeding,
That would assure the victory: my angell
Direct and help me.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: The State in Combustion,
Part of the Cittadell forc'd, the treasure seiz'd on;
The guards corrupted, arme themselves against
Their late protected Master; Ferrant fled too,
And with small strength, into the Castles Tower,
The onely Aventine, that now is left him?
And yet the undertakers, nay, performers,
Of such a brave and glorious enterprize,
Are yet unknown: they did proceed like men,
I like a childe; and had I never trusted
So deep a practise unto shallow fools,
Besides my soules peace, in my Iuliana,
The honour of this action had been mine,
In which, accurs'd, I now can claime no share.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Ronvere! 'tis he, a thing, next to the devill
I most detest, and like him terrible;
Martia's right hand, the Instrument I feare too,
That is to put her bloody will into act.
Have I not will enough, and cause too mighty?
Weake womens fear, fly from me.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Sure this habit,
This likenesse to Ronvere which I have studied,
Either admits me safe to my designe,
Which I too cowardly have halted after,
And suffer'd to be ravish't from my glory;
Or sincks me and my miseries together;
Either concludes me happy.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: He stands musing,
Some mischiefe is now hatching:
In the full meditation, of his wicknesse,
I'le sink his cursed soule: guid my hand heaven,
And to my tender arm give strength and fortun,
That I may doe a pious deed all ages
Shall blesse my name for; all remembrance Crown me.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: It shall be so.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: It shall not, take that token,
And beare it the lustfull Arms of Martia,

Tell her, for
~irolets deare sake, I sent it.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: O I am happy, let me see thee,
That I may blesse the hand that gave me liberty,
O courteous hand, nay, thou hast done most nobly,
And heaven has guided thee, 'twas their great justice;
O blessed wound, that I could come to kisse thee!
How beautifull, and sweet thou shewest!

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Sighe not,
Nor weep not Deare, shed not those soveraign Balsoms
Into my blood; which must recover me;
Then I shall live again, to doe a mischiefe,
Against the mightinesse of love and vertue,
Some base unhallowed hand shall rob thy right off.
Help me, I faint: so.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: O unhappy wench!
How has my zeale abus'd me? you that guard vertue,
Were ye asleep? or doe you laugh at innocence?
You suffer'd this mistake? O my deare Virolet!
An everlasting curse follow that forme
I strook thee in his name ever blasted;
For his accursed shadow has betrayed
The sweetnesse of all youth, the noblenesse,
The honour, and the valor; wither'd for ever
The beauty and the bravery of all mankind:
O my dull, devils eyes.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: I doe forgive you,
By this, and this I doe; I know you were cozend;
The shadow of Ronvere, I know you aym'd at,
And not at me; but 'twas most necessary,
I should be struk, some hand above directed you,
For Juliana could not shew her justice
Without depriving high heaven of his glory,
Or any subject fit for her, but Virolet;
Forgive me too, and take my last breath sweet one,
This the new marriage of our soules together;
Thinke of me Iuliana, but not often,
For feare my faults should burthen your affections,
Pray for me, for I faint.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: O stay a little,
A little little Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Fye Iuliana.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Shall I outlive the vertue, I have murderd?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Hold, or thou hatest my peace; give me the dagger;
On your obedience, and your love, deliver it.
If you doe thus, we shall not meet in heaven sweet;
No guilty blood comes there; kill your intentions,
And then you conquer: there where I am going,
Would you not meet me Deare?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: And still love me?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: And still behold you.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Live then till heaven cals you,
Then ripe and full of sweetnesse you rise Sainted.
Then I that went before you to prepare,
Shall meet and welcome you, and daily court you
With Hymnes of holy Love— I goe out,
Give me your hand, farewell, in peace farewell,
Remember me, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Sleep you sweet glasses,
An everlasting slumber Crown those Christals,
All my delight adue, farewell, Deare Virolet,
Deare, Deare, most Deare; O I can weep no more,
My body now is fire, and all consuming,
Here will I sit, forget the world, and all things,
And onely waite what heaven shall turne me to,
For now me thinkes, I should not live,

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: O my sweet daughter,
The worke is finisht now, I promis'd thee:
Here are thy vertues shewed, here register'd,
And here shall live for ever.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Blot it, burne it.
I have no vertue, hatefull I am as hell is.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse:
Is not this
~irolet?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Aske no more questions,
Mistaking him, I kil'd him.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: O my Sonne,
Nature turnes to my heart again, my deare Sonne,
Sonne of my age, would'st thou goe out so quickly?
So poorly take thy leave, and never see me?
Was this a kind stroake daughter? could you love him?
Honour his Father, and so deadly strike him?
O wither'd timelesse youth, are all thy promises,
Thy goodly growth of Honors come to this?
Doe I halt still ith' world, and trouble nature,
When her maine pieces founder, and faile daily?
Boy he does weep certain: what bodies that lies by him?
How doe you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: O look there Lucio,
Thy Master, thy best Master.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Woe is me.
They have kill'd him, slaine him basely, O my Master,

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Well daughter well; what heart you had to do this;
I know he did you wrong; but 'twas his fortune,
And not his fault, for my sake that have lov'd you,
But I see now, you scorne me too.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: O Mistrisse?
Can you sit there, and his cold body breathlesse?
Basely upon the earth?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Let her alone Boy,
She glories in his end.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: You shall not sit here,
And suffer him you loved- ha; good Sir come hither,
Come hither quickly, heave her up; O heaven Sir,
O God, my heart, she's cold; cold and stiffe too.
Siffe as a stake, she's dead.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: She's gone, ne re bend her,
I know her heart, she could not want his company:
Blessing goe with thy soule, sweet Angels shadow it
O, that I were the third now, what a happinesse?
But I must live, to see you layed in earth both,
Then build a Chapell to your memories,
Where all my wealth shall fashion out your storyes.
Then digge a little grave besides, and all's done.
How sweet she looks, her eyes are open smiling,
I thought she had been alive; you are my charge Sir,
And amongst you, I'le see his goods distributed.
Take up the bodies, mourn in heart my friends,
You have lost two Noble succors; follow me,
And thou sad Country, weepe this misery.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Keep the Ports strongly mand, and let none enter,
But such as are known Patriots.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Liberty, liberty.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: 'Tis a substantiall thing, and not a word
You men of Naples, which if once taken from us,
All other blessings leave us; 'tis a Jewell
Worth purchasing, at the dear rate of life,
And so to be defended. O remember
What you have suffer'd, since you parted with it;
And if again you wish not to be slaves,
And properties to Ferrands pride and lust,
Take noble courage, and make perfect what
Is happily begun.

speeches.speaker: 1. Cit.
verse: Our great preserver,
You have infranchis'd us, from wretched bondage.

speeches.speaker: 2. Cit.
verse: And might be known, to whom we owe our freedome,
We to the death would follow him.

speeches.speaker: 3. Cit.
verse: Make him King,
The Tyrant once remov'd.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: That's not my end.
'Twas not ambition that brought me hither,
With these my faithfull friends, nor hope of spoile;
For when we did possesse the Tyrants treasure,
By force extorted from you, and employed
To load you with most miserable thraldome,
We did not make it ours, but with it purchas'd
The help of these, to get you liberty,
That for the same price kept you in subjection.
Nor are we Switzers, worthy Country-men,
But Neapolitans; now eye me well:
And tho the reverend Emblems of mine age,
My Silver locks are shorne, my beard cut off,
Partaking yet of an adulterate Colour;
Tho 14. yeares you have not seen this face,
You may remember it, and call to mind,
There was a Duke of Sess, A much wrong'd Prince,
Wrong'd by this Tyrant Ferrand.

speeches.speaker: 1. Cit.
verse: Now I know him.

speeches.speaker: 2. Cit.
verse: 'Tis he, long live the Duke of Sess.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: I thank you.
The injuries I receiv'd, I must confesse,
Made me forget the love I owed this Country,
For which I hope, I have given satisfaction,
In being the first that stir'd, to give it freedome;
And with your loves and furtherance, will call back,
Long banisht peace, and plenty, to this people;

speeches.speaker: 2. Cit.
verse: Lead where you please, we'l follow.

speeches.speaker: 1. Cit.
verse: Dare all dangers.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: What solemne funeral's this?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: There rest a while,
And if't be possible there can be added
Wings to your swift desire of just revenge,
Hear, (if my teares will give way to my words)
In briefe a most sad story.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Speake, what are they?
I know thee well Pandulfe.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: My best Lord?
As farre as sorrow will give leave, most welcome;
This Virolet was, and but a Sonne of mine,
I might say, the most hopefull of our Gentry;
And though unfortunate, never Ignoble:
But I'le speake him no further. Look on this,
This face, that in a Savage would move pitty,
The wonder of her Sex; and having said
'Tis Iuliana, Eloquence will want words
To set out her deservings; this blest Lady
That did indure the Rack, to save her Husband,
That Husband, who, in being forc'd to leave her,
Indur'd a thousand tortures; By what practise,
I know not, (bur 'twas sure a cunning one)
Are made, the last I hope, but sad examples
Of Ferrands Tyranny. Convey the bodies hence.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Expresse your sorrow
In your revenge, not teares, my worthy Souldiers:
That fertile earth, that teem'd so many children,
To feed his cruelty, in her wounded wombe,
Can hardly now receive 'em.

speeches.speaker: Boatsw.
verse: We are cold,
Cold walls shall not keep him from us.

speeches.speaker: Gun.
verse: Were he cover'd with mountaines, and roome onely for a
Bullet to be sent levell at him, I would speed him.

speeches.speaker: Mr.
verse: Let's scale this petty Towre; at Sea we are Falcons,
And fly unto the maine top in a moment.
What then can stop us here?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: We'l teare him peece-meale.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: Or eat a passage to him.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Let discretion
Direct your anger; that's a victory,
Which is got with least losse, let us make ours such:
And therefore friends, while we hold parly here,
Raise your scalado, on the other side,
But enter'd weake, your suffrings.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: In our wrongs.
There was no meane.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: Nor in our full revenge
Will we know any.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Be appeas'd good man,
No sorrow can redeem them from deaths Prison;
What his inevitable hand hath seiz'd on,
The world cannot recover. All the comfort
That I can give to you, is to see vengeance
Pour'd dreadfully upon the Authors head,
Of which their ashes may be sensible,
That have falne by him.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: They appeare.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: 'Tis not that we esteme rebellious Traytors
Worthy an answer to their proudest Sommons
That we vouchsafe our presence; or to exchange
One syllable with 'em: but to let such know,
Though Circled round with treason, all points bent
As to their Center at my heart, 'tis free,
Free from feare villaines, and in this weake Tower
Ferrand commands as absolute, as when
He trod upon your necks, and as much scornes you.
And when the Sunne of Majesty shall breake through
The clouds of your rebellion, every beame
Instead of comfortable heate, shall send
Consuming plagues among you; and you call
That government which you term'd tyrannous
Hereafter, gentle.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Flatter not thy selfe
With these deluding hopes, thou cruell beast,
Thou art ith' toyle, and the glad Huntsmam prouder,
By whom thou art taken, of his prey, then if
(Like thee) he should command, and spoile his Forrest.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: What art thou?

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: To thy horror, Duke of Sesse.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: The Divel.

speeches.speaker: Sess.
verse: Reserv'd for thy damnation.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Why shakes my love?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: O I am lost for ever;
Mountains divide me from him; some kind hand
Prevent our fearfull meeting: Or lead me
To the steep rock, whose rugged brows are bent
Upon the swelling main; there let me hide me:
And as our bodies then shall be divided,
May our soules never meet.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: Whence grows this, Sweetest?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: There are a thousand furies in his looks;
And in his deadly silence more loud horror,
Then when in Hell the tortur'd and tormentors
Contend whose shreeks are greater. Wretched me!
It is my father.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Yes, and I wil own her, Sir,
Till my revenge. It is my daughter, Ferrand;
My daughter, thou hast whor'd.

speeches.speaker: Fer.
verse: I triumph in it:
To know she's thine, affords me more true pleasure,
Then the act gave me, When even at the height,
I crack'd her Virgin zone. Her shame dwell on thee,
And all thy family; may they never know
A female issue, but a whore, Ascanio.
Ronvere, look cheerfully; be thou a man too,
And learn of me to die. That we might fall,
And in our ruines swallow up this Kingdom,
Nay the whol world, and make a second Chaos.
And if from thence a new beginning rise,
Be it recorded this did end with us;
And from our dust hath embryon.

speeches.speaker: Ron.
verse: I liv'd with you,
And wil die with you; your example makes me
Equally bold.

speeches.speaker: Ase
verse: And I resolv'd to beare
What ere my fate appoints me.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: They are ours,
Now to the spoyle.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Pity the Lady; to all else be deaft.
Within, Kill, kill, kill.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Cruell beginnings meet with cruell ends;
And the best sacrifice to Heaven for peace,
Is tyrants blood: and those that stuck fast to him,
Flesh'd instruments in his commands to mischiefe,
With him dispatch'd.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: They are all cut off.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Tis well.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Thanks to the Duke of Sesse.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Pay that to Heaven,
And for a generall joy, give generall thanks:
For blessings nere descend from Heaven, but when
A gratefull Sacrifice ascends from men.
To your devotion; leave me; there's a Scene,
Which I would act alone; yet you may stay,
For wanting just spectators, twill be nothing.
The rest forbeare me.

speeches.speaker: Citizens.
verse: Liberty liberty, liberty.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I would I were as far beneath the Centre,
As now I stand above it; how I tremble!
Thrice happy they that dyed; I dying live
To stand the whirlwind of a fathers fury.
Now it moves toward me.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Thou, I want a name,
By which to stile thee: All articulate sounds
That do expresse the mischiefe of vile woman,
That are, or have been, or shall be, are weak
To speak thee to the height. Witch, parricide,
For thou, in taking leave of modesty,
Hast kild thy father, and his honour lost;
He's but a walking shadow, to torment thee.
To leave, and rob thy father; then set free
His foes, whose slavery he did prefer
Above all treasure, was a strong defeazance
To cut off, even the surest bonds of mercy.
After all this, having given up thy selfe,
Like to a sensuall beast, a slave to lust,
To play the whore, and then (high Heaven it racks me)
To finde out none to quench thy appetite,
But the most cruell King, whom next to Hell,
Thy father hated; and whose black imbraces
Thou shouldst have fled from, as the whips of furies;
What canst thou look for?

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Death; and tis not in you
To hurt me further: my old resolution,
Take now the place of feare; in this I liv'd,
In this Ile die, your daughter.

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: Look but here;
You had, I know, a guilty hand in this;
Repent it Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Juliana dead?
And Virolet?

speeches.speaker: Pand.
verse: by her unwilling hand.

speeches.speaker: Mart.
verse: Fates you are equall. What can now fall on me,
That I wil shrink at? now unmov'd I dare
Look on your anger, and not bend a knee
To aske your pardon: let your rage run higher
Then billows rais'd up by a violent Tempest,
And be as that is, deafe to all intreaties:
They are dead, and I prepar'd; for in their fall
All my desires are sum'd up.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Impudent too?
Die in it wretch.

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: Stay sir.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: How dar'st thou villaine,
Snatch from my sword the honour of my justice?

speeches.speaker: Bots.
verse: I never did you better service sir,
Yet have been ever faithfull. I confesse
That she deserv'd to die; but by whose hand?
Not by a fathers. Double all her guilt,
It could not make you innocent, had you done it.
In me tis murder, in you twere a crime
Heaven could not pardon. Witnesse that I love you,
And in that love I did it.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: Thou art Noble,
I thank thee for't; the thought of her die with her.

speeches.speaker: Ascan.
verse: My turn is next: since she could finde no mercy,
What am I to expect?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: With one voyce, sir,
The Citizens salute you, with the stile
Of King of Naples.

speeches.speaker: Ses.
verse: I must be excus'd,
The burden is too heavy for my shoulder,
Bestow it where tis due. Stand forth Ascanio,
It does belong to you; live long and weare it,
And warn'd by the example of your Unkle,
Learn that you are to govern men, not beasts:
And that it is a most improvident head,
That strives to hurt the limbs that do support it.
Give buriall to the dead; for me, and mine,
We wil again to Sea, and never know,
The place, which in my birth first gave me woe.

speeches.speaker: Curio.
verse: SIgnor Alphonso, ye are too rugged to her,
Believe too full of harsnesse.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Yes, it seemes so.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: A father of so sweet a child, so happy,
(Fy Sir) so excellent in all endowments,
In blessednesse of beauty, such a mirror.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: She is a foole, away.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Can ye be angry?
Can any wind blow rough, upon a blossom
So faire, and tender? Can a Fathers nature,
A noble Fathers too?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: All this is but prating:
Let her be rul'd; let her observe my humor,
With tny eyes let her see; with my eares listen;
I am her Father: I begot her, bred her,
And I will make her.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: No doubt ye may compell her,
But what a misceivous, unhappy fortune
May wayt upon this wil of yours, as commonly
Such forcings ever end in hates, and ruines.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Is't not a man I wish her to? a strong man?
What can she have? what could she have? a Gentleman?
A yong man? and an able-man? a rich man?
A handsome man? a valiant man? do you marke me?
None of your peeced-companions, your pin'd-Gallants,
That flie to fitters, with every flaw of weather:
None of your impt bravados: what can she ask more?
Is not a mettal'd-man fit for a woman?
A strong chindman? i'le not be foold, nor flurted.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I grant ye Rodorgio is all these
And a brave Gentleman: must it therefore follow
Upon necessity she must doate upon him?
Will ye allow no liberty in choosing?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Alas she is tender yet.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Enough enough, enough Sir:
She is malliable; shee'l endure the hammer,
And why not that strong workeman that strikes deepest?
Let me know that? she is fifteen, with the vantage,
And if she be not ready now for mannage—

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: You know he is a banish'd man: an out-Law;
And how he lives: his nature rough, and bloody
By customary rapines: now, her sweet humor
That is as easy as a calme, and peacefull,
All her affections, like the dewes on Roses,
Faire as the flowers themselves: as sweet, and gentle:
How would you have these meet?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: A bed, a bed sir:
Let her be the fairest Rose, and the sweetest,
Yet I know this faire rose must have her prickles:
I grant ye Rodorigo is an out-Law,
An easie composition cals him in again,
He is a valiant man, and he is a rich man,
And loves the foole: a little rough by custome:
Shee'l like him ten times better. Shee'l doat upon him,
If ere they come to grapling, run mad for him;
But there is an other in the wind, some castrell
That hovers over her, and dares her dayly,
Some flickring slave.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: I dare not think so poorely.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Something there is, and must be: but I shall sente it
And hunt it narrowly.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I never saw her yet
Make offer at the least glance of affection,
But still so modest, wise.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: They are wise to gull us,
There was a fellow, old Ferandos son,
I must confesse handsome, but my enemy,
And the whole family, I hate yong Pedro:
That fellow I have seen her gaze upon,
And turn, and gaze again, and make such offers
As if she would shoot her eyes like meteors at him:
But that cause stands removed.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: You need not doubt him.
For long since as 'twas thought on a griev'd conscience,
He left his father, and his friends: more pitty:
For truth reports he was a noble Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Let him be what he wil: he was a begger,
And there i'le leave him.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: The more the Court must answer;
But certainly I think, though she might favour him,
And love his goodnesse, as he was an honest man:
She never with loose eyes stuck on his person.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: She is so full of conscience too, and charity,
And outward holinesse, she will undoe me:
Relieves more beggers, then an hospitall;
And all poor rogues, that can but say their prayers,
And tune their pipes to Lamentations,
She thinks she is bound to dance to: good morrow to you,
And that's as ye deserve too: you know my mind,
And studdy to observe it: doe it cheerfully.
And readily, and home.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I shall obey ye.
But noble sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Come, come, away with your flatteries,
And your fine phrases,

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Pray ye be gentle to her:

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I know 'em; and know your feates: if you will find me
Noble and loving, seek me in your duty,
You know I am too indulgent.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Alas poor Lady.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: To your devotions: I take no good thing from you
Come Gentlemen; leave pittying, and moaning of her,
And praysing of her vertues: and her whym-whams,
It makes her proud, and sturdy:

speeches.speaker: Seb. Cur.
verse: Good houres wait on ye.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I thank ye Gentlemen: I want such comforts:
I would thank you too father: but your cruelty
Hath almost made me senselesse of my duty,
Yet still I must know: would J had known nothing;
What Poor attend my charity to day, wench?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Of all sorte, Madam; your open handed bounty
Makes 'em flock every houre: some worth your pitty,
But others that have made a trade of begging.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Wench, if they ask it truly, I must give it:
It takes away the holy use of charity
To examine wants.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I would you would be merry:
A cheerfull-giving hand, as I think, Madam,
Requires a heart as cheerfull.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Alas Iuletta,
What is there to be merry at? what joy now,
Unlesse we foole our own afflictions,
And make them shew ridiculous?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Sure Madam,
You could not seeme thus serious, if you were married,
Thus sad, and full of thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Married? to whom, wench?
Thou thinkst if there be a yong handsome fellow
As those are plentifull, our cares are quenched then.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Madam, I think a lusty handsome fellow
If he be kind, and loving, and a right one,
Is even as good a pill, to purge this melancholy,
As ever Galen gave, I am sure more naturall:
And merrier for the heart, then Wine and Saffron:
Madam, wantone youth is such a Cataplasme.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Who has bin thy tutor wench?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Even my own thoughts, Lady:
For though J be bard the liberty of talking,
Yet I can think unhappily, and as near the mark, Madam,
'Faith, marry, and be merry.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Who wil have me?
Who wil be troubled with a tettish Girle?
It may be proud, and to that vice expencefull?
Who can assure himselfe, I shall live honest?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Let every man take his fortune:

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: And o' my conscience
If once I grow to breeding, a whole Kingdome
Wil not containe my stock.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: The more the merrier:
'Tis brave to be a mother of new Nations.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Why, I should bury a hundred husbands.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Tis no matter:
As long as ye leave sufficient men to stock ye.

speeches.speaker: Alm.
verse: Is this thy mirth? are these the joyes of marriage?
Away light-headed foole; are these contentments?
If I could finde a man.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: You may a thousand.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Meere men I know I may: and there a woman
Has liberty, (at least shee'l venture for it,)
To be a monster and become the time too;
But to enjoy a man, from whose example
(As from a compasse) we may steer our fortunes,
Our actions, and our age; and safe arive at
A memory that shall become our ashes,
Such things are few, and far to seek; to finde one
That can but rightly mannage the wild beast, woman,
And sweetly govern with her. But no more of this, wench,
Tis not for thy discourse: Lets in, and see
What poor afflicted wait our charity.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Stand off, and keep your Rancks: twenty foot further:
There Iouse your selves with reason, & discretion.
The Sun shines warm: the farther still the better,
Your beasts wil bolt anon, and then tis dangerous.

speeches.speaker: 1. Beg.
verse: Heaven blesse our Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Does the crack go that way?
'Twil be o'th o'ther side anon.
Pray ye friend.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Your friend? and why your friend? why, goodman turncoat
What dost thou see within me, or without me,
Or what itch dost thou know upon me, tell me,
That I should be thy friend? what do I look like
Any of thy acquaintance hoong in Gibbets?
Hast thou any Friends, Kindred, or Alliance,
Or any higher ambition, then an almes-basket?

speeches.speaker: 2. Beg.
verse: I would be your worships friend.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: So ye shall Sirra,
When I quarter the same louse with ye.
Tis twelve o'clock.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Tis ever so with thee, when thou hast done scratching,
For that provokes thy stomach to ring noon;
O the infinite Seas of porridge thou hast swallowd!
And yet thou lookst as if they had bin but Glisters;
Thou feedst abundance; thou hadst need of sustenance;
Almes do you call it to relieve these Rascals?
No^hing but a generall rot of sheep can satisfie'em.

speeches.speaker: Al
verse: Did not I tel you, how she would undo me?
What Marts of Rogues, and Beggers?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Tis charity
Methinks, you are bound to love her for—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Yes, I warrant ye,
If men could sale to heaven in porridge pots,
With masts of Beef, and Mutton, what a voyage should I make?
What are all these?
Poore people, and 't like your worship.
Wretched poor people.
Very hungry people.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: And very Lousy.
Yes forsooth, so, so.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: I'le undertake five hundred head about 'em,
And that's no needy Grasier.

speeches.speaker: Al
verse: What are you?

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: Strangers that come to wonder at your charity,
Yet people poore enough to beg a blessing.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Use them with favour, sir, their shews are reverent,
It seemes ye are holy Pilgrimes?

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: Ye ghesse right sir,
And bound far off, to offer our devotions.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: What make ye this way? we keep no Reliques here,
Nor holy Shrines.

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: The holiest we ere heard of;
Ye keep a living monument of goodnesse,
A Daughter of that pious excellence,
The very Shrines of Saints sinck at her vertues,
And swear they cannot hold pace with her pieties,
We come to see this Lady: not with prophane eyes,
Nor wanton bloods, to do at upon her beauties,
But through our tedious wayes to beg her blessings.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: This is a new way of begging, and a neat one,
And this cries money for reward: good store too;
These commendations beg not with bag, and bottle;
Well, well, the sainting of this woman (Gentlemen)
I know what it must come too: these women saints
Are plaguy heavy saints: they out-waigh a he-saint
Three thousand thick; I know: I feele.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Ye are more afraid then hurt sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Have you your commendations ready too?
He bowes, and nods.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: A handsome well built person.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: What Country-craver are you? nothing but motion?
A puppet-Pilgrim?

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: Hee's a stranger sir;
This foure dayes I have traveld in his company,
But little of his busines, or his Language
As yet, I have understood.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Both yong, and handsome,
Only the Sun has bin too saucy with him.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Would ye have money sir, or meat? what kind of blessing
Does your devotion looke for? Still more ducking?
Be there any saints, that understand by signes only?
More motion yet? this is the prettiest Pilgrim,
The pinck of pilgrims: ile be for ye sir;
Do ye discourse with signes? ye are hartly welcome:
A poor viaticum; very good gold sir;
But holy men affect a better treasure.
I kept it for your goodnes, but neerthelesse
Since it can prove but burthen some to your holines,
And you affect light prayer, fit for carriage,
I'le put this up againe.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Ye are too unreverent..

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Ye talk too broad; must I give way, and wealth too
To every toy, that carries a grave seeming?
Must my good angels wait on him? if the proud hilding
Would yeild but to my wil, and know her duty
I knew what I would suffer.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Good sir, be patient,
The wrongs ye do these men, may light on you,
Too heavy too: and then you wil wish you had said lesse;
A comly and sweet usage becomes strangers.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: We shall have half the Kingdom strangers shortly,
And this fond prodigality be sufferd;
But I must be an asse, see 'hem relieved, sirah;
If I were yong again, I would sooner get beare whelps,
And safer too, them any of these She-saints,
But I will break her,

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Such a face for certain.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Me thinks I have seen it too: but we are cozend;
But fair befall thee Pilgrim, thou lookst lovely.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Will ye troop up, ye porridge Regiment?
Captain Poors quarter wil ye move?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Ye dull Knave,
Are not these wretches served yet?

speeches.speaker: Beg.
verse: 'Blesse my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Do you make sport sir, with their miseries?
Ye drousie rogue.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: They are too high fed, Madam,
Their stomacks are a'sleep yet.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Serve 'hem plentifully,
Or i'le serve you out next: even out o' dores, sirah;
And serve 'em quickly too.

speeches.speaker: Beg.
verse: Heaven blesse the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Blesse the good end I meane it for.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I would I knew it:
If it be for any mans sake, i'le cry amen too,
Well Madam, ye have even as pretty a port of pentioners.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Vain-glory would seek more, and handsomer.
But I appeale to vertue what my end is;
What men are these?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: It seems they are holy Pilgrims:
That handsome youth should suffer such a pennance,
Would I were even the saint they make their vowes too,
How easily I would grant.

speeches.speaker: Pil,
verse: Heavens grace in-wheele ye:
And all good thoughts, and prayers dwell about ye,
Abundance be your friend; and holy charity
Be ever at your hand' to crown ye glorious.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I thank ye sir; peace guid your travels too,
And what you wish for most, end all your trobles;
Remember me by this: and in your prayers
When your strong heart melts, mediate my poor fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: All my devotions wait upon your service.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Are ye of this Country, sir?

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: Yes, worthiest Lady,
But far off bred: my fortunes farther from me.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Gentle, I dare believe.

speeches.speaker: Pil.
verse: I have liv'd freer.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I am no inquisitor, that were too curious:
What ever vow, or pennance puls ye on sir;
Conscience, or love, or stubborn disobedience,
The saint ye kneel too, hear, and ease your travels.

speeches.speaker: Pil.
prose: Yours neer begin: and thus I seal my prayers.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: How constantly this man looks? how he sighes?
Some great affliction hatches his devotions,
Right holy sir: how yong, and sweet he suffers?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Would I might suffer with him.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: He turns from us:
Alas he weeps too: something presses him
He would reveale, but dare not; sir, be comforted,
Ye come for that: and take it: if it be want, sir,
To me yee appear so worthy of relieving,
I am your steward: speak, and take: he's dumb still:
Now as I have a faith this man so stirs me,
His modesty makes me affraid I have trespassed.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Would he would stir me too: I like his shape well.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: May be he would speak alone: go off Iuletta,
Afflicted hearts fear their own motions,
Be not far off.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Would I were neerer to him,
A yong smug handsome holines has no fellow.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Why do you grieve? do you find your pennance sharp?
Orare the vowes ye have made, too mighty for ye?
Do's not the world allure ye to look back
And sorrow for the sweet time ye have lost?
Ye are yong, and fair; be not deluded, sir;
A manly made up heart contemnes these shadows,
And yours appeares no lesse: greifes for your fears,
For houres ill-spent, for wrongs don rash, and rudely,
For fowle contempts for faiths ill violated,
Become fears well: I dare not task your Goodnes:
And then a sorrow shewes in his true glory
VVhen the whole heart is excellently sorry.
I pray ye be comforted.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I am, deer Lady,
And such a comfort ye have cast upon me,
That though I struggle with mine own calamities
Too mighty, and too many for my mannage,
And though, like angry waves, they curld upon me
Contending proudly who should first devour me,
Yet I would stem their danger.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: He speaks nobly:
What do ye want?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: All that can make me happy:
I want my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Your self? who rob'd ye Pilgrim?
Why does he look so constantly upon me?
I want my selfe: indeed, you holy wounderers
Are said to seek much: but to seek your selves.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I seek my self; and am but my selfs-shadow:
Have lost my self; and now am not so noble.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I seek my self: something I yet remember
That bears that Motto; 'tis not he: he is yonger,
And far more tender: for that self-sake (Pilgrim)
Be who it will, take this.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Your hand I dare take,
That be far from me, Lady, thus I kisse it,
And thus I blesse it too; be constant fair still:
Be good, and live to be a great example.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: One word more (Pilgrim) has amazd me strangly,
Be constant faire still: tis the posse here:
And here without, Be good: he wept to see me
Juletta:

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Take this Key, and fetch me
The Marygold Jewell that lies in my little Cabinet:
I think tis that: what eyes had I, to misse him?
O' me, what thoughts? he had no beard then, and
As I remember well, he was more ruddy.
If this be he, he has a manly face yet
A goodly shape.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Here Madam?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Let me see it:
Tis so, too true: It must be he, or nothing,
He spak the words just as they stand engraved here:
I seek my self, and am but my selfes-shadow:
Alas poor man: didst thou not meet him, Iuletta?
The Pilgrim wench?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: He went by long ago, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I forgot to give him something.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: 'Twas ill done Lady:
For, o' my troth, he is the handsomest man
I saw this many a day: would he had all my wealth,
And me to boote: what ayles she to grow sullen?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
prose: Come, I forgot; but I will recompence it.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Can she slip through a cat-hole? tel me that: resolve me;
Can the sly ith ayre? is she a thing invisible?
Gon, and none know it?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Ye amaz your servants.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Some pelting rogue has watch'd her houre of itching,
And clawd her; clawd her: do you mark me, clawd her;
Some that I foster up.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: They are all here, sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Let 'em be where they will, they are arrant rascals,
And by this hand i'le hang 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Deale calmely:
You will not give 'em time to answer ye.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I'le choak 'hem: famish 'em: what say you wag-taile?
You knew her mind: you were of councell with her,
Tell me: and tell me true.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Aske with discretion.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Discretion? hang discretion, hang ye all:
Let me know where she is.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Would you know o' me sir?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: O' thee sir: I, o' thee sir: what art thou sir?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Hir woman sir, and 't like your worship, sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Her band, her fidle-stick.
Her Lady-fayry, to oyl the dores o' nights,
That they may open with discretion,
Her Gin, her Nut-crack,

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Tis very well sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Thou liest; tis dan nal le ill, tis most abhominaable:
Will ye confes (Thing)

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Say I were gulty, sir?
I would be hangd before I would confesse:
Is this a World to confesse in?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Deale directly.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Yes, if my matter lie direct before me:
But when I am forc'd, and ferryted.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Tell me the truth,
And as I live, i'le give thee a new petticote.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: And you would give me ten, I would not tell ye,
Truths bear a greater price, then you are aware of.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Deale modestly.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I doe not pluck my cloths up.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: What say you sirha? you? or you? are ye dumb all?

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: I saw her last night, and 't shall like your worship
When I serv'd in her Livery.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: What's that, sirha?

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: Her Chamber pot, and 't please ye.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: A new Livery.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Where lay she? who lay with her?

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: In truth not I sir:
I lay with my fellow Fredrick, in the flea-chamber
And 't like your worship, we are almost worried.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I left her by her self, in her own closet,
And there I thought she had slept.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Why lay you from her?

speeches.speaker: Iu.
verse: It was her will I should: she is my Mistris,
And my part is obedience.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Were all the dores lockt?

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: All mine.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: And mine: she could not get out those wayes
Unles she lept the wals: and those are higher
Then any womans courage dare aspire at.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Come, you must know.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Conceale it not, but deale plaine.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: If I did know, and her trust lay upon me,
Not all your angers, nor your flatteries
Should make me speak, but having no more interest
Then I may well deliver to the aire,
I'le tell ye what I know: and tell it liberally,
I think she is gon, because we cannot find her;
I think she is weary of your tyranny,
And therefore gon: may be she is in love:
May be in love, where you show no great liking,
And therefore gon: May be, some point of conscience,
Or vowd devotion.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: These are nothing, minion;
You that can aime at these, must know the truth too.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Any more truth then this if I know, hang me,
Or where to search for it, if I make a lie
To gaine your love, and envy my best Mistris,
Pin me against a wall, with my heel's upwards.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Out of my dores.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: That's all my poor petition:
For if your house were gold, and she not in it,
Sir, I should count it but a cage to whistle in.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Whore, if she be above ground, I wil have her.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I would live in a cole-pit, then, were I your daughter.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Certaine she dos not know Sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Hang her, hang her:
She knowes too much: search all the house; all corners,
And where tis possible she may goe out,
If I do finde your tricks.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Reward me for 'hem.
Or if I had such tricks, you could discover
So weak, and sleightly woven, you might look through,
All the young Girles should hoot me out oth' Parish.
You are my Master, but ye owne an anger
Becomes a School-boy, that hath lost his Apples;
Will ye force things into our knowledges?

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Come hither Juletta; thou didst love me.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: And do still:
You are my Ladies father, and I reverence ye.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Thou wouldst have pleas'd my humor.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Any good way,
That carried not suspition in't: or flattery,
Or faile of trust.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Come, come, thou wouldst have.—

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Stay sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: And thou hast felt my bounty for't, and shalt doe.
Dost thou want Clothes or Money?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Both.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Shalt have both.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: But not this way: I had rather be an Adamite
And bring Fig-leaves into fashion again.
If you were young sir,
Handsome, and fitted to a womans appetite;
And I a giddy-headed girle, that car'd for nothing,
Much might be done; then you might fumble with me,
And thinke to grope out matters of some moment,
Which now you will put too short for:
For what you have seen hitherto,
And know by me, has been but honest service,
Which I dare pin ith' market-place to answer;
And let the world, the flesh and divell examine it,
And come you in too, I dare stand your strictest.
And so much good may doe you, with your dreames of curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: This is most monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Sure she do's not know sir:
She durst not be so confident and guilty.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How now; what newes? what hopes and steps discovered?
Speake any thing thats good, that tends to th' matter;
Doe you stand staring still?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: We are no Gods sir,
To say she is here, or there: and what she is doing;
But we have search'd.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: I am sure she is not ith' Cellar;
For looke you sir, if she had been ith' Cellar—

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I am sure thou hast been there.

speeches.speaker: Por.
verse: As I carried the matter,
For I search'd every piece of Wine; yes sure sir,
And every little Teresse that could but testifie:
And I drew hard to bolt her out.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Away with him;
Fling him ith' Haymow, let him lie a mellowing;
He stinks of Muskadel like an English Christmas:
Are these your cares? your services?

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Pray ye heare sir,
We have found where she went out; her very footing.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Where where? goe on.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Observe then wth more slaiednesse.

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: Searching the garden: at the little Posterne
That opens to the Parke, we first discovered it.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: A little foot?

speeches.speaker: 1 Ser.
verse: It must be hers, or none sir.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How far beyond that?

speeches.speaker: 2 Ser.
verse: To the Parke it leads us,
But there the ground being hard, we could not marke it.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: She alwaies kept that Key: I was a coxcomb,
A foole, an asse, to give a girle that liberty:
Saddle my Horses, rogues, ye drunken varlets:
Your precious diligence lies in Pint-pots,
Your brains in Butts, my horses, ye pin-buttocks.
You'l beare me company?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: We dare not leave ye,
Unlesse we found a quieter soule within ye.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: If we may do the Lady any service,
Sweet, gentle soule.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: I say againe, my horses:
Are ye so hot? have ye your private pilgrimages?
Must ye be Jumping-Jone? Ile wander with ye:
Ile jump ye, and Ile joggle ye: my horses;
And keep me this young Lirry-poope within dores,
I will discover, dame.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: 'Tis fit you should sir,
If ye knew what: Well Love, if thou bee'st with her,
Or what power else that armes her resolution,
Conduct her faire, and keepe her from this mad man,
Direct her to her wishes: dwell about her
That no dishonourable end ore-take her,
Danger, or want: and let me try my fortune.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: You know the place we meet in?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: We shall hit it.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: And as ye are honest Gentlemen, endeavour.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
prose: We'l search the best we can: if she light in our hands.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Tie her to th' horse taile.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: We know how to use her,
But not your way, for all your state.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Make haste there:
And get you in, and looke to th'house. If you stir out, Damsell,
Or set o' foot any new motion this way,
When I come home, (which shall be suddenly)
You know my mind: if you doe play the rascall,
I have my eyes and eares in sundry places,
If ye doe praunce.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I shall doe that, that's fit, sir:
And fit to crosse your fooleries; Ile faile else.
And so Ile to my chamber.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: To your prayers,
And leave your stubborne tricks: She is not far yet,
She cannot be; and we dividing suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Keep her from thy hands, I beseech.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Our horses;
Come cheerfully. Ile teach her to run gadding.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: Captaine, y'are not merry.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: We get nothing,
We have no sport; whoring, apd drinking spoiles us,
We keep no guards.
There come no passengers,
Merchants, nor Gentlemen, nor whosoever,
But we have Tribute.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: And whilst we spend that idlely,
We let those passe that carry the best purchase.
Ile have all search'd & brought in; Rogues, and Beggars,
Have got the tricke now to become Banck-masters.
Ile have none scape: onely my friends, and neighbours,
That may deliver to the King my innocence;
Those I would have regarded; tis policy.
But otherwise nor gravities, nor shadows,
Appeare they how they will, that may have purses,
For they shall pay.
Ye speake now like a Captaine.
And if we spare, flea us, and coyn our Cassoks;
Will ye looke blith?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You heare no preparation
The King intends against us yet?
Not a word sir.
Good man, he's troubled with matter of more moment,
Hummings of higher nature vex his braines, sir;
Doe not we fee his garrisons?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Who are out now?
Good fellows sir, that if there be any purchase stirring
Will strike it dead; Jaques and Loper, Lads
That know their quarters, as they know their knapsaks;
And will not off.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Where is the boy ye brought me?
A pretty lad, and of a quicke capacity,
And bred up neatly.
He's within at meat, sir,
The knave is hungry: yet he seasons all
He eates or drinkes with many teares and sighings,
The saddest appetite I ever look'd on;
The boy is young, tis feare and want of company
He knows and loves: use him not rough, nor harshly,
He will be quickly bold; Ile entertaine him:
I want a pretty Boy to waite upon me,
And when I am sad or sleepy, to prate to me;
Besides there's something in his face, I like well.
And still the more I looke, more like; let him want nothing,
And use him gently, all.
Here's a small Box, sir,
We tooke about him, which he griev'd to part with,
May be some wealth.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Alas, some little money
The poore knave carried to defray his lodgings,
Ile give it him againe, and adde unto it.
'Twere sin to open such a petty purchase.
How now, who is this? what have you brought me Souldiers?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We know not wel what: a strange staving fellow,
Sullen enough I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Where tooke ye him?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Upon the skirt o'th wood, veiwing, and gaping,
And sometime standing still, as if he had meant
To view the best accesses to our quarters;
Money he has enough: and when we threatned him,
He smil'd, and yeilded; but not one word utter'd.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: His habit saies he's holy: if his heart
Keep that proportion too, 'tis best ye free him,
We keep his Wallet here: I am sure tis heavy.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Pilgrime: come hither sir; Are you a Pilgrime?
A piece of pretty holinesse: doe you shrinke sir?
A smug young Saint. What Countrey were you born in?
Ye have a Spanish face: In a dumb Province?
And had your mother too this excellent vertue?
No tongue do you say? sure she was a matchlesse woman;
What a sine family is this man sprung from!
Certaine he was begotten in a calme,
When all was husht: the Midwife was dumb Midnight;
Are ye seal'd up? or doe you scorne to answer?
Ye are in my hands, and I have medicines for ye
Can make ye speake: pull off his Bonnet, Souldiers;
Ye have a speaking face.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I am sure a handsome:
This Pilgrime cannot want She-Saints to pray to.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Stand neerer: ha?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Come, do your worst; I am ready.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Is your tongue found? go off, and let me talk with him;
An keepe your watches round.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We are ready Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: So: now what are ye?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Am I?
My habit shewes me what I am.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Thy heart
A desperate foole, and so thy fate shall tell thee;
What devill brought thee hither? for I know thee.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I know thou dost: and since it is my fortune
To light into thy fingers; I must thinke too
The most malicious of all devils brought me,
Yet some men say thou art Noble.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Not to thee,
That were a benefit to mocke the giver:
Thy father hates my friends, and family,
And thou hast been the heire of all this malice.
Can two such stormes meet then, and part with kissing?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: You have the mightier hand.

speeches.speaker: Rod
verse: And so Ile use it.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I cannot hinder ye: lesse can I beg
Submissive at his knees that knows not honour;
That bears the stamp of man, and not his nature;
Ye may doe what ye please.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I will doe all.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: And when you have done all, which is my poore ruine,
(For farther your base malice cannot venture)
Dishonours selfe will cry you out a coward.
Hadst thou been brave, and noble and an Enemy,
Thou wouldst have sought me whilst I carried Armes,
Whilst my good Sword was my profession,
And then have cried out Pedro, I defie thee;
Then stuck Alphonso's quarrell on the point,
The mercenary anger thou serv'st under
To get his daughter. Then thou shouldst have brav'd me,
And arm'd with all thy families hate upon me,
Done something worthy feat: Now poore and basely
Thou setst Toyles to betray me; and like the Pesant,
That dares not meet the Lyon in the face,
Digst crafty pit-fals: Thou sham'st the Spanish honour:
Thou hast neither poynt of man, nor conscience in thee.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Sir, sir, y'are brave; ye plead now in a Sanctuary;
You think your Pilgrimes bulwarke can defend ye:
You will not finde it so.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I looke not for't.
The more unhallowed soule hast thou to offer it.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: When you were bravest, sir, and your Sword sharpest,
I durst affront ye: when the Court Sunne guilded ye,
And every cry was the young hopefull Pedro,
Alonsos sprightly sonne; then durst I meet ye,
When you were Master of this fame, and fashion,
And all your glories in the full Meridian,
The Kings proof-favour buckled on your body;
Had we then come to competition,
Which I have often sought.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: And I desired too.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You should have seen this Sword, how ere you sleight it,
And felt it too; sharper then sorrow felt it,
In execution quicker then thy scornes;
Thou shouldst have seen all this, and shrunke to see it.
Then like a Gentleman I would have us'd thee,
And given thee the faire fortune of thy being,
Then with a Souldiers Arme I had honour'd thee;
But since thou stealst upon me like a Spie,
And thiefe-like thinkst that holy case shall carry thee
Through all my purposes, and so betray me,
Base as you act, thy end be, and I forget thee.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: What poore evasions thou buildst on, to abuse me?
The goodnesse of a man nere taught these principles.
I come a Spie? durst any Noble spirit
Put on this habit, to become a Traitor?
Even in an Enemy shew me this antipathy
Where there is Christian faith, and this not reverenced:
I come a Spie? no Roderigo, no,
A hater of thy person, a maligner?
So far from that, I brought no malice with me,
But rather when I meet thee, teares to soften thee;
When I put on this habit, I put off
All fires, all angers, all those starts of youth
That clapt too ranke a biasse to my being,
And drew me from the right marke all should aime at;
In stead of stubborne steele, I put on prayers;
For rash and hasty heats, a sweet repentance:
Long weary steps, and vows, for my vain-glories.
O Roderigo.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: If thy tongue could save thee,
Prating be thy baile, thou hast a rare benefit.
Souldiers, come out, and bring a halter with ye;
Ile forgive your holy habit sir, but Ile hang you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: Wherefore this halter Captaine?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: For this traytor.
Go, put it on him, and then tie him up:
Do you want a Band sir? this is a course wearing,
Twill fit but scurvily upon this collar;
But patience is as good as a French Pickadell.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: What's his fault, Captaine?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Tis my will he perish,
And thats his fault.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: A Captaine of good government.
Come Souldiers, come, ye are roughly bred, and bloody,
Shew your obedience, and the joy ye take
In executing impious commands;
Ye have a Captaine seales your liberall pardons,
Be no more Christians, put religion by,
Twill make ye cowards: feele no tendernesse,
Nor let a thing call'd conscience trouble ye;
Alasse, twill breed delay. Beare no respect
To what I seem: were I a Saint indeed,
Why should that stagger ye? you know not holinesse:
To be excellent in evill, is your goodnesse;
And be so, twill become ye: have no hearts,
For feare you should repent: that will be dangerous:
For if there be a knocking there, a pricking,
And that pulse beate backe to your considerations,
How ye have laid a stiffe hand on Religion—

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Trusse him I say.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: And violated faith,

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: heare him not prate.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Why, what a thing will this be?
What strange confusion then will breed among ye?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Will none of ye obey?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: What devils vex ye?
The feares ye live in and the hourely dangers
Will be delights to these: those have their ends,
But these outlive all time, and all repentance:
And if it creep into your conscience once,
Be sure ye locke that close.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Why stand ye gazing?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Farewell sleep, peace, all that are humane comforts,
Better ye had been Trees, or Stones, and happier;
For those die here, and seeke no further being,
Nor hopes, nor punishments.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Rots take ye Rascals.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: What would you have us do?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Dispatch the prater.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: And have religious blood hang on our consciences?
We are bad enough already: sins enough
To make our graves even loath us.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: No man love me?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Although I be a thiefe, I am no hangman;
They are two mens trades, and let another execute.
Lay violent hands on holy things?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Base Cowards,
Put to your powers, ye Rascals, I command ye.
Holy, or unholy, if I say it,
Ile have it done.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: If I do't, let me starve for't.
Or I.
Or I: we will obey things handsome,
And bad enough, and over doe obedience:
But to be made such instruments of mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I have done as many villanies as another,
And with as little reluctation,
Let me come cleare of these, and wipe that score off.
Put me upon a felt and known perdition?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Have ye conspir'd, ye slaves?

speeches.speaker: Ped
verse: How vildly this showes,
In one that would command another temper,
And beare no bound in's own?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Am I thus jaded?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Is it my life thou long'st for Roderigo?
And can no sacrifice appease thy malice,
But my blood spilt? doe it thy selfe, dispatch it;
And as thou takst the whole revenge unto thee,
Take the whole sin upon thee; and be mighty,
Mighty in evill, as thou art in anger:
And let not these poore wretches houle for thy sake.
Those things that in thine owne glasse seeme most monstrous,
Wouldst thou abuse their weak sights with, for amiable?
Is it, thou thinkst to feare me with thy terrors,
And into weake condition draw my vertue?
If I were now to learn to die I would sue to thee:
Or did I feare death, then I would make thee glorious.
But knowing what, and how far I can suffer;
And all my whole life being but deaths preface,
My sleep but at next doore.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Are ye so valiant?
