Ile make ye feele: Ile make ye know, and feele too;
And Rascals, you shall tremble. Keepe him here,
And keep him safe too: if he scape your guards—

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Feare not, I will not.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: As I live, ye die for't;
I will not be thus baffled.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: What a divel have ye done, Pilgrim? or what mischief
Have you conspir'd, that he should rage and rave thus?
Have you kild his father, or his mother? or strangled any of his kindred?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Has he no sisters? have you not been bouncing
About their belly pieces?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Why should that be dangerous
Or any way deserve death? is it not naturall?
Bar us the Christian liberty of women,
And build us up with bricK, take away our free-stone.

speeches.speaker: 1 Outl.
verse: Because thou art holier then he, upon my conscience
He dos not envy thee: that's not his quarrell;
For, look you, that might be co~pounded without praiers.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Nor that thou seemst an honester man: for here
We have no trading with such Tinsell-stuffe;
To be an excellent thiefe, is all we aime at.
Wilt thou take a spit: and stride, and see if thou canst outrun us?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I scorn to shift his fury, keepe your obedience;
For though your government admit no president,
Keep your selves carefull in't.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Thou will be hang'd then.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I cannot die with fewer faults upon me.

speeches.speaker: 2 Out-l.
verse: Tis ten to one he wil shoot him: for the devil's in him
If he hang him himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He has too proud a nature:
He will compell some one.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I am confident.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And so are all I thinke.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Be not molested,
If I must die, let it not trouble you;
It stirs not me: It is the end I was born for.
Onely this honest office I desire ye,
(If there be curtesie in men of your breed)
To see me buried; not to let his fury
Expose my body to the open violence
Of beasts, and fowles: so far I urge humanity.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: He shall not deny us that: we'l see ye under ground
And give ye a volley of as good cups of Sacke,
For that's our Discipline.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He comes againe,
As high in rage as ever; the boy with him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: Will he compell the child?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He is bent to doe it,
And must have some body.

speeches.speaker: Red.
verse: If thou lov'st me doe it:
Love me, or love me not, I say thou shalt doe it:
Stare not, nor stagger, sirra; if ye deny me,
Doe you see this Rogue?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: What would ye have me doe sir?
Heavens goodnesse blesse me.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Doe? why hang a Rascall,
That would hang me.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I am a boy, and weake, sir.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Thou art strong enough to tie him to a Bough,
And turn him off: come, thou shalt be my Jewell,
And Ile allow thee horse, and all thy pleasures,
And twenty gallant things: Ile teach thee armes too;
Make thee mine heire.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Let me inherit death first.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Make me not angry, sirha.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Which is the man, sir?
Ile pluck up the best heart I can yet.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Feare not,
It is my will: That in the Pilgrimes coate there,
That devill in the Saints skin.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Guard me goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Dispatch him presently.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I wait your worst, sir.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: will the boy doe it? is the rogue so confident?
So young, so deep in blood?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He shakes, and trembles.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Dost thou seeke more coles still to sear thy conscience,
Worke sacred innocence, to be a devill?
Doe it thy selfe for shame, thou best becomst it.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Sirha, I scorn my finger should be filde with thee;
And yet Ile have it done: this child shall strangle thee,
A crying Girle, if she were here should master thee.

speeches.speaker: Ali.
verse: How should I save him? how my self from violence?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Leave your tongue-valour, & dispatch your hate, sir;
The patience of my death, shall more torment thee,
(Thou painted honour, thou base man made backward)
Then all my life has fear'd thee.

speeches.speaker: Rod
verse: Gag him, sirha.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: The Boy looks cheerfully now: sure he will do it.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: He will mall him else.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Are ye prepar'd to die, sir?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Yes boy, and ready; prethee to thy businesse.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Why are ye then so angry? so perplext, sir?
Patience wins Heaven, and not the heat of passion.
Why doe you rayle?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: The boy's a pretty Priest.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I thank ye gentle child, you teach me truely.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: You seem to feare too.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Thou seest more, then I feel, boy.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: You tremble sure.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: No sure boy, tis thy tendernesse:
Prethee make haste, and let that gulph be satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Are ye so willing to goe to it?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Most willing:
I would not borrow from his curtesie
One houre of life, to gaine an age of glory.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: And is your reckoning straight sir?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: As straight as truth, boy:
I cannot go more joyfully to a wedding.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Then to your prayers: Ile dispatch ye presently.
Now guid my tongue, thou blessednesse.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: A good boy.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: But harke ye sir, one word; and pray ye resolve me.
Let me speake privately.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: What wouldst thou have child?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Shall this man die?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Why dost thou make that question?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Pray ye be not angry: if he must, Ile doe it.
But must he now?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: What else? who dare reprieve him?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Pray ye thinke againe; and as your injuries
Are great, and full, you suffer from this fellow,
Doe not ye purpose so to suit your vengeance?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I doe, and must.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: You cannot if he die now.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Cannot?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: No, cannot: be not vext, you'l finde it.
I have considered, and I know it certaine,
Ye suffer below him: lose all your angers.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Why my best boy?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I love, and tender ye,
I would not tell ye else. Is that revenge,
To sleight your cause, and Saint your enemy,
Clap the Doves wings of downy peace unto him,
And let him soare to Heaven, whilst you are sighing?
Is this revenge?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I would have him die.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Prepar'd thus?
The blessing of a father never reach'd it:
His contemplation now scornes ye, contemnes ye,
And all the tortors ye can use. Let him die thus;
And these that know and love revenge will laugh at ye:
Here lies the honour of a wel-bred anger,
To make his enemy shake and tremble under him;
Doubt: nay, almost despaire, and then confound him.
This man ye rocke asleep, and all your rages
Are Requiems to his parting soule, meere Anthems.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Indeed he is strongly built.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: You cannot shake him;
And the more waight ye put on his foundation,
Now as he stands, ye fixe him still the stronger;
If ye love him, honour him, would heape upon him
Friendships and benefits beyond example,
Hope him a Star in Heaven, and there would stick him,
Now take his life.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I had rather take mine own, Boy.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Ile ease him presently.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Stay, be not hasty.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Blesse my tongue still.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: What has the boy done to him?
How dull, and still he lookes?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: You are a wise man.
And long have buckled with the worlds extremities,
A valiant man, and no doubt know both fortunes,
And would ye work your Master-peece thus madly,
Take the bare name of honour, that will pitty ye
When the world knows ye have prey'd on a poor Pilgrim?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: The Boy has staggard me: what would'st thou have me?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Have ye? do you not feel Sir? do's it not stir ye?
Doe you aske a child? I would have ye do most bravely,
Because I most affect ye: like your selfe Sir,
Scorn him, and let him goe; seem to contemne him,
And now ye have made him shake, seale him his pardon,
When he appears a subject fit for Anger,
And fit for you, his pious Armour off,
His hopes no higher then your sword may reach at
Then strike, and then ye know revenge; then take it.
I hope I have turn'd his mind.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Let the foole goe there,
I scorn to let loose so base an anger
May light on thee: See me no more, but quit me;
And when we meet again.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I'le thank ye Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Why this was like your selfe: but which way goes he?
Shall we ne're happy meet?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I am drowsie; Boy,
Goe with me, and discourse: I like thy company
O Child! I love thy Tongue.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I shall waite on ye.

speeches.speaker: Lo.
verse: The Boy has don't: a Plaguey witty Rascall.
And I shall love him terribly.

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: 'Twas he most certaine,
For if ye marke, how earnest he was with him,
And how he labour'd him.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A cutting villaine,
But a good Rogue; This Boy will make's all honest.

speeches.speaker: 1. Outl.
verse: I scarce beleeve that: but I like the Boy well
Come, let's to Supper; then upon our watches.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: This Pilgrim scap'd a joyfull one.

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: Let's Drink round,
To the Boyes health, and then about our businesse.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: None of you know her?

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: Alas Sir, we never saw her:
Nor ever heard of her, but from your report.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: No happy eye?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I doe not think 'tis she, Sir,
Me thinks a woman dares not.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Thou speak'st poorely,
What dares not woman, when she is provok'd?
Or what seemes dangerous to Love, or fury?
That it is she, this has confirm'd me certain,
These Jewels here, a part of which I sent her,
And though unwilling, yet her Father wrought her
To take, and weare.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A wench, and we not know it?
And among us? where were our understandings?
I could have ghess'd unhappily: have had some feeling
In such a matter: Here are as pretty fellowes,
At the discovery of such a Jigambob:
A handsome wench too? sure we have lost our faculties,
We have no motions: what should she doe here, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: That's it that troubles me: O that base Rascall!
There lies the misery: how cunningly she quit him,
And how she urg'd? had ye been constant to me,
I ne're had suffer'd this.

speeches.speaker: 1. Outl.
verse: Ye might have hang'd him:
And would he had been hang'd, that's all we care for't:
So our hands had not don't.

speeches.speaker: Rod
verse: She is gone again too,
And what care have ye for that? gone, and contemn'd me;
Master'd my will, and power, and now laughs at me.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: The devill that brought her hither, Sir I thinke
Has carryed her back again invisible,
For we ne're knew, nor heard of her departure.

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: No living thing came this night through our watches
She went with you:

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Was by me till I slept,
But when I wak'd, and call'd: O my dull pate here,
If I had open'd this when it was given me,
This Roguy Box.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: We could but give it ye.

speeches.speaker: Rod
verse: Pilgrime? a Pox O Pilgrimes there the game goes,
There's all my fortune fled; I know it, I feele it.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Bring me unto thy Captain: where's thy Captain?
I am founder'd, melted, some fairy thing or other
Has led me dauncing; the devill has haunted me
Ith' likenesse of a voyce: give me thy Captaine.

speeches.speaker: 2. Outl.
verse: He's here Sir, there he stands.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: How do'st thou Captain?
I have been fool'd and jaded, made a dogge bolt.
My daughters runne away: I have been haunted too,
I have lost my horse; I am hungry, & out of my wits also.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Come in; I'le tell you what I know: strange things
And take your ease; I'le follow her recovery,
These shall be yours the whil'st, and do ye service.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Let me have drinke enough: I am almost choak'd too.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You shall have any thing; what think you now, Souldiers?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I think a woman, is a woman that's any thing.
The next we take, we'l search a little neerer,
We'l not be boyed again with a paire of breeches.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: He's gone in here: This is Roderigo's quarter,
And i'le be with him soone: I'le startle him,
A little better then I have done: All this long night againe,
I have led him out o'th way, to try his patience,
And made him sweare, and curse; and pray, and sweare
And cry for anger; I made him leave his horse too,
Where he can never find him more; whistled to him,
And then he would run through thick & thin, to reach me,
And down in this ditch; up again, and shake him,
And swear some certaine blessings; then into that bush
Pop goes his pate, and all his face is comb'd over,
And I sit laughing: a hundred tricks, I have serv'd him:
And I will double em, before I leave him;
I'le teach his anger to dispute with women,
But all this time, I cannot meet my Mistresse,
I cannot come to comfort her; that grieves me,
For sure she is much afflicted: till I doe,
I'le haunt thy Ghost Alphonso; I'le keep thee waking,
Yes, I must get a Drum: I am villanous weary,
And yet i'le trot about these villages
Till I have got my will, and then have at ye.
I'le make your anger drop out at your elbowes ere I leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: 'Tis strange, in all the circuit we have ridden,
We cannot crosse her: no way light upon her:

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: I doe not think she is gone thus far, or this way,
For certain if she had, we should have reach'd her
Made some discovery: heard some news; we have seen, nothing.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Nor passe by any body that could promise any thing.
She is certainly disguis'd, her modesty
Durst never venture else.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Let her take any shape,
And let me see it once, I can distinguish it.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: So should I think too: has not her father found her?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: No, i'le be hang'd then; he has no patience
Unlesse she light in's teeth, to looke about him.
He guesses now, and chafes and frets like Tinsell.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Let him goe on, he cannot live without it.
But keep her from him, heaven: where are we Curi?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: In a wood I think, hang me if I know else.
And yet I have ridden all these Coasts, at all houres,
And had and aime.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: I would we had a guid,

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: And if I be not much awry Seberto,
Not far off should be Rodorigo's quarter,
For in this Fastwes if I be not cozen'd,
He and his Out-laws live.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: This is the place then
We appointed him to meet in.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Yes, I thinke so:

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Would we could meet some living thing: what's that there?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: A Boy, I think, stay; why may not he direct us.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I am hungry, and I am weary, and I cannot find him.
Keep my wits heaven, I feele 'em wavering,
O God my head.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Boy, dost thou heare, thou stripling?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Now they will teare me, torture me, now Roderigo
Will hang him without mercy; ha:

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Come hither.
A very pretty Boy: what place is this, child?
And whether dost thou travell? how he stares!
Some stubborn Master has abu'd the Boy,
And beaten him: how he complaines! whether goest thou?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I goe to Segonia Sir, to my sick Mother,
I have been taken here by drunken theeves,
And (O my bones;) I have been beaten Sir.
Mis-us'd, & rob'd: extreamly beaten Gentlemen,
O God, my side!

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: What beasts would use a Boy thus?
Look up, and be of good cheer:

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: O, I cannot.
My back, my back, my back.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: What theeves?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I know not.
But they call the Captaine Roderigo.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Look ye,
I know we were there abouts;

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Do'st thou want any thing?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Nothing but ease, but ease, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: There's some mony,
And get thee to thy Mother.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I thank ye Gentlemen:

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: This was extreamely foule, to vex a Child thus.
Come, let's along, we cannot loose our way now.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Though ye are honest men, I feare your fingers,
And glad I am got off; O how I tremble!
Send me but once within his armes dear Fortune,
And then come all the world: what shall I do now?
'Tis almost night again, and where to lodge me,
Or get me meat, or any thing, I know not.
These wild woods, and the fancies I have in me,
Will run me mad.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Boy, Boy:

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: More set to take me?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Do'st thou heare Boy; thou pointer.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: 'Tis a Boy too,
A Lacky Boy: I need not feare his feircenesse.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Canst thou beat a Drum?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: A Drum?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: This thing, a drum here.
Didst thou never see a Drum: Canst thou make this grumble?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Iulettas face, and tongue; Is she run mad too?
Here may be double craft: I have no skill in't.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I'le give thee a Royall but to goe along with me.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I care not for thy Royall, I have other businesse,
Drum to thy selfe, and daunce to it.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Sirha, Sirha.
Thou scurvy Sitha; thou snotty-nos'd scab, do'st thou heare me?
If I lay downe my Drum.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Here comes more Company,
I feare a plot, heaven send me fairely from it.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Basto; who's here?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Captain, do you need me Father?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: No not a foot: give me the gowne: the sword now.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: This is the devill theef, and if he take me,
Woe be to my Gally-gaskins.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Certaine Sir,
She will take her patches of, and change her habit.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Let her do what she please: No, no Alinda
You cannot cozen me againe in a Boyes figure,
Nor hide the beauty of that face in patches,
But I shall know it.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: A Boy his face in patches?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Nor shall your tongue againe bewitch mine Anger,
If she be found ith' woods, send me word presently,
And i'le returne; she cannot be farre gone yet,
If she be not, expect me, when ye see me,
Use all your service to my friend Alphonso,
And have a care to your businesse: farewell,
No more, farewell. Exeunt.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I am heartily glad thou art gone yet.
This Boy in patches, was the Boy came by me,
The very same, how hastily it shifted?
What a mopp'-eyed asse was I, I could not know her,
This must be she, this is she, now I remember her,
How loth she was to talk too, how she fear'd me?
I could now pisse mine eyes out for meer anger:
I'le follow her, but who shall vex her father then?
One flurt at him, and then I am for the voyage,
If I can crosse the Captain too: Come Tabor. Exit.

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: Are they all set?

speeches.speaker: 1 Outl.
verse: All, and each quarter quiet.

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: Is the old man asleep?

speeches.speaker: 1 Outl.
verse: An houre agoe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: We must be very carefull in his absence,
And very watchfull.

speeches.speaker: 1 Outl.
verse: It concerns us neerely,
He will not be long from us.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: No, he cannot,

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: A little heate of love, which he must wander out.
And then again: harke.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: What?

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: Tis not the wind sure:
That's still and calme. no noyse, nor flux of waters.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I heare a Drum, I thinke.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: That that;
It beats againe now.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Now it comes neerer: sure we are surprized, sir;
Some from the Kings command: we are lost, we are
dead all.

speeches.speaker: 1 Out-l.
verse: Hark, hark, a charge now: my Captaine has betray'd us.
And left us to this ruine, run away from us.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Another beates o'that side.

speeches.speaker: 2 Out-l.
verse: Fly, flie, Jaques,
We are taken in a toyle: snapt in a pitfall;
Methinks I feele a Sword already shave me.

speeches.speaker: 3 Out-l
verse: A thousand horse and foot, a thousand pioners,
If we get underground, to fetch us out againe;
And every one an Axe to cut the woods downe.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: This is the dismalst night—

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Where's my nag now?
And what make I here to be hang'd? What devill
brought me into this danger? Is there nere a hole?
That I may creep in deep enough, and the quickly?
Nere an old ditch to choke in? I shall be taken
For their Commander now, their Generall,
And have a commanding Gallows set up for me
As high as a May-pole; and nasty Songs made on me,
Be printed with a Pint-pot and a dagger.
They are all kill'd by this time: Can I pray?
Let me see that first: I have too much feare to be faithfull.
Where's all my State now? I must go hunt for daughters;
Daughters, and damsels of the Lake, damned daughters.
A hundred Crownes for a good tod of Hay,
Or a fine hollow Tree, that would containe me;
I heare 'em comming: I feele the nooze about me.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Why do you fear, and fly? here are no Souldiers;
None from the King to vex ye.

speeches.speaker: 1 Outl.
verse: The Drum, the Drum, sir.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: I never saw such Pigeon-hearted people:
What Drum? what danger? who's that that shakes behind there:
Mercy upon me sir, why are ye fear'd thus?

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Are we all kill'd, no mercy to be hoped for?
Am I not shot do you think?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: You are strangely frighted,
Shot with a fiddle stick: who's here to shoot ye?
A Drum we saw indeed, a boy was beating it,
And hunting Squirrels by Moon-light.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Nothing else, sir?

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Not any thing: no other person stirring.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: O that I had that boy: this is that Devill,
That fairy rogue, that haunted me last night;
H'as sleeves like Dragons wings.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: A little Foot-boy.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Come, let's go in, and let me get my clothes on;
If ere I stay here more to be thus martyr'd -
Did ye not meet the wench?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: No sure, we met her not.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: She has been here in boyes apparrell, Gentlemen,
A gallant thing, and famous for a Gentlewoman,
And all her face patcht over for discovery:
A pilgrime too, and thereby hangs a circumstance,
Tha she hath playd her master-prize, a rare one.
I came too short.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Such a young boy we met sir.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: In a gray hat.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: The same: his face all patcht too.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Twas she, a rot run with her; she: that ranck she;
Walk in, Ile tell ye all: and then we'l part again,
But get some store of Wine: this fright sits here yet.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: What a fright I have put 'em in; what a brave hurry.
If this doe bolt him, Ile be with him againe
With a new part, was never play'd; Ile ferk him.
As he hunts her, so ile hunt him: Ile claw him.
Now will I see if I can crosse her footing:
Yet still ile watch his water, he shall pay for't;
And when he thinks most malice, and meanes worse,
Ile make him know the Mare's the better Horse.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Ye are a stranger sir, and for humanity,
Being come within our walls, I would shew you something.
Ye have seen the Castle?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Yes sir, tis astrong one,
And well maintain'd.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Why are you still thus sad, sir?
How doe ye like the walkes?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: They are very pleasant;
Your Town stands coole and sweet.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: But that I would not
Affect you with more sadnesse, I could shew ye
A place worth view.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Showes seldome alter me sir;
Pray ye speake it, and then shew it.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Tis a house here
Where people of all sorts, that have been visited
With lunacies and follies waite their cures,
Their's fancies of a thousand stamps and fashions,
Like flies in severall shapes buze round about ye,
And twice as many gestures; some of pitty,
That it would make ye melt to see their passions:
And some as light againe, that would content ye.
But I see sir, your temper is too modest,
Too much inclin'd to contemplation,
To meet with these?

speeches.speaker: Ped
verse: You could not please me better;
And I beseech you sir, doe me the honour
To let me waite upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Since ye are willing,
To me it shall be a pleasure to conduct ye.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: I never had such a mind yet to see misery.

speeches.speaker: 1 Keep.
verse: Carry mad Besse some meat, she rores like Thunder;
And tie the Parson short, the Moone's ith full,
H'as a thousand Pigs in's braines: Who lookes to the Prentize?
Keep him from women, he thinks h'as lost his Mistris,
And talke of no silke stuffes, 'twill runne him horn mad.

speeches.speaker: 2 Keep.
verse: The Justice keeps such a stirre yonder with his Charges,
And such a coyle with warrants,

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: Take away his Statutes;
The divell has possest him in the likenesse
Of penall Lawes: keep him from Aquavite,
For if that spirit creep into his corum,
He will commit us all: how is it with the Scholler?

speeches.speaker: 2 K.
verse: For any thing I see, he's in his right wits.

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: Thou art an asse; in's right wits, goodman coxcomb?
As though any man durst be in's right wits, and be here.
It is as much as we dare be that keep 'em.

speeches.speaker: Engl.
verse: Give me some drink.

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: O, there's the English man.

speeches.speaker: Engl.
verse: Fill me a thousand pots, and froth 'em, froth 'em.
Down o' your knees, ye rogues, and pledge me roundly;
One, two, three, and foure; we shall be an merry within this houre.
To the great Turke.

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: Peace, peace, thou Heathen drunkard;
These English are so Malt-mad, there's no medling with 'em;
When they have a fruitfull yeere of Barly there,
All the whole Island's thus.

speeches.speaker: Engl.
verse: A Snuff, a snuff, a snuff.
A lewd notorious snuff: giv't him againe, boy.

speeches.speaker: Fool.
verse: God-ye-good even, Goffer.

speeches.speaker: 2 K.
verse: Who let the Foole loose?

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: If any of the mad-men take her, she is pepper'd,
They'l bounce her loynes.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Will ye walke into the cole house?

speeches.speaker:
1
^p.
verse: She is as leacherous too as a she-ferret.

speeches.speaker: 2 K.
verse: Who a vengeance looks to her? go in Kate,
Ile give thee a fine Apple.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Will ye busse me?
And tickle me, and make me laugh?

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: Ile whip ye.

speeches.speaker: Engl.
verse: Foole, foole, come up to me foole.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Are ye peeping?

speeches.speaker: Engl.
verse: Ile get thee with five fooles.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: O fine, O dainty.

speeches.speaker: Eng.
verse: And thou shalt lie in in a horse-cloth, like a Lady

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: And shall I have a Coach?

speeches.speaker: Engl.
verse: Drawn with foure Turkeys,
And they shall tread thee too.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: We shall have egges then;
And shall I sit upon 'em?

speeches.speaker: Engl.
verse: I, I, and they shall be all addle,
And make an admirable Tanzey for the divell.
Come come away, I am taken with thy love foole,
And will mightily belabour thee.

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: How the foole bridles? how she twitters at him?
These Englishmen would stagger a wise-woman.
If we should suffer her to have her will now,
We should have all the women in Spaine at mad as she here,

speeches.speaker: 2 K.
prose: They would strive who should be most fool: away with her.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
prose: Pray ye stay a little: lets heare him sing, h'as a fine breast.

speeches.speaker: 1 K.
verse: Here comes my Master, to the spit ye whore,
And stir no more abroad, but tend your businesse;
Your shall have no more sops ith' pan else, nor no porrige:
Besides, Ile whip your breech.

speeches.speaker: Foole.
verse: Ile goe in presently.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Ile assure ye sir, the Cardinal's angry with ye
For keeping this young man.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I am heartily sorry.
If ye allow him sound, pray ye take him with ye.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: This is the place, and now observe their humors:

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: We can find nothing in him light, nor tainted;
No startings, nor no rubs, in all his answers,
In all his Letters nothing but discretion,
Learning, and handsome stile.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Be not deceived sir,
Marke but his looke.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: His griefe, and his imprisonment
May stamp that there.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Pray talke with him again then.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: That will be needlesse, we have tride him long enough,
And if he had a taint we should have met with't.
Yet to discharge your care —

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: A sober youth:
Pity so heavy a crosse should light upon him.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: You finde no sicknesse?

speeches.speaker: Schol.
verse: None sir, I thank Heaven,
Nor nothing that diverts my understanding.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Doe you sleep a nights?

speeches.speaker: Schol.
verse: As sound, and sweet, as any man:

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Have ye no fearfull dreams?

speeches.speaker: Schol.
verse: Sometimes, as all have
That go to bed with raw and windy stomacks;
Else, I am all one piece.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Is there no unkindnesse
You have conceiv'd from any friend or parent?
Or scorne from what ye lov'd?

speeches.speaker: Schol.
verse: No, truely sir:
I never yet was master of a faith
So poore, and weake, to doubt my friend or kindred,
And what love is, unlesse it lie in learning
I thinke I am ignorant.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: This man is perfect,
A civiller discourser I nere talk'd with.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: You'l finde it otherwise.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I must tell ye true sir,
I thinke ye keep him here to teach him madnesse.
Here's his discharge from my Lord Cardinall;
And come sir, goe with us.

speeches.speaker: Schol.
verse: I am bound unto ye,
And farewell Master.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Farewell Stephano,
Alas poore man.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: What flaws, and whirles of weather,
Or rather storms have been aloft these three daies;
How darke, and hot, and full of mutiny!
And still grows lowder.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: It has been stubborn weather.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Strange work at Sea, I fear me there's old tumbling.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Blesse my old unkles Barke, I have a venture.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: And I more then I would wish to lose.

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: Doe you feare?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Ha! how he lookes?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Nay, marke him better Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Mercy upon me: how his eyes are altered?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Now tell me how ye like him: whether now
He be that perfect man ye credited?

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: Doe's the Sea staggger ye?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Now ye have hit the nick.

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: Doe ye feare the billowes?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: What ailes him? who has stir'd him?

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: Be not shaken,
Nor let the singing of the storm shoot through ye,
Let it blow on, blow on: let the clouds wrastle,
And let the vapours of the earth turn mutinous,
The Sea in hideous niountaines rise and tumble
Upon a Dolphins back, Ile make all tremble,
For I am Neptune.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Now what think ye of him?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: A las poore man.

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: Your Barke shall plough through all,
And not a Surge so saucy to disturbe her.
Ile see her safe, my power shall saile before her.
prose:
Down ye angry waters all,
Ye loud whistling whirlwinds fall;
Down ye proud Waves, ye stormes cease;
I command ye, be at peace.
Fright not with your churlish Notes,
Nor bruise the Keele of Bark that flotes:
No devouring Fish come nigh,
Nor Monster in my Empery,
Once shew his head, or terror bring;
But let the weary Saylor sing:
Amphitrite with white armes
Srike my Lute, Ile sing Charmes.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: He must have Musicke now: I must observe him.
His fit will grow to full else.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: I must pitty him.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Now he will in himselfe most quietly,
And clean forget all, as he had done nothing.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: We are sorry, sir: and we have seen a wonder;
From this houre we'l believe, and so we'l leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: This was a strange fit.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Did ye marke him sir?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: He might have cozen'd me with his behaviour.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Many have sworn him right, and I have thought so:
Yet on a sudden, from some word, or other,
When no man could expect a sit, he has flown out:
I dare not give him will.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Pray Heaven recover him.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Must I come in too?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: No, my pretty Lad;
Keep in thy chamber Boy: 'shalt have thy supper.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I pray ye what is he sir?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: A strange boy, that last night
Was found i'th' Town, a little craz'd, distracted,
And so sent hither.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: How the pretty knave looks,
And playes, and peepes upon me! sure such eyes
I have seen, and lov'd: what fair hands? certainly—

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Good sir, you'l make him worse.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I pray believe not.
Alas, why should I hurt him? how he smiles?
The very shape, and sweetnesse of Alinda:
Let me look once againe: were it in such clothes
As when I saw her last; this must be she.
How tenderly it stroakes me?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Pray ye be mild sir;
I must attend elsewhere.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Pray ye be secure sir,
What would ye say? how my heart beates and trembles?
He holds me hard by th' hand; O my life, her flesh too!
I know not what to think: her teares, her true ones;
Pure orient teares: Hark, doe you know me little one?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: O Pedro Pedro!

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: O my soule!

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: What fit's this?
The Pilgrimes off the hooks too.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Let me hold thee,
And now come all the world, and all that hate me.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Be wise, and not discovered: O how I love ye!
How doe ye now?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I have been miserable;
But your most vertuous eyes have cur'd me, Pedro:
Pray ye thinke it no immodesty, I kisse ye,
My head's wild still.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Be not so full of passion,
Nor do not hang so greedily upon me;
Twill be ill taken.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Are ye weary of me?
I will hang here eternally, kisse ever,
And weep away for joy.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I told ye sir,
What ye would doe: for shame doe not afflict him;
You have drawn his fit upon him fearfully:
Either depart, and presently; Ile force ye else.
Who waits within?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Alas good sir.
This is the way never to hope recovery.
Stay but one minute more, Ile complaine to the Governour.
Bring in the boy: doe you see how he swels, and teares himselfe?
Is this your cure? Be gon; if the boy miscarry
Let me nere find you more, for ile so hamper ye —

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: You were too blame: too rash.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Farewell for ever.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: You are now within a mile oth' Towne sir: if my businesse
Would give me leave, I would turne and waite upon ye;
But for such Gentlemen as you enquire of,
Certaine, I saw none such: But for the boy ye spoke of,
I will not say tis he, but such a one;
Just of that height.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: In such clothes?

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: I much mistake else,
Was sent in th'other night, a little maddish,
And where such people waite their cures.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I understand ye.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: There you may quickly know.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I thanke ye sir.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: So doe I to: and if there be such a place,
I aske no more; but you shall heare more of me.
She may be there, and you may play the tyrant;
Ile see what I can doe: I am almost foundred
In following him; and yet Ile never leave him,
Ile crawle of all foure first; my cause is meritorious,
And come what can come.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: All you have told me is certaine;
Complexion, and all else.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: It may be she then;
And ile so fumble her: Is she growne mad now?
Is her blood set so high? ile have her madded,
Ile have her worm'd.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Marke but the end, old Master,
If thou beest not sicke oth' Bots within these five hours,
And kickst and roar'st; Ile make ye fart fire, Signior,

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Here's one oth' house, a foole, an idiot sir;
May be she is going home; she'l be a guide to ye;
And so I kisse your hand.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: I am your servant.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: O now I am lost, lost, lost, Lord, how I tremble!
My father, arm'd in all his hates and angers;
This is more misery then I have scap'd yet.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Foole, foole.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: He knows me not; will ye give me two-pence?
And gaffer, here's a Crow-flower, and a Dazie;
I have some pie in my pocket too.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: This is an arrant foole,
An ignorant thing.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Believe so, and I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Dost thou dwell in Sigonia, foole?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: No no, I dwell in Heaven.
And I have a fine little house, made of Marmalad.
And I am a lone woman, and I spin for Saint Peter;
I have a hundred little children, and they sing Psalmes with me.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Tis pity this pretty thing should want understanding.
But why doe I stand talking with a coxcombe?
If I doe finde her, if I light upon her,
Ile say no more. Is this the way to th' Town, foole?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: You must goe over the top of that high steeple, Gaffer.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: A plague o' your fooles face.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: No, take her counsell.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: And then you shall come to a River twenty mile over,
And twenty mile & ten: and then you must pray, Gaffer;
And still you must pray, and pray.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Pray Heaven deliver me
From such an asse, as thou art.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Amen, sweet Gaffer.
And fling a sop of Suger-cake into it;
And then you must leap in naked.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Would he would believe her.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: And sink seven daies together; can ye sinck gaffer?

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Yes coxcombe, yes; prethee farewell: a pox on thee.
A plague o' that foole too, that set me upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: And then Ile bring you a sup of Milke shal sarve ye:
I am going to get Apples.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Go to th' devill:
Was ever man tormented with a puppy thus?
Thou tell me news? thou be a guide?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: And then Nunkle —

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Prethee keepe on thy way (good Naunt) I could rayle now
These ten houres at mine owne improvidence:
Get Apples, and he choak'd: farewell.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Farewell Nuncle.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I rejoyce in any thing that vexes him;
And I shall love this foole extreamly for't:
Could I but see my Mistris now, to tell her
How I have truely, honestly wrought for her,
How I have worne my selfe away, to serve her.
Foole, there's a Royall for the sport thou mad'st me,
In crossing that old foole, that parted from thee.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Thou art honest sure; but yet thou must not see me:
I thanke ye little Gentleman: Heaven blesse ye
And ile pray for ye too: pray ye keep this Nutmeg,
Twas sent me from the Lady of the Mountaine.
A golden Lady.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: How prettily it prattles.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Tis very good to rub your understanding:
And so good night: the Moone's up.

speeches.speaker: Jul
verse: Pretty innocent.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Now fortune, if thou dar'st do good, protect me.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ile follow him to yond Towne: he shall not scape me:
Stay, I must counterfeit a Letter by the way first,
And one that must carry some credit with it: I am wide else,
And all this to no purpose that I ayme at.
A Letter must be had, and neatly handled:
And then if Goodwife fortune doe not faile me,
Have at his skirts: I shall worse anger him
Then ever I have done, and worse torment him.
It do's me good to thinke how I shall conjure him.
And crucifie his crabbednesse: he's my Master,
But that's all one: Ile lay that on the left hand.
He would now persecute my harmlesse Mistris,
A fault without forgivenesse, as I take it;
And under that bold banner flies my vengeance,
A meritorious war, and so Ile make it.
I'th' name of Innocence, what's this the foole gave me?
She said twas good to rub my understanding.
What strange concealment? Bread or Cheese, or a Chesnut?
Ha! tis a Ring: a pretty Ring, a right one:
A ring I know too! the very same Ring:
O admirable Blockhead! O base eyes!
A Ring my Mistris tooke from me, and wore it;
I know it by the Posie: Prick me, and heale me.
None could deliver this, but she her selfe too:
Am I twice sand-blind? twice so neer the blessing
I would arive at? and block-like never know it?
I am veng'ance angry, but that shal light on thee,
And heavily, and quickly, I pronounce it:
There are so many crosse waies, there's no following her:
And yet I must not now: I hope she is right still,
For all her outward shew, for sure she knew me;
And in that hope, some few houres Ile forget her.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: She is not to be recovered, which I vex at;
And he beyond my veng'ance, which torments me:
O! I am fool'd and sleighted, made a Rascall;
My hopes are flatterd, as my present fortunes:
Why should I wander thus and play the coxcomes?
Tire out my peace and pleasure for a Girle?
A Girle that scorns me too? a thing that hates me?
And considered at the best, is but a short breakfast
For a hot appetite: why should I walke, and walke thus,
And fret my selfe, and travell like a Carrier,
And peep, and watch? want Meat, and Wine, to cherish me,
When thousand women may be had, ten thousand,
And thank me too, and I sit still: well, trim Beauty
And Chastity, and all that seem to ruin me,
Let me not take ye; let me not come neer ye,
For Ile so trim ye: Ile so bussell with ye;
Tis not the name of Virgin shall redeem ye,
Ile change that property: nor teares, nor angers:
I beare a hate about me scorns those follies.
To finde this villaine too, for there's my main prize;
And if he snap me then.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Is not that Pedro?
Tis he, tis he: O!

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: What art thou?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Ha? now, now, now,
O now most miserable.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: What a' devill art thou?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: No end of my mis-fortunes, Heaven?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: What Anticke?
Speake Puppet, speake.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: That habit to betray me?
Ye holy Saints, can ye see this?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: It danceth:
The devill in a fooles Coat, is he turn'd Innocent?
What mops, and mowes it makes: heigh, how it frisketh,
Is't it not a Faiery? or some small hobgoblin?
It has a mortall face, and I have a great mind to it,
But if it should prove the devill then.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Come hither.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I think 't will ravish me,
It is a handsome thing, but horribly Sun-burnt,
What's that it points at?

speeches.speaker: Alin,
verse: Do'st thou see that Starre there,
That, just above the Sunne;
Prethe goe thither, and light me this Tobacco,
And stop it with the hornes o'th' Moone.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: The thing's mad,
Abhominably mad, her braines are butter'd,
Goe sleep, foole, sleep.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Thou canst not sleep so sweetly:
For so I can say my Prayers, and then slumber.
prose:
I am not proud, nor full of wine,
This little Flowre will make me fine:
Cruell in heart, for I shall crie,
If I see a Sparrow dye:
I am not watchfull to due ill,
Nor glorious to pursue it still:
Nor pittilesse to those that weepe;
Such as are, bid them goe sleep.

Doe, doe, do, and see if they can.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: It said true,
I feele it sinke into me forcibly.
Sure 'tis a kind of Sibill, some mad Prophet.
I feel my wildnesse bound, and fetter'd in me.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Give me your hand, and i'le tell you what's your fortune.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Here: prethee speake.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Fie, fie, fie, fie, fie.
Wash your hands, and pare your Nailes, and look finely
You shall never kisse the Kings daughter else.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I wash 'em daily.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: But still you fowle 'em faster.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: This goes neerer.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: You'll have two wives.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Two wives?

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I two fine gentle-women.
M^ke much of 'em: for they'l stick close to you Sir.
And these two, in two dayes.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: That's a fine Riddle.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: To day you shall wed sorrow,
And repentance will come to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Sure she's inspired.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I'le sing ye a fine Song Sir.
He called down his merry men all
By one, by two, by three,
William would faine have been the first,
But now the last is he.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: This the meer Chronicle of my mis-hap.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I'le bid you good ev'n: for my Boat staies for me yonder,
And I must Sup with the Moone to night in the Mediterraneum.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: When fools, and mad-folks shall be tutors to me,
And feele my sores, yet I unsensible;
Sure it was set by Providence upon me
To steer my heart right: I am wondrous weary.
My thoughts too, which adde more burthen to me:
I have been ill, and (which is worse) pursu'd it,
And still runne on: I must thinke better, nobler,
And be another thing, or not at all.
Still I grow heavier, heavier heaven defend me:
I'le lye down, and take rest: and goodnes guard me.

speeches.speaker: Pes. 1
verse: We have scap'd to day well: certain, if the Out-laws
Had known we had been stirring, we had paid for't,
Plague on 'em, they have rob'd me thrice,
And me five times:
Beside they made my daughter one of us too
An arrant Drum: O, they are the lewdest Rascals,
The Captaine such a damn'd peece of iniquitie:
But we are farre enough of on 'em, that's the best on't,
They cannot heare.
They'le come to me familiarly
And eat up all I have: drinke up my wine too,
And if there be a Servant that content 'em,
Let her keele hold, they'll give her Stowage enough:
We have no Children now, but Theeves, and Outlawes.
The very Brats in their Mothers bellies have their qualities.
They'll steale into the world.
Would we had some of 'em here,
I, O' that condition we could Master 'em,
They are sturdy knaves.
A devill take their sturdinesse,
We can neither keep our wives from 'em, nor our States,
We pay the Rent, and they possesse the benefit.
What's this lies here? is it drunk, or sober?
It sleeps, and soundly too.
'Tis an old woman
That keepes sheepe hereabouts: it turns, and stretches.
Do's she keep sheep with a sword?
It has a Beard too.
Peace, peace: It is the devill Roderigo,
Peace of all hands, and looke.
'Tis he
Speake softly,
Now we may fit him.
Stay, stay: let's be provident.
Kill him, and wake him then.
Let me come to him,
Ev'n one blow at his pate, if ere he wake more.
So, so, so, lay that by.
I must needs kill him.
It stands with my reputation
Stand off, I say:
And let us some way make him sure; then torture him.
To kill him presently, has no pleasure in't.
Has been tormented of us, at least this twelve moneth.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Oh me!

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: He comes: he comes.
Has he no Guns about him?
Softly again: no, no: take that hand easily,
And tye it fast there: that to th' other bough there.
Fast, fast, and easie least he wake.
Have we got ye?
This was a benefit we never aym'd at.
Out with your knives, and let's carve this Cock-theefe,
Daintily carve him.
I would he had been used thus
Ten year agoe; we might have thought we had children.
O, that Sir Nicholas now our Priest were here.
What a sweet Homily would he say over him,
For ringing all in with his wife in the Bell-frey?
He would stand up stiffe girt: Now pounce him lightly,
And as he rores, and rages, let's goe deeper:
Come neere: you are dym ey'd: on with your spectacles.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: O, what torments me thus? what slaves, what villaines?
O spare me, doe not murther me.
We'll but tickle ye,
You have tickled us at all points.
Where are his Emblemes?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: As ye are men, and Christians
Yes we hear ye,
And you shall here of us too.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Oh no mercy.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: What noyse is this? what rore? I cannot find her,
She is got free again: but where, or which way?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: O' villains, beasts.

speeches.speaker: Pedro.
verse: Murdring a man, ye rascals?
Ye inhumane slaves, off, off, and leave this cruelty,
Or as I am a Gentleman: do ye brave me?
Then have among ye all, ye slaves, ye cowards,
Take up that sword, and stand: stay ye base rascals,
Ye cut-throate rogues.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Ye dog-whelps:

speeches.speaker: Rod
verse: O' I am how more wretched far, then ever.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: A violence to that habit? ha? Roderigo,
What makes he here, thus lad? is it repentance,
Or only a fair shew to guid his mischiefes?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: This benefit has made me shame to see him,
To know him, blush?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: You are not much hurt?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: No Sir;
All I can call a hurt, sticks in my conscience,
That pricks, and tortuers me.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Have ye considerd
The nature of these men, and how they us'd ye?
Was it fair play? did it appear to you handsom?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I dare not speak: or if I do, tis nothing
Can bring me off, or justifie me.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Was it noble
To be o're-layd with odds, and violence?
Manly, or brave in these thus to oppresse ye?
Do you blush at this, in such as are meer rudenes,
That have stopt soules, that never knew things gentle?
And dare you glorifie worse in your self sir?
Ye us'd me with much honour, and I thank ye,
In this I have requited some: ye know me:
Come turne not back, ye must, and ye shall know me;
Had I bin over seasond with base anger,
And suited all occasions to my mischiefes,
Bore no respect to Honesty, Religion,
No faith, no common tie of man, humanity,
Had I had in me, but given reines, and licence
To a tempestuous will, as wild as winter,
This day, know Roderigo, I had set
As small a price upon thy life, and fortunes,
As thou didst lately on mine innocence;
But I reserve thee to a nobler service.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I thank ye, and i'le studdy more to honour ye:
You have the nobler soule, I must confesse it,
And are the greater master of your goodnes.
Though it be impossible I should now recover,
And my rude will grow handsome in an instant,
Yet touching but the purenes of your mettle,
Something shall shew like gold, at least shall glister,
That men may hope, although the mine be rugged,
Stony, and hard to work: yet time, and honour
Shall find and bring forth that, that's rich and worthy.

speeches.speaker: Ped
verse: I'le trie that: and to 'th purpose: ye told me sir
In noble emulation, so I take it;
I'le put your hatred far off, and forget it,
You had a faire desire to try my valour:
You seemd to court me to it; you have found a time,
A weapon in your hand, an equall enemy,
That, as he puts this off, puts of all injuries,
And only now for honors sake defies ye:
Now, as you are a man, I know you are valiant,
As you are gentle bred, a souldier fashioned.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: His vertue startles me. I dare fight Pedro.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: And as you have a Mistris that you honor,
Mark me, a Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: A handsome Mistris,
As you dare hold your self deserving of her.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Deserving? what a word was that to fire me?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I could compell ye now without this circumstance,
But i'le deale free, and fairely, like a Gentleman:
As ye are worthy of the name ye carry,
A daring man.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: O that I durst not suffer:
For all I dare do now, implies but pennance.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Now do me noble right.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I'le satisfy ye:
But not by th'word: pray ye hear me, and allow me;
I have bin rude: but shall I be a monster,
And teach my sword to hurt that that preserved me?
Though I be rough by nature, shall my name
Inherit that eternall staine of barbarous?
Give me an enemy, a thing that hates ye,
That never heard of yet, nor felt your goodnes,
That is one main antipathy to sweetnes;
And set me on, you cannot hold me coward:
If I have ever err'd, 'th as in hazard:
The temper of my sword starts at your vertue,
And will flie off, nay it will weep to light ye;
Things excellently mingled, and of pure nature,
Hold sacred love, and peace with one another.
See how it turnes.

speeches.speaker: Ped
verse: This is a strange conversion:
And can ye faile your Mistris? can ye grow cold
In such a case?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Those heats that they adde to us,
(O noble Pedro) let us feele 'em rightly,
And rightly but consider how they move us.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Is not their honour ours?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: If they be vertuous;
And then the sword ads nothing to their lustre,
But rather cals in question what's not doubted:
If they be not: the best swords, and best valours
Can never fight 'em up to fame again:
No, not a Christian war, and that's held pious.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: How bravely now he is tempered? I must fight,
And rather make it honorable, then angry,
I would not taske those sins to me committed.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You cannot sir: you have cast those by; decarded 'em,
And in a noble mind, so low and loosely
To look back, and collect such lumps, and lick 'em
Into new horrid formes agen.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Still braver.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: To fight, because I dare, were worse, and weaker
Then if I had a woman in my cause, sir,
And more proclaim'd me foole; yet I must confesse
I have bin covetous of all occasions,
And this I have taken upon trust, for noble,
The more shame mine; devise a way to fight thus,
That like the wounded aire no blood may issue,
Nor where this sword shall enter, no lost spirit,
And set me on: I would not scar that body,
That vertuous, valiant body, nor deface it
To make the Kingdom mine: if one must bleed,
Let me be both the sacrifice, and altar,
And you the Priest: I have deserv'd to suffer.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: The noble Roderigo, now I call ye,
And thus my love shall ever count, and hold ye,
I am your servant sir: and now this habit,
Devotion, not distrust shall put upon me,
I'le wait upon your fortunes, that's my way now,
And where your grieve, or joy, i'le be a partner.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I thank ye sir, I shall be too proud of ye,
O I could tell ye strange things.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I ghesse at 'em,
And I could curse my self, I made 'em stranger;
Yet my mind sayes, you are not far from happines.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: It shall be welcome; come, lets keep us thus still,
And be as we appear: Heavens hand may blesse us.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Yes sir, here be such people: but how pleasing,
They will appear to you.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Pray let me see'm,
I come to that end: pray let me see'em all.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: They will confound ye sir, like bels rung backward
They are nothing but confusion, and meer noyses.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: May be I love a noyse: but hark ye sir,
Have ye no boyes, handsome yong boyes?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Yes one sir,
A very handsome boy.

speeches.speaker: Alp
verse: Long here?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: But two dayes;
A little crazed: but much hope of recovery.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I that boy, let me see: may be I know him;
That boy, I say: this is the boy he told me of,
And it must needs be she: that boy I beseech ye sir,
That boy I come to see.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: And ye shall see him:
Or any els, but pray be not too violent.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I know what to do, I warrant ye: I am for all fancies:
I can talk to'em, and dispute.

speeches.speaker: 1 Keep.
verse: As madly:
For they be very madde sir.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Let 'em be horne mad.

speeches.speaker: 1. Keep.
verse: We have few Citizens: they have bedlames of their own sir,
And are mad at their own charges.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Who lies here?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Pray ye do not disturb'em sir, here lie such youths
Will make you start if they but dance their trenchmores.
Fetch out the boy, sirha: hark.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Heigh boyes.

speeches.speaker: Eng.
verse: Bownce,
Clap her o'th Star-bord: bounce: top the can, Jenkin.

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: Dead ye dog, dead: do ye quarrell in my Kingdom?
Give me my trident.

speeches.speaker: Eng.
verse: Bownce, 'twixt wind and water,
Loaden with Mackrels: O brave meat.

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: My Sea horses.
I'le charge the Northern wind, and break his bladder.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: I'le sell my bels, before I be out-brav'd thus.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: What's he? what's he?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: A parson sir, a parson,
That run madde for tythe Goslings.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Green sawte cure him.

speeches.speaker: Pars.
verse: I'le curse ye all, i'le excommunicate ye:
Thou English heretique, give me the tenth pot.

speeches.speaker: Eng.
verse: Sue me, i'le drink up all, bownce I say once more,
O, have I split your mizen? blow, blow thou West wind,
Blow till thou rive, and make the Sea run roaring.
I'le hisse it down againe with a bottle of Ale.

speeches.speaker: Scho.
verse: Triton, why Triton.

speeches.speaker: Eng.
verse: Tritons drunk with metheglin.

speeches.speaker: Sch.
verse: Strike, strike the surges, strike.

speeches.speaker: Eng.
verse: Drink, drink, tis day light;
Drink, didle, didle, didle, drink, Parson, proud Parson:
A pigs tayle in thy teeth, and I defie thee.

speeches.speaker: Par.
verse: Give me some porridge, or i'le damne thee English.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: How comes this English madde man here?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Alas thats no question:
They are mad every where sir;
Their fits are coole now: let 'em rest.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Madde Gallants:
Most admirable mad: I love their faces.

speeches.speaker: 1. K.
verse: Ye stinking whore: who knew of this? who lookd to him?
Pox take him, he was sleepy when I left him,

speeches.speaker: 2. K.
verse: Certain he made the foole drunk.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: How now who's this here?
Where is the boy?

speeches.speaker: 1. Keep.
verse: The boy sir?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I the boy, sir.

speeches.speaker: 1. K.
verse: Here's all the boyes we founde.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: These are his cloths.
But wher's the boy?

speeches.speaker: She-f.
verse: The boy is gone a maying,
Hee'l bring me home a Cuckowes nest; do ye hear Master
I put my cloths off, and I dizend him,
And pind a plumb in's forehead, and a feather,
And buss'd him twice, and bid him go seek his fortune:
He gave me this fine money, and fine wine too,
And bid me sop: and gave me these trim cloths too,
And put 'em on.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Is this the boy you would shew?

speeches.speaker: She-f.
verse: I'le give you two pence Master.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Am I foold of all sidies?
I met a foole i'th woods, they said she dwelt here,
In a long pied coat.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: That was the very boy, sir.

speeches.speaker: She.f.
verse: I, I, I, I gave him leave to play forsooth,
Hee'l come again to morrow, and bring pescods.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I'le bring your bones.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Pox o' your fooles, and bedlams,
Plague o' your owls and apes.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Pray ye sir, be tamer,
We cannot help this presently: but we shal know;
I'le recompence your cares too.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Know me a pudding.
You juggle, and ye fidle: fart upon ye:
I am abused.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Pray ye sir.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: And I will be abused sir,
And yon shall know I am abused.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Whaw, Mr. Keeper.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Pox o' thy whawes, and thy whyms,
Pox o' thy urship.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Give me some Ceeze, and Onions: give me some wash-brew,
I have — in my bellies: give me abundance,
Pendragon was a Shentleman, marg you sir,
And the Organs at Rixum were made by revelations,
There is a spirit blowes, and blowes the bellowes,
And then they sing.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: What Moon-cals's this? what dreame?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Pray ye sir observe him,
He is a mountaineere, a man of Goteland.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: I will beate thy face as black as a blew-clout,
I will leave no more sheet in thine eyes.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: He will not hurt ye.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Give me a great deale of guns: thou art the devils,
I know thee by thy tayles: poor Owei.'s hungry,
I will pig thy bums full of bullets.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: This is the rarest rascall,
He speakes as if he had butter-milk in's mouth,
Is this any thing a kin to th' English?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: The elder brother, sir,
He run mad because a rat eate up's cheese.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: H'ad a great deale of reason sir.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: Basilus manus, is for an old codpice, mark ye,
I will borrow thy unships whore, to seale a Letter.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Now he growes villanous.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Me thinks he's best now.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Away with him.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: He shall not.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Sir, he must.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: I will sing, and dance:
Do any thing.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Wilt thou declaime in greek?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Away with the foole,
And whip her soundly sirah.

speeches.speaker: She-f.
verse: I'le tell no more tales.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Or wilt thou fly i'th ayre?

speeches.speaker: Eng.
verse: Do, and i'le catch thee,
And like a wisp of hay, i'le whirle, and whirle thee,
And pusse thee up: and puff thee up.

speeches.speaker: Sch.
verse: I'le save thee,
And thou shalt fall into the Sea, soft, softly.

speeches.speaker: Wel.
verse: I'le get upon a mountaine and call my Countrymen.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: They all grow wild: away with him for heaven sake,
Sir, ye are much too blame.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: No, no, tis brave sir,
Ye have cozend me; i'le make you madde.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: In with him,
And lock him fast.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I'le see him in his lodging.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: What meanes this Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: He's in: have at him,
Are you the Master, sir?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: What would you with him?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I have a busines from the Duke of Medina,
Is there not an old Gentleman come lately in?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Yes, and a wild one too; But not a prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Did you observe him well? tis like he may be.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I have seen younger men of better temper.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: You have hit the cause I come for: ther's a letter
Pray ye peruse it well: I shall be wi' ye;
And sodainly, I fear not: finley, daintely,
I shall so feed your fierce vexation,
And raise your worships stormes: J shall so niggle ye,
And juggle ye, and fiddle ye, and firck ye:
I'le make ye curse the houre yet vext a woman;
I'le make ye stake, when our sex, are but sounded:
For the Lords sake, we shall have him at; I long to see it
As much as for my wedding night: I gape after it.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: This Letter sayes the Gentleman is lunatique
I half suspected it.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Tis very true sir,
And such prancks he has plaid.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: He's some great man,
The Duke commands me with such care to look to him,
And if he grow too violent, to correct him,
To use the speediest meanes for his recovery,
And those he must finde sharpe.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: The better for him:

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: How got ye him hither?

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: With a train, I told him:
He's in love with a boy, there lies his mellancholly.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Hither he came to seek one.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Yes, J sent him,
Now had we dealt by force, we had never brought him.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Here was a boy.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: He saw him not?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: He was gon first.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: It is the better; looke you to your charge well:
Ile see him lodged, for so the duke commanded me
He will be very rough.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We are usd to that sir,
And we as rough as he, if he give occasion.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: You will find him gainfull, but be sure ye curb him,
And get him if ye can fairely to his lodging,
I am afraid ye will not.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: We must sweat then.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: What dost thou talk to me of noyses? i'le have more noyse
I'le have all loose, and all shall play their prizes;
Thy Master has let loose the boy I lookt for
Basely convaid him hence.

speeches.speaker: Keep.
verse: Will ye go out sir?

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I will not out: I will have all out with' me,
I'le have thy Master in; he's only madde here.
And rogues, ile have ye all whipt: heigh mad boyes, mad boyes.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Do you perceive him now?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Tis too apparant.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: I am glad she is gon: he raves thus.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Do you hear sir,
Pray will ye make lesse stir, and see your chamber,
Call in more help; and make the closset ready.

speeches.speaker: Keep.
verse: I thought he was mad: ile have on^ long lash at ye.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: My chamber? where my chamber why my chamber
Wher's the young boy?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Nay pray ye sir be more modest
For your own credit sake: the people see ye,
And I would use ye with the best.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Best, hang ye
What dost thou think me madde?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Pray, and be civill,
Heaven may deliver ye.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Into a rogues hands.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: You do but draw more misery upon ye,
And adde to your disease.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Get from me.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: No sir,
You must not be left so: bear your self civilly,
And twill be better for ye: swell not, nor chafe not.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I am a Gentleman, and a neighbour, rascall.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: A great deale the more pity: I have heard of ye.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: Excellent Master.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: The Duke is very tender too.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Am I lunatique? am I run madde?
What dost thou talk to me of Dukes, and Devils,
Why do the people gape so?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Do not anger 'em,
But go in quietly, and slip in softly
They will so tew ye, els, I am commanded sir.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Why, prethee why?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Ye are dog-mad: you perceive it not
Very far madde: and whips wil scant recover ye.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Ha. whips?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: I whips, and sore whips, and ye were a Lord sir,
If ye be stubborne here:

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Whips? what am I grown.

speeches.speaker: Iul.
verse: O I could burst: hold, hold, hold, hold o'both ends,
How h^ lookes, pray heaven, he be not madde indeed.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: I do not perceive I am so; but if you think it,
Nor I.le be hangd if't be so.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Do you see this sir?
Down with that devill in ye.

speeches.speaker: Alp.
verse: Indeed I am angry,
But ile containe my selfe: O I could burst now,
And teare my selfe, but these rogues will torment me,
Madde in mine old dayes? make mine owne afflictions?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: What doe you mutter sir?

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Nothing, sir, nothing;
I will goe in, and quietly, most civilly:
And good sir, let none of your tormentors come about me,
You have a gentle face; they look like Dragons.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Be civill and be safe: come, for these two daies
Ye must eate nothing neither: twill ease your fits sir.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Twill starve me sir; but I must beare it joyfully.
I may sleepe?

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Yes, a little: go in with these men.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: O miserable me!

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Ile follow presently.
You see tis done sir.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Ye have done it handsomely,
And ile inform the Duke so: Pray ye attend him;
Let him want nothing, but his will.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: He shall not,
And if he be rebellious—

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Never spare him:
H'as flesh, and hide enough, he loves a whipping.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: My service to his Grace.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I shall commend it.
So, thou art fast: I must goe get some fresh roome
To laugh, and caper in: O how it tickles me!
O how it tumbles me with joy! thy mouths stopt:
Now if I can doe my Mistris good, I am Sainted.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: Now, o' my conscience, we have lost him utterly,
He's not gon home: we heard from thence this morning,
And since our parting last at Rodorigo's,
You know what ground we have travel'd.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: He's asleep sure:
For if he had been awake, we should have met with him:
'Faith let's turn back, we have but a fruitlesse journey;
And to hope further of Alindas recovery,
(For sure she'l rather perish then returne)
Is but to seeke a Moth i'th Sunne.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: We'l on sure;
Something we'l know, some cause of all this fooling,
Make some discovery.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Which way shall we cast then,
For all the Champion Country, and the villages,
And all those sides?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: We'l crosse these woods a while then:
Here if we faile, we'l gallop to Segonia
Add if we light of no news there, heare nothing;
We'l even turn fairly home, and coast the other side.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: He may be sicke, or faln into some danger;
He has no guide, nor no man to attend him.

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: He's well enough, he has a travel'd body,
And though he be old, he's tough, and will endure well;
But he is so violent to finde her out,
That his anger leads him a thousand wild goose chases:
Ile warrant he is well.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Shall we part company?

speeches.speaker: Seb.
verse: By no means, no: that were a sullen businesse:
No pleasure in our journey: Come, let's crosse here first,
And where we finde the paths, let them direct us.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Why are you still so fearfull of me, Lady?
So doubtfull of my faith, and honest service?
To hide your selfe from me, to fly my company?
Am I not yours? all yours? by this light you shake still;
Do ye suspect me false? did I ever faile ye?
Doe you think I am corrupted? base? and treacherous?
Lord, how ye look! Is not my life tyde to ye?
And all the power I have to serve, and honour ye?
Still do ye doubt? still am I terrible?
I will not trouble ye: good Heaven preserve ye,
And send ye what ye wish: I will not see ye,
Nor once remember I had such a Misiris.
I will not speak of ye, nor name Alinda,
For feare you should suspect I would betray ye:
Goodnesse and peace conduct ye.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Prethee pardon me,
I know thou art truly faithfull: and thou art welcome,
A welcome partner to my miseries;
Thou knowst I love thee too.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I have thought so, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Alas, my feares have so distracted me
I durst not trust my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Come, pray ye think better,
And cast those by: at least consider, Lady,
How to prevent 'em: pray ye put off this fooles coate;
Though it have kept ye secret for a season,
Tis known now, and will betray ye; your arch enemy
Roderigo is abroad: many are looking for ye.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I know it: and those many I have cozen'd:

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: You cannot still thus.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: I have no meanes to shift it.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I have: and shift you too. I lay last night
At a poore widows house here in the Thicket,
Whether I will conduct ye, and new shape ye,
My selfe too to attend ye.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: What meanes hast thou?
For mine are gone.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Feare not, enough to serve ye;
I came not out so empty.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Prethee tell me;
(For thou hast stroke a kind of comfort through me.)
When saw'st thou Roderigo?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Even this morning,
And in these woods: take heed, h'as got a new shape.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: The habit of a Pilgrime? yes, I know it,
And I hope shall prevent it; was he alone?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: No Madam, and which made me wonder mightily,
He was in company with that handsome Pilgrime,
That sad sweet man.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: That I forgot to give to?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: The same, the very same, that you so pittied,
A man as fit to suit his villanies.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: And did they walke together?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Wondrous civilly.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Talke, and discourse?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: I thinke so, for I see 'em
Make many stands, and then embrace each other.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: The Pilgrime is betraid, a Judas dwels with him,
A Simon, that will seem a Saint to choake him.
Canst thou but shew me this?

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Lord how she trembles!
Not thus, for all the world, ye are undone then;
But let's retire, and alter, then we'l walke free;
And then ile shew ye any things.

speeches.speaker: Alin.
verse: Come, good wench,
And speedily: for I have strang faiths working,
As strange feares too, ile tell thee all my life then.

speeches.speaker: Jul.
verse: Come quick, ile conduct ye, and still serve ye,
And doe not feare; hang feare, it spoiles all projects.
This way; Ile be your guide.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Use all your sports,
All your solemnities; tis the Kings day to morrow.
His birth day, and his marriage, a glad day,
A day we ought to honour, all.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: We will sir,
And make Segonia ring with our rejoycings.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Be sumptuous, but not riotous; be bounteous,
But not in drunken Bacchanals: free to all strangers,
Easie, and sweet in all your entertainments,
For tis a Royall day admits no rudenesse.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: Your Lordship will do us the honour to be here your selfe,
And grace the day?

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Tis a maine part of my service.

speeches.speaker: 3 Cit.
verse: I hope your honour has taken into your consideration
The miseries we have suffered by these Out-laws,
The losses, howrly feares; the rude abuses
Strangers that travell to us are daily loaden with
Our daughters, and our wives complaints.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: I am sorry for't,
And have Commission from the King to ease it:
You shall not be long vext.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cit.
verse: Had we not wals, sir,
And those continually man'd too with our watches,
We should not have a bit of meat to feed us.
And yet they are our friends, and we must think so,
And entertaine 'em so sometimes, and feast 'em,
And send 'em loden home too, we are lost else.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
verse: They'l come to Church amongst us, as we hope Christians,
When all their zeale is but to steale the Chalices;
At this good time now, if your Lordship were not here,
To awe their violence with your authority,
They would play such gambals.

speeches.speaker: Gov.
verse: Are they grown so heady?

speeches.speaker: 2 Cit.
