Where there no Rose, nor Lilly but her Cheek,
No Musick but her tongue; vertue but hers;
She must not rest near me, my vow is graven,
Here in my heart, irrevocably breath'd
And when I break it,

speeches.speaker: Ast.
verse: This is rudenesse Spaniard,
Unseasonably you play the Timonist,
Put on a disposition is not yours,
Which neither fits you, nor becomes you.

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: We cannot force you but we would perswade.

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: Beseech you Sir, no more I am resolv'd
To forsake Malta, tread a Pilgrimage
To faire Jerusalem, for my Ladies soule,
And will not be diverted.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You must beare
This Child along 'we then.

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: VVhat Child?

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: How's this?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Nay then Gomera, thou art injurious,
This child is thine, and this rejected Lady
Thou hast as often known, as thine own wife,
And this I'le make good on thee, with my sword.

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: Thou durst as well blaspheme: if such a scandall
(I crave the rights due to a Gentleman)
Women unvaile.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Will you refuse me yet?

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: My wife!

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: My sister!

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: Some body, thank Heaven
I cannot speak.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: All praise be ever given:

speeches.speaker: Mount.
verse: This saves our lives, yet would she had bin dead;
The very sight of her afflicts me more
Then fear of punishment, or my disgrace.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: How came you to the Temple?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Sir, to do
My poor devotions, and to offer thanks
For scaping a temptation ne'r perform'd
VVith this faire virgin. I restore a wife
Earth cannot paralell: and busie nature
If thou wilt still make women, but remember
To work 'em by this sampler; take heed sir,
Henceforth you never doubt sir.

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: VVhen I do
Death take me sodainly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: To encrease your happinesse
To your best wife, take this addition.

speeches.speaker: Gom.
verse: Alack, my poor knave.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: The confession
The Moor made 't seemes was truth.

speeches.speaker: Nor.
prose: Mary was it sir; the only truth that ever issud out of hell, which her black jawes resemble; a plague o' your bacon-face, you must be giving drinks with a vengance; ah thou branded bitch: do'ye stare, gogles, I hope to make winter bootes o' thy hide yet, she feares not damning: hell fire cannot parch her blacker then she is: do'ye grin, chimney sweeper.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: VVhat is't Mranda?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: That you would please Lucinda might attend you.

speeches.speaker: Col.
verse: That suit sir, I consent not to.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: My husband?
My deerest Angelo?

speeches.speaker: Nor.
verse: More liggam bobs; is not this the fellow that swom
Like a duck to th'shoare in our sea-service?

speeches.speaker: Col.
verse: The very same, do not you know me now sir,
My name is Angelo, though Colonna vaild it,
Your Countryman, and kinsman born in Florence,
VVho from the neighbour Island here of Goza
VVhas captive lead, in that unfortunate day
VVhen the Turk bore with him three thousand soules;
Since in Constantinople have I liv'd
VVhere I beheld this Turkish Damosell first.
A tedious suitor was I for her love,
And pittying such a beauteous case should hide
A soule prophan'd with infidelity,
I labourd her conversion with my love,
And doubly won her, to faire faith her soule
She first betroth'd, and then her faith to me,
But fearfull there to consummate this contract
VVe fled, and in that flight were tane againe
By those same Gallies, fore Valletta fought.
Since in your service I attended her,
VVhere, what I saw, and heard, hath joy'd me more
Then all my past afflictions greiv'd before.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Wonders crown wonders: take thy wife Miranda.
Be henceforth called our Malta's better angell,
And thou her evill Mountferrat.

speeches.speaker: Nor.
prose: Wee'l call him Cacodemon, with his block gib there, his Succuba, his devils seed, his spawn of Phlegeton, that o' my conscience was bred o' the spume of Cocitus; do ye snarle you black jill? she looks lie the Picture of America.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Why stay we now.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This last petition to the Court,
I may bequeath the keeping of my Fort
To this my kinsman, toward the maintenance
Of him, and his faire vertuous wife; discreet,
Loyall, and valiant I dare give him you.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: You must not ask in vaine, sir.

speeches.speaker: Col.
verse: My best thanks
To you my noble Cozen, and my service
To the whole Court; may I deserve this bounty.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: Proceed to th'ceremony, one of our Esguard
Degrade Mountferrat first

speeches.speaker: Mount.
verse: I will not sue
For mercy, 'twere in vaine; fortune thy worst.
See see, the staine of honor, vertues foe,
Of Virgins fair fames, the foule overthrow,
That broken hath his oath of chastity
Dishonor'd much this holy dignity,
Off with his Roab, expell him forth this place,
Whilst we rejoyce, and sing at his disgrace.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Since by thy actions thou hast made thy self
Unworthy of that worthy signe thou wear^st,
And of our sacred order, into which
For former vertues, we receiv'd thee first,
According to our Statutes, Ordinances,
For praise unto the good, a terror to
The bad, and an example to all men;
We here deprive thee of our habit, and
Declare thee unworthy our society,
From which we do expell thee, as a rotten
Corrupted, and contagious member.

speeches.speaker: Esq.
verse: Using th'authority th'Superiour
Hath given unto me, I unty this knot,
And take from thee the pleasing yoak of heaven:
We take from off thy breast this holy crosse,
Which thou hast made thy burthen, not thy prop;
Thy spurs we spoile thee off, eleaving thy heeles
Bare of thy honour, that have kick'd against
Our orders precepts: next we reave thy sword,
And give thee armelesse to thy enemies,
For being foe to goodnesse, and to God,
Last, 'bout thy stiff neck, we this halter hang,
And leave thee to the mercy of the Court.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Invest Miranda.
Faire child of vertue, honors bloome
That here with burning zeale dost come
With joy to ask the white crosse cloak,
And yeild unto this pleasing yoake
That being yong, vowes chastity,
And choosest wilfull poverty;
As this flame mounts, so mount thy zeale, thy glory
Rise past the Stars, and fix in Heaven thy story.

speeches.speaker: 1. Bish.
verse: What crave you gentle sir?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Humble admittance
To be a brother of the holy Hospitall
Of great Jerusalem.

speeches.speaker: 2. Bish.
verse: Breath out your vow.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: To heaven and all the bench of Saints above
Whose succour I implore t'enhable me,
I vow henceforth a chaste life, not to enjoy
Any thing proper to my self; obedience
To my superiours, whom Religion,
And Heaven shall give me: ever to defend
The vertuous fame of Ladies, and to oppugne
Even unto death the Christian enemy,
This do I vow to accomplish.

speeches.speaker: Esq.
verse: Who can tell,
H'as he made other vow, or promis'd marriage
To any one, or is in servitude?

speeches.speaker: All
verse: He's free from all these.

speeches.speaker: 1. Bish.
verse: Put on his spurs, and girt him with the sword,
The scourge of infidels, and tipes of speed.
Buildst thy faith on this

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: On him that di'd
On such a sacred figure, for our sins.

speeches.speaker: 2. Bish.
verse: Here, then we fix it on thy left side, for
Thy encrease of faith, Christian defence, and service
To th'poor, and thus near to thy heart we plant it
That thou maist love it even with all thy heart,
With thy right hand protect, preserve it whole,
For if thou fighting 'gainst heavens enemies
Shall fly away, abandoning the crosse
The Ensigne of thy holy Generall,
With shame thou justly shalt be rob'd of it
Chas'd from our company, and cut away
As an infectious putrified limb.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I aske no favour.

speeches.speaker: 1 Bish.
verse: Then receive the yoak
Of him that makes it sweet, and light, in which
Thy soule find her eternall rest.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Most welcome.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Welcome, our noble brother.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Break up the Court; Mountferrat, though your deeds
Conspiring 'gainst the lives of innocents
Hath forfeited your own, we will not staine
Our white Crosse with your blood: your doom is then
To marry this coagent of your mischiefes
Which done, we banish you the continent,
If either, after three dayes here be found
The hand of Law, layes hold upon your lives.

speeches.speaker: Nor.
prose: Away French stallion, now you have a Barbary mare of your own, go leap her, and engender young devillings.

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: VVe will find something, noble Norandine
To quit your merit: so to civill feasts,
According to our customes; and all pray
The dew of grace, blesse our new Knight to day.

plays.play_title: THE WOMANS PRIZE: OR, The Tamer Tamed.

speeches.speaker: Moroso.
verse: GOd give 'em joy.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Amen.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Amen, say I to:
The Puddings now i'th proof; alas poor wench,
Through what a mine of patience must thou worke,
Ere thou know'st good houre more?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Tis too true: Certaine,
Me thinks her father has dealt harshly with her,
Exceeding harshly, and not like a Father,
To match her to this Dragon; I protest
I pity the poore Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Me thinks now,
He's not so terrible as people think him.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: This old thiefe flatters, out of meere devotion,
To please the father for his second daughter.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: But shall he have her?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Yes, when I have Rome.
And yet the father's for him.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Ile assure ye,
I hold him a good man.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Yes sure a wealthy,
But whether a good womans man, is doubtfull.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Would 'twere no worse.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: What though his other wife,
Out of her most abundant sobernesse,
Out of her daily huy and cries upon him,
(For sure she was a Rebell) turn'd his temper,
And forc'd him blow as high as she? do'st follow
He must retain that long since buried Tempest,
To this soft maid?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: I feare it.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: So do I too:
And so far, that if God had made me woman,
And his wife that must be—

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: What would you doe sir?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I would learn to eate Coales with an angry Cat,
And spit fire at him: I would (to prevent him)
Do all the ramping, roaring tricks, a whore
Being drunke, and tumbling ripe, would tremble at:
There is no safety else, nor morall wisdome,
To be a wife, and his.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: So I should think too.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: For yet the bare remembrance of his first wife
(I tell ye on my knowledge, and a truth too)
Will make him start in's sleep, and very often
Cry out for Cudgels, Colstaves, any thing;
Hiding his Breeches, out of feare her Ghost
Should walk, and weare 'em yet. Since his first marriage,
He is no more the still Petruchio,
Then I am Babylon.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: He's a good felloW,
And on my word I love him: but to think
A fit match for this tender soule—

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: His very frowne, if she but say her prayers
Louder then men talk treason, makes him tindar;
The motion of a Diall, when he's testy,
Is the same trouble to him as a water-worke;
She must do nothing of her selfe; not eate,
Drink, say sir how do ye, make her ready, unready,
Unlesse he bid her.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: He will bury her
Ten pound to twenty shillings, within these three weeks.

speeches.speaker: Tra:
verse: Ile be your halfe.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: He loves her most extreamly,
And so long 'twil be honey-moon. Now Jaques
You are a busie man I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Yes certaine,
This old sport must have egges,

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Not yet this ten daies.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Sweet Gentlemen with Muskadell.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: That's right sir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: This fellow broods his Master: speed ye Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: We shall be for you presently.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Your worships
Shal have it rich and neat: and o' my conscience
As welcom as our Lady day: O my old sir,
When shall we see your worship run at Ring?
That houre a standing were worth money

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: So sir.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Upon my little honesty, your Mistris,
If I have any speculation, must thinke
This single thrumming of a Fiddle,
Without a Bow, but ev'n poore sport.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Y'are merry.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Would I were wise too: so God bless your worship.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: The fellow tels you true.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: When is the day man?
Come, come, you'l steale a marriage.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Nay believe me:
But when her father pleases I am ready,
And all my friends shall know it.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Why not now?
One charge had serv'd for both.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: There's reason in't.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Call'd Rowland.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Will ye walke?
They'l think we are lost: Come Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: You have wip't him now.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: So will he never the wench I hope.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I wish it.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Now Livia, if you'l goe away to night,
If your affections be not made of words.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I love you, and you know how dearly Rowland,
Is there none neere us? my affections ever
Have been your servants; with what superstition
I have ever Sainted you—

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Why then take this way.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Twill be a childish and a lesse prosperous course,
Then his that knows not care: why should we do
Our honest and our hearty love such wrong,
To over-run our fortunes?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Then you flatter.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Alas you know I cannot.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: What hopes left else
But flying to enjoy ye?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: None so far,
For let it be admitted we have time,
And all things now in other expectation,
My father's bent against us; what but ruine,
Can such a by-way bring us? if your feares
Would let you look with my eyes, I would shew you,
And certain, how our staying here would win us
A course, though somewhat longer, yet far surer.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: And then Moroso h'as ye.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: No such matter:
For hold this certaine, begging, stealing, whoring,
Selling, (which is a sin unpardonable)
Of counterfeit Cods, or musty English Crac^s,
Switches, or stones for th'toothache sooner finds me,
Then that drawn Fox and Moroso.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: But his money,
If wealth may win you—

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: If a Hog may be
High Priest among the Jewes: his money Rowland?
Oh Love forgive me, what faith hast thou?
Why, can his money kisse me?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Behind,
Lasd out upon a Petticote: or graspe me
While I cry, O good thank you? o' my troth
Thou makst me merry with thy feare: or lie with me,
As you may do? alas, what fooles you men are?
His mouldy money? half a dozen Riders,
That cannot sit but stampt fast to their Saddles?
No Rowland, no man shall make use of me;
My beauty was born free, and free Ile give it
To him that loves, not buys me. You yet doubt me.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I cannot say I doubt ye.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Goe thy waies,
Thou art the prettiest puling piece of passion:
Y faith I will not faile thee.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I had rather—

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Prethee believe me, if I do not carry it,
For both our goods—

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: But—

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: What but?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I would tell you.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I know all you can tell me; all's but this,
You would have me, and lie with me; is't not so?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Why you shall; will that content you? Goe.

speeches.speaker: Row.
prose: I am very loth to goe.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Now o' my conscience
Thou art an honest fellow: here's my sister;
Go, prethee goe; this kisse, and credit me,
Ere I am three nights older, I am for thee:
You shall heare what I do.
Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Alas poore foole, how it looks?
It would ev'n hang it selfe, should I but crosse it.
For pure love to the matter I must hatch it.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Nay never look for merry houre Maria,
If now you make it not; let not your blushes,
Your modesty, and tendernesse of spirit,
Make you continuall Anvile to his anger:
Believe me, since his first wife set him going,
Nothing can bind his rage: Take your own Councell,
You shall not say that I perswaded you.
But if you suffer him—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay, shall I do it?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Have you a stomack to't?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I never shew'd it.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Twill shew the rarer, and the stronger in you.
But do not say I urg'd you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am perfect,
Like Curtius to redeeme my Countrey, have I
Leap'd into this gulph of marriage, and Ile do it.
Farewell all poorer thoughts, but spight & anger,
Till I have wrought a miracle. Now cosen,
I am no more the gentle tame Maria;
Mistake me not; I have a new soule in me
Made of a North-wind, nothing but tempest;
And like a tempest shall it make all ruins,
Till I have run my will out.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: This is brave now,
If you continue it; but your own will lead you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Adieu all tendernesse, I dare continue;
Maides that are made of feares and modest blushes,
View me, and love example.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Here is your sister.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Here is the brave old mans love.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: That loves the young man.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I and hold thee there wench: what a grief of heart is't,
When Papbos Rebels should up rowse old night,
To sweat against a Cork; to lie and tell
The clock o'th longs, to rise sport-starv'd?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Deere sister,
Where have you been you talke thus?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why at Church, wench;
Where I am tide to talke thus: I am a wife now.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: It seems so, and a modest.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: You are an asse;
When thou art married once, thy modesty
Will never buy thee Pins.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: 'Blesse me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: From what?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: From such a tame foole as our cozen Livia?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: You are not mad.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes wench, and so must you be,
Or none of our acquantance, marke me Livia.
Or indeed sit for our sex: Tis bed time.
Pardon me yellow Hymen, that I meane
Thine offrings to protract, or to keepe fasting
My valiant Bridegroome.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Whether will this woman?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: You may perceive her end.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Or rather feare it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Dare you be partner in't?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Leave it Maria,
I feare I have mark'd too much, for goodnesse leave it;
Devest you with obedient hands to bed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To bed? No Livia, there are Comets hang
Prodigious over that yet; there's a fellow
Must yet before I know that heat (nere start wench)
Be male a man, for yet he is a monster;
Here must his head be Livia.

speeches.speaker: Liv
verse: Never hope it.
Tis as easie with a Sive to scoope the Ocean, as
To tame Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay: Lucina heare me,
Never unlock the treasure of my womb
For humane fruit, to make it capable;
Nor never with thy secret hand make briefe
A mothers labour to me; if I doe
Give way unto my married husbands will,
Or be a wife, in any thing but hopes,
Till I have made him easie as a child,
And tame as feare, he shall not win a smile,
Or a pleas'd look, from this austerity,
Though it would pull another Joynture from him,
And make him ev'ry day another man;
And when I kisse him, till I have my will,
May I be barren of delights, and know
Onely what pleasures are in dreams, and guesses.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: A strange Exordium.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: All the severall wrongs
Done by Emperious husbands to their wives
These thousand yeeres and upwards, strengthen thee:
Thou hast a brave cause.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And Ile doe it bravely
Or may I knit my life out ever after.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: In what part of the world got she this spirit?
Yet pray Maria, looke before you truly,
Besides the obedience of a wife,
Which you will finde a heavy imputation,
Which yet I cannot thinke your own, it shews
So distant from your sweetnesse.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Tis I sweare.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Weigh but the person, and the hopes you have,
To worke this disperate cure.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A weaker subject
Would shame the end I aime at, disobedience.
You talk too tamely: By the faith I have
In mine own Noble will, that childish woman
That lives a prisoner to her husbands pleasure,
Has lost her making, and becomes a beast,
Created for his use, not fellowship.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: His first wife said as much.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: She was a foole,
And took a scurvy course; let her be nam'd
'Mongst those that wish for things, but dare not do 'em:
I have a new daunce for him.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Are you of this faith?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Yes truly, and wil die in't.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Why then let's all weare breeches.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now thou comst neere the nature of a woman;
Hang these tame hearted Eyasses, that no sooner
See the Lure out, and heare their husbands halla,
But cry like Kites upon 'em: The free Haggard
(Which is that woman, that hath wing, and knowes it,
Spirit, and plume) wil make an hundred checks,
To shew her freedome, saile in ev'ry ayre,
And look out ev'ry pleasure; not regarding
I ure, nor quarry, till her pitch command
What she desires, making her foundred keeper
Be glad to fling out traines, and golden ones,
To take her down again.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: You are learned sister;
Yet I say still take heed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A witty saying;
Ile tell thee Livia, had this fellow tired
As many wives as horses under him,
With spurring of their patience; had he got
A Patent, with an Office to reclaime us
Confirm'd by Parliament; had he all the malice
And subtilty of Devils, or of us,
Or any thing that's worse then both.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Hey, hey boyes, this is excellent.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Or could he
Cast his wives new again, like Bels to make 'em
Sound to his will; or had the fearfull name
Of the first breaker of wilde women: yet,
Yet would I undertake this man, thus single,
And spight of all the freedom he has reach'd to,
Turn him and bend him as I list, and mold him
Into a babe again; that aged women,
Wanting both teeth & spleen, may Master him.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Thou wilt be chronicl'd.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: That's all I aime at.

speeches.speaker: Liv
verse: I must confesse, I do with all my heart
Hate an Emperious husband, and in time
Might be so wrought upon.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: To make him cuckold?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If he deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Then Ile leave ye Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Thou hast not so much Noble anger in thee.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Goe sleep, goe sleep, what we intend to do,
Lies not for such starv'd soules as thou hast Livia.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Good night: the Bridegroom will be with you presently.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: That's more then you know.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: If ye worke upon him,
As you have promised, ye may give example,
Which no doubt will be followed.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: So.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Good night: we'l trouble you no further.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If you intend no good, pray doe no harm.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: None, but pray for you.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: 'Cheere wench?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Now Byancha,
Those wits we have let's wind 'em to the height,
My rest is up wench, and I pull for that
Will make me ever famous. They that lay
Foundations, are halfe builders all men say.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: My Master forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Oh how do's thy Master? prethee commend me to him.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: How's this? my Master staies forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why let him stay, who hinders him forsooth?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: The Revel's ended now,
To visit you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am not sick.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I mean to see his chamber, forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Am I his Groom? where lay he last night, forsooth?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: In the low matted Parlour.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: There lies his way by the long Gallery.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I mean your chamber: y'ar very merry Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Tis a good signe I am sound hearted Jaques:
But if you'l know where I lie, follow me;
And what thou seest, deliver to thy Master.

speeches.speaker: Bja.
verse: Do gentle Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Ja.
verse: Ha, is the wind in that dore?
By'r Lady we shall have foule weather then:
I doe not like the shuffling of these women,
They are mad beasts when they knock their heads together:
I have observ'd them all this day; their whispers,
One in anothers eare, their signes, and pinches,
And breaking often into violent laughters:
As if the end they purpos'd were their own.
Call you this weddings? Sure this is a knavery,
A very trick, and dainty knavery,
Marvellous finely carried, that's the comfort:
What would these women doe in waies of honour,
That are such Masters this way. Well, my Sir
Has been as good at finding out these toyes,
As any living; if he lose it now,
At his own perill be it. I must follow.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: You that are married, Gentlemen, home at ye
For a round wager now.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Of this nights Stage?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: I am your first man: a paire of Gloves of twenty shillings.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Done: who takes me up next? I am for all bets.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Well lusty Laurence, were but my night now,
Old as I am, I would make you clap on Spurs,
But I would reach you, and bring you to your trot too:
I would Gallants.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Well said good Will; but where's the staffe boy, ha?
Old father time, your houre-glasse is empty.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: A good tough traine would break thee all to pieces;
Thou hast not breath enough to say thy prayers.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Set how these boyes despise us. Will you to bed sonne?
This pride will have a fall.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Upon your daughter;
But I shall rise again, if there be truth
In Egges, and butter'd Pasnips.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Wil you to bed son, & leave talking;
To morrow morning we shall have you looke,
For all your great words, like St. George at Kingston,
Running a foot-back from the furious Dragon,
That with her angry tayle belabours him
For being lazie.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: His courage quench'd, and so far quench'd—

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Tis well sir.
What then?

speeches.speaker: Saph.
verse: Fly, fly, quoth then the fearfull dwarfe;
Here is no place for living man.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: How now is my faire Bride a bed?
prose: Well my masters, if I doe sinke under my businesse, as I finde tis very possible, I am not the first that has miscarried; So that's my comfort, what may be done without impeach or waste, I can and will doe.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: No truly sir.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
prose: Not a bed yet? body o' me: we'l up and rifle her: here's a coyle with a mayden-head, tis not intayl'd, is it?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: If it be, ile try all the Law i'th Land, but Ile cut it off: let's up, let's up, come.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: That you cannot neither.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Unlesse you'll drop through the Chimney like a Daw, or force a breach i'th windows: you may untile the house, tis possible.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: What dost thou meane?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: A morall sir, the Ballat will expresse it:
The wind and the rain has turnd you back again,
And you cannot be lodged there. The truth is all the doores
Are baracadoed; not a Cathole, but holds a murd'rer in't.
She's victual'd for this moneth.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Art not thou drunk?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: He's drunk, he's drunk; come, come, let's up.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Yes, yes, I am drunke: ye may goe up, ye may Gentlemen, but take heed to your heads: I say no more.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Ile try that.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: How dost thou say? the door fast lock'd fellow?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Yes truly sir, tis lock'd, and guarded too; and two as desperate tongues planted behind it, as ere yet batterd: they stand upon their honours, and will not give up without strange composition, Ile assure you; marching away with their Pieces cockt, and Bullets in their mouthes will not satisfie them.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: How's this? how's this they are?
Is there another with her?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Yes marry is there, and an Engineir.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Who's that for Heavens sake?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
prose: Colonell Byancha, she commands the workes: Spinala's but a ditcher to her, there's a halfe-moon; I am but a poore man, but if you'l give me leave, Ile venture a yeeres wages, draw all your force before it, and mount your ablest piece of battery, you shall not enter it these three nights yet.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I should laugh at that good Jaques.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Beat back again, she's fortified for ever.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Am I drunk now sir?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: He that dares most, goe up now, and be cool'd.
I have scap'd a pretty scowring.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: What are they mad? have we another Bedlam? They doe not talke I hope?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: Oh terribly, extreamly fearfull, the noise at London-bridge is nothing neere her.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: How got she tongue?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: As you got taile, she was born to't.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Lock'd out a doors, and on my wedding-night?
Nay, and I suffer this, I may goe graze:
Come Gentlemen, Ile batter; are these vertues?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: Do, and be beaten off with shame, as I was: I went up, came to th' doore, knockd, no body answered; knock'd lowder, yet heard nothing: would have broke in by force; when suddenly a water-worke flew from the window with such violence, that had I not duck'd quickly like a Fryer, caetera quis nescit? The chamber's nothing but a meere Ostend, in every window Pewter cannons mounted, you'l quickly finde with what they are charg'd, sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Why then tantara for us.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
prose: And all the lower works lin'd sure with small shot, long tongues with Fire-locks, that at twelve score blanke hit to the heart: now and ye dare go up

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: The window opens, beat a parley first;
I am so much amaz'd my very haire stands.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Why how now daughter: what intrenc'd?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A little guarded for my safety sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: For your safety Sweet-heart why who offends you?
I come not to use violence.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I thinke you cannot sir, I am better fortified.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I know your end,
You would faine reprieve your Maiden-head
A night, or two.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, or ten, or twenty, or say an hundred;
Or indeed, till I list lie with you.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: That's a shrewd saying; from this present houre,
I never will believe a silent woman.
When they break out they are bonfires.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Till you list lie with him? why who are you Madam?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: That trim Gentlemans wife, sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Cry you mercy, do you command too?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes marry do's she, and in chiefe.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: I doe command, and you shall go without:
(I mean your wife, for this night)

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And for the next too wench, and so as't follows.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Thou wilt not, wilt 'a?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes indeed deere father,
And till he seale to what I shall set down,
For any thing I know, for ever.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Indeed these are Bugs-words.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: You heare sir, she can talke, God be thanked.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I would I heard it not sir.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: I finde that all the pity bestowd upon this woman,
Makes but an Anagram of an ill wife,
For she was never vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Youl let me in I hope, for all this jesting.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Hope still Sir.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: You will come down I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am sure I will not.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Ile fetch you then.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: The power of the whole County cannot sir,
Unlesse we please to yeild, which yet I thinke
We shal not; charge when you please, you shall
Heare quickly from us.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Blesse me from a Chicken of thy hatching,
Is this wiving?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Prethee Maria tell me what's the reason,
And do it freely, you deale thus strangely with me?
You were not forc'd to marry, your consent
Went equally with mine, if not before it:
I hope you do not doubt I want that mettle
A man should have to keepe a woman waking;
I would be sorry to be such a Saint yet:
My person, as it is not excellent,
So tis not old, nor lame, nor weak with Physick,
But wel enough to please an honest woman,
That keeps her house, and loves her husband.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Tis so.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: My means and my conditions are no shamers
Of him that owes 'em, all the world knows that,
And my friends no reliers on my fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: All this I believe, and none of all these parcels
I dare except against; nay more, so far
I am from making these the ends I aime at,
These idle outward things, these womens feares,
That were I yet unmarried, free to choose
Through all the Tribes of man, i'ld take Petruchio
In's shirt, with one ten Groats to pay the Priest,
Before the best man living, or the ablest
That ev'r leap'd out of Lancashire, and they are right ones.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Why do you play the foole then, and stand prating
Out of the window like a broken Miller!

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: If you wil have me credit you Maria,
Come down, and let your love confirme it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay there sir, that bargain's yet to make.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Play sure wench, the pucks in thine own hand.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Let me die lowsie, it these two wenches
Be not brewing knavery to stock a Kingdome.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Why this is a Riddle:
I love you, and I love you not.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: It is so:
And till your own experience do untie it,
This distance I must keep.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: If you talk more,
I am angry, very angry.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am glad on't, and I wil talke.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Prethee peace,
Let me not think thou art mad. I tell thee woman,
If thou goest forward, I am still Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And I am worse, a woman that can feare
Neither Petruchio Furius, nor his fame,
Nor any thing that tends to our allegeance;
There's a short method for you, now you know me.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: If you can carry't so, tis very wel.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: No you shall carry it, sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Peace gentle Low-bel.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Use no more words, but come down instantly,
I charge thee by the duty of a child.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Prethee come Maria, I forgive all.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay there; That duty, that you charge me by
(If you consider truly what you say)
Is now another mans, you gave't away
I'th Church, if you remember, to my husband:
So all you can exact now, is no more
But onely a due reverence to your person,
Which thus I pay: Your blessing, and I am gone
To bed for this night.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: This is monstrous:
That blessing that St. Dunstan gave the Devil,
If I were neere thee, I would give thee—
Pull thee down by th' nose.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Saints should not rave, sir;
A little Rubarb now were excellent.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Then by that duty you owe to me Maria,
Open the doore, and be obedient: I am quiet yet.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I do confesse that duty; make your best on't.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Why give me leave, I will.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Sir, there's no learning
An old stiffe Jade to trot: you know the morall.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yet as I take it sir, I owe no more
Then you owe back again.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: You wil not Article?
All I owe, presently, let me but up, ile pay.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Y'are too hot, and such prove Jades at length;
You do confesse a duty or respect to me from you again:
That's very neere, or full the same with mine?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Then by that duty, of respect, or what
You please to have it, goe to bed and leave me,
And trouble me no longer with your fooling;
For know, I am not for you.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Well, what remedy?

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: A fine smart Cudgell. Oh that I were neer thee.

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: If you had teeth now, what a case were we in?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
prose: These are the most authentique Rebels, next Tyrone, I ever read of.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: A weeke hence, or a fortnight, as you beare you,
And as I finde my will observ'd, I may
With intercession of some friends be brought
May be to kisse you; and so quarterly
To pay a little rent by composition,
You understand me?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Thou Boy, thou.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Well there are more Maides then Maudlin, that's my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, and more men then Michael.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I must not to bed with this stomach, and no meat Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Feed where you will, so it be sound, and wholsome,
Else live at livery, for i'le none with you.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: You had best back one of the dairy maids, they'l carry.
But take heed to your girthes, you'l get a bruise else.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Now if thou would'st come down, and tender me:
All the delights due to a marriage bed,
Studdy such kisses as would melt a man,
And turne thy selfe into a thousand figures,
To adde new flames unto me, I would stand
Thus heavy, thus regardlesse, thus despising
Thee, and thy best allurings: all thy beauty
That's laid upon your bodies, mark me well,
For without doubt your mind's are miserable,
You have no maskes for them: all this rare beauty,
Lay but the Painter, and the silke worme by,
The Doctor with his dyets, and the Taylor,
And you appeare like flead Cats, not so handsome.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And we appeare like her that sent us hither,
That onely excellent and beauteous nature;
Truly our selves, for men to wonder at,
But too divine to handle; we are Gold,
In our own natures pure; but, when we suffer
The husbands stamp upon us then alayes,
And bas ones of you, men are mingled with us,
And make us blush like Copper.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Then, and never
Till then are women to be spoken of,
For till that time you have no soules I take it:
Good night: come Gentlemen; i'le fast for this night,
But by this hand—well: I shall come up yet?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Noe.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: There will I watch thee like a wither'd Jewry,
Thou shalt neither have meat, fire, nor Candle,
Nor any thing that's easie: doe you rebell so soone?
Yet take mercy.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Put up your Pipes; to bed sir; i'le assure you
A moneths seige will not shake us.

speeches.speaker: Moro.
verse: Well said Colonell.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To bed to bed Petruchio: good night Gentlemen,
You'l make my Father sicke with sitting up:
Here you shall finde us any time these ten dayes,
Unlesse we may march off with our contentment.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Ile hang first.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And i'le quarter if I doe not,
Ile make you know, and feare a wife Petruchio,
There my cause lies.
You have been famous for a woman tamer,
And beare the fear'd-name of a brave wife-breaker:
A woman now shall take those honours off,
And tame you; nay, never look so bigge, she shall beleeve me,
And I am she: what thinke ye; good night to all,
Ye shall finde Centines.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: If ye dare sally.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
prose: The devill's in 'em, ev'n the very devill, the downe right devill.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
prose: Ile devill 'em: by these ten bones I will: i'le bring it to the old Proverb no sport no pie: — taken down i'th top of all my speed; this is fine dancing: Gentlemen, stick to me. You see our Freehold's touch'd, and by this light, we will beleaguer'em, and either starve 'em out, or make 'em recreant.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Ile see all passages stopt, but those about 'em:
If the good women of the Towne dare succour 'em,
We shall have warres indeed.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Ile stand perdue uppn 'em.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: My regiment shall lye before.

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: I think so, 'tis grown too old to stand.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Let's in, and each provide his tackle,
We'l fire'em out, or make'em take their pardons,
Heare what I say, on their bare knees —
Am I Petruchio, fear'd, and spoken of,
And on my wedding night am I thus jaded?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Now Pedro?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Very busie Master Rowland.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: What haste man?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: I beseech you pardon me,
I am not mine own man.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Thou art not mad?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: No; but beleeve me, as hasty—

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: The cause good Pedro?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: There be a thousand sir; you are not married?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Not yet.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Keepe your selfe quiet then.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: You'l finde a Fiddle
That never will be tun'd else: from all women—

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: What ailes the fellow tro? Iaques?

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: Your friend sir.
But very full of businesse.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Nothing but businesse?
Prethee the reason, is there any dying?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I would there were sir.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: But thy businesse?

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: Ile tell you in a word,
I am sent to lay
An imposition upon Sowse and Puddings,
Pasties, and Penny Custards, that the women
May not releeve you Rebels: Fare ye well sir.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: How does my Mistresse?

speeches.speaker: Iaq.
verse: Like a resty jade.
She's spoil'd for riding.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: What a devill ayle they?
Custards, and penney Pasties, Fooles and Fiddles,
What's this to'th purpose? O well met.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Now Rowland.
I cannot stay to talk long.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: What's the matter?
Here's stirring, but to what end? whether goe you?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: To view the works.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: What workes?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: The womens Trenches.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Trenches? are such to see?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: I doe not jest sir.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I cannot understand you.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Doe not you heare
In what a state of quarrell the new Bride
Stands with her husband?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Let him stand with her, and there's an end.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: It should be, but by'r Lady
She holds him out at Pikes end, and defies him,
And now is fortifide; such a Regiment of Rutters
Never defied men braver: I am sent
To view their preparation.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: This is newes
Stranger then Armes in the ayre, you saw not
My gentle Mistresse?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Yes, and meditating
Upon some secret businesse, when she had found it
She leapt for joy, and laugh'd, and straight retir'd
To shun Moroso.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: This maybe for me.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Will you along?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Farewell sir.
What should her musing meane, and what her joy in't,
If not for my advantage? stay ye; may not
That Bob-taile Jade Moroso, with his Gold,
His gew-gaudes, and the hope she has to send him
Quickly to dust, excite this? here she comes,
And yonder walkes the Stallion to discover:
Yet i'le salute her: save you beauteous mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Livi.
verse: The Fox is kennell'd for me: save you sir.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Why doe you looke so strange?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I use to looke sir
Without examination.

speeches.speaker: Moro.
verse: Twenty Spur-Royals for that word.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Belike then
The object discontents you?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Yes it does.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Is't come to this? you know me, doe you not?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Yes as I may know many by repentance.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Why doe you breake your faith?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Ile tell you that too,
You are under age, and no band holds upon you.

speeches.speaker: Moro.
verse: Excellent wench.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Sue out your understanding,
And get more haire, to cover your bare knuckle
(For Boyes were made for nothing, but dry kisses,)
And if you can, more manners.

speeches.speaker: Moro.
verse: Better still.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: And then if I want Spanish gloves, or stockings,
A ten-pound waste-coate, or a Nag to hunt on,
It may be I shall grace you to accept 'em.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Farewell, and when I credit women more,
May I to Smith-field, and there buy a Jade,
(And know him to be so) that breakes my neck.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Because I have knowne you, Ile be thus kinde to you;
Farewell, and be a man, and i'le provide you,
Because I see y'are desperate, some stai'd Chamber-maid
That may relieve your youth, with wholesome doctrin.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: She's mine from all the world: ha wench?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
prose: Ha Chicken? —

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: How's this? I do not love these favours: save you.

speeches.speaker: Row.
prose: The devill take thee—

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: There's a love token for you: thank me now.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Ile thinke on some of ye, and if I live,
My nose alone shall not be plaid withall.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: A Box o'th eare doe you say?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Yes sure a sound one,
Beside my nose blown to my hand; if Cupid
Shoot Arrows of that waight, i'le sweare devoutly,
Has sude his liverie, and no more a Boy.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: You gave her some ill language?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Not a word,

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Or might be you weare fumbling?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Would I had sir.
I had been a forehand then; but to be baffel'd,
And have no feeling of the cause—

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Be patient,
I have a medicine clapt to her back will cure her.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: No sure it must be afore sir.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: O' my Conscience,
When I got these two wenches (who till now
Ne'r shew'd their riding) I was drunck with Bastard,
Whose nature is to forme things like it selfe
Heady, and monstrous: did she slight him too?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: That's all my comfort: a meere Hobby-horse
She made childe Rowland: s'foot she would not know him,
Not give him a free look, not reckon him
Among her thoughts, which I held more then wonder,
I having seene her within's three dayes kisse him
With such an appetite as though she would eat him.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: There is some trick in this: how did he take it?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Ready to cry; he ran away.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: I feare her.
And yet I tell you, ever to my anger,
She is as tame as Innocency; it may be
This blow was but a favour.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Ile be sworne
'Twas well tye'd on then.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Goe too, pray forget it,
I have bespoke a Priest: and within's two houres
Ile have ye married; will that please you?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Ile see it done my selfe, and give the Lady
Such a sound exhortation for this knavery
Ile warrant you, shall make her smell this Moneth on't,

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Nay good sir, be not violent.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Neither—

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: It may be
Out of her earnest love, there grew a longing
(As you know women have such toyes) in kindnesse,
To give me a box o'th eare or so.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: It may be.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: I reckon for the best still: this night then
I shall enjoy her.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: You shall hansell her.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Old as I am, i'le give her one blow for't
Shall make her groane this twelve-moneth.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Where's your joynture?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: I have a joynture for her.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Have your Councell
Perus'd it yet?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: No Councell, but the night, and your sweet daughter
Shall ere peruse that Joynture.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Very well sir.

speeches.speaker: Moro.
verse: Ile no demurrers on't nor no rejoynders.
The other's ready seal'd.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Come then lets' comfort
My Son Petruchio, he's like little Children
That loose their Bables, crying ripe.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Pray tell me,
Is this stern woman still upon the flaunt
Of bold defiance?

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Still, and still she shall be
Till she be starv'd out: you shall see such justice,
That women shall be glad after this tempest
To tye their husbands shooes, and walke their horses;
That were a merry world: doe you heare the rumour,
They say the women are in Insurrection,
And meane to make a —

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: They'l sooner
Draw upon walls as we doe: Let 'em, let 'em,
We'l ship 'em out in Cuck-stooles, there they'l saile
As brave Columbus did, till they discover
The happy Islands of obedience.
We stay too long, Come.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Now Saint George be with us.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Now if I can but get in hansomely,
Father I shall deceive you, and this night
For all your private plotting, i'le no wedlock;
I have shifted saile, and finde my Sisters safety
A sure retirement; pray to heaven that Rowland
Do not beleeve too farre, what I said to him,
For y'on old Foxcase forc'd me, that's my feare.
Stay, let me see, this quarter fierce Petruchio
Keepes with his Myrmidons: I must be suddaine,
If he seize on me, I can looke for nothing
But Marshall Law; to this place have I scap'd him;
Above there.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Cheval'a.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: A Friend.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Who are you?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Looke out and know.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Alas poore wench who sent thee,
What weake foole made thy tongue his Orator?
I know you come to parly.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Y'are deceiv'd,
Urg'd by the goodnes of your cause I come
To doe as you doe.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Y'ar too weake, too foolish,
To cheat us with your smoothnesse: doe not we know
Thou hast been kept up tame?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Beleeve me.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No, prethee good Livia
Utter thy Eloquence somewhere else.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Good Cosen
Put up your Pipes; we are not for your palat,
Alas we know who sent you.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: O' my word —

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Stay there; you must not thinke your word,
Or by your Maydenhead, or such Sonday oathes
Sworne after Even-Song, can inveigle us
To loose our hand-fast: did their wisdomes thinke
That sent you hither, we would be so foolish,
To entertaine our gentle Sister Sinon,
And give her credit, while the woodden Jade
Petruchio stole upon us: no good Sister,
Goe home, and tell the merry Greekes that sent you,
I^ium shall burn, and I, as did Aeneas,
will on my back, spite of the Myrmidons,
Carry this warlike Lady, and through Seas
Unknown, and unbeleev'd, seek out a Land,
Where like a race of noble Amazons,
We'le root our selves and to our endlesse glory
Live, and despise base men.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Ile second ye.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: How long have you been thus?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: That's all one Cosen.
I stand for freedome now.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Take heed of lying;
For by this light, if we doe credit you,
And finde you tripping, his infliction
That kill'd the Prince of Orenge, will be sport
To what we purpose.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Let me feele the heaviest.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Swear by thy Sweet-heart Rowland (for by your mayden-head,
I feare 'twill be too late to swear) you meane
Nothing but faire and safe, and honourable
To us, and to your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I sweare.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Stay yet,
Sweare as you hate Moroso, that's the surest,
And as you have a certaine feare to finde him
Worse then a poore dride Jack, full of more Aches
Then Autumne has; more knavery, and usury,
And foolery, and brokery, then doggs-ditch:
As you doe constantly beleeve he's nothing
But an old empty bagge with a grey beard,
And that beard such a Bob-taile, that it lookes
Worse then a Mares taile eaten off with Fillyes:
As you acknowledge, that young hansome wench
That lyes by such a Bilbo blade, that bends
With ev'ry passe he makes to'th hilts, most mis^rable,
A dry nurse to his Coughes, a fewterer
To such a nasty fellow, a rob'd thing
Of all delights youth lookes for: and to end,
One cast away on course beef, born to brush
That everlasting Cassock that has worne
As many Servants out, as the Northeast passage
Has consum'd Saylors: if you sweare this, and truly
Without the reservation of a gowne
Or any meritorious Petticoate,
'Tis like we shall beleeve you.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I doe sweare it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Stay yet a little; came this wholesome motion
(Deale truly Sister) from your own opinion,
Or some suggestion of the Foe?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Nev'r feare me,
For by that little faith I have in husbands,
And the great zeale I beare your cause, I come
Full of that liberty, you stand for, Sister.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If we beleeve, and you prove recreant Livia,
Think what a maym you give the noble Cause
We now stand up for: Thinke what women shall
An hundred yeare hence speak thee, when examples
Are look'd for, and so great ones, whose relations
Spoke as we doe th'em wench, shall make new customs.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: If you be false, repent, goe home, and pray,
And to the serious women of the City
Confesse your selfe; bring not a sinne so heynous
To load thy soule, to this place: mark me Livia,
If thou bee it double, and betray'st our honours,
And we fail in our purpose: get thee where
There is no women living, nor no hope
There ever shall be.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: If a Mothers daughter,
That ever heard the name of stubborn husband
Found thee, and know thy sinne.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Nay, if old age,
One that has worne away the name of woman,
And no more left to know her by, but railing,
No teeth, nor eyes nor legges, but woodden ones
Come but i'th wind-ward of thee, forsure she'l smell thee
Thou'lt be so ranck, she'l ride thee like a night-mare,
And say her Prayers back-ward to undoe thee,
She'l curse thy meat and drink, and when thou marriest,
Clap a sound spell for ever on thy pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Children of five yeare old, like little Fayries
Will pinch thee into motley, all that ever
Shall live, and heare of thee, I meane all women;
Will (like so many furies) shake their Keyes,
And tosse their flaming distaffes o're their heads,
Crying Revenge: take heed, 'tis hideous:
Oh 'tis a fearefull office, if thou had'st
(Though thou bee'st perfect now) when thou cam'st, hither,
A false Imagination, get thee gone,
And as my learned Cozen said repent,
This place is sought by soundnesse.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: So I seeke it,
Or let me be a most despis'd example.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I doe beleeve thee, be thou worthy of it.
You come not empty?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: No, Here's Cakes, and cold meat,
And tripe of proofe: behold here's wine, and beere,
Be suddaine, I shall be surpriz'd else.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Meet at the low Parlor doore, there lyes a close way:
What fond obedience you have living in you,
Or duty to a man, before you enter,
Fling it away, 'twill but defile our Offrings.

speeches.speaker: By.
verse: Be wary as you come,

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: 1 Mai.
verse: How goes your businesse Girles?
A foot, and faire.
If fortune favour us: away to your strength
The Country Forces are ariv'd, be gone.
We are discover'd else.
Arme? and be valiant.
Think of our cause.
Our Justice.
'Tis sufficient.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Now Rowland?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: How yoe you?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: How do'st thou man,
Thou look'st ill:

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Yes, pray can you tell me Tranio,
Who knew the devill first?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: A woman.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Thou hast heard I am sure of Esculapius.
So were they not well acquainted?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: May be so,
For they had certaine Dialogues together.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: He sold her fruit, I take it?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Yes, and Cheese
That choak'd all mankinde after.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Canst thou tell me
Whether that woman ever had a faith
After she had eaten?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: That's a Schoole question

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: No
'Tis no question, for beleeve me Tranio,
That cold fruit after eating bread naught in her
But windy promises, and chollick vowes
That broke out both wayes.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Thou ha'st heard I am sure
Of Esculapius, a farre famed Surgeon,
One that could set together quarter'd Traytors,
And make 'em honest men.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: How do'st thou Rowland?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Let him but take, (if he dare doe a cure
Shall get him fame indeed) a faithlesse woman,
There will be credit for him, that will speake him,
A broken woman Tranio, a base woman,
And if he can cure such a rack of honour
Let him come here, and practise.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Now for honours sake
Why what ayl'st thou Rowland?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I am ridden Tranio.
And Spur-gald to the life of patience
(Heaven keepe my wits together) by a thing
Our worst thoughts are too noble for, a woman.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Your Mistresse has a little frown'd it may be?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: She was my Mistresse.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Is she not?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: No Tranio.
She has done me such disgrace, so spitefully,
So like a woman bent to my undoing,
That henceforth a good horse shall be my Mistresse,
A good Sword, or a Booke: and if you see her,
Tell her I doe beseech you, even for love sake.—

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: I will Rowland.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: She may sooner
Count the good I have thought her,
Our old love and our friend-ship,
Shed one true teare, meane one houre constantly,
Be old, and honest, married, and a maide,
Then make me see her more, or more beleeve her:
And now I have met a Messenger, farewell sir.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Alas poore Rowland, I will doe it for thee:
This is that dogge Moroso, but I hope
To see him cold i'th mouth first 'er he enjoy her:
Ile watch this young man, desperate thoughts may seize him,
And if my purse, or councell can, i'le ease him.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: For looke you Gentlemen, say that I grant her
Out of my free and liberall love, a pardon,
Which you and all men else know she deserves not,
(Teneatis amici) can all the world leave laughing?

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: I thinke not.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: No by — they cannot;
For pray consider, have you ever read,
Or heard of, or can any man imagine.
So stiffe a Tomb boy, of so set a ma ice,
And such a brazen resolution,
As this young Crab-tree? and then answer me,
And marke but this too friends, without a cause,
Not a foule word comes crosse her, not a feare,
She justly can take hold on, and doe you thinke
I must sleepe out my anger, and endure it,
Sow pillows to her ease, and lull her mischiefe?
Give me a Spindle first: no, no my Masters,
Were she as faire as Nell a Greece, and house-wife,
As good as the wife Saylors wife, and young still,
Never above fifteene; and these tricks to it,
She should ride the wild Mare once a week, she should.
(Believe me friends she should) I would tabor her,
Till all the Legions that are crept into her,
Flew out with fire i'th tailes.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Me thinks you erre now,
For to me seems, a little sufferance
Were a far surer cure.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Yes, I can suffer,
Where I see promises of peace and amendment.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Give her a few conditions.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Ile be hangd first.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Give her a crab-tree-cudgell.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: So I will;
And after it a flock-bed for her bones.
And hard egges, till they brace her like a Drum,
She shall be pamperd with —
She shall not know a stoole in ten moneths Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: This must not be.

speeches.speaker: Jaq
verse: Arme, arme, out with your weapons,
For all the women in the Kingdom's on ye;
They swarm like waspes, and nothing can destroy 'em,
But stopping of their hive, and smothering of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Stand to your guard sir, all the devils extant
Are broke upon us, like a cloud of thunder;
There are more women, marching hitherward,
In rescue of my Mistris, th^n ere turn'd taile
At Sturbridge Faire; and I believe, as fiery.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: The forlorn-hope's led by a Tanners wife,
I know her by her hide; a desperate woman:
She flead her husband in her youth, and made
Raynes of his hide to ride the Parish. Take 'em all together,
They are a genealogy of Jennets, gotten
And born thus, by the boysterous breath of husbands;
They serve sure, and are swift to catch occasion,
(I meane their foes, or husbands) by the fore-locks,
And there they hang like favours; cry they can,
But more for Noble spight, then feare: and crying
Like the old Gyants that were foes to Heaven,
They heave ye stoole on stoole, and fling main Potlids
Like massie rocks, dart ladles, tossing Irons,
And tongs like Thunderbolts, till overlayd,
They fall beneath the waight; yet still aspiring
At those Emperious Godsheads, that would tame 'em.
There's nere a one of these, the worst and weakest,
(Choose where you will) but dare attempt the raysing
Against the soveraigne peace of Puritans,
A May-pole, and a Morris, maugre mainly
Their zeale, and Dudgeon-daggers: and yet more,
Dares plant a stand of battring Ale against 'em,
And drinke 'em out o'th Parish

speeches.speaker: Saph.
prose: Lo you fierce Petruchio, this comes of your impatience.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: There's one brought in the Beares against the Canons
Of the Town, made it good, and fought 'em.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Another, to her everlasting fame, erected
Two Ale-houses of ease: the quarter-sessions
Running against her roundly; in which businesse
Two of the disannullers lost their night-caps:
A third stood excommunicate by the cudgell.
The Cunstable, to her eternall glory,
Drunke hard, and was converted, and she victor.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Then are they victualed with pies and puddings,
(The trappings of good stomacks) noble Ale
the true defendor, Sawsages, and smoak'd ones,
If need be, such as serve for Pikes; and Porke,
(Better the Jewes never hated:) here and there
A bottle of Metheglin, a stout Bricaine
That wil stand to 'em, what else they want, they war for.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Come to councell,

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Now you must grant conditions or the Kingdom
Will have no other talke but this.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Away then, and let's advise the best.

speeches.speaker: Soph:
verse: Why doe you tremble?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Have I liv'd thus long to be knockt o'th head,
With halfe a washing beetle? pray be wise sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Come, something Ile doe; but what it is I know not.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: To councel then, and let's avoyd their follies.
Guard all the doors, or we shal not have a cloke left.
How goes the businesse, girles?
A foot, and faire.
If fortune favour us: away to your strength,
The Country forces are ariv'd; be gon we are discovered else.
Arme, and be valiant.
Think of our cause.
Our iustice.
Tis sufficient.

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: I am indifferent, though I must confesse,
I had rather see her carted.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: No more of that sir.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Are ye resolv'd to give her fair conditions?
Twill be the safest way.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I am distracted,
Would I had run my head into a halter
When I first woo'd her: if I offer peace,
She'l urge her own conditions, that's the devil.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Why say she do?

speeches.speaker: Petru:
verse: Say, I am made an Asse, then;
I know her aime: may I with reputation
(Answer me this) with safety of mine honour,
(After the mighty mannage of my first wife,
Which was indeed a fury to this Filly,
After my twelve strong labours to reclaime her,
Which would have made Don Hercules horn mad,
And hid him in his hide) suffer this Sicely,
Ere she have warm'd my sheets, ere grappel'd with me,
This Pinck, this painted Foyst, this Cockle-boat,
To hang her Fights out, and defie me friends,
A wel known man of war? if this be equal,
And I may suffer, say, and I have done?

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: I do not think you may.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: You'l make it worse sir.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Pray heare me good Petruchio: but ev'n now,
You were contented to give all conditions,
To try how far she would carry: Tis a folly,
(And you wil find it so) to clap the curb on,
Er you be sure it proves a naturall wildnesse,
And not a forc'd. Give her conditions,
For on my life this tricke is put into her.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: I should believe so too.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: And not her own.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: You'l finde it so.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Then if she flownder with you,
Clap spurs on, and in this you'l deale with temperance,
Avoyd the hurry of the world.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: And loose

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: No honour on my life, sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I wil do it.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: It seems they are very merry.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Why God hold it.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Now Jaques?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: They are i'th flaunt, sir.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Yes we heare 'em.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: They have got a stick of Fiddles, and they firke it
In wondrous waies, the two grand Capitanos,
(They brought the Auxiliary Regiments)
Daunce with their coats tuckt up to their bare breeches,
And bid them kisse 'em, that's the burden;
They have got Metheglin, and audacious Ale,
And talke like Tyrants.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: How knowest thou?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I peep't in
At a loose Lansket.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Harke.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: A Song, pray silence.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: They look out.

speeches.speaker: Petru
verse: Good ev'n Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Good you good ev'n sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: How have you slept to night?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Exceeding well sir.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Did you not wish me with you?

speeches.speaker: Mar:
verse: No, believe me,
I never thought upon you.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Is that he?

speeches.speaker: Bya.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: She has drunk hard, mark her hood.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You are —

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Learuedly drunk, Ile hang else: let her utter.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And I must tell you, viva voce friend,
A very foolish fellow.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: There's an Ale figure.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: I thank you Susan Brotes.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Forward sister.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You have espoused here a hearty woman,
A comely, and couragious.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Wel I have so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And to the comfort of distressed damsels,
Weomen out-worn in wedlock, and such vessels,
This woman has defied you.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: It should seem so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And why?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Yes, can you tell?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: For thirteen causes.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Pray by your patience Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Forward sister.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Do you mean to treat of all these?

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Who shall let her?

speeches.speaker: Petro.
verse: Doe you heare, Velvet-hood, we come not now
To heare your doctrine.

speeches.speaker: Cunt.
verse: For the first, I take it,
It doth divide it selfe into seven branches.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Harke you good Maria,
Have you got a Catechiser here?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Good zeale.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: Good three pil'd predication, will you peace,
And heare the cause we come for?

speeches.speaker: Cunt.
verse: Yes Bob-tailes
We know the cause you come for, here's the cause,
But never hope to carry her, never dream
Or flatter your opinions with a thought
Of base repentance in her.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Give me sack,
By this, and next strong Ale.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sweare forward sister.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: By all that's cordiall, in this place we'l bury
Our bones, fames, tongues, our triumphs; and then all
That ever yet was chronicl'd of woman;
But this brave wench, this excellent despiser,
This bane of dull obedience, shall inherit
His liberall wil, and march off with conditions
Noble, and worth her selfe.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She shall Tom Tilers,
And brave ones too; My hood shal make a hearse-cloth,
And I lie under it, like Jone o Gaunt,
Ere I goe lesse, my Distaffe stucke up by me,
For the eternall Trophce of my conquests;
And loud fame at my head, with two main Bottles,
Shall fill to all the world the glorious fall
Of old Don Gillian.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Yet a little further,
We have taken Armes in rescue of this Lady;
Most just and Noble: if ye beat us off
Without conditions, and we recant,
Use us as we deserve; and first degrade us
Of all our ancient chambring: next that
The Symbols of our secrecy, silke Stockings,
Hew of our heeles; our petticotes of Armes
Teare of our bodies, and our Bodkins breake
Over our coward heads.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And ever after
To make the tainture most notorious,
At all our Crests, videlicet our Plackets.
Let Laces hang, and we returne againe
Into our former titles, Dayry maids.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: No more wars: puissant Ladies, shew conditions,
And freely I accept 'em.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Call in Livia;
She's in the treaty too.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: How, Livia?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Heare you that sir?
There's the conditions for ye, pray peruse 'em.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Yes, there she is: t'had been no right rebellion,
Had she held off; what think you man?

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: Nay nothing.
I have enough o'th prospect: o'my conscience,
The worlds end, and the goodnesse of a woman
Will come together.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: Are you there sweet Lady?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: Cry you mercy sir, I saw you not: your blessing.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
prose: Yes when I blesse a jade, that stumbles with me. How are the Articles?

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: This is for you sir;
And I shal think upon't.

speeches.speaker: Mor.
verse: You have us'd me finely.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: There's no other use of thee now extant,
But to be hung up; cassock, cap, and all,
For some strange monster at Apothecaries.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: I heare you whore.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: It must be his then sir,
For need wil then compell me.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Blessing on thee.

speeches.speaker: Liv.
verse: He wil undoe me in meere pans of Coles
To make him lustie.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: There's no talking to 'eni;
How are they sir?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: As I expected: Liberty and clothes,
When, and in what way she wil: continuall moneys,
Company, and all the house at her dispose;
No tongue to say, why is this? or whether wil it;
New Coaches, and some buildings, she appoints here,
Hangings, and hunting-horses: and for Plate
And Jewels for her private use, I take it,
Two twousand pound in present: then for Musick,
And women to read French;

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: This must not be.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: And at the latter end a clause put in,
That Livia shal by no man be importun'd.
This whole moneth yet, to marry.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: This is monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: This shall be done, Ile humor her awhile:
If nothing but repentance, and undoing
Can win her love, Ile make a shift for one.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: When ye are once a bed, all these conditions
Lie under your own seale.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Do yo like 'em?

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Yes.
And by that faith I gave you fore the Priest
Ile ratifie 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Stay, what pledges?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No, Ile take that oath;
But have a care you keep it.

speeches.speaker: Cit.
verse: Tis not now
As when Andrea liv'd.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: If you do juggle,
Or alter but a Letter or these Articles
We have set down, the self-same persecution.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Mistrust him not.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: By all my honesty —

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Enough I yield.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: What's this
Inserted here?

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: That the two valiant women that command here
Shall have a Supper made em, and a large one,
And liberall entertainment without grudging,
And pay for all their Souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: That shall be too;
And if a tun of Wine wil serve to pay 'em,
They shall have justice: I ordaine ye all
Pay-masters, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Then we shall have sport boyes.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: We'l meet you in the Parlour.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Ne'r looke sad sir, for I will doe it.

speeches.speaker: Soph.
verse: There's no danger in't.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: For Livia's Article, you shall observe it,
I have tyde my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Petron.
verse: I wil.

speeches.speaker: Petru.
verse: Along then: now
Either I break, or this stiffe plant must bow.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: Come, you shall take my counsell.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: I shall hang first.
Ile no more love, that's certaine, tis a bane,
(Next that they poyson Rats with) the most mortall:
No, I thank Heaven, I have got my sleep again,
And now begin to write sence; I can walk ye
A long howre in my chamber like a man,
And think of something that may better me;
Some serious point of Learning, or my state;
No more ay-mees, and miseries Tranio
Come neer my brain. Ile tell thee, had the devil
But any essence in him of a man,
And could be brought to love, and love a woman,
Twould make his head ake worser then his hornes doe;
And make him with a fire he never felt yet,
Would make him dance. I tell thee there is nothing
(It may be thy case Tranio, therefore heare me:)
Under the Sun (reckon the masse of follies
Crept into th'world with man) so desperate,
So madde, so sencelesse, poor and base, so wretched,
Roguy, and scurvy.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: VVhether wilt thou Rowland?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: As tis to be in love.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: And why for vertues sake?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: And why for vertues sake? do'st thou not conceive me?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: No by my troth.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Pray then, and hartely
For fear thou fall into 't: I'le tell thee why too,
(For I have hope to save thee) when thou lovest,
And first beginst to worship the gilt calfe,
Imprimis, thou hast lost thy gentry,
And like a prentice flung away thy freedom.
Forthwith thou art a slave.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: That's a new Doctrine.

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: Next thou art no more man.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: VVhat then?

speeches.speaker: Row.
verse: A Fryppery;
