Beare ye up your point there; pick his teeth: Oh' base.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Fie: you are the most untoward Scholler: beare
Your body gracefully: what a posture's there?
You lie too open breasted.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Oh!

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: You'ld never
Make a good States-man:

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Pray no more.
I hope to breath in peace, and therefore need not
The practise of these dangerous qualities,
I doe not meane to live by't; for I trust
You'l leave me better able.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Not a Button:

speeches.speaker: Eugenia,
verse: Let's goe get us a new heire.

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: I by my troth: your daughter's as untoward.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: I will breake thee bone by bone, and bake thee,
Ere i'le ha' such a woodden Sonne, to inherit:
Take him a good knock; see how that will work.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Now, for your life Signior:

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Oh: alas, I am kill'd
My eye is out: looke Father: Zancho: —
Ile play the foole no more thus, that I will not.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Heart: nere a rogue in Spaine shall wrong my brother
Whil'st I can hold a sword.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Hold, Maddam, Maddam.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Clara.

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Mistresse:

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Bradamante.
Hold, hold I pray.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: The devil's in her, o'the other side: sure,
There's Gold for you: they have chang'd what ye calt's:
Will no cure help? well, I have one experiment,
And if that faile, Ile hang him, then here's an end on't.
Come you along with me: and you sir:

speeches.speaker: Bob.
prose: Now are you going to drowning.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Ile ev'n along with ye: she's too great a Lady
For me, and would prove more then my match.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You'r he spoke of Vitelli to the Steward?

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Yes: and I thank you, you have beat me for't.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: But are you sure you doe not wrong him?

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Sure?
So sure, that if you please venture your selfe
Ile show you him, and his Cockatrice together,
And you shall heare 'em talke.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Will you? by — sir
You shall endeere me ever: and I ask
You mercy.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: You were somewhat boystrous.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: There's Gold to make you amends: and for this paines,
Ile gratifie you further: i'le but masque me
And walke along with ye: faith let's make a night on't.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
prose: Come on my brave water-Spanlels: you that hunt Ducks in the night: and hide more knavery under your gownes then your betters: observe my precepts, and edifie by my doctrine: at yond corner will I set you; if drunkards molest the street, & fall to brabling, knock you down the malefactors, and take you up their cloaks and hats, and bring them to me: they are lawfull prisoners, and must be ransom'd ere they receive liberty: what else you are to execute upon occasion, you sufficiently know: and therefore I abbreviat my Lecture.

speeches.speaker: Met.
prose: We are wise enough, and warme enough.

speeches.speaker: Men.
prose: Vice this night shall be apprehended.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: The terror of rug-gownes shall be known: and our bils
Discharge us of after recknings.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
prose: I will doe any thing, so I may eat.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
prose: Lazarillo, We will spend no more; now we are growne worse, we will live better: let us follow our calling faithfully.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Away, then the Common-wealth is our Mistresse: and who
Would serve a common Mistresse, but to gaine by her?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I pray you see the Masque, my Lord,

speeches.speaker: Ana.
verse: 'Tis early night yet.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: O if it be so late, take me along:
I would not give advantage to ill tongues
To tax my being here, without your presence
To be my warrant.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: You might spare this, Sister,
Knowing with whom I leave you; one that is
By your allowance, and his choice, your Servant,
And may my councell and perswasion work it,
Your husband speedily: For your entertainement
My thankes; I will not rob you of the meanes
To doe your Mistresse some acceptable service
In waiting on her to my house.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: My Lord,

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: As you respect me, without further trouble
Retire, and taste those pleasures prepar'd for you,
And leave me to my own wayes.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: When you please sir.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: You'l leave my Chamber?

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Let us but bill once,
My Dove, my Sparrow, and I, with my office
Will be thy slaves for ever.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Are you so hot?

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: But taste the difference of a man in place,
You'l finde that when authoritie pricks him forward,
Your Don, nor yet your Diego comes not neere him
To doe a Lady right: no men pay deerer
For their stolne sweetes, then we: three minutes trading
Affords to any sinner a protection
For three yeeres after: thinke on that, I burne;
But one drop of your bounty.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Hence you rogue,
Am I fit for you? is't not grace sufficient
To have your staffe, a bolt to bar the doore
Where a Don enters, but that you'l presume
To be his taster?

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Is no more respect
Due to this rod of justice?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Doe you dispute?
Good Doctor of the Dungeon, not a word more,
— If you doe, my Lord Vitelli knowes it.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Why I am bigge enough to answer him,
Or any man.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: 'Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Malroda.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: You know the voice, and now crowch like a Cur
Tane worrying sheepe: I now could have you guelded
For a Bawd rampani: but on this submission
For once I spare you

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: I Will be reveng'd
My honourable Lord.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: There's for thy care

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: I am mad, starck mad: proud Pagan scorn her host
I would I were but valiant enough to kick her,
Il'd wish no manhood else.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: You see, I have kept my word.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: But in this object
Hardly deserv'd my thanks.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Is there ought else
You will command me?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Onely your sword
Which I must have: nay willingly I yet know
To force it, and to use it.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: 'Tis yours Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I ask no other guard.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: If so I leave you:
And now, if that the Constable keepe his word,
A poorer man may chance to gull a Lord.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: By this good — you shall not.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: By this—
I mu^, and will, Malroda; What doe you make
A stranger of me?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Ile be so to you,
And you shall find it.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: These are your old arts
T'endeere the game you know I come to hunt for,
Which I have borne too coldly.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Doe so still,
For if I h at you, hang me.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: If you doe not
I know who'll starve for't: why, thou shame of women,
Whose folly, or whose impudence is greater
Is doubtfull to det^rmine; this to me
That know thee for a whore.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: And made me one,
Remember that.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Why should I but grow wise
And tye that bounty up, which nor discretion
Nor honour can give way too; thou wouldst be
A Bawd e're twenty, and within a moneth
A barefoot, lowzie, and diseased whore,
And shift thy lodgings oftner then a rogue
That's whipt from post to post.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Pish: all our Colledge
Know you can raile well in this kinde.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: For me
He never spake so well.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: I have maintain'd thee
The envy of great fortunes, made thee shine
As if thy name were glorious: stuck thee full
Of jewels, as the firmament of Starrs,
And in it made thee so remarkable
That it grew questionable, whether vertue poore,
Or vice so set forth as it is in thee,
Were even by modesties selfe to be prefer'd,
And am I thus repaid?
You are still my debtor;
Can this (though true) be weigh'd with my lost honour,
Much lesse my faith? I have liv'd private to you,
And but for you, had ne're known what lust was,
Nor what the sorrow for't.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: 'Tis false.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: 'Tis true,
But how return'd by you, thy whole life being
But one continued act of lust, and Shipwrack
Of womens chastities.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: But that I know
That she that dares be damn'd dares any thing,
I should admire thy tempting me: but presume not
On the power you thinke you hold o're my affections,
It will deceive you: yeeld, and presently
Or by the inflamed blood, which thou must quench
Ile make a forcible entrie.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Touch me not:
You know I have a throat, — if you doe
I will cry out a rape, or sheath this here,
Ere i'le be kept, and us'd for Julip-water
T'allay the heate which lushious meats and wine
And not desire hath rais'd.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: A desperate devill,
My blood commands my reason: I must take
Some milder way.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: I hope (deere Don) I fit you.
The night is mine, although the day was yours
You are not fasting now: this speeding trick
Which I would as a principle leave to all,
That make their maintenance out of their own Indies
As I doe now; my good old mother taught me,
Daughter, quoth she, contest not with your lover
His stomach being empty; let wine heat him,
And then you may command him: 'tis a sure one:
His lookes shew he is coming.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Come this needs not,
Especially to me: you know how deere
I ever have esteemed you.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Lost again.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: That any sight of yours, hath power to change
My strongest resolution, and one teare
Sufficient to command a pardon from me,
For any wrong from you, which all mankinde
Should kneel in vaine for.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Pray you pardon those
That need your favour, or desire it

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Prethee.
Be better temper'd: Ile pay as a forfeit
For my rash anger, this purse fil'd with Gold.
Thou shalt have servants, gownes, attires, what not?
Only continue mine.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: 'Twas this I fish'd for

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Look on me, and receive it.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Well, you know
My gentle nature, and take pride t'abuse it:
You see a trifle pleases me, we are friends;
This kisse, and this confirmes it.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: With my ruine.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: I'le have this dyamond; and this pearle.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: They are yours.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: But wil you not, when you have what you came for,
Take them from me to morrow? tis a fashion
Your Lords of late have us'd.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: But Ile not follow.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: That any man at such a rate as this
Should pay for his repentance.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Shall we to bed now?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Instantly, Sweet: yet now I think on't better
Ther's something first that in a word or two
I must acquaint you with.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Can I cry ayme,
To this against my selfe? Ile break this match,
Or make it stronger with my bloud.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: I am yours,
A Don's not priviledgd here more then yourself,
Win her, and weare her.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Have you a Priest ready?

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: I have him for thee, Lad; and when I have
Married this scornefull whore to this poor gallant.
She wil make suit to me; there is a trick
To bring a high-priz'd wench upon her knees:
For you my fine neat Harpyes stretch your tallons
And prove your selves true night-Birds.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: Take my word
For me and all the rest.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: If there be meat
Or any banquet stirring, you shall see
How ile bestow my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: When they are drawn,
Rush in upon 'em: al's faire prize you light on:
I must away: your officer may give way
To the Knavery of his watch, but must not see it.
You all know where to finde me.

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: There look for us.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: My Piorato, welcome, welcome:
Faith had you not come when you did, my Lord
Had done I know not what to me.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: I am gul'd,
First cheated of my Jewels, and then laugh'd at:
Sirha, what make you here?

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: A businesse brings me,
More lawfull then your own,

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: How's that, you slave?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: He's such, that would continue his a whore
Whom he would make a wife of.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Ile trea'd upon
The face you doat on, strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: Keep the peace there.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: A plot upon my life too?

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: Down with him.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Show your old valour, and learn from a woman,
One Eagle has a world of odds against
A flight of Dawes, as these are.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Get you off,
Ile follow instantly.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
prose: Run for more help there.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Losse of my gold, & jewels, & the wench too
Afflicts me not so much, as th'having Clara
The witnesse of my weaknesse.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: He turns from me,
And yet I may urge merit, since his life
Is made my second gift.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: May I ne'r prosper
If I know how to thank her.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Sir, your pa don
For pressing thus beyond a Virgins bounds
Upon your privacies: and let my being
Like to a man, as you are, be th'excuse
Of my solliciting that from you, which shall not
Be granted on my part, although desir'd
By any other: sir, you understand me,
And 'twould shew nobly in you, to prevent
From me a farther boldnesse, which I must
Proceed in, if you prove not mercifuil,
Though with my losse of blushes, and good name.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Madam, I know your wil, and would be thankfull
If it were possible I could affect
The Daughter of an enemy.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: That faire false one
Whom with fond dotage you have long pursu'd
Had such a father: she to whom you pay
Deerer for your dishonour, then all titles
Ambitious men hunt for are worth.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: 'Tis truth.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Yet, with her, as a friend you still exchange
Health for diseases, and to your disgrace
Nourish the rivals to your present pleasures,
At your own charge, us'd as a property
To give a safe protection to her lust,
Yet share in nothing but the shame of it.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Grant all this so, to take you for a wife
Were greater hazard, for should I offend you
(As tis not easy still to please a woman)
You are of so great a spirit, that I must learn
To weare your petticoat, for you wil have
My breeches from me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Rather from this houre
I here abjure all actions of a man,
And wil esteem it happinesse from you
To suffer like a woman: love, true love
Hath made a search within me, and expel'd
All but my naturall softnesse, and made perfect
That which my parents care could not begin.
I wil show strength in nothing, but my duty,
And glad desire to please you, and in that
Grow every day more able.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Could this be,
What a brave race might I beget? I finde
A kind of yeelding; and no reason why
I should hold longer out: she's yong, and faire,
And chast for sure, but with her leave the Devil
Durst not attempt her: Madam, though you have
A Souldiers arme, your lips appear as if
They were a Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: They dare sir from you
Endure the tryall.

speeches.speaker: ~it.
verse: Ha: once more I pray you:
The best I ever tasted; and tis said
I have prov'd many, 'tis not safe I feare
To aske the rest now: wel, I will leave whoring
And luck herein send me with her: worthiest Lady,
Ile wait upon you home, and by the way
(If ere I many, as ile not forswear it)
Tell you, you are my wife.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Which if you do,
From me all man-kinde women, learne to woe.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: A cloak? good purchase, and rich hangers? well,
Wee'l share ten Pistolets a man

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Yet still
I am monstrous hungry: could you not diduct
So much out of the grosse some, as would purchase
Eight loynes of Veale, and some two dozen of Capons?

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: O strange proportion for five.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: For five? I have
A legion in my stomach that have kept
Perpetuall fast these ten years: for the Capons,
They are to me but as so many black Birds:
May I but eate once, and be satisfied,
Let the fates call me, when my ship is fraught,
And I shall hang in peace.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Steale well to night,
And thou shalt feed to morrow; so now you are
Your selves againe, ile raise another watch
To free you from suspition: set on any
You meet with boldly: Ile not be far off,
T'assist you, and protect you.

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: O brave officer.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: Would every ward had one but so well given,
And we would watch for rug, in gownes of velvet.

speeches.speaker: Mend.
verse: Stand close: a prize.

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: Satten, and gold Lace, Lads.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Why do'st thou hang upon me?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: 'Tis so darke
I dare not see my way: for heaven sake father
Let us go home.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: No, ev'n here wee'l leave you:
Let's run away from him, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Oh 'las.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Thou hast made me mad: and I wil beat thee dead
Then bray the in a morter, and now mold thee
But I wil alter thee.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: 'Twill never be:
He has bin three dayes practising to drink,
Yet still he sips, like to a waiting woman,
And looks as he were murdring of a fart
Among wild Irish swaggerers.

speeches.speaker: Luc
verse: I have still
Your good word, Zancho, father.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Milk-sop coward;
No house of mine receives thee: I disclam thee,
Thy mother; on her knees shall not entreat me
Hereafter to acknowledge thee.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Pray you speak for me.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: I would; but now I cannot with mine honour.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Ther's only one course left, that may redeem thee,
Which is, to strike the next man that you meet,
And if we chance to light upon a woman,
Take her away, and use her like a man,
Or I wil cut thy hamstrings.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: This makes for us

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: What do'st thou do now?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Sir, I am saying my prayers;
For being to undertake what you would have me,
I know I cannot live.

speeches.speaker: Lam
verse: Madam, I fear
You'l wish you had usd your coach: your brothers house
Is yet far off.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: The better sir: this walk
Will help digestion after your great supper,
Of which I have fed largely.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: To your task,
Or els you know what followes:

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I am dying:
Now Lord have mercy on me: by your favour,
Sir I must strike you.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: For what cause?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I know not:
And I must likewise talke with that young Lady,
An houre in private.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: What you must, is doubtfull,
But I am certain sir, I must beat you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Help, help.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Not strik againe?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How, Alvarez?

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: This for my Lord Vitell's love.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: Break out,
And like true theeves, make pray on either side,
But seem to help the stranger.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Oh my Lord,
They have beat him on his knees.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Though I want courage:
I yet have a sons duty in me, and
Compassion of a fathers danger; that,
That wholy now possesses me.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Lucio.
This is beyond my hope.

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: So Lazarillo,
Take up all boy: well done.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: And now steale off
Closely, and cunningly.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: How? have I found you?
Why Gentlemen, are you madde, to make your selves
A prey to Rogues?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Would we were off.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Theeves, theeves.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Defer our own contention: and down with them.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Ile make you sure.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Now he playes the Devil.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: This place is not for me.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Ile follow her
Half of my pennance is past ore.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: What noyse?
What tumult's there? keep the Kings peace I charge you.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: I am glad he's come yet.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: O, you keep good Guard
Upon the City, when men of our ranck
Are set upon in the streetes.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: The assistance
Shall heare os't be assur'd.

speeches.speaker: An.
verse: And if he be
That carefull Governour he is reported,
You will smart for it.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Patience, good Signiours:
Let me survey the Rascals: O, I know them,
And thank you for them: they are pillfring rogues
Of Andaluzia, that have perus'd
All Prisons in Castile: I dare not trust
The dungeon with them: no, ile have them home
To my own house.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: We had rather go to prison.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Had you so dog-holts? yes, I know you had:
You there would use your cunning fingers on
The simple locks; you would: but ile prevent you.

speeches.speaker: Lam
verse: My Mistris lost? good night.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Your Son's gon to,
What should become of him?

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Come of him, what will:
Now he dares fight, I care not: i'le to bed:
Look to your prisoners Alguazier.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Al's cleer'd:
Droop not for one disaster: let us hug,
And triumph in our knaveries.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: This confirmes
What was reported of him.

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: 'Twas done bravely.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: I must a little glory in the meanes
We officers have, to play the Knaves, and safely:
How we breake through the toyles, pitch'd by the Law,
Yet hang up them that are far lesse delinquents:
A simple shopkeeper's carted for a baud
For lodging (though unwittingly) a smock-Gamster:
Where, with rewards, and credit I have kept
Malroda in my house, as in a cloyster,
Without taint, or suspition.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: But suppose
The Governour should know't?

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: He? good Gentleman,
Let him perplex himself with prying into
The measures in the market, and th'abuses
The day stands guilty of: the pillage of the night
Is only mine, mine own feesimple;
Which you shall hold from me, tennants at will,
And pay no rent for't.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: Admirable Landlord.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Now wee'l go search the taverns, commit such
As we finde drinking: and be drunk our selves
With what we take from them: these silly wretches
Whom I for forme sake only have brought hither
Shall watch without, and guard us.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: And we wil.
See you sase lodg'd, most worthy Alguazier,
With all of you his comrads.

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: Tis the Governour.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: We are betray'd?

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: My guard there: bind them fast:
How men in high place, and authority
Are in their lives and estimation wrong'd
By their subordinate Ministers? yet such
They cannot but imploy: wrong'd justice finding
Scarce one true servant in ten officers.
'T'xpostulate with you, were but to delay
Your crimes due punishment, which shall fall upon you
So speedily, and severely, that it shall
Fright others by th'example: and confirme
How ever corrupt officers may disgrace
Themselves, 'tis not in them to wrong their place.
Bring them away.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: Wee'l suffer nobly yet,
And like to Spanish Gallants.

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: And wee'l hang so.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: I have no stomach to it: but i'le endeavour.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Nay you are rude; pray you forbeare; your offer now
More then the breeding of a Gentleman
Can give you warrant for.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Tis but to kisse you,
And think not ile receive that for a favour
Which was enjoyn'd me for a pennance, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: You have met a gentle confessor, and for once
(So men you wil rest satisfied) I vouchsafe it.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Rest satisfide with a kisse? why can a man
Desire more from a woman? is there any
Pleasure beyond it? may I never live
If I know what it is.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Sweet Innocence.

speeches.speaker: Luc
verse: VVhat strange new motions do I feele? my veines
Burn with an unknown fire: in every part
I suffer alteration: I am poysond,
Yet languish with desire againe to taste it,
So sweetly it works on me.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: I ne'r saw
A lovely man, till now.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: How can this be?
She is a wom^n, as my mother is,
And her I have kiss'd often, and brought off
My lips unscortch'd; yours are more lovelie, Lady,
And so should be lesse hurtfull: pray you vouchsafe
Your hand, to quench the heat tane from your Lip,
Perhaps that may restore me.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: VVillinglie.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: The flame increases: if to touch you, burne thus,
VVhat would more strict embraces do? I know not,
And yet methinks to die so; were to ascend
To Heaven, through Paradise.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: I am wounded too,
Though modesty forbids that I should speake
VVhat ignorance makes him bold in: why do you fix
Your eyes so stronglie on me?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Pray you stand still,
There is nothing els, that is worth the looking on:
I could adore you, Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Can you love mee?

speeches.speaker: Luo.
verse: To waite on you, in your chamber, and but touch
VVhat you, by wearing it, have made divine,
Were such a happinesse. I am resov'd,
Ile sell my libertie to you for this glove,
And write my selfe your slave.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: On easier termes,
Receive it as a friend.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How! giving favour!
I'le have it with his heart.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: VVhat will you doe?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: As you are mercifull, take my life rather.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: VVill you depart with't so?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Do's that grieve you?

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: I know not: but even now you appeare valiant.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Twas to preserve my father: in his cause
I could be so again.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Not in your own? Kneel to thy rivall and thine enemy?
Away unworthy creature, I begin
To hate my selfe, for giving entrance to
A good opinion of thee: For thy torment,
If my poore beauty be of any power,
Mayst thou doat on it desperately: but never
Presume to hope for grace, till thou recover
And weare the favour that was ravish'd from thee.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: He weares my head to then.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Poore foole, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: My womanish soul, which hitherto hath governd
This coward flesh, I feele departing from me;
And in me by her beauty is inspir'd
A new, and masculine one: instructing me
What's fit to doe or suffer; powerfull love
That hast with loud, and yet a pleasing thunder
Rous'd sleeping manhood in me, thy new creature,
Perfect thy worke so that I may make known
Nature (though long kept back) wil have her owne.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Can it be possible, that in six short houres
The subiect still the same, so many habits
Should be remov'd? or this new Lucio, he
That yesternight was baffeld and disgrac'd,
And thankt the man that did it, that then kneeld
And blubberd like a woman, should now dare
One terme of honour seeke reparation
For what he then appear'd not capable of?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Such miracles, men that dare doe injuries
Live to their shames to see, and for punishment
And scourge to their proud follies.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Prethee leave me:
Had I my Page, or foot-man here to flesh thee,
I durst the better heare thee.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: This scorn needs not:
And offer such no more.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Why say I should,
You'l not be angry?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Indeed I think I shal,
Would you vouchsafe to shew your selfe a Captaine,
And lead a little further, to some place
That's lesse frequented.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: He looks pale.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: If not,
Make use of this.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: There's anger in his eyes too:
His gesture, voyce, behaviour, all new fashion'd;
Wel, if it does endure in act the triall
Of what in show it promises to make good,
~lysses Cyclops, Io's transformation,
Eurydice fetcht from Hell, with all the rest
Of Ovids Fables, ile put in your Creed;
And for proofe, all incredible things may be
Writ down that Lucio, the coward Lucio,
The womanish Lucio fought.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: and Lamorall,
The stil imployd great duellist Lamorall.
Took his life from him.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Twill not come to that sure:
Methinks the onely drawing of my Sword
Should fright that confidence.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: It confirmes it rather.
To make which good, know you stand now oppos'd
By one that is your Rivall, one that wishes
Your name and title greater, to raise his;
The wrong you did, lesse pardonable then it is,
But your strength to defend it, more then ever
It was when justice friended it. The Lady
For whom we now contend, Genevora
Of more desert, (if such incomparable beauty
Could suffer an addition) your love
To Don Vitelli multipli'd, and your hate
Aagainst my father and his house increas'd;
And lastly, that the Glove which you there wear,
To my dishonour, (which I must force from you)
Were deerer to you then your life.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You'l finde
It is, and so ile guard it:

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: All these meet then
With the black infamy, to be foyld by one
That's not allowd a man: to help your valour,
That falling by your hand, I may, or die,
Or win in this one single opposition
My Mistris, and such honour as I may
Inrich my fathers Armes with.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Tis said Nobly;
My life with them are at the stake.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: At all then.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: She's yours: this, and my life, to follow your fortune;
And give not onely back that part the looser
Scorns to accept of —

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: My poor life,
Which do not leave me as a further torment,
Having dispoild me of my Sword, mine honour,
Hope of my Ladies grace, fame, and all else
That made it worth the keeping.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I take back
No more from you, then what you forc'd from me;
And with a worser title: yet think not
That Ile dispute this, as made insolent
By my successe, but as one equall with you,
If so you wil accept me; that new courage,
Or call it fortune if you please, that is
Confer'd upon me by the onely sight
Of fair Genevora, was not bestow'd on me
To bloody purposes: nor did her command
Deprive me of the happinesse to see her
But till I did redeem her favour from you;
Which onely I rejoyce in, and share with you
In all you suffer else.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: This curtesie
Wounds deeper then your Sword can, or mine owne;
Pray you make use of either, and dispatch me.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: The barbarous Turke is satisfied with spoile;
And shall I, being possest of what I came for,
Prove the more Infidell?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You were better be so,
Then publish my disgrace, as tis the custome,
And which I must expect.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Judge better on me:
I have no tongue to trumpet mine owne praise
To your dishonour: tis a bastard courage
That seekes a name out that way, no true born one;
Pray you be comforted, for by all goodnesse
But to her vertuous selfe, the best part of it,
I never wil discover on what termes
I came by these: which yet I take not from you,
But leave you in exchange of them, mine own,
With the desire of being a friend; which if
You wil not grant me, but on further triall
Of manhood in me, seeke me when you please,
(And though I might refuse it with mine honour)
Win them again, and weare them: so good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I nere knew what true valour was till now;
And have gain'd more by this disgrace, then all
The honours I have won: they made me proud,
Presumptuous of my fortune; a meere beast,
Fashion'd by them, onely to dare and doe:
Yeelding no reasons for my wilfull actions
But what I stuck on my Swords point, presuming
It was the best Revenew. How unequall
Wrongs wel maintain'd makes us to others, which
Ending with shame teach as to know our selves,
I wil think more on't.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Lamorall.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: My Lord?

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: I came to seeke you.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: And unwillingly;
You nere found me till now: your pleasure sir?

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: That which wil please thee friend: thy vowd love to me
Shall now be put in action: means is offer'd
To use thy good Sword for me; that which still
Thou wearst, as if it were a part of thee.
Where is it?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Tis changd for one more fortunate:
Pray you enquire not how.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Why, I nere thought
That there was musick int, but ascribe
The fortune of it to the arme.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Which is grown weaker too. I am not (in a word)
Worthy your friendship: I am one new vanquish'd,
Yet shame to tell by whom.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: But Ile tell thee
Gainst whom thou art to fight, and there redeeme
Thy honour lost, if there be any such:
The King, by my long suit, at length is pleas'd
That Alvarez and my self, with eithers Second,
Shall end the difference between our houses,
Which he accepts of I make choice of thee;
And where you speak of a disgrace, the means
To blot it out, by such a publique triall
Of thy approved valour, wil revive
Thy ancient courage. If you imbrace it, doe;
If not, Ile seeke some other.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: As I am
You may command me.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Spoke like that true friend
That loves not onely for his private end.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: This from Madona Clara?

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: Yes, and 't please you.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Alvarez daughter?

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: The same, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: She,
That sav'd my brothers life?

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: You are still in the right,
She wil'd me wait your walking forth: and knowing
How necessary a discreet wise man
Was in a businesse of such weight, she pleas'd
To think on me: it may be in my face
Your Ladiship not acquainted with my wisdome
Finds no such matter: what I am, I am;
Thought's free: and think you what you please.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Tis strange,

speeches.speaker: Bob.
verse: That I should be wise, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: No, thou art so;
There's for thy paines: and prethee tell thy Lady
I wil not faile to meet her: Ile receive
Thy thanks and duty in thy present absence:
Farewell, farewel, I say, now thou art wise.
She writes here, she hath something to impart
That may concerne my brothers life; I know not,
But generall fame does give her out so worthy,
That I dare not suspect her: yet wish Lucio
Were Master of her mind: but fie upon't;
Why do I think on him? see, I am punish'd for it,
In his unlookd for presence: Now I must
Endure another tedious piece of Courtship,
Would make one forsweare curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Gracious Madam,
The sorrow paid for your just anger towards me
Arising from my weaknesse, I presume
To presse into your presence, and dispaire not
An easie pardon.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: He speaks sende: oh strange.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: And yet believe, that no desire of mine,
Though all are too strong in me, had the power
For their delight, to force me to iufringe
What you commanded, it being in your part
To lessen your great rigour when you please,
And mine to suffer wirh an humble patience
What you'l impose upon it.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Courtly too.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Yet hath the poore, and contemn'd Lucio, Madam,
(Made able onely by his hope to serve you)
Recover'd what with violence, not justice,
Was taken from him: and here at your feet
With these, he could have laid the conquer'd head
Of Lamorall (tis all I say of him)
For rudely touching that, which as a relique
I ever would have worship'd, since twas yours.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Valiant, and every thing a Lady could
Wish in her servant.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: All that's good in me,
That heavenly love, the opposite to base lust,
Which would have all men worthy, hath created;
Which being by your beames of beauty form'd,
Cherish as your own creature.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: I am gone
Too far now to dissemble: rise, or sure
I must kneele with you too: let this one kisse
Speake the rest for me: tis too much I doe,
And yet, if chastity would, I could wish more.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: In overjoying me, you are grown sad;
What is it Madam? by—
There's nothing that's within my nerves (and yet
Favour'd by you, I should as much as man)
But when you please, now or on all occasions
You can think of hereafter, but you may
Dispose of at your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: If you breake
That oath again, you lost me. Yet so wel
I love you, I shall never put you to't;
And yet forget it not: rest satisfied
With that you have receiv'd now: there are eyes
May be upon us, till the difference
Between our friends are ended: I would not
Be seen so private with you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I obey you.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: But let me heare oft from you, and remember
I am Vitellies sister.

speeches.speaker: Luc:
verse: What's that Madam?

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Nay nothing, fare you well: who feeles loves fire,
Would ever aske to have means to desire.

speeches.speaker: Assis.
verse: Are they come in?

speeches.speaker: Har.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Assis.
verse: Read the Proclamation,
That all the people here assembled may
Have satisfaction, what the Kings deere love,
In care of the Republique, hath ordained;
Attend with silence: read aloud.

speeches.speaker: Herald
prose:
FOrasmuch as our high and mighty Master, Philip, the potent and most Catholique King of Spaine, hath not onely in his own Royall person, been long, and often sollicited, and grieved, with the deadly and uncurable hatred, sprung up betwixt the two ancient and most honourably discended Houses of these his two deerely and equally beloved Subjects, Don Ferdinando de Alrarez, and Don Pedro de Vitelli: (all which in vaine his Majesty hath often endeavoured to reconcile and qualifie:) But that also through the debates, quarrels, and outrages daily arising, falling, and flowing from these great heads, his publique civill Government is seditiously and barbarously molested and wounded, and many of his chiefe Gentry (no lesse tender to his Royall Majesty then the very branches of his own sacred blood) spoyld, lost, and submerged, in the impious inundation and torrent of their still-growing malice: It hath therefore pleased His sacred Majesty, out of His infinite affection to preserve his Common-wealth, and generall peace, from farther violation, (as a sweet and heartily loving father of his people) and on the earnest petitions of these Arch-enemies, to Order, and Ordaine, That they be ready, each with his wel-chosen and beloved friend, arm'd at all points like Gentlemen, in the Castle of St. Jago, on this present Munday morning betwixt eight and nine of the clocke; where (before the combatants be allowed to commence this granted Duell) This to be read aloud for the publique satisfaction of his Majesties welbeloved Subjects.

'Save the King.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Hark how their Drums speak their insatiate thirst
Of blood, and stop their eares 'gainst pious peace,
Who gently whispering, implores their friendship?

speeches.speaker: Assis.
verse: Kings, nor authority can master fate;
Admit 'em then, and blood extinguish hate.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Stay, yet be pleasd to think, and let not daring
Wherein men nowadaies exceed even beasts,
And think themselves not men else, so transport you
Beyond the bounds of Christianity:
Lord Alvarez, Vitelli, Gentlemen,
No Town in Spaine, from our Metropolis
Unto the rudest hovell, but is great
With your assured valours daily proofes:
Oh wil you then, for a superfluous fame,
A sound of honour, which in these times, all
Like heretiques professe (with obstinacy)
But most erroneously, venture your soules,
Tis a hard tasque, thorough a Sea of blood
To saile, and land at Heaven?

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: I hope not
If justice be my Pilot: but my Lord,
You know, if argument, or time, or love,
Could reconcile, long since we had shook hands;
I dare protest, your breath cooles not a veine
In any one of us, but blowes the fire
Which nought but blood reciprocall can quench.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Vitelli, thou sayst bravely, and sayst right,
And I wil kill thee for't, I love thee so.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Ha, ha, old man: upon thy death Ile build
A story (with this arme) for thy old wife
To tell thy daughter Clara seven yeeres hence
As she sits weeping by a wintet fire,
How such a time Vitelli slew her husband
With the same Sword his daughter favour'd him,
And lives, and weares it yet: Come Lamorall,
Redeeme thy selfe.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Lucio, Genevora
Shall on this Sword receive thy bleeding heart,
For my presented hat, laid at her feet.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Thou talkst wel Lamorall, but tis thy head
That I wil carry to her to thy hat:
Fie father, I do coole too much.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Oh boy:
Thy fathers true sonne:
Beat Drums,—and so good morrow to your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Brave resolutions.

speeches.speaker: Anast.
verse: Brave, and Spanish right.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Lucio.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Vitelli.

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: Alvarez.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: How the devill
Got these Cats into th' gutter? my pusse too?

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: Heare us.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: We must be heard.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: We will be heard
Vitelli; looke, see Clara on her knees
Imploring thy compassion: Heaven, how sternly
They dart their emulous eyes, as if each scorn'd
To be behind the other in a look!
Mother, death needs no Sword here: oh my sister
(Fate faine would have it so) perswade, entreat,
A Ladies teares are silent Orators
(Or should be so at least) to move beyond
The honest tongu'd-Rethoritian:
Why will you fight? why do's an uncles death
Twentie yeare old, exceed your love to me
But twentie daies? whose forc'd cause, and faire manner
You could not understand, onely have heard.
Custome, that wrought so cunningly on nature
In me, that I forgot my sex, and knew not
Whether my body femall were, or male,
You did unweave, and had the power to charme
A new creation in me, made me feare
To think on those deeds I did perpetrate,
How little power though you allow to me
That cannot with my sighes, my teares, my prayers
Move you from your own losse, if you shoule gaine.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: I must forget you Clara, 'till I have
Redeem'd my uncles blood, that brands my face
Like a pestiferous Carbuncle: I am blinde
To what you doe: deafe to your cries: and Marble
To all impulsive exorations.
When on this point, I have pearch'd thy fathers soule,
Ile tender thee this bloody reeking hand
Drawne forth the bowels of that murtherer:
If thou canst love me then, i'le marry thee,
And for thy father lost, get thee a Sonne;
On no condition else.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Most barbarous.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Savage.

speeches.speaker: Anast.
verse: Irreligious.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Oh Lucio!
Be thou more mercifull: thou bear'st fewer yeers,
Art lately wean'd from soft effeminacy,
A maidens manners, and a maidens heart
Are neighbours still to thee: be then more milde,
Proceed not to this combat; bee'st thou desperate
Of thine owne life? yet (deerest) pitty mine
Thy valour's not thine owne, I gave it thee,
These eyes begot it, this tongue bred it up,
This breast would lodge it: doe not use my gifts
To mine own ruine: I have made thee rich,
Be not so thanklesse, to undoe me for't.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Mistresse, you know I doe not weare a vaine.
I would not rip for you, to doe you service:
Life's but a word, a shadow, a melting dreame,
Compar'd to essentiall, and eternall honour.
Why, would you have me value it beyond
Your brother: if I first cast down my sword
May all my body here, be made one wound,
And yet my soule not finde heaven thorough it.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: You would be catter-walling too, but peace,
Goe, get you home, and provide dinner for
Your Sonne, and me: we'l be exceeding merry:
Oh Lucio, I will have thee cock of all
The proud Vitellies that doe live in Sprine:
Fie, we shall take cold: hunch:— I am hoarse
Already.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How your Sister whets my spleene!
I could eate Lucio now:

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Lamorall: you have often sworne
You'ld be commanded by me.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Vitelli, Brother,
Ev'n for your Fathers soule, your uncles blood,
As you doe love my life: but last, and most
As you respect your own Honour, and Fame,
Throw downe your sword; he is most valiant
That herein yeelds first.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Peace, you foole.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Why Lucio,
Doe thou begin; 'tis no disparagement:
He's elder, and thy better, and thy valour
Is in his infancy.

speeches.speaker: Gen
verse: Or pay it me,
To whom thou ow'st it: Oh, that constant time
Would but goe back a week, then Lucio
Thou would'st not dare to fight.

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: Lucio, thy Mother,
Thy Mother beggs it: throw thy sword down first.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Ile throw his head downe after then.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Lamorall.
You have often swore you'ld be commanded by me.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Never to this: your spight, and scorn Genevora,
H'as lost all power in me:

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: Your hearing for six words.

speeches.speaker: Ass.
verse: Say. An. Strange obstinacy!

speeches.speaker: Al. Vit. Lu. Lam.
verse: We'l stay no longer.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Then by thy oath Vitelli,
Thy dreadfull oath, thou wouldst returne that sword
When I should aske it, give it to me, now,
This instant I require it.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: By thy vow,
As dreadfull, Lucio, to obey my will
In any one thing I would watch to challenge,
I charge thee not to strike a stroake: now he
Of our two brothers that loves perjurie
Best, and dares first be damn'd, infringe his vow.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: Excellent Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Pish you tyrannize.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: We did equivocate.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: On.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Then Lucio,
So well I love my husband, for he is so,
(wanting but ceremony) that I pray
His vengefull sword may fall upon thy head
succesfully for false-hood to his Sister.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: I likewise pray (Vitelli) Lucio's sword
(who equally is my husband, as thou hers)
May finde thy false heart, that durst gage thy faith,
And durst not keepe it.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Are you men, or stone.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Men, and we'l prove it with our swords:

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: Your hearing for six words, and we have done,
Zancho come forth—we'l fight our challenge too:
Now speake your resolutions.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: These they are,
The first blow given betwixt you, sheathes these swords
In one anothers bosomes.

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: And rogue, looke
You at that instant doe discharge that Pistoll
Into my breast: if you start back, or quake,
Ile stick you like a Pigge.

speeches.speaker: A^v.
verse: — hold: you are mad.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: This we said: and by our hope of bliffe
This we will doe: speake your intents.

speeches.speaker: Cla. Gen.
verse: Strike.

speeches.speaker: Eug.
verse: Shoot.

speeches.speaker: Al.
verse: Vit. Lu. La. Hold, hold: all friends.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Come downe.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: These devillish women
Can make men friends and enemies when they list.

speeches.speaker: Say.
verse: A gallant undertaking and a happie;
Why this is noble in you: and will be
A well comer present to our Master Philip
Then the returne from his Indies.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Father your blessing.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Take her: if he bring not
Betwixt you, boyes that will finde out new worlds,
And win 'em too I'm a false Prophet.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Brother.
There is a Sister: long divided streames
Mix now at length, by fate.

speeches.speaker: Bob.
prose: I am not regarded: I was the carefull Steward that provided these Instruments of peace, I put the longest weapon in your Sisters hand, (my Lord) because she was the shortest Lady: For likely the shortest Ladies, love the longest—men: And for mine own part, I could have discharged it: my Pistoll is no ordinary Pistoll, it has two ramming Bullets; but thought I, why should I shoot my two bullets into my old Lady? if they had gon, I would not have staid long after: I would ev'n have died too, bravely y'faith, like a Roman-Steward: hung my selfe in mine owne Chaine; and there had been a story of Bobadilla, Spindola, Zancho, for after ages to lament: hum: I perceive I am not onely not regarded, but also not rewarded.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Prethee peace: 'shalt have a new chaine, next
Saint Iaques day, or this new gilt:

speeches.speaker: Bob.
prose: I am satisfied: let vertue have her due: And yet i am melancholy upon this atonement: pray heaven the State rue it not: I would my Lord Vitellies Steward, and I could meet: they should finde it should cost 'em a little more to make us friends: well, I will forsweare wine, and women for a yeere: and then I will be drunk to morrow, and runne a whoring like a dogge with a broken bottle at's taile; then will I repent next day, and forsweare 'em againe more vehemently: be for-sworne next day againe, and repent my repentance: for thus a melancholy Gentleman doth, and ought to live.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Nay, you shall dine with me: and afterward
Ile with 'ye to the King: But first, I will
Dispatch the Castles businesse, that this day
May be compleat. Bring forth the malefactors.
You Alguazier, the Ringleader of these
Poore fellowes, are degraded from your office,
You must restore all stolne goods you receiv'd,
And watch a twelve moneth without any pay:
This, if you faile of, (all your goods confiscate)
You are to be whipt, and sent into the Gallies.

speeches.speaker: Alg.
verse: I like all, but restoring that Catholique doctrine
I doe dislike: Learn all ye officers
By this to live uprightly (if you can)

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: You Cobler, to translate your manners new,
Are doom'd to th' Cloyster of the Mendicants,
With this your brother; botcher there, for nothing
To cobble, and heel hose for the poor Friers,
Till they allow your pennance for sufficient,
And your amendment; then you shall be freed,
And may set up againe,

speeches.speaker: Pach.
verse: Mendoza, come.
Our soules have trod awry, in all mens sight,
We'l underlay 'em, till they goe upright.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Smith, in those shackles you for your hard heart
Must lye by th'heeles a yeer.

speeches.speaker: Met.
verse: I have shod your horse, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Away: for you, my hungry white-loaf'd face,
You must to th' Gallies, where you shall be sure
To have no more bits, then you shall have blowes.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Well, though herrings want, I shall have rowes.

speeches.speaker: Assist.
verse: Signior, you have prevented us, and punish'd
Your selfe severeller then we would have done.
You have married a whore: may she prove honest.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: 'Tis better my Lord, then to marry an honest woman
That may prove a whore.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: 'Tis a hansome wench: and thou canst keepe her tame:
Ile send you what I promis'd.

speeches.speaker: Pio.
verse: Ioy to your Lordships.

speeches.speaker: Alv.
verse: Here may all Ladies learne, to make of foes
The perfect'st friends: and not the perfect'st foes
Of deerest friends, as some doe now a dayes.

speeches.speaker: Vit.
verse: Behold the power of love, to nature lost
By custome irrecoverably, past the hope
Of friends restoring, love hath here retriv'd
To her own habit, made her blush to see
Her so long monstrous metamorphoses,
May strange affaires never have worse successe.

speeches.speaker: Ame.
prose: MOrrow my Lord of Orleance.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: You salute me like a stranger; brother Orleance were to me a Title more belonging, whom you call the husband of your sister.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Would the circumstances of your brotherhood had never offer'd cause to make our conversation lesse familiar: I meet you like a hinderance in your way: your great law suit is now upon the tongue, and ready for a judgement.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Came you from the Hall now?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Without stay; the Court is full, and such a presse of people does attend the issue, as if some great man were brought to his araignment.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Every mothers sonne of all that multitude of hearers went to be a witnesse of the misery your sisters fortunes must have come to, if my adversary who did love her first, had been her husband.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: The successe may draw a testimony from them to confirme the same opinion, but they went prepar'd with no such hope or purpose.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: And did you intreat, the number of them that are come with no such hope or purpose.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Tush, your own experience of my heart can answer ye.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: This doubtfull, makes me clearly understand your disposition.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: If your cause be just,
I wish you a conclusion like your cause.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: I can have any common charity to such a prayer
From a friend I would expect a love to prosper in;
Without exceptions such a love as might
Make all my under takings thankfull to't;
Precisely just is seldome faithfull in our wishes
To another mans desires: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Here comes your adversaries brother in law.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: The Lord of Amiens.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: From the Hall I thinke.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I did so: save your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: That's a wish my Lord, as courteous to my present state,
As ever honest mind was thankfull for;
For now my safety must expose it selfe
To question: yet to look for any free
Or hearty salutation (sir from you)
Would be unreasonable in me.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Your sister is my adversaries wife;
That neernesse needs must consequently draw
Your inclination to him.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I will grant
Him all the neernesse his alliance claimes,
And yet be nothing lesse impartiall
My Lord of Montague.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Lord of Montague yet:
But (sir) how long the dignity or state
Belonging to it will continue, stands
Upon the dangerous passage of this houre,
Either for ever more to be confirm'd,
Or like the time wherein twas pleaded, gone:
Gone with it, never to be call'd again.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Justice direct your processe to the end;
To both your persons my respect shall stil
Be equall; but the righteous cause is that
Which bears my wishes to the side it holds,
Where, ^ver may it prosper.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then my thanks
Are proper to you, if a man may raise
A confidence upon a lawfull ground
I have no reason to be once perplexed
With any doubtfull motion, Longueville,
That Lord of Amiens, (didst observe him?) has
A worthy nature in him.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Either tis his nature or his cunning.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: That's the vizard of most mens actions,
Whose dissembled lives
Do carry onely the similitude
Of goodnesse on 'em, but for him
Honest behaviour makes a true report,
What disposition does inhabit him,
Essentiall vertue.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Then tis pitty that
Injurious Orleance is his brother.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: He is but his brother in law.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Law? that's as bad.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: How is your Law as bad? I rather wish
The hangman thy executor then that
Equivocation should be ominous.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Some of your Lawyers.—

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: What is ominous?

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: Let no distrust trouble your Lordships thought.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: The evidences of your question'd land
Ha' not much as any literall
Advantage in 'em to be made against
Your title.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: And your Councell understands
The businesse fully.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: Th'are industrious, just.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: And very confident.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: Your state endures
A voluntary tryall; like a man
Whose honours are maliciously accus'd.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: The Accusation serves to cleare his cause.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: And to approve his truth more.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: So shall all
Your adversaries pleadings strengthen your
Possession.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: And be set upon record
To witnesse the hereditary right
Of you and yours.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: Courage, you have the law.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And you the profits.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: If discouragement
Could worke upon me, your assurances
Would put me strongly into heart again;
But I was never fearfull: and let fate
Deceive my expectation, yet I am
Prepared against dejection.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: So are we.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
verse: We have received a comfortable hope
That all will speed well.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: What is he Duboys?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: A Creditor.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I thought so, for he speaks
As if he were a partner in his state.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Sir, I am largely indebted to your loves.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: More to their purses.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Which you shall not lose.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Your Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: That's another creditor.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Has interest in me.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: You have more of him.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: And I have had so many promises
From these and all your learned Councellors,
How certainly your cause wil prosper: that—

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: You brought no Serjeants with you?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: To attend his ill successe.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Good sir, I will not be
Unthankfull either to their industries
Or your affections.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: All your land (my Lord)
Is at the bar now, give me but ten Crowns
Ile save you harmlesse.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Take him at his word;
If he does lose, you're sav'd by miracle,
For I never knew a lawyer yet undone.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: Then now you shall sir, if this prospers not.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Sir, I beseech you doe not force your voyce
To such a loudnesse, but be thrifty now;
Preserve it till you come to plead at bar
It wil be much more profitable in
The satisfaction then the promise.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: Is not this a satisfaction to engage
My selfe for this assurance, if he—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: No sir, my ruine never shall import
Anothers losse, if not by accident,
And that my purpose is not guilty of:
You are engaged in nothing but your care.
Attend the Procurator to the Court,
Observe how things incline, and bring me word.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I dare not sir; if I be taken there,
Mine eares will be in danger.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why? hast thou
Committed something that deserves thine eares?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: No, but I feare the noyse; my hearing will be
Perished by the noise; tis as good 't want
A member, as to loose the use —

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: The ornament is excepted.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Well my Lord
Ile put 'em to the hazzard.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Your desires be prosperous to you.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
verse: Our best prayers waite
Upon your fortune.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: For your selves, not him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Thou canst not blame 'em: I am in their debts.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: But had your large expence (a part whereof
You owe 'em) for unprofitable Silkes
And Laces, been bestowed among the poore,
That would have prayd the right way for you:
Not upon you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: For unprofitable Silkes
And Laces? now believe me honest boy
Th'ast hit upon a reprehension that belongs
Unto me.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: By—my Lord,
I had not so unmannerly a thought,
To reprehend you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why I love thee for't.
Mine own acknowledgement confirmes thy words:
For once I do remember, comming from
The Mercers, where my Purse had spent it selfe
On those unprofitable toyes thou speakst of,
A man halfe naked with his poverty
Did meet me, and requested my reliefe:
I wanted whence to give it, yet his eyes
Spoke for him, those I could have satisfied
With some unfruitfull sorrow, (if my teares
Would not have added rather to his griefe,
Then eas'd it) but the true compassion that
I should have given I had not: this began
To make me think how many such mens wants
The vaine superfluous cost I wore upon
My outside would have clothed, and left my selfe
A habit as becomming: to encrease
This new consideration there came one
Clad in a garment plaine and thrifty, yet
As decent as these faire deare follies; made
As if it were of purpose to despise
The vanity of show: his purse had still
The power to doe a charitable deed,
And did it.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Yet your inclination, sir,
Deservd no lesse to be commended, then his action.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Prethee do not flatter me;
He that intends well, yet deprives himselfe
Of means to put his good thoughts into deed,
Deceives his purpose of the due reward
That goodnesse merits: O antiquity
Thy great examples of Nobility
Are out of imitation, or at least
So lamely follow'd, that thou art as much
Before this age in vertue, as in time.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Sir, it must needs be lamely followed, when
The chiefest men love to follow it
Are for the most part cripples.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Who are they?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Souldiers, my Lord, souldiers.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Tis true Duboys: but if the Law disables me no more
For Noble actions, then good purposes,
Ile practice how to exercise the worth
Commended to us by our ancestors;
The poore neglected souldier shall command
Me from a Ladies Courtship, and the forme
Ile study shall no more be taught me by
The Taylor, but the Scholler; that expence
Which hitherro has been to entertaine
Th' intemperate pride and pleasure of the taste
Shall fill my Table more to satisfie,
And lesse to surfeit.
What an honest worke it would be; when we finde
A Virgin in her poverty, and youth
Inclining to be tempted, to imploy
As much perswasion, and as much expence
To keep her upright as men use to do upon her falling.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Tis charity that many mayds wil be unthankful for,
And some will rather take it for a wrong,
To buy 'em out of their inheritance,
The thing that they were born to.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Longueville thou bringst a cheerfull promise in thy face.
There stands no pale report upon thy cheeke,
To give me feare or knowledge of my losse, tis red and lively.
How proceeds my suit?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: That's with labour sir, a labour that to those of Hercules
May adde another; or (at least) be cald
A imitation of this burning shirt:
For twas a paine of that unmercifull
Perplexity, to shoulder through the throng
Of people that attended your successe:
My sweaty linnen fixt upon my skin,
Still as they puld me, tooke that with it; 'twas
A feare I should have left my flesh among 'em:
Yet I was patient, for (me thought) the toyle
Might be an emblem of the difficult
And weary passage to get out of Law.
And to make up the deare similitude,
When I was forth seeking my handkircher
To wipe my sweat off, I did finde a cause
To make me sweat more, for my Purse was lost
Among their finger.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: There twas rather found.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: By them.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I mean so.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Well, I will restore
Thy dammage to thee: how proceeds my suit?

speeches.speaker: Lang.
verse: Like one at Brokers; I thinke forfeited.
Your promising councell at the first
Put strongly forward with a labour'd speed,
And such a violence of pleading, that
His fee in Sugar-candie scarce will make
His throat a satisfaction for the hurt
He did it, and he carried the whole cause
Before him with so cleare a passage, that
The people in the favour of your side
Cried Montague, Montague: in the spight of him
That cryed out silence, and began to laugh
Your adversaries Advocate to scorn:
Who like a cunning foot-man? set me forth
With such a temperate easie kind of course
To put him into exercise of strength,
And follow'd his advantages so close,
That when your hot mouthed pleader thought 'had wonne,
Before he reacht it, he was out of breath,
And then the other stript him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So all is lost.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: But how I know not; for (me thought) I stood
Confounded with the clamour of the Court,
Like one embarqued upon a storm at Sea,
Where the tempestuous noise of Thunder mixt
With roaring of the billows, and the thick
Imperfect language of the Sea-men, takes
His understanding and his safety both
Together from him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Thou dost bring ill news

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Of what I was unwilling to have been
The first reporter.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Didst observe no more?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: At least no better.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then th' art not inform'd
So well as I am; I can tell thee that
Will please thee, for when all else left my cause,
My very adversaries tooke my part.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: —whosoever told you that abused you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Credit me, he took my part
When all forsook me.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Took it from you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes I meane so, and I think he had just cause
To take it when the verdict gave it him.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: His Spirit would ha' sunke him, ere he could
Have carried an ill fortune of this waight so lightly.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Nothing is a misery unlesse our weaknesse apprehend it so;
We cannot be more faithfull to our selves
In any thing that's manly, then to make
Ill fortune as contemptible to us
As it makes us to others.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Here come they
Whose very countenances will tell you how
Contemptible it is to others.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: The sir of Knighthood may be given him, ere
They heare you now.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Good sir but a word.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: How soon the losse of wealth makes any man
Grow out of knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Let me see I pray sir,
Never stood you upon the pillory?

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: The Pillory?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: O now I know you did not.
Y'ave eares, I thought ye had lost 'em; pray observe,
Here's one that once was gracious in our eyes.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: O my Lord, have an eye upon him.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: But ha' you nere a Counsell to redeeme
His Land yet from the judgement?

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
verse: None but this, a writ of errour to remove the cause.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: No more of errour, we have been in that too much already.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
prose: If you will reverse the judgement, you must trust to that delay.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Delay? Indeed he's like to trust to that,
With you has any dealing.

speeches.speaker: 2 Law.
prose: Ere the Law proceeds to an habere facias possessionem.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: That's a language sir, I understand not.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Th'art a very strange unthankfull fellow to have taken Fees of such a liberall measure, and then give a man hard words for's money.

speeches.speaker: 1 Law.
verse: If men will hazzard their salvations,
What should I say? I've other businesse.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Y'are ith' right;
That's it you should say now prosperity has left me.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Have an eye upon him; if
We lose him now, he's gone for ever; stay
And dog him: Ile goe fetch the officers.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Dog him you blood-hound: by this point thou shalt more safely dog an angry Lion then attempt him.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Doe but steere to fetch a Serjeant; and (besides your losse
Of labour) Ile have you beaten, till
Those casements in your faces be false lights.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Falser then those you sell by.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Who gave you Commission to abuse my friends thus?

speeches.speaker: Lon.
verse: Sir, are those your friends that would betray you?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Tis to save themselves rather then betray me.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Your Lordship makes a just construction of it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
verse: All our desire is but to get our own.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Your wives desires and yours do differ then.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So far as my ability will goe
You shall have satisfaction Longeville,

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And leave your selfe neglected; every man
Is first a debtor to his own demands, being honest.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: As I take it sir, I did
Not entertaine you for my counsellor.

speeches.speaker: Ilong.
verse: Counsel's the office of a servant,
When the master fals upon a danger: as
Defence is never threaten with your eyes,
They are no cockatrices; do you heare?
Talke with a Girdler, or a Milner,
He can informe you of a kind of men
That first undid the profit of those trades
By bringing up the forme of carrying
There morglachs in their hands: with some of those
A man may make himselfe a priviledge
To aske a question at the prison gates,
Without your good permission.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
verse: By your leave.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Stay sir, what one example since the time
That first you put your hat off to me, have
You noted in me to encourage you
To this presumption? by the justice now
Of thine own rule, I should begin with thee,
I should turn thee away ungratified
For all thy former kindnesse, forget
Thou ever didst me any service: tis not feare
Of being arrested makes me thus incline
To satisfie you; for you see by him,
I lost not all defences with my state;
The curses of a man to whom I am
Beholding terrifie me more, then all
The violence he can pursue me with.
Duboys, I did prepare me for the worst;
These two small Cabinets doe comprehend
The sum of all the wealth that it hath pleased
Adversity to leave me, one as rich
As th' other, both in Jewels; take thou this,
And as the Order put within it shall
Direct thee, distribute it half between
Those Creditors, and th' other halfe among
My servants: for (sir) they are my creditors
As well as you are, they have trusted me
With their advancement: if the value faile,
To please you all, my first increase of meanes
Shall offer you a fuller payment; be content
To leave me something, and imagine that
You put a new beginner into credit.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
prose: So prosper our own blessings, as we wish you to your merit.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Are your silences of discontent, or of sorrow?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Sir, we would not leave you.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Do but suffer us to follow you, and what our present means, or industries hereafter can provide, shall serve you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: O desire me not to live
To such a basenesse, as to be maintained
By those that serve me; pray be gone, I wil
Defend your honesties to any man
That shal report you have forsaken me;
I pray be gone.
Why dost thou weep my boy,
Because I doe not bid thee goe too?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: No, I weep (my Lord) because I would not goe;
I feare you will command me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: No my child,
I wil not; that would discommend th'intent
Of all my other actions: thou art yet
Unable to advise thy selfe a course,
Should I put thee to seeke it; after that
I must excuse or at the least forgive
Any uncharitable deed that can be done against my selfe.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: Every day (my Lord) I tarry with you, Ile account
A day of blessing to me; for I shall
Have so much lesse time left me of my life
When I am from you: and if misery
Befall you (which I hope so good a man
Was never born to) I wil take my part,
And make my willingnesse increase my strength
To beare it. In the Winter I will spare
Mine own clothes from my selfe to cover you;
And in the Summer, carry some of yours
To ease you: Ile doe any thing I can.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why, thou art able to make misery
Ashamed of hurting, when thy weaknesse can
Both beare it, and despise it: Come my boy
I will provide some better way for thee
Then this thou speakst of; tis the comfort that
Ill fortune has undone me into the fashion:
For now in this age most men do begin,
To keep but one boy, that kept many men.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Where is she? call her.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I attend you sir.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Your friend sweet Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: What friend, good my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Your Montague, Madam, he will shortly want
Those Courtly graces that you love him for;
The means wherewith he purchased this, and this,
And all his own provisions to the least
Proportion of his feeding or his clothes,
Came out of that inheritance of land
Which he unjustly lived on: but the law
Has given me right in't, and possession; now
Thou shalt perceive his bravery vanish, as
This Jewell does from thee now, and these Pearles
To him that owes 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Ye are the owner sir of every thing that does belong to me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: No, not of him, sweet Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: O good God!

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: But in a while your mind will change, and be
As ready to disclaime him; when his wants
And miseries have perish'd his good face,
And taken off the sweetnesse that has made
Him pleasing in a womans understanding.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: O Heaven, how gratious had Creation been
To women, who are borne without defence,
If to our hearts there had been doores through which
Or husbands might have lookt into our thoughts,
And made themselves undoubtfull.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Made 'em madde.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: With honest women.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Thou dost stile pretend
A title to that vertue: prethee let
Thy honesty speak freelie to me now.
Thou knowest that Montaigue of whose Land
I am the master, did affect three first,
And should have had thee, if the strength of friends
Had not prevail'd above thine own consent.
I have undone him; tell me how thou doest
Consider his ill fortune and my good.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Ile tell you justly his iundoing is
An argument for pitty? and for teares
In all their dispositions that have known
The honour and the goodnesse of his life:
Yet that addition of prosperity,
Which you have got by't, no indifferent man
Will malice or repine at, if the Law
Be not abused in 't; howsoever since
You have the upper fortune of him, 'twill
Be some dishonour to you to beare your selfe
With any pride or glory over him.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: This may be truly spoken, but in thee
It is not honest.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Yes, so honest, that I care not if the chast Penelope
Were now alive to hear me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Who comes there?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: My brother.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Save yee.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Now sir, you have heard of prosperous Montague.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: No sir, I have heard of Montague,
But of your prosperity.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Is he distracted.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: He does beare his losse with such a noble strength
Of patience that,
Had fortune eyes to see him, she would weepe
For having hurt him, and pretending that
Shee did it but for triall of his worth:
Hereafter ever love him.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: I perceive you love him, and because (I must confesse)
He does deserve that though for some respects,
I have not given him that acknowledgement,
Yet in mine honour I did still conclude to use him nobly.

speeches.speaker: Am.
prose: Sir, that will become your reputation and make me grow proud of your alliance.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: I did reserve the doing of this friendship till I had
His fortunes at my mercy, that the world
May tell him 'tis a willing courtesie.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: This change wil make me happy.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Tis a change; thou shalt behold it, then observe me when
That Montague had possession of my Land,
I was his rivall, and at last obtain'd
This Lady who by promise of her own
Affection to him, should ha bin his wife;
I had her, and withheld her like a pawne,
