Till now my Land is rendred to me againe,
And since it is so, you shall see I have
The conscience not to keep her—give him her— draws
For by the faithfull temper of my sword, shee shall not tarry with me.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Give me way —
Thou most unworthy man—give me way
Or by the wrong he does the Innocent,
Ile end thy misery and his wickednesse, together.

speeches.speaker: Lady
verse: Stay and let me justifie
My husband in that, I have wrong'd his bed
Never—all shames that can afflict me fall
Upon me if I ever wrong'd you;

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Didst thou not confesse it?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Twas to save your bloud from shedding, that has
Turn'd my brothers edge;
He that beholdes our thoughts as plainely as
Our faces, knowes it, I did never hurt
My honesty but by accusing it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Womens consents are sonner credited
Then their denials: and Ile never trust
Her body that prefers any defence
Before the safety of her honour—here—
Show forth that stranger—give me not a word
Thou seest a danger readie to be tempted.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Cast that upon me rather then my shame,
And as I am now dying I wil now—
That I am honest.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Put her out of dores; but that I feare my land
May go againe to Montague, I would kill thee, I am loth,
To make a beggar of him that way; or else—
Go now you have the liberty of flesh,
And you may put it to a double use,
One for your pleasure, th'other to maintaine
Your welbeloved, he wil want.
In such a charitable exercise
The vertue wil excuse you for the vice.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What meanes your Lordship?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: For the love of God—

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Thou hast advantage of mee, cast away this buckler.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So he is Sir, for he lives
With one that is undone—a voyd us boy.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: Ile first avoid my safety,
Your Rapier shall be button'd, with my heade before it touch my Master.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Montague?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: You know my sister?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes sir.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: For a whore?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: You lye, and shall lie lower if you dare abuse her honor.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: I am honest.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: Honest!

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Upon my faith I am.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: What did then perswade thee to condemn thy self?

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Your safety.

speeches.speaker: Am.
verse: I had rather be expos'd
To danger, then dishonor; th'ast betray'd
The reputation of my familie
More basely by the falsenesse of that word,
Then that thou hast delivered me asleepe
Into the hands of base enemie.
Reliefe will never make thee sensible
Of thy disgraces; let thy wants compell thee to it.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: O I am a miserable woman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why Madam? are you utterly without means to relieve you?

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: I have nothing sir, unlesse by changing of these cloaths for worse, and then at last the worst for nakednesse.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Stand off boy, nakednesse would be a change
To please us Madam, to delight us both.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: What nakednesse sir?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why the nakednesse of body Madam, we were Lovers once.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Never dishonest Lovers.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Honestie has no allowance now to give our selves.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: Nor you allowance against honestie.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Ile send my Boy hence, opportunitie
Shall be our servant, come and meet me first
With kisses like a stranger at the doore,
And then invite me neerer to receive
A mor^ familiar inward welcome—where,
Instead of tapers made of Virgins wax
Th'increasing flames of our desires shall light
Us to a banquet: and before the taste
Be dull with satisfaction, Ile prepare
A nourishment compos'd of every thing
That beares a naturall friendship to the bloud,
And that shall set another edge upon't,
Or else between the courses of the feast
Wee'l dallie out an exercise of time,
That ever as one appetite expires another may succeede it.

speeches.speaker: La.
verse: O my Lord, how has your nature lost her worthinesse?
When our affections had their liberty,
Or kisses met as temperatelie as
The hands of sisters, or of brothers, that
Our blouds were then as moving; then you were
So noble, that I durst have trusted your
Embraces in an opportunity
Silent enough to serve a ravisher,
And yet come from you—undishonor'd—how
You think me altered, that you promise your
Attempt successe I know not; but were all
The sweet temptations that deceive us set
On this side, and one that side all the waiters,
These neither should perswade me nor the force.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then misery may waste your body.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Yes, but lust shall never.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I have found you still as uncorrupted as I left you first
Continue so; and I wil serve you with
As much devotion as my word, my hand
Or purse can show you; and to justifie
That promise, here is half the wealth I have,
Take it, you owe me nothing, till you fall
From vertue, which the better to protect
I have bethought me of a present meanes
Give me the Letter; this commends my Boy
Into the service of a Lady, whose
Free goodnesse you have bin acquainted with Lamira.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sir I know her.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then believe her entertainment wil be noble to you;
My boy shall bring you thither: and relate
Your manner of misfortune if your own
Report needs any witnesse: so I kisse your hand good Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Sir, I know not how to promise, but I cannot be unthankfull.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: All that you can implore in thankfulnesse
Be yours, to make you the more prosperous.
Farwell my boy,— I am not yet oppress'd.
Having the power to helpe one that's distress'd.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: What shall we do now: swords are out of use,
And words are out of credit.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: We must serve.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: The meanes to get a service will first spend
Our purses; and except we can allow
Our selves an entertainment, service will
Neglect us; now tis grown into a doubt
Whether the Mr. or the servant gives the countenance.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Then fall in with Mistresses.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: They keep more servants now (indeed) then men,
But yet the age is grown so populous
Of those attendants, that the women are
Grown full to.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: What shall we propund our selves?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I'le think on't.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Do; Old occupations have too many setters up to prosper, some uncommon trade would thrive now.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Wee'l ee'n make up some half a dozen proper men,
And should not we get more
Then all your female sinners?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: If the house be seated as it should be privately.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I but that would make a multitude of witches.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: VVitches? how prethee?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Thus the bands would all turn witches to revenge
Themselves upon; us and the women that
Come to us, for disguises must wear beards,
And that's they say, a token of a witch.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: VVhat shall we then do.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: VVe must study on't,
VVith more consideration; stay Duboyes
Are not the Lord of Orleans and the Lord
Of Amiens enemies?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Yes, what of that.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Methinks the factions of two such great men.
Should give a promise of advanc^ment now
To us that want it.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Let the plot be thine, and in the enterprize Ile second thee.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I have it, wee will first set down our selves
The Method of a quarrell; and make choyce
Of some frequented Taverne; or such a place
Of common notice to perform it in
By way of undertaking to maintaine
The severall honours of those enemies.
Thou for the Lord of Orleanes; I for Amiens.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I like the project, and I think 'twill take
The better, since their difference first did rise
From his occasion whom we followed once.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: We cannot hope lesse after the report,
Then entertainment or gratuity,
Yet those are ends, I do not aime at most;
Greater spirits that are needy, and will thrive,
Must labour whiles such troubles are alive.

speeches.speaker: La p.
prose: Slander is sharper then the sword. I have fed this three dayes upon leafe Tobacco, for want of other Victuals.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: You have liv'd the honester Captaine; but be not so dejected, but hold up thy head, and meate wil sooner fall i'thy mouth.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: I care not so much for meat, so I had but good liquor, for which my guts croak like so many Frogs for raine.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: It seemes, you are troubled with the wind-Collick Captaine, swallow a bullet: tis present remedy i'le assure you.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: A bullet; if you be Captain, my panch is nothing but a pile of bullets; when I was in any service I stood between my Generall and the shot, like a mud-wall; I am all lead, from the crown of the head to the soale of the foot, not a sound bone about me.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: It seems you have bin in terrible hot service Captaine.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: It has ever bin the fate of the low Country wars to spoile many a man, I ha' not bin the first nor shall not be the last: but ile tell you sir, (hunger has brought it in to minde) I served once at the Siege of Braste 'tis memorable to this day, where we were in great distresse for victuals, whole troops fainted more for want of food then for blood, and died, yet we were resolved to stand it out; I my self was but then Gentleman of a Company, and had as much need as any man, and indeed I had perished had not a miraculous providence preserved me.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: As how good Captaine?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Marry sir ee'n as I was fainting and falling down for want of sustenance, the enemy made a shot at me, and struck me full ith' paunch with a penny loaf.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Instead of a bullet!

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: In stead of a bullet.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: That was miraculous in deed; and that loaf sustained you.

speeches.speaker: Lap-p.
prose: Nourished me or I had famished with the rest.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: You have done worthy acts being a souldier, and now you shall give me leave to requite your tale, and to acquaint you with the most notorious deeds that I have done being a Courtier. I protest Captain I wil lie no more then you have done.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: I can indure no lies.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I know you cannat Captaine, therefore ile only tell you of strange things, I did once a deed of charity for it self; I assisted a poor widdow in a sute, and obtained it, yet I protest I took not a penny for my labour.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Tis no such strange thing.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: By Mars Captaine, but it is, and a very strange thing too in a Courtier, it may take the upper hand of your penny loaf for a miracle. I could ha' told you how many Ladies have languished for my love, and how I was once sollicited by the mother, the daughter, and grand-mother out of the least of which I might have digg'd my selfe a fortune; they were all great Ladies, for two of them were so big I could hardly embrace them: but I was sluggish in my rising courses, and therefore let them passe; what meanes I had is spent upon such as had the wit to cheat me; That wealth being gon, I have only bought experience with it, with a strong hope to cheat others; but see here comes the much declined Montague, who had all the Man or houses, which were the body of his estate overthrowen by a great winde.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: How by a great winde? was he not over thrown by law?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Yes, marry was he: but there was terrible puffing and blowing before he was overthrown, if you observ'd, and believe it Captain, ther's no wind so dangerous to a building as a lawyers breath.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: What's he with him?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: An eminent Citizen. Mounsier Mallicorne, lets stand a side and listen their design.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Sir, profit is the Crown of labour, it is the life, the soule of the industrious Merchant, in it he makes his paradise, and for it neglects Wife, Children, Friends, Parents, nay all the world, and delivers up himselfe to the violence of stormes, and to be tos'd into unknown ayres; as there is no faculty so perillous, so ther's none so worthy profitable.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Sir, I am very well possest of it, and what of my poore fortunes remaines, I would gladly hazzard upon the Sea; it cannot deale worse with me then the Land, though it sinck or throw it in the hands of Pirats. I have yet five hundred pounds left, and your honest and worthy acquaintance may make me a young Merchant; th'one moity of what I have I would gladly adventure.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: How adventure? you shall hazzard nothing: you shall only joyne with me in certaine commodities that are safe arrived unto the Key; you shall neither be in doubt of danger nor dammage; But so much mony disburst, so much receive; sir I would have you conceive I pursue it not for any good your money wil do me, but meerly out of mine own freenesse and courtesie to pleasure you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I can believe no lesse, and you expresse a noble nature, seeking to build up a man so ruin'd as my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Captaine here is subject for us to worke upon if we have wit; you hear that there is money yet left, and it is going to be layd out in Rattels, Bels, Hobby-Horses, brown paper, or some such like sale commodities; now it would do better in our purses, upon our backs in good Gold-lace, and Scarlet, and then we might pursue our projects, and our devices towards my Lady Annabella; go to, ther's a conceit newly landed; harck I stand in good reputation with him, and therefore may the better cheat him: Captaine, take a few instructions from me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: What monies I have is at your disposing, and upon twelve I will meete you at the Pallace with it.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: I wil there expect you, and so I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: You apprehend me?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Why do ye think I am a dunce?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Not a dunce Captaine, but you might give me leave to misdoubt that pregnancy in a Souldier, which is proper and hereditary to a Courtier; but prosequute it, I wil both second, and give credit to it. Good Mounsier Montague, I would your whole revenues lay within the circuit of mine armes, that I might as easily bestow, or restore it unto you as my curtesie.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: My zealous wishes sir, do accompany his for your good fortunes.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Believe it sir, our affection towards you is a strong band of friendship.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: To which I shall most willingly seale. But believe me Gentlemen in a broken estate, the bond of friendship oft is forfeited, but that it is your free and ingenuous nature to renew it.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Sir, I wil amply extend my self to your use, and am very zealously afflicted as not one of your least friends for your croocked fate; But let it seise you with any dejection, you have as I hear a sufficient competency left, which wel disposed may erect you as high in the worlds account as ever.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose:
I cannot live to hope it, much lesse injoy it, nor
is it any part of my endeavour; my study is to render every man his own, and to containe my self within the limits of a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I have the grant of an Office given me by some noble favorites of mine in Court, there stands but a small matter between me and it, if your ability be such to lay down the present sum, out of the love I bear you, before any other man, it shall be confirmed yours.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I have heard you often speak of such a thing; if it be assur'd to you I wil gladly deale in it that portion I have, I would not hazard upon one course, for I see the most certainest is incertain.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Having money sir, you could not light upon men that could give better direction; there is at this time a friend of mine upon the Seas; to be plain with you, he is a Pyrate, that hath wrote to me to work his fredom, and by this Gentlemans meanes, whose acquaintance is not small at Court; we have the word of a worthy man for it, only there is some money to be suddainly disburst, and if your happinesse be such to make it up you shall receive treble gaine by it, and good assurance for it.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Gentlemen out of the weaknesse of my estate you seem (to have some knowledge of my brest) that wood if it were possible advance my declined fortunes, to satisfie all men of whom I have had credit, and I know no way better then these which you propose; I have some money ready under my command, some part of it is already promis'd, but the remainder is yours to such uses as are propounded.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Appoint some certain place of meeting, for these affaires requires expedition.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I wil make it my present businesse: at twelve, I am to meet Mallicorne the Marchant at the Pallace, you know him sir, about some negotiation of the same nature, there I wil be ready to tender you that money, upon such conditions as wee shall conclude off.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: The care of it be yours, so much as they affaire concernes you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Your caution is effectuall, and till then I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Good Mr Montague.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Nay Gentlemen what meane you pray be quiet, have some respect unto the house.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: A treacherous slave.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Thou dost revile thy self base Longavile.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I say thou art a villaine and a corrupt one, that hast some seaven years fed on thy masters trencher, yet never bredst good bloud towards him: for if, thou hadst have a sounder heart.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: So sir, you can use your tongue something nimbler then your sword.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Wood you cood use your tongue well of your Master, friend you might have better imployment for your sword.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: I say againe and I wil speak it loud and often, that Orleans is a noble Gentleman with whom Amiens is to light to poyse the scale.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: He is the weaker for taking of a prayse out of thy mouth.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: This hand shall seale his merit at thy heart.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Part them my masters part them.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: Part them sir, why do you not part them, you stand by with your sword in your hand, and cry part 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Why you must know my friend my cloaths are better then yours, and in a good suit, I do never use to part any body.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And it is discretion.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I marry is it Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Duboies though this place priviledge thee, know where next we meet, the bloud which at thy heart flowes drops at thy feet.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: I would not spend it better then in this quarrell, and on such a hazard.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: What uprores this, must my name here be question'd in Tavern brawels, and by affected Ruffins?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Not we indeed sir.

speeches.speaker: Du.
prose: Fear cannot make me shrink out of your fury, though you were greater then your name doth make you, I am one, and the opposer; if your swoln rage have ought in mallice to inforce expresse it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I seek thee not nor shalt thou ever gaine
That credit, which a blow from me wood give thee,
By my —I more detest that fellow
Which took my part then thee, that he durst offer
To take my honour in his feeble armes,
And spend it in a drinking room; which way went he?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: That way sir, I wood you wood after for I do fear we shall have some more scuffling.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Ile follow him, and if my speed o're take him,
I shall ill thank him for his forwardnesse.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I am glad he's gon, for I do not love to see a sword drawn in the hand of a man that lookes so furious, ther's no jesting with edge tooles, how say you Captaine?

speeches.speaker: Cap.
prose: I Say tis better jesting then to be in earnest with them.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: How now? what's the difference? they say there have bin swords drawn, and in my quarrell, let me know that man, whose love is so sincere to spend his bloud for my sake, I will bounteously requite him.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: We were all of your side, but there he stands begun it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: What's thy name?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Duboyes?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Give me thy hand, thou hast receaved no hurt?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Not any, nor wear this body stuck full of wounds, I should not count them hurts, being taken in so honorable a cause as the defence of my most worthy Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: The dedication of thy love to me requires my ample bounty, thou art mine, for I do finde thee made unto my purposes. Mounsieur Laverdine, pardon my neglect I not observed you, and how runs rumour.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Why, it runs my Lord like a foot man without a cloak, to show that what's once rumour'd it cannot be hidde.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: And what say the rable, am not I the subject of their talk?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Troth my Lord the common mouth speakes foule words.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Of me, for turning away thy wife do they not?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Faith the men do a little murmer at it and say, 'tis an ill president in so great a man, marry the women they rayle, out right.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose:
Out upon them rampallions Ile keepe my selfe safe enough out of their fingers, but what say my prity
Jelly composed gallant that censure every thing more desperate then it is dangerous; what say they?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Marry they are laying wagers, what death you shall die; one offers to lay five hundred pounds; And yet he had but a groat about him, & that was in two two-pences too to any man that wo'd make it up a shilling; that you were kil'd with a Pistoll charg'd with white Powder; another offerd to pawne his soule for five shillings, and yet no body wo'd take him, that you were stab'd to death and sho'd die with more wounds then Cesar.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: And who sho'd be the Butchers that sho'd do it? Montague and his associates?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: So tis conjectured.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And believe it, sweet Prince, it is to be feared, and therefore prevented.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: By turning his purpose on himself, were not that the way?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: The most direct path for your safety. For where doth danger sit more furious then in a desperate man?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And being you have declined his meanes, you have increast his malice.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Besides the generall report that steems in every mans breath, and staines you all over with infamy, that Time the devourer of all things cannot eat out.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: I, for that former familiarity, which he had with your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Men speak it as boldly as words of complement; good morrow, good even, or God save you sir, are not more usuall; if the word cuckold had been written upon your forehead in great Capitall Letters, it could not have been dilated with more confidence.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: He shall not sleepe another night, I will have his blood, though it be required at my hands again.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Your Lordship may, and without hazzarding your own person; he's a Gentleman in whose looks I see a resolution to perform it.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Let his Lordship give me but his honourable word for my life, Ile kill him as he walks.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Or pistoll him as he sits at meat.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Or at game.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Or as he is drinking.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Any way.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Wot thou? call what is mine thine own, thy reputation shall not be brought in question for it, muchlesse thy life; it shall be namd a deed of valour in thee, not murder: Farewell.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: I need no more encouragement, it is a worke I will perswade my selfe that I was borne to.

speeches.speaker: Laver.
prose: And you may perswade your selfe to that you shall be sav'd by it, being that it is for his honourable Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: But you must yield me means, how, when and where.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: That shall be bur taskes;
Nay more, we will be agents with thee:
This houre we are to meet him, on the receipt of certain moneys,
Which indeed we purpose honestly to cheat him of,
And that's the many causes I wo'd have him slain,
Who works with safety makes a double gain.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Stay sir, I have took some pains to overtake you.
—You name is Longaville?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I have the word of many honest men for't, I crave your Lordships pardon, your sudden apppehension on my steps made me to frame an answer unwitting and unworthy your respect.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Doe you know me?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Yes, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: I know not you; nor am I well pleased to make this time, as the affaire now stands, the induction of your acquaintance; you are a fighting fellow?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: How my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: I thinke I too much grace you; rather you are a fellow dares not fight, but spet and puffe and make a noyse whilst your trembling hand drawes out your Sword, to lay it upon Andirons, stooles or tables, rather then on a man.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Your honour may best speake this; yet— with little safety, if I thought it serious.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Come, you are a merry braggart, and you have given me cause to tell you so: what weaknesse have you ever seen in me to prompt your selfe, that I could need your helpe, or what other reasons could induce you to it? you never yet had a meales meat from my Table, nor as I remember from my Wardrop any cast Suite.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: Tis true, I never durst yet have such a service spirit, to be the minion of a full swolne Lord; but alwaies did detest such slavery: a meales meat, or a cast sute? I wo'd first eate the stones, and from such rags the dunghils does afford pick me a garment.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: I have mistook the man, his resolute spirit
Proclaimes him generous, he has a noble heart
As free to utter good deeds as to act them;
For had he not been right, and of one piece,
He would have crumpled, curled, and struck himselfe
Out of the shape of man into a shaddow.
But prethee tell me, if no such fawning hope
Did lead thee on to hazzard life for my sake;
What was it that incited thee?
Tell me; speak it without the imputation of a Sicophant.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Your own desert, and with it was joyn'd the unfained friendship that I judged you ever held unto my former Lord.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: The noble Montague?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Yes, the noble and much injured Montague.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: To such a man as thou art, my heart shall be
A Casket: I will lock thee up there,
And esteem thee as a faithfull friend,
The richest Jewell that a man enjoyes;
And being thou didst follow once my friend,
And in thy heart still dost, not with his fortunes casting him off,
Thou shalt goe hand in hand with me, and share
As well in my ability as love; tis not my end
To gaine men for my use, but a true friend.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: There's no such thriving way to live in grace,
As to have no sence of it; his backe nor belly
Shall not want warming that can practise me mischiefe;
I walke now with a full purse, grow high and wanton,
Prune and briske my selfe in the bright shine
Of his good Lordships favours; and for what vertue?
For fashioning my selfe a murderer.
O noble Montague, to whom I owe my heart,
With all my best thoughts, tho my tongue have promisd
To exceed the malice of thy destiny,
Never in time of all my service knew I
Such a sinne tempt thy bounty; those that did feed
Upon thy charge had merit or else need.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Duboys, most prosperously met.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: How now? will he come this way.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: This way, immediately; therefore thy assistance, deere Duboys.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: What have you cheated him of the money you spoke of?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Fough, as easily as a filly Countrey wench of her maydenhead; we had it in a twinkling.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Tis well Captaine, let me helpe you, you must be our leader in this action.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Tut, feare not, Ile warrant you if my Sword hold, we'l make no sweating sicknesse of it.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Why that's well said, but let's retire a little, that we may come on the more bravely; this way, this way.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cre.
prose: Officers look to him, and be sure you take good security before he part from you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why but my friends, you take a strange course with me; the sums I owe you are rather forgetfulnesse they are so slight, then want of will or honesty to pay you.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: I sir, it may be so; but we must be paid, and we will be paid before you scape: we have wife and children, and a charge, and you are going down the wind, as a man may say; and therefore it behooves us to looke to't in time.

speeches.speaker: 2 Cred.
prose: Your cloak here wo'd satisfie me, mine's not above a three pound matter, besides the arrest.

speeches.speaker: 3 Cred.
prose: Faith and mine is much about that matter too; your Girdle and Hangers, and your Beaver, shall be sufficient baile for't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: If you have ever a plain black sute at home, this Silken one, with your Silke-stockings, Garters, and Roses shall pacifie me too; for I take no delight, if I have a sufficient pawne, to cast any Gentleman in prison; therefore tis but an untrussing matter, and you are free, we are no unreasonable creatures you see; for mine own part, I protest I am loth to put you to any trouble for security.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Is there no more of you? he wo'd next demand my skinne.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: No sir, here's no more of us, nor do any of us demand your skin, we know not what to doe with it: but it may be if you ow'd your Glover any money, he knew what use to make of it.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Ye dregs of basenesse, vultures amongst men,
That tyer upon the hearts of generous spirits.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: You doe us wrong sir, we tyre no generous spirits, we tyre nothing but our hackneys.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: But here comes one made of another piece;
A man well meriting that free born name
Of Citizen; welcome my deliverer, I am falne
Into the hands of blood-hounds, that for a sum
Lesser then their honesties, which is nothing,
Wo'd teare me out of my skin.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Why sir, what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: 1 Cre.
prose: Why sir, the matter is, that we must have our money, which if we cannot have, we'l satisfie our selves with his carcasse, and be payd that waies: you had as good sir not have been so peremptory. Officer, hold fast.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offi.
prose: The strenuous fist of vengeance now is clutcht; therefore feare nothing.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: What may be the debt in grosse?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Some forty Crowns, nay rather not so much, tis quickly cast.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Tis strange to me, that your estate sho'd have so low an ebbe, to sticke at such sleight sums: why my friends, you are too strict in your accounts, and call too sudden on this Gentleman, he has hopes left yet to pay you all.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
prose: Hopes? I marry bid him pay his friends with hopes, and pay us with currant Coyne: I knew a gallant once that fed his creditors still with hopes, and bid 'em they sho'd feare nothing, for he had 'em tyed in a string; and trust me so he had indeed, for at last he and all his hopes hopt in a haltar.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Good sir, with what speed you may free out the company of these slaves, that have nothing but their names to show 'em men.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: What wo'd you wish me do sir? I protest I ha' not the present summe (small as it is) to lay down for you; and for giving my word, my friends no latter then yesternight made me take bread and eate it, that I sho'd not do it for any man breathing ith' world; therefore I pray bold me excused.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: You doe not speake this seriously?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: As ever I said my prayers, I protest to you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: What may I think of this?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Troth sir thought is free for any man; we abuse our betters in it, I have done it my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Trust me, this speech of yours doth much amaze me, pray leave this language, and out of that same sum you lately did receive of me, lay down as much as may discharge me.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: You are a merry man sir, and I am glad you take your crosses so temperately; fare you well sir, and yet I have something more to say to ye, a word in your eare I pray; to be plaine with you I did lay this plot to arrest you to enjoy this money I have of yours, with the more safety. I am a foole to tell you this now; but in good faith I could not keepe it in. And the money wo'd a done me little good else. An honest Citizen cannot wholly enjoy his own wife for you, they grow old before they have true use of them, which is a lamentable thing, and truely much hardens the hearts of us Citizens against you: I can say no more, but am heartily sorry for your heavinesse, and so I take my leave.

speeches.speaker: 1 Cred.
verse: Officers take hold on him againe, for Mounsier
Mallycorne will doe nothing for him I perceive.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Nay come my masters, leave dauncing of the old measures, and let's assault him bravely.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: By no means; for it goes against my stomacke to kill a man in an unjust quarrell.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: It must needs be a clog to a mans conscience all his life time.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: It must indeed Captaine: besides doe ye not see he has gotten a guard of friends about him, as if he had some knowledge of our purpose?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Had he a guard of Devils as I think them little better, my Sword should doe the message that it came for.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: If you will be so desperate, the blood lie upon your own neck, for we'l not meddle in't.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I am your friend and servant,
Struggle with me and take my Sword;
Noble sir make your way, you have slaine an Officer.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Some one of them has certainly
Requited me; for I do lose much blood.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offic.
prose: Udsprecious, we have lost a brother, pursue the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: 2 Offic.
prose: Ile not meddle with him: you see what comes on't; besides I know he will be hang'd ere he be taken.

speeches.speaker: 1 Offic.
prose: I tell thee yeoman he must be taken ere he be hanged; he is hurt in the guts, run afore therefore and know how his wife will rate his Sawsiges a pound.

speeches.speaker: 3 Offic.
prose: Stay brother, I may live, for surely I finde i'm but hurt in the leg a dangerous kick on the shin-bone.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You see Lady
What harmlesse sports ous Countrey life affords;
And though you meet not here with City dainties,
Or Courtly entertainment, what you have
Is free and hearty.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Madam, I finde here
What is a stranger to the Court, content,
And receive curtesies done for themselves,
Without an expectation of returne,
Which binds me to your service.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Oh your love;
My homely house built more for use then shew
Observes the Golden mean equally distant
From glittering pompe, and sordid avarice;
For Maskes we will observe the workes of nature
And in the place of visitation read.
Our Physick shall be wholsome walkes, our viandes,
Nourishing not provoking: for I finde
Pleasures are tortures, that leave stings behind.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: You have a great estate.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A competency
Sufficient to maintaine me and my ranke,
Nor am I, I thank Heaven, so Courtly bred
As to imploy the utmost of my Rents
In paying Tailors for phantastick Roabes;
Or rather then be second in the fashion,
Eate out my Officers and my Revenues
With grating usury; my back shall not
Be the base on which your soothing Citizen
Erects his Summer-houses; nor on the other side
Will I be so penuriously wise,
As to make money (thats my slave) my Idoll,
Which yet to wrong, merits as much reproof,
As to abuse our servant.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Yet with your pardon
I thinke you want the Crown of all contentment.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: In what good Madam?

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: In a worthy husband.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: — It is strange the galley-slave should praise
His Oare, or stroakes; or you, that have made shipwracke
Of all delight upon this Rock cal'd marriage,
Should sing Encomions o't.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Madam, though one fall
From his horse and breake his neck, will you
Conclude from that it is unfit to ride?
Or must it follow, because Orleance
My Lord's pleased to make his passionate triall
Of my suspected patience, that my brother,
(Were he not so, I might say, worthy Amiens)
Will imitate his ills, that cannot fancy
What's truely Noble in him?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I must grant
There's as much worth in him as can be lookt for
From a young Lord, but not enough to make
Me change my golden liberty and consent
To be a servant to it, as wives are
To the Imperious humors of their Lords:
Me thinks I'm well, I rise and goe to bed
When I thinke fit, eate what my appetite
Desires without controle, my servants study
Is my contentment, and to make me merry
Their farthest ayms; my sleeps are enquired after,
My rising up saluted with respect:
Command and liberty now waite upon
My Virgin state; what would I more? change all,
And for a husband? no; these freedomes die,
In which they live with my Virginity;
Tis in their choice that's rich to be a wife,
But not being yoakt to chuse the single life.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: How like you the Countrey?

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: I like the ayre of it well Madam, and the rather because as on Irish Timber your Spiders will not make his web, so for ought I see yet your Cheater, Pander, and Informer being in their dispositions too foggy for this piercing climate, shun it, and choose rather to walk in mists in the City.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Who did you serve first boy?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: A rich Merchants widdow, and was by her preferred to a young Court-lady.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
prose: And what difference found you in their service?

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: Very much: for looke how much my old City Madam gave to her-young visitants, so much my Lady received for her hoary Court-servants.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: And what made you to leave her?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: My father (Madam) had a desire to have me a tale-man, took me from thence.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Well, I perceive you inherit the wag, from your father.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Doves beget Doves; and Eagles, Eagles, Madam: A Citizen here, tho left never so rich, seldome at the best proves a Gentleman: the sonne of an Advocate, tho dub'd like his father, will shew a relish of his discent, and the fathers thriving practice, as I have heard: she that of a Chambermayd is metamorphosed into a Madam, will yet remember how oft her daughter by her mother ventured to lie upon the rushes before she could get in that which makes many Ladies.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
prose: But what think you of your late Master?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Oh Madam —

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Why doe you sigh? you are sorry that you left him,
He made a wanton of you.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Not for that:
Or if he did, for that my youth must love him.
Oh pardon me, if I say liberty
Is bondage, if compared with his kind service;
And but to have power now to speake his worth
To its desert; I should be well content
To be an old man when his praise were ended:
And yet, if at this instant you were pleased,
I should begin, the livery of age
Would take his lodging upon this head
Ere I should bring it to a period.
In briefe he is a man (for God forbid
That I should ever live to say he was
Of such a shape as would make one beloved,
That never had good thought;) and to his body
He hath a mind of such a constant temper
In which vertues throng to have a room:
Yet 'gainst this noble Gentleman, this Montague,
For in that name I comprehend all goodnesse,
Wrong, and the wrested law, false witnesses,
And envy sent from hell, have rose in Armes,
And tho not pierced, battered his honourd shield.
What shall I say? I hope you will forgive me,
That if you were but pleas'd to love,
I know no Juno worthy such a Jove.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Tis well yet that I have the second place
In your affection: From whence?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: From the Lord Amiens, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Tis welcome, though it beare his usual language:
I thought so much, his love-suit speake his health.
What's he that brought it?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: A Gentleman of good ranke, it seems.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Receiving entertainment in your house
Sorting with his degree.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: He waites your Ladiships pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: He shall not waite long:
Ile leave you for a while; nay stay you boy,
Attend the Lady.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Would I might live once
To waite on my poore Master.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: That's a good boy:
This thankfulnesse looks lovely on thy forehead,
And in it, as a book, me thinks I read
Instructions for my selfe, that am his debtor,
And wo'd do much that I might be so happy
To repaire that which to our griefe is ruin'd.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: It were a worke a King might glory in,
If he saw with my eyes: If you please Madam,
For sure to me you seem to me unapt to walke,
To sit, although the churlish Birds deny
To give us musicke in this grove, where they
Are prodigall to others: Ile strain my voyce
For a sad Song, the place is safe and private.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Twas my desire; begin good Viramour.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: What's he Viramour?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: A goodly personage.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Am I yet safe? or is my flight a dream?
My wounds and hunger tell me that I wake:
Whither have my feares borne me? no matter where,
Who hath no place to goe to, cannot erre:
What shall I doe? cunning calamity
That others grosse wits uses to refine,
When I most need it duls the edge of mine.

speeches.speaker: L O^l.
verse: Is not this Montagues voyce?

speeches.speaker: V^
verse: My Masters? fie.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What sound was that, pish,
Feare makes the wretch think every leafe oth' Jury:
What course to live, beg? better men have done it,
But in another kind: steale? Alexander
Though stiled a Conquerour, was a proud thiefe
Though he robd with an Army; fie how idle
These meditations are: though thou art worse
Then sorrows tongue can speak thee, thou art still
Or shouldst be, honest Montague.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Tis too true.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Tis he: what villaines hands did this? oh that my flesh
Were Balme; in faith sir, I would plucke it off
As readily as this; pray you accept
My will to doe you service: I have heard
The Mouse once sav'd the Lyon in his need,
As the poore Scarab spild the Eagles seed.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: How do you?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: As a forsaken man.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Do not say so, take comfort,
For your misfortunes have been kind in this,
To cast you on a hospitable shoare,
Where dwels a Lady—

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: She to whom, good Master,
You prefer'd me.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: In whose house, whatsoere
Your dangers are, Ile undetake your safety.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I feare that I am pursued, and doubt that I
In my defence have kild an Officer.

speeches.speaker: ~ir.
verse: Is that all? there's no law under the Sunne
But will I hope confesse, one drop of blood
Shed from this arme is recompence enough
Though you had cut the throats of all the Catchpoles
In France, nay in the world.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I would be loth
To be a burthen, or feed like a drone
On the industrious labour of a Bee,
And baser far I hold it to owe for
The bread I eate, what's not in me to pay;
Then since my full fortunes are declined,
To their low ebb Ile fashion my high mind.
It was no shame to Hecuba to serve
When Troy was fired: ift be in your power
To be a means to make her entertainment,
And far from that I was; but to supply
My want with habit fit for him that serves,
I shall owe much to you.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Leave that care to me.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
prose: Good sir, leaue on my shoulder; helpe good Madam ^ oh that I were a horse for halfe an houre, that I might carry you home on my backe: I hope you wil love me still?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Thou dost deserve it boy, that I should live
To be thus troublesome.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Good sir, tis none.

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: Trouble most willingly; I would be changd
Like Apuleius, weare his Asses eares,
Provided I might still this burthen beare.

speeches.speaker: L. Orl.
verse: Tis a kind boy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I finde true proofe of it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: You'l carry it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: As I live although my packet were like Bellerophons, what have you seen in me or my behaviour since your favours so plentifully showed upon my wants, that may beget distrust of my performance?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Nay, be not angry, if I entertained
But the least scruple of your love, or courage,
I would make of one which my state
Should do me right in this, nor can you blame me
If in a matter of such consequence
I am so importunate.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Good my Lord tell me, prevent your further conjurations
To rayse my spirit, I know this is a challenge
To be delivered unto Orleance hand,
And that my undertaking ends not there,
But I must be your second, and in that
Not alone search your enemy, measure weapons,
But stand in all your hazzards, as our blouds
Ran in the self same veines, in which if I
Better not your opinion, as a limbe
That's putrifyed and uselesse, cut me off,
And underneath the Gallons bury it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: At full you understand me, and in this
Binde me and what's mine to you and yours,
I wil not so much wrong you as to adde
One sylable more, let it suffice I leave
My honor to your guard: and in that prove
You hold the first place in my heart and love.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: The first place in a Lords affection? very good; and how long doth that last? perhaps the changing of some three shirts in the Tennis Court; wel it were very necessary that an order were taken (if it were possible,) that younger brother, might have more wit, or more money: for now how ever the foole hath long bin put upon him that inherits his revenew hath brought him a spunge, and wip't off the imputation, and for the understanding of the younger, let him get as much rhetorick as he can to grace his language.
They wil see he shall have glosse little enough to set out his barck; stand Dubois look about all safe.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Approach not neer me but with reverence
Lawrell and adorations, I have done more then deserve a 1^0 thanks.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: How now what's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: With this hand only aided by this brain,
Without an Orpheus Harp redeem'd from hels
Three headed Porter, our Euridice.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Nay prithee speak sence, this is like the stale braggart in a Play.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Then in plaine Prose thus, and with as little action as thou canst desire, the three headed Porter, were three unexorable Catch-poles out of whose jawes with out the help of Orpheus Harp, baite or bribe, for those too stringes, makes the Musique that mollifies those flinty furies, I rescued our Euridice, I meane my old Master Montague.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: And is this all, a poor rescue, I thought thou hadst reverst the judgement for his overthrow, in his sute, or wrought upon his adversary Orleance, taken the shape of a Ghost, frighted his mind into distraction, and for the appeasing of his conscience forc'd him to make restitution of Montagues Lands, or such like rescued; slight I would have hired Crohi^ture for two Cardekues to have done so much with his whip.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: You wood sir, and yet tis more then three on their foot-cloathes durst do for a sworne Brother, in a Coach.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Besides what proofs of it, for ought I know this may be a trick, I had rather have him a Prisoner, where I might visit him, and do him service, then not at all, or I know not where.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Well sir, the end wil shew it, what's that a challenge?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Yes, wher's Orleance? though we fight in jest he must meet with Amiens in earnest, —fall off, we are discovered; my horse garcon ha'.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Were it not in a house and in his presence,
To whom I owe all duty—

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: What would it do? prate as it do's? but be as far from stricking as he that owes it Orleans.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I think thou art his Porter,
Set here to answer creditors, that his Lordship
Is not within or takes the diet. I am sent,
And wil grow here untill I have an answer,
Not to demand a debt of money, but
To call him to a strict account for wrong
Done to the honors of a Gentleman,
Which nothing but his heart-bloud shall wash off.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Shall I hear this?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And more, that if I may not
Have accesse to him, I will six this here
To his disgrace and thine.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: And thy life with it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Then have the coppies of it pasted on posts,
Like Phamplet titles that sue to be sold;
Have his disgrace talk for Tobacco shops,
His picture bafful'd.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: All respect away, wer't in a Church—draw both

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: This is the book I pray with.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Forbear upon your lives.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: What are you rous'd? I hope your Lordship can read (though he staine not his birth with scholler-ship) doth it not please you now? if you are a right Mounsier, muster up the rest of your attendance, which is a page, a cook, a pander, coach-man, and a foot man, in these dayes a great Lords traine, pretending I am unworthy to bring you a challenge, in stead of answering it, have me kik't.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: If he does thou deserv'st it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I dare you all to touch me, I'le not stand still,
What answer you?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: That thou hast done to Amience
The office of a faithfull friend which I
Would cherish in thee were he not my foe,
How ever since on honorable tearmes
He cals me forth, say I will meet with him,
And by Dubois ere Sun-set make him know
The time and place, my swords length, and what ever
Scruple of circumstance he can expect.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: This answer comes unlookt for, far you well,
Finding your temper thus, wood I had sayd lesse.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Now Comes thy love to the test.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: My Lord 'twill hold,
And in all dangers prove it selfe true gold.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I wil acquaint my Lady with your comming.
Please you repose your selves here.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Ther's a tester, nay now I am a woer I must be bountifull.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: If you would have two three-pences for it sir, To give some of your kindred as you ride, I'le see if I can get them; we use not (tho Servants) to take Bribes.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Then thou art unfit, to be in office either in Court or City.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Indeed corruption is a Tree whose branches are of an unmeasurable length they spread every where, and the dew that drops from thence have infected some chayres and stooles of authority.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose:
Ah Captaine, lay not all the fault upon Officers
you know you can shark though you be out of action, witnesse Montague.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Hang him, hee's safe enough; you had a hand in it to and have gained by him; but I wonder you Citizens that keep so many bookes, and take such strict accounts for every farthing due to you from others, reserve not so much as a memorandum for the curtesies you receive.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Would you have a Citizen book those? thankfulnes is a thing we are not sworn to in our indentures: you may as well urge conscience.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Talke no more of such vanities. Montague is irrecoverably sunk, I would we had twenty more to send after him; the Snake that would be a Dragon and have wings must eate; and what imployes that but this, that in this Canniball age he that would have the sute of wealth must not care—whom he feeds on? and as I have heard no flesh battens better, then that of a profest friend; and he that would mount to honour must not make dainty to use the head of his mother, back of his father, or neck of his brother, for ladders to his preferment; for but observe, and you shall finde for the most part cunning villany sit at a feast as principall guest, and Innocent honesty waite as a contemn'd servant with a trencher.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: The Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Do yee smell nothing?

speeches.speaker: Cha.
verse: Not I sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: The carrion of knaves is very strong in my nostrels.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: We came to admire, and finde fame was a niggard
Which we thought prodigall in our report
Before we saw you.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Tush sir, this Courtship's old.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Ile fight for thee sweet wench,
This is my tongue and woes for me?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Good man of War,
Hands of; if you take me it must be by siege,
Not by an onset; and for your valour, I
Think that I have deserved few enemies,
And therefore need it not.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Thou needst nothing sweet Lady, but an obsequious husband, and where wilt thou finde him, if not in the City: we are true Moscovits to our Wives, and are never better pleased, then when they use us as slaves, bridle and saddle us; have me, thou shalt command all my wealth as thine own, thou shalt sit like a Queen in my ware house; And my factors at the returne with my ships shall pay thee tribute of all the rarities of the earth; thou shalt wear gold, feed on delicates, the first peascods-strauberies, grapes, cherries shall—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Be mine; I apprehend what you would say,
Those dainties which the City payes so dear for,
The Country yeilds for nothing, and as early;
And credit me your far fet viandes please not
My appetite better then those that are neer hand.
Then for your promis'd service and subjection
To all my humors, when I am your wife,
Which as it seemes is frequent in the City,
I cannot finde what pleasure they receive
In using there fond husbands like their Maydes;
But of this more hereafter; I accept
Your proffer kindly, and yours; my house stands open
To entertain you; take your pleasure in it,
And ease after your journey.

speeches.speaker: La. Orl.
prose: Do you note the boldnesse of the fellowes?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Alas Madam, a virgin must in this be like a lawyer,
And as he takes all fees, shee must hear all suitors; the
One for gaine, the other for her mirth; stay with the
Gentlemen, wee'l to the Orchards.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: —what art thou?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: An honest man, though poor;
And look they like to monsters, are they so rare?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Rose from the dead.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Do you heare Mounsier Serviture, didst thou never heare of one Montague a prodigall gull, that lives about Paris?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: So s^r.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: One that after the losse of his maine estate in a
Law sute, bought an Office in the Court.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: And should have letters of Mart, to have the Spanish treasure as it came from the Indies; were not thou and he twins? put of thy hat, let me see thy forehead.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Though you take priviledge to use your tongues,
I pray you hold your fingers,
'Twas your base cozenage made me as I am,
And were you some where else I would take off
This proud filme from your eyes, that will not tell you,
Know I am Montague.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: I will observe this better.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: And art thou he? I wil do thee grace; give me thy hand; I am glad thou hast taken so good a course; serve God and please thy Mistris; if I prove to be thy Master as I am very likely, I will do for thee.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Faith the fellow's well made for a servingman, and will no doubt carry a chyne of Beefe with good grace.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Prithee be carefull of me in my chamber, I will remember thee at my departure.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: All this I can indure under this roof,
And so much owe I her, whose now I am,
That no wrong shall incense me to molest
Her quiet house; while you continue here,
I will not be ashamed to do you service
More then to her, because such is her pleasure.
But you that have broke thrice, and foureteen times
Compounded for two shillings in the pound,
Know I dare kick you in your shop; do ye hear?
If ever I see Paris, though an army
Of musty Murrions, rusty brown bils and clubs,
Stand for your guard— I have heard of your tricks,
And you that smell of Amber at my charge,
And triumph in your cheat; well I may live
To meet thee, be it among a troop of such
That are upon the faire face of the Court
Like running ulcers, and before thy whore
Trampell upon thee.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: This a language for a livery? take heed, I am a Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: A Gox-comb are you not? that thou and I
To give proof, which of us dares most, were now
In mid'st of a rough Sea, upon a piece
Of a split ship, where only one might ride,
I would —but foolish anger makes me talke
Like a Player.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Indeed you act a part
Doth ill become you my servant; is this your duty?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I crave your pardon, and wil hereafter be more circumspect.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose:
Oh the power of a Womans tongue! it had
done more then we three with our swords durst undertake: put a madde man to silence.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Why Sirra these are none of your comrades
To drink with in the celler; one of them
For ought you know may live to be your Master.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Ther's some comfort yet.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Here's choyce of three, a wealthy Merchant.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Hem, shee's taken, she hath spy'd my good Calf,
And many Ladies chuse their husbands by that.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A Courtier that's in grace, a valiant Captaine,
And are these mates for you? away be gon.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I humbly pray you will be pleased to pardon,
And to give satisfaction to you Madam.
(Although I break my heart) I will confesse
That I have wrong'd them too, and make submission.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: No I'le spare that; goe bid the Cook haste Supper.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Oh brave Lady thou art worthy to have servants, to be commandresse of a Family, that knowst how to use and govern it.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: You shall have many Mistresses that will so mistake as to take their horse keepers, and footemen insteed of their Husbands, thou art none of those.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: But she that can make distinction of men, and knowes when she hath gallants, and fellowes of rank and quality in her house—

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Gallants indeed, if it be the Gallants fashion
To triumph in the miseries of a man,
Of which they are the cause: one that transcends
(In spight of all that fortune hath, or can be done)
A million of such things as you, my doores
Stand open to receive all such as wear
The shape of Gentlemen, and my gentlier nature
(I might say weaker) weighes not the expence
Of entertainment; think you i'le forget yet
What's due unto my selfe? do not I know,
That you have dealt with poor Montague, but like
Needy Commanders, cheating Citizens,
And perjured Courtiers? I am much mov'd, else use not
To say so much, if you will bear your selves
As fits such you would make me think you are,
You may stay; if not the way lies before you.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: What think you of this Captaine?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: That this is a baudy house, with Pinacles and Turrets, in which this disguised Montague goes to rut grat is, and that this is a landed pandresse, and makes her house a brothell for charity.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Come, that's no miracle; but from whence derive you the supposition?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Observe but the circumstance; you all know that in the height of Montagues prosperity, hee did affect and had his love return'd by this Lady Orleans; since her divorcement, and his decay of estate, it is knowne, they have met not so much as his boy is wanting; and that this can be any thing else then a meer plot for their night work, is above my imagination to conceive.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Nay it carries probability, let us observe it better, but yet with such caution as our prying be not discovered: here's all things to be had without cost, and therefore good staying here.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Nay that's true, I would we might woe her twenty years like Penelopes sutors; come Laverdine.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I follow instantly, yonder he is.
The thought of this Boy hath much coold my affection to his Lady, and by all conjectures, this is a disguised whore; I will try if I can search this Mine. Page—

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Your pleasure sir?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Thou art a pritty Boy.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: And you a brave man: now I am out of your debt.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Nay prithy stay.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: I am in haste sir.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: By the faith of a Courtyer.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: Take heed what you say, you have taken a strange Oath.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I have not seene a youth that hath pleased me better, I would thou could'st like me, so far as to leave thy Lady and waite on me, I would maintaine thee in the bravest Cloaths.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Though you took them up on trust, or bought 'em at the brokers.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Or any way: then thy imployments should bee so neate and cleanly, thou shouldst not touch a payre of Pantables in a Moneth, and thy lodging—

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: Should be in a brothell.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: No, but in mine armes.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: That my be the circle of a Baudy house, or worse.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I meane thou shouldest lie with me.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: Lie with you? I had rather lie with my Ladies Monkey; 'twas never a good World since our French Lords learned of the Neopolitans; to make their Pages their Bed-fellowes, doth more hurt to the Suburbe Ladies then tweenty dead Vacations; Tis Supper time sir.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I thought so, I know by that 'tis a Woman, for because peradventure she hath made tryall of the Monkey, she preferrs him before me, as one unknown; well these are standing Creatures, and have strange desires; And men must use strange meanes to quench strange fires.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Now Montague, who discerns thy spirit now?
Thy breeding or thy bloud? here's a poor cloud
Ecclipseth all thy splendor; who can reade
In thy pale face, dead eye, or lenten shute,
The liberty thy ever giving hand
Hath bought for others, manacling it selfe
In gives of parchment indissoluble?
The greatest hearted man supplyed with meanes,
Nobility of birth and gentlest parts,
I though the right hand of his Soveraigne,
If vertue quit her seat in his high soule,
Glitters but like a Pallace set on fire,
Whose glory whilst it shines, but ruins him,
And his bright show each houre to ashes tending
Shall at the last be rak't up like a sparkle,
Unlesse mens lives and fortunes feede the flame.
Not for my own wants though blame I my Stars,
But suffering others to cast love on me,
When I can neither take nor thankfull be.
My Ladies woman, faire and vertuous
Young as the present moneth, sollicits me
For love and marriage now being nothing worth —

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Oh Master, I have sought you a long hour,
Good faith, I never joyd out of your sight;
For Gods sake sir be merry, or else beare
The Buffets of your fortunes with more scorn;
Do but begin to raile, teach me the way,
And Ile sit down and help your anger forth:
I have known you weare a suit full worth a Lordship,
Give to a man whose need nere frighted you
From calling of him friend, five hundred Crowns
Ere sleep had left your sences to consider
Your own important present uses; yet
Since I have seen you with a trencher waite,
Voide of all scorne, therefore Ile waite on you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Would God thou wert lesse honest.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Would to God you were lesse worthy: I am even w'ee sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Is not thy Master strangely fallen, when thou
Servest for no wages, but for charity?
Thou dost surcharge me with thy plenteous love:
The goodnesse of thy vertue shown to me,
More opens still my disability
To quit thy pains: Credit me loving boy,
A free and honest nature may be opprest,
Tir'd with curtesies from a liberall spirit,
When they exceed his means of gratitude.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: But tis a due in him that to that end
Extends his love or duty.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Little world
Of vertue, why dost love and follow me?

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: I will follow you through all Countries,
Ile run (fast as I can) by your horse side,
Ile hold your stirrop when you doe alight,
And without grudging waite till you returne:
Ile quit offerd meanes, and expose my selfe
To cold and hunger still to be with you;
Fearlesse Ile travell through a wildernesse,
And when you are weary, I will lay me down
That in my bosome you may rest your head,
Where whilst you sleep, Ile watch that no wild beast
Shall hurt or trouble you: and thus we'l breed a story
To make every hearer weep,
When they discourse our fortunes and our loves.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Oh what a scoffe might men of Wormes make,
If they did know this boy? but my desire
Is that thou wouldest not (as thou usest still
When like a servant I'mong servants sit)
Waite on my Trencher, fill my cups with wine:
Why shouldst thou doe this boy? prethee consider,
I am not what I was.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Curst be the day when I forget that Montague was my Lord, or not remember him my Master still.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Rather curse me, with whom thy youth hath spent
So many houres, and yet untaught to live
By any worldly qualitie.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Indeed you never taught me how to handle Cards
To cheat and coz in men with oathes and lies;
Those are the wordly qualities to live:
Some of our Scarlet Gallants teach their boyes
These worldly qualities.
Since stumbling fortune then leaves vertue thus
Let me leave fortune, ere be vicious.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Oh lad, thy love will kill me.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: In truth, I think in conscience I shall die for you:
Good Master weep not, doe you want aught sir?
Will you have any money? here's some Silver;
And here's a little Gold, 'twill serve to play,
And put more troublesome thoughts out of your mind:
I pray sir take it, Ile get more with singing.
And then Ile bring it you; my Lady ga't me,
And — it was not covetousnesse,
But I forgot to tell you sooner on't.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Alasse boy, thou art not bound to tell it me,
And lesse to give it, buy thee Scarfes and Garters,
And when I have money, I will give thee a Sword:
Nature made thee a beauteous Cabinet
To lock up all the godnesse of the Earth.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: I have lost my voyce with the very sight of this Gentlewoman: good sir steale away, you were wont to be a curious avoyder of womens company.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why boy, thou darst trust me any where, darst thou not?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: I had rather trust you by a roaring Lyon, then a ravening woman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why boy.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Why truly she devoures more mans flesh—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: I, But she roares not boy.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: No sir, why she is never silent but when her mouth is full.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Mounsier Montague.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: My sweet fellow, since you please to call me so.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Ah my conscience she would be pleased well enough to call you bedfellow: oh Master, do not hold her by the hand so: a woman is a lyme-bush, that catcheth all she toucheth.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: I do most dangerously suspect this boy to be a wench; art thou not one? come hither, let me feele thee.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: With all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Why dost thou pull off thy glove?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Why, to feele whether you be a boy, or no.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Fie boy, goe too, Ile not looke your head, nor combe your locks any more, if you talke thus.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: Why, ile sing to you no more then.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: Fie upon't, how sad you are? a young Gentleman that was the very Sunne of France.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: But I am in the eclipse now.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: A Noble soule is like a ship at Sea,
That sleepes at Anchor when the Ocean's calme;
But when she rages, and the wind blows high,
He cuts his way with skill and Majesty.
prose: Suffer himselfe to be over-run with a Lethargy of melancholy and discontent! rouze up thy spirit, man, and shake it off:
I would turn a foole, or Poet, or any thing, or marry, to make you merry; prethee let's walke: good Veramour leave thy Master and me, I have earnest businesse with him.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: What have you to do with him? come sir will you goe?
And ile sing to you again:
prose: Pray doe you leave my Master, and me; we were very merry before you came, he does not covet womens companie.
I'faith his mind is stronger then to credit womens vows, and too pure to be capable of their loves.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
prose: The boy is jealous; sweet lad leave us; my Lady call'd for you I sweare: that's a good child, there's a piece of Gold for thee, go buy a Feather.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose:
There's two pieces for you, do you goe and buy one, or what you will, or nothing so you goe. Nay then I see you would have me go sir; why, 'faith I will; now I perceive you love her better then you doe me; but
God blesse you whatever you do, or intend; I know you are a very honest man.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Still shall I woe thee, whilst thy eares reply
I cannot, or I will not marry thee?
Why hast thou drawn the blood out of my cheekes,
And given a quicker motion to my heart?
Oh thou hast bred a fever in my veines
Call'd love, which no Physitian can cure;
Have mercy on a maid whose simple youth—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: How your example fairest teacheth me
A ceremonious Idolatry!
By all the joy of love I love thee better
Then I or any man can tell another;
And will expresse the mercy which thou crav'st,
I will forbeare to marry thee: consider
Thou art natures heire in feature, and thy parents
In faire inheritances; rise with these thoughts,
And look on me; but with a womans eye,
A decayd fellow, voyd of means and spirit.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Of spirit?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes, could I tamely live,
Forget my fathers blood, waite and make legs,
Staine my best breeches, with the servile drops
That fall from others draughts:

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: This vizard wherewith thou wouldst hide thy spirit
Is perspective, to shew it plainlier.
This under-value of thy life is but
Because I should not buy thee; what more speaks
Greatnesse of man, then valiant patience,
That shrinks not under his fates strongest strokes?
These Roman deaths, as falling on a Sword,
Opening of veines, with poyson quenching thirst,
(Which we erroneously doe stile the deeds
Of the heroicke and magnanimous man)
Was dead-eyd cowardise, and white cheeke feare,
Who doubting tyranny, and fainting under
Fortunes false Lottery, desperately runne
To death for dread of death; that soules most stout,
That bearing all mischance, dares last it out;
Will you performe your word, and marry me,
When I shall call you to't?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I'faith I will.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Who's this alights here?

speeches.speaker: Long,
prose: With leave faire creature, are you the Lady Mistris of the house?

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Her servant sir.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: I pray then favour me, to inform your Lady, and
Duke Orleans wife,
A businesse of emport awaites 'em here,
And craves for speedy answer.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: Are you in post sir?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: No, I am in Satin Lady; I would you would be in post.

speeches.speaker: Charl.
verse: I will returne. Sweet.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Honest friend, doe you belong to the house?
I pray be covered.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Sir, I doe.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Ha, dreamst thou Longaville? sure tis not he: sir
I should know you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So should I you, but that I am asham'd.
But though thou knowst me, prethee Longaville,
Mock not my poverty, pray remember your selfe;
Showes it not strangely for thy cloathes to stand
Without a hat to mine? mocke me no more.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: She—embroyder me all over sir,
If ever I began to mocke you yet.
The — on me, why should I weare Velvet
And Silver Lace,—I will teare it off.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why mad-man?

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Put on my Hat? yes, when I am hangd I will:
— I could break my head
For holding eyes that knew not you at first:
But time and fortune run your courses with him,
He'l laugh and storm you, when you shew most hate.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You're a fair Mounsier.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Doe you mocke me Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Your businesse sir, I mean.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Regard your selfe good Mounsier Longueville.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You are too negligent of your selfe and place,
Cover your head sweet Mounsier.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Mistake me not faire Ladies,
Tis not to you, nor you, that I stand bare.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Nay sweet deere Mounsier, let it not be to us then.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: — a complement.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: And — of manners.
Pray hide your head, your gallants use to do't.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: And you your foreheads, why you needful accessary rascals,
That cannot live without your mutuall knaveries,
More then a Bawd, a Pandor, or a Whore
From one another; how dare you suspect
That I stand bare to you? what make you here?
Shift your house Lady of 'em, for I know 'em,
They come to steale Napkins, and your Spoons;
Look to your Silver-bodkin, (Gentlewoman)
Tis a dead utensil, and Page 'ware your pockets;
My reverence is unto this man, my master,
Whom you with protestations, and oaths
As high as Heaven, as deep as hell, which would
Deceive the wisest man of honest nature,
Have cozned and abus'd; but I may meet you,
And beate you one with t'other.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Peace, no more.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Not a word sir.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: I am something thicke of hearing; what said he?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I heare him, but regard him not.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Nor I, I am never angry fasting.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: My love keeps back my duty, noblest Lady;
If husband or brother merit love from you,
Prevent their dangers, this houre brings to triall
Their hereto sleeping hates; by this time each
Within a yerd is of the others heart,
And met to prove their causes and their spirits
With their impartiall Swords points; haste and save,
Or never meet them more but at the grave.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Oh my distracted heart, that my wrackt honour Should for a brothers, or a husbands life, through thy undoing die.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Amiens engagd; if he miscarry all my hopes and joys,
I now confesse it loudly, are undone:
Caroch, and haste, one minute may betray
A life more worth then all time can repay.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Hump: Mounsier Laverdine pursues this boy extreamly. Captaine what will you doe?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
