prose: Any thing but follow to this Sea-service; I am a Sea-captaine you know, and to offer to part 'em, without we could do't like water-men with long staves, a quarter of a mile off, might be dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Why then let's retire and pray for 'em, I am resolv'd to stop your intent; abus'd more then we have been we cannot be, without they fall to flat beating o'us.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: And that were unkindly done i'faith.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: — but you are the troublesomest Asse that ere I met with; retire, you smel like a womans chamber, that's newly up, before she have pinsht her vapours in with her cloathes.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I will haunt thee like thy Grandames ghost, thou shalt never rest for me.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: Well, I perceive tis vaine to conceale a secret from you: believe it sir, indeed I am a woman.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Why la; I knew't, this Propheticall tongue of mine never faild me; my mother was halfe a witch, never any thing that she forespake, but came to passe: a woman? how happy am I? now we may lawfully come together without feare of hanging; Sweet wench, be gracious, in honourable sort I woe, no otherwise.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: Faith the truth is I have loved you long.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: See, see.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: But durst not open it.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: — I think so.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
prose: But briefly, when you bring it to the test, if there be not one Gentleman in this house, wil challenge more interest in me, then you can, I am at your disposure.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Oh Fortunatus, I envie thee not
For cap, or pouch, this day Ile prove my Fortune,
In which your Lady doth elect her husband,
Who will be Amiens, 'twill save my wedding dinner,
Povera, La-poop and Malicorne: if all faile,
I will turne Citizen, a beauteous wife
Is the horn-booke to the richest Tradesmans life.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: Here's a good even piece of ground my Lords:
Will you fix here?

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Yes any where; Lacquey, take off my spurs;
Upon a bridge, a raile but my Swords bredth, upon a battlement,
Ile fight this quarrell.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: O' the ropes, my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Upon a line.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: So all our Countrie Duels are carried, like a fire-worke on a thred.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Go now stay with the horses, and doe you heare
Upon your lives, till some of us come to you,
Dare not to looke this way.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Except you see strangers or others that by chance or purpose are like to interrupt us.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Then give warning.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Who takes a Sword? the advantage is so small,
As he that doubts hath the free leave to choose.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Come give me any, and search me; tis not
The ground, weapon, or seconds that can make
Oddes in those fatall trials: but the cause.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Most true, and but it is no time to wish
When men are come to do, I would desire
The cause 'twixt us were other then it is;
But where the right is, there prevaile our Swords.
And if my sister have outliv'd her honour,
I doe not pray I may outlive her shame.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Your sister Amiens, is a whore, at once.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: You oft have spoke that sence to me before,
But never in this language Orleance;
And when yov spoke it faire, and first, I told you
That it was possible you might be abus'd:
But now, since you forget your manners, you shall finde,
If I transgresse my custome, you doe lie,
And are a villaine, which I had rather yet
My Sword had prov'd, then I been forc'd to speake:
Nay give us leave, and since you stand so haughtily
And highly on your cause, let you and I,
Without engaging these two Gentlemen, singly determine it.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: My Lord, you'l pardon us.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: I trust your Lordships may not doe us that affront.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: As how?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: We kisse your Lordships hand, and come to serve you here with Swords.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: My Lord, we understand our selves.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: We have had the honour to be call'd unto the businesse, and we must not now quit it on terms.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Not terms of reason?

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: No, no reason for the quitting of our calling.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: True if I be call'd to't I must aske no reason.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Nor heare none neither, which is lesse:
It is a favour if my throat be cut,
Your Lordship does me; which I never can,
Nor must have hope how to requite: what noise,
What cry is that my Lord upon your guard?
Some treachery is a foot.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: O here they are:
My Lord (deare Lady helpe me) helpe me all;
I have so woefull interest in both,
I know not which to feare for most: and yet
I must prefer my Lord. Deare brother,
You are too understanding, and too Noble
To be offended, when I know my duty,
Though scarce my teares will let me so to do it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Out loathed strumpet.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: O my dearest Lord,
If words could on me cast the name of whore,
I then were worthy to be loath'd; but know,
Your unkindnesse cannot make me wicked;
And therefore should lesse use that power upon me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Was this your art to have these actors come,
To make this interlude? withdraw, cold man,
And if thy spirit be not frozen up,
Give me one stroke yet at thee for my vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Thou shalt have stroakes, and stroakes, thou glorious man,
Till thou breathst thinner ayre then that thou talkest.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: My Lord Count Amiens.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Princely husband.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Whore.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You wrong her impudent Lord; O that I had the bulke
Of those dull men; look how they stand, and no man
Will revenge an innocent Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: You hinder it Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: I would hinder you; is there none else to kill him?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Kill him Madam? have you learn'd that bad Language? O repent,
And be the motive, rather both kill me.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Then die my infamy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Hold bloody man.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Art thou their Basiliske?

speeches.speaker: Mont:
prose: To strike thee dead, but that thy fate deserves some weightier hand.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Sweet my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: O here's a plot; you bring your champions with you; the adultresse with the adulterer: Out howling—

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose:
Are you her Graces countenance Lady, the
receiver to the poore vicious couple.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Sweet my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Sweet rascall, didst not thou tell me, false fellow,
This Montague, here was murdered?

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: I did so; but he was falser, and a worthlesse Lord,
Like thy foule selfe, that would have had it so.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: Orleance tis true, and shall be prov'd upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Thy malice Duke, and this thy wicked nature, are all as visible as thou; but I borne to contemne thy iniuries, doe know, that though thy greatnesse may corrupt a Jury, and make a Judge afraid, and carry out a world of devils with thy title: yet thou art not quiet at home, thou bearest about thee that, that doth charge thee, and condemne thee too. The thing that grieves me more, and doth indeed displease me, is, to thinke that so much basenesse stands here to have encountered so much honour: Pardon me my Lord what late my passion spake, when you provok'd my innocence.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Yes doe, O flattery becomes him better then the sute he weares; give him a new one Amiens.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Orleance, tis here no time nor place, to jest or raile
Poorely with you, but I will finde a time to
Whisper you forth to this or some fit place,
As shall not hold a second interruption.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I hope your Lordships honour, and your life
Are destined unto higher hazzards; this is of
A meaner arme.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Yes faith, or none.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: He is not fit to fall by an honest Sword,
A Prince and lie!

speeches.speaker: Dub.
verse: And slander, and hire men
To publish the false rumours he hath made.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: And sticke 'em on his friends, and innocents.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: And practice against their lives after their fames.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: In men that are the matter of all leudnesse,
Bands, thieves, and cheaters, it were monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: But in a man of blood, how more conspicuous?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Can this be?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: They doe slander him.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Hang them, a paire of railing hangbies.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: How? stand Orleance; stay, give me my Pistols boy,
Hinder me not, by—
I will kill him.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: O stay his fury,

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Longueville, my friend.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Not for my selfe, my Lord, but for mankind,
And all that have an interest to vertue,
Or title unto innocence.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Why heare me.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: For justice sake.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: That cannot be.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: To punish his wives, your honour, and my Lords wrongs here, whom I must ever call so; for your loves Ile sweare, Ile sacrifice—

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Longaville, I did not thinke you a murtherer before.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: I care not what you thought me.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: By —If thou attempt
His life, thy own is forfeit.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Foolish frantick man, the murder will be of us, not him.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: O God.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: We could have kild him, but we would not take
The justice out of fates. —
Singe but a haire of him, thou diest.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: No matter, shoot.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Villaine.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: My Lord, your sister is slaine.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Biancha?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: O haplesse and most wretched chance.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Standst thou looking upon the mischief thou hast made
Thou Godlesse man, feeding thy blood-shot eyes
With the red spectacle, and art not turn'd to stone
With horrour? hence and take the wings of thy blacke
Infamy, to carry thee beyond the shoot of looks,
Or sound of curses, which will pursue thee still:
Thou hast out-fled all but thy guilt.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: O wish it off again, for I am crack'd
Under the burden, and my heart will breake.
How heavy guilt is, when men come to feele
If you could know the mountaine I sustaine
With horror, you would each take off your part,
And more, to ease me: I cannot stand,
Forgive where I have wrong'd I pray.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Looke to him Montague.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: My Lords and Gentlemen, the Lady is well, but for feare,
Unlesse that have shot her;
I have the worst on't, that needs would venture
Upon a tricke had like to ha' cost my guts:
Look to her, she'l be well, it was but Powder
I chargd with, thinking that a guilty man
Would have been frighted sooner; but I am glad
He's come at last.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: How is Byancha? well?

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Lives she? see sister, doth she breath?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: O Gentlemen, thinke you I can breath,
That am restored to the hatefull sense
Of feeling in me my deare husbands death?
O no, I live not; life was that I left;
And what you have cal'd me to, is death indeed;
I cannot weep so fast as he doth bleed.

speeches.speaker: Dub.
prose: Pardon me Madam, he is well.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: Ha my husband.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: I cannot speake whether my joy or shame
Be greater, but I thank the Heavens for both.
O look not black upon me, all my friends,
To whom I will be reconciled, or grow unto
This earth, till I have weept a trench
That shall be great enough to be my grave,
And I will think them too most manly teares,
If they do move your pities: it is true,
Man should do nothing that he should repent;
But if he have, and say that he is sorry,
It is a worse fault if he be not truly.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: My Lord, such sorrow cannot be suspected:
Here take your honoured wife, and joyn your hands.
— she hath married you again:
And Gentlemen, I do invite you all,
This night to take my house, where on the morrow,
To heighten more the reconciling feast,
Ile make my selfe a husband and a guest.

speeches.speaker: Char.
prose: Well now I am sure you are mine.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I am sure I am glad
I have one to own then; you'l finde me honest
As these daies go, enough; poore without question,
Which beggars hold a vertue; give me meat, and I
Shall do my worke, else knock my shooes off,
And turn me out again.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: You are a merry fellow.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I have no great cause.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Yes thy love to me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: That's as we make our game.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Why you repent then.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: Faith no wors then I am I cannot be;
Much better I expect not: I shall love you,
And when you bid me goe to bed, obey,
Lie still or move, as you shall minister,
Keep a foure-nobles Nag, and a black
Merling, learn to love Ale, and play at two-hand Irish,
And there's then all I aime at.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Nay sweet fellow, Ile make it something better.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: If you doe, you'l make me worse:
Now I am poore, and willing to doe wel,
Hold me in that course, of all the Kings creatures,
I hate his coyne, keep me from that, and save me;
For if you chance out of your housewifery
To leave a hundred pound or two, bestow it
In Plum-broth ere I know it, else I take it;
Seeke out a hundred men that want this money,
Share it among 'em, they'l cry noble Montague,
And so I stand again at livery.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: You have pretty fancies sir, but married once,
This charity will fall home to your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I would it would, I am afraid my loosenesse
Is yet scarce stopt, though it have nought to worke on
But the meere aire of what I have had.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Pretty.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: I wonder sweet heart why you'l marry me,
I can see nothing in my selfe deserves it,
Unlesse the handsome wearing of a band,
For that's my stocke now, or a paire of garters,
Necessity will not let me loose.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: I see sir a great deale more, a hansome man, a husband
To make a right good woman truely happy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Lord, where are my eyes? either you are foolish
As wenches once a yeere are, or far worse,
Extreamly vertuous, can you love a poore man
That relies on cold meat and cast stockings,
One onely suit to his backe, which now is mewing?
But what will be the next coate will pose Tristram.
If I should leavy from my friends a fortune:
I could not raise ten groats to pay the Priest now.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Ile do that duty; tis not means nor money
Makes me pursue your love; were your mind bankrupt,
I would never love you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Peace wench, here's my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Nay never shrinke i'th wetting, for my presence;
D'ee finde her willing Montague?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Willing Madam?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How dainty you make of it, doe not I know
You two love one another?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Certaine Madam, I thinke ye'ave revelations of these matters:
Your Ladyship cannot tell me when I kist her.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: But she can, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: But she will not Madam;
For when they talke once, tis like fairy-money,
They get no more close kisses.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Thou art wanton.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: God knows I need not, yet I would be lusty:
But — my provender scarce pricks me.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: It shall be mended Montague, I am glad you are grown so merry.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: So am I too Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You two will make a pretty hansome consort.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Madam, if my fiddle faile me not.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Your Fiddle? why your Fiddle? I warrant thou meanest madly:

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Can you blame me? alasse I am in love.

speeches.speaker: Char.
verse: Tis very well sir.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: How long have you been thus?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: How thus in love?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You are very quick sir: no, I mean thus pleasant.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: —Ever since I was poore.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: A little wealth would change you then.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Yes Lady into another suit, but never more
Into another man: Ile bar that mainly,
The wealth I get henceforward shal be charm'd
For ever hurting me, Ile spend it fasting:
As I live noble Lady there is nothing
I have found directly cures the melancholy,
But want and wedlocke; when I had store of money
I simper'd sometime, and spoke wondrous wise,
But never laught out-right; now I am empty
My heart sounds like a bell, and strikes at both sides.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: You are finely temper'd Montague.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Pardon Lady, if any way my free mirth have offended,
Twas meant to please you: if it prove too sawsie,
Give it a frown, and I am ever silenc'd.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: I like it passing well; pray follow it:
This is my day of choice, and shall be yours too,
Twere pity to delay ye: call to the Steward,
And tell him tis my pleasure he should give you
500 Crowns: make your selfe hansome Montague,
Let none weare better cloathes, tis for my credit;
But pray be merry still.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: If I be not, and make a foole of twice as many hundreds,
Clap me in Canvas Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: I am strangely glad, I have found the mystery
Of this disguised boy out: I ever trusted
It was a woman, and how happily
I have found it so; and for my selfe, I am sure
One that would offer me a thousand pound now
(And that's a pretty sum to make one stagger)
In ready Godl for this concealment, could not
Buy my hope of her, she's a dainty wench,
And such a one I finde. I want extreamly
To bring me into credit: beauty does it.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Say we should all meach here, and stay the feast, now what can the worst be? we have plai'd the knaves, that's without question.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: True, and as I take it this is the first truth
We told these ten yeeres, and for any thing
I know may be the last: but grant we are knaves,
Both base and beastly knaves —

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Say so then.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Well.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: And likewise let it be considered, we have wrongd
And most maliciously, this Gentlewoman,
We cast to stay with, what must we expect now?

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: I there's the point, we would expect good eating.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I know we would, but we may find good beating.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: You say true Gentlemen, and by—
Though I love meat as well as any man,
I care not what he be, if a eate a Gods name;
Such crab-sauce to my meat wil turn my pallate.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: There's all the hazzard, for the frozen Montague
Has now got spring againe, and warmth in him,
And without doubt dares beat us terribly.
For not to mint the matter, we are cowards,
And have and shall be beaten when men please
To call us into cudgelling.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I feele we are very prone that way.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: The sonnes of Adam.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Now here then rests the state o'th question?
Whether we yeild our bodies for a dinner
To a sound dog-whip, for I promise ye
If men be given to correction,
We can expect no lesse, or quietly
Take a hard Egge or two, and ten mile hence
Baite in a ditch, this we may do securely;
For to stay here about will be all one,
If once our morall mischiefes come in memory.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: But pray ye hear me, is not this the day
The Virgin Lady doth elect her husband?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: The dinner is to that end.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Very well then, say we all stay, and say we all scape this whipping, and be well entertained, and one of us carry the Lady.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: 'Tis a seemly saying, I must confesse, but if we stay, how fitly
We may apply it to our selves (i'th end)
Will aske a Christian feare; I cannot see
If I say true, what spetiall ornaments
Of art or nature, lay aside our lying
Whoring and drinking, which are no great vertues,
We are endued withall to win this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Yet women go not by the best parts ever; that I have found directly.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Why should we fear then? they choose men
As they feed; some times they settle
Upon a white broth'd face, a sweet smooth gallant,
And him they make an end of in a night;
Sometimes a Goose, sometimes, a grosser meat,
A rump of beef will serve 'em at some season,
And fill their bellies too: though without doubt
They are great devourers: stock fish is a dish,
If it be well drest, for the tufnesse sake
Wil make the proud'st of 'em long and leap for't.
They'l run mad for a pudding ere they'l starve,

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: For my own part I care not, come what can come,
If I be whipt, why so be it; if cudgel'd,
I hope I shall out live it, I am sure
'Tis not the hundreth time I have bin serv'd so,
And yet I thank God I am here.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Here's resolution.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: A little patience, and a rotten Apple
Cures twenty worse diseases; what say you sir?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Marry I say sir, if I had bin acquainted
With lamming in my youth, as you have bin
With whipping, and such benefits of nature,
I should do better: as I am, i'le venture,
And if it be my luck to have the Lady,
I'le use my fortune modestly; if beaten
You shall not hear a word, one I am sure of,
And if the worst fall she shall be my physick.
Lets go then, and a merry winde be with us.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Captaine your shooes are old, pray put 'em off,
And let one fling 'em after us; be bold sirs,
And howosever our fortune fals, lets beare
An equall burden; if there be an odde lash,
Wee'l part it afterwards.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: I am arm'd at all points.

prose: Then my Lady will have a bedfellow to night.
So she sayes, heaven what a danty armefull shall he enjoy that has the launching of her, what a fight shee'l make.
I mary boyes, there will be sport indeed, there will be grapling, she has a murderer lies in her prow, I am affraid will fright his maine mast Robin.
Who dost thou think shall have her of thy conscience, thou art a wise man.
If she go the old way, the way of lot, the longest cut sweeps all without question?
She has lost a friend of me else; what think yee of the Courtier.
Hang him hedgehogge, h'as nothing in him but a piece of Euphues, and twenty dozen of twelve penny riband all about him, he is but one Pedlers shop of gloves and garters, pickteeth and pomander.
The Courtier! marry God blesse her Steven, she is not mad yet, she knowes that trindle tayle too well, he's crest falne, and pinbuttock't with leaping Landresses.
The Merchant sure shee will not be so base to have him.
I hope so Rohin, hee'l sell us all to the Moors to make mummy; nor the Captaine.
Who Potgun, that's a sweet youth indeed, will he stay thinke ye?

Yes, without question, and have half din'd too ere the grace be done; he's good for nothing in the world but eating, lying and sleeping; what other men devour in drink, he takes in Pottage, they say has bin at Sea, a Herring fishing, for without doubt he dares not hayle an Ele-boate, ith way of War.
I think so, they would beate him off with Butter.

When he brings in a prize, unlesse it be Cockles, or Callis sand to scoure with, I'le renounce my five mark a year, and all the hidden art I have in carving, to teach young Birds to whistle Walsingham; leave him to the lime boates; now, what think you of the brave Amiens?
That's a thought indeed.
I marry ther's a person fit to feed upon a dish so danty, and hee'l do't I warrant him ith nick boyes, has a body world without end.
And such a one my Lady will make no little off; but is not Montague married to day?
Yes faith, honest Montague must have his bout too.
Hee's as good a lad as ever turnd a trencher; must we leave him?
Hee's to good for us Steven, I'le give him health to his good luck to night ith old Beaker, and it shall be sack too.
I must have a Garter; and boyes I have bespoke, a a Posset, some body shall give me thanks for't, 'tas a few toyes in't will rase commotions in a bed lad.
Away; my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Stur your selves noble Lords and Gentlemen,
You know your places; many royall welcomes
I give your grace; how lovely shewes this change?
My house is honor'd in this reconcilement.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Thus Madam must you do, my Lady now shall see
You made a Woman;
And give you some short lessons for your voyage.
Take her instructions Lady, she knowes much.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: This becomes you sir.

speeches.speaker: La.
prose: My Lord must have his will.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Tis all I can do now sweet heart, faire Lady;
This to your happy choyce brother Amiens,
You are the man I meane it to.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: I'le pledge you.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: And with my heart.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: With all my love I take it.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
verse: Noble Lords I am proud ye have done this day,
so much content, and me such estimation that this hour
(In this poor house) shall be a league for ever,
For so I know ye mean it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: I do Lady.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: And I my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Y'ave done a work of honor.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Give me the Cup, where this health stops, let
That man be either very sick, or very simple;
Or I am very angry; sir, to you;
Madam me thinks this Gentleman might sit to;
He would become the best on's.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Pray sit down sir, I know the Lady of the feast expects not this day so much old custom.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Sit down Mountague; nay never blush for the matter.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: Noble Madam, I have too reasons against it, and I dare not; duty to you first, as you are my Lady, and I your poorest servant; next the custome of this dayes ceremony.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: As you are my servant, I may command you then.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: To my life Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Sit down, and here, i'le have it so.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Sit down man, never refuse so faire a Ladies offer.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: It is your pleasure Madam, not my pride,
And I obey; ile pledge yee now my Lord, Mounsier Longavile.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: I thank you sir.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
prose: This to my Lady, and her faire choyce to day, and happinesse.

speeches.speaker: Lon.
prose: Tis a faire health, i'le pledge you though I sinke for't.

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Montague you are too modest; come i'le adde a little more wine t'ee, 'twill make you merry, this to the good I wish.—

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Honord Lady, I shall forget my selfe with this great bounty.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: You shall not sir; give him some Vine.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: By heaven you are a worthy woman, and that.
Man is blest can come neer such a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Such a blessing wet weather washes.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: At all, I will not go a lip lesse my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Tis well cast sir.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: If Montague get more Wine, we are like to heare on't.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: I do not like that sitting there.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Nor I, me thinks he looks like a Judge.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Now have I a kinde a grudging of a beating on me, I fear my hot sit.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Drink apace, ther's nothing allays a cudgell like it.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Montague, now I'le put my choyce to you; who do you hold in all this honor'd company a husband fit to enjoy thy Lady? speak directly.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Shall I speak Madam?

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Montague, you shall.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Then as I have a soule i'le speak my conscience,
Give me more wine, in vino veritas,
Here's to my self, and Montague have a care.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Speak to th'cause.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Yes, Madam; first i'le begin to thee.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Have at us.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Now for a Psalme of mercy.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: You good Mounsier, you that bely the noble Name of Courtier, and think your claime good here, hold up your hand; your VVorship is endited here, for a vaine glorious foole.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Good, oh sir.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: For one whose wit
Lies in a ten pound wastcoat, yet not warme;
Ye have travel'd like a Fidler to make faces,
And brought home nothing but a case of tooth-picks.
You would be married, and no lesse then Ladies,
And of the best sort can serve you; thou silke worm
What hast thou in thee to deserve this woman?
Name but the poorest piece of man, good manners,
Ther's nothing sound about thee, faith thou'ast none,
It lies pawn'd at thy silke mans, for so much lace;
Thy credit which is worse cannot redeem it,
Thy cloaths are all the soule thou hast, for so
Thou sav'st them hansome for the next great tilting
Let who wil take the t'other, thou wert never christen'd
Upon my conscience (but in barbers water)
Thou art never out o'th basen, thou art rotten,
And if thou darst tell truth, thou wilt confesse it;
—thy skin
Looks of a Chestnut colour, greas'd with Amber
All women that on earth do dwell thou lov'st,
Yet none that understand love thee again,
But those that love the Spittle, get thee home
Poor painted butter fly, thy summers pa'st;
Go sweat and eat dry Mutton, thou mayst live
To do so well yet; a bruis'd Chamber Maide
May fall upon thee, and advance thy follies.
You have your sentence; now it followes Captaine,
I treat of you.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Pray God I may deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
verse: Beshrow my heart he speaks, plaine.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: That's plain dealing.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: You are a rascall Captaine.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: A fine calling.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: A water coward.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: He would make a prety stuffe.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Nay I speak freely Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Her's none ties you.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why should'st thou dare come hither with a thought
To finde a wife here fit for thee? are all
Thy single money whores that fed on Carrots,
And fild the high grasse with familiars
Falne of to footmen? prethee tell me truly,
For now I know thou dar'st not lie, couldst thou not
Wish thy selfe beaten well with all thy heart now,
And out of paine? say that I broke a rib,
Or cut thy nose off, wert not mercifull for this ambition?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Do your pleasure sir, beggars must not be choosers.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: He longs for beating.

speeches.speaker: Mon.
verse: But that I have nobler thoughts possesse my soule,
Then such brown bisket, such a peice of dog-fish,
Such a most mangy Mackrell eater as thou art
That dares do nothing that belongs toth'Sea,
But spue, and catch rats, and fear men of war,
Though thou hast nothing in the world to loose
Abord thee, but one piece of beefe, one Musket
Without a cock for peace sake, and a pitch barrell,
I'le tell thee if my time were not more pretious
Then thus to loose it, I would rattle thee,
It may be beat thee, and thy pure fellow,
The Merchant there of Catskins, till my words,
Or blowes, or both, made ye two branded wretches
To all the world hereafter; you would faine to
Venture your bils of lading for this Lady;
What would you give now for her? some five frayle
Of rotten Figs good, Godson, would you not sir?
Or a Parrat that speaks high Dutch? can all thou ever saw'st
Of thine own fraughts from Sea, or cosonage
(At which thou art as expert as the devill)
Nay sell thy soul for wealth to, as thou wilt do,
Forfeit thy friends, and raise a mint of Money,
Make thee dream all these double could procure
A kisse from this good Lady? can'st thou hope
She would lie with such a nook of hell as thou art,
And hatch young Merchant-furies? oh ye dog-bolts
That fear no God but Dunkirks, I shall see you
Serve in a lowsy Lime boat, ere I die,
For mouldy cheese and butter Billingsgate
Would not endure, or bring in rotten Pippins
To cure blew eyes, and swear they came from China.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Vex 'em no more, alas they shake:

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Down quickly on your marrow bones. and thank this Lady.
I would not leave you thus else, there are blankets,
And such delights for such knav s; but fear still;
'Twill be revenge enough, to keep you waking.
Ye have no minde of Marriage, ha' ye?

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: Surely no great mind now.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Nor you.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Nor I, I take it.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Two eager sutors.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
prose: Troth tis wonderous hot, God blesse us from him

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: You have told me Montague
Who are not fit to have me, let me know
The man you would point out for me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: There he sits; my Lord of Amiens, Madam, is my choyce, hee's noble every way, and worthy a wife with all the dowries of—

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Do you speak sir out of your friendship to me?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Yes, my Lord, and out of truth, for I could never flatter.

speeches.speaker: Ami
verse: I would not say how much I owe you for it,
For that were but a promise, but Ile thank ye,
As now I find you, in despite of fortune,
A faire and noble Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: My Lords I must confesse the choyce this man hath made
Is every way a great one, if not too great,
And no way to be slighted: yet because
We love to have our own eyes, sometimes now
Give me a little liberty to see,
How I could fit my selfe, if I were put to't.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Madam we must.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Are yee all agreed?

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: We be?

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Then as I am a maid, I shall choose here.
Montague, I must have thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Why Madam I have learnt to suffer more then you can (out of pitty) mock me with this way especially.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Thou think'st I jest now;
But by the love I bear thee, I will have thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: If you could be so weak, to love a falne man,
He must deserve more then I ever can,
Or ever shall (deer Lady;) look but this way
Upon that Lord and you will tell me then
Your eyes are no true choosers of good men.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
prose: Do you love him truely?

speeches.speaker: Lam.
prose: Yes my Lord, I will obey him truly, for I'le marry him, and justly thinke he that has so well serv'd mee with his obedience being borne to greatnesse, must use mee nobly of necessity when I shall serve him.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: 'Twere a deepe sin to crosse ye, noble Montague,
I wish ye all content, and am as happy
In my friends good as it were meerly mine.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Your Lordship does ill to give up your right;
I am not capable of this great goodnesse,
There sits my wife that holds my troth.

speeches.speaker: Cha.
prose: I'le end all, I wooed you for my Lady, and now give up my title, alas poor wench, my aimes are lower far.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: How's this sweet heart?

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: Sweet heart tis so, the drift was mine to hide
My purpose till it struck home.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: God give you joy.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
prose: Prethee leave wondring, by this kisse i'le have thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: Then by this kisse, and this i'le ever serve ye.

speeches.speaker: Long.
prose: This Gentleman and I sir must needs hop once more to follow yee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: As friends and fellows, never as servants more.

speeches.speaker: Long. Dub.
prose: You make us happy.

speeches.speaker: Orl.
prose: Friend Montague, ye have taught mee so much honor, I have found a fault in my self, but thus I'le purge my conscience of it, the late land I took by false play, from you with as much Contrition, and entirenesse of affection to this most happy day again, I render; be Master of your own, forget my malice, and make mee worthy of your love, L. Montague.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
prose: You have won me and honor to your name.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
prose: Since your Lordship has begun good deeds, wee'l follow; good sir forgive us, we are now those men fear you for goodnes sake; those sums of money unjustly we detaine from you, on your pardon shall bee restord again, and we your servants.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
prose: You are very forward sir, it seems you have money, I pray you lay out, i'le pay you or pray for you, as the Sea works.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Their pennance sir i'le undertake, so please ye
To grant me on concealement.

speeches.speaker: Long.
verse: Right courtier, still a begging.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: What is it sir?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: A Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: In my gift?

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Yes sir, in yours.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why bring her forth and take her.

speeches.speaker: Lami.
verse: What wench would he have?

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Any wench I think.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: This is the Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: 'Tis my Page sir.

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: No sir, I am a poor disguis'd Lady?
That like a Page have followed you full long for love god-wot.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: A Lady—Laverdine—yes, yes, tis a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: It may be so, and yet we have laine together,
But by my troth I never found her, Lady.

speeches.speaker: L Orl.
verse: Why wore you boyes cloathes?

speeches.speaker: Vir.
verse: I'le tell you Madam,
I took example by 2 or 3. playes, that methought
Concernd me.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Why made you not me acquainted with it.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: Indeed sir I knew it not my selfe,
Untill this Gentleman opend my dull eyes,
And by perswasion made me see it.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Could his power in words make such a change?

speeches.speaker: ~er.
verse: Yes, as truly woman as your selfe my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: Why but hark you, are not you a woman?

speeches.speaker: Ver.
prose: If hands and face make it not evident, you shall see more.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Breeches, breeches, Laverdine.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Tis not enough, women may wear those cases.
Search further Courtier.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: La-p.
verse: Oh thou freshwater Gudgeon, wouldst thou come
To point of Marriage with an Ignoramus?
Thou shouldst have had her urin to the doctors,
The foolishest Phisitian could have made plaine
The liquid Epicaene; a blind man by the hand
Could have discoverd the ring from the stone.
Boy, come, to Sea with me, ile teach thee to climb,
And come down by the rope, nay to eate Rats.

speeches.speaker: Ver.
verse: I shall devour my Master before the prison then,
Sir, I have began my Trade.

speeches.speaker: Mal.
verse: Trade? to the Citie, child, a flatcap will become thee.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Gentlemen I beseech you molest your selves no further,
For his preferment it is determin'd.

speeches.speaker: Lav.
verse: I am much ashamed, and if my cheek
Gives not satisfaction, break my head.

speeches.speaker: Mont.
verse: Your shame's enough sir.

speeches.speaker: Ami.
verse: Montague, much joy attend thy marriage Bed;
By thy example of true goodnesse, envie is exil'd,
And to all honest men that truth intend,
I wish good luck, faire fate be still thy friend.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: THe Generall is returned then?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: With much honour.

speeches.speaker: Sol.
verse: And peace concluded with the Prince of Argos?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: To the Queens wishes: the conditions sign'd
So farre beyond her hopes, to the advantage
Of Corinth, and the good of all her Subjects;
That though Leonidas our brave Generall
Ever came home a faire and great example,
He never yet return'd, or with lesse losse
Or more deserved honour.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Have you not heard
The motives to this generall good?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: The maine one
Was admiration first in young Agenor,
(For by that name we know the Prince of Argos)
Of our Leonidas wisedome, and his valour,
Which though an enemy, first in him bred wonder;
That liking, Love succeeded that, which was
Followed by a desire to be a friend
Upon what termes soever to such goodnesse;
They had an enterview; and that their friendship
Might with our peace be ratified, 'twas concluded,
Agenor yeelding up all such stronge places
As he held in our Territories, should receive
(With a sufficient Dower, paid by the Queene)
The faire Merione for his wife.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: But how
Approves the Queene of this? since we well know,
Nor was her Highnesse ignoant, that her Sonne
The Prince Theanor made love to this Lady,
And in the noblest way.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Which she allowed of,
And I have heard from some familiar with
Her neerest secrets, she so deeply priz'd her
Being from an Infant train'd up in her service,
(Or to speake better, rather her owne Creature)
She once did say, That if the Prince should steale
A Marriage without her leave, or knowledge,
With this Merione, with a little suit
She should grant both their pardons: where as now
To shew her selfe forsooth a Spartan Lady,
And that 'tis in her power, now it concernes
The common good, not alone to subdue
Her owne affections, but command her Sons;
She has not onely forc'd him with rough threats
To leave his Mistris, but compell'd him when
Agenor made his entrance into Corinth
To wait upon his Rivall.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Can it be
The Prince should sit downe with this wrong?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: I know not,
I am sure I should not.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Trust me nor I,
A Mother is a name, but put in ballance
With a yong wench 'tis nothing; where did you leave him?

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Neere Vesta's Temple, for there he dismiss'd me,
And full of troubled thoughts, calling for Crates:
He went with him, but whither or to what purpose
I am a stranger.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: They are come backe Neanthes.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I like the place well.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Well Sir? it is built
As if the Architect had been a Prophet,
And fashion'd it alone for this nights action;
The vaults so hollow, and the walls so strong,
As Dian there might suffer violence,
And with loud shrikes in vaine call Jove to helpe her;
Or should he heare, his thunder could not finde
An entrance to it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I give up my selfe
Wholly to thy direction, worthiest Crates;
And yet the desperate cure that we must practice
Is in it selfe so foule, and full of danger,
That I stand doubtfull whether 'twere more manly
To dye not seeking helpe, or that helpe being
So deadly, to pursue it.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: To those reasons
I have already urg'd, I will adde these.
For but consider Sir—

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: It is of weight
What ere it be, that with such vehement action,
Of eye, hand, foot, nay all his bodies motion,
Crates incites the Prince to.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Then observe,
With what variety of passions he
Receives his reasons; now he's pale, and shakes
For feare or anger; now his naturall red
Comes backe againe, and with a pleasing smile
He seemes to entertaine it; 'tis resolv'd on
Be it what 'twill: to his ends may it prosper
Though the State sinke for't.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Now you are a Prince
Fit to rule others, and in shaking off
The Bonds in which your Mother fetters you
Discharge your debt to nature, she's your guide,
Follow her boldly Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am confirm'd,
Fall what may fall,

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Yet still disguise your malice
In your humility.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am instructed.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Though in your heart there rage a thousand tempests,
All calmenesse in your lookes.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I shall remember.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: And at no hand, though these are us'd as agents
Acquaint them with your purpose till the instant
That we employ them; tis not fit they have
Time to consider, when 'tis done, reward
Or feare will keep them silent: yet you may
Grace them as you passe by, 'twill make them surer,
And greedier to deserve you.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Ile move onely
As you would have me: Good day gentlemen;
Nay, spare this ceremonious forme of duty
To him that brings love to you, equall love,
And is in nothing happier, then in knowing
It is return'd by you; we are as one.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: I am ore-joyd, I know not
How to reply: but—

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Hang all buts; my Lord,
For this your bounteous favour—

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Let me speake,
If to feed Vultures hereafter the halter
Has done his part, or if there be a Hell
To take a swindge or two there, may deserve this.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: We are ready.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Try us any way.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Put us to it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What jewels I have in you?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Have these soules,
That for a good looke, and a few kinde words
Part with their essence?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Since you will compell me
To put that to the tryall, which I doubt not,
Crates may be suddenly will instruct you
How, and in what to shew your loves; obey him
As you would binde me to you.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Tis well grounded;
Leave me to reare the building.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: We will doe.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I know it.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Any thing youl put us to.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Sister, I reape the harvest of my labours
In your preferment, be you worthy of it,
And with an open bosome entertaine
A greater fortune then my love durst hope for;
Be wise, and welcome it: play not the coy
And foolish wanton, with the offerd bounties
Of him that is a Prince. I was woo'd for you,
And won Merione: then if you dare
Beleeve the object that tooke me was worthy,
Or trust my judgement, in me think you were
Courted, sued to, and conquerd.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Noble brother,
I have, and still esteeme you as a Father,
And will as farre obey you; my heart speakes it:
And yet without your anger give me leave
To say, That in the choice of that on which
All my lifes joyes or sorrowes have dependance,
It had been fit ere you had made a full
And absolute grant of me to any other,
I should have us'd mine owne eyes, or at least
Made you to understand, whether it were
Within my power to make a second gift
Of my poore selfe.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I know what tis you point at,
The Prince Theanos love; let not that cheat you;
His vowes were but meere courtship; all his service
But practise how to entrap a credulous Lady:
Or grant it serious, yet you must remember
He's not to love but where the Queene his Mother
Must give allowance, which to you is barr'd up:
And therefore study to forget that ever
You cherisht such a hope.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I would I could.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: But brave Agenor, who is come in person
To celebrate this Marriage, for your love
Forgives the forfeit of ten thousand lives,
That must have falne under the sword of war
Had not this peace been made; which generall good
Both Countries owe to his affection to you:
O happy Sister, aske this noble Lady
Your bosome friend (since I faile in my credit)
What palme Agenors name above all Princes
That Greece is proud of carries, and with lustre.

speeches.speaker: Rel.
verse: Indeed fame gives him out of excellent;
And friend, I doubt not but when you shall see him
He'l so appeare to you. Art sure 'tis he?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: As I live Madam—

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Vertue enable me to containe my joy.
'Tis my Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: And he's in health?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Most certainly Madam,

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Ile see him instantly.
So prethee tell him.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I yeeld my selfe too weake
In argument to oppose you: you may leade me
Whither you please.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: 'Tis answer'd like my Sister;
And if in him you finde not ample cause
To pray for me, and daily on your knees,
Conclude I have no judgement.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: May it prove so:
Friend, shall we have your company?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Two houres hence
I will not faile you.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: At your pleasure Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Could I in one word speake a thousand welcomes
(And hearty ones) you have 'em: Fie, my hand,
We stand at no such distance, by my life
The parting kisse you tooke before your travell
Is yet a virgin on my lips, preserv'd
With as much care as I would doe my fame,
To entertaine your wish'd returne.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Best Lady,
That I doe honour you, and with as much reason
As ever man did vertue; that I love you,
Yet looke upon you with that reverence
As holy men behold the Sun, the Starrs,
The Temples, and their gods, they all can witnesse;
And that you have deserv'd this duty from me;
The life, and meanes of life, for which I owe you,
Commands me to professe it, since my fortune
Affords no other payment.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Good Euphanes, where benefits are ill conferr'd,
I had thought,
That for the trifling courtesies as I call them,
(Though you give them another name) you had
Made ample satisfaction in th' acceptance,
And therefore did presume you had brought home
Some other Language.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: No one I have learn'd
Yeelds words sufficient to expresse your goodnesse;
Nor can I ever chuse another theame
And not be thought unthankfull.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Pray you no more
As you respect me.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: That charme is too powerfull
For me to disobey it: 'Tis your pleasure,
And not my boldnesse Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Good Euphanes,
Beleeve I am not one of those weak Ladies,
That (barren of all inward worth) are proud
Of what they cannot truly call their owne,
Their birth or fortune, which are things without them,
Nor in this will I imitate the world,
Whose greater part of men think when they give
They purchase bondmen, not make worthy friends:
By all that's good I sweare, I never thought
My great estate was an addition to me,
Or that your wants took from you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: There are few
So truly understanding or themselves
Or what they doe possesse.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Good Euphanes,
Where benefits
Are ill conferr'd as to unworthy men,
That turne them to bad uses, the bestower
For wanting judgement how, and on whom to place them,
Is partly guilty: but when we do favours
To such as make them grounds on which they build
Their noble actions, there we improve our fortunes
To the most faire advantage. If I speake
Too much, though I confesse I speak well,
Prethee remember 'tis a womans weaknesse,
And then thou wilt forgive it.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You speake nothing
But what would well become the wisest man:
And that by you deliver'd is so pleasing
That I could heare you ever.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Fly not from
Your word, for I arrest it: and will now
Expresse my selfe a little more, and prove
That whereas you professe your selfe my debtor,
That I am yours.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Your Ladiship then must use
Some Sophistry I ne're heard of.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: By plaine reasons,
For looke you, had you never sunk beneath
Your wants, or if those wants had found supply
From Crates, your unkinde and covetous brother,
Or any other man, I then had miss'd
A subject upon which I worthily
Might exercise my bounty: whereas now
By having happy opportunity
To furnish you before, and in your travells,
With all conveniencies that you thought usefull,
That Gold which would have rusted in my Coffers
Being thus imploy'd, has rendred me a partner
In all your glorious actions. And whereas
Had you not been, I should have di'd a thing.
Scarce knowne, or soone forgotten: there's no Trophy
In which Euphanes for his worth is mentioned,
But there you have been carefull to remember,
That all the good you did came from Beliza.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: That was but thankfulnesse.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Twas such an honour,
And such a large returne for the poore trash.
I ventur'd with you, that if I should part
With all that I possesse, and my selfe too
In satisfaction for it, 'twere still short
Of your deservings.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You o're-prize them Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: The Queen her selfe hath given me gracious thanks
In your behalfe, for she hath heard Euphanes
How gallantly you have maintain'd her honour
In all the Courts of Greece: and rest assur'd,
(Though yet unknown) when I present you to her,
Which I will doe this evening, you shall finde
That she intends good to you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Worthiest Lady,
Since all you labour for is the advancement
Of him that will live ever your poore servant,
He must not contradict it.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Here's your Brother,
'Tis strange to see him here.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: You are welcome home Sir,
(Your pardon Madam) I had thought my house,
Considering who I am, might have been worthy
Of your first visit.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: 'Twas not open to me
When last I saw you; and to me 'tis wonder
That absence which still renders men forgotten
Should make my presence wish'd for.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: That's not it,
Your too kinde Brother understanding that
You stand in no need of him, is bold to offer
His entertainment.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: He had never wanted,
Or yours, or your assistance, had he practiz'd
The way he might have tooke, to have commanded
What ever I call mine,

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I studied many,
But could finde none.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: You would not finde your selfe Sir,
Or in your selfe what was from you due to me:
The priviledge my birth bestow'd upon me
Might challenge some regard.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You had all the Land Sir,
What else did you expect? and I am certaine
You kept such strong Guards to preserve it yours
I could force nothing from you.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Did you ever
Demand helpe from me?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: My wants have, and often,
With open mouthes, but you nor heard, nor saw them;
May be you look'd I should petition to you
As you went to your Horse; flatter your servants,
To play the Brokers for my furtherance,
Sooth your worse humours, Act the Parasite
On all occasions, write my name with theirs
That are but one degree remov'd from slaves,
Be drunk when you would have me, then wench with you,
Or play the Pander; enter into Quarrels
Although unjustly grounded, and defend them
Because they were yours; these are the tyrannies
Most younger Brothers groane beneath; yet beare them
From the insulting Heire, selling their freedomes
At a lesse rate then what the State allowes,
The sallary of base and common Strumpets:
For my part, ere on such low termes I feed
Upon a Brothers trencher, let me dye
The Beggers death, and starve.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: 'Tis bravely spoken,
Did what you doe ranke with it.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Why, what does he
You would not wish were yours?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Ile tell you Lady,
Since you rise up his Advocate, and boldly,
(For now I finde, and plainly, in whose favour
My love and service to you was neglected)
For all your wealth, nay, adde to that your beauty,
And put your vertues in if you have any,
I would not yet be pointed at, as he is,
For the fine Courtier, the womans man,
That tells my Lady stories, dissolves riddles,
Ushers her to Coach, lyes at her feet
At sollemne Maskes, applauding what she laughs at;
Reads her asleep a nights, and takes his oath
Upon her Pantoffles, that all excellence
In other Madams doe but zany hers:
These you are perfect in, and yet these take not
Or from your birth or freedome.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Should another
Say this, my deeds, not lookes should shew—

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Contemne it:
His envie faines this, and he's but reporter,
Without a second, of his owne dry fancies.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Yes Madam, the whole City speakes it with me,
And though it may distaste, 'tis certaine you
Are brought into the sceane, and with him censur'd;
For you are given out for the provident Lady,
That not to be unfurnish'd for her pleasures
(As without them to what vaine use is greatnesse)
Have made choyce of an able man, a young man
Of an Herculean back to doe you service,
And one you may command too, that is active,
And does what you would have him.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You are foule mouth'd.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: That can speake well, write Verses too, and good ones,
Sharp and conceited, whose wit you may lie with
When his performance failes him; one you have
Maintain'd abroad to learne new waies to please you.
And by the gods you well reward him for it,
No night (in which while you lye sick and panting)
He watches by you but is worth a tallent:
No conference in your Coach which is not paid with
A scarlet Suit; this the poore people mutter,
Though I beleeve, for I am bound to doe so,
A Lady of your youth, that feeds high too,
And a most exact Lady, may doe all this
Out of vertuous love, the last bought vizard
That Leachery purchas'd.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Not a word beyond this,
The reverence I owe to that one wombe
In which we both were embrions, makes me suffer
What's past; but if continued—

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Stay your hand,
The Queene shall right mine honour.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Let him doe it,
It is but marrying him; and for your anger
Know that I slight it: when your Goddesse here
Is weary of your sacrifice, as she will be,
You know my house, and there amongst my servants
Perhaps youl finde a livery.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Be not mov'd,
I know the rancour of his disposition,
And turne it on himselfe by laughing at it,
And in that let me teach you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I learne gladly.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: You are met unto my wishes, if you ever
Desir'd true mirth so far as to adventure
To dye with the extreamity of laughter,
I come before the object that will doe it;
Or let me live your foole.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Who is't Neanthes?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Lamprias the Usurers sonne.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Lamprias? the youth
Of six and fifty?

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: That was sent to travell
By rich Beliza, till he came to age,
And was fit for a Wife?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: The very same,
This gallant with his Guardian, and his Tutor,
(And of the three who is most foole I know not)
Are newly come to Corinth, ile not stale them
By giving up their characters, but leave you
To make your owne discoveries: here they are Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tutor.
verse: That legge a little higher; very well.
Now put your face into the Travellors posture;
Exceeding good.

speeches.speaker: Vnckle.
verse: Doe you mark how they admire him?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: They will be all my Schollars, when they know
And understand him truly.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Phoebus guard me
From this new Python.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: How they have trimm'd him up
Like an old Reveller?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Curl'd him and perfum'd him,
But that was done with judgement, for he lookes
Like one that purg'd perpetually; trust me,
That Witches face of his is painted too,
And every ditch upon it buries more
Then would set off ten Bawds, and all their tenants.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: See how it moves towards us.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: There's a salutation:
'Troth Gentlemen, you have bestowed much travell
In trayning up your Pupill.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Sir, great buildings
Require great labours, which yet we repent not,
Since for the Countries good we have brought home
An absolute man.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: As any of his yeares,
Corinth can shew you.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: He's exceeding meagre.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: His contemplation—

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Besides, 'tis fit
Learners should be kept hungry.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: You all contemplate;
For three such wretched pictures of leane famine
I never saw together.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: We have fat minds Sir,
And travell'd to save charges. Doe you thinke
'Twas fit a young and hopefull Gentleman
Should be brought up a glutton? he's my Ward,
Nor was there ever where I bore the bagg
Any superfluous waste.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Pray you can it speake?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: He knowes all Languages, but will use none,
They are all too big for his mouth, or else too little
T'expresse his great conceits: and yet of late
With some ippulsion he hath set downe
In a strange method by the way of question,
And briefly, to all businesse whatsoever
That may concerne a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Good Sir, let's heare him.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Come on Sir.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: They have taught him like an Ape,
To doe his tricks by signes: now he begins.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: When shall we be drunke together?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: That's the first.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Where shall we whore to night?

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
verse: That ever followes.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: 'Odds me, he now lookes angry.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Shall we quarrell?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: With me at no hand Sir.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Then let's protest.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Is this all?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: These are Sir, the foure new Vertues
That are in fashion: many a mile we measur'd
Before we could arrive unto this knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: You might have spar'd that labour, for at home here
Ther's little else in practice: Ha? the Queene?
Good friends, for halfe an houre remove your motion,
To morrow willingly when we have more leasure
We'l looke on him againe.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Did I not rarely?

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
verse: Excellent well.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: He shall have sixe Plumbs for it.

speeches.speaker: Queene.
verse: How much my Court is honour'd princely Brother
In your vouchasing it your long'd for presence
Were tedious to repeat, since 'tis already
(And heartily) acknowledg'd; may the gods
That looke into Kings actions smile upon
The league we have concluded; and their justice
Finde me out to revenge it if I breake
One article.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: Great miracle of Queenes,
How happy I esteeme my selfe in being
Thought worthy to be numbred in the rank
Of your confederates, my love and best service
Shall teach the world hereafter: but this gift
With which you have confirm'd it, is so farre
Beyond my hopes and meanes ere to returne,
That of necessity I must dye oblig'd
To your unanswer'd bounty.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: The sweet Lady
In blushes gives your Highnesse thankes.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Beleeve it
On the Queenes word, she is a worthy one,
And I am so acquainted with her goodnesse,
That but for this peace that hath chang'd my purpose,
And to her more advancement, I should gladly
Have call'd her Daughter.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Though I am depriv'd of
A blessing 'tis not in the Fates to equall,
To shew my selfe a subject as a sonne,
Here I give up my claime, and willingly
With mine owne hand deliver you what once
I lov'd above my selfe; and from this houre
(For my affection yeelds now to my duty)
Vow never to sollicite her.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: 'Tis well cover'd
Neanthes, and the rest.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Nay, for this night
You must (for 'tis our Country fashion Sir)
Leave her to her devotions, in the morning
We'l bring you to the Temple.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How in this
Your Highnesse honours me?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Sweet rest to all.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: This kisse, and I obey you.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Please it your Highnesse,
This is the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: You are welcome home Sir,
(Now as I live, one of a promising presence)
I have heard of you before, and you shall finde
Ile know you better: finde out something that
May doe you good, and rest assur'd to have it.
Were you at Sparta lately?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Three daies since
Madam I came from thence.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: 'Tis very late,
Good night my Lord; doe you Sir follow me,
I must talke further with you.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: All rest with you.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: She must passe through this Cloyster, suddainly
And boldly seaze upon her.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Where's the Prince?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: He does expect us at the place I shew'd you.
I heare ones footing, peace, 'tis she;

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Now leave me,
I know the way, though Vesta witnesse with me
I never trod it with such feare: helpe, helpe.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Stop her mouth close, out with the Light, ile guide you.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: TO whom now shall I cry? What pow'r thus kneele to?
And beg my ravisht honour back upon me?
Deafe, deafe, you gods of goodnesse, deafe to me,
Deafe Heaven to all my cryes; deafe hope, deafe justice,
I am abus'd, and you that see all saw it;
Saw it, and smil'd upon the villaine did it:
Saw it, and gave him strength: why have I pray'd to ye,
When all the worlds eyes have been sunk in slumbers?
Why have I then powr'd out my teares? kneel'd to ye?
And from the Altar of a pure heart sent ye
Thoughts like, your selves, white, innocent, vowes purer
And of a sweeter flame then all earths odours?
Why have I sung your praises, strew'd your Temples,
And Crown'd your holy Priests with Virgin Roses?
Is it we hold ye powerfull, to destroy us?
Beleeve, and honour ye, to see us ruin'd?
These teares of anger thus I sprinckle toward ye,
You that dare sleep secure whilst Virgins suffer,
These stick like Comets, blaze eternally,
Till with the wonder they have wak't your justice,
And forc't ye feare our curses, as we yours.
My shame still followes me, and still proclames me;
He turnes away in scorne, I am contemned too,
A more unmanly violence then the other;
Bitten, and flung away? What ere you are
Sir, you that have abus'd me, and now most basely
And sacrilegiously rob'd this faire Temple,
I fling all these behinde me, but looke upon me,
But one kinde loving look, be what ye will,
So from this hower you will be mine, my Husband;
And you his hand in mischiefe, I speake to you too,
Counsell him nobly now; you know the mischief,
The most unrighteous act he has done, perswade him,
Perswade him like a friend, knock at his Conscience
Till faire Repentance follow: yet be worthy of me,
And shew your self, if ever good thought guided ye,
You have had your foul will, make it yet fair with marriage;
Open your self and take me, wed me now:
More fruits of Villany? your Dagger? come
Ye are mercifull, I thank ye for your medicine:
Is that too worthy too?
Devill, thou with him,
Thou penny Bawd to his Lust, will not that stir thee?
Do you work by tokens now? Be sure I live not,
For your owne safeties knaves. I will sit patiently:
But as ye are true Villaines, the Devills owne servants,
And those he loves and trusts, make it as bloody
An Act, of such true horrour Heaven would shake at,
'Twill shew the braver: goodnesse hold my hope fast,
And in thy mercies looke upon my ruines,
And then I am right: my eyes grow dead and heavy:
Wrong me no more as ye are men.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: She is fast.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Away with her.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Now Gentlemen, the time's come now t'enjoy
That fruitfull happinesse my heart has long'd for:
This day be happy call'd, and when old Time
Brings it about each yeare, crown'd with that sweetnesse
It gives me now, see every man observe it,
And laying all aside beares shew of businesse,
Give this to joy and triumph: How sits my cloaths?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Handsome, and wondrous well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Do they shew richly?
For to those curious eyes even beauty envies,
I must not now appeare poore, or low fashion'd;
Me thinks I am younger then I was, farre younger;
And such a promise in my bloud I feele now,
That if there may be a perpetuall youth
Bestowed on man, I am that soule shall win it:
Do's my haire stand well, Lord how ill-favourdly
You have drest me to day? how baldly? why this Cloke?

speeches.speaker: 2 G^n.
verse: Why 'tis the richest Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: And here ye have put me on
A paire of Breeches look like a paire of Bagpipes.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Beleeve Sir, they shew bravely.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Why these Stockings?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent
verse: Your Legg appeares—

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Peuh I would have had 'em peach collour,
All young, and new about me: and this Scarfe here
A goodly thing: you have trickt me like a Puppet.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Ile undertake to rig forth a whole Navie,
And with lesse labour then one man in love,
They are never pleas'd.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Me thinks he lookes well.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Well
As man can looke, as handsome: now do I wonder
He found not fault his Nose was put on ugly,
Or his Eyes lookt too gray, and rayle at us,
They are the waywards things, these Lovers.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: All will be right
When once it comes to th' push.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: I would they were at it
For our owne quiet sake.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Come, wait upon me,
And beare your selves like mine, my friends, and nobly.

speeches.speaker: Erat.
verse: This is her Brothers Doore.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: There lay her downe then.
Lay her along: she is fast still.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: As forgetfulnesse.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Be not you stirr'd now, but away to your Mother,
Give all attendance, let no staine appeare
Of feare, or doubt in your face: carry your selfe confidently.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: But whither runs your drift now?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: When she wakes,
Either what's done will shew a meere dreame to her,
And carry no more credit: or say she finde it,
Say she remember all the circumstances,
Twenty to one the shapes in which they were acted,
The horrours, and the still affrights we shew'd her,
Rising in wilder figures to her memory
Will run her mad, and no man ghesse the reason:
If all these faile, and that she rise up perfect,
And so collect her selfe, beleeve this Sir,
Not knowing who it was that did this to her,
Nor having any power to ghesse; the thing done too,
Being the utter undoing of her Honour
If it be knowne, and to the worlds eye publish'd,
Especially at this time when Fortune courts her,
She must and will conceale it; nay, forget it,
The woman is no Lucrece; get you gone Sir,
And as you would have more of this sport, feare not.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am confirm'd, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Farewell, away Sir:
Disperse your selves, and as you love his favour,
And that that crowns it, Gold, no tongues amongst ye.
You know your charge, this way goes no suspition.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: You are stirring early Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: It was my duty
To wait upon your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: How fares your Sister,
My beauteous Mistris, what is she ready yet?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: No doubt she'l lose no time Sir, yong Maids in her way
Tread upon thornes, and think an houre an age
Till the Priest has done his part, that theirs may follow:
I saw her not since yesterday ith' evening:
But Sir, I am sure she is not slack; beleeve me,
Your grace will finde a loving soule.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: A sweet one,
And so much joy I carry in the thought of it,
So great a happinesse to know she is mine;
Beleeve me noble Brother, that to expresse it
Me thinkes a Tongue's a poore thing, can do nothing,
Imagination lesse: who's that that lies there?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Where Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Before the doore, it lookes like a woman:

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: This way I came abroad, but then there was nothing,
One of the Maids o're-watch'd belike.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: It may be.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: But me thinks this is no fit place to sleep in.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: 'Tis sure a woman Sir, she has Jewels on too:
She feares no foule play sure.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Bring a Torch hither,
Yet 'tis not perfect day: I should know those Garments.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: How sound she sleepes?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I am sorry to see this.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Do you know her?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And you now I am sure Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: My Mistris, how comes this?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: The Queene and her traine?

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: You know my pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Eup.
verse: And will be most carefull.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Be not long absent, the suit you preferr'd
Is granted.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: This fellow mounts apace, and will
Towre o're us like a Falcon.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Good morrow to ye all, why stand ye wondring?
Enter the house Sir, and bring out your Mistris,
You must observe our Ceremonies: what's the matter?
What's that ye stand at? How Merione?
Asleep i'th street? belike some sudden Palsie
As she stept out last night upon devotion,
To tooke her farewell of her Virgin state,
The Ayre being sharp and piercing, struck her suddenly:
See if she breath.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: A little.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Wake her then,
'Tis sure a fit.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: She wakes her selfe,
Give roome to her.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: See how the spirits struggle to recover,
And strongly re-inforce their strengths; for certaine
This was no naturall sleep.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I am of your minde Madam.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: No Sonne, it cannot be.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Pray Heaven no trick in't;
Good soule she little merits such a mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: She is broad awake now, and her sence clears up,
'Twas sure a fit; stand off.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: The Queene, my Love here,
And all my noble friends? Why where am I?
How am I traunc'd, and moaped? i'th street? Heaven blesse me,
Shame to my Sex; o'th ground too? O, I remember—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How wilde she lookes?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Oh my cold heart, how she trembles?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: O I remember, I remember.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: My shame, my shame, my shame: O I remember
My never-dying shame.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Here has been villainie.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: I feare so to.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: You are no Furies are ye?
No horrid shapes sent to affright me?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: No sweet,
We are your friends: looke up, I am Agenor,
O my Merione, that loves you dearely:
And come to marry ye.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Sister, what ayle ye?
Speake out your griefes, and boldly—

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Something sticks here
Will choake ye else.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I hope it will.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Be free Lady,
You have your loving friends about ye.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Deare Merione,
By the unspotted love I ever bore ye,
By thine owne goodnesse—

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: O 'tis gone, 'tis gone Sir,
I am now I know not what: pray ye look not on me,
No name is left me, nothing to inherit
But that detested, base, and branded —

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Speake it,
And how; diseases of most danger
Their causes once discover'd are easily cur'd:
My faire Merione.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I thanke your love Sir;
When I was faire Merione, unspotted,
Pure, and unblasted in the bud you honour'd,
White as the heart of truth, then Prince Agenor,
Even then I was not worthy of your favour;
Wretch that I am, lesse worthy now of pitty:
Let no good thing come neare me, vertue fly me;
You that have honest noble names despise me,
For I am nothing now but a maine pestilence
Able to poyson all. Send those unto me
That have forgot their names, ruin'd their fortunes,
Despis'd their honours; those that have been Virgins
Ravish'd and wrongd, and yet dare live to tell it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Now it appeares too plaine.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Send those sad people
That hate the light, and curse society;
Whose thoughts are Graves, and from whose eyes continually
Their melting soules drop out, send those to me;
And when their sorrowes are most excellent,
So full that one griefe more cannot be added,
My Story like a torrent shall devoure 'em.
Hark, it must out; but pray stand close together,
And let not all the world heare.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Speake it boldly.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: And Royall Lady, think but charitably,
Your Grace has known my breeding.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Prethee speake it.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Is there no stranger here? send off your servants,
And yet it must be knowne: I shake.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Sweet Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I am abus'd, basely abus'd; do you ghesse yet?
