Come close ile tell ye plainer; I am Whor'd,
Ravish'd, and robb'd of Honour.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: O the Divell.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: What hellish Slave was this?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: A wretch, a wretch,
A damned wretch: do you know the Villaine Lady?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: No.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Not by ghesse?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: O no.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: It must be knowne.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Where was the place?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I know not neither.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: O Heaven,
Is this the happy time? my hope to this come?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Neither the man, nor circumstances?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: His tongue,
Did you not heare his tongue, no voice?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: None, none Sir:
All I know of him was his violence.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: How came ye hither Sweet?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I know not neither.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: A cunning piece of Villany.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: All I remember
Is onely this: Going to Vestas Temple
To give the Goddesse my last Virgin prayers,
Neere to that place I was suddenly surpris'd,
By five or sixe disguis'd, and from thence violently
To my dishonour hal'd: that Act perform'd,
Brought back, but how, or whether, till I wak'd here.—

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: This is so monstrous the gods cannot suffer it;
I have not read in all the villanies
Committed by the most obdurate Rascalls,
An act so truly impious.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Would I knew him.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: He must be known, the Devill cannot hide him.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: If all the Art I have, or power can do it,
He shall be found, and such a way of justice
Inflicted on him: A Lady wrong'd in my Court,
And this way rob'd, and ruin'd?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Be contented Madam,
If he be above ground I will have him.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Faire vertuous Maid, take comfort yet and flourish,
In my love flourish: the staine was forc'd upon ye
None of your wills, nor yours; rise, and rise mine still,
And rise the same white, sweet, faire soule, I lov'd ye,
Take me the same.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I kneele and thank ye Sir,
And I must say ye are truly honourable,
And dare confesse my will yet still a Virgin;
But so unfit and weak a Cabinet
To keep your love and vertue in am I now,
That have been forc'd and broken, lost my lustre,
I meane this body, so corrupt a Volume
For you to study goodnesse in, and honour,
I shall intreat your Grace, conferre that happinesse
Upon a beauty sorrow never saw yet:
And when this griefe shall kill me, as it must do,
Only remember yet ye had such a Mistris;
And if ye then dare shed a teare, yet honour me:
Good Gentlemen expresse your pitties to me,
In seeking out this villany; and my last suit
Is to your Grace, that I may have your favour
To live a poore recluse Nun with this Lady,
From Court and Company, till Heaven shall heare me,
And send me comfort, or death end my misery.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: Take your own will, my very heart bleeds for thee.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Farewell Merione, since I have not thee
Ile wed thy goodnesse, and thy memory.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And I her faire revenge.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Away: let's follow it,
For he is so rank i'th wind we cannot misse him.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Conon you are welcome home, yee are wondrous welcome,
Is this your first arrivall?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Sir, but now
I reacht the Towne.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Ye'ar once more welcome then.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I thanke ye noble Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Pray ye do me the honour
To make my poore house first—

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Pray Sir excuse me,
I have not seene mine owne yet; nor made happy
These longing eyes with those I love there: what's this a Taverne?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: It seemes so by the outside.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Step in here then,
And since it offers it selfe so freely to us,
A place made only for liberall entertainment,
Let's seeke no further but make use of this,
And after the Greek fashion, to our friends,
Crown a round cup or two.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Your pleasure Sir.
Drawers, who waits within?

speeches.speaker: Draw.
verse: Anon, anon Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: Look into the Lilly-pot: why Mark there;
You are welcome Gentlemen; heartily welcome
My noble friend.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Let's have good Wine mine Host,
And a fine private roome.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: Will ye be there Sir?
What is't you'l drink? ile draw your Wine my selfe:
Quissions ye knaves: why when?

speeches.speaker: Dra.
verse: Anon, anon Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: Chios, or Lebos, Greek?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Your best and neatest.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: Ile draw ye that shall dance.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Away, be quick then.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: How does your Brother Sir, my noble friend
The good Euphanes? in all my course of travell
I met not with a Gentleman so furnish'd
In gentlenesse and courtesie; beleeve Sir,
So many friendly Offices I receiv'd from him,
So great, and timely, and enjoy'd his company
In such an open and a liberall sweetnesse,
That when I dare forget him—

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: He's in good health Sir,
But you will finde him a much alter'd man,
Growne a great Courtier Sir.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: He's worthy of it.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: A man drawne up, that leaves no print behind him
Of what he was: those goodnesses you speake of
That have been in him, those that you call freedomes,
Societies, and sweetnesse, looke for now Sir,
You'le finde no shadowes of them left, no sound,
The very Ayre he has liv'd in alter'd: now behold him,
And you shall see a thing walk by, looke big upon ye,
And cry for place; I am the Queenes, give roome there:
If you bow low, may be he'l touch the Bonnet,
Or fling a forced smile at ye for a favour.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: He is your brother Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: These formes put off,
Which travell, and Court Holy-water sprinkle on him,
I dare accept, and know him: you'l think it strange Sir,
That even to me, to me his naturall Brother,
And one by birth he owes a little honour too—
(But that's all one) come give me some Wine, mine Host,
Here's to your faire returne.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I wonder at it,
But sure he has found a nature not worth owning
In this way; else I know he is tender carried.
I thank ye Sir: and now durst I presume
For all you tell me of these alterations,
And stops in his sweet nature, which till I finde so,
I have known him now so long, & look'd so through him,
You must give me leave to be a little faithlesse:
I say for all these, if you please to venter
Ile lay the Wine we drink, let me send for him
(Even I that am the poorest of his fellowship)
But by a Boy oth' house too, let him have businesse,
Let him attend the Queene, nay let his Mistris
Hold him betwixt her armes, he shall come to me,
And shall drink with me too; love me, and heartily,
Like a true honest man bid me welcome home.
I am confident.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: You will lose.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: You'l stand toth' wager?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: With all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Go Boy, and tell Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: He's now gone up the street Sir,
With a great traine of Gallants.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: What think you now Sir?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Go, and overtake him,
Commend my love unto him: my name is Conon,
Tell him I am new arriv'd, and where I am,
And would request to see him presently:
Ye see I use old dudgen phrase to draw him.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Ile hang and quarter when you draw him hether.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Away Boy.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: I am gone Sir.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Here's to you now,
And you shall finde his travell has not stopt him
As you suppose, nor alter'd any freedome,
But made him far more cleare and excellent;
It drawes the grosnesse off the understanding,
And renders active and industrious spirits:
He that knowes most mens manners, must of necessity
Best know his owne, and mend those by example:
'Tis a dull thing to travell like a Mill-horse,
Still in the place he was borne in, lam'd and blinded;
Living at home is like it: pure and strong spirits
That like the Fire still covet to fly upward,
And to give fire as well as take it; cas'd up, and mewd here
I meane at home, like lusty metled Horses,
Onely ty'd up in Stables, to please their Masters,
Beat out their fiery lives in their owne Litters,
Why doe not you travell Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I have no beliefe in't
I see so many strange things, halfe unhatcht, to
Returne, those that went out men, and good men,
They looke like potch'd Eggs with the soules suckt out,
Empty and full of wind: all their affections
Are bak'd in Rye crust, to hold carriage
From this good Towne toth' other: and when they are open'd,
They are so ill cooked and mouldy—

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Ye are pleasant.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Ile shew ye a pack of these: I have 'em for ye,
That have been long in travell too.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Please you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: You know the Merchants walk, Boy?

speeches.speaker: 2 Boy.
verse: Very well.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: And you remember those Gentlemen were here
The other day with me?

speeches.speaker: 2 Boy.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Then go thither,
For there I am sure they are, pray 'em come hither,
(And use my name) I would be glad to see 'em.

speeches.speaker: 1 Boy.
verse: Your Brother's comming in Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: Odds my passion,
Out with the Plate ye knaves: bring the new Quishions,
And wash those Glasses I set by for high dayes,
Perfume the roomes along, why Sirrah.

speeches.speaker: 1 Boy.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: Bid my Wife make her selfe ready handsomely,
And put on her best Apron: it may be
The noble Gentleman will looke upon her.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Where is he Boy?

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: Your worship's heartily welcome,
It joyes my very heart to see ye here Sir.
The Gentleman that sent for your Honour—

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: O good mine Host.

speeches.speaker: Vint.
verse: To my poor homely house, and't like your honor.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I thank thine honour good mine Host, where is he?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: What think ye now? my best Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Conon, welcome my friend, my noble friend how is it?
are you in safety come, in health?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: All health, all safety,
Riches, and all that makes content and happinesse
Now I am here I have: how have you far'd Sir?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Well, I thank Heaven, and never nearer friend
To catch at great occasion.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Indeed I joy in't.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Nor am I for my selfe borne in these fortunes,
In truth I love my friends.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: You were noble ever.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I thought you have not knowne me.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Yes, ye are my Brother,
My elder Brother too, would your affections
Were able but to aske that love I owe to ye,
And as I give, preserve it: here friend Conon,
To your faire welcome home.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Deare Sir, I thank ye,
Fill it toth' brim, Boy: Crates.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Ile pledge you,
But for that glorious Comet lately fired.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Fie, fie Sir, fie.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Nay, let him take his freedomes,
He stirs not me I vow to ye: much lesse staines me.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Sir, I cannot talke with that neat travelling tongue.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: As I live, he has the worst beleefe in men abroad.
I am glad I am come home.

speeches.speaker: 2 Boy.
verse: Here are the Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: O let 'em enter: now you that trust in travell,
And make sharp Beards, and little Breeches Deities,
You that inhaunce the daily price of Tooth-picks,
And hold there is no homebred hapinesse,
Behold a modell of your minds and actions.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Though this be envious, yet done ith' way of mirth,
I am content to thank ye for't.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: 'Tis well yet.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Let the Maske enter.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: A pretty Taverne 'faith, of a fine structure.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Beare your selfe like a Gentleman, here's six pence,
And be sure you breake no Glasses.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Harke ye Pupill,
Go as I taught you, hang more upon your hams,
and put your knees out bent: there, yet a little:
Now I beseech ye, be not so improvident
To forget your travelling pace, 'tis a maine posture,
And to all unayr'd Gentlemen will betray you:
Play with your Pisa Beard: why, where's your brush Pupil?
He must have a Brush Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: More charge yet?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Here, take mine,
These elements of travell he must not want Sir.

speeches.speaker: Vnc.
verse: Ma' foy, he has had some nineteene pence in elements,
What would you more?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Durus me hercle pater.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: What Mounsieur Onos, the very pump of travell,
Sir, as I live you have done me the greatest kindnesse,
O my faire Sir, Lampree, the carefull Unckle
To this young hopefull issue; Mounsieur Tutor too,
The father to his minde; Come, come, let's hug Boyes,
Why what a bunch of travell doe I embrace now,
Me thinkes I put a Girdle about Europe;
How has the Boy profited?

speeches.speaker: Vnc.
verse: He has enough Sir,
If his too fiery mettle doe not mar it.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Is he not thrifty yet?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: That's all his fault,
Too bounteous minded being under age too,
A great consumer of his stock in Pippins.
Had ever a hot stomack.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Come hither Onos,
Will you love me for this fine Apple?

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: We.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: And will ye be rul'd by me sometimes?

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: 'Faith I will.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: That's a good Boy.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Pray give me not the childe so much fruit,
He's of a raw Complexion.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You Mounsieur hard egge,
Do you remember me? Doe you remember
When you and your Consort travell'd through Hungary?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: He's in that circuit still.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Do you remember
The cantell of immortall Cheese ye carried with ye,
The halfe cold Cabbedge, in a leather Sachell,
And those invincible Eggs that would lye in your bowells
A fortnight together, and then turne to bedstaves;
Your sowre milk that would choak an Irish man,
And bread was bak'd in Caesars time for the Army?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Providence, providence.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: The soule of travell.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Can the Boy speak yet?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Yes, and as fine a Gentleman,
I thanke my able knowledge, he has arriv'd at,
Only a little sparing of his Language,
Which every man of observation—

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: And of as many tongues.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Pray be content Sir,
You know you are for the bodily part, the Purse,
I for the magazine, the minde.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Come hither springall.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: That in the Almain Tongue signifies a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fuph.
prose: What think you of the formes of Italy or Spain?

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: I love mine owne Country Pippin.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Nobly answer'd,
Borne for his Country first.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: A great Philosopher:
What Horses do you prefer?

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: The White horse Sir,
There were I lye; honest and a just beast,

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: O Caput lepidum: a Childe to say this,
Are these figures for the mouthes of Infants?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Onos, what wenches?
Come, tell me true.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: I cannot speake without booke.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: When shall we have one, ha?

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Steale me from mine Unckle,
For looke you, I am broke out horribly
For want of fleshly Phisick: they say I am too yong,
And that 'twill spoyle my growth. but could you help me?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Meet me to morrow man, no more.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You thinke now
Ye have open'd such a shame to me of travell,
By shewing these thin Cubbs: ye have honour'd us
Against your will, proclam'd us excellent:
Three Frailes of Sprats carried from Mart, to Mart,
Are as much meat as these, to more use travell'd;
A bunch of bloted fooles: me thinkes your judgement
Should looke abroad sometimes without your envie.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Such are most of you: so I take my leave,
And when you finde your womens favour faile,
'Tis ten to one yoa'l know your selfe, and seeke me
Upon a better Muster of your manners.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: This is not hansome Sir.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Pray take your pleasure,
You wound the wind as much—

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Come you with me,
I have businesse for you presently: there's for your Wine,
I must confesse I lost it.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Shall I steale to ye
And shall we see the Wench?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: A dainty one.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: And have a dish of Pippins?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: What a peck man.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Will you wait Sir.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Pray let's meet oftner Gentlemen,
I would not lose ye.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: O sweet Sir.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Do you thinke I would,
Such noted men as you?

speeches.speaker: Onos, ~nc. Tut.
verse: We are your Servants.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: That thing they would keep in everlasting nonage,
My Brother for his owne ends has thrust on
Upon my Mistris, 'tis true, he shall be rich
If ever he can get that Rogue his Unckle
To let him be of yeares to come to inherit it,
Now what the maine drift is—

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Say ye so? no more words,
Ile keepe him company till he be of yeares,
Though it be a hundred yeares, but ile discover it;
And ten to one ile crosse it too.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You are honest,
And I shall study still your love: farewell Sir,
For these few houres I must desire your pardon,
I have businesse of importance: once a day
At least I hope you'l see me: I must see you else:
So, once more ye are welcome.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: All my thankes Sir,
And when I leave to love you, life go from me.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: WHy Sir, the Kingdomes his, and no man now
Can come to Corinth, or from Corinth goe
Without his Licence; he puts up the tithes
Of every Office through Achaia;
From Courtier to the Carter hold of him:
Our Lands, our Liberties, nay very lives
Are shut up in his Closet, and let loose
But at his pleasure; Bookes, and all discourse
Have now no Patron, nor direction.
But glorifi'd Euphanes: our Cups are guilty
That quench our thirsts, if not unto his health:
Oh, I could eat my heart, and fling away
My very soule for anguish: gods, nor men
Should tollerate such disproportion.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And yet is he belov'd: whether't be vertue,
Or seeming vertue which he makes the cloake
To his ambition.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Be it which it will:
Your Highnesse is to tame, your eyes too film'd
To see this, and sit still: the Lion should not
Tremble to heare the bellowing of the Bull;
Nature excuse me, though he be my Brother,
You are my Countries Father, therefore mine:
One paralell line of Love I bend on him,
All lines of love and duty meet in you
As in their Center: therefore heare, and weigh
What I shall speake: You know the Queen your Mother
Did from a private state your Father raise,
So all your Royalty you hold from her;
She is older then she was, therefore more doating,
And what know we but blindnesse of her love
(That hath from underneath the foot of fortune
Set, even Euphanes foot, on fortunes head)
Will take him by the hand, and cry, Leap now
Into my bed; 'tis but a trick of age;
Nothing impossible.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What do you infer on this?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Your pardon Sir:
With reverence to the Queen; yet why should I
Feare to speak plaine what pointeth to your good?
A Good old Widow is a hungry thing,
(I speak of other Widows, not of Queens.)

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Speak to thy purpose.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I approach it: Sir,
Should young Euphanes claspe the Kingdome thus,
And please the good old Lady some one night;
What might not she be wrought to put on you,
Quite to supplant your birth? neither is she
Past children, as I take it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Crates, Thou shak'st me;
Thou, that dost hate thy Brother for my love,
In my love finde one; henceforth be my brother:
This Gyant I will fell beneath the earth;
I will shine out, and melt his artfull wings:
Euphanes, from my mothers sea of favours
Spreads like a River, and runs calmly on,
Secure yet from my stormes; like a young pine
He growes up planted under a faire Oake,
Whose strong large branches yet do's shelter him,
And every Traveller admires his beauty;
But like a winde, ile work into his crancks,
Trouble his streame, and drowne all Vessells that
Ride on his Greatnesse: under my mothers armes,
Like to a stealing tempest will I search,
And rend his root from her protection.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
prose: I, now Theanor speaks like Prince Theanor.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: But how shall we provoke him to our snares?
He has a temper malice cannot move
To exceed the bounds of judgement; he is so wise,
That we can pick no cause to affront him.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: No?
What better then his crossing your intent?
The suit I had to ye? Conons forfeit state
(Before he travel'd) for a Riot, he
Hath from your Mother got restor'd to him:

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Durst he? What is this Conon?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: One that hath,
As people say, in forraigne pleasur'd him.
But now no more;
They have brought the Travellors I told you of,
That's the sweet youth, that is my Brothers Rivall,
That curles his head, for he has little haire,
And paints his vizor, for it is no face,
That so desires to follow you, my Lord:
Show 'em some countenance, and it will beget
Our sport at least.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What villanous Crab-tree legs he makes?
His shins are full of true-love knots.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: His leggs were ever villanous, since I knew him.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Faith his Uncles shanks are somewhat the better.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: But is't possible he should believe he is not of age?
He is 50, man, in's Jubile I warrant: s'light, he
Looks older then a groat, the very stamp on's face is why
Worne out with handling.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Why I tell you all men believe it when they heare him speake,
He utters such single matter in so infantly a voice.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: He looks as like a fellow that I have seen accommodate
Gentlemen with Tobacco in our Theaters.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Most illustrious Prince.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: A pox on him, he is guelt, how he trebles?

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: I am a Gentleman a both sides.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
prose: He meanes (so't please your highnesse) both by Father & Mother.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Thou a Gentleman? thou an Asse.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: He is nere the farther from being a Getl. I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: May it please your Grace, I am another.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: He is another Asse he saies, I believe him.

speeches.speaker: ~ncle.
verse: We be three, Heroicall Prince.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Nay then we must have the Picture of 'em, and the
Word Nos sumus.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: That have travail'd all parts of the Globe together.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
prose: For my part, I have seen the vicissitude of fortune before.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
prose:
Peace
~ncle, for though you speak a little better then I—

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: 'Tis a very little, in truth.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Yet we must both give place, as they say, to the best Speaker
The Tutor.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Yet since it hath pleas'd your radience to decline so low, as on us,
Poore and unworthy dunghils.—

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: What a stinking knaves this?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
prose: Our Perigrination was nere so felicitated, as since we enter'd the line of your gracious favour, under whose bea-my aspect, and by which infallible Mathematicall compasse, may we but hereafter presume to saile, our industries have reach't their desir'd termination and period; and we shall voluntarily sacrifice our lives to your resplendent eyes, both the Altars and fires of our devoted offrings.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Oh divine Tutor!

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Can you hold Sir?

speeches.speaker: Era.
prose: He ha's spoken this very speech to some Whore in Corinth.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
prose:
A plague on him for a sustain Dictionary; on my conscience this is the
~lissean Travellor that sent home his Image riding upon Elephants to the great Magoll.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
prose: The same: his wit is so huge, nought but an Elephant could carry him.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: So heavy you meane.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
prose: These three, are ev'n the finest one foole tripartite, that was ere discovered.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Or a Treatise of famine divided into three branches.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: The Prince speakes.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I thank ye for your loves; but as I told you,
I have so little meanes, to do for those
Few followers I have already, that
I would have none shiprack themselves, and fortune,
Upon my barren shelf: Sue to Euphanes.
For he is Prince, and Queen, I would have no man
Curse me in his old age.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Alas Sir, they desire to follow you
But a farre off, the farther off the better.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
prose: I Sir, and't be seven mile off, so we may but follow you, onely to countenance us in the confronts and affronts, which (according to your Highnesse will) we meane on all occasions to put upon the Lord Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
prose: He shall not want gibing nor jeering, I warrant him; if he do, i'le forsweare wit.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
prose: It has forsworne thee, 'ile sweare, it is the ancient enemy to thy house.

speeches.speaker: The.
prose: Well, be it so; I here receive ye, for my followers a great way off.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Seven miles, my Lord, no further.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
prose: By what time, Sir, (by this measure) may I come to follow him in his Chamber?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Why when his Chamber, Sir, is seven miles long.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Make way there, for my Lord Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Cro.
verse: Looke Sir, Jove appeares,
The Peacock of our State, that spreads a traine
Brighter then Iris blushes after raine.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: You need not thank me Conon, in your love
You Antidated what I can do for you,
And I in gratitude was bound to this,
And am to much more: and what ere he be
Can with unthankfulnesse assoile me, let him
Dig out mine eyes, and sing my name in verse.
In Balland verse at every drinking-house,
And no man be so charitable to lend me
A Dogg to guide my steps.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Haile to Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: Mighty Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: The great Prince Euphanes.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Key of the Court, and Jewell of the Queen.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Sol in our Firmament.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Pearl in the States eye.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Being a black man.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: Mistris of the Land.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Our humble, humble poore Petitions are,
That we may hold our places.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: May we?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Yes; be you malicious knaves still: and you fooles.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: This is the Princes, and your Brothers spight.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I know't, but will not know't it.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Yonder they are,
Who's fine childe's this?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Unckle, le' be,
Let him alone, he is a mighty Prince.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I aske your Highnesse pardon: I protest
By Jupiter I saw you not.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Humh, it may be so,
You have rais'd such mountaines 'twixt your eyes and me,
That I am hidden quite: what do ye meane Sir?
You much forget your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I should much more,
Not to remember my due duty to your Grace;
I know not wherein I have so transgress'd
My service to your Highnesse, to deserve
This rigour and contempt, not from you only
But from your followers, with the best of whom
I was an equall in my lowest ebbe:
Beseech you Sir, respect me as a Gentleman,
I will be never more in heart to you:
Five faire Discents I can derive my selfe,
From Fathers worthy both in Arts and Armes.
I know your goodnesse companies your greatnesse
But that you are perverted: Royall Sir,
I am your humblest subject, use your pleasure,
But do not give protection to the wrongs
Of these subordinate Slaves, whom I could crush
By that great destin'd favour, which my Mistris
And your majestick Mother deignes to me,
But in respect of you: I know leane envie
Waites ever on the steps of vertue advanc'd:
But why your Mothers grace gets me disgrace,
Or renders me a slave to beare these wrongs
I do not know.
Oh Mediocrity,
Thou prizelesse jewell, only meane men have
But cannot value; like the precious Jem,
Found in the Mukhill by the ignorant Cock.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Your creamy words but cozen: how durst you
Intercept me so lately to my Mother?
And what I meant your Brother, you obtain'd
Unto the forfeiture againe.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Your answer to that my Lord, my Brother.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: May I perish
If ere I heard you intended such a Suit,
Though 'twould have stuck an ignominious brand
Vpon your Highnesse, to have given your servant
A Gentlemans whole state of worth and quality,
Confiscate only for a youthfull brawle.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Your rudiments are too sawcy: teach your Page.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I, so are all things but your flatterers.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Hold you your prating.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: You know where you are, you fleeten face.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Yet Sir to appease and satisfie your anger,
Take what you please from me, and give it him
In lieu of this: you shall not take it neither,
I freely will impart it, halfe my state,
Which Brother if you please—

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Ile starve in Chaines first,
Eat my owne armes.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Oh that you saw your selfe:
You ne're made me such offer in my poorenesse,
And 'cause (to do you ease) I sought not to you
You thus maligne me; yet your nature must not
Corrupt mine, nor your rude examples lead me:
If mine can mend you, I shall joy; you know
I feare you not: you have seene me prov'd a man
In every way of fortune, 'tis my comfort
I know no more such Brothers in the world
As Crates is.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Nor I such as Euphanes:
The temper of an Angell raignes in thee.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Your Royall Mother Sir, (I had forgot)
Entreates your presence.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: You have done her errand,
I may do yours.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Let it be truth my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Crates, ile question you for this.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Pish, your worst.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Away you hounds after your sent.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Come, we'l scorn to talk to 'm: now they are gone,
We'l away too.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Why beare you this my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: To shew the passive fortitude the best;
Vertues a solid Rock, whereat being aym'd
The keenest darts of envie, yet unhurt
Her Marble Heroes stand, built of such Bases,
Whilst they recoyle, and wound the Shooters faces.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: My Lord, the Queene.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Gentle Euphanes, how,
How do'st thou honest Lord? oh how I joy
To see what I have made, like a choyce Workman,
That having fram'd a Master-peece, doth reape
An universall comendations.
Princes are Gods in this. Ile build thee yet,
(The good foundation so pleases me)
A story or two higher; let Doggs barke,
They are fooles that hold them dignifi'd by blood,
They should be only made great that are good.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Oraculous Madam.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Sirra, I was thinking
If I should marry thee, what merry tales
Our neighbour Islands would make of us;
But let that passe, you have a Mistris
That would forbid our Banes: troth I have wish'd
A thousand times that I had been a man,
Then I might sit a day with thee alone,
And talke,
But as I am I must not; there's no skill
In being good, but in not being thought ill.
Sirrah, who's that?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: So't please your Majesty
Conon, the friend I su'd for.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: 'Tis dispatch'd.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Gracious Madam,
I owe the gods and you my life.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: I thanke you,
I thank you heartily; and I do think you
A very honest man, he sayes you are:
But now ile chide thee; what's the cause my Son,
For my eye's every where, and I have heard,
So insolently do's thee Contumelies
Past sufferance (I am told) yet you complaine not,
As if my justice were so partiall
As not to right the meanest: credit me,
Ile call him to a strict accompt, and fright
By his example, all that dare curb me
In any thing that's just: I sent you for him.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Humbly he did returne, he would wait on you:
But let me implore your Majesty, not to give
His Highnesse any check, for worthlesse me;
They are Court canckers, and not Counsellors
That thus informe you: they do but hate the Prince,
And would subvert me: I should curse my fortune
Even at the highest, to be made the ginne
To unscrew a Mothers love unto her Son:
Better had my pale flame in humble shades
Been spent unseene, then to be rais'd thus high,
Now to be thought a meteor to the State,
Portending ruine and contagion:
Beseech you then rest satisfi'd, the Prince
Is a most noble natur'd Gentleman,
And never did to me but what I tooke
As favours from him, my blown billowes must not
Strive 'gainst my shore, that should confine me; nor
Justle with Rocks to break themselves to peeces.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Well, thou'rt the composition of a god:
My Lion, Lamb, my Eaglet, and my Dove,
Whose soule runs clearer then Dianas Fount,
Nature pick'd severall flowers from her choyce banks
And bound 'em up in thee, sending thee forth
A Posie for the bosome of a Queene.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: The Prince attends you.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Farewell my good Lord,
My honest man; Stay, hast no other suit?
I prethee tell me; Sirrah, thine eye speakes
As if thou hadst: out with it modest foole.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: With favour Madam, I would crave your leave
To Marry, where I am bound in gratitude,
The immediat meanes she was to all my being:
Nor do I think your wisedome sacred Queen
Fetters in favours, taking from me so
The liberty that meanest men enjoy.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: To marry? you are a foole: thou'st anger'd me:
Leave me, ile think on't:
Only to try thee this, for though I love thee,
I can subdue my selfe: but she that can
Enjoy thee, doth enjoy more then a man.
Nay rise without a blessing, or kneele still:
What's Sir the reason you oppose me thus,
And seeke to darken what I would have shine?
Ecclipse a fire much brighter then thy selfe,
Making your Mother not a competent Judge
Of her owne actions?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Gracious Madam, I
I have done no more then what in royalty
(And to preserve your fame) was fit to do:
Heard you the peoples talke of you, and him
You favour so, his greatnesse, and your love,
The pitty given to me, you would excuse me,
They prate as if he did dishonour you:
And what know I, but his owne lavish tongue
Has utter'd some such speeches; he is call'd
The King of Corinth.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: They are traitors all:
I weare a Christall casement 'fore my heart,
Through which each honest eye may looke in to't:
Let it be prospect unto all the world,
I care not this.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: This must not be my way;
Your pardon gracious Madam: these incitements
Made me not shew so cleare a countenance
Upon the Lord Euphanes as I would:
Which since your Majesty affects so grievously
Ile cleare the black cloud of it, and henceforth
Uow on this knee all love and grace to him.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Rise with my blessing, and to prove this true,
Beare him from me this Cabinet of Jewells
In your owne person, tell him, for his marrying
He may dispose him how, and when he please.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: I shall discharge my duty and your will.
Crates?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I have heard all my Lord, how luckely
Fate pops her very spindle in our hands:
This marriage with Beliza you shall crosse,
Then have I one attempt for Lamprias more
Upon this Phaeton: where's Merione's Ring,
That in the Rape you tooke from her?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis here.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: In and effect our purpose: you my Lord
Shall disobey your Mothers charge, and send
This Cabinet by some servant of her owne,
That what succeeds may have no reference
Unto your Highnesse.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: On, my engine on.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Now, if we be not struck by Heavens owne hand,
We'l ruine him, and on his ruines stand.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: These heavie Ayres feed sorrow in her Lady,
And nourish it too strongly; like a Mother
That spoiles her Childe with giving on't the will.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Some lighter note.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How like a hill of Snow she sits, and melts
Before the unchast fire of others lust?
What heart can see her passion and not break?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Take comfort gentle Madam; you know well
Even actuall sins committed without will,
Are neither sins nor shame, much more compell'd;
Your Honour's no whit lesse, your Chastity
No whit impair'd, for faire Merione
Is more a Virgin yet then all her Sex:
Alas, 'tis done; why burne these Tapers now?
Wicked and frantick Creatures joy in night.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Imagine faire Merione had dream'd
She had been ravish'd, would she si^ thus then
Excruciate?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Fye, fye, how fond is this?
What reason for this surfet of remorse?
How many that have done ill, and proceed,
Women that take degrees in wantonnesse,
Commence, and rise in rudiments of Lust,
That feele no scruple of this tendernesse?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Pish.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Nor are you matches in mishap, even I
Doe beare an equall part of misery;
That love, belov'd, a man, the Crowne of men,
Whom I have friended, and how rais'd 'tis better
That all doe know and speak it then my selfe:
When he sail'd low I might have made him mine,
Now at his full gale, it is questionable
If ever I o're-take him.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Wherefore sits
My Phebe shadowed in a sable could?
Those pearly drops which thou lets't fall like beades,
Numbring on them thy vestall Orisons
Alas are spent in vaine: I love thee still,
In mid'st of all these showres thou sweetlier sent'st,
Like a green Meadow on an April day,
In which the Sun and West-wind play together,
Striving to catch and drink the balmy drops.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: The Lord Euphanes Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Poore Merione,
She loathes the light, and men.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: The vertuous gods preserve my Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: O my most honour'd Lord, those times are chang'd.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Let times and men change, could Heaven change, Euphanes
Should never change, to be devoted ever
To faire Beliza, should my load of honours,
Or any Grace which you were Author of
Detract mine honour, and diminish Grace?
The gods forbid: you here behold your Servant,
Your Creature, gentle Lady, whose sound sleepes
You purchas'd for him: whose food you paid for,
Whose garments were your charge, whose first preferment
You founded: then, what since the gracious Queene
Hath, or can reare, is upon your free Land,
And you are Mistris of.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Mock me not gentle Lord,
You shine now in too high a spheare for me,
We are Plannets now disjoyn'd for ever: yet
Poore superstitious innocent that I am,
Give leave that I may lift my hands, and love
Not in Idolatry, but perfect zeale:
For credit me, I repent nothing I have done,
But were it to begin would do the same.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: There are two Seas in Corinth, and two Queens,
And but there, not two such in the spacious Universe;
I came to tender you the man you have made,
And like a thankfull streame to retribute
All you my Ocean have enrich'd me with.
You told me once you'ld marry me.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Another mock? you were wont to play faireplay,
You scorne poore helps; he that is sure to win,
May slight mean harts, whose hand commands the Queen

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Let me be held the Knave through all the Stock
When I doe slight my Mistris; you know well
The gracious inclination of the Queene,
Who sent me leave this morning to proceed
To marry, as I saw convenience,
And a great gift of Jewels: Three daies hence
The generall sacrifice is done to Vesta,
And can you by then be accommodated
Your servant shall wait on you to the Temple.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Till now
I never felt a reall joy indeed.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Here then I seale my duty, here my love,
Till which vouchsafe to weare this Ring, deare Mistris;
Twas the Queens Token, and shall celebrate
Our Nuptialls.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Honour still raise, and preserve
My honour'd Lord, as he preserves all honour.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Why shift you places thus Merione,
And will not lend a word? Could'st thou so soone
Leave sorrow as the place, how blest were I,
But 'twill not be; griefe is an impudent guest,
A follower every where, a hanger on,
That words nor blowes can drive away.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Deare Sister.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Who can be sad? out with these Tragick Lights,
And let day repossesse her naturall howres:
Teare downe these blacks, cast ope' the Casements wide,
That we may jocondly behold the Sun.
I did partake with sad Merione
In all her mourning: let her now rejoyce
With glad Beliza, for Euphanes is
As full of love, full of humility
As when he wanted.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh — that.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Help, she faints:
Her griefe has broke her heart.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: No— that — that.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Mistris, what point you at?
Her lamps are out, yet still she extends her hand
As if she saw something antipathous
Unto her vertuous life.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Still, still she points,
And her lips move, but no articulate sound
Breathes from 'em: Sister, speak, what moves you thus?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Her spirits returne.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Oh, hide that fatall Ring,
Where had it you Beliza?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: What hid fate
Depends on it? Euphanes gave it me
As holy pledge of future Marriage.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Then is Euphanes the foule Ravisher?
Let me speake this and dye. That dismall night
Which seal'd my shame upon me, was that Ring,
The partner of my rob'd virginity.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Euphanes?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Strange.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Impossible.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Impossible. to have redresse on him,
Chiefe servant to the Queene—ha! I have read
Somewhere I am sure, of such an injury
Done to a Lady: and how she durst dye.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Oh follow her Beliza

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: To assure her,
The unlikelihood of this

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Love hides all sins.
What's to be done Leonidas?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Why this:
Amazement takes up all my faculties;
The plagues of gods and men will muster all
To avenge this tyranny. Oh frontlesse man,
To dare doe ill, and hope to beare it thus:
First let's implore, then cure.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Who, who can trust
The gentle lookes and words of two-fac'd man?
Like Corinths double torrent, you and I
Will rush upon the Land; nor shall the Queene
Defend this Villaine in his villany:
Lusts violent flames can never be withstood
Nor quench'd, but with as violent streames of blood.

speeches.speaker: Ono.
verse: THinkes he to carry her and live?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: It seemes so,
And she will carry him the story sayes.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Well, hum—
Have I for this thou faire but falsest faire
Stretch'd this same simple legge over the Sea?
What though my bashfulnesse, and tender yeares,
Durst ne're reveale my affection to thy teeth?
Deep love ne're tatles, and (say they) loves bit
The deeper dip'd, the sweeter still is it.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Oh, see the power of Love: he speakes in ryme.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Oh, love will make a Dog howle in rime:
Of all the Lovers yet I have heard or read
This is the strangest: but his Guardian,
And you his Tutor should informe him better,
Thinkes he, that Love is answer'd by instinct?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: He should make meanes.
For certaine Sir his bashfulnesse undo's him,
For from his Cradle h'had a shamefull face.
Thus walkes he night and day. eates not a bit,
Nor sleepes one jot, but's growne so humorous;
Drinkes Ale, and takes Tobacco as you see;
Weare's a Steeleto at his Codpeece close,
Stabs on the least occasion: stroakes his beard,
Which now he puts i'th posture of a T.
The Roman T. your T. beard is the fashion,
And twifold doth expresse the enamour'd Courtier,
As full as your fork-carving Travellour.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Oh, black clouds of discontent invellop me,
Garters fly off: go Hatband, binde the browes
Of some dull Citizen that feares to ake:
And Leg appeare now in simplicity
Without the trappings of a Courtier:
Burst Buttons, burst, your Bachelor is worm'd.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: A worm-eaten Batchelor th'art indeed.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: And Devill melancholly possesses me now.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Crosse him not in this fit I advise you Sir.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Dye crimson Rose, that didst adorne these cheeks, scabby.
For ytch of love is now broke forth on me.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Poore Boy, 'tis true: his wrists and hands are scabby.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Burne eyes out in your sockets, sinck and stink:
Teeth I will pick ye to the very bones,
Hang haire like Hemp, or like the Isling Curs,
For never Powder, nor the Crisping-iron
Shall touch these dangling locks—oh—Ruby lips,
Love hath to you been like Wine-vinegar,
Now you look wan and pale, lips, ghosts ye are,
And my disgrace sharper than Mustard-seed.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: How like a Chaundler he do's vent his passions,
Risum teneatis?

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Well sung the Poet,
Love is a golden bubo, full of Dreames:
That ripen'd breakes, and fills us with extreames.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: A gold buble, pupill, Oh grosse solaecisme
To chaster eares, that understand the Latine.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: I will not be corrected now:
I am in love, revenge is now the Cud
That I do chaw: Ile challenge him.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I marry Sir.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Your Honour bids you Nephew, on, and prosper.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: But none will beare it from me, times are dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Carry it your selfe man.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Tutor, your counsell: Ile do nothing Sir
Without him.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: This may rid thee, (valiant Cuz)
Whom I have kept this forty yeare my Ward:
Faine would I have his state, and now of late
He did enquire at Ephesus for his age,
But the Church Booke being burnt with Dians Temple
He lost his ayme: I have try'd to famish him,
Marry he'l live o' stones: and then for Poysons,
He is an Antidote 'gainst all of 'em;
He sprung from Mithridates; he is so dry and hot,
He will eat Spiders faster then a Monkey:
His Maw (unhurt) keeps Quicksilver like a bladder,
The largest dosse of Camphire, Opium,
Harmes not his braine; I think his Skul's as empty
As a suckt Egge; Vitrioll, and Oyle of Tartar
He will eat tosts of: Henbane I am sure
And Hemblock I have made his Pot-hearbs often.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: If he refuse you, yours is then the honour:
If he accept, he being so great, you may
Crave both to chuse the Weapon, time, and place,
Which may be ten yeares hence, and Calicut,
Or underneath the lyne to avoid advantage.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: I am resolved.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: By your favour Pupill,
Whence shall this challenge rise? for you must ground it
On some such fundamentall base, or matter
As now the Gentry set their lives upon.
Did you ere cheat him at some Ordinary,
And durst he say so, and be angry? if thus,
Then you must challenge him hath he call'd your whore,
Whore; though she be (beside yours) twenty mens?
Your honour, reputation is touch'd then,
And you must challenge him: Has he deny'd
On thirty damne me's to accommodate money,
Though he have broke threescore before to you?
Here you must challenge him: Durst he ever shun
To drink two pots of Ale wi' ye? or to wench,
Though weighty businesse otherwise importun'd?
He is a proud Lord,
And you may challenge him: Has he familiarly
Dislik'd your yellow Starch or said your Dublet
Was not exactly frenchifi'd? or that, that report
In faire tearmes was untrue? or drawn your Sword,
Cry'd 'twas ill mounted? Has he given the lye
In circle, or oblique, or semy-circle,
Or direct paralell? you must challenge him.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: He never gave my direct apparrell the lye in's life.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: But for the crown of all, Has he refus'd
To pledge your Mistris health though he were sick?
And crav'd your pardon? you must challenge him,
There's no avoyding: one or both must drop.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Exquisi^e Tutor.

speeches.speaker: Nean.
verse: Crates, I have sought you long, what make you here
Fooling with these three farthings, while the Towne
Is all in unproare, and the Prince our Master
(Ceas'd by Leonidas, and Agenor) carried
And Prisoner kept i'the Castle, flanckes
The west part of the City, where they vow
To hold him, till your Brother, Lord Euphanes
Be rendr'd to 'em, with his life to satisfie
The Rape, by him suspected to Merione?
The Queene refuses to deliver him,
Pawning her knowledge for his innocency,
And dares 'em do their worst on Prince Theanor,
The whole State's in combustion.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Fatall Ring.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: What will become of us?

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: And she hath given Commission to Euphanes
And Conon (who have leavied men already)
With violence to surprize the Towre, and take 'em.
What will you doe?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Along wi' ye, and prevent
A further mischiefe: Gentlemen, our intents
We must defer: you are the Princes followers.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: Will ye walk with us?

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: You shall pardon us.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: We are his followers afarre off you know.
And are contented to continue so.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Sir Boy.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Sir Foole? a Challenge to my Lord?
How dar'st thou, or thy ambs—ace here think of him,
Ye Crow-pick'd heads, which your thin shoulders beare
As doe the poles on Corinth Bridge the Traitors:
Why you three Ninc-pins, you talke of my Lord,
And Challenges? you shall not need: come draw,
His Page is able to swindge three such whelpes:
Unckle, why stand ye off: long-man advance.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: S'light, what have we done Tutor?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: He is a Boy,
And we may run away with honour.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: That ye shall not,
And being a Boy I am fitter to encounter
A Childe in Law as you are, under twenty:
Thou Sot, thou three-score Sot, and that's a Childe
Againe I grant you.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Nephew, here's an age:
Boyes are turn'd men, and men are Children.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Away you Pezants with your bought Gentry;
Are not you he, when your fellow Passengers,
Your last transportment being assayl'd by a Galley
Hid your selfe i'the Cabbin: and the Fight done
Peep'd above Hatches, and cry'd, Have we taken,
Or are we tane? Come, I doe want a slipper,
But this shall serve: Sweare all as I would have you,
Or I will call some dozen brother Pages,
(They are not farre off I am sure) and we will blancket
You untill you pisse againe.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: Nay, we will sweare Sir.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: 'Tis your best course:
First, you shall sweare never to name my Lord,
Or heare him nam'd hereafter, but bare-headed.
Next, to begin his health in every place,
And never to refuse to pledge it, though
You surfeit to the death. Lastly, to hold
The poorest, litlest Page in reverence;
To think him valianter, and a better Gentleman
Then you three stamp'd together: and to give him
Wine and Tobacco wheresoe're you meet,
And the best meat if he can stay.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We sweare it loyally.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: Then I dismisse you
True Leigmen to the Pantaffle:
I had more Articles, but I have businesse
And cannot stay now: so adieu deare Monsieur,
Tres nobles & tres puissant.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Adieu Monsieur.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: A vostre service & commaundement.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: I told you Pupill, you'ld repent this foolery.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Who, I repent? you are mistaken Tutor,
I ne're repented any thing yet in my life,
And scorne to begin now: Come, let's be melancholly.

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: 'Twere better treat with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: I will no Treaties
With a League-breaker and a Rebell; shall I
Article with a Traitor? be compell'd
To yeeld an innocent unto their fury
Whom I have prov'd so to you?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Gracious Queene,
Though your owne god-like disposition
Would succour vertue, and protect the right,
Yet for the publike good, for the deare safety
Of your most Royall onely Son, consent
To give me up the sacrifice to their malice:
My life is aym'd at, and 'twere better farre
The blood of twenty thousand such as I
Purpled our Seas, then that your Princely Son
Should be endanger'd.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Still well said honest Foole,
Were their demand but one haire from thy head,
By all the gods il'd scorne 'em: were they here,
The Majesty that dwels upon this brow
Should strike 'em on their knees: As for my Son,
Let 'em no more dare then they'l answer, I
An equall Mother to my Country, am,
And every vertuous Son of it is son
Unto my bosome, tender as mine owne.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Oh, you are heavenly Madam, and the gods
Can suffer nothing passe to injure you:
The life that Conon promis'd, he stands now
Ready to pay with joy.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Farewell both,
Successe attend you: you have Souldiers been,
Tam Marte quam Mercurio: if you bring not peace
Bring me their heads.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I will put faire for one.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Double the Guard upon her Highnesse Person;
Conon, you must performe a friendly part,
Which I shall counsell you.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I am your Servant

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Make good that Fortification, and the Watch
Keepe still upon the Battlements: Royall Sir,
Weigh but our injuries, we have told you fully
The manner and the matter hales us thus;
Nor shall this upstart Mushrum bred i'ch night,
Sit brooding underneath your Mothers wings
His damn'd impieties.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: For your selfe, brave Prince,
Feare nothing that this face of Armes presents:
We aske the Ravisher, and have no meanes
To win him from your most indulgent Mother
But by this practice.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Stout Leonidas,
Princely Agenor, your wrongs cry so loud,
That who so would condemne you is not heard:
I blame you not, who but Euphanes durst
Make Stories like to this? My wrong's as strong
Aske my revengefull arme to strengthen yours:
As for my feare, know you, and Greece throughout,
Our Mother was a Spartan Princesse borne,
That never taught me to spell such a word.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Sir, you doe tempt your life.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Conon, no more.
Doe thus as thou wouldst save it.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: What Trumpet's this?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Beneath I doe perceive
Two armed men, single, that give us summons
As they would treat.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Let us descend.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: My Lord,
I would you would excuse me, and proceed
According to the Queenes directions.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Friend,
As thou wouldst weare that title after death
Performe my charge: no Souldier on his life
Approach us nearer.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Safety to both the Princes, loyalty
To you Lord Generall, the Queene, your Mistris
As well as ours, though not to feare, to cut
Civill dissention from her Land, and save
Much guiltlesse blood, that uprore ever thirsts,
And for the safe-guard of her Son, by me
(As you demand) hath sent the Lord Euphanes
To plead his owne cause, or to suffer death
As you shall finde him worthy; so delivering
The Prince back, I shall leave him to your Guard.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: The Queene is good and gracious: kisse her hand.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: And seale our duties: Sir, depart in peace.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Oh Sir, you now perceive, when in the scales
Nature, and fond affection weigh together,
One poyzes like a feather, and you know my Lords
What's to be done.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Your Highnesse is unarm'd,
Please you to use mine, and to lead the Army
Back to your Mother: Conon, march you with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: I will my Lord: But not so farre as not
To bring you help if danger looke upon you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Why doe you looke so strangely, fearefully,
Or stay your deathfull hande, be not so wise
To stop your rage: looke how unmoov'dly, here
I give my selfe my Countries sacrifice,
An innocent sacrifice: Truth laughs at death,
And terrifies the killer more then kill'd;
Integrity thus armelesse seekes her foes,
And never needs the Target, nor the Sword,
Bow, nor invenom'd shafts.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: We are amaz'd,
Not at your eloquence, but impudence,
That dare thus front us.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Kill him, who knowes not
The iron forehead that bold mischiefe weares.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Forbeare a while Agenor, I doe tremble,
And something sits like vertue in his face,
Which the gods keep.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Agenor, strike Leonidas
You that have purchas'd fame on certaine grounds,
Loose it on supposition? smeare your hands
In guiltlesse blood, laugh at my Martyrdome:
But yet remember, when Posterity
Shall read your Volumes fill'd with vertuous acts,
And shall arrive at this black bloody leafe,
Noting yout foolish barbarisme, and my wrong,
(As time shall make it plaine) what followes this
Disciphering any noble deed of yours
Shall be quite lost, for men will read no more.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Why? dare you say you are innocent?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: By all the gods, as they
Of this foule crime, why Gent. pry clean through my life,
Then weigh these circumstances: think you that he
Which made day night, and men to furies turn'd,
Durst not trust silence, vizors, nor her sence
That suffer'd; but with Charmes and Potions
Cast her asleep, (for all this I have enquir'd)
Acted the Fable of Proserpines Rape,
The place (by all description) like to Hell:
And all to perpetrate unknowne his Lust,
Would fondly in his Person bring a Ring,
And give it a betrothed Wife, ith' same house
Where the poore injur'd Lady liv'd, and groan'd.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Hell gives us Art to reach the depth of sin,
But leaves us wretched Fooles, when we are in.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Had it given me that Art, and left me so,
I would not thus into the Lyons jawes
Have thrust my selfe (defencelesse) for your good,
The Princes safety, or the Common-weales:
You know the Queene deny'd me, and sent us
Commanders to surprize you, and to race
This Tower down, we had power enough to doe it,
Or starve you, as you saw, and not to tender
My Person to your wrath, which I have done,
Knowing my heart as pure as infants sleep.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: What think you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: No harme I am sure: I weepe.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: The gods are just, and mighty: but to give you
Further assurance, and to make your selves
Judges, and witnesses of my innocency,
Let me demand this question: On what night
Was this foule deed committed?

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: On the Eave
Before our Marriage meant.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Leonidas,
(Your rage being off, that still drownes memory)
Where was your selfe and I that very night,
And what our conference?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: By the gods 'tis true:
Both in her Highnesse Chamber conferring
Even of this Match untill an houre of day,
And then came I to call you: we are sham'd.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Vtterly lost, and sham'd.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Neither, be chear'd,
He that could finde this out can pardon it,
And know this Ring was sent me from the Queene,
How she came by it, yet is not exquir'd,
Deeper occurrents hang on't: and pray Heaven
That my suspicions prove as false as yours,
Which (for the world) till I have greater proofe
I dare not utter what, nor whom they touch;
Only this build upon, with ail my nerves
Ile labour with ye, till time waken truth.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: There are our swords Sir, turne the points on us,

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Punish Rebellion, and revenge your wrong.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Sir, my revenge shall be to make your peace,
Neither was this Rebellion, but rash love.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: How's this? unarm'd left, now found doubly arm'd?
And those that would have slaine him at his feet?
Oh Truth, thou art a mighty Conqueresse:
The Queene (my Lord) perplex'd in care of you,
That crosse to her command hazard your selfe
In person, here is come into the Field,
And like a Leader, marches in the head
Of all her Troopes, vowes that she will demolish
Each stone of this proud Tower be you not safe:
She chafes like stormes in Groves, now sighs, now weepes,
And both sometimes, like Raine and Wind commixt,
Abjures her Son for ever, lesse himselfe
Do fetch you off in person, that did give
Your selfe to save him of your owne free will,
And sweares he must not, nor is sit to live.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Oh she's a Mistris for the gods.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: And thou
A godlike servant fit for her.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Wide Greece
May boast because she cannot boast thy like.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Thus Conon tell her Highnesse.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: My joy flyes.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Let's toward her march: sterne Drum speake gentle peace.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: We are prisoners, lead us, ne're was knowne
A president like this: one unarm'd man
(Suspected) to captive with golden words
(Truth being his sheild) so many arm'd with swords.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: We are not lucky Crates, this great torrent
Beares all before him.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Such an age as this
Shall ne're be seene againe: vertue growes fat,
And villany pines; the Furies are asleep,
Mischiefe 'gainst goodnesse aym'd is like a stone,
Unnaturally forc'd up an imminent hill,
Whose weight falls on our heads and buries us,
We springe our selves, we sink in our owne bogs.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: What's to be done?

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Repent and grow good.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Pish,
'Tis not the fashion (foole) till we grow old:
The peoples love to him now scares me more
Then my fond Mothers: both which like two floods
Bearing Euphanes up; will o're-flow me,
And he is worthy, would he were in Heaven,
Be that hereafer: Crates helpe me now,
And henceforth be at ease.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Your will my Lord?

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Beliza is to marry him forth-with,
I long to have the first touch of her too,
That will a little quiet me.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Fie Sir,
You'l be the tyrant to virginity;
To fall but once is manly, to persevere
Beastly, and desperate.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Crosse me not but do't:
Are not the meanes, the place, the instruments
The very same? I must expect you suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: I must obey you.
Who is in evill once a companion
Can hardly shake him off, but must run on.
Here I appointed Conon to attend
Him, and his sword: he promis'd to come single
To avoyd prevention: he is a man on's word.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: You are well met Crates.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: If we part so Conon.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Come, we must doe these mutuall offices,
We must be our owne seconds, our owne Surgeons,
And fairely fight, like men, not on advantage.

speeches.speaker: Caa.
verse: You have an honest bosome.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Yours seemes so.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Let's paire our swords: you are a just Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: You might be so: now shake hands if you please,
Though't be the cudgell fashion, 'tis friendly one.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: So, stand off.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: That's my que to beckon 'em.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Crates, to expostulate your wrongs to me
Were to doubt of 'em, or wish your excuse
In words, and so returne like maiden Knights:
Yet freely thus much I professe, your spleene
And rugged carriage toward your honour'd Brother
Hath much more stirr'd me up, then mine owne cause,
For I did ne're affect these bloody men,
But hold 'em fitter be made publike Hangmen,
Or Butchers call'd, then valiant Gentlemen:
'Tis true stamp'd valour do's upon just grounds,
Yet for whom justlier should I expose my life
Than him, unto whose vertue I owe all.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Conon, you think by this great deed of yours
To insinuate your selfe a lodging nearer
Unto my Brothers heart: such men as you
Live on their undertakings for their Lords,
And more disable them by answering for 'em
Then if they sate still, make 'em but their Whores,
For which end Gallants now adayes do fight:
But here we come not to upbraid; what men
Seeme, the rash world will judge; but what they are
Heaven knowes: and this—Horses, we are discry'd,
One stroak for feare of laughter.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Halfe a score.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Hold, hold: on your allegeance hold.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: He that strikks next—

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Falls like a Traytor on our swords.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Oh Heaven, my Brother bleeds: Conon, thou art
A villaine, an unthankfull man, and shalt
Pay me thy blood for his, for his is mine:
Thou wert my friend, but he is still my Brother;
And though a friend sometimes be nearer said
In some gradation, it can never be
Where that same Brother can be made a friend,
Which dearest Crates thus low I implore;
What in my poverty I would not seeke,
Because I would not burthen you, now here
In all my height of blisse I beg of you,
Your friendship; my advancement Sir is yours;
I never held it strange, pray use it so:
We are but two, which number Nature fram'd
In the most usefull faculties of man,
To strengthen mutually and releeve each other:
Two eyes, two eares, two armes, two leggs and feet,
That where one fail'd the other might supply;
And I, your other eye, eare, your arme and legge,
Tender my service, helpe and succour to ye.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Leo, A most divine example.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: For deare Brother,
You have been blind, and lame, and deafe to me,
Now be no more so: in humility
I give ye the duty of a younger Brother,
Which take you as a Brother, not a Father,
And then you'l pay a duty back to me.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Till now I have not wept these thirty yeares.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Discording Brothers are like mutuall leggs
Supplanting one another: he that seekes
Aid from a stranger and forsakes his Brother,
Do's but like him that madly lops his arme,
And to his body joynes a wooden one:
Cuts off his naturall legge, and trusts a Crutch,
Plucks out his eye to see with Spectacles.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Most deare Euphanes, in this crimson floud
Wash my unkindnesse out: you have ore-come me,
Taught me humanity and brotherhood;
Full well knew Nature thou wert fitter far
To be a Ruler ore me then a Brother,
Which henceforth be: Jove surely did descend
When thou wert gotten in some heavenly shape
And greet my Mother, as the Poets tell
Of other women.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Be this Holy-day.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And noted ever with the whitest stone.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: And pardon me my Lord, looke you, I bleed
Faster then Crates; what I have done I did
To reconcile your loves, to both a friend,
With my blood ciment, never to part or end.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Most worthy Conon.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Happy rise, this day
Contracts more good then a whole age hath done.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Royall Agenor, brave Leonidas,
You are maine causes, and must share the fame.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Which in some part this hower shall requight,
For I have aym'd my black shafts at white markes,
And now ile put the clew into your hands
Shall guide ye most perspicuously to the depth
Of this dark Laborinth, where so long ye were lost
Touching this old Rape, and a new intent,
Wherein your counsell, and your active wit
My dearest Brother will be necessary.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: My Prophecy is come, prove my hopes true
Agenor shall have right, and you no wrong,
Time now will pluck her daughter from her Cave:
Let's hence to prevent rumour; my deare Brother,
Natures divided streames the highest shelfe
Will over-run at last, and flow to it selfe.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I Have won the Lady to it, and that good
Which is intended to her, your faith onely
And secrecie must make perfect: Thinke not Sir,
I speake as doubting it, for I dare hazard
My soule upon the tryall.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: You may safely,
But are Agenor, and Leonidas ready
To rush upon him in the Act, and seize him
In the height of his security?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: At all parts
As you could wish them.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Where's the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: There
Where you appointed her to stay.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: 'Tis wisely order'd.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Last, when you have him sure compell him this way,
For as by accident here ile bring the Queene
To meet you, 'twill strike greater terrour to him,
To be tane unprovided of excuse,
And make more for our purposes.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Come Neanthes,
Our fames and all are at the stake.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: 'Tis fit
That since relying on your skill we venture
So much upon one game, you play with cunning
Or we shall rise such losers: as—

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: The Prince.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: The plot is laid Sir, howsoe're I seem'd
A little scrupulous, upon better judgement
I have effected it.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: 'Tis the last service
Of this foule kinde I will employ you in.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: We hope so Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And I will so reward it—

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: You are bound to that; in every Family
That do's write lustfull, your fine Bawd gaines more
(For like your Broker, he takes fees on both sides)
Then all the Officers of the house.

speeches.speaker: Sos.
verse: For us then
To be a great mans Panders, and live poore,
That were a double fault.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: Come, you lose time Sir,
We will be with you instantly: the deed done,
We have a Mask that you expect not.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Thou art ever carefull: for Joves Mercury
I would not change thee.

speeches.speaker: Era.
verse: There's an honour for you.

speeches.speaker: Nea.
verse: To be compar'd with the celestiall Pimp,
Joves smock-sworne Squire, Dan Hermes.

speeches.speaker: Cra,
verse: Ile deserve it,
And Gentlemen be assur'd, though what we do now
Will to the Prince Theanor looke like treason
And base disloyalty, yet the end shall prove,
When he's first taught to know himselfe, then you,
In what he judg'd us false we were must true.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Only make haste (my Lords) in all things else
You are instructed: you may draw your swords
For shew if you thinke good, but on my life
You will finde no resistance in his servants,
And he's himselfe unarm'd.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: I would he were not,
My just rage should not then be lost.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Good Sir,
Have you a care no injury be done
Unto the Person of the Prince: but Conon,
Have you an eye on both, it is your trust
That I relye on.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Which I will discharge,
Assure your selfe most faithfully.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: For the Lady,
I know your best respect will nor be wanting:
Then to avoyd suspition and discovery,
I hold it requisite, that as soone as ever
The Queene hath seene her, she forsake the place,
And fit her selfe for that which is projected
For her good, and your honour.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: If this prosper,
Beleeve it you have made a purchase of
My service and my life.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Your love I ayme at.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Here I shall finde you?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: With the Qteene.

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Enough Sir.

speeches.speaker: Page.
verse: The Queene enquires for you my Lord, I have met
A dozen Messengers in search of you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I knew I should be sought for, as I wish'd
She's come her selfe in person.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Are you found Sir?
I wonder where you spend your houres, me thinkes
Since I so love your company, and professe
'Tis the best comfort this life yeelds me; mine
Should not be tedious to you.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Gracious Madam,
To have the happinesse to see and heare you,
Which by your bounty is conferr'd upon me,
I hold so great a blessing, that my honours
And wealth compar'd to that are but as Cyphers
To make that number greater: yet your pardon
For borrowing from my duty so much time
As the provision for my sudden Marriage
Exacted from me.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: I perceive this Marriage
Will keepe you often from me: but ile beare it.
She's a good Lady, and a faire, Euphanes,
Yet by her leave I will share with her in you:
I am pleas'd that in the night she shall enjoy you,
And that's sufficient for a Wife: the day time
I will divorce you from her.

speeches.speaker: Leo. within.
verse: We will force you if you resist.

speeches.speaker: Queen.
verse: What noyce is that?

speeches.speaker: The. within.
verse: Base Traytors.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: It moves this way.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: What ere it be ile meet it,
I was not borne to feare: Who's that Beliza?

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: My worthiest, noblest Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Stay her, ha?
All of you looke as you were rooted here,
And wanted motion: what new Gorgons head
Have you beheld, that you are all turn'd Statues?
This is prodigious: ha's none a tongue
To speake the cause?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Could every haire great Queene
Upon my head yeeld an articulate sound,
And all together speake, they could not yet
Expresse the villany we have discover'd,
And yet, when with a few unwilling words
I have deliver'd what must needs be knowne,
You'l say I am too eloquent, and wish
I had been borne without a tongue.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Speak boldly,
For I unmov'd with any losse will heare.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Then know, we have found out the Ravisher
Of my poore Sister, and the place, and meanes
By which th' unfortunate though faire Beliza
Hath met a second violence.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: This confirmes
What but before I doubted, to my ruine
My Lady ravish'd.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Point me out the villaine,
That guilty wretched monster that hath done this,
That I may looke on him, and in mine eye
He read his Sentence.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: That I truly could
Name any other but the Prince, that heard
You have it all.

speeches.speaker: Queen.
verse: Wonder not that I shake,
The miracle is greater that I live,
Having endur'd the thunder that thy words
Have throwne upon me: dar'st thou kneele, with hope
Of any favour, but a speedy death,
And that too in the dreadfull'st shape that can
Appeare to a dispairing leaprous soule,
If thou hast any? no, libidinous beast,
Thy Lust hath alter'd so thy former being,
By Heaven I know thee not.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Although unworthy
Yet still I am your Son.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Thou lyest, lyest falsly,
My whole life never knew but one chaste bed,
Nor e're desir'd warmth but from lawfull fires,
Can I be then the Mother to a Goat,
Whose lust is more insatiate then the grave,
And like infectious ayre engenders plagues,
To murder all that's chaste, or good in woman?
The Gods I from my youth have serv'd and fear'd,
Whose holy Temples thou hast made thy Brothells;
Could a Religious Mother then bring forth
So damn'd an Atheist? read but o're my life,
My actions, manners, and made perfect in them
But looke into the story of thy selfe
As thou art now, not as thou wert Theanor,
And Reason will compell thee to confesse,
Thou art a stranger to me.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: Note but how heavie
The weight of guilt is: it so low hath sunke him
That he wants power to rise up in defence
Of his bad cause.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Perswade me not Euphanes,
This is no Prince, nor can claime part in me:
My Son was borne a Free-man, this a Slave
To beastly passions, a fugitive,
