And run-away from vertue: bring bonds for him.
By all the honour that I owe to Justice
He loses me for ever that seekes to save him:
Binde him I say, and like a wretch that knowes
He stands condemn'd before he heares the Sentence,
With his base Agents, from my sight remove him,
And lodge them in the Dungeon: As a Queene
And Patronesse to Justice I command it:
Thy teares are like unseasonable showres,
And in my heart now steel'd can make no entrance:
Thou art cruell to thy selfe (Foole) 'tis not want
In me of soft compassion; when thou left'st
To be a Son, I ceas'd to be a Mother;
Away with them: The children I will leave
To keepe my name to all posterities
Shall be the great examples of my Justice,
The government of my Country, which shall witnesse
How well I rul'd my selfe: bid the wrong'd Ladies
Appeare in Court to morrow, we will heare them;
And by one Act of our severity
For feare of punishment, or love to vertue,
Teach others to be honest: all will shun
To tempt her Lawes, that would not spare her Son.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Nay Nephew.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Pupill, heare but reason.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: No, I have none, and will heare none; oh my honor,
My honour blasted in the bud, my youth,
My hopefull youth, and all my expectation
Ever to be a man are lost for ever.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: Why Nephew, we as well as you are dub'd
Knights of the Pantofle.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: And are shouted at,
Kick'd, scorn'd, and laugh'd at by each Page and Groome,
Yet with erected heads we beare it.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Alas,
You have yeares, and strength to doe it; but were you
(As I) a tender grisle, apt to bow,
You would like me with Cloakes envelloped,
Walke thus, then stamp, then stare.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: He will run mad
I hope, and then all's mine.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Why looke you Pupill,
There are for the recovery of your honour
Degrees of Medicines, for a tweak by the Nose
A man's to travell but fixe moneths, then blow it
And all is well againe: the Bastinado
Requires a longer time, a yeare or two,
And then 'tis buried: I grant you have been bafful'd,
'Tis but a journey of some thirty yeares
And it will be forgotten.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: Thinke you so?

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Assuredly.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: He may make a shorter cut,
But hange, or drowne himselfe, and on my life
'Twill no more trouble him.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: I could ne're endure
Or Hemp or Water, they are dangerous tooles
For youth to deale with: I will rather follow
My Tutors counsell.

speeches.speaker: Tut.
verse: Do so.

speeches.speaker: Onos.
verse: And put in
For my security, that ile not returne
In thirty yeares, my whole state to my Unckle.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: That I like well of.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Still provided Unckle,
That at my comming home you will allow me
To be of age, that I may call to accompt
This Page, that hath abus'd me.

speeches.speaker: ~nc.
verse: 'Tis a march.

speeches.speaker: On.
verse: Then Corinth, thus the bashfull Lamprias
Takes leave of thee: and for this little time
Of thirty yeares will labour all he can,
Though he goes yong forth, to come home a man.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Are your Prisoners ready?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: When it shall please the Queene
To call them forth my Lord.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: Pray you doe me the favour
To tell me how they have borne themselves this night
Of their imprisonment?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Gladly Sir; your Brother
With the other Courtiers willingly receiv'd
All courtesies I could offer; eat, and drank,
And were exceeding merry, so dissembling
Their guilt, or confident in their innocence,
That I much wonder'd at it. But the Prince,
That (as borne highest) should have grac'd his fall
With greatest courage, is so sunck with sorrow,
That to a common judgement ye would seeme
To suffer like a woman: but to me,
That from the experience I have had of many
Looke further in him, I doe finde the deep
Consideration of what's past, more fright him
Then any other punishment.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: That is indeed
True magnanimity: the other but
A desperate bastard vallour.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I pressed to him,
And notwithstanding the Queenes strict command,
(Having your Lordships promise to secure me)
Offer'd to free him from his bonds, which he
Refus'd, with such a sorrow mixt with scorne
That it amaz'd me; yet I urg'd his Highnesse
To give one Reason for't: he briefly answer'd,
That he had sate in Judgement on himselfe,
And found that he deserv'd them: that he was
A Ravisher, and so to suffer like one,
Which is the reason of my teares: he addeth,
For were't not I againe should breake the Lawes,
By scorning all their rigour can inflict,
I should dye smiling.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: I forbeare to wonder
That you were mov'd that saw this: I am strooke
With the relation so. 'Tis very well;
See all things ready. I doe wish I could
Send comfort to the Prince; be ready with him;
'Tis in the Queenes breast only, which for us
To search into were sawcinesse, to determine
What she thinkes fit.

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: Make way there for the Queene.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Read first the Law, and what our Ancestors
Have in this case provided, to deter
Such like offenders: To you gentle Ladies
This onely, Would I could as well give comfort,
As bid you be secure from feare or doubt
Of our displeasure: be as confident
As if your plea were 'gainst a common man,
To have all right from us; I will not grieve
For what's not worth my pitty: Read the Law.

speeches.speaker: Clerke
prose: Lycurgus the nineteenth against Rapes: It is provided, and publiquely enacted and confirmed, That any man of what degree soever, offering violence to the chastity of a Virgin, shall (Ipso facto) be lyable to her accusation, and according to the said Law be censur'd; Ever provided, that it shall be in the choyce of the said Virgin so abused, either to compell the Offender to Marry her without a Dowre, if so she will be satisfied, or demanding his head for the offenoe, to have that accordingly performed.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: You heare this: what doe you demand?

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: The benefit
The Law allowes me.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: For the injury
Done to mine Honour, I require his head.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I likewise have an eye upon mine Honour,
But knowing that his death cannot restore it
I aske him for my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I was Ravish'd,
And will have Justice.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: I was Ravish'd too,
I kneele for mercy.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I demand but what
The Law allowes me.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: That which I desire
Is by the same Law warranted.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: The Rape
On me, hath made a forfeit of his life,
Which in revenge of my disgrace I plead for.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: The Rape on me gives me the priviledge
To be his wife, and that is all I sue for.

speeches.speaker: Age.
verse: A doubtfull case.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Such pretty Lawyers, yet
I never saw, nor read of.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: May the Queene
Favour your sweet plea, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Is that justice?
Shall one that is to suffer for a Rape
Be by a Rape defended? Looke upon
The publike enemy of chastity,
This lustfull Satyre, whose enrag'd desires
The ruine of one wretched Virgins honour
Would not suffice; and shall the wrack of two
Be his protection? May be I was ravish'd
For his lust onely, thou for his defence;
O fine evasion! shall with such a sleight
Your justice be deluded? your Lawes cheated?
And he that for one fact deserv'd to die,
For sinning often finde impunity?
But that I know thee, I would sweare thou wert
A false impostour, and subornd to this;
And it may be thou art Merione:
For hadst thou suffer'd truly what I have done,
Thou wouldst like me complaine, and call for vengeance,
And our wrongs being equall, I alone
Should not desire revenge: But be it so,
If thou prevaile, even he will punish it,
And foolish mercy shew'd to him undoe thee,
Consider, foole, before it be too late,
What joyes thou canst expect from such a husband,
To whom thy first, and what's more, forc'd embraces,
Which men say heighten pleasure, were distastefull.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: 'Twas in respect, that then they were unlawfull,
Unbless'd by Hymen, and left stings behind them,
Which from the marriage bed are ever banish'd.
Let this Court be then the image of Joves throne,
Upon which grace and mercy still attend,
To intercede betweene him and his Justice;
And since the Law allowes as much to me
As she can challenge, let the milder sentence,
Which best becomes a Mother, and a Queene
Now overcome; nor let your wisdome suffer,
In doing right to her, I in my wrong
Indure a second Ravishment.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You can free him
Onely from that which do's concerne your selfe,
Not from the punishment that's due to me:
Your injuries you may forgive, not mine;
I plead mine owne just wreak, which will right both,
Where that which you desire robs me of Justice;
'Tis that which I appeale to.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: Bloody woman,
Dost thou desire his punishment? Let him live then;
For any man to marry where he likes not
Is still a lingring torment.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: For one Rape
One death's sufficient, that way cannot catch me.

speeches.speaker: Mer.
verse: To you I fly then, to your mercy Madam,
Exempting not your Justice, be but equall;
And since in no regard I come behind her,
Let me not so be undervalu'd in
Your highnesse favour, that the world take notice
You so prefer'd her, that in her behalf
You kil'd that Son, you would not save for me;
Mercy, O mercy Madam.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Great Queen, Justice.

speeches.speaker: Age.
prose: With what a Masculine constancy the grave Lady hath heard them both?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Yet how unmov'd she sits
In that which most concernes her?

speeches.speaker: Con.
verse: Now she rises,
And having well waigh'd both their arguments,
Resolves to speak.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: And yet againe she pauses;
O Conon, such a resolution once
A Roman told me he had seene in Cato
Before he kill'd himself.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: 'Tis now determin'd.
Merione, I could wish I were no Queene,
To give you satisfaction; no Mother
Beliza, to content you; and would part,
Even with my being, both might have their wishes;
But since that is impossible, in few words
I will deliver what I am resolved on:
The end for which all profitable Lawes
Were made, looks two waies onely, the reward
Of innocent good men, and the punishment
Of bad Delinquents: Ours, concerning Rapes,
Provided that same latter clause of Marriage
For him that had falne once, not then foreseeing
Mankinde could prove so monstrous, to tread twice
A path so horrid. The great Law-giver
Draco, That for his strange severity
Was said to write his sterne Decrees in blood,
Made none for Parricides, presuming that
No man could be so wicked: Such might be,
Lycurgus answere (did he live) for this.
But since I finde that in my Sonne, which was not
Doubted in any else, I will adde to it;
He cannot marry both, but for both dying,
Both have their full revenge: You see Beliza
You have your wish; with you Merione
Ile spend a teare or two, so Heaven forgive thee.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Upon my knees I do approve your judgement,
And beg that you would put it into act
With all speed possible; onely that I may,
Having already made peace with my self,
Part so with all the world: Princely Agenor
I aske your pardon; yours my Lord Euphanes;
And Crates, with the rest too, I forgive you;
Do you the like for me: Yours, gracious Mother,
I dare not ask, and yet if that my death
Be like a Son of yours, though my life was not,
Perhaps you may vouchsafe it: Lastly that
Both these whom I have wrong'd, may wish my ashes
No heavy burden, ere I suffer death,
For the restoring of Meriones honour,
Let me be married to her, and then dye
For you Beliza.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: Thou hast made in this
Part of amends to me, and to the world,
Thy suit is granted, call a Flamyn forth
To do this holy work; with him a Headsman.
Raise up thy weeping eyes Merione,
With this hand I confirme thy Marriage,
Wishing that now the Gods would shew some miracle,
That this might not divorse it.

speeches.speaker: Cra.
verse: To that purpose
I am their Minister; stand not amaz'd,
To all your comforts I will do this wonder,
Your Majesty (with your pardon I must speak it)
Allow'd once heretofore of such a Contract,
Which you repenting afterwards, revok'd it,
Being fully bent to match her with Agenor,
The griev'd Prince knowing this, and yet not daring
To crosse what you determin'd, by an Oath
Bound me and these his followers to doe something
That he might once enjoy her, we sworne to it,
And easily perswaded, being assur'd
She was his Wife before the face of Heaven,
Although some Ceremonious formes were wanting,
Committed the first Rape, and brought her to him,
Which broke the Marriage; but when we perceiv'd
He purpos'd to abuse our ready service
In the same kinde, upon the chaste Beliza,
Holding our selves lesse ty'd to him then goodnesse;
I made discovery of it to my Brother,
Who can relate the rest.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: It is most true.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: I would it were.

speeches.speaker: Euph.
verse: In every circumstance
It is upon my soule: For this knowne to me,
I wan Merione in my Ladies habit,
To be againe (but willingly) surpriz'd,
But with Agenor, and her noble Brother,
With my approv'd friend Conon, with such speed
She was pursu'd, that the lewd act scarce ended,
The Prince (assur'd he had enjoy'd Beliza,
For all the time Meriones face was cover'd)
Was apprehended, and b^ought to your presence,
But not till now discover'd, in respect
I hop'd the imminent danger of the Prince,
To which his loose unquenched heats had brought him,
Being pursu'd unto the latest tryall
Would worke in him compunction, which it has done;
And these two Ladies in their feign'd contentions,
To your delight I hope have serv'd as Maskers
To their owne Nuptialls.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: My choyce was worthy
When first I look'd on thee, as thou hast order'd
All shall be done, and not the meanest that
Plaid in this unexpected Comedy,
But shall pertake our bounty: And my Lord,
That with the rest you may seeme satisfi'd,
If you dare venture on a Queene, not yet
So farre in debt to yeares. but that she may
Bring you a lusty Boy, I offer up
My selfe and Kingdome during my life to you.

speeches.speaker: Ag.
verse: It is a blessing which I durst not hope for,
But with all joy receive.

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: We all applaud it.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Then on unto the Temple, where the rights
Of Marriage ended, we'l finde new delights.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: TIs true she is a right good Princes, and a just one;
And Florence when she sets has lost a Planet.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: My Mistris? I tell thee gentle Nephew,
There is not such another friend to goodnesse,
To down-right dealing, to faith and true heart
Within the Christian confines: Before she blest us,
Justice was a Cheese-monger; a meere Cheese-monger,
Weigh'd nothing to the World but mytes and maggots,
And a maine stinke: Law like a Horse-courser,
Her rules, and precepts hung with gawdes and ribbonds,
And pamper'd up to cousen him that bought her,
When she her selfe was hackney lame and founder'd.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: But the sweet Lady,
Belvidere the bright one—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I, there's a face indeed: O my deare Nephew;
Could a young fellow of thy fiery mettle
Freeze, and that Lady in his armes?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I think not.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Thou hast a parlous judgement; but let that passe,
She is as truly vertuous, faire, and noble,
As her great Mother's good; and that's not ordinary.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: But why (so many Princes, and so great ones
Being Suitors) should the Dutchesse deny to match her?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: She is a Jewell man, hangs in her bosome,
Her only Childe: with her eyes she sees all things,
Discourses with her tongue, and pluck her from her
(So dotingly the old one loves her young one)
You pluck her heart out too: Besides, of late daies,
The Duke of Millaine, who could never win her
By love, nor treaty, laid a close traine for her
In her owne private walkes: some forty Horse-men,
So to surprize her; which we found, and dealt with,
And sent 'em running home to the Duke their Master,
Like Doggs with bottles at their tailes.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Since that, I heard Sir,
She has sent her to your Cittadell to secure her,
My cousen Rodope, your wife attending her.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You heare a truth, and all convenient pleasures
Are there proportion'd for her.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I would faine Sir,
Like one that owes a dutious service to her
Sometimes, so please you—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Gentle Cousen pardon me,
I must not, nor you must not dare to offer,
The last Edict lyes on his life pu^sues it;
Your friend Sir to command, abroad to love you,
To lend ye any thing I have, to wait upon ye,
But in the Cittadell where I stand charg'd,
Not a bit upon a march: no service Sir,
No, good Sir by no meanes: I kisse your hands Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: To your keeping only? none else to look upon her?
None but Bartello worthy her attendance?
No faith but his to serve her? O Belvidere,
Thou Saint to whom my youth is sacrific'd,
Thou point to which my life turnes, and my fortune,
Art thou lock'd from me now? from all my comforts,
Art thou snatch'd violently? thou hear'st me not,
Nor canst thou see (faire soule) thy Servants mournings,
Yet let thy gentle heart feele what is absence,
The great divorse of minds so truly loving,
So long, and nurs'd in one affection
Even from our infant eyes, suck'd in and nourish'd:
O let it feele but that, and there stand constant
And I am blest. My deare Neece Rodope,
That is her Governesse, did love me dearely,
There's one hope yet to see her: when he is absent
It may be ventur'd, and she may work it closely:
I know the Ladies will goes equall with me,
And so the danger of the Edict avoyded;
Let me think more, for I must try all hazards.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Will ye go yonder Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Yes marry will I Sir.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: And by this Ladder?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: By that Ladder, coxcomb.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Have ye any more necks at home when this is broken,
For this will crack with the best friend he has Sir?
Or can you pitch of all foure, like an Ape now?
Let me see you tumble.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You are very pleasant Sir.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: No truly Sir, I should be loath to see ye
Come fluttering down like a yong Rooke, cry squab,
And take ye up with your brains beaten into your buttocks

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Hold your peace Asse: who's this stands musing here?
Silvio?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Who calls me?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: One most glad to see you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: My dearest Claudio? what make you thus private,
And with a preparation of this nature?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
prose: We have leave to play, and are going to climbe Birds nests.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Prethee what is it friend? why start ye from me?
Is your old Mistris growne so coy and cruell,
She must be scal'd? it seemes you are loath to tell me,
Since twenty yeares continuance of our friendship
May not be worth the weight of such a secret,
'Twill be but rude to aske againe: 'save ye.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nay stay, deare Silvio, if you love me take it:
For till you know it, never woman labour'd
As I do now.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Ile do my best to ease it.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You have heard the Lady Belvidere—

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: What heard Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Heard to the Cittadell, upon some feares
She is confin'd.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Why dreames he on this beauty?
'Tis true, I have heard it.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And that no accesse,
No blessing from those eyes but with much hazard,
Even hazard of a life.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: He dares not love her;
I have heard that too: but whither points your purpose?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: O Silvio, let me speake that none may heare me,
None but thy truth: I have lov'd this Lady long,
Long given away my life to her devotion,
Long dwelt upon that beauty to my ruine.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Do's she know this?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: No, there begins my misery,
Ixion-like, I have onely yet clasp'd Clouds,
And fed upon poore empty dreames that starve me.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: And what do you meane to do now?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Though I dye for't,
Though all the tortures in the world hung on me,
Arm'd with imperious Love, I stand prepar'd now,
With this to reach her Chamber: there to see her,
And tell her boldly with what truth I love her.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: 'Twill not be easily done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: O my Silvio,
The hardest things are sweetest in possession.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Nor will shew much discretion.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Love is blinde man,
And he that lookes for reason there far blinder.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Have ye consider'd ripely?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: All that may fall,
And arm'd against that all.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Her honour too?
What she may suffer in this rash adventure?
The beauty of her name?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ile do it closely,
And only at her window, with that caution—

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Are there no Guards?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Corruption chokes their service.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Or do you hold her bred so light a woman
To hold commerce with strange tongues?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Why this service,
This only hazard of my life must tell her,
Though she were Vestas selfe, I must deserve her.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I would not have ye go: pray let it sinke here,
And think a nobler way to raise your service,
A safer, and a wiser.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Tis too late Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Then I must say, You shall not go.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I shall not?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: You shall not go: that part bred with ye, friendship
Bids me say boldly so, and you observe me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You stretch that tye too far.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Ile stretch it farther:
The honour that I beare that spotlesse vertue
You fouly seeke to taint, unnobly covet,
Bids me command ye stay: if not, thus force ye.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: This will be worse then climbing.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Why do ye draw Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: To kill thee, if thy base will be thy Master.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I ever was your friend.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Whilst thou wert honest,
And not a Night-theife of anothers honour;
I never call'd a Foole my friend, a mad-man,
That durst expose his fame to all opinions,
His life to unhonest dangers: I never lov'd him,
Durst know his name, that sought a Virgins ruine,
Nor ever tooke I pleasure in acquaintance
With men, that give as loose raynes to their fancies
As the wilde Ocean to his raging fluxes:
A noble soule I twin with, and my love
Followes, his life dares master his affections.
Will ye give off, or fight?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I will not fight with ye:
The sacred name of friend tyes up that anger,
Rather ile study.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Do, to be a friend still.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: If this way, I shall never hold.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Ile watch ye:
And if I catch ye false: by Heaven ye dye for't,
All love forgot.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: When I feare that I am fit for't.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Whilst prodigall yong gaudy Fools are banqueting,
And launching out their states to catch the giddy,
Thus do I study to preserve my fortune,
And hatch with care at home the wealth that Saints me.
Here's Rubies of Bengala, rich, rich, glorious;
These Diamonds of Ormus bought for little,
Here vented at the price of Princes Ransomes;
How bright they shine like constellations,
The South seas treasure here, Pearle, faire and orient
Able to equall Cleapatra's Banket,
Here chaines of lesser stones for Ladies lustres,
Ingotts of Gold, Rings, Brooches, barrs of Silver,
These are my studies to set off in sale well,
And not in sensuall surfeits to consume 'em;
How rosts mine egg? he heats apace, ile turne him:
Penurio, where you knave do you wait? Penurio,
You lazie knave.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Did you call Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Where's your Mistris?
What vanity holds her from her attendance?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The very sight of this egge has made him cockish,
What would a dozen butter'd do? She is within Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Within Sir, at what thrift ye knave? what getting?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Getting a good stomack Sir, & she knew where to get meat to it,
She is praying heartily upon her knees Sir,
That Heaven would send her a good bearing dinner.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Nothing but gluttony and surfeit thought on,
Health flung behinde: had she not yesternight firrah
Two Sprats to supper, and the oyle allowable?
Was she not sick with eating? Hadst not thou,
(Thou most vngratefull knave, that nothing satisfies)
The water that I boyl'd my other egge in
To make thee hearty broth?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: 'Tis true, I had Sir;
But I might as soone make the Philosophers Stone on't,
You gave it me in water, and but for manners sake,
I could give it you againe in wind, it was so hearty
I shall turne pissing Conduit shortly: my Mistris comes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Welcome my Dove.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Pray ye keep your welcome to ye,
Unlesse it carries more then words to please me,
Is this the joy to be a Wife? to bring with me,
Besides the noblenesse of blood I spring from,
A full and able portion to maintaine me?
Is this the happinesse of youth and beauty,
The great content of being made a Mistris,
To live a Slave subject to wants, and hungers,
To jealousies for every eye that wanders?
Unmanly jealousie.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Good Isabella.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Too good for you: do you think to famish me,
Or keep me like an Almes-woman in such rayment,
Such poore unhandsome weeds? am I old, or ugly?
I never was bred thus: and if your misery
Will suffer wilfull blindnesse to abuse me,
My patience shall be no Bawd to mine owne ruine.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Tickle him Mistris: to him.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Had ye love in ye,
Or any patt of man—

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Follow that Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Or had humanity but ever knowne ye,
You would shame to use a woman of my way thus,
So poore, and basely: you are strangly jealous of me
If I should give ye cause.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: How Isabella?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: As do not venture this way to provoke me.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Excellent well Mistris,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: How's this Isabella?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: 'Twill stir a Saint, and I am but a woman,
And by that tenure may.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: By no meanes Chicken,
You know I love ye: fie, take no example
By those young gadding Dames: (you are noted vertuous)
That stick their Husbands wealth in trifles on 'em
And point 'em but the way to their owne miseries:
I am not jealous, kisse me, — I am not:
And for your diet, 'tis to keep you healthfull,
Surfits destroy more then the sword: that I am carefull
Your meat should be both neat, and cleanly handled
See, Sweet, I am Cook my selfe, and mine owne Cater.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A — of that Cook cannot lick his fingers.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Ile adde another dish: you shall have Milke to it,
'Tis nourishing and good.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: With Butter in't Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: This knave would breed a famine in a Kingdom:
And cloths that shall content ye: you must be wise then,
And live sequestred to your selfe and me,
Not wandring after every toy comes crosse ye,
Nor strooke with every spleene: what's the knave doing? Penurio.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Hunting Sir, for a second course of flyes here,
They are rare new Sallads.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: For certaine Isabella
This ravening fellow has a Woolf in's belly:
Untemperate knave, will nothing quench thy appetite?
I saw him eat two Apples, which is monstrous.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: If you had given me those 'thad bin more monstro~s.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Tis a maine miracle to feed this villaine,
Come Isabella, let us in to Supper,
And think the Romane dainties at our Table,
'Tis all but thought.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Would all my thoughts would do it:
The Devill should think of purchasing that Egge-shell,
To vittle out a Witch for the Burmoothes:
'Tis treason to any good stomack living now
To heare a tedious Grace said, and no meat to 't,
I have a Radish yet, but that's but transitory.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Can any living man unlesse a Rascall
That neither knowes himselfe, nor a fashion'd Gentleman
Take me for a worse man then my Master now?
I am naturally proud in these cloths: but if pride now
Should catch a fall in what I am attempting,
'Tis but a Proverb sound, and a Neck broken,
That's the worst can come on't: a Gentleman's gone then,
A Gentleman oth' first house, there's the end on't:
My Master lyes most pittifully complaining,
Wringing and kicking up toth' eares in love yonder,
And such a lamentable noyse he keepes, it kills me:
I have got his cloths, and if I can get to her
By hooke or crooke here, such a song ile sing her—
I think I shall be hang'd, but that's no matter,
What's a hanging among friends: I am valiant now as an Elephant;
What's a hanging among friends: I am valiant now as an
I have consider'd what to say too: let me see now,
This is the place, 'tis plaguy high: stay at that lower window
Let me ayme finely now, like a good Gunner,
It may prove but a whipping.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I saw some-body
Passe by me now, and though it were dark, me thought yet
I knew the clothes: ha, let me not be cozen'd,
The Ladder too, ready to fling it? monstrous,
'Tis he, 'tis Claudio: most voluptuous villaine,
Scandall to womans credit: Love, I forget thee.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: What will he do ith' name of heaven, what's that there?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: And all the friendship that I bore thee, bury here.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: What has he in's hand? I hope but a Cudgell.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Thy fault's forgive O Heaven: farewell thou traitor.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: I am slaine: I am slaine.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: He's downe, and dead: dead certaine,
'Twas too rash, too full of spleene, stark dead:
This is no place now to repent in, onely
Would I had given this hand that shot the Pistoll
I had miss'd thee, and thou wert once more Claudio.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Why should I love thus foolishly? thus desperatly?
And give away my heart where no hope's left me?
Why should not the true counsell of a friend restraine me?
The Devills mouth I run into affright me,
The honour of the Lady charme my wildnesse;
I have no power, no being of my selfe,
No reason strong enough now left within me
To binde my will: O Love, thou God, or Devill,
Or what thou art that playes the tyrant in me.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Oh.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What's that cry?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: A Surgeon, a Surgeon,
Twenty good Surgeons.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Tis not far from me,
Some Murther o' my life,

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Will you let me dye here?
No drink come, nor no Surgeon?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Tis my man sure,
His voyce, and here he lyes: how is it with thee?

speeches.speaker: Sot.
verse: I am slaine, Sir, I am slaine.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Slaine? Who has slaine thee?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Kill'd, kill'd, out-right kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Where's thy hurt?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: I know not,
But I am sure I am kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Canst thou sit up,
That I may finde the hurt out?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: I can sit up,
But ne're the lesse I am slaine.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Tis not o'this side?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: No Sir, I thinke it be not.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nor o' this side,
Was it done with a Sword?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: A Gun, a Gun sweet Master.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: The devill a' bullet has been here: thou art well, man.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: No sure, I am kill'd.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Let me see thy thighes, and belly,
As whole as a Fish for any thing I see yet:
Thou bleed'st no where.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: I thinke I do not bleed Sir,
But yet I am afraid I am slaine.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Stand up Foole,
Thou hast as much hurt as my naile: who shot thee,
A Pottle, or a Pinte?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Signiour Silvio shot me
In these clothes, taking me for you, and seeing
The Ladder in my hand here, which I stole from ye,
Thinking to have gone to the Lady my selfe, & have spoke for ye

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: If he had hit ye home, he had serv'd ye right sirra,
You sawcy rogue, how poore my intent showes to me,
How naked now, and foolish?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Are ye sure he has not hit me,
It gave a monstruous bounce?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You risse of your right side,
And said your prayers too, you had been payed else:
But what need'st thou a Bullet when thy feare kills thee?
Sirrah, keep your own counsell for all this, you'l be hang'd else,
If it be knowne.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: If it be by my meanes let me;
I am glad I am not kill'd, and far more gladder
My gentleman-like humours out: I feele 'tis dangerous,
And to be a gentleman, is to be kill'd twice a week.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Keepe your selfe close ith' Country for a while sirra.
There's Money, walk to your friends.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: They have no Pistolls,
Nor are no Gentlemen, that's my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I will retire too, and live private; for this Silvio
Inflam'd with noblenesse will be my death else;
And if I can forget this love that loades me,
At least the danger: and now I think on't better,
I have some conclusions else invites me to it.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: NEphew.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: My deare Ant.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Would you goe by thus slily
And never see me, not once send in to me
Your loving Neece? she that above all those
I call my Kindred honour'd you, and placed you
Nearest my heart?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I thanke you worthy Cousen,
But such at this time are my occasions—

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You shall not goe yet, by my faith you shall not,
I will not be denyd: why looke ye sad Nephew?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I am seldome other: O, this blood sits heavy:
As I walk't this way late last night,
In meditation of some things concern'd me—

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: What Nephew?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Why me thought I heard a Peece, Lady,
A peece shot off, much about this place too,
But could not judge the cause, nor what it boaded,
Under the Castle wall.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: We heard it too,
And the Watch pursu'd it presently, but found nothing,
Not any tract.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I am right glad to heare it:
The Ruffians surely, that command the night
Have found him, stript him: and into the River
Convey'd the body.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You looke still sadder, Nephew,
Is any thing within these walls to comfort ye?
Speake, and be master of it.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Ye are a right Courtier,
A great Professor, but a poore performer.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Do you doubt my faith: you never found me that way
I dare well speake it boldly, but a true friend.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Continue then.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Try me, and see who falters.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I will, and presently: 'tis in your power
To make me the most bound man to your courtesie.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Let me know how, and if I faile—

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: 'Tis thus then,
Get me accesse to the Lady Belvidere
But for a minute, but to see her: your Husband now
Is safe at Court, I left him full employ'd there.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You have ask'd the thing without my power to grant ye,
The Law lyes on the danger: if I lov'd ye not
I would bid ye goe, and there be found, and dye for't.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I knew your love, and where there shew'd a danger
How far you durst step for me: give me a true friend,
That where occasion is to doe a benefit
Aymes at the end, and not the rubs before it;
I was a foole to aske ye this, a more foole
To thinke a woman had so much noble nature
To entertaine a secret of this burthen;
Ye had best to tell the Dutchesse I perswaded ye,
That's a fine course, and one will win ye credit;
Forget the name of Cousen, blot my blood out,
And so you raise your selfe, let me grow shorter.
A woman friend? he that beleeves that weaknesse
Steeres in a stormy night without a Compasse.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: What is't I durst not do might not impeach ye?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Why this ye dare not do, ye dare not thinke of.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: 'Tis a maine hazard.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: If it were not so
I would not come to you to seeke a favour.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You will lose your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: The losse ends with my selfe then.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: You will but see her?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Onely looke upon her.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Not stay?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Prescribe your time.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Not traffique with her
In any close dishonourable actions?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Stand you your selfe by.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: I will venture for ye,
Because ye shall be sure I am a touch'd friend,
Ile bring her to ye: come walke, you know the Garden,
And take this key to open the little Posterne,
There stand no guards.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I shall soone finde it Cousen.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: Is the Captaine come home?

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: No, who commands the Guard to night?

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: I thinke Petruchio.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: What's the Word?

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: None knowes yet.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: I would this Lady were married out oth' way once,
Or out of our custodies; I wish they wold take in more com~panies,
For I am sure we feel her in our duties shrewdly.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: 'Tis not her fault I warrant ye, she is ready for't,
And that's the plague, when they grow ripe for marriage
They must be slipt like Hawkes.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: Give me a meane wench,
No State doubt lyes on her, she is alwaies ready.

speeches.speaker: 1 Sol.
verse: Come to the Guard, 'tis late, and sure the Captaine
Can not be long away.

speeches.speaker: 2 Sol.
verse: I have watch'd these three nights,
To morrow they may keep me tame for nothing.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: This is the place I think; what Light is that there?
The Lady and my Cousen?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Is this the Garden?

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Yes Madam.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: O my blessed Mistris,
Saint of my soule.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Speake softly: take me to ye,
O Silvio I am thine, thine ever Silvio.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Is this your promise Sir? Lady your honour?
I am undone if this be seene, disgrac'd,
Fallen under all discredit.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Do you love still?
Deere, do you keepe your old faith?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Ever Lady;
And when that failes me, all that's good forsake me.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Do not you shame? Madam, I must not suffer this,
I will not suffer it; men call you vertuous,
What do you meane to lose your selfe thus? Silvio
I charge thee get away, charge you retire ye,
Ile call the watch else.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Call all the world to see us,
We live in one anothers happinesse,
And so will die.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Here will I hang for ever.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: As ye respect me, as hereafter Madam
You would enjoy his love—nothing prevaile with ye?
Il'e try my strength then; get thee gone thou villain,
Thou Promise-breaker.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I am tide, I cannot.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Ile ring the Bell then.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Ring it to death, I am fixt here.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: I saw a light over the Garden walke,
Hard by the Ladies Chamber, here's some knavery
As I live, I saw it twice.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: The Guard, the Guard there;
I must not suffer this, it is too mischievous.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Light up the torch, I fear'd this, ha? young Silvio?
How got he in?

speeches.speaker: 1. Sold.
verse: The Divell brought him in sure
He came not by us.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: My wife between 'em busling?
Guard, pull him off.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Now, now, ye feele the misery.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: You, Madam, at an houre so far undecent?
Death, O my soule! this is a foule fault in ye,
Your mothers care abusd too, light's to her Chamber,
I am sorry to see this.

speeches.speaker: Bell.
verse: Farewell my Sylvio,
And let no danger sink thee.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Nor death Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Are ye so hot? I shall prepare ye Phisick
Will purge ye finely, neatly; you are too fiery,
Think of your prayers, Sir, and you have not forgot 'em;
Can ye fly i'th ayre, or creepe ye in at key-holes?
I have a gyn will catch ye though you conjur'd:
Take him to Guard to night, to strong and sure Guard;
Ile back to'th Dutchesse presently: no lesse sport serve ye,
Then the Heire to a Dukedom? play at push-pin there Sir?
It was well aim'd, but plague upon't, you shot short,
And that will lose your game.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I know the losse then.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Now, in this habit may I safely see
How my incensed friend carries my murther,
Who little I imagin'd had been wrought
To such a height of rage; and much I grieve now
Mine owne blinde passion had so master'd me,
I could not see his love, for sure he loves her,
And on a nobler ground then I pretended.
It must be so, it is so; what Penurio,
My shotten friend, what winde blew you?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Faith 'tis true,
Any strong winde will blow me like a feather,
I am all Ayre, nothing of earth within me,
Nor have not had this moneth, but that good Dinner
Your Worship gave me yesterday, that staies by me,
And gives me ballasse, else the Sun would draw me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: But do's my Mistris speake still of me?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Yes Sir,
And in her sleep, that makes my Master mad too,
And turne and fart for anger.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Art sure she saw me?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: She saw ye at a window.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: 'Tis most true,
In such a place I saw a Gentlewoman,
A young, sweet hansome woman.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: That's she, that's she Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And well she view'd me, I view'd her.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Still she Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: At last she blush'd, and then look't off.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: That blush Sir,
If you can read it truly—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: But didst thou tell her,
Or didst thou foole me, thou knew'st such a one?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I told her, and I told her such a sweet tale—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: But did she heare thee?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: With a thousand eares Sir,
And swallow'd what I said as greedily,
As great-bellyed women do Cherries, stones and all Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Methinkes she should not love thy Master?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Hang him Pilcher,
There's nothing loves him: his owne Cat cannot endure him,
She had better lye with a Beare, for he is so hairie,
That a tame warren of flyes frisk round about him.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And wilt thou worke still?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Like a Miner for ye.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And get accesse.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Or conjure you together,
'Tis her desire to meet: she is poyson'd with him,
And till she take a sweet fresh ayre, that's you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: There's money for thee: thou art a precious Varlet,
Be fat, be fat, and blow thy Master backward.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Blow you my Mistris Sir, as flat as a flounder,
Then blow her up againe as Butchers blow their Veales;
If she dye upon the same
Bury her, bury her in Gods name.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Thou art a merry knave: by this hand ile feed thee,
Till thou crack'st at both ends, if thou dar'st do this
Thou shalt eat no fantasticall Porredge,
Nor lick the dish where oyle was yesterday,
Dust, and dead flyes to day; Capons, fat Capons—

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: O hearty sound.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Cramb'd full of itching Oysters.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Will ye have the Dutchesse?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And Lobsters big as Gauntlets,
Thou shalt despise base Beefe.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I do despise it,
And now me thinkes I feele a Tart come sliding.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Leaping into thy mouth: but first deale faithfully.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: When will ye come?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: To morrow.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Ile attend ye,
For then my Master will be out in businesse.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What newes abroad?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: 'Mas as I was comming to you,
I heard that Signiour Silvio, a good Gentleman,
Many a good meale I have eaten with him—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What of him?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Was this day to be Arraigned before the Duchesse,
But why I could not heare.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Silvio arraign'd?
Go, get ye gone, and thinke of me.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I fly Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Arraign'd? for what? for my supposed death? no,
That cannot be sure, there's no rumour of it,
Be it what it will, I will be there and see it,
And if my help will bring him off he has it.

speeches.speaker: Du.
verse: Read the Edict last made,
Keepe silence there.

speeches.speaker: Clerk.
prose: If any man of what condition soever, and a subject, after the publishing of this Edict, shall without speciall Licence from the great Duchesse, attempt or buy, offer, or make an attempt, to solicite the love of the Princesse Belvidere, the person so offending shall forfeit his life.

speeches.speaker: Counsellour.
verse: The reason why my Royall Mistris here
In her last Treaty with Siennas Duke,
Promis'd her beauteous Daughter there in marriage,
The Duke of Millaine, rivall in this fortune,
Un-nobly sought by practise to betray her;
Which found, and cross'd, the Cittadell receiv'd her
There to secure her Mothers word; the last cause
So many Gentlemen of late enamour'd
On this most beauteous Princesse, and not brooking
One more then other, to deserve a favour,
Blood has been spilt, many brave spirits lost,
And more unlesse she had been kept close from their violence
Had like to have followed: therefore for due prevention
Of all such hazards and unnoble actions,
This last Edict was publish'd, which thou Silvio
Like a false man, a bad man, and a Traitor
Hast rent a peeces, and contemn'd; for which cause
Thou standest a guilty man here now.

speeches.speaker: Clark.
verse: Speak Silvio,
What canst thou say to avoyd the hand of Justice?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: Nothing, but I confesse, submit, & lay my head to it.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Have ye no eyes my Lords, no understandings?
The Gentleman will cast himselfe away,
Cast himselfe wilfully: are you, or you guilty?
No more is he, no more taint sticks upon him:
I drew him thether, 'twas my way betray'd him,
I got the entrance kept, I entertain'd him,
I hid the danger from him, forced him to me,
Poore gentle soule, he's in no part transgressing,
I wrot unto him.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Do not wrong that honour,
Cast not upon that purenesse these aspersions,
By Heaven it was my love, my violence,
My life must answer it: I broke in to her,
Tempted the Law, sollicited unjustly.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: As there is truth in Heaven I was the first cause,
How could this man have come to me, left naked
Without my counsell and provision?
What hower could he finde out to passe the Watchs,
But I must make it sure first? Reverend Judges,
Be not abus'd, nor let an innocent life lye
Upon your shaking Conscience; I did it,
My love the maine wheele that set him a going:
His motion but compell'd.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Can ye beleeve this,
And know with what a modesty and whitenesse
Her life was ever ranck'd? Can you beleeve this
And see me here before ye young, and wilfull?
Apt to what danger Love dares thrust me on,
And where Law stops my way, apt to contemne it?
If I were bashfull, old, or dull, and sleepy
In Loves allarmes, a woman might awake me,
Direct, and clew me out the way to happinesse:
But I like fire, kindled with that bright beauty,
Catch hold of all occasions, and run through 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I charge ye as your honest soules will answer it.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I charge ye, as you are the friends to vertue,
That has no patterne living but this Lady.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Let not his blood—

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Let not her wilfulnesse—
For then you act a scene Hell will rejoyce at.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: He is cleare.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: She is as white in this as infants.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: The god of Love protect your cause, and help ye,
Two nobler peeces of affection
These eyes ne're look'd on, if such goodnesse perish,
Let never true hearts meet againe, but break.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: A strange example of strong love, a rare one.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lord.
verse: Madam, we know not what to say to think on.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: I must confesse it strikes me tender too,
Searches my Mothers heart: you found 'em there?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Yes certaine Madam.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: And so linked together?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: As they had been one peece of Alablaster.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Nothing dishonourable?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: So let my soule have happinesse,
As that thought yet durst never seeke this bosome.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: What shall I do? 'has broke my law, abus'd me,
Faine would I know the truth, either confesse it,
And let me understand the maine offender,
Or both shall feele the torture.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Are ye a Mother?
The Mother of so sweet a Rose as this is?
So pure a Flower? and dare ye lose that nature?
Dare ye take to your selfe so great a wickednesse,
(O holy Heaven) of thinking what may ruine
This goodly building? this temple where the gods dwell?
Give me a thousand tortures, I deserve 'em,
And shew me death in all the shapes imagin'd.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No death but I will answer it, meet it, seeke it;
No torture but ile laugh upon't, and kisse it.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: This is no way.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lord.
verse: They say no more for certaine
Then their strong hearts will suffer.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: I have bethought me;
No Lords, although I have a Childe offending,
Nature dares not forget she is a Childe still;
Till now I never look'd on love imperious:
I have bethought me of a way to breake ye,
To separate, though not your loves your bodies:
Silvio attend, ile be your Judge my selfe now,
The sentence of your death (because my Daughter
Will beare an equall part in your afflictions)
I take away and pardon: this remaines then
An easie, and a gentle punishment,
And this shall be fulfill'd: because unnobly
You have sought the love, and marriage of a Princesse,
The absolute and sole Heire of this Dukedome,
By that meanes as we must imagine strongly,
To plant your selfe into this Rule hereafter,
We here pronounce ye a man banish'd from us.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: For ever banish'd Lady?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Yet more mercy,
But for a yeare: and then againe in this place
To make your full appearance: yet more pitty,
If in that time you can absolve a question,
Writ down within this scrowle, absolve it rightly,
This Lady is your wife, and shall live with ye;
If not, you loose your head.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I take this honour,
And humbly kisse those Royall hands.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Receive it: Bartello, to your old guard take the Princesse,
And so the Court break up.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Farewell to all,
And to that spotlesse heart my endlesse service.

speeches.speaker: 1. Lord.
verse: What will this prove?

speeches.speaker: 2. Lord.
verse: Ile tell you a yeare hence, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Are you pleas'd now? have I not wrought this wonder
Non eben fatto Signieur.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Rarely Penurio.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Close, close then, and work wax.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I am studying for thee
A dinner, that shall victuall thee for ten yeare.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Do you heare Mistris?
You know what a dundier whelp my Master is,
I need not preach to ye, how unfit and wanting
To give a woman satisfaction:
How he stinks, and snores, a Bull's a better bed-fellow;
And for his love never let that deceive ye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Nay sure he loves me not.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: If he could coyne ye,
Or turne ye into mettle much might be then;
He loves not any thing but what is traffique:
I have heard him sweare he would sell ye to the grand Signior.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: The Turk.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The very Turke, and how they would use ye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ile fit him fort: the Turke?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I know the price too:
Now ye have time to pay him, pay him home Mistris;
Pay him o'th pate, clout him for all his curtesies;
Here's one that daunces in your eyes, young delicate
To work this vengeance; if ye let it slip now,
There is no pittying of ye, od's precious, Mistris,
Were I his wife, I would so mall his Mazard,
'Tis charity, meere charity, pure charity,
Are you the first? has it not been from Eves time,
Women would have their safe revenges this way?
And good, and gracious women, excellent women;
Is't not a handsome Gentleman? a sweet Gentleman?
View him from head to foot, a compleat Gentleman;
When can ye hope the like againe? I leave ye,
And my revenge too, with ye; I know my Office,
Ile not be farre off, be not long a fumbling,
When danger shall appeare, Ile give the larme.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: You are welcome Sir, and would it were my fortune
To afford a Gentleman of your faire seeming,
A freer entertainment then this house has,
You partly know Sir.—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Know, and pitty Lady,
Such sweetnesse in the bud, should be so blasted;
Dare you make me your Servant?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Dare you make Sir,
That service worthy of a womans favour
By constancy and goodnesse?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Here I sweare to ye,
By the unvalued love I beare this beauty,
(And kisse the Book too) never to be recreant,
To honour ye, to truly love, and serve ye,
My youth to wait upon ye, what my wealth has.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: O make me not so poore, to sell affection,
Those bought love's Sir, weare faster then the moneys;
A handsome Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: A most delicate sweet one,
Let my truth Purchase then.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I should first try it,
But you may happily.—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: You shall not doubt me,
I hope she loves me; when I prove false shame take me;
Will ye believe a little?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I feare, too much, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: And will ye love a little?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: That should be your part.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Thus I begin then, thus and thus.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: A good beginning,
We have a Proverbe saies, makes a good ending.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Say ye so? 'tis well infer'd.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Good Sir, your patience:
Me thinks I have ventur'd now, like a weak Bark
Upon a broken billow, that will swallow me,
Upon a rough sea of suspitions,
Stuck round with ieallous rocks.

speeches.speaker: Pen. within.
verse: A hem, a hem there.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: This is my man; my feares too soone have found me,
Now what's the newes?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A pox of yonder old Rigell,
The Captaine, the old Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: What old Captaine?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Captaine couragious yonder of the Castle,
Captaine dondeigo, old Bartello.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Where is he?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: He's comming in:
'Twould vex the Divell, that such an old Potgun as this,
That can make no sport, should hinder them that can do it.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I would not have him see the Gentleman
For all the world, my credit were undone then.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Shall I fling a pisse-pot on's head as he comes in,
And take him into'th Kitchin, there to dry him.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: That will not do; and he is so humerous too
He will come in.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What is he?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: One much troubles me.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: And can do nothing, cannot eat.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Your sight now,
Out of a driveling dotage he beares to me,
May make him tell my husband, and undo me.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What would ye have me do?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: But for a while Sir,
Step here behind this hanging, presently
I'le answer him, and then.—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I will obey ye.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Where's my rich Jeweller? I have stones to set.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: He is abroad, and sure Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Ther's for your service:
Wher's the faire Lady? all alone sweet beauty?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: She's never much alone Sir, that's acquainted
With such companions as good honest thoughts are.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ile sit down by thee, and ile kisse thy hand too,
And in thine eare sweare by my life I love thee.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ye are a merry Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And a mad one, Lady;
By th'mas thou hast goodly eyes, excellent eyes, wench,
Ye twinkling rogue, look what thy Captain brings thee,
Thou must needs love me, love me heartily,
Hug me, and love me, hug me close.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Fye Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Nay, I have strength, and I can straine ye sirrah,
And vault into my seat as nimbly, little one.
As any of your smooth chinn'd boyes in Florence,
I must needs commit a little folly with ye,
Ile not be long, a brideling case, and away wench;
The hobnaile thy husband's as fitly out o'th way now.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Do you think he keeps a bawdy house?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: That's all one.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Or did you ever see that lightnesse in my carriage,
That you might promise to your self —

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Away foole,
A good turn's a good turne; I am an honest fellow.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: You have a handsome wife, a vertuous Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They are not for this time o'th yeer.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: A Lady,
That ever bore that great respect to you,
That noble constancy.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: That's more then I know.

speeches.speaker: Maid.
verse: O Mistris, ye are undone, my Master's coming.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Coming hard by here.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Plague Consume the Rascall,
Shall I make petty-patties of him?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Now what love Sir?
Feare of your comming made him jealous first;
Your finding here, will make him mad and desperate,
And what in that wilde mood he will execute—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I can think of nothing, I have no wit left me,
Certaine my heads a mustard-pot.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I have thought Sir.
And if you'l please to put in execution
What I conceive—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I'le do it, tell it quickly.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Draw your Sword quickly, and go down inrag'd,
As if you had pursu'd some foe up hither,
And grumble to your self extremely, terribly,
But not a word to him, and so passe by him.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ile do it perfectly.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Stand you still good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Rascall, slave, villaine, take a house so poorely,
After thou hast wrong'd a Gentleman, a Souldier,
Base Poultroon boy, you will forsake your neast sirrah.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: The matter, good sweet Captain?

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Run-away rogue,
And take a house to cover thy base cowardize,
Ile whip ye, Ile so scourge ye.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Mercy upon me,
What's all this matter wife?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Did you meet the mad man?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I never saw the Captain so provok't yet.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: O he's a Devill sure, a most bloody devill,
He follow'd a young Gentleman, his sword drawne,
With such a fury, how I shake to think on't,
And foyn'd, and flash't at him, and swore he'd kill him,
Drove him up hither, follow'd him still bloodily,
And if I had not hid him, sure had slaine him;
A mercilesse old man.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Most vertuous Lady,
Even as the giver of my life, I thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: This fellow must not stay here, he is too hansom;
He is gone Sir, and you may passe now with all security,
Ile be your guide my selfe, and such a way
Ile lead ye, none shall crosse, nor none shall know ye.
The doore's left open Sirrah, ile starve you for this trick,
Ile make thee fast o' Sondayes; and for you Lady,
Ile have your lodgings farther off, and closer,
Ile have no street lights to you; will you go Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I thank ye Sir; the Devill take this fortune;
And once more all my service to your goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Now could I eat my very arms for madnesse,
Cross'd in the nick o'th matter? vengeance take it,
And that old Cavalier that spoil'd our Cock-fight;
Ile lay the next plot surer.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I am glad and sorry;
Glad, that I got so fairely off suspition;
Sorry I lost my new lov'd friend.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Not lost Mistris;
Ile conjure once againe to raise that spirit;
In, and looke soberly upon the matter,
Wee'l ring him one peale more, and if that fall,
The Devill take the clappers, bells, and all.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: NOw, Rhodope, How do you finde my daughter?

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: Madam, I finde her now what you would have her,
What the State wishes her; I urg'd her fault to her,
Open'd her eyes, and made her see the mischiefe
She was running with a headlong will into,
Made her stait at her folly, shake and tremble,
At the meere memory of such an ignorance,
She now contemnes his love, hates his remembrance,
Cannot endure to heare the name of Silvio;
His person spits at.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: I am glad to heare this.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: And humbly now to your will, your care, Madam,
Bends her affections, bowes her best obedience;
Syennas Duke, with new eyes now she looks on,
And with a Princely love, sit for his person,
Returnes that happinesse and joy he look't for;
The generall good of both the neighbour Dukedoms,
Not any private end, or rash affection
She aims at now: hearing the Duke ariv'd too,
(To whom she owes all honour, and all service,)
She charg'd me kneele thus at your Graces feet,
And not to rise without a generall pardon.

speeches.speaker: Du h.
verse: She has it, and my love againe, my old love,
And with more tendernesse I meet this penitence,
Then if she ne're had started from her honour;
I thank ye Rhodopc, am bound to thank ye,
And dayly to remember this great service,
This honest faithfull service; go in peace,
And by this Ring, delivered to Bartello,
Let her enjoy our favour, and her liberty,
And presently to this place, with all honour,
See her conducted.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: Your Grace has made me happy.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: Syennas noble Duke, craves his admittance.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Go, wait upon his Grace; fair Sir, you are welcome,
Welcome to her ever admir'd your vertues:
And now, me thinks, my Court looks true nobly;
You have taken too much pains, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Syen.
verse: Royall Lady,
To wait upon your Grace is but my service.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Keep that Sir, for the Saint ye have vow'd it to.

speeches.speaker: Syen.
verse: I keep a life for her: Since your Grace pleases
To jump so happily into the matter,
I come indeed to claime your royall promise,
The beauteous Belvidere in marriage,
I come to tender her my youth, my fortune,
My everlasting love.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: You are like to win Sir:
All is forgot, forgiven too; no sadnesse
My good Childe, you have the same heart still here,
The Duke of Syenna, Childe, pray use him nobly.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: An Angell beauty.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Your Grace is fairely welcome,
And what in modesty a blushing maid may
Wish to a Gentleman of your great goodnesse;
But wishes are too poore a pay for Princes.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: You have made me richer then all States and Titles,
One kisse of this white hand's above all honours,
My faith deare Lady, and my fruitfull service,
My duteous zeale—

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Your Grace is a great Master,
And speake too powerfully to be resisted:
Once more you are welcome Sir, to me you are welcome,
To her that honoures ye; I could say more Sir,
But in anothers tongue 'twere better spoken,

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: As wise as faire, you have made your Servant happy;
I never saw so rich a Mine of sweetnesse.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Will your Grace please, after your painfull journy
To take some rest? Are the Dukes Lodgings ready?

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: All Madam.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Then wait upon his Grace, all, and to morrow Sir
We'l shew ye in what high esteeme we hold ye,
Till then a faire repose.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: My fairest service

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: You have so honour'd me, my dearest Daughter,
So truly pleas'd me in this entertainment,
I meane your loving carriage to Syenna,
That both for ever I forget all trespasses,
And to secure you next of my full favour,
Aske what you will within my power to grant ye,
Aske freely: and if I forget my promise—
Aske confidently.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You are too royall to me,
To me that have so foolishly transgress'd you,
So like a Girle, so far forgot my vertue,
Which now appeares as base and ugly to me,
As did his Dream, that thought he was in Paradice,
Awak'd and saw the Devill; how was I wander'd?
With what eyes could I look upon that poore, that course thing,
That wretched thing call'd Silvio? that (now) despis'd thing?
And lose an object of that gracefull sweetnesse,
That god-like presence as Syenna is?
Darknesse, and cheerfull day had not such difference:
But I must ever blesse your care, your wisedome,
That led me from this labirinth of folly,
How had I sunk else? what example given?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Prethee no more, and as thou art my best one,
Aske something that may equall such a goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Why did ye let him go so slightly from ye,
More like a man in triumph, then condemn'd?
Why did ye make his pennance but a question,
A riddle, every idle wit unlocks.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: 'Tis not so,
Nor do not feare it so: he will not finde it,
I have given that (unlesse my selfe discover it)
Will cost his head.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Tis subject to construction?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: That it is too.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: It may be then absolv'd,
And then are we both scorn'd and laugh'd at, Madam;
Beside the promise you have ty'd upon it,
Which you must never keepe.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: I never meant it.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: For heaven sake let me know it, 'tis my Suit to ye,
The Boone you would have me aske; let me but see it,
That if there be a way to make't so strong,
No wit nor powerfull reason can run through it,
For my disgrace, I may beg of heaven to grant it.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Feare not, it has been put to sharper judgements
Then ere he shall arrive at: my deare Father,
That was as fiery in his understanding,
And ready in his wit as any living,
Had it two yeares; and studied it, yet lost it:
This night ye are my Bed-fellow, there Daughter
Into your bosome ile commit this secret,
And there we'l both take counsell.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I shall finde
Some trick I hope too strong yet for his minde.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Methinks I am batten'd well of late, growne lusty,
Fat, high, and kicking, thankes to the bounteous Rugio;
And now, methinkes I scorne these poore repasts,
Cheese parings, and the stinking tongues of Pilchers;
But why should I remember these? they are odious,
They are odious in mine eyes; the full fat dish now,
The bearing dish is that I reverence,
The dish an able Serving-man sweats under,
And bends ith' hams, as if the house hung on him,
That dish is the dish: hang your bladder Bankets,
Or halfe a dozen of Turnop, and two Mushrumps,
These when they breed their best, hatch but two Belches;
The state of a fat Turkey, the decorum
He marches in with, all the traine and circumstance;
'Tis such a matter, such a glorious matter,
And then his sauce, with Orenges and Onions,
And he display'd in all parts, for such a dish now,
And at my need I would betray my father,
And for a roasted Conger, all my Country.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: What my friend Lean-gut, how do's thy beauteous Mistris?
And where's your Master Sirra? where's that horn-pipe?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: My Mistris Sir, do's as a poore wrong'd Gentlewoman,
Too much heaven knows opprest with injuries,
May do and live.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Is the old foole still jealous?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: As old fooles are, and will be still the same Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He must have cause: he must have cause.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: 'Tis true Sir,
And would he had with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: He shall have.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: For then he had Salt to his Saffron Porredge.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Why do not I see thee sometime? why thou starv'd rascal?
Why do not ye come to me, you precius bow-case?
I keepe good meat at home, good store:

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Yes Sir,
I will not faile ye all next weeke.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Thou art welcome,
I have a secret I would faine impart to thee,
But thou art so thin the wind will blow it from thee,
Or men will read it through thee.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Wrapt up in beefe Sir,
In good grosse beefe, let all the world looke on me,
The English have that trick to keep intelligence.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: A witty knave, first there's to tye your tongue up,

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Dumbe as a Dog Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Next, hark in your eare. Sirra.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Well, very well, excellent well: 'tis done Sir,
Say no more to me.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Say and hold.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: 'Tis done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: As thou lov'st butter'd eggs, sweare.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Let me kisse the Booke first,
But here's my hand, brave Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Looke ye hold, sirra.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: O the most precious vanity of this world
When such dry Neats-tongues must be sok'd and larded
With young fat supple wenches? O the Devill,
What can he do, he cannot suck an egge off
But his back's loose ith' hilts: go thy waies Captaine,
Well may thy Warlike name work Miracles,
But if e're thy founder'd courser win match more,
Or stand right but one traine—

speeches.speaker: 1. Gent.
verse: Now Signiour Shadow,
What art thou thinking of, how to rob thy Master?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Of his good deeds? the Thief that undetakes that
Must have a hook will poze all Hell to hammer:
Have ye dined Gentlemen, or do you purpose?

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Dined, two long houres ago.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Pray ye take me with ye.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
verse: To supper do'st thou meane?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: To any thing
That has the smell of meat in't: tell me true, Gentlemen,
Are not you three now going to be sinfull,
To jeabard a joynt, or so? I have found your faces,
And see whore written in your eyes.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: A parlous Rascall,
Thou art much upon the matter.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Have a care Gentlemen,
'Tis a sore age, very sore age, lewd age,
And women now are like old Knights adventures,
Full of inchanted flames, and dangerous.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent,
verse: Where the most danger is, there's most honour.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I grant ye, honour most consists in sufferance,
And by that rule you three should be most honourable.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
verse: A subtle Rogue: but canst thou tell Penurio
Where we might light upon—

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A learned Surgeon?

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
verse: Pox take ye foole; I meane good wholsome wenches.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: 'Faith wholsome women will but spoyle ye too,
For you are so us'd to snap-haunces: But take my counsell,
Take fat old women, fat, and five and fifty,
The Dog-dayes are come in.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Take fat old women?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The fatter and the older, still the better,
You do not know the pleasure of an old Dame,
A fat old Dame, you do not know the knack on't:
They are like our Country grotes, as coole as Christmas,
And sure ith' keeles.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Hang him starv'd foole, he mocks us.

speeches.speaker: 3. Gent.
verse: Penurio, thou know'st all the hansome wenches?
What shall I give thee for a Merchants wife now?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I take no money Gentlemen, that's base,
I trade in meat, a Merchants wife will cost ye
A glorious Capon, a great shoulder of Mutton,
And a Tart as big as a Conjurers circle.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
verse: That's cheap enough.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: And what a Haberdashers?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Worse meat will serve for her: a great Goose Pye,
But you must send it out oth' Country to me,
It will not do else: with a peece of Bacon,
And if you can a pot of Butter with it.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Now do I ayme at horse-flesh: what a Parsons?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A tithe Pig has no fellow, if I fetch her,
If she be Puritane, Plumb-porridge do's it,
And a fat loyne of Veale well sawc'd and rosted.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Wee'l meet one night, and thou shalt have all these,
O' that condition we may have the wenches,
A dainty rascall.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: When your stomacks serve ye,
(For mine is ever ready) ile supply ye.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gent.
verse: Farewell, and there's to fill thy paunch.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Brave Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gent.
verse: Hold sirrah, there.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Any young wench ith' Towne Sir.

speeches.speaker: 3 Gent.
verse: It shall go round.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Most honourable Gentlemen,
All these are Courtiers, but they are meere Coxcombs,
And only for a wench, their purses open,
Nor have they so much judgement left to chuse her;
If e're they call upon me ile so fit 'em,
I have a pack of wry-mouth'd mackrell Ladies,
Stinke like a standing ditch, and those deare Damsels;
But I forgot my businesse, I thank ye Mounsieurs,
I have a thousand whimsies in my braines now.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Your Grace shall now perceive how much we honor ye
And in what deare regard we hold your friendship
Will you sit Sir, and grace this homely Banquet?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Madam, to your poor friend you are too magnificent.

speeches.speaker: Duc.
verse: To the Dukes health, and all the joyes I wish him,
Let no man misse this cup: have we no Musick?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Your noble favours still you heap upon me,
But where's my vertuous Mistris, such a Feast,
And not her sparkling beauty here to blesse it?
Me thinkes it should not be, it shewes not fully.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Young Ladies Sir, are long, and curious
In putting on their trims, forget how day goes,
And then 'tis their good morrow when they are ready:
Go some and call her, and wait upon her hither,
Tell her the Duke and I desire her company:
I warrant ye, a hundred dressings now
She has survey'd, this, and that fashion look'd on,
For Ruffs and Gowns; cast this away, these Jewels
Suited to these and these knots: o' my life Sir,
She feares your curious eye will soone discover else:
Why stand ye still, why gape ye on one another?
Did I not bid ye go and tell my Daughter?
Are ye nayled here? nor stir? nor speake? who am I,
And who are you?

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: Pardon me, gracious Lady,
The feare to tell you that you would not hear of
Makes us all dumb, the Princesse is gone, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Gone? whither gone? some wiser fellow answer me.

speeches.speaker: 2 Lord.
verse: We sought the Court all over, and beleeve Lady,
No newes of where she is, nor how convey'd hence.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: It cannot be, it must not be.

speeches.speaker: 1 Lord.
verse: 'Tis true Madam,
No roome in all the Court but we search'd through it,
Her women found her want first, and they cry'd to us.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Gone? stolne away? I am abus'd, dishonour'd.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: 'Tis I that am abus'd, 'tis I dishonour'd,
Is this your welcome, this your favour to me?
To foyst a trick upon me, this trick too,
To cheat me of my love? Am I not worthy?
Or since I was your Guest, am I growne odious?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
