verse: Your Grace mistakes me, as I have a life, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: And I another, I will never beare this,
Never endure this dor.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: But heare me patiently.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Give me my love.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: As soone as care can find her,
And all care shall be used.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: And all my care too,
To be reveng'd; I smell the trick, 'tis too ranke,
Fie, how it smells oth' Mother.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: You wrong me, Duke.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: For this disgrace ten thousand Florentines
Shall pay their dearest bloods, and dying curse ye,
And so I turne away, your mortall enemy.

speeches.speaker: Duc.
verse: Since ye are so high and hot Sir, ye have half arm'd us,
Be carefull of the Towne, of all the Castles,
And see supplyes of Souldiers every where,
And Musters for the Field, when he invites us,
For he shall know 'tis not high words can fright us.
My Daughter gone? has she so finely cozen'd me?
This is for Silvio's sake sure, O cunning false one;
Publish a Proclamation thorough the Dukedome.
That whosoe're can bring toth' Court young Silvio,
Alive or dead, beside our thankes and favour,
Shall have two thousand Duckets for his labour;
See it dispatch'd, and sent in haste: O base one.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Was't thou with Rugio?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Yes marry was I closely.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: And do's he still remember his poore Mistris?
Do's he desire to see me?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Yes, and presently:
Puts off all businesse else, lives in that memory,
And will be here according to directions.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: But where's thy Master?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Where a coxcombe should be,
Waiting at Court with his Jewells,
Safe for this night I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I am bound to thee.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I would ye were; as close as I could tye ye,

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Thou art my best, my truest friend.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I labour,
I moyle and toyle for ye: I am your hackney.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: If ever I be able—

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Steale the great Cheese Mistris,
Was sent him out oth' Country.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Any thing.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: That's meat, 'tis lawfull Mistris: where's the Castle Custard
He got at Court?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: He has lock't it in's study.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Get a warrant to search for counterfeit gold.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Give me thy Candle,
Ile finde a time to be thy carefull Cater.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: And many a time Ile finde to be his Cook,
And dresse his Calves head to the sweetest sauce Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: To bed Penurio, go, the rest is my charge,
Ile keep the Watch out.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Now if you spare him—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Peace foole,
I hope my Rugio will not faile, 'twould vexe me:
Now to my string; so, sure he cannot misse now,
And this end to my finger: ile lye downe,
For on a suddaine I am wondrous heavy,
'Tis very late too; if he come, and finde this,
And pull it, though it be with easie motion
I shall soone waken, and as soone be with him.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Thou secret friend, how am I bound to love thee,
And how to hug thee for thy private service?
Thou art the Star all my suspitions saile by,
The fixed point my wronged honour turnes to,
By thee I shall know all, finde all the subtilties
Of devillish women, that torment me daily:
Thou art my Conjurer, my Spell, my Spirit,
All's hush'd and still, no sound of any stirring,
No tread of living thing: the Light is in still,
And there's my wife, how prettily the foole lyes,
How sweet, and handsomely, and in her clothes too,
Waiting for me upon my life; her fondnesse
Would not admit her rest till I came to her:
O carefull foole, why am I angry with thee?
Why do I think thou hat'st thy loving Husband?
I am an Asse, an over-doating Coxcombe,
And this sweet soule the mirrour of perfection:
How admirable faire and delicate,
And how it stirs me, ile sing thy sweets a Requiem,
But will not waken thee.
Now will I steale a kisse, a deare kisse from her,
And suck the Rosie breath of this bright beauty;
What a Devill is this? ty'd to her finger too?
A string, a damned string to give intelligence
O my lov'd key, how truly has'st thou serv'd me;
Ile follow this: soft, soft, toth' doore it goes,
And through toth' other side; a damned string 'tis,
I am abus'd, topt, Cuckolded, fooled, jaded,
Ridden to death, to madnesse; stay, this helps not:
Stay, stay, and now invention help me,
Ile sit downe by her, take this from her easily,
And thus upon mine owne: Dog, I shall catch ye,
With all your cunning Sir: I shall light on ye,
I felt it pull sure: yes, but wondrous softly,
'Tis there againe, and harder now, have at ye:
Now and thou scap'st, the Devills thy ghostly father.
prose:
Song.
O Faire sweet face, O eyes celestiall bright,
Twin-stars in Heaven that now adorn the night;
O fruitfull lips, where Cherries ever grow,
And Damask cheeks, where all sweet beauties blow;
O thou from head to foot divinely faire,

Cupids most cunning Nets made of that haire,
And as he weaves himselfe for curious eyes,
O me, O me, I am caught my selfe, he cryes:
Sweet rest ahout this sweets and golden sleepe,
Soft peacefull thoughts your how' rely watches keepe,
Whilst I in wonder sing this sacrifice,
To beauty sacred, and those Angell-eyes.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Sure 'twas my Husbands voyce: The string is gone to,
He has found the trick on't: I am undone, betray'd,
And if he meet my friend he perishes,
What fortune followes me, what spightfull fortune?
Hoa, Jaquenet.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Here Mistris, do you call me?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Didst thou heare no noise?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: I heare my Master mad yonder,
And sweares, and chafes—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Dar'st thou do one thing for me?
One thing concernes mine honour, all is lost else?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Name what you will.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: It can bring but a beating,
Which I will recompence so largely—

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Name it.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Sit here, as if thou wert asleep.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Is that all?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: When he comes in, what e're he do unto thee
(The worst will be but beating) speak not a word,
Not one word as thou lovest me.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Ile run through it.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ile carry away the Candle.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: And I the blowes Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Have you put your light out? I shall stumble to ye,
You whore, you cunning whore, I shal catch your rogue to,
Has light leggs else: I had so Ferret-claw'd him:
O have I found ye? do ye play at dog-sleep still whore?
Do you think that can protect ye? yes, I will kill thee,
But first ile bring thy friends to view thy villanies,
Thy whorish villanies: and first ile beat thee,
Beat thee to pin-dust, thou salt whore, thou varlet,
Scratch out thine eyes; ile spoile your tempting visage;
Are ye so patient? ile put my nayles in deeper,
Is it good whoring? whoring ye base rascall?
Is it good tempting men with strings to ride ye?
So, ile fetch your kindred, and your friends, whore,
And such a Justice I will act upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: What is he gone?

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: The Devill go with him Mistris,
Has harrowed me, plow'd land was ne're so harrowed:
I had the most ado to save mine eyes.

speeches.speaker: Isah.
verse: Has paid thee,
But ile heale all againe with good gold Jaquenet;
Has damned nayles.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: They are ten-penny nayles I think Mistris:
Ile undertake he shall strike 'em through an inch board.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Go up, and wash thy selfe: take my Pomatum,
And now let me alone to end the Tragedy.

speeches.speaker: Joq.
verse: You had best beware.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I shall deale stoutly with him,
Reach me my book, and see the doore made fast wench,
And so good night: now to the matter politick.

speeches.speaker: Lop. within
verse: You shall see what she is, what a sweet jewell.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Who's there, what mad-man knocks? is this an hower
And in mine husbands absence?

speeches.speaker: Lop. within.
verse: Will ye open?
You know my voyce ye whore, I am that husband:
Do you mark her subtlety? but I have paid her,
I have so ferk'd her face: here's the blood Gentlemen,
Ecce signum: I have spoyl'd her Goatish beauty,
Observe her how she lookes now, how she is painted,
O 'tis the most wicked'st whore, and the most treacherous-

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Here walkes my Cousen full of meditation,
Arm'd with religious thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Is this the monster?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
verse: Is this the subject of that rage you talk't of,
That naughty woman you had pull'd a peeces?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Here's no such thing.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gentlew.
verse: How have ye wrong'd this beauty?
Are not you mad my friend? what time o'th Moon is't?
Have not you Maggots in your braines?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: 'Tis she sure.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Where's the scratch'd face ye spoke of, the torne garments,
And all the haire pluck'd off her head?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Beleeve me,
'Twere better far you had lost your paire of pibbles,
Then she the least adornment of that sweetnesse.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Is not this blood?

speeches.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
verse: This is a monstrous folly,
A base abuse.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Thus he do's ever use me,
And stickes me up a wonder, not a woman,
Nothing I do but subject to suspition;
Nothing I can do able to content him.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Lopez, you must not use this.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
verse: 'Twere not amisse Sir,
To give ye sauce to your meat, and suddainly.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
verse: You that dare wrong a woman of her goodnesse,
Thou have a wife, thou have a Beare ty'd to thee,
To scratch thy jealous itch, were all o' my minde,
I meane all women, we would soone disburthen ye
Of that that breeds these fits, these dog-flawes in ye,
A Sow-guelder should trim ye.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: A rare cure Lady,
And one as fit for him as a Thief for a halter,
You see this youth: will you not cry him quittance,
Body' me, I would pine, but I would pepper him,
Ile come anon, he, hang him, poore pompillion:
How like a wench bepist he lookes, ile come Lady:
Lopez, the Law must teach ye what a wife is,
A good, a vertuous wife.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ile ne're live with him,
I crave your loves all to make knowne my cause,
That so a faire Divorce may passe between us,
I am weary of my life: in danger hourely.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You see how rude you are, I will not misse ye,
Unsufferable rude: ile pay him soundly,
You should be whipt in Bedlam: ile reward him.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
verse: Whipping's too good.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I think I am alive still,
And in my wits.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ile put a trick upon him,
And get his goods Confiscate: you shall have 'em;
I will not faile at nine.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I think I am here too,
And once I would have sworn I had taken her napping,
I think my name is Lopez.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: Fie for shame Sir,
You see you have abus'd her, foulely wrong'd her,
Hung scandalous and course opinions on her,
Which now you finde but children of suspition:
Aske her forgivenesse, shew a penitence,
She is my Kins-woman, and what she suffers
Under so base and beastly jealousies,
I will redresse else, ile seeke satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Why, every Boy ith' Towne will pisse upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I am sorry for't.

speeches.speaker: 1 Gentlew.
verse: Downe o' your marrow-bones.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Even sorry from my heart: forgive me sweet wife,
Here I confesse most freely I have wrong'd ye,
As freely here I beg a pardon of ye,
From this hower no debate, no crosse suspition—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: To shew ye Sir I understand a wives part,
Thus I assure my love, and seale your pardon.

speeches.speaker: 2 Gentlew.
verse: 'Tis well done, now to bed and there confirm it.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: And so good night.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Aware relapses, Lopez.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Now Isabella tell me truth, and suddainly,
And do not juggle with me, nor dissemble,
For as I have a life ye dye then: I am not mad,
Nor do's the Devill work upon my weaknesse,
Tell me the trick of this, and tell me freely.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Will then that satisfie ye?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: If ye deale ingenuously.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ile tell ye all, and tell ye true and freely,
Bartello was the end of all this jealousie,
His often visitations brought by you, first
Bred all these fits, and these suspitions:
I knew your false key, and accordingly
I fram'd my plot, to have him take him finely,
Too poore a pennance for the wrong his wife beares,
His worthy vertuous wife: I felt it sensibly
When ye tooke off the string, and was much pleas'd in't,
Because I wish'd his importunate dotage paid well,
And had you staid two minutes more, ye had had him.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: This sounds like truth.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Because this shall be certaine,
Next time he comes, as long he cannot tarry,
Your self shall see, and heare, his lew'd temptations.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Till then I am satisfied, and if this prove true,
Henceforward Mistris of your self I give ye,
And I to serve ye: For my lusty Captaine,
Ile make him daunce, and make him think the Devill
Clawes at his breech, and yet I will not hurt him:
Come now to bed, and prove but constant this way,
Ile prove the man you ever wished.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: You have blest me.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: WHat labour and what travell have I runne Through?
And through what Cities to absolve this Riddle?
Diviners, Dreamers, Schoolemen, deep Magitians,
All have I tride, and all give severall meanings,
And from all hope of any future happinesse,
To this place am I come at length, the country,
The people simple, plaine, and harmlesse witty,
Whose honest labours Heaven rewards with plenty
Of Corne, Wine, Oyle, which they againe, as thankfull,
To their new Cropps, new pastimes celebrate,
And crowne their joyfull harvests with new voyces;
By a rich farmer here I am entertain'd,
And rank't among the number of his Servants,
Not guessing what I am, but what he would have me,
Here may be so much wit (though much I feare it)
To undo this knotty question; and would to Heaven
My fortunes had been hatch'd with theirs, as innocent,
And never knowne a pitch above their plainnesse.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: That it is, that it is, what's this word now? this
Is a plaguy word, that it is, r. e. a. that it is, reason,
By your leave, Mr. Soto, by your leave, you are too quick, Sir,
Ther's a strange par'lous T. hefore the reason,
A very tall T. which makes the word High Treason.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
prose: What Treason's that? do's this fellow understand Himselfe?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Pitch will infect, ile meddle no more with this geere;
What a Devill ayles this fellow? this foolish fellow,
Being admitted to be one of us too,
That are the masters of the Sports proceeding,
Thus to appeare, before me too, unmorriss'd?
Do you know me friend?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: You are my Matters Son, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: And do you know what sports are now in season?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I heare there are some a foot.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Where are your Bells then?
Your Rings, your Ribanes, friend? & your clean Napkins?
Your nosegay in your hat, pinn'd up, am not I here?
My fathers eldest Son, and at this time, Sir,
I would have ye know it, though ye be ten times his servant,
A better man then my father far, Lord of this Harvest, Sir,
And shall a man of my place want attendance?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: 'Twas want of knowledge, Sir, not duty, bred this,
I would have made suit else for your Lordships service.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: In some sort I am satisfied now, mend your maners,
But thou art a melancholly fellow, veng'ance melancholly,
And that may breed a insurrection amongst us;
Go too, Ile lay the best part of two pots now
Thou art in love, and I can guesse with whom too,
I saw the wench that twir'd and twinkled at thee,
The other day; the wench that's new come hither,
The young smug wench.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: You know more then I feele Sir.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Go too, Ile be thy friend, ile speak a good word for thee,
And thou shalt have my Lordships countenance to her;
May be I have had a snap my self, may be I, may be no,
We Lords are allow'd a little more.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: 'Tis fit Sir;
I humbly thank ye, you are too too tender of me,
But what Sir, I beseech ye, was that paper,
Your Lordship was so studiously Imployed in,
When ye came out a doores?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Thou meanest this paper.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: That Sir, I think.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Why, 'tis a Proclamation,
A notable piece of villany, as ever thou heard'st in thy life,
By mine honour it is.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: How Sir? or what concernes it?

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: It comes ye from the Duchesse, a plaguy wise woman,
To apprehend the body of one Silvio,
As arrant a Rascall as ever pist against post,
And this same Silvio, or this foresaid rascall,
To bring before her, live or dead; for which good service
The man that brings him, has two thousand Duckets;
Is not this notable matter now?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: 'Tis so indeed,
This Proclamation beares my bane about it;
Can no rest finde me? no private place secure me?
But still my miseries like blood-hounds haunt me?
Unfortunate young man, which way now guides thee,
Guides thee from death? the Countrey's laid round for thee;
O Claudio, now I feele thy blood upon me,
Now it speaks lowdly here, I am sure against me,
Time now has found it out, and truth proclam'd it,
And Justice now cries out, I must die for it.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Hast thou read it?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: And dost thou know that Silvio.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I never saw him, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: I have, and know him too,
I know him as well as I know thee, and better,
And if I light upon him, for a trick he plaid me once,
A certaine kinde of dog-trick, ile so fiddle him,
Two thousand Duckets, ile so pepper him,
And with that money ile turne Gentleman,
Worth a browne Bakers dozen of such Silvio's.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: There is no staying here, this rogue will know me,
And for the money sake betray me too;
I must bethink me suddenly and safely.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Mine owne deare Lady, have at thy honey-comb,
Now, for the honour of our Towne, Boyes, trace sweetly,
What a vengeance ayles this whobub? pox refuse 'em,
Cannot they let us dance in our owne defence here?

speeches.speaker: Capt.
verse: Arme, honest friends, arme suddenly & bravely,
And with your antient resolutions follow me;
Look how the Beacons show like comets, your poor neighbours
Run maddingly affrighted through the Villages;
Syennas Duke is up, burnes all before him,
And with his sword, makes thousand mothers childlesse,

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: What's this to our Morrisdancers?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: This may serve my turne.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Theres ne're a Duke in Christendome but loves a May-game.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: At a Horse you were alwaies ceaz'd, put your Son on him,
And arme him well i'th States name, I command ye;
And they that dare go voluntary, shall receive reward.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: I dare go no way, Sir, this is strange, Master Captaine,
You cannot be content to spoile our sport here,
Which I do not think your Worship's able to answer,
But you must set us together by the ears, with I know not who to?
We are for the bodily part o'th dance.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Arme him suddenly,
This is no time to foole, I shall returne ye else,
A rebell to the Generall, State, and Duchesse,
And how you'l answer then—

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: I have no more Sons, Sir,
This is my onely boy; I beseech ye Master Captain.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: I am a rank coward too, to say the truth, Sir,
I never had good luck at buffets neither.

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: Here's vorty shillings, spare the childe.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: I cannot.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Are ye a man? will ye cast away a May-Lord?
Shall all the wenches in the Country curse ye?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: An't please you Captaine, ile supply his person,
'Tis pitty their old custome should be frighted,
Let me have Horse, and good Armes, ile serve willingly,
And if I shrink a foot of ground, Hell take me.

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: A promising aspect, face full of courage,
Ile take this man, and thank ye too.

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: Ther's for thee,
'Tis in a clout, but good old gold.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I thank ye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: Goe saddle my fore-horse, put his feather on too,
Hee'l praunce it bravely, friend, he feares no Colours,
And take the Armour down, and see him dizin'd,

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Farewell, & if thou carriest thy self well in this matter,
I say no more, but this, there must be more May-Lords,
And I know who are sit.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Dance you, Ile fight, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cap.
verse: Away, away.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Farewell, I am for the Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: Now to this matter againe, my honest fellowes,
For if this go not forward, I foresee friends,
This war will fright our neighbours out o'th villages;
Cheere up your hearts, we shall heare better news, boyes.

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: Surely, I will daunce no more, 'tis most ridiculous,
I finde my wives instructions now meere verities,
My learned wives, she often hath pronounc'd to me
My safety Bomby, defie these sports, thou art damn'd else,
This Beast of Babylon, I will never back againe,
His pace is sure prophane, and his lewd wihies
The Sons of Hymyn, and Gymyn, in the wildernesse.

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: Fie neighbour Bomby, in your fits againe,
Your zeale swets, this is not carefull, neighbour,
The Hobby-Horse, is a seemely Hobby-Horse.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: And as pretty a Beast on's inches, though I say it.

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: The Beast is an unseemely, and a lew'd Beast,
And got at Rome by the Popes Coach-Horses,
His mother was the Mare of ignorance.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Cobler, thou lyest, and thou wert a thousand Coblers,
His mother was an honest Mare, & a Mare of good credit,
I know the Mare, and if need be, can bring witnesse;
And in the way of honesty I tell thee,
Scorn'd any Coach-Horse the Pope had, thou art foolish,
And thy blind zeale makes thee abuse the Beast.

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: I do defie thee, and thy foot-cloth too,
And tell thee to thy face, this prophaine riding
I feele it in my conscience, and I dare speake it,
This unedified ambling, hath brought a scourge upon us,
This Hobby-horse sincerity we liv'd in
War, and the sword of slaughter: I renounce it,
And put the Beast off; thus, the Beast poluted,
And now no more shall hope on high Bomby,
Follow the painted Pipes of worldly pleasures,
And with the wicked daunce the Devills measures;
Away thou pamper'd jade of vanity,
Stand at the Livery of lewd delights now,
And eat the provender of prickear'd folly,
My daunce shall be to the pipe of persecution.

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: Will you daunce no more Neighbour?

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: Surely no,
Carry the Beast to his Crib: I have renounc'd him,
And all his workes.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Shall the Hobby-horse be forgot then?
The hopefull Hobby-horse? shall he lye founder'd?
If thou do'st this, thou art but a cast-away Cobler:
My anger's up, think wisely, and think quickly,
And look upon the quondam beast of pleasure,
If thou dost this (mark me, thou serious Sowter)
Thou Bench-whistler of the old tribe of toe-peeces,
If thou do'st this there shall be no more Shooe-mending,
Every man shall have a speciall care of his owne soule:
And in his pocket carry his two Confessors,
His Yugell, and his Nawle: if thou do'st this—

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: He will dance againe for certaine.

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: I cry out on't,
'Twas the fore-running sin brought in those Tilt-staves,
They brandish 'gainst the Church, the Devill calls May-poles,
Take up your Horse againe, and girth him to ye,
And girth him handsomely good neighbour Bomby.

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: I spit at him.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Spit in the Horse face, Cobler?
Thou out of tune-Psalm-singing Slave; spit in his visnomy?

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: I spit againe, and thus I rise against him:
Against this Beast: that signifi'd destruction,
Fore-shew'd ith' falls of Monarchies.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Ith' face of him?
Spit such another spit, by this hand Cobler
Ile make ye set a new peece o' your nose there,
'Tak't up I say, and dance without more bidding,
And dance as you were wont: you have been excellent
And art still, but for this new nicity,
And your wives learned Lectures: take up the Hobby-horse
Come, 'tis a thing thou hast lov'd with all thy heart Bomby
And would'st do still but for the round-breecht Brothers:
You were not thus in the morning, tak't up I say,
Do not delay but do it: you know I am officer,
And I know 'tis unfit all these good fellowes
Should wait the cooling of your zealous porridge;
Chuse whether you will dance, or have me execute:
Ile clap your neek ith' Stocks, and there ile make ye
Dance a whole day, and dance with these at night too,
You mend old Shooes well, mend your old manners better,
And suddenly see you leave off this sincerenesse.
This new hot batch borrowed from some brown Baker,
Some learned Brother, or ile so bait ye for't,
Take it quickly up.

speeches.speaker: Hob.
verse: I take my persecution,
And thus I am forced a by-word to my Brethren.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Strike up, strike up: strike merrily.

speeches.speaker: Far.
verse: To it roundly,
Now to the harvest feast: then sport againe Boyes.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: What shall I do? live thus unknown, and base still?
Or thrust my self into the head oth' Battell?
And there, like that I am, a Gentleman,
And one that never fear'd the face of danger,
(So in her angry eyes she carried honour)
Fight nobly, and (to end my cares) dye nobly?
What heavenly voice is this that followes me?
This is the second time 't has waited on me,
Since I was arm'd, and ready for the Battell;
It names me often, steeles my heart with courage,
And in a thousand sweet noates comforts me;
What Beldom's this? how old she is, and ugly,
Why do's she follow me?
prose:
Song within.


SIlvio go on, and raise thy noble minde
To noble ends; fling course base thoughts behinde:

Silvio, thou Sonne of everliving fame,
Now aime at vertue, and a Noble Name.

Silvio consider, Honour is not wonne,
Nor vertue reach't, till some brave thing be done:
Thy Country calls thee now; she burnes, and bleeds,
Now raise thy self, young man, to noble deeds.
Into the Battell Silvio, there seeke forth
Danger, and blood, by them stands sacred worth.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Be not dismaid, Son,
I wait upon thee, for thy good, and honour,
'Twas I that now sung to thee, stir'd thy minde up,
And rais'd thy spirits to the pitch of noblenesse.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Though she be old, and of a crooked carkasse,
Her voice is like the harmony of Angels.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Thou art my darling, all my love dwells on thee
The Son of vertue, therefore I attend thee;
Enquire not what I am, I come to serve thee,
For if thou beest inquisitive, thou hast lost me:
A thousand long miles hence my dwelling is,
Deep in a Cave, where but mine owne, no foot treads,
There by mine Art, I found what danger (Silvio)
And deep distresse of heart, thou wert growne into,
A thousand leagues I have cut through empty aire,
Far swifter then the sayling tack that gallops
Upon the wings of angry winds, to seeke thee.
Sometimes 'ore a swelling tide, on a Dolphins back I ride,
Sometimes passe the earth below, and through the unmoved Center go;
Sometimes in a flame of fire, like a Meteor I aspire,
Sometimes in mine own shape, thus, when I helpe the vertuous,
Men of honourable minds, command my Art in all his kinds;
Pursue the noble thought of war, from thy Guard ile not be far,
Get thee worship on thy foe, lasting fame is gotten so.
Single Syennas Duke alone, heare thy friends, thy Country grone,
And with thy manly arme strike sure, then thou hast wrought thine owne free cure.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Some Sybell sure, some soule heaven loves, and favours.
And lends her their free powers, to worke their wonders?
How she incites my courage?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Silvio,
I knew thee many daies a go,
Foresaw thy love to Belvidere, the Duchesse Daughter, and her Heire;
Knew she lov'd thee, and know what past, when you were found i'th Castle fast
In one anothers armes; foresaw the taking of ye, and the Law;
And so thy innocence I loved, the deepest of my skill I proved;
Be rul'd by me, for to this houre I have dwelt about thee with my powre.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I will, and in the course of all observe thee,
For thou art sure an Angell good sent to me.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Get thee gone then to the fight, longer stay but robs thy right;
When thou grow'st weary ile be neere, then think on beauteous Belvidere,
For every precious thought of her, ile lend thine honour a new spurre;
When all is done, meet here at night; Go and be happy in the fight.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I certainly believe I shall do nobly,
And that Ile bravely reach at too, or die.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Is she so loving still?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: She is mad with love,
As mad as ever unworm'd dogge was, Signior,
And do's so weep, and curse, for your prevention,
Your crosses in your love; it frets me too,
I am falne away to nothing, to a spindle,
Growne a meere man of mat, no soule within me,
Pox o' my Master, Sir, will that content ye?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: This rogue but cozens me, and she neglects me,
Upon my life there are some other gamsters,
Neerer the winde then I, and that prevents me,
Is there no other holds acquaintance with her?
Prethee be true, be honest, do not mock me,
Thou knowest her heart, no former interest
She has vow'd a favour to? and cannot handsomly
Go off, but by regaining such a friendship?
There are a thousand handsom men, young, wealthy,
That will not stick at any rate, nor danger,
To gaine so sweet a prize; nor can I blame her,
If where she finds a comfort she deale cunningly,
I am a stranger yet.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Ye are all she looks for,
And if there be any other, she neglects all,
And all for you: I would you saw how grievously
And with what hourely lamentations.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I know thou flatter'st me; tell me but truth,
Looke here, look well, the best meat in the Dukedom,
The rarest, and the choicest of all diets,
This will I give thee, but to satisfie me;
That is, not to dissemble; this rare Lobster,
This Pheasant of the sea, this dish for Princes,
And all this thou shalt enjoy, eat all thy selfe,
Have good Greeke wine, or any thing belongs to it,
A wench if it desire one.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: All this, Signior?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: All, and a greater far then this.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A greater?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: If thou deserve by telling truth.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: A wench too?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Or any thing, but if you play the knave now,
The Cozening knave besides the losse of this,
In which thou hast parted with a paradise,
I neare will give thee meat more, not a morsell,
No smell of meat by my meanes shall come neere thee,
Nor name of any thing that's nourishing,
But to thy old part Tantalus againe,
Thou shalt returne, and there snap at a shadow.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Upon this point, had I intended Treason,
Or any thing might call my life in question,
Follow'd with all the tortures time could think on,
Give me but time to eat this lovely Lobster,
This Alderman o'th Sea, and give me wine to him,
I would reveale all, and if that all were too little,
More then I knew; Bartello holds in with her,
The Captain of the Cittadell, but you need not fear him,
His tongue's the stiffest weapon that he carries.
He is old, and out of use; there are some other,
Men young enough, handsome, and bold enough,
Could they come to make their game once; but they want Sir,
They want the unde quare, they are laid by then,
You onely are the man shall knock the nayle in—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: How now Penurio?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Your Worship's fairely met, Sir.
You shall heare further from me, steale aside Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Remember your Master for those Chaines.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: They are ready, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: What young thing's this? by his habit hee's a Merchant;
I feare he trades my way too, you dryed dog-fish,
What bait was that?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Who Sir, the thing went hence now?
A notable young whelp.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: To what end Sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Came to buy Chaines and Rings, is to be married,
An Asse, a Coxcomb, has nothing in his house, Sir;
I warrant you think he came to see my Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: I doubt it shrewdly.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Away, away, 'tis foolish;
He has not the face to look upon a Gentlewoman,
A poore skym'd thing, his Mothers maids are faine, Sir,
To teach him how to kisse, and against he is married,
To shew him on which side the stirrop stands.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: That's a fine youth.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Thou wouldst hang thy self, that thou hadst half his power,
Thou empty Potgun.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Am I come fit Penurio?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: As fit as a fiddle,
My Matter's now abroad about his businesse.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: When thou cam'st to me home to day, I half suspected
My wife was jealous, that she whispered to thee.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: You deserve well the whil'st, ther's no such matter,
She talk'd about some toyes my Master must bring to her,
You must not know of.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Ile take noat, Penurio.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: No, Nor you shall not, till you have it soundly.
This is the bravest Capitano Pompo,
But I shall pump ye anon Sir.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: O my Bartello?

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Ye pretty Rogue, you little Rogue, you sweet Rogue,
Away Penurio, go and walk i'th Horse-Fayre.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: You do not love me?

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Thou lyest thou little Rascall;
There Sirrah, to your Centry.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: How the Colt itches?
Ile help ye to a Curry-comb shall claw ye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: And how much dost thou love me?

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Let's go in quickly,
Ile tell thee presently, ile measure it to thee.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: No busses first? sit 'o my knee, my brave boy,
My valiant boy; do not look so fiercely on me,
Thou wilt fright me with thy face; come busse againe Chick,
Smile in my face you mad thing.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: I am mad indeed wench,
Precious I am all o' fire.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ile warrant thee better.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Ile warme thee too, or ile blow out my bellowes;
Ha, ye sweet rogue, you loving rogue, a Boy now,
A Souldier I will get shall prove a fellow.

speeches.speaker: Jaq.
verse: Mistris, looke to your selfe, my Master's comming.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: The Devill come, and go with him.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The Devill's come indeed, he brings your wife, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: We are undone, undone then.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: My wife with him?
Why this is a dismall day.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: They are hard by too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I must not, dare not see her.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Nor my Husband,
For twenty thousand pound.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: That I were a Cat now,
Or any thing could run into a Bench-hole,
Saint Anthonies Fire upon the Rogue has brought her;
Where shall I be? just in the nick oth' matter?
When I had her at my mercy: think for heaven sake,
My wife, all the wilde furies hell has.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Up the Chimney.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: They'l smoke me out there presently.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: There, there, it must be there,
We are all undone else: it must be up the Chimney.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Give me a Ladder.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: You must use your Art Sir,
Alas, we have no Ladders.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Pox o' thy husband,
Do's he never mend his house?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: No, nor himselfe neither:
Up nimbly Sir, up nimbly.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Thou know'st I am fat,
Thou mercilesse leane Rogue.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Will ye be kill'd?
For if he take ye—

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Lend me thy shoulder.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Soft Sir,
You'l tread my shoulder-bones into my sides else,
Have ye fast hold oth' barrs?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: A vengeance bar 'em.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Patience good Captain, patience: quickly, quickly.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Do you think I am made of smoke?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Now he talkes of smoke,
What if my Master should call for fire?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Will ye Martyr me?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: He must needs have it.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Will ye make me Bacon?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: We'l do the best we can, are all things ready?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: All, all, I have 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Go, let 'em in then,
Not a word now on your life.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I hang like a Meteor.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: You are welcome Lady.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: You are too too curteous,
But I shall make amends, faire Isabella.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Welcome my worthy friend, most kindely welcome.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: I heare on't, and ile fit him for his foolery.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Some sweet meats wife: some sweet meats presently.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: O my sowre sauce.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Away quick Isabella.
Did you heare him?

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: Yes, yes, perfectly, proceed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Speake loud enough: Dare ye at length but pitty me?

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: 'Faith Sir, you have us'd so many reasons to me,
And those so powerfully—

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Keep this kisse for me.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And do I stand and heare this?

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: This for me Sir,
This is some comfort now: Alas my Husband—
But why Do I think of so poore a fellow,
So wretched, so debosh'd?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: That's I, I am bound to heare it.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: I dare not lye with him, he is so ranke a Whore-master.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And that's a dangerous point.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: Upon my conscience Sir,
He would stick a thousand base diseases on me.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And now must I say nothing.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I am sound Lady.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: That's it that makes me love ye.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Let's kisse againe then.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: Do, do.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Do, the Devill.
And the grand Pox do with ye.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Do ye heare him? well—
Now, what's the newes with you?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The sound of War Sir,
Comes still along: The Duke will charge the City,
We have lost they say.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: What shall become of me then,
And my poore wealth?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Even hang'd, I hope.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: Remove your Jewells presently,
And what you have of wealth into the Cittadell,
I here all's secure.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I humbly thank ye Lady:
Penurio, get me some can climbe the Chimney,
For there my Jewells are, my best, my richest,
I hid 'em, fearing such a blow.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Most happily:
I have two Boyes, that use to sweep fould Chimnies,
Truly I brought 'em Sir, to mock your worship,
For the great Fires ye keep, and the full diet.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I forgive thee knave, where are they?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Here Sir, here:
Mounsieur Black will your small worship mount?

speeches.speaker: 1 Boy.
verse: Madam è be com to creep up into your Chimney, and make you.
Cleane, as any Lady in de world: Ma litla, litla frera, and è,
Chanta, frere, chanta.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Come Mounsieur, mounte, mountè, mount Mounsieur Musterd-pot.

speeches.speaker: 1 Boy.
verse: Mounsieur è have dis for votra barba, ple ta von Mounsieur.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
prose: Mòunte Mounsieur, mountè dere be some fine tings.

speeches.speaker: 1 Boy.
verse: Me will creep like de Ferret Mounsieur.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Dere in the Chimney.

speeches.speaker: 1 Boy.
verse: He be de sheilde due shauson, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: There's a Birds-neast, I wound have ye climbe it Mounsieur,
Up my fine singing Mounsieur: that's a fine Mounsieur.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Watch him, he do not steale.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I warrant ye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: These Boyes are knavish.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Ile looke to him tithly

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Lord, what comes here,
A walking apparition?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Saint Christopher.

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: Mercy o' me, what is it?
How like my Husband it lookes?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Get ye downe Devill,
Ile breake your neck else: was ever man thus chimnied?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Go pay the Boyes well: see them satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Come Mounsieur Devills, come my Black-berries
Ile butter ye o' both sides.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Nay, ev'n look Sir, are you cooled now, Captaine?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: I am Cuckolled, and fool'd to boot too:
Fool'd fearefully, fool'd shamefully.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: You are welcome Sir,
I am glad I have any thing within these doores Sir
To make ye merry; you love my wife, I thank ye,
You have shew'd your love.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Wife, am I this? this odde matter,
This monstrous thing?

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: You ought, but yet you are not:
I have been bold with you Sir, but yet not basely,
As I have faith I have not.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Sir, beleeve it;
'Twas all meant but to make you feele your trespasse;
We new your howre, and all this fashion'd for it.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Were you oth' plot too?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Yes by my troth, sweet Captaine.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: You will forgive me wife?

speeches.speaker: Rho.
verse: You will deserve it?

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: Put that toth' venture.

speeches.speaker: Rho:
verse: Thus am I friends againe then,
And as you ne're had gone astray, thus kisse ye.

speeches.speaker: Bar.
verse: And ile kisse you, and you too ask forgivenesse;
Kisse my wife Lopez, 'tis but in jest remember;
And now all friends together to my Castle,
Where we'l all dine, and there discourse these stories,
And let him be Chimney-swept in's lust that glories.

segments.head: Actus Quartus. | Scaena Q a ta.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Haile reverent Dame, heaven wait upon thy studies.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You are well met Son: what is the Battell ended?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Mother, 'tis done.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: How has thy honour prosper'd?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: The Dutchesse has the day, Syenna's Prisoner:
Arm'd with thy powrefull Art, this arme dismounted him,
Receiv'd him then on foot, and in faire valour
Forc'd him mine owne, this Jewell I tooke from him,
It hung upon his cask, the Victors triumph:
And to the Dutchesse now a Prisoner
I have renderd him: Come off againe unknown, Mother.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Tis well done, let me see he jewell Son;
'Tis a rich one, curious set, fit a Princesse Burgonet:
This rich token late was sent, by the Dutchesse with intent
The Marriage next day to begin: Do'st thou know what's hid within?
Wipe thine eyes, and then come neere, see the beautious Belvidere:
Now behold it.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: O my Saint.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: We are it nobly, do not faint.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: How blest am I in this rich spoile, this picture,
For ever will I keep it here, here Mother,
For ever honour it: how oft, how chastly
Have I embrac'd the life of this, and kist it?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: The day drawes on that thou must home returne,
And make thy answer to the Dutchesse quest on
I know it troubles thee, for if thou faile in't—

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: O, I must dye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Feare not, feare not, ile be nigh,
Cast thy trouble on my back, art nor cunning shal not lack
To preserve thee, still to keepe, what thy envious foemen seeke;
Go boldly home, and let thy minde, no distrustfull crosses finde:
All shall happen for the best; souls walk through sorrowes that are blest.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Then I go confident.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: But first my Son, a thankfull service must be done,
The good old woman for her paine, when every thing stands faire againe,
Must ask a poore Boon, and that granting, there's nothing to thy journey wanting.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Except the triall of my soul to mischief,
And as I am a Knight, and love mine honour,
I grant it whatsoever.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Thy pure soule
Shall never sinke for me, nor howle.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Then any thing.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: When I shall aske remember.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: If I forget, heavens goodnesse forget me.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: On thy journey then a while, to the next crosse way and stile
Ile conduct thee, keepe thee true, to thy Mistris and thy vow,
And let all their envies fall, ile be with thee and quench all.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: LAdy, the stubborn war's more milde then you are,
That allowes Ransome, and the Prisoner taken—

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: We must not be too hasty: Remember Sir,
The wrong and violence you have offer'd us,
Burnt up our Frontire Townes, made prey before ye
Both of our Beasts, and Corne; slaine our deare Subjects,
Open'd the fountaine eyes of thousand widowes,
That daily fling their curses on your fury;
What ordinary satisfaction can salve this?
What hasty thought-on Ransome give a remedy?
You must excuse us yet, we'l take more counsell:
In the meane time, not as a Prisoner,
But as a noble Prince we entertaine ye.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: I am at your mercy Lady, 'tis my fortune,
My stubborne fate; the day is yours, you have me,
The valour of one single man has cross'd me,
Crost me and all my hope; for when the Battells
Were at the hottest game of all their furies,
And conquest ready then to crowne me Victor,
One single man broke in, one sword, one vertue,
And by his great example thousands followed,
O how I shame to think on't, how it shakes me!
Nor could our strongest head then stop his fury,
But like a tempest 'bore the field before him,
Till he arriv'd at me, with me he buckell'd,
A while I held him play; at length his violence
Beat me from my Saddle, then on foot pursu'd me,
There triumph'd once againe, then tooke me Prisoner:
When I was gone a feare possest my people.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: One single arme, in a just dause, heaven prospers.
Is not this stranger Knight as yet discover'd,
That we may give his vertue a doe honour?

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: Not yet that we hear Madam, but to that purpose,
Two dayes ago we publish'd Proclamations

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: O dainty Duchesse, here I bring that Knight
Before thy fragrant face, that warlike wight,
He that Syenna's Duke, and all his Louts
Beat (as the Proverb seemly sayes) to clouts:
He that unhorss'd the man of fame to boot,
And bootlesse taught his Grace to walk afoot:
He that your writings (pack'd to every pillar)
Promis'd promotion to, and store of filler,
That very man I set before thy Grace,
And once againe pronounce this man it was.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: A pretty foolish Squire, what must the Knight be?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Some Jugler, or some Mad-man.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I was not so,
When thy faint Troopes in flockes I beat before me,
When through the thickest of thy warlike horse
I shot my selfe, even to thy Standard Duke,
And there found thee, there fingled thee, there shew'd thee
The temper of my Sword. 'Tis true, thou stood'st me,
And like a noble Souldier bid'st me welcome;
And this ile say, More honour in that arme
I found and tryed, then all thy Army carried:
What followes thy Imprisonment can tell thee.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: His faire relation carries truth and vertue,
And by those Armes I see (for such were his,
So old, so rusty) this may be he that forc'd me.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Do you know this Jewell, from your Cask I rent it,
Even as I clos'd, and forced ye from your saddle;
Do you now remember me?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: This is the valour
Madam, for certaine he, it must be he,
That day I wore this Jewell, you remember it.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Yes, very well; not long before I sent it.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: That day I lost this Jewell, in fight I lost it,
I felt his stroakes, and felt him take it from me,
I wore it in my Cask; take it againe Sir,
You won it nobly, 'tis the prize of honour.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: My Father, and my selfe are made for ever.

speeches.speaker: Duc.
verse: Kneele down brave Sir, thus my Knight first I raise ye,
Gird on a Sword; next Generall of my Army,
Give him a Staffe; last, one in Counsell neare me.
Now, make us happy with your sight: how? Silvio?
Have I on thee bestow'd this love, this honour?
The Treasons thou hast wrought set off with favours?
Unarme him presently: O thou foule Traitor,
Traitor to me, mine honour, and my Country,
Thou kindler of these Warres.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Mistake not Madam.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Away with him to prison,
See him safe kept, the Law shall shortly Sirra,
Finde fitter titles for ye, then I gave ye.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: This is the youth that kild me, ile be quit with him,
What a blinde rogue was I, I could never know him?
And't please your Grace, I claime the benefit
Of the Proclamation that proclam'd him Traitor,
I brought him in.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Thou shalt have thy reward for't.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Let him be hang'd, or drown'd then.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Away with him.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Madam, I crave your promise first; you are tyed to it,
You have past your Princely word.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Prove it, and take it.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: This is the day appointed,
Appointed by your Grace for my appearance,
To answer to the Question.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: I remember it.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I claime it then,

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: If you performe it not,
The penalty you claime too.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I not repent it;
If I absolve the words?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Your life is free then,
You have drawne a speedy course above my wishes,
To my rezenge, be sure ye hit it right,
Or ile be sure you shall not scape the danger.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: My rest is up now Madam.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Then play it cunningly.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Now, where's the Hag? where now are all her promises,
She would be with me, strengthen me, informe me?
My death will now be double death, ridiculous:
She was wont still to be neare, to feele my miseries,
And with her Art, I see her no where now;
What have I undertaken? now she failes me,
No comfort now I finde, how my soule staggers?
Till this houre never fear, nor doubt possest me,
She cannot come, she will not come, she has fool'd me;
Sure, she is the Devill, has drawne me on to ruine,
And now to death bequeaths me in my danger.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: He stands distracted, and his colour changes.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: I have given him that will make his blood forsake him;
Shortly his life.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: His hands and contemplation
Have motion still, the rest is earth already.

speeches.speaker: Duc.
verse: Come, will ye speak or pray? your time growes out Sir;
How every where he looks? he's at last cast.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: His colour comes againe fresh.

speeches.speaker: Duc.
verse: 'Tis a flash, Sir,
Before the flame burnes out; can ye yet answer?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Yes Madam, now I can.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: I feare you'l faile in't.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: And do not think my silence a presage,
Or Omen to my end, you shall not finde it;
I am bred a Souldier, not an Orator,
Madam, peruse this scrowle, let that speake for me,
And as you are Royall, wrong not the construction.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: By Heaven you shall have faire play.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I shall looke for't.
Tell me what it that onely thing,
For which all women long;
Yet having what they most desire,
To have it do's them wrong.
Tis not to be chaste, nor faire,
Such gifts malice may impaire;
Richly trim'd, to walke or ride,
Or to wanton unespi'd;
To preserve an honest name,
And so to give it up to fame;
These are toyes. In good or ill
They desire, to have their will;
Yet when they have it, they abuse it,
For they know not how to use it.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: You have answer'd right, and gain'd your life,
I give it.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: O happy Hag! But my most gracious Madam,
Your promise tide a nobler favour to me.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: 'Tis true, my daughter too.

speeches.speaker: Sil
verse: I hope you will keep it.

speeches.speaker: Duc.
verse: 'Tis not in my powre now, she is long since wanderd,
Stolne from the Court, and me; and what I have not
I cannot give: no man can tell me of her,
Nor no search finde her out: and if not Silvio,
Which strongly I beleeve—

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Mock me not Lady,
For as I am a servant to her vertue,
Since my first howre of exile, I ne're saw her

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: That she is gone 'tis too too true, and lamentable,
Our last hope was in you.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: What do I heare then,
And wherefore have I life bestow'd and honour?
To what end do I walk? for men to wonder at,
And fight, and foole? pray ye take your honours from me,
(My sorrowes are not fit companions for 'em)
And when ye please my life: Art thou gone Mistris,
And wander'st heaven knowes where? this vow I make thee,
That till I finde thee out, and see those faire eyes,
Those eyes that shed their lights, and life into me,
Never to know a friend, to seeke a kindred,
To rest where pleasure dwells, and painted glory,
But through the world, the wide world thus to wander,
The wretched world alone, no comfort with me,
But the meere meditations of thy goodnesse:
Honour and greatnesse, thus adieu.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Stay Silvio,
And Lady sit againe, I come for Justice.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: What would she now?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: To claime thy promise Silvio,
The Boone thou swor'st to give me.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: What may this be,
A woman, or a Devill?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: 'Tis a Witch sure,
And by her meanes he came to untwist this Riddle,

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: That I am bound to her for my liffe, mine honour,
And many other thousand waies for comfort
I here confesse: Confesse a promise too,
That what she would aske me to requite these favours,
Within the endeavour of my life to grant,
I would; and here I stand my words full master.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I wish no more: great Lady, witnesse with me,
The Boone I crave for all my service to thee,
Is now to be thy wife, to grant me marriage.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: How? for to marry thee? aske againe woman,
Thou wilfull woman, aske againe.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No more Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Aske land, and life.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I aske thee for a Husband.

speeches.speaker: Soto.
verse: Marry her, and beat her into Gun-powder,
She would make rare Crackers.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Aske a better fortune,
Thou art too old to marry: I a Souldier,
And alwaies married to my sword.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Thy word Foole,
Breake that, and ile breake all thy fortunes yet.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: He shall not,
I am witnesse to his faith: and ile compell it.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: 'Tis fit ye hold your word, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: O most wretched.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: This was a fortune now beyond my wishes,
For now my Daughter's free, if e're I finde her.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: But not from me.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: You are sharer in this happinesse,
My selfe will wait upon this marriage,
And do the old woman all the honour possible.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Ile lead the Knight, and what there wants in dalliance,
Wee'l take it out in drinke.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: O wretched Silvio.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Hast thou sent for him?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Yes,

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: A young man, saist thou?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Yes, very young, and very amarous.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And handsom?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: As the Town affords.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: And dar'st thou
Be so farre good, and Mistris of thine honour,
To sleight these?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: For my husbands sake to curse 'em,
And since you have made me Mistris of my fortune,
Never to point at any ioy, but husband,
I could have cozen'd ye, but so much I love ye,
And now so much I weigh the estimation
Of an unspotted wife—

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I dare believe thee,
And never more shall doubt torment my spirit.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: How now Penurio?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: The thing is comming, Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Ile take my standing.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Do, and ile take mine.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Where didst thou leave him?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I left him in a Cellar,
Where he has paid me titely, paid me home Mistris,
We had an hundred & fifty healths to you, sweet Mistris,
And three score and ten damnations to my Master;
Mistris, shall I speak a foolish word to ye?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: What's that Penurio?
The fellow's drunke.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I would faine know your body.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: How's that? how's that prethee?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: I would know it carnally,
I would conglutinate.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: The reason sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Lobster, sweet Mistris, Lobster.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Thy Master heares.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Lobster, sweet Master, Lobster.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Thou art the most precious rogue.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
verse: Most pretious Lobster.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Do you see who's here? go sleep ye drunken rascall.

speeches.speaker: Pen.
prose: Remember you refuse me arm'd in Lobster.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: O my lost Rugio, welcome, welcome, welcome,
A thousand welcomes here Ile seale.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Pray ye stay, Lady,
Do you love me ever at this rate? or is the fit now,
By reason of some wrong done by your husband,
More fervent on ye?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Can I chuse but love thee?
Thou art my Martyr, thou hast suffered for me,
My sweet, sweet Rugio.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Do you do this seriously?
'Tis true, I would be entertained thus.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: These are nothing,
No kisses, no embraces, no endeerements,
To those—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Do what you will.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Those that shall follow,
Those I will crowne our love withall; why sigh ye?
Why look ye sad my deere one?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nay faith nothing,
But me thinks so sweet a beauty, as yours showes to me,
And such an innocence as you may make it,
Should hold a longer Siege.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ha, you speake truth, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I would not have it so.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: And now methinkes,
Now I consider truly what becomes me,
I have been cozen'd, fearefully abus'd,
My reason blinded.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nay, I did but jest with ye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Ile take ye at your word, and thank ye for't Sir;
And now I see no sweetnesse in that person,
Nothing to stir me to abuse a Husband,
To ruine my faire fame.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Good Isabella.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: No hansome man, no any thing to doat on,
No face, no tongue to catch me, poore at all points,
And I an asse.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Why do ye wrong me Lady?
If I were thus, and had no youth upon me,
My service of so meane a way to win ye,
(Which you your selfe are conscious must deserve ye,
If you had thrice the beauty you possesse, must reacht ye)
If in my tongue your fame lay wrack't, and ruin'd
With every cup I drink: if in opinion
I were a lost, defam'd man: but this is common
Where we love most, where most we stake our fortunes,
There least and basest we are rewarded: fare ye well,
Know now I hate you too as much, contemne ye,
And weigh my credit at as high a value.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: May be I did but jest.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ye are a woman,
And now I see your wants, and mine owne follies,
And task my selfe with indiscretion,
For doating on a face so poore.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Say ye so Sir,
(I must not lose my end) I did but jest with you,
Only fool'd thus to try your faith: my Rugio,
Do you think I could forget?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Nay, 'tis no matter.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Is't possible I should forsake a constancy,
So strong, so good, so sweet?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: A subtle woman.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: You shall forgive me, 'twas a trick to try ye,
And were I sure ye lov'd me—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Do you doubt now?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I do not doubt, but he that would professe this,
And beare that full affection you make shew of,
Should do—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: What should I do?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I cannot shew ye.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ile try thee damnedst Devill: hark ye Lady,
No man shall dare do more, no service top me,
Ile marry ye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: How Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Your husbands sentenc'd,
And he shall dye.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Dye?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Dye for ever to ye,
The danger is mine owne.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Dye did ye tell me?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: He shall dye, I have cast the way.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: O foule man,
Malicious bloody man.

speeches.speaker: Lop,
verse: When shall he dye Sir,
By whom, and how?

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Hast thou betray'd me, woman?

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Base man, thou wouldst have ruin'd me, my name too,
And like a Toad, poyson'd my vertuous memory:
Further then all this, dost thou see this friend here,
This only friend, shame take thy lust and thee,
And shake thy soule, his life, the life I love thus,
My life in him, my only life thou aim'dst at.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Am I catch's thus?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: The Law shall catch ye better.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: You make a trade of betraying womens honours,
And think it noble in ye to be lustfull,
Report of me hereafter—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Fool'd thus finely?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I must intreat ye walk, Sir, to the Justice,
Where if hee'l bid ye kill me—

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Pray stay a while, Sir,
I must use a Players shift, do you know me now Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Your brother Claudio sure.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: O me, 'tis he Sir,
O my best brother.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: My best sister now too,
I have tryed ye, found ye so, and now I love ye,
Love ye so truly nobly.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Sir, I thank ye,
You have made me a most happy man.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Thank her Sir,
And from this houre preserve that happinesse,
Be no more fool'd with jealousie.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: I have lost it,
And take me now new borne againe, new natur'd.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: I do, and to that promise tye this faith,
Never to have a false thought tempt my vertue.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Enough, enough, I must desire your presence,
My Cozen Rhodope has sent in all hast for us,
I am sure you will be welcome.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Ile wait on ye.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: What the Project is—

speeches.speaker: Isab.
prose: We shall know when we are there, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Joy to you Silvio, and your young faire Bride,
You have stolne a day upon us; you cannot wooe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: The joyes of Hell hang over me, O mischiefe,
To what a fortune has the Devill driven me?
Am I reserv'd for this?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Beshrew me Sir,
But you have gotten you a right faire bedfellow,
Let you alone to chuse.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I beseech your Grace,
'Tis misery enough to have met the Devill,
Not mens reproches too.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: How old is she?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: A very Girle, her eye delivers it.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: Her teeth are scarce come yet.

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: What goodly children
Will they two have now? she is rarely made to bread on,
What a sweet timberd body?

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Knotty i'th back,
But will hold out the stronger; What a nose?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: I marry, such a nose, so rarely mounted,
Upon my conscience, 'twas the part he doted on.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: And that fine little eye to it, like an Elephants.

speeches.speaker: Lord.
verse: Yes, if her feet were round, and her ears sachells.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: For any thing we know.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Have ye no mercy?
No pitty in your bloods, to use a wretch thus?
You Princes, in whose hearts the best compassions,
Neerest to those in Heaven, should finde fit places,
Why do you mock at misery? Fling scornes and basenesse
Upon his broken back, that sinks with sorrowes?
Heaven may reward you too, and an houre come,
When all your great designes shall shew ridiculous,
And your hearts pinch'd like mine.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Fye Sir, so angry
Upon your wedding day? go smug your selfe,
The Maid will come anon: what Musick's this?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: I warrant you some noble preparation.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Let's take our places then.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: More of these Devills dumps?
Must I be ever haunted with these witchcrafts?

speeches.speaker: 1. Pre.
verse: Roome, roome for merry spirits, roome,
Hether on command we come,
From the good old Beldam sent,
Cares and sorrowes to prevent.
Looke up Silvio, smile, and sing,
After winter comes a spring.
Feare not faint foole what may follow,
Eyes that now are sunk and hollow,
By her Art may quick returne
To their flames againe, and burne.
Art commands all youth, and blood,
Strength and beauty it makes good.
Feare not then, dispaire not, sing
Round about as we do spring:
Cares and sorrowes cast away,
This is the old wives holy-day.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Who is this?

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: The shape of Belvidere.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Now Silvio,
How do'st thou like me now?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Thus I kneele to thee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Stand up, and come no nearer, mark me well too,
For if thou troublest me I vanish instantly:
Now chuse wisely or chuse never,
One thou must enjoy for ever.
Do'st thou love me thus?

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: Most dearely.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Take heed foole, it concernes thee nearely.
If thou wilt have me young and bright,
Pleasing to thine eye and sight,
Courtly, and admir'd of all,
Take heed least thy fame do fall,
I shall then be full of scorne,
Wanton, proud, beware the horne,
Hating what I lov'd before,
Flattery apt to fall before,
All consuming, nothing getting,
Thus thy faire name comes to setting.
But if old and free from these
Thou shalt chuse me, I shall please:
I shall then maintaine thee still,
With my vertue and my skill:
Still encrease and build thy name,
Chuse now Silvio, here I am.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I know not what to say, which way to turne me,
Into thy Soveraigne will I put my answer.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I thank ye Sir, and my will thus rewards ye,
Take your old Love, your best, your dearest Silvio:
No more Spells now, nor further shapes to alter me,
I am thy Belvidere indeed, Deare Mother,
There is no altering this; heavens hand is with it:
And now you ought to give me, he has fairely won me.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: But why that Hag?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: In that shape most secure still,
I followed all your fortunes, serv'd, and counsell'd ye,
I met ye at the Farmers first a Country wench,
Where fearing to be knowne I tooke that habit,
And to make ye laughing sport at this mad marriage,
By secret ayde of my friend Rhodope
We got this Maske.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: And I am sure I have ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: For ever now, for ever.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: You see it must be,
The wheele of destiny hath turn'd it round so.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: It must, it is, and curs'd be he that breakes it.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Ile put a choyce to you Sir: ye are my Prisoner.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: I am so, and I must be so, till it please you—

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: Chuse one of these, either to pay a Ransome,
At what rate I shall set it, which shall be high enough,
And so returne a Free-man, and a Bachellor,
Or give me leave to give you a fit wife,
In honour every way your Graces equall,
And so your Ransom's paid.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: You say most nobly,
Silvio's example's mine, pray chuse you for me.

speeches.speaker: Duc.
verse: I thank ye Sir, I have got the mastry too,
And here I give your Grace a husbands freedome,
Give me your hand, my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Sy.
verse: You much honour me,
And I shall ever serve ye for this favour.

speeches.speaker: Bart.
verse: Come Lopez, let us give our wives the breeches too,
For they will have 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lop.
verse: Whilst they rule with vertue
Ile give 'em, skin and all.

speeches.speaker: Isab.
verse: Wee'l scratch it off else.

speeches.speaker: Sil.
verse: I am glad ye live, more glad ye live to honour,
And from this houre a stronger love dwell with us;
Pray you take your man againe.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: He knowes my house Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duch.
verse: 'Tis sin to keep you longer from your Loves,
Wee'l lead the way; and you young men that know not
How to preserve a wife, and keep her faire,
Give 'em their soveraign wills, & pleas'd they are.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: WIll your Grace speak?

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: Let me alone Sorano,
Although my thoughts seeme sad, they are welcome to me.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: You know I am private as your secret wishes,
Ready to fling my soule upon your service,
Ere your command be on't.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: Bid those depart.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: You must retire my Lords.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: What new design in hammering in his head now?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Lets pray heartily
None of our heads meet with it, my wife's old,
That's all my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Mine's ugly, that I am sure on,
And I think honest too, 'twould make me start else.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Mine's troubled in the Country with a feaver,
And some few infirmities else; he looks againe,
Come le'ts retire, certaine 'tis some she businesse,
This new Lord is imployed.

speeches.speaker: Val.
prose: I'le not be far off, because I doubt the cause.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: Are they all gone?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: All but your faithfull servant.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I would tell thee,
But 'tis a thing thou canst not like.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Pray ye speak it, is it my head? I have it ready for ye, Sir:
Is't any action in my powre? my wit?
I care not of what nature, nor what followes.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: I am in love.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: That's the least thing of a thousand,
The easiest to atchieve.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: But with whom Sorano?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: With whom you please, you must not be deny'd, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Say it be with one of thy Kinswomen.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Say withall,
I shall more love your Grace, I shall more honour ye,
And would I had enough to serve your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why 'tis thy Sister then, the faire Evanthe,
Ile be plaine with thee.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Ile be as plaine with you Sir,
She brought not her perfections to the world,
To lock them in a case, or hang 'em by her,
The use is all she breeds 'em for, she is yours, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Dost thou meane seriously?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: I meane my Sister,
And if I had a dozen more, they were all yours:
Some Aunts I have, they have been handsome women,
My mother's dead indeed, and some few cozens
That are now shooting up, we shall see shortly.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No, 'tis Evanthe.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: I have sent my man unto her,
Upon some businesse to come presently
Hither, she shall come; Your Grace dare speak unto her?
Large golden promises, and sweet language, Sir,
You know what they worke, she is a compleat Courtier,
Besides Ile set in.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She weights upon my Queene,
What jealousie and anger may arise,
Incensing her?

speeches.speaker: Sora.
verse: You have a good sweet Lady,
A woman of so even and still a temper,
She knows not anger; say she were a fury,
I had thought you had been absolute the great King,
The fountaine of all honours, playes and pleasures,
Your will and your commands unbounded also;
Go get a paire of beads and learne to pray, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: My Lord, your servant staies.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Bid him come hither, and bring the Lady with him.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I will wooe her,
And either lose my selfe, or win her favour.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: She is comming in.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: Thy eyes shoot through the doore,
They are so piercing, that the beames they dart
Give new light to the roome.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Whether dost thou go?
This is the Kings side, and his private lodgings,
What businesse have I here?

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: My Lord sent for ye.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: His lodgings are below, you are mistaken,
We left them at the staire-foot.

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: Good sweet Madam,

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I am no Counsellor, nor important Sutor.
Nor have no private businesse through these Chambers,
To seek him this way, o' my life thou art drunke,
Or worse then drunke, hir'd to convey me hither
To some base end; now I looke on thee better,
Thou hast a bawdy face, and I abhor thee,
A beastly bawdy face, Ile go no further.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Nay shrink not back, indeed you shall good Sister,
Why do you blush? the good King will not hurt ye,
He honours ye, and loves ye.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Is this the businesse?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
prose: Yes, and the best you ever will arive at, if you be wise.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: My Father was no bawd Sir,
Nor of that worshipfull stock as I remember.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: You are a foole.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: You are that I shame to tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Gentle Evanthe.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: The gracious Queen Sir
Is well and merry, heaven be thanked for it,
And as I think she waites you in the Garden.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Let her wait there, I talk not of her Garden,
I talk of thee sweet flower.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Your Grace is pleasant,
To mistake a nettle for a rose.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: No Rose, nor Lilly, nor no glorious Hyacinth
Are of that sweetnesse, whitenesse, tendernesse,
Softnesse, and satisfying blessednesse
As my Evanthe.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Your Grace speakes very feelingly,
I would not be a hansome wench in your way Sir,
For a new gowne.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Thou art all hansomnesse,
Nature will be asham'd to frame another
Now thou art made, thou hast rob'd her of her cunning,
Each severall part about thee is a beauty.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Do you heare this Sister?

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Yes unworthy Brother, but all this will not do.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: But love Evanthe,
Thou shalt have more then words, wealth, ease, and honors
My tender wench.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Be tender of my credit,
And I shall love you Sir, and I shall honour ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I love thee to injoy thee my Evanthe,
To give thee the content of love.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Hold, hold Sir, ye are to fleet,
I have some businesse this way, your Grace can nere content.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: You stubborne toy.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Good my Lord Bawd I thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Thou shalt not go, beleeve me sweet Evanthe,
So high I will advance thee for this favour,
So rich and potent I will raise thy fortune,
And thy friends mighty.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Good your Grace be patient,
I shall make the wo^st honourable wench that ever was,
Shame your discretion, and your choyce.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Thou shalt not.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Shall I be rich do you say, and glorious,
