And shine above the rest, and scorne all beauties,
And mighty in command?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Thou shalt be any thing.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Let me be honest too, and then ile thank ye.
Have you not such a title to bestow too?
If I prove otherwise, I would know but this Sir;
Can all the power you have or all the riches,
But tye mens tongues up from discoursing of me,
Their eyes from gazing at my glorious folly,
Time that shall come from wondering at my impudence,
And they that read my wanton life from curses?
Can you do this? have ye this magick in ye?
This is not in your powre, though you be a Prince Sir,
No more then evill is in holy Angels,
Nor I, I hope; get wantonnesse confirm'd
By Act of Parliament an honesty,
And so receiv'd by all, ile hearken to ye.
Heaven guide your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Evanthe, stay a little,
Ile no more wantonnesse, ile marry thee.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: What shall the Queene do?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ile be divorsed from her.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Can you tell why? what has she done against ye?
Has she contrived a treason gainst your Person?
Abus'd your bed? does disobedience urge ye?

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: That's all one, 'tis my will.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: 'Tis a most wicked one,
A most absurd one, and will show a Monster;
I had rather be a Whore, and with lesse sin,
To your present lust, then Queen to your unjustice.
Yours is no love, Faith and Religion fly it,
Nor has no taste of faire affection in it,
Some hellish flame abuses your faire body,
And hellish furies blow it; looke behinde ye,
Divorse ye from a woman of her beauty,
Of her integrity, her piety?
Her love to you, to all that honours ye,
Her chast and vertuous love, are these fit causes?
What will you do to me, when I have cloyd ye?
You may finde time out in eternity,
Deceit and violence in heavenly Justice,
Life in the grave, and death among the blessed,
Ere staine or brack in her sweet reputation.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: You have fool'd enough, be wise now, and a woman,
You have shew'd a modesty sufficient,
If not too much for Court.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: You have shew'd an impudence,
A more experienc'd bawd would blush and shake at;
You will make my kindred mighty.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Prethee heare me.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I do Sir, and I count it a great offer.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: Any of thine.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: 'Tis like enough you may clap honour on them,
But how 'twill sit, and how men will adore it,
Is still the question. Ile tell you what they'l say Sir,
What the report will be, and 'twill be true too,
And it must needs be comfort to your Master,
These are the issues of her impudence:
Ile tell your Grace, so deare I hold the Queene,
So deare that honour that she nurs'd me up in,
I would first take to me, for my lust, a Moore,
One of your Gally-slaves, that cold and hunger,
Decrepid misery, had made a mock-man,
Then be your Queene.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You are bravely resolute.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I had rather be a Leopar, and be shun'd,
And dye by peeces, rot into my grave,
Leaving no memory behind to know me,
Then be a high Whore to eternity.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You have another Gamster I perceive by ye,
You durst not slight me else.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Ile finde him out,
Though he lye next thy heart hid, Ile discover him,
And ye proud peat, Ile make you curse your insolence.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Tongue of an Angell, and the truth of Heaven,
How am I blest?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Podramo go in hast
To my Sisters Gentlewoman, you know her well,
And bid her send her Mistris presently
The lesser Cabinet she keeps her Letters in,
And such like toyes, and bring it to me Instantly. Away.

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: I am gone.

speeches.speaker: Sora.
verse: The Queene.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
prose: Lets quit the place, she may grow jealous.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: So suddenly departed, what's the reason?
Doe's my approach displease his Grace? are my eyes
So hatefull to him? or my conversation
Infected, that he flies me? faire Evanthe,
Are you there? then I see his shame.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: 'Tis true Madam,
'Thas pleas'd his Goodnesse to be pleasant with me,

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis strange to finde thy modesty in this place,
Doe's the King offer faire? doe's thy face take him?
Nere blush Evanthe, 'tis a very sweet one,
Doe's he raine gold, and precious promises
Into thy lap? will he advance thy fortunes?
Shalt thou be mighty wench?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Never mock Madam;
'Tis rather on your part to be lamented,
At least reveng'd, I can be mighty Lady,
And glorious too, glorious and great, as you are.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: He will marry thee.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Who would not be a Queene, Madam?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis true Evanthe, 'tis a brave ambition,
A golden dreame, that may delude a good minde,
What shall become of me?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: You must learne to pray,
Your age and honour will become a Nunnery.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Wilt thou remember me?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: She weeps. Sweet Lady
Upon my knees I aske your sacred pardon,
For my rude boldnesse; and know, my sweet Mistris,
If e're there were ambition in Evanthe,
It was and is to do you faithfull duties;
'Tis true I have been tempted by the King,
And with no few and potent charmes, to wrong ye,
To violate the chaste joyes of your bed;
And those not taking hold, to usurpe your state,
But she that has been bred up under ye,
And daily fed upon your vertuous precepts,
Still growing strong by example of your goodnesse,
Having no errant motion from obedience,
Flyes from these vanities, as meere illusions;
And arm'd with honesty, defies all promises.
In token of this truth, I lay my life downe
Under your sacred foot, to do you service.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Rise my true friend, thou vertuous, bud of beauty,
Thou Virgins honour, sweetly blow and flourish,
And that rude nipping winde, that seeks to blast thee,
Or taint thy root, be curst to all posterity;
To my pro^ection from this houre I take ye,
Yes, and the King shall know—

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Give his heat way, Madam,
And 'twill go out againe, he may forget all.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: What have we to do with the times? we cannot cure 'em;
Let 'em go on, when they are swolne with surfets
They'le burst and stink, then all the world shall smell 'em

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: A man may live a bawd, and be an honest man.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Yes, and a wise man too, 'tis a vertuous calling.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: To his owne wife especially, or to his sister,
The neerer to his owne blood, still the honester;
There want such honest men, would we had more of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: To be a villaine is no such rude matter.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: No, if he be a neat one, and a perfect,
Art makes all excellent, what is it Gentl.
In a good cause to kill a dozen coxcombs?
That blunt rude fellowes call good Patriots?
Nothing, nor ne're look'd after.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: 'Tis ene as much, as easie too, as honest, & as cleer,
To ravish Matrons, and deflowre coy wenches,
But here they are so willing, 'tis a complement.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: To pull downe Churches with pretention,
To build 'em fairer, may be done with honour,
And all this time beleeve no God.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: I think so, 'tis faith enough if they name him in their angers,
Or on their rotten Tombs ingrave an Angell;
Well, brave Alphonso, how happy had we been,
If thou had'st rain'd?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Would I had his disease,
Tyed like a Leprosie to my posterity,
So he were right againe.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: What is his Melady?

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Nothing but sad and silent melancholly,
Laden with griefes and thoughts, no man knows why neither;
The good Brandino Father to the Princesse,
Used all the art and industry that might be,
To free Alphonso from this dull calamity,
And seat him in his rule, he was his eldest
And noblest too, had not faire nature stopt in him,
For which cause this was chosen to inherit,
Frederick the yonger.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Doe's he use his brother
With that respect and honour that befits him?

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: He is kept privately, as they pretend,
To give more ease and comfort to his sicknesse;
But he has honest servants, the grave Rugio,
And Fryer Marco, that waight upon his Person,
And in a Monastery he lives.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: 'Tis full of sadnesse,
To see him when he comes to his fathers Tombe,
As once a day that is his Pilgrimage,
Whilst in devotion the Quire sings an Antheme:
How piously he kneeles, and like a Virgin
That some crosse fate had cozen'd of her Love,
Weeps till the stubborne Marble sweats with pitty,
And to his grones the whole Quire beares a Chorus.

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: So do I too. The King with his contrivers,
This is no place for us.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: This is a Jewell,
Lay it aside, what Paper's that?

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: A Letter,
But 'tis a womans, Sir, I know by the hand,
And the false authography, they write old Saxon.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: May be her ghostly mothers, that instructs her.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: No, 'tis a cozens, and came up with a great Cake.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Sora.
verse: A paire of Gloves the Duchesse gave her,
For so the outside saies:

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: That other Paper?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
prose: A charme for the tooth-ach, here's nothing but Saints and Crosses.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: Look in that box, me thinks that should hold secrets,

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: 'Tis paint and curles of haire, she begins to exercise.
A glasse of water too, I would faine taste it,
But I am wickedly afraid 'twill silence me,
Never a Conduit Pipe to convey this water.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: These are all Rings, deaths heads, and such me~mentoe^
Her Grandmother, and worme-eaten Aunts left to her,
To tell her what her beauty must arive at.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: That, that.

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: They are written Songs Sir, to provoke young Ladies;
Lords, here's a prayer booke, how these agree?
Here's a strange Union.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
prose: Ever by a safest you have a julip set to coole the Patient.

speeches.speaker: Fred
verse: Those, those.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: They are Verses to the blest Evanthe.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Those may discover,
Reade them out Sorant.

prose:
To the blest Evanthe,

LEt those complaine, that feeles Loves cruelty,
And in sad Legents write their woes,
With Roses gently 'has corrected me;
My war is without rage or blowes;
My Mistris eyes shine faire on my desires,
And hope springs up inflam'd with her new fires.

No more an Exile will I dwell,
With folded armes, and sighs all day,
Reckoning the torments of my hell,
And flinging my sweet joyes away;
I am call'd home againe to quiet peace,
My Mistris smiles, and all my sorrowes cease.
Yet what is living in her eyes?
Or being blest with her sweet tongue,
If these no other joyes imply?
A golden Give, a pleasing wrong:
To be your owne but one poore Moneth, I'd give
My youth, my fortune, and then leave to live.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: This is my rivall, that I knew the hand now.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: I know it, I have seene it, 'tis Valerio's,
That hopefull Gentlemans that was brought up with ye,
And by your charge nourisht and fed
At the same Table, with the same allowance.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And all this curtesie to ruine me?
Crosse my desires? had better have fed humblier,
And stood at greater distance from my fury:
Go for him quickly, finde him instantly,
Whilst my impatient heart swells high with choller;
Better have lov'd despaire, and safer kist her.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Thou old weak foole, dost thou know to what end,
To what betraying end he got this Casket?
Durst thou deliver him without my Ring?
Or a command from mine own mouth? that Cabinet
That holds my heart, you unconsiderate asse,
Thou brainlesse Ideot.

speeches.speaker: Cas.
verse: I saw you go with him,
At their first word commit your person to him,
And made no scruple; he is your brothers Gentleman,
And for any thing I know, an honest man;
And might not I upon the same security deliver him a box?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: A Bottle-head.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You shall have cause to chafe, as I will handle it.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: I had rather thou hadst delivered me to Pirats,
Betraid me to uncurable diseases,
Hung up my Picture in a Market place,
And sold me to wilde bawds.

speeches.speaker: Cassan.
verse: As I take it Madam,
Your Maidenhead lyes not in that Cabinet,
You have a Closer, and you keep the key too,
Why are you vext thus?

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: I could curse thee wickedly,
And wish thee more deformed then age can make thee,
Perpetuall hunger, and no teeth to satisfie it,
Waight on thee still, nor sleep be found to ease it:
Those hands that gave the Casket, may the Palfie
For ever make unusefull, even to feed thee;
Long winters, that thy bones may turne to Isicles
No Hell can thaw againe, inhabit by thee.
Is thy care like thy body, all on crookednesse?
How scurvily thou criest now? like a drunkard,
Ile have as pure teares from a durty spout:
Do, sweare thou didst this ignorantly, sweare it,
Sweare and be damn'd, thou halfe witch.

speeches.speaker: Cassan.
verse: These are fine words, well Madam, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: 'Tis not well thou mummy,
'Tis impudently, basely done, thou durty—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Has your young sanctity done railing, Madam,
Against your innocent Squire? do you see this Sonnet?
This loving Script? do you know from whence it came too?

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: I do, and dare avouch it pure and honest.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You have private Visitants, my noble Lady,
That in sweet numbers court your goodly vertues,
And to the height of adoration.

speeches.speaker: Evan,
verse: Well Sir,
There's neither Heresie nor Treason in it.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: A Prince may beg at the doore; whilst these feast with ye;
A favour or a grace, from such as I am.
Course, common things. You are welcome; pray come neer, Sir,
Do you know this paper?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I am betray'd; I do Sir,
'Tis mine, my hand and heart, if I die for her,
I am thy Martyr, Love, and time shall honour me.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: You sawcy Sir, that came in my Ladies name,
For her guilt Cabinet, you cheating Sir too,
You scurvy Usher, with as scurvy leggs,
And a worse face, thou poore base hanging holder,
How durst thou come to me with a lye in thy mouth?
An impudent lye?

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: Hollow, good Jill, you hobble.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: A stinking lye, more stinking then the teller,
To play the pilfring knave, there have been rascals
Brought up to fetch and carry like your Worship,
That have been hang'd for lesse, whipt there are daily
And if the Law will do me right—

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: What then old Maggot?

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Thy mother was carted younger; Ile have thy hide,
Thy mangy hide, embroder'd with a dog-whip,
As it is now with potent Pox, and thicker.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Peace, good antiquity, Ile have your bones else
Ground into Gunpowder to shoot at Cats with;
One word more, and Ile blanch thee like an Almond,
There's no such cure for the she-falling-sicknesse,
As the powder of a dried bawds skin, be silent,
You are very prodigall of your service here, Sir,
Of your life more it seems.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I repent neither,
Because Your Grace shall understand it comes
From the best part of love, my pure affection,
And kindled with chaste flame, I will not fly from it,
If it be error to desire to marry,
And marry her that sanctity would dote on,
I have done amisse; if it be a Treason
To graft my soule to vertue, and to grow there,
To love the tree that beares such happinesse;
Conceive me, Sir, this fruit was ne're forbidden;
Nay, to desire to taste too, I am Traytor;
Had you but plants enough of this blest Tree, Sir,
Set round about your Court to beautifie it,
Deaths twice so many, to dismay the aproachers,
The ground would scarce yeeld graves to noble Lovers,

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis well maintain'd, you wish and pray to fortune,
Here in your Sonnet, and she has heard your prayers,
So much you dote upon your owne undoing,
But one Month to injoy her as your wife,
Though at the expiring of that time you die for't.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I could wish many, many ages Sir,
To grow as old as time in her imbraces,
If heaven would grant it, and you smile upon it;
But if my choice were two houres, and then perish,
I would not pull my heart back.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You have your wish,
To'morrow I will see you nobly married,
Your Month take out in all content and pleasure;
The first day of the following Month you dye for't;
Kneele, not, not all your prayers can divert me;
Now marke your sentence, mark it scornfull Lady,
If when Valerio's dead, within twelve houres,
For thar's your latest time, you finde not out
Another husband on the same condition
To marry you againe, you dye your self too.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Now you are mercifull, I thank your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Fre.
verse: If when you are married, you but seek to scape
Out of the Kingdome, you, or she, or both,
Or to infect mens minds with hot commotions,
You dye both instantly; will you love me now Lady?
My tale will now be heard, but now I scorne ye.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Is our faire love, our honest, our intire,
Come to this hazard?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Tis a noble one, and I am much in love with malice for it,
Envy could not have studied me a way,
Nor fortune pointed out a path to honour,
Straighter and nobler, if she had her eyes:
When I have once injoyed my sweet Evanthe,
And blest my youth with her most deere Imbraces,
I have done my journey here, my day is out,
All that the world has else is foolery,
Labour, and losse of time, what should I live for?
Think but mans life a moneth, and we are happy.
I would not have my joyes grow old for any thing;
A paradise, as thou art my Evanthe,
Is only made to wonder at a little,
Enough for humane eyes, and then to wander from.
Come do not weep, sweet, you dishonour me,
Your teares and griefes but question my ability,
Whether I dare dye: Do you love intirely?

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: You know I do.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Then grudge not my felicity.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Ile to the Queene.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Do any thing that's honest,
But if you sue to him in death, I hate you.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: WAs there ever heard of such a marriage?

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Marriage and hanging go by destiny,
'Tis the old proverb, now they come together.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: But a month married, then to lose his life for't?
I would have a long month sure that payes the Souldiers,

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Or get all the Almanacks burnt, that were a rare trick,
And have no month remembred. How now Tony?
Whose water are you casting?

speeches.speaker: Tony.
verse: A sick Gentlemans,
Is very sick, much troubled with the stone,
He should not live above a month by his Urine,
About Saint Davids day it will go hard with him,
He will then be troubled with a paine in his neck too.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: A pestilent foole; when wilt thou marry Tony?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: When I mean to be hangd, & 'tis the surer contract.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: What think you of this marriage of Valerios?

speeches.speaker: Tony.
prose: They have given him a hot custard, and meane to burne his mouth with it; had I knowne he had been given to die honourably, I would have helpt him to a wench, a rare one, should have kill'd him in three weeks, and sav'd the sentence.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: There be them would have spared ten daies of that too.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: It may be so, you have women of all vertues;
There be some Guns that I could bring him too,
Some Morter-peeces that are plac'd i'th Suburbs,
Would teare him into quartets in two houres;
There be also of the race of the old Cockatrices,
That would dispatch him with once looking on him.

speeches.speaker: Men.
prose: What Month wouldst thou chuse Tony, if thou hadst the like fortune?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
prose: I would chuse a mull'd Sack month, to comfort my belly, for sure my back would ake for't, and at the months end I would be most dismally drunk, & scorn the gallows.

speeches.speaker: Me.
prose: I would chuse March, for I would come in like a Lion.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: But you'ld go out like a Lamb, when you went to hanging.

speeches.speaker: Ca.
verse: I would take April, take the sweet o'th year,
And kisse my wench upon the tender flowrets,
Tumble on every Greene, and as the birds sung,
Embrace and melt away my soule in pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: You would go a Maying gayly to the gallowes.

speeches.speaker: Clean.
verse: Prethee tell us some newes.

speeches.speaker: Tony.
verse: Ile tell ye all I know,
You may be honest and poore fooles, as I am,
And blow your fingers ends.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: That's no newes foole.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: You may be knaves then, when you please, starke knaves,
And build faire houses, but your heires shall have none of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: These are undoubted.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Truth is not worth the hearing,
Ile tell you newes then, There was a drunken Saylor,
That got a Marmaid with childe as she went a milking,
And now she sues him in the bawdy Court for it,
The infant Monster is brought up in fish-street.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: I, this is somthing.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Ile tell you more, There was a fish taken,
A monstrous fish, with a sword by his side, a long sword,
A pike in's neck, and a gun in's nose, a huge gun,
And letters of Mart in's mouth, from the Duke of Florence.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: This is a monstrous lye.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: I do confesse it;
Do you think I would tell you truths, that dare not heare 'em?
You are honest things, we Courtiers scorn to converse with

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: A plaguy foole, but lets consider Gentl.
Why the Queen strives not to oppose this sentence,
The Kingdomes honour suffers in this cruelty.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: No doubt the Queen, though she be vertuous,
Winks at the marriage, for by that only meanes
The Kings flame lessens to the youthfull Lady,
If not goes out, within this month, I doubt not,
She hopes to rock a sleep his anger also;
Shall we go see the preparation?
'Tis time, for strangers come to view the wonder.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
prose: Come, lets away, send my friends happier weddings.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: You shall be merry, come, Ile have it so,
Can there be any nature so unnoble?
Or anger so unhumane to pursue this?

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: I feare there is.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: Your feares are poore and foolish,
Though he be hasty, and his anger death,
His will like torrents, not to be resisted,
Yet Law and Justice go along to guide him;
And what Law or what Justice can he finde
To justifie his will? what Act or Statute,
By Humane or Divine establishment,
Left to direct us, that makes marriage death?
Honest faire wedlock? 'twas given for increase,
For preservation of mankinde I take it;
He must be more then man then, that dare break it;
Come dresse ye handsomly, you shall have my Jewels,
And put a face on that contemnes base fortune,
'Twill make him more insult to see you fearfull,
Outlooke his anger.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: O my Valerio!
Be witnesse my pure minde, 'tis thee I grieve for.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: But shew it not, I would so crucifie him
With an innocent neglect of what he can do,
A brave strong pious scorne, that I would shake him;
Put all the wanton Cupids in thine eyes,
And all the graces on that nature gave thee,
Make up thy beauty to that height of excellence,
Ile help thee, and forgive thee, as if Venus
Were now againe to catch the God of Warre,
In his most rugged anger, when thou hast him
(As 'tis impossible he should resist thee)
And kneeling at thy conquering feet for mercy,
Then shew thy vertue, then againe despise him
And all his power, then with a looke of honour,
Mingled with noble chastity, strike him dead.

speeches.speaker: Eva.
verse: Good Madam dresse me,
You arme me bravely.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: Make him know his cruelty
Begins with him first, he must suffer for it,
And that thy sentence is so welcome to thee,
And to thy noble Lord, You long to meet it.
Stamp such a deep impression of thy beauty
Into his soule, and of thy worthinesse,
That when Valerio and Evanthe sleep
In one rich earth, hung round about with blessings,
He may run mad, and curse his act; be lusty,
Ile teach thee how to die too, if thou fear'st it.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I thank your Grace, you have prepar'd me strongly,
And my weak minde.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: Death is unwelcome never,
Unlesse it be to tortur'd mindes and sick soules,
That make their own Hells; 'tis such a benefit
When it comes crown'd with honour, shews so sweet too,
Though they paint it ugly, that's but to restraine us,
For every living thing would love it else,
Fly boldly to their peace, ere nature call'd 'em;
The rest we have from labour, and from trouble,
Is some incitement, every thing alike,
The poore slave that lies private has his liberty,
As amply as his Master, in that Tombe,
The earth as light upon him, and the flowers
That grow about him, smell as sweet, and flourish,
But when we love with honour to our ends,
When memory and vertues are our mourners,
What pleasure's there? they are infinite Evanthe;
Onely, my vertuous wench, we want our sences,
That benefit we are barr'd, 'twould make us proud else,
And lazy to look up to happier life,
The blessings of the people would so swell us.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Good Madam dresse me, you have drest my soul,
The merriest Bride ile be for all this misery,
The proudest to some eyes too.

speeches.speaker: Que.
verse: 'Twill do better, come shrink no more.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I am too confident.

speeches.speaker: Sora.
verse: You are too remisse and wanton in your angers,
You mold things hansomly, and then neglect 'em;
A powerfull Prince should be constant to his power still,
And hold up what he builds, then people feare him;
When he lets loose his hand, it shewes a weaknesse,
And men examine or contemne his greatnesse;
A scorne of this high kinde should have cal'd up
A revenge equall, not a pitty in you.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She is thy sister.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: And she were my mother,
Whilst I conceive she has you wrong'd, I hate her,
And shake her neernesse off; I study, Sir,
To satisfie your angers that are just,
Before your pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I have done that already,
I feare has pull'd to many curses on me.

speeches.speaker: Sora.
verse: Curses or envies, on Valerio's head,
Would you take my counsell, Sir, they should all light,
And with the weight, not only crack his scull,
But his faire credit; the exquisite vexation
I have devis'd, so please you give way in't,
And let it worke, shall more afflict his soule,
And trench upon that honour that he brags of,
Then feare or death in all the frights he carries;
If you sit downe here they will both abuse ye,
Laugh at your poore relenting powre, and scorne ye;
What satisfaction can their deaths bring to you,
That are prepar'd and proud to dye, and willingly,
And at their ends will thank you for that honour?
How are you nearer the desire you aim at?
Or if it be revenge your anger covets,
How can their single deaths give you content, Sir?
Petty revenges end in blood, sleight angers,
A Princes rage should finde out new diseases,
Death were a pleasure too, to pay proud fooles with.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: What should I do?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Adde but your power unto me,
Make me but strong by your protection,
And you shall see what joy, and what delight,
What infinite pleasure this poore mouth shall yeeld him,
Ile make him wish he were dead on's marriage day,
Or bedrid with old age, ile make him curse,
And cry and curse, give me but power.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You have it,
Here take my Ring, I am content he pay for't.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: It shall be now revenge, as I will handle it,
He shall live after this to beg his life too,
Twenty to one by this thread, as ile weave it,
Evanthe shall be yours.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Take all authority, and be most happy.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Good Sir, no more pitty.

speeches.speaker: 1. Wife.
verse: Good Master Tony, put me in.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Where do you dwell?

speeches.speaker: 1. Wife.
verse: Forsooth, at the sign of the great shoulder of Mutton,

speeches.speaker: To.
prose: A hungry man would hunt your house out instantly, Keep the dogs from your doore; Is this Lettice Ruffe your husband? a fine sharp sallet to your signe.

speeches.speaker: 2. Wife.
verse: Will you put me in too?

speeches.speaker: 3. Wife.
verse: And me, good Master Tony.

speeches.speaker: Tony.
verse: Put ye all in? you had best come twenty more; you
Think 'tis easie, a trick of legerdemaine, to put ye all in,
'Twould pose a fellow that had twice my body,
Though it were all made into chines and fillets.

speeches.speaker: 2. W.
verse: Puts into'th wedding, Sir, we would fain see that.

speeches.speaker: 1. W.
verse: And the brave Masque too.

speeches.speaker: To.
verse: You two are pretty women, are you their husbands?

speeches.speaker: 2. Citiz.
verse: Yes, for want of better.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: I think so too, you would not be so mad else
To turne 'em loose to a company of young Courtiers,
That swarme like Bees in May, when they see young wenches;
You must not squeak.

speeches.speaker: 3. W.
verse: No Sir, we are better tutor'd.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Nor if a young Lord offer you the curtesie—

speeches.speaker: 2. W.
verse: We know what 'tis, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Nor you must not grumble,
If you be thrust up hard, we thrust most furiously.

speeches.speaker: 1. W.
verse: We know the worst.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Get you two in then quietly,
And shift for your selves; we must have no old women,
They are out of use, unlesse they have petitions,
Besides they cough so loud they drown the Musick,
You would go in too, but there is no place for ye,
I am sorry for't, go and forget your wives,
Or pray they may be able to suffer patiently.
You may have Heires may prove wise Aldermen,
Go, or ile call the Guard.

speeches.speaker: 3 Citi.
verse: We will get in, wee'l venture broken pates else.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: 'Tis impossible,
You are too securely arm'd; how they flock hether,
And with what joy the women run by heapes
To see this Marriage? they tickle to think of it,
They hope for every moneth a husband too;
Still how they run, and how the wittals follow 'em,
The weake things that are worne between the leggs,
That brushing, dressing, nor new naps can mende,
How they post to see their owne confusion?
This is a merry world.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Looke to the doore sirra,
Thou art a foole, and may'st do mischiefe lawfully.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Give me your hand, you are my brother Foole,
You may both make the Law, and mar it presently.
Do you love a wench?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Who does not foole?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
prose: Not I, unlesse you will give me a longer lease to marry her.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
prose: What are all these that come, what businesse have they?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Some come to gape, those are my fellow fooles;
Some to get home theit wives, those be their own fooles;
Some to rejoyce with thee, those be the times fooles;
And some I feare to curse thee, those are poore fooles.
A set people calls them honest. Looke, looke King, look,
A weather-beaten Lady new carin'd.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: An old one.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: The glasses of her eyes are new rub'd over,
And the worme-eaten records in her face are daub'd up neatly;
She layes her breasts out too, like to poch'd eggs
That had the yelkes suckt out; they get new heads also,
New teeth, new tongues, for the old are all worne-out,
And as 'tis hoped, new tayles.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: For what?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: For old Courtiers,
The young ones are too stirring for their travells.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: God leave your knavery, and helpe to keepe the doore well,
I will have no such presse.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Lay thy hand a thy heart King.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ile have ye whipt.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: The Foole and thou are parted.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Sorano work, and free me from this spell,
'Twixt love and scorne there's nothing felt but hell.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Tye on my Scarfe, you are so long about me,
Good my Lords help, give me my other Cloke,
That Hat and Feather, Lord what a Taylor's this,
To make me up thus straight, one sigh would burst me,
I have not roome to breath, come button, button,
Button, apace.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: I am glad to see you merry Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Twould make you merry had you such a wife,
And such an age to injoy her in.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: An age Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: A moneth's an age to him that is contented,
What should I seeke for more? give me my sword.
Ha my good Lords, that every one of you now
Had but a Lady of that youth and beauty
To blesse yourselves this night with, would ye not?
Pray ye speak uprightly.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: We confesse ye happy,
And we could well wish such another Banquet,
But on that price my Lord—

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Twere nothing else,
No man can ever come to aime at Heaven,
But by the knowledge of a Hell. These shooes are heavy,
And if I should be call'd to dance they'l clog me,
Get me some pumps; ile tell ye brave Camillo,
And you deare friends, the King has honour'd me,
Out of his gracious favour has much honour'd me,
To limit me my time, for who would live long?
Who would be old? 'tis such a wearinesse,
Such a disease, that hangs like lead upon us
As it increases, so vexations,
Griefes of the minde, paines of the feeble body,
Rhumes, coughs, catarrs, we are but our living coffines;
Beside, the faire soules old too, it growes covetous,
Which shewes all honour is departed from us,
And we are earth againe.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: You make faire use Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I would not live to learne to lye Cleanthes
For all the world, old men are prone to that too;
Thou that hast been a Souldier, Menallo
A noble Souldier, and defied all danger,
Adopted thy brave arme the heire to victory,
Would'st thou live so long till thy strength forsooke thee?
Till thou grew'st only a long tedious story
Of what thou hadst been? till thy sword hang by,
And lazie Spiders fill'd the hilt with cobwebs?

speeches.speaker: Men:
verse: No sure, I would not.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Tis not fit ye should,
To dye a young man is to be an Angell,
Our great good parts, put wings to our soules:
Wee'l have a rouse before we go to bed friends,
Pray ye tell me, ist a hansome Maske we have?

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: We understand so.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: And the young gent. dance?

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: They do Sir, and some dance well.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: They must before the Ladies,
Wee'l have a rouse before we go to bed friends,
A lusty one, 'twill make my blood dance too.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Ten if you please.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: And wee'l be wondrous merry,
They stay sure, come, I heare the Musick forward,
You shall have all Gloves presently.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: We attend Sir, but first we must looke to'th
Doores.
The King has charged us.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: What a noyse do you keepe there, call my fellowes
A the Guard; you must cease now untill the King be
Enter'd, he is gone to'th Temple now.

speeches.speaker: 2 Serv.
verse: Looke to that back doore, and keep it fast,
They swarme like Bees about it,

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Keepe back those Citizens, and let their wives in,
Their hansome wives.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: They have crowded me to Vergis,
I sweat like a Butter-box.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: Stand further off there.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Take the women aside, and talk with 'em in privat,
Give 'em that they came for.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: The whole Court cannot do it;
Besides, the next Maske if we use 'em so,
They'l come by millions to expect our largesse;
We have broke a hundred heads.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Are they so tender?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: But 'twas behinde, before they have all murrions.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Let in those Ladies, make 'em roome for shame there.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: They are no Ladies, there's one bald before 'em,
A gent. bald, they are curtall'd queanes in hired clothes,
They come out of Spaine I think, they are very sultry.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: Keep 'em in breath for an Embassadour.
Me thinks my nose shakes at their memories,
What bounsing's that?

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: I am one of the Musick Sir.

speeches.speaker: Within.
verse: I have sweet-meats for the banquet.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Let 'em in.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: They lye my Lord, they come to seeke their wives,
Two broken Citizens.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Breake 'em more, they are but brusled yet.
Bold Rascalls, offer to disturbe your wives.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
verse: Lock the doores fast; the Musick, hark, the King comes.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: Unbinde me, my delight, this night is mine,
Now let me looke upon what Stars here shine,
Let me behold the beauties, then clap high
My cullor'd wings, proud of my Deity;
I am satisfied, binde me agen, and fast,
My angry Bow will make too great a waste
Of beauty else, now call my Maskers in,
Call with a Song, and let the sports begin;
Call all my servants the effects of love,
And to a measure let them nobly move.
Come you servants of proud love,
Come away:
Fairely, nobly, gently move,
Too long, too long you make us stay;
Fancy, Desire, Delight, Hope, Feare,
Distrust and Jealousie, be you too here;
Consuming Care, and raging Ire,
And Poverty in poore attire,
March fairely in, and last Despaire;
Now full Musick strike the Aire.

speeches.speaker: Cup.
verse: Away, I have done, the day begins to light,
Lovers, you know your fate, good night, good night.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: Come to the Banquet, when that's ended Sir,
Ile see you a bed, and so good night; be merry,
You have a sweet bed-fellow.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I thanke your Grace,
And ever shall be bound unto your noblenesse.

speeches.speaker: King.
verse: I pray I may deserve your thankes, set forward.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: THe night growes on, lead softly to the Tombe,
And sing not till I bid ye; let the Musick
Play gently as he passes.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: O faire picture,
That wert the living hope of all our honours;
How are we banisht from the joy we dreamt of?
Will he ne're speak more?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: 'Tis full three moneths Lord Rugio,
Since any articulate sound came from his tongue,
Set him downe gently.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: What should the reason be Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: As 'tis in nature with those loving Husbands,
That sympathize their wives paines, and their throwes
When they are breeding, and 'tis usuall too,
We have it by experience so in him Sir,
In this most noble spirit that now suffers;
For when his honour'd Father good Brandino
Fell sick, he felt the griefes, and labour'd with them,
His sits and his disease he still inherited,
Grew the same thing, and had not nature check'd him,
Strength, and ability, he had dyed that houre too.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: Embleme of noble love!

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: That very minute
His fathers breath forsooke him, that same instant,
A rare example of his piety,
And love paternall, the Organ of his tongue
Was never heard to sound againe; so neare death
He seekes to waite upon his worthy Father,
But that we force his meat, he were one body.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: He points toth' Tombe.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: That is the place he honours,
A house I feare he will not be long out of.
He will toth' Tombe, good my Lord lend your hand;
Now sing the Funerall Song, and let him kneele,
For then he is pleas'd.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: Heaven lend thy powerfull hand,
And ease this Prince.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: He will passe back againe.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: They drink abundantly, I am hot with wine too,
Lustily warme, ile steale now to my happinesse,
'Tis midnight, and the silent houre invites me,
But she is up still, and attends the Queene;
Thou dew of wine and sleep hang on their eye-lids,
Steep their dull sences in the healths they drink,
That I may quickly finde my lov'd Evanthe.
The King is merry too, and dranke unto me,
Signe affaire peace, O this nights blessednesse!
If I had forty heads I would give all for it.
Is not the end of our ambitions,
Of all our humane studies, and our travells,
Of our desires, the obtaining of our wishes?
Certaine it is, and there man makes his Center.
I have obtain'd Enanthe, I have married her,
Can any fortune keep me from injoying her?
I have my wish, what's left me to accuse now?
I am friends with all the world, but thy base malice;
Go glory in thy mischiefes thou proud man,
And cry it to the world thou hast ruin'd vertue;
How I contemne thee and thy petty malice,
And with what scorne I looke downe on thy practice.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse:
You'l sing me a new Song anon
~alerio,
And wish these hot words—

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I despise thee fellow,
Thy threats, or flatteries, all I fling behinde me;
I have my end, I have thy noble Sister,
A name too worthy of thy blood; I have married her,
And will injoy her too.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: 'Tis very likely.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: And that short moneth I have to blesse me with her
Ile make an age, ile reckon each embrace
A yeare of pleasure, and each night a Jubilee,
Every quick kisse a Spring; and when I meane
To lose my selfe in all the delightfulnesse,
Twenty sweet Summers I will tye together
In spight of thee, and thy malignant Master:
I will dye old in love, though young in pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: But that I hate thee deadly, I could pitty thee,
Thou art the poorest miserable thing
This day on earth; ile tell thee why Valerio,
All thou esteemest, and build'st upon for happinesse,
For joy, for pleasure, for delight is past thee,
And like a wanton dreame already vanisht.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Is my love false?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: No, she is constant to thee,
Constant to all thy misery she shall be,
And curse thee too.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Is my strong body weakn'd,
Charm'd, or abus'd with subtle drink? speak villaine.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Neither, I dare speake, thou art still as lusty
As when thou lovsdst her first, as strong and hopefull,
The month thou hast given thee is a month of misery,
And where thou think'st each hower shall yeeld a pleasure
Looke for a killing paine, for thou shalt finde it
Before thou dyest, each minute shall prepare it,
And ring so many knells to sad afflictions;
The King has given thee a long moneth to dye in,
And miserably dye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Undo thy Riddle,
I am prepar'd what ever fate shall follow.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Dost thou see this Ring?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I know it too.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Then marke me,
By vertue of this Ring this I pronounce to thee,
'Tis the Kings will.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Let me know it suddenly.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: If thou dost offer to touch Evanthes body
Beyond a kisse, though thou art married to her,
And lawfully as thou think'st may'st injoy her,
That minute she shall dye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: O Devill—

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: If thou discover this command unto her,
Or to a friend that shall importune thee,
And why thou abstainest, and from whose will, ye all perish,
Upon the self-same forfeit are ye fitted Sir,
Now if ye love her, ye may preserve her life still,
If not, you know the worst, how falls your month out?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: This tyranny could never be invented
But in the schoole of Hell, earth is too innocent;
Not to injoy her when she is my wife?
When she is willing too?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: She is most willing,
And will run mad to misse; but if you hit her,
Be sure you bit her home, and kill her with it;
There are such women that will dye with pleasure:
The Axe will follow else, that will not faile
To fetch her Maiden-head, and dispatch her quickly;
Then shall the world know you are the cause of Murther,
And as 'tis requisite your life shall pay for't.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Thou dost but jest, thou canst not be so moostrous
As thou proclaim'st thy selfe; thou art her Brother,
and there must be a feeling heart within thee
Of her afflictions; wert thou a stranger to us,
And bred amongst wilde rocks, thy nature wilde too,
Affection in thee as thy breeding, cold,
And unrelenting as the rocks that nourisht thee,
Yet thou must shake to tell me this; they tremble
When the rude sea threatens divorce amongst 'em,
They that are sencelesse things shake at a tempest;
Thou art a man—

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Be thou too then, 'twill try thee,
And patience now will best become thy noblenesse.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Invent some other torment to afflict me,
All, if thou please, put all afflictions on me,
Study thy braines out for 'em, so this be none
I care not of what nature, nor what cruelty,
Nor of what length.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: This is enough to vex ye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: The tale of Tantalus is now prov'd true,
And from me shall be registred Authentick;
To have my joyes within my armes, and lawfull,
Mine owne delights, yet dare not touch.
Even as thou hatest me Brother, let no young man know this,
As thou shalt hope for peace when thou most needest it,
Peace in thy soule, desire the King to kill me,
Make me a traitor, any thing, ile yeeld to it,
And give thee cause so I may dye immediatly;
Lock me in Prison where no Sun may see me,
In walls so thick no hope may ere come at me;
Keep me from meat, and drink, and sleep, ile blesse thee;
Give me some damned potion to deliver me,
That I may never know my selfe againe, forget
My Country kindred, name and fortune; last,
That my chaste love may never appeare before me,
This were some comfort.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: All I have I have brought ye,
And much may it do ye with it my deare Brother,
See ye observe it well; you will finde about ye
Many eyes set, that shall o're-looke your actions,
If you transgresse ye know, and so I leave ye,

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Heaven be not angry, and I have some hope yet,
And when you please, and how allay my miseries.
To whom I kneele be mercifull unto me,
Looke on my harmelesse youth Angels of pitty,
And from my bleeding heart wipe off my sorrowes,
The power, the pride, the malice and injustice
Of cruell men are bent against mine innocence.
You that controwle the mighty wills of Princes,
And bow their stubborne armrs, look on my weaknesse,
And when you please, and how, allay my miseries.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Hast thou been with him?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Yes, and given him that Sir
Will make him curse his Birth; I told ye which way,
Did you but see him Sir, but look upon him,
With what a troubled and dejected nature
He walkes now in a mist, with what a silence,
As if he were the shrowd he wrapt himselfe in,
And no more of Valerio but his shadow,
He seekes obscurity to hide his thoughts in,
You would wonder and admire for all you know it,
His jollity is downe, valed to the ground Sir,
And his high hopes of full delights and pleasures
Are turn'd tormenters to him, strong diseases.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: But is there hope of her?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: It must fall necessary
She must dislike him, quarrell with his person,
For women once deluded are next Devills,
And in the height of that opinion Sir,
You shall put on againe, and she must meet ye,

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I am glad of this.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Ile tell ye all the circumstance
Within this houre, but sure I heard your Grace
To day as I attended, make some stops,
Some broken speeches, and some fighs between,
And then your Brothers name I heard distinctly,
And some sad wishes after.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ye are i'th right Sir,
I would he were as sad as I could wish him,
Sad as the earth.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Would ye have it so?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Thou hearest me,
Though he be sick with small hope of recovery,
That hope still lives, and mens eyes live upon it,
And in their eyes their wishes; my Soram,
Were he but cold once in the tombe he dotes on,
As 'tis the fittest place for melancholly,
My Court should be another Paradice,
And flow with all delights.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Go to your pleasures, let me alone with this,
Hope shall not trouble ye, nor he three dayes.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I shall be bound unto thee.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Ile do it neatly too, no doubt shall catch me.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Be gone, they are going to bed, ile bid good night to 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
prose: And mark the man, you'le scarce know 'tis Valerio.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Cheere up my noble Lord, the minutes Come,
You shall injoy the abstract of all sweetnesse,
We did you wrong you need no wine to warme ye,
Desire shoots through your eyes like sudden wild-fires.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Beshrew me Lo^ds, the wine has made me dull,
I am I know not what.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Good pleasure to ye,
Good night and long too, as you finde your appetite
Yon may fall too.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I do beseech your Grace,
For which of all my loves and services
Have I deserved this:

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I am not bound to answer ye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Nor I bound to obey in unjust actions.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Do as you please, you know the penalty,
And as I have a soule it shall be executed;
Nay look not pale, I am not used to feare Sir,
If you respect your Lady, good night to ye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: But for respect to her and to my duty,
That reverent duty that I owe my Soveraigne,
Which anger has no power to snatch me from,
The good night should be thine; good night for ever,
The King is wanton Lords, he would needs know of me
How many nick chases I would make to night.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: My Lord, no doubt you'l prove a perfect gamester.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Faith no, I am unacquainted with the pleasure,
Bungle a set I may, how my heart trembles,
And beats my breast as it would breake his way out
Good night my noble friends.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: Nay we must see you toward your bed my Lord:

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Good faith it needs not,
'Tis late, and I shall trouble you.

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: No, no, till the Bride come Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I beseech you leave me,
You will make me bashfull else, I am so foolish,
Besides, I have some few devotions Lords,
And he that can pray with such a book in's armes —

speeches.speaker: Cam.
verse: Wee'l leave ye then, and a sweet night wait upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Men.
verse: And a sweet issue of this sweet night crown ye.

speeches.speaker: Cle.
verse: All nights and dayes be such till you grow old Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I thank ye, 'tis a curse sufficient for me,
A labour'd one too, though you meane a blessing.
What shall I do, I am like a wretched Debtor,
That has a summe to tender on the forfeit
Of all he is worth, yet dare not offer it.
Other men see the Sun, yet I must wink at it;
And though I know 'tis perfect day, deny it:
My veines are all on fire, and burne like Aetna,
Youth and desire beat larums to my blood,
And adde fresh fuell to my warme affections.
I must injoy her, yet when I consider,
When I collect my selfe, and weigh her danger,
The Tyrants will, and his powre taught to murther,
My tender care controlls my blood within me,
And like a cold fit of a peevish Ague
Creepes to my soule, and flings an Ice upon me.
That locks all powres of youth up but prevention;
O what a blessednesse 'twere to be old now,
To be unable, bed-rid with diseases,
Or halt on Crutches to meet holy Hymen;
What a rare benefit, but I'am curst
That that speakes other men most freely happy,
And makes all eyes hang on their expectations,
Must prove the bane of me youth, and ability.
She comes to bed, how shall I entertaine her?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Nay I come after too, take the foole with ye,
For lightly he is ever one at Weddings.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Evanthe, make ye unready, our Lord staies for ye,
And prethee be merry.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Be very merry, Chicken,
Thy Lord will pipe to thee anon, and make thee dance too.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Will he so, good-man asse.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Yes goody filly,
And you had such a Pipe, that piped so sweetly,
You would dance to death, you have learnt your sinque a pace.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Your Grace desires that that is too free in me,
I am merry at the heart.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
prose: Thou wilt be anon, the young smug Boy will give thee a sweet cordiall.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I am so taken up in all my thoughts,
So possest Madam with the lawfull sweets
I shall this night partake of with my Lord,
So far transported (pardon my immmodesty)

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Alas poore wench, how shall I recompence thee?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: That though they must be short, and snatcht away too,
E're they grow ripe, yet I shall far prefer 'em
Before a tedious pleasure with repentance.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: O how my heart akes.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Take off my Jewells Ladies,
And let my Ruffe loose, I shall bid good night to ye,
My Lord staies here.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: My wench, I thank thee heartily,
For learning how to use thy few houres hansomly,
They will be yeares I hope; off with your Gowne now,
Lay downe the bed there?

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Shall I get into it and warme it for thee, a Fooles fire is a fine thing,
And I'll so busse thee.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Ile have ye whipt ye rascall.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: That will provoke me more, ile talke with thy husband,
He's a wise man I hope.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Good night deare Madam,
Ladies, no further service, I am well,
I do beseech your Grace to give us this leave,
My Lord and I to one another freely,
And privately, may do all other Ceremonies,
Women and Page wee'l be to one another,
And trouble you no farther.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Art thou a wise man?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I cannot tell thee Tony, aske my neighbours.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: If thou beest so, go lye with me to night,
The old foole will lye quieter then the young one,
And give thee more sleep, thou wilt looke to morrow else
Worse then the prodigall foole the Ballad speakes of,
That was sqeez'd through a horne.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I shall take thy counsell.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Why then good night, good night my best Evanthe,
My worthy maid, and as that name shall vanish,
A worthy wife, a long and happy; follow sirra.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: That shall be my care,
Goodnesse rest with your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Be lusty Lord, and take your Lady to ye,
And that power that shall part ye be unhappy.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Sweet rest unto ye, to ye all sweet Ladies;
Tony good night.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: Shall not the Foole stay with thee?

speeches.speaker: Quee.
verse: Come away Sirra.

speeches.speaker: Ton.
verse: How the Foole is sought for, sweet Malt is made of easie fire,
A hasty horse will quickly tire, a sudden leaper sticks i'th mire,
Phlebotomy and the word lye nier, take heed of friend I thee require;
This from an Almanack I stole, and learnt this Lesson from a foole.
Good night my Bird.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Good night wise Master Tony;
Will ye to bed my Lord? Come, let me help ye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: To bed Evanthe, art thou sleepy?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: No, I shall be worse if you look sad upon me,
Pray ye let's to bed.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I am not well my love.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Ile make ye well, there's no such Phisick for ye
As your warme Mistris armes.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Art thou so cunning?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I speake not by experience, pray ye mistake not;
But if you love me—

speeches.speaker: ~al.
verse: I do love so dearely,
So much above the base bent of desire
I know not how to answer thee.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: To bed then,
There I shall better credit yea; sie my Lord,
Will ye put a maid too't, to teach ye what to do?
An innocent maid? Are ye so cold a Lover?
Intruth you make me blush, 'tis midnight too,
And 'tis no stolne love, but authorised openly,
No sin we covet, pray let me undresse ye,
You shall help me; prethee sweet Valerio;
Be not so sad, the King will be more mercifull.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: May not I love thy minde?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: And I yours too,
'Tis a most noble one, adorn'd with vertue;
But if we love not one another really,
And put our bodies and our mindes together,
And so make up the concord of affection,
Our love will prove but a blinde superstition:
This is no schoole to argue in my Lord,
Nor have we time to talke away allow'd us,
Pray let's dispatch, if any one should come
And finde us at this distance, what would they think?
Come, kisse me and to bed.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: That I dare do, and kisse againe.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Spare not, they are your owne Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: But to injoy thee is to be luxurious,
Too sensuall in my love, and too ambitious;
O how I burne! to pluck thee from the stalke,
Where now thou grow'st a sweet bud and a beauteous,
And bear'st the prime and honour of the Garden,
Is but to violate thy spring, and spoile thee.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: To let me blow, and fall alone would anger ye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Let's sit together thus, and as we sit
Feed on the sweets of one anothers soules,
The happinesse of love is contemplation,
The blessednesse of love is pure affection,
Where no allay of actuall dull desire,
Of pleasure that partakes with wantonnesse,
Of humane fire that burnes out as it kindles,
And leaves the body but a poore repentance,
Can ever mix, let's sixe on that Evanthe,
That's everlasting, the tother casuall;
Eternity breeds one, the other Fortune,
Blinde as her selfe, and full of all afflictions.
Shall we love vertuously?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I ever loved so.

speeches.speaker: Val
verse: And only think our love; the rarest pleasure,
And that we most desire, let it be humane,
If once injoyed growes stale, and cloyes our appetites;
I would not lessen in my love for any thing,
Nor finde thee but the same in my short journey,
For my loves safety.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Now I see I am old Sir,
Old and ill-favour'd too, poore and despis'd,
And am not worth your noble Fellowship,
Your fellowship in Love, you would not else
Thus cunningly seeke to betray a maid,
A maid that honours you thus piously;
Strive to abuse the pious love she brings ye.
Farewell my Lord, since ye have a better Mistris,
For it must seeme so, or ye are no man,
A younger, happier, I shall give her roome,
So much I love ye still.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Stay my Evanthe;
Heaven beare me witnesse, thou art all I love,
All I desire, and now have pitty on me,
I never lyed before; forgive me Justice,
Youth and affection stop your eares unto me.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Why do you weep? if I have spoke too harshly,
And unbeseeming my beloved Lord,
My care and duty, pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: O heare me,
Heare me Evanthe; I am all on torture
And this lye tears my conscience as I vent it;
I am no man.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: How Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: No man for pleasure, no womans man,

speeches.speaker: Evan.
prose: Goodnesse forbid my Lord, sure you abuse your selfe:

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Tis true Evanthe;
I shame to say you will finde it.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: He weepes bitterly,
'Tis my hard fortune, blesse all young maids from it;
Is there no help my Lord in Art will comfort ye?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I hope there is.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: How long have you been destitute?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Since I was young.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: 'Tis hard to dye for nothing,
Now you shall know 'tis not the pleasure Sir,
(For I am compell'd to love you spiritually)
That women aime at I affect ye for,
'Tis for your worth; and kisse me, be at peace,
Because I ever loved ye I still honour'd ye,
And with all duty to my Husband follow ye;
Will ye to bed now? ye are asham'd it seemes;
Pigmalion prayed and his cold stone took life,
You do not know with what zeale I shall aske Sir,
And what rare miracle that may worke upon ye;
Still blush? prescribe your Law.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I prethee pardon me,
To bed, and ile sit by thee, and mourne with thee,
Mourne both our fortunes, our unhappy ones:
Do not despise me, make me not more wretched,
I pray to heaven when I am gone Evanthe,
As my poore date is but a span of time now,
To recompence thy noble patience,
Thy love and vertue with a fruitfull husband,
Honest and honourable.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Come, you have made me weep now,
All fond desire dye here, and welcome chastity,
Honour and chastity, do what you please Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: WHat ailes this peece of mischief to looke sad?
He seemes to weep too.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Something is a hatching,
And of some bloody nature too Lord Rugio,
This Crocadile mournes thus cunningly.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Haile holy Father,
And good day to the good Lord Rugio,
How fares the sad Prince I beseech ye Sir?

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: 'Tis like you know, you need not aske that question,
You have your eyes and watches on his miseries
As neare as ours, I would they were as tender.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Can you do him good? as the King and you appointed him,
So he is still, as you desir'd I think too,
For every day he is worse (Heaven pardon all)
Put off your sorrow, you may laugh now Lord,
He cannot last long to disturbe your Master,
You have done worthy service to his Brother,
And he most memorable love.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: You do not know Sir
With what remorse I aske, nor with what wearinesse
I grone and bow under this load of honour,
And how my soule sighs for the beastly services,
I have done his pleasures, these be witnesse with me,
And from your piety beleeve me Father,
I would as willingly unclothe my selfe
Of title, that becomes me not I know;
Good men, and great names best agree together;
Cast off the glorious favours, and the trappings
Of sound and honour, wealth and promises,
His wanton pleasures have flung on my weaknesse,
And chuse to serve my Countries cause and vertues,
Poorely and honestly, and redeeme my rulnes,
As I would hope remission of my mischiefes.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: Old and experienc'd men my Lord Sorano,
Are not so quickly caught with gilt hypocrisie,
You pull your clawes in now and fawne upon us,
As Lyons do to intice poore foolish beasts;
And beasts we should be too if we beleeved ye,
Go exercise your Art.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: For heaven sake scorne me not,
Nor adde more hell to my afflicted soule
Then I feele here; as you are honourable,
As you are charitable looke gently on me,
I will no more to Court, be no more Devill.
I know I must be hated even of him
That was my Love now, and the more he loves me
For his foule ends, when they shall once appeare to him,
Muster before his conscience and accuse him,
The fouler and the more falls his displeasure,
Princes are fading things, so are their favours.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: He weeps agen, his heart is toucht sure with remorce.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: See this, and give me faire attention good my Lord,
And worthy Father see, within this violl
The remedy and cure of all my honour,
And of the sad Prince lyes.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: What new trick's this?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: 'Tis true, I have done Offices abundantly
Ill, and prodigious to the Prince Alphonso,
And whilst I was a knave I sought his death too.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: You are too late convicted to be good yet.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: But Father, when I felt this part afflict me,
This inward, and call'd me to an audit
Of my misdeeds and mischiefes—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Well, go on Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: O then, then, then, what was my glory then Father?
The favour of the King, what did that ease me?
What was it to be bow'd to by all creatures?
Worshipt, and courted, what did this availe me?
I was a wretch, a poore lost wretch.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Still better.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Till in the midst of all my griefe I found
Repentance, and a learned man to give the meanes to it,
A Jew, an honest and a rare Phisition,
Of him I had this Jewell; 'tis a Jewell,
And at the price of all my wealth I bought it:
If the King knew it I must lose my head,
And willingly, most willingly I would suffer,
A childe may take it, 'tis so sweet in working.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To whom would you apply it too?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: To the sick Prince,
It will in halfe a day dissolve his melancholly.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: I do beleeve, and give him sleep for ever.
What impudence is this, and what base malice,
To make us instruments of thy abuses?
Are we set here to poison him?

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Mistake not, yet I must needs say, 'tis a noble care,
And worthy vertuous servants; if you will see
A flourishing estate againe in Naples,
And great Alphonso reigne that's truly good,
And like himselfe able to make all excellent;
Give him this drink, & this good health unto him.
I am not so desperate yet to kill my selfe,
Never looke on me as a guilty man,
Nor on the water as a speedy poison:
I am not mad, nor laid out all my treasure,
My conscience and my credit to abuse ye;
How nimbly and how cheerefully it workes now
Upon my heart and head, sure I am a new man
There is no sadnesse that I feele within me,
But as it meets it like a lazie vapour
How it flyes off. Here, give it him with speed,
You are more guilty then I ever was,
And worthier of the name of evill subjects:
If but an houre you hold this from his health.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: 'Tis some rare vertuous thing sure, he is a good man,
It must be so, come, let's apply it presently,
And may it sweetly work.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Pray let me heare on't, and carry it close my Lords.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Yes, good Sorano.

speeches.speaker: Sor.
verse: Do my good fooles, my honest pious coxcombs,
My wary fooles too, have I caught your wisedomes,
You never dream't I knew an Antidote,
Nor how to take it to secure mine owne life;
I am an asse, go, give him the fine cordiall,
And when you have done go dig his grave, good Frier,
Some two houres hence we shall have such a bawling,
And roaring up and downe for Aquavitae,
Such rubbing, and such nointing, and such cooling,
I have sent him that will make a bonefire in's belly,
If he recover it, there is no heat in Hell sure.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Podrano?

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Call hither Lord Valerio, and let none trouble us.

speeches.speaker: Pod.
verse: It shall be done Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I know he wants no additions to his tortures,
He has enough for humane blood to carry,
Yet I must vex him further;
So many that I wonder his hot youth
And high-bred spirit breakes not into fury;
I must yet torture him a little further,
And make my selfe sport with his miseries,
My anger is too poore else. Here he comes,
Now my young married Lord, how do you feele your self?
You have the happinesse you ever aimed at
The joy and pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Would you had the like Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You tumble in delights with your sweet Lady,
And draw the minutes out in deare embraces,
You live a right Lords life.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Would you had tryed it,
That you might know the vertue but to suffer,
Your anger though it be unjust and insolent,
Sits hansomer upon you then your scorne,
To do a wilfull ill and glory in it,
Is to do it double, double to be damn'd too.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Hast thou not found a loving and free Prince,
High in his favours too; that has confer'd
Such hearts ease, and such heapes of comfort on thee,
All thou coudest aske.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: You are too growne a tyrant
Upon so suffering, and so still a subject;
You have put upon me such a punishment,
That if your youth were honest it would blush at:
But you are a shame to nature, as to vertue.
Pull not my rage upon ye, 'tis so just,
It will give way to no respect; my life,
My innocent life, I dare maintaine it Sir,
Like a wanton prodigall you have flung away,
Had I a thousand more I would allow 'em,
And be as carelesse of 'em as your will is;
But to deny those rights the Law has given me,
The holy Law, and make her life the pennance,
Is such a studied and unheard of malice,
No heart that is not hyred from Hell dare think of;
To do it then too, when my hopes were high,
High as my blood, all my desires upon me,
My free affections ready to embrace her,
And she mine owne; do you smile at this, ist done well?
Is there not heaven above you that sees all?
Come hither Time, how does your noble Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: As a Gentlewoman may do in her case that's newly married Sir:
Sickly sometimes, and fond on't, like your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She is breeding then?

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: She wants much of her cullour,
And has her qualmes as Ladies use to have Sir,
And her disgusts.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And keeps her chamber?

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Yes Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And eats good Brooths and Jellies.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: I am sure she sighs Sir, and weepes, good Lady.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Alas good Lady for it,
She should have one could comfort her Cassandra,
Could turne those teares to joyes, a lusty comforter.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: A comfortable man does well at all houres,
For he brings comfortable things.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Come hither, & hold your face between, you have eaten Onions,
Her breath stinks like a Fox, her teeth are contagious,
These old women are all Elder-pipes, do ye mark me.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Yes Sir, but does your Grace think I am fit,
That am both old and vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Therefore the fitter, the older still the better,
I know thou art as holy as an old Cope,
Yet upon necessary use.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: 'Tis true Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Her feeling sence is fierce still, speake unto her,
You are familiar; speake I say unto her,
Speake to the purpose; tell her this, and this.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Alas, she is honest, Sir, she is very honest,
And would you have my gravity—

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I, I, your gravity will become the cause the better,
Ile looke thee out a Knight shall make thee a Lady too,
A lust Knight, and one that shall be ruled by her;
And adde to these, ile make 'em good, no mincing,
Nor ducking out of nicity good Lady,
But do it home, wee'l all be friends to tell her;
And such a joy—

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: That's It that stirs me up Sir,
I would not for the world attempt her chastity,
But that they may live lovingly hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: For that I urge it too.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: A little evill may well be suffered for a generall good, Sir,
Ile take my leave of your Majesty.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Go fortunately, be speedy too, here comes Valerio,
If his affliction have allayed his spirit
My work has end. Come hither Lord Valerio,
How do you now?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Your Majesty may ghesse,
Not so well, nor so fortunate as you are,
That can tye up mens honest wills and actions.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You have the happinesse you ever aim'd at,
The joy, and pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Would you had the like Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: You tumble in delights with your sweet Lady,
And draw the minutes out in deare embraces,
You lead a right Lords life.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Would you had tryed it,
That you might know the vertue but to suffer,
If anger, though it be unjust and insolent
Sits hansomer upon you then your scorne, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yon cleerly see now brave Valerio
What 'tis to be the rivall to a Prince,
To interpose against a raging Lion;
I know you have suffer'd, infinitely suffer'd,
And with a kinde of pitty I behold it,
And if you dare be worthy of my mercy,
I can yet heale you; yeeld up your Evanthe,
Take off my sentence also.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I fall thus low Sir,
My poore sad heart under your feet I lay,
And all the service of my life.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Do this then, for without this 'twill be impossible,
Part with her for a while.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: You have parted us,
What should I do with that I cannot use Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis well consider'd, let me have the Lady,
And thou shalt see how nobly ile befriend thee,
How all this difference.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Will she come, do you think Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She must be wrought, I know she is too modest,
And gently wrought, and cunningly.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'I is fit Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And secretly it must be done.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: As thought.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ile warrant ye, her honour shall be faire still,
No foyle nor staine shall appeare on that, Valerio,
You see a thousand that beare sober faces,
And shew of as in-imitable modesties;
You would be sworn to that they were pure Matrons,
And most chaste maids; and yet to augment their fortunes
And get them noble friends—

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: They are content Sir,
In private to bestow their beauties on 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: They are so, and they are wise, they know no want for't,
Nor no eye sees they want their honesties.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: If it might be carried thus.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: It shall be Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Ile see you dead first, with this caution,
Why sure I think it might be done.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Yes, easily.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: For what time would your Grace desire her body?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: A moneth or two, it shall be carried still
As if she kept with you, and were a stranger,
Rather a hater of the Grace I offer:
And then I will returne her with such honour—

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Tis very like I dote much on your honour.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: And load her with such favour to Valerio—

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: She never shall claw off, I humbly thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ile make ye both the happiest, and the richest,
And the mightiest too—

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: But who shall work her Sir,
For on my conscience she is very honest,
And will be hard to cut as a rough Diamond?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why you must work her, any thing from your tongue,
Set off with golden and perswasive language,
Urging your dangers too.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: But all this time
Have you the conscience Sir to leave me nothing,
Nothing to play withall?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: There be a thousand, take where thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: May I make bold with your Queene,
She is uselesse to your Grace as it appeals Sir,
And but a loyall wife that may be lost too;
I have a minde to her, and then 'tis equall?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: How Sir?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: 'Tis so Sir, thou most glorious impudence,
Have I not wrongs enow to suffer under,
But thou must pick me out to make a monster?
A hated wonder to the world? Do you start
At my intrenching on your private liberty,
And would you force a hye-way through mine honour,
And make me pave it too? but that thy Queene
Is of that excellence in honesty,
And guarded with Divinity about her,
No loose thought can come neare, nor flame unhollowed,
I would so right my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why take her to ye,
I am not vext at this, thou shalt injoy her,
Ile be thy friend if that may win thy courtesie.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I will not be your Bawd though for your Royalty
Was I brought up, and nourisht in the Court,
With thy most Royall Brother and thy selfe,
Upon thy Fathers charge, thy happy Fathers,
And suckt the sweetnesse of all humane Arts,
Learnt armes and honour to become a rascall;
Was this the expectation of my youth,
My growth of honour? Do ye speak this truly,
Or do ye try me Sir? for I beleeve not,
At least I would not, and me thinks 'tis impossible
There should be such a Devill in a Kings shape,
Such a malignant Fiend.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I thank ye Sir,
To morrow is your last day, and looke to it,
Get from my light, away.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Ye are, Oh, my heat's too high and full to think upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: You think it fit then mortified Cassandra,
That I should be a Whore?

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Why a whore, Madam?
If every woman that upon necessity
Did a good turne, for there's the maine point, mark it,
Were term'd a whore, who would be honest, Madam?
Your Lords life and your owne are now in hazard,
Two precious lives may be redeem'd with nothing,
Little or nothing; say an houres or dayes sport,
Or such a toy, the end to it is wantonnesse.
(That we call lust that maidens lose their fame for)
But a compell'd necessity of honour,
