Faire as the day, and cleare as innocence,
Upon my life and conscience a direct way.—

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: To be a rascall.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: 'Tis a kinde of Rape too,
That keeps you cleare, for where your will's compell'd,
Though you yeeld up your body you are safe still.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Thou art grown a learned Bawd, I ever look'd
Thy great sufficiency would breake out.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: You may,
You that are young and faire scorne us old creatures,
But you must know my yeares ere you be wise Lady,
And my experience too; say the King loved ye?
Say it were nothing else?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I marry wench, now thou comest to me.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: Doe you thinke Princes favours are such sleight things,
To fling away when you please? there be young Ladies
Both faire and honourable, that would leap to reach 'em,
And leap aloft too.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Such are light enough;
I am no Valter, wench, but canst thou tell me,
Though he be a King, whether he be sound or no?
I would not give my youth up to infection.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: As found as honour ought to be, I think Lady;
Go too, be wise, I do not bid you try him;
But if he love you well, and you neglect him,
Your Lords life hanging on the hazard of it,
If you be so wilfull proud.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Thou speakest to the point still;
But when I have lyen with him, what am I then, Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: What are you? why the same you are now, a Woman,
A vertuous woman, and a noble woman,
Touching at what is noble, you become so.
Had Lucrecee e're been thought of, but for Tarquin?
She was before a simple unknowne woman,
When she was ravisht, she was a reverent Saint;
And do you think she yeeldee not a little?
And had a kinde of will to have been re-ravisht?
Believe it yes: There are a thousand stories
Of wondrous loyall women, that have slipt,
But it has been on the ice of tender honour,
That kept 'em coole still to the world, I think you are blest,
That have such art occasion in your hands to beget a Chronicle,
A faithfull one.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: It must needs be much honour.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: As you may make it, infinite and safe too,
And when ;tis done, your Lord and you may live
So quietly and peaceably together,
And be what you please.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: But suppose this, wench,
The King should so delight me with his company,
I should forget my Lord, and no more look on him.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: That's the maine hazard, for I tell you truly,
I have heard report speak, is an infinite pleasure,
Almost above beliefe: there be some Ladies,
And modest to the world too, wondrous modest,
That have had the blessednesse to try his body,
That I have heard proclaime him a new Hercules.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: So strongly able?

speeches.speaker: Cassan.
verse: There will be the danger,
You being but a young and tender Lady,
Although your minde be good, yet your weak body,
At first encounter too, to meet with one
Of his unconquer'd strength.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Peace thou rude bawde,
Thou studied old corruptnesse, tye thy tongue up,
Your hired base tongue; is this your timely counsell?
Dost thou seeke to make me dote on wickednesse?
Because 'tis ten times worse then thou deliver'st it?
To be a whore, because he has sufficiency,
To make a hundred? O thou impudence,
Have I relieved thy age to mine owne ruine?
And worne thee in my bosome to betray me?
Can yeares and impotence win nothing on thee
That's good and honest, but thou must go on still?
And where thy blood wants heat to sin thy selfe,
Force thy decreped will to make me wicked.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: I did but tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: What the damned'st woman,
The cunning'st and the skilful'st bawd comes short of:
If thou had'st liv'd ten ages to be dam'd in,
And exercised this art the Devill taught thee,
Thou could'st not have exprest it more exactly.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: I did not bid you sin.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Thou wood'st me to it,
Thou that art fit for prayer and the grave,
Thy body earth already, and corruption,
Thou taught'st the way; go follow your fine function,
There are houses of delight, that want good Matrons,
Such grave instructors, get thee thither monster,
And read variety of sins to wantons,
And whey they rore with paines, learne to make playsters.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: This we have for our good wills.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: If e're I see thee more,
Or any thing that's like thee, to affright me,
By this faire light ile spoile thy bawdery,
Ile leave thee neither eyes nor nose to grace thee,
When thou wantest bread, and common pitty towards thee,
And art a starving in a ditch, think of me,
Then die, and let, the wandering bawds lament thee;
Be gone, I charge thee, leave me.

speeches.speaker: Cass.
verse: You'l repent this.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: She's angry, and t'other crying too, my suit's cold;
Ile make your heart ake, stubborne wench, for this;
Turne not so angry from me, I will speak to you,
Are you growne proud with your delight, good Lady,
So pamper'd with your sport, you scorne to know me?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I scorne ye not, I would you scorn'd not me, Sir,
And forc't me to be weary of my duty,
I know your Grace, would I had never seene ye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Because I love you, because I dote upon ye,
Because I am a man that seeke to please ye.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I have man enough already to content me,
As much, as noble, and as worthy of me,
As all the world can yeeld.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: That's but your modesty,
You have no man, nay never look upon me,
I know it Lady, no man to content ye,
No man that can, or at the least that dare,
Which is a poorer man, and neerer nothing.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Be nobler, Sir, inform'd.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Ile tell thee, wench,
The poore condition of this poorer fellow,
And make thee blush for shame at thine owne errour,
He never tendred yet a husbands duty,
To thy ^rme longing bed.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: How should he know that?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I am sure he did not, for I charg'd him no,
Upon his life I charg'd him, but to try him;
Could any brave or noble spirit stop he e?
Was life to be preser'd before affection?
Lawfull, and long'd for too?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Did you command him?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I did in policy to try his spirit.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: And could he be so dead cold to observe it?
Brought I no beauty? nor no love along with me?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Why what is it that makes me scorne to name him?
I should have lov'd him, if he had venter'd for't,
Nay, doted on his bravery.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Onely charg'd?
And with that spell sit downe? dare men fight bravely
For poore slight things, for drink or ostentation?
And there indanger both their lives and fortunes,
And for their lawfull Loves fly off with feare?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: 'Tis true, and with a cunning base feare too to abuse thee;
Made thee believe, poore innocent Evanthe,
Wretched young girle it was his impotency;
Was it not so? deny it.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: O my anger, at my yeares to be cozen'd with a young man!

speeches.speaker: Fred,
verse: A strong man too, certaine he lov'd ye deerly.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: To have my shame and love mingled together,
And both flung on me like a wait to sinke me,
I would have dyed a thousand times.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: So would any,
Any that had the spirit of a man;
I would have been kill'd in your armes.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I would he had been,
And buried in mine armes, that had been noble,
And what a monument would I have made him?
Upon this breast he should have slept in peace,
Honour, and everlasting love his mourners;
And I still weeping till old time had turn'd me,
And pittying powers above into pure christall.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Hadst thou lov'd me, and had my way been stuck
With deaths, as thick as frosty nights with stars,
I would have ventur'd.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
prose: Sure there is some trick in't; Valerio ne're was coward.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Worse then this too,
Tamer, and seasoning of a baser nature,
He set your woman on ye to betray ye,
Your bawdy woman, or your sin solicitor:
I pray but think what this man may deserve now,
I know he did, and did it to please me too.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Good Sir afflict me not too fast, I feele
I am a woman, and a wrong'd one too,
And sensible I am of my abuses,
Sir, you have loved me.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
prose: And I love thep still, pitty thy wrongs, and dote upon thy person.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: To set my woman on me 'twas too base Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Abominable vilde.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: But I shall fit him.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: All reason and all Law allowes it to ye,
And ye are a foole, a tame foole, if you spare him.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: You may speake now, and happily prevaile too,
And I beseech your Grace be angry with me.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I am at heart. She staggers in her faith,
And will fall off I hope, Ile ply her still.
Thou abused innocence, I suffer with thee
If I should give him life, he would still betray thee;
That foole that feares to dye for such a beauty,
Would for the same feare sell thee unto misery?
I do not say he would have been bawd himself too.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Follow'd thus far? nay then I smell the malice,
It tasts too hot of practis'd wickednesse,
There can be no such man, I am sure no Gentleman:
Shall my anger make me whore, and not my pleasure?
My sudden unconsiderate rage abuse me?
Come home againe, my frighted faith, my vertue,
Home to my heart againe: he be a bawd too?

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: I will not say, he offered faire Evanthe.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Nor do not dare, 'twill bean impudence,
And not an honour for a Prince to lye;
Fie Sir, a person of your ranke to trifle,
I know you do lye.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Lye shamefully, and I could wish my selfe a man but one day,
To tell you openly you lye too, basely.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Take heed wilde foole.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Take thou heed thou tame Devill,
Thou all Pandora's box in a Kings figure,
Thou hast almost whor'd my weake beliefe already,
And like an Engineer blowne up mine honour;
But I shall countermine, and catch your mischiefe,
This little Fort you seeke, I shall man nobly,
And strongly too, with chaste obedience
To my deere Lord, with vertuous thoughts that fsorne ye.
Victorious Tameris nere won more honour
In cutting off the Royall head of Cyrus,
Then I shall do in conquering thee; farewell,
And if thou canst be wise, learne to be good too,
'Twill give thee nobler lights then both thine eyet do;
My poore Lord and my selfe are bound to suffer,
And when I see him faint under your sentence,
Ile tell ye more, it may be then Ile yeeld too.

speeches.speaker: Fred.
verse: Foole, unexampled, shall my anger follow thee?

speeches.speaker: Rugio.
verse: Curst on our sights, our fond credulities,
A thousand curses on the slave that cheated us.
The damn'd slave.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: We have e'ne sham'd our service,
Brought our best care and loyalties to nothing,
'Tis the most fearefull poyson, the most potent,
Heaven give him patience; oh it works most srongly,
And teares him Lord.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: That we should be so stupid,
To trust the arrant'st villaine that e're flatter'd,
The bloodiest too, to believe a few soft words from him,
And give way to his prepar'd teares.

speeches.speaker: Within Alpbonso.
verse: Oh, oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: Harke Fryer Marco, harke, the poore Prince, that we should he such blockheads,
As to be taken with his drinking first?
And never think what Antidotes are made for?
Two wooden sculls we have, and we deserve to be hang'd for't;
For certainly it will be laid to our charge;
As certaine too, it will dispatch him speedily,
Which way to turne, or what to—

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Lets pray, Heavens hand is strong.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: The Poysons strong, you would say.
Would any thing—He comes, let's give him comfort.

speeches.speaker: Alphon.
verse: Give me more ayre, ayre, more ayre, blow, blow,
Open thou Easterne gate, and blow upon me,
Distill thy cold dewes, O thou icy Moone,
And rivers run through my afflicted spirit,
I am all fire, fire, fire, the raging dog star
Raines in my blood, oh which way shall I turne me?
AEtna and all his flames burne in my head,
Fling me into the Ocean or I perish:
Dig, dig, dig, till the springs fly up,
The cold, cold springs, that I may leap into 'em,
And bathe my scorcht limbs in their purling pleasures;
Or shoot me up into the higher Region,
Where treasures of delicious snow are nouirisht,
And banquets of sweet haile.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: Hold him fast Fryer, O how he burnes!

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: What will ye sacrifice me?
Upon the Altar lay my willing body?
And pile your wood up, fling your holy incense?
And as I turne me you shall see all flame,
Consuming flame, stand off me, or you are ashes.

speeches.speaker: Both.
verse: Most miserable wretches.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Bring hither charity
And let me hug her, Flyer, they say she's cold,
Infinite cold, devotion cannot warme her;
Draw me a river of false lovers teares
Cleane through my brest, they are dull, cold, and forgetfull,
And will give ease, let Virgins sigh upon me,
Forsaken soules, the sighs are precious,
Let them all sigh: oh hell, hell, hell, oh horror.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To bed, good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alpha.
verse: My bed will burne about me,
Like Phaeton, in all consuming flashes
I am inclosed, let me fly, let me fly, give roome;
Betwixt the cold beare, and the raging Lyon
Lyes my safe way; O for a cake of ice now,
To clap unto my heart to comfort me;
Decrepid winter hang upon my sholders,
And let me we are thy frozen Isicles
Like Jewels round about my head, to coole me;
My eyes burne out, and sinke into their sockets,
And my infected braine like brimtstone boyles,
I live in hell, and severall furies vex me;
O carry me where no Sun ever shew'd yet
A face of comfort, where the earth is christall,
Never to be dissolv'd, where nought inhabits
But night and cold, and nipping frosts, and winds
That cut the stubborne rocks, and make them shiver;
Set me there friends.

speeches.speaker: Rug.
prose: Hold fast, he must to bed Fryer, what scalding sweats he has?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: He'le scalld in hell for't, that was the cause.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Drinke, drinke, a world of drinke,
Fill all the cups, and all the antick vessels,
And borrow pots, let me have drinke enough,
Bring all the worthy drunkards of the time,
The experienc'd drunkards, let me have them all,
And let them drinke their worst, Ile make them Ideots,
Ile lye upon my Back and swallow Vessels;
Have Rivers made of cooling wine run through me,
Not stay for this mans health, or this great Princes,
But take an Ocean, and begin to all; oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: He cooles a little, now away with him,
And to his warme bed presently.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: No drinke? no winde? no cooling aire?

speeches.speaker: Rug.
verse: You shall have any thing.
His hot fit lessens, Heaven put in a hand now,
And save his life; there's drink Sir in your chamber,
And all coole things.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Away, away, lets fly to'em.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: To say you were impotent, I am asham'd on't,
To make your self no man, to a fresh maid too,
A longing maid, upon her wedding night also,
To give her such a dor.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I prethee pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Had you been drunke, 'thad been excusable,
Or like a Gentleman under the Surgeons hands,
And so not able, there had been some colour,
But wretchedly to take a weaknesse to ye,
A fearefull weaknesse, to abuse your body,
And let a lye worke like a spell upon ye,
A lye, to save your life.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Will you give me leave sweet?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: You have taken too much leave, and too base leave too,
To wrong your Love; hast thou a noble spirit?
And canst thou looke up to the peoples loves,
That call thee worthy, and not blush Valerio?
Canst thou behold me that thou hast betraid thus?
And no shame touch thee?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Shame attend the sinfull, I know my innocence.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Ne're think to face it, that's a double weaknesse,
And shewes thee falser still; the King himselfe,
Though he be wicked, and our Enemy,
But juster then thine, in pitty of my injuries,
Told me the truth.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: What did he tell Evanthe?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: That but to gaine thy life a fortnight longer,
Thy lov'd poore life, thou gav'st up all my duties.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I sweare 'tis false, my life and death a recitall,
I have weir'd 'em both, and finde'em but one fortune,
But Kings are men, and live as men, and dye too,
Have the affections men have, and their falsehoods;
Indeed they have more power to make 'em good;
The King's to blame, it was to save thy life wench,
Thy innocent life, that I forbore thy bed,
For if I had toucht thee thou hadst dyed, he swore it.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: And was not I as worthy to dye nobly?
To make a story for the times that follows,
As he that married me? what weaknesse, Sir,
Or dissability do you see in me,
Either in minde or body? to defraud me
Of Such an opportunity? Do you think I married you
Only for pleasure, or content in lust?
To lull you in mine armes, and kise you hourely?
Was this my end? I might have been a Queen, Sir,
If that had caught me, and have knowne all delicates;
There's few that would have shun'd so faire an offer,
O thou unfaithfull fearefull man, thou hast kill'd me,
In saving me this way, thou hast destroy'd me,
Rob'd me of that thy love can never give more;
To be unable to save me? O misery!
Had I been my Valerio, thou Evanthe,
I would have lyen with thee under a Gallowes,
Though the Hangman had been my Hymen, and the furies
With iron whips and forks, ready to torter me,
I would have hug'd thee too, though hell had gap'd at me;
Save my life! that expected to dye bravely,
That would have woo'd it too? Would I had married
An Eun^h, that had truly no ability,
Then such a fearefull lyar, thou hast done me
A scurvy curtesie, that has undone me.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Ile do no more, since you are so nobly fashion'd,
Made up so strongly, Ile take my share with ye,
Nay Deere, Ile learne of you.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: He weeps too tenderly;
My angers gone, good my Lord pardon me,
And if I have offended, be more angry,
It was a womans flash, a sudden valour,
That could not lye conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I honour ye by all the rights of holy marriage,
And pleasures of chaste love, I wonder at ye,
You appeare the vision of a Heaven unto me,
Stuck all with stars of honour shining cleerly,
And all the motions of your minde celestiall;
Man is a lumpe of earth, the best man spiritlesse,
To such a woman; all our lives and actions
But counterfeits in Arras to this vertue;
Chide me againe, you have so brave an anger,
And flowes so nobly from you, thus deliver'd,
That I could suffer like a childe to heare ye,
Nay make my self guilty of some faults to honour ye.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Ile chide no more, you have rob'd me of my courage.
And with a cunning patience checkt my impudence;
Once more forgivenesse?

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Will this serve Evanthe?
And this my love? Heavens mercy be upon us;
But did he tell no more?

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Only this trifle: You set my woman on me, to betray me;
'Tis true, she did her best, a bad old woman,
It stir'd me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I cannot blame thee, Jewell.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: And me thought when your name was sounded that way—

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: He that will spare no fame, will spare no name Sweet;
Though as I am a man, I am full of weaknesse,
And may slip happily into some ignorance,
Yet at my yeeres to be a bawd, and cozen
Mine owne hopes with my Doctrine—

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: I beleeve not, nor never shall; our time is out to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: Let's be too night then full of fruitfulnesse,
Now we are both of one minde, let's be happy,
I am no more a wanting man Evanthe,
Thy warme embraces shall dissolve that impotence,
And my cold lye shall vanish with thy kisses;
You houres of night be long, 'as when Alemena
Lay by the lusty side of Jupiter;
Keep back the day, and hide his golden beames,
Where the chaste watchfull morning may not finde 'em;
Old doting Tython hold Aurora fast,
And though she blush the day-break from her cheeks,
Conceale her still; thou heavy Walne stand firme,
And stop the quicker revolutions;
Or if the day must come, to spoile our happinesse,
Thou envious Sunne peepe not upon our pleasure,
Thou that all Lovers curse, be farre off from us.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Then let's to bed, and this night in all joyes
And chaste delights —

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Stay, I must part ye both;
It is the Kings command, who bids me tell ye,
To morrow is your last houre.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I obey, Sir,
In Heaven we shall meet, Captaine, where King Frederick
Dare not appeare to part us.

speeches.speaker: Cast.
verse: Mistake me not, though I am rough in doing of my Office,
You shall finde, Sir, you have a friend to honour ye.

speeches.speaker: Val.
verse: I thank ye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Evan.
verse: Pray Captaine tell the King,
They that are sad on Earth, in Heaven shall sing.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: SIr i'me no Boy, i'me deepe in one and twenty,
The second yeare's approaching.

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: A fine time
For a youth to live by his wits then I should thinke,
If e're he meane to make account of any.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Wits Sir?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: I wits Sir, if it be so strange to thee,
I'me sorry I spent that time to get a Foole,
I might have imploy'd my paines a great deale better;
Thou know'st all that I have I ha got by my wits,
And yet to see how urgent thou art too;
It grieves me thou art so degenerate
To trouble me for meanes, I never offer'd it:
My Parents from a Schoole-boy, past nineteen once,
See what these times are growne too, before twenty
I rusht into the world, which is indeed
Much like the Art of Swimming, he that will atteine to't
Must fall plumpe, and duck himselfe at first,
And that will make him hardy and adventurous,
And not stand putting in one foot and shiver,
And then draw tother after, like a quake-buttock;
Well he may make a padler i' the world,
From hand to mouth, but never a brave swimmer,
Borne up by th' chin as I bore up my self.
With my strong industry that never fayl'd me;
For he that lyes borne up with Patrimonies,
Lookes like a long great Asse that swims with bladders,
Come but one prick of adverse fortune to him
He sinkes, because he never try'd to swim
When wit playes with the billowes that choackt him.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Why is it not a fashion for a Father Sir,
Out of his yearely thousands, to allow
His only sonne a competent brace of hundreds,
Or such a toy?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Yes, if he meane to spoyle him,
Or mar his wits he may, but never I
This is my humour Sir, which you'le finde constant;
I love wit so well because I liv'd by't,
That ile give no man power out of my meanes to hurt it,
And that's a kinde of gratitude to my rayser,
Which great ones oft forget; I admire much
This Ages dulnesse, when I scarce writ man,
The first degree that e're I tooke in thriving,
I lay intelligencer close for wenching,
Could give this Lord or Knight a true Certificate
Of all the Maiden-heads extant, how many lay
'Mongst Chamber-maids, how many 'mongst Exchange Wenches,
Though never many there I must confesse,
They have a trick to utter ware so fast;
I knew which Lady had a minde to fall,
Which Gentlewoman new divorc'st, which Trades-man breaking,
The price of every sinner to a haire,
And where to raise each price; which were the Tearmers
That would give Velvet Petty-coates, Tissue Gownes,
Which Peeces, Angells, Suppers, and Halfe crownes;
I knew how to match and make my market,
Could give intelligence where the Pox lay ledger,
And then to see the Letchers shift a point,
'Twas sport and profit too; how they would shun
Their ador'd Mistris chambers, and run fearefully,
Like Rats from burning houses, so brought I
My Clyents a the game still safe together,
And noble Gamesters lov'd me, and I felt it:
Give me a man that lives by his wits say I,
And never left a Groat, there's the true Gallant.
When I grew somewhat pursie, I grew then
In mens opinions too, and confidences,
They put things call'd Executorships upon me,
The charge of Orphans, little sencelesse creatures,
Whom in their Childe-hoods I bound forth to Felt-makers,
To make 'em lose and work away their Gentry,
Disguise their tender natures with hard custome,
So wrought 'em out in time, there I rizze ungently,
Nor do I feare to discourse this unto thee,
I'me arm'd at all points against treachery,
I hold my humour firme, if I can see thee thrive by
Thy wits while I live, I shall have the more courage
To trust thee with my Lands when I dye; if not,
The next best wit I can heare of carries 'em:
For since in my time and knowledge so many rich Children
Of the City conclude in beggery, i'de rather
Make a wise stranger my Executor, then a foolish
Sonne my Heire, and to have my Lands call'd after my
Wit, thou after my name; and that's my nature.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: 'Tis a strange harsh one, must I still shift then?
I come brave cheates, once to my trade agen,
And i'le ply't harder now then e're I did for't,
You'le part with nothing then, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Old K.
verse: Not a jot Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: If I should aske you blessing e're I go Sir,
I think you would not give't me.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Let me but heare thou liv'st by thy wits once
Thou shalt have any thing, thou'rt none of mine else,
Then why should I take care for thee?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: 'Thanke your bounty.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: So wealth love me, and long life, I beseech it,
As I do love the man that lives by his wits,
He comes so neare my nature; i'me growne old now,
And ev'n arriv'd at my last cheat I feare me,
But 'twill make shift to bury me, by day-light too,
And discharge all my Legacies, 'tis so wealthy,
And never trouble any Interest money:
Iv'e yet a Neece to wed, over whose steps
I have plac'st a trusty watchfull Gardinesse,
For feare some poore Earle steale her, 't has bin threatned
To redeem morgag'd Land, but he shall misse on't;
To prevent which, I have sought out a match for her,
Fop of Fop-hall, he writes himselfe, I take it,
The antient, st Fop in England, with whom i'me privately
Compounded for the third part of her Portion,
And she seemes pleas'd, so two parts rest with me,
Hee's come; Sir Gregory, welcome, what's he Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Young Cunningham, a Norfolke Gentleman,
One that has liv'd upon the Fops, my kinred,
Ever since my remembrance; hee's a wit indeed,
And we all strive to have him, nay, 'tis certaine
Some of our name has gone to Law for him;
Now 'tis my turne to keep him, and indeed
Hee's plaguy chargeable as all your wit, are,
But I will give him over when I list,
I ha us'd wits so before.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Hope when y'are married Sir you'le shake him off.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why what do you take me to be, old Father i'Law that shall be, do you think ile have any of the Wits hang upon nie after I am married once? none of my kinred ever had before me; but where's this Neece? ist a fashion in London to marry a woman and never see her?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Excuse the nicenesse Sir, that care's your friend,
Perhaps had she Been seen, you had never seen her;
There's many a spent-thing call'd an't like your honour,
That lyes in wait for her at first snap, she's a Countesse,
Drawne with sixe Mares through Fleet-streete, and a Coach-man,
Sitting Bare-headed to their Flaunders buttocks,
This whets him on.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Pray let's clap up the businesse Sir,
I long to see her, are you sure you have her,
Is she not there already? Hark, O hark.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: How now, what's that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir. Greg.
verse: Every Caroach goes by,
Goes ev'n toth' heart of me.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Ile have that doubt eas'd Sir,
Instantly cas'd, Sir Gregory, and now I think on't
A toy comes i' my minde, seeing your friend there,
Wee'l have a little sport, give you but way to't,
And put a trick upon her, I love wit pretiously,
You shall not be seene yet, wee'le stale your friend first,
If't please but him to stand for the Anti-maske.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Puh, he shall stand for any thing, why his supper
Lyes i' my breeches here, ile make him fast else.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Then come you forth more unexpectedly
The Maske it selfe, a thousand a yeare joynture,
The cloud your friend will be then drawne away,
And only you the beauty of the Play.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: For Red and Black Ile put downe all your Fuller
Let but your Neece bring White, and we have three Cullours.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I'me given to understand you are a Wit Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cunning.
verse: I'me one that Fortune shewes small favour to Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why there you conclude it, whether you will or no Sir;
To tell you truth, i'me taken with a wit.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Fowlers catch Woodcocks so, let not them know so much,

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: A Pestilence mazard, a Duke Humphrey sparke
Had rather lose his Dinner then his Jest,
I say, I love a wit the best of all things.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: AlwaieS except your selfe.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Has gin't me twice now,
All with a breath, I thank him; but that I love a wit
I should be heartily angry; cuds, my Neece,
You know the businesse with her,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: With a woman?
'Tis ev'n the very same it was i'me sure
Five thousand yeares a go, no foole can misse it.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: This is the Gentleman I promist Neece,
To present to your affection.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Ware that Arrow.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Deliver me the truth now of your liking.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'me spoyl'd already, that such poore leane Game
Should be found out as I am.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Go set too her Sir—ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: How noble is this vertue in you Lady,
Your eye may seeme to commit thousand slaughters
On your dull servants, which truly tasted
Conclude all in comforts.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Puh.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: It rather shewes what a truth worth can make,
Such as yours is.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: And that's not worth a groat,
How like you him Neece?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: It shall appeare how well Sir,
I humbly thanke you for him.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Hah? ha, good gullory, he does it well ifaith,
Light, as if he meant to purchase lip-land there:
Hold, hold, beare off I say, slid your part hangs too long.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: My joyes are mockcries.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Y'ave ^th exprest a worthy care and love Sir,
Had mine owne eye been set at liberty,
To make a publike choyce (beleeve my truth Sir)
It could not ha done better for my heart
Then your good providence has.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: You will say so then,
Alasse sweet Neece, all this is but the scahbard,
Now I draw forth the weapon.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Sir Gregory,
Approach thou Lad of thousands.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Who calls me?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What motion's this? the Modell of Ninivie?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Accost her daintily now, let me advise thee.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I was advis'd to bestow dainty cost on you.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: You were ill advis'd, back, and take better counsell;
You may have good for an Angell, the least cost
You can bestow upon a woman Sir
Trebles ten Counsellors Fees, in Lady-ware,
Y'are over head and eares ere you be aware,
Faith keep a Batchelour still, and go to bowles Sir,
Follow your Mistris there, and prick and save Sir,
For other Mistresses will make you a slave Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: So, so, I have ray lerrepoop already.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why how now Neece, this is the man I tell you.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: He, hang him Sir, I know you do but mocke,
This is the man you would say.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: The Devill rides I think.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I must use cunning here.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Make me not mad, use him with all respect,
This is the man I sweare.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Would you could perswade me to that;
Alasse, you cannot go beyond me Unckle.
You carry a lest well I must confesse,
For a man of your yeares, but—

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I'me wrought beside my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I never beheld comlinesse till this minute.

speeches.speaker: Guar.
verse: O good sweet Sir, pray offer not these wards
To an old Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Away fifteene,
Here's fifty one exceeds thee.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What's the businesse?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Give me these motherly creatures, come, ne're smother it,
I know you are a teeming woman yet.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Troth a young Gent. might do much I think Sir

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Go too then.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: And I should play my part, or I were ingratefull.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Can you so soone neglect me?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Hence, i'me busie.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: This crosse point came in luckely, impudent Baggage.
Hang from the Gentleman, art thou not asham'd
To be a Widowes hinderance?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Are you angry Sir?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: You're welcome, pray court on, I shall desire
Your honest wise acquaintance; vexe me not
After my care and paines to finde a match for thee,
Lest I confine thy life to some out chamber,
Where thou shalt waste the sweetnesse of thy youth,
Like a consuming light in her owne socket,
And not allow'd a male creature about thee;
A very Munckey thy necessity
Shall prize at a thousand pound a Chimney-sweeper
At fifteene hundred.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: But are you serious Unckle?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Serious.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Pray let me looke upon the gentleman
With more heed, then I did but hum him over
In haste, good faith, as Lawyers Chancery sheetes;
Beshrew my blood a tollerable man,
Now I distinctly read him.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Hum, hum, hum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Say he be black, hee's of a very good pitch,
Well anckled, two good confident calves, they looke
As if they would not shrink at the ninth childe;
The rednesse ith' face, why that's in fashion,
Most of your high bloods have it, signe of greatnesse marry;
'Tis to be taken downe too with May butter,
Ile send to my Lady Spend-tayle for her Medicine.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Lum te dum, dum, dum, de dum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Hee's qualified too, beleve me.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Lum to dum, de dum, de dum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Where was my judgement?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Lum te dum, dum, dum, te dum, te dum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Perfections cover'd messe.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Lum te dum, te dum, te dum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: It smoakes apparantly, pardon sweet Sir
The errour of my Sex.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why well said Neece,
Upon submission you must pardon her now Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Ile do't by course, do you think i'me an asse Knight?
Here's first my hand, now't goes to the Seale Office.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Formally finisht, how goes this Suit forward?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'me taking measure of the widowes minde Sir,
I hope to fit her heart.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: Who would have dreamt
Of a young morsell now? things come in minutes.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Trust him not widow, hee's a younger Brother,
Hee'le sweare and lye; beleeve mo hee's worth nothing.

speeches.speaker: Guard.
verse: He brings more content to a woman with that nothing,
Then he that brings his thousands without any thing,
We have presidents for that amongst great Ladies.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Come, come, no Language now shall be in fashion,
But your Love-phrase the bell to procreation.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Pax, there's nothing puts me besides my wits, but this fourth,
This lay illiterate share, there's no conscience in 't.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Sir, it has ever been so where I have practis'd, and must be
Sill where I am, nor has it been undeserv'd at the yeares
End, and shuffle the Almanack together, vacations and
Terme-times one with another, though I say't, my wife is a
Woman of a good spirit, then it is no lay-share.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Faith for this five yeare, Ego possum probare, I have had
A hungry penurious share with em, and she has had as much
As I alwayes.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Present or not present?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Residens aut non residens, perfidem.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: And what president's this for me? because your Hic & hac, Turpis and Qui mihi discipulus braines (that never got any thing but by accidence and uncertainty) did allow it, therefore I must, that have grounded conclusions of wit, hereditary rules for my Father to get by.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Sir be compendious, either take or refuse, I will bate no token of my wives share, make even the last reckonings, and either so unite or here devide company.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: A good resolution, profecto, let every man beg his owne way, and happy man be his dole.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Well, here's your double share, and single brains Pol, edipo, here's toward, a Caster ecastor for you, I will endure it a forthnight longer, but by these just five ends—

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Take heed, five's odde, put both hands together or severally they are all odde unjust ends.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose:
Medeius sidius, hold your tongue, I depose you from halfe a share presently else, I will make you a participle and decline you, now you understand me, be you a quiet conjunction amongst the undeclined; you and your Latine ends shall go shift, Solus cum solo together else, and then if ever they got ends of gold and silver enough to
serve that Gerundine maw of yours, that without Do will end in Di & Dum instantly.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Inough, ynough, here comes company, we lose five shares in wrangling about one.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: My Father, put on Priscian, he has Latine fragments too, but I feare him not, ile case my face with a little more haire and releive.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Tush Nephew (ile call you so) for if there be
No other obstacles then those you speake of
They are but powder charges without pellets,
You may safely front 'em; and warrant your owne danger.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: No other that I can perceive ifailh Sir, for I put her to't, and felt her as far as I could, and the strongest repulse was, she said, she would have a little Souldier in me, that (if need were) I should defend her reputation.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: And surely Sir, that is a principle
Amongst your principall Ladies, they require
Vallour either in a friend or a husband.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: And I allow their requests ifaith, as well as any womans heart can desire, if I knew where to get valour, I would as willingly entertaine it as any man that blowes.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Breathes, breathes Sir, that's the sweeter phrase.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Blowes for a Souldier, ifaith Sir, and i'me in
Practise that way.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: For a Souldier, I grant it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Slid ile swallow some bullets, and good round ones too, but ile have a little Souldier in me.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Will you on and beg, or steale and be hang'd.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: And some Schollar she would have me besides,
Tush, that shall be no bar, 'tis a quality in a
Gentleman, but of the least question.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Salvete Domini benignissimi, munificentissimi.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Salvete dicis ad nos? fubeo te salvere,
Nay Sir, we have Latine and other mettall in us too,
Sir, you shall se talke with this fellow now.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I could finde in my heart to talk with him too,
If I could understand him.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Charissimi, Doctissimiq. Domini, ex abundantia,
Charitatis vestrae estote poopitii in me junenem,
Miserum, pauperem, & omni consolatione exulem.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: A pretty Schollar by my faith Sir, but ile to him agen.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Does he beg or steale in this Language can you tell Sir?
He may take away my good name from me, and I ne're
The wiser.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: He begs, he begs Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Ecce, ecce, in oculis lacrymarum flumen, in ore
Fames, sitisq. ignis in vultu, pudor & impudentia,
In omni parte necessitas & indigentia.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Audi tu bonus socius, tu es Scolasticus, sic intelligo,
Ego faciam argumentum, mark now Sir, now I fetch
Him up.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I have been fetcht up a hundred times for this,
Yet I could never learne halfe so much.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Audi, & responde, hoc est Argumentum, nomen est
Nomen, ergo, quod est tibi nomen, Responde nunc,
Responde argumentum meum. Have I not put him to't Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Yes Sir, I think so.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Step in, the rascall is put out of his pen'd speech,
And he can go no farther.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Cur non respondes?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Oh Domine, tanta mea est miseria.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: So he's almost in agen.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: ~t nocte mecum pernoctat egestas, luce quotidie
Paupertat habitat.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Sed quid est tibi nomen, & quis dedit? Responde
Argumentum.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Hem, hem.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: He's dry, he hems, on quickly.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Courteous Gentlemen, if the brow of a Military face may not be offensive to your generous eye-balls, let his wounds speake better then his words, for some branch or small sprig of charity to be planted upon this poore barren soyle of a Souldier.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: How now, what Armes and Arts both go a beging?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Such is the poast-progresse of cold charity now a dayes, who (for heat to her frigid limbs) passes in so swift a motion, that two at the least had need be to stay her.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Sir, let's reward um I pray you and be gone, if any quarrell should arise amongst us, I am able to answer neither of them, his Iron and Steele tongue is as hard as the tothers Latine one.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Stay, stay Sir, I will talke a little with him first,
Let me alone with both, I will try whether they
Live by their wits or no; for such a man I love,
And what? you both beg together then?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Conjunctis manibus, profecto, Domine.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: With equall fortunes equall distribution, there's not the breadth of a swords point uneven in our division.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: What two qualities are here cast away upon two poore fellowes, if a man had um that could maintaine um, what a double man were that, if these two Fellowes might be bought and sodden, and boyl'd to a jelly, and eaten fasting every morning, I do not thinke but a man should finde strange things in his stomack.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Come Sir, joyne your charity with mine, and we'le make up a couple of pence betwixt us.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: If a man could have a penny-worth for his penny, I would bestow more money with 'em.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Save you Gentlemen, how now? what are you encountred here? what fellowes are these?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: 'Faith Sir, here's Mars and Mercury, a paire of poore Planets it seemes, that Jupiter has turn'd out to live by their wits, and we are e'ne about a little sparke of charity to kindle um a new fire.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Stay, pray you stay Sir, you may abuse your charity, nay make that goodnesse in you no better then a vice, so many deceivers walke in these shadowes now a dayes, that certainly your bounties were better spilt then reserv'd to so lewd and vicious uses; which is he that professes the Souldier?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: He that professes his owne profession Sir, and the dangerous life he hath led in it this paire of halfe score yeares.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: In what services have you been Sir?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: The first that flesht me a souldier Sir, was that great battell at Aleazar in Barbarie, where the noble English Stukely fell, and where that royall Portugall Sebastian ended his untimely dayes.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Are you sure Sebastian dyed there?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Faith Sir, there was some other rumour hop't a-amongst us, that he wounded escap't, and touch't on his Native shore agen, where finding his Country at home more distrest by the invasion of the Spaniard then his losse abroad, forsooke it, still supporting a miserable and unfortunate life, which (where he ended) is yet uncertaine.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: By my faith Sir, he speakes the nearest same of truth in this.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Since Sir, I serv'd in France, the Low Countries, lastly, at that memorable Skirmish at Newport, where the forward and bold Scot there spent his life so freely, that from every single heart that there fell, came home from his resolution a double honour to his country.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: This should be no counterfeit, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: I do not thinke he is, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: But Sir, me thinkes you do not shew the markes of a Souldier, could you so freely scape, that you brought home no scarres to be your chronicle?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: Sir, I have wounds and many, but in those parts where nature and humanity bids me shame to publish.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: A good Souldier cannot want those badges.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Now am not I of your minde in that, for I hold him the best souldier that scapes best, alwaies at a Cocke-fencing I give him the best that has the fewest knocks.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nay ile have a bout with your Schollar too,
To aske you why you should be poore (yet richly learn'd)
Were no question, at least you can easily
Answer it; but whether you have learning enough,
To deserve to be poore or no (since poverty is
Commonly the meed of Learning) is yet to be trye'd;
You have the Languages, I meane the chiefe,
As the Hebrew, SyriacK, Greeke, Latine, &c.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Aliquantulum, non totaliter, Domine.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: The Latine I have sufficiently tryed him in,
And I promise you Sir he is very well grounded.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I will prove him in some of the rest.
Tois miois fatherois iste Cock-scomboy?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Kay yonkeron niggitton oy fouleroi Asinisoy.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Cheateron ton biton?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Tous pollous strikerous, Angelo to peeso.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Certainely Sir, a very excellent Schollar in the Greeke.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: I do note a wonderous readinesse in him.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I do wonder how the Trojans could hold out ten yeares Seige (as 'tis reported) against the Greekes, if Achilles spoke but this Tongue? I do not thinke but he might have shaken downe the walls in a seventh-night, and ne're troubled the wooden horse.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I will try him so far as I can in the Syriack.
Kircom bragmen, shag a dou ma dell mathou.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Hashagath rabgabash shobos onoriadka.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Colpack Rubasca, gnawerthem shigshag.
Napshamothem Ribsbe bongomosh lashemech nagothi.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Gentlemen I have done, any man that can, go further,
I confesse my selfe at a Nonplus.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Faith not I Sir, I was at my farthest in my naturall Language, I was never double-tongu'd I thanke my hard fortune.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Well Gentlemen, 'tis pitty (walke further off a little my friends) I say, 'tis pitty such fellowes so endow'd, so qualified with the gifts of Nature and Arts, yet should have such a scarcity of fortunes benefits, we must blame our Iron-hearted age for it.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: 'Tis pitty indeed, and our pitty shall speake a little for 'em;
Come Sir, here's my Groat.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: A Groat Sir? oh fie, give nothing rather, 'twere better you rayl'd on um for begging and so quit your selfe, I am a popre Gentleman, that have little but my wits to live on.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Troth and I love you the better, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Yet ile begin a better example then so, here fellowes, there's between you, take Purse and all, and I would it were heavier for your sakes, there's a paire of Angells to guide you to your lodgings, a poore Gentlemans good will.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Gratias, maximas gratias, benignissime Domine.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: This is an ill example for us, Sir, I would this bountifull Gentleman had not come this way to day.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Pox, we must not shame our selves now, Sir, ile give as much as that Gentleman, though I never be Souldier or Schollar while I live; here friends, there's a piece, that if he were divided would make a paire of Angells for me too, in the love I beare to the Sword and the Tongues.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: My largesse shall be equall too, and much good doe you, this bounty is a little abatement of my wit though, I feele that.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: May souldiers ever defend such charities.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: And Schollars pray for their encrease.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Fare you well Sir, these fellowes may pray for you, you have made the Schollars commons exceed to day, and a word with you, Sir, you said you liv'd by your wits, if you use this bounty you'le begger your wits beleeve it.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Oh Sir, I hope to encrease 'em by it, this seed never wants his harvest, fare you well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I thinke a man were as good meer with a reasonable Thiefe, as an unreasonable Begger sometimes, I could finde in my heart to beg halfe mine back agen, can you change my piece my friends?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Tempora mutantur, & nos mutamur in illis.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: My Gold is turn'd into Latine,
Looke you good fellowes, here's one round
Shilling more that lay conceal'd.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Sir, away, we shall be drawn farther into dammage else.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: A pox of the Foole, he live by his wits? if his wits leave him any money but what he beggs or steales very shortly, ile be hang'd for him.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: This breakfast parcell was well fetcht of ifaith.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Tush, a by-blow for mirth, we must have better purchase, we want a fourth for another project that I have ripen'd.

speeches.speaker: Ruin,
prose: My wife, she shares, and can deserve it.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: She can change her shape, and be masculine.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
prose: 'Tis one of the free'st conditions, she feares not the crack of a Pistoll, she dares say stand to a Grazier.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Probatum fuit, profecto, Domine.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Good, then you Sir Bacchus, Appollo shall be dispatcht with her share, and some contents to meete us to morrow (at a certaine place and time appointed) in the masculine Gender, my Father has a Nephew, and I an owne Cousen comming up from the University, whom he loves most indulgently, easie Master Credulous Oldcraft, (for you know what your meere Academique is) your Carrier never misses his houre, he must not be rob'd (because he has but little to lose) but he must joyne with us in a devise that I have, that shall rob my Father of a hundred pieces, and thanke me to be rid on't, for there's the ambition of my wit to live upon his profest wit, that has turn'd me out to live by my wits.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Cum hirundinis alis tibi regratulor.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: A male habit, a bag of a hunder'd weight, though it be counters (for my Alchimy shall turne 'em into Gold of my Fathers) the houre, the place, the action shall be at large set downe, and Father, you shall know, that I put my portion to use, that have given me to live by;
And to confirme your selfe in me renate,
I hope you'le finde my wits legitimate.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: NAy Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Put me not in minde on't prethee,
You cannot do a greater wrong to women,
For in our wants, 'tis the most chiefe affliction
To have that name remembred; 'tis a title
That misery workes us by, and the worlds malice,
Scorne and contempt has not where with to work
On humble Callings; they are safe, and lye
Levell with pitty still, and pale distresse
Is no great stranger to 'em; but when fortune
Lookes with a stormy face on our conditions,
We finde affliction worke, and envie pastime,
And our worst enemy then that most abuses us,
Is that we are call'd by, Lady, O my spirit,
Will nothing make thee humble? I am well methinkes,
And can live quiet with my fate sometimes,
Untill I looke into the world agen,
Then I begin to rave at my stars bitternesse,
To see how many muck hills plac'd above me;
Peasants and Droyles, Caroches full of Dunghills,
Whose very birth stinkes in a geenerous nostrill,
Glistring by night like Glow-wormes through the High-streets,
Hurried by Torch-light in the Foot-mans hands
That shew like running Fire-drakes through the City,
And I put to my shifts and wits to live,
Nay sometimes danger too; on Foot, on Horse-back,
And earne my supper manfully ere I get it,
Many a meale I have purchas'd at that rate,
Fed with a wound upon me, stampt at midnight.
Hah, what are you?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Now you rnay tell your selfe Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh Mr. Priscian, what's the project,
For you ne're come without one.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: First, your Husband,
Sir Ruinous Gentry greetes you with best wishes,
And here has sent you your full share by me
In five Cheates, and two Robberies.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: And what comes it too?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Neare upon thirteene pound.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: A goodly share.
'Twill put a, Lady scarce in Philip and Cheyney,
VVith three small Bugle Laces, like a Chamber-maid,
Here's pretious lifing.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: 'Lasse you must consider, Lady,
'Tis but young Tearm, Atturnies ha small doings yet,
Then High-way Lawyers, they must needs ha little,
Wee'ne had ho great good luck to speake troth Beauty,
Since your stout Lady-ship parted from 's at Hye-gate,
But there's a faire hope now for a present hunder'd,
Here's mans Apparrell, your Horse stands at doore.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: And what's the vertuous plot now?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Marry Lady,
You like a bvave young Gallant must be rob'd.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I rob'd?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Nay then—

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Well, well, go on, let's heare Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Here's a seal'd bag of a Hunder'd, which indeed
Are Counters all, only some sixteen Groates
Of white money i'the mouth on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: So, what Saddle have I?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Mounsieur Laroon's the French-mans.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: That agen,
You know so well itis not for my stride,
How oft have I complain'd on't?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: You nay have Jockey's then, the little Scotch one,
You must dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Ile soone by ready Sir,
Before you ha shifted Saddles, many women
Have their wealth flow to 'em, I was made I see
To help my fortune, not my fortune me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: My wayes are Goblin-led, and the night Else
Still drawee me from my home, yet I follow,
Sure 'tis not altogether fabulous,
Such Haggs do get dominion of our tongues
So soone as we speake, the Inchantment bindes;
I have dissembled such a trouble on me,
As my best wits can hardly cleare agen;
Piping through this old Reede, the Gardianesse,
With purpose that my harmony shall reach
And please the Ladies eare, she stops below,
And ecchoes back my love unto my lips,
Perswaded by most violent arguments
Of selfe-love in her selfe; I am so selfe-foole,
To do at upon her hunder'd-wrinckl'd face;
I could begger her to accept the gifts
She would throw upon me; 'twere charity,
But for pitties sake I will be a niggard
And undo, her, refusing to take from her;
I'me haunted agen, if it take not now
I'le breake the Spell.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Sweet Cuningame, welcome;
What? a whole day absent? Birds that build Nests
Have care to keep 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: That's granted,
But not continually to sit upon 'em;
Lesse in the youngling season, else they desire
To fly abroad, and recreate their labours,
Then they returne with fresher appetite
To worke agen.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Well, well, you have built a nest
That will stand all stormes, you need not mistrust
A weather-wrack, and one day it may be
The youngling season too, then I hope
You'le ne're fly out of sight.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There will be paines,
I see to shake this Bur off, and sweetest,
Prethee how fares thy charge? has my good friend
Sir Gregory the countenance of a Lover?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: No by my troth, not in my minde, me thinkes
(Setting his Worship aside) he lookes like a foole.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay ifaith, ne're divide his Worship from him for that
Small matter; Foole and Worship are no such
Strangers now adaies, but my meaning is,
Has he thy Ladies countenance of love?
Lookes she like a welconie on him? plainely,
Have they as good hope of one another,
As Cupid blesse us, we have ?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Troth I know not,
I can perceive no forwardnesse in my charge,
But I protest I wish the Knight better
For your sake, Bird.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why thanks sweet Bird, and with my heart I wish,
That he had as strong and likely hope of her
As thou haste of me.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Well, he's like to speed
Ne're the worse for that good wish, and ile tell you
Bird (for secrets are not to be kept betwixt us two)
My charge thinkes well of you.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Of me? for what?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: For my sake, I meane so, I have heard her
A hundred times since her. Unckle gave her
The first bob about you, that she'de do somewhat
For my sake if things went well together,
We have spoke of doores and bolts, and things and things,
Go too, Ile tell you all, but you'le finde
Some advancement for my sake I do beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Faith be not sparing, tell me.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: By my Lady
You shall pardon me for that, 'twere a shame
If men should heare all that women speakes behinde
Their backes sometimes.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You must give me leave yet,
At least to give her thankes.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Not that neither,
She must not take a notice of my blabbing,
It is sufficient you shall give me thankes,
For 'tis for my sake if she be bountifull,
She loves me, and loves you too for my sake.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: How shall I knowing this but be ingrate,
Not to reapy her with my dearest duty.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I, but you must not know it, if you tell
All that I open to you, you'le shame us both;
A far off you may kisse your hand, blush, or so,
But I'le allow no nearer conference.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Whoope! you'le be jealous I perceive now.

speeches.speaker: Gad.
verse: Jealous? why there'e no true love without it, Bird,
I must be jealous of thee, but for her,
(Were it within my duty to my Master)
I durst trust h er with the strongest tempter,
And I dare sweare her now as pure a Virgin
As e're was welcom'd to a marriage bed,
If thoughts may be untainted, hers are so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And where's the cause of your feare then?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Well, well;
When things are past, and the wedding Torches
Lighted at matches, to kindle better fire,
Then Ile tell you more.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Come, come, I see further,
That if we were married you'de be jealous.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I protest I should a little, but not of her,
It is the married woman (if you mark it)
And not the maid that longs, the appetite
Followes the first taste, when we have relisht
We wish cloying, the taste once pleas'd before,
Then our desire is whetted on to more,
But I reveale too much to you, ifaith Bird.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Not a whit 'faith, Bird, betwixt you and I,
I am beholding for bettering of my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Nay you shall know more of me if you'le be rul'd,
But make not things common.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Vd' so, your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I, 'tis no matter, she'le like well of this,
Our familiarity is her content.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: This present from Sir Gregory?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: From my Master, the Worshipfull right Sir Gregory Fop

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: A Ruffe? and what might be his high conceit
In sending of a Ruffe?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I thinke he had two conceits in it forsooth, too high too
Low, Ruffe high, because as the Ruffe does embrace yout
necke all day, so does he desire to throw his Knightly armes.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: But then I leave him off a nights.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Why then he is ruffe low, a ruffian, a bold adventerous errant to do any rough service for his Lady.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: A witty and unhappy conceit, do's he meane
As he seemes to say unto that reverence?
He does wooe her sure.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: To tell you truth Lady, his conceit was far better then I have blaz'd it yet.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Do you think so, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Nay I know it forsooth, for it was two dayes ere he compass'd it, to finde a fitting present for your Ladyship, was sending once a very fine Puppy to you.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: And that he would have brought himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: So he would indeed, but then he alter'd his devise, and sent this Ruffe, requesting withall, that whensoever it is foule, you (with your owne hands) would bestow the starching of it.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Else she wooes him, now his eyes shoots this way; And what was the reason for that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: There lyes his maine conceit, Lady, for sayes he, In so doing she cannot chuse but in the starching to clap it often between her hands, and so she gives a great liking and applause to my present, whereas if I should send a Puppy; she ever calls it to her with Irist, hisse, hisse, which js a fearefull disgrace, he drew the devile from a Play, at the Bull tother day.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I marry Sir, this was a rich conceit indeed.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: And far fetch'd, therefore good for you Lady-

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: How now? which way looke you, Bird?

speeches.speaker: Can.
verse: At the Fdole Bird shall I hot look at the Foole?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: At the Foole and I here? what need that? pray look this way.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Ile fit him aptly, either ile awake
His wits (if he have any) or force him
To app^are (as yet I cannot think him)
Without any, Sirrah, tell me one thing true
That I sahall aske you now, Was this devise
Your Masters owne? I doubt his wit in it;
He's not so ingenious.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: His owne I assure you, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Nay, you must not lye.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Not with a Lady, i'de rather lye with you then lye with my Master, by your leave in such a case as this.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Yet agen your eye?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The Foole makes mirth ifaith,
I would heare some.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Come, you shall heare none but me.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Come hither friend, nay come neare me; did
Thy Master send thee to me? he may be wise,
But did not shee it much in that; men sometimes
May wrong themselves unawares, when they least thinke on 't;

Was
~ulcan ever so unwise, to send Mars
To be his spokesman when he went a wooing ?
Send thee? heigh-ho, a pretty rowling eye.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I can turne up the white and the black too, and need be, forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Why, here's an amorous nose.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: You see the worst of my nose, forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: A cheek, how I could put it now in dalliance,
A paire of lips, oh that we were uney'd,
I could suck Sugar from 'em, what a beard's here?
When will the Knight thy Master have such a
Stampe of man-hood on his face? nay, do not blush.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Tis nothing but my flesh and blood that rises so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Death, she courts the Foole.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Away, away, 'tis sport, do not minde it.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Give me thy hand, come be familiar;
I, here's a promising palme; what a soft
Handfull of pleasure's here, here's Downe compar'd
With Flocks and quilted Straw, thy Knights fingers
Are leane mattrice rubbers to these Feathers,
I prethee let me leane my cheeke upon't,
What a soft pillow's here?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, umh, hu, hum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why there's a courage in that lively passion,
Measure thee all o're, there's not a limbe
But has his full proportion; it is my voyce,
There's no compare betwixt the Knight and thee,
The goodlier man by halfe, at once now
I see thee all over.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: If you had seen me swim tother day on my back, you would have sed you had seene, there was two Chambermaids that saw me, and my leggs by chance were tangled in the flags, and when they saw how I was hang'd, they cryed out, O help the man for feare he be drown'd.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: They could do no lesse in pitty, come, thine arme, wee'le walke together.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Blindnesse of Love and Women, why she dotes upon the Foole.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: What's that to you, minde her not.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Away you Burre.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Hang of Fleshook, fasten thine itchy claspe
On some dry Toad-stoole that will kindle with thee,
And burne together.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh abominable,
Why do you not love me?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No, never did?
I tooke thee downe a little way to
Enforce a Vomit from my offended stomack,
Now thou'rt up agen I loath thee filthily.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh Villaine.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why dost thou not see a sight
Would make a man abjure the sight of women.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, he's vext; ha, ha, ha,
Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Why dost thou laugh?
Because thou laugh'st, nothing else ifaith.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She has but mockt my folly, else she findes not
The bosome of my purpose, some other way
Must make me know; ile try her, and may chance quit
The fine dexterity of her Lady-wit.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Yes introth, I laught to think of thy Master,
Now, what he would think if he knew this?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: By my troth I laugh at him too, faith Sirrah, hee's but a foole to say the truth, though I say't that should not say't.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Yes, thou shouldst say truth, and I beleeve thee;
Well, for this time wee'le part, you perceive something,
Our tongues betray our hearts, there's our weaknesse,
But pray be silent.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: As Mouse in Cheese, or Goose in Hay ifaith.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: Looke, we are cut off, there's my hand where my lips would be.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ile wink and think 'em thy lips, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Now Gardionesse, I need not aske where you have been.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: O Lady, never was woman so abus'd

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Do'st thou heare Lady sweet-heart, I had forgot to tell thee, if you will I will come back in the Evening?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: By no meanes, come not till I send for you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: If there be any need, you may think of things when I am gone, I may be convey'd into your chamber, ile lye under the bed while midnight, or so, or you shall put me up in one of your little boxes, I can creep in at a small hole.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: These are things I dare not venter, I charge you on my love never come till I send for you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Verbum insapienti, 'tis enough to the wise, nor I think it is not fit the Knight should know any thing yet.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: By no meanes, pray you go now, we are suspected.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: For the things that are past, let us use our secrets.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Now ile make a firme triall of your love,
As you love me, not a word more at this time,
Not a sillable, 'tis the seale of love, take heed.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, hum, hum, hum —
Hum's loath to depart.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: So, this pleasant trouble's gone, now Gardianesse,
What? your eyes easing your heart, the cause woman?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: The cause is false man, Madam, oh Lady,
I have been gub'd in a shining Carbuncle,
A very Glo-worme, that I thought had sire in't,
And 'tis as cold as Ice.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: And justly serv'd,
Would'st thou once think that such an erring Spring
Would dote upon thine Autumne?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh, had you heard him
But protest.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I would not have beleev'd him,
Thou might'st have perceiv'd how I mockt thy folly,
In wanton imitation with the Foole,
Go weepe the sin of thy credulity,
Not of thy losse, for it was never thine,
And it is gaine to misse it; wert thou so dull?
Nay yet thou'rt stupid and uncapable,
Why thou wert but the bait to fish with, not
The prey, the stale to catch another Bird with.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Indeed he call'd me Bird.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Yet thou perceiv'st not,
It is your Neece he loves, would'st thou be made
A stakling Jade? 'tis she, examine it,
Ile hurry all awry, and tread my path
Over unbeaten grounds, go levell to the mark,
Not by circuler bouts, rare things are pleasing,
And rare's but seldome in the simple sence,
But has her Emphasis with eminence

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: My Neece? she the rivall of my abuse?
My flesh and blood wrong me? ile Aunt her for't;
Oh opportunity, thou blessest me
Now Gentlewoman, are you parted so soone?
Where's your friend I pray? your Cuningame?

speeches.speaker: M^r.
verse: What say you Aunt?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Come, come, your Cuningame?
I am not blinde with age yet, nor deafe.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Dumbe I am sure you are not, what ayld you Ant?
Are you not well?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: No, nor sick, nor mad, nor in my wits, nor sleeping, nor walking, nor nothing, nor any thing; I know not what I am, nor what I am not.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Mercy cover us, what do you meane Aunt?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I meane to be reveng'd.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: On whom?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: On thee, Baggage.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Revenge should follow injury,
Which never reacht so far as thought in me
Towards you Aunt.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Your cunning, minion,
Nor your Cuningame can either blinde me,
The gentle Begger loves you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Beseech you,
Let me stay your errour, I begin to heare,
And shake off my amazement; if you think
That ever any passage treating love
Hath been betwixt us yet commenc't, any
Silent eye-glance that might but sparkle fire,
So much as brother and sister might meet with,
The lip-salute, so much as strangers might
Take a farewell with, the commixed hands,
Nay, but the least thought of the least of these;
In troth you wrong your bosome, by that truth
(Which I thinke yet you durst be bayle for in me,
If it were offered ye) I am as free
As all this protestation.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: May I believe this?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: If ever you'l believe truth: why, I thought he had spake love to you, and if his heart prompted his tongue, sure I did heare so much.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh falsest man, Ixions plague fell on me,
Never by woman (such a masculine cloud)
So airy and so subtle was embrac't.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: By no cause in me, by my life deere Aunt.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I believe you, then help in my revenge,
And you shall do't, or loose my love for ever,
Ile have him quitted at his equall weapon,
Thou art young, follow him, bait his desires
With all the Engines of a womans wit,
Stretch modesty even to the highest pitch;
He cannot freeze at such a flaming beauty;
And when thou hast him by the amorous gills,
Thinke on my vengeance, choke up his desires,
Then let his banquettings be Tantalisme,
Let thy disdaine spurne the dissembler out;
Oh I should clime my stars, and sit above,
To see him burne to ashes in his love.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This will be a strange taste, Aunt, and an
Unwilling labour, yet in your injunction
I am a servant to't.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: Thou'lt undertak't?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Yes, let the successe commend it selfe hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Effect it Girle, my substance is thy store,
Nothing but want of will makes woman poore.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Why Pompey, thou art not starke mad, art thou?
Wilt thou not tell me how my Lady doe's?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Did she receive the thing that I sent her kindly, or no?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: The thing that you sent her, Knight, by the thing that you sent, was for the things sake that was sent to carry the thing that you sent, very kindly received, first, there is your Indenture, now go seeke you a servant: secondly, you are a Knight: thirdly and lastly, I am mine owne man: and fourthly, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Why Pompey? prethee let me speak with thee,
Ile lay my life some Haire has crost him.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Knight, if you be a Knight, so keep you; as for the Lady, who shall say that she is not a faire Lady, a sweet Lady, an honest and a vertuous Lady, I will say he is a base fellow, a blab of his tongue, and I will make him eat these fingers ends.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why here's no body saies so Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Whatsoever things have past betweene the Lady and the other party, whom I will not name at this time, I say she is vertuous, and honest, and I will maintaine it, as long as I can maintaine my selfe with bread and water.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why I know no body thinks otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Any man that doe's but thinke it in my hearing, I will make him thinke on't while he has a thought in his Bosome; shall we say that kindnesses from Ladies are common? or that favours and protestations are things of no moment betwixt parties and parties? I say still, whatsoever has been betwixt the Lady and the party which I will not name, that she is honest, and shall be honest, whatsoever she doe's by day or by night, by light or by darknesse, with cut and long tale.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why I say she is honest.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Is she honest? in what sense do you say she is honest, Knight?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: If I could not finde in my heart to throw my Dagger at thy head, hilts and all, I'me an asse, and no Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Throw your Dagger at me! do not Knight, I give you faire warning, 'tis but cast away if you do, for you shall have no other words of me, the Lady is an honest Lady, whatsoever reports may go of sports and toyes, and thoughts, and words, and deeds, betwixt her and the party which I will not name; this I give you to understand, That another man may have as good an eye, as amorous a nose, as faire a stampt beard, and be as proper a man as a Knight, (I name no parties) a Servingman may be as good as a Sir, a Pompey as a Gregory, a Doodle as a Fop; so Servingman Pompey Doodle may be respected as well with Ladies (though I name no parties) as Sir Gregory Fop; so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: If the fellow be not out of his wits, then will I never have any more wit while I live; either the sight of the Lady has gaster'd him, or else he's drunke, or else he walks in his sleepe, or else he's a foole, or a knave, or both, one of the three I'me sure 'tis; yet now I think on't, she has not us'd me so kindly as her Uncle promis'd me she should, but that's all one, he saies I shall have her, and I dare take his word for the best Horse I have, and that's a weightier thing then a Lady, I'me sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady Ruin.
verse: Nay, I am your owne, 'tis in your pleasure
How you'l deale with me; yet I would intreat,
You will not make that which is bad enough,
Worse then it need be, by a second ill,
When it can render you no second profit;
