If it be coyne you seeke, you have your prey,
All my store, I vow, (and it weighs a hundred)
My life, or any hurt you give my body,
Can inrich you no more.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: You may pursue.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: As I am a Gentlewoman, I never will,
Onely wee'l binde you to quiet behaviour
Till you call out for Bayle, and on th'other
Side of the hedge leave you; but keep the peace
Till we be out of hearing, for by that
We shall be out of danger, if we come back,
We come with a mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You need not feare me.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Come, wee'l bestow you then.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
prose: Why law you Sir, is not this a swifter Revenue then Sic probas ergo's & igitur's can bring in? why is not this one of your Syllogismes in Barbara? Omne utile est honestum.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Well Sir, a little more of this acquaintance,
Will make me know you fully I protest.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: You have (at first sight) made me conscious
Of such a deed my dreames ne're prompted, yet
I could almost have wisht rather ye'ad rob'd me
Of my Cloake, (for my Purse 'tis a Schollers)
Then to have made me a robber.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: I had rather have answered three difficult questions,
Then this one, as easie as yet it seems.

speeches.speaker: W^tty.
verse: Tush, you shall never come to further answer for't;
^an you confesse your penurious Uncle,
^ his full face of love, to be so strict
^ Nigard to your Commons, that you are faine
To size your belly out with shoulder fees?
With Rumps and Kidneyes, and cues of single Beere,
And yet make Dayn^y to feed more daintily,
A^ this easier rate? fie Master Credulous,
I blush for you.

speeches.speaker: C^ed.
verse: This is a truth undeniable.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Why go to then, I hope I know your Uncle,
How doe's he use his Sonne, nearer then you?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith like his Jade, upon the bare Commons,
Turn'd out to pick his living as he can get it;
He would have been glad to have shar'd in such
A purchase, and thankt his good fortune too;
But mum no more — is all safe, Bullies?
Secure? the Gentleman thinks him most happy in his losse,
With his safe life and limbs. and redoubles
^ first vow, as he is a Gentleman,
Never to pursue us.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Well away then,
Disperse you with Master Credulous, who still
Shall beare the purchase, Priscian and I
Will take some other course: You know our meeting
At the Three Cups in Saint Gyles, with this proviso,
(For 'tis a Law with us) that nothing be open'd
Till all be present, the looser saies a hundred,
And it can weigh no lesse.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Come, Sir, wee'l be your guide.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: My honesty, which till now was never forfeited,
All shall be close till our meeting.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Tush, I believ't,
And then all shall out; where's the theefe that's rob'd?

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Here Master Old^raft, all followes now.

speeches.speaker: W^t.
prose: 'Twas neatly done, wench, now to turne that bag ^ counterfets to current pieces, & actum est.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: You are the Chymist, wee'l blow the fire still,
If you can mingle the ingredients.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I will not misse a cause, a quantity, a dram,
You know the place.
I have told her that, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Good, turne Ruinous to be a Constable, I'me sure
^ not beards of all sorts, from the
Worshipfull Magistrate to the under Watchman;
^ecause we must have no danger of life,
^ cleanly cheat, attach Credulous,
^ cause is plaine, the theft found about him;
^en fall I in his owne Cozens shape

^
^eere accident, where finding him distrest,
^ w^h some difficulty must fetch him off,
With promise that his Uncle shall shut up all
With double restitution: Master Constable, Ruinous
His mouth shall be stop't; you, Mistris rob theef^,
Shall have your share of what we can pull my father of;
Is't plaine enough?

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: As plaine a cozenage as can be, saith.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Father, I come againe, and againe when this is
Past too, Father, one will beget another;
I'de be loath to leave your posterity barren,
You were best to come to composition Father,
Two hundred pieces yearly allow me yet,
It will be cheaper (Father) then my wit,
For I will cheate none but you, deare Father.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: NAy Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Put me not in minde on't prethee,
You cannot do a greater wrong to women,
For in our wants, 'tis the most chiefe affliction
To have that name remembred; 'tis a title
That misery workes us by, and the worlds malice,
Scorne and contempt has not where with to work
On humble Callings; they are safe, and lye
Levell with pitty still, and pale distresse
Is no great stranger to 'em; but when fortune
Lookes with a stormy face on our conditions,
We finde affliction worke, and envie pastime,
And our worst enemy then that most abuses us,
Is that we are call'd by, Lady, O my spirit,
Will nothing make thee humble? I am well methinkes,
And can live quiet with my fate sometimes,
Untill I looke into the world agen,
Then I begin to rave at my stars bitternesse,
To see how many muck hills plac'd above me;
Peasants and Droyles, Caroches full of Dunghills,
Whose very birth stinkes in a geenerous nostrill,
Glistring by night like Glow-wormes through the High-streets,
Hurried by Torch-light in the Foot-mans hands
That shew like running Fire-drakes through the City,
And I put to my shifts and wits to live,
Nay sometimes danger too; on Foot, on Horse-back,
And earne my supper manfully ere I get it,
Many a meale I have purchas'd at that rate,
Fed with a wound upon me, stampt at midnight.
Hah, what are you?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Now you rnay tell your selfe Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Oh Mr. Priscian, what's the project,
For you ne're come without one.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: First, your Husband,
Sir Ruinous Gentry greetes you with best wishes,
And here has sent you your full share by me
In five Cheates, and two Robberies.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: And what comes it too?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Neare upon thirteene pound.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: A goodly share.
'Twill put a, Lady scarce in Philip and Cheyney,
VVith three small Bugle Laces, like a Chamber-maid,
Here's pretious lifing.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: 'Lasse you must consider, Lady,
'Tis but young Tearm, Atturnies ha small doings yet,
Then High-way Lawyers, they must needs ha little,
Wee'ne had ho great good luck to speake troth Beauty,
Since your stout Lady-ship parted from 's at Hye-gate,
But there's a faire hope now for a present hunder'd,
Here's mans Apparrell, your Horse stands at doore.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: And what's the vertuous plot now?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Marry Lady,
You like a bvave young Gallant must be rob'd.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: I rob'd?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Nay then—

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Well, well, go on, let's heare Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Here's a seal'd bag of a Hunder'd, which indeed
Are Counters all, only some sixteen Groates
Of white money i'the mouth on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: So, what Saddle have I?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Mounsieur Laroon's the French-mans.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: That agen,
You know so well itis not for my stride,
How oft have I complain'd on't?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: You nay have Jockey's then, the little Scotch one,
You must dispatch.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Ile soone by ready Sir,
Before you ha shifted Saddles, many women
Have their wealth flow to 'em, I was made I see
To help my fortune, not my fortune me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: My wayes are Goblin-led, and the night Else
Still drawee me from my home, yet I follow,
Sure 'tis not altogether fabulous,
Such Haggs do get dominion of our tongues
So soone as we speake, the Inchantment bindes;
I have dissembled such a trouble on me,
As my best wits can hardly cleare agen;
Piping through this old Reede, the Gardianesse,
With purpose that my harmony shall reach
And please the Ladies eare, she stops below,
And ecchoes back my love unto my lips,
Perswaded by most violent arguments
Of selfe-love in her selfe; I am so selfe-foole,
To do at upon her hunder'd-wrinckl'd face;
I could begger her to accept the gifts
She would throw upon me; 'twere charity,
But for pitties sake I will be a niggard
And undo, her, refusing to take from her;
I'me haunted agen, if it take not now
I'le breake the Spell.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Sweet Cuningame, welcome;
What? a whole day absent? Birds that build Nests
Have care to keep 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: That's granted,
But not continually to sit upon 'em;
Lesse in the youngling season, else they desire
To fly abroad, and recreate their labours,
Then they returne with fresher appetite
To worke agen.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Well, well, you have built a nest
That will stand all stormes, you need not mistrust
A weather-wrack, and one day it may be
The youngling season too, then I hope
You'le ne're fly out of sight.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There will be paines,
I see to shake this Bur off, and sweetest,
Prethee how fares thy charge? has my good friend
Sir Gregory the countenance of a Lover?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: No by my troth, not in my minde, me thinkes
(Setting his Worship aside) he lookes like a foole.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay ifaith, ne're divide his Worship from him for that
Small matter; Foole and Worship are no such
Strangers now adaies, but my meaning is,
Has he thy Ladies countenance of love?
Lookes she like a welconie on him? plainely,
Have they as good hope of one another,
As Cupid blesse us, we have ?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Troth I know not,
I can perceive no forwardnesse in my charge,
But I protest I wish the Knight better
For your sake, Bird.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why thanks sweet Bird, and with my heart I wish,
That he had as strong and likely hope of her
As thou haste of me.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Well, he's like to speed
Ne're the worse for that good wish, and ile tell you
Bird (for secrets are not to be kept betwixt us two)
My charge thinkes well of you.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Of me? for what?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: For my sake, I meane so, I have heard her
A hundred times since her. Unckle gave her
The first bob about you, that she'de do somewhat
For my sake if things went well together,
We have spoke of doores and bolts, and things and things,
Go too, Ile tell you all, but you'le finde
Some advancement for my sake I do beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Cur.
verse: Faith be not sparing, tell me.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: By my Lady
You shall pardon me for that, 'twere a shame
If men should heare all that women speakes behinde
Their backes sometimes.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You must give me leave yet,
At least to give her thankes.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Not that neither,
She must not take a notice of my blabbing,
It is sufficient you shall give me thankes,
For 'tis for my sake if she be bountifull,
She loves me, and loves you too for my sake.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: How shall I knowing this but be ingrate,
Not to reapy her with my dearest duty.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I, but you must not know it, if you tell
All that I open to you, you'le shame us both;
A far off you may kisse your hand, blush, or so,
But I'le allow no nearer conference.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Whoope! you'le be jealous I perceive now.

speeches.speaker: Gad.
verse: Jealous? why there'e no true love without it, Bird,
I must be jealous of thee, but for her,
(Were it within my duty to my Master)
I durst trust h er with the strongest tempter,
And I dare sweare her now as pure a Virgin
As e're was welcom'd to a marriage bed,
If thoughts may be untainted, hers are so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And where's the cause of your feare then?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Well, well;
When things are past, and the wedding Torches
Lighted at matches, to kindle better fire,
Then Ile tell you more.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Come, come, I see further,
That if we were married you'de be jealous.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I protest I should a little, but not of her,
It is the married woman (if you mark it)
And not the maid that longs, the appetite
Followes the first taste, when we have relisht
We wish cloying, the taste once pleas'd before,
Then our desire is whetted on to more,
But I reveale too much to you, ifaith Bird.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Not a whit 'faith, Bird, betwixt you and I,
I am beholding for bettering of my knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Nay you shall know more of me if you'le be rul'd,
But make not things common.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Vd' so, your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I, 'tis no matter, she'le like well of this,
Our familiarity is her content.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: This present from Sir Gregory?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: From my Master, the Worshipfull right Sir Gregory Fop

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: A Ruffe? and what might be his high conceit
In sending of a Ruffe?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I thinke he had two conceits in it forsooth, too high too
Low, Ruffe high, because as the Ruffe does embrace yout
necke all day, so does he desire to throw his Knightly armes.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: But then I leave him off a nights.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Why then he is ruffe low, a ruffian, a bold adventerous errant to do any rough service for his Lady.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: A witty and unhappy conceit, do's he meane
As he seemes to say unto that reverence?
He does wooe her sure.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: To tell you truth Lady, his conceit was far better then I have blaz'd it yet.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Do you think so, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Nay I know it forsooth, for it was two dayes ere he compass'd it, to finde a fitting present for your Ladyship, was sending once a very fine Puppy to you.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: And that he would have brought himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: So he would indeed, but then he alter'd his devise, and sent this Ruffe, requesting withall, that whensoever it is foule, you (with your owne hands) would bestow the starching of it.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: Else she wooes him, now his eyes shoots this way; And what was the reason for that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: There lyes his maine conceit, Lady, for sayes he, In so doing she cannot chuse but in the starching to clap it often between her hands, and so she gives a great liking and applause to my present, whereas if I should send a Puppy; she ever calls it to her with Irist, hisse, hisse, which js a fearefull disgrace, he drew the devile from a Play, at the Bull tother day.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I marry Sir, this was a rich conceit indeed.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: And far fetch'd, therefore good for you Lady-

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: How now? which way looke you, Bird?

speeches.speaker: Can.
verse: At the Fdole Bird shall I hot look at the Foole?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: At the Foole and I here? what need that? pray look this way.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Ile fit him aptly, either ile awake
His wits (if he have any) or force him
To app^are (as yet I cannot think him)
Without any, Sirrah, tell me one thing true
That I sahall aske you now, Was this devise
Your Masters owne? I doubt his wit in it;
He's not so ingenious.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: His owne I assure you, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Nay, you must not lye.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Not with a Lady, i'de rather lye with you then lye with my Master, by your leave in such a case as this.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Yet agen your eye?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The Foole makes mirth ifaith,
I would heare some.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Come, you shall heare none but me.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Come hither friend, nay come neare me; did
Thy Master send thee to me? he may be wise,
But did not shee it much in that; men sometimes
May wrong themselves unawares, when they least thinke on 't;

Was
~ulcan ever so unwise, to send Mars
To be his spokesman when he went a wooing ?
Send thee? heigh-ho, a pretty rowling eye.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I can turne up the white and the black too, and need be, forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Why, here's an amorous nose.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: You see the worst of my nose, forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: A cheek, how I could put it now in dalliance,
A paire of lips, oh that we were uney'd,
I could suck Sugar from 'em, what a beard's here?
When will the Knight thy Master have such a
Stampe of man-hood on his face? nay, do not blush.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Tis nothing but my flesh and blood that rises so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Death, she courts the Foole.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Away, away, 'tis sport, do not minde it.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Give me thy hand, come be familiar;
I, here's a promising palme; what a soft
Handfull of pleasure's here, here's Downe compar'd
With Flocks and quilted Straw, thy Knights fingers
Are leane mattrice rubbers to these Feathers,
I prethee let me leane my cheeke upon't,
What a soft pillow's here?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, umh, hu, hum.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why there's a courage in that lively passion,
Measure thee all o're, there's not a limbe
But has his full proportion; it is my voyce,
There's no compare betwixt the Knight and thee,
The goodlier man by halfe, at once now
I see thee all over.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: If you had seen me swim tother day on my back, you would have sed you had seene, there was two Chambermaids that saw me, and my leggs by chance were tangled in the flags, and when they saw how I was hang'd, they cryed out, O help the man for feare he be drown'd.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: They could do no lesse in pitty, come, thine arme, wee'le walke together.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Blindnesse of Love and Women, why she dotes upon the Foole.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: What's that to you, minde her not.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Away you Burre.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: How's that?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Hang of Fleshook, fasten thine itchy claspe
On some dry Toad-stoole that will kindle with thee,
And burne together.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh abominable,
Why do you not love me?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No, never did?
I tooke thee downe a little way to
Enforce a Vomit from my offended stomack,
Now thou'rt up agen I loath thee filthily.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh Villaine.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why dost thou not see a sight
Would make a man abjure the sight of women.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, he's vext; ha, ha, ha,
Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Why dost thou laugh?
Because thou laugh'st, nothing else ifaith.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She has but mockt my folly, else she findes not
The bosome of my purpose, some other way
Must make me know; ile try her, and may chance quit
The fine dexterity of her Lady-wit.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Yes introth, I laught to think of thy Master,
Now, what he would think if he knew this?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: By my troth I laugh at him too, faith Sirrah, hee's but a foole to say the truth, though I say't that should not say't.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Yes, thou shouldst say truth, and I beleeve thee;
Well, for this time wee'le part, you perceive something,
Our tongues betray our hearts, there's our weaknesse,
But pray be silent.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: As Mouse in Cheese, or Goose in Hay ifaith.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: Looke, we are cut off, there's my hand where my lips would be.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ile wink and think 'em thy lips, farewell.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Now Gardionesse, I need not aske where you have been.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: O Lady, never was woman so abus'd

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Do'st thou heare Lady sweet-heart, I had forgot to tell thee, if you will I will come back in the Evening?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: By no meanes, come not till I send for you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: If there be any need, you may think of things when I am gone, I may be convey'd into your chamber, ile lye under the bed while midnight, or so, or you shall put me up in one of your little boxes, I can creep in at a small hole.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: These are things I dare not venter, I charge you on my love never come till I send for you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Verbum insapienti, 'tis enough to the wise, nor I think it is not fit the Knight should know any thing yet.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: By no meanes, pray you go now, we are suspected.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: For the things that are past, let us use our secrets.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Now ile make a firme triall of your love,
As you love me, not a word more at this time,
Not a sillable, 'tis the seale of love, take heed.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, hum, hum, hum —
Hum's loath to depart.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: So, this pleasant trouble's gone, now Gardianesse,
What? your eyes easing your heart, the cause woman?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: The cause is false man, Madam, oh Lady,
I have been gub'd in a shining Carbuncle,
A very Glo-worme, that I thought had sire in't,
And 'tis as cold as Ice.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: And justly serv'd,
Would'st thou once think that such an erring Spring
Would dote upon thine Autumne?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh, had you heard him
But protest.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I would not have beleev'd him,
Thou might'st have perceiv'd how I mockt thy folly,
In wanton imitation with the Foole,
Go weepe the sin of thy credulity,
Not of thy losse, for it was never thine,
And it is gaine to misse it; wert thou so dull?
Nay yet thou'rt stupid and uncapable,
Why thou wert but the bait to fish with, not
The prey, the stale to catch another Bird with.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Indeed he call'd me Bird.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Yet thou perceiv'st not,
It is your Neece he loves, would'st thou be made
A stakling Jade? 'tis she, examine it,
Ile hurry all awry, and tread my path
Over unbeaten grounds, go levell to the mark,
Not by circuler bouts, rare things are pleasing,
And rare's but seldome in the simple sence,
But has her Emphasis with eminence

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: My Neece? she the rivall of my abuse?
My flesh and blood wrong me? ile Aunt her for't;
Oh opportunity, thou blessest me
Now Gentlewoman, are you parted so soone?
Where's your friend I pray? your Cuningame?

speeches.speaker: M^r.
verse: What say you Aunt?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Come, come, your Cuningame?
I am not blinde with age yet, nor deafe.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Dumbe I am sure you are not, what ayld you Ant?
Are you not well?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: No, nor sick, nor mad, nor in my wits, nor sleeping, nor walking, nor nothing, nor any thing; I know not what I am, nor what I am not.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Mercy cover us, what do you meane Aunt?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I meane to be reveng'd.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: On whom?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: On thee, Baggage.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Revenge should follow injury,
Which never reacht so far as thought in me
Towards you Aunt.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Your cunning, minion,
Nor your Cuningame can either blinde me,
The gentle Begger loves you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Beseech you,
Let me stay your errour, I begin to heare,
And shake off my amazement; if you think
That ever any passage treating love
Hath been betwixt us yet commenc't, any
Silent eye-glance that might but sparkle fire,
So much as brother and sister might meet with,
The lip-salute, so much as strangers might
Take a farewell with, the commixed hands,
Nay, but the least thought of the least of these;
In troth you wrong your bosome, by that truth
(Which I thinke yet you durst be bayle for in me,
If it were offered ye) I am as free
As all this protestation.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: May I believe this?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: If ever you'l believe truth: why, I thought he had spake love to you, and if his heart prompted his tongue, sure I did heare so much.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Oh falsest man, Ixions plague fell on me,
Never by woman (such a masculine cloud)
So airy and so subtle was embrac't.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: By no cause in me, by my life deere Aunt.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I believe you, then help in my revenge,
And you shall do't, or loose my love for ever,
Ile have him quitted at his equall weapon,
Thou art young, follow him, bait his desires
With all the Engines of a womans wit,
Stretch modesty even to the highest pitch;
He cannot freeze at such a flaming beauty;
And when thou hast him by the amorous gills,
Thinke on my vengeance, choke up his desires,
Then let his banquettings be Tantalisme,
Let thy disdaine spurne the dissembler out;
Oh I should clime my stars, and sit above,
To see him burne to ashes in his love.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This will be a strange taste, Aunt, and an
Unwilling labour, yet in your injunction
I am a servant to't.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: Thou'lt undertak't?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Yes, let the successe commend it selfe hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Effect it Girle, my substance is thy store,
Nothing but want of will makes woman poore.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Why Pompey, thou art not starke mad, art thou?
Wilt thou not tell me how my Lady doe's?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Did she receive the thing that I sent her kindly, or no?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: The thing that you sent her, Knight, by the thing that you sent, was for the things sake that was sent to carry the thing that you sent, very kindly received, first, there is your Indenture, now go seeke you a servant: secondly, you are a Knight: thirdly and lastly, I am mine owne man: and fourthly, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Why Pompey? prethee let me speak with thee,
Ile lay my life some Haire has crost him.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Knight, if you be a Knight, so keep you; as for the Lady, who shall say that she is not a faire Lady, a sweet Lady, an honest and a vertuous Lady, I will say he is a base fellow, a blab of his tongue, and I will make him eat these fingers ends.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why here's no body saies so Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Whatsoever things have past betweene the Lady and the other party, whom I will not name at this time, I say she is vertuous, and honest, and I will maintaine it, as long as I can maintaine my selfe with bread and water.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why I know no body thinks otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Any man that doe's but thinke it in my hearing, I will make him thinke on't while he has a thought in his Bosome; shall we say that kindnesses from Ladies are common? or that favours and protestations are things of no moment betwixt parties and parties? I say still, whatsoever has been betwixt the Lady and the party which I will not name, that she is honest, and shall be honest, whatsoever she doe's by day or by night, by light or by darknesse, with cut and long tale.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Why I say she is honest.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Is she honest? in what sense do you say she is honest, Knight?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: If I could not finde in my heart to throw my Dagger at thy head, hilts and all, I'me an asse, and no Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Throw your Dagger at me! do not Knight, I give you faire warning, 'tis but cast away if you do, for you shall have no other words of me, the Lady is an honest Lady, whatsoever reports may go of sports and toyes, and thoughts, and words, and deeds, betwixt her and the party which I will not name; this I give you to understand, That another man may have as good an eye, as amorous a nose, as faire a stampt beard, and be as proper a man as a Knight, (I name no parties) a Servingman may be as good as a Sir, a Pompey as a Gregory, a Doodle as a Fop; so Servingman Pompey Doodle may be respected as well with Ladies (though I name no parties) as Sir Gregory Fop; so farewell.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: If the fellow be not out of his wits, then will I never have any more wit while I live; either the sight of the Lady has gaster'd him, or else he's drunke, or else he walks in his sleepe, or else he's a foole, or a knave, or both, one of the three I'me sure 'tis; yet now I think on't, she has not us'd me so kindly as her Uncle promis'd me she should, but that's all one, he saies I shall have her, and I dare take his word for the best Horse I have, and that's a weightier thing then a Lady, I'me sure on't.

speeches.speaker: Lady Ruin.
verse: Nay, I am your owne, 'tis in your pleasure
How you'l deale with me; yet I would intreat,
You will not make that which is bad enough,
Worse then it need be, by a second ill,
When it can render you no second profit;
If it be coyne you seeke, you have your prey,
All my store, I vow, (and it weighs a hundred)
My life, or any hurt you give my body,
Can inrich you no more.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: You may pursue.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: As I am a Gentlewoman, I never will,
Onely wee'l binde you to quiet behaviour
Till you call out for Bayle, and on th'other
Side of the hedge leave you; but keep the peace
Till we be out of hearing, for by that
We shall be out of danger, if we come back,
We come with a mischiefe.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
prose: You need not feare me.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
prose: Come, wee'l bestow you then.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
prose: Why law you Sir, is not this a swifter Revenue then Sic probas ergo's & igitur's can bring in? why is not this one of your Syllogismes in Barbara? Omne utile est honestum.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Well Sir, a little more of this acquaintance,
Will make me know you fully I protest.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: You have (at first sight) made me conscious
Of such a deed my dreames ne're prompted, yet
I could almost have wisht rather ye'ad rob'd me
Of my Cloake, (for my Purse 'tis a Schollers)
Then to have made me a robber.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: I had rather have answered three difficult questions,
Then this one, as easie as yet it seems.

speeches.speaker: W^tty.
verse: Tush, you shall never come to further answer for't;
^an you confesse your penurious Uncle,
^ his full face of love, to be so strict
^ Nigard to your Commons, that you are faine
To size your belly out with shoulder fees?
With Rumps and Kidneyes, and cues of single Beere,
And yet make Dayn^y to feed more daintily,
A^ this easier rate? fie Master Credulous,
I blush for you.

speeches.speaker: C^ed.
verse: This is a truth undeniable.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Why go to then, I hope I know your Uncle,
How doe's he use his Sonne, nearer then you?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith like his Jade, upon the bare Commons,
Turn'd out to pick his living as he can get it;
He would have been glad to have shar'd in such
A purchase, and thankt his good fortune too;
But mum no more — is all safe, Bullies?
Secure? the Gentleman thinks him most happy in his losse,
With his safe life and limbs. and redoubles
^ first vow, as he is a Gentleman,
Never to pursue us.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Well away then,
Disperse you with Master Credulous, who still
Shall beare the purchase, Priscian and I
Will take some other course: You know our meeting
At the Three Cups in Saint Gyles, with this proviso,
(For 'tis a Law with us) that nothing be open'd
Till all be present, the looser saies a hundred,
And it can weigh no lesse.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Come, Sir, wee'l be your guide.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: My honesty, which till now was never forfeited,
All shall be close till our meeting.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Tush, I believ't,
And then all shall out; where's the theefe that's rob'd?

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Here Master Old^raft, all followes now.

speeches.speaker: W^t.
prose: 'Twas neatly done, wench, now to turne that bag ^ counterfets to current pieces, & actum est.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: You are the Chymist, wee'l blow the fire still,
If you can mingle the ingredients.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I will not misse a cause, a quantity, a dram,
You know the place.
I have told her that, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Good, turne Ruinous to be a Constable, I'me sure
^ not beards of all sorts, from the
Worshipfull Magistrate to the under Watchman;
^ecause we must have no danger of life,
^ cleanly cheat, attach Credulous,
^ cause is plaine, the theft found about him;
^en fall I in his owne Cozens shape

^
^eere accident, where finding him distrest,
^ w^h some difficulty must fetch him off,
With promise that his Uncle shall shut up all
With double restitution: Master Constable, Ruinous
His mouth shall be stop't; you, Mistris rob theef^,
Shall have your share of what we can pull my father of;
Is't plaine enough?

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: As plaine a cozenage as can be, saith.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Father, I come againe, and againe when this is
Past too, Father, one will beget another;
I'de be loath to leave your posterity barren,
You were best to come to composition Father,
Two hundred pieces yearly allow me yet,
It will be cheaper (Father) then my wit,
For I will cheate none but you, deare Father.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: WHy now you take the course Sir Gregory Fop:
I could enforce her and I list, but love
That's gently wonne, is a mans owne for ever,
Have you prepar'd good musick?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: As fine a noyse, Uncle, as heart can wish.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why that's done like a Suitor,
They must be woo'd a hundred severall waies,
Before you obtaine the right way in a woman,
'Tis an odde creature, full of creeks and windings.
The Serpent has not mo^e; for sh'as all his,
And then her owne beside came in by her mother.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A fearefull portion for a man to venter on.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: But the way found once by the wits of men,
There is no creature lyes so tame agen.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I promise you, not a house-Rabbit, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: No sucker on 'em all.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What a thing's that?
They're pretty Fooles I warrant, when they're tame
As a man can lay his lips to.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: How were you bred, Sir?
Did you never make a foole of a Tenants daughter?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Never i'faith, they ha' made some fooles for me,
And brought 'em many a time under their aprons.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: They could not shew you the way plainlier, I thinke,
To make a foole againe.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: There's fooles enough, Sir,
Lesse they were wiser.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: This is wondrous rare,
Come you to London with a Maiden-head, Knight?
A Gentleman of your ranke ride with a Cloak-bag?
Never an Hostesse by the way to leave it with?
Nor Tapsters sister? nor head Ostlers wife?
What no body?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Well mockt old Wit Monger,
I keep it for your Neece.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Do not say so for shame, shee'l laugh at thee,
A wife ne're looks for't, 'tis a Batchellors penny,
He may giv't to a beggar-wench, i'th progresse time,
And never call'd to account for't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Would I'de knowne so much,
I could ha' stopt a beggars mouth by'th way,
That rail'd upon me 'cause I'de give her nothing—
What, are they come?

speeches.speaker: Pag.
verse: And plac'd directly, Sir,
Under her window.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What may I call you Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: A poore servant to the Violl, I'me the Voyce, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: In good time Master Voyce.

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Indeed good time doe's get the mastery.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What Countryman Master Voyce?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir, borne at Ely, we all set up in Ely,
But our house commonly breakes in Rutland Shire.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A shrewd place by my faith, it may well break your voyce,
It breaks many a mans back; come, set to your businesse.
FAine would I wake you, Sweet, but feare
I should invite you to worse cheare;
In your dreames you cannot fare
Meaner then Musick; no compare;
None of your slumbers are compil'de
~nder the pleasure makes a childe;
Your day-delights, so well compact,
That what you think, turnes all to act:
I'de wish my life no better play,
Your dreame by night, your thought by day.
Wake gently, wake,
Part softly from your dreames;
The morning flies
To your faire eyes,
To take her speciall beames.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I heare her up, here Master Voyce,
Pay you the Instruments, save what you can,
To keep you when you're crackt.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Who should this be?
That I'me so much beholding to, for sweetnesse?
Pray Heaven it happens right.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Good morrow Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: An ill day and a thousand come upon thee.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: 'Light that's sixe hundred more then any Almanack has.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Comes it from thee? it is the mangiest Musick
That ever woman heard.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Nay say not so Lady,
There's not an itch about 'em.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I could curse
My attentive powers, for giving entrance to't;
There is no boldnesse like the impudence
That's lock't in a fooles blood, how durst you do this?
In conscience I abus'd you as sufficiently
As woman could a man; insatiate Coxcombe,
The mocks, and spitefull language I have given thee,
Would a' my life ha' serv'd ten reasonable men,
And rise contented too, and left enough for their friends.
You glutten at abuses, never satisfied?
I am perswaded thou devour'st more flouts
Then all thy body's worth, and still a hungred!
A mischiefe of that mawe; prethee seeke elsewhere,
Introth I am weary of abusing thee;
Get thee a fresh Mistris, thou'^ make worke enough;
I do not thinke there's scorne enough in Towne
To serve thy turne, take the Court Ladies in,
And all their women to 'em, that exceed 'em.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is this in earnest, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Oh unsatiable!
Dost thou count all this but an earnest yet?
I'de thought I'de paid thee all the whole summe, trust me;
Thou't begger my derision utterly
If thou stai'st longer, I shall want a laugh:
If I knew where to borrow a contempt
Would hold thee tack, stay and be hang'd thou should'st then,
But thou'st no conscience now to extort hate from me,
When one has spent all she can make upon thee;
Must I begin to pay thee hire againe?
After I have rid thee twice? faith 'tis unreasonable.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Say you so? I'le know that presently.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Now he runs
To fetch my Uncle to this musty bargaine,
But I have better ware alwaies at hand.
And lay by this still when he comes to cheapen.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I met the Musick now, yet cannot learne
What entertainment he receiv'd from her.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: There's some body set already, I must to't, I see,
Well, well, Sir Gregory.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Hah, Sir Gregory?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Where e're you come you may well boast your conquest.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She's lost y'faith, enough, has fortune then
Remembred her great boy? she seldome failes 'em.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: He was the unlikeliest man at first, me thought,
To have my love, we never met but wrangled,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A pox upon that wrangling, say I still,
I never knew it faile yet, where er't came;
It never comes but like a storme of haile,
'Tis sure to bring fine weather at the tayle on't,
There's not one match 'mongst twenty made without it,
It fights i'th tongue, but sure to agree i'th haunches.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: That man that should ha' told me, when time was,
I should ha' had him, had been laught at pitteously,
But see how things will change?

speeches.speaker: Cun,
verse: Here's a heart feeles it — O the deceitfull promises of love!
What trust should a man put i'th lip of woman?
She kist me with that strength, as if sh'ad meant
To ha' set the faire print of her soule upon me.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I would ha' sworne 'twould ne're ha' beene a match once.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Ile heare no more, I'me mad to heare so much,
Why should I aime my thoughts at better fortunes
Then younger brothers have? that's a Maid with nothing,
Or some old Soap-boylers Widow, without teeth,
There waits my fortune for me, seeke no farther.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: You tell me things, Sir Gregory, that cannot be,
She will not, nor she dares not.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Would I were whipt then.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Ile make as little show of love, Sir Gregory,
As ever woman did, you shall not know
You have my heart a good while.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Heard you that?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Man will insult so soone, 'tis his condition,
'Tis good to keep him off as long as we can,
I've much a do, I sweare; and love i'th end
Will have his course, let Maids do what they can,
They are but fraile things, till they end in man.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: What say you to this, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: This is somewhat handsome.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: And by that little wrangling that I fain'd,
Now I shall try how constant his love is,
Although't went sore against my heart to chide him.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Alas poore Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Now y'are sure of truth,
You heare her owne thoughts speak.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: They speake indeed.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Go, you're a brainelesse Coxe, a Toy, a Fop,
Ile go no farther then your name, Sir Gregory,
Ile right my self there; were you from this place,
You should perceive I'me heartily angry with you,
Offer to sowe strife 'twixt my Neece and I?
Good morrow Neece, good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Many faire ones to you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Go, your'e a Coxcombe. How dost Neece this morning?
An Idle shallow foole: Slep'st thou well, Girle?
Fortune may very well provide thee Lordships,
For honesty has left thee little manners.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: How am I bang'd a' both sides?

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: Abuse kindnesse? Wil't take the ayre to day Neece?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: When you please, Sir,
There stands the Heyre behinde you I must take,
(Which I'de as live take, as take him I sweare.)

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: La' you; do you hear't continued to your teeth now?
A pox of all such Gregories; what a hand
Have I with you?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: No more y'feck, I ha' done, Sir:
Lady, your Scarfe's falne downe.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: 'Tis but your luck, Sir,
And doe's presage the Mistris must fall shortly,
You may weare it, and you please.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: There's a trick for you,
You'r parlously belov'd, you should complaine.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Yes, when I complaine, Sir,
Then do your worst, there Ile deceive you Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: You are a Dolt, and so I leave you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Ah sirra, Mistris, were you caught y'faith?
We overheard you all; I must not know
I have your heart, take heed a that, I pray,
I knew some Scarfe would come.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: He's quite gone, sure:
Ah you base Coxcomb, couldst thou come againe?
And so abus'd as thou wast?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: 'Twould ha' kill'd
A sensible man, he would ha' gone to his Chamber,
And broke his heart by this time.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Thank you heartily.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Or fixt a naked rapier in a wall,
Like him that earn'd his Knighthood e're he had it,
And then refus'd upon't, ran up to'th hilts.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Yes, let him run for me, I was never brought up to't,
I never profest running i' my life.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What art thou made on? thou tough villanous vermin,
Will nothing destroy thee?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Yes, yes, assure your selfe
Unkinde words may do much.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why, dost thou want 'em?
I've e'ne consum'd my spleene to help thee to 'em,
Tell me what sort of words they be would speed thee?
Ile see what I can do yet.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I'me much beholding to you,
Your'e willing to bestow huge paines upon me.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I should account nothing too much to rid thee.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I wonder you'd not offer to destroy me,
All the while your Uncle was here?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why there thou betray'st thy house, we of the Old-Crafts
Were borne to more wit then so.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I weare your favour here.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Would it might rot thy arme off: if thou knewst
With what contempt thou hast it, what hearts bitternesse,
How many cunning curses came along with it,
Thoud'st quake to handle it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A pox, tak't againe then;
Who'd be thus plagu'd of all hands?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: No, weare't still,
But long I hope thou shalt not, 'tis but cast
Upon thee, purposely to serve another
That has more right to't, as in some Countries they convey
Their treasure upon Asses to their friends,
If mine be but so wise and apprehensive
As my opinion gives him to my heart,
It stayes not long on thy desertlesse arme;
Ile make theee're I ha' done not dare to weare
Any thing of mine, although I give't thee freely;
Kisse it you may, and make what shew you can,
But sure you carry't to a worthier man,
And so good morrow to you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Hu hum, ha hum;
I han't the spirit now to dash my braines out,
Nor the audacity to kill my selfe,
But I could cry my heart out, that's as good,
For so't be out no matter which way it comes,
If I can dye with a fillip, or depart
At hot cockles, what's that to any man?
If there be so much death that serves my turne there.
Every one knowes the state of his owne body,
No Carrion kills a Kite, but then agen
There's Cheese will choak a Daw; time I were'dead ifaith,
If I knew which way without hurt or danger.
I am a Maiden-Knight, and cannot looke
Upon a naked weapon with any modesty,
Else 'twould go hard with me, and to complaine
To Sir Perfidious the old Knight agen,
Were to be more abus'd; perhaps he would beat me well,
But ne're beleeve me;
And few men dye a beating, that were lost too:
Oh, here's my friend, ile make my moane to him.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I cannot teare her memory from my heart,
That treads mine downe, was ever man so fool'd
That profest wit?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: O Cuningame?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sir Gregory?
The choyce, the Victor, the Townes happy man?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Sniggs, what dost meane? come I to thee for comfort, and dost abuse me too?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Abuse you? how Sir?
With justifying your fortune, and your joyes?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Pray hold your hand, Sir i've bin bold enough,
You come with a new way now; strike me merrily,
But when a man's sore beaten a both sides already,
Then the least tap in jest goes to the guts on him;
Wilt ha the truth? i'me made the ranckest asse
That e're was borne to Lordships.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What? no Sir;

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I had not thought my body could a yeelded
All those foule scurvie names that she has call'd me,
I wonder whence she fecht 'em?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Is this credible?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: She pin'd this scarfe upon me afore her Unckle,
But his back turn'd, she curst me so for wearing on't,
The very brawne of mine arme has ak'd ever since,
Yet in a manner forc't me to weare't still,
But hop't I should not long; if good luck serve
I should meet one that has more wit and worth
Should take it from me, 'twas but lent to me,
And sent to him for a token.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I conceit it, I know the man
That lyes in wait for't, part with't by all meanes,
In any case, you are way-laid about it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: How Sir? way-laid?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Pox of a Scarfe say I,
I prize my friends life 'bove a million on 'em,
You shall be rul'd, Sir, I know more then you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: If you know more then I, let me be rid on't,
Lasse 'tis not for my wearing, so she told me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No, no, give me't, the knave shall misse his purpose,
And you shall live.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I would, as long as I could, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No more replyes, you shall, Ile prevent this,
Pompey shall march without it.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What, is't he?
My man that was?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Call him your deadly Enemy;
You give him too faire a name, you deale too nobly,
He beares a bloody minde, a cruell foe, Sir,
I care not if he heard me.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: But do you heare, Sir?
Can't sound with reason she should affect him?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Do you talk of reason? I never thought to have heard
Such a word come from you; reason in love?
Would you give that, no Doctor could e're give?
Has not a Deputy married his Cooke-maid?
An Aldermans Widow one that was her turne broach?
Nay, has not a great Lady brought her Stable
Into her Chamber: lay with her Horse-keeper?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Did ever love play such Jades tricks, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Oh thousands, thousands: Beware a sturdy Clown ere while you live, Sir;
'Tis like a huswifery in most Shires about us;
You shall ha' Farmers widowes wed thinne Gentlemen,
Much like your selfe, but put'em to no stresse;
What worke can they do, with small trap-stick leggs?
They keep Clownes to stop gaps, and drive in peggs,
A drudgery fit for Hindes, e'ne back agen, Sir,
You'r safest at returning.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Thinke you so, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: But how came this Clowne to be cal'd Pompey first?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Push, one good man Caesar, a Pump-maker kersen'd him;
Pompey he writes himselfe, but his right name's Pumpey,
And stunke too when I had him, now he's cranke.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I'me glad I know so much to quell his pride, Sir,
Walke you still that way, Ile make use of this,
To resolve all my doubts, and place this favour
On some new Mistris, only for a try,
And if it meet my thoughts, Ile sweare 'tis I.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is Pompey growne so malepert? so frampell?
The onely cutter about Ladies honours?
And his blade soonest out?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Now, what's the newes, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gre.
verse: I dare not say but good; oh excellent good, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I hope now you'r resolv'd she loves you, Knight?

speeches.speaker: Sir Gr.
verse: Cuds me, what else Sir? that's not to do now.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: You would not think how desperately you anger'd me,
When you belyed her goodnesse; oh you vext me,
Even to a Palsey.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What a thing was that, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: 'Tis, that 'tis; as I have hope of sweetnes, the Scarfe's gone;
Worthy wise friend, I doat upon thy cunning,
We two shall be well matcht, our Issue male, sure
Will be borne Counsellors; is't possible?
Thou shalt have another token out of hand for't;
Nay since the way's found, pitty thou shouldst want, y'faith,
O my best joy, and dearest.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Well said, Neece,
So violent fore your Uncle? what will you do
In secret then?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Marry call me slave, and rascall.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Your Scarfe — the Scarfe I gave you—

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Masse that's true Neece,
I ne're thought upon that; the Scarfe she gave you- Sir?
What dumbe? no answer from you? the Scarfe?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I was way-laid about it, my life threatned;
Life's life, Scarfe's but a Scarfe, and so I parted from't.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Unfortunate woman! my first favour too?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Will you be still an asse? no reconcilement
Twixt you and wit? are you so far fallen out,
You'l never come together? I tell you true,
I'me very lowsily asham'd on you,
That's the worst shame that can be;
Thus bayting on him: now his heart's hook't in,
Ile make him, e're I ha' done, take her with nothing,
I love a man that lives by his wits a life;
Nay leave, sweet Neece, 'tis but a Scarfe, let it go.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: The going of it never grieves me, Sir.
It is the manner, the manner—

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: O dissembling Marmaset! if I durst speake,
Or could be believ'd when I speake,
What a tale could I tell, to make haire stand upright now?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Nay, Sir, at your request you shall perceive, Uncle,
With what renewing love I forgive this?
Here's a faire Diamond, Sir, Ile try how long
You can keep that?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Not very long, you know't too,
Like a cunning witch as you are.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Y'are best let him ha' that too.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: So I were, I think, there were no living else,
I thank you, as you have handled the matter.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why this is musicall now, and Tuesday next
Shall tune your Instruments, that's the day set.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: A match, good Uncle.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Sir, you heare me too?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Oh very well, I'me for you.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: What e're you heare, you know my minde.

speeches.speaker: Sir Gre.
prose: I a — on't, too well, if I do not wonder how we two shall come together, I'me a beare whelpe? he talks of Tuesday next, as familiarly as if we lov'd one another, but 'tis as unlikely to me, as 'twas seven yeare before I saw her; I shall try his cunning, it may be he has a way was never yet thought on, and it had need to be such a one, for all that I can thinke on will never do't; I looke to have this Diamond taken from me very speedily, therefore Ile take it off a my finger, for if it be seene, I shall be way-laid for that too.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: OH torture! torture! thou carriest a sting i'thy taile,
Thou never brought'st good news i'thy life yet,
And that's an ill quality, leave it when thou wilt.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Why you receive a blessing the wrong way, Sir,
Call you not this good newes? to save at once Sir
Your credit and your kinsmans life together;
Would it not vexe your peace, and gaule your worth?
T' have one of your name hang'd?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Peace, no such words, boy.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Be thankfull for the blessing of prevention then.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: Le' me see, there was none hang'd out of our house since Brute,
I ha' search't both Stowe, and Hollinshead.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: O Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Ile see what Polychronicon saies anon too.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: 'Twas a miraculous fortune that I heard on't.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I would thou'dst never heard on't,

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: That's true too,
So it had ne're been done; to see the luck on't,
He was ev'n brought to Justice Aurums threshold,
There had flewen sorth a Mittimus straight for Newgate;
And note the fortune too, Sessions a Thursday,
Jury cul'd out a Friday, Judgement a Saturday,
Dungeon a Sunday, Tyburne a Munday,
Miseries quotidian ague, when't begins once,
Every day puls him, till he pull his last.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: No more, I say, 'tis an ill theame: where left you him?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: He's i'th Constables hands below i'th Hall, Sir,
Poore Gentleman, and his accuser with him.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: What's he?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: A Judges Sonne, 'tis thought so much the worse too,
He'l hang his enemy, an't shall cost him nothing,
That's a great priviledge.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Within there?

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Call up the folks i'th Hall. I had such hope on him,
For a Scholler too, a thing thou ne're wast fit for,
Therefore erected all my joyes in him;
Got a Welch Benefice in reversion for him,
Deane of Cardigan, has his grace already,
He can marry and bury, yet ne're a haire on's face;
Like a French Vicar, and doe's he bring such fruits to Town with him?
A thiefe at his first lighting? Oh good den to you.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Nay, sweet Sir, you'r so vext now, you'l grieve him,
And hurt your selfe.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Away, Ile heare no counsell;
Come you but once in seven yeare to your Uncle,
And at that time must you be brought home too?
And by a Constable?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Oh speake low, Sir,
Remember your owne credit, you professe
You love a man a' wit, begin at home, Sir,
Expresse it i' your self.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Nay, Master Constable,
Shew your self a wise man, 'gainst your nature too.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Sir, no Dish-porridgement, we have brought home
As good men as ye.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Out, a North-Brittaine Constable, that tongue
Will publish all, it speaks so broad already;
Are you the Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: The unfortunate one, Sir,
That fell into the power of mercilesse thieves,
Whereof this fellow, whom I'de call your kinsman,
As little as I could, (for the faire reverence
I owe to fame and yeares) was the prime villaine.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: A wicked prime.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Nay, not so loud, sweet father.

speeches.speaker: Lad.
verse: The rest are fled, but I shall meet with 'em,
Hang one of 'em I will certaine, I ha' swore it,
And 'twas my luck to light upon this first.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: A Cambridge man for this? these your degrees, Sir?
Nine yeares at University for this fellowship?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Take your voyce lower, deare Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: What's your losse, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: That which offends me to repeat, the Money's whole, Sir,
'Tis i' the Constables hands there, a seal'd hundred,
But I will not receive it.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: No? not the money, Sir,
Having confest 'tis all?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: 'Tis all the Money, Sir,
But 'tis not all I lost, for when they bound me,
They tooke a Diamond hung at my shirt string,
Which feare of life made me forget to hide;
It being the sparkling witnesse of a Contract
'Twixt a great Lawyers daughter and my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I told you what he was; what does the Diamond
Concerne my Cozen, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: No more did the Money,
But he shall answer all now.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: There's your conscience,
It shewes from whence you sprung.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sprung? I had leapt a thiefe,
Had I leapt some of your alliance.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Slave!

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: You prevent me still.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: 'Slid, sonne are you mad?

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Come, come, Ile take a legall course.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Will you undo us all? what's your demand, Sir?
Now we're in's danger too.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: A hundred Marke, Sir,
I will not bate a doit.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: A hundred rascals.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: Sir, finde 'em out in your own blood, and take 'em.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Go take your course, follow the Law, and spare not.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Does fury make you drunke? know you what you say?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: A hundred dogs dungs, do your worst.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: You do I'me sure; whose loud now?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: What his owne asking?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Not in such a case?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: You shall have but three score pound; spite a your teeth,
Ile see you hangd first.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: And whats seven pound more man?
That all this coyle's about? stay, I say, he shall ha't.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: It is your owne, you may do what you please with it;
Pardon my zeale, I would ha sav'd you money;
Give him all his owne asking?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: What's that to you, Sir?
Be sparing of your owne, teach me to pinch
In such a case as this? go, go, live by your wits, go.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I practise all I can.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Follow you me, Sir,
And Master Constable come from the knave,
And be a witnesse of a full recompence.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Pray stop the Constables mouth, what ere you do. Sir

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Yet agen? as if I meant not to do that my selfe,
Without your counsell? As for you, precious kinsman,
Your first years fruits in Wales shall go to rack for this,
You lye not in my house, Ile pack you out,
And pay for your lodging rather.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Oh fie Cozen,
These are ill courses, you a Scholler too,

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: I was drawne into't most unfortunately,
By filthy deboyst company.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I, I, I,
'Tis even the spoile of all our youth in England;
What were they Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith so like, some on 'em,
They were ev'n the worse agen.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Hum.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Great Tobacco swivers,
They would go neere to rob with a pipe in their mouths.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: What, no?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith leave it Cozen, because my rascals use it,

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: So they do meat and drinke, must worthy Gentlemen
Refraine their food for that? an honest man
May eat of the same pig some Parson dines with,
A Lawyer and a foole feed of one Woodcock,
Yet one ne're the simpler, t'other ne're the wiser;
'Tis not meat, drinke, or smoak, dish, cup, or pipe,
Co-operates to the making of a knave,
'Tis the condition makes a slave, a slave,
There's London Philosophy for you; I tell you cozen,
You cannot be too cautelous, nice, or dainty,
In your society here, especially
When you come raw from the University,
Before the world has hardned you a little,
For as a butter'd loafe is a Schollers breakfast there,
So a poacht Scholler is a cheaters dinner here,
I ha' knowne seven of 'em supt up at a Meale.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Why a poacht Scholler?

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Cause he powres himself forth,
And all his secrets, at the first acquaintance,
Never so crafty to be eaten i'th shell,
But is outstript of all he has at first,
And goes downe glibb, he's swallowed with sharp wit,
Stead of Wine Vinegar.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: I shall think, Cozen,
A' your poch't Scholler, while I live.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Master Credulous,
Your Uncle wills you to forbeare the House,
You must with me, I'me charg'd to see you plac'd
In some new lodging about Theeving Lane,
What the conceit's, I know not, but commands you
To be seene here no more, till you heare further.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Here's a strange welcome, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: This is the World, Cozen;
When a mans fame's once poyson'd, fare thee well Lad.
This is the happiest cheat I e're claim'd share in,
It has a two fold fortune, gets me coyne,
And puts him out of grace, that stood between me,
My fathers Cambridge Jewell, much suspected
To be his Heyre, now there's a barre in's hopes.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: It chinks, make haste.

speeches.speaker: Lady.
verse: The Goat at Smithfield Pens.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Zo, zo, zufficient. Master Cunningame?
I never have ill luck when I meet a wit.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A wit's better to meet, then to follow then,
For I ha' none so good I can commend yet,
But commonly men unfortunate to themselves,
Are luckiest to their friends, and so may I be.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I run o're so much worth, going but in haste from you,
All my deliberate friendship cannot equall.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis but to shew that you can place sometimes,
Your modesty a top of all your vertues.
This Gentleman may pleasure me yet agen;
I am so haunted with this broad brim'd hat,
Of the last progresse block, with the young hat-band,
Made for a sucking Devill of two yeare old,
I know not where to turne my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Mir,
verse: Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: More torture?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Tis rumor'd that you love me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A my troth Gentlewoman,
Rumour's as false a knave as ever pist then,
Pray tell him so from me; I cannot faine
With a sweet Gentlewoman, I must deale downe right.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I heard, though you dissembled with my Aunt, Sir,
And that makes me more confident.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There's no falshood,
But paies us our owne some way, I confesse
I fain'd with her, 'twas for a weightier purpose,
But not with thee, I sweare.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Nor I with you then,
Although my Aunt enjoyn'd me to dissemble,
To right her splene, I love you faithfully.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Light, this is worse then 'twas.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I finde such worth in you,
I cannot, nay I dare not dally with you,
For feare the flame consume me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Here's fresh trouble,
This drives me to my conscience, for 'tis fowle
To injure one that deales directly with me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I crave but such a truth from your love, Sir,
As mine brings you, and that's proportionable.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A good Geometrician, shrew my heart;
Why are you out a' your wits, pretty plumpe Gentlewoman,
You talk so desperately? 'tis a great happinesse,
Love has made one on's wiser then another,
We should be both cast away else;
Yet I love gratitude, I must requite you,
I shall be sick else, but to give you me,
A thing you must not take, if you meane to live,
For a' my troth I hardly can my selfe;
No wise Physitian will prescribe me for you.
Alas your state is weake, you had need of Cordials
Some rich Electuary, made of a Sonne an Heire,
An elder brother in a Cullisse, whole,
'T must be some wealthy Gregory, boyl'd to a Jelly,
That must restore you to the state of new Gownes,
French Ruffs, and mutable head tires,

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: But where is he, Sir?
One that's so rich will ne're wed me with nothing.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Then see thy conscience and thy wit together,
Wouldst thou have me then, that has nothing neither?
What say you to Fop Gregory the first yonder?
Will you acknowledge your time amply recompenc'd?
Full satisfaction upon loves record?
Without any more suit, if I combine you?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, by this honest kisse.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You'r a wise Clyent,
To pay your fee before hand, but all do so,
You know the worst already, that's thee best too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I know he's a foole,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You'r shrewdly hurt then;
This is your comfort, your great wisest women
Pick their first husband still out of that house,
And some will have 'em to chuse, if they bury 20.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I'me of their mindes, that like him for a first husband,
To run youths race with him, 'tis very pleasant,
But when I'me old, I'de alwaies wish a wiser.
You may have me by that time; for this first businesse,
Rest upon my performance.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: With all thankfulnesse.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I have a project you must aid me in too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You binde me to all lawfull action, Sir,
Pray weare this scarfe about you;
I conjecture now—

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There's a Court principle for't, one office must help another;
As for example, for your cast a Manchits out a'th Pantry,
Ile allow you a Goose out a'th Kitchin.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Tis very sociably done, Sir, farewell performance,
I shall be bold to call you so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Do, sweet confidence,
If I can match my two broad brim'd hats;
'Tis he, I know the Maggot by his head;
Now shall I learne newes of him, my pretious chiefe.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I have been seeking for you i'th bowling Greene,
Enquir'd at Nettletons, and Anthonies Ordinary,
T'ha's vext me to the heart, looke, I've a Diamond here,
And it cannot finde a Master.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No? That's hard y'faith.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: It does belong to some body, a — on him,
I would he had it, do's but trouble me,
And she that sent it, is so waspish too,
There's no returning to her till't be gone.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Oh, ho, ah sirrah, are you come?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What's that friend?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Do you note that corner sparkle?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Which? which? which Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: At the West end a'the Coller.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Oh I see't now.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis an apparent marke; this is the stone, Sir,
That so much blood is threatned to be shed for.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I pray?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A tunne at least.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: They must not find't I'me then, they must
Go where 'tis to be had.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis well it came to my hands first, Sir Gregory,
I know where this must go.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Am I discharg'd on't?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: My life for yours now.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: What now?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis discretion, Sir,
Ile stand upon my Guard all the while I ha't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Troth thou tak'st too much danger on thee still,
To preserve me alive.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis a friends duty, Sir,
Nay, by a toy that I have late thought upon,
Ile undertake to get your Mistris for you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Thou wilt not? wilt?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Contract her by a trick, Sir,
When she least thinks on't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: There's the right way to't,
For if she thinke on't once, shee'l never do't.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She doe's abuse you still then?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A —damnably,
Every time worse then other; yet her Uncle
Thinks the day holds a tuesday; say it did, Sir,
She's so familiarly us'd to call me rascall,
She'l quite forget to wed me by my owne name,
And then that marriage cannot hold in Law, you know.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Will you leave all to me?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Who should I leave it to?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Tis our luck to love Neeces; I love a Neece too.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I would you did y'faith.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: But mine's a kinde wretch.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I marry Sir, I would mine were so too.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No rascall comes in her mouth.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Troth, and mine has little else in hers.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Mine sends me tokens,
All the world knows not on.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Mine gives me tokens too, very fine tokens,
But I dare not weare 'em.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Mine's kinde in secret.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: And there mine's a hell-cat.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: We have a day set too.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: 'Slid, so have we man,
But there's no signe of ever comming together.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Tell thee who 'tis, the old womans Neece.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is't she?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I would your luck had been no worse for mildnesse;
But mum, no more words on't to your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Foh!

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: No blabbing as you love me.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: None of our blood
Were ever bablers.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Prethee convey this Letter to her,
But at any hand let not your Mistris see't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Yet agen Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: There's a Jewell in't,
The very art would make her doat upon't.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Say you so?
And she shall see't for that trick onely.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Remember but your Mistris, and all's well.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Nay if I do not hang me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I believe you;
This is the onely way to returne a token,
I know he will do't now, cause he's charg'd to'th contrary.
He's the nearest kin to a woman, of a thing
Made without substance, that a man can finde agen,
Some petticoat begot him, Ile be whipt else,
Engendring with an old paire of pawnde hose,
Lying in some hot chamber o're the Kitchin,
Very steame bred him,
He never came where Rem in Re e're grew;
The generation of a hundred such
Cannot make a man stand in a white sheet,
For 'tis no act in Law, nor can a Constable
Pick out a bawdy businesse for Bridewell in't;
A lamentable case, he's got with a mans Urine, like a Mandrake.
How now? hah? what prodigious bravery's this?
A most preposterous Gallant, the Doublet sits
As if it mockt the breeches.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Save you, Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Has put his tongue in the fine suit of words too.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: How doe's the party?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Takes me for a Scrivener. Which of the parties?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Hum, simplicity betide thee—
I would faine heare of the party; I would be loath to go
Further with her; honour is not a thing to be dallied withall,
No more is reputation, no nor fame, I take it, I must not
Have her wrong'd when I'me abroad, my party is not
To be compell'd with any party in an oblique way;
'Tis very dangerous to deale with women;
May prove a Lady too, but shall be namelesse,
Ile bite my tongue out, e're it prove a Traitor.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Upon my life I know her.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Not by me,
Know what you can, talke a whole day with me,
Y'are ne're the wiser, she comes not from these lips.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The old Knights Neece.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Slid he has got her, pox of his heart that told him,
Can nothing be kept secret? let me entreat you
To use her name as little as you can, though.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: 'Twill be small pleasure, Sir, to use her name.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I had intelligence in my solemne walks,
'Twixt Paddington and Pancridge, of a Scarfe,
Sent for a token, and a Jewell follow'd,
But I acknowledge not the receipt of any,
How e're 'tis carried, believe me Sir,
Upon my reputation I received none.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What, neither Scarfe nor Jewell?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Twould be seene
Some where about me, you may well think that,
I have an arme for a Scarfe, as others have,
And dare to hang a Jewell too, and that's more
Then some men have, my betters a great deale,
I must have restitution, where e're it lights.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And reason good.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: For all these tokens, Sir,
Passe i' my name.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: It cannot otherwise be.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Sent to a worthy friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I, that's to thee.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I'me wrong'd under that title.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I dare sweare thou art,
'Tis nothing but Sir Gregories circumvention,
His envious spite, when thou'rt at Paddington,
He meets the gifts at Pancridge.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Ah false Knight?
False both to honour, and the Law of Arms?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What wilt thou say if I be reveng'd for thee?
Thou sit as witnesse?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I should laugh in state then.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Ile fobb him, here's my hand.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I should be as glad as any man alive, to see him well fob'd, Sir; but now you talk of fobbing, I wonder the Lady sends not forme according to promise? I ha' kept out a Towne these two daies, a purpose to be sent for; I am almost starv'd with walking.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Walking gets men a stomack.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: 'Tis most true, Sir, I may speake it by experience, for I ha' got a stomack six times, and lost it agen, as often as a traveller from Chelsy shall lose the sight of Pauls, and get it agen.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Go to her, man.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Not for a Million, enfringe my oath? there's a toy call'd a vowe, has past betweene us, a poore trifle, Sir; Pray do me the part and office of a Gentleman, if you chance to meet a Footman by the way, in orange tawny ribbands, running before an empty Coach, with a Buzzard i'th Poope on't, direct him and his horses toward the new River by Islington, there they shall have me looking upon the Pipes, and whistling.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: A very good note; this love makes us all Monkeyes,
But to my work: Scarfe first? and now a Diamond? these
Should be sure signes of her affections truth;
Yet Ile go forward with my surer proofe.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is't possible?
Nay here's his Letter too, there's a fine Jewell in't,
Therefore I brought it to you.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: You tedious Mongrill! Is't not enough
To grace thee, to receive this from thy hand,
A thing which makes me almost sick to do,
But you must talke too?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I ha' done

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Fall back,
Yet backer, backer yet, you unmannerly puppy,
Do you not see I'me going about to reade it?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Nay these are golden daies, now I stay by't,
She was wont not to endure me in her sight at all,
The world mends, I see that.

speeches.speaker: N^ece.
verse: What an ambiguous Superscription's here?
To the best of Neeces. Why that title may be mine,
And more then her's:
Sure I much wrong the neatnessed of his art;
'Tis certaine sent to me, and to requite
My cunning in the carriage of my Tokens,
Us'd the same Fop for his.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: She nodded now to me, 'twill come in time.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
