verse: What's here? an entire Rubye, cut into a heart.
And this the word, Istud Amoris opus?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Yes, yes, I have heard him say that love is the best stone-cutter.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Why thou sawcy issue of some travelling Sow-gelder,
What makes love? thy mouth? is it a thing
That ever will concerne thee? I do wonder
How thou dar'st think ont? hast thou ever hope
To come i' the same roome where lovers are;
And scape unbrain'd with one of their velvet slippers?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Love tricks breake out I see, and you talk of slippers once,
'Tis not farre off to bed time.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Is it possible thou canst laugh yet?
I would ha' undertooke to ha' kill'd a spider
With lesse venome far, then I have spit at thee.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: You must conceive,
A Knight's another manner a peece of flesh.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Back, Owles face.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Do, do.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: 'Tis my Uncles voyce, that:
Why keep you so farre off, Sir Gregory?
Are you afraid, Sir, to come neare your Mistris?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Is the proud heart come downe? I lookt for this still.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: He comes not this way yet: Away, you dog-whelp;
Would you offer to come neare me, though I said so?
Ile make you understand my minde in time;
Your running greedily like a hound to his breakfast,
That chops in head and all to beguile his fellowes;
I'me to be eaten, Sir, with Grace and leisure,
Behaviour and discourse, things that ne're trouble you;
After I have pelted you sufficiently,
I tro you will learne more manners.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I'me wondring still when we two shall come together?
Tuesday's at hand, but I'me as farre off, as I was at first,
I sweare.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Now Cuningame, Ile be reveng'd at large:
Lady, what was but all this while suspition,
Is truth, full blowne now, my Neece weares your Scarfe.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Hah?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Do but follow me, Ile place you instantly
Where you shall see her courted by Cuningame.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I go with greedinesse; we long for things
That break our hearts sometimes, there's pleasures misery,

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Where are those gad-flies going? to some Junket now;
That some old humble-bee toles the you~g one forth
To sweet meats after kinde, let 'em looke to't,
The thing you wot on, be not mist or gone,
I bring a Maiden-head, and I looke for one.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Yes, yes.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Too manifest now, the Scarfe and all.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: It cannot be, you're such a fearefull soule.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Ile give her cause of feare e're I part from her.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Will you say so? Is't not your Aunts desire too?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: What a dissembling groane's that? shee'l forswear't now.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I see my project takes, yonder's the grace on't.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Who would put confidence in wit againe,
I'me plagu'd for my ambition, to desire
A wise man for a husband, and I see
Fate will not have us go beyond our stint,
We are allow'd but one dish, and that's Woodcock,
It keeps up wit to make us friends and fervants of,
And thinks any thing's good enough to make us husbands
Oh that whores hat a' thine, a' the riding block,
A shade for lecherous kisses.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Make you doubt on't?
Is not my love of force?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Yes, me it forces
To teare that sorcerous strumpet from th'imbraces.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Oh thou hast wrong'd the exquisit'st love—

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What meane you Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Mine, you'l answer for't.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Alas, what seek you?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Sir, mine owne with losse.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: You shall.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: I never made so hard a bargaine.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sweet Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Unjust man, let my wrath reach her,
As you owe vertue duty; your cause trips you,
Now Minion, you shall feele what loves rage is,
Before you taste the pleasure; smile you false, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: How can I chuse? to see what paines you take,
Upon a thing will never thank you for't?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: See what things you women be, Lady,
When cloathes are taken for the best part of you?
This was to show you, when you think I love you not,
How y'are deceiv'd still, there the Morall lyes,
'Twas a trap set to catch you, and the only bait
To take a Lady nibling, is fine clothes;
Now I dare boldly thank you for your love,
I'me pretty well resolv'd in't by this fit,
For a jealous ague alwaies ushers it.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Now blessings still maintaine this wit of thine,
And I'me an excellent fortune comming in thee,
Bring nothing else I charge thee.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Not a groat I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Thou shalt be worthily welcome, take my faith for't,
Next opportunity shall make us.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The old Gentlewoman has fool'd her revenge sweetly.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Lasse 'tis her part, she knowes her place so well yonder;
Alwaies when women jumpe upon three score,
Love shoves 'em from the chamber to the doore.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Thou art a precious she-wit.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: FRiend, met in the harvest of our designes,
Not a thought but's busle.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: I knew it man,
that made me provide these needfull Reapers,
Hooks, Rakers, Gleaners; wee'l sing it home
With a melodious Horne-pipe; this is the Bond,
That as we further in your great affaire,
You'l suffer us to gleane, pick up for crums,
And if we snatch a handfull from the sheafe,
You will not looke a churle on's.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Friend, wee'l share
The sheaves of gold, only the Love Aker
Shall be peculiar.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Much good do you, Sir,
Away, you know your way, and your stay; get you
The Musick ready, while we prepare the dancers.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: We are a consort of our selves.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: And can strike up lustily.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: You must bring Sir Fop.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: That's perfect enough.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Bring all the Fops you can, the more the better fare,
So the proverbe runs backwards.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Ile bring the Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Wit.
verse: Do so first, and then the Fops will follow;
I must to my father, he must make one.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: While I dispatch a businesse with the Knight,
And I go with you. Well sed, I thank you,
This small Banquet will fusnish our few Guests
With taste and state enough; one reach my Gowne,
The action craves it rather then the weather.

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: There's one staies to speake with you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: What is he?

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: Faith I know not what, Sir, a foole I thinke,
That some Brokers shop has made half a Gentleman;
Has the name of a Worthy too..

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Pompey? is't not?

speeches.speaker: 1 Serv.
verse: That's he, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Alas poore fellow, prethee enter him, he will need too,
He shall serve for a Witnesse. Oh Gramercy:
If my friend Sir Gregory comes, you know him,
Entertaine him kindly. Oh Master Pompey, how is't man?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Snailes, I'me almost sstarv'd with love, and cold, and one thing or other;
Has not my Lady sent for me yet?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Not that I heare, sure some unfriendly Messenger Is imployed betwixt you,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I was ne're so cold in my life, in my conscience I have been seven mile in length, along the new River; I have seene a hundred stickle bags; I do not thinke but there's gudgeons too; 'twill ne're be a true water.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why thinke you so?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I warrant you, I told a thousand Millers thumbs in it,
Ile make a little bold with your Sweet-meats.
And welcome Pompey.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: 'Tis is a strange thing, I have no taste in any thing.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Oh, that's Love, that distasts any thing but it selfe.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: 'Tis worse then Cheese in that point, may not a man breake his word with a Lady? I could finde in my heart and my hose too.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: By no meanes Sir, that breakes all the Lawes of Love.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Well, ile ne're passe my word without my deed to Lady, while I live agen, I would faine recover my taste.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Well, I have newes to tell you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Good newes, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Happy newes, I help you away with a Rivall your Master bestow'd

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Where for this plumbs sake—

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay listen me.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I warrant you, Sir, I have two eares to one mouth,
I heare more then I eat, i'de ne're row by Queen Hive
While lived else.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: I have a wife for him, and that shall witnesse the Contract.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: The old one I hope, 'tis not the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Choak him first, 'tis one which thou shalt see,
See him, see him deceiv'd, see the deceit, only
The injunction is, you shall smile with modesty.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ile simper ifaith, as cold as I am yet, the old one I hope.

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Sir, here's Sir Gregory.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Ud' so shelter, shelter, if you be seene
All's ravell'd out agen; stand there private,
And you'le finde the very opportunity
To call you forth, and place you at the Table.
You are welcome Sir, this Banquet will serve,
When it is crown'd with such a dainty as you
Expect, and must have.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Tush, these sweet-meats are but sauce to that,
Well, if there be any honesty or true word in a dreame,
She's mine owne, nay, and chang'd extreamely,
Not the same woman.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Who? not the Lady?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg,
verse: No, not to me, the edge of her tongue is taken off,
Gives me very good words, turn'd upside downe to me,
And we live as quietly as two Tortusses, if she hold on
As she began in my dreame.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay, if Love send forth such Predictions,
You are bound to beleeve 'em, there's the watch-word
Of her coming, to your practis'd part now,
If you hit it, Aequus Cupido nobis.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: I will warrant you Sir, I will give armes to
Your Gentry, looke you forward to your businesse,
I am an eye behind you, place her in that Chaire,
And let me alone to grope her out.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Silence, Lady, your sweet presence illustrates
This homely roofe, and as course entertainment;
But where affections are both Host and Guest,
They cannot meet unkindly, please you fit,
Your something long stay made me unmannerly,
To place before you, you know this friend here,
He's my Guest, and more especially,
That this our meeting might not be too single,
Without a witnesse to't.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
verse: I came not unresolv'd, Sir,
And when our hands are clasp'd in that firme faith
Which I expect from you; fame shall be bold
To speake the lowdest on't: oh, you graspe me.
Somewhat too hard friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: That's Loves eager will,
Ile touch it gentlier.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
verse: That's too low in you,
Lesse it be doubly recompenc'd in me.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Puh, I must stop my mouth, I shall be choakt else.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Come, wee'le not play and trifle with delayes,
We met to joyne these hands, and willingly
I cannot leave it till confirmation.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
prose: One word first, how does your friend, kinde Sir Gregory?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why do you mention him? you love him not?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I shall love you the lesse if you say so, Sir,
In troth I love him, but 'tis you deceive him,
This flattering hand of yours does rob him now,
Now you steale his right from him, and I know
I shall have hate for't, his hate extreamly.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why I thought you had not come so weakly arm'd,
Upon my life the Knight will love you for't,
Exceedingly love you, for ever love you.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I, you'le perswade me so.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Why he's my friend,
And wishes me a fortune equall with him,
I know, and dare speake it for him.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Oh, this hand betrayes him, you might remember him in some courtesie yet at least.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I thank your help in't, here's to his health
Where e're he be.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Ile pledge it were it against my health.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Oh. oh, my heart hops after twelve mile a day, upon a good returne, now could I walke three hundred mile a foot, and laugh forwards and backwards.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You'le take the Knights health Sir,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Yes, yes forsooth, oh my sides! such a Banquet once a weeke, would make me grow fat in a fortnight.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Well, now to close our meeting, with the close
Of mutuall hands and hearts, thus I begin,
Here in Heavens eye, and all loves sacred powers,
(Which in my prayers stand propitious)
I knit this holy hand fast, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
By force of this initiating Contract
Both heart and hand in love, faith, loyalty,
Estate, or what to them belongs, in all the dues;
Rights and honours of a faithfull husband,
And this firme vow henceforth till death to stand
Irrevocable, seal'd both with heart and hand.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Which thus I second, but oh, Sir Gregory.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Agen? this interposition's ill, beleeve me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Here in Heavens eye, and all Loves sacred powers
I knit this holy hand fast, and with this hand
The heart that owes this hand, ever binding
Both heart and hand in love, honour, loyalty,
Estate, or what to them belongs in all the dues,
Rights, and duties of a true faithfull wife;
And this firme Vow henceforth till death to stand,
Irrevocable seal'd both with heart and hand.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A full agreement on both parts.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I, here's witnesse of that.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Nay, I have over-reacht you Lady, and that's much,
For any Knight in England to over-reach a Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I rejoyce in my deceit, I am a Lady
Now, I thanke you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Good morrow Lady Fop.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: 'Snailes, i'me gull'd, made a worshipfull asse, this is not my Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: But it is Sir, and true as your dreame told you,
That your Lady was become another woman.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Ile have another Lady Sir, if there were no more Ladies in London, blinde-man buffe is an unlawfull Game.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Come, downe on your knees first, and thanke your stars.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: A fire of my stars, I may thanke you I think.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: So you may pray for me, and honour me,
That have preserv'd you from a lasting torment,
For a perpetuall comfort; did you call me friend?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I pray pardon me for that, l did miscall you, I confesse.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: And should I receiving such a thankfull name
Abuse it in the act? should I see my friend
Bafful'd, disgrac'd, without any reverence
To your title to be call'd slave, rascall?
Naay curst to your face, fool'd, scorn'd, beaten downe
With a womans peevish hate, yet I should stand
And suffer you to be lost, cast away?
I would have seene you buried quick first,
Your spurrs of Knight-hood to have wanted rowels,
And to be kickt from your heeles; slave, rascall?
Heare this tongue?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: My dearest Love, sweet Knight, my Lord, my Husband.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: So, this is not slave and rascall then.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What shall your eye command, but shall be done,
In all the duties of a loyall wife?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Good, good, are not curses fitter for you? wer't not better
Your head were broke with the handle of a fanne,
Or your nose bor'd with a silver bodkin?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why, I will be a servant in your Lady.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Pox, but you shall not, she's too good for you,
This contract shall be a nullity, ile breake't off,
And see you better bestow'd.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: 'Slid, but you shall not Sir, she's mine owne, And I am hers, and we are one anothers lawfully, and let me see him that will take her away by the Civill Law, if you be my friend keepe you so, if you have done me a good turne, do not hit me ith' teeth with't, that's not the part of a friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: If you be content —

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Content? I was never in better contention in my life,
Ile not change her for both the Exchanges, New or the Old;
Come, kisse me boldly.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Give you joy, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Oh Sir, I thanke you as much as though I did, you are beloved of Ladies, you see we are glad of under women.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ladies? let not Ladies be disgrac'd, you are as it were a married man, and have a Family, and for the parties sake that was unnam'd before, being Pese-cod time, I am appeas'd, yet I would wish you make a ruler of your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Nay, no dissention here, I must bar that,
And this (friend) I entreat you, and be advis'd,
Let this private contract be yet conceal'd,
And still support a seeming face of love
Unto the Lady; marke how it availes you,
And quits all her scornes, her Unckle is now hot
In pursuit of the match, and will enforce her
Bend her proud stomack, that she shall proffer
Her selfe to you, which when you have flouted,
And laught your fill at, you shall scorne her off
With all your disgraces trebled upon her,
For there the pride of all her heart will bow,
When you shall foot her from you, not she you.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Good ifaith; ile continue it, i'de faine laugh at the old fellow too, for he has abus'd me as scurvily as his Neece, my Knight-hood's upon the spur, wee'le go to Bed, and then to Church as fast as we can.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I do wonder I do not heare of the Lady yet.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: The good minute may come sooner then you are aware of,
I do not thinke but 'twill e're night yet as neare as 'tis.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Oh Knight that thou should'st be gull'd so; ha, ha, it does me good at heart,
But oh Lady, thou tak'st downe my merry part. Exit
prose: Well, I will go walke by the new River in that meditation, I am o're shooes I'me sure upon the dry bank, this gullery of my Master will keepe me company this two houres too, if love were not an enemy to laughter I should drive away the time well enough; you know my walke Sir, if she sends, I shall be found angling, for I will try what I can catch for luck sake, I will fish faire for't.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Friend.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Here friend.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: All's afoot, and will go smooth away,
The woman has conquer'd the women, they are gone,
Which I have already complain'd to my Father,
Suggesting that Sir Gregory is falne off
From his charge, for neglects and ill usage,
And that he is most violently bent
On Gentries wife (whom I have call'd a widow)
And that without most sudden prevention
He will be married to her.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Foot, all this is wrong,
This wings his pursuit, and will be before me; I am lost for ever.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: No, stay, you shall not go
But with my Father, on my wit let it lye,
You shall appeare a friendly assistant,
To helpe in all affaires, and in execution
Helpe your selfe only.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Would my beleefe
Were stronge in this assurance.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: You shall credit it,
And my wit shall be your slave if it deceive you.
My Father —

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Oh Sir, you are well met, where's the Knight your friend?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Sir, I thinke your Sonne has told you.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Shall I stand to tell't agen? I tell you he loves,
But not my Kins-woman, her base usage,
And your slack performance which he accuses most
Indeed, has turn'd the Knights heart upside downe.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Ile curbe her for't, can he be but recover'd,
He shall have her, and she shall be dutifull,
And loue him as a wife too.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: With that condition Sir,
I dare recall him were he enter'd the Church,
So much interest of love I assure in him.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Sir, it shall be no losse to you if you do.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: I, but these are words still, will not the deeds Be wanting at the recovery, if it should be agen?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why here foole, I am provided, five hunder'd in earnest,
Of the thousands in her Dower, but were they married once,
I'de cut him short enough, that's my agreement.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I, now I perceive some purpose in you, Father.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: But wherefore is she then stolne out of doores to him?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: To him? oh fye upon your errour, she has another objett, beleeve it Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I never could perceive it.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I did Sir, and to her shame I should speake it,
To my owne sorrow I saw it, dalliance,
Nay dotage with a very Clowne, a Foole.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: Wit and wantons? nothing else? nothing else?
She love a Foole? she'le sooner mate a foole
Of a wise man.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I, my friend complaines so,
Sir Gregory sayes flatly she makes a foole of him,
And these bold circumstances are approv'd;
Favours have been sent by him, yet he ignorant
Whither to carry 'em; they have been understood,
And taken from him, certaine Sir, there is
An unsuspected fellow lyes conceal'd,
What, or where e're he is, these slight neglects
Could not be of a Knight else.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Well Sir, you have promis'd (if we recover him Unmarried) to salve all these old bruises?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Ile do my best Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: I shall thanke you, costly Sir, and kindly too.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Will you talke away the time here Sir, and come behirtde all your purposes?

speeches.speaker: O.K.
verse: Away good Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Then stay a little good Sir, for my advise,
Why Father are you broke? your wit begger'd,
Or are you at your wits end? or out of
Love with wit? no trick of Wit to surprize
Those designes, but with open Hue and Cry,
For all the world to talke on? this is strange,
You were not wont to slubber a project so.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Can you helpe at a pinch now? shew your selfe
My sonne, go too, I leave this to your wit,
Because ile make a proofe on't.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: 'Tis thus then,
I have had late intelligence, they are now
Buxsome as Bachus Froes, revelling, dancing,
Telling the Musicks numbers with their feet,
Awaiting the meeting of premonisht friends,
That's questionlesse, little dreading you,
Now Sir, with a dexterous trick indeed, suddaine
And sufficient were well, to enter on um
As something like the abstract of a Masque;
What though few persons? if best for our purpose
That commends the project.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: This takes up time.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Not at all, I can presently furnish
With loose disguises that shall fit that Scene.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why what wants then?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nothing but charge of Musick,
That must be paid you know.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: That shall be my charges, ile pay the Musick,
What e're it cost.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: And that shall be all your charge,
Now on, I like it, there will be wit in't Father.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: I will neither distrust his wit nor friendship,
Yet if his master braine should be o're-throwne
My resolution now shall seize mine owne.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Nay, let's have Musick, let that sweet breath at least
Give us her ayrie welcome, 'twill be the best
I feare this ruin'd receptacle will yeeld,
But that most freely.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: My welcome followes me,
Else I am ill come hither, you assure me
Still Mr. Cuningame will be here, and that it was
His kinde entreaty that wisht me meet him.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Else let me be that shame unto my Sex,
That all beleefe may fly um.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Continue still
The Knights name unto my Gardianesse,
She expects no other.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: He will, he will assure you
Lady, Sir Gregory will be here, and suddainely
This Musick fore-ran him, is't not so consorts?

speeches.speaker: Ruin,
verse: Yes Lady, he staies on some device to bring along
Such a labour he was busie in, some witty device.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: 'Twill be long e're he comes then, for wit's a great Labour to him.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Well, well, you'le agree better one day.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Scarce two I think.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Such a mock-begger suit of clothes as led me
Into the fooles paire of Dice, with dewze ace,
He that would make me Mistris Cun, Cun, Cunnie,
He's quite out of my minde, but I shall ne're
Forget him while I have a hole in my head,
Such a one I think would please you better,
Though he did not abuse you.

speeches.speaker: Ruin,
verse: Fye, speake well of him now,
Your Neece has quitted him.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I hope she has,
Else she looses me for ever; but for Sir Gregory,
Would he were come. I shall ill answer this
Unto your Unckle else.

speeches.speaker: Nei.
verse: You know 'tis his pleasure
I should keepe him company.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: I, and should be your owne
If you did well too, Lord, I do wonder
At the nicenesse of you Ladies now a dayes,
They must have Husbands with so much wit forsooth.
Worship and wealth were both wont to be
In better request I'me sure, I cannot tell,
But they get ne're the wiser children that I see.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: La, la, la, la, Sol, this Musick breathes in vaine,
Me thinks 'tis dull to let it move alone,
Let's have a female motion, 'tis in private,
And wee'le grace't our selves how ever it deserves.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: What say you Gardianesse?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: 'Lasse i'me weary with the walke,
My jaunting dayes are done.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Come, come, we'le fetch her in by course, or else,
She shall pay the Musick.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Nay, ile have a little for my money then.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Hark? upon my life the Knight; 'tis your friend,
This was the warning-peece of his approach.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Ha? no words but mum? well then,
We shall need no counsell-keeping

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Cuningame?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Yes, feare nothing.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Feare? why do you tell me of it?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Your Unckles here.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Aye me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Peace.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: We have caught 'em.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Thanke my wit Father.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Which is the Knight thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: I know not, he will be found when be speakes,
No Maske can disguise his tongue.

speeches.speaker: Wity.
verse: Are you charg'd?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Are you awake?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: I'me answer'd in a question.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Next change we meet, we loose our hands no more.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Are you prepar'd to tye 'em?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: Yes,
You must go with me.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Whether Sir? not from my charge beleeve me.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: She goes a long.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
verse: Will you ventur and my Unckle here?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: His stay's prepar'd for.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: 'Tis the Knight sure, ile follow.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: How now, the Musick tyr'd before us?

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: Yes Sir, we must be paid now.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Oh, that's my charge Father.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: But stay, where are our wanton Ladies gone?
Sonne, where are they?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Onely chang'd the roome in a change, that's all sure.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Ile make 'em all sure else, and then returne to you.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: You must pay for your Musick first, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Must? are there musty Fidlers? are Beggers choosers now?
Ha? why Witty-pate, Sonne, where am I?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: You were dancing e'ne now, in good measure Sir,
Is your health miscarried since? what ayle you, Sir?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Death, I may be gull'd to my face, where's my Neece?
What are you?

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: None of your Neece, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: How now? have you loud Instruments too? ile heare
No more I thanke you, what have I done tro
To bring these feares about me? Sonne, where am I?

speeches.speaker: VVitty.
verse: Not where you should be, Sir, you should be paying
For your Musick, and you are in a maze.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Oh, is't so, put up, put up, I pray you,
Here's a crowne for you.

speeches.speaker: L. Ruin.
verse: Pish, a crowne?

speeches.speaker: Ru. Pris.
verse: Ha, ha, ha, a crowne?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Which way do you laugh? I have seene a crowne
Has made a Consort laugh heartily.

speeches.speaker: VVitty.
verse: Father,
To tell you truth, these are no ordinary
Musitians, they expect a bounty
Above their punctuall desert.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: A — on your Puncks, and their deserts too.
Am I not cheated all this while thinke you?
Is not your pate in this?

speeches.speaker: VVitty.
verse: If you be cheated,
You are not to be Indicted for your owne goods,
Here you trifle time to market your bounty
And make it base, when it must needs be free
For ought I can perceive.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Will you know the lowest price, Sir?

speeches.speaker: VVitty.
verse: That I will Sir, with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Unlesse I was discover'd, and they now fled
Home agen for feare, I am absolutely beguil'd,
That's the best can be hop'd for.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Faith 'tis somewhat too deare yet, Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Ruin.
verse: There's not a Denier to be bated, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Now Sir, how deare is it?

speeches.speaker: VVitty.
verse: Bate but the tother ten pound?

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Not a Bawbee, Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. R.
verse: How? bate ten pound? what's the whole summe then?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Faith Sir, a hundred pound, with much a doe,
I got fifty bated, and faith Father, to say truth,
'Tis reasonable for men of their fashion.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: La, la, la, downe, a hunder'd pound? la, la, la,
You are a Consort of Theeves, are you not?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: No Musitians Sir, I told you before.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Fiddle faddle, is it not a robbery? a plaine robbery?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: No, no, no, by no meanes Father, you have receiv'd
For your money, nay, and that you cannot give back,
'Tis somewhat deare I confesse, but who can helpe it?
If they had been agreed with before hand,
'Twas ill forgotten.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: And how many shares have you in this? I see my force,
Case up your Instruments, I yield, here, as rob'd and
Taken from me, I deliver it.

speeches.speaker: VVitty.
prose: No Sir, you have perform'd your promise now, which was, to pay the charge of Musick, that's all.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: I have heard no Musick, I have receiv'd none, Sir, There's none to be found in me, nor about me.

speeches.speaker: VVitty.
verse: Why Sir, here's witnesse against you, you have danc'd,
And he that dances acknowledges a receit
Of Musick.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: I deny that Sir, looke you, I can dance without Musick, do you see Sir? and I can sing without it too; you are a consort of Theeves, do you heare what I do?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Pray you take heed Sir, if you do move the Musick agen, it may cost you as much more.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
prose: Hold, hold, ile depart quietly, I need not bid you farewell, I think now, so long as that hundred pound lasts with you.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
verse: Ha, ha, am I snapt ifaith?
Oh, Sir, Perfidious.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: I, I, some howling anotherwhile, Musick's too damnable deare.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: Oh Sir, my heart-strings are broke, if I can but live to tell you the tale I care not, your Neece my charge is —

speeches.speaker: O.K.
prose: What, is she sick?

speeches.speaker: Gard,
prose: No, no Sir, she's lustity well married.

speeches.speaker: O.K.
prose: To whom?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: Oh, to that cunning dissembler, Cuningame.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Ile hang the Priest, first, what was he?

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: Your Kinsman Sir, that has the Welch Benefice.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: I sav'd him from the Gallowes to that end, good, is there any more?

speeches.speaker: Garde
prose: And Sir Gregory is married too.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: To my Neece too, I hope, and then I may hang her.

speeches.speaker: Gard.
prose: No Sir, to my Neece, thank Cupid; and that's all that's likely to recover me, she's Lady Fop now, and I am One of her Aunts I thanke my promotion.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
prose: I hate perform'd your behest Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: What have you perform'd Sir?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Faith Sir, I must excuse my Cousen in this act,
If you can excuse your selfe for making him
A Priest, there's the most difficult answer
I put this practise on him as from your desire,
A truth, a truth Father.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
prose: I protest Sir, he tells you truth, he mov'd me to't in your name.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: I protest Sir, he told you a lye in my name, and were you so easie Mr. Credulous to beleeve him?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
prose: If a man should not beleeve his Cousen Sir, whom should he beleeve?

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Godden to you good Mr. Cousen Cuningame,
And your faire Bride, my Cousen Cuningame too,
And how do you, Sir Gregory, with your faire Lady?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: A little better then you would have had me, I thanke you Sir, the dayes of Puppy, and Slave, and Rascall are pretty well blowne over now, I know Crabs from Verjuyce, I have tryed both, and thoud'st give me thy Neece for nothing i'de not have her.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: I thinke so Sir Gregory, for my sake you would not.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: I wo'd thou had'st scap'd her too, and then she had dyed of the greene sicknesse, know this, that I did marry in spight, and I will kisse my Lady in spight, and love her in spight, and beget children of her in spight, and when I dye they shall have my Lands in spight; this was my resolution, and now 'tis out.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: How spightfull are you now, Sir Gregory?
Why looke you, I can love my dearest Husband,
With all the honours, duties, sweet embraces,
That can be throwne upon a loving man.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: — This is afore your Unckles face, but behinde his back in private you'le shew him another tale.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: You see Sir, now the irrecoverable state of all these things before you, come out of your muse, they have been but wit weapons, they were wont to love the play.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
prose: Let me alone in my muse a little Sir, I will wake to you anon.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: U'd so, your friend Pompey, how will you answer him?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: Very well, if you'le but second it, and help me.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I do heare strange stories, are Ladies things obnoxious?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: Oh, the dissembling falsest wretch is come.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: How now Lady?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Let me come to him, and in stead of love
Let me have revenge.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Pray you now, will you first examine, whither he be guilty or no.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: He cannot be excus'd,
How many Messengers (thou perjur'd man)
Hast thou return'd with Vowes and Oathes? that thou
Wouldst follow, and never till this unhappy houre
Could I set eye of thee, since thy false dye
Drew my heart to it? oh I could teare thee now,
In stead of soft embraces, pray give me leave—

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Faith this was ill done of you Sir, if you promis'd otherwise.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: By this hand, never any Messenger came at me since the first time I came into her company; that a man should be wrong'd thus?

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Did not I send thee Scarfes and Diamonds?
And thou returnd'st me letters, one with a faife heart in't.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: On fye to receive favours, returne false-hoods, and hold a Lady in hand —

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Will you believe me Sir? if ever I receiv'd Diamonds, or Scarfe, or sent any Letter to her, would this Sword might ne're go through me.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Some bad Messengers have gone betweene you then.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: Take him from my fight, if I shall see to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Pray you forbeare the place, this discontent may impaire her health much.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Foot, if a man had been in any fault 'twould ne're have griev'd him, Sir, if you'le beleeve.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nay, nay, protest no more, I do believe you,
But you see how the Lady is wrong'd by't;
She has cast away her selfe it is to be fear'd,
Against her Unckles will, nay, any consent,
But out of a meere neglect, and spight to her selfe,
Married suddenly without any advice.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Why who can helpe it? if she be cast away she may thanke her selfe, she might have gone further and far'd worse; I could do no more then I could do, 'twas her owne pleasure to command me that I should not come till I was sent for, I had been with her every minute of an houre else.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Truly I believe you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Night and day she might have commanded me, and that she knew well enough; I said as much to her between her and I, yet I protest she's as honest a Lady for my part, that i'de say if she would see me hang'd, if she be cast away I cannot helpe it, she might have stay'd to have spoke with a man.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Well, 'twas a hard misse on both parts.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: So 'twas, I was within one of her, for all this crosse luck, I was sure I was between the Knight and home.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: Not gone yet? oh my heart! none regard my health?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: Good Sir, forbeare her sight a while, you heare how ill she brookes it.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Foolish woman, to over-throw her fortunes so; I shall thinke the worse of a Ladies wit while I live for't— I could almost cry for anger, if she should miscarry now, 'twould touch my conscience a little, and who knowes what love and conceit may do? what would people say as I go along? there goes he that the Lady dyed for love on, lam sure to heare on't ith' streets. I shall weepe before hand; foolish woman, I do grieve more for thee now then I did love thee before; well, go thy waies, would'st thou spare thy Husbands head and breake thine owne heart? if thou hadst any wit, I would some other had been the cause of thy undoing, I shall be twitted i'th teeth with't, i'me sure of that, foolish Lady.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
prose: So, so, this trouble's well shooke off, Unckle, how dee? there's a Dowrie due, sir.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
verse: We have agreed it, sweetest,
And finde your Unckle fully recover'd, kinde to both of us.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose: To all the rest I hope;

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Never to thee, nor thee, easie cousen Credulous,
Was your wit so raw?

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: Faith yours Sir, so long season'd
Has been faulty too, and very much to blame,
Speaking it with reverence, Unckle.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Yes faith, Sir, you have paid as deare for your time as any man here.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
prose:
I Sir, and ile reckon it to him. Imprimis, The first preface cheat of a paire of peeces to the Beggers, you
remember that I was the example to your bounty there, I spake Greeke, and Syriacke, Sir, you understand me now. Next, the Robbery put upon your indulgent Cousen, which indeed was no Robbery, no Constable, no Justice, no Thiefe, but all Cheaters; there was a hunder'd Mark, mark you that. Lastly, this memorable 100. pounds worth of Musick, this was but cheats and wit too, and for the assistance, this Gentleman to my Cousen (for which I am to have a Fee) that was a little practice of my wit too, Father; will you come to composition yet, Father?

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Yes faith Sir, do, two hunder'd a yeare will be easier then so much weekly, I do not think he's barren if he should be put to't agen.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Why this was the day I look'd for, thou shalt have't,
And the next cheat makes it up three hunder'd;
Live thou upou thy ten pound Vicarage,
Thou get'st not a penny more, here's thy full
Hire now.

speeches.speaker: Cred.
verse: I thanke you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Why there was the summe of all my wit Father,
To shove him out of your favour, which I fear'd
Would have dis-inherited me.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Most certaine it had,
Had not thy wit recover'd it; is there any here
That had a hand with thee?

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Yes, all these Sir.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Nephew, part a hunder'd pound amongst 'em,
Ile repay it; wealth, love me as I love wit;
When I dye,
Ile build an Almes-house for decay'd wits.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
prose: Ile entertaine one in my life time; Schollar, you shall be my Chaplaine, I have the gift of twenty Benefices, simple as I am here.

speeches.speaker: Pris.
verse: Thankes my great Patron.

speeches.speaker: Cun.
prose: Sir, your Gentry and your name shall both be rais'd as high as my fortunes can reach 'em, for your friends sake.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Something will be in my present power, the future more,
You shall share with me.

speeches.speaker: Ruin. and VVife.
verse: Thankes worthy Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Neece.
verse: Sir, I would beg one thing of you?

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: You can beg nothing of me.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Oh Sir, if she begs, there's your power over her.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: She has begg'd me for a foole already, but 'tis no matter,
I have begg'd her for a Lady that she might have been,
That's one for another.

speeches.speaker: Witty.
verse: Nay, but if she beg—

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Let her beg agen then.

speeches.speaker: Nee.
prose: That your man Pompeyes Coat may come over his eares backe agen, I would not he should be lost for my sake.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Well, 'tis granted, for mine owne sake.

speeches.speaker: Mirab.
verse: Ile entreat it Sir.

speeches.speaker: Sir Greg.
verse: Why then 'tis granted for your sake.

speeches.speaker: O. K.
verse: Come, come, downe with all weapons now, 'tis
Musicke time,
So it be purchas'd at an easie rate;
Some have receiv'd the knocks, some given the hits,
And all concludes in love, there's happy wits.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: I Never saw the like, shee's no more stirr'd,
No more another woman, no more alter'd,
With any hopes or promises layd to her
(Let 'em be nev'r so waighty, nev'r so winning,
Then I am with the motion of my owne legs.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Chilax.
You are a stranger yet in these designes,
At least in Rome; tell me, and tell me truth,
Did you ere know in all your course of practise,
In all the wayes of woman you have runne through
(For I presume you have been brought up Chilax,
As we to fetch and carry.)

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: True I have so:

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Did you I say againe in all this progresse,
Ever discover such a peece of beauty,
Ever so rare a Creature, and no doubt
One that must know her worth too, and affect it,
I and be flatter'd, else tis none: and honest?
Honest against the tide of all temptations,
Honest to one man, to her husband only,
And yet not eighteene, not of age to know
Why she is honest?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I confesse it freely,
I never saw her fellow, nor er'e shall,
For all our Graecian Dames, all I have tri'd,
(And sure I have tri'd a hunderd, if I say two
I speake within my compasse) all these beauties,
And all the constancy of all these faces,
Mayds, Widdows, Wives, of what degree or calling,
So they be Greekes, and fat, for there's my cunning,
I would undertake and not sweat sor't, Proculus,
Were they to try againe, say twice as many,
Vnder a thousand pound, to lay 'em bedrid;
But this Wench staggers me.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: Doe you see these Iewells?
You would thinke these pretty baytes; now Ile assure ye
Here's halfe the wealth of Asia.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: These are nothing
To the full honours I propounded to her;
I bid her think, and be, and presently
What ever her ambition, what the Councell
Of others would adde to her, what her dreames
Could more enlarge, what any President
Of any woman rising up to glory,
And standing certaine there, and in the highest,
Could give her more, nay to be Empresse.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: And cold at all these offers?

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Cold as Christall,
Never to be thaw'd again,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I trid her further,
And so farre, that I think she is no woman,
At least as women goe now.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: Why what did you?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I offerd that, that had she been but Mistris
Of as much spleene as Doves have, I had reach'd her.
A safe revenge of all that ever hates her,
The crying down for ever all beauties
That may be thought come neare her.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: That was pretty.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I never knew that way faile, yet Ile tell ye
I offerd her a gift beyond all yours,
That, that had made a Sainct start, well considerd,
The Law to be her creature, she to make it,
Her mouth to give it, every creature living
From her aspect, to draw their good or evill
Fixd in'em spight of Fortune; a new Nature
She should be called, and mother of all ages,
Time should be hers, and what she did lame vertue
Should blesse to all posterities: her aire
Should give us life, her earth and water feed us.
And last, to none but to the Emperour,
(And then but when she pleas'd to have it so,)
She should be held for mortall.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: And she heard you?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Yes, as a Sick man heares a noise, or he
That stands condemn'd his Iudgment, let me perish,
But if there can be vertue, if that name
Be any thing but name and emptie title,
If it be so as fooles have been pleas'd to saigne it,
A power that can preserve us after ashes,
And make the names of men out-reckon ages,
This Woman has a God of vertue in her.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: I would the Emperor were that God.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: She has in her
All the contempt of glory and vaine seeming
Of all the Stoicks, all the truth of Christians,
And all their Constancy: Modesty was made
When she was first intended: When she blushes
It is the holyest thing to looke upon;
The purest temple of her sect, that ever
Made nature a blest Founder.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Is there no way
To take this Phenix?

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: None but in her ashes.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: If she were fat, or any way inclining
To ease or pleasure, or effected glory,
Proud to be seene and worship'd, t'were a venture;
But on my soule she is chaster then cold Camphire.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: I thinke so too; for all the wayes of woman,
Like a full saile she bears against: I aske her
After my many offers, walking with her,
And her as many down-denyals, how
If the Emperor grown mad with love should force her;
She pointed to a Lucrece, that hung by,
And with an angry looke, that from her eyes
Shot Vestall fire against me, she departed.

speeches.speaker: Bro.
verse: This is the first wench I was ever pos'd in,
Yet I have brought young loving things together
This two and thirty yeare.

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: I find by this wench
The calling of a Bawd to be a strange,
A wise, and subtile calling; and for none
But staid, discreet, and understanding people:
And as the Tutor to great Alexander,
Would say a young man should not dare to read
His morall books, till after five and twenty;
So must that he or she, that will be bawdy,
(I meane discreetly bawdy, and be trusted)
If they will rise, and gaine experience,
Wel steept in yeares, and discipline, begin it,
I take it tis no boys play.

speeches.speaker: Bal.
verse: Well, what's thought off?

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: The Emperour must know it.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: If the women should chance to faile too,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: As tis ten to one,

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Why what remaines, but new nets for the purchase?

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Let's goe consider then: and if all faile,
This is the first quick Eele, that sav'd her taile.

speeches.speaker: Ardelia.
verse: You still insist upon that Idoll, Honour,
Can it renue your youth, can it adde wealth,
That takes off wrinkles: can it draw mens eyes,
To gaze upon you in your age? can honour,
That truly is a Saint to none but Souldiers,
And lookd into, beare no reward but danger,
Leave you the most respected person living?
Or can the common kisses of a husband,
(Which to a sprightly Lady is a labour)
Make ye almost Immortall? ye are cozend,
The honour of a woman is her praises;
The way to get these, to be seene, and sought too,
And not to bury such a happy sweetnesse
Vnder a smoaky roofe.

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Ile heare no more:

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: That white, and red, and all that blessed beauty,
Kept from the eyes, that make it so, is nothing;
Then you are rarely faire, when men proclaime it;
The Phenix, were she never seene, were doubted,
That most unvalued Horne the Vnicorne
Beares to oppose the Huntsman, were it nothing
But tale, and meere tradition, would help no man,
But when the vertue's knowne, the honor's dobled:
Vertue, is either lame, or not at all,
And Love a sacriledge, and not a Saint,
When it bars up the way to mens Petitions.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Nay ye shal love your husband too; we come not
To make a Monster of yee;

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Are ye women?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: You'l find us so, and women you shall think too,
If you have grace to make your use.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Eye on yee,

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Alas poore bashfull Lady, by my soule,
Had ye no other vertue, but your blushes,
And I a man, I should run mad for those;
How daintlily they set her off, how sweetly?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Come Goddesse, come, you move too neer the earth,
It must not be, a better orbe staies for you:
Here: be a mayd, and take'en,

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Pray leave me.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: That were a sin sweet Lady, and a way
To make us guilty of your melancholly;
You must not be alone; In conversation
Doubts are resolvd, and what sticks neer the conscience
Made easie, and allowable.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Ye are Devills,

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: That you may one day blesse for your damnation.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I charge ye in the name of Chastity,
Tempt me no more; how ugly ye seem to me?
There is no wonder men defame our Sex,
And lay the vices of all ages on us,
When such as you shall beare the names of women;
If ye had eyes to see your selves, or sence
Above the base rewards ye play the bawds for:
If ever in your lives ye heard of goodnesse,
(Though many Regions off, as men heare thunder)
If ever ye had Mothers, and they soules:
If ever Fathers, and not such as you are;
If ever any thing were constant in you,
Beside your sins, or comming but your curses,
If ever any of your Ancestors
Dyde worth a noble deed, that would be cherishd,
Soule-frighted with this black infection,
You would run from one another, to repentance,
And from your guilty eyes drop out those sins,
That made ye blind, and beasts.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Ye speak well Lady;
A signe of fruitfull education,
If your religious Zeale had wisdome with it.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: This Lady was ordain'd to blesse the Empire,
And we may all give thanks for't.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: I beleive ye,

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: If any thing redeem the Emperour,
From his wild flying courses, this is she;
She can instruct him if ye mark; she is wise too.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Exceeding wise, which is a wonder in her,
And so religious, that I well believe,
Though she would sinne she cannot.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: And, besides
She has the Empires cause in hand, not loves;
There lies the maine consideration,
For which she is chiefly borne.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: She finds that point
Stronger then we can tell her, and believe it
I look by her meanes for a reformation,
And such a one, and such a rare way carried
That all the world shall wonder at.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Tis true;
I never thought the Emperor had wisdom,
Pittie, or faire affection to his Country,
Till he profest this love: gods give'em Children,
Such as her vertues merit, and his zeale.
I looke to see a Numa from this Lady,
Or greater then Octavius.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Do you mark too,
Which is a Noble vertue, how she blushes,
And what a flowing modesty runs through her,
When we but name the Emperour?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: But mark it,
Yes, and admire it too, for she considers,
Though she be faire as heaven, and vertuous
As holy truth, yet to the Emperour
She is a kind of nothing but her service,
Which she is bound to offer, and she'l do it,
And when her Countries cause commands affection;
She knows obedience is the key of vertues,
Then flye the blushes out like Cupids arrowes,
And though the tye of marriage to her Lord,
Would faine cry stay Lucina, yet the cause
And generall wisdom of the Princes love,
Makes her find surer ends and happier,
And if the first were chaste, this is twice dobled.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Her tartnes unto us too.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: That's a wise one.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: I rarely like, it shewes a rising wisdom,
That chides all common fooles as dare enquire
What Princes would have private.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: What a Lady
Shall we be blest to serve?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Goe get ye from me.
Ye are your purses Agents, not the Princes:
Is this the vertuous Lore yee traind me out too?
Am I a woman fit to imp your vices?
But that I had a Mother, and a woman
Whose ever living fame turnes all it touches,
Into the good it selfe is, I should now
Even doubt my selfe, I have been search't so neere
The very soule of honour: why should you two,
That happily have been as chast as I am,
Fairer, I think, by much, for yet your faces,
Like ancient well built piles, shew worthy ruines,
After that Angell age, turne mortall Devills?
For shame, for woman-hood, for what ye have been,
For rotten Cedars have borne goodly branches,
If ye have hope of any Heaven, but Court,
Which like a Dreame, you'l find hereafter vanish,
Or at the best but subject to repentance,
Study no more to be ill spoken of;
Let women live themselves, if they must fall,
Their owne destruction find 'em, not your sevours.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Madam, yee are so excellent in all,
And I must tell it you with admiration,
So true a joy ye have, so sweet a feare,
And when ye come to anger, tis so noble,
That for mine own part, I could still offend,
To heare you angry; women that want that,
And your way guided (else I count it nothing)
Are either Fooles, or Cowards.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: She were a Mistris for no private greatnesse,
Could she not frowne a ravishd kisse from anger,
And such an anger as this Lady learnes us,
Stuck with such pleasing dangers. Gods (I aske ye)
Which of ye all could hold from?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: I perceive ye,
Your owne dark sins dwell with yee, and that price
You sell the chastitie of modest wives at
Runs to diseases with your bones: I scorne ye,
And all the nets ye have pitcht to catch my vertues
Like Spiders Webs, I sweep away before me.
Goe tell the Emperour, yee have met a woman,
That neither his owne person, which is God-like,
The world he rules, nor what that world can purchase,
Nor all the glories, subject to a Cesar,
The honours that he offers for my body,
The hopes, gifts, everlasting flatteries,
Nor any thing that's his, and apt to tempt me,
No not to be the Mother of the Empire,
And Queene of all the holy fires he worships,
Can make a Whore of.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: You mistake us Lady.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
verse: Yet tell him this ha's thus much weakend me,
That I have here his knaves, and you his Matrons,
Fit Nurses for his sins, which gods forgive me,
But ever to be leaning to his folly,
Or to be brought to love his lust, assure him,
And from her mouth, whose life shal make it certain
I never can: I have a Noble husband,
Pray tell him that too, yet a noble name,
A Noble Family, and last a Conscience:
Thus much for your answer: For your selves,
Ye have liv'd the shame of women, dye the better,

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: What's now to doe?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: Ev'n as she said, to dye,
For ther's no living here, and women thus,
I am sure for us two.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Nothing stick upon her?

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: We have lost a masse of mony; wel Dame vertue,
Yet ye may halt if good luck serve.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: Wormes take her,
She has almost spoil'd our trade.

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: So godly;
This is ill breeding Phorba.

speeches.speaker: Phor.
verse: If the women
Should have a longing now to see this Monster,
And she convert 'em all,

speeches.speaker: Ard.
verse: That may be Phorba,
But if it be, Ile have the young men gelded:
Come, let's goe think, she must not scape us thus;
There is a certain season, if we hit,
That women may be rid without a bit.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I cannot blame the Nations noble friend,
That they fall off fo fast from this wild man,
When (under our Allegeance be it spoken,
And the most happy tye of our affections)
The worlds weight groanes beneath him; where lives vertue,
Honour, discretion, wisdom? who are cald
And chosen to the stleering of the Empire
But Baudes, and singing Girles? ô my Aecius,
The glory or a Souldier, and the truth
Of men made up for goodnesse sake, like shells
Grow to the ragged walls for want of action:
Only your happy selfe, and I that love ye,
Which is a larger meanes to me then favour.

speeches.speaker: Aecius
verse: No more my worthy friend, though these be truths,
And though these truthes would aske a Reformation,
At least a little squaring; yet remember,
We are but subjects Maximus; obedience
To what is done, and griefe for what is ill done,
Is all we can call ours: the hearts of Princes
Are like the Temples of the gods; pure incense,
Vntill unhallowed hands defile those off^ings,
Burnes ever there; we must not put 'em out,
Because the Priests that touch those sweetes are wicked;
We dare not deerest friend, nay more we cannot,
While we consider why we are, and how,
To what lawes bound, much more to what Law-giver;
Whilest majestie is made to be obeyed,
And not inquired into, whilest Gods and Angels
Make but a rule as we do, though a stricter;
Like desperate and unseason'd fooles let fly
Our killing angers, and forsake our honors.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: My noble Freind, from whose Instructions
I never yet tooke surfet, weigh but thus much,
Nor thinke I speake it with ambition,
For by the Gods I do not, why Aecius,
Why are we thus, or how become thus wretched?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: You'l fall againe into your fit.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I will not.
Or are we now no more the sons of Romanes,
No more the followers of their happy fortunes,
But conquer'd Gaules, or Quivers for the Parthians?
Why is this Emperor, this man we honor,
This God that ought to be?

speeches.speaker: Aecius.
verse: You are too curious.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Good, give me leave, why is this Author of us?

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: I dare not heare ye speake thus.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Ile be modest,
Thus led away, thus vainly led away,
And we beholders, misconceive me not,
I sow no danger in my words; but wherefore
And to what end, are we the sonnes of Fathers
Famous, and fast to Rome? Why are their vertues
Stampt in the dangers of a thousand Battailes,
For goodnesse sake, their honors, time out daring,
I thinke for our example.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Ye speake nobly.

speeches.speaker: Mac.
verse: Why are we seeds of these then, to shake hands
With Bawdes and base Informers, kisse discredit,
And court her like a Mistris? pray, your leave yet;
You'l say the Emperor is young, and apt
To take impression rather from his pleasures
Then any constant worthynsse, it may be.
But why do these, the people call his pleasures,
Exceed the moderation of a man?
Nay to say justly freind, why are they vices
And such as shake our worthes with forraigne Nations?

speeches.speaker: Aec.
verse: You search the soare too deep, and I must tel ye,
In any other man this had been boldnesse,
And so rewarded; pray depresse you spirit,
For though I constantly beleeve ye honest,
Ye were no freind for me else, and what now
Ye freely spake, but good ye owe toth Empire,
Yet take heed worthy Maximus, all eares
Heare not with that distinction mine doe, few
You'l find admonishers, but urgers of your actions,
And to the heaviest (freind;) and pray consider
We are but shadowes, motions others give us,
And though our pitties may become the times,
Iustly our powers cannot; make me worthy
To be your ever freind in faire allegiance,
But not in force: For durst mine own soule urge me
(And by that soule, I speake my just affections)
To turn my hand from truth, which is obedience,
And give the helme my vertue holds, to Anger,
Though I had both the blessings of the Brutij,
And both their Instigations, though my cause
Carried a face of Iustice beyond theirs,
And as I am a servant to my fortunes,
That daring soule, that first taught disobedience,
Should feele the first example: Say the Prince,
As I may well beleeve, seemes vitious,
Who justly knowes tis not to try our honors?
Or say he be an ill Prince, are we therefore
Fit fires to purge him? No, my dearest freind
The Elephant is never won with anger,
Nor must that man that would reclaime a Lyon,
Take him by'th teeth.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I pray mistake me not.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Our honest actions, and the light that breakes
Like morning from our service, chaste and blushing
Is that, that pulls a Prince backe; then he sees,
And not till then truly repents his errors,
When subjects Chrystall soules are glasses to him.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: My ever honored freind, Ile take your councel:
The Emperor appeares, Ile leave ye to him,
And as we both affect him, may he flourish.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
prose: Is that the best newes?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Yet the best we know Sir.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: Bid Maximus come to me, and be gone then:
Mine own head be my helper, these are fooles;
How now Aecius, are the Souldiers quiet?

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Better I hope Sir, then they were.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: They are pleas'd I heare,
To censure me extremely for my pleasures,
Shortly the'l fight against me.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Gods defend Sir.
And for their censures they are such shrew'd Iudgers;
A donative of ten Sesterties
Ile undertake shall make 'em ring your praises,
More then they sang your pleasures.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: I beleeve thee.
Art thou in love Aecius yet?

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: O no Sir.
I am too course for Ladies; my embraces
That only am acquainted with Alarums,
Would break their tender bodies.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: Never feare it,
They are stronger then ye think, they'le hold the hammer
My Empresse sweares thou art a lusty Souldier,
A good one I beleeve thee.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: All that goodnesse
Is but your Graces creature.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: Tell me truly,
For thou darst tell me.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Any thing concernes ye,
That's fit for me to speake and you to pardon.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: What say the soldiers of me, and the same words,
Mince 'em not good Aecius, but deliver
The very forms and tongues they talke withall,

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Ile tell your Grace, but with this caution
You be not stirr'd, for should the Gods live with us,
Even those we certainly beleeve are righteous.
Give 'em but drinke, they would censure them too.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: Forward.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Then to begin, they say you sleep too much
By which they judge your Majesty too sensuall,
Apt to decline your strength to ease and pleasures,
And when you do not sleepe, you drink too much,
From which they feare suspitions first, then ruines;
And when ye neither drinke nor sleepe, ye wench much,
Which they affirm first breakes your understanding,
Then takes the edge of honor, make us seeme,
That are the ribbes, and rampires of the Empire,
Fencers, and beaten Fooles, and so regarded;
But I beleive 'em not; for were these truths,
Your vertue can correct them.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: They speake plainly.

speeches.speaker: Aec.
verse: They say moreover (since your grace wil have it,
For they will talke their freedoms, though the sword
Were in their throat) that of late time, like Nero,
And with the same forgetfullnes of glory,
You have got a vaine of filing, so they terme it.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: Some drunken dreames Aecius.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: So I hope Sir.
And that you rather study cruelty,
And to be feared for blood, then lov'd for bounty.
Which makes the Nations, as they say, despise ye,
Telling your yeares and actions by their deathes,
Whose truth, and strength of duty made you Caesar.
They say besides you nourish strange devourers,
Fed with the fat o'th Empires, they call Bawdes,
Lazie and lustfull creatures that abuse ye,
A people as they terme 'em, made of paper,
In which the secret sins of each mans monyes
Are sealed and sent a working.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: What sin's next?
For I perceive they have no mind to spare me.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: Nor hurt ye ô my soule Sir; but such people
(Nor can the power of man restraine it)
When they are full of meat and ease, must prattle.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: Forward.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: I have spoken too much Sir.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: Ile have all.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: It fits not
Your eares should heare their vanities; no profit
Can justly rise to you from their behaviour,
Vnlesse ye were guilty of those crimes.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: It may be
I am so, therefore forward.

speeches.speaker: Aeci
verse: I have ever
Learn'd to obey, nor shall my life resist it.

speeches.speaker: Empe.
verse: No more Apologies.

speeches.speaker: Aeci.
verse: They greive besides Sir,
To see the nations, whom our ancient vertue
With many a weary march and hunger conquer'd,
With losse of many a daring life subdude,
Fall from their faire obedience, and even murmure
To see the warlike Eagles mew their honors
In obscure Townes, that wont to prey on Princes,
They cry for enemies, and tel the Captaines
The fruits of Italy are luscious, give us Aegypt,
Or sandy Affrick to display our valours,
There where our Swords may make us meat, and danger
Digest our well got Vyands: here our weapons
And bodyes that were made for shining brasse,
Are both unedg'd and old with ease, and women;
And then they cry agen, where are the Germaines,
Linde with hot Spaine, or Gallia, bring 'em on,
And let the son of war, steel'd Mithridates,
Lead up his winged Parthians like a storme,
Hiding the face of Heaven with showres of arrowes;
Yet we dare fight like Romanes; then as Souldiers
Tyr'd with a weary march, they tell their wounds
Even weeeping ripe they were no more nor deeper,
And glory in those scarrs that make 'em lovely,
And sitting where a Campe was, like sad Pilgrims
They reckon up the times, and living labours
Of Julius or Germanicus, and wonder
That Rome, whose turrets once were topt with honours,
Can now forget the Custome of her conquests:
And then they blame your Grace, and say who leads us,
Shall we stand here like Statues? were our Fathers
The Sonnes of lazie Moores, our Princes Persians,
Nothing but silkes, and softnesse? curses on 'em
That first taught Nero wantonnesse, and bloud,
Tiberius doubts, Caligula all vices;
For from the spring of these succeeding Princes
Thus they talke Sir;

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Well,
Why doe you heare these things?

speeches.speaker: Aec.
verse: Why do you do 'em?
I take the gods to witnesse, with more sorrow,
And more vexation, doe I heare these taintures,
Then were my life dropt from me through an hour-glasse

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Belike then you beleeve 'em, or at least
Are glad they should be so; take heed, you were better
Build your own Tomb, and runne into it living,
Then dare a Princes anger.

speeches.speaker: Aec.
verse: I am old Sir,
And ten yeares more addition, is but nothing:
Now if my life be pleasing to ye, take it,
Vpon my knees, if ever any service,
As let me brag, some have bin worthy notice,
If ever any worth, or trust ye gave me,
Deserv'd a faire respect, if all my actions,
The hazards of my youth, colds, burnings, wants,
For you and for the Empire, be not vices,
By that stile ye have stampt upon me, Souldier,
Let me not fall into the hands of wretches.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: I understand ye not.

speeches.speaker: Aec.
verse: Let not this body,
That has lookd bravely in his bloud for Cesar,
And covetous of wounds, and for your safety,
After the scape of Swords, Speares, Slings, and Arrows,
Gainst which my beaten body was mine Armour,
The Seas, and thirstie deserts, now be purchase
For Slaves, and base Informers: I see anger,
And death look through your eyes: I am markt for slaughter
And know the telling of this truth has made me
A man cleane lost to this world; I embrace it;
Only my last Petition sacred Cesar,
Is, I may dye a Roman.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Rise my friend still,
And worthy of my love; Reclaime the Souldier,
Ile study to doe so upon my selfe too,
Goe keep your command, and prosper.

speeches.speaker: Aec.
prose: Life to Cesar

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: Lord Maximus attends your Grace.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Goe tell him,
Ile meete him in the gallery.
The honesty of this Aecius
Who is indeed the Bull-wark of the Empire,
Has div'd so deep into me, that of all
The sins I covet, but this womans beautie,
With much repentance, now I could be quit of:
But she is such a pleasure, being good,
That though I were a god, she would fire my bloud.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: NAY ye shall set my hand out, tis not just
I should neglect my fortune, now tis prosperous.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: If I have any thing to set your Grace,
But Clothes or good conditions, let me perish,
You have all my mony Sir;

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: And mine,

speeches.speaker: Chi.
verse: And mine too.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Vnlesse your Grace will credit us,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: No bare boord,

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: Then at my Garden-House;

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: The Orchard too.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: And't please your Grace,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Have at 'em,

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: They are lost;

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: Why farewell Fig-trees,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Who sets more?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: At my Horse Sir,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: The dapl'd Spaniard?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: He.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: He's mine,

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: He is so;

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Your shorthorse is soone curried:

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: So it seemes Sir,
So may your Mare be too, if luck serve.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Ch.
verse: Nothing my Lord but grieving at my fortune,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Come Maximus, you were not wont to flinch thus

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: By Heaven Sir, I have lost all.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Ther's a ring yet,

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: This was not made to loose Sir,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Some love token;
Set it I say;

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I doe beseech your Grace,
Rather name any house I have.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: How strange,
And curious you are growne of toyes? redeem't
If so I win it, when you please, to morrow,
Or next day as ye will, I care not,
But only for my luck sake: Tis not Rings
Can make me richer.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Will you throw Sir? there 'tis:

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Why then have at it fairely: myne.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Your Grace
Is only ever fortunate: to morrow,
An't be your pleasure Sir, Ile pay the price on't;

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: To morrow you shall have it without price Sir,
But this day 'tis my victory: good Maximus,
Now I bethink my selfe, goe to Aecius,
And bid him muster all the Cohorts presently;
They mutiny for pay I heare, and be you
Assistant to him; when you know their numbers,
Ye shall have monyes for 'em, and above
Something to stop their tongues withall.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: I will Sir,
And gods preserve you in this mind still.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Shortly Ile see 'em march my selfe.

speeches.speaker: Max.
verse: Gods ever keep ye.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: To what end doe you think this ring shall serve now?
For you are fellowes only know by roate,
As birds record their lessons.

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: For the Lady,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: But how for her?

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: That I confesse I know not,

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Then pray for him that do's: fetch me an Eunuch
That never saw her yet: and you two see.
The Court made like a Paradise.

speeches.speaker: Lyc.
verse: We will Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: Full of faire shewes and Musiques; all your arts
(As I shall give instructions) screw to'th highest,
For my maine peece is now a doing: and for feare
You should not take, Ile have an other engine,
Such as if vertue be not only in her,
She shall not choose but leane to, let the women
Put on a graver shew of welcome.

speeches.speaker: Pro.
verse: Well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
prose: They are a thought too eager.—

speeches.speaker: Chil.
verse: Here's the Eunuch,

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Long life to Cesar.

speeches.speaker: Emp.
verse: I must use you Lycias:
Come let's walk in, and then Ile shew ye all:
If women may be fraile, this wench shall fall.

speeches.speaker: Claudia.
verse: Sirrha, what ayles my Lady, that of late
She never cares for company?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I know not,
Vnlesse it be that company causes Cuckolds.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: That were a childish feare;

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: What were those Ladyes,
Came to her lately,
From the Court?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: The same wench.
Some grave Instructors on my life, they look
For all the world like old hactht hilts.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Tis true wench.
For here and there, and yet they painted well too,
One might discover where the gold was worne
Their Iron ages.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: If my judgment faile not,
They have been sheathed like rotten ships,

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: It may be.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: For if ye mark their rudders, they hang weakly.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: They have past the line belike: wouldst live Clau.
Till thou wert such as they are?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Chimney pieces.
Now heaven have mercy on me, and young men,
I had rather make a drallery till thirty,
While I were able to endure a tempest,
And beare my fights out bravely, till my tackle.
Whistled i'th wind, and held against all weathers,
While I were able to beare with my tyres
And so discharg 'em, I would willingly
Live Marcellina, not till barnacles
Bred in my sides.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Thou art i'th right wench.
For who would live, whom pleasures had forsaken,
To stand at marke, and cry a bow short signeur?
Were there not men came hither too?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Brave fellowes.
I feare me Bawdes of five i'th' pound.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: How know you?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: They gave me great lights to it.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Take heed Claudia.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Let them take heed, the spring comes on.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: To me now,
They seem'd as noble visitants.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: To me now
Nothing lesse Marcellina, for I marke 'em,
And by this honest light, for yet tis morning,
Saving the reverence of their guilded doublets
And Millan skins.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Thou art a strange wench Claudia.

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: Ye are deceived, they shew'd to me directly
Court crabbs that creepe a side way for their living
I know 'em by the breeches that they beg'd last,

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Peace, my Lady comes; what may that be?

speeches.speaker: Clau.
verse: A Sumner
That cites her to appeare.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No more of that wench.

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Madam, what answer to your Lord?

speeches.speaker: Luci.
verse: Pray tell him, I am subject to his will,

speeches.speaker: Eun.
verse: Why weepe you Madam?
