speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: We will instantly be with you;
Now we are all fellowes.
Nine a clock, and no clyents come
Yet, sure thou dost not set up bills enough.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: I have set up bills in abundance.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: What bills?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Marry for curing of all diseases,
Recovery of stolne goods,
And a thousand such impossibilities.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: The place is unlucky,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No certaine, tis scarcity of mony; doe not you here the Lawyers complain of it? men have as much malice as ever they had to wrangle, but they have no mony: whether should this mony be tralaunct?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: To the Devill I think.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Tis with his cofferer I am certaine, that's the Vsurer.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Our cheating does not prosper so well as it was wont to doe.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No sure, why in England we coo'd cozen 'em as familiarly, as if we had travaild with a Briefe, or a Lotterie.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: I'th Low-countries we did prety well.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: So so, as long as we kept the Mop-headed butter-boxes sober; marry when they were drunke, then they grew buzards: You should have them reel their heads together, and deliberate; your Dutchman indeed when he is foxt, is like a Fox; for when hee's sunke in drink, quite earth to a mans thinking, tis full Exchange time with him, then hee's subtlest; but your Switzert, was nothing to cheate him.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Nothing?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No nor conscience to bee made of it; for since nature afore-hand cozend him of his wit, 'twas the lesse sinne for us to cozen him of his mony.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: But these Italians are more nimble-pated, wee must have some new trick for them, I protest but that our Hostisse daughter is a sweet lasse, and drawes great resort to'th house, we were as good draw teeth a horseback.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I told 'em in the Market place you could conjure, and no body would beleeve me: but ere long I will make'em beleeve you can conjure with such a figuary.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: What language shal's conjure in? high Dutch
I thinke, that's full i'th mouth.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No, no, Spanish, that roares best; and will appeare more dreadfull.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Prethee tell me thy conceit thou hast to gull them.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No, no, I will not steale it; but my dear Iews-trump, for thou art but my instrument, I am the plotter, and when we have cozen'd 'em most titely, thou shalt steale away the Inn-keepers daughter, I'le provide my selfe of another moveable: and wee will most purely retire our selues to Geneva.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Thou art the compasse I saile by.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Was ever expectation of so Noble
A requitall answered with such contumely!
A wild Numidian that had suck't a Tigresse,
Would not have bin so barbarous; did he threat
To cut thy hand off?

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Yes Sir, and his slaves were ready to perform't.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: What hindred it?

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Onely his sonnes intreaty.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: Noble youth,
I wish thou wert not of his blood; thy pitty
Gives me a hope thou art not.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You mistake Sir,
The injury that followed from the sonne,
prose: Was worse then the fathers; he did first disarme and tooke from me a Iewell which I prize above my hand or life.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Take thy sword from thee?
He stole it like a thiefe rather, he could not
I'th field deprive thee of it.

speeches.speaker: Ment
verse: He tooke it from me,
And sent me forth so thinne, and so unmade up,
As if I had bin a Foote-boy.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: O my fury!
I must now aske thee forgivenesse, that my rashnesse
Bred out of too much friendship, did expose thee
To so eminent a danger; which I vowe
I will revenge on the whole Family:
All the calamities of my whole life,
My banishment from Genoa, my wifes losse
Compar'd to this indignity is nothing;
Their Family shall repair't; it shall be to them
Like a plague, when the Dog-star reignes most hot:
An Italians revenge may pause, but's ne're forgot.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I would I had conceal'd this from my father,
For my interest in Clarissa; my care now
Must be to untangle this division,
That our most equall flames may be united;
And from these various and perturbed streames
Rise like a sweet morne after terrible dreames.—

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I am happy in your recovery,
And I Sister, am ever best pleased in your happinesse:
But I wish a toy should be on your finger.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: My Ring this morning when I wash't
I put it off, ti's in my windowe.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Wher's your Looking-glasse?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: T'is a faire one.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: T'is pure Chrystall.

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Can a Diamond cut in Crystall? let me see,
I'le grave my name in't.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Oh, you'l spoyl my glasse.
Would you not have your brother in your eye?

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: I had thougt he had bin Planted in your heart,
Looke you, the Diamond cuts quaintly, you are cozen'd,
Your Crystall is too britle.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: T'is the Ring
I gave unto Mentivole, sure the same.
You put me to amazement Sir, and horror;
How came you by that ring?

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Does the blood rise?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Pray Sir resolve me, ô for pitty doe;
And take from me a trembling at the heart,
That else will kill me: for I too much feare
Nothing but Death could ravish ir from his hand
That wore it.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Was it given to Mentivola on that condition?

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Tell me of his health first.
And then I'le tell you any thing.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: By my life he's well,
In better health then I am.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Then it was Sir.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Then shall I ever hate thee, oh thou false one;
Hast thou a Faith to give unto a friend,
And breake it to a brother? did I not
By all the tyes of blood importune thee
Never to part with it without my knowledge?
Thou might'st have given it to a Muliter,
And made a contract with him in a stable
At as cheap a price of my vengeance: never more
Shall a Womans trust beguile me; You are all
Like Reliques: you may well be look't upon,
But come a man to'th handling of you once,
You fall in peeces.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Dear Sir, I have no way
Look't either beneath reason or my selfe
In my election; there's parity in our blood,
And in our fortunes, ancient amity
Betwixt our parents: to which wants nothing,
But the fruit of blest marriage between us,
To add to their posterities: nor does now
Any impeachment rise, except the sad
And unexpected quarrell which divided
So noble and so excellent a friendship,
Which as I ner'e had Magick to foresee
So I could not prevent.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Well you must give me leave
To have a hand in your disposing, I shall
In the absence of my father be your Guardian;
His Suit must passe through my office. Mentivole,
He has too much of my blood already; he has,
And he gets no more of't—
Wherefore weep you mother?

speeches.speaker: Marian.
verse: T'is occasion'd by a sorrow,
Wherein you have a childs part, and the mainest,
Your Father's dead.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Dead?

speeches.speaker: Marian.
verse: There's one can relate the rest.

speeches.speaker: Sailor.
verse: I can Sir, your Father's drown'd,
Most unfortunately drownd.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: How? in a tempest?

speeches.speaker: Sailor.
verse: No Sir, in a calme,
calme as this evening; the Gunner being drunk,
Forgot to fasten the Ordnance to their ports,
When came a suddain gust which tumbled them
All to the starboord side, o'returnd the ship,
And sunck her in moment, some six men
That were upon the deck were saved: the rest
Perish't with your Father.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: O my dearest Father—

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I pray thee leave us.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: I have a sorrow of another nature, equall to the former.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: And most commonly they come together.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: The Family of the Baptisti
Are growne to faction, and upon distast
Of the injury late offerd in my house,
Have vowd a most severe, and fell revenge
'Gainst all our family, but especially
'Gainst you my deere Caesario.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Let them threat, I am prepard to oppose them.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: And is your losse then
Of so easie an estimation, what comfort
Have I but in your life, and your late danger
Presents afore me what I am to suffer,
Should you miscarry; therefore ile advise you
When the Funerall is over, you would travaile,
Both to prevent their fury, and weare out the injury.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: No Mother, I will not travaile,
So in my absence he may marry my Sister,
I will not travaile certaine.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: O my Caesario,
Whom I respect and love 'bove my owne life,
Indeed with a kind of dotage, he shall never
Goe forth a doores, but the contrary faction
Will indanger's life, and then am I most wretched.
I am thinking of a strange prevention,
Which I shall witnesse with a bleeding eye,
Fondnesse sometimes is worse then cruelty.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: HAunted, my house is hanted with goblins. I shal be frighted out of my wits, and set up a signe only to invite carriers and Foot-posts; scar-crows to keep off the Cavelrie, and Gentry of the best rank. I will naile up my doors, and wall up my girle (wife) like an Anchoresse; or she will be ravisht before our faces, by rascalls and cacafugo's (wife) cacafugo's.

speeches.speaker: Hostesse.
prose: These are your In-comes, remember your own proverb, the savour of every gaine smelt sweet; thank nobody but your selfe for this trouble.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: No gaulling (deere Spouse) no gaulling, every dayes new vexation abates mee two inches in the wast, terrible pennance for an Host, Girle, girle, girle, which of all this gally-maufry of mans flesh appears tolerable to thy choice; speak shortly, and speak truly: I must and will know, must and will; here ye that?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Sir, be not jealous of my care and duty;
I am so far from entertaining thoughts
Of liberty, that much more excellent objects
Then any of such course contents as these are,
Could not betray mine eye to force my heart;
Conceive a wish of any deerer happinesse
Then your direction warrants. I am yours sir.

speeches.speaker: Hostesse
prose: What thinks the man now? is not this strange at 13.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Very good words, ther's a tang in 'em, and a sweet one, tis musicke (wife) and now I come t'ee. Let us a little examine the severall conditions of our Paragraphisticall suitors. The first, a travailing Tailor, who by the mistery of his needle and thimble, hath surveyd the fashions of the French, and English; this Signior Ginger-bread stitcht up in the shreds of a gaudy outside, sowes lineings with his crosse legd complement, like an Ape doing tricks over a staffe, cringes, and crouches, and kisses his fore-finger.

speeches.speaker: Hostesse.
prose: Out upon him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: A second, a lavolteteere, a saltatory, a dancer with a Kit at his bum, one that by teaching great Madonuas to foot it, has miraculously purchast a ribanded wastcote, and foure cleane paire of socks; a fellow that skips as hee walkes, and instead of sensible discourse vents the curious conceit of some new tune stolne from a Maske, or a bawdie dittie elevated for the Pole Artick of a Ladies chamber, in that fyle stands another of your inamoratoes

speeches.speaker: Hostesse.
prose: Hang him and his fiddle together, hee never fidles any child of ours.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: The third, a Mongrell, got by a Switzer on an Italian, this puppy, being left well estated, comes so Florence, that the world may take notice, how impossible it is for experience to alter the course of nature, a foole (wife) and indeed a Clown turnd gallant, seldom or never proves other then a gallant foole, this toy prates to little purpose other then what's a clock, shall's go drink, de'e forsooth, and thank ye heartily; I feare no art in him to catch thee, and yet wee must bee tormented with this buzzard amongst the rest.

speeches.speaker: Hostesse.
prose: Tis your owne folly, forbid him the house.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: The 4th, a Mule-driver, a stubborn & a harsh knave: the fifth a School-Master, a very amorous Pedant, run almost mad with study df Sonnets and Complements out of old play-ends, the last an Advocates clerk, that speaks pure Fustion in Law termes, excellent Courtiers all, and all as neate as a Magnifico's post new painted at his entrance to an office; thou shalt have none of 'em. Laugh at 'em doe. I say thou shalt have none of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
prose: Still your command to me shall stand a Law.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Now they throng like so many horse-coursers at a faire, in clusters about the man of art, for love powders, ingredients, potions, counsailes, postures, complements, philters: the devill and the—how now? tumults? batteries, noise? ha, get from my sight.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Murther me, do, pound me to Mummye, doe; see what will come on't.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Dog, leave thy snarling, or i'le cut thy tongue out,
Thou unlikt beare, darst thou yet stand my fury,
My generous rage? yet! by the sulpherous damps
That feed the hungry and incessant darknesse,
Which curles round the grim Alastors back,
Mutter againe, and with one powerfull word,
Ile call an Host up from the Stygian lakes,
Shall waft thee to the Acherontick fennes;
Where choak't with mists as black as thy impostors,
Thou shalt live still a dying.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Conjure mee to the devill and you can. I live in hell upon earth 'em already, and you had any mercy, you would not practise upon a kind heart thus.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: You have drawne blood from him Signior, Is his offence unpardonable?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A lump of ignorance, pray speak not for him,
A drowsie grossenesse, in all christian kingdomes,
The mention of my art, my name, my practise
Merit and glory hath begot at once
Delight and wonder; ile not be entreated;
Spare intercession for him,—ô thou scorne
Of learning, shame of duty; must thy sloth
Draw my just fame in question? I discharge thee
From my service; see me no more henceforth.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Discharge me, is that my yeares wages!
Ile not be so answerd.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Not Camell, sirra I am liberall to thee;
Thou hast thy life, begon.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Vengeance, sweet vengeance.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Do'e mumble?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ile be revengd, monstrously, sudainly, and insatiably; my bulke begins to swell.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Homotolenton, Pragmatophoros, Heliostycorax.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Call up your spirits, I defie 'em; well have law for my broken pate, twelve ounces of pure bloud; Troy-weight. In despight of thee my Master, and thy Master the grand devill himselfe, vindicta, vindicta.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Signior you are exceeding mov'd.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
verse: Mercy upon us, what terrible words thou talk't?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A slave, a curre—but be not you affrighted
Young Virgin, 'twere an injury to sweetnesse:
Should any rough sound draw from your cheekes,
The pretious tincture which makes nature proud
Of her own workmanship.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Wife, Marke, mark that wife.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Shake then your anger off Sir;

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: You command it
Faire one, mine Host and Hostesse, with your leaves
I have a motion joyntly to you all.

speeches.speaker: Hostesse.
verse: An honest one I hope.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Well put in wife.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A very necessary one, the Messe
Stooles out. And halfe of suiters, that attend tousher
Their loves sit reverence to your daughter, waite
With one consent, which can best please her eye;
In offering at a dance, I have provided
Musick. And 'twill be something I dare promise
Worthy your laughter, shal they have admittance?

speeches.speaker: H.
verse: By any means, for I am perswaded the manner will be so
Ridiculous, that it will confirm the assurance of their
Miserable fooleries, but no longer trouble with 'em here,
Then they are in these May-games.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: So I am resolvd.

speeches.speaker: Hostesse.
verse: Nor any wise word of sencelesse love.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Not any; I have charm'd them, did you see
How they prepared themselves, how they stroak up
Their foretops, how they justle for the Looking-glasse,
To set their Faces by it;
You would look for some most impossible antick.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: So, so, so, so, here flutter the nest of hornets, the hotch-potch of rascallity, now, now, now, now, the dung-hill of corruption hath yawnd forth the burthen of abhomination. I am vext, vext to the soule, will rid my house of this unchristend fry, and never open my doores again.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Some other time, ile give no answer now,
But have preferred your suits, here shew your cunning.
First every one in order do his honour
To the faire mark you shoot at; courtly, courtly,
Convay your severall loves in lively measure:
Come, let us take our seates, some sprightly musick.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Dance all and part, tis a very necessary farewell.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Well done my lusty blouds, preciously well done,
One lusty rouse of wine, and take leave on all sides.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Thanks for your revells Gentlemen; accept
This Gold, and drink as freely as you danc'd.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: My noble Lord Cesario, cleer the rooms sirs.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Away. Attend your answers.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
prose: With your favour Rolando, I would change a word or two with your faire daughter.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: At your Lordships pleasure, come wife, no muttering, have a care girle, my love, service, and duty to your good Lordship.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: My often visits (sweet Bianca) cannot
But constantly inform thy judgment, wherein
Thy happinesse consists, for to steale minutes
From great imployments, to converse with beauty,
Lodg'd in so meane a fortune, to lay by
Consideration of the unequall distance
Between my blood and thine, to shun occasions
Of courtship with the Ladies of the time:
Noble, and faire, only for love to thee,
Must of necessity invite a tendernesse;
As low as nature could have stampt a bond womans.
To entertaine quick motions of rare gratitude
For my uncommon favours.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Deed my Lord, as far as my simplicity can leade mee,
I freely thank your curtesies.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: To thank them, is to reward them pretty one.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Then teach me
How I may give them back again; in truth
I never yet receiv'd a paire of Gloves:
A trifling ring from any that expected
An equall satisfaction, but as willingly
I parted with the gift unto the owner, as he bestowd it.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: But I pow're before thee
Such plenties, as it lyes not in the ability
Of thy whole kindred to returne proportionable
One for a thousand.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: You my Lord conclude
For my instruction, to ingage a debt
Beyond a possibilitie of paiment,
I ever thought a sinne; and therefore justly
Without conceit of scorne or curious rudenesse,
I must refuse your bounty.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Canst thou love?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Love! is there such a word in any language
That carries honest sence?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Never dwelt ignorance
In so sweet-shap't a building, love Bianca,
Is that firme knot which tyes two hearts in one,
Shall ours be tyed so?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Vse a plainer word,
My Lord. Insteed of tyes, say marries hearts,
Then I may understand.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Their hearts are married
Whose enterchange of pleasures and embraces,
Soft kisses, and the privacies of sweetes,
Keeps constant league together, when temptation
Of great mens oathes and gifts shall urge contempt,
Rather then batter resolution, novelty
Of sights, or taste of new delights in wantonnesse,
Breeds surfeit more then appetite in any
Reserv'd to noble vowes; my excellent maide
Live thou but true to me, and my contents,
Mine only, that no partner may pertake
The treasure of those sweets thy youth yet glories in
And I will raise thy lownesse to abundance
Of all varieties, and more triumph
In such a mistris, then great Princes doating
On truth-betraying wives.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Thus to yeeld up then
The cottage of my vertue to be swallow'd
By some hard-neighboring landlord such as you are
Is in effect to love, a Lord so vicious!
O where shall innocence find some poore dwelling
Free from temptations tirrany.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Nay prethee;

speeches.speaker: Byan.
verse: Gay clothes, high feeding, easie beds of lust,
Change of unseemly sights; with base discourse,
Draw curses on your Pallaces; for my part
This I will be confirmd in, I will eate
The bread of labour, know no other rest
Then what is earnd from honest paines, ere once more
Lend eare to your vild toyles; Sir, would you were
As noble in desires, as I could be in knowing vertue.
Pray doe not afflict a poore soule thus.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
prose: I sweare.—to me?

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: The Duke my Lord commands your speedy presence
For answering agreivances late urg'd
Against you by your Mother.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: By my Mother.

speeches.speaker: Gent.
verse: The Court is neere on sitting.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I waite on it Sir,

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What wast of bloud, what tumults, what divisions,
What outrages, what uprores in a state,
Factions though issuing from meane springs at first
Have (not restraind) flowed to, the sad example

At Rome betweene the
~rsins and Columnies,
Nay here at home in Florence, twixt the Neers
And the Bianchi can too mainly witnesse.
I sit not at the helme (my Lords) of soveraignty
Deputed Pilot for the Common-wealth,
To sleep whiles others steere (as their wild fancies
Shall councell) by the compasse of disorders.
Baptista, This short Preface is directed
Chiefly to you, the petty brawles and quarrels
Late urg'd betwixt th' Alberti and your family
Must, yes and shall like tender unknit joynts
Fasten againe together of themselves:
Or like an angry Chyrurgion, we will use
The roughnesse of our justice, to cut off
The stubborne rancour of the limbes offending.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Most gracious Florence.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Our command was signified,
That neither of the followers of each party
Should appeare here with weapons.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Tis obeyd Sir, on my side.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: We must leave the generall cause
Of State employments to give eare to brawles
Of some particular grudges, pollitick government
For tutord Princes, but no more henceforth.
Our frowne shall check presumption, not our clemency,

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: All blessings due to unpartiall Princes,
Crowne Florence with eternity of happinesse.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: If double praiers can double blessings (great Sir)
Mine joyne for your prosperity with my mothers.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Rise both; now briefly (Lady) without circumstance
Deliver those agrievances which lately
Your importunity possest our counsaile
Were fit for audience, wherein you petitiond,
You might be heard without an Advocate
Which boone you find is granted.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Though divided.
I stand between the laws of truth and modesty,
Yet let my griefes have vent: Yet the cleernesse
Of strange necessity requires obedience
To nature and your mercy, in my weeds
Of mourning, emblems of too deer misfortunes,
Badges of griefes, and Widdowhood, the burthen
Of my charg'd soule must be layd downe before you;
Wherein if strict opinion cancell shame,
My frailty is my plea;
Stand forth young man,
And heare a story that will strike all reason
Into amasement.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I attend.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Alberto (peace dwell upon his ashes) still the husband
Of my remembrance and unchanging vowes,
Has by his death left to his heire possession
Of faire revenew, which this young man claymes
As his inheritance. I urgd him gently,
Friendly, and privately to grant a partage
Of this estate to her who ownes it all
This his supposed Sister.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: How supposed?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Pray Madam recollect your selfe.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: The relish
Of a strange truth begins to work like Physick
Already: I have bitternesse to mingle
With these preparatives, so deadly loathsome;
It will quite choake digestion; shortly heare it
Cesario, for I dare not rob unjustly
The poore soule of his name; this, this Cesario
Neither for Father had Alberto, me
For Mother, nor Clarissa for his Sister.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: Mother, ô Mother.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I am in a Dream sure.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: No interruptions. Lady on,

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: How ever

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: A Faulkners sonne:

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Mistake not
Great Duke of Tuscany or the beginning
Or processe of this novelty; my husband
The now deceasd Alberto, from his youth
In-urd to an impatiency, and roughnesse
Of disposition, when not many monthes
After our marriage were worne out, repin'd
At the unfruitfull barrennesse of youth,
Which as he pleasd to terme it, cut our hops off
From blessing of some issue, to prevent it;
I grew ambitious of no fairer honor
Then to preserve her love, and as occasions
Still call'd him from me, studied in his absence
How I might frame his welcome home with comfort.
At last I faynd my selfe with child; the Message
Of freedome or reliefe to one halfe stervd
In prison is not utter'd with such greedinesse;
Of expectation and delight as this was
To my much affected Lord, his care, his goodnesse;
(Pardon me that I use the word) exceeded
All former feares, the houre of my deliverance
As I pretended drawing nee'r, I fashiond
My birth-rights at a Country Garden house,
Where then my Faulkners wife was brought a bed
Of this Cesario; him I ownd for mine;
Presented him unto a joyfull Father.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Can you prove this true?

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Proofes I have most evident;
But O the curse of my impatiency; shortly
Ere three new Moones had spent their borrowed lights,
I grew with child indeed, so just is Heaven,
The issue of which burthen was this daughter;
Iudge now most gracious Prince my Lords and you,
What combats then and since I have indur'd
Between a mothers piety and weakenesse
Of a Soul trembling wife; to have reveal'd
This secret to Alberto, had bin danger
Of ruine to my fame, besides the conflict
Of his distractions; now to have supprest it,
Were to defeate my child, my only child,
Of her most lawfull honors, and inheritance.
Caesario, th'art a man still, Education
Hath moulded thee a Gentleman, continue so;
Let not this fall from greatnesse, sinke thee lower
Then worthy thoughts may warrant, yet disclaime
All interest in Albertos blood, thou hast not
One drop of his or mine.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Produce your witnesse.

speeches.speaker: Marian.
verse: The Faulconers wife his mother,
And such women as waited then upon me,
Sworne to the privacy of this great secret.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Give them all their oathes.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: O let me crave forberance, gracious Sir,
Vouchsafe me hearing.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Speake Caesario.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Thus long
I have stood silent, and with no unwillingnesse,
Attended the relation of my fall,
From a fair expectation; what I fear'd
(Sinc the first sillable this Lady utter'd
Of my not being hers) benevolent Fates
Have eas'd me off; for to be basely born,
If not base-born, detracts not from the bounty
Of natures freedom or an honest birth.
Nobilitie claym'd by the right of blood,
Sh^wes chiefly that our Ancestors desir'd
What we inherit; but that man whose actions
Purchase a reall merit to himselfe,
And rancks him in the file of of prayse and honour,
Creates his own advancement; let me want
The fuell which best feedes the fires of greatnesse,
Lordly possessions, yet shall still my gratitude
By some attempts of mention not unworthy
Indeavour to returne a fit acquittance
To that large debt I owe your favours (Madam)
And great Alberto's memory and goodnesse;
O that I could as gently shake off passion
For the losse of what great brave man as I can shake off
Remembrance of that once I was reputed;
I have not much to say, this Princely presence
Needs not too strictly to examine farther
The truth of this acknowlegment; a mother
Dares never disavowe her only sonne,
And any woman must come short of Piety,
That can or dis-inherit her own issue,
Or feares the voice of rumor for a stranger.
Madam, you have confest, my Father was
A servant to your Lord and you: by interest
Of being his sonne, I cannot but claime justly
The honour of continuing still my service
To you and yours; which granted, I beg leave
I may for this time be dismist.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Bold spirit.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I love thee now with pitty;

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Goe not yet—
A suddain tempest that might shake a rock,
Yet he stands firm against it; much it moves me,
He not Alberto's sonne, and she a widdow,
And she a widdow,— Lords your eare.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: Your pleasure.—

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: So, Lady, what you heard avouch't is truth.

speeches.speaker: Mari.
verse: Truth onely, gracious Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Heare then our Sentence.
Since from his cradle you have fed and fostered
Caesario as your sonne, and train'd him up
To hopes of greatnesse; which now in a moment
You utterly againe have ruin'd, this way
We with our Councell are resolv'd, you being
A widdow shall accept him for a husband.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Husband to me Sir?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: T'is in us to raise him
To honours, and his vertues will deserve 'em.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: But Sir, 'tis in no Prince nor his preogative,
To force a womans choice against her heart.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: True, if then you appeale to higher justice,
Our doome includes this clause upon refusall
Out of your Lords revenues shall Caesario
Assure to any whom he takes for wife
The inheritance of three parts; the lesse remainer
Is dowry large enough to marry a daughter;
And we by our prerogative which you question
Will publiquely adopt him into'th name
Of your deceas'd Alberto, that the memory
Of so approv'd a Peer may live in him
That can preserve his memory lesse you find out
Some other meanes which may as amply satisfie
His wrong, our Sentence stands irrevocable:
What think you Lords?

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: The Duke is just and honorable.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Let me embrace Caesario, henceforth ever
I vow a constant friendship.

speeches.speaker: Mentivole.
verse: I remit all former difference.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: I am too poore
In words to thanke this Iustice. Madam alwayes
My studies shall be love to you, and duty.
Duke Replyes we admit none. Caesario waite on us.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Mentivole.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: My Lord.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Looke on Clarissa, shee's noble, rich, young, faire.

speeches.speaker: Mentivole.
verse: My Lord, and vertuous.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Mentivole and vertuous.—Madam.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Tyranny of justice, I shall live reports derision,
That am compeld to exchange a gracefull widdow-hood
For a continuall Martyrdome in marriage,
With one so much beneath me.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I'le plead for ye
Boldly and constantly, let you^ daughter only
Admit my sonne her servant, at next visit
Madam ile be a messenger of comfort.
Mentivole, be confident and earnest.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Married again, to him too! better t'had been
The young man should have still retain'd the honors
Of old Albertos son, then I the shame
Of making him successor of his bed; I was too blam,

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Indeed without offence,
Madame I thinke you were,

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: You urge it fairely, and like a worthy freind.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: can you say any thing
In commendation of a Mushroome withered
Assoone as started up?

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You scorne an Innocent
Of noble growth, for whiles your husband liv'd
I have heard you boast Cesario in all actions
Gave matter of report of Imitation,
Wonder and envy; let not discontinuance
Of some few dayes estrange a sweet opinion
Of vertue, cheifely when in such extremity,
Your pitty not contempt will argue goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: O Sir,

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: If you would use a thriving courtship,
You cannot utter a more powerfull language
That I shall listen to with greater greedinesse
Then th'argument you prosecute; this speakes you
A man compleat and excellent;

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I speake not, they are his owne deserts.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Good Sir forbeare,
I am now fully sensible of running
Into a violent Lethargy, whose deadlinesse
Locks up all reason, I shall never henceforth
Remember my past happinesse.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: These clouds may be disperst,

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: I feare continuall night
Will over-shroud me, yet poore youth his trespasse
Lies in his fortune, not the cruelty
Of the Dukes sentence.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I dare thinke it does,

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: If all faile I will learne thee to conquer
Adversity with sufferance.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: You resolve Nobly.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Let any freind have entrance,

speeches.speaker: Servant.
verse: Sir a'shall.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Any, I except none,

speeches.speaker: Serv.
verse: Wee know, your minde Sir

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Pleasures admit no bounds.
I am pitcht so high
To such a growth of full prosperities
That to conceale my fortunes were an injury?
To gratfulnesse and those more liberall favours
By whom my glories prosper. He that flowes
In gracious and swolne tydes of best abundance,
Yet will be Ignorant of his owne fortunes,
Deserves to live contemn'd, and dye forgotten;
The harvest of my hopes is now already
Ripen'd and gather'd, I can fatten youth
With choice of plenty, and supplies of comforts,
My fate springs in my owne hand, and Ile use it.
Tis my place,
Yours- here faire one, Ile aquaint my Lord,
He's here, go to him boldly.
Please you to let him understand how readily
I waited on your errand?
Saucy fellow, you must excuse his breeding,

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Whats the matter
Biancha, my Biancha, to your offices.
This visit (Sweet) from thee (my pretty deere)
By how much more twas unexpected, comes
So much the more timely: witnes this free welcome,
What ere occasion led thee?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: You may gusse Sir,
Yet indeed tis a rare one,

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Prethee speake it, my honest vertuous maide,

speeches.speaker: Bian,
verse: Sir I have heard
Of your misfortune, and I cannot tell you
Whether I have more cause of joy or sadnesse,
To know they are a truth.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: What truth Bianca! misfortunes, how, wherein?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: You are disclaym'd
For being the Lord Albertos sonne, and publickly
Acknowledg'd of as meane a birth as mine is,
It cannot chuse but greive thee

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Greive me, ha ha ha ha? is this all?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: This all.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Thou art sorry for't
I warrant thee, alas good soule, Biancha,
That which thou call'st misfortune is my happines,
my happines Biancha.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: If you love me, it may prove mine too,
May it, I will love thee.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: My good good maid,
If that can make thee happy,
Better and better love thee,

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Without breach then
Of modesty I come to claime the Interest
Your protestations both by vowes and letters
Have made me owner of, from the first houre
I saw you, I confesse I wisht J had beene
Or not so much below your ranke and greatnesse,
Or not so much above those humble flames
That should have warm'd my bosome with a temperate
Equality of desires in equall fortunes.
Still as you utter'd Language of affection,
I courted time to passe more slowly on
That I might turne more food to lend attention
To what I durst not credit nor yet hope for:
Yet still as more I heard, I wisht to heare more,

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Didst thou introth wench

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Willingly betraid
My selfe to hopelesse bondage.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: A good girle,
I thought I should not misse
What eare thy answer was.

speeches.speaker: Biancha.
verse: But as I am a maid Sir, and I'faith
You may beleeve me, for I am a maid,
So deerely I respected both your fame
And quality, that I would first have perisht
In my sicke thoughts then ere have given consent
To have undone your fortunes by inviting
A marriage with so meane a one as I am,
I should have dyed sure, and no creature knowne
The sicknesse that had kill'd me.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Pretty heart, good soule, alas. alas.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Now since I know
There is no difference twixt your birth and mine.
Not much twixt our estates, if any bee,
The advantage is on my side, I come willingly
To tender you the first fruits of my heart,
And am content t'accept you for my husband,
Now when you are at lowest.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: For a husband?
Speake sadly, dost thou meane so?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: In good deed Sir,
Tis pure love makes this proffer.

speeches.speaker: Ces
verse: I beleeve thee,
What counsaile urg'd thee on, tell me, thy Father
My worshipfull smug Host? wast not he wench?
Or mother Hostesse? ha?

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: D'ee mock my parentage?
I doe not scorne yours.
Meane folkes are as worthy
To be well spoken of if they deserve well,
As some whose only fame lies in their bloud.
O y'are a proud poore man: all your oathes falshood,
your vowe deceite, your letters forg'd, and wicked.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Thou'dst be my wife. J dare sware,

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Had your heart,
Your hand and tongue been twins, you had reputed
This courtesy a benefit,

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Simplicity,
How prettily thou mov'st me? why Biancha
Report has cozned thee, I am not fallen
From my expected honors, or possessions.
Though from the hope of birthright.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Are you not?
Then I am lost againe, I have a suit too;
Youle grant it if you be a good man.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Any thing,

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Pray doe not talke of ought what I have said tee.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: As I wish health I will not.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Pitty me, but never love me more.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Nay now y'are cruell,
Why all these teares?—Thou shalt not goe.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Ile pray for yee
That you may have a vertuous wife, a faire one,
And when I am dead—

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Fy, fy,

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Thinke on me sometimes,
With mercy so this trespasse.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Let us kisse
At parting as at comming.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: This I have
As a free dower to a virgins grave,
All goodnesse dwell with yee.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Harmelesse Biancha? unskild,
What hansome toyes are maids to play with?
How innocent. but I have other thoughts
Of nobler meditation.—my felicity,
Thou commest as I could wish, lend me a lip
Soft, as melting as when old Alberto
After his first nights triall taking farewell
Of thy youthes conquest tasted.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: You are uncivill.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: I will be Lord of my owne pleasures, Madame
Y'are mine, mine freely,
Come, no whimpering henceforth
New con the lessons of loves best experiencd,
That our delights may meet in equal measure
Of resolutions and desires; this sullenes
Is scurvy, I like it not,

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Be modest.
And doe not learne Cesario how to prostitute
The riot of thy hopes to common folly;
Take a sad womans word, how ere thou doatest
Vpon the present graces of thy greatnes,
Yet I am not falne so belowe my constancy
To vertue, nor the care which I once tendred
For thy behoof that I prefer a sentence
Of cruelty before my honor.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Honor!

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Hear me, thou seest this girle! now the comfort
Of my last dayes. She is the onely pledge
Of a bed truly noble, shee had a father
(I need not speake him more then thou remembrest)
Whom to dishonor by a meaner choice,
Were injury and infamy,

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: to goodnes,
To time and vertuous mention.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I have vow'd,
Observe me now Cseario, that how ere
I may be forc't to marry, yet no tyranny,
Perswasions, flattery, guifts, intreats, or tortures,
Shall draw me to a second bed.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Tis Iust too

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Yes and tis Iust Clarissa. I allow
The Dukes late sentence, am resolv'd young man
To be thy wife, but when the ceremony
Of marriage is perform'd, in life I wil bee
Though not in name a widdow.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Pray a word Tee,
Shall I in earnest never be your bedfellow?

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Never, ô never; and tis for your good too.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Prove that.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Alas too many yeares are numbred
In my account to entertaine the benefit
Which youth in thee Cesario and ability
Might hope for and require, it were Injustice
To rob a gentleman deserving memory
Of Issue to preserve it.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: No more herein,
You are an excellent patterne of true piety,
Let me now turne your advocate. Pray looke into
The order of the Duke, Jnjoynd, admit
J satisfie the sentence without mariage
with you, how then?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Cesario.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: If I know
How to acquit your feares, yet keepe th'injunction
In every clause whole and entire, your charity
Will call me still your servant.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Still my son.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Right Madam, now you have it, still your son.
The Genius of your blessings hath instructed
Your tongue oraculously, wee wil forget
How once I and Clarissa enterchangd
The tyes of brother and of sister, henceforth
New stile us man and wife.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: By what authority

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Heavens great appointment, yet in all my dotage
On thy perfections, when I thought Clarissa
Wee had beene pledges of one wombe, no loose
No wanton heat of youth, desir'd to claime
Priority in thy affections, other
Then nature might commend. Chastly I tendred
Thy farewell as a brother ought; but since
Our bloods are strangers, let our hearts contract
A long life-lasting unity, for this way
The sentence is to be observd or no way.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Then no way.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: I expected other answer Madam from you.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: No, every age shall curse me,
The monster, and the prodigie of nature,
Horrors beyond extremity,

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Pray mother confine the violence of greife

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Yes mother, pray do.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Thus some catch at a matrons honor
By flying lust to plot Incestuous witchcrafts,
More terrible then whoredomes; cruell mercy
When to preserve the body from a death
The soule is strangled.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: This is more then passion.
It comes neere to distraction.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I am quieted.
Cesario, thou maiest tell the Duke securely
Albertos titles, honors and revenues,
The Duke may give away, Injoy them thou.
Clarissas birthright, Marianas dower
Thou shalt be Lord of; turne us to the world
Vnpittyed and unfreinded, yet my bed
Thou never sleep'st in; as for her; she heares me,
If she as much as in a thoughts consent;
That thou may'st call her wife, a Mothers curse
Shall never leave her.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: As a brother once
I lov'd you, as a noble freind yet honor ye,
But for a husband sir, I dare not owne you,
My faith is given already.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: To a Villaine, Ile cut his throat.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why this is more then passion?
It comes neere a distraction.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: Call to minde Sir.
How much you have abated of that goodnesse
Which once raign'd in ye, they appear'd so lovely
That such as freindship led to observation
Courted the great example.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Left and flatterd into abroad derision

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Why dee thinke so?
My Lord Baptista, is your sonne growne cold
In hasting on the marriage, which his vowes
Have seald to my wrongd daughter?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Wee come Lady, to consummate the contract.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: With Mentivole? is he the man?

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Clarissas, troth and mine,
Cesario are recorded in a character
So plaine and certaine, that except the hand
Of heaven, which writ it first, would blot it out againe,
No human power can raze it.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: But say you so too? young Lady,

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: I should els betray
My heart to falshood, and my tongue to perjury.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Madam, you know the sentence.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: From the Duke,
I have particular comforts which require
A private eare.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: I shall approve it gladly,
Wee are resolvd Cesario.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Be not insolent upon a Princes favour.

speeches.speaker: Cla.
verse: Loose no glory,
Your younger yeares have purchast.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: And deservd too y'have many worthy freinds.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
prose: Preserve and use them.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Good, very good, why heres a complement
Of mirth in desperation, I could curse
My fate. ô with what speed men tumble downe
From hopes that soare to high. Biancha now
May scorne me justly too, Clarissa married,
Albertos widdow resolute, Biancha
Refusd, and I forsaken, let me study,
I can but dye a Batchelor thats the worst on't.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Come Gentlemen,
This is the day that our great artist hath
Promist to give all your severall suites satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Dancer.
verse: Is he stirring?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: He hath beene at his booke these two houres.

speeches.speaker: Pedant.
verse: Hees a rare Physitian.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Why Ile tell you,
Were Paracelsus the German now
Living, heed take up his single rapier against his
Terrible long sword, he makes it a matter of nothing
To cure the goute, sore eyes he takes out as familiarly,
Washes them, and puts them in againe,
As you'd blanch almonds.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: They say he can make gold.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: I, I, he learnt it of Kelly in Germany.
Theres not a Chimist
In christendome can goe beyond him for multiplying.

speeches.speaker: Pedant.
verse: Take heed then,
He get not up your daughters belly my Host.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: You are a merry Gentleman
And the man of art will love you the better.

speeches.speaker: Dancer.
verse: Does he love mirth and crotchets?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: O hees the most courteous Physitian,
You may drink or drab in's company freely,
The better he knowes how your disease growes,
The better he knowes how to cure it.

speeches.speaker: Danc.
verse: But I wonder my Host
He has no more resort of Ladyes to him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Why Sir?

speeches.speaker: Dan.
verse: O divers of them have great beleife in conjurers
Lechery is a great helpe to the quality.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Hee's scarce knowne to be in towne yet,
Ere long we shall have em come
hurring hither in Fetherbeds.

speeches.speaker: Dan.
verse: How? bedridden.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: No sir, in fetherbeds that move upon 4 wheeles in Spanish caroches.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Pray acquaint him we give attendance.

speeches.speaker: Host,
verse: I shall gentlemen. I would faine be rid
Of these rascalls, but that they raise profit
To my wine-seller;
When I have made use of them sufficiently,
I will intreat the conjurer to tye crackers to their tailes,
And send them packing.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Come hither mine Host looke here.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Whats that?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A challenge from my man.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: For breakings pate?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: He writes here if I meet him not
Ith Feild within this halfe houre,
I shall heare more from him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: O sir, minde your profit,
Nere thinke of the rascall, here are the gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Morrow my worthy clients,
What are you all prepard of your questions?
That I may give my resolution upon them,

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
verse: We are sir.

speeches.speaker: Pedant,
verse: And have brought our mony.

speeches.speaker: Foro
verse: Each then in order,
And differ not for precedency.

speeches.speaker: Dan.
verse: I am buying of an office sir,
And to that purpose I would faine learne
to dissemble cunningly.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Doe you come to me for that? you should rather
Have gone to a cunning woman.

speeches.speaker: Danc.
verse: I sir but their Instructions are but like women,
Pretty well but not to the depth, as I'do have it,
You are a conjurer, the devils master,
And I would learn it from you so exactly,

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: That the divill himselfe
Might not go beyond you,

speeches.speaker: Danc.
verse: You are ith right sir.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: And so your mony for your purchase
Might come in againe within a 12 month.

speeches.speaker: Danc.
verse: I would be a Graduate sir, no freshman.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Heres my hand sir,
I will make you dissemble so methodically,
As if the divell should be sent from the great Turke,
In the shape of an Embassador
To set all the christian princes at variance.

speeches.speaker: Danc.
verse: I cannot with any modesty desire any more,
Theres your mony sir,

speeches.speaker: Foco.
verse: For the art of dissembling.

speeches.speaker: Cox.
verse: My suite sir will be newes to you when I tell it,

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Pray on.

speeches.speaker: Cox.
verse: I would set up a presse here in Italy,
To write all the Caranta for Christendome.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Thats newes indeed,
And how would you imploy me in't?

speeches.speaker: Cox.
verse: Marry sir, from you
I would gaine my intelligence.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: I conceave you, you would have me furnish you
With a spirit to informe you.

speeches.speaker: Cox.
verse: But as quiet a Divell as the woman,
The first day and a halfe after she's married,
I can by no meanes indure a terrible one.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: No, no, Ile qualifie him,
He shall not fright you,
It shall be the ghost of some lying Stationer,
prose: A Spirit shall looke as if butter would not melt in his mouth, A new Mercurius Gallobelgicus.

speeches.speaker: Coxc.
verse: O there was a captaine was rare at it,

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Nere thinke of him,
Though that captaine writ a full hand gallop,
And wasted indeed more harmelesse paper then
Ever did laxative Physick,
Yet wil I make you to out-scribble him,
And set downe what you please,
The world shall better beleeve you.

speeches.speaker: Cox.
verse: Worthy sir I thanke you, there's mony.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A new office
For writing pragmaticall Curranto's

speeches.speaker: Pedant.
verse: I am a schoole-master sir,
And would faine conferre with you
About erecting 4 new sects of religion at Amsterdam.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: What the Divell should
New sects of religion doe there?

speeches.speaker: Pedaot.
verse: I assure you I would get
A great deale of mony by it.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: And what are the 4 new sects
Of religion you would plant there?

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Why thats it I come about sir,
Tis a Divel of your raising must invent 'em,
I confesse I am too weake to compasse it.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: So sir, then you make it a matter of no difficulty
To have them tolerated.

speeches.speaker: Pedant.
verse: Trouble not your selfe for that,
Let but your Divel set them a foot once,
I have Weavers, and Ginger-bread makers,
And mighty Aquavitae-men, shall set them a going.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: This is somewhat difficult,
And will aske some conference with the divell.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Take your owne leasure sir,
I have another busines too, because I meane
To leave Jtaly, and bury my selfe in those neather parts
Of the low countries.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Whats that sir.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
prose: Marry I would faine make 9 dayes to the weeke, for the more ample benefit of the captaine.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: You have a shrewd pate sir.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: But how this might be compasd?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Compasd easily; tis but making
A new Almanacke, and dividing the compasse
Of the yeare into larger penny-worths,
As a Chandler with his compasse makes
A Geometrick proportion of the Holland cheese
He retailes by stivers.
But for getting of it licenc'd.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Trouble not your selfe with that sir,
Theres your mony,

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: For foure new sects of religions,
And 9 dayes to the weeke.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: To be brought in at generall pay-dayes,
Write I beseech you.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: At generall pay-dayes.

speeches.speaker: Taylor.
verse: I am by profession a taylor,
You have heard of me.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Yes sir, and will not steale from you
The least part of that commendation I have heard utterd.

speeches.speaker: Taylor.
verse: I take measure of your worth sir,
And because I will not afflict you with any large bill
Of circumstances, I will snip off particulars.
I would faine invent some strange
And exquisite new fashions.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Are you not travel'd sir.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: Yes sir, but have observ'd all we can see
Or invent are but old ones with new names to'em,
Now I would some way or other grow more curious.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Let me see to devise new fashions.
Were you never in the Moone?

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: In the Moone taverne! yes sir: often.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: No, I do meane in the new world,
In the world thats in the Moone yonder.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: How? a new world ith moone?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Yes I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: And peopled?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: O most fantastically peopled.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: Nay certaine then ther's worke for taylors?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: That there is I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: Yet I have talked with a Scotch taylor
That never discover'd so much to me,
Though he has travail'd far, and was a pedlar in Poland.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: That was out of his way,
This lies beyond China,
You would study new fashions you say?
Take my councell, make a voyage,
And discover that new world.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: Shall I be a moon-man?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: I am of opinion, the people of that world
(Jf they be like the nature of that climate they live in)
Do vary the fashion of their cloathes oftner then any
Quick-silver'd nation in Europe.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: Not unlikely, but what should that be we call
The man in the moone then?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Why tis nothing but an Englishman
That stands there starke naked,
With a paire of sheires in one hand,
And a great bundle of broad cloath in the other
(Which resembles the bush of thornes)
Cutting out of new fashions.

speeches.speaker: Taylor
verse: I have heard somewhat like this,
But how shall I get thither?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Ile make a new compasse shall direct you.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: Certaine?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Count me else for no man of direction.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
verse: Theres 20 duckats in hand, at my returne
Ile give you a 100.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A new voyage to discover new fashions.

speeches.speaker: Mul.
verse: I have been a travailer too sir,
That have shewed strange beasts in Christendome,
And got mony by them, but I finde the trade to decay.
Your Camelion, or East-Indian hedg-hog
Gets very little mony, and your Elephant devoures
So much bread, brings in so little profit,
His keeper were better every morning
Cram 15 Taylors with white manchet,
I would have some new spectacle,
And one that might be more attractive.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Let me see, were you ever in Spaine?

speeches.speaker: Mule.
prose: Not yet Sir.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: I would have you go to Madrill, and against some great festivall, when the court lies there, provide a great and spacious Engilsh Oxe, and rode him whole, with a pudding in's belly; that would be the eight wonder of the world in those parts I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Mule.
prose: A rare project without question.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Goe beyond all their garlike olla Podrithoes, though you sod one in Garquentuas cauldron, bring in more mony, then all the monsters of Affrick.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Good Sir do your best for him; he's of my acquaintance, and one if ye knew him—

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: What is he?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: He was once a man of infinite letters.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: A Scholler?

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: No sir, a packet carrier, which is alwaies a man of many letters, yon know: then he was Mule-driver, now hee's a gentleman, and feedes monsters.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: A most ungratefull calling.

speeches.speaker: Mule.
prose: Ther's mony for your direction; the price of the Oxe Sir.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: A hundred French crownes, for it must be a Lincolne shire Oxe, and a prime one:
For a rare and monstrous spectacle, to be seen at Madrill.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
prose: Pray forbeare sir, we shall have a new quarrell.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: You durst not meet me ith' field, I am therefore come to spoyle your market.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Whats the newes with you sir.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Gentlemen, you that come hither to be most abominably cheated, listen, and be as wise as your plannet will suffer you, keep your mony, be not guld, be not laught at.

speeches.speaker: Pedant.
prose: What meanes this? would I had my mony againe in my pocket.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: The fellow is full of malice, do not mind him.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: This profest cheating rogue was my master, and I confesse my selfe a more preternotorious rogue then himselfe, in so long keeping his villainous counsell.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Come, come, I will not heare you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No couzner, thou wouldest not heare me, I do but dare thee to suffer me to speake, and then thou and all thy divells spit fire, and spoute Aqua fortis.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Speake on, I freely permit thee.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Why then know all you simple animals, you whose purses are ready to cast the calfe, if they have not cast it already, if you give any credit this jugling rascal, you are worse then simple widgins, and will be drawne into the net by this decoy ducke, this tame cheater.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, pray marke him.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: He does professe Physicke, and counjuring; for his Physicke; he has but two medicins for all manner of diseases; when he was i'th low countryes, he us'd nothing but butterd beere, colourd with Allegant, for all kind of maladies, and that he called his catholick medcine; sure the ducth smelt out it was butterd beere, else they would never have endur'd it for the names sake: then does he minister a grated dogs turd instead of Rubarbe, many times of Vnicornes horne, which working strongly with the conceit of the Patient, would make them bescummer to the height of a mighty purgation.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: The rogue has studied this invective.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Now for his conjuring, the witches of Lapland are the divells chaire-women to him, for they will sell a man a winde to some purpose; he sells winde, and tells you fortye lyes over and over.

speeches.speaker: Hostess.
prose: I thought what we should find of him.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Hold your prating, be not you an hereticke.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Conjure! Ile tell you, all the divells names he calls upon, are but fustian names, gatherd out of welch heraldry; in breife, he is a rogue of six reprieves, foure pardones of course, thrice pilloried, twince sung Lacrymae to the Virginalls of a carts taile, h'as five times been in the Gallies, and will never truly run himselfe out of breath, till he comes to the gallowes.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: You have heard worthy gentlemen, what this lying detracting rascall has vomited.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
prose: Yes certaine, but we have a better trust in you, for you have taine our mony.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: I have so, truth is he was my servant, and for some chastisement I gave him, he does practise thus upon me; speake truly sirra, are you certaine I cannot conjure?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Conjure! ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Nay, nay, but be very sure of it.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Sure of it? why Ile make a bargaine with thee, before all these gentlemen, use all thy art, all thy roguery, and make me do any thing before al this company I have not a mind to, Ile first give thee leave to claime me for thy bond slave, and when thou hast done hang me.

speeches.speaker: Foro,
prose: Tis a match, sirra, Ile make you caper ith' aire presently.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I have too solid a body, and my beleife is like a Puritans on Good-Friday, too high fed with capon.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: I will first send thee to Greeke land for a haunch of venison, just of the thicknesse of thine own tallow.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ha, ha, ha, Ile not stir an inch for thee.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Thence to Amboyna ith' East-Jndies, for pepper to bake it.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: To Amboyna? so I might be pepperd.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Then will I conveigh thee strark naked to Develing to beg a paire of brogs, to hide thy mountainous buttocks.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: And no doublet to 'em?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: No sir, I intend to send you of a sleevelesse errand; but before you vanish, in regard you say I cannot conjure, and ar so stupid, and opinionated a slave, that neither I, nor my art can compell you to do any thing thats beyond your own pleasure, the gentlemen shall have some sport; you cannot endure a cat sirra?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Whats that to thee Iugler?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Nor you'l do nothing at my entreaty?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Ile be hang'd first.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Sit Gentlemen, and whatsoever you see, be not frighted;

speeches.speaker: Hostess:
prose: Alas I can endure no coniuring.

speeches.speaker: Host:
prose: Stir not wife.

speeches.speaker: Bian:
prose: Pray let me go sir, I am not fit for these fooleryes.

speeches.speaker: Host:
prose: Move not daughter.

speeches.speaker: For:
prose: I wil make you dance a new dance calld leap-frog.

speeches.speaker: Clow:
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Fro:
prose: And as naked as a frog.

speeches.speaker: Clow:
prose: Ha, ha, ha, I defye thee.

speeches.speaker: Pedant:
verse: Spirits of the water in the likenes of frogs.
Tay: he has fisht faire beleeve me.

speeches.speaker: Mule:
prose: See, see, he sweats and trembles.

speeches.speaker: Foro:
prose: Are you come to your quavers?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Oh, oh, oh.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Ile make you run division on that o's ere I leave you; looke you, here are the playfellowes that are so indeerd to you; come sir, first unease, and then dance, nay Ile make him daunce stark naked.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Oh let him have his shirt on, and his Mogols breeches, here are women ith' house.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Well for their sakes he shall.

speeches.speaker: Tay.
prose: He daunces, what a lying rogue was this to say the gentleman could not conjure?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: He does prettily well, but tis voluntary, I assure you, I have no hand in't.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: As you are a Counjurer, and a rare Artist, free me from these couplets; of all creatures I cannot endure a Frog.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: But your dauncing is voluntary, I can compell you to nothing.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
prose: O me, danghter, lets take heed of this fellow, he'le make us dance naked, an' we vex him.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Now cut capers sirra, Ile plague that chin of yours.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Oh, oh, oh, my kidneys are rosted, I drop away like a pound of butter rosted.

speeches.speaker: Tayl.
prose: He will daunce himselfe to death.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: No matter Ile sell his fat to the Pothecaries, and repaire my injury that way.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Enough in conscience.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Well, at your entreaty vanish. And now I wil only make him breake his neck in doing a sommerset, and thats all the revenge I meane to take of him.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: O gentlemen, what a rogue was I to belye so an approved Master in the noble datk science? you can witnesse, this I did only to spoyle his practise and deprive you of the happynesse of injoying his worthy labours; rogue that I was to do it, pray sir forgive me.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: With what face canst thou ask it?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: With such a face as I deserve, with a hanging looke, as all here can testifie.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Well gentlemen, that you may perceive the goodnes of my temper, I will entertain this rogue again in hope of amendment, for should I turn him off, he would be hanged.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: You may read that in this foule coppy.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Only with this promise, you shall never cozen any of my patients.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Never.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: And remember hence forward, that though I cannot counjure, I can make you daunce sirra, go get your selfe into the cottage againe.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I will never more daunce leape Frog: now I have got you into credit, hold it up, and cozen them in abundance.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Oh rare rascall

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
prose: How now, a Frankford mart here, a Mountebanke, and his worshipfull auditory.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: They are my ghuests Sir.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
prose: A—upon them, shew your jugling tricks in some other roome.

speeches.speaker: Host,
prose: And why not here Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
prose: Hence, or sirra I shall spoile your figure flinging, and all their radicall questions.

speeches.speaker: Omnes
prose: Sir we vanish.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Signior Caesario, you make bold with me,
And somewhat I must tell you to a degree
of ill manners, they are my ghuests, and men I live by,
And I would know by what authority
You command thus far.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
prose: By my interest in your daughter.

speeches.speaker: Host.
prose: Interest do you call't? as J remember I never put her out to Vsury on that condition.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
prose: Pray thee be not angry.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
verse: I am come to make thee happy, and her happy:
Shee's here; alas my pretty soule, I am come
To give assurance thats beyond thy hope,
Or thy beleife, I bring repentance 'bout me,
And satisfaction, I will marry thee.

speeches.speaker: Bianca.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: As I live I will, but do not entertain't
With too quick an apprehension of joy,
For that may hurt thee, I have heard some dye of't,

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Do not feare me.

speeches.speaker: Caesar
verse: Then thou think'st I faigne
This protestation, I will instantly
Before this testimony, my new alliance,
Contract my selfe unto thee, then I hope
We may be more private.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: But thou shalt not sir,
For so has many a maiden-head been lost, and many a bastard gotten,

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Then to give you the best of any assurance in the world,
Entreat thy father to goe fetch a Preist
Wee will instantly to bed, and there be married.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Pride hath not yet fosaken you I see,
Though prosperity has.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Sir you are too confident
To fashion to your selfe a dreame of purchase
When you are a begger,

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: you are bold with me.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
verse: Doe we not know your value is cried downe
Fourescore i'th hundred.

speeches.speaker: Bian
verse: Oh sir I did love you
With such a fixed heart, that in that minute
Wherein you slighted, or contemn'd me rather,
I tooke a vow to obey your last decree,
And never more looke up at any hope
Should bring me comfort that way, and though since
Your Foster-mother, and the faire Clarissa
Have in the way of marriage despis'd you,
That hath not any way bred my revenge,
But compassion rather. I have found
So much sorrow in the way to a chaste wedlock
That here I will set downe, and never wish
To come to'th journies end. Your suite to mee
Henceforth be ever silenc't.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: My Bianca.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
verse: Henceforward pray forbeare her and my house:
She's a poore vertuous wench, yet her estate
May weigh with yours in a gold balance.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Yes, and her birth in any Heralds office in Christendome.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
verse: It may prove so:
When you'l say, you have leapt a Whiteing.

speeches.speaker: Ces,
verse: How far am I growne behind hand with fortune?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Here's Cesario.
My son sir is to morrow to be married
Vnto the faire Clarissa,

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: So.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Wee hope youle be a gueste there?

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: No I will not grace your triumph so much.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I will not tax your breeding.
But it alters not your birth sir, fare you well.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Oh sir doe not greive him,
He has to much affliction already.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: Every way scorn'd and lost,
Shame follow you
For I am growne most miserable.

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: Sir doe you know a Ladies son in towne here
They cal Cesario?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Ther's none such I assure thee;

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: I was told you were the man.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Whats that to thee?

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: A—on't. You are melancholy, will you drink Sir?

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: With whom?

speeches.speaker: Sail.
prose: With mee Sir; despise not this pitcht Canvas; the time was wee have knowne them lined with Spanish Duckets: I have news for you:

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: For me!

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: Not unlesse you'l drink;
We are like our Sea provision, once out of pickle,
We require abundance of drink; I have news to tell you
That were you Prince,
Would make you send your mandate
To have a thousand bonfires made 'ith City,
And pist out agen with nothing but Greek wine.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: Come, I wil drink with thee howsoever,

speeches.speaker: Sail.
prose: And upon these terms I wil utter my mind to you.

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: SHall we bring your necessaries ashore my Lord?

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Do what you please, I am land-sicke, worse by far
Then ere I was at sea.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Collect your selfe

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: O my most worthy Prospero, my best friend,
The noble favor I receivd from thee
In freeing me from the Turks I now accompt
Worse than my death; for I shall never live
To make requitall; what doe you attend for?

speeches.speaker: Sail.
verse: To understand your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: They doe mock me;
I doe protest I have no kind of pleasure
In any thing i'th world, butin thy friendship,
I must ever except that.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
prose: Pray leave him, leave him.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: The newes I heard related since my landing
Of the division of my Family,
How is it possible for any man
To bear't with a set patience?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: You have suffer'd
Since your imprisonment more waighty sorrowes.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I, then I was a man of flesh and bloud,
Now I am made up of fire, to the full height
Of a deadly Calenture; ô these vild women
That are so ill preservers of mens honors,
They cannot governe their own honesties.
That I should thirty and odde winters feed
My expectation of a noble heire,
And by a womans falshood finde him now
A fiction, a meare dreame of what he was;
And yet I love him still.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: In my opinion
The sentence (on this tryall) from the Duke
Was noble, to repaire Cesarios losse
With the marriage of your wife, had you been dead.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: By your favor but it was not, I conceive
T'was disparagment to my name, to have my widdow
Match with a Faulkners son, and yet beleev't
I love the youth still, and much pitty him.
I doe remember at my going to Sea,
Vpon a quarrell, and a hurt receiv'd
From young Mentivole, my rage so farre
Oretopt my nobler temper, I gave charge
To have his hand cut off, which since I heard,
And to my comfort, brave Caesario,
Worthyly prevented.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: And 'twas nobly done.

speeches.speaker: Albert.
verse: Yet the revenge, for this intent of min^
Hath bred much slaughter in our families,
And yet my wife (which infinitly moanes me)
Intends to marry my sole heire Clarissa
To the head branch of the other faction.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Tis the meane to work reconcilement.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Betweene whom?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Your selfe, and the worthy Baptista.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Never.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: O you have been of a noble and remarkable freindship,
And by this match tis generally in Florence
Hop'd, twill fully be reconcild; to me
'Twould be absolute content.

speeches.speaker: Iulia.
verse: And to my selfe, I have maine interest in it.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: Noble Sir, you may command my heart to breake for you
But never to bend that way; poore Caesario
When thou puft'st on thy mournfull willow garland,
Thy enemy shall be suted (I do vow)
In the same livery, my Caesario
Loved as my foster child, though not my sonne,
Which in some countryes formerly were barbarous,
Was a name held most affectionate; thou art lost,
Vnfortunate young man, not only slighted
Where thou received'st thy breeding, but since scorn'd
Ith' way of marriage, by the poore Bianca
The In-keepers daughter.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: I have heard of that too;
But let not that afflict you; for this Lady
May happily deliver at more leasure
A circumstance may draw a faire event,
Better then you can hope for.
For this present we must leave you,
And shall visit you againe within these two houres.

speeches.speaker: Albert.
verse: Ever to me most welcome,—O my Caesario.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I am none of yours Sir, so tis protested;
And I humbly beg,
Since tis not in your power to preserve me
Any longer in a noble course of life,
Give me a worthy death.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: The youth is mad.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Nay Sir, I will instruct you in a way
To kill me honorably.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: That were most strange.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: I am turning Pirate, You may be imployed
By the Duke to fetch me in; and in a sea-fight
Give me a noble grave.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Questionlesse he's mad; I would give any Doctor
A thousand crownes to free him from this sorrow.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
prose: Here's the Physitian.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Hold Sir, I did say
To free you from the sorrow, not from life.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Why life and sorrow are unseparable.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Be comforted Caesario, Mentivole
Shall not marry Clarissa.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: No Sir, ere he shall, Ile kill him.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: But you forfeit your own life then.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: Thats worth nothing.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Caesario, be thy selfe, be mine Caesario,
Make not thy selfe uncapable of that portion
I have full purpose to confer upon thee;
By falling into madnesse, beare thy wrongs
With noble patience, the afflicted freind
Which ever in all actions crownes the end.

speeches.speaker: Ces.
verse: You well awake me. nay recover'd me
Both to sence and full life, ô most noble sir,
Though I have lost my fortune, and lost you
For a worthy Father: yet I will not loose
My former vertue, my integrity
Shall not yet forsake me; but as the wilde Ivy,
Spredds and thrives better in some pittious ruin
Of tower, or defac'd Temple, then it does
Planted by a new building- so shall I
Make my adversity my instrument
To winde me up into a full content.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Tis worthily resolv'd; our first adventure
Is to stop the marriage; for thy other losses,
Practis'd by a womans malice, but account them
Like conjurers windes rais'd to a fearefull blast,
And doe some mischeife, but do never last.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Now sir, will you not acknowledge that I have mightily advancte your practice?

speeches.speaker: Forobos.
prose: Tis confest, and I will make thee a great man for't.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
