prose: I take a course to do that my selfe, for I drinke sack in abundance.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: O my rare rascall. We must remove.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Whither?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Any whither: Europe is to little to be cozned by us, I am ambitious to goe to the East-Indies, thou and I to ride on our brace of Elephants.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: And for my part I long to be in England agen; you wil never get so much as in England, we have shifted many countryes, and many names: but traunce the world over you shall never purse up so much gold as when you were in England, and call'd your selfe Doctor Lambestones.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Twas an atractive name I confesse, women were then my only admirers.

speeches.speaker: Clow,
prose: And all their visits was either to further their lust, or reveng injuries.

speeches.speaker: Foro
prose: You should have forty in a morning beleager my closett, and strive who should be cozend first, amongst fourescore love-sick waighting women that has come to me in a morning to learne what fortune should betide them in their first marriage, I have found above 94 to have lost their maidenheads.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: By their owne confession, but I was faine to be your male midwife, and worke it out of them by circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Thou wast, and yet for all this frequent resort of women and thy handling of their urinalls and their cases, thou art not given to lechery, what should be the reason of it? thou hast wholsome flesh enough about thee; me thinkes the divell should tempt thee too't.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: What need he do that, when he makes me his instrument to tempt others.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Thou canst not chuse but utter thy rare good parts; thou wast an excellent baude I acknowledge.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Well, and what I have done that way I will spare to speake of all you and I have done sir, and though we should—

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: We will for England, thats for certaine.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: We shall never want there.

speeches.speaker: Foro,
prose: Want? the Court of Wards shall want mony first, for I professe my selfe Lord Paramount over fooles and madfolkes.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Do but store your selfe with lyes enough against you come thither,

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: VVhy thats all the familarity I ever had with the Divell, my guift of lying, they say hees the Father of lyes, and though I cannot conjure, yet I professe my selfe to be one of his poore gossips. I will now reveale to thee a rare peece of service.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: VVhat is it my most worshipful Doctor Lambstones.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: There is a Captaine come lately from Sea,
They call Prosper I saw him this morning
Through a chincke of wainscote that divides my lodging
prose: And the Host of the house, withdraw my Host, and Hostesse, the faire Biancha, and an antient gentlewoman into their bedchamber; I could not overheare their conference, but I saw such a masse of gold & Iewels, & when he had done he loc't it up into a casket; great joy there was amongst them & forth they are gone into the city, and my Host told me at his going forth he thought he should not returne till after supper; now sir, in their absence will we fall to our picklocks, enter the chamber, seize the Iewels, make an escape from Florence, and wee are made for ever.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: But if they should goe to a true conjurer, and fetch us back in a whirle winde?

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Doe not beleeve there is any such fetch in Astrology, and this may be a meanes to make us live honest hereafter.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Tis but an ill road too't that lyes through the high way of theeving.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: For indeed I am weary of this trade of fortune-telling, and meane to give all over, when I come into England, for it is a very ticklish quality.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: And ith end will hang by a twine thred.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Besides the Island has too many of the profession, they hinder one anothers market.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: No, no, the pillory hinders their market.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: You know there the jugling captaine.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: I theres a sure carde.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Onely the fore-man of their jury is dead, but he dyed like a Roman.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Else tis thought he had made worke for the hangman.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: And the very Ball of your false prophets, hee's quasht too.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: He did measure the starres with a false yard, and may now travaile to Rome with a morter on's head to see if he can recover his mony that way.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Come, come, lets fish for this casket, and to Sea presently.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: We shall never reach London I feare;
My minde runs so much of hanging landing at wapping.
This well may be a day of joy long wish'd for
To my Clarissa, shee is innocent.
Nor can her youth but with an open bosome
Meet Himens pleasing bounties, but to me
That am invirond with black guilt and horror
It does appeare a funerall though promising much
Jn the conception were hard to mannage
But sad in the event, it was not hate
But fond indulgence in me to preserve
Cesarios threatned life in open court
That forc'd me to disclaime him, choosing rather
To rob him of his birth-right, and honor
Then suffer him to run the hazard of
Inrag'de Baptistas fury, while he lives;
I know I have a sonne, and the Dukes sentence
A while deluded, and this tempest over,
When he assures himselfe despaire hath seizd him.
I can relieve and raise him—speake, who is it
That presses on my privacies? Sir your pardon.
You cannot come unwelcome, though it were
To reade my secret thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Lady to you
Mine shall be ever open; Lady said I,
That name keeps too much distance, sister rather
I should have stilde you, and I now may claime it,
Since our divided families are made one
By this blessed marriage; to whose honor comes
The Duke in person, waited on by all
The braveries of his Coutt, to witnesse it,
And then to be our ghests, is the bride ready
To meet and entertaine him?

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: She attends the comming of your sonne.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Pray you bring her forth.
The Dukes at hand—Musick in her loud voyce,
Speakes his arrivall.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Shee's prepard to meet it.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: It were impertinent to wish you joy,
Since all joyes dwell about you, Himens torch
Was never slighted with a luckier omen,
Nor burnt with so much splendor, to defer
With fruitlesse complement, the meanes to make
Your certain pleasures lawfull to the world;
Since in the union of your hearts they are
Confirmd already: would but argue us
A boaster of our favours; to the Temple
And there the sacred knot once tyde, all t'riumphs
Our Dukedome can affoord, shall grace your nuptialls.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: On there.

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: I hope it is not in the power
Of any to crosse us now.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: But in the breath
Of a wrongd Father I forbid the bands.

speeches.speaker: Cesar.
verse: What, doe you stand at gaze?

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Risen from the dead!

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Although the sea had vomitted up the figure
In which thy better part livd long imprisond,
True love despising feare, runs thus to meete it.

speeches.speaker: Claris.
verse: In duty I kneele to it.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Hence vile wretches,
To you I am a substance incorporeall,
And not to be prophand, with your vile touch?
That could so soone forget me, but such things
Are neither worth my anger, nor reproofe.
To you great sir, I turne my selfe and these
Immediate Ministers of your government,
And if in my rude language I transgresse;
Ascribe it to the cold remembrance of
My services, and not my rugged temper.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Speake freely, be thy language ne're so bitter,
To see thee safe Alberto, signes thy pardon.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: My pardon? I can need none, it it be not
Receivd for an offence. I tamely beare
Wrongs, which a slave-born Muscovite would check at.
Why if for treason I had beene deliverd
Vp to the hangmans Axe, and this dead trunck
Vnworthy of a Christian Sepulcher;
Exposd a prey to feed the ravenous vulture,
The memory of the much I oft did for you,
Had you but any touch of gratitude,
Or thought of my deservings, would have stopd you
From these unjust proceedings.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Heare the motives that did induce us.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I have heard them all,
Your highnesse sentence, the whole Court abusd,
By the perjuries, and practise of this woman.
(Wee pest thou Crocodile) my hopefull son,
Whom I dare sweare mine owne, degraded of
The honors that descend to him from me:
And from that in his love scornd by a creature
Whose base birth though made eminent by her beauty,
Might well have markd her out Cesarios servant,
All this I could have pardond and forgot;
But that my daughter with my whole estate
So hardly purchasd, is assignd a dower;
To one whose Father, and whose family
I so de^est; that I would loose my essence
And be transformed to a Basiliske
To look them dead, to mee's an injury,
Admits no satisfaction.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Ther's none offerd.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Nor would not be accepted,
Though upon thy knees twere tenderd.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Now the storme grows high.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: But that I thought thee dead, and in thy death
The brinie Ocean had entombd thy name;
I would have sought a wife in a Bordello
For my Mentivole, and gladly hugd
Her spurious Issue as my lawfull Nephewes,
Before his blood should ere have mixd with thine;
So much I scorne it.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I'll not bandy words, but thus dissolve the contract.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: There I meet thee, and seize on whats mine owne.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: For all my service,
Great Sir grant me the combat with this wretch,
That I may scourge his insolence.

speeches.speaker: Baptist.
verse: I kneele for it.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
verse: And to approve my selfe Albertos sonne,
Ile be his second upon any odds,
Gainst him that dare most of Baptistas race.

speeches.speaker: Menti.
verse: Already upon honorable termes,
In me thou hast met thy better, for her sake
I'le adde no more.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: Sir, let our swords decide it.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: O stay Sir, and as you would hold the title
Of a just Prince, ere you grant licence to
These mad-mens fury, lend your private eare
To the most distres'd of women.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Speake, tis granted.

speeches.speaker: Clar.
verse: In the meane time, let not Clarissa be
A patient looker on, though as yet doubtfull,
To whom to bend her knee first, yet to all
I stoop thus low in duty, and would wash
The dust of fury with my Virgin teares,
From his blessd feete, and make them beautifull
That would move to conditions of peace,
Though with a snaile like pace, they all are wingd
To beare you to destruction: reverend sirs,
Think on your ancient friendship caemented
With so much bloud, but shed in noble action,
Divided now in passion for a brawle;
The makers blush to own, much lov'd Caesario.
Brother, or friend, (each title may prevaile,)
Remember with what tendernesse from our child-hood
Wee lov'd together, you preferring me
Before your selfe, and I so fond of you
That it begot suspition in ill mindes
That our affection was incestuous.
Thinke of that happy time, in which I know
That with your deerest blood you had prevented
This showre of teares from me Mentivole,
My husband, registred in that bright star-chamber,
Though now on earth made strangers, be the example
And offer in one hande the peacefull Olive
Of concord. or if that can be denyed
By powerfull intercession in the other
Carry the Hermian rod and force atonement,
Now we will not bee all marble. Deaths the worst then
And hee shall be my bridegroome,

speeches.speaker: Ment.
verse: Hold Clarissa, his loving violence needs must
Offer inspite of honor

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Was it to that end then on your religion?

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: And my hope in heaven Sir.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Wee then will leave entreaties, and make use
Of our authority, must I cry ai-me
To this unheard of insolence? in my presence
To draw your swords, and as all reverence
Thats due to majesty were forfeited,
cherish this wildernesse! sheath them instantly,
and shew an alteration in your lookes, or by my power

speeches.speaker: Alber,
verse: Cut of my head

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: And mine, rather then heare of peace with this bad man.
I'le not alone give up my throat, but suffer
Your rage to reach my family.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: And my name to be no more remembred.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What are these?

speeches.speaker: Caes.
prose: Biancha, tis Biancha, still Biancha: but strangely alter'd.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: If that thirteene yeares
Of absence could raze from my memory
The figure of my freind, I might forget thee;
But if thy Image be graven on my heart,
Thou art my Prospero.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Thou my Baptista?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: A suddaine change!

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: I dare not aske deere freind
If Juliana live! for thats a blessing
I am unworthy of, but yet deny not
To let me know the place she hath made happy
By having there her sepulcher.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: If your highnesse please to vouchsafe a patient
Eare wee shall make a true relation of a story
That shall call on your wonder.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Speake, wee heare you.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Baptistas Fortune in the Genoa court,
His banishment, with his faire wifes restraint
You are acquainted with; what since hath follow'd
I faithfully will deliver, ere eight moones
After Baptistas absence were compleate,
Faire Juliana founde the pleasures that
They had injoy'd together were not barren,
And blushing at the burthen of her wombe,
No father neere to owne it, it drew on
A violent sicknesse, which call'd downe compassion
From the angry Duke, then carefull of her health.
Physitians were enquir'd of, and their judgment
Prescrib'd the Bathes of Luca as a meanes
For her recovery; to my charge it pleas'd her
To be committed; but as on the way
Wee journy'd, those throwes only knowne to women
Came thick upon her, in a private village.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Shee died?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Have patience, she brought to the world
A hopefull daughter; for her bodies sicknesse
It soone decai'd, but the greife of her minde
Hourely increas'd, and life grew tedious to her,
And desperate ere to see you; she injoyn'd me
To place her in a Greeekish Monastery,
And to my care gave up her pretty daughter.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: What monastery? as a Pilgrim bare-foot,
Ile search it out.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: Pray you interrupt me not,
Now to my fortunes; the girle well dispos'd off
With a faithfull freind of mine, my cruell fate
Made me a prisoner to the Turkish gallies,
Where for 12 yeares, these hands tugd at the oare,
But fortune tyr'd at length with my afflictions,
Some ships of Malta mett the Ottaman fleete,
Charg'd them and boorded them, and gave me freedome
With my deliverers I serv'd, and gott
Such reputation with the great Master
That he gave me command over a tall
And lusty ship, where my first happy service
Was to redeeme Alberto rumor'd dead,
But was like me surpris'd by Cortugogly.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: I would I had dyed there.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: And from him learning
Baptista liv'd, and their dissolved freindship,
I hois'd up sailes for Greece, found Iuliana
A votary at her beades; having made knowne
Both that you liv'd, and where you were, she borrow'd
So much from her devotion as to wish me
To bring her to you; if the object please you,
With joy receave her.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: Rage and fury leave me-
I am so full of happines, theres no room left
To entertaine you, O my long lost Iewell,
Light of mine eyes, my soules strength.

speeches.speaker: Julia.
verse: My best Lord, having Embrac'd you thus,
Death cannot fright me.

speeches.speaker: Bapt.
verse: Live long to do so though J should fix here.
Pardon me Prospero though I enquire my daughters fortune.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: That your happinesse
May be at all parts perfect, here she is!

speeches.speaker: Caes.
verse: Biancha daughter to a princesse.

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: True with my faithfull Host I left her,
And with him till now she hath resided,
Ignorant both of her birth and greatnesse.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: O my blest one. Ioy upon joy over-whelmes me.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Above wonder.

speeches.speaker: Alb.
verse: I doe begin to melt too, this strange story
Workes much upon me.

speeches.speaker: Duke
verse: Since it hath ples'd heaven
To grace us with this miracle, I that am
Heavens instrument here, determine thus; Alberto
Be not unthankefull for the blessings showne you,
Nor you Baptista; discord was yet never
A welcome sacrifice; therefore rage layd by,
Embrace as freinds, and let pass'd difference
Be as a dreame forgotten.

speeches.speaker: Bap.
verse: Tis to me.

speeches.speaker: Alber.
verse: And me, and thus confirme it.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: And to tye it
In bonds not to be broken, with the marriage.
Of young Mentivole, and faire Clarissa,
So you consent great Lady, your Biancha
Shall call Caesario Husband.

speeches.speaker: Iulia.
verse: Tis a motion I gladly yeeld too.

speeches.speaker: Caesar.
prose: One in which you make a sadd man happy.

speeches.speaker: Bian.
verse: Kneele not, all forgiven.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: With the Duke your Vnkle I will make attonement, and will have no denyall.

speeches.speaker: Mar.
verse: Let this day be still held sacred.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Now if you can conjure, let the Divell unbind you,

speeches.speaker: Foro.
verse: Wee are both undone,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
verse: Already wee feele it.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Iustice sir,

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: What are they?

speeches.speaker: Pros.
verse: I can resolve you, slaves freed from the Gallyes
By the Viceroy of Sicilia.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: Whats their offence?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: The robbing me of all my plate and Iewels,
I meane the attempting of it,

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Please your grace I will now discover this varlet in earnest, this honest pestilent rogue, profest the art on conjuring, but all the skill that ever he had in the black art was in making a seacole fire; only with wearing strange shapes he begot admiration amongst fooles and women.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Wilt thou preach thou varlet?

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: Why does he gogle with his eyes, and stauke so?

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: This is one of his Magicall raptures.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: I doe vilifie your censure, you demand if I am guilty, whir sayes my cloake by a tricke fo legerdemaine, now I am not guilty, I am guarded with innocence, pure silver lace I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: Thus have I read to you your vertues, which notwithstanding I would not have you proud of.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: Out thou concealement of tallow, and counterfeit Mummia.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
prose: To the Gallyes with them both.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: The onely sea physick for a knave ia to be basted in a gally with the oyle of a Bulls peesell.

speeches.speaker: Foro.
prose: And will not you make a soure face at the same sauce, sirra? I hope to finde thee so leane, in one fortnight thou mayest be drawne by the eares through the hoop of a firkin.

speeches.speaker: Duke,
prose: Divide them and away with them to'th Gallyes.

speeches.speaker: Clow.
prose: This will take downe your pride Iugler.

speeches.speaker: Duke.
verse: For blessings nere discend from thence, but when
A sacrifice in thankes ascends from men.
prose: This day that hath given birth to blessings; beyond hope, admits no criminall sentence, to the Temple and there with humblenesse praise heavens bounties;

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: SIgnior Don Diego, and mine Host, save thee.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I thank you Mr Bayly.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: O the block.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Why, how should I have answered?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Not with that
Negligent rudeness: But I kiss your hands
Signior Don Incubo de Hambre, and then
My titles; Master Bayly of Castil-blanco:
Thou nere wilt have the elegancy of an Host;
I sorrow for thee, as my friend and gossip:
No smoak, nor steam out-breathing from the kitchen?
There's litle life i'th harth then.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I, there, there,
That is his friendship, hearkning for the spit,
And sorrow that he cannot smel the pot boil.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Strange
An Inne should be so curst, and not the sign
Blasted, nor withered; very strange, three days now,
And not an egg eat in it, or an onyon.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I think they ha' strew'd the high-wayes with cal-traps, I,
No horse dares pass 'em; I did never know
A week of so sad doings, since I first
Stood to my sign-post.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Gossip, I have found
The root of all; kneel, pray, it is thy self
Art cause thereof: each person is the founder
Of his own fortune, good, or bad; but mend it,
Call for thy cloak, and rapier.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Do, call,
And put 'em on in haste: Alter thy fortune,
By appearing worthy of her: Dost thou think
Her good face ere wil know a man in cuerpo?
In single body, thus? in hose, and doblet?
The horse boyes garb? base blank, and half blank cuerpo?
Did I, or Mr Dean of Civil our neighbor
Ere reach our dignities in cuerpo, thinkst thou,
In squirting hose, and doublet? Signior, no,
There went more to't: there were cloaks, gowns, cassocks
And other paramentos; Call, I say,
His cloak, and rapier here.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
verse: What means your worship?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Bring forth thy husbands Sword: so hang it on,
And now his cloak, here, cast it up; I mean
Gossip, to change your luck, and bring you guests.

speeches.speaker: Hostes.
verse: Why? is there charm in this?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Expect; now walk,
But not the pace of one that runs on errands;
For want of gravity in an Host, is odious:
You may remember Gossip, if you please,
(Your wife being then th' Infanta of the Gipsies,
And your self governing a great mans Mules then)
Me a poor Squire at Madrid attending
A Master of Ceremonies; But a man, beleeve it,
That knew his place to the gold weight, and such
Have I heard him oft say, ought every Host
Within the Catholique kings dominions
Be in his own house.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: A Master of Ceremonies:
At least vice-master, and to do nought in cuerpo,
That was his maxime; I wil tell thee of him:
He would not speak with an Ambassadors Cook,
See a cold bake-meat from a forreign part
In cuerpo: had a dog but staid without,
Or beast of quality, as an English cow,
But to present it self, he would put on
His Savoy chain about his neck, the ruff
And cuffs of Holland, then the Naples hat
With the Rome hat-band, and the Florentine agat,
The Millain Sword, the Cloak of Genua, set
With Flemish buttons, all his given peeces
To entertain 'em in, and complement
With a tame Coney, as with the Prince that sent it.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: List, who is there?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: A guest and 't be thy wil.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Look Spowse, cry luck, and we be encounter'd: ha?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Luck then, and good, for 'tis a fine brave guest,
With a brave horse.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Why now, beleeve of cuerpo
As you shal see occasion: go, and meet him.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Look to my horse, I pray you, wel.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: He shal Sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Oh how beneath his rank and call was that now?
Your horse shal be entreated as becomes
A horse of fashion, and his inches.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: O.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Look to the Cavalier: what ailes he? stay
If it concern his horse, let it not trouble him,
He shal have all respect the place can yeeld him
Either of barley, or fresh straw.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Good Sir
Look up.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: He sincks, somewhat to cast upon him,
Hee'l go away in cuerpo else.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: What, wife!
O your hot waters quickly, and some cold
To cast in his sweet face.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Alas, fair flowre?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Do's any body entertain his horse?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Yes, Lazaro has him.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Go you see him in person.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Sir, taste a litle of this, of mine own water,
I did distil't my self; sweet Lilly look upon me,
You are but newly blown, my pretty Tulip.
Faint not upon your stalk, 'tis firme and fresh
Stand up, so, bolt upright, you are yet in growing.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Pray you let me have a chamber.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: That you shall Sir.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: And where I may be private, I intreat you.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: For that introth Sir, we ha' no choice: our house
Is but a vent of need, that now and then
Receives a guest, between the greater towns
As they come late; onely one room,

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: She means Sir, it is none
Of those wild, scatter'd heaps, call'd Innes, where scarce
The Host is heard, though he wind his horn t'his people,
Here is a competent pile, wherein the man,
Wife, Servants, all doe live within the whistle

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Onely one room.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: A pretty modest quadrangle
She will describe to you.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Wherein stands two Beds Sir
We have, and where, if any guest do come,
He must of force be lodg'd, that is the truth Sir.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: But if I pay you for both your beds, methinks
That should alike content you.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: That it shall Sir.
If I be paid, I am praid.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Why, ther's a Ducket
Will that make your content?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: O the sweet face on you:
A Ducket? yes, and there were three beds Sir,
And twice so many rooms, which is one more,
You should be private in 'em all, in all Sir,
No one should have a peece of a bed with you
Not Master Deane of Civill himself, I swear
Though he came naked hither, as once he did
When h'had like t'have been tane a bed with the Moore
And guelt by her Master: you shall be as private,
As if you lay in's owne great house, that's haunted,
Where no body comes, they say:

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I thank you Hostesse.
Pray you will you shew me in.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Yes marry will I Sir,
And pray that not a flea, or a chink vex you

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: You forget supper: Gossip: move for supper

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: 'Tis strange what love to a beast may do, his Horse
Threw him into this fit.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: You shall excuse me
It was his being in Cuerpo, meerly caus'd it.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Do you think so Sir?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Most unlucky Cuerpo,
Naught els, he looks as he would eat partridge,
This guest; ha' you em ready in the house?
And a fine peece of kid now? and fresh garlick,
With a Sardina, and Zant oile? how now?
Has he bespoke? what will he have a brace,
Or but one partridge, or a short leg'd hen,
Daintyly carbonado'd?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: 'Lasse the dead
May be as ready for a Supper as he.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: He has no mind to eat, more then his shadow:

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Say you.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: How do's your worship

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I put on
My left shoo first to day, now I perceive it,
And skipt a bead in saying 'em ore; els
I could not be thus cross'd: He cannot be
Above seventeen; one of his years, and have
No better a stomach?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: And in such good clothes too

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Nay, those do often make the stomach worse, wife,
That is no reason.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I could at his years Gossips
(As temperate as you see me now) have eaten
My brace of ducks, with my half goose, my cony,
And drink my whole twelve Marvedis in wine
As easie as I now get down three olyffs.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: And with your temperance-favour, yet I think
Your worship would put to't at six and thirty
For a good wager; and the meal in too.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I do not know what mine old mouth can do,
I ha not prov'd it lately

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: That's the grief Sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: But is he without hope then gone to bed?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: I fear so Sir, has lock'd the door close to him
Sure he is very ill.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: That is with fasting,
You should ha told him Gossip, what you had had,
Given him the inventury of your kitchen,
It is the picklock in an Inne, and often
Opens a close barr'd stomach: what may he be trob?
Has he so good a Horse?

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Oh a brave Jennet,
As ere your worship saw.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: And he eats

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Strongly,

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: A mighty solascisme, heaven give me patience,
What creatures has he?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: None.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: And so well cloath'd,
And so well mounted?

speeches.speaker: Di g.
verse: That's all my wonder Sir,
Who he should be; he is attir'd and hors'd
For the Constables son of Spaine.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: My wonders more
He should want appetite: well a good night
To both my Gossips: I will for this time
Put off the thought of supping; In the morning
Remember him of breakfast pray you,

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: 'T shall Sir,

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: A hungry time Sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: We that live like myce
On others meat, must watch when we can get it

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Yes, but I would not tell him: Our fair guest
Says, though he eat no supper, he will pay for one.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Good news: we'l eat it spouse, 't his health,
'Twas politickly done t'admit no sharers.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Look to the Mules there, wher's mine Host?

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Here Sir.
Another Fayerie.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Blesse me.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: From what sweet Hostesse?
Are you affraid o' your guests?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: From Angels Sir,
I think ther's none but such come here to night,
My house had never so good luck afore
For brave fine guests; and yet the ill luck on't is
I cannot bid you welcome.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: No?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Not lodge you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Not, Hostesse?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: No in troth Sir, I do tell you
Because you may provide in time: my beds
Are both tane up by a yong Cavalier
That wil, and must be private.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: He has paid Sir
For all our Chambers.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Which is one: and Beds
Which I already ha' told you are two: But Sir,
So sweet a creature, I am very sorry
I cannot lodge you by him; you look so like him
Yo'are both the loveliest peeces.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What train has he?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: None but himself.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: And wil no less then both deds
Serve him?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: H'as given me a ducket for 'em.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: O.
You give me reason Hostesse: Is he handsome,
And yong do you say?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: O Sir, the delicat'st flesh
And finest clothes withall, and such a horse,
With such a Sadle.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Shee's in love with all.
The horse, and him, and Sadle, and clothes: good woman,
Thou justifiest thy Sex; lov'st all that's brave:
Sure though I lye o'th ground, ile stay here now
And have a sight of him: you'l give me house-room,
Fire, and fresh meat for money: gentle Hostesse
And make me a pallat?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Sir shee shal do reason:
I understood you had another guest: Gossips
Pray you let his Mule be lookt too: have good straw,
And store of bran: And Gossip do you hear,
Let him not stay for supper: what good fowle ha' you?
This gentleman would eat a pheasant.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: 'Lass Sir;
We ha' no such.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I kiss your hands fair Sir.
What ha' you then? speak what you have? I 'me one Sir
Here for the Catholique King, an Officer
T' enquire what guests come to these places; you Sir
Appear a person of quality, and 'tis fit
You be accommodated: why speak you not,
What ha' you woman? are you afraid to vent
That which you have?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: This is a most strange man;
'T appoint my meat.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: The half of a cold hen Sir,
And a boil'd quarter of kid, is all i'th house.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Why all's but cold; let him see it fourth,
Cover, and give the eye some satisfaction,
A Travellers stomach must see bread and salt,
His belly is nearer to him, then his kindred:
Cold hen 's a pretty meat Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What you please;
I am resolv'd t' obey.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: So is your kid,
With pepper, garlick, and the juice of an Orenge,
She shal with sallads help it, and cleane lynnen;
Dispatch: what news at Court Sir?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Faith new tires
Most of the Ladies have: the men old Suits,
Only the Kings fool has a new coat
To serve you.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I did ghess you came from thence Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: But I do know I did not.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I mistook Sir.
What hear you of the Archdukes?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Troth your question.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Of the French business, What?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: As much.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: No more?
They say the French: O that's wel: come I'le help you:
Have you no jibblets now? or a broild rasher
Or some such present dish t'assist?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Not any Sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: The more your fault; you nev'r should be without
Such aydes: what cottage would ha' lackt a pheasant
At such a time as this? wel, bring your hen,
And kid forth quickly.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: That should be my prayer
To scape his inquisition.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Sir, the French,
They say are divided 'bout their match with us,
What think you of it.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: As of naught to me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Nay it's as litle to me too: but I love
To ask after these things, to know the affections
Of States, and Princes, now and then for bettring.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Of your own ignorance.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Yes Sir:

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Many do so.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I cannot live without it: what do you hear
Of our Indian Fleet; they say they are well return'd.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I had no venture with 'em Sir; had you?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Why do you ask Sir?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: 'Cause it might concern you,
It do's not me.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: O here's your meat come.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Thanks,
I welcome it at any price.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Some stools here,
And bid mine Host bring Wine, ile try your kid,
If he be sweet: he looks wel: yes, he is good;
Ile carve you sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: You use me too too princely:
Tast, and carve too.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I love to do these offices.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I think you do: for whose sake?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: For themselves sir,
The very doing of them is reward.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: 'Had little faith would not beleeve you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
prose: Gossip some wine.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Here 'tis: and right St Martyn.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Measure me out a glass.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I love the humanity
Us'd in this place:

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Sir, I salute you here.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I kiss your hands Sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Good wine; it wil beget an appetite:
Fil him; and sit down, Gossip, entertain
Your noble guest here, as becomes your title.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Please you to like this wine Sir?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: J dislike
Nothing mine Host, but that I may not see
Your conceal'd guest: here's to you.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: In good faith Sir,
I wish you as wel as him: would you might see him.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: And wherefore may he not:

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: 'Has lock'd himself Sir
Up, and has hir'd both the beds o' my wife
At extraordinary rate.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Ile give as much
If that will do't, for one, as he for both;
What say you mine Host, the door once open
Ile fling my self upon the next bed to him
And there's an end of me till morning; noise
I will make none.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: I wish your worship well —but

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: His honour is engag'd: And my she Gossip
Hath past her promise, hath she not?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Yes truely:

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: That toucheth to the credit of the house:
Well, I will eate a little, and think: how say you sir
Unto this brawn o'th hen?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I ha' more minde
To get this bed sir.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Say you so: Why then
Giv't me agen, and drink to me: mine Host
Fill him his wine: thou'rt dull, and do'st not praise it,
I eate but to teach you the way Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Sir:
Find but the way to lodge me in this chamber
Ile give mine Host two duckets for his bed,
And you sir two realls: here's to you

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Excuse me,
I am not mercenary: Gossip pledge him for me,
Ile think a little more; but ev'n one bit
And then talke on: you cannot interrupt me.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: This peece of wine sir cost me

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Stay: I have found:
This little morcell: and then: here's excellent garlick:
Have you not a bunch of grapes now: or some Bacon
To give the mouth a rellish?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Wife, do you hear?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: It is no matter. Sir, give mine Host your duckets.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: How Sir?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Do you receive 'em: I will save
The honesty of your house: and yours too Gossip,
And I will lodge the Gentleman: shew the Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Good Sir do you hear.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Shew me the Chamber.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Pray you Sir,
Do not disturb my guests.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Disturb? I hope
The Catholique King sir, may command a lodging
Without disturbing in his vassails house,
For any Minister of his, emploid
In business of the State. Where is the door?
Open the door, who are you there? within?
In the Kings name.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: What would you have?

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Your key sir,
And your door open: I have here command
To lodge a Gentleman, from the Justice, sent
Upon the Kings affairs.

speeches.speaker: Theod.
verse: Kings and necessities
Must be obey'd:' the key is under the door.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: How now sir, are you fitted? you secur'd?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Your two reals are grown a peece of eight.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: Excuse me Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: 'Twill buy a hen; and wine
Sir, for to morrow.

speeches.speaker: Inc.
verse: I do kisse your hands Sir
Well this will bear my charge yet to the Gallies
Where I am owing a ducket: whither this night
By the Moons leave Ile march: for in the morning
Early they put from Port S. Maries.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Lazaro
How do the horses?

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Would you would go and see Sir,
A — of all Jades, what a clap h'as given me:
As sure as you live master he knew perfectly
I couzend him on's Oats: he lookt upon me
And then he sneerd, as who should say take heed sirrah:
And when he saw our half peck, which you know
Was but an old Court dish: lord how he stampt:
I thought 't had been for joy, when suddenly
He cuts me a back caper with his heels
And takes me just o'th' crupper: down came I
And all my ounce of Oates: Then he neigh'd out
As though he had had a Mare by'th taile.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Faith Lazaro
We are to blame to use the poor dumb serviters
So cruelly.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Yonder's this other gentlemans horse
Keeping our Lady eve: the devill a bit
Has got since he came in yet: there he stands
And looks, and looks, but 'tis your pleasure sir
He shall look lean enough: has hay before him
But 'tis as big as hemp, and will as soon choak him,
Unless he eate it butter'd: he had four shoos
And good ones when he came: 'tis a strange wonder
With standing still he should cast three.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: O Lazaro
The devils in this trade: truth never knew it
And to the devill we shall travell Lazaro
Unless we mend our manners: once every week
I meet with such a knock to molefie me
Sometimes a dozen to awake my conscience
Yet still I sleep securely.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: Certain Master
We must use better dealing.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: 'Faith for mine own part
Not to give ill example to our issues,
I could be well content to steal but two girths,
And now and then a saddle cloth: change a bridle
Onely for exercise.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: If we could stay there
There were some hope on's Master: but the devill is
We are drunk so early we mistake whole Saddles
Sometimes a horse; and then it seems to us too
Every poore Jade has his whole peck, and tumbles
Up to his ears in clean straw, and every bottle
Shews at the least a dozen; when the truth is Sir
Ther's no such matter, not a smell of provinder,
Not so much straw, as would tye up a horse tail,
Nor any thing ith' rack, but two old cobwebs
And so much rotten hay as had been a hens nest.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Well, these mistakings must be mended Lazaro,
These apparitions, that abuse our sences,
And make us ever apt to sweep the manger
But put in nothing; these fancies must be forgot
And we must pray it may be reveal'd to us
Whose horse we ought in conscience to couzen,
And how, and when: A Parsons horse may suffer
A little greazing in his teeth, 'tis wholsome;
And keeps him in a sober shuffle: and his Saddle
May want a stirrop, and it may be sworn
His learning lay on one side, and so brok it:
Has ever Oates in's cloak-bag to prevent us
And therefore 'tis a meritorious office
To tythe him soundly.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: And a Grazier may
For those are pinching puckfoysts and suspitious:
Suffer a myst before his eyes sometimes too,
And think hee sees his horse eat half a bushel:
When the truth is, rubbing his gums with salt,
Till all the skin come off: he shal but mumble
Like an old woman, that were chewing brawn,
And drop 'em out again.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: That may do wel too,
And no doubt 'tis but venial: But good Lazaro
Have you a care of understanding horses,
Horses with angry heels, gentlemens horses,
Horses that know the world: let them have meat
Till their teeth ake; and rubbing till their ribbs
Shine like a wenches forehead; they are devils

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: And look into our dealings: as sure as we live
These Courtiers horses are a kind of Welsh prophets,
Nothing can be hid from 'em: For mine own part
The next I cozen of that kind, shal be founderd,
And of all four too: Ile no more such complements
Upon my crupper.

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Steal but a litle longer
Till I am lam'd too, and wee'l repent together,
It wil not be above two daies.

speeches.speaker: Laz.
verse: By that time
I shal be wel again, and all forgot Sir.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Why then ile stay for thee.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Oh,—ho-? oh—ho?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Oh—oh? heart—heart—heart—heart?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What's that?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: When wilt thou break?— break, break, break?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Ha?
I would the voice were strong, or I neerer,

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Shame, shame, eternal shame? what have I done?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Done?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: And to no end: what a wild Jorney
Have I more wildly undertaken?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Jorney?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: How without counsel? care? reason? or fear?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Whither wil this fit carry?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: O my folly:

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: This is no common sickness.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: How have I left
All I should love, or keep? ô heaven.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: How do you gentle Sir?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Alas my fortune

speeches.speaker: Ph.
verse: It seems your sorrow oppresses: please your goodness
Let me bear half Sir: a divided burthen
Is so made lighter.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Oh,

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: That sigh betrayes
The fulness of your grief:

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I, if that grief
Had not bereft me of my understanding,
I should have wel remembred where I was,
And in what company; and clapt a lock
Upon this tongue for talking.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Worthy Sir
Let it not add to your grief, that I have heard
A sigh, or groan come from you: That is all Sir:

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Good Sir no more: you have heard too much I fear,
Would I had taken poppy when I spake it.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: It seems you have an ill belief of me
And would have feard much more, had you spoke ought
I could interpret. But beleeve it Sir
Had I had means to look into your breast,
And tane you sleeping here, that so securely
I might have read, all that your woe would hide
I would not have betrayd you.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Sir that speech
Is very noble, and almost would tempt
My need to trust you.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: At your own election,
I dare not make my faith so much suspected
As to protest again: nor am I curious
To know more then is fit.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Sir I wil trust you
But you shal promise Sir to keep your bed,
And whatsoe'er you hear, not to importune
More I beseech you from me.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Sir I wil not.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Then I am proan to utter.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: My faith for it.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: If I were wise, I yet should hold my peace
You wil be noble.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: You shal make me so
If you'l but think me such.

speeches.speaker: Theo
verse: I do: then know
You are deceiv'd with whom you have talk so long.
I am a most unfortunate lost woman.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Ha?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Do not stir Sir: I have here a Sword.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Not I sweet Lady: of what blood, or name.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: You'l keep your faith.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Ile perish else.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Beleeve then
Of birth too noble for me, so descended—
I am ashamd, no less then I am affrighted.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Fear not: by all good things, I will not wrong you.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I am the daughter of a noble Gentleman
Born in this part of Spain: my fathers name Sir:
But why should I abuse that reverence
When a childs duty has forsaken me.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: All may be mended: in fit time too: speak it

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Alphonso, sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Alphonso? what's your own name?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Any base thing you can invent.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Deal truely.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: They call me Theodosia

speeches.speaker: Phi^.
verse: Ha? and love
Is that that hath chang'd you thus?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Ye have observ'd me
Too neerly Sir, 'tis that indeed: 'tis love Sir.
And love of him (oh heavens) why should men deal thus?
Why should they use their arts to cozen us?
That have no cunning, but our fears about us?
And ever that too late to; no dissembling
Or double way but doating: too much loving?
Why should they find new oaths, to make more wretches?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What may his name be?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Sir a name that promises
Me thinks no such ill usage: Mark-antonio
A noble neighbours Son: Now I must desire ye
To stay a while: else my weak eyes must answer.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I will: —Are ye yet ready? what is his quality?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: His best a theef Sir: that he would be known by;
Is, heir to Leonardo, a rich Gentleman:
Next, of a handsome body, had heaven made him
A minde fit to it. To this man, my fortune,
(My more then purblind fortune) grave my faith.
Drawn to it by as many shews of service
And signs of truth, as ever false tongue utter'd:
Heaven pardon all.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: 'Tis wel said: forward Lady.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Contracted Sir, and by exchange of rings
Our souls deliver'd: nothing left unfinish'd
But the last work, enjoying me, and Ceremony.
For that I must confess was the first wise doubt
I ever made: yet after all this love sir,
All this profession of his faith; when dayly
And hourly I expected the blest priest
Hee left me like a dream, as all this story
Had never been, nor thought of, why I know not;
Yet I have called my conscience to confession,
And every sillable that might offend
I have had in shrift: yet neither loves law Signiour,
Nor ty of maidens duty, but desiring
Have I transgrest in: left his father too,
Nor whither he is gone, or why departed
Can any tongue resolve mee: All my hope
(Which keeps mee yet alive, and would perswade mee
I may be once more happy, and thus shapes mee
A shame to all my modest sex) is this Sir,
I have a Brother and his old Companion,
Studient in Sallimanca, there my last hope
If hee bee yet alive, and can be loving
Is left mee to recover him: For which travel
In this Sute left at home of that dear Brothers
Thus as you find mee, without fear, or wisdom,
I have wander'd from my father, fled my friends,
And now am only child of hope and danger:
You are now silent Sir: this tedious story
(That ever keeps mee waking) makes you heavy:
'Tis fit it should do so: for that, and I
Can be but troubles.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: No, I sleep not Lady:
I would I could: oh heaven is this my comfort.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: What aile you gentle Sir?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Oh.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Why do you groan so?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I must, I must; oh misery.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: But now Sir
You were my comfort: if any thing afflict yee
Am not I fit to bear a part on't? and by your own rule.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: No; if you could heal, as you have wounded me,
But 'tis not in your power.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I fear intemperance.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Nay do not seek to shun mee: I must see you:
By heaven I must: hoa, there mine Host: a Candle:
Strive not, I wil not stir ye.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Noble Sir
This is a breach of promise.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Tender Lady
It shal be none but necessary: hoa, there,
Some light, some light for heavens sake.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Wil ye betray mee?
Are ye a gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Good woman:

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: If I be prejudicial to you, curse mee.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Ye are early stirring sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Give mee your Candle
And so good morrow for a while.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Good morrow Sir.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: My Brother Don Philippo: nay Sir, kil mee
I ask no mercy Sir, for none dare know me,
I can deserve none: As ye look upon me
Behold in infinite these foul dishonors
My noble father, then your self: last all
That bear the name of kindred, suffer in mee:
I have forgot whose child I am, whose Sister:
Do you forget the pity tyed to that:
Let not compassion sway you: you wil be then
As foul as I, and bear the same brond with me,
A favourer of my fault: ye have a sword sir,
And such a cause to kil me in.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Rise Sister:
I wear no sword for women: nor no anger
While your fair chastity is yet untouch'd.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: By those bright starrs, it is Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: For my Sister
I do beleeve ye: and so neer blood has made us
With the dear love I ever bore your vertues
That I wil be a Brother to your griefs too:
Be comforted, 'tis no dishonor Sister
To love, nor to love him you do: he is a gentleman
Of as sweet hopes, as years, as many promises,
As there be growing truths, and great ones.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: O sir!

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Do not despair.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Can ye forgive?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Yes Sister,
Though this be no smal error, a far greater.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: And think me stil your Sister?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: My dear Sister.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: And wil you counsel mee?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: To your own peace too:
Ye shal love stil.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: How good ye are?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: My business,
And duty to my father, which now drew mee
From Salimanca, I wil lay aside
And only be your Agent to perswade ye
To leave both love, and him, and wel retyre ye.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Oh gentle Brother.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: I perceive 'tis folly:
Delayes in love, inore dangerous.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Noble Brother.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Fear not, ile run your own way: and to help you,
Love having rackt your passions beyond counsel:
Ile hazard mine own fame: whither shal we venture?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Alas, I know not Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Come, 'tis bright morning
Let's walk out, and consider: you'l keep this habit.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I would sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Then it shal be: what must I cal ye?
Come, do not blush: pray speak, I may spoil all else.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Pray cal me Theodoro.

speeches.speaker: Dieg.
verse: Are ye ready?
The day draws on a pace: once more good morrow.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Good morrow gentle Host: now I must thank ye:

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Who do'st thou think this is?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Were you a wench Sir
I think you would know before me.

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: Mine own Brother.

speeches.speaker: Diego.
verse: By'th Masse your noses are a kin: should I then
Have been so barbarous to have parted Brothers?

speeches.speaker: Phi.
verse: You knew it then.

speeches.speaker: Diego.
verse: I knew 'twas necessary
You should be both together: Instinct Signior
Is a great matter in an Host.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I am satisfied.

speeches.speaker: Ped.
verse: Is not mine Host up yet?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Die.
verse: Ile see.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Sister, withdraw your self.

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
verse: Signiour Philippo

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Noble Don Pedro, where have you been this way?

speeches.speaker: Pedr
verse: I came from Port St Maries, whence the Gallyes
Put this last tide, and bound for Barcellona,
I brought Mark-antonie upon his way.

speeches.speaker: Phil
verse: Marc-antonie?

speeches.speaker: Pedr
verse: Who is turn'd Soldier
And entertain'd in the new Regiment,
For Naples.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Is it possible?

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
verse: I assure you.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: And put they in at Barcellona?

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
verse: So
One of the Masters told me.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Which way go you Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
verse: Home:

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: And I for Civill: pray you Sir, say not
That you saw me, if you shall meet the question,
I have some little businesse

speeches.speaker: Pedr.
verse: Were it lesse Sir.
It shall not become me, to loose the caution:
Shall we break-fast together?

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Ile come to you Sir:
Sister you hear this: I beleeve your fortune
Begins to be propitious to you: we will hire
Mules of mine host here: if we can himself
To be our guid, and streight to Barcellona,
This was as happy news, as unexpected
Stay you, till I rid him away.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I will.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: KNock at the door.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: 'Tis open Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: That's all one
Knock when I bid you.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Will not your worship enter.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Will not you learn more manners Sir, and do that
Your Master bids ye; knock ye knave, or ile knock
Such a round peal about your pate; I enter
Under his roofe, or come to say god save ye
To him, the Son of whose base dealings has undone me.
Knock lowder, lowder yet: ile starve, and rot first,
This open ayr is every mans.

speeches.speaker: 2. Ser.
verse: Come in Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: No, no Sir, I am none of these come in Sirs
None of those visitants: bid your wise Master
Come out, I have to talk unto him: go Sir

speeches.speaker: 2. Ser.
verse: Your worship may be welcome.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Sir, I will not,
I come not to be welcome: good my three duckets
My pickell'd sprat a day, and no oyl to't,
And once a year a cotten coat, leave prating
And tell your Master, I am here.

speeches.speaker: 2. Ser.
verse: I will Sir.
This is a strange old man.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: I welcome to him!
Ile be first welcome to a Pesthouse: Sirhah
Lets have your valour now casde up, and quiet
When an occasion calls, 'tis wisdom in ye,
A Serving mans discretion: if you do draw
Draw but according to your entertainment;
Five nobles worth of fury.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Signiour Alphonso.
I hope no discontent from my will given,
Has made ye shun my house: I ever lov'd ye.
An credit me amongst my fears 'tis greatest
To minister offences.

speeches.speaker: Alph
verse: O good Signiour
I know ye for Italian breed, fair tongu'd,
Spare your Appologies, I care not for'em,
As little for your love Sir; I can live
Without your knowledge; eat mine own, and sleep
Without dependances, or hopes upon ye.
I come to aske my daughter.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Gentle Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: I am not gentle Sir, nor gentle will be
Till I have justice, my poor child restor'd
Your caper-cutting boy has run away with
Yong Signior-smooth-face, he that takes up wenches
With smiles, and sweet behaviours, songs, and sonnets,
Your high fed Jennet, that no hedge can hold
They say you bred him for a Stallion.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Fie Signiour, there be times, and terms of honour
To argue these things in, descidements able
To speak ye noble gentlemen, ways punctuall
And to the life of credit, ye are too rugged.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: I am too tame Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Will ye hear but reason?

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: No, I will hear no reason: I come not hither
To be popt off with reason; reason then.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Why Signior, in all things there must be method
Ye choak the child of honour els, discretion,
Do you conceive an injury?

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: What then Sir?

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Then follow it in fair terms, let your sword bite
When time calls, not your tongue.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: I know Sir
Both when and what to do without directions,
And where, and how, I come not to be tutur'd,
My cause is no mans but mine own: you Signior
Will ye restore my daughter?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Who detains her?

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: No more of these sleight shifts

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ye urge me Signior
With strange unjustice: because my Son has err'd

speeches.speaker: Zanch
verse: Mark him.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Out of the heat of youth: do'st follow
I must be father of his crimes.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: I say still
Leave off your rhetorick, and restore my daughter.
And sodainly: bring in your rebell too,
Mountdragon, he that mounts without commission
That I may see him punished, and severely,
Or by that holy heaven, ile fire your house,
And ther's my way of honour.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Pray give me leave
Was not man made the noblest creature

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Should not his mind then answer to his making,
And to his mind his actions, if this ought to be,
Why do we run a blind way from our worths,
And cancell our discretions, doing those things
To cure offences, are the most offences?
We have rules of justice in us; to those rules
Let us apply our angers: you can consider
The want in others of these terminations,
And how unfurnish'd they appear.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Hang others,
And where the wrongs are open, hang respects,
I come not to consider.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Noble Sir,
Let us argue cooly, and consider like men.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Like men!

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ye are too sodain still.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Like men Sir?

speeches.speaker: Zanch
verse: It is fair language, and ally'd to honour.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Why, what strange beast would your grave reverence
Make me appear? like men!

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Taste but that point Sir,
And ye recover all.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: I tell thy wisdome
I am as much a man, and as good a man.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: All this is granted Sir.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: As wise a man.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Ye are not tainted that way.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: And a man
Dares make thee no man; or at best, a base man.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Fy, Fy, here wants much carriage.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Hang much carriage.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Give me good language sirrah Signiour.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Give me my daughter.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I am as gentle as your self, as free born.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Observe his way.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: As much respect ow'd to me.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: This hangs together nobly.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And for Civill
A great deal more it seems: go look your daughter.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: There ye went well off Signiour.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: That rough tongue
You understand at first: you never think Sir
Out of your mightinesse, of my losse: here I stand
A patient anvill, to your burning angers
Made subject to your dangers; yet my losse equall:
Who shall bring home my son?

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: A whipping Beadle.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Why, is your daughter whorish?

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Ha, thou dar'st not,
By heaven I know thou dar'st not.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: I dare more Sir
If you dare be uncivill.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Laugh too, Pidgeon.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: A fitter time for fames sake: two weak Nurses
Would laugh at this; are there no more days coming,
No ground but this to argue on? no swords left
Nor friends to carry this, but your own furies?
Alas! it shows too weakly.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Let it show,
I come not here for shews: laugh at me sirrah?
Ile give ye cause to laugh.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ye are as like Sir
As any man in Spaine.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: By heaven I will,
I will brave Leonardo.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Brave Alphonso,
I will expect it then.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Hold ye there both,
These terms are noble.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Ye shall hear shortly from me.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Now discreetly.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: Assure your self ye shall: do ye see this sword Sir?
He has not cast his teeth yet.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Rarely carried.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: He bites deep: most times mortall: Signiour
Ile hound him at the fair and home.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Still nobly.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: And at all those that dare maintain ye.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Excellent.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: How you shall please Sir, so it be fair, though certain,
I had rather give you reason.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Fairly urg'd too.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
verse: This is no age for reason, prick your reason
Upon your swords point.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: Admirably follow'd.

speeches.speaker: Alph.
prose: And there ile hear it: so till I please, live Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: And so farewell, you'r welcome.

speeches.speaker: Zanch.
verse: The end crowns all things
Signiour, some little businesse past, this cause ile argue
And be a peace between ye, ift so please ye,
And by the square of honour to the utmost:
I feel the old man's master'd by much passion,
And too high rackt, which makes him overshoot all.
His valour should direct at, and hurt those
That stand but by as blenchers: this he must know too,
As necessary to his judgement, doting women
Are neither safe nor wise adventures: conceive me,
If once their wills have wander'd; nor is't then
A time to use our rages: for why should I
Bite at the stone, when he that throws it wrongs me?
Do not we know that women are most wooers
Though closest in their carriage? Do not all men know,
Scarce all the compasse of the globe can hold 'em
If their affections be afoot? shall I then covet
The follys of a she-fool, that by nature
Must seek her like, by reason be a woman,
Sink a tal ship because the sales defie me?
No, I disdain that folly; he that ventures
Whilst they are fit to put him on, has found out
The everlasting motion in his scabbard.
I doubt not to make peace: and so for this time
My best love, and remembrance.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Your poor Servant.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Where will our Horses meet us?

speeches.speaker: Host Dieg.
verse: Fear not you Sir,
Some half mile hence, my worships man will stay us,
How is it with my young bloods? come, be joviall,
Let's travell like a merry flock of wild geese,
Every tongue talking.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: We are very merry;
But do you know this way Sir?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Is't not dangerous?
Methinks these woody thickets should harbour knaves.

speeches.speaker: Host Die.
verse: I fear none but fair wenches: those are theeves
May quickly rob me of my good conditions
If they cry stand once: but the best is Signiours
They cannot bind my hands; for any else,
They meet an equall knave, and there's my pasport:
I have seen fine sport in this place, had these trees tongues,
They would tell ye pretty matters: do not you fear though
They are not every days delights.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What sport Sir?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Why to say true, the sport of all sports.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What was't?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Such turning up of taffataes; and you know
To what rare whistling tunes they go, far beyond
A soft wind in the shrowds: such stand there,
And down ith thother place; such supplications
And subdivisions for those toys their honours,
One, as ye are a gentleman in this bush,
And oh sweet Sir, what mean ye? ther's a bracelet,
And use me I beseech ye like a woman,
And her petition's heard: another scratches,
And crys she will die first, and then swones: but certain
She is brought to life again, and does well after.
Another save mine honour, oh mine honour,
My husband serves the Duke, Sir, in his kitchen;
l have a cold pie for ye; fy, fy, fy gentlemen,
Will nothing satisfie ye, where's my husband?
Another crys, do ye see Sir how they use me,
Is there no law for these things?

speeches.speaker: The^.
verse: And good mine Host,
Do you call these fine sports?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: What should I call 'em,
They have been so call'd these thousand years & upwards.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: But what becomes o'th' men?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: They are stript and bound,
Like so many Adams, with fig leafs afore 'em,
And there's their innocence.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Would we had known this?
Before we reacht this place.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Come, there's no danger,
These are but sometimes chances.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Now we must through.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Who's that?

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Stand to it Signiors.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: No it needs not,
I know the face; 'tis honest.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: What mine Host:
Mine everlasting honest Host.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Masse Bayly:
Now in the name of an ill reckoning
What make you walking this round?

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: A — of this round,
And of all businesse too, through woods, and rascalls,
They have rounded me away a dozen duckets,
Besides a fair round cloke: Some of 'em knew me,
Els they had cased me like a cony too,
As they have done the rest, and I think rosted me,
For they began to baste me soundly: my young Signiors,
You may thank heaven, and heartily, and hourly,
You set not out so early; ye had been smoak'd els
By this true hand ye had Sirs, finely smoakt,
Had ye been women, smockt too.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Heaven defend us.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: Nay, that had been no prayer, there were those
That run that prayer out of breath, yet fail'd too:
There was a Fryer, now ye talk of prayer,
With a huge bunch of beads, like a rope of onyons;
I am sure as big, that out of fear and prayer,
In half an houre wore 'em as small as bugles,
Yet he was flea'd too.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: At what houre was this?

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: Some two houres since.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Do you think the passage sure now.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: Yes, a rope take 'em, as it will, and blesse 'em,
They have done for this day sure.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Are many riffled?

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: At the least a dozen,
And there left bound.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: How came you free?

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: A curtesie
They use out of their rogueships, to bequeath
To one, that when they give a signe from far
Which is from out of danger; he may presently
Release the rest, as I met you, I was going,
Having the signe from yonder hill to do it.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Alas poor men.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Mine Host, pray go untie'em.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Let me alone for cancelling: where are they?

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: In every bush like black birds, you cannot misse 'em

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: I need not stalk unto 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: No, they'l stand ye,
My busy life for yours Sir: you would wonder
To see the severall tricks, and strange behaviors
Of the poor rascals in their miseries,
One weeps, another laughs at him for weeping,
A third is monstrous angry he can laugh
And crys, go too, this is no time; he laughs still,
A fourth exhorts to patience: him a fift man
Curses for tamenesse; him a Fryer schools,
All hoot the Fryer: here one sings a Ballad,
And there a little Curat confutes him,
And in this linsey woolsey way, that would make a dog
Forget his dinner, or an old man fire
They rub out for their ransoms: Amongst the rest,
There is a little Boy rob'd, a fine child,
It seems a Page: I must confesse my pitty
(As 'tis a hard thing in a man of my place)
To shew compassion, stir'd at him; so finely
And without noyse he carrys his afflictions,
And looks as if he had but dreamt of loosing.
This boy's the glory of this robbery,
The rest but shame the action: now ye may hear 'em.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Come lads, 'tis holy-day: hang clothes, 'tis hot,
And sweating agues are abroad.
It seems so;
For we have met with rare Phisitians
To cure us of that mallady.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Fine footing,
Light and deliver: now my boys: Master Fryer,
How do's your holinesse, bear up man; what
A cup of neat sack now and a toast: ha, Fryer,
A warm plaister to your belly Father,
There were a blessing now.

speeches.speaker: Fryer.
verse: Ye say your mind Sir.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Where my fine Boy: my poynter.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: Ther's the wonder.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: A rank whore scratch their sides till the pox follow
For robbing thee, thou hast a thousand ways
To rob thy self boy, dyce, and a chamber devill.

speeches.speaker: Leoc.
verse: Ye are deceiv'd Sir.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: And thy Master too Boy.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: A sweet fac'd Boy indeed: what rogues were these?
What barbarous brutish slaves to strip this beauty?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Come hither my boy: alas! he's cold, mine Host,
We must intreat your Cloak.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Can ye intreat it.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: We do presume so much, you have other garments.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Will you intreat those too?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Your Mule must too,
To the next town, you say 'tis neer; in pity
You cannot see this poor Boy perish.
I know ye have a better soul, we'l satisfie ye.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: 'Tis a strange foolish trick I have, but I cannot help it,
I am ever cozen'd with mine own commendations;
It is determin'd then I shall be robb'd too.
To make up vantage to this dozen: here Sir,
Heaven has provided ye a simple garment
To set ye off: pray keep it hansomer
Then you kept your own, and let me have it render'd,
Brush'd, and discreetly folded.

speeches.speaker: Leoc.
verse: I thank ye Sir.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Who wants a doblet?
I.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Where will you have it?
From you Sir, if you please.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Oh, there's the poynt Sir.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: My honest friends, I am sorry for your fortunes,
But that's but poor relief; here are ten Duckets,
And to your distribution holy Sir,
I render 'em: and let it be your care
To se 'em, as your wants are, well divided.

speeches.speaker: Hos.
verse: Plain dealing now my friends: and Father Fryer,
Set me the sadle right; no wringing Fryer,
Nor tithing to the Church, these are no duties;
Scowre me your conscience, if the Devill tempt ye
Off with your cord, and swing him.

speeches.speaker: Fry.
verse: Ye say well Sir.

speeches.speaker: all.
verse: Heaven keep your goodnesse.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Peace keep you, farewell friends

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Farewell light horse-men.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Which way travell you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: To the next town.

speeches.speaker: The.
verse: Do you want any thing.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: Only discretion to travell at good houres,
And some warm meat to moderate this matter,
For I am most outragious cruell hungry

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: I have a stomach too such as it is
Would pose a right good pasty, I thank heaven for't.

speeches.speaker: Bayl.
verse: Chees that would break the teeth of a new hand-saw,
I could endure now like an Eastrich, or salt beeffe
That Cesar left in pickell.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Take no care,
Wee'l have meat for you and enough: I th' mean time
Keep you the horse way lest the fellow misse us,
We'l meet ye at the end o'th wood.

speeches.speaker: Host.
verse: Make hast then.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: My pretty Sir, till your necessities
Be full supplied, so please you trust our friendships,
We must not part.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ye have pull'd a charge upon ye,
Yet such a one, as ever shall be thankfull.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Ye have said enough: may I be bold to ask ye,
What Province you were bred in? and of what parents?

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Ye may Sir: I was born in Andoluzia,
My name Francisco, son to Don Henriques
De Cardinas.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Our noble neighbour.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Son to Don Henriques:
I know the gentleman: and by your leave Sir,
I know he has no son.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: None of his own Sir,
Which makes him put that right upon his brother
Don Zanchio's children: one of which I am,
And therefore do not much err.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Still ye do Sir,
For neither has Don Zanchio any son;
A daughter, and a rare one is heire,
Which though I never was so blest to see,
Yet I have heard great good of.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Urge no further,
He is ashamed, and blushes.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Sir,
If it might import you to conceal your self,
I ask your mercy, I have been so curious:

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: Alas! I must ask yours Sir: for these lies,
Yet they were usefull ones; for by the claiming
Such noble parents, I beleev'd your bounties
Would shew more gracious: The plain truth is gentlemen,
I am Don Sanchios stewards son, a wild boy,
That for the fruits of his unhappinesse,
Is faigne to seek the wars.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: This is a lie too.
If I have any ears.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Why?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: Mark his language,
And ye shall find it of too sweet a relish
For one of such a breed: ile pawn my hand,
This is no boy.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: No boy? what would you have him?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: I know, no boy: I watcht how fearfully,
And yet how sodainly he cur'd his lies,
The right wit of a woman: Now I am sure.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: What are ye sure?

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: That 'tis no boy: ile burn in't.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Now I consider better, and take councell,
Methinks he shows more sweetnesse in that face,
Then his fears dare deliver.

speeches.speaker: Theo.
verse: No more talk on't,
There hangs some great waight by it: soon at night
Ile tell ye more.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
verse: Come Sir, what ere you are
With us, embrace your liberty, and our helps
In any need you have.

speeches.speaker: Leo.
verse: All my poor service
Shall be at your command Sir, and my prayers.

speeches.speaker: Phil.
prose: Let's walke a pace; hunger will cut their throats els.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Call up the Master.

speeches.speaker: Mast.
verse: Here Sir.

speeches.speaker: Rod.
verse: Honest Master,
