Your love to Mirabell; your blushes tell it:
'Tis too much known, and spoken of too largely;
And with no little shame I wonder at it.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Is it a shame to love?

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: To Love undiscreetly:
A Virgin should be tender of her honour,
Close, and secure.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I am as close as can be,
And stand upon as strong and honest guards too,
Unless this Warlike Age need a Port-cullis:
Yet I confess, I love him.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Hear the people.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Now I say hang the people: He that dares
Believe what they say, dares be mad, and give
His Mother, nay his own Wife up to Rumor;
All grounds of truth they build on, is a Tavern,
And their best censure's Sack, Sack in abundance:
For as they drink, they think: they ne'r speak modestly
Unless the wine be poor, or they want money.
Beleeve them? beleeve Amadis de Gaul,
The Knight o'th' Sun, or Palmerin of England;
For these, to them, are modest, and true stories.
Pray understand me; if their tongues be truth,
And if in Vino veritas be an Oracle,
What woman is, or has been ever honest?
Give 'em but ten round cups, they'll swear Lucretia
Dy'd not for want of power to resist Tarquine,
But want of Pleasure, that he stayd no longer:
And Portia, that was famous for her Pietie
To her lov'd Lord, they'll face ye out, dy'd o'th' pox.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Well, there is something, Sister.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: If there be, Brother,
'Tis none of their things, 'tis not yet so monstrous;
My thing is Mariage: And at his return
I hope to put their squint-eyes right again.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Mariage? 'tis true: his father is a rich man;
Rich both in land and money: he his heir,
A young and handsom man, I must confess too;
But of such qualities, and such wild flings,
Such admirable imperfections, Sister,
(For all his travaile, and bought experience)
I should be loth to own him for my brother:
Me thinks a rich mind in a state indifferent
Would prove the better fortune.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: If he be wild,
The reclaming him to good, and honest (brother)
Will make much for my honor; which, if I prosper,
Shall be the study of my love, and life too.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Ye say well; would he thought as well, and loved too.
He mary? he'll be hang'd first: he knows no more
What the conditions and the ties of Love are,
The honest purposes and grounds of Mariage,
Nor will know, nor be ever brought t' endeavour,
Than I do how to build a Church; he was ever
A loose and strong defier of all order,
His Loves are wanderers, they knock at each door,
And tast each dish, but are no residents:
Or say he may be brought to think of Mariage
(As 't will be no small labour) thy hopes are strangers.
I know there is a labour'd match, now follow'd,
(Now at this time, for which he was sent for home too)
Be not abus'd, Natolet has two fair daughters,
And he must take his choice.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Let him take freely;
For all this I despair not: my mind tells me
That I, and onely I, must make him perfect;
And in that hope I rest.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Since y' are so confident
Prosper your hope: I'll be no adversary:
Keep your self fair and right, he shall not wrong ye.

speeches.speaker: Or.
prose: When I forget my vertue, no man know me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Welcom to Paris once more, Gentlemen:
We have had a merry, and a lusty Ord'nary,
And wine, and good meat, and a bounsing Reckning;
And let it go for once; 'Tis a good physick:
Only the wenches are not for my dyet,
They are too lean and thin; their embraces brawn-fall'n.
Give me the plump Venetian, fat, and lusty,
That meets me soft and supple; smiles upon me,
As if a cup of full wine leap'd to kiss me;
These slight things I affect not.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: They are ill built;
Pin-buttockt, like your dainty Barbaries,
And weak i'th pasterns; they'l endure no hardness.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: There's nothing good, or handsom, bred amongst us;
Till we are travail'd, and live abroad, we are coxcombs:
Ye talk of France, a slight, unseason'd Country;
Abundance of gross food, which makes us block-heads:
We are fair set-out indeed, and so are fore-horses.
Men say we are great Courtiers, men abuse us:
We are wise, and valiant too, non credo Signior:
Our women the best Linguists, they are Parrats;
O' this side the Alpes they are nothing but meer Drollaries:
Ha Roma la Santa, Italie for my money:
Their policies, their customs, their frugalities,
Their curtesies so open, yet so reserved too,
As when ye think y' are known best, ye are a stranger;
Their very pick-teeth speak more man than we do,
And season of more salt.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: 'Tis a brave Country;
Not pester'd with your stubborn precise puppies,
That turn all usefull, and allow'd contentments
To scabs and scruples; hang 'em Capon-worshippers.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I like that freedom well, and like their women too,
And would fain do as others do; but I am so bashfull,
So naturally an Ass: Look ye, I can look upon 'em,
And very willingly I go to see 'em,
(There's no man willinger) and I can kiss 'em,
And make a shift—

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: But if they chance to flout ye,
Or say ye are too bold; fie Sir remember;
I pray sit farther off;—

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Tis true, I am humbled,
I am gone, I confess ingenuously I am silenced,
The spirit of Amber cannot force me answer.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Then would I sing and dance.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You have wherewithall, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: And charge her up again.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I can be hang'd first:
Yet where I fasten well, I am a tyrant.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why, thou darst fight?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Yes, certainly, I dare fight;
And fight with any man, at any weapon,
Would th' other were no more; but, a pox on't,
When I am sometimes in my height of hope,
And reasonable valiant that way, my heart harden'd,
Some scornfull jest or other, chops between me
And my desire: What would ye have me to do then, Gentlemen?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Belvere, ye must be bolder: Travell three years,
And bring home such a baby to betray ye
As bashfulness? a great fellow, and a souldier?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You have the gift of impudence, be thankful;
Every man has not the like talent: I will study
And if it may be reveal'd to me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Learn of me,
And of Pinac: no doubt you'll find imployment;
Ladies will look for Courtship.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: 'Tis but fleshing,
But standing one good brunt or two: ha'st thou any mind to mariage?
Wee'll provide thee some soft-natur'd wench, that's dumb too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Or an old woman that cannot refuse thee in charity.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: A dumb woman, or an old woman, that were eager,
And car'd not for discourse, I were excellent at.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You must now put on boldness, there's no avoyding it;
And stand all hazards; fly at all games bravely;
They'll say you went out like an Ox, and return'd like an Ass else.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I shall make danger sure.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I am sent for home now,
I know it is to mary, but my father shall pardon me,
Although it be a witty ceremony,
And may concern me hereafter in my gravitie;
I will not lose the freedom of a Traveller;
A new strong lusty Bark cannot ride at one anchor;
Shall I make divers suits to shew to the same eyes?
'Tis dull, and home-spun: Study severall pleasures,
And want employments for 'em? I'll be hang'd first;
Tie me to one smock? make my travels fruitless?
I'll none of that: For every fresh behaviour,
By your leave, father, I must have a fresh Mistris,
And a fresh favour too.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I like that passingly;
As many as you will, so they be willing;
Willing, and gentle, gentle.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: There's no reason
A Gentleman, and a Traveller, should be clapt up,
For 'tis a kind of Baeboes to be maryed
Before he manifest to the world his good parts:
Tug ever like at a rascall at one oar?
Give me the Italian liberty.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: That I study;
And that I will enjoy: Come, go in Gentlemen,
There mark how I behave my self, and follow.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: You and your beauteous daughters are most welcom,
Beshrew my blood they are fair ones; welcom Beauties,
Welcom sweet birds.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: They are bound much to your curtesies.

speeches.speaker: La Ca.
verse: I hope we shall be nearer acquainted.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: That's my hope too.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: For certain, Sir, I much desire your Alliance.
You see 'em, they are no Gipscies; for their breeding,
It has not been so coarse, but they are able
To rank themselves with women of fair fashion;
Indeed they have been trained well.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Thank me.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: Fit for the heirs of that state I shall leave 'em;
To say more, is to sell 'em. They say your son
Now he has travail'd must be wondrous curious,
And choice in what he takes: These are no coarse ones;
Sir, here's a merry wench, let him look to himself,
(All heart, y'faith) may chance to startle him;
For all his care, and travail'd caution,
May creep into his eye; if he love Gravitie,
Affect a solemn face, there's one will fit him.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: So young, and so demure?

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: She is my daughter,
Else I would tell you, Sir, she is a Mistris
Both of those manners, and that modesty,
You would wonder at: She is no often speaker,
But when she does, she speaks well; Nor no Reveller,
Yet she can dance, and has studied the Court Elements,
And sings, as some say, handsomly; if a woman,
With the decencie of her sex, may be a Scholar,
I can assure ye, Sir, she understands too.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: These are fit Garments, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Thank them that cut 'em:
Yes, they are handsom women; they have handsom parts too;
Prettie becoming parts.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: 'Tis like they have, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Yes, yes, and handsom Education they have had too:
Had it abundantly; they need not blush at it;
I taught it, I'll avouch it.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: Ye say well, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: I know what I say, Sir, and I say but right, Sir.
I am no trumpet of their commendations
Before their father; else I should say farther.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: Pray ye, what's this Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: One that lives with me, Sir;
A man well bred and learn'd, but blunt and bitter,
Yet it offends no wise man; I take pleasure in't:
Many fair gifts he has, in some of which
That lie most easie to their understandings,
Has handsomly bred up my girls, I thank him.
I have put it to 'em, that's my part, I have urg'd it,
It seems they are of years now to take hold on't.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: He's wondrous blunt.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: By my faith I was afraid of him:
Does he not fall out with the Gentlewomen sometimes?

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: No, no; he's that way moderate, and discreet, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: If he did, we should be too hard for him.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Well said Sulphur:
Too hard for thy husbands head, if he wear not armour.

speeches.speaker: Na.
prose: Many of these bickrings, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: I am glad they are no Oracles:
Sure, as I live, he beats them, he's so puisant.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Well, if ye do forget—

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Pre'thee hold thy peace;
I know thou art a prettie wench; I know thou lov'st me,
Preserve it till we have a fit time to discourse on't,
And a fit place: I'll ease thy heart, I warrant thee:
Thou seest I have much to do now.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I am answer'd, Sir:
With me ye shall have nothing on these conditions.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Your father, and your friends.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: You are welcom home, Sir;
'Bless ye, ye are very welcom.
'Pray know this Gentleman,
And these fair Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: Monsieur Mirabell,
I am much affected with your fair return, Sir:
You bring a generall joy.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I bring you service,
And these bright beauties, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: Welcom home, Gentlemen,
VVelcom, with all my heart.

speeches.speaker: Bel. Pi.
verse: VVe thank ye, Sir.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: Your friends will have their share too.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Sir, we hope
They'll look upon us, though we shew like strangers.

speeches.speaker: Na.
verse: Monsieur de-Gard, I must salute you also,
And this fair Gentlewoman: you are welcom from your Travell too.
All welcom, all.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: VVe render ye our loves, Sir;
The best wealth we bring home: By your favours, Beauties,
One of these two: you know my meaning.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: VVell Sir;
They are fair and handsom, I must needs confess it;
And let it prove the worst, I shall live after it,
Whilst I have meat & drink, Love can not starve me;
For if I dye o'th' first fit, I am unhappy,
And worthy to be buried with my heels upward.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: To mary, Sir?

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: You know I am an old man,
And every hour declining to my grave,
One foot already in, more sons I have not,
Nor more I dare not seek whilst you are worthy,
In you lies all my hope, and all my name,
The making good or wretched of my memory,
The safety of my state.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And you have provided
Out of this tenderness this handsom Gentlewoman,
Daughters to this rich man, to take my choice of?

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: I have, dear son.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Tis true, ye are old, and feebled;
Would ye were young again, and in full vigor;
I love a bounteous fathers life, a long one,
I am none of those that when they shoot to ripeness,
Do what they can to break the boughs they grew on:
I wish ye many years, and many riches,
And pleasures to enjoy 'em: But for Mariage,
I neither yet beleeve in't, nor affect it,
Nor think it fit.

speeches.speaker: La. C.
verse: You will render me your reasons?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, Sir, both short and pithy; and these they are:
You would have me mary a Mayd?

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: A Mayd? what else?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, there be things called Widdows, dead-mens Wills,
I never lov'd to prove those; nor never long'd yet
To be buried alive in anothers mans cold Monument.
And there be Maids appearing, and Maid ^ing:
The appearing, are fantastick things, meer shadows;
And if you mark 'em well, they want their heads too;
Onely the world, to cosen mystie eyes,
Has clapt 'em on new faces. The Mayds being,
A man may venture on, if he be so mad to mary;
If he have neither fear before his eyes, nor fortune;
And let him take heed how he gather these too;
For look ye, father, they are just like Melons,
Musk-Melons are the Emblems of these Mayds;
Now they are ripe, now cut 'em, they taste pleasantly,
And are a dainty fruit, digested easily:
Neglect this present time, and come to morrow,
They are so ripe they are rotten gon, their sweetness
Run into humour, and their taste to surfeit.

speeches.speaker: La. C.
verse: Why these are now ripe son.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I'll try them presently,
And if I like their taste—

speeches.speaker: La. C.
verse: 'Pray ye please your self, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: That liberty is my due, and I'll maintain it.
Lady, what think you of a handsom man now?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: A wholsom too, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: That's as you make your bargain.
A handsom, wholsom man then, and a kind man,
To chear your heart up, to rejoyce ye, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yes, Sir, I love rejoycing.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: To ly close to ye?
Close as a cockle? keep the cold nights from ye?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: That will be lookt for too, our bodies ask it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And get two Boyes at every birth?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: That's nothing,
I have known a Cobler do it, a poor thin Cobler;
A Cobler out of mouldy cheese perform it,
Cabbage, and coarse black bread: me thinks a Gentleman
Should take foul scorn to have a Nawl out-name him.
Two at a birth? why every House-dove has it:
That man that feeds well, promises as well too,
I should expect indeed something of worth from
Ye talk of two?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: She would have me get two dozen,
Like Buttons, at a birth.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: You love to brag, Sir.
If you proclame these offers at your Mariage,
Ye are a pretty timber'd man, take heed,
They may be taken hold of, and expected,
Yes, if not hoped for at a higher rate too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I will take heed, and thank ye for your counsell:
Father, what think ye?

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: 'Tis a merry Gentlewoman;
Will make, no doubt, a good wife.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Not for me:
I mary her, and happily get nothing;
In what a state am I then? Father, I shall suffer

For any thing I hear t^
^he contrary, more majorum,
I were as sure to be a Cuckold, Father,
A Gentleman of Antler.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: Away, away fool.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: As I am sure to fail her expectation,
I had rather get the pox than get her babies.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: Ye are much too blame; if this do not affect ye,
Pray try the other; she is of a more demure way.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: That I had but the audacitie to talk thus!
I love that plain-spoken Gentlewoman admirably,
And certain I could go as near to please her,
If down-right doing— she has a per'lous countenance,
If I could meet one that would beleeve me,
And take my honest meaning without circumstance.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You shall have your will, Sir, I will try the other,
But 'twill be to small use. I hope, fair Lady
(For methinks in your eyes I see more mercy)
You will enjoyn your Lover a less penance;
And though I'll promise much, as men are liberall,
And vow an ample sacrifice of service,
Yet your discretion, and your tenderness,
And thriftiness in Love, good houswives carefulnes
To keep the stock entire—

speeches.speaker: Lyl.
verse: Good Sir, speak louder,
That these may witness too ye talk of nothing,
I should be loth alone to bear the burthen
Of so much indiscretion.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Heark ye, heark ye;
Od's-bobs, you are angry, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lyl.
verse: Angry? no, Sir;
I never own'd an anger to lose poorly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: But you can love, for all this, and delight too,
For all your set-austeritie, to hear
Of a good husband, Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lyl.
verse: You say true, Sir:
For by my troth, I have heard of none these ten year,
They are so rare, and there are so many, Sir,
So many longing-women on their knees too,
That pray the droping down of these good husbands,
The droping down from heaven: for they are not bred here,
That you may ghess at all my hope, but hearing—

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why may not I be one?

speeches.speaker: Lyl.
verse: You were near 'em once, Sir,
When ye came ore the Alpes; those are near heaven:
But since ye mist that happiness, there's no hope of ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Can ye love a man?

speeches.speaker: Lyl.
verse: Yes, if the man be lovely;
That is, be honest, modest: I would have him valiant,
His anger slow, but certain for his honor;
Travail'd he should be, but through himself exactly;
For 'tis fairer to know manners well, than Countries;
He must be no vain talker, nor no Lover
To hear himself talk, they are brags of a wanderer,
Of one finds no retreict for fair behaviour;
Would ye learn more?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Lyl.
verse: Learn to hold your peace then,
Fond girls are got with tongues, women with tempers.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Women, with I know what; but let that vanish:
Go thy way good wife Bias; sure thy husband
Must have a strong Philosophers stone, he will ne'r please thee else.
Heer's a starcht peece of Austeritie: do you hear, father?
Do you hear this morall Lecture?

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: Yes, and like it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why there's your judgment now; there's an old bolt shot:
This Thing must have the strangest observation,
Do you mark me (father?) when she is maryed once,
The strangest custom too of admiration
On all she do's and speaks, 'twill be past sufferance;
I must not lie with her in common language,
Nor cry, have at thee Kate, I shall be hist then;
Nor eat my meat without the sawce of Sentences,
Your powder'd beef, and problemes, a rare dyet;
My first son, Monsieur Aristotle, I know it,
Great Master of the Metaphysicks, or so;
The second Solon, and the best Law-setter;
And I must look Egyptian God-fathers,
Which will be no small trouble: My eldest daughter
Sapho, or such a fidling kind of Poetess,
And brought up, invita Minerva, at her needle.
My dogs must look their names too, and all Spartan,

Lelaps, Mel^
: no more Fox and Baudiface.

I maryed to ^
^llen set of Sentences?
To one that weighs her words and her behaviours
In the Gold-weights of discretion? I'll be hang'd first.

speeches.speaker: La C.
verse: 'Pre'thee reclame thy self.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Pray ye give me time then;
If they can set me any thing to play at,
That seems fit for a Gamester, have at the fairest
Till I see more, and try more.

speeches.speaker: L. C.
verse: Take your time then,
I'll bar ye no fair liberty: Come Gentlemen,
And Ladies, come; to all once more a welcom,
And now let's in to supper.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: How do'st like 'em?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: They are fair enough, but of so strange behaviors.

speeches.speaker: Mir
verse: Too strange for me; I must have those have mettle,
And mettle to my mind: Come lets be merry.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Bless me from this woman: I would stand the Cannon
Before ten words of hers.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: Do you find him now?
Do you think he will be ever firm?

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I fear not.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: NE'r tel me of this happiness, 'tis nothing;
The state they bring with being sought to scurvey,
I had rather make mine own play, and I will do.
My happiness is in mine own content,
And the despising of such glorious trifles,
As I have done a thousand more. For my humour
Give me a good free fellow, that sticks to me,
A joviall fair companion; there's a Beauty:
For women, I can have too many of them;
Good women too, as the Age reckons 'em,
More than I have employment for.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: You are happy.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: My only fear is, that I must be forced
Against my nature, to conceal my self.
Health, and an able body are two jewels.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: If either of these two women were offer'd to me now,
I would think otherwise, and do accordingly:
Yes, and recant my heresies, I would Sir;
And be more tender of opinion,
And put a little off my travail'd Libertie
Out of the way, and look upon 'em seriously.
Me-thinks this grave-carried wench.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Me-thinks the other,
The home-spoken Gentle-woman, that desires to be fruitfull,
That treats of the full mannage of the matter,
For there lies all my aim; that wench, me-thinks
If I were but well set-on; for she is a fable,
If I were but hounded right, and one to teach me;
She speaks to th' matter, and comes home to th' point:
Now do I know I have such a body to please her,
As all the kingdom cannot fit her with, I am sure on't,
If I could but talk my self into her favour.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: That's easily done.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: That's easily said, would 'twere done;
You should see then how I would lay about me;
If I were vertuous, it would never grieve me,
Or any thing that might justifie my modesty,
But when my nature is prone to do a charitie,
And my calfs-tongue will not help me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Will ye go to 'em?
They cannot but take it curteously.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I'll do my part,
Though I am sure 'twil be the hardest I e'r plaid yet,
A way I never try'd too, which will stagger me,
And if it do not shame me, I am happy.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Win 'em, and wear 'em, I give up my interest.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: What say ye, Monsieur Bellure?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Would I could say,
Or sing, or any thing that were but handsom,
I would be with her presently.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Yours is no venture;
A merry ready wench.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: A vengeance squibber;
She'll fleer me out of faith too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I'll be near thee;
Pluck up thy heart, I'll second thee at all brunts;
Be angry if she abuse thee, and beat her a little,
Some women are won that way.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Pray be quiet,
And let me think: I am resolv'd to go on;
But how I shall get off again—

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I am perswaded
Thou wilt so please her, she will go neer to ravish thee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I would 'twere come to that once: Let me pray a little.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Now for thine honor Pinac; board me this modesty,
Warm but this frozen snow-ball, 'twill be a conquest
(Although I know thou art a fortunate Wencher,
And hast done rarely in thy daies) above all thy ventures.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You will be ever neer?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: At all necessities,
And take thee off, and set thee on again, Boy;
And cherish thee, and stroak thee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Help me out too?
For I know I shall stick 'ith' mire: if ye see us close once,
Be gone, and leave me to my fortune, suddainly,
For I am then determin'd to do wonders.
Farewell, and fling an old shooe: how my heart throbs?
Would I were drunk: Farewell Pinac; heaven send us
A joyfull and a merry meeting, man.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Farewell,
And chear thy heart up; and remember Bellure
They are but women.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I had rather they were Lyons.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: About it; Ill be with you instantly.
Shall I ne'r be at rest? no peace of conscience?
No quiet for these creatures? Am I ordain'd
To be devour'd quick by these she-Canibals?
Here's another they call handsom, I care not for her,
I ne'r look after her: When I am half tipled
It may be I should turn her, and peruse her,
Or in my want of women, I might call for her;
But to be haunted when I have no fancie,
No maw to th' matter—Now, why do you follow me?

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I hope, Sir, 'tis no blemish to my vertue,
Nor need you (out of scruple) ask that question,
If you remember ye, before your Travell
The contract you ty'd to me: 'tis my love, Sir,
That makes me seek ye, to confirm your memory,
And that being fair and good, I cannot suffer:
I come to give ye thanks too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: For what 'prethee?

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: For that fair peece of honesty ye shew'd, Sir,
That constant nobleness.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: How? for I am short headed.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I'll tell ye then; for refusing that free offer
Of Monsieur Nantolets; those handsom Beauties,
Those two prime Ladies, that might well have prest ye,
If not to have broken, yet to have bow'd your promise.
I know it was for my sake, for your faith sake,
You slipt 'em off: your honesty compell'd ye.
And let me tell ye, Sir, it shew'd most handsomly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And let me tell thee, there was no such matter:
Nothing intended that way of that nature;
I have more to do with my honesty than to fool it,
Or venture it in such leak-barks as women;
I put 'em off; because I lov'd 'em not,
Because they are too queazie for my temper,
And not for thy sake, nor the Contract sake,
Nor vows, nor oathes; I have made a thousand of 'em,
They are things indifferent, whether kept or broken;
Meer veniall slips, that grow not near the Conscience;
Nothing concerns those tender parts; they are trifles;
For, as I think, there was never man yet hop'd for
Either constancie, or secrecie, from a woman,
Unless it were an Ass ordain'd for sufferance;
Nor to contract with such can be a Tiall;
So let them know again; for 'tis a Justice,
And a main point of civill policie,
Whate're we say or swear, they being Reprobates,
Out of the state of faith, we are clear of all sides,
And 'tis a curious blindness to beleeve us.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: You do not mean this sure?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes sure, and certain,
And hold it positively, as a Principle,
As ye are strange things, and made of strange fires and fluxes,
So we are allow'd as strange wayes to obtain ye,
But not to hold; we are all created Errant.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: You told me other tales.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I not deny it;
I have tales of all sorts for all sorts of women,
And protestations likewise of all sizes,
As they have vanities to make us coxcombs;
If I obtain a good turn, so it is,
I am thankfull for it: if I be made an Ass,
The mends are in mine own hands, or the Surgeons,
And there's an end on't.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Do not you love me then?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: As I love others, heartily I love thee,
When I am high and lusty, I love thee cruelly
After I have made a plenteous meal, and satisfi'd
My senses with all delicates, come to me,
And thou shalt see how I love thee.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Will not you mary me?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No, certain, no, for any thing I know yet;
I must not lose my liberty, dear Lady,
And like a wanton slave cry for more shackles.
What should I mary for? Do I want any thing?
Am I an inch the farther from my pleasure?
Why should I be at charge to keep a wife of mine own,
When other honest maryed men will ease me?
And thank me too, and be beholding to me:
Thou thinkst I am mad for a Maiden-head, thou art cozen'd;
Or if I were addicted to that diet
Can you tell me where I should have one? thou art eighteen now,
And if thou hast thy Maiden-head yet extant,
Sure 'tis as big as Gods-head: and those grave dishes
I never love to deal withall: Do'st thou see this book here?
Look over all these ranks; all these are Women,
Mayds, and pretenders to Maiden-heads; these are my conquests,
All these I swore to mary, as I swore to thee,
With the same reservation, and most righteously,
Which I need not have don neither; for alas they made no scruple,
And I enjoy'd 'em at my will, and left 'em:
Some of 'em are maried since, and were as pure mayds again,
Nay o' my conscience better than they were bred for;
The rest fine sober women.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Are ye not asham'd, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No by my troth, Sir; there's no shame belongs to it;
^ hold it as commendable to be wealthy in pleasure,
As others do in rotten sheep, and pasture.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Are all my hopes come to this? is their no faith?
No troth? nor modesty in men?

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: How now Sister,
Why weeping thus? did I not prophesie?
Come tell me why—

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I am not well; 'pray ye pardon me.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: Now Monsieur Mirabell, what ails my Sister?
You have been playing the wag with her.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: As I take it,
She is crying for a cod-peece; is she gone?
Lord, what an Age is this? I was calling for ye,
For as I live I thought she would have ravish'd me.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: Ye are merry Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Thou know'st this book, de Gard, this Inventory.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: The Debt-book of your Mistrisses, I remember it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why this was it that anger'd her; she was stark mad
She found not her name here, and cry'd down-right,
Because I would not pitty her immediately,
And put her in my list.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Sure she had more modesty.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Their modesty is anger to be over-done;
They'll quarrell sooner for precedence here,
And take it in more dudgen to be slighted,
Than they will in publique meetings; 'tis their natures:
And alass I have so many to dispatch yet,
And to provide my self for my affairs too,
That in good faith—

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: Be not too glorious foolish;
Summe not your Travails up with vanities,
It ill becomes your expectation:
Temper your speech, Sir; whether your loose story
Be true, or false (for you are so free, I fear it)
Name not my Sister in't; I must not hear it;
Upon your da^er name her not: I hold her
A Gentlewom^n of those happy parts and carriage,
A good mans tongue may be right proud to speak her.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Your Sister, Sir? d'ye blench at that? d'ye cavill?
Do you hold her such a peece, she may not be play'd withall?
I have had an hundred handsomer and nobler,
Has su'd to me too for such a curtesie:
Your Sister comes i'th' rear: since ye are so angry,
And hold your Sister such a strong Recusant,
I tell ye I may do it, and it may be will too,
It may be have too; there's my free confession;
Work upon that now.

speeches.speaker: de G.
verse: If I thought ye had, I would work,
And work such stubborn work, should make your heart ake;
But I beleeve ye, as I ever knew ye,
A glorious talker, and a Legend maker
Of idle tales, and trifles; a depraver
Of your own truth; their honours fly about ye;
And so I take my leave, but with this caution,
Your sword be surer than your tongue, you'll smart else.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I laugh at thee, so little I respect thee;
And I'll talk louder, and despise thy Sister;
Set up a Chamber-maid that shall out-shine her,
And carry her in my Coach too, and that will kill her.
Go get thy Rents up, go.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: Ye are a fine Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Now have at my two youths, I'll see how they do,
How they behave themselves, and then I'll study
What wench shall love me next, and when I'll loose her.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Art thou her servant, saist thou?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Her poor creature,
But servant to her horse, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Canst thou shew me
The way to her chamber? or where I may conveniently
See her, or come to talk to her?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: That I can, Sir;
But the question is whether I will or no.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Why I'll content thee.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Why I'll content thee then; now ye come to me.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: There's for your diligence.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: There's her chamber, Sir;
And this way she comes out; stand ye but here, Sir,
You have her at your prospect, or your pleasure.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Is she not very angry?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: You'll find that quickly:
'May be she'll call ye sawcy scurvey fellow,
Or some such familiar name: 'may be she knows ye,
And will fling a Piss-pot at ye, or a Pantofle,
According as ye are in acquaintance: if she like ye,
'May be she'll look upon ye, 'may be no,
And two moneths hence call for ye.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: This is fine.
She is monstrous proud then?

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: She is a little haughtie;
Of a small body, she has a mind well mounted.
Can ye speak Greek?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: No certain.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Get ye gon then;
And talk of stars, and firmaments, and fire-drakes,
Do you remember who was Adams School-master,
And who taught Eve to spin? she knowes all these,
And will run ye over the beginning o'th' world
As familiar as a Fidler.
Can ye sit seven hours together, and say nothing?
Which she will do, and when she speaks speak Oracles;
Speak things that no man understands, nor her self neither.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Thou mak'st me wonder.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Can ye smile?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Yes willingly:
For naturally I bear a mirth about me.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: She'll ne'r endure ye then; she is never merry;
If she see one laugh, she'll swound past Aquavitae;
Never come near her, Sir; if ye chance to venture,
And talk not like a Doctor, you are damn'd too;
I have told ye enough for your Crown, and so good speed ye.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I have a pretty task, if she be thus curious,
As sure it seems she is; if I fall off now,
I shall be laugh'd at fearfully; if I go forward,
I can but be abus'd, and that I look for,
And yet I may hit right, but 'tis unlikely.
Stay, in what mood and figure shall I attempt her?
A careless way? no, no, that will not waken her;
Besides, her gravity will give me line still,
And let me lose my self; yet this way often
Has hit, and handsomly. A wanton method?
I, if she give it leave to sink into her consideration;
But there's the doubt: if it but stir her blood once,
And creep into the crannies of her phansie,
Set her a gog: but if she chance to slight it,
And by the pow'r of her modesty fling it back,
I shall appear the arrantst Rascal to her,
The most licentious knave, for I shall talk lewdly.
To bear my self austerely? rate my words,
And fling a generall gravitie about me,
As if I meant to give Laws? but this I cannot do,
This is a way above my understanding;
Or if I could, 'tis ods she'll think I mock her;
For serious and sad things are ever still suspicious.
Well, I'll say something.
But learning I have none, and less good manners,
Especially for Ladies; well, I'll set my best face;
I hear some coming; this is the first woman
I ever fear'd yet, the first face that shakes me.

speeches.speaker: Li.
verse: Give me my hat Petella, take this veil off,
This sullen cloud, it darkens my delights;
Come wench be free, and let the Musick warble,
Play me some lusty measure.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: This is she sure,
The very same I saw, the very woman,
The Gravitie I wonder'd at: Stay, stay,
Let me be sure; ne'r trust me, but she danceth,
Summer is in her face now, and she skippeth:
I'll go a little nearer.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Quicker time fellows,
I cannot find my legs yet, now Petella.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I am amaz'd, I am founder'd in my fancie.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Hah, say ye so; is this your gravitie?
This the austeritie ye put upon ye?
I'll see more o'this sport.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: A Song now;
Call in for a merry, and a light Song,
And sing it with a liberall spirit.

speeches.speaker: Man.
verse: Yes, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: And be not amaz'd sirha, but take us for your own company.
Let's walk our selves; come wench, would we had a man or two.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Sure she has spi'd me, and will abuse me dreadfully,
She has put on this for the purpose; yet I will try her.
Madam, I would be loth my rude intrusion,
Which I must crave a pardon for—

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: O ye are welcom,
Ye are very welcom, Sir, we want such a one;
Strike up again: I dare presume ye dance well:
Quick, quick, Sir, quick, the time steals on.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I would talk with ye.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Talk as ye dance.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: She'll beat him off his legs first.
This is the finest Masque.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Now how do ye, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: You have given me a shrew'd heat.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: I'll give ye a hundred.
Come sing now, sing; for I know ye sing well.
I see ye have a singing face.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: A fine Modesty!
If I could she'd never give me breath,
Madam would I might sit and recover.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Sit here, and sing now,
Let's do things quickly, Sir, and handsomly,
Sit close wench, close, begin, begin.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I am lesson'd.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: 'Tis very pretty y'faith, give me some wine now.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I would fain speak to ye.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: You shall drink first, believe me:
Here's to ye a lusty health.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I thank ye Lady.
Would I were off again; I smell my misery;
I was never put to this rack; I shall be drunk too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: If thou be'st not a right one, I have lost mine aim much:
I thank heaven that I have scap'd thee: To her Pinac;
For thou art as sure to have her, and to groan for her—
I'll see how my other youth does; this speeds trimly:
A fine grave Gentlewoman, and worth much honour.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Now? how do ye like me, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I like ye rarely.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Ye see, Sir, though sometimes we are grave and silent,
And put on sadder dispositions,
Yet we are compounded of free parts, and sometimes too
Our lighter, airie, and our fierie mettles
Break out, and shew themselves; and what think you of that Sir?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Good Lady sit, for I am very weary;
And then I'll tell ye.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Fie, a young man idle:
Up, and walk; be still in action.
The motions of the body are fair beauties,
Besides 'tis cold; ods-me Sir, let's walk faster.
What think ye now of the Lady Felicia?
And Bella-fronte the Dukes fair daughter? ha?
Are they not handsom things? thereis Duarta,
And brown Olivia.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I know none of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: But brown must not be cast away, Sir; if young Lelia
Had kept her self till this day from a husband,
Why what a Beauty, Sir? you know Ismena
The fair Jem of Saint Germins?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: By my troth I do not.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: And then I know you must hear of Brisac,
How unlike a Gentleman—

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: As I live I have heard nothing.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Strike me another Galliard.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: By this light I cannot;
In troth I have sprain'd my leg, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Now sit ye down, Sir,
And tell me why ye came hither, why ye chose me out?
What is your business? your errant? dispatch, dispatch;
'May be ye are some Gentlemans man, and I mistook ye,
That have brought me a Letter, or a haunch of Venison,
Sent me from some friend of mine.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Do I look like a Carrier?
You might allow me what I am, a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Cry 'ye mercie, Sir, I saw ye yesterday,
You are new come out of Travail, I mistook ye;
And how do's all our impudent friends in Italie?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Madam, I came with duty, and fair curtesie,
Service, and honour to ye.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Ye came to jeer me:
Yee see I am merry, Sir, I have chang'd my coppy:
None of the Sages now, and 'pray ye proclame it,
Fling on me what aspersion you shall please, Sir,
Of wantonness, or wildness, I look for it;
And tell the world I am an hypocrite
Mask in a forc'd and borrow'd shape, I expect it;
But not to have you beleev'd; for mark ye, Sir,
I have won a nobler estimation,
A stronger tie by my discretion
Upon opinion (how ere you think I forced it)
Than either tongue or art of yours can slubbber,
And when I please I will be what I please, Sir,
So I exceed not Mean; and none shall brand it
Either with scorn or shame, but shall be slighted.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Lady, I come to love ye.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Love your self, Sir.
And when I want observers, 'll send for ye:
Heigh, ho; my fit's almost off, for we do all by fits, Sir:
If ye be weary, sit till I come again to ye.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: This is a wench of a dainty spirit; but hang me if I know yet
Either what to think, or make of her; She had her will of me,
And baited me abundantly, I thank her.
And I confess I never was so blurted,
Nor never so abus'd; I must bear mine own sins;
Ye talk of Travails, here's a curious Country,
Yet I will find her out, or forswear my facultie.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ne'r vex your self, nor grieve; ye are a fool then.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I am sure I am made so: yet before I suffer
Thus like a girl, and give him leave to triumph—

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: You say right; for as long as he perceives ye
Sink under his proud scornings, he'll laugh at ye:
For me, secure your self; and for my Sister,
I partly know her mind too: howsoever
To obey my Father we have made a tender
Of our poor beauties to the travail'd Monsieur;
Yet two words to a bargain; he slights us
As skittish things, and we shun him as curious.
May be my free behaviour turns his stomach,
And makes him seem to doubt a loose opinion.
I must be so sometimes, though all the world saw it.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Why should not ye? Are our minds only measur'd?
As long as here ye stand secure.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ye say true;
As long as mine own conscience makes no question,
What care I for Report: That woman's miserable
That's good or bad for their tongues sake: Come let's retire.
And get my veil wench: By my troth your sorrow,
And the consideration of mens humorous maddings,
Have put me into a serious contemplation.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Come 'faith, let's sit and think.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: That's all my business.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: Why standst thou peeping here? thou great slug, forward.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: She is there, peace.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why standst thou here then,
Sneaking, and peaking, as thou would'st steal linnen?
Hast thou not place and time?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I had a rare speech
Studied, and almost ready, and your violence
Has beat it out of my brains.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Hang your rare speeches,
Go me on like a man.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Let me set my Beard up.
How has Pinac performed?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: He has won already:
He stands not thrumming of caps thus.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Lord, what should I ail?
What a cold I have over my stomack; would I had some Hum.
Certain I have a great mind to be at her:
A mighty mind.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: On fool.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Good words, I beseech ye;
For I will not be abused by both.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Adieu, then,
I will not trouble you, I see you are valiant,
And work your own way.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Hist, hist, I will be rul'd
I will y'faith, I will go presently:
Will ye forsake me now and leave me i'th' suds:
You know I am false-hearted this way; I beseech ye,
Good sweet Mirabell; I'll cut your throat if ye leave me,
Indeed I will sweet heart.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I will be ready,
Still at thine elbow; take a mans heart to thee,
And speak thy mind: the plainer still the better.
She is a woman of that free behaviour,
Indeed that common curtesie, she cannot deny thee;
Go bravely on.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Madam—keep close about me,
Still at my back. Madam, sweet Madam.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ha;
What noise is that, what saucy sound to trouble me?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What sayd she?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I am saucy.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Tis the better.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: She comes; must I be saucie still?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: More saucie.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Still troubled with these vanities? heaven bless us;
What are we born to? would ye speak with any of my people?
Go in, Sir, I am busie.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: This is not she sure:
Is this two children at a Birth? I'll be hang'd then:
Mine was a merry Gentlewoman, talkt daintily,
Talkt of those matters that befitted women;
This is a parcell-pray'r-book; I'm serv'd sweetly;
And now I am to look too; I was prepar'd for th' other way.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Do you know that man?

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Sure I have seen him, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Me-thinks 'tis pitty such a lusty fellow
Should wander up and down and want employment.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: She takes me for a Rogue: you may do well Madam,
To stay this wanderer, and set him a work, forsooth,
He can do something that may please your Ladiship.
I have heard of women that desire good breedings,
Two at a birth, or so.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: The fellow's impudent.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Sure he is crazed.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I have heard of men too that have had good manners;
Sure this is want of grace; indeed 'tis great pitty
The young man has been bred so ill; but this lewd Age
Is full of such examples.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I am founder'd,
And some shall rue the setting of me on.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Ha? so bookish, Lady, is it possible?
Turn'd holy at the heart too? I'll be hang'd then:
Why this is such a feat, such an activitie,
Such fast and loose: a veyl too for your knavery?
O dio, dio!

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: What do you take me for, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: An hypocrite, a wanton, a dissembler,
How e're ye seem, and thus ye are to be handled.
Mark me Bellure, and this you love, I know it.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Stand off, bold Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You wear good clothes to this end,
Jewels, love Feasts, and Masques.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ye are monstrous saucie.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: All this to draw on fools? and thus, thus Lady,
Ye are to be lull'd.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Let her alone, I'll swinge ye else,
I will y'faith; for though I cannot skill o'this matter
My self, I will not see another do it before me,
And do it worse.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Away, ye are a vain thing;
You have travail'd far Sir, to return again
A windy and poor Bladder: you talk of women,
That are not worth the favour of a common one;
The grace of her grew in an Hospitall:
Against a thousand such blown fooleries
I am able to maintain good womens honours,
Their freedoms, and their fames, and I will do it.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: She has almost struck me dumb too.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: And declame
Against your base malicious tongues; your noyses;
For they are nothing else: You teach behaviours?
Or touch us for our freedoms? teach your selves manners,
Truth and sobriety, and live so clearly
That our lives may shine in ye; and then task us:
It seems ye are hot, the suburbs will supply ye,
Good women scorn such Gamesters; so I'll leave ye.
I am sorry to see this; 'faith Sir live fairly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This woman, if she hold on, may be vertuous,
'Tis almost possible: we'll have a new day.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Ye brought me on, ye forced me to this foolery;
I am sham'd, I am scorn'd, I am flurted; yes, I am so:
Though I cannot talk to a woman like your worship,
And use my phrases, and my learned figures,
Yet I can fight with any man.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Fie.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I can, Sir,
And I will fight.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: With whom?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: With you, with any man;
For all men now will laugh at me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Pre'thee be moderate.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: And I'll beat all men. Come.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I love thee dearly.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I beat all that love, Love has undone me;
Never tell me, I will not be a History.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Thou art not.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Sfoot I will not; give me room,
And let me see the proudest of ye jeer me,
And I'll begin with you first.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Pre'thee Bellure;
If I do not satisfie thee —

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Well, look ye do:
But now I think on't better, 'tis impossible;
I must beat some body, I am maul'd my self,
And I ought in Justice—

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No, no, no, ye are couzen'd;
But walk, and let me talk to thee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Talk wisely,
And see that no man laugh upon no occasion;
For I shall think then 'tis at me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I warrant thee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Nor no more talk of this.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Do'st think I am maddish?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I must needs fight yet; for I find it concerns me,
A pox on't, I must fight.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Y'faith thou shalt not.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: I Know ye are a Scholar, and can do wonders.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: There's no great Scholarship belongs to this, Sir;
What I am, I am; I pitty your poor Sister,
And heartily I hate these Travellers,
These Gim-cracks, made of Mops, and Motions:
There's nothing in their houses here but humings;
A Bee has more brains. I grieve, and vex too
The insolent licentious carriage
Of this out-facing fellow, Mirabell,
And I am mad to see him prick his plumes up.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: His wrongs you partly know.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Do not you stir, Sir,
Since he has begun with wit, let wit revenge it;
Keep your sword close, wee'll cut his throat a new way.
I am asham'd the Gentlewoman should suffer
Such base lewd wrongs.

speeches.speaker: de Ga.
verse: I will be rul'd, he shall live,
And left to your revenge.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: I, I, I'll fit him:
He makes a common scorn of handsom women;
Modesty, and good manners are his May-games:
He takes up Maidenheads with a new Commission;
The Church, warrant's out of date: follow my Counsell
For I am zealous in the Cause.

speeches.speaker: de Gr.
verse: I will, Sir;
And will be still directed: for the truth is
My Sword will make my sister seem more monstrous:
Besides there is no honor won on Reprobates.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: You are ith' right: The slight he has shew'd my Pupills
Setts me a fire too: goe Ile prepare your Sister,
And as I told ye.

speeches.speaker: de Gr.
verse: Yes all shalbe fit, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: And seriously, and handsomely.

speeches.speaker: de Gr.
verse: I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: A little councell more.

speeches.speaker: de Gr.
verse: 'Tis well.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: Most stately.
See that observ'd; and then.

speeches.speaker: de Gr.
verse: I have ye every way.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: Away then and be ready.

speeches.speaker: de Gr.
verse: With all speed Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: Wee'll learne to travell too, may be beyond him
Good day, Faire beauties.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: You have beautified us.
We thank ye Sir, ye have set us off most gallantly
With your grave precepts.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: We expected Husbands
Out of your Documents, and taught behaviours;
Excellent Husbands, thought men would run starck mad on us
Men of all Ages, and all States: we expected
An Inundation of desires, and Offers,
A Torrent of trym Suitors: all we did,
Or said, or purpos'd to be Spels about us,
Spells to provoake.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Ye have provoak'd us finely,
We follow'd your directions, we did rarely,
We were Stately, Coy, Demure, Careless, Light, Giddy,
And plai'd at all points: This you swore would Carry.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: We made Love, and Contemn'd Love. Now seemd holy
With such a reverent put-on Reservation
Which could not misse according to your Principles,
Now gave more hope again. Now close, Now publick,
Still up and down, we beate it like a Billowe;
And ever those Behaviours you read to us,
Subtile, and new. But all this will not help us.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: They help to hinder us of all Acquaintance,
They have frighted off all Friends: what am I better
For all my Learning, if I love a Dunce,
A handsome dunce? to what use serves my Reading,
You should have taught me what belongs to Horses,
Doggs, dice, Hawkes, Banketts, masks, free and faire Meetings
To have studied Gownes and Dressings.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: Ye are not mad sure,

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: We shalbe if we follow your encouragements;
I'le take mine own way now:

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: And I my Fortune.
We may live Maids else till the Moon drop Milstones;
I see your modest Women are tak'en for Monsters,
A Dowry of good breeding is worth nothing.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: Since ye take it so toth' heart, pray'ye give me leave yet
And ye shall see how I'le convert this Heretique;
Mark how this Mirabell.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Name him no more:
For, though I long for a husband, I hate him,
And would be marryed sooner to a Monkey,
Or to a Jack of Straw, then such a Juggler.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I am of that minde too; he is too nimble,
And plays at fast and loose too learnedly
For a plain-meaning Woman; thats the truth on't.
Here's one too, that we love well, would be angry;
And reason why: No, no, we will not trouble ye
Nor him, at this time: may he make you happy.
We'll turn our selves loose now, to our faire Fortunes,
And the down-right way.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: The winning-way wee'll follow,
Wee'll bait, that men may bite fair, and not be frighted;
Yet wee'll not be carryed so cheap neither: wee'll have som sport,
Some mad-Morrysse or other for our money (Tutor.)

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: 'Tis like enough: prosper your own Devices;
Ye are old enough to Choose: But for this Gentlewoman
So please her, give me leave.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: I shall be glad Sir,
To finde a Friend, whose pity may direct me.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: Ile doe my best, and faithfully deale for ye;
But then ye must be ruled.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: In all, I vo^ to ye.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Doe, doe: he has a lucky hand somtimes, Ile assure ye:
And hunts the recovery of a lost Lover deadly.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: You must away straight.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: And Ile instruct ye:
Here ye can know no more.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: By your leave, sweet Ladies,
And all our Fortunes, arive at our own wishes.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Amen, Amen.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: I must borrow your man.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: 'Pray take him;
He is within: to doe her good, take any thing,
Take us, and all.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: No doubt ye may finde Takers;
And so wee'll leave ye to your own disposes.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Now which way, Wench.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Wee'll goe a brave way; fear not:
A safe, and sure way too: and yet a by-way,
I must confess I have a great minde to be marryed.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: So have I too, a grudging of good-will that way;
And would as fain be dispatch'd. But this Monsieur Quicksilver.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: No, no: we'll bar him, by, and Mayne: Let him trample;
There is no safety in his Surquedrie:
An Army-Roiall of Women, are too few for him,
He keeps a Journall of his Gentleness,
And will go near to print his fair Dispatches,
And call it his Triumph over Time and Women:
Let him pass out of memory: what think ye
Of his two Companions?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Pinac methinks is reasonable;
A little Modestie he has brought home with him,
And might be taught in time some handsome duty.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: They say he is a Wencher too.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I like him better:
A free light Touch or two becomes a Gentleman,
And sets him seemly off: so he exceed not,
But keep his Compass, clear he may be lookt at;
I would not marry a man that must be taught,
And conjur'd up with Kisses; the best Game
Is plaid still by the best Gamesters.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Fie upon thee!
What talk hast thou?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Are not we alone, and merry?
Why should we be asham'd to speak what we think? thy Gentleman
The tall fat: Follow; he that came to see thee.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Is't not a goodly man?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: A wondrous goodly!
'Has weight enough I warrant thee: Mercy upon me;
What a Serpent wilt thou seem under such a St George.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Thou art a Fool; give me a man brings Mettle.
Brings substance with him; needs no Brothes to Lare him:
These little Fellows shew like Fleas in boxes,
Hop up and down, and keep a stir to vex us;
Give me the puissant Pike, take you the small Shot.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Of a great thing I have not seen a Duller,
Therefore methinks, sweet Sister.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Peace: he's modest:
A bashfulness, which is a point of grace, Wench:
But when these Fellows come to moulding, Sister,
To heat, and handling: as I live, I like him;
And methinks I could form him.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Peace: the Fire-drake.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Bless ye sweet Beauties: sweet incomparable Ladies:
Sweet wits: sweet humours: 'Bless you, Learned Lady,
And you, most holy Nun; 'Bless your Devotions,

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: And 'bless your brains, Sir, your most pregnant brains, Sir,
They are in Travail, may they be delivered
Of a most hopefull Wild-Goose.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: 'Bless your manhood:
They say ye are a Gentleman of Action,
A fare accomplish'd man; and a rare Engineer,
You have a trick to blow-up Maidenheads,
A subtle trick, they say abroad.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I have Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: And often glory in their Ruines.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes forsooth;
I have a speedy trick: please you to try it:
My Engine will dispatch ye instantly.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I would I were a Woman, Sir, fit for ye,
As there be such, no doubt, may Engine you too;
May with a Counter-mine blow up your valour:
But in good faith, Sir, we are both too honest;
And the plague is, we cannot be perswaded:
For, look ye: if we thought it were a glory
To be the last of all your lovely Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Come, come; leave prating: this has spoil'd your Market;
This pride, and pufft-up heart, will make ye fast (Ladies)
Fast, when ye are hungry too.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: The more our pain, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: The more our health, I hope too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Your behaviours
Have made men stand amaz'd; those men that lov'd ye;
Men of fair States and parts; your strange conventions
Into I know not what, nor how, nor wherefore;
Your scorns of those that came to visit ye;
Your studied Whim-whams; and your fine set Faces:
What have these got ye? proud, and harsh opinions:
A Travail'd-Monsieur, was the strangest Creature,
The wildest Monster to be wondred at:
His Person made a publique Scoff, his Knowledge,
(As if he had been bred 'mongst Bears or Bandoggs)
Shunn'd and avoided: his conversation snuft at.
What Harvest brings all this?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I pray ye proceed, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Now ye shall see in what esteem a Travailer,
An under standing Gentleman, and a Monsieur
Is to be held, and to your greifes confes it,
Both to your greifes, and gaules.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: In what I pray ye, Sir?
We would be glad to understand your Excellence

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Goe on, (sweet Ladies) it becomes ye rarely
For me, I have blest me from ye, scoff on, seriously,
And note the Man ye mock'd: you, (Lady Learning)
Note the poore Traveller, that came to visit ye,
That flat unfurnish'd Fellow: note him throughly,
You may chance to see him anon.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: 'Tis very likely

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And see him Courted, by a Travell'd Lady,
Held deer, and honour'd by a vertuous virgin,
May be a Beautie, not far short of yours, neither
It may be, cleerer.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Not unlikely

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Younger:
As killing eyes as yours: a wit as poynant
May be, a State to that may top your Fortune;
Enquire how she thinks of him, how she holds him;
His good parts; in what precious price already;
Being a stranger to him, how she courts him;
A stranger to his Nation too, how she dotes on him:
Enquire of this; be sick to know: Curse, Lady,
And keep your Chamber: cry, and curse, a sweet one,
A thousand in yearly land; well bred; well friended:
Travell'd, and highly followed for her fashions.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: 'Bless his good Fortune, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This scurvy fellow;
I think they call his name Pinac; this serving-man
That brought ye Venison, as I take it, Madam;
Note but this Scab; 'tis strange that this course creature,
That has no more set off, but his jugglings,
His travell'd tricks.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Good, sir, I grieve not at him,
Nor envy not his Fortune: yet I wonder,
He's handsom; yet I see no such perfection.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Would I had his Fortune: for 'tis a woman
Of that sweet temper'd nature, and that judgment,
Besides her state, that care, clear understanding,
And such a wife to bless him.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Pray ye whence is she?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Of England and a most accomplish'd Lady,
So modest that mens eies are frighted at her,
And such a noble carriage. How now Sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Sir, the great English Lady.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What of her, sir?

speeches.speaker: Boy.
verse: Has newly left her Coach, and coming this way,
Where you may see her plain: Monsieur Pinac,
The onely man that leades her.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: He is much honored;
Would I had such a favour: now vex Ladies,
Envy, and vex, and raile.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ye are short of us, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Bless your fair Fortune, sir.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I Nobly thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Is she married, friend?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: No, no.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: A goodly Lady;
A sweet and delicate Aspect: mark, mark, and wonder!
Hast thou any hope of her?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: A little.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Follow close then:
Loose not that hope.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: To you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Gentle Lady.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: She is fair indeed.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I have seen a fairer, yet
She is well.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Her clothes sit handsome too.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: She dresses prettily.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: And by my faith she is rich; she looks stil sweeter.
A well-bred woman, I warrant her.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Do you hear, Sir;
May I crave this Gentlewomans name?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Mariana, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I will not say I ow ye a quarel Monsieur
For making me your Stale: a noble Gentleman
Would have had more curtesie; at least, more faith,
Then to turn of his mistris at first trial:
You know not what respect I might have shew'd ye;
I finde ye have worth.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I cannot stay to answer ye;
Ye see my charge: I am beholding to ye
For all your merry tricks ye put upon me,
Your bobs, and base accounts: I came to love ye,
To woo ye, and to serve ye; I am much endebted to ye
For dancing me off my legs; and then for walking me;
For telling me strange tales I never heard of,
More to abuse me; for mistaking me,
When ye both knew I was a Gentleman,
And one deserv'd as rich a match as you are.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Be not so bitter, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: You see this Lady:
She is young enough, and fair enough to please me,
A woman of a loving minde, a quiet,
And one that weighs the worth of him that loves her,
I am content with this, and bless my Fortune,
Your curious Wits, and Beauties.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Faith see me once more.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I dare not trouble ye.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: May I speak to your Lady?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I pray ye content your self: I know ye are bitter,
And in your bitterness, ye may abuse her;
Which if she comes to know, (for she understands ye not)
It may breed such a quarrel to your kindred,
And such an indiscretion fling on you too;
For she is Nobly friended.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I could eat her.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Rest as ye are, a modest noble Gentlewoman,
And afford your honest neighbours som of your prayers.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What think you now?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Faith she's a pretty Whiting;
She has got a pretty catch too.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You are angry;
Monstrous angry now; grievously angry;
And the pretty heart does swell now.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: No in troth, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And it will cry anon; a pox upon it:
And it will curse it self: and eat no meat, Lady;
And it will fight.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Indeed you are mistaken;
It will be very merry.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Why, sir, do you think
There are no more men living, nor no handsomer
Then he, or you; By this light there be ten thousand
Ten thousand thousand: comfort your self, dear Monsieur,
Faces, and Bodies, Wits, and all Abilliments
There are so many we regard 'em not.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: That such a noble Lady, I could burst now.
So far above such triffles?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You did laugh at me,
And I know why ye laughed.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gen.
verse: I pray ye be satisfied;
If we did laugh, we had some private reason,
And not at you.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gen.
verse: Alas, we know you not, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I'll make you know me; set your faces soberly;
Stand this way, and look sad; I'll be no May-game;
Sadder; demurer yet.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: What's the matter?
What ailes this Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: go off now backward, that I may behold ye;
And not a simper on you lives.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: He's mad sure.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Do you observe me too?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I may look on ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Why do you grin? I know your minde.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You do not.
You are strangely humorous: Is there no mirth, nor pleasure,
But you must be the object?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Mark, and observe me;
Where ever I am nam'd;
The very word shall raise a general sadness,
For the disgrace this scurvy woman did me;
This proud pert thing; take heed ye laugh not at me;
Provoke me not, take heed.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I would fain please ye;
Do any thing to keep ye quiet.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Hear me,
Till I receive a satisfaction
Equal to the disgrace, and scorn ye gave me:
Ye are a wreatched woman; till thou woo'st me,
And I scorn thee asmuch, as, seriously,
Gear, and abuse thee; ask what Gill thou art;
Or any baser name; I will proclaim thee;
I will so sing thy vertue; so be-paint thee,

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Nay, good sir, be more modest.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Do you laugh again?
Because ye are a woman ye are lawless,
And out of compass of an honest anger.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Good sir, have a better belief of me.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Away deare sister.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Is not this better now, this seeming madness,
Then falling out with your friends.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Have I not frighted her?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Into her right wits, I warrant thee: follow this humor,
And thou shalt see how prosperously 'twil guide thee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I am glad I have found a way to woo yet, I was afraid once
I never should have made a civill Suiter.
Well, I'le about it still.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Doe, doe, and prosper.
What sport do I make with these fools? What pleasure
Feeds me, and fats my sides at their poor innocence?
Wooing and wiving, hang it: give me mirth,
Witty and dainty mirth: I shall grow in love sure
With mine own happy head. Who's this? To me, Sir?
What youth is this?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Yes, Sir, I would speak with you,
If your name be Monsieur Mirabel.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Ye have hit it.
Your businesse, I beseech yee.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: This it is, Sir.
There is a Gentlewoman hath long time affected yee,
And lov'd ye dearly.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Turn over, and end that story,
'Tis long enough: I have no faith in women, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: It seems so, Sir: I do not come to woo for her,
Or sing her praises, though she well deserve 'em.
I come to tell ye, ye have been cruel to her,
Unkind and cruell, falser of faith, and carelesse,
Taking more pleasure in abusing her,
Wresting her honour to your wild disposes,
Then noble in requiting her affection:
Which, as ye are a man, I must desire ye
(A Gentleman of rank) not to persist in;
No more to load her fair name with your injuries.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Why, I beseech ye, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Leu.
verse: Good Sir, I'le tell ye.
And I'le be short: I'le tell yee, because I love ye,
Because I would have you shun the shame may follow:
There is a noble man, new come to Town, Sir,
A noble and a great man that affects her,
A Countreyman of mine, a brave Savoyan,
Nephew to th'Duke, and so much honours her,
That 'twill be dangerous to pursue your old way,
To touch at any thing concerns her honour,
Believe, most dangerous; her name is Oriana,
And this great man will marry her: take heed, Sir;
For howsoev'r her brother, a staid Gentleman,
Lets things passe upon better hopes, this Lord, Sir,
Is of that fiery, and that poynant metall,
(Especially provok'd on by affection)
That 'twill be hard: but you are wise.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: A Lord, sir?

speeches.speaker: Lev.
verse: Yes, and a noble Lord.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Send her good fortune.
This will not stir her Lord; a Barronness,
Say ye so; say ye so: by'r Lady, a brave title;
Top, and top gallant now; 'save her great Ladiship.
I was a poor servant of hers, I must confess, Sir,
And in those daies, I thought I might be jovy,
And make a little bold to call into her:
But Basto, now; I know my rules and distance;
Yet, if she want an Usher; such an implement;
One that is throughly pac'd; a clean made gentleman;
Can hold a hanging up; with approbation
Plant his Hat formally, and wait with patience
I do beseech you, sir.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Sir, leave your scoffing;
And as ye are a Gentleman, deal fairly:
I have given ye a friends councel, so I'll leave ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: But hark ye, hark ye, sir; is't possible
I may beleeve what you say?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: You may chuse, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No Baites? No Fish-hooks, sir? No Gins? No Nooses?
No Pitfals to catch Puppies?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: I tell ye certain;
You may beleeve; if not, stand to the danger.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: A Lord of Savoy saies he? The Dukes Nephew?
A man so mighty? By 'Lady a fair marriage;
By my faith, a handsom Fortune: I must leave prating;
For to confess the truth, I have abused her,
For which I should be sorry; but that will seem scurvy;
I must confess, she was ever since I knew her
As modest, as she was fair: I am sure she lov'd me;
Her means good; and her breeding excellent;
And for my sake she has refus'd fair matches:
I may play the fool finely. Stay who are these?
'Tis she, I am sure; and that the lord it should seem,
He carries a fair Port; is a handsom man too:
I do begin to feel, I am a Coxcomb.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Good my Lord, chuse a nobler: for I know
I am so far below your rank and Honor,
That what ye can say this way, I must credit,
But spoken to beget your self sport: Alas, Sir,
I am so far off, from deserving you,
My Beauty so unfit for your Affection,
That I am grown the scorn of common Railers,
Of such injurious Things, that when they cannot
Reach at my person, lie with my reputation:
I am poor besides.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Ye are all wealth and goodness;
And none but such as are the scum of men,
The Ulcers of an honest State; Spight-weavers,
That live on poyson onely, like swoln Spiders,
Dare once profane such excellence, such sweetness.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This man speaks loud indeed.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Name but the men, Lady;
Let me but know these poor, and base depravers;
Lay but to my revenge their persons open,
And you shall see how suddenly, how fully
For your most Beautious sake, how direfully
I'll handle their despights. Is this thing one?
Be what he will.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Dare your malicious tongue, sir?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I know you not; nor what ye mean.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Good my Lord.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: If he, or any he.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I beseech your Honor.
This Gentleman's a stranger to my knowledge,
And no doubt, sir, a worthy man.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Your mercy;
But had ye been attaint of your Honor;
A blaster of those beauties raign within ye;
But we shall finde a fitter time: dear Lady,
As soon as I have freed ye from your Guardian,
And done some honour'd offices unto ye,
I'll take ye with those faults the world flings on ye;
And dearer then the whole world I'll esteem ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This is a thundring Lord; I am glad I scap'd him:
How lovingly the wench disclaim'd my villany?
I am vext now heartily that he shall have her;
Not that I care to marry, or to lose her;
But that this Bilbo-Lord shall reap that Maiden-head
That was my due; that he shall rig and top her;
Ide give a thousand Crowns now, he might miss her.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Nay, if I bear your blowes, and keep your councel,
You have good luck, Sir; I'll teach ye to strike lighter.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Come hether, honest Fellow; canst thou tell me
Where this great Lord lies? This Savoy Lord? Thou met'st him;
He now went by thee certain.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Yes, he did, Sir;
I know him; and I know you are fool'd.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Come hether.
Here's all this, give me truth.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Not for your money;
(And yet that may do much) but I have been beaten:
And by the worshipful Contrivers beaten, and I'll tel ye;
This is no Lord, no Savoy Lord.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Go forward.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: This is a Trick, and put upon ye grosly
By one Lugier; the Lord is Monsieur De-Gard, Sir;
An honest Gentleman, and a neighbour here;
Their ends you understand better then I, sure.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Now I know him.
Know him now plain.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I have discharg'd my Colours; so God by ye, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What a purblinde Puppy was I; now I remember him.
All the whole cast on's face, though 'twere umber'd,
And mask'd with patches: what a dunder-whelp
To let him domineer thus: how he strutted,
And what a load of Lord he clapt upon him?
Would I had him here again, I would so bounce him,
I would so thank his Lordship for his lewd plot:
Do they think to carry it away, with a great band made of bird-pots.
And a pair of pin-buttockt breeches? Ha! 'Tis he again
He comes, he comes, he comes; have at him.

speeches.speaker: Sings.
verse: My Savoy Lord, why dost thou frown on me?
And will that favour never sweeter be?
Wilt thou I say, for ever play the fool?
De-Gard, be wise, and Savoy go to School.
My Lord De-Gard, I thank ye for your Antick,
My Lady bright, that will be sometime Frantick;
You worthy Train, that wait upon this Pair,
'Send you more wit, and they a bouncing Baire;
And so I take my humble leave of your honors.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: We are discover'd, there's no remedy;
Lelia, Biancha's man upon my life,
