In stubbornness, because Lugier corrected him.
(A shameless Slaves-plague on him for a Rascal.)

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I was in a perfect hope; the bane on't is now;
He will make mirth on mirth, to persecute us.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: We must be patient; I am vext to the proof too.
I'll try once more; then if I fail: Hear's one speaks.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Let me be lost, and scorn'd first.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Well, we'll consider.
Away, and let me shift; I shall be hooted else.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: FAint not; but do as I direct ye, trust me;
Beleeve me too, for what I have told ye, (Lady)
As true as you are Lelia, is Authentick;
I know it; I have found it; 'tis a poor courage
Flies off for one repulse; these Travellers
Shall finde before we have done, a home-spun wit,
A plain French understanding may cope with 'em;
They have had the better yet, thank your sweet Squire, here;
And let 'em brag: You would be reveng'd?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Yes surely.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: And married too?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I think so.

speeches.speaker: Leug.
verse: Then be Counsel'd;
You know how to proceed: I have other Irons
Heating as well as yours: and I will strike
Three blowes with one Stone home, be rul'd, and hapie;
And so I leave yee. Now is the time.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I am ready.
If he doe come to do me.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Will ye stand here,
And let the people think, ye are God knows what, Mistris;
Let Boyes, and Prentizes presume upon ye.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Pre'thee hold thy peace.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: Stand at his dore, that hates ye?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Pre'thee leave prating.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: 'Pray ye goe to th' Tavern. Ile give ye a Pint of wine there;
If any of the Mad-cap Gentlemen should come by
That take up women upon speciall warrant,
You were in a wise case now.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Give me the Garland,
And wait you here.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: She is here to seeke thee, Sirrah.
I told thee what would follow; she is mad, for thee;
Shew, and advance. So early stirring Lady,
It shewes a busie mind, a fancie troubled:
A willowgh Garland too. Is't possible,
'Tis pitty so much Beautie should lie mustie,
But 'tis not to be help'd now.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: The more's my Miserie
Good fortune to ye (Ladie) you deserve it:
To me: too late Repentance; I have sought it:
I doe not envy, though I greive a little,
You are Mistris of that happines, those Joyes
That might have bin, had I bin wise: but fortune.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: She understands ye not, 'pray ye doe not trouble her;
And do not crosse me like a Hare thus, 'tis as ominous.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I come not to upbraid, your Levitie
Though ye made shew of Love, and though I lik'd ye
To claime an Interest; we are yet both Strangers,
But what we might have bin, had you persever'd, Sir,
To be an eye-sore to your loving Lady;
This garland shewes, I give my self forsaken;
(Yet She must pardon me, 'tis most unwillingly:)
And all the power and interest I had in ye?
As I perswade my self, somewhat ye Lov'd me;
Thus patiently I render up, I offer
To her that must enjoy ye: and so blesse ye;
Onely, I heartily desire this Courtesie,
And would not be denide: to wait upon ye
This day, to see ye tide, then no more trouble ye.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: It need not, Ladie.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Good, Sir, grant me so much.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: 'Tis privat, and we make no Invitation.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: My presence, sir, shall not proclaim it publick.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: May be 'tis not in Town.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I have a Coach, sir.
And a most ready will to do you service.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Strike now or never; make it sure: I tell thee,
She will hang her self; if she have thee not.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: 'Pray ye, sir,
Entertain my noble mistris: onely a word or two
With this importunate woman, and I'll relieve ye.
Now ye see what your flings are, and your fancies,
Your States, and your wild stubbornes, now ye finde
What 'tis to gird and kick at mens fair services,
To raise your pride to such a pitch, and glory
That goodness shews like Gnats, scorn'd under ye,
'Tis ugly, naught, a self-will in a woman,
Chain'd to an over-weening thought, is Pestilent,
Murthers fair Fortune first; Then fair opinion?
There stands a Patern, a true patient Patern,
Humble, and sweet.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I can but grieve my ignorance.
Repentance some say too, is the best Sacrifice;
For sure, Sir, if my chance had been so happy,
(As I confess I was mine own destroyer)
As to have arrived at you; I will not prophesie,
But certain, as I think, I should have pleas'd ye;
Have made ye as much wonder at my curtesie,
My love, and duty, as I have dishearten'd ye,
Some hours we have of youth, and some of folly;
And being free-born Maides, we take a liberty,
And to maintain that, sometimes we strain highly.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Now ye talk reason.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: But being yoak'd, and govern'd,
Married, and those light vanities purg'd from us;
How fair we grow, how gentle, and how tender
We twine about those loves that shoot-up with us?
A sullen woman fear, that talks not to ye;
She has a sad and darkn'd soul, loves dully:
A merry and a free wench, give her liberty;
Beleeve her in the lightest form she appears to ye;
Beleeve her excellent, though she despise ye;
Let but these fits and flashes pass, she will shew to ye;
As Jewels rub'd from dust, or Gold new burnish'd:
Such had I been, had you beleev'd.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Is't possible.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: And to your happiness, I dare assure ye
If True love be accounted so; your pleasure,
Your will, and your command had tyed my Motions:
But that hopes gone; I know you are young, and giddy,
And till you have a Wife can govern with ye,
You saile upon this world-Sea, light and empty;
Your Bark in danger daily; 'tis not the name neither
Of Wife can steer ye; but the noble nature,
The dilligence, the Care, the Love, the Patience,
She makes the Pilat, and preserves the Husband,
That knowes, and reckons every Ribb, he is built on;
But this I tell ye, to my shame.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I admire ye,
And now am sorry, that I ayme beyond ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: So, so, so: faire and softly. She is thine own (Boy)
She comes now, without Lure.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: But that it must needes
Be reckon'd to me as a wantonnesse,
Or worsse, a Madnesse, to forsake a Blessing,
A Blessing of that hope.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I dare not urge ye;
And yet deare, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: 'Tis most certain, I had rather,
If 'twere in mine owne Choice, for you are my Country-woman,
A Neighbour here borne by me, She a Stranger;
And who knowes how her Friends?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Doe as you please, Sir,
If ye be fast: not all the world: I love ye,
'Tis most true: and cleer, I would perswade ye;
And I shall love ye still.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Goe, ^et before me:
So much ye have won upon me: doe it presently:
Here's a Preist ready: Ile have you.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: not now, Sir,
No, you shall pardon me: advance your Lady,
I dare not hinder your most high preferment,
'Tis honor enough for me, I have unmask'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: How's that.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: I have caught ye, Sir; alas, I am no States-woman,
Nor no great Traveller, yet I have found ye,
I have found your Lady too: your beauteous Lady;
I have found her Birth, and Breeding too: her disciplin:
Who brought her over, and who kept your Lady:
And when he laid her by, what vertuous Nunnery
Received her in: I have found all these: are ye blanck now,
Methinks such travel'd wisdomes should not foole thus:
Such excellent Indiscretions.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: How could she know this?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: 'Tis true she is English borne: but most part French now,
And so I hope you will find her, to your comfort,
Alas, I am ignorant of what, She cost ye:
The price of these hired Clothes I doe not know Gentlemen;
Those Jewells are the Broakers, how ye stand bound for 'em.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Will you make this good?

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Yes, yes, and to her face, Sir,
That she is an English whore, a kind of fling dust
One of your London Light o'Loves: a right one,
Came over in thin Pumps; and half a Petcicote,
One faith, and one Smock, with a broken Haberdasher;
I know all this, without a Conjurer:
Her name is Jumping-Jone, an ancient Sin-Weaver;
She was first a Ladies Chamber-maid, there slip'd
And broke her leg above the knee: departed
And set up shop her self. Stood the fierce Conflicts
Of many a furious Tearme; there lost her Colours,
And last shipt over hither.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: We are betray'd.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Doe you come to fright me with this Misterie?
To stirre me with a stink none can endure, Sir?
I pray ye proceed, the Wedding will becom ye,
Who gives the Lady? you? an excellent Father:
A carefull man, and one that knows a Beautie,
'Send ye faire shipping, Sir, and so Ile leave ye;
Be wise and manly, then I may chance to love ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: As I live I am asham'd, this wench has reach'd me,
Monstrous asham'd, but there's no remedie,
This skew'd-eyde Carren.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: This I suspected ever,
Come, Come, uncase, we have no more use of ye;
Your Clothes, must back againe.

speeches.speaker: Maria.
verse: Sir, ye shall pardon me:
'Tis not our English use to be degraded:
If you will visit me and take your venture,
You shall have pleasure for your properties;
And so sweet heart.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Let her goe, and the Devill goe with her:
We have never better luck with these preludiums:
Come, be not daunted: think she is but a woman,
And let her have the devills witt, wee'll reach her.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ye have now redeem'd my good opinion (Tutor)
And ye stand faire again.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: I can but labour,
And sweat in your Affaires: I am sure Bellure:
Wilbe here instantly, and use his Anger
His wonted harshness.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I hope he will not beate me.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: No sure; he has more manners: be you ready.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yes, yes, I am: and am resolv'd to fit him,
With patience to out-doe all he can offer;
But how do's Oriana?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Worse, and worse still:
There is a sad house for her: she is now
Poore Ladie, utterly distracted.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Pittie:
Infinite pittie: 'tis a handsom Ladie,
That Mirabel's a Beast, worse then a Monster.
If this affliction work not.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Are ye readie?
Bellure is comming on, here, hard behind me,
I have no leysure to relate my Fortune.
Onely I wish you may come off as handsomely,
Upon the sign you know what.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Well, well, leave me,

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: How now?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ye are welcome, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Tis well ye have manners:
That Curt'sy again, and hold your Countenance staidly;
That looks too light; take heed: so, sit ye down now,
And to confirm me that your gall is gone,
Your bitterness dispers'd, for so I'll have it;
Look on me stedfastly; and whatsoe'er I say to ye,
Move not, nor alter in your face, ye are gon then;
For if you do express the least distaste,
Or shew an angry wrinkle; mark me, woman,
We are now alone, I will so conjure thee:
The third part of my Execution
Cannot be spoke.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I am at your dispose, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Now rise, and woo me a little, let me hear that faculty;
But touch me not; nor do not lie, I charge ye.
Begin now.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: If so mean and poor a Beauty
May ever hope the grace.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Ye Cog, ye flatter
Like a lew'd thing, ye lie: may hope that grace?
Why, what grace canst thou hope for? Answer not,
For if thou dost, and lyest again, I'll swindge thee;
Do not I know thee, for a pestilent woman?
A proud at both ends? Be not angry;
Nor stir not o' your life?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I am counseld, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Art thou not now, (confess, for I'll have the truth out)
As much unworthy of a man of merit,
Or any of ye all? Nay of meer man?
Though he were crooked, cold, all wants upon him;
Nay of any dishonest thing, that bears that figure;
As Devils are of mercy?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: We are unworthy.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Stick to that truth, and it may chance to save thee;
And is it not our bounty that we take ye?
That we are troubled, vex'd, or tortur'd with ye?
Our meer, and special bounty?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Our pitty,
That for your wickedness we swindge ye soundly;
Your stubbornness and stout hearts, we be-labour ye?
Answer, to that?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I do confess your pitty.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: And dost not thou deserve in thine own person?
(Thou Impudent, thou Pert; do not change countenanance?)

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I dare not, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: For if ye do.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I am setled.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Thou Wag-tail, Peacock, Puppy; look on me:
I am a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: It seems no less, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: And darest thou in thy Surquedry?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I beseech ye.
It was my weakness, sir; I did not view ye;
I took not notice of your noble parts;
Nor call'd your person, nor your proper fashion.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: This is some amendes yet.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I shall mend, sir, daily.
And study to deserve.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Come a little neerer:
Canst thou repent thy Villany?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Most seriously.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: And be asham'd?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I am asham'd.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Cry.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: It will be hard to do, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Cry now instantly;
Cry monstrously, that all the Town may hear thee;
Cry seriously; as if thou hadst lost thy Monkey;
And as I like thy Tears.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Now.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: How? How? do ye jear me?
Have ye broke your bounds again Dame?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yes, and laugh at ye;
And laugh most heartily.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: What are these, Whirl-winds?
Is Hell broke loose, and all the Furies flutter'd?
Am I greas'd once again?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yes indeed are ye;
And once again ye shall be, if ye quarrel:
Do you come to vent your fury on a Virgin?
Is this your manhood, sir?

speeches.speaker: 1. VVo.
verse: Let him do his best:
Let's see the utmost of his indignation:
I long to see him angry: come, proceed, sir.
Hang him, he dares not stir; a man of Timber.

speeches.speaker: 2. Wo.
verse: Come hither to fright Maids, with thy Bul-faces?
To threaten Gentlewomen? Thou a man? A May-pole.
A great dry Pudding.

speeches.speaker: 3. Wo.
verse: Come, come, do your worst, sir;
Be angry if thou dar'st.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: The Lord deliver me.

speeches.speaker: 4. Wo.
verse: Do but look scurvily upon this Lady,
Or give us one foul word. We are all mistaken;
This is some mighty Dairy-Maid in mans clothes.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: I am of that minde too.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: What will they do to me?

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: And hired to come and abuse us; a man has manners;
A Gentleman, Civility, and Breeding:
Some Tinkers Trull with a beard glew'd on.

speeches.speaker: 1. VVo.
verse: Let's search him;
And as we finde him.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Let me but depart from ye,
Sweet Christian women.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Hear the Thing speak, Neighbours.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Tis but a small request: if ere I trouble ye,
If ere I talk again of beating Women,
Or beating any thing that can but turn to me;
Of ever thinking of a handsom Lady
But vertuously and well: of ever speaking
But to her honor: This I'le promise ye,
I will take Rhubarb; and purge Choler mainly,
Abundantly Ile purge.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Ile send ye Brothes, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I will be laugh'd at, and endure it patiently,
I will doe any thing.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ile be your Bayle then:
When ye com next to woo, 'pray ye com not boistrously
And furnish'd like a Bear-ward.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No in truth, forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I sented ye long since.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I was to blame, sure;
I will appear a Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: 'Tis the best for ye,
For a true noble Gentleman's a brave thing;
Upon that hope we quit ye: You fear seriously?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Yes truly do I; I confess I fear ye,
And honor ye, and any thing.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Farewel then.

speeches.speaker: Wo.
prose: And when ye come to woo next bring more mercy.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: A Dary-Maid? A Tinkers-Trull: Heaven bless me:
Sure if I had provok'd 'em, they had quarter'd me.
I am a most ridiculous Ass, now I perceive it:
A Coward, and a Knave too.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gen.
verse: 'Tis the mad Gentleman.
Let's set our Faces right.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No, no, laugh at me;
And laugh aloud.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gen.
verse: We are better manner'd, sir.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I do deserve it; call me Patch, and Puppy,
And beat me if you please.

speeches.speaker: 1. Gen.
verse: No indeed: We know ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: 'Death, do as I would have ye.

speeches.speaker: 2. Gen.
verse: Ye are an Ass then;
A Coxcomb, and a Calf.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I am a great Calf:
Kick me a little now: Why, when? Sufficient:
Now laugh aloud, and scorn me; so good buy'ye;
And ever when ye meet me laugh.

speeches.speaker: Gen.
verse: We will, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Your Patience, Gentlemen; why do ye bait me?

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: Is't not a shame you are so stubborn-hearted,
So stony and so dull to such a Lady,
Of her Perfections, and her Misery?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Does she not love ye? does not her distraction
For your sake only, her most pityed Lunacie
Of all but you, shew ye? does it not compell ye?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Soft and fair, Gentlemen, pray ye proceed temperately.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: If ye have any feeling, any sense in ye,
The least touch of a noble heart.

speeches.speaker: le-Cast.
verse: Let him alone;
It is his glory that he can kill Beauty,
Ye bear my Stamp, but not my Tenderness;
Your wild unsavoury Courses set that in ye!
For shame be sorry, though ye cannot Cure her,
Shew something of a Man, of a fair Nature.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Ye make me Mad.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Let me pronounce this to ye,
You take a strange felicity in slighting
And wronging Women; which my poor sister feels now,
Heavens hand be gentle on her: Mark me, Sir,
That very hour she dyes; there's small hope otherwise,
That minute you and I must grapple for it;
Either your life or mine.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Be not so hot, Sir,
I am not to be wrought on by these Policies;
In truth I am not; Nor do I fear the Tricks,
Or the high sounding Threats of a Savoyen:
I glory not in Cruelty; ye wrong me;
Nor grow up water'd with the Tears of Women;
This let me tell ye, howsoe're I shew to ye
Wilde, as you please to call it; or self-will'd;
When I see cause, I can both doe, and suffer,
Freely, and feelingly, as a true Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: O pity, pity; thousand thousand pities!

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Alas, poor soul! she will die; she is grown sensless;
She will not know, nor speak now.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Die for Love,
And Love of such a Youth? I would die for a Dog, first.
He that kils me, Ile give him leave to eat me;
Ile know men better ere I sigh for any of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Ye have don a worthy act, Sir; a most famous;
Ye have kild a Maid the wrong way; ye are a conqueror.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: A Conqueror? a Cobler; hang him Sowter;
Goe hid thy self for shame; go lose thy Memory;
Live not 'mongst Men; thou art a Beast, a Monster;
A Blatant Beast.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: If ye have yet any honestie,
Or ever heard of any; take my Counsell;
Off with your Garters; and seek out a Bough,
A handsom Bough; (for I would have ye hang like a Gentleman;)
And write some dolefull matter to the world,
A warning to hard-hearted men.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Out Kitlings:
What Catterwalling's here? what gibbing?
Do you think my heart is softned with a black Santis;
Shew me some Reason.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Here then, here is a reason.

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: Now, if ye be a man, let this sight shake ye.

speeches.speaker: la-C.
verse: Alas poor Gentlewoman! do ye know me Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: How she looks up and stares.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: I know ye very well:
You are my Godfather; and that's the Monsieur.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: And who am I?

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: You are Amadis de Gaule, Sir.
Oh, oh, my heart! were you never in love, sweet Lady?
And do you never dream of Flowres and Gardens;
I dream of walking Fires: take heed, It comes now,
Who's that? pray stand away; I have seen that face sure;
How light my head is.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Take some rest.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: I cannot.
For I must be up to morrow, to go to Church:
And I must dress me, put my new Gown on,
And be as fine to meet my Love: Heig ho!
Will not you tell me where my Love lies buried?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: He is not dead: beshrew my heart she stirs me.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: He is dead to me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Is't possible my Nature
Should be so dampnable, to let her suffer;
Give me your hand.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: How soft you feel; how gentle?
Ile tell ye your fortune, Friend.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: How she stares on me?

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: You have a flattring face; but 'tis a fine one;
I warrant you may have a hundred Sweet-hearts:
Will ye pray for me? I shall die to morrow;
And will ye ring the Bells?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I am most unworthy;
I doe confess unhappy; doe you know me?

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: I would I did.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Oh fair tears; how ye take me.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Do you weep too? you have not lost your Lover?
You mock me: Ile go home and pray.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Pray ye pardon me:
Or if it please ye to consider justly,
Scorn me; for I deserve it: Scorn, and shame me:
Sweet Oriana.

speeches.speaker: Lel.
verse: Let her alone; she trembles.
Her fits will grow more strong, if ye provoke her;

speeches.speaker: Ca-Last.
verse: Certain she knowes ye not, yet loves to see ye
How she smiles now:

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Where are ye? oh, why doe not ye laugh: come laugh at me;
Why a devill, art thou sad, and such a subject,
Such a ridiculous subject, as I am
Before thy face?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Pre'thee put off this Lightnes,
This is no time for mirth, nor place: I have us'd too much on't:
I have undon my self and a sweet Ladie,
By being too Indulgent to my Foolery
Which truly I repent: looke here.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: What ayles she.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Alas she is mad.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Mad.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, too sure for me too.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Dost thou wonder at that? by this good light, they are all so;
They are coz'ning mad, they are brawling mad, they are proud mad.
They are all, all mad: I came from a world of mad women,
Mad as march Haires: get 'em in Chaines, then deale with 'em.
There's one that's mad: she seemes well, but she is dog mad:
Is she dead, do'st think?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Dead? heaven forbid.

speeches.speaker: Bel
verse: Heaven further it.
For till they be key-cold dead, there's no trusting of 'em
What ere they seeme, or howsoere they carry it,
Till they be chap-falne, and their Tongues at peace,
Nayl'd in their Coffins sure, Ile ne're beleeve 'em,
Shall I talk with her.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No, deer friend, be quiet;
And be at peace a while.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Ile walk a side,
And come again anon: But take heed to her
You say she is a woman?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Take great heed:
For if she doe not Cozen thee, then hang me:
Let her be mad, or what she will, shee'll cheate thee

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Away wild Foole: how vild this shewes in him now?
Now take my faith, before ye all I speake it,
And with it, my repentant Love.

speeches.speaker: La-Cast.
verse: This seemes well.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Were but this Lady cleere again, whose sorrowes
My very hart melts for; were she but perfect
(For thus to marry her, would be two Miseries,)
Before the rishest, and the noblest Beautie,
France, or the world could shew me; I would take her
As she is now, my Teares, and praires shall wed her.

speeches.speaker: de-Ga.
verse: This makes some small amends.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: She beckens to ye.
To us too, to goe off.

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: Let's draw aside all.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Oh my best friend: I would faine.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What? she speakes well,
And with another voice.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: But I am fearfull,
And shame a little, stops my tongue.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Speake boldly.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Tell ye, I am well, I am perfect well. 'pray ye mock not;
And that I did this to provoke your Nature,
Out of my infinite, and restles Love,
To win your pitty: pardon me.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Goe forward;
Who set ye on?

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: None, as I live, no Creature.
Not any knew, or ever dreamt, what I meant:
Will ye be mine?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Tis true, I pittie ye;
But when I marry ye, ye must be wiser;
Nothing but Tricks? devises?

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Will ye shame me?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, marry will I: Come neer, Come neer, a Miracle,
The Womans well: she was only mad for Mariage,
Stark mad to be ston'd to death; give her good Councel,
Will this world never mend? are ye caught, Damsell?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: How goes it now?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Thou art a kind of Prophet,
The woman's well again; and would have gull'd me,
Well, excellent well: and not a Taynt upon her.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Did not I tell ye? Let'em be what can be;
Saints, Devills, any thing, they will abuse us;
Thou wert an Asse to beleeve her so long: a Coxcomb;
Give 'em a minute, they'll abuse whole Millions.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And am not I a rare Phisitian, Gentlemen?
That can cure desperate mad Mindes?

speeches.speaker: de-Ga.
verse: Be not insolent.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Well, goe thy waies: from this howre, I disclame thee,
Unles thou hast a Trick above this: then Ile love thee.
Ye owe me for your Cure; pray have a Care of her,
For fear she fall into Relaps; Come Bellure
We'll set up Bills, to Cure diseased virgins.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Shall we be merry?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: But Ile no more projects;
If we could make 'em mad, it were some Mastery.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: I am glad she is well again.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: So am I, certain
Be not ashamed.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: I shall never see a man more.

speeches.speaker: de-G.
verse: Come ye are afoole: had ye but told me this Trick,
He should not have gloried thus.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: He shall not long neither.

speeches.speaker: la-Cast.
verse: Be rul'd, and be at peace: ye have my Consent,
And what powre I can work with.

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: Come, leave blushing;
We are your Friends; an honest way compell'd ye;
Heaven will not see so true a love unrecompenc'd;
Come in, and slight him too.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: The next shall hit him.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: 'TWill be discover'd.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: That's the worst can happen:
If there be any way, to reach, and work upon him;
Upon his nature suddenly, and catch him: That he loves,
Though he dissemble it, and would shew contrary,
And will at length relent: I'll lay my Fortune,
Nay more, my life.

speeches.speaker: De G.
verse: Is she won?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Yes, and ready,
And my designments set.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: They are now for Travel,
All for that Game again: they have forgot wooing.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Let 'em; we'll travel with 'em.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Where's his Father?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Within; he knows my minde too, and allows it;
Pitties your Sisters Fortune most sincerely;
And has appointed, for our more assistance,
Some of his secret Friends.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: 'Speed the plowgh.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Well said;
And be you serious too.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: I shall be diligent.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Let's break the Ice for one, the rest will drink too
(Beleeve me, sir) of the same Cup; my young Gentlewomen
Wait but who sets the Game a foot; though they seem 'stubborn,
Reserv'd, and proud now, yet I know their hearts,
Their pulses, how they heat, and for what cause, Sir;
And how they long to venture their Abilities
In a true Quarrel; Husbands they must, and will have,
Or Nunneries, and thin Collations
To cool their bloods; Let's all about our business,
And if this faile, let Nature work.

speeches.speaker: De-G.
verse: Ye have arm'd me.

speeches.speaker: La Cast.
verse: Will ye be wilful then?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: 'Pray, sir, your pardon,
For I must Travel: lie lazy here;
Bound to a Wife; Chain'd to her subtleties,
Her humors, and her wills, which are meer Fetters;
To have her today pleas'd, to morrow peevish,
The third day mad, the fourth rebellious;
You see, before they are married, what Moriscoes,
What Masques, and Mummeries they put upon us,
To be ty'd here, and suffer their Lavalto's?

speeches.speaker: Nan.
verse: 'Tis your own seeking.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, to get my freedom;
Were they as I could wish 'em.

speeches.speaker: la-Cast.
verse: Fools, and Meacocks,
To endure what you think fit to put upon 'em:
Come, change your minde.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Not before I have chang'd air (Father)
When I know women worthy of my company,
I will return again and wait upon 'em;
Till then (dear Sir) I'll amble all the world over,
And run all hazards, misery, and poverty,
So I escape the dangerous Bay of Matrimony.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Are ye resolv'd?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes certain; I will out again.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: We are for ye, sir; we are your servants once more;
Once more we'll seek our fortune in strange Countries;
Ours is too scornful for us.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Is there ne'er a Land
That ye have read, or head of, (for I care not how far it be,
Nor under what Pestiferous Star it lies)
A happy Kingdom, where there are no Women?
Nor have been ever? Nor no mention
Of any such lewd Things, with lewder qualities?
For thether would I Travel; where 'tis Fellony
To confess he had a Mother: a Mistris, Treason?

speeches.speaker: la-Cast.
verse: Are you for Travel too?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: For any thing;
For living in the Moon, and stopping hedges,
E'er I stay here to be abus'd, and baffell'd.

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: Why did ye not break your minds to me? They are my daughters;
And sure I think I should have that command over 'em?
To see 'em well bestow'd: I know ye are Gentlemen,
Men of fair Parts and States; I know your Parents;
And had ye told me of your fair Affections:
Make but one Tryal more; and let me second ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No I'll make Hob-nailes first, and mend old Kettles:
Can ye lend me an Armor of high proof, to appear in,
And two or three field pieces to defend me?
The Kings Guard are meer Pigmeys.

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: They will not eat ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Yes, and you too, and twenty fatter Monsieurs,
If their high stomacks hold: They came with Chopping-knives,
To cut me into Rands, and Surloyns, and so powder me.
Come, shall we go?

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: You cannot be so discurteous
(If ye intend to go) as not to visit 'em,
And take your leaves.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: That we dare do, and civilly,
And thank 'em too.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Yes, sir, we know that honesty.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I'll come i'th Rear, forty foot off, I'll assure ye,
With a good Gun in my hand; I'll no more Amazous,
I mean, no more of their frights; I'll make my three legs,
Kiss my hand twice; and if I smell no danger;
If the enterview be clear, may be I'll speak to her;
I'll ware a privy coat too; and behind me,
To make those parts secure, a Bandog.

speeches.speaker: la-Cast.
verse: You are a merry Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: A wary Gentleman; I do assure ye,
I Have been warn'd, and must be arm'd.

speeches.speaker: la-Cast.
verse: Well, Son,
These are your hasty thoughts, when I see you are bent to it,
Then I'll beleeve, and joyn with ye; So we'll leave ye:
There's a Trick will make ye stay.

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: I hope so.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: We have won immortal Fame now, if we leave 'em.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: You have, but we have lost.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Pinac, Thou art cozen'd;
I know they Love ye; and to gain ye handsomly,
Not to be thought to yeeld, they would give millions;
Their Fathers willingness, that must needs shew ye.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: If I thought so.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Ye shall be hang'd, ye Recreant,
Would ye turn Renegado no?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No lets away, Boyes,
Out of the Air, and tumult of their Villanies;
Though I were married to that Grashopper,
And had her fast by th' legs I should think she would cozen me.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
prose: Monsieur Mirabel, I take it?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Y'are ith' right, sir.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: I am come to seek ye, sir; I have been at your Fathers,
And understanding you were here.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Ye are welcome:
May I crave your name?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Fosse, Sir, and your servant;
That you may know me better; I am Factor
To your old Merchant, Levordare.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: How do's he?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Well, sir, I hope: he is now at Orleance,
About some business.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You are once more welcom.
Your Master's a right honest man; and one
I am much beholding too, and must very shortly
Trouble his love again.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: You may be bold, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Your business if you please now?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: This it is, sir.
I know ye well remember in your Travel
A Genea Merchant.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I remember many.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: But this man, sir, particularly; your own benefit
Must needs imprint him in ye: one Alberto;
A Gentleman you sav'd from being Murther'd
A little from Bollonia,
I was then myself in Italie, and supplide ye,
Though happely, you have forgot me now.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No, I remember ye,
And that Alberto too: a noble Gentleman:
More to remember, were to thanck myself, Sir.
What of that Gentleman?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: He is dead:

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I am sorry.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: But on his death bed, leaving to his Sister.
All that he had beside some Certaine Jewells,
Which with a Ceremony, he bequeathd to you,
In gratefull memory: he commanded strictly
His Sister, as she lov'd him and his peace,
To see those Jewells safe, and true deliverd;
And with them, his last Love. She, as tender
To observe this wil, not trusting friend, nor Servant,
With such a weight, is come her self to Paris
And at my Masters House.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You tell me a wonder.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: I tell ye a truth, Sir: She is young, and handsom,
And well attended: of much State, and Riches;
So loving, and obedient to her Brother;
That on my Conscience, if he had given her also,
She would most willingly have made her tender.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: May not I see her?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: She desires it hartily.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And presently?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: She is now about some Business,
Passing Accompts of some few debts here owing,
And buying Jewells of a Merchant,

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Is she wealthie.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: I would ye had her, Sir, at all adventure.
Her Brother had, a main State.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And faire too?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: The prime of all those parts of Italie,
For Beautie, and for Curtesie.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I must needs see her.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: 'Tis all her Business, Sir. Ye may now see her,
But to morrow will be fitter for your visitation;
For she is not yet prepared.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Onely, her sight, Sir.
And when you shall think fit for further visit.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Sir, ye may see her; and Ile wayt your Coming.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: And Ile be with ye instantly. I know the house,
Mean time, my love, and thanks, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Your poore Servant

speeches.speaker: Pi.
prose: Thou hast the strangest Luck: What was that Alberto?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: An honest noble Marchant, 'twas my chance
To rescue from some Rogues had almost slain him;
And he in kindness to remember this.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Now we shall have you:
For all your protestations, and your forwardness,
Finde out strange Fortunes in this Ladies eyes,
And new entirements to put off your journey;
And who shall have honor then?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No, no, never fear it:
I must needs see her, to receive my Legacy.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: If it be tide up in her smock, Heaven help thee:
May not we see too?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Yes, afore we go:
I must be known my self e'er I be able
To make thou welcom: wouldst thou see more women?
I thought you had been out of love with all:

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I may be,
I finde that with the least encouragement,
Yet I desire to see whether all Countries
Are naturally possess'd with the same spirits;
For if they be, I'll take a Monastery,
And never Travel; for I had rather be a Frier,
And live mewed up, then be a fool and flouted.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Well, well, I'll meet ye anon; then tell you more, Boys;
How e'er, stand prepar'd, prest for our journey;
For certain, we shall go, I think, when I have seen her.
And view'd her well.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Go, go, and we'll wait for ye;
Your fortune directs ours.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You shall finde us ith' Tavern,
Lamenting in Sack and Suger for our losses;
If she be right Italian, and want servants,
You may prefer the properest man,
How I could worry a woman now?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Come, come, leave prating;
Ye may have enough to do, without this boasting

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: This is the last adventure.

speeches.speaker: de-G.
verse: And the happiest,
As we hope too.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: We should be glad to finde it.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Who shall conduct us thither?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Your man is ready.
For I must not be seen; no, nor this Gentleman;
That may beget suspition: all the rest
Are people of no doubt; I would have ye, Ladies,
Keep your old liberties, and as we instruct ye:
Come, look not pale; you shall not lose your wishes;
Nor beg 'em neither: but be your selves, and happy.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I tell ye true, I cannot hold off longer,
Nor give no more hard language.

speeches.speaker: de-G.
verse: You shall not need.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I love the Gentleman, and must now show it;
Shall I beat a propper man out of heart?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: There's none advises ye.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: 'Faith I repent me too.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Repent, and spoil all.
Tell what ye know, ye had best.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: I'll tell what I think;
For if he ask me now, if I can love him,
I'll tell him yes, I can: The man's a kinde man;
And out of his true honesty affect me;
Although he plaid the fool, which I required;
Must I still hold him at the staves end?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: You are two strange woman.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: We may be, if we fool still.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Dare ye beleeve me?
Follow but this advice I have set you in now,
And if ye lose: would ye yeeld now so basely?
Give up without your honors saved?

speeches.speaker: de-G.
verse: Fie, Ladies.
Preserve your freedom still.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Well, well, for this time.

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: And carry that full state.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: That's as the winde stands:
If it begin to chop about, and scant us;
Hang me, but I know what Ile do: come direct us,
I make no doubt, we shall do handsomly.

speeches.speaker: de-G.
verse: Some part o' th' way, we'll wait upon ye, Ladies;
The rest your man supplies:

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: Do well, I'll honor ye.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Look ye, Sir, there she is, you see how busie;
Methinks you are infinitely bound to her, for her journey.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: How gloriously she shews? She is a tall woman.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Of a fair Size, sir. My Master not being at home,
I have been so out of my wits, to get her company:
I mean, sir, of her own fair Sex, and fashion.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: A far off, she is most fair too.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Neer, most Excellent.
At length, I have entreated two fair Ladies,
And happily you know 'em: the young daughters
Of Monsieur Nantolet.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I know 'em well, sir.
What are those? Jewels?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: All.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: They make a rich shew?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: There is a matter of ten thousand pounds too
Was owing here: you see those Merchants with her;
They have brought it in now.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: How handsomly her shape shews?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Those are still neate: your Italians are most curious.
Now she looks this way.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: She has a gooly presence.
How full of curtesie? Well, sir, I'll leave ye.
And if I may be bold to bring a friend or two;
Good noble Gentlemen.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: No doubt, ye may, sir.
For you have most command.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I have seen a wonder.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Is he gon?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Yes.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: How?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Taken to the utmost.
A wonder dwels about him.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: He did not guess at me?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: No, be secure; ye shew another woman.
He is gone to fetch his friends.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Where are the Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Here, here, now they are come,
Sit still, and let them see ye.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Pray ye, where's my friend, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: She is within, Ladies, but here's another Gentlewoman;
A stranger to this Towne: so please you visit her,
'Twill be well taken.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Where is she?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: There, Above; Ladies.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: 'Bless me: what Thing is this? two Pinacles,
Upon her pate! Is't not a glode to catch Wood-cocks?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Peace, ye rude, knave.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: What a bouncing Bum she has too?
There's Saile enough for a Carreck.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: What is this Lady?
For as I live, she's a goodly woman.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Ghess, ghess.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: I have not seen a nobler Presence.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: 'Tis a lustie wench: now could I spend my forty-pence,
With all my heart, to have but one fling at her;
To give her but a washing blow.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Ye Rascall.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: I that's all a man has, for's goodwill: 'twil be long enough,
Before ye cry come Anthonie, and kiss me.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Ile have ye whipt.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Has my friend seen this Lady?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Yes, yes, and is well known to her.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I much admire her Presence.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Soe do I too:
For I protest, she is the handsomest,
The rarest, and the newest to mine eie
That ever, I saw yet.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I long to know her;
My friend shall doe that kindness.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: So she shall Ladies.
Come, pray ye come up.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: O, me,

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Hang me if I knew her:
Were I a man my self, I should now love ye;
Nay, I should doate.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I dare not, trust mine eies;
For as I live ye are the strangest alter'd
I must come up to know the truth.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
verse: So must I, Lady;
For I am a kind of unbeleever too.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Get ye gon, Sirrah;
And what ye have seen, be secret in: you are paid else;
No more of your long tongue.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Will ye goe in Ladies,
And talke with her. These venturers will come strait:
Away with this fellow.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: There, Sirrah, goe, disport ye.

speeches.speaker: Ser.
prose: I would the Trunck-hos'd-woman, would goe with me.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Is she so glorious handsome?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: You would wonder:
Our Women look like Gipsies, like Gills to her:
Their Clothes and fashions beggerly, and Bankrupt:
Base, old, and scurvy.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: How lookes her face?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Most heavenly:
And the becoming-motion of her Bodie
So setts her off.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Why then we shall stay.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Pardon me:
That's more then I know: if she be that Woman,
She appeares to be.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: As 'tis impossible.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I shall then tell ye more.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Did ye speake to her?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No, no, I onely saw her: She was busie
Now I goe for that end: And mark her (Gentlemen)
If she appear, not to ye, one of the sweetest,
The handsomest: the fayrest, in behaviour,
We shall meet the two wenches there too, they come to visit her,
To wonder, as we doe.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Then we shall meet 'em.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I had rather meet two Beares.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: There you may take your leaves, dispatch that business,
And as ye find their humours.

speeches.speaker: Pi
verse: Is your Love there too?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: No certain, she has no great heart to set out againe.
This is the house, Ile usher ye?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Ile bless me,
And take a good heart if I can:

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Come, nobly

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: They are come in: Sit you two off, as Strangers,
There Ladie: where's the Boy? be readie, Sirrha
And cleere your Pipes, the Musick now: they enter.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: What a State she keepes? how far off they sit, from her?
How rich she is, I marry, this shewes bravely.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: She is a lusty wench: and may allure a good man,
But if she have a Tongue, Ile not give two pence for her:
There fits my Fury: how I shake to see her.

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: Madam this is the Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Mir,
verse: How sweet she kisses?
She has a Spring dwells on her lipps: a paradize
This is the Legacie.
From the honor'd dead I bring
Thus his love and last offring.
From a faith &c.
Take it nobly, 'tis your due,
From a friendship ever true.

speeches.speaker: Ori.
verse: Most noble, Sir.
This from my now dead Brother, as his love,
And gratefull memory of your great benefit:
From me my thanks, my wishes, and my Service,
Till I am more acquainted I am silent,
Onely I dare say this, you are truly noble.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What should I think?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Think ye have a handsome fortune,
Would I had such another.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Ye are well mett Gentlemen,
We heare ye are for Travell?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Ye heare true, Ladie,
And come to take our Leaves.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Wee'll along with ye,
We see you are growne so witty by your Journey,
We cannot choose but step out too: This Lady,
We mean to wait upon as far as Italy.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I'll travel into Wales, amongst the Mountains;
I hope they cannot finde me.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: If you go further;
So good, and free society we hold ye,
We'll jog along too.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Are ye so valiant Lady?

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: And we'll be merry, Sir, and laugh.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: It may be
We'll go by Sea.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Why 'tis the the onely voyage;
I love a Sea-voyage, and a blustring Tempest;
And let all split.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: This is a dainty Damosel:
I think 'twill tame ye: can ye ride post?

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: 'O excellently: I am never weary that way:
A hundred mile a day is nothing with me.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I'll travel under ground: do you hear (sweet Lady?)
I finde it will be dangerous for a woman.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
prose: No danger, sir, I warrant; I love to be under.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I see she will abuse me all the world over:
But say we pass through Germany, and drink hard?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: We'll learn to drink and swagger too.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: She'll beat me.
Lady, I'll live at home.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: And I'll live with thee;
And We'll keep house together.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I'll keep hounds first;
And those I hate right hartily.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: I go for Turky,
And so it may be up into Persia.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: We cannot know to much, I'll travel with ye.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: And you'll abuse me?

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Like enough.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: 'Tis dainty.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I will live in a bawdy-house.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I dare come to ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Say, I am dispos'd to hang my self?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: There I'll leave ye:

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I am glad I know how to avoid ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: May I speak yet?

speeches.speaker: Fac.
verse: She beckons to ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Lady, I could wish, I know to recompence,
Even with the service of my life, those paines,
And those high favours you have thrown upon me;
Till I be more desertful in your eye;
And till my duty shall make known I honor ye:
Noblest of Women, do me but this favour,
To accept this back again, as a poor testimony.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I must have you too with 'em; else the Will,
That says they must rest with ye, is infring'd, sir,
Which pardon me, I dare not do.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Take me then;
And take me with the truest love.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: 'Tis certain,
My Brother lov'd ye dearly, and I ought
As dearly to preserve that love. But, Sir;
Though I were willing; these are but your Ceremonies.

speeches.speaker: Mir,
verse: As I have life, I speak my soul.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I like ye.
But how you can like me, without I have Testimony,
A Stranger to ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I'll marry ye immediately.
A fair State, I dare promise ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Yet she'll cozen thee.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Would some fair Gentlemen durst promise for ye.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
prose: By all that's good

speeches.speaker: All.
verse: And we'll make up the rest, Lady.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Then Oriana takes ye; nay, she has caught ye;
If ye start now let all the World cry shame on ye:
I have out Travell'd ye.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: did not I say she would cheat thee?

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: I thank ye, I am pleas'd, ye have deceived me;
And willingly I swallow it, and joy in't;
And yet perhaps I know ye: whose plot was this?

speeches.speaker: Lug.
verse: He is not asham'd that cast it: he that executed
Followed your Fathers will.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: What a world's this, nothing but craft, and cozenage?

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: Who begun, sir.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: Well; I do take thee upon meer Compassion;
And I do think, I shall love thee. As a Testimony,
I'll burn my book, and turn a new leafe over.
But these fine clothes you shall wear still.

speeches.speaker: Or.
verse: I^ obey you, sir, in all.

speeches.speaker: Nant.
verse: And how! How, daughters! What say you to these Gentlemen?
What say ye, Gentlemen, to the Girles?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: By my troth—if she can love me.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: —How long?

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Nay, if once ye love.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: Then take me,
And take your chance.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Most willingly, ye are mine, Lady:
And if I use ye not, that ye may love me.

speeches.speaker: Lil.
verse: A Match y' faith.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Why now ye travel with me.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: How that thing stands?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: It will, if ye urge it.
'Bless your five wits.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Nay, 'prethe stay, I'll have thee.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: You must ask me leave first.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Wilt thou use me kindly;
And beat me but once a week?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: If ye deserve no more.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: And wilt thou get me with child?

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Dost thou ask me seriously?

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: Yes indeed do I.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: Yes, I will get thee with child: Come presently,
And 't be but in revenge, I'll do thee that curtesie.
Well, if thou wilt fear God, and me; have at thee.

speeches.speaker: Ros.
verse: I'll love ye, and I'll honor ye:

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: I am pleas'd then.

speeches.speaker: Mir.
verse: This Wild-Goose-Chase is done, we have won o' both sides.
Brother, your love: and now to Church of all hands;
Let's lose no time.

speeches.speaker: Pi.
verse: Our Travelling, lay by.

speeches.speaker: Bel.
verse: No more for Italy; for the Low-Countries,
